# PREFACE TO THE THIRD TOME

I. In the writings of the holy Fathers, the part comprising homilies or sermons commonly appears less polished and exact than their other monuments of intellect. In this respect St Bernard claims for himself, before others, or at least before nearly all, the distinction that his sermons possess no less sharpness of language, variety of thought, and loftiness of conception, nor any less piety of feeling, than his other works. As I considered the reason, there came to mind not only his ingenuity and quick movements of mind, ready to expound matters and move the affections, but also the diversity of hearers for whose benefit such sermons were composed. For when those ancient most holy Fathers delivered sermons to instruct peoples in the doctrine and piety of the Christian religion, wisely consulting the needs of their hearers, they fashioned them in a humble style suited to popular understanding and mostly common subjects. Bernard, however, addressed persons trained in spiritual matters and knowledge of Scripture, most of whom had formerly excelled in secular learning and rank; his discourse therefore had to be suited to their learning and perfection [Note: [Col. 0010] See book III of the *Life*, chapter 3, no. 1.]. Hence it happened that not only his distinguished sermons on the Song of Songs, composed with greater care, but also the others, whether for annual feasts and days or on various subjects, which we present in this tome, are customarily preferred by devout and learned men to the popular homilies and sermons of the Fathers.

II. This opinion of Bernard’s sermons is not mine alone or singular; it is that of distinguished literary men who have expressed their judgment in speech or writing. I call upon only two of them for honour’s sake, whose authority is no less than their learning and erudition. The first is Justus Lipsius, in Letter 49 to Aubertus Miraeus, where, speaking of sacred preaching, he says: “Among the Latins Bernard carries me away and has the power to stir, because of his sharpness and warmth everywhere; and also to teach and impress, because of the acuteness of his thoughts, which he frequently and wholesomely intermingles.” Thus this most learned man, after diligently seeking an outstanding model from the Fathers to propose for forming a sacred orator, believed that he had found none more suitable than Bernard, whom he judged should be preferred to the other Latins. It would be remarkable if this palm were likewise assigned to Bernard before the Greek Fathers who excelled in that kind of eloquence. I would not have dared to declare myself author of that opinion had Henry Valesius, a man of the highest rank, not already [Col. 0011] commended it with his own vote. Of him his brother Adrian Valesius, worthy of so great a brother, records this in his life: “Three or four years before he died, whenever, ill on feast days, he was obliged to remain at home, he ordered the sermons of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, to be read to him by his reader; he listened attentively and drank them in with eager ears. He thought, and commonly said to his friends, that Sundays and feast days ought to be spent in the praises of God, not in literary studies; and that Bernard’s sermons were much better suited to arouse and kindle piety in our minds than the homilies and sermons of any of the ancient Fathers, Greek as well as Latin.” I cite this testimony the more willingly because the authority of so great a man strongly serves to recommend Bernard’s sermons and because the memory of that man, who once honoured me with his friendship and familiarity, is most pleasing to me.

III. To these two testimonies of recent men, which may stand in place of the rest, one could easily add the opinions of writers before our age who spoke of Bernard no otherwise than of a truly apostolic preacher. Among them Erasmus seems not to be passed over, though elsewhere more lavish in invective than praise. In book II of *On the Method of Preaching* he says of Bernard: “Bernard is a preacher by nature rather than art, lively and pleasing, and not sluggish in moving the affections.” But I fear that if I should try to prove at greater length a matter not at all doubtful, I might be hindered or delayed from considering other things that could be more useful. Therefore, as I hasten to other matters, it remains to inquire: first, why Bernard spoke to his own more often than his Order’s rule allowed; second, at what time—that is, on which days and at which hours of the day—he did so; third, in what idiom; and finally, what principles of Christian and religious life he chiefly impressed upon his hearers. In addition, we shall discuss certain points both to expound some heads of his doctrine and to distinguish his genuine sermons from those known to be spurious or falsely attributed.

IV. The days on which sermons “in chapter” were formerly customarily held among the Cistercians are stated by the Cistercian Usages in chapter 67: namely, the days “of the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, Palm Sunday, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, all feasts of Holy Mary, the Nativity of St John the Baptist, the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the Solemnity of St Benedict, All Saints, and the first Sunday of Advent.” So far as I know, there is nowhere any mention of private or weekday days, on which Bernard nevertheless preached very frequently. Hence in Sermon 1 for Septuagesima, no. 2, he says: “I speak to you more often, even beyond the custom of our Order.”

V. I find altogether two reasons why this most religious man and zealous observer of regular discipline did so. One was the command of the first Fathers of the Order, who imposed this spiritual work upon Bernard, scarcely able to bear bodily labour, in compensation. He himself explains this reason at the end of Sermon 10 on Psalm 90: “That we sometimes speak to you beyond the custom of our Order, we do not do by our own presumption, but by the will of our venerable brethren and fellow abbots, who even impose it upon us—though they do not at all wish it everywhere to be permitted to themselves … For I would not now speak to you if I could labour with you. That would perhaps be a more effective word for you and more acceptable to my conscience. But since this is denied me, as you know, through my sins and the manifold weakness of this burdensome body, and also by the necessity of the time, may I at least, though speaking and not doing, merit to be found even the least in the kingdom of God!” This was the reason and occasion for expounding Psalm 90 on the weekdays of Lent, which he followed in consecutive sermons, insofar as the troublesome pressure of business and arriving guests allowed. Both impediments repeatedly called him away from sermons; the authority of fellow abbots urged him to preach frequently, but so too did—this being the second reason—his ardent charity for his brethren’s progress and his zeal. Hence in Sermon 5 for Lent, no. 1: “The charity by which I am concerned for you, my brethren, compels me to speak to you; and, urged by it, I would speak much more often if I were not hindered by so many occupations.” And at the beginning of Sermon 8 on Psalm 90: “At times, beloved, we would speak to you more briefly if it were allowed more frequently … But when the evil of the day itself, taking possession beforehand, has perhaps caused us to endure for several days the most troublesome silence from your exhortation and consolation, I think none of you should wonder if, when we wish to redeem the time itself, the rarer sermon sometimes seems prolonged.” By “the evil of the day” he means the crowd of business and guests, of which he complains more than once in the sermons on the Song of Songs, as we shall see in the preface to the following tome. Yet however much Bernard was hindered from frequent sacred preaching, the sermons were not so infrequent that he did not fear his brethren might be surfeited with spiritual things. “One thing I fear,” he says in Sermon 2 for the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, no. 1, “that the words of salvation heard so often may begin to grow cheap to us, as mere words.” For the same holy Doctor observes in Sermon 35 on the Song of Songs, no. 9: “If bodily food, when you take it without appetite and already full, not only does no good but causes great harm, much more the bread of the soul, taken with disgust, will bring not nourishment of knowledge but rather torment of conscience.”


VI. Bernard himself indicates at various places when this treatment of spiritual matters took place. He allowed scarcely a day to pass without these conferences unless something elsewhere detained him. This is proved by the many sermons for the seasons and saints’ days, the very varied sermons on diverse subjects, the outstanding sermons on the Song of Songs, to say nothing of the brief sayings and sentences that were first outlines of sermons. When spiritual thoughts occurred to his mind [Col. 0013] and he could not immediately express them in full speech, he committed such sacred offspring to wax tablets, to perfect them when time and leisure allowed. Thus Ernaldus wrote of him in book II of his *Life*, no. 51: “The man of God dictated, and sometimes wrote on wax tablets, and did not allow what had been divinely inspired in him to perish.”

VII. He spent the hours for delivering sermons sometimes in the morning after Prime and before the common work or before Mass, sometimes in the evening. He indicates the first time in Sermon 10 on Psalm 90, no. 6: “I fear being caught out. For that great and common abbot of ours and yours is known to have assigned this hour not to leisure for sermons but to manual labour.” He marks the approaching time of Mass in Sermon 1 on the feast of St Michael, at the end: “But the hour is already passing; we must go to Mass.” And in Sermon 1 on the feast of All Saints, no. 3: “For the present we have food in his deeds and words; after this, God being propitious, we shall receive the undefiled sacrament of the Lord’s body on the most holy table of the altar.” At the end of the second sermon: “But the sermon must now be closed, for the solemnities of Mass still to be celebrated call us.” That evening hours were used for the same sermons is proved by Sermon 1 on St Malachy, no. 8: “The day has already declined, and the sermon has proceeded farther than I had hoped.” More distinctly, Sermon 38 on diverse subjects, no. 3: “We must go, for we have already heard the bell and the time of evening prayer has come.” The sermons on the Song of Songs prove the same, as we shall see in their place.

VIII. We must now inquire in order whether Bernard delivered his sermons in Latin or in the common tongue. The difficulty is no light one. Lay brethren, illiterate and wholly ignorant of Latin, seem to have attended these sermons; their only habitual language was the vernacular, commonly and corruptly called “Roman” by authors of those times—Nithard in his *History*, Gerard in the *Life of Abbot Adalard*, and the Chronicler of St Trond, where it is called “corruptly Roman, Walloon in German.” Hence Peter, clerk of Louis the Younger, king of the Franks, says in a letter to the abbot of Lagny: “A certain boy, my kinsman, was sent to me from England to learn the Roman language” [Note: [Col. 0013] Duchesne, tome IV, p. 742.]—that is, the French vernacular. Yet those who knew this language did not therefore understand Latin, not even in the ninth century, still less in the eleventh, as is clear from the booklet on the vision of Flotilda or Chlotilda, in which certain priests are reproved “who were ignorant even of the letters which they read” [Note: [Col. 0013] The same, tome II, p. 625.]. If then illiterate brethren attended Bernard’s sermons, it is by no means likely that those sermons were delivered in Latin. Indeed Bernard’s sermons for the seasons are held in the convent of the Feuillants at Paris, written in French in the time, it seems, of St Bernard himself; both the handwriting and the antiquity of the idiom point to this. Add that Bernard, at the beginning of Letter 17 to Peter the cardinal deacon, testifies that his sermons were taken down in his disciples’ “style”—as though to say that they were endowed not in the manner in which they had been delivered but in another’s style. His words are: “Certain brethren wrote down in their own style some things which they heard me say before them.” Nearly the same words occur at the end of Letter 18, where he adds: “And they keep them with themselves.” From this one might perhaps infer that Bernard spoke in his native or country speech, adapting himself to lay brethren, and that his disciples translated his words into Latin.

IX. Many things show that lay brethren were wholly illiterate and ignorant of the Latin language. These brethren were joined to the choir but lacked clerical tonsure, and were entirely distinct from the *conversi*. They are discussed in book VII of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 23: “They who were trained under our blessed Father Bernard in the disciplines of heavenly philosophy imitated this form of divine knowledge”—namely, “Let him not glory in his wisdom” (Jeremiah 9:23), and so forth—“more perfectly: not only many learned men trained in the mysteries of the sacred law, but also very many lay and illiterate men. Although they had by no means attained the structure of human learning by which they might strive toward the summit of perfection, they nevertheless possessed illuminating grace and the life-giving Spirit, who taught them incomparably more effectively than secular learning concerning all things necessary. One such was a lay monk, not taught by the letter but by the spirit,” and so forth. Such was the condition of these laymen: wholly illiterate and ignorant of Latin, as John the Hermit testifies in his letter to Peter of Tusculum on the *Life of St Bernard*, no. 2: “A certain monk, a true and sincere lover of the venerable abbot, was walking by chance through the brushwood adjoining Clairvaux monastery with a lay brother named Humbert, holding in his hands a book of the holy Father’s miracles and explaining them in the idiom of the Roman language for his own and that man’s edification.” Why explain them in the Roman or French tongue unless this lay brother did not know Latin? Such was another layman praised soon afterward by John himself, no. 3. Although he had previously not known even “the alphabet,” “God illuminating his understanding, and certain brethren assisting, he shortly progressed so far that he knew not only how to read but even how to sing quite properly and suitably. Thereafter, by use cooperating with grace, he began somewhat to understand the meanings of words and gradually to advance in learning of that kind.” No one fails to see that this is said of Latin.


Nor were lay brethren [Col. 0015] of this sort admitted only among Cistercians; they were also admitted among other monks, as was the one mentioned by Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, in book III, letter 8, who “because he was a layman spoke not Latin, which he had not learned, but his mother tongue.” We are not here speaking of *conversi*, although the same arguments that apply to lay brethren apply also to them and prove that they likewise lacked understanding of Latin. This is confirmed by Herbert’s testimony in book I, chapter 16, of *On the Miracles of Clairvaux*: he speaks of a certain *conversus* “who, when he came to death, began to speak in Latin speech though he had never learned Latin letters.” Thus one may state generally that ordinary people did not have common use of Latin, even though public acts were commonly drawn up in Latin. Indeed Peter the Venerable writes in book IV, letter 18 to Pope Celestine that he received a letter concerning the pope’s election and, when it had been read in chapter, “expounded it,” he says, “to the learned and the unlearned whom we call *conversi*”—that is, explained it in the vernacular. This would have been useless had all known Latin. Finally, that each province of Gaul had its own idioms, as now, is shown by Bernard’s Letter 67 to the monks of Flavigny in the district of Beauvais, where he says that they and his own men of Clairvaux use “dissimilar languages.”

X. Such indeed was the state of affairs, but nevertheless we hold without doubt that Bernard’s sermons were conceived in Latin, delivered in Latin, and taken down by his disciples in exactly that manner. First, this is shown by the continual and natural play on Latin words. Next, it is shown by the equality of style in the sermons and in his other books and treatises. Further, the Carthusians of that period, who also admitted lay brethren, spoke Latin in public sermons to the brethren, and retain that practice even now. The same must be judged of Bernard’s other sermons and of his exposition on the Song of Songs: the sermons of that exposition were written in exactly the way they were delivered, as he says in Sermon 54, no. 1: “They were written as they were spoken, and taken down by the pen like the other sermons, so that what may perhaps have slipped away can easily be recovered.”

XI. This explains the testimony above from Letter 18, objected against us, where certain brethren who used to hear Bernard speaking in person are said to have “taken down his sermons in their own *stylo*”; *stylus* means pen or writing, not a style of expression. Thus Nicholas of Clairvaux says in Letter 39: “The hand is not sufficient to hold the stylus.” The same sense is required for the word at the end of Letter 304: “Let the reader recognize the stylus, because I myself dictated.” Here *stylus* plainly means autograph writing and *dictare* means to write. So at the end of Letter 310: “I myself dictated this, being so disposed that by the familiar hand you may recognize the affection.” Nothing is clearer. A manner of speech does not indicate the hand, but one’s own writing does. Add William’s authority in book I of the *Life of Bernard*, no. 70: “His writings bear witness, those he himself wrote or others wrote as they took them down from his mouth.” These considerations move us to believe that Bernard’s sermons have reached us in no other style or mode of speech than that in which he delivered them, and that the Feuillant manuscript contains not their native language but a translation from Latin. That manuscript, which we believe autograph, was not written before Bernard’s death, as is proved by its heading, in which Bernard is called saint, as we shall later see. Bernard also more than once calls his hearers trained in sacred letters: in Sermon 3 on Peter and Paul, no. 6, “You remember, I think; for I speak to those who know the law”; in Sermon 7 on Psalm 90, no. 5, “I mean Balaam—recall it, you who know the histories”; at Sermon 10 for Easter, “These are the words of Revelation: let those who have not read learn, and those who know remember”; and more openly in Sermon 4 on the Nativity, no. 1, “I speak to those who know the Scriptures.” Compare Sermon 10 on Psalm 90, no. 2. From all this it is understood that Bernard’s hearers were learned and knew Latin.

XII. The objection from lay brethren cannot move us from this conclusion: perhaps other sermons, more familiar, were delivered to them, unless they attended with the *conversi* in their private chapter—which, for their benefit, according to the Order’s custom, took place every Sunday with a vernacular sermon. Yet Nicholas of Clairvaux’s Letter 24, to be considered below, causes some difficulty.

XIII. In exhortations addressed either to *conversi* or to outsiders and secular people, however, the holy man without doubt used the vernacular idiom. To the former belongs the saying of a dying *conversus*, encouraged by Bernard to Christian hope, who answered that he was secure in Christ’s mercy. Reproved by Bernard, he said: “If that preaching of yours which you have often impressed upon us is true—namely, that the kingdom of God is possessed neither by nobility of flesh nor earthly riches, but acquired by the virtue of obedience alone—I have kept this one saying, as a shortened word from the Lord, in diligent remembrance.” [Note: [Col. 0015] *Life of St Bernard*, book VII, chapter 26.] Bernard therefore preached to the *conversi*, and did so on Sundays in their private chapter, as the ancient Cistercian definitions prescribe, distinction 14, chapter 4.


[Col. 0017]

XIV. Nor did the holy Doctor fail secular people and outsiders when charity or occasion seemed to require it. Geoffrey testifies in book III, chapter 3, no. 8, of his *Life*: “He always studied to benefit the people of God, never endured to rule them. Yet he rarely went out to preach except perhaps to nearby places. But whenever some necessity drew him, he sowed upon all waters, publicly and privately announcing God’s word; and he did this by command of the supreme pontiff and at the request of other prelates wherever he happened to be present.” The same Geoffrey reports, no. 7, what happened when Bernard proclaimed the holy expedition in German lands at the command of Eugenius III: “Honey and milk were under his tongue … Thus, even when speaking to German peoples, he was heard with wondrous affection; and their devotion seemed to be edified more by his sermon, which as people of another language they could not understand, than by the understood speech of any most skilled interpreter speaking after him; they seemed rather to feel the power of his words. The certain proof was beating of breasts and pouring forth of tears.” That the Germans could not understand his sermon “as people of another language” proves that he used his native, or French, speech. Philip the monk says in book VI, no. 16, of *His Miracles* that he spoke in the “Roman language,” that is, French, among Germans. Ekkehard the Younger, in his book on the fortunes of St Gall monastery, writes of an illiterate ninth-century monk that Tutilo addressed his companions “in Latin, so that it might be hidden from the man who understood nothing.” The same must be said of the English, for whom Alfred in the ninth century caused Gregory the Great’s *Pastoral Rule* and Bede’s *History* to be translated into Saxon; hence translations in that age of the Gospels and the Rule of St Benedict into German.

XV. Perhaps we have lingered on this longer than the effort merits; still, we do not regret it, since it commends the apostolic zeal and office of the holy man. In his preaching, Geoffrey testifies in the passage just cited, Bernard “used the Scriptures so freely and aptly that he seemed not so much to follow them as to go before them, and, following the author of them, the guiding Spirit, to lead them himself wherever he wished.”

XVI. It will not be useless briefly to consider what principal rules of religious life Bernard was accustomed to impress from sacred letters upon monks in his sermons. One of the chief, from the Apostle, was that they should count themselves strangers in this world. Two passages provide evidence: Sermon 1 on Epiphany, no. 1, “We take care frequently to warn you of this, that it never escape your mind that we are strangers, far from our homeland, driven from our inheritance. For whoever does not know desolation cannot know consolation; whoever does not know consolation to be necessary has no grace of God.” The other is Sermon 7 for Lent, no. 1: “Happy are those who show themselves strangers and pilgrims in this present wicked world, keeping themselves unstained from it,” and so forth.

XVII. Bernard’s second maxim was that it is especially profitable for monks—indeed, for all striving toward virtue—to forget what lies behind and stretch themselves forward, after the Apostle’s example. “Our progress,” he says in Sermon 2 on the Purification, no. 3, “consists in this, as I remember often saying: that we never think we have apprehended, but always stretch toward what lies ahead, continually strive for better, and constantly expose our imperfection to the gaze of divine mercy.” The same thought is in Sermon 4 on Psalm 90, no. 3: “This too is surely great virtue and highest security: when you live piously, yet attend more to what you lack than to what you seem to have obtained, forgetting what is behind and stretching yourself forward.” Related is the passage there saying that perfection greatly depends on professing ourselves unprofitable servants when we have fulfilled every part of our religion and duty; that too is to be forgetful of what is behind.

XVIII. The third axiom is that we should always fear lest we fall from grace. “For the present,” he says in Sermon 5 for All Saints, no. 3, “our whole blessedness is to fear God.” In Sermon 1 after the octave of Epiphany, no. 5, after setting out a twofold fear—“perhaps to be cast into Gehenna, perhaps to be excluded from eternal life”—he adds: “It is good to add a third, known to spiritual persons … Those who know spiritual food fear perhaps being deprived of it. Those perhaps need food who have put their hand to strong things … This is the third measure, which he significantly put under a disjunction because it is not for all: for a hundredfold reward is promised not to all but only to those who have left everything.” In the following sermon, nos. 8–9, he adds that this third fear “fills the soul with every anxious concern lest it be abandoned by grace … lest it happen that a person loses grace and, left to himself, daily falls from bad to worse, from lesser sin into a graver fault.” He pursues this more fully in Sermon 54 on the Song of Songs, no. 9: “In truth I have learned that nothing is as effective for meriting, retaining, and recovering grace as to be found at all times before God not thinking highly, but fearing.”

XIX. A fourth saying of Bernard’s may be added to these, greatly and frequently commended by him: those whom God has drawn out from the world’s storms should flee with all their heart the vice of ingratitude toward God and strive to show themselves as grateful as possible. He develops this in Sermon 2 on the Seven Mercies for the sixth Sunday after Pentecost, no. 2: “Therefore a person who desires the gifts of grace received not only to remain with him but also to be multiplied must be grateful and devout … But especially we, whom he has set apart for himself and taken up to serve him alone,” and so forth. He presses the same point in Sermon 27 on diverse subjects, [Col. 0019] “Against the most wicked vice of ingratitude,” no. 6: “How many brethren do we see and mourn who, provided habit and tonsure remain, judge everything safe for themselves! The wretches do not consider how the worm of ingratitude, gnawing their inward parts, for this very reason refrains from boring through the visible bark, lest they perhaps reflect and blush and be corrected by that very shame.” And below: “You see, then, that it does not profit all to be cleansed from the leprosy of secular living, whose sins are manifest; in some a worse hidden ulcer of ingratitude arises, the more dangerous the more inward it is.” I would be excessive if I wished to treat arguments of this kind as far as possible. Let these things suffice as a sample and aid for devout readers.

**XX.** The teaching of these sermons is not only full of piety, but also plain, easy, and free from difficulty. If anything in them may nevertheless delay the less learned reader, it will be explained in its proper place. One point is useful to explain here: Bernard’s opinion concerning the state of holy souls released from their bodies, as expressed in the second, third, and fourth sermons for All Saints’ Day, in the fourth sermon for the Dedication of a Church, and elsewhere. At the outset the holy doctor sets forth his mind on this subject not lightly or cursorily, but deliberately and after prayer, though “without prejudice, of course, if perhaps something else has been revealed to another”; nevertheless, as he says in sermon 4 on the saints, nos. 1 and 2, he thinks that he has “the mind” of God on this matter. Then, after laying down the threefold state of souls—“in a corruptible body,” “without a body,” and “in a body now glorified”—he treats of the middle state and establishes his opinion under four heads.

First, those holy souls released from the body are immediately admitted into heaven, according to the same sermon 4, no. 1, and therefore “into the fellowship of angels,” as he writes of Saint Malachy in the second sermon, no. 5. Secondly, there they dwell “in great light,” as in the same sermon 4, no. 1. Thirdly, they see Christ’s humanity, there no. 2, but not his divinity, which is to be granted them only after the resurrection. “Meanwhile,” under the altar—that is, “under Christ’s humanity”—the saints happily rest, “into which, indeed, the angels themselves desire to look.” Fourthly and finally, they “have joy in their spirit and much gladness in their heart, though not full,” in the second sermon on the saints, no. 4; and therefore are not without a wrinkle, in the third sermon, no. 2, namely because of the desire to take up their bodies again. “For this natural desire is so vigorous in them that their whole affection does not yet freely press onward into God; rather, it is in some way contracted and makes a wrinkle while they are bent by that desire.” The same opinion occurs in the book *On Loving God*, no. 32. This is, in substance, Bernard’s teaching, which he expounded only as an opinion, as is clear from book V of *On Consideration*, chapter 4, no. 9, where he considers the holy souls of martyrs in Abraham’s bosom “and under the altar, whatever that may be, patiently awaiting the second robe in the first.”

**XXI.** Although this was Bernard’s opinion, in certain passages he nevertheless attributes the vision of God to holy souls. Thus he says that Malachy rejoices “in glory and happiness equal to that of the angels,” in sermon 2 on him, no. 5; that certain saints have already deserved to be introduced into the holy of holies, “where they see the face of the One standing, that is, the brightness of the unchangeable God,” in a sermon on the *Song of Songs*; and that martyrs are “immersed” “in the immense sea of eternal light and luminous eternity,” near the end of the book *On Loving God*. More clearly, in the second sermon on Saint Victor, no. 4: “Now having entered the heavens, which he had previously beheld open with blessed eyes, he truly now beholds the glory of God with unveiled face, absorbed indeed, but not forgetful of the cry of the poor. Blessed is the vision by which he is transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.” But how can these passages be reconciled with Bernard’s preceding opinion, when in explicit words, in sermon 4 on the saints, no. 2, where he treats this question expressly, he asserts that after the resurrection the Son will provide his elect with “the new delights, certainly, and wholly untried until that time, of his manifest contemplation”? Or did he perhaps later retract and correct this opinion? It is not easy to affirm this, since the dates on which the apparently conflicting sermons were delivered cannot be accurately determined.

**XXII.** Here Thomas the Englishman presents himself, in his little work *On the Intermediate State of Souls*, distinction 4. There he judges Bernard to have been the first of the Fathers to assign a seat in heaven to the blessed souls released from the body, whereas the other, earlier Fathers assigned it to the blessed only after the Last Judgment; and that Bernard denied those souls the vision of the Godhead before the resurrection, whereas those Fathers granted it to them. Thomas certainly errs in the first point. We offer only three witnesses to his error: Cyprian, Alcuin, and Florus, deacon of the Church of Lyons, all far earlier than Bernard in time. Cyprian, near the end of the book *On Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 12, says: “How great is the dignity, and how great the security . . . to close in an instant the eyes by which men and the world were seen, and immediately to open those same eyes so that Christ God may be seen! You are suddenly withdrawn from earth, to be placed in the heavenly kingdoms.” More briefly, in the book *On the Praise of Martyrdom*: “The martyrs rejoice in heaven.” In the former passage, moreover, he asserts that not martyrs alone, but also patriarchs and prophets together with the apostles, already possess heaven. Alcuin, in letter 81, testifies that in his time some people had indeed entertained a doubt on this matter, but secretly, not openly, as though they feared to disclose their error because it was contrary to everyone’s opinion. “There is also,” he says, “a secret doubt in certain persons whether the souls of the holy apostles, martyrs, and other perfect persons are received into the heavenly kingdom before the day of judgment.” Alcuin condemns this opinion and counts it among the Spanish heresies. But Florus’s opinion is more explicit in his exposition of the Mass, on the words of the Canon, “Remember also, Lord, thy servants,” etc., where [Column 21] Florus comments thus: “It is clearer than light that the souls of perfect righteous persons, as soon as they leave the bonds of this flesh, are received into heavenly abodes.” Nothing is clearer than these testimonies against Thomas the Englishman and in favor of Bernard’s opinion—indeed, of the Church’s opinion.


**XXIII.** On the second point, namely the vision of God: as to the ancients who place the souls of the blessed in heaven only after the Last Judgment, and before that in hidden retreats, I am not sure whether they grant those souls the vision of the divine essence before that time. But, not to digress into a superfluous question, Bernard does indeed assign to released souls the manifest contemplation of Christ’s humanity alone; yet even in this he differs from the commonly received opinion of John XXII and his followers. Indeed, he seems in substance not to differ even from those who attribute the sight of the Godhead to the blessed, though less perfectly than after the resurrection. For the whole reason that moves Bernard is the very reason why these latter attribute to released souls a vision of God that is not so perfect: namely, their vehement desire to take up their bodies again. They hold with Bernard that perfect contemplation of God is of such force and power that it absorbs and utterly extinguishes every affection, which will belong even to the saints only after the resurrection. Read Augustine, sermons 280, no. 5, and 318, nos. 5 and 6. Bernard’s words in sermon 19 *On Various Subjects*, no. 3, are worthy of notice. Explaining the prerogatives of the blessed, he says: “Thirdly, they now draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior and, with bare eyes, so to speak, gaze upon the essence of the Godhead, deceived by no image of bodily phantasms.” If he says this of the present state, as indeed he seems to do, he unquestionably attributes here to the saints before the resurrection an intuitive vision of the divine essence.

**XXIV.** But leaving these matters at last, we must come to the final chapter of this preface, which concerns the criticism of Bernard’s genuine sermons. Discussion of this will not be very long, since the judgment on most of them is certain and established. Of the sermons *On the Seasons* that Horst had admitted, we have rejected as spurious the second sermon for the Lord’s Supper, on “When you sit at the table of a rich man.” It neither savors of Bernard’s genius nor occurs in any ancient codices that I have seen, nor even in the old Lyons edition of 1514.

**XXV.** This sermon was followed by a *Meditation on the Life or Passion of the Lord*, beginning with the words “Jesus of Nazareth,” etc. This too is absent from the same codices and from the Lyons edition, and is more rightly assigned to Saint Anselm under the title *Stimulus of Love* by Trithemius and Bellarmine.

**XXVI.** A sermon on David’s battle with Goliath—for so they wrote it—for the fourth Sunday after Pentecost is placed after the sermons of Nicholas of Clairvaux in the codex used by the religious Bertrand Tissier, author of the *Cistercian Library*. But because this sermon occurs in many codices of good standing, such as those of Clairvaux, Anchin, and the White Mantles at Paris, and is cited in the *Flowers of Bernard* compiled four hundred years ago, it did not seem right to take it away from Bernard.

**XXVII.** Since mention has here arisen of Nicholas of Clairvaux’s sermons, it is useful to observe that this Nicholas, formerly a monk of Arremar, became a monk of Clairvaux and Saint Bernard’s secretary, then an apostate. He dedicated nineteen sermons composed by himself to Henry, count palatine of Troyes. They were printed in volume III of the aforementioned *Cistercian Library*, together with Nicholas’s preface to Count Henry, where these words occur: “Henceforth I send to your glory nineteen sermons, from the feast of Saint John the Baptist to the feast of Saint John the Evangelist, other sermons, and certain verses of the Psalter discovered by my own understanding and dictated in my own style, except that in a few places I have drawn upon another’s revenues.” That is, upon the revenues of Bernard, his master, whose style he had almost attained. For in the sermon on the Nativity of the Lord he says of Bernard: “But the whole wealth of the thought will be borrowed from his treasury, whose counsel is as the counsel of God. He is the very man whose religious devotion and discretion, wisdom and eloquence, life and renown deservedly range throughout all Latin-speaking lands.” This is certainly a splendid eulogy of Bernard. But Nicholas’s so cool mention of him in the foregoing preface resulted from the fact that it was addressed to Count Henry of Troyes after Nicholas’s apostasy.

Moreover, after those nineteen sermons the manuscript codex contains four sermons which Nicholas rather clearly indicates in his preface: the first, “On the words of Wisdom, ‘The Lord guided the righteous man,’” etc. (Wisdom 10:10); the second, “On five stones against Goliath”; the third, “On flesh, skin, and bones”; the fourth, “On the threefold glory,” on the Apostle’s words, “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17). All are attributed to Bernard: the second, as I have just said, for the fourth Sunday after Pentecost; the other three among the *Various Sermons*, not only in the first Lyons edition, but also in all or nearly all manuscripts. I therefore judged it unsuitable to deny them to Bernard, especially since Nicholas, his secretary and in other matters not sufficiently scrupulous, may have attributed them to himself, as was observed in the notes on letter 298.

**XXVIII.** Among the sermons on the saints, the second sermon for the Conversion of Saint Paul is absent from most manuscripts, including the French Feuillant manuscript. It is, however, found in Vatican manuscript no. 663, and I do not at all doubt that it is truly Bernard’s. The sermon for the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, one of Nicholas’s nineteen sermons, was rejected into volume VI after having been omitted in volume V, where, together with certain other sermons of Nicholas, occur also sermon 5 for the Assumption and the panegyric sermon on the Blessed Virgin, which had formerly been placed among Bernard’s works. We have deliberately passed over quite a number of sermons attributed to Bernard, both in the new Cologne edition [Column 23] and in Homey’s *Supplement of the Fathers*, as well as in certain manuscript codices, since they are foreign to Bernard’s style and genius; nor did it seem worthwhile to place them in the class of spurious works.


**XXIX.** Of the *Various Sermons*, which in some codices are entitled “Extracts from the sayings of Saint Bernard,” some are attributed to Guerric, abbot of Igny, and some to Nicholas of Clairvaux. Three are attributed to Nicholas, those mentioned above: the sixth, seventh, and twenty-first. Six sermons are attributed to Guerric: 8, 28, 71, 73, 76, and 79. Yet since these sermons, according to Horst’s testimony, do not occur among Guerric’s sermons in the Cologne codex, while they occur in most copies of Bernard, it seemed right to retain them among the *Various Sermons*. This is especially so because all these streams flowed from Bernard’s fountain, as is read at the end of the royal codex of the College of Navarre at Paris, which contains Bernard’s sermons *On the Seasons* and *On the Saints*. At its end occurs this clause: “Afterwards follows the sermon on conversion to clerics, which has thirty-one sections. This book is followed by certain abbreviated extracts from various sermons of that saint himself, which he delivered in different places and times, briefly and usefully collected by those who clung inseparably to his side night and day. Afterwards follows the treatise of Lord Geoffrey, the secretary, which he composed and sent to Lord Henry, bishop and cardinal, on ‘Simon Peter said to Jesus.’ Finally follow the letters of Saint Bernard which he wrote to various persons. But although these writings were handed down by a hand other than his own, all these streams flowed from his fountain.” Those extracts are the *Various Sermons*, many of which are summaries of sermons rather than full sermons.

**XXX.** Of five parables attributed to Bernard, which occur after the *Various Sermons*, the first is genuine; the second and third seem fabricated in imitation of the first; the fourth and fifth have their place among spurious works in the ancient editions. The hortatory poem to Rainald seems wholly unworthy of Bernard. The published rhymes on the name of Jesus, and others as well, must be denied to him for the reasons I set forth at the end of volume V, where they now occur.

**XXXI.** What we have said of the holy Father’s sermons is also supported both by the books of extracts which William of Tournai, monk of Saint-Martin, composed almost five hundred years ago and entitled the *Bernardine*, as was said in the preface to volume I; and by the French manuscript which Nicholas Faber, tutor of Louis the Just, granted to the reverend Fathers of the convent of Saint-Bernard at Paris. For the *Bernardine* mentions nearly all the sermons *On the Seasons* and *On the Saints*, and most of the *Various* and *Short Sermons*, which we shall identify in their places. For Holy Thursday it cites one sermon only, and likewise only one for the Wednesday of the Lord’s Passion—precisely those shown to be genuine, not the other two that we rejected. For the Conversion of Saint Paul, fragments from the first sermon are cited once and again; this designation as first indicates a second, even though no fragments from it are adduced.

**XXXII.** Yet the Feuillant manuscript has only one sermon on that conversion, namely the first. It contains forty-four sermons in all, which it is useful to list here because of the codex’s uniqueness and antiquity, reaching back to Bernard’s own time. They are: six on Advent; six on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord; five on the Nativity itself; one each on Saints Stephen, John, and the Innocents; three on the Circumcision; three on the Epiphany; one on the Octave; two for the Sunday after the Octave; one on the Conversion of Saint Paul; three on the Purification; two on Septuagesima; and six on Lent. Of the latter, the first four occur in the same order as in the printed editions; the fifth is on the pilgrim, the dead man, and the crucified man. After it is inserted the sermon on Saint Benedict, and after that the sixth Lenten sermon, on threefold prayer, which is fifth in the printed editions; the sermon on the Lord’s Prayer, sixth in the published editions, is omitted. Then follows one sermon called *Common*, which is sermon 35 of the *Various Sermons*, addressed to abbots; likewise one *Common* sermon, which is the preface to the exposition of Psalm 90; and finally three sermons on the Annunciation.

**XXXIII.** Nicholas of Clairvaux sent all these and the other sermons of volume III, contained in two volumes, to Peter of Celle, as his letter 24 testifies: “I who had renounced the stylus, worthy of hiding places and solitude, after I perceived and fully understood your eagerness for the words and concerning the words of that man whose eloquence and wisdom, life and renown have deservedly spread throughout all Latin-speaking lands, took up my tablets and did what I could and what I did.” The same words occur in the same Nicholas’s sermon on the Nativity of the Lord.

**XXXIV.** The words which follow in the preceding letter deserve attention: “But you say: You could have done all this in silence, and rather with silence. It is strange if you say this in earnest. For who is more amid a crowd than one occupied in composing writings? For, in order that the truth of meanings may be discovered worthily, the variety of words, what best suits the sequence, finally what ought to be brought forth, when, where, and how, make a noise. Will you call this silence and rest, especially for an unskilled man, to whom no thought is present and whose speech is neither graceful nor easy for clothing thoughts?” By these words Nicholas seems to indicate plainly that he expended much labor in dictating, composing in writing, and arranging in order the arguments of the sermons that he sends. But what sermons does he send? Surely Bernard’s. For after a few words he [Column 25] adds: “Yet I have compelled myself against myself, and send you two volumes of sermons of the man of God. In one of them I dictated that which begins thus: ‘The Apostle Paul is wont to be brief in words, dense in meanings.’ The other volume was long ago dictated, and gnawed and scraped. But seek someone who may write it carefully and wisely, for it is full of many meanings.” If I understand the sense of these words correctly, it seems possible to infer from them that Nicholas dictated in his own words—that is, in Latin—the sermons contained in the other volume, which began with “The Apostle,” etc.; this beginning is that of sermon 19 *On Various Subjects*. If this is so, the arguments return which we above tried to refute: that Bernard delivered his sermons not in Latin but in French, and that his disciples afterward clothed them in Latin. And indeed there is sometimes great variation in the sermons, especially the *Various Sermons*; that variation would arise from different persons translating these sermons into Latin in different ways. Moreover, Geoffrey, secretary of the holy man, says that he composed his little work on the dialogue of Simon and Jesus “from many sermons of our Father.” Why should other secretaries not have done the same? But if this were so, why would they not also have attributed these sermons to themselves?


**XXXV.** On closer consideration, however, Nicholas’s difficulty concerning writing and dictating seems to refer not to Bernard’s sermons but to letters, from the writing of which Nicholas tries to excuse himself by this circuit of words. The title of the letter supports this interpretation: “To the abbot of Celle, an excuse concerning writing or dictating.” Or rather, he wished to express both, seeking to free himself from the duty both of writing letters and of dictating sermons from a codex, or at least to advertise his labor in both. Finally, Nicholas borrowed these words almost word for word from Bernard’s letter 89 to Ogerius, no. 1, in which Bernard excuses himself from letter-writing; Nicholas must not be supposed to have applied them here to another use. Nicholas’s corrupt text may be restored from Bernard’s letter, written twenty years before Nicholas moved to Clairvaux. As we have observed elsewhere, Nicholas habitually transfers Bernard’s words to his own purposes. Since knowledge of this Nicholas contributes considerably to the illumination of Bernard’s history, it will be worth depicting the man here in his own colors.

[Column 25]

## Second part of the preface: on Nicholas, Saint Bernard’s secretary

**XXXVI.** Nicholas was French by nation, and from early youth a monk in the monastery of Arremar, in the diocese of Troyes, four leagues from the city itself. He was a man of ready and versatile talent, easily entering into the feelings of others, very well cultivated in letters for his time, and placed over the instruction of others among his brethren at Arremar. He was dear to the foremost men of that age: Atto, bishop of Troyes; Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny; Peter of Celle; Henry, brother of Louis the Younger; and others.

**XXXVII.** Captivated no less by Bernard’s fame and genius than by his holiness, he went to Clairvaux, approved the monks’ religious life, and appealed to the affection of the elders, asking them to admit him to their company: wearied of a laxer life and most eager for a stricter one. In almost a single interview he carried and obtained the matter. Returning to his own house, he pressed the business. During Bernard’s absence he approached the prior and elders of Clairvaux by letter—his letter 7—addressed “To the reverend lords and fathers, Prior R.,” that is, Rualen, “and his council.” In it he assumes every posture and feeling. He praises Clairvaux’s religious life and expresses his desire to see them again and join himself to them. “Your humility,” he says, “and our necessity, and that third thing in which you gave me hope, the reception of our littleness, all give me confidence.” A little later he marks the time at which he wrote the letter: “What joy it will be for me who sit in darkness, who do not see the light of heaven, the light of Clairvaux! O light descending from the Father of lights! Where the lights shine in the firmament of heaven, whence was taken, namely Pope Eugenius, the greater light to enlighten the earth.” This occurred, therefore, under Pope Eugenius, and in the first year of his pontificate, since Rualen was transferred that same year from the priorate of Clairvaux to govern the Roman monastery at Acquas-Salvias, of which Eugenius had been abbot before his pontificate, after Nicholas had already been admitted to Clairvaux, as his letter 43 proves. The words “namely Pope Eugenius,” however, seem to have crept from the margin into the text.

**XXXVIII.** Besides the foregoing letter to the prior and elders of Clairvaux, he soon added two others: one to Brother Gaucher of Clairvaux, into whose affection he had insinuated himself, and the other to Fromund, the hospitaller there—letters 44 and 46. In the former he explains his vows more fully and ardently, saying that he is held by such a desire for his conceived purpose that he counts “a day as a year.” He says that he did [Column 27] not fail to be present at the appointed time, but suffered much from his Arremar brethren, now through importunity, now through blandishments, now through threats, and could scarcely at last tear himself from their company. Yet, having finally escaped their hands, he arrived “without clothes, without money, without servants, without horses, scarcely at Arrouaise,” a Cistercian monastery in the territory of Troyes, and then at Clairvaux. But he says he was dragged thence “to the ends of the earth,” evidently at the objection of the abbot of Arremar—this was Guy, at whose request Bernard composed the office of Saint Victor—who perhaps shut him up in a certain priory. From there Nicholas wrote these letters full of impatient longing, and others to Fromund which he sent through a certain cleric who had withdrawn thither with him.

In the earlier letter to Gaucher he depicts himself thus: “Entering and leaving under the rags of Christ’s humility, I leapt into the gulf of pleasures; and from the patrimony of the Crucified, from the price of my Lord’s wounds, I showed myself not merely within the sanctuary but within the holy of holies as a monk without rule and a priest without reverence. For, going and returning too curiously to the Roman curia [Note: [Column 27] See Peter the Venerable, book II, letter 49, and book III, letter 2], I had made myself a great name, beside the name of the great who are on earth; and I remember that in all my life I had scarcely lived a single day.” These are modest words indeed, if he uttered them sincerely.

**XXXIX.** At last, after reconciliation with his abbot—such is the title and subject of letter 40—he was admitted to Clairvaux together with Prior Theobald, whom, after he later left, Nicholas vainly tries to recall in letter 6. This conversion moved Brocard, or Burchard, abbot of Balerne in the Cistercian order, to congratulate him in a letter on the matter, letter 9 among Nicholas’s letters. There one reads: “I give thanks to God, who makes all things new, for the new wonder of the new transformation of renewed Nicholas. He who made white from black made something new and wonderful; but this is more wonderful than all new things, that from such blackness such whiteness has been made.” Such, indeed, were the Cistercians’ applause for such a proselyte.

**XL.** Hardly had he been established in their fellowship when the office of secretary was entrusted to him. Bernard had several secretaries because of the varied affairs continually referred to him. Geoffrey was the principal one, and Nicholas was joined to him. Nicholas complains, whether sincerely or not, of the duty assigned him in letter 15 to a certain companion from Arremar: “You know that I am among men in whom flourish the rigor of discipline, gravity of conduct, maturity of counsel, weight of authority, and distinction of silence. I do not wish to be accused of singularity: while they are free and see that he is God, I turn over stylus and tablets, that I may fly back to the trappings and glory of words. Yet from the morning watch until night I do nothing else. Let it not be imputed to those who laid this burden upon me and set me to write much and rewrite for many.”


**XLI.** In another letter, namely 35, he describes his “little writing room” thus: “I have a little writing room in my Clairvaux, surrounded on every side by heavenly workshops that conceal it. Its door opens into the novices’ cell, where a numerous company of noble and learned men bring forth the new man in newness of life. . . . On the right rises the monks’ cloister, where that more flourishing convent walks about. . . . There, under the most exact discipline, they open one by one the books of divine eloquence, not to display the treasures of their learning, but to draw out love, compunction, and devotion. On the left projects the house and ambulatory of the infirm, where bodies wearied and battered by regular disciplines are refreshed with more generous food, until, healed or improved, they fly back to the flock of laborers and pray-ers who do violence to the kingdom of heaven and seize it by force. Do not think my little house contemptible, for it is desirable to the affection, delightful to the sight, and fit for retreat. It is full of the choicest and divine books. From their pleasing inspection I learn contempt for this worldly vanity, considering that vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, and that nothing is vainer than vanity. It has been entrusted to me for reading, writing, dictating, meditating, praying, and worshipping the Lord of majesty.”

Nicholas was occupied not only in copying books but also in conducting business, as letter 49 to Peter of Celle testifies. Among other things he writes: “I dictated these things for you, sweetest of friends, at least by leaps, since I could not do so continuously, being drawn and drawn back by many affairs; and I wrote them with my own hands. For all who have business come to us; yet I alone can say with holy Jacob: ‘All these evils have fallen upon me’ (Gen. 42:36).”

**XLII.** From this it appears that Nicholas also had secretaries under him. One was Gerard of Péronne, his singular friend, “the inseparable companion,” he says in letter 10, “of my writing,” and praised by him in several other letters. Nicholas himself dedicated his letters to this Gerard and to Henry, a monk of royal descent.

**XLIII.** He frequently exchanged books with Peter of Celle and others. Of this kind is letter 34 to Amadeus, bishop of Lausanne, containing these words: “I send you Master Anselm’s book on the Holy Spirit, well punctuated, unless I am mistaken, and corrected.” He customarily sent copies of books on the condition that, when the copy was returned, another copy should be sent him free of charge. Thus he asks Peter of Celle in letter 24, after sending him two volumes of Bernard: “Make haste to copy these quickly, and return the copies to me; and have them copied for my use according to our agreement. [Column 29] Send me also the things which I sent you and the copies made from them, as has been said, and see that I lose not one iota.” Such are his words to Peter. He also repeatedly asked others to lend books, as in letter 17 to Peter, dean of Troyes: “Return to us the letters of the lord of Le Mans, for we wish to transcribe them.”

He even wrote to Philip, provost of the Church of Cologne and chancellor of the emperor, in the person of Brother Philip, congratulating him on his journey to Jerusalem; and he asks for Philip’s very rich library in these words of letter 29: “And see that you leave to Christ’s poor that singular treasure of yours—I mean the noble library which you have assembled as wonderfully as it is incomparably—so that they may pray and weep for you, that the God of our salvation may make your journey prosperous.”


**XLIV.** To show himself religious, Nicholas not only refused to read verses, following the example of his brethren of Clairvaux, but also returned a tunic sent him by a friend, as insufficiently suited to his order. On verses he says in letter 15: “I have not yet received the verses of my Walter—indeed, yours too. But even if I had seen them, I would not have read them through, because we receive nothing that is bound by metrical laws.” Odo, abbot of Pulteney, one of the Black Monks, had given him the tunic as a token of friendship. Nicholas returns it with many thanks in letter 27 because it was “too beautiful and precious; for this one reason not good, because too good.” He then adds: “I neither wish nor am able—indeed, I ought not—to wear it. Among those dressed in little rags and half-girdles, I shall walk neither purple-clad nor un-tunicked. Far be it, far be it, that a splendid garment should again be fitted to sinful flesh, lest it be carried away to its follies. Therefore I return it to you, since among us there is no one who either dares or ought to wear it. Wear it yourself, lord Father, to whom it is permitted both by your order and by your dignity. For when you put on a tunic, you do something beyond your customary practice. But you know who said: ‘Whatever you spend beyond this, I will repay you when I return’ (Luke 10:35).”

**XLV.** Three things in these words deserve notice. First is the reference to half-girdles. If Nicholas retained the proper use of the word, we infer that the Cistercians used half-girdles. What a half-girdle was can be understood from Herbert’s book I *On the Miracles of the Cistercians*, chapter 6. Speaking there of Schocelin, hermit of the district of Trier, he explains it thus: “That exceedingly wealthy man also had tied about his loins a shabby and very short half-girdle, which could scarcely cover the shameful parts of his body alone when that unavoidable necessity compelled him to appear before men.” The ancients called it a loincloth. It is indeed most likely that the Cistercians initially used such half-girdles, particularly since they wore only a tunic next to the skin; and it seemed necessary for decency when, having put aside the cowl, they worked with their hands.

The second point to note is why Nicholas says that putting on the tunic was beyond the custom and order of the abbot of Pulteney. The abbot professed the Rule of Saint Benedict, which grants monks a tunic among other things in chapter 55. This is true; but in those times monks commonly wore a long robe, not a tunic, which fell scarcely to the middle of the shin, such as the Cistercians wore. Or was it that tunic—undoubtedly white—which Abbot Odo sent Nicholas—and this is the third point to note—which Nicholas says Odo was permitted to wear “both by order and by dignity”? What then? Did the Black Monks at that time use white garments? Why, then, was there such great contention between them and the Cistercians concerning black and white clothing? The Benedictines did use a white tunic, at least in some places, but a black cowl, whereas the Cistercians wore a white one. Certainly in the Aniane Ceremonial, then in use among the Black Monks, monks are depicted in more than one place wearing a white robe and a somewhat black cowl. We have observed both likewise in other pictures, especially in Rabanus Maurus’s book *On the Cross*, where he is depicted in a white tunic.

Although the Cluniacs and Cistercians disputed not only about the color of the cowl, but also about that of the tunic, as may be gathered from Peter the Venerable’s letter 229 here, no. 22, this practice was by no means uniform among our brethren. But after the practice prevailed among those who wore a white tunic of adding a robe to the tunic, and, once the cowl had been put aside outside choir—though formerly this was not permitted even in bed—the robe alone with the scapular seemed sufficient to retain the monk’s distinguishing dress. Then at last the robe everywhere came to be made even of black cloth, while the tunic’s white color was retained. It was succeeded by a woolen garment, and later by an outer tunic which in our own time has also changed to black. The Cistercians, however, in their earliest period, content with a tunic and cowl alone, or with a scapular in place of the cowl, rejected robes, whether plain or woolen.

XLVI. Let us return to Nicholas. He took sufficient care to retain through literary service the friends he had gained in his earlier monastery of Arrémar, especially the two Peters, abbots of Cluny and of La Celle. We have only two letters to the abbot of Cluny among those he wrote before his defection from the Cistercian Order, namely the last two; but far more to Peter of La Celle. The first is Letter 20, in the person of Adam, a monk who had migrated from La Celle to Clairvaux. The other is Letter 24, addressed in Nicholas’s own name “to the most friendly lord Peter, abbot of La Celle, friend among friends,” in which he begs the duty of frequent letters. Letter 28 has a similar heading: “To Peter, abbot of La Celle, a special and almost singular friend”; so too Letter 48. Shorter but more familiar is the next letter, “His own to his own”; and, to omit Letter 51, Letter 52: “His own of La Celle to his own of Clairvaux, because his own.” Why I observe this more carefully will appear below: I shall maintain that before his desertion Nicholas had been well known and intimate with Peter of La Celle, and consequently that he is different from that Nicholas the Englishman against whom [Col. 0031] Peter of La Celle wrote a defence of Bernard, then dead, as against a man unknown to him by face.

XLVII. While the French Nicholas lived at Clairvaux, he wrote various letters in other persons’ names: those of Bernard himself, Prior Rualen, and other monks—more than fifty-five in all—which he addressed to “most beloved brethren Gerard and Henry,” that is, Gerard of Péronne and Henry, son of Louis the Fat and brother of Louis the Younger, then monks at Clairvaux. He also wrote some letters in their persons. Among those composed in Rualen’s name, the heading of Letter 23 is corrupt: “To the lord and worthily reverend Hugh, archbishop of Tours, Brother R.” Whoever supplied the heading made it: “In the person of the prior of Rievaulx to the archbishop of Tours.” John Picard notes in the margin that Rievaulx is a Cistercian abbey in England in the diocese of York. Correct enough; but what had the archbishop of Tours to do with Rievaulx? The letter was certainly written in the name of Prior Rualen; the abbreviation of his name in its address gave the heading’s author occasion for error. The same error occurs in Letter 23.

XLVIII. As we have said, Nicholas was a friend of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, even to affection; Bernard repeatedly sent him to Peter so that the mutual secrets of their hearts and reciprocal affections might be deposited with this mediator. On this see Peter’s Letter 264 among Bernard’s letters. But at last—O unhappy condition of mortals!—Nicholas abused Bernard’s indulgence and easiness, falsified his seal for evil uses, and finally fell into a dreadful defection which it is doubtful whether he ever seriously repaired. On the corrupted seal Bernard, concealing Nicholas’s name as charity befitted a holy man, informed Eugenius in Letter 284: “We have been in peril among false brethren, and many forged letters under our forged seal have gone into many hands; and, what I fear more, the falsehood is said to have flown even as far as you.” He laments the same man’s ruin in Letter 298 to the same Eugenius, no longer concealing the author because the crime was public: “That Nicholas went out from us because he was not of us; but he went out leaving foul traces behind him. I had known the man long before, yet waited either for God to convert him or for him, like Judas, to betray himself.” Behold the holy man’s patience! “And this happened. Besides books, money, and much gold, at his departure three seals were found upon him: one his own, another the prior’s, the third ours … Concerning his shameful acts, by which the earth is defiled and all have made them a byword, I refrain from polluting my lips and your ears.” Bernard adds that if he dared go to Eugenius’s court, as he boasted, he deserved, more than anyone, “perpetual confinement.” This fall happened in 1151, as appears from Bernard’s Letter 298 to Eugenius written that year and Peter the Venerable’s Letter 388 on the election of Grenoble in the same year; there Nicholas is praised as still dear to Bernard and Peter and as their faithful messenger.

XLIX. Everyone supposes that he fled to England and took refuge in St Albans monastery; that he was the Nicholas who publicly censured and attacked Bernard’s opinion on the Conception of the Mother of God, and had Peter of La Celle as adversary. This man was indeed called Nicholas, but that he was English is certain from Peter’s two letters to him, book VI, letter 23 and book IX, letter 10. In the former Peter says: “Let not English levity be indignant if Gallic maturity is more solid … Certainly I have found more dreamers English than French.” In the latter: “The Frenchman will keep the Englishman shut up and bound in his caverns.” These prove that that Nicholas was English; the last words of the letter show Peter did not know him by face: “Would that I saw face to face you whom the well-adorned habit of your writings has more than once enabled me to hear.” I pass over the difference of style between Nicholas the Englishman and Nicholas of Clairvaux: the Englishman’s is harsher and rougher; that of Clairvaux is brighter, more humane, and more polished. Yet the foregoing proves that Nicholas of Clairvaux was very well known and intimate with Peter before his flight, and was not English but Gaul or French; he must therefore be distinguished from that Englishman.


L. “But where,” you ask, “did Nicholas the Frenchman take refuge?” After wandering here and there, he finally settled in his own monastery of Arrémar, where after Bernard had been taken from the living he could live safely and without fear. This is clear both from Letter 59 of Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, to Nicholas himself and from Nicholas’s own letter to William, bishop of Reims, recently published by the most distinguished Étienne Baluze in volume II of his *Miscellanies*. That letter was not written before 1176, when William took the see of Reims. In it Nicholas praises him for admitting him into the “sanctuary” of his friendship and for giving no place to whisperers and detractors—for these Nicholas feared. He then excuses himself for having so long stayed away from William’s presence, and these words concern our matter: “Shall I excuse myself by the difficulty of the journey, by the length of country between the city of Reims and the church of Arrémar?” Nicholas therefore lived there at that time. “But the journey is short, the road level, and all around full of my friends.”

LI. What position or person Nicholas occupied in the monastery of Arrémar is indicated in what follows; from it we note only this: “Shall I add that I could not have permission to come, when I go and come, depart and return, throughout the whole day? I would say these things if I were so placed under authority that I could not have command of myself.” Nicholas therefore lived among the men of Arrémar in such a way as to be his own master. A miserable condition indeed for one who had been Bernard’s disciple and secretary! But who should wonder, when angels fell from heaven itself? [Col. 0033] He shows his vanity especially in boasting of a multitude of friends, as he did elsewhere. Thus in a letter to Henry, count of Champagne, published in the same volume of *Miscellanies* and written at nearly the same time as the preceding, he says: “From my earliest age I have pleased the great and highest princes of this world; but to you, by the dominion of nature, I owe uniquely whatever I am, and by the duty of friendship whatever I can do.” From this it is inferred that Nicholas was born in Champagne, which was subject to Henry’s lordship; but the cause of his fall must be sought in nothing other than vainglory and pride, which drive most people mad. That he was especially devoted to Henry, count of Champagne or Troyes, is understood from two letters of Nicholas to the count. One, by which he dedicates his sermons to him, published in tome III of the *Cistercian Library*, is addressed “to his singular lord and benefactor Henry,” and so forth; the other to the same man as “his most serene prince and dearest lord,” and is found in Baluze’s tome II. There he says: “I send to Your Highness certain letters which I remember, with some care, dedicating in the past two years to the lord pope, the chancellor, and other distinguished men.” Yet he seems to have abused the authority of the same prince, as appears from Arnulf of Lisieux’s Letter 59 “to Nicholas, monk of the monastery of Arramatus”—where *Arremarus* must be read. That letter concerns a bad canon, Nicholas’s disciple, for whom Nicholas says he had received “a further favour” through Arnulf’s intercession, though Arnulf denies it.

LII. From all these things Nicholas’s character appears: vain, inconstant, restless—a sort of person of whom scarcely any good can ever be hoped. We do not know what end he had. It remains, as I promised above, to present here as a specimen a fragment of St Bernard’s first sermon, rendered in French in an ancient manuscript of the Feuillant Fathers at Paris. Its title and beginning are these:


**CI ENCOMENCENT LI SERMON SAINT BERNAVT KIL FAIT DE LAVENT ET LES ALTRES FESTES PARMEI LAN.**

*Here begin the sermons which Saint Bernard made for Advent and the other feasts through the year.*

1. Today, dear brethren, we begin Advent, whose name, like the names of other solemnities, is well famed and known in the world, though the reason for the name is perhaps not so well known. For the wretched children of Adam care not for truth or for those things that belong to their salvation, but seek … failing and passing things. To what people shall we liken the people of this generation, or with what people shall we compare those whom we see so fixed and rooted in earthly and bodily comforts that they cannot be torn away from them? Certainly they are like those plunged in some great water and in danger of drowning. You would see them holding what they hold and for no reason willing to release whatever they can first put their hands upon, whatever it may be, even though it be something unable to help them at all, such as roots of herbs or other such things. If anyone comes to help them, they drag down with themselves everyone whom they can seize, so that neither they nor those others can give any aid. Thus the wretches perish in this great and wide sea, because, following things that perish, they let go the solid things by which they might be delivered from the danger in which they are and save their souls. For it is said of truth, not vanity: “You shall know it, and it shall deliver you.” But you, dear brethren, to whom God reveals, as to little ones, the things hidden from the wise and prudent, attend diligently to the things that truly belong to your salvation. Think carefully about the meaning of this Advent; ask and seek who it is that comes, whence he comes, where he comes, why he comes, when he comes, and by what way he comes. This inquiry is most praiseworthy and most healthful. For the whole holy Church would not celebrate this Advent so devoutly unless a great sacrament were hidden in it.

2. First, see how the Apostle is altogether amazed at this Advent, etc.

3. For God’s sake, dear brethren, flee pride, and flee it forcefully. Pride is the beginning of every sin, and so cruelly cast down Lucifer, who shone more brightly than all the stars; it changed not merely an angel into a devil, but the prince of angels. He especially envied humanity and put into it the wickedness he had conceived in himself when he persuaded it that it would be like God, knowing good and evil, [Col. 0034] if it ate the forbidden tree. Wretched and evil promise! Since the Son of the Most High has the key of knowledge—indeed he himself is the key of David, who shuts and no one opens, and in him are hidden all treasures of wisdom and knowledge—will you steal these in order to give them to humanity? Now you may see that this man is a liar and his father, according to our Lord’s sentence. He was a liar when he said he would be like the Most High, and father of lies when he poured the poisoned seed of falsehood into man, saying that they would be like God. You too, O human being, see the thief and run with him. You have heard, dear brethren, what was read tonight in the prophet Isaiah, where our Lord says: “The princes of your people are disobedient and companions of thieves.”

Truly our first rulers, Adam and Eve, the beginning of our race, were disobedient and companions of thieves. By the serpent’s counsel—or rather the devil’s counsel through the serpent—they wickedly wished to steal for themselves that which belongs only to the Son of God. The Father did not then delay punishment, as he did for the Son; for the Father loves the Son. Rather, he immediately avenged the Son upon humanity and laid his hand upon us all. For we all sinned in Adam and in him all received the sentence of condemnation. What would the Son do, seeing the Father so moved to avenge him that he spared no creature? “For me,” he says, “my Father loses all his creatures. The first angel wished to rise to my height and had a great company agreeing with him; but the Father’s love for me immediately avenged this, striking him and all his with cruel chastisement and an incurable wound. Humanity likewise wished to seize the knowledge that is mine, and he neither pitied it nor spared it. Does God care for beasts? He had made only two noble rational creatures capable of blessedness—angel and man. But for me he has lost a great part of the angels and all people. Therefore, that they may know that I too love the Father, it is right that he receive through me those whom he seems in some manner to have lost through me. If this tempest has arisen because of me, as Jonah says, take me and cast me into the sea. All envy me; but behold, I come and show myself such to them that all who put aside their envy and wish to follow me shall be blessed,” etc.

## SERMONS FOR THE SEASONS OF ST BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX

[Col. 0035]

### FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD


### SERMON I. On the Advent of the Lord and its six circumstances

[Col. 0035A]

1. Today, brethren, we celebrate the beginning of Advent. Its name, like that of the other solemnities, is certainly famous and known to the world, but perhaps the reason for the name is not so well known. For the unhappy children of Adam, abandoning true and saving pursuits, seek instead fleeting and passing things. To what shall we liken people of this generation, or to whom shall we compare those whom we see unable to be torn and separated from earthly and bodily consolations? They are certainly like persons submerged and in danger in waters. You may see them holding fast and on no account abandoning whatever first comes to hand, whatever it may be, even though it be something wholly unable [Col. 0035B] to help them, such as roots of plants and other things of that kind. If some come to them to help, they sometimes draw those whom they have seized down with them, so that they are no longer able to bring aid either to themselves or to others. Thus the wretched perish in this great and broad sea: following perishable things, they lose the solid things by grasping which they could rise up from their danger and save their souls. For it is said not of vanity but of truth: “You shall know it, and it shall set you free” (John 8:32). Therefore, brethren, to whom God reveals, as to little ones, what is hidden from the wise and prudent, turn diligent thought to things that are truly saving. Carefully weigh the meaning of this Advent, asking who comes, whence [Col. 0035C], where, for what purpose, when, and by what way. This inquiry is undoubtedly praiseworthy and healthful; for the universal Church would not celebrate this present Advent so devoutly unless a great mystery were hidden in it.

2. First, then, together with the Apostle in astonishment and wonder, consider how great is he who enters. For according to Gabriel’s testimony he is the Son of the Most High (Luke 1:32), and consequently is himself coequal with the Most High. It is not lawful to suppose that the Son of God is degenerate; rather, it is necessary to confess that he is of equal height and exactly the same dignity. For who does not know that the sons of princes are princes, and the sons of kings kings? Nevertheless, what does it mean that, of the [Col. 0036A] three persons whom we believe, confess, and adore in the supreme Trinity, neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit came, but the Son? I certainly do not think that this happened without cause. But “who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Romans 11:34). For it was not without the most exalted counsel of the Trinity that the Son came; and if we consider the cause of our exile, perhaps we can perceive at least in part how fitting it was that we should be delivered especially by the Son. That Lucifer who rose in the morning, because he attempted to usurp the likeness of the Most High and regarded equality with God as something to seize—which belongs properly to the Son—was immediately cast down and fell, because the Father was zealous for the Son and seemed to say by his deed: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” [Col. 0036B] (Romans 12:19). “Immediately I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). Why, then, are you proud, earth and ashes? If God did not spare the angels when they grew proud, how much less will he spare you, corruption and a worm?
