Lucifer did nothing and carried nothing out; he merely conceived pride, and in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, was irreparably cast down, because according to the Evangelist “he did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44).

3. Flee pride, my brethren; I beg you, flee it greatly. Pride is the beginning of every sin. It so swiftly darkened with eternal gloom even Lucifer, who shone more brightly than all the stars; it changed not merely an angel but the first of the angels into a devil. Hence, immediately envying humanity, he produced [Col. 0036C] in it the iniquity he had conceived in himself, persuading it that by tasting the forbidden tree it would become like God, knowing good and evil. What are you promising, what are you pledging, wretch, when the Son of the Most High possesses the key of knowledge—indeed, is himself the key of David, “who shuts and no one opens” (Revelation 3:7)? In him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians 2:3). Will you then wickedly steal them in order to give them to humanity? You see that, according to the Lord’s judgment, he is a liar and the father of falsehood (John 8:44). He was a liar when he said, “I shall be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14), and the father of the lie when he poured the poisoned seedbed of his falsehood into humanity, saying, “You shall be like gods” (Genesis 3:5). You too, O human being, if you see a thief, run with him. You heard, brethren, [Col. 0037A] what was read tonight in Isaiah, when the Lord said: “Your princes are faithless”; or, as another translation has it, “disobedient, companions of thieves” (Isaiah 1:23).

4. Truly our rulers, Adam and Eve, the beginnings of our stock, were disobedient and companions of thieves: by the serpent’s counsel—or rather the devil’s through the serpent—they tried to steal what belongs to the Son of God. The Father does not conceal the injury to the Son, for “the Father loves the Son” (John 5:20); he immediately exacts vengeance upon humanity and lays his hand heavily upon us. For all sinned in Adam, and all received in him the sentence of condemnation. What does the Son do, seeing the Father zeal for him and spare no creature? “Behold,” he says, “because of me the Father loses his creatures. The first angel desired [Col. 0037B] my height and had a people who believed him; but the Father’s zeal immediately avenged this grievously, striking him and all his with an incurable wound and cruel chastisement. Humanity likewise wanted to steal the knowledge that is mine, and his eye neither pitied nor spared it. Does God care for oxen? (1 Corinthians 9:9.) He had made only two noble creatures, sharing reason and capable of blessedness—angel and human—but behold, because of me he lost many angels and all humans. Therefore, that they may know that I also love the Father, let him receive through me those whom he seems in some manner to have lost because of me. If this tempest has arisen because of me,” as Jonah says, “take me and cast me into the sea” (Jonah 1:12). [Col. 0037C] “All envy me. Behold, I come and show myself to them in such a way that whoever wishes to envy, whoever longs to imitate, may find that rivalry turned to good. Yet I know that the deserting angels passed into an affection of malice and wickedness and sinned not through ignorance or weakness; therefore, unwilling to repent, they must perish. For the Father’s love and the King’s honour love judgment.”

5. For this reason he created humans from the beginning to fill that place and restore Jerusalem’s ruins. He knew that no way of return lay open to angels. “He knows the pride of Moab, that he is very proud” (Isaiah 16:6); pride admits no remedy of repentance, and therefore [Col. 0037D] no forgiveness. But after humanity he created no further creature, thereby indicating that humanity was still to be redeemed; it was overthrown by another’s malice, and another’s love can therefore benefit it. “So, Lord, may it please you to deliver me, for I am weak; for I was secretly taken from my land, and here I was cast innocent into the pit” (Genesis 40:15). Not wholly innocent, indeed, but in some degree innocent in relation to the one who seduced me. A lie was persuaded to me, Lord: let Truth come, that falsehood may be discovered; let me know truth, and truth set me free—provided I wholly renounce falsehood once discovered and cling to truth once known. Otherwise the temptation and sin will not be human but diabolical obstinacy. To persevere in evil is diabolical; all who remain in sin in the devil’s likeness deserve to perish with him. [Col. 0038A]

6. Behold, brethren, you have heard who comes; now consider whence he comes and where. He comes from the heart of God the Father into the womb of the Virgin Mother; he comes from highest heaven into the lower parts of the earth. What then? Must we not also live on earth? Yes, provided he remains in it. Where can it be well without him, or where can it be ill with him? “What have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you on earth? God of my heart and my portion, God for ever” (Psalm 72:25). “Though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, if you are with me” (Psalm 22:4). Now, as I see, he descends even to the earth and [Col. 0038B] to hell itself, not as a captive but as free among the dead, like light shining in darkness which darkness did not comprehend. Hence his soul is not left in hell nor his holy body see corruption on earth. Christ who descended is also he who ascended, that he might fill all things. Of him it is written: “He went about doing good and healing all oppressed by the devil” (Acts 10:38); and elsewhere: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his way: his going out is from the highest heaven and his return to its summit” (Psalm 18:6). The Apostle therefore rightly cries: “Seek the things above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:1). He would labour in vain to raise our hearts unless he taught that the author of our salvation is placed [Col. 0038C] in heaven. Yet let us see what follows. The matter is indeed copious and most abundant, but the narrowness of time does not admit so great a length of discourse. To those considering who comes, a great and ineffable majesty has appeared; to those considering whence he comes, a truly great way has opened, as he testifies who, inspired by prophetic spirit, says: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar” (Isaiah 30:27). And to those considering where he comes, an inestimable and wholly unthinkable condescension appears: so great a height deigned to descend into the horror of this prison.


7. Who can now doubt that some great matter was involved [Col. 0038D], for so great a Majesty deigned to descend from so far away into so unworthy a place? It was surely something great: great mercy, much compassion, abundant love. For what purpose should he be believed to have come? This is what the order we proposed requires us now to investigate. Nor is labour needed here, since both his words and works openly proclaim the cause of his advent. He hastened down from the mountains to seek the hundredth sheep that had strayed; and, that people might more openly confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men, he came for us. Wonderful is the condescension of God who seeks; great is the dignity of humanity thus sought. Whoever wishes to glory in this will not be foolish—not because humanity appears to be anything from itself, but because its Maker has made it of such worth. All the riches and glory of the world, and all desired in it, are less than this glory; indeed they are nothing by comparison. “Lord, what is man that you magnify him, or set your heart upon him?” [Col. 0039A]

8. Yet I would know why he came to us, or why we did not rather go to him. Need was ours; but it is not the custom of the rich to come to the poor, even when they intend to bestow. It was more fitting, brethren, that we should come to him, but there was a twofold impediment. Our eyes were dark, while he inhabits inaccessible light (1 Timothy 6:16); and, lying paralysed upon a bed, we could not [Col. 0039B] reach that divine height. Therefore the most gracious Saviour and physician of souls descended from his height and tempered his brightness for weak eyes. He clothed himself with a lantern, namely that glorious and unstained body which he assumed. This is the very light and shining cloud upon which the prophet foretold he would ascend in descending into Egypt (Isaiah 19:1).

9. It is now time to consider the time when the Saviour came. He came, as you surely know, not at the beginning or middle of time but at its end. This was not unsuitable: Wisdom truly and wisely arranged to bring help first [Col. 0039C] when it was more necessary, not unaware that Adam’s children are prone to ingratitude. The day was indeed drawing toward evening and already declining; the sun of righteousness had almost departed, so that there was very little brightness or warmth on earth. The light of divine knowledge was extremely small, and, as iniquity abounded, love’s fervour had grown cold. Angel no longer appeared, prophet no longer spoke; as if overcome by despair, they ceased because of humanity’s excessive hardness and obstinacy. Then the Son says: “Behold, I come” (Psalm 39:8). Thus, while all things held deep silence and night in its course ran through its way (Wisdom 18:14), your almighty Word, Lord, came from royal thrones. The Apostle indicates this: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Galatians [Col. 0039D] 4:4). The fullness and abundance of temporal things had made oblivion and scarcity of eternal things. Eternity therefore came fittingly when temporality prevailed most; and at that time temporal peace was so great that the whole world was enrolled at one person’s decree (Luke 2:1).

10. You now have the person who comes, both places—from which and to which he comes—the cause, and the time. One thing remains, the way by which he came, and this too must be carefully sought, so that we may worthily meet him. But as he once came visibly in flesh to work salvation in the midst of the earth, so daily [Col. 0040A] he comes invisibly in spirit to save the souls of individuals: “Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face.” To show that this spiritual advent is hidden: “In his shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lamentations 4:20). Therefore, if the sick person cannot go far out to meet so great a physician, he should at least strive to raise his head and rise somewhat to meet the one who comes. You need not, O human being, cross seas, penetrate clouds, or go beyond the Alps. The way shown you is not great: meet your God as far as yourself. “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Romans 10:8). Meet him in compunction of heart and confession of mouth, that you may at least leave the dung-heap of miserable conscience [Col. 0040B], for it is unworthy that the author of purity enter there. These things have been said of the advent by which he deigns invisibly to illuminate individual minds with his presence.

11. But it delights us to consider the way of the manifest advent, for “his ways are beautiful ways and all his paths are peace” (Proverbs 3:17). “Behold,” says the bride, “he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills” (Song 2:8). You see him coming, O beautiful one, but before you could not see him reclining; for you said: “Tell me, whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you recline” (Song 1:6). Reclining, he feeds angels in their everlasting eternities, satisfying them with sight of his eternity and immutability. But lest you fail to know yourself, O beautiful one: “That vision has been made wonderful from [Col. 0040C] you; it has been strengthened, and you cannot attain it.” Yet behold, he has gone out from his holy place; and he who reclining feeds angels has come and will heal us. He will be seen coming and feeding, though before he could not be seen reclining and feeding. Behold, he comes leaping upon mountains and skipping over hills. Understand the mountains and hills as patriarchs and prophets; read the book of generations to see how he came leaping and skipping: “Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob” (Matthew 1:2), and so forth. From these mountains came, as you find, the root of Jesse; from it, according to the prophet, a rod came forth and from it a flower ascended, on which rested the sevenfold Spirit (Isaiah 11:1–3). The same prophet explains it more clearly elsewhere: [Col. 0040D] “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which means “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14). He first called him flower and then Emmanuel; and, explaining more plainly the rod he had named, he called it a virgin. But the consideration of this most high mystery must be reserved for another day, for the matter deserves its own sermon, especially since today’s discourse has already grown long.

### SERMON II. On Isaiah’s words to Ahaz: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth of hell or in the height above,” etc. (Isaiah 7:11–16).

**1.** We have heard Isaiah urging King Ahaz to ask a sign of the Lord, whether in the depth [Column 41A] of hell or in the height above. We have heard his answer, having indeed the form of piety but not its power. Therefore he deserved to be rejected by him who sees the heart and to whom human thought confesses itself. “I will not ask,” he says, “and I will not tempt the Lord.” Ahaz was exalted by the height of a royal throne and cunning in the words of human wisdom. Isaiah had heard from the Lord: “Go, say to that fox that he should ask himself a sign from the Lord in the depth.” For the fox has its hole; but even if he descends to hell, one is present who catches the wise in their cunning. Again the Lord says: “Go, say to that bird that he should ask a sign in the height above.” For the bird has its nest; but if he ascends to heaven, there is one there who, resisting the proud, tramples by his own power upon the necks of the proud and lofty [Column 41B].

Yet Ahaz pretends not to seek a sign of exalted power or unfathomable depth of wisdom. Therefore the Lord himself promises the house of David a sign of goodness and love, so that those whom neither power nor wisdom frightened may at least be attracted by love’s manifestation. But in the words “in the depth of hell,” love itself may rightly be signified—the love than which none was greater, so that, dying for friends, it descended even into hell. Ahaz is thus commanded either to fear the majesty of the reigning One in the height, or to embrace the love of the One descending to hell. Therefore anyone is burdensome not only to human beings but also to God who neither considers majesty with fear nor meditates on love with love [Column 41C]. “Therefore,” he says, “the Lord himself will give you a sign,” in which both majesty and love are plainly made known. “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted “God with us.” Do not flee, Adam, for God is with us. Do not fear, O man, and do not be terrified when you hear God’s name, for God is with us: with us by likeness of flesh, with us by unity [alias, usefulness]. For us he came as one of us, like us, capable of suffering.

**2.** “He shall eat butter and honey,” he says. It is as though he said: “He shall be a little child and shall feed on infant foods.” “That he may know,” he says, “to reject evil and choose good.” Here too you hear good and evil, as in the forbidden tree, as in the tree of transgression. But this second Adam makes a far better division than the first [Column 41D]. Choosing good, he rejects evil, unlike him who “loved cursing, and it came upon him; he did not desire blessing, and it was far from him” (Ps. 108:18). In the words which preceded, “He shall eat butter and honey,” you may observe this little child’s choice. May his grace be present, so that he may grant us worthily to perceive, however imperfectly, what he bestows and to set it forth suitably to understanding.

There are two things in sheep’s milk: butter and cheese. Butter is rich and moist; cheese, by contrast, dry and hard. Thus our little child rightly knows how to choose: eating butter, he certainly does not eat cheese. For what is the hundredth sheep that went astray (Matt. 18:12), and speaks in the Psalm: “I have gone astray like a lost sheep” [Column 42A] (Ps. 118:176)? It is surely the human race, which the most gracious shepherd seeks, leaving the other ninety-nine sheep upon the mountains. In this sheep, therefore, you find a sweet nature, a good nature, and very good, like butter; and the corruption of sin, like cheese. See then how excellently our child chose: he took our nature without any corruption of sin. For you read of sinners: “Their heart has curdled like milk” (ibid., 70); in them the leaven of malice, the curdling of iniquity, had corrupted the purity of milk.

**3.** So too the bee has the sweetness of honey and also the sting’s wound. The bee is she who feeds among lilies and dwells in the flower-bearing country of angels [Column 42B]. Thus she flew to the city of Nazareth, which is interpreted “flower,” and came to the sweet-smelling flower of perpetual virginity; she settled on her and clung to her. He knows the honey and sting of this bee who sings to her of mercy and judgment with the Prophet (Ps. 100:1). Yet when she came to us, she brought honey only, not the sting: that is, mercy and not judgment. Thus when the disciples at one time urged him to command a city which would not receive him to be consumed by fire, he answered that the Son of Man had not come to judge but to save the world (Luke 9:54–56). Our bee did not have the sting; in some manner she had laid it aside when, suffering so many indignities, she displayed mercy and not judgment.

But do not hope in iniquity; do not sin in hope [Column 42C]. For our bee will someday take up her sting and drive it very sharply into the marrow of sinful men, because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). But now our little child eats butter and honey, when he so united in himself the good of human nature with divine mercy that he was true man and had no sin, merciful God and did not exercise judgment.


**4.** From these things, I think, it is now clear what the rod proceeding from Jesse’s root is, and who is the flower upon whom the Holy Spirit rests. The Virgin Mother of God is the rod; her Son is the flower. The Son of the Virgin is indeed a flower, “white and ruddy, chosen from thousands” (Song 5:10); the flower into which [Column 42D] angels desire to look; the flower at whose fragrance the dead revive; and, as he himself testifies, he is the flower of the field (Song 2:1), not of a garden. A field flowers without any human aid: sown by none, dug with no hoe, enriched by no manure. So altogether, so did the Virgin’s womb flower; so did Mary’s inviolate, whole, and chaste entrails, like pastures of eternal verdure, bring forth a flower whose beauty sees no corruption and whose glory never fades.

O Virgin, lofty rod, to what a height you raise your holy summit! To the One seated on the throne, to the Lord of majesty. Nor is this wonderful, since you send the roots of humility down deep. O truly heavenly plant, more precious than all things, [Column 43A] holier than all! O truly tree of life, alone worthy to bear the fruit of salvation! You have been caught, malicious serpent; your cunning has been laid bare, your falsehood plainly uncovered. You had accused the Creator on two charges, falsehood and envy; but in both you have been convicted of lying. For from the beginning, he dies to whom you said, “You shall not die at all” (Gen. 3:4), and “the truth of the Lord remains forever” (Ps. 116:2). Now answer, if you can, what tree—whose fruit he might have envied—was denied by him who did not deny even this chosen rod and exalted fruit. For “he who did not spare his own Son, how did he not also give us all things together with him?” (Rom. 8:32).

**5.** But you have now noticed, I think, that the royal Virgin herself is the way by which the Savior came, proceeding [Column 43B] from her womb like a bridegroom from his chamber. Holding, then, the way which, if you remember, we began to seek in the preceding sermon, let us also, dearly beloved, strive to ascend through her to him who descended through her to us; through her to come into the grace of him who came through her into our misery. Through you may we have access to the Son, O blessed finder of grace, bearer of life, mother of salvation, so that he who was given to us through you may receive us through you. May your integrity excuse before him the guilt of our corruption; may your humility, pleasing to God, obtain pardon for our vanity. May your abundant love cover the multitude of our sins, and your glorious fruitfulness confer on us fruitfulness in merits. Our Lady, our mediatrix, our advocate, reconcile us to your Son; commend us to your Son; present us to your Son [Column 43C]. Make it so, O blessed one, by the grace you found, by the prerogative you deserved, by the mercy you bore [alias, received], that he who through you deigned to become a participant in our weakness and misery may also, through your intercession, make us participants in his glory and blessedness—Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord, who is God above all, blessed forever. Amen.

## Sermon III: On the threefold coming of the Lord and the seven columns which we must raise in ourselves

**1.** In the Advent of the Lord which we celebrate, if I consider the person [Column 43D] who comes, I cannot comprehend the excellence of his majesty. If I attend to those to whom he came, I tremble at the greatness of his condescension. The angels surely marvel at the novelty, seeing beneath themselves him whom they always worship above themselves; they are now plainly ascending and descending upon the Son of Man. If I consider why he came, I embrace as far as I can the immeasurable breadth of his love. If I consider the manner, I recognize the exaltation of the human condition. For the Creator and Lord of the universe came; he came to human beings, for human beings, and as a human being.

But someone will say: How is he said to have come who was always everywhere? He was indeed in the world, and the world was made through him, but the world did not know him (John 1:10). Thus one who was absent did not come; one who was hidden appeared. Therefore he put on the human form by which he might be known, he who dwells in divine inaccessible light [Column 44A] (1 Tim. 6:16). Nor is it dishonorable for majesty to appear in its own likeness, which it had made from the beginning, nor unworthy of God to be shown in an image to those by whom he could not be known in his substance, so that he who made man in his own image and likeness might become known to men by becoming man.

**2.** The whole Church solemnly commemorates once a year this coming of such majesty, such humility, such love, and such glorification of us. But would that it were done once in such a way as to be done always; that would be more fitting. For how great the madness that, after the coming of so great a King, people should wish [Column 44B] or dare to be occupied with any other affairs, rather than, putting all things aside, devote themselves to his worship alone and remember no one else in his presence. But the Prophet’s saying is not for everyone: “They shall utter the memory of the abundance of your sweetness” (Ps. 144:7); for not everyone is fed by this memory. Certainly no one utters what he has not tasted, nor even what he has merely tasted. Utterance proceeds only from fullness and satiety. Therefore those whose mind and life are worldly, though they celebrate this remembrance, do not utter it; without devotion and affection they observe these days with a certain dry custom.

Indeed, what is more blameworthy, the very remembrance of this inestimable condescension is made an occasion for the flesh. You may see them preparing with such care in these days the glory of clothes [Column 44C] and the pleasures of food, as if Christ sought these and similar things at his birth, and were received more worthily where they are displayed more meticulously. But hear him himself say: “With a proud eye and insatiable heart I did not eat” (Ps. 100:5). Why do you prepare clothes with such ambition for my Nativity? I detest pride; I do not embrace it. Why do you store such abundance of food for that time with such anxiety? I condemn pleasures of the flesh; I do not accept them. You are plainly insatiable in heart, preparing so much and so long in advance; surely fewer things, and things more readily found, would suffice for the body. Thus when you celebrate my Advent, you honor me with your lips, but your heart is far from me. You do not worship me: your god is your belly, [Column 44D] and your glory is in your shame. Completely unhappy is one who worships bodily pleasure and the vanity of worldly glory. But “blessed is the people whose God is the Lord” (Ps. 143:15).


**3.** Brothers, “do not envy evildoers, nor be jealous of those who do iniquity” (Ps. 36:1). Rather consider their latter end, pity them from the heart, and pray for those overtaken in sin. These wretches act thus because they have ignorance of God. Had they known him, they would never in such madness have provoked the Lord of glory against themselves. But we, dearly beloved, have no excuse of ignorance. Whoever you are who are here, you certainly know him; if you say, “I do not know him,” you will be a liar like worldly people. For if you do not know him, who brought you here [Column 45A], or how did you come here? How otherwise could you be persuaded voluntarily to renounce the affections of loved ones, the pleasures of the body, the vanities of the world, to cast your care upon the Lord, and to throw every anxiety upon him, from whom, as conscience bears witness, you deserved nothing good but so much evil? Who, I say, could persuade you of this, unless you knew that “the Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him”; unless you too had known that the Lord is sweet, gentle, abundant in mercy, and true? And how do you know these things, unless he came not only to you but also into you?

**4.** For we know his threefold coming: to human beings, into human beings, and against human beings. He comes to all indiscriminately [Column 45B], but not in the same way into all, nor against all. Since the first and third are known because manifest, hear him himself speak of the second, which is spiritual and hidden: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Blessed is he with whom you make your dwelling, Lord Jesus. Blessed is the one in whom Wisdom builds herself a house, hewing out seven columns. Blessed is the soul which is Wisdom’s seat. What soul is that? Surely the soul of the righteous. Rightly so, because “justice and judgment are the preparation of your seat.” Which of you, brothers, desires to prepare Christ a seat in his soul? See what silks, tapestries, and cushion [Column 45C] must be prepared for him: “Justice,” he says, “and judgment are the preparation of your seat” (Ps. 88:15).

Justice is the virtue that gives to each what is his. Give, therefore, what belongs to them to three classes. Return to superior, inferior, and equal each what you owe; thus you worthily celebrate Christ’s coming by preparing his seat in justice. Return, I say, reverence and obedience to your superior: one belongs to the heart and the other to the body. For it is not enough outwardly to obey our elders unless from the innermost affection of our heart we think highly of them. Even if a superior’s unworthy life becomes so manifest that it allows neither concealment nor excuse, nevertheless, for the sake of him from whom all authority comes, we must deem high the one we know to be such [Column 45D], yielding not to the present merits of the person but to divine ordination and the dignity of the office itself.

**5.** So also to our brothers among whom we live, by the very right of brotherhood and human fellowship, we owe counsel and assistance. We desire them to render us these same things: counsel, by which our ignorance is instructed; assistance, by which our weakness is helped. Yet perhaps someone among you silently answers: “What counsel shall I give a brother when I may not say even a single word without permission? What assistance can I give him when I may not do even the smallest thing without obedience?” To this I answer: there will surely be something for you to do, provided brotherly love is not lacking. I judge that no counsel is better than striving by your example to teach your brother what should and should not be done, urging him to better things and counseling him not by word or tongue, but by deed and truth [Column 46A]. Is there any assistance more useful or effective than devoutly praying for him, not neglecting to rebuke his faults, not only placing no stumbling block before him, but also being solicitous, to the extent of your power, like an angel of peace, to remove from God’s kingdom scandals and every occasion of scandal? If you show yourself such a helper and counselor to your brother, you render him what you owe and he has no ground for complaint.

**6.** Moreover, if you happen to be set over someone, you are without doubt bound to him by the debt of greater solicitude. He demands from you both custody [Column 46B] and discipline: custody, so that he may avoid sin; discipline, so that what he did not sufficiently avoid may by no means remain unpunished. Even if you seem to preside over none of the brethren, you nevertheless have under you someone to whom you must give this custody and discipline. I mean your body, which your spirit has undoubtedly received to govern. You owe it custody, so that sin may not reign in it and your members may not become weapons of iniquity. You owe it discipline too, so that, chastised and reduced to servitude, it may bear fruits worthy of repentance.

Yet those bound to give account for many souls are held by a far more grave and dangerous debt. Woe to me! Where shall I turn if I should keep negligently so great a treasure, this precious deposit which Christ judged more precious to himself than his own blood? If I had collected the blood dripping on the Lord’s cross and it had been entrusted to me in a glass vessel that had often to be carried, what would my mind be in such danger? And surely I have received to keep that for which the merchant who was not foolish—Wisdom itself—gave that blood. Yet I have this treasure in earthen vessels [Column 46C], and dangers far more numerous than those threatening glass seem to threaten them. To the accumulation of solicitude and weight of fear is added the fact that, since I must guard both my own conscience and my neighbor’s, neither is sufficiently known to me. Each is an unsearchable abyss, each a night to me; nevertheless the custody of both is required of me, and the cry is raised: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what [Column 46D] of the night?” (Isa. 21:11). I may not say with Cain, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Gen. 4:9), but must humbly confess with the Prophet that “unless the Lord keeps the city, the watchman watches in vain” (Ps. 126:1). Still, I seem excusable if, as I said, I give the custody and discipline that are due. If the preceding four things also are not lacking—reverence and obedience toward superiors, counsel and assistance toward brothers—Wisdom will find a seat prepared, not unready, in what belongs to justice.


**7.** Perhaps these seem to be the six columns that Wisdom cut out in the very house which she built for herself; and a seventh must be sought, if perhaps she may deign to make it known to us also. What [Column 47A] prevents us from understanding judgment as the seventh, just as the six are understood in justice? For he does not say justice alone, but “justice and judgment are the preparation of your seat” (Ps. 88:15). Finally, if we give superiors, equals, and inferiors what is fitting, shall God receive nothing? Yet no one can repay God what is owed him, because he has heaped his mercy so abundantly upon us, because we have sinned so much against him, because we are so frail and nothing, and because he is so full and self-sufficient, needing none of our goods. Yet I have heard one to whom the uncertain and hidden things of divine wisdom had been revealed say that “the honor of the king loves judgment” (Ps. 98:4). God requires nothing more from us than what lies within our power: only let us confess our iniquities, and he will justify us freely, so that grace may be commended.

For he loves the soul that considers itself in his sight without interruption and judges itself without pretense [Column 47B]. He requires that judgment from us only for our sake, because if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. Therefore the wise man fears all his works, searches, examines, and judges everything. He honors truth who both truly recognizes himself and all his things in the condition in which truth finds them and humbly confesses them. Hear, finally, that judgment is plainly required of you after justice: “When you have done all that was commanded you, say, ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke 17:10). This, as far as humanity is concerned, is a worthy preparation of a seat for the Lord of majesty: to strive to observe the commands of justice and always to judge oneself unworthy and unprofitable [Column 47C].

## Sermon IV: On the twofold coming and the pursuit of true virtues [alias, On the twofold coming and silvered wings]

**1.** It is fitting, brothers, that you celebrate the Lord’s Advent with all devotion, delighted by so great a consolation, astonished by so great a condescension, and inflamed by so great a love. Consider not only the coming by which he came to seek and save what was lost, but also the one by which he will come and take us to himself. Would that you were occupied with continual meditation on these two comings, pondering in your hearts how much he bestowed in the first and how much he promised in the second. Would that you might sleep between the two portions [Column 47D]. These are the bridegroom’s two arms, between which the bride, sleeping, said: “His left hand is under my head, and his right shall embrace me” (Song 2:6). For in his left hand, as we read elsewhere, are riches and glory; in his right, length of life (Prov. 3:16).

“In his left hand,” he says, “are riches and glory.” Sons of Adam, avaricious and ambitious race, listen. What have you to do with earthly riches and temporal glory, which are neither true nor yours? Gold and silver: are they not red and white earth, which human error alone makes, or rather considers, precious? Finally, if these are yours, take them with you. But when man dies, he will not take all things, and his glory will not go down with him.

**2.** True riches, therefore, are not wealth but virtues [Column 48A], which conscience carries with itself so that it may be rich forever. The Apostle also says concerning glory: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). This is indeed true glory, which comes from the Spirit of truth. For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God (Rom. 8:16). But the glory received from one another by those who do not seek the glory that comes from God alone is vain, because the children of men are vain. Fool, you gather wages into a pierced bag and place your treasure in another’s mouth! Do you not know that this chest is not closed and has no locks? How much more wisely do those act who keep their treasure themselves and do not entrust it to others. But will they always keep it? Will they always conceal it [Column 48B]?

The time will come when the hidden things of the heart will be made manifest; what has been displayed will not appear. Thus, when the Lord comes, the lamps of the foolish virgins are extinguished (Matt. 25:1–12), and those who have received their reward (Matt. 6:16) are unknown to the Lord. Therefore I tell you, dearest ones, it is more useful to conceal than to display whatever good we have. So beggars asking alms do not show costly clothes, but half-naked limbs or, if they have them, sores, so that the mind of the beholder may more quickly incline to mercy. That rule the Publican observed much better than the Pharisee, and therefore “went down justified from him” (Luke 18:14), that is, before him.

**3.** It is time, brothers, for judgment to begin from [Column 48C] the house of God. What will be the end of those who do not obey the Gospel? What judgment awaits those who do not rise in this judgment? Whoever neglects to be judged in the judgment that is now, in which the prince of this world is cast out, should await—or rather fear—the Judge by whom they too will be cast out with their prince. But if we are judged perfectly now, let us safely await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who “will reform the body of our humility, configured to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:21). Then the righteous will shine so that learned and unlearned alike may see them, for “they shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43). The brightness of the sun will be sevenfold (Isa. 30:26), that is, like the light of seven days.


[Column 48D] **4.** When the Savior comes, he will reform the body of our humility, configuring it to the body of his glory—provided that the heart has first been reformed and configured to the humility of his heart. Therefore he said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). Consider in these words that humility is twofold: one of knowledge, the other of affection, which is here called humility of heart. By the first we know that we are nothing; we learn it from ourselves and our own weakness. By the second we trample worldly glory; we learn it from him who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), who fled when sought for kingship, yet willingly offered himself when sought for such shame and the ignominious [Column 49A] punishment of the cross. If we wish to sleep between the two portions—that is, the two comings—let our wings therefore be silvered (Ps. 67:14), so that we may hold the form of virtues which Christ, present in flesh, commended by word and example. In silver his humanity is fittingly understood, as his divinity is in gold.

**5.** Every virtue of ours is as far from true virtue as it is from that form, and every wing of ours is worthless unless it is silvered. Poverty is a great wing by which one flies so quickly to the kingdom of heaven. In the other virtues that follow, the promise is stated in the future; to poverty it is not so much promised as given [Column 49B]. Hence it is stated in the present: “For theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” whereas of the others it is said: “They shall inherit,” “they shall be comforted,” and the like (Matt. 5:3–9). Yet we see certain poor persons who, if they had true poverty, would not be so fainthearted and sad, being kings, and kings of heaven. These are the people who want to be poor on condition that they lack nothing, and so love poverty that they endure no want. Others are meek so long as nothing is said or done except as they wish; but should a slight occasion arise, it will appear how far they are from true meekness. How will this meekness inherit, which fails before inheritance?

I see others mourning, but if those tears proceeded from the heart, they would not so easily [Column 49C] immediately dissolve into laughter. Now when idle and jesting words flow more abundantly than the tears before, I do not think those tears are of the kind to which divine consolation is promised, since cheap consolation is so easily admitted after them. Others are so vehemently zealous against others’ offenses that they might seem to hunger and thirst for justice, if the same judgment were present in them concerning their own sins. But now “weight and weight, both are an abomination to God” (Prov. 20:23). Against others they boil as shamelessly as vainly; themselves they flatter as foolishly as uselessly.

**6.** Others are merciful with things that do not belong to them. They are scandalized if everything is not given abundantly to all [Column 49D], yet so that they themselves are not burdened even slightly. If they were merciful, they ought to show mercy from their own goods; if unable to do so from earthly substance, they should give pardon from good will to those whom they see perhaps sinning against them. They should give a sweet sign, a good word, which is above the best gift, to urge their minds to repentance. Finally, to these and to all whom they know to be in sin, they should give compassion and prayer. Otherwise their mercy is none, and they receive no mercy.

Likewise, some confess their sins in such a way that they might seem to do it from a desire to cleanse their heart—for all things are washed in confession—except that they cannot patiently hear from others what they themselves voluntarily tell others [Column 50A]. If they truly desired cleansing, as they seem to, they would not be angered, but would thank those who showed them their stains. There are also those who, if they see anyone even lightly scandalized, are very anxious how they may restore him to peace and would seem peaceable, except that their own disturbance, should anything be done or said against them, can be calmed by all only more slowly and with greater difficulty. If they truly loved peace, they would undoubtedly seek it for themselves.

**7.** Let us therefore silver our wings in Christ’s conduct [Column 50B], as the holy martyrs washed their robes in his Passion. Let us imitate, as far as we can, him who so loved poverty that, although the ends of the earth were in his hand, he had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58), so that we read that his disciples, clinging to him, compelled by hunger, rubbed ears of grain in their hands as they passed through fields (Luke 6:1). Let us imitate him who was led like a sheep to slaughter and, like a lamb before his shearer, was silent and did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7); whom we read to have wept over Lazarus and over the city (John 11:35; Luke 19:41), and to have spent the night in prayer (Luke 6:12), but nowhere to have laughed or jested [Note: [Column 49D] Alias, *jocatum*. But the manuscripts have *jocasse*. Although few would readily have used *joco* for *jocor* in this age, Vossius says that it occurs more often [Column 50D] in earlier centuries.]; who so hungered for justice that, although he had no sins of his own, he exacted from himself such great satisfaction for our sins [Column 50C]. Thus on the cross he thirsted for nothing but justice: he did not hesitate to die for his enemies and prayed for his crucifiers; he committed no sin and patiently heard things laid upon him by others, he who suffered so much to reconcile sinners to himself.


## Sermon V: On the intermediate coming and threefold renewal

**1.** We said recently that those who have silvered their wings ought to sleep between the two portions, signifying the two comings; but we did not say where they ought to sleep. There is a third coming, intermediate between those two, in which those who know it sleep delightfully. The two are manifest, but this one is not [Column 50D]. In the first, he was seen on earth and conversed with human beings, when, as he himself testifies, “they both saw and hated” (John 15:24). In the last, “all flesh shall see the salvation of our God” (Luke 3:6), and “they shall look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19:37). The intermediate coming is hidden, in which the elect alone see him within themselves and their souls are saved. In the first, therefore, he came in flesh and weakness; in this intermediate one, in spirit and power; in the last, in glory and majesty. For through power one reaches glory, because “the Lord of powers, he is the King of glory” (Ps. 23:10). The same prophet says elsewhere: “That I might see [Column 51A] your power and your glory” (Ps. 62:3). This intermediate coming is a way by which one passes from the first to the last. In the first, Christ was our redemption; in the last, he will appear as our life; in this one, so that we may sleep between the two portions, he is our rest and consolation.

**2.** But lest what we say of this intermediate coming seem invented to anyone, hear him himself: “If anyone loves me,” he says, “he will keep my words; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him” (John 14:23). But what does it mean: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words”? I have read elsewhere: “He who fears God will do good” (Ecclus. 15:1). Yet I perceive something more said of the one who loves: he will keep God’s words. Where then are they to be kept? Undoubtedly in the heart [Column 51B], as the Prophet says: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118:11). But how are they to be kept in the heart? Is it enough to keep them in memory alone? To one who keeps them thus the Apostle says: “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1). Besides, forgetfulness easily erases memory.

Keep the word of God in the same way in which you can best keep the food of your body. For it too is living bread and food of the mind. While earthly bread is in the chest, it can be stolen by a thief, gnawed by a mouse, or spoiled by age. But once you have eaten it, what of these things need you fear? Keep God’s word in this manner, for “blessed are those who keep it” (Luke 11:28). Let it therefore pass into the inward parts of your soul; let it pass into your affections and your conduct. Eat good, and your soul will delight in abundance [Column 51C]. Do not forget to eat your bread, lest your heart dry up; instead let your soul be filled with fat and richness.

3. If you preserve the word of God in this way, there can be no doubt that you will be preserved by it. For the Son will come to you with the Father; the great Prophet will come, who will renew Jerusalem, and he will make all things new. For this is what this coming will accomplish: that, as we have borne the image of the earthly man, so we may also bear the image of the heavenly man (1 Cor. 15:49). As the old Adam was diffused throughout the whole human being and took possession of the whole, so now may Christ take possession of the whole—he who created the whole, redeemed the whole, and will also glorify the whole, and who made the whole human being whole on the Sabbath. Once the old man was in us: that transgressor was in us, in hand, mouth, and heart alike. In the hand in two ways: through crime and disgraceful conduct. In the mouth likewise through arrogance and detraction. In the heart also through desires of the flesh and desires for temporal glory. But now, if anyone is a new creation in him, the old things have passed away; and, opposed to crime in the hand, there is innocence; opposed to disgraceful conduct, self-restraint. In the mouth, opposed to arrogance, the word of confession; opposed to detraction, the word of edification, so that old things may depart from our mouth. In the heart, however, opposed to fleshly desires, charity; opposed to temporal glory, humility. And see whether each of the elect does not receive Christ, the Word of God, in these three places—those to whom it was said: “Set me as a seal upon your arm, as a sign upon your heart” (Song 8:6); [Col. 0052A] and elsewhere: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Rom. 10:8).

## SERMON VI. On the Threefold Coming and the Resurrection of the Flesh

1. Brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant of the time of your visitation; nor, indeed, of what is visited in you at this time. For this season has been assigned to souls, not to bodies, since the soul, being far worthier than the body, claims prior care for itself by its natural dignity. It must also be repaired first, since it is acknowledged to have fallen first. For the soul, corrupted into guilt, caused the body also to be corrupted as punishment. Therefore, if we wish to be found members of Christ, [Col. 0052B] we must without doubt follow our Head: namely, our first concern must be the restoration of souls, for whose sake he has already come, and whose corruption he first endeavoured to heal. Let us reserve the care of the body rather for that time, and defer it until that day on which he will come with the grace of restoring the body, as the Apostle recalls when he says: “We await the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:19–20).

For at the first coming John the Baptist cries out as a herald—or rather, truly as Christ’s own herald—saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). He does not say, “Diseases of the body”; nor, “Afflictions of the flesh”; but “sin,” which is [Col. 0052C] the disease of the soul and the corruption of the mind. “Behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” From where? Certainly from the hand, from the eye, from the neck, and finally even from the flesh itself, where it is more deeply implanted.

2. He takes sin from the hands by blotting out sins committed; he takes it from the eye by purifying the intention of the mind; he takes it from the neck by removing its violent domination, as it is written: “You have broken the sceptre of his oppressor, as in the day of Midian” (Isa. 9:4); and likewise: “The yoke shall rot away because of the oil” (Isa. 10:27). The Apostle too says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6:12). For elsewhere the same Apostle says: “I know that no good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7:18); and elsewhere: [Col. 0052D] “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (ibid., 24).

He knew, indeed, that he would not first be delivered from that most evil root implanted in the flesh—from the law of sin that is in our members—until he should be released from the body itself. Hence he desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 1:23), knowing that sin, which separates us from God, cannot be entirely taken away until we are freed from the body. You have heard of one whom the Lord healed of a demon: the demon, throwing him down and tearing him violently, went out of him at the Lord’s command (Mark 9:16–25). Therefore I tell you that that kind of sin which so often disturbs us—I mean evil desires and concupiscences—must indeed be restrained, and can be restrained by the grace of God, so that it may not reign in us and [Col. 0053A] we may not offer our members to sin as weapons of iniquity (Rom. 6:13); and thus there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Yet it is not cast out except in death, when we are so torn apart that the soul is separated from the body.

3. You have learned for what purpose Christ came and to what the Christian ought to direct attention. Therefore, O body, do not seize the times beforehand: you can impede your soul’s salvation, but you cannot bring about your own. “All things have their time” (Eccl. 3:1). Allow the soul now to labour for itself; indeed, cooperate with it, because if you suffer with it, you will also reign with it. To the extent that you impede its restoration, you impede your own, since you cannot be restored before God sees his own image restored in it. You have a noble guest, O flesh, exceedingly noble; and your whole salvation depends upon that guest’s salvation. Give such a guest honour. You dwell indeed in your own country; but the soul is a stranger and exile lodging with you.

I ask you: what peasant, if some noble and very powerful person should wish to lodge with him, would not gladly lie in a corner of his house, or beneath his stairs, or even among the ashes, yielding to his guest the more honourable place, as is fitting? Do likewise, then. Do not reckon your own injuries or discomforts, provided only that your guest may be able to remain with you honourably. It is an honour to you that, for the present, you make yourself dishonoured for that guest’s sake.

4. And lest perhaps you despise or make little of your guest because he appears to you a stranger and newcomer, [Col. 0053C] attend carefully to what the presence of this guest bestows upon you. He is the one who gives sight to the eyes, grants hearing to the ears, supplies the tongue with speech, the palate with taste, and all the limbs with movement. Whatever life, whatever sensation, whatever beauty there is in you, acknowledge it as this guest’s benefit. Finally, his departure proves what his presence was giving. For as soon as the soul departs, the tongue falls silent, the eyes see nothing, the ears become deaf, the whole body grows rigid, and the face turns pale. Shortly thereafter, the entire corpse will become at once rotten and foul-smelling, and all beauty will be turned to corruption.

Why, then, for any temporary pleasure do you grieve and injure this guest, when you could not in any way even perceive that pleasure [Col. 0053D] except through him? Moreover, if, while he is an exile cast out from the presence of his Lord because of enmity, he bestows so much upon you, how much will he provide when reconciled? O body, do not impede that reconciliation, because great glory is thereby being prepared for you. Patiently—indeed, willingly—expose yourself to all things; conceal nothing that may seem able to benefit this reconciliation. Say to your guest: “Because the Lord will remember you and restore you to your former station, remember me also” (Gen. 40:13).

5. For he will surely remember you for good if you serve him well. When he comes to his Lord, he will speak to him concerning you and will say good things for a good host:

> While your servant was exiled in punishment for his fault, a certain poor man with whom I lodged showed me mercy; and may my Lord repay him on my account. First he gave all his possessions, and then even himself, for my benefit. He did not spare himself for my sake: in many fasts, frequent labours, vigils beyond measure, hunger and thirst, even cold and nakedness.

What then? Surely Scripture will not lie, where it says: “He will fulfil the desire of those who fear him, and will hear their prayer” (Ps. 144:19). Oh, if perhaps you could taste this sweetness, if perhaps you could assess this glory! For I am about to say something marvellous, yet true and wholly beyond doubt for believers. The Lord of Sabaoth himself—the Lord of hosts and King of glory—will himself descend to reform our bodies and conform them to the body of his glory. How great will be that glory, how inexpressible [Col. 0054B] that exultation, when the Creator of the universe, who previously came lowly and hidden to justify souls, comes lofty and manifest to glorify you, O wretched flesh—not now in weakness, but in his glory and majesty! Who can conceive that day of his coming, when he descends with the fullness of light, angels running before him, the sound of the trumpet awakening the helpless body from the dust, and carrying it away to meet Christ in the air?

6. How long, then, will wretched flesh—foolish, blind, senseless, and utterly insane flesh—seek transient and perishable consolations, indeed desolations, at the risk of being rejected and judged unworthy of this glory, and yet nevertheless being tortured eternally with unspeakable punishment? Not so, I beg you, my brothers, [Col. 0054C] not so. Rather, let our soul delight in meditations of this kind; indeed, let our flesh also rest in hope, awaiting the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform it, conforming it to the body of his glory.

For thus the Prophet says: “My soul thirsted for you; in how many ways has my flesh thirsted for you” (Ps. 62:2). The prophetic soul desired the first coming, by which it knew that it would be redeemed; but the flesh desired much more the second coming and its own glorification. Then our desires will be fulfilled, and the whole earth will be filled with the majesty of the Lord. To that glory, to that blessedness, and finally to that peace which surpasses all understanding, may he by his mercy bring us; and may the Saviour whom we await not disappoint us in our expectation—Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all, blessed for ever and ever.

## SERMON VII. On the Threefold Benefit of the Lord’s Advent

1. If we devoutly celebrate the Advent of the Lord, we do what is fitting. For he came not only to us, but also for us; he who has no need of our goods. Yet the very greatness of his condescension makes the extent of our need more clearly manifest. The danger of disease is made known not only by the price of the remedy, but the number of illnesses also by the multitude of remedies. Why, indeed, are there divisions of graces if no diversity of needs is apparent? [Col. 0055A] It is difficult to pursue in a single discourse all the needs that we experience; but meanwhile three common and, in a sense, principal needs occur to me. For no one is found among us who does not, at least for the present, appear to need counsel, assistance, and protection.

Certainly the human race has a threefold general misery; and all of us who dwell in the region of the shadow of death, in bodily weakness and in a place of temptation, suffer pitiably from this threefold disadvantage, if we consider it carefully. For we are easily deceived, weak in action, and fragile in resistance. If we wish to distinguish good from evil, we are deceived; if we attempt to do good, we fail; if we try to resist evil, we are cast down and overcome.

2. The coming of the Saviour is therefore necessary; the presence of Christ is necessary for persons thus beset. And would that he may come in such a way that, by his most abundant condescension, dwelling in us through faith, he may enlighten our blindness; remaining with us, may help [Col. 0056A] our weakness; and standing for us, may protect and defend our frailty. For if he is in us, who will now deceive us? If he is with us, what can we not henceforth do in him who strengthens us? If he is for us, who is against us? (Rom. 8:31). He is a faithful counsellor, who can neither be deceived at all nor deceive; a strong helper, who does not grow weary; an effective advocate, who will swiftly crush Satan himself beneath our feet and shatter all his schemes.

Surely he is the wisdom of God, always ready to instruct the ignorant; he is the power of God, able easily both to restore those who fail and to rescue those in danger. Therefore, my brothers, let us run to this teacher alone in every deliberation; let us call upon this so vigorous helper in every undertaking; [Col. 0056B] let us entrust our souls to this so faithful defender in every struggle. For this very purpose he came into the world: that, dwelling in human beings, with human beings, and for human beings, he might enlighten our darkness, lighten our labours, and drive away our dangers.

[Col. 0055]

# IN PRAISE OF THE VIRGIN MOTHER  
On the words of the Gospel, “The angel Gabriel was sent,” etc. FOUR HOMILIES.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING HOMILIES

The following four homilies, which are among Bernard’s earliest works, although commonly entitled “On *Missus est*,” ought nevertheless, according to the author’s own intention—that is, Bernard’s—to be entitled “In Praise of the Virgin Mother.” For he himself says in the present Preface and in Letter 18 to Peter, cardinal deacon: “I know that I have written four Homilies in praise of the Virgin Mother; for this is their title,” etc. Again, in Letter 89, to Ogerius: “I am sending you another little book recently published by me, *In Praise of the Virgin Mother*.” Moreover, Bernard’s treatise *On Baptism*, addressed to Hugh, chapter 5, should be consulted, where he explains and defends from calumny a certain statement in this first sermon.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0055C]

Devotion commands me to write something, and occupation forbids it. Yet, because bodily infirmity presently prevents me from joining the brothers’ assembly, I will not allow the small amount of leisure that I am permitted to steal during the nights, even at the expense of sleep, to remain idle. I therefore wish to attempt precisely that undertaking which has often pressed upon my mind: namely, to say something in praise of the Virgin Mother, upon that Gospel reading in which Luke recounts the history of the Lord’s Annunciation.

Although no necessity of the brothers—whose advancement I am bound to serve—urges me to perform this work, nor does any usefulness move [variant: “admonish”] me to it, nevertheless, provided that I am not thereby hindered in being less prepared for whatever they need, I do not think they ought to be troubled if I satisfy my own devotion.

#  HOMILY I  
“The angel Gabriel was sent by God into a city of Galilee, named Nazareth, to a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the Virgin’s name was Mary” (Luke 1:26–27).

1. Why did the Evangelist intend by so pointedly naming, in this passage, so many proper names of things? [Col. 0056C] I believe he did not wish us to hear negligently what he took such care to narrate. He names the messenger who is sent, the Lord by whom he is sent, the Virgin to whom he is sent, and also the Virgin’s spouse; and he designates the lineage of both, the city, and the region by their proper names. Why is this? Do you suppose that any of these details has been included superfluously? By no means. For if not even a leaf falls from a tree without cause, nor one of the sparrows falls to the ground without the heavenly Father (Matt. 10:29), should I suppose that a superfluous word flows from the mouth of the holy Evangelist, especially in the sacred history of the Word? I do not think so.

For all things are full of heavenly mysteries and each overflows with celestial sweetness—provided that they have an attentive observer who knows how to draw honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone. Certainly, on that day the mountains dripped sweetness and the hills flowed with milk and honey (Joel 3:18), when the heavens rained dew from above and the clouds poured down the Just One; when the earth was opened, joyfully bringing forth the Saviour (Isa. 45:8); when, the Lord giving kindness and our earth yielding its fruit, mercy and truth met together upon that mountain of mountains, the rich and fertile mountain; righteousness and peace kissed each other (Ps. 84:11).

At that time, too, this one mountain among the other mountains, by no means insignificant—the blessed Evangelist himself—commended to us in his honeyed discourse the longed-for beginning of our salvation; and, as though the south wind were blowing and the sun of righteousness shining nearby, certain spiritual fragrances flowed forth from it. Would that God would now send forth his word and melt them for us; that his Spirit would blow and the Gospel words become intelligible to us; that they might become in our hearts more desirable than much gold and precious stone, and sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.

2. Thus he says: “The angel Gabriel was sent by God.” I do not think that this angel was among the lesser ones, who are accustomed to carry out embassies to earth frequently and for any reason whatever. This is plainly suggested by his name, which when interpreted means “strength of God,” and because he is said to have been sent not by some other, perhaps more excellent spirit—as is customary—but by God himself. [Col. 0057B] Therefore “by God” was inserted, or “by God” was said, lest anyone think that God revealed his plan to any blessed spirit before revealing it to the Virgin, except only to the archangel Gabriel. Among his fellow angels, Gabriel was surely found to possess such excellence that he was worthy both of such a name and of such a message.

Nor is the name discordant with the message. For whom was it more fitting to announce Christ, the power of God, than him whom a similar name honours? For what else is strength but power? It should not seem unfitting or incongruous that the Lord and the messenger are denoted by a common designation, since, although the name is similar in both, the reason for the designation is not similar in each. Christ is called the strength or power of God in one way; the angel in another. [Col. 0057C] The angel is so called merely by designation; Christ, however, both is called and truly is the power of God (1 Cor. 1:24), which, coming as one stronger upon the strong man armed who used to guard his courtyard in peace, defeated him by its own arm and mightily snatched away from him the vessels of captivity.

But the angel was called the strength of God either because he merited the privilege of such an office, by which he might announce the coming of that same Power; or because he ought to strengthen the Virgin—timid by nature, simple, and modest—lest she be terrified by the newness of the miracle. And this he did, saying: “Do not fear, Mary; you have found favour with God.” Perhaps the same angel also, not without reason, strengthened her spouse—a man likewise humble and God-fearing—although the Evangelist does not name him on that occasion. “Joseph, son of David,” he says, “do not fear to take Mary your wife” (Matt. 1:20). Gabriel, then, is fittingly chosen for this task; indeed, because such a commission is assigned to him, he is rightly designated by such a name.

3. Therefore the angel Gabriel was sent by God. Where? Into a city of Galilee named Nazareth. Let us see whether, as Nathanael says, anything good can come from Nazareth (John 1:46). Nazareth means “flower.” It seems to me that the divine addresses and promises made from heaven to the fathers—namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—were a certain seed of divine knowledge, as though cast down from heaven to earth. Of this seed it is written: “Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom and would have resembled Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:9).

This seed flowered in the miracles shown during Israel’s departure from Egypt; in the figures and riddles throughout the journey in the wilderness to the land of promise; and afterward in the visions and prophecies of the prophets, and likewise in the establishment of kingdom and priesthood until Christ. Christ, however, is rightly understood to be the fruit of this seed and of these flowers, David saying: “The Lord will give kindness, and our land will yield its fruit” (Ps. 84:13); and again: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11). Therefore Christ’s birth is announced in Nazareth because from the flower the fruit is expected to proceed. But when the fruit comes forth, the flower falls away, because, when truth appeared in the flesh, the figure passed away.

Hence Nazareth is called a city of Galilee—that is, of “passing over” or “transmigration”—because, at Christ’s birth, all those things which I have enumerated above passed away, which, as the Apostle says, happened to them in figure (1 Cor. 10:11). We too, who now possess the fruit, see these flowers to have passed away; and even while they still seemed to bloom, they were foreseen as destined to pass. Hence David says: “In the morning, like grass, let it pass away; in the morning let it flourish and pass away; in the evening let it fall, harden, and wither” (Ps. 89:6). For in the evening—that is, when the fullness of time came, in which God sent his Only-begotten Son, made of a woman, made under the law (Gal. 4:4)—he himself said: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5). The old things passed away and disappeared, just as flowers fall and wither when the growing fruit succeeds them. Hence it is again written: “The grass has withered and the flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord remains for ever.” I think you do not doubt that the word is the fruit; and the Word is Christ.

4. Christ, then, is the good fruit that remains for ever. But where is the grass that has withered? Where is the flower that has fallen? Let the Prophet answer: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:8). If all flesh is grass, then that carnal people of the Jews withered like grass [variant: “was grass”]. Did not the grass wither when that people, empty of every richness of the Spirit, clung to the dry letter? Did not the flower also fall when the boast that they had in the law did not remain? If the flower did not fall, where then are the kingdom, priesthood, prophets, temple, and finally those mighty deeds in which they used to boast and say: “How great are the things we have heard and known, and our fathers have related to us?” And again: “How great are the things he commanded our fathers to make known to their children?” (Ps. 77:3). These things have been said on account of the phrase: “into a city of Galilee, named Nazareth.”

5. Therefore the angel Gabriel was sent by God into that city. To whom? To a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph. Who is this Virgin, so venerable that she is greeted by an angel, so humble that she is betrothed to a craftsman? A beautiful union of virginity and humility: and not moderately does that soul please God in which humility commends virginity and virginity adorns humility. But how great, do you think, is the reverence due to her in whom fruitfulness exalts humility and childbearing consecrates virginity? You hear “virgin”; you hear “humble.” If you cannot imitate the virginity of the humble one, imitate the humility of the Virgin.

Virginity is a praiseworthy virtue, but humility is more necessary. The former is counselled; the latter commanded. You are invited to the former; compelled to the latter. Of virginity it is said: “Who can receive this, let him receive it” (Matt. 19:12); of humility: “Unless someone becomes like this little child, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). Thus virginity is rewarded, but humility is required. In short, you can be saved without virginity; you cannot be saved without humility. Humility can please even when it mourns virginity lost; but without humility, I dare say, not even Mary’s virginity would have pleased.

“Upon whom,” he says, [Col. 0059B] “will my Spirit rest, but upon the humble and quiet?” (Isa. 66:2). He said, “upon the humble,” not “upon the virgin.” Therefore, if Mary had not been humble, the Holy Spirit would not have rested upon her; if he had not rested upon her, she would not have conceived. For how could she conceive from him without him? It is plain, then, that in order to conceive from the Holy Spirit, God—as she herself declares—“regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48), rather than her virginity. And if she was pleasing by reason of virginity, nevertheless she conceived by reason of humility. It is therefore clear that humility undoubtedly made virginity pleasing as well.

6. What do you say, proud virgin? Mary, forgetful that she is a virgin, glories in humility; and do you, neglecting humility, flatter yourself because of virginity? “He regarded,” she says, [Col. 0059C] “the humility of his handmaid.” Who is she? Certainly a holy virgin, a sober virgin, a devout virgin. Are you more chaste than she? More devout? Or is your purity perhaps more pleasing than Mary’s chastity, so that you may suffice to please by yours without humility, whereas she could not do so by hers? Indeed, the more honourable you are because of the singular gift of chastity, the greater injury you inflict upon yourself by defiling its beauty in you through the admixture of pride. Otherwise, it is better for you not to be a virgin than to become insolent because of virginity.

Virginity is not for everyone; yet humility together with virginity belongs to far fewer. Therefore, if you can do no more than admire virginity in Mary, strive to imitate humility, and that is enough for you. But if you are both virgin and humble, whoever you are, you are great.

7. Yet there is something greater to admire in Mary: namely, fruitfulness together with virginity. For from the beginning of time it has not been heard that anyone was both mother and virgin. And if you consider whose mother she is, where will your admiration at her wondrous exaltation lead you? Surely to the recognition that you cannot admire enough. In your judgment—or rather, in the judgment of Truth—will not she who had God as her Son be exalted above even all the choirs of angels? Does Mary not boldly call God and Lord of the angels her own Son, saying: “Son, why have you done this to us?” (Luke 2:48). Which of the angels would dare this? It is enough for them, and they count it a great thing, that although they are spirits by creation, they have by grace been made and called angels, as David testifies: “He makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103:4).

Mary, however, recognizing herself as mother, calls with confidence her own Son that Majesty whom they serve with reverence. Nor does God disdain to be called what he deigned to be. For shortly afterward the Evangelist adds: “And he was subject to them” (Luke 2:51). Who was subject to whom? God to human beings—God, I say, to whom angels are subject and principalities and powers obedient—was subject to Mary, and not only to Mary but also to Joseph for Mary’s sake. Wonder, then, at either, and choose which you more admire: the Son’s most gracious condescension or the Mother’s most excellent dignity. On both sides there is astonishment; on both sides, miracle. That God obeys a woman is humility without example; that a woman has authority over God is exaltation without equal. In the praises of virgins it is sung uniquely that “they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4). What praises, then, do you judge worthy of her who even goes before him?

8. Learn, O human being, to obey; learn, O earth, to be subject; learn, O dust, to comply. Speaking of your Maker, the Evangelist says: “And he was subject to them”—without doubt, to Mary and Joseph. Blush, proud ash! God humbles himself, and you exalt yourself? God subjects himself to human beings, and you, eager to rule over human beings, set yourself above your Maker? Would that, whenever I think something of this sort, God might deign to answer me as he answered his Apostle in rebuke: “Get behind me, Satan, for you do not savour the things that are of God” (Matt. 16:23). For as often as I desire to preside over human beings, I strive to go before my God; and then truly I do not savour the things that are of God. For of him it was said: “And he was subject to them.”

If, O human being, you disdain to imitate a human example, it certainly will not be unworthy of you to follow your Maker. If perhaps you cannot follow him wherever he goes, deign at least to follow him where he descended to meet you. That is: if you cannot walk the lofty path of virginity, follow God at least on the safest path of humility. If any even among virgins have deviated from its straightness, then, to confess the truth, neither do they follow the Lamb wherever he goes. The defiled but humble person follows the Lamb, and the proud virgin follows him too; but neither follows wherever he goes. For the former cannot ascend to the Lamb’s purity, who is without spot; nor does the latter deign to descend to his meekness, because the Lamb was silent not before the shearer but before the killer. Yet the sinner has chosen the healthier part of following in humility than the proud person in virginity: for the humble sinner’s satisfaction cleanses his impurity, while pride defiles the latter’s chastity.

9. But Mary is blessed, for neither humility nor virginity was lacking to her: indeed, a singular virginity, which fruitfulness did not violate but honour; likewise a special humility, which fruitful virginity did not take away but exalt; and an altogether incomparable fruitfulness, accompanied at once by virginity and humility. What of these is not wonderful?

> **[Note: From these words to the end of this homily, and the whole beginning of the following one down to the words “By these, indeed,” no. 2, are lacking in most ancient manuscripts, in [Col. 0062D] which the first and second homilies are joined together and only three homilies on “*Missus est*” are found.]**

What is not [Col. 0061A] incomparable? What is not singular? Yet it would be strange if, in weighing them, you did not hesitate which you should judge more worthy of admiration: whether fruitfulness in a virgin is more astonishing, or integrity in a mother; sublimity in the child, or humility combined with such sublimity. Unless, indeed, it is beyond doubt that all these things together should be preferred to each singly, and that it is incomparably more excellent and blessed to have received all of them than some of them.

And what wonder if God, who is said and seen to be wonderful in his saints (Ps. 67:36), showed himself more wonderful in his Mother? Therefore, married persons, reverence the integrity of flesh in corruptible flesh; sacred virgins, admire fruitfulness in a virgin; all people, imitate the humility of the Mother of God. Holy angels, honour the Mother of your King—you who adore the offspring of our Virgin, indeed the King both of us and of you, the restorer of our race and the renewer of your city. To him, so exalted among you and so humble among us, may reverence due to his dignity be given alike by you and us, and honour and glory to his condescension for ever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY II  
On Luke 1:26–27

1. No one doubts that the new song, which only virgins will be allowed to sing in the kingdom of God, will be sung by the Queen of virgins along with the rest—indeed, first among the rest. Yet I think that, besides that song which, as I said, will be common to her with all the virgins, she will gladden the city of God with some sweeter and more elegant melody. Surely no one, not even among the virgins themselves, will be found worthy to bring forth or express its sweet-sounding measures, because it will rightly be reserved for her alone to sing of childbirth—and of divine childbirth. I say that she glories in childbirth, not in herself, but in him whom she bore. For he whom she bore is God.

God, intending to endow his Mother with singular glory in heaven, took care to anticipate her on earth with singular grace: namely, that she might conceive ineffably while untouched, and give birth while remaining incorrupt. Such a birth, moreover, was fitting for God, who could be born only from a Virgin; and such childbirth was fitting for the Virgin, who was to bear none but God. Therefore the maker of human beings, when about to become human and be born from a human being, ought from among all women to choose—or rather, create—for himself such a mother as he knew befitted him and would please him.

He therefore willed that she should be a virgin, from whom the spotless one might proceed spotless, to cleanse the stains of all; and he willed her also to be humble, from whom he who is meek and humble of heart might come forth, showing in himself the necessary and most saving example of these virtues for all. Therefore he gave the Virgin childbirth, after already inspiring in her the vow of virginity and granting her the merit of humility. Otherwise, how does the angel later declare her full of grace if she possessed anything, even a small good, that was not from grace?

2.
