Therefore, in order that she who was to conceive and bear the Holy of Holies might be holy in body, she received the gift of virginity; and in order that she might be holy also in mind, she received humility. Adorned with these two jewels of virtue, and shining with the twofold beauty of mind and body, the royal Virgin became known in heaven through her beauty and loveliness; she drew to herself the gaze of the citizens of heaven, so that she inclined the King’s heart to desire her and brought the heavenly messenger down to herself from above. This is what the Evangelist here commends to us when he says that the angel was sent by God to the Virgin: “By God,” he says, “to the Virgin”—[Col. 0062B] that is, from the high one to the lowly, from the Lord to the handmaid, from the Creator to the creature. How great is God’s condescension! How great the Virgin’s excellence!

Run, mothers; run, daughters; run, all you who come after Eve and from Eve, who conceive in sorrow and give birth in sorrow. Approach the virginal bridal chamber; enter, if you can, the chaste room of your sister. For behold, God sends to the Virgin; behold, the angel addresses Mary. Put your ear to the wall; listen to what he announces to her, so that perhaps you may hear wherefrom you may receive consolation.

3. Rejoice, father Adam; but still more, you, mother Eve, exult: you who, as you were the parents of all, were also the destroyers of all; and, what is more unhappy, destroyers before you were parents. Be comforted, both of you [Col. 0062C] over a daughter—such a daughter; but especially she from whom evil first sprang, whose reproach passed upon all women. For the time is at hand when that reproach shall be removed, and man shall have no ground for accusation against woman—he who, when he imprudently tried to excuse himself, did not hesitate cruelly to accuse her, saying: “The woman whom you gave me gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12). Therefore run, Eve, to Mary; run, mother, to daughter. Let the daughter answer for the mother; let her [variant: “thus”] remove her mother’s reproach; let her make satisfaction to the father on behalf of the mother. For behold, if man fell through woman, he is now raised only through woman. What were you saying, Adam? “The woman whom you gave me gave me from the tree, and I ate.” These are words of malice, by which [Col. 0062D] you increase rather than erase your fault. Yet Wisdom overcame malice, when it found in the treasury of its inexhaustible mercy the occasion for pardon which God, by questioning you, sought to draw forth from you but could not.

For woman is given in return for woman: the prudent for the foolish, the humble for the proud; she who, instead of the tree of death, offers you the taste of life, and instead of that poisonous food of bitterness, brings forth the sweetness of eternal fruit. Change, therefore, the language of wicked excuse into a voice of thanksgiving, and say: “Lord, the woman whom you gave me has given me from the tree of life, and I ate; and it became sweeter than honey to my mouth, because in it you gave me life.” [Col. 0063A] For this purpose the angel was sent to the Virgin. O Virgin admirable and most worthy of every honor! O woman singularly worthy of reverence, wonderful above all women: restorer of parents, giver of life to descendants!

4. “The angel,” he says, “was sent to the Virgin.” A virgin in body, a virgin in mind, a virgin by profession; in short, a virgin such as the Apostle describes, holy in mind and body (1 Cor. 7:34). She was not newly or accidentally found, but chosen from eternity, foreknown by the Most High and prepared for himself, guarded by angels, prefigured by the fathers, promised by the prophets. Search the Scriptures [p. 738] and prove what I say. Do you wish me also to insert here some testimonies from them? To speak of a few among many: of what other [Col. 0063B] woman does God seem to have prophesied to you when he said to the serpent, “I will put enmities between you and the woman”? And if you still doubt that he spoke of Mary, hear what follows: “She shall crush your head” (Gen. 3:15). For whom was this victory reserved, if not for Mary? Beyond doubt she crushed the venomous head, she who reduced to nothing every suggestion of the Evil One, both the enticement of the flesh and the pride of the mind.

5. Whom else was Solomon seeking when he said: “Who shall find a valiant woman?” For the wise man knew the weakness of this sex, the frailty of its body, the instability of its mind. Yet because he had read that God had promised this, and saw that it was fitting that he who had conquered through woman should be conquered through her, he cried out in great wonder: “Who shall find a valiant woman?” [Col. 0063C] That is to say: If both the salvation of us all, the restoration of innocence, and victory over the enemy depend upon a woman’s hand, then a strong woman must surely be provided [variant: “foreseen”], fit for so great a work. But who shall find a valiant woman? Yet, lest he be thought to have sought her in despair, he adds prophetically: “Her price is from afar and from the uttermost bounds” (Prov. 31:10). That is, her worth is not cheap, small, mediocre, or earthly; but heavenly—not from the heaven nearest the earth, but her going forth is from the highest heaven.

What, further, did that Mosaic bush of old signify, emitting flames indeed but not burning (Exod. 3:2), except Mary giving birth yet not feeling pain? [Col. 0063D] What, I ask, did Aaron’s rod flowering without being watered signify (Num. 17:8), except her who conceived although she knew no man? Isaiah explains the greater mystery of this great miracle, saying: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1), understanding the rod as the Virgin and the flower as the Virgin’s offspring.

6. But if Christ’s being understood now by the flower appears to you to conflict with the earlier statement, in which he was said to be signified not by the flower of the rod but by the fruit of the flower, know that in the same Aaronic rod—which not only flowered, but also put forth leaves and bore fruit—he is signified not only by the flower or fruit, but also by the leaves themselves. Know also that in Moses he is shown neither by the fruit of the rod nor by its flower, but by the rod itself—[Col. 0064A] that rod, namely, by whose striking the water was either divided for those passing through (Exod. 14:16), or struck forth from the rock for those who were to drink (Exod. 17:6).

There is no inconsistency in Christ’s being prefigured by different things for different reasons: in the rod, his power; in the flower, his fragrance; in the fruit, the sweetness of his savor; and in the leaves, his diligent protection, by which he does not cease to shelter beneath the shadow of his wings little ones fleeing to him, whether from the heat of fleshly desires or from the face of the wicked who have afflicted them. Good and desirable is the shade beneath the wings of Jesus, where there is a safe refuge for fugitives and grateful refreshment for the weary. “Have mercy on me, Lord Jesus, have mercy on me; for my soul trusts in you, and in the shadow of your wings I shall hope, [Col. 0064B] until iniquity passes away” (Ps. 56:2 [Vulgate]).

In this testimony of Isaiah, however, understand the flower as the Son and the rod as the Mother: for the rod flowered without a shoot, and the Virgin conceived not from a man. Neither did the putting forth of the flower harm the rod’s freshness, nor did the birth of the sacred offspring injure the Virgin’s chastity.

7. Let us bring forward other testimonies from the Scriptures fitting for the Virgin Mother and God the Son. What does Gideon’s fleece signify—that fleece shorn from flesh, yet placed upon the threshing-floor without injury to the flesh, and now the wool, now the floor itself drenched with dew (Judg. 6:37–40)—except flesh assumed from the Virgin’s flesh without loss of virginity? [Col. 0064C] Upon this flesh, as the heavens distilled, the whole fullness of divinity poured itself; so that from this fullness we all have received [variant: “might receive”], who without her are truly nothing but dry earth.

The prophetic saying also seems very suitably to correspond to this Gideonic event, where it is written: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece.” For the words which follow, “and like drops falling upon the earth” (Ps. 71:6 [Vulgate]), convey the same meaning as the discovered [p. 739] threshing-floor wet with dew. For the voluntary rain which God set apart for his inheritance descended first, gently and without the noise of human operation, into the virginal womb by its own most peaceful flowing-in [variant: *elapsu*, “flowing out”]. Afterwards it was spread abroad throughout all lands through the mouths of preachers, no longer as rain upon fleece but as drops falling upon the earth, accompanied by a certain [Col. 0064D] sound of words and the report of miracles. For those clouds which bore the rain remembered the command given them when they were sent: “What I tell you in darkness, say in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matt. 10:27). And this they did: “Their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5 [Vulgate]).

8. Let us hear Jeremiah prophesying new things to the ancients; what he could not show as present, he ardently desired as future and confidently promised: “The Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). Who is this woman? And who is this man? Or, if he is a man, how is he encompassed by a woman? Or, if he can be encompassed by a woman, how is he a man? Or, to speak more plainly, [Col. 0065A] how can he be both a man and in his mother’s womb? For that is what it is for a man to be encompassed by a woman.

We know [variant: “We say”] men who, having passed through infancy, childhood, adolescence, and youth, have arrived at an age near old age. How, then, can one already so grown be encompassed by a woman? Had he said, “A woman shall encompass an infant,” or, “A woman shall encompass a little child,” it would seem neither new nor wonderful. But since he said nothing of the sort and said “a man,” we ask what is this new thing which God has made upon earth: that a woman should encompass a man, and a man should restrain himself within the members of one little female body? What miracle is this? Can a man, as Nicodemus says, enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born again? [Col. 0065B] (John 3:4).

9. But I turn to virginal conception and birth, to see whether, among the many new and wonderful things which one surely observes there if one inquires carefully, I may find also this new thing which I have drawn from the Prophet. There one recognizes length that is short, breadth that is narrow, height that is lowly, depth that is level [variant: “full”]. There one recognizes light not shining, the Word an infant, water thirsty, bread hungry. If you attend, you will see power ruled, wisdom instructed, strength sustained: in short, God nursing, yet refreshing angels; crying, yet consoling the wretched. If you attend, you will see joy made sorrowful, confidence afraid, salvation suffering, life dying, strength becoming weak. But, no less wonderful, [Col. 0065C] there also appears sorrow giving joy, fear giving strength, suffering saving, death giving life, weakness strengthening.

Who, then, will not also think of that which I was seeking? Is it not easy for you, amid these things, to recognize a woman encompassing a man, when you see Mary embracing in her womb Jesus, a man approved by God? I call Jesus a man not only when he was already called “a prophet, mighty in deed and word” (Luke 24:19), but even while the Mother of God gently cherished his still tender infant limbs in her lap or bore him in her womb. Thus Jesus was a man even before he was born—not by age, but by wisdom; not by bodily strength, but by vigor of mind; not by the bulk of his limbs, but by maturity of understanding. For Jesus conceived had no less wisdom—or rather, was no less Wisdom [variant: “was lesser Wisdom”]—[Col. 0065D] than Jesus born; Jesus small than Jesus great.

Whether hidden in the womb, crying in the manger, asking the teachers in the temple when somewhat older, or teaching the people at mature age, he was assuredly equally full of the Holy Spirit. There was no hour at any age of his in which anything was either diminished from, or added to, that fullness which he received in the womb at his conception. Rather, from the beginning he was perfect; from the beginning, I say, he was full of the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11:2–3).

10. Nor should you be troubled by what you read of him elsewhere [Col. 0066A]: [p. 740] “But Jesus advanced in wisdom and age and grace before God and men” (Luke 2:52). For what is here said about wisdom and grace must be understood not according to what he was, but according to what he appeared to be: not because something new was added to him which he did not previously possess, but because it appeared to be added when he himself wished to appear [variant: “that he might appear”]. You, a human being, when you advance, do not advance when or as much as you wish; rather, without your knowing it, your progress is governed and your life ordered. But the child Jesus, who orders your life—[“life” absent in other witnesses]—ordered his own life; and when he wished, and to whom he wished, he appeared wise; when and to whom he wished, wiser; when and to whom he wished, wisest, although in himself [Col. 0066B] he was never anything but wisest.

Likewise, although he was always full of every grace that he ought to have, whether before God or before human beings, he nevertheless showed it now more, now less, according to his own will, as he knew this either suited the merits or served the salvation of those who saw him. It is therefore clear that Jesus always had a manly mind, although he did not always appear as a man in body. Why, then, do I hesitate to say that he was a man in the womb, when I do not doubt that there he was God? For it is less to be a man than to be God.

11. But see whether Isaiah does not also most clearly explain this new thing of Jeremiah—Isaiah who above expounded the new Aaronic flowers. “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” There you have the woman, namely the Virgin. Do you wish to hear who the man is? [Col. 0066D] “And his name,” he says, “shall be called Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14). [Col. 0066C] Therefore the woman encompassing the man is the Virgin conceiving God.

You see how beautifully and harmoniously the wondrous deeds and mystical sayings of the saints sound together. You see how astounding is this one miracle accomplished concerning and in the Virgin, which so many miracles preceded and so many oracles promised. For the prophets had one Spirit; and although in diverse ways, signs, and times, different persons both foresaw and foretold the same thing—not by a different Spirit. What was shown to Moses in the bush and fire, to Aaron in the rod and flower, to Gideon in the fleece and dew, Solomon openly foretold in the valiant woman and her price; Jeremiah proclaimed more plainly concerning the woman and the man; Isaiah declared most plainly concerning the Virgin and God; finally Gabriel presented the Virgin herself [absent in other witnesses] by greeting her. For she is the one of whom the Evangelist now says: “The angel Gabriel was sent by God to a virgin betrothed to Joseph.”

12. “To a virgin betrothed,” he says. Why betrothed? Since she was, I say, a chosen virgin and, as has been shown, a virgin to conceive and a virgin to give birth, it is remarkable why she was betrothed, though not to marry. Can anyone say that even this occurred by chance? What is commended by a rational cause did not occur by chance—a cause exceedingly useful and necessary, and wholly worthy of the contrivance of divine counsel. I shall state not my own view, but what seemed right to the Fathers before me.

[Col. 0067A] The reason for Mary’s betrothal was the same as the reason for Thomas’s doubt. For it was the custom of the Jews that, from the day of their betrothal until the time of marriage, brides should be entrusted to their betrothed for safekeeping, so that the men might guard their chastity more carefully as they proved more faithful to themselves. Therefore, as Thomas, by doubting and touching, became the most steadfast confessor of the Lord’s resurrection, so Joseph, by betrothing Mary to himself and more diligently proving her conduct during the period of guardianship, became the most faithful witness to her chastity. Beautiful is the correspondence of both matters: Thomas’s doubt and Mary’s betrothal.

They could indeed have laid for us a snare of similar error—bringing the truth of faith in his case and of chastity in hers into suspicion. But it was done most wisely and piously by the opposite means, so that where suspicion was feared, firm [Col. 0067B] certainty might result. For concerning the Son’s resurrection, I, weak as I am, would sooner believe Thomas when doubting and touching than Cephas when hearing and believing; and concerning the Mother’s continence, I would more readily believe her betrothed, guarding and experiencing it, than the Virgin herself defending herself only from her own conscience. Tell me, I ask: who, seeing her unbetrothed and pregnant, would not call her a harlot [variant: “corrupted”] rather than a virgin? Yet this ought not to be said of the Lord’s Mother. It was more tolerable and honorable for Christ to be thought, for a time, born of marriage than of fornication.

13. But, you say, could not God show some manifest [Col. 0067C] sign by which neither his birth would be defamed nor his mother accused? He certainly could; but what people knew could not be hidden from demons. Yet the mystery of the divine plan had to be concealed for a time from the prince of this world—not because God feared that, if he wished to do his work openly, he could be hindered by him, but because he who has done whatever he willed not only powerfully but wisely, and who in all his works customarily observes certain correspondences of things and times for the beauty of order, wished in this also—his most magnificent work, namely our restoration—to show not only his power but also his wisdom.

Although he could have accomplished it otherwise, as he wished, it pleased [Col. 0067D] him rather to reconcile humankind to himself by the mode and order in which he knew humankind had fallen: so that, as the devil first deceived the woman and afterward conquered the man through the woman, so he might first be deceived by a virgin woman and afterward openly defeated by the man Christ. Thus, while the art of mercy mocked the guile of malice and Christ’s power crushed the strength of the Evil One, God would appear to the devil both wiser and stronger. For it was fitting that incarnate Wisdom should conquer spiritual malice in such a way as not only to “reach mightily from end to end,” but also to “order all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1).

It reaches from end to end, that is, from heaven to hell. “If I ascend into heaven,” he says, “you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138:8 [Vulgate]). In both places it does so mightily: when it cast the proud one from the heights and despoiled the greedy one in the lower world. [Col. 0068A] It was fitting, therefore, that it should also order all things sweetly, both heavenly and earthly: so that, while casting down the restless one from there, it might establish the others in peace; and while about to overcome the envious one here, it might first leave us the very necessary example of its humility and gentleness. Thus, by the wondrous governance of Wisdom, it might appear gentle to its own and strong against its enemies. For what profit would there be in the devil’s being conquered by God if we remained proud?

Therefore Mary was necessarily betrothed to Joseph, since thereby the holy thing is hidden from dogs, her virginity is proved by her betrothed, and provision is made both for the Virgin’s modesty and [Col. 0068B] for her reputation. What could be wiser or more worthy of divine providence? By one such design, a witness is admitted into heavenly secrets, an enemy is excluded, and the reputation of the Virgin Mother is kept intact. Otherwise, when would a just man have spared an adulteress? Yet it is written: “Joseph her husband, being just and unwilling to expose her, wished to dismiss her secretly” (Matt. 1:19). Rightly, because he was just, he was unwilling to expose her: for as he would by no means have been just if he had consented to a woman known to be guilty, so neither would he have been just if he had condemned one proved innocent. Therefore, because he was just and unwilling to expose her, he wished to dismiss her secretly.

14. Why did he wish to dismiss her? Receive here too not my own view but that of the Fathers. Joseph wished to dismiss her for the same [Col. 0068C] reason that Peter drove the Lord away from himself, saying: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8); and for the same reason that the centurion kept him from his house, saying: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter beneath my roof” (Matt. 8:8). So Joseph too, judging himself unworthy and sinful, said within himself that he ought no longer to be granted familiar cohabitation with one of such and so great dignity, whose marvelous eminence above him he regarded with awe. He saw and trembled before the most certain sign of the divine presence which she bore; and because he could not penetrate the mystery, he wished to dismiss her. Peter feared the greatness of power; the centurion feared the majesty of presence. Joseph too, as a man, recoiled from the novelty of so great [Col. 0068D] a mystery and its depth; and therefore wished secretly to dismiss her.

[p. 742] Are you surprised that Joseph judged himself unworthy of companionship with the pregnant Virgin, when you hear that even holy Elizabeth could not bear her presence except with trembling and reverence? For she said: “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43). Joseph therefore wished to dismiss her. But why secretly, and not openly? So that the cause of the separation would not be investigated and an explanation demanded. What could a just man answer to a stiff-necked people, a people unbelieving and gainsaying? If he said what he felt, what he had proved concerning her unstained purity, would not the unbelieving and cruel Jews immediately mock [Col. 0069A] him and stone her? When would they believe Truth silent in the womb, when later they despised it crying out in the Temple? What would they do to one not yet appearing, when later they laid impious hands even upon one radiant with miracles? Thus the just man rightly wished secretly to dismiss her, lest he be compelled either to lie or to defame an innocent woman.

15. But if anyone thinks otherwise and maintains that Joseph doubted as a man, but, because he was just, did not wish to live with her on account of suspicion, nor yet, because he was pious, wished to expose one he suspected, and therefore wished secretly to dismiss her: I reply briefly that, even so, Joseph’s doubt was necessary, since it deserved confirmation by a divine oracle. For it is written: “While he thought these [Col. 0069B] things”—namely, that he would secretly dismiss her—“an angel appeared to him in a dream, saying: Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife; for that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20).

Therefore for these reasons Mary was betrothed to Joseph—or rather, as the Evangelist puts it, to “a man whose name was Joseph.” He calls him a man not because he was a husband, but because he was a man of virtue. Or rather, because according to another Evangelist he is called not simply a man but “her man,” he is rightly so called because he was necessarily thought to be so. Therefore he ought to be called her man because it was necessary that he be thought so, just as he deserved to be called—not to be—the Savior’s father, in order that he might be thought to be so. Thus the same Evangelist says: “And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph” [Col. 0069C] (Luke 3:23). He was therefore neither the Mother’s husband nor the Son’s father, although by a certain, as has been said, necessary dispensation he was for a time both called and supposed to be both.

16. Yet infer from this designation, by which he deserved to be honored by God—so as to be both called and believed to be the Father of God—and also from his own name, which you do not doubt is interpreted “increase,” what and what sort of man this Joseph was. Remember at the same time that great patriarch of old, sold into Egypt (Gen. 37:27), and know that this Joseph not only received his name but also attained his chastity, innocence, and grace.

For that Joseph, sold through his brothers’ envy [Col. 0069D] and brought into Egypt, prefigured Christ’s sale; this Joseph, fleeing Herod’s envy, carried Christ into Egypt (Matt. 2:14). The former kept faith with his master and refused intercourse with his mistress (Gen. 39:12); the latter, recognizing his mistress—the Mother of his Lord—to be a virgin, faithfully guarded her and himself remained continent. To the former was given understanding of the mysteries of dreams (Gen. 40–41); to the latter it was given to become aware of and share in heavenly sacraments (Matt. 1:20). The former stored grain not for himself but for all the people (Gen. 40–41); the latter received for safekeeping the living bread from heaven, for himself and for the whole world.

There is no doubt that this Joseph, to whom the Savior’s Mother was betrothed, was a good and faithful man: faithful, I say, and prudent servant, [Col. 0070A] whom the Lord appointed as a comfort to his Mother, a nourisher of his flesh, and finally his most faithful fellow-worker on earth in the great counsel. To this is added that he is said to have been of the house of David. Truly this Joseph was of David’s house, truly descended from a royal stock: noble in birth, nobler in mind. Certainly a son of David, not degenerating from his father David. Indeed, I say, a son of David not only in flesh but in faith, holiness, and devotion: one whom the Lord found, as another David, according to his heart, to whom he could safely entrust the most secret and most sacred mystery of his heart; to whom, as to [p. 743] another David, he revealed the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom; and to whom he gave knowledge of the mystery [Col. 0070B] which none of the rulers of this age knew. To him was granted what many kings and prophets, though they wished to see, did not see, and to hear, did not hear: not only to see and hear, but also to carry, lead, embrace, kiss, nourish, and guard.

Nor should only Joseph, but Mary also, be believed to have descended from the house of David. Otherwise she would not have been betrothed to a man of David’s house unless she too were of David’s house. Both, then, were of the house of David; but in one the truth which the Lord swore to David was fulfilled, while the other knew and witnessed the promise’s fulfillment.

17. At the end of the verse he says: “And the Virgin’s name was Mary.” Let us say a few words also about this name, which is interpreted “star of the sea” and is most fittingly applied to the Virgin Mother. [Col. 0070C] For she is most aptly compared to a star: just as a star emits its ray without corruption of itself, so the Virgin gives birth to her Son without injury to herself. Neither does the star’s ray lessen its brightness, nor does the Son lessen the Virgin’s integrity.

She, therefore, is that noble star risen from Jacob, whose ray illumines the whole world, whose brightness both shines beforehand in the heavens and penetrates the lower regions; which also illuminates the earth and, warming minds more than bodies, nourishes virtues and burns away vices. She, I say, is that brilliant and exceptional star, necessarily raised above this great and spacious sea, shining by merits and illuminating by examples. O whoever you are, who understand that in the flood of this age you are tossed more amid storms and tempests [Col. 0070D] than you walk upon land, do not turn your eyes from the splendor of this star, if you do not wish to be overwhelmed by storms.

If the winds of temptations rise, if you strike the rocks of tribulations, look to the star; call upon Mary. If you are tossed by the waves of pride, ambition, detraction, or envy, look to the star; call upon Mary. If anger, avarice, or the enticement of the flesh shakes the little ship of your mind, look to Mary. If, troubled by the enormity of your sins, confused by the foulness of conscience, terrified by the dread of judgment, you begin to be swallowed by the abyss of sorrow and the gulf of despair, think of Mary. In dangers, in distresses, in doubtful matters, think of Mary; call upon Mary. Let her not depart from your mouth; let her not depart from your heart. And, that you may obtain the help of her prayer, do not forsake the example of her way of life. [Col. 0071A] Following her, you do not go astray; asking her, you do not despair; thinking of her, you do not err. With her holding you, you do not fall; with her protecting you, you do not fear; with her leading you, you do not grow weary; with her favorable to you, you arrive. And thus you experience in yourself how deservedly it was said: “And the Virgin’s name was Mary.”

But now we must pause a little, lest we too gaze, as we pass by, upon the brightness of so great a light. For, to use apostolic words, “It is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:4); and it is pleasant sweetly to contemplate in silence that which laborious speech cannot adequately unfold. Meanwhile, from devout contemplation of the shining star, the discussion which follows will be renewed with greater fervor.

## HOMILY III. On Luke, chapter 1, verses 28–32

[Col. 0071B] 1. Whenever I see that it is suitable, I gladly borrow the words of the saints, so that whatever I set before the reader in them may be more pleasing by the beauty of the vessels. But now, to begin with prophetic words: “Woe is me”—not indeed, as with the prophet, because I have kept silent, but because I have spoken—“for I am a man of unclean lips!” (Isa. 6:5). Alas! How many vain, false, and shameful things I remember vomiting forth through this very foul mouth of mine, in which I now presume to turn over heavenly words! I greatly fear lest I shall presently hear said to me: “Why do you recount my just judgments and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49:16 [Vulgate]).

Would that from the heavenly altar there might be brought to me not one coal indeed, but a huge fiery globe, sufficient completely to burn away the abundant and long-standing rust of my itching [p. 744] mouth! [Col. 0071C] Then I might be deemed worthy to recount in my poor manner, with words, the pleasing and chaste reciprocal conversation of the angel with the Virgin and of the Virgin with the angel himself. The Evangelist therefore says: “And the angel entered in to her”—without doubt, to Mary—and said: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.”

Where did he enter in to her? I suppose into the inner chamber of her chaste room, where perhaps, with the door closed upon herself, she was praying to her Father in secret. Angels are accustomed to stand beside those who pray and to delight in those whom they see lifting pure hands in prayer; they rejoice to offer God the holocaust of holy devotion as a sweet odor. How pleasing Mary’s prayers were in the sight of the Most High was shown by the angel, who entered to her and greeted her with such reverence.

Nor was it difficult for the angel to penetrate through the closed door into the Virgin’s hidden chamber, since by the subtlety of his substance he has by nature this property: no iron bars can bar his entrance wherever his impulse carries him. Walls do not resist angelic spirits; all visible things give way to them, and all bodies alike, however solid or dense, are penetrable and passable to them. We should not suppose, therefore, that the angel found the Virgin’s little door open; for it was her intention to flee human crowds and avoid conversation, lest either the silence of her prayer be disturbed or the chastity of her continence be tempted. Thus at that hour the most prudent Virgin had shut her dwelling upon herself [Col. 0072A]—but against people, not angels. Therefore, although the angel could enter to her, access was open to no human being.

2. The angel, therefore, entering in to her, said: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” We read in the Acts of the Apostles that Stephen too was full of grace (Acts 6:5), and that the apostles were filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:4); but in a way far unlike Mary. For the fullness of divinity did not dwell bodily in Stephen as it did in Mary; nor did they conceive by the Holy Spirit as Mary did. “Hail,” he says, “full of grace, the Lord is with you.” What wonder that she was full of grace, with whom the Lord was? But this is rather to be wondered at: how he who had sent the angel to the Virgin was found by the angel to be with the Virgin.

Was God swifter than the angel, so that he himself, more swift, hastened [Col. 0072B] ahead of his speeding messenger to earth? It is no wonder. For while the King was at his table, the Virgin’s nard gave forth its fragrance; the smoke of its spices ascended before the sight of his glory; and she found grace before the Lord’s eyes, while those standing around cried: “Who is this that comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke, from spices of myrrh and frankincense?” (Song 3:6). Immediately the King, going forth from his holy place, rejoiced as a giant to run his course; and though “his going forth is from the summit of heaven” (Ps. 18:6–7 [Vulgate]), yet, flying with exceeding desire, he forestalled his messenger in reaching the Virgin whom he loved, whom he chose for himself, whose beauty he desired. Beholding him coming from afar, rejoicing and exulting, the Church says [Col. 0072C]: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills” (Song 2:8).

3. The King deservedly desired the Virgin’s beauty. For she had done all that her father David had long beforehand enjoined upon her, saying: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house. And if you do this, the king shall desire your beauty” (Ps. 44:11–12 [Vulgate]). For she heard and saw—not as some who, hearing, do not hear and, seeing, do not understand—but she heard and believed, saw and understood. She inclined her ear to obedience and her heart to instruction; she forgot her people and her father’s house, because she took no care either to increase her people through succession of offspring [Col. 0072D] or to leave an heir to her father’s house. Rather, whatever honor she could have among her people, whatever earthly possessions from her paternal house, she counted all as dung, that she might gain Christ. Nor did her intention deceive her, since she claimed Christ as her Son without violating her purpose of chastity. Rightly, therefore, was she full of grace: she retained the grace of virginity and acquired besides the glory of fruitfulness.

745 4. “Hail,” he says, “full of grace, the Lord is with you.” He did not say, “The Lord is in you,” but, “The Lord is with you.” For God, who by his simple substance is wholly and equally everywhere, is nevertheless present by his operation differently in rational creatures than in the rest, and differently in the good than in the evil among rational creatures. He is indeed [Col. 0073A] in irrational creatures in such a way that he is not comprehended by them. But he can be comprehended by all rational creatures through knowledge; yet he is comprehended through love only by the good. Therefore he is in the good alone in such a way that he is also with them, through harmony of will. For while they submit their wills to righteousness in such a manner that it is not unfitting for God to will what they will, by not departing from his will they join God to themselves in a special way.

Yet although he is thus with all the saints, he is with Mary in a special way. With her there was indeed so great a concord that he united to himself not only her will but also her flesh; and from his own substance and that of the Virgin he made one Christ—or rather, the one Christ came to be: who, though not wholly from God nor wholly from the Virgin, [Col. 0073B] was nevertheless wholly God’s and wholly the Virgin’s; not two sons, but the one Son of both.

Therefore he says: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” And not only the Lord the Son is with you, whom you shall clothe with your flesh; but also the Lord the Holy Spirit, by whom you shall conceive; and the Lord the Father, who begot him whom you shall conceive. The Father, I say, is with you, who makes his Son yours also. The Son is with you, who, in order to accomplish within you a wonderful mystery, wonderfully opens to himself the secret place of generation and preserves for you the seal of virginity. The Holy Spirit is with you, who, together with the Father and the Son, sanctifies your womb. Therefore the Lord is with you.

5. “Blessed are you among women.” I gladly add what Elizabeth—whose words these are—went on to say: “And blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke [Col. 0073C] 1:42). It is not because you are blessed that the fruit of your womb is blessed; rather, because he preceded you with blessings of sweetness, you are blessed. For truly blessed is the fruit of your womb, in whom all nations are blessed, and from whose fullness you too have received with the rest, though differently from the rest. Therefore you are blessed, but among women; whereas he is blessed not among human beings, not among angels, but is, as the Apostle says, “God blessed above all things for ever” (Rom. 9:5).

A blessed man is spoken of, blessed bread, a blessed woman, blessed land—or whatever else among creatures is said to be blessed. But uniquely blessed is the fruit of your womb, since he is God blessed above all things for ever [Col. 0073D].

6. Blessed, therefore, is the fruit of your womb: blessed in fragrance, blessed in taste, blessed in appearance. He who said, “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field, which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27), perceived the fragrance of this fragrant fruit. Is he not truly blessed whom the Lord has blessed?

One who had tasted of this fruit [variant: “what he had tasted”] poured forth concerning its flavor, saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9); and elsewhere: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. 30:20). And another says: “If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” (1 Pet. 2:3). And the Fruit himself, inviting us to himself, says: “Whoever eats me will still hunger, and whoever drinks me will still thirst” (Ecclus. 24:29) [Col. 0074A]. Certainly he said this because of the sweetness of his taste: once tasted, he awakens appetite all the more. A good fruit, who is both food and drink for souls hungering and thirsting for righteousness.

You have heard of his fragrance; you have heard of his taste: hear also of his appearance. For if that fruit of death was not only pleasant to eat but also, Scripture testifying, delightful to look upon (Gen. 3:6), how much more ought we to seek the life-giving beauty of this vital fruit, into whom, according to another Scripture, even angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1:12). He who said, “From Zion is the beauty of his splendor” (Ps. 49:2), beheld his beauty in the spirit and desired to behold it in the body. And lest you suppose that he commended only an ordinary beauty to you, recall what you read in another psalm: “Fairer in form than the children of men; grace has been poured out upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you for ever” (Ps. 44:3) [Col. 0074B].

746 7. Blessed, therefore, is the fruit of your womb, whom God has blessed for ever; through whose blessing you too are blessed among women, because a bad tree cannot bear good fruit. Blessed, I say, are you among women, who escaped that general curse by which it was said, “In sorrow you shall bear children” (Gen. 3:16), and likewise that which followed it: “Cursed is the barren woman in Israel” (Exod. 23:26; Deut. 7:14). You have obtained a singular blessing: that you might neither remain barren nor give birth in pain.

A harsh necessity and grievous yoke lay [Col. 0074C] upon all the daughters of Eve! If they give birth, they are tormented; if they do not give birth, they are cursed. Pain forbids childbearing, and failure to bear children brings a curse. What will you do, Virgin, who hear and read these things? If you give birth, you are distressed; if you remain barren, you will be cursed. What will you choose, prudent Virgin?

“Distresses surround me on every side,” she says. “Yet it is better for me to incur the curse and remain chaste than first to conceive through desire, only then deservedly to give birth in pain. In the one case I see a curse, but not sin; in the other, both sin and torment. For what else, finally, is this curse but human reproach? Nor indeed is the barren woman called cursed for any other reason than because she is to be regarded with reproach and [Col. 0074D] contempt, as useless and unfruitful—and this only in Israel. But it is a small thing to me that I displease human beings, provided I may present myself as a chaste virgin to Christ.”

O prudent Virgin, O devoted Virgin, who taught you that virginity pleases God? What law, what righteousness, what page of the Old Testament either commands, counsels, or exhorts one to live in the flesh without living carnally, and on earth to lead an angelic life? Where had you read, blessed Virgin, “The wisdom of the flesh is death” (Rom. 8:6), and, “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14)? Where had you read of virgins that they sing a new song which no one else can sing, and that they follow the Lamb wherever he goes? (Rev. 14:4.) Where had you read that those are praised who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of [Col. 0075A] heaven? (Matt. 19:12.) Where had you read: “Though walking in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh” (2 Cor. 10:3); and, “He who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her does better”? Where had you heard: “I wish you all to be as I myself am,” and, “It is good for a man to remain thus, according to my counsel”? “Concerning virgins,” he says, “I have no command, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7:38, 7, 40, 25).

But you had not, I say, a command, nor even counsel, nor an example—unless it was that the anointing taught you concerning all things, and the word of God, living and effective, became your teacher before becoming your son, first instructing your mind before clothing himself with flesh. You therefore vow to present yourself as a virgin to Christ, and do not know that you must also present yourself to him as a mother. You choose to be despised in Israel and, in order to please him to whom you have committed yourself, to incur the curse of barrenness; and behold: the curse is changed into blessing, barrenness is repaid with fruitfulness [Col. 0075B].

8. Open your bosom, Virgin; spread out your lap; prepare your womb. For behold, he who is mighty will do great things for you—so great that, instead of Israel’s curse, all generations will call you blessed. Do not, prudent Virgin, regard fruitfulness with suspicion, for it will not take away your integrity. You will conceive, but without sin; you will be pregnant, but not burdened; you will give birth, but not in sorrow. You will not know a man, yet you will bear a son.

What sort of son? You will be the mother of him whose Father is God. The Son of the Father’s radiance [variant: “love”; variant: “majesty”] will be the crown of your chastity. The Wisdom of the Father’s heart [Col. 0075C] will be the fruit of your virginal womb. In short, you will give birth to God and conceive from God. Take courage, then, fruitful Virgin, chaste woman in childbirth, untouched Mother; for you will no longer be cursed in Israel, nor counted among the barren. And if you are still cursed by Israel according to the flesh, it will not be because they see you as barren, but because they envy you as fruitful. Remember that Christ too bore the curse of the cross: he who blessed you as his mother in heaven. On earth also you are blessed by the angel and deservedly proclaimed blessed by all generations of the earth. Therefore blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.

9. “When she had heard this, she was troubled at his saying, and considered 747 what manner of greeting this might be.” Virgins who are true virgins are accustomed always to be fearful [Col. 0075D] and never self-assured; and, in order that through fearfulness they may take precautions, they fear even what is safe. They know that they carry a precious treasure in earthen vessels, and that it is exceedingly difficult to live angelically among human beings, to conduct oneself on earth in the manner of heavenly beings, and to lead a celibate life in the flesh. Therefore whatever novel or sudden thing arises, they regard as a suspected snare; they judge everything to have been contrived against them.

For this reason Mary too was troubled at the angel’s speech. She was troubled, but not disturbed. “I was troubled,” he says, “and did not speak; but I considered the days of old and kept eternal years in mind” (Ps. 76:5–6). Thus Mary too was troubled and did not speak, but considered what manner of greeting this might be. That she was troubled belonged to virginal modesty; that she was not disturbed, to fortitude; that she kept silence and considered, to prudence. She considered, then, what manner of greeting this might be. The prudent Virgin knew that often an angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light; and because she was assuredly humble and simple, she expected nothing of the sort at all from a holy angel. Therefore she considered what manner of greeting this might be [Col. 0076A].

10. Then the angel looked upon the Virgin and, readily perceiving the various thoughts she was turning over within herself, comforted the fearful one, strengthened the doubtful one, and, calling her familiarly by name, kindly persuaded her not to fear. “Do not fear,” he says, “Mary; you have found grace with God.” There is no deceit here, no fraud here. Suspect no trickery, no snares here. I am not a human being but a spirit; and I am an angel of God, not of Satan [Col. 0076B]. “Do not fear, Mary; you have found grace with God.”

Oh, if you knew how greatly your humility pleases the Most High, how great an exaltation awaits you with him, you would not judge yourself unworthy either of angelic speech or of angelic service. Why should you call the grace of angels undeserved for yourself, when you have found grace with God? You have found what you sought; you have found what no one before you was able to find; you have found grace with God. What grace? Peace between God and human beings, the destruction of death, the restoration of life. This, then, is the grace which you have found with God.

And this is the sign for you: “Behold, you will conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.” Understand, prudent Virgin, from the name of the promised Son how great and how special the grace is that you have found with God. “And you shall call,” he says, “his name Jesus.” Another Evangelist gives the reason for this name, with the angel interpreting it thus: “For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21) [Col. 0076C].

11. I read that two men named Jesus, as types of the one now in our hands, went before him, both having governed peoples. One led his people out of Babylon (Hag. 1; 3 Esdr. 5:5); the other brought his people into the land of promise (Josh. 1:11). Those men indeed defended the peoples under their charge from enemies; but did they save them from their sins? Our Jesus, however, both saves his people from their sins and brings them into the land of the living. “For he shall save his people from their sins.”

Who is this who also forgives sins? May the Lord [Col. 0076D] Jesus deem me also, a sinner, worthy to be numbered among his people, so that he may save me from my sins! Truly blessed is the people whose Lord and God is this Jesus, because he himself shall save his people from their sins. Yet I fear that many profess themselves to belong to his people whom he nevertheless does not count as his people. I fear that to many who appear, as it were, more religious within his people, he will one day say: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15:8).

For the Lord Jesus knows who are his (2 Tim. 2:19); he also knows whom he chose from the beginning. “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’” he says, “and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46). Do you wish to know whether you belong to his people—or rather, do you wish to be among his people? Do what Jesus says, and he will number you among his people [Col. 0077A]. Do what the Lord Jesus commands in the Gospel, what he commands in the Law and the Prophets, what he commands through his ministers who are in the Church. Obey the vicars set over you—not only the good and gentle, but also the harsh. Learn from Jesus himself, because he is meek and humble of heart; and 748 you will belong to his blessed people, whom he chose for his inheritance. You will belong to his praiseworthy people, whom the Lord of hosts blessed, saying: “You are the work of my hands, my inheritance Israel” (Isa. 19:25). And, lest perhaps you envy carnal Israel, he also bears witness to this people, saying: “A people whom I did not know has served me; at the hearing of the ear it obeyed me” (Ps. 17:45).

12. But let us hear what the same angel thinks of him to whom, before he was yet conceived, he gave such a name. For he says: “He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Most High” [Col. 0077B]. Rightly great, he who deserves to be called the Son of the Most High. Is not he great “whose greatness has no end”? (Ps. 144:3.) And, “Who is great,” he says, “like our God?” (Ps. 76:14.) He is plainly great who is as great as the Most High, because he himself is the Most High. For the Son of the Most High will not deem it robbery to be equal with the Most High (Phil. 2:6).

He rightly is judged to have conceived robbery who, having been made from nothing into angelic form, compared himself to his Creator and claimed for himself what belongs properly to the Son of the Most High. That Son, indeed, being in the form of God, was not made by God but begotten from God. For God the Father, though omnipotent, could neither create a creature equal to himself nor beget a son unequal to himself [Col. 0077C]. Thus he made an angel great, but not as great as himself; and therefore not most high. But the Almighty did not make, but begot, the only-begotten Son: the Omnipotent begot one omnipotent, the Most High one most high, the Eternal one coeternal. He does not deem it robbery or injury that this Son is in every respect compared with himself. Rightly, therefore, “he shall be great,” who shall be called the Son of the Most High.

13. But why “he shall be” great, rather than “he is” great, since he is always equally great, has nothing by which to grow, and will be no greater after conception than he is or was before it? Perhaps he said “he shall be” because he who was great God would become great man. Rightly, therefore: “He shall be great.” Great man, great teacher, great prophet. Thus it is said of him in the Gospel: “A great prophet has arisen among us” (Luke 7:16). And likewise a great prophet is promised as coming by a lesser prophet: “Behold,” he says, “a great prophet will come, and he himself will renew Jerusalem.”

And you, Virgin, will give birth to a little one, nourish a little one, nurse a little one. But when you see the little one, think of the great one. For he shall be great, because God will magnify him in the sight of kings, so that all kings may worship him and all nations serve him. Therefore let your soul magnify the Lord, because he shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High. He shall be great, and he who is mighty shall do great things for you, and holy is his name. For what name is holier than that by which he shall be called the Son of the Most High?

Let the great Lord be magnified also by us little ones. In order to make us great, he became little [Col. 0078A]. “A little one,” he says, “has been born to us, and a son has been given to us” (Isa. 9:6). To us, I say, not to himself; for, having been born from the Father before times in a far nobler manner, he had no need to be born temporally from a mother. Nor was he born for angels, who, possessing the great one, did not require the little one. Therefore he was born to us and given to us, because he was necessary to us.

14. Let us now make use, for the end for which he was born and given, of him who was born and given to us. Let us use what is ours for our own benefit; let us work out salvation from the Savior. Behold, a little one is set in the midst. O little one, desired by little ones! O truly little, but in malice, not in wisdom! Let us strive to become like this little one; let us learn from him, because he is meek and humble of heart. Let not the great God have become a little human being [Col. 0078B] without cause, nor have died in vain, nor been crucified to no purpose.

Let us learn his humility, imitate his meekness, embrace his love, share in his sufferings, and be washed in his blood. Let us offer him as a propitiation for our sins, because for this end he himself was born and given to us. Let us offer him to the eyes of the Father—and to his own eyes as well—because the Father “did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us” (Rom. 8:32), and the Son himself emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7). He gave his life over to death and was numbered with criminals; and he bore the sins of 749 many and prayed for transgressors, that they might not perish (Isa. 53:12).

Those for whom the Son prays that they may not perish cannot perish; nor can those for whom the Father delivered the Son to death, that they might live. Therefore pardon is equally to be hoped for from both, since equal in both is mercy in compassion, equal in will is power, and one in divinity is the substance in which the one Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God with them through all ages of ages. Amen [Col. 0078C].

## HOMILY IV. On Luke, chapter 1, verses 32–38

1. There is no doubt that whatever we offer in praise of the Mother pertains to the Son; and, conversely, when we honor the Son, we do not depart from the Mother’s glory. For if, according to Solomon, “a wise son is the glory of his father” (Prov. 10:1), how much more glorious is it to become the mother of Wisdom itself? But what am I attempting in the praises of her whom the prophets proclaim praiseworthy, the angel attests, and the Evangelist recounts? I therefore do not praise her, because I do not dare; I merely repeat devoutly what the Holy Spirit has already expounded through the Evangelist’s mouth.

For the text continues: “And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father.” These are the angel’s words to the Virgin about the promised Son, promising that he is to possess David’s kingdom. No one doubts that the Lord Jesus drew his origin from David’s stock. But I ask how God gave him the throne of David his father, since he did not reign in Jerusalem; indeed, when the crowds wished to make him king, he did not consent (John 6:15), and before Pilate he declared: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).

Finally, what great thing is promised [Col. 0079A] to him who sits above the cherubim (Ps. 79:2), whom the prophet saw sitting upon a high and exalted throne (Isa. 6:1), in being seated upon the throne of David his father? But we know that another Jerusalem, more noble and far richer than the present Jerusalem in which David reigned, is signified. I think that this is what is signified here, according to that manner of speech frequently found in Scripture whereby the sign is put for the thing signified. God indeed gave him the throne of David his father when he established him as king upon Zion, his holy mountain (Ps. 2:6).

But the prophet seems to have disclosed more expressly what kingdom he meant by saying not “in Zion” but “above Zion.” Perhaps “above” was used because David reigned in Zion, while above Zion is the kingdom of him of whom it was said to David: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11); and of whom another prophet said: “He shall sit upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom” (Isa. 9:7) [Col. 0079B]. Do you see that everywhere you find “above”? Above Zion, above the throne, above the royal seat, above the kingdom. Therefore the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father—not a figurative throne, but a true one; not temporal, but eternal; not earthly, but heavenly. As has already been said, it is called David’s because the throne on which David sat temporally bore the image of that eternal throne.

2. “And he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end.” Here too, if we understand the temporal house of Jacob, how shall he reign for ever in that which is not eternal [Col. 0079C]? We must therefore seek the eternal house of Jacob, in which he will reign for ever and whose kingdom will have no end. Did not that house of Jacob bitterly and impiously deny him and foolishly reject him before Pilate, when, Pilate declaring, “Shall I crucify your king?”, it cried out with one voice in reply: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15)?

Seek, then, the Apostle, and he will distinguish for you the Jew who is one inwardly from the Jew who is one outwardly, and the circumcision which is in the spirit from that performed in the flesh (Rom. 2:28); spiritual Israel from carnal Israel, and Abraham’s children of faith from children of the flesh. “For,” he says, “not all who are of Israel are Israelites, nor are all who are Abraham’s seed children” (Rom. 9:6–7) [Col. 0079D].

Proceed, therefore, and say: likewise, not all who are from Jacob are to be counted in the house of Jacob. Jacob himself is Israel. Count, then, as [750] in the house of Jacob only those who are found perfect in Jacob’s faith; or rather, know that they themselves are to be the spiritual and eternal house of Jacob, in which the Lord Jesus will reign for ever. Which of us is there who, according to the interpretation of Jacob’s name, supplants the devil from his heart and wrestles with his vices and desires, so that sin may not reign in his mortal body but Jesus may reign in him—now indeed by grace, and for ever by glory? Blessed are those in whom Jesus will reign for ever, because they too will reign with him and this kingdom will have no end.

O how glorious is that kingdom in which kings are gathered together [Col. 0080A] and meet as one, namely to praise and glorify him who is above all, King of kings and Lord of lords. From the most resplendent contemplation of him, the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. 13:43). Oh, may Jesus remember even me, a sinner, in the favor shown to his people when he comes into his kingdom! Oh, may he deign on that day, when he will deliver the kingdom to God the Father, to visit me with his salvation: that I may behold the prosperity of his elect, rejoice in the joy of his people, and myself praise him with his inheritance!

Meanwhile, come, Lord Jesus: remove the scandals from your kingdom, which is my soul, so that you may reign in it—as you ought. For avarice comes and claims a seat in me; boasting desires to rule me; pride wishes to be my king. Lust says, “I will reign”; ambition, detraction, envy, and anger contend within me, concerning me myself, to determine whose I shall chiefly appear to be. But as far as I can, I resist; I struggle as far as I am helped. I call upon my Lord Jesus; I defend myself for him, because I acknowledge that I belong by right to him. I hold him as my God and Lord, and say: “I have no king except the Lord Jesus.” Come, therefore, Lord; scatter them in your power, and you shall reign in me, because you are yourself my King and my God, who commands the deliverances of Jacob [Col. 0080B].

3. “But Mary said to the angel: How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” At first she wisely kept silence while she was still doubtful and considered what manner of greeting this might be. For she judged it better humbly not [Col. 0080C] to answer than rashly to speak of what she did not know. But now, strengthened and having carefully reflected—while the angel spoke outwardly, but God persuaded inwardly, for the Lord was with her, as the angel said, “The Lord is with you”—thus strengthened, with faith driving away fear and joy driving away modesty, she said to the angel: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?”

She does not doubt the event, but asks for its manner and order. For she does not ask whether this will happen, but how. As though she said: “Since my Lord, the witness of my conscience, knows that it is the vow of his handmaid not to know a man, by what law, by what order, will it please him that this should take place? If I must break my vow in order to bear such a son, I rejoice in the son and grieve for my resolution; nevertheless, let his will [Col. 0080D] be done. But if I conceive as a virgin and give birth as a virgin—which, if it pleases him, will assuredly not be impossible—then I know truly that he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid. How, therefore, shall this be, since I do not know a man?”

“And the angel answered and said to her: The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.” Above she was said to be full of grace; and now how is it said, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you”? Could she be filled with grace and not yet have the Holy Spirit, since he himself is the giver of graces? But if the Holy Spirit was already in her, how is he promised as still to come upon her as though newly?

Perhaps for this reason he did not say simply, “He will come into you,” but added “upon”: because he was indeed already in her through abundant grace, but is now announced as coming upon her because of the fullness of more abundant grace which he is about to pour out upon her. Yet, if she is already full, how can she receive anything more? And if she can receive something more, how should she be understood to have been full before? Perhaps her earlier grace had filled only her mind, whereas the later grace was to overflow into her womb as well, so that the fullness of divinity, which had formerly dwelt spiritually in her, as in many saints, might [751] begin to dwell bodily in her as in no saint [Col. 0081A].

4. Therefore he says: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.” What is meant by, “the power of the Most High shall overshadow you”? Let the one who can receive it, receive it [Col. 0081B]. For who, except perhaps she alone who most blessedly deserved to experience this in herself, can comprehend by understanding or distinguish by reason how that inaccessible splendor poured itself into virginal entrails; and how, so that she might be able to endure its inaccessible approach, he made a shadow for the rest of the mass from that small portion of the same body to which he joined himself as to an animate body?

And perhaps this is especially why it was said, “shall overshadow you”: because the matter was indeed a mystery, and what the Trinity alone willed to accomplish in the Virgin alone and with the Virgin alone was granted to be known only by her to whom it was granted to be experienced. Therefore let it be said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you,” who will assuredly make you fruitful by his power. “And the power of the Most High shall overshadow you”: that is, the power of God and the [Col. 0081C] wisdom of God, Christ, will cover and conceal under shadow in his most secret counsel the manner in which you will conceive by the Holy Spirit, so that it may be known only to himself and to you.

It is as though the angel replied to the Virgin: “Why do you ask of me what you will shortly experience in yourself? You will know, you will know, and know blessedly—but with him as your teacher who is also its author. I have been sent to announce a virginal conception, not to create it. It cannot be taught except by him who gives it; it cannot be learned except by her who receives it.”

“Therefore also that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God.” This is to say: because you will conceive not from a man but from the Holy Spirit [variant: “because what you shall conceive is not from a man but from the Holy Spirit”], and will conceive the power of the Most High, that is, the Son of God, therefore also that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God. That is, not only he who, coming from the bosom of the Father into your womb, shall overshadow you, but also that which he will unite to himself from your substance will from this time be called the Son of God. Just as he who was begotten from the Father before the ages will henceforth also be counted your son, so what is born from the Father will be yours, and what shall be born from you will be his. Yet there will not be two sons, but one. And though one thing is from you and another from him, they will nevertheless no longer each have his own son: one Son will belong to both [Col. 0081D].

5. “Therefore also that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God.” Consider, I beg you, how reverently he said, “that holy thing which shall be born from you.” Why did he say simply “the Holy,” without qualification? I think it was because he had nothing by which properly or worthily to name that exceptional, magnificent, and venerable reality: namely, that which from the most pure flesh of the Virgin, together with its own soul, was to be united with the Only-begotten of the Father. If he had said “holy flesh,” or “holy man,” or “holy infant,” or anything of that kind, he would have seemed to himself to have said too little. Therefore he used the indefinite expression, “the Holy,” because whatever that was which the Virgin bore was undoubtedly holy, and uniquely holy, both through the Spirit’s sanctification and through the Word’s assumption [Col. 0082A].

6. And the angel added: “And behold, Elizabeth, your kinswoman, has herself also conceived a son in her old age.” Why was it necessary to announce to the Virgin the conception of this barren woman too? Was it perhaps that he wished to strengthen one still doubtful and unbelieving concerning the oracle by a more recent miracle [Col. 0082B]? Far be it! We read that Zechariah’s unbelief was rebuked by this very angel; but we do not read that Mary was reproved in any respect. Rather, we know that her faith was praised when Elizabeth prophesied: “Blessed is she who believed, because those things which were spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled in you” (Luke 1:45).

But the conception of her barren kinswoman is announced to the Virgin so that, as miracle is added to miracle, joy may be heaped upon joy. Moreover, she who was shortly to conceive the Son of the Father’s love with the joy of the Holy Spirit had to be kindled beforehand with no small fire of joy and love. For such an abundance of sweetness and gladness could be received only in a heart most devout and most joyful.

Or Elizabeth’s conception is announced [Col. 0082C] to Mary because it was fitting, of course, [752] that the Virgin should first learn from an angel the news which would shortly be published everywhere, rather than hear it from a human being; lest the Mother of God seem excluded from her Son’s counsels if she remained ignorant of things taking place so near at hand on earth. Or rather, Elizabeth’s conception was announced to Mary so that, being taught now of the Savior’s coming and now of the Forerunner’s, and keeping hold of the time and order of events, she might later disclose the truth more fully to the writers and preachers of the Gospel—she who had been instructed from heaven from the beginning in all mysteries.

Or Elizabeth’s conception is still announced to Mary so that, hearing of her aged and pregnant kinswoman, the young woman may think of service; and so, as she hastens to visit her, the little prophet may be given the place and occasion in which he can offer the first fruits of service to his Lord, though he is still the lesser one. And while the devotion of mothers and infants, stirred by each other, comes together reciprocally, a miracle may more wonderfully arise from a miracle [Col. 0082D].

7. But take care not to expect these great things which you hear the angel foretelling to be accomplished by the angel himself. If you ask by whom, listen to the angel himself. “For,” he says, “no word shall be impossible with God.” It is as though he said: “These things which I promise so faithfully I presume upon not through my own power, but through the power of him who sent me.” “For no word shall be impossible with God.”

For what word could be impossible to him who made all things in the Word? This too moves me in the angel’s words: he pointedly [Col. 0083A] did not say, “No deed shall be impossible with God,” but, “No word.” Did he use “word” because, just as human beings can easily say what they wish, even what they are wholly unable to do, so God can just as easily—indeed, incomparably more easily—fulfill in action whatever they are able to express in words? I shall put it more plainly. If it were as easy for human beings to do as to say what they wish, no word would be impossible for them either.

But now, although it is an ordinary and ancient saying that there is a great difference between speaking and doing, this is true among human beings, not with God. For with God alone doing is the same as speaking, and speaking the same as willing. Therefore no word shall be impossible with God. For example: the prophets could foresee and foretell that a virgin or a barren woman would conceive and give birth; but could they make her conceive and give birth? Yet God, who gave them power to foresee, could as easily then foretell through them what he willed as he can now, when he wills, fulfill by himself what he promised. For with God the word does not differ from intention, because he is truth; nor does the deed differ from the word, because he is power; nor does the manner differ from the deed, because he is wisdom. Therefore no word shall be impossible with God [Col. 0083B].

8. You have heard, Virgin, the deed; you have heard also the manner: both wonderful, both joyful. “Rejoice, daughter of Zion; exult exceedingly, daughter of Jerusalem” (Zech. 9:9). And since joy and gladness have been given to your hearing, let us also hear from you the answer of joy which we desire, so that the bones that have been humbled may now exult [Col. 0083C]. You have heard, I say, the deed, and have believed it: believe also what you have heard concerning the manner. You have heard that you shall conceive and bear a son; you have heard that this will be not through a man, but through the Holy Spirit. The angel awaits your answer, for it is time that he return to God who sent him. We too await from you, O Lady, the word of mercy—we whom the sentence of condemnation grievously oppresses. And behold: the price of our salvation is offered to you; we shall immediately be delivered if you consent. In the eternal Word of God we were all made, and behold, we die; by your brief answer we are to be restored, so that we may be recalled to life. This Adam, sorrowing in exile from Paradise with his wretched offspring, entreats of you, O gracious Virgin; this Abraham, this David. This the other holy Fathers [Col. 0083D] demand—your own fathers, that is—who likewise dwell in the region of the shadow of death. The whole world, prostrate at your knees, awaits this. Nor without reason, since upon your mouth depend the consolation of the afflicted, the redemption of captives, the liberation of the condemned—indeed, the salvation of all the sons of Adam, of your whole race.

Give your answer quickly, Virgin. O Lady, utter the word for which earth, hell, and heaven itself are waiting. The King and Lord of all, who so greatly desired your beauty, equally desires your consenting reply; for through it he has determined to save the world. And you who pleased him in silence will please him still more by your word, when he himself [Col. 0084A] cries to you from heaven: “O fairest among women, let me hear your voice.” If, then, you make him hear your voice, he will make you see our salvation. Is this not what you sought, for which you groaned, for which you sighed in prayer by day and night? What then? Are you she to whom this was promised, or are we to await another? Indeed, you yourself, and no other. You, I say, are she who was promised, awaited, and desired; from you your holy father Jacob, already approaching death, hoped for eternal life when he said: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49:18). In you, finally, and through you, God himself, our King, purposed before the ages to work salvation in the midst of the earth. Why hope from another for what is offered to you? Why await through another what will shortly be supplied through you, provided only [Col. 0084B] that you give consent and utter the word?

Therefore answer the angel quickly—or rather, answer the Lord through the angel. Speak your word, and receive the Word; bring forth yours, and conceive the divine one; send forth what is passing, and embrace what is eternal. Why do you delay? Why do you tremble? Believe, confess, and receive. Let humility take courage; let modesty take confidence. It is by no means fitting now that virginal simplicity should forget prudence. In this one matter, prudent Virgin, do not fear presumption: for although modesty is pleasing in silence, yet at this moment mercy is more necessary in speech. Open, blessed Virgin, your heart to faith, your lips to confession, your womb to the Creator. Behold, the Desired of all nations stands outside and knocks at the door. Oh, if through your delay he should pass by, and you should [Col. 0084C] again begin sorrowfully to seek him whom your soul loves! Rise, run, open. Rise through faith, run through devotion, open through confession.

[Note: [Col. 0083] You will find similar material in the Appendix to vol. V of St Augustine, Sermon 120, no. 7.]

9. “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” Humility is always a virtue closely allied with divine grace. For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” Therefore she answers humbly, that a seat may be prepared for grace. “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord.” What is this humility, so exalted, which knows not how to yield to honours and does not know how to become insolent through glory? She is chosen as Mother of God, yet calls herself a handmaid. Truly, this is no slight mark of humility: not to forget humility when such glory is offered. It is no great thing to be humble in lowliness; humility when honoured is indeed a great and rare virtue.

If the Church, deceived by my pretences, should advance me, a wretched little man, to some even moderate dignity [Col. 0084D]—God, undoubtedly, permitting this either because of my sins or those of my subjects—would I not immediately forget what I had been, and think myself such as I am thought by men who do not see the heart? I believe my reputation [otherwise: “indeed”]; I pay no attention to conscience. Reckoning not that honour is due to virtues, but that virtues are due to honour, I deem myself holier in proportion as I deem myself higher. You may see many in the Church, made noble from lowly birth and rich from poverty, suddenly swell with pride, forget their former abjection, blush at their own lineage, and scorn their humble parents. You may see wealthy [Col. 0085A] [otherwise: “ruinous”] men hasten toward every ecclesiastical dignity, soon congratulating themselves upon a holiness consisting solely in changed clothes, not changed minds. They judge themselves worthy of the office which they attained by ambition, and attribute to merits what, if I may dare say it, they acquired with money. I pass over those whom ambition blinds, and for whom honour itself becomes material for pride.

10. But I see—what pains me more—that after rejecting worldly pomp, some learn pride more thoroughly in the school of humility; beneath the wings of a gentle and humble master they grow more insolent, and in the cloister become more impatient than they had been in the world. What is more perverse, many cannot endure contempt in the house of God [Col. 0085B] who in their own homes could be nothing but contemptible: because, apparently, where honours are sought by many, they did not deserve to have a place; so at least they may appear honourable there where honours are despised by all.

I see others also—something that should not be seen without grief—who, after undertaking Christ’s warfare, again become entangled in worldly business and again sink into earthly desires; taking great care to raise walls while neglecting character; under the pretext of common usefulness selling words to the rich and greetings to ladies; moreover, contrary to their Emperor’s edict, coveting what belongs to others and pursuing their own possessions through litigation. They do not hear the apostle sounding the trumpet under the King’s command: “Indeed, it is already a fault among you that you have lawsuits. Why do you not rather suffer wrong?” (1 Cor. 6:7) [Col. 0085C]. Is this how they have crucified the world to themselves and themselves to the world: that men scarcely known formerly in their own village or town now roam through provinces, frequent courts, and obtain the acquaintance of kings and intimacy with princes? What shall I say of dress, in which warmth is no longer sought but colour, and more attention is paid to the adornment of clothes than to virtues? Shameful to say: frivolous women are surpassed in their own pursuit when monks seek price, not necessity, in clothing. Without even retaining the outward form of religion, Christ’s soldiers desire to be adorned, not armed, in their dress.
