Whereas they ought to prepare for battle and display the badge of poverty against the powers of the air—which their adversaries greatly fear—they instead show in their soft [Col. 0085D] garments the mark of peace, and voluntarily deliver themselves unarmed to their enemies without bloodshed. These evils arise from no other source than this: abandoning the humility by which we abandoned the world, we are compelled once again to follow the foolish pursuits of secular people, and become dogs returning to their vomit.

11. Let us therefore hear, all of us who are such, what she answered who was chosen as Mother of God but did not forget humility. “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” *Let it be done* is a sign of desire, not an indication of doubt. And [lacuna] in saying, “Let it be done to me according to your word,” she is to be understood as expressing the affection of one who desires, rather than seeking an effect in the manner of one who doubts. [Col. 0086A] Yet nothing prevents us from understanding *let it be done* as the word of one praying. For no one prays except for what he believes and hopes. But God wishes even what he promises to be asked of him. And so he perhaps first promises many things which he has determined to give, in order that devotion may be aroused by the promise, and thus devout prayer may merit what he was going to give freely. Thus the gracious Lord, who wills all people to be saved, draws merits from us; and while he goes before us by bestowing what he may repay, he acts freely, lest he bestow freely.

The prudent Virgin undoubtedly understood this when, to the gift of a gratuitous promise that went before her, she joined the merit of her prayer, saying: “Let it be done to me according to your word.” Let it be done to me from the Word according to your word. Let the Word which was in the beginning with God become flesh from my flesh [Col. 0086B] according to your word. Let the Word, I beseech you, be made for me—not uttered so as to pass away, but conceived so as to remain; clothed, indeed, in flesh and not in air. Let it be made for me not merely audible to the ears, but visible to the eyes, tangible to the hands, borne upon the shoulders. Let it not be made for me as a written and mute word, but as one incarnate and living: that is, not traced in mute figures upon dead skins, but livingly impressed in human form within my chaste womb; and this not by the drawing of a dead pen, but by the operation of the Holy Spirit. Let it be made for me in the manner in which it was made for no one before me and shall be made for no one after me.

Formerly, indeed, God spoke to the Fathers in many portions and in many ways through the prophets; and it is recorded that the word of the Lord came to some in the ear, to others in the mouth, and even to others in the hand [Col. 0086C]; but I pray that it may be made in my womb according to your word. I do not wish it to be made for me as something declaimed in preaching, figuratively signified, or imagined in a dream; but silently inspired, personally incarnate, bodily implanted in my inmost being. Therefore, may the Word—which in himself could neither be made nor needed to be made—deign to be made in me and for me according to your word. Let it indeed be made for the whole world generally, but for me especially according to your word.

## St Bernard’s apology for undertaking to treat this passage of the Gospel after other interpreters

I have expounded the Gospel reading as I could, and I do not fail to know that it will not please everyone. Yet I know that on this account I shall be exposed to the indignation of many, and [Col. 0086D] shall be judged either superfluous or presumptuous, because, after the Fathers who have expounded this very passage most fully, I have dared as a new interpreter to lay my hand once more upon the same subject. But if anything has been said after the Fathers which is not against the Fathers, I think it ought to displease neither the Fathers nor anyone else. Where I have said what I received from the Fathers, provided that the swelling of presumption is absent and the fruit of devotion is present, I shall patiently hear those who complain of superfluity.

Yet let those who censure me as offering an idle and unnecessary explanation know that I have aimed not so much at expounding the Gospel as at taking from the Gospel an occasion to speak of what delighted me to speak. But if I have sinned in stirring up from this passage my own devotion more than in seeking common usefulness, the gracious Virgin will be able to excuse this sin of mine with her merciful Son, to whom I have most devoutly dedicated this little work of mine, such as it is.

[Col. 0087]

## ON THE VIGIL OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

### SERMON I. On the proclamation of the Martyrology: “Jesus Christ, Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judah.”

[Note: [Col. 0087] These words are found in Usuard’s *Martyrology*, which at that time was used by all, or almost all, of the Gallican Churches, and even by the Roman Church.]

[Col. 0087A]

1. A voice of joy has sounded in our land, a voice of exultation and salvation in the dwellings of sinners. A good word has been heard, a consoling word, a discourse full of delight, worthy of all acceptance. Mountains, sing praise with jubilation; and all trees of the forest, clap your hands before the Lord, for he comes. [Col. 0087B] Hear, heavens; give ear, earth; be astonished and give praise, all creation—but you most of all, O human being: “Jesus Christ, Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judah.”

Whose heart is so stony that his soul is not melted by this word? What sweeter announcement could be made? What more delightful declaration could be offered? What like it was ever heard, or what similar thing has the world ever received? “Jesus Christ, Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judah.” O brief word concerning the abbreviated Word, yet filled with heavenly sweetness! Loving affection strains, eager to pour forth more broadly an abundance of honeyed sweetness, yet finds no words. So great is the grace of this utterance that it immediately begins to seem less savoury if I alter a single iota: “Jesus Christ, [Col. 0087C] Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judah.”

O birth unsullied in holiness, honourable to the world, lovable to humankind because of the greatness of the benefit bestowed, unfathomable even to angels because of the depth of its sacred mystery, and in all these respects admirable by the singular excellence of its novelty: a birth which has had no similar predecessor and shall have no successor. O delivery alone without pain, alone knowing no shame, ignorant of corruption; not opening but consecrating the temple of the virgin womb! O birth above nature, yet for nature; surpassing by the excellence of miracle, yet restoring by the power of mystery! Brothers, who shall recount this generation? An angel announces; the power of the Most High overshadows; the Spirit comes upon her; the Virgin believes; as a virgin she conceives by faith, as a virgin gives birth, and remains a virgin: who would not wonder? The Son of the Most High is born [Col. 0087D], God begotten from God before the ages; the Word is born as an infant: who can wonder sufficiently?

2. Nor is this birth idle, nor is this condescension of majesty without fruit. “Jesus Christ, Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judah.” You who are in the dust, awake and give praise. Behold, the Lord comes with salvation, comes with ointments, comes with glory. For Jesus does not come without salvation, Christ not without anointing, nor the Son of God without glory. He himself is salvation, he himself is anointing, he himself is glory, as it is written: “A wise son is the glory of his father” (Prov. 10:1). Happy is the soul which, having tasted the fruit of salvation, is drawn and runs after the fragrance of the ointments, in order to see his glory, glory as of [Col. 0088A] the only-begotten from the Father.

Take breath again, you who are lost: Jesus has come to seek and save what was lost. You who are sick, be restored to health: Christ has come, who heals the broken-hearted by the anointing of his mercy. Exult, all who desire great things: the Son of God has come down to you, that he may make you co-heirs of his kingdom. Thus, I beseech you, heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved; glorify me, and I shall be glorious. For in this way my soul shall bless the Lord, and all that is [Col. 0088B] within me his holy name, when you have forgiven all my iniquities, healed all my infirmities, and satisfied my desire with good things (Ps. 102:1, 3, 5).

These three things, beloved, are what I understand in hearing that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is born. Why do we call his name Jesus, unless because “he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21)? Or why did he wish to be called Christ, unless because “the yoke shall rot away because of the oil” (Isa. 10:27)? Why did the Son of God become human, unless to make human beings children of God? And who can resist his will? Jesus justifies: who is there to condemn? Christ heals: who is there to wound? The Son of God exalts: who is there to humble?

[Col. 0088C]

3. Therefore Jesus is born: let whoever has been condemned by the conscience of sins as guilty of everlasting damnation rejoice. For the mercy of Jesus exceeds every magnitude and multitude of crimes. Christ is born: let whoever was assailed by long-standing vices be glad. For before the anointing of Christ no sickness of the soul, however inveterate, can stand at all. The Son of God is born: let one accustomed to desire great things exult, because the great Giver has come.

Brothers, this is the heir; let us receive him devoutly, for then his inheritance will be ours also. “He who did not spare his own Son, how has he not also given us all things together with the Son?” (Rom. 8:32). Let no one disbelieve; let no one hesitate. We have testimony [Col. 0088D] most worthy of belief: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The Only-begotten of God wished to have brothers, that he himself might be the firstborn among many brethren. And so that even the faintheartedness of human frailty might not hesitate at all, he first became the brother of human beings, became the son of a human being, became human. If a human being judges even this incredible, the eyes establish faith.

4. “Jesus Christ is born in Bethlehem of Judah.” Observe his condescension. Not in Jerusalem, the royal city, but in Bethlehem, which is the least among the thousands of Judah. O little Bethlehem, yet now magnified by the Lord! He has magnified you who, though great, became little in you. Rejoice, Bethlehem; let a festal Alleluia be sung today through all [Col. 0089A] your streets. What city, if it hears this, will not envy you that most precious stable and the glory of that manger? Your name is now famous throughout the whole earth, and all generations call you blessed. Everywhere glorious things are spoken of you, city of God; everywhere it is sung that “a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5). Everywhere, I say, it is preached and proclaimed: “Jesus Christ, Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judah.”

Nor is the addition “of Judah” idle, since it recalls to us the promise made to the fathers: “The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.” For salvation is from the Jews, but it is salvation unto the ends of the earth [Col. 0089B]. “Judah,” he says, “your brothers shall praise you. Your hands shall be upon the necks of your enemies,” and the other things said concerning that Judah which we read nowhere as fulfilled in Judah himself, but see fulfilled in Christ. For he is the Lion from the tribe of Judah, of whom it is further said: “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son” (Gen. 49:8, 10). Christ is a great plunderer, who before he knows how to call father or mother carries off the spoils of Samaria (Isa. 8:4). Christ is a great plunderer, who, ascending on high, led captivity captive; yet he took nothing away, but rather himself gave gifts to human beings. Thus, the phrase “Bethlehem of Judah” calls to mind these and other similar prophecies fulfilled in Christ—for they were also foretold concerning him—and leaves no room at all to ask whether anything good can come from [Col. 0089C] Bethlehem.

5. Indeed, so far as concerns us, we learn also from this how he wishes to be received, who chose to be born in Bethlehem. Someone might perhaps have thought that lofty palaces should be sought for him, where the King of glory might be received with glory; yet it was not for this that he came from those royal dwellings. “In his left hand are riches and glory; in his right, length of days” (Prov. 3:16). An eternal abundance of all these things was available in heaven, but poverty was not to be found there. Yet on earth this condition abounded and overflowed, while humanity did not know its worth. Therefore the Son of God, desiring it, came down in order to choose it for himself and, by his own esteem, make it precious for us also.

Adorn [Col. 0089D] your bridal chamber, Zion—but with humility, with poverty. For he takes delight in these rags, and, as Mary bears witness, delights in being wrapped in these silks. Sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to your God.

6. Consider, finally, that he is born in Bethlehem of Judah, and be zealous to be found yourself as Bethlehem of Judah; he does not disdain to be received even in you. For Bethlehem means “house of bread,” and Judah signifies “confession.” Therefore, if you fill your soul with the nourishment of the divine word and faithfully receive—although unworthily, yet with as much devotion as you can—that bread which came down from heaven and gives life to the world, namely the Lord’s body of Jesus, so that the new flesh of the resurrection may restore and sustain the old wineskin of your body, in order that the new wine within may be able, strengthened by this bond [Col. 0090A], to contain it; if, finally, you live by faith and need never groan because you have forgotten to eat your bread: you have become Bethlehem, plainly worthy to receive the Lord, provided confession is not lacking.

Let Judah therefore be your sanctification. Put on confession and beauty; Christ especially accepts this garment in his ministers. Finally, the Apostle briefly commends both to you: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). For righteousness is in the heart, bread in the house. Righteousness is bread: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6). Therefore let righteousness, the righteousness that is from faith, be in the heart; for that alone has glory before God. Let confession unto salvation also be in the mouth [Col. 0090B]; and now receive with confidence him who is born in Bethlehem of Judah, Jesus Christ, Son of God.

### SERMON II. On what is written: “O Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear; tomorrow you shall go forth, and the Lord will be with you.” 2 Chronicles, chapter 20, verse 17

1. We address true Jews, not according to the letter but according to the Spirit: the seed of Abraham, whose multiplication, as it is read to have been promised, is seen to have been fulfilled. For it is not the children of the flesh, but the children of promise, who are reckoned as the seed (Rom. 9:8). Nor do we call that Jerusalem which kills the prophets. How could we console that city over which the Lord wept (Luke 19:41), which was given over to destruction? We speak to that Jerusalem which comes down new from heaven: Do not fear, O Judah and Jerusalem [Col. 0090C]. Do not fear, true confessors, who confess the Lord not only with the mouth but wholly and in every part, clothed in confession as in a garment; indeed, whose every inward part confesses the Lord, and whose every bone says, “Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. 34:10)—not like those who profess to know God but deny him by their deeds (Titus 1:16).

True confession is this: that all your works, brothers, should be his works and should confess him. Let them confess him with a twofold confession, that you may be “clothed doubly”: namely, with confession of your sins and confession of divine praise. Then you will be true Jews, if your whole life confesses that you are sinners and deserving of much greater punishments, while God is the highest good, who remits the eternal torments which you have deserved in exchange for these light and transitory punishments [Col. 0090D]. For whoever does not ardently desire repentance appears by his deeds to say either that he has no need of repentance—and thus does not confess his own fault—or that repentance cannot benefit him—and thus does not confess divine goodness.

But you must be true Jews, and also true Jerusalem, so that you may fear nothing further. For Jerusalem is a vision of peace: vision, not possession. The Lord has appointed peace as its boundaries—not, indeed, as its beginning or its middle. Therefore, if you do not have peace—or rather, since you cannot have it perfectly in this world—at least see it, behold it, consider it, and desire it. Let the eyes of your heart be directed there; let your intention turn toward peace, so that whatever you do, you may do from desire for that peace [Col. 0091A] “which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4:7); in all things aim at this: that, reconciled, you may have peace with God.

2. To these we say, “Do not fear”; these we console—not those who have not known the way of peace. For if it were said to them, “Tomorrow you shall go forth,” this would be a threat, not consolation. Only those who desire to be dissolved and long to depart see peace, and know that, if their earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, they have a building from God; not those who, turned to madness, delight in their own fetters. Such people, indeed, ought in dying to be called not so much those who have gone forth as those who have entered: for they go not into light or freedom, but into prison, darkness, and hell.

But to you it is said [Col. 0091B]: “Do not fear; tomorrow you shall go forth,” and there shall no longer be fear within your boundaries. You indeed have many enemies: the flesh, than which none can be a nearer enemy; the present evil world, which surrounds you on every side; and the princes of darkness, stationed in the air to block your path. Yet do not fear: tomorrow, that is, shortly, you shall go forth. For tomorrow is near. Thus holy Jacob also says: “Tomorrow my righteousness shall answer for me” (Gen. 30:33).

There are three days, of which we also read: “After two days he shall revive us; on the third day he shall raise us up” (Hos. 6:3). One is under Adam, another in Christ, the third with Christ. Thus it is added there: “We shall know and follow on, that we may know the Lord”; and here it is said: “Tomorrow you shall go forth, [Col. 0091C] and the Lord will be with you.” For this is spoken to those who have cut short their days, in whom the day on which they were born has perished: the day of Adam, the day of sin, which Jeremiah also cursed, saying: “Cursed be the day on which I was born” (Jer. 20:14). For we are all born in that day. Would that this day might perish in all of us: the day of cloud and darkness, the day of gloom and tempest, which Adam made for us, which the enemy made, who said: “Your eyes shall be opened” (Gen. 3:5).

3. But behold, the day of new redemption, of ancient restoration, of eternal blessedness, has dawned upon us. “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117:24), because tomorrow we shall go forth. From where, except from the inner chamber of this world, the prison of this body, the fetters of necessity, curiosity, vanity, [Col. 0091D] and pleasure, which hold the feet of our affections even against our will? What has our spirit to do with earthly things? Why does it not desire, seek, and relish spiritual things? O spirits who are from above, what have you to do with the lowest things? “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth” (Col. 3:1–2).

But “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind full of many thoughts” (Wis. 9:15). The many necessities of this wretched body restrain us. A certain glue of perverse desire and earthly delight prevents flight, and swiftly draws the mind back if perhaps it is ever lifted up. But do not fear: tomorrow you shall go forth from the pit of misery and the mire of filth. For in order to bring you forth from it, he too was fixed in the deep mire. Do not fear, therefore: tomorrow you shall go forth from the body of death [Col. 0092A] and from every corruption of sin.

Spend this day in Christ, that you may walk as he himself walked. “Whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). Therefore do not fear, because tomorrow you shall go forth, and so you shall always be with the Lord. Or, since it is expressly said, “and the Lord will be with you,” let us understand it thus: while we are in the body, we may be with the Lord—that is, adhere to his will—but he is not with us in the sense of consenting to our will. For we would already be free; we long to be dissolved and desire to depart, but he still delays for a certain reason. Tomorrow we shall go forth, and the Lord will be with us, so that whatever [Col. 0092B] we shall will, he will will, and in nothing will he differ from our will.

4. Therefore, O Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear if you cannot yet attain the perfection which you desire. Let the humility of confession supply what the imperfection of your conduct lacks; and the eyes of God have seen your imperfection. For this reason he commanded his commandments to be kept exceedingly (Ps. 118:4): so that, seeing our failure and imperfection, and our inability to fulfil what we ought, we may flee to mercy and say, “Your mercy is better than lives” (Ps. 62:4); and, unable to appear clothed in the garment of innocence or righteousness, we may appear clothed in confession. For “confession and beauty are [Col. 0092C] before the Lord” (Ps. 95:6), provided that it is—as we have said—the confession not only of the mouth but also of the whole person, so that all our bones may say, “Lord, who is like you?”—and all this solely with a view to peace and from desire for reconciliation with God.

To such people it is said: “O Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear; tomorrow you shall go forth.” That is: as soon as the soul leaves the body, all the affections and all the desires by which it was meanwhile scattered and bound throughout the whole world will be dissolved, and it will go forth from this glue; and the Lord will be with us. This may seem too much to you, if you look at yourselves rather than at those who await you. Does not the whole world await this? For creation has been subjected to vanity; and when the human being fell, whom the Lord had appointed lord of his household [Col. 0092D] and ruler of all his possession, the entire inheritance was corrupted together. Hence the air was thrown into disorder, the earth cursed in Adam’s works, and all things subjected to vanity.

5. Nor indeed will the inheritance be restored until the heirs are restored. Therefore, according to the Apostle’s testimony, it too groans and labours in childbirth until now (Rom. 8:22). And we have become a spectacle not only to this world, but also to angels and human beings. “The righteous await me,” he says, “until you repay me” (Ps. 141:8). And when the martyrs sought the day of judgment—not as persons eager for vengeance, but desiring the perfection of the blessedness they will then possess—they received the divine reply: “Wait a little time, until the number [Col. 0093A] of your brothers is completed” (Rev. 6:11).

They have already received individual robes, but they will not be clothed doubly until we too are clothed. We hold pledges and hostages: their very bodies, without which they cannot be perfected, nor will they receive them without us. Thus the Apostle says concerning the patriarchs and prophets: “God having provided something better for us, that they should not be made perfect without us” (Heb. 11:40). Oh, if we too knew how they await and how greatly they desire our coming! How anxiously they seek news, how gladly they hear good reports concerning us!

6. Yet why do I speak of those who have learned compassion from the things which they suffered, when even the holy angels themselves desire us? Are not the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem to be rebuilt from these little worms and this dust? Do you suppose how much the citizens of heaven desire the ruins of their city to be restored? How anxious they are for living stones to come, to be built together with them! How they run to and fro as intermediaries between us and God, most faithfully carrying our groanings to him and most devoutly bringing back his grace to us! Surely they will not disdain that we become their companions, since they have already become our ministers. For are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service for the sake of those who shall receive the inheritance [Col. 0093B] of salvation? (Heb. 1:14).

Let us hasten, I beseech you, beloved; let us hasten. The entire multitude of the heavenly court awaits us. We caused the angels to rejoice when we were converted to repentance; let us make progress and hasten to complete their joy concerning us. Woe to you, whoever you are, who [Col. 0093C] deliberate about returning to the mire, returning to vomit! Do you think that at judgment you will find appeased those whom you seek to deprive of so great and so hoped-for a joy? They exulted when we came to repentance, as over people whom they saw recalled from the very gate of hell. What, then, will happen if they see those who have already set one foot in Paradise turn back from the very gate of Paradise and depart backward? For although their bodies are below, their hearts are above.

7. Run, brothers, run. Not angels alone, but the Creator of angels himself awaits you. The wedding is prepared, but the house is not yet full; those through whom the wedding shall be filled are still awaited. The Father awaits and desires you, not only because of his exceeding [Col. 0093D] love with which he loved you—whence the Only-begotten, who is in the Father’s bosom, has himself declared it, saying, “The Father loves you” (John 16:27)—but for his own sake, as he speaks through the prophet: “For my own sake I will act, not for your sakes” (Ezek. 36:22). For who can doubt that he will fulfil what he promised the Son, saying: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8)? And elsewhere: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 109:1).

Not all his enemies will be crushed while they can still assail us, who are his members in any degree. This promise will not be fulfilled until death, the last enemy, is destroyed. For who does not know how greatly the Son desires the fruit of his birth and of the whole life which he lived in the flesh—in short, the fruit of his cross and death [Col. 0094A], the price of his precious blood? Will he not hand over to God the Father the kingdom which he acquired? Will he not restore to him his creatures, for whom the Father sent him into the world? The Holy Spirit also awaits us. For he is love and kindness, in which we were predestined from eternity; nor is there doubt that he wills his predestination to be fulfilled.

8. Therefore, since the wedding is prepared, and the entire multitude of the heavenly court desires and awaits us, let us run, not as though toward an uncertainty; let us run in our desires and in the progress of virtues. To make progress is to set out. Let each of us say: “Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment [ordinance] for those who love your name” (Ps. 118:132). Have mercy, not as I have deserved, but as they have decreed. Let us likewise say, “As your will has been in heaven, so let it be”; and likewise, “Your will be done” (Matt. 6:10). We know that it is written: “If God is for us, who is against us? Or who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect?” (Rom. 8:31, 33). “Is it not lawful for me,” he says, “to do what I will?” (Matt. 20:15).

Let this meanwhile be our consolation, dearest brethren, until we go forth and the Lord is with us. May he in his great mercy bring us to that blessed going-forth and to that bright tomorrow; and may he deign also to visit us and be with us on this coming tomorrow: so that, if anyone perhaps is detained in any temptation, through the mercy of him who came to preach release to those imprisoned, he may go forth tomorrow; so that with saving joy we may receive the crown of our little King, [Col. 0094C] he himself granting it, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. On the text: “Today you shall know that the Lord is coming, and in the morning you shall see his glory.” Exodus, chapter 16, vv. 6–7.

1. “All you earthborn, and sons of men, hear: you who are in the dust, awake and praise.” For the physician is coming to the sick, the redeemer to those who have been sold, the way to those who wander, life to the dead. For he comes who will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea, who will heal all our infirmities, who will carry us back upon his own shoulders to the original source of our proper dignity. [761] Great is this power; but still more to be wondered at is the mercy—that he who could have brought aid chose to come in this way.

“Today,” he says, “you shall know that the Lord is coming.” These words were indeed set in Scripture in their own place and time; yet Mother Church has fittingly adapted them to the Vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. I mean that Church which has within herself the counsel and Spirit of her Bridegroom and God, in whom the Beloved abides between her breasts, chiefly possessing and preserving the principal seat of her heart. Surely she is the one who wounded his heart and immersed the eye of contemplation in the very abyss of God’s secrets, so as to establish for him in hers, and for herself in his heart, a perpetual dwelling-place.

Therefore, when she either alters or varies words in the divine Scriptures, that arrangement is stronger than the original placing of the words; and perhaps stronger by as much as figure differs from truth, light from shadow, mistress from handmaid.

> [Note: [Col. 0095D] How highly Bernard valued the decrees of the universal Church: he recognized such great authority for her even in an accommodated interpretation [Col. 0096D] of Scripture—an authority which certainly she herself does not claim.]

2. “Today you shall know that the Lord is coming.” In my judgment, two days are more expressly indicated to us in these words. The first is that which runs from the fall of the first man until the end of the world, the day which the saints are known often to have cursed. For Adam was cast out from that most radiant day in which he had been created; thrust into these narrow straits of things, he entered a dark day and was almost extinguished from the light of truth. We are all born in this day—if indeed it ought to be called a day rather than a night—except that unconquerable mercy has left us the light of reason as a kind of little spark.

But the second day will be amid the splendors of the saints for everlasting ages, when that most serene morning has dawned, which is the promised mercy, and death has been swallowed up in victory; when shadows and darkness have been removed, the splendor of the true light will at once occupy all things above and below, within and without. “Make me hear your mercy in the morning,” says the saint (Ps. 142:8); and, “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy” (Ps. 89:14, 9).

But let us return to our day, which is called like a watch in the night because of its brevity, and which is termed a nothing and an emptiness by that familiar instrument of the Holy Spirit when he says, “For all our days have failed”; “My days have vanished like smoke”; and, “My days have declined like a shadow” (Ps. 101:4, 12). “Few and evil are all the days of my life,” says that holy patriarch [Col. 0095C] who saw the Lord face to face and spoke with him so familiarly (Gen. 47:9).

And indeed on this very day God grants human beings reason and bestows understanding; yet when one goes forth from this world, it is necessary that he be illumined by the light of God’s knowledge, lest, if he departs extinguished from the house of imprisonment and the shadow of death, he be unable to be illumined for ever.

For this reason the Only-begotten of God, the sun of righteousness, like a torch of immeasurable and splendid light, was brought into the prison of this world and kindled, so that all who wish to be illumined may approach and be joined to him, with nothing between themselves and him. For our sins separate between us and God. But once they have been removed, we are joined in one to the true light, to be illumined and, as it were, made one body with it; just as an extinguished light is joined, without any intervening medium, to a shining and burning light in order to be illuminated, so that through the example of visible things we may know the effects of invisible things.

3. Therefore, before we depart from the darkness of this world, let us, according to the prophet, kindle for ourselves the light of knowledge in relation to this great and most radiant star (Hos. 10:12, according to the LXX), lest we pass from darkness into darkness, and into everlasting darkness. What, then, is this knowledge? Surely, to know that the Lord is coming, although we cannot know when he will come. This is the whole thing required of us.

“But,” you say, [Col. 0096A] “this knowledge belongs to everyone. For who, even if faithful only in name, does not know that the Lord is coming, that he will come to judge the living and the dead and render to each according to his works?” This knowledge, my brothers, does not belong to everyone—not even to many. It belongs to few, because truly few are saved.

Do you suppose that those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in wicked things (Prov. 2:14) either know or consider that the Lord is coming? If they themselves say so, do not believe them. For “whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4). “They profess,” says the Apostle, “that they know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1:16), because “faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:20). For they would not so defile themselves with every impurity if they knew [Col. 0096B] or feared that the Lord was coming; rather, they would surely keep watch and would not permit their consciences to be so grievously pierced.

4. In its first stage this knowledge produces repentance and sorrow, so that it turns laughter into mourning, song into lamentation, and joy into grief; and things which formerly pleased you intensely begin to displease you, while you particularly dread those things you particularly desired. For it is written: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18), so that ensuing sorrow is the proof of true and holy knowledge.

But in the second stage it produces amendment, so that you no longer offer your members to sin as weapons of iniquity, but restrain gluttony, slay lust, cast down pride, and make the body serve holiness, when before it served iniquity. For repentance without amendment will not profit, as the Wise Man says: “One building and another destroying—what profit have they except labor? One praying and another cursing—whose voice will God hear? He who is washed by a dead person and touches him again—his washing profits him nothing” (Ecclus. 34:28–30); rather, according to the Savior’s judgment, one must fear lest something worse happen to him (John 5:14).

But because these things cannot be maintained for long unless the tireless mind watches and attends to itself with much circumspection, in the third stage it produces watchful care: so that one now begins, in such care, to walk with his God and searches on every side lest in even the slightest matter he offend the gaze of that dreadful Majesty. In repentance it is kindled, in amendment it burns, [Col. 0096D] in watchful care it shines, so that it may be renewed within and without.

5. Here it begins at last to breathe again after the affliction and grief caused by evils, and to temper the greatness of its fear with spiritual joy, lest it be swallowed up by excessive sorrow at the enormity of its own crimes. Hence, though it fears the Judge, it hopes in the Savior. Since fear and joy now yield to and meet each other in its soul, fear often overcomes joy, while joy more often excludes fear and encloses it within the secret place of its own gladness. Happy the conscience in which such a struggle is continually waged, until what is mortal is swallowed up by life, until the fear which is partial is done away and joy, which is perfect, succeeds it; for not everlasting fear but everlasting joy will be its portion.

Yet one who thus burns and shines should not suppose that he is already in the house where a kindled light can ordinarily be carried without any fear of winds. Rather, let him remember that he is out in the open and strive to shield with both hands what he carries; nor let him trust the air, even if it seems calm. For suddenly, at an hour when he does not expect it, it will change; and if he relaxes his hands even a little, the light will be extinguished. And if the heat of the hands carrying it should also burn them, as sometimes happens, let him choose to suffer rather than withdraw his hands, because it can be blown out in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.

If we were in that house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens, where no enemy enters and no friend departs, there would be nothing to fear. But now we are exposed to three most evil and powerful winds: the flesh, the devil, and the world. They endeavor to extinguish the illumined conscience, breathing into our hearts evil desires and unlawful impulses, and troubling you so suddenly that you can scarcely know beforehand whence you come or whither you go.

Of these, although two often cease, no one has ever extorted a respite from the third’s blowing. Therefore the soul must be sheltered with both hands, those of heart and body, lest what has already been illumined be extinguished. Nor must one yield or draw back, [763] even if the severe heat of temptations violently assails the condition of both the inner and outer person; but one must say with the saint: “My soul is always in my hands” (Ps. 118:109).

Let us choose rather to burn than to yield. And just as we do not readily forget what we hold in our hands, so let us never forget the business of our souls, and let that care flourish chiefly in our hearts.

6. Therefore, when our loins have thus been girded and our lamps are burning, we must keep the watches of the night over the flock of our thoughts and actions, so that, if the Lord comes in the first watch, or the second, or the third, he may find us ready.

The first watch is uprightness in action: that throughout your life you strive to conform to this Rule which you have vowed, and do not overstep the bounds set by your fathers in all the exercises of this way and life, turning neither to the right nor to the left.

The second is purity of intention: that the single eye may make the whole body full of light, so that whatever you do, you do for God, and that the graces may return to the place from which they proceed, in order to flow forth again.

The third is the keeping of unity: that, being placed in the community, you put the wills of others before your own; that you remain among the brethren not only without complaint, but also graciously, bearing all, praying for all, so that it may likewise be said of you: “This is a lover of the brethren and of the people of Israel; this is he who prayed much for the people and for the holy city Jerusalem” (2 Macc. 15:14).

Thus, on this day, the advent of the Only-begotten kindles in us true knowledge—namely, that knowledge which teaches us that the Lord is coming, and which is to be the perpetual and steadfast foundation of our conduct.

7. “And in the morning,” he says, “you shall see his glory.” O morning! O day, better in the courts of the Lord than thousands, when there shall be month after month and Sabbath after Sabbath, when the brightness of light and the ardor of charity shall illumine the inhabitants of the earth even unto those loftiest wonders! Who could think of you, much less presume to recount anything about you?

Meanwhile, however, brothers, let us build up our faith, so that, if we cannot see those wonders reserved for us, we may at least contemplate a little the wonders wrought on earth for our sake. In the assumption of our flesh that almighty Majesty accomplished three works, three mixtures, so uniquely wonderful and wonderfully unique that such things have neither been done nor will be done again upon earth. For God and man, mother and virgin, faith and the human heart, have been joined together. These mixtures are admirable and more wonderful than every miracle: how things so different and so divided from one another could be united with one another.

8. First, then, consider the creation, placing, and ordering of things: how great is the power in creation, how great the wisdom in placing, how great the kindness in composition. In creation see how many and how great things have been powerfully created; in placing, how wisely all things have been situated; in composition, how kindly the highest and lowest things have been joined together by charity as lovable as it is admirable.

For he mingled vital power with this earthly clay, so that in trees there arise beauty in leaves, loveliness in flowers, flavor in fruits, and healing power. Not content with this, he added also sentient power to our clay, so that there might be animals which not only live but also perceive, flourishing in fivefold sensation.

Further, to honor our clay, he implanted in it rational power, so that there might be human beings who not only live and feel, but also discern between advantage and disadvantage, good and evil, truth and falsehood.

He also willed to exalt our weaker nature with more abundant glory, and Majesty contracted itself, so as to join to our clay that which it had better—namely, itself. Thus in one person God and clay, majesty and weakness, such lowliness and such sublimity, were united to each other. For nothing is higher than God, nothing baser than clay; and yet with such condescension did God descend into clay, [Col. 0098D] and with such dignity did clay ascend into God, [764] that whatever God did in it is believed to have been done by clay, and whatever clay suffered, God is said to have suffered in it—by a sacrament as ineffable as it is incomprehensible.

And observe that, just as in that singular divinity there is a Trinity in persons and unity in substance, so in this special mixture there is a trinity in substances and unity in person. And just as there the persons do not divide the unity, nor does the unity diminish the Trinity, so here the person does not confuse the substances, nor do the substances themselves destroy the unity of the person.

That supreme Trinity has displayed to us this trinity: a marvelous work, a singular work among and above all his works. For Word, soul, and flesh came together in one person; and these three are one, and this one is three, not through confusion of substance but through unity of person.

This is the first and surpassing mixture, and the first among the three. Take heed, O human being, that you are clay, and do not be proud; that you are joined to God, and do not be ungrateful.

9. The second mixture is virgin and mother, plainly admirable and unique. Since the beginning of time it has not been heard that she who gave birth was a virgin, or that she who remained a virgin was a mother. According to the order of things, virginity is never found where fruitfulness is proclaimed, nor fruitfulness where intact virginity is preserved. This woman alone is she in whom virginity and fruitfulness met each other.

There occurred once what had not occurred before and will not occur through eternity, because she was seen to have neither a like predecessor nor a successor.

The third is faith and the human heart. This is indeed inferior to the first and second, but perhaps not less powerful. For it is wondrous how the human heart granted faith to these two things, how it could be believed that God was man and that she who had borne a child remained a virgin.

Just as iron and earthenware cannot be joined, so neither can these two be mingled unless the adhesive of the Spirit of God unites them.

Must it then be believed that he who is laid in a manger, who cries in a cradle, who suffers all the affronts of infant need, who is scourged, spat upon, crucified, laid in a tomb, and shut in between two stones, is the exalted and immeasurable God? Will she be a virgin who gladdens the child, who has a husband as her continual companion, at table and [Col. 0099C] in the marriage chamber; who takes her to Egypt, brings her back from Egypt, and alone with her alone completes a journey so long and so secluded?

How could this have been persuaded to the human race, to the whole world? And yet it was persuaded so easily and so powerfully that the multitude of believers makes it credible to me. Young men and virgins, old people with the young, chose to die a thousand deaths rather than fall away from this faith for even a moment.

10. This mixture, indeed, is excellent; but the second is more excellent, and the third most surpassing of all. The ear heard the first, but the eye did not see it: for that great mystery of godliness was heard and believed to the ends of the earth, but no eye, O God, saw apart from you how you joined yourself, within the narrow confines of a virgin womb, to a human body.

The eye saw the second, for that unique Queen saw herself fruitful and virgin, she who kept all these words, pondering them in her heart; and Joseph too knew it, no less a witness than guardian of so great a virginity.

The third entered into the human heart when what was done was believed as it was done; when we believe more by oracle than by eye; when we hold most firmly to what has been said or done, doubting it in no way.

In the first, see what; in the second, through whom; in the third, for what purpose God gave to you. He gave you Christ through Mary for healing. In the first is the remedy, because a poultice was prepared from God and man which would heal all your infirmities. These two ingredients were blended and mingled in the Virgin’s womb as in a little mortar, while the Holy Spirit, like a pestle, gently mixed them.

But because you were unworthy for it to be given directly to you, it was given to Mary, so that through her you might receive whatever you possessed. For in that she is mother, she bore God for you; in that she is virgin, she was heard, because of her reverence, in your cause and that of the whole human race.

If she were mother only, it would suffice for her salvation that she should be saved through the bearing of children; if virgin only, she would suffice for herself, nor would the blessed fruit of her womb be the price of the world. Therefore, as there is remedy in the first, so in the second there is help, because God willed us to possess nothing which did not pass through Mary’s hands. But in the third is merit, because when we firmly believe these things, we already possess merit; and [Col. 0100B] in faith is healing, because “he who believes shall be saved” (Mark 16:16).

## SERMON IV. On the medicine of the left hand and the delights of the right hand of the Most High.

1. The custom of our Order does not require a sermon today; but tomorrow it will be necessary to be occupied longer with the solemnities of the Masses, and the short hour will not allow a lengthy sermon. Therefore I think it not out of place to prepare your hearts today for so great a solemnity, especially since the depth of this mystery is most profound and incomprehensible, and, like a fountain of life, the more it is drawn from, the more it overflows and can never be exhausted.

For I know how your tribulation abounds for Christ; and may your consolation through him abound also. For I neither wish nor am permitted to offer you worldly consolation. Such consolation is worthless and of no use; and, what is more to be feared, it is even an impediment to true and health-giving consolation.

Therefore he who is the delight and glory of angels has himself become the salvation and consolation of the wretched; he who in his city, great and exceedingly exalted, makes citizens blessed, himself, little and very humble in exile, gladdens exiles; and he who in the highest is the glory of the Father has become on earth peace to people of good will.

For the little one was given to little ones, that the great one might be given to the great, and that those whom the little one justifies, the great and glorious one might afterward magnify and glorify. Hence without doubt the Vessel of Election, who had received from the fullness of this little one—for though little, he was full, full of grace and truth, and in him dwells bodily all the fullness of divinity (Col. 2:9)—hence, indeed, Paul pours forth that good word which you have often heard in these days: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4:4).

Rejoice, he says, in the gift bestowed; rejoice again in the promise, because both the thing itself is full of joy and the hope is full of joy. Rejoice because you have already received the gifts of the left hand; rejoice because you await the rewards of the right hand. “His left hand,” he says, “is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6). The left hand raises up; the right receives. The left heals and justifies; the right embraces and makes blessed. In his left hand merits are contained; in his right, rewards; in the right hand, I say, are delights; in the left are medicines.

2. But consider the loving physician; consider the wise physician. Examine more carefully what new remedies he bears; see how he has brought not merely precious but beautiful medicines, not only highly useful for the fruit of health, but pleasing to the sight and sweet to the taste.

Finally, consider his first medicine, the first thing he bears in his left hand, and you will find conception without seed. Observe, I beg you, what sort of thing this is: how new, how admirable, how lovable, how delightful! For what is more beautiful than a chaste generation? What more glorious than a holy and pure conception, in which there is nothing shameful, nothing foul, nothing corrupt?

Yet perhaps the welcome wonder of novelty would hold us less strongly if consideration of its saving and useful fruit did not also delight the mind. This conception is not only glorious in its, as it were, outward appearance, but precious in its inward power; so that, according to what is written, in the Lord’s left hand glory and [766] riches are found together (Prov. 3:16)—riches, I mean, of salvation together with the glory of novelty.

For who can make clean a conception from unclean seed except he alone who was conceived without any unlawful or unclean pleasure? At my very root and origin I have been infected and defiled; my conception is unclean, but there is one by whom this shame may be removed. He removes it, he alone upon whom it does not fall.

3. I have riches of salvation with which I may redeem the impurity of my own conception: Christ’s most pure conception. Add yet more, Lord Jesus: renew signs; alter wonders, for the former ones have become cheap through familiarity itself.

Indeed the rising and setting of the sun, the fruitfulness of the earth, and the succession of the seasons are miracles—and great miracles—but we have seen them so often that no one now pays attention. “Renew signs and alter wonders. Behold,” he says, “I make all things new.” Who says this? Surely the Lamb who sat on the throne (Rev. 21:5). A Lamb altogether sweet, altogether delightful, indeed altogether anointed. For this is the meaning of his name, Christ.

To whom can he seem harsh or hard, he who did not bring upon even his Mother in giving birth anything harsh, anything injurious?

O truly new miracles! He was conceived without shame and born without pain. In our Virgin the curse of Eve was changed: for she bore a son without pain. The curse, I say, was changed into blessing; and, as was foretold by the angel Gabriel, “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28).

O blessed one, alone among women blessed and not cursed; alone free from the general curse and exempt from the pain of women giving birth! Nor is it surprising, brothers, if he brought no pain upon his Mother, he who bore the pains of the whole world, as Isaiah says: “Truly he himself bore our infirmities” (Isa. 53:4).

There are two things which human frailty fears: shame and pain. Christ came to take both away; therefore he assumed both, when—to pass over other things—he was condemned to death, and to the most shameful death, by the wicked. Thus, in order to give us confidence that he would take these things away from us, he first kept his Mother exempt from both: so that there might be no shame in conception and no pain in childbirth.

4. Still more riches are heaped up, glory increases, signs are renewed, and miracles are altered. Not only conception without shame and birth without pain: she is a mother without corruption. O truly unheard-of novelty! A virgin bore a child, and after childbirth remained inviolate, possessing the fruitfulness of offspring together with soundness of flesh, and a mother’s joy together with the honor of virginity.

Now I confidently await the glory of incorruption promised me in my flesh, since through him incorruption was preserved even in his Mother. He through whom his Mother herself did not lose incorruption by giving birth will easily cause this corruptible thing also to put on incorruption in rising again.

5. Yet you have still greater riches; you have fuller glory. The Mother is without corruption of virginity; the Son is without every stain of sin. Eve’s curse does not fall upon the mother; nor does that universal condition fall upon the offspring, of which it was said through the prophet: “No one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon earth is one day” (Job 14:4–5, according to the LXX).

Behold an infant without defilement, alone among human beings true—indeed, Truth itself. Behold the Lamb without spot, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29). For who could take away sins better than he upon whom sin does not fall? He can without doubt wash me, since it is certain that he is not defiled.

Let that hand which alone is without dust cleanse my eye covered with mud. Let him remove the speck from my eye, he who has no beam in his own; indeed, let him remove the beam from mine, he who does not have even a tiny particle of dust in his own.

6. We have surely seen the riches of salvation and life; we have seen his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father. You ask, from what Father? “And he shall be called Son of the Most High.” It is clear who the Most High is. But lest any place remain for evasion, the angel Gabriel says to Mary: “That holy thing which is born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:32, 35). [767]

O truly holy one! “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10), he who did not take incorruption away even from his Mother.

Miracles increase, riches multiply, the treasury is opened. She who gives birth is both mother and virgin; he who is born is both God and man. But shall what is holy be given to dogs, or pearls to swine? Let our treasure certainly be hidden in a field, and our money laid away in a bag. Let conception without seed be covered by the Mother’s betrothal; childbirth without pain by the cries and sorrow of the little child. Let the incorruption of the woman giving birth be hidden by legal purification; the infant’s innocence by customary circumcision.

Hide, I say, hide, Mary, the splendor of the new sun. Place the infant in a manger; wrap him in swaddling clothes. For even the swaddling clothes themselves are our riches. The Savior’s clothes are more precious than every purple garment, and this manger more glorious than the gilded thrones of kings; indeed, Christ’s poverty is richer than all riches and all treasures.

For what is richer than humility? What is found more precious, by which, surely, the kingdom of heaven is bought and divine grace acquired? As it is written: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3); and in the Apostle: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). You have humility commended by God in the Nativity. For in it he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being found in appearance as a human being.

7. Do you wish to find still more precious riches and surpassing glory? You have love in the Passion. “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). These are the riches of salvation and glory: the precious blood by which we were redeemed, and the Lord’s cross, in which we glory with the Apostle: “But far be it from me,” he says, “to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). And he said: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2).

Christ Jesus, and he crucified, is the left hand itself; Christ Jesus, and he glorious, is the right hand. “Jesus Christ,” he says, “and him crucified.” Perhaps we ourselves are the cross upon which Christ is said to have been fixed. For the human being has the form of a cross, which, if he stretches out his hands, he expresses more plainly.

Christ speaks in the Psalm: “I am fixed in the mud of the deep” (Ps. 28:3). That we are mud is plain, since we were fashioned from mud. But then we were the mud of paradise; now, however, the mud of the deep.

“I am fixed,” he says: I did not pass through, I did not withdraw. “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). For he is Emmanuel, God with us. He is with us, indeed, but by the left hand. Thus, when Tamar was giving birth, Zerah first put forth only a hand, bound with a scarlet thread in the mystery of the Lord’s Passion (Gen. 38:27).

8. Therefore we now hold the left hand, but still must cry: “Stretch forth your right hand to the work of your hands” (Job 14:15); for “delights are at your right hand forever” (Ps. 15:11). Lord, stretch out to us your right hand [otherwise, show it], and that is enough for us.

“Glory and riches are in his house” (Ps. 15:11), namely, in the house of him who fears the Lord. But what is in your house, Lord? Surely thanksgiving and the voice of praise. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord” (Ps. 83:5), and so forth.

For “eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of humankind, what things you have prepared, O God, for those who love you” (1 Cor. 2:9). It is inaccessible light; it is peace which surpasses every understanding; it is a fountain that knows no ascent, but descent. The eye has not seen inaccessible light; the ear has not heard incomprehensible peace.

“Beautiful indeed are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Rom. 10:15); but although their sound has gone out into all the earth, the peace which surpasses every understanding could not be comprehended in its greatness even by them, much less communicated to others’ ears. For Paul himself says: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have comprehended it” (Phil. 3:13).

“Faith comes by hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (Rom. 10:17); but it is faith, not sight; promise, not the actual bestowal of peace. Indeed, even now there is peace on earth for people of good will; but what is this peace in comparison with the fullness and supereminence of that peace?

Hence the Lord himself says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave with you” [768] (John 14:27). For you are not yet capable of my peace, which surpasses every understanding and is peace above peace; therefore I give you the homeland of peace, and meanwhile leave you the way of peace.

9. But what is this that we said: “It has not ascended into the heart of man”? Surely because it is a fountain and knows no ascent. For we know that it is the nature of springs to follow the streams of valleys [Col. 0104B] and to avoid the steep heights of mountains, as it is written: “You send forth springs in the valleys; waters shall pass through the midst of the mountains” (Ps. 103:10). This is what I frequently strive to impress upon your charity: that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. For a spring does not rise higher than the place from which it issues.

Yet it may seem, by this rule, that pride does not obstruct the paths of grace—especially since that first proud one, who according to Scripture is king over all the children of pride (Job 41:25), is not recorded as having said, “I shall be higher,” but, “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). Nevertheless the Apostle does not lie, since he is exalted above everything believed to be God or worshipped as God (2 Thess. 2:4). Human hearing shudders at the expression [Col. 0104C]; but would that the mind likewise shuddered at the evil thought and its corresponding desire. For I tell you that not only he, but every proud person, exalts himself above God. God wills that his own will be done, and the proud person wills that his own will be done. Equality now seems to appear; but observe the ill-matched proportion. God wills his will to be done only in those things that reason approves; the proud person wills his will both with reason and against reason. You see, then, that this is a height to which the streams of grace do not reach.

“Unless you are converted,” he says, “and become like this little child”—that is, like himself, who is the fountain of life, in whom dwells and from whom flows the fullness of every grace—“you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). Therefore prepare channels; scatter the embankments of earthly and lofty thought; be conformed to the Son of Man, not to the first man. For the fountain of grace does not ascend into the heart of man—that is, of the fleshly and earthly man. Cleanse also your eye, that you may be able to see the most pure light; incline your ear to obedience, that you may one day attain everlasting rest and peace beyond peace. It is light because of its serenity, peace because of its tranquility, and a fountain because of its abundance and eternity.

Assign the fountain to the Father, from whom the Son is born and the Holy Spirit proceeds; the light to the Son, who is indeed the radiance of eternal life and the true light enlightening every person coming into this world; peace to the Holy Spirit, who surely rests upon the humble and quiet person. I do not say this as though these belonged exclusively [Col. 0105A] to each one: for the Father too is light, so that the Son may be light from light; the Son too is peace—our peace, who made both one; and the Holy Spirit is the fountain of water springing up into eternal life.

10. But when shall we attain this? When will you fill me, Lord, with joy in your presence? We rejoice in you because you, the dawn from on high, have visited us; again we rejoice, awaiting the blessed hope at the second coming. But when will the fullness of joy come—not from remembrance but from presence; from actual manifestation, not expectation? “Let your moderation,” says the Apostle, “be known to all men; the Lord is near” (Phil. 4:5). It is fitting that our moderation should be known, just as the moderation of the Lord our God became known to all. For what could be more unfitting [Col. 0105B] than that a man conscious of his own weakness should act without moderation, when the modest Lord of majesty has appeared among men? “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29), so that your moderation too may become known to others.

What follows—“the Lord is near”—must be understood with reference to the right hand. For he speaks of the left hand when he says: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20). The Lord is near, my brothers; be anxious about nothing. He is close at hand and will appear soon. Do not fail; do not grow weary. Seek him while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. 33:19); he is near to those who await [Col. 0105C] him, who await him in truth. Finally, do you wish to know how near he is? Hear the bride singing of the bridegroom: “For behold, he stands behind the wall” (Song 2:9). Understand this wall as your body, an obstacle preventing you from yet being able to behold him who is near. Hence Paul himself desires “to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23), and cries out most pitiably: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). Thus too the prophet says in the Psalm: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Ps. 141:8).

## SERMON V. On the words: “Sanctify yourselves today, and be ready; for tomorrow you shall see the majesty of God in yourselves.” Responsory at the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0105D]

1. Since we are about to celebrate the ineffable mystery of the Lord’s Nativity, we are rightly admonished, brothers, to prepare ourselves in every sanctification. For the Holy of holies is at hand; he is at hand who said: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. 19:2). Otherwise, how shall that which is holy be given to dogs, or pearls to swine, unless the former are first cleansed from wickedness, the latter from unlawful pleasure, and henceforth flee with all diligence—the former their vomit, the latter the wallowing in mud?

Carnal Israel, when once it was to receive the divine commandments, was sanctified by carnal ordinances, various washings, gifts, and sacrifices, which could not make the worshipper perfect according to conscience. But all these things have passed away, having plainly been imposed only until [Col. 0106A] the time of correction—which has now indeed come. Appropriately, therefore, perfect sanctification is now enjoined upon us; inward washing is commanded; spiritual purity is required, as the Lord says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). For this we live, brothers; for this we were born; for this we were called; for this the present day has dawned upon us. There was once night, when no one could perform these works. Night lay over the whole world before the rising of the true light, before Christ’s birth. There was likewise night for each of us before his own conversion and inward regeneration.

2. Was not the deepest night and the thickest darkness over the whole face of the earth when our fathers of old worshipped fabricated gods and, in utterly mad sacrilege, adored wood and stone? Was there not also a dark night for each of us when we lived in this world as though without God; when we walked after our own desires; pursued the enticements of the flesh; obeyed worldly appetites; presented our members as weapons of iniquity to sin; and served iniquity unto iniquity—things of which we now rightly blush as works of darkness? “Those who sleep sleep at night,” says the Apostle, “and those who are drunk are drunk at night” (1 Thess. 5:7). And these things you indeed were; but you have been awakened, you have been sanctified—provided, however, that you are children of light and children of day, not of night nor of darkness.

For the herald of day is also the one who cries: “Be sober and watch” (1 Pet. 5:8). And at Pentecost he spoke to the Jews concerning his fellow disciples: “How can these men be drunk, since it is the third hour of the day?” (Acts 2:15). This is what his fellow Apostle says: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably, as in the day” (Rom. 13:12–13). “Cast off,” he says, “the works of darkness”: namely drowsiness and drunkenness—for, as we recalled above, “those who sleep sleep at night, and those who are drunk are drunk at night”—so that, as in daylight, we may not sleep but walk, and do so honorably, not drunkenly.

Do you see a man whose soul drowses from weariness toward every good thing? He is still in darkness. Do you see someone drunk with wormwood, wise beyond what is fitting and not unto sobriety; whose eye is not satisfied with seeing nor his ear with hearing; who, loving money or something similar, is not satisfied, drinking a prolonged thirst like a dropsical man? He is a child of night and darkness. Nor are these two easily separated, for Scripture says: “Every idle person is in desires”; that is, every sleepy person is in [Col. 0106D] drunkenness. Therefore let us be sanctified today and be ready: ready today by shaking off nocturnal sleep, and likewise sanctified, as in the day, by restraining the frenzied violence of harmful desire, that nocturnal drunkenness. For on these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets: turning away from evil and doing good.

3. But this is for today; for tomorrow will be neither sanctification [Col. 0107A] nor preparation, but the vision of majesty. “Tomorrow,” it says, “you shall see the majesty of God in yourselves.” This is what the patriarch Jacob says: “Tomorrow my righteousness shall answer for me” (Gen. 30:33). Today righteousness is cultivated; tomorrow it will answer. Today it is exercised; tomorrow it will bear fruit. Otherwise, a man will not reap what he has not sown. For he will not then see majesty who meanwhile has despised holiness; nor will the Sun of glory rise for one for whom the Sun of righteousness has not risen; nor will tomorrow’s day dawn upon one for whom today has not shone.

Indeed, he who today has been made righteousness for us by God the Father will tomorrow appear as our life, so that we too may appear with him in glory. Today a little child is born to us, so that man may not presume to magnify himself, but may rather be converted and become like little children. Tomorrow the Lord, great and exceedingly praiseworthy, will be revealed, so that we too may be magnified in praise, when each shall have praise from God. Those whom he justifies today, he will glorify tomorrow; and the vision of majesty will follow the completion of holiness. Nor is it an empty vision, which consists only in likeness: “for we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” Hence here too it is not simply said, “You shall see the majesty of God,” but the significant addition is made: “in yourselves.”

Today, as in a mirror, we see ourselves in him while he takes up what is ours; tomorrow we shall see him in ourselves, when he grants us what is his, when he shows us himself and takes us [Col. 0107C] up to himself. This is what he promised: that, passing by, he would minister to them (Luke 12:37). From his fullness we now receive, not indeed glory for glory, but grace for grace, as it is written: “The Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 83:12). Therefore do not despise the earlier gifts if you desire those that follow; do not loathe the first dish if you wish to receive what comes after; nor refuse, on account of the vessel in which it is served, to take what is served. For our Prince of Peace made for himself an incorruptible vessel, fitting to himself an incorruptible body, in which he might serve the banquet of salvation. “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10). This is he of whom Gabriel said to Mary: “That holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

[Col. 0107D]

4. Therefore let us today be sanctified by this Holy One, that when that day breathes upon us we may see his majesty. For a sanctified day has dawned upon us: a day of salvation, not of glory or blessedness. Thus, until the Passion of the Holy of holies is proclaimed—he who suffered on the *parasceve*, that is, the day of preparation—it is rightly said to all: “Sanctify yourselves today, and be ready.” Be sanctified more and more, advancing from virtue to virtue; and be ready by persevering. Yet in what shall we be sanctified? I read of one of whom Scripture says that God “sanctified him in his faithfulness and meekness” (Sir. 45:4). For it is no more possible for people to please without meekness than for anyone to please God without faith. We are rightly admonished to be ready in those things by which we are fitted both for God, whose majesty we are to behold, and for one another, so that together we may behold it in ourselves. Therefore we ought to provide what is good not only before God but also before men, that we may be pleasing not only to our King but also to our fellow citizens and fellow soldiers.

5. First of all, faith must be sought, of which it is written: “Purifying their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see the majesty of God” (Matt. 5:8). Therefore entrust yourself to God, commit yourself to him, cast your care upon him, and he will sustain you, so that you may say confidently: “The Lord is mindful of me” (Ps. 39:18). For those who love themselves do not think thus—those pretentious wise people, anxious [Col. 0108B] on their own behalf, making provision for the flesh in its desires, deaf to the voice that says: “Casting all your care upon him, for he cares for you” (1 Pet. 5:7).

To trust oneself is not faith but faithlessness; to have confidence in oneself is not confidence but rather distrust. He is truly faithful who neither trusts himself nor hopes in himself, who has become to himself like a lost vessel, yet loses his soul in such a way as to preserve it unto eternal life. Now only humility of heart causes a soul that does not trust itself to lean upon God. Leaving itself behind, it ascends from the wilderness, leaning upon the Beloved, and therefore abounding in delights.

6. Moreover, that sanctification may be perfect, we must also learn meekness and the grace of common life from the Holy of holies, as he himself says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). What prevents us from calling such a person one abounding in delights: sweet and gentle, rich in mercy, made all things to all people, and bathing all in a certain oil of meekness and gentleness? He is so filled, so saturated, and even so overflowing with it that he seems to drip with it on every side.

Blessed is he who, prepared by this twofold sanctification, can say: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” (Ps. 56:8). For today he has his fruit unto sanctification, and tomorrow he will have everlasting life as his end. For he shall see the majesty of God, which is eternal life, as Truth himself says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). The righteous Judge will render to him the crown of righteousness on that day, to which no other day will succeed. Then he shall see and overflow; his heart shall wonder and be enlarged. How far shall it be enlarged? Until it sees within itself the majesty of God. Do not suppose, brothers, that we can explain that promise to you in words.

7. “Sanctify yourselves today, and be ready: tomorrow you shall see and rejoice, and your joy shall be filled.” What could that majesty fail to fill? Indeed, it will overfill and overflow, when “they shall give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing” (Luke 6:38). It will so overflow as to exceed beyond measure in sublimity not only merits but even desires, for he is truly able to do beyond what we can understand or hope.

For our desires seem chiefly to concern three things: what is honorable, what is useful, and what is pleasant. These are what we desire—all of us all of them, but one person this more, another that. One is so given over to pleasure that he gives little heed either to honorableness or usefulness. Another, intent rather upon gain, disregards both what is honorable and what is pleasant. Another, less concerned alike for pleasure and utility, seeks honor alone or chiefly. Yet the desire for these things is not blameworthy, if we sought them where they are truly found. For where they truly are, they are one; and that one is the supreme good, supreme usefulness, supreme glory, supreme pleasure. [Col. 0109B] So far as we can at present grasp it, this is our expectation and the vision of majesty in ourselves promised to us: that God may be all in all—everything pleasant, everything useful, everything honorable.

## SERMON VI. On the Annunciation of the Lord

1. We have heard a report full of grace and worthy of reception: “Jesus Christ, Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judah.” My soul has melted at this saying, and my spirit also glows within my breast, hastening to pour forth to you, with its customary desire, this joy and exultation. Jesus means “Savior.” What is so necessary to the lost? What is so desirable to the wretched? What is so useful to the despairing? Otherwise, whence could salvation come, or even some slender hope of salvation, amid the law of sin, the body of death, this evil of the day, and place of affliction, unless something new and unexpected were born for us?

But perhaps you desire salvation, yet, conscious alike of your frailty and your sickness, you dread the severity of treatment. Do not fear: Christ is plainly gentle and mild and rich in mercy, anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions—those, indeed, who, though they do not receive the fullness itself, nevertheless receive from the fullness of this anointing. But lest, on hearing that the Savior is gentle, you should suppose him to be ineffective, “Son of God” is added. For as is the Father, so is the Son, who possesses power whenever he wills.

Or perhaps, having heard of the usefulness of salvation and the sweetness of anointing, you murmur something—I suppose you are also concerned about honorableness. You rejoice that the Savior is at hand for you, like a paralytic lying upon a bed, or rather like one left half-dead on the road between Jerusalem and Jericho. Moreover, you rejoice that the physician is neither harsh nor uses severe remedies, lest perhaps the brief cure itself appear to you more unbearable than a long illness. Thus, indeed, even today many perish by fleeing the physician: they know Jesus, but do not know Christ, judging by human reasoning the burden of the remedy prepared for them from the multitude and malignity of their diseases.

2.
