But if you are certain of the Savior, and likewise know that he is Christ, healing not by cautery but by ointment, not by burning but by anointing, I think one thing still can trouble a noble creature: lest—God forbid—the person of this Savior appear insufficiently worthy of such a work. Yet I suppose you are not so ambitious and eager for glory, or so jealous for honor, that you would refuse to receive this favor from one of your fellow servants, if he could bestow it. For if he were an angel or archangel, or belonged to any higher order of blessed spirits, your pride would have still less cause for complaint. But now you ought to receive this Savior with all the greater devotion because, more distinctively than all others, he has inherited the name Jesus Christ, Son of God.

See whether the angel, speaking to the shepherds, did not more clearly commend these same three things when he explained the great joy that he announced: “For,” he says, “there is born to you this day a Savior, who is Christ the Lord” (Luke 2:11). Therefore let us rejoice, brothers, in this Nativity and rejoice in it in many ways, since the usefulness of salvation, the sweetness of anointing, and the majesty of the Son of God so elegantly illuminate it that nothing is lacking of all that is desired—neither what is advantageous, nor pleasant, nor honorable. Let us rejoice, I say, pondering within ourselves and pouring forth to one another the sweet word, the delightful utterance: “Jesus Christ, Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judah.”

3. Let no irreverent, ungrateful, or impious person answer me in these matters: “This is not new; it was heard long ago, it happened long ago, Christ was born long ago.” I say: long ago, and before long ago. He will not wonder at “long ago and before long ago” who recalls that prophetic expression: “For ever and beyond” (Exod. 15:18). Christ was born, therefore, not only before our times, but before all times. Yet that birth “made darkness its hiding place”; or rather, he dwells in inaccessible light. He lies hidden in the Father’s heart, upon the shadowy and thick mountain.

Therefore, that he might in some measure become known, he was born; and born in time from flesh, born in flesh, the Word was made flesh. What wonder, then, if even today it is said in the Church, “Christ, Son of God, is born,” when long before it was said—undoubtedly concerning him—“A child is born to us” (Isa. 9:6)? This word began to be heard long ago, and none of the saints ever grew weary of it. For Jesus Christ, Son of God, is yesterday, today, [Col. 0110D] and forever. Hence the first man, father of all the living, uttering the great mystery which the Apostle later more clearly commended as being in Christ and the Church, says: “A man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24; Eph. 5:31–32).

4. Abraham likewise, father of all believers, rejoiced to see this day, and saw it and was glad (John 8:56). Otherwise, when he ordered his servant, swearing to him by the God of heaven, to place his hand under his thigh (Gen. 24:2–3), would he not have foreseen that the God of heaven himself was to be born from that same thigh? God also revealed this counsel of his heart to the man after his own heart: he who “swore truth and will not disappoint him,” saying, “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11). Hence he is born in Bethlehem of Judah, as the angel says, in the city of David (Luke 2:4, 11), surely for the truthfulness of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.

This too was revealed in many portions and in many ways to the other fathers and prophets (Heb. 1:1). Far be it that those who loved God should ever have heard it negligently! Unless perhaps he seemed negligent who said: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. 4:13); or seemed weary of it who cried: “Oh, that you would rend the heavens” (Isa. 64:1) “and come down,” and other similar words. Then the holy Apostles themselves saw and heard this same thing, and their hands handled the Word of life; and to them he said in a special manner: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke 10:23). Finally, this same thing has been preserved also for us believers, entrusted to the treasures of faith, he likewise saying: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29).

This is our portion in the Word of life. Nor is it contemptible, since by it we live and by it the world is conquered. “The righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. 2:4), and “this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith” (1 John 5:4). It is faith that, like a kind of image of eternity, embraces past, present, and future together in an exceedingly vast bosom, so that nothing passes beyond it, nothing perishes, and nothing goes before it.

5. Rightly, therefore, as a testimony to your faith, when the voice of this announcement sounded in your ears, you rejoiced with joy, gave thanks, and fell prostrate upon the ground in adoration, gathering together as under the shadow of his wings and hoping beneath his feathers. Did not each of you, hearing of the Savior’s birth, cry in your hearts: “But for me, it is good to cleave to God” (Ps. 72:28); or rather what the same prophet says: “Be subject to God, O my soul” (Ps. 61:6)?

Wretched indeed is anyone who, prostrating himself falsely, humbles his body while retaining a hard heart. “There is one who humbles himself wickedly, but his inward parts are full of deceit” (Sir. 19:23). Whoever gives less thought to his need, feels his miseries less, fears dangers less, flees with less devotion to the remedies of the salvation that has arisen, subjects himself to God less affectionately, and sings less faithfully, “Lord, you have been our refuge” (Ps. 89:1)—his worship is less acceptable, his prostration less genuine, his humility less profound, his faith also less victorious—indeed, less living.

Yet what does he say? “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed”—as though believing were not in some fashion already seeing. But note carefully to whom and when this was said: namely, to the one reproved because he had believed after seeing. For to see and therefore believe is not the same as to see by believing. Otherwise, in what way are we to believe that Abraham your father saw this day of the Lord, except by believing? And how are we to understand what was sung to us this night: “Sanctify yourselves today, and be ready; for tomorrow you shall see the majesty of God in [Col. 0112A] yourselves,” unless to see with the mind is to set before oneself and recall in devout devotion and unfeigned faith that great mystery of great godliness: “manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the Gentiles, believed in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16)?

6. It is always new because it always renews minds; never old because it never ceases to bear fruit and never withers forever. For this is the Holy One who is not allowed to see corruption. This is the new man, capable of no oldness whatever, who transfers even those whose every bone has grown old into the true newness of life. Hence, even in this most joyful present announcement, if you observed it, it is fittingly said not so much that he has been born as that he is being born: “Jesus Christ, Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judah.” For just as he is in some manner still sacrificed daily until we proclaim his death, so he also appears to be born while we faithfully represent his Nativity.

Tomorrow, therefore, we shall see the majesty of God, but indeed in ourselves, not in himself: majesty in humility, power in weakness, God in man. For he is Emmanuel, which means “God with us.” Hear it more plainly: “The Word,” he says, “was made flesh and dwelt in us” (John 1:14). Thus from then onward we have seen his glory, but glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father; that is, we have seen him full of grace and truth. We have not seen the glory of power or splendor, but the glory [Col. 0112C] of fatherly compassion, the glory of grace, of which the Apostle says: “To the praise of the glory of his grace” (Eph. 1:6).

7. Thus he is born. But where, do you think? “In Bethlehem of Judah” (Luke 2:15). For it is not fitting that we should pass Bethlehem by in this way. “Let us go as far as Bethlehem,” say the shepherds, not, “Let us pass through Bethlehem.” What if it is a poor village? What if it seems the least in Judah? This too is not unfitting for him who, though rich, became poor for our sake; and though he was the Lord, great and exceedingly praiseworthy, was born a little child to us; and said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3); and again: “Unless you are converted and become like this child, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). Thus he chose even a stable and a manger: a house of clay and lodging for beasts, so that you may know him to be the one who raises the poor from the dung heap and saves humans and beasts.

8. Would that we too may be found in Bethlehem of Judah, so that he may deign to be born in us also and we may deserve to hear: “For you who fear God, the Sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. 4:2). Perhaps this is what we recalled above: that both sanctification and preparation are needed in order to see in ourselves the Lord’s majesty. For, according to the prophet, “Judah became his sanctification” (Ps. 113:2), because all things are washed in confession; and “house of bread,” which is what Bethlehem means, may perhaps seem especially to pertain to preparation. For how is someone prepared to receive so great a guest if he says: “There is no bread in my house” (Isa. 3:7)? Finally, because a certain man was unprepared, he had to knock at his friend’s closed door at midnight and say: “My friend has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him” (Luke 11:6).

The Prophet says, “His heart is ready to hope in the Lord,” doubtless speaking of the righteous man. “His heart is established; he shall not be moved” (Ps. 111:8). A heart that is not established is not ready. But we know, on the testimony of the same prophet, that bread strengthens the heart of man (Ps. 103:15). Therefore the heart of one who has forgotten to eat his bread is not ready, but dry and bloodless. He is ready and untroubled to keep the commandments of life who, forgetting what is behind, stretches himself toward what lies ahead.

You see how some forgetfulness must be avoided and how some must be desired. For not all Manasseh crossed the Jordan, nor did all of it choose its dwelling on this side (Josh. 13). One person has forgotten the Lord his creator; another, keeping him always before his eyes, has forgotten his people and his father’s house. The former forgets heavenly things; the latter, earthly things. The latter forgets present things; the former, future things. The latter, things seen; the former, things unseen. Finally, the latter, his own interests; the former, the interests of Jesus Christ. Both are Manasseh; both are forgetful. But one has forgotten Jerusalem and the other Babylon: the one who has forgotten the things that impede him is ready; the other has rather forgotten the things that help him and which it is not expedient to forget. The latter is altogether unprepared to see in himself the Lord’s majesty. Nor is he the house of bread in which the Savior may arise; he is not that Manasseh to whom he who rules Israel and sits above the cherubim appears: “Appear,” he says, “before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh” (Ps. 79:3). I think these are the three who are saved, whom another prophet named Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. 14:14); and who are also designated by those three shepherds to whom the angel announced great joy when the Angel of great counsel was born.

9. See, moreover, whether perhaps these are also the three Magi, now coming not merely from the East but from the West also, that they may recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For it may perhaps suitably seem that the offering of incense belongs to Ephraim—whose name means fruitfulness—because it belongs to those whom the Lord appointed to go and bear fruit, that is, the prelates of the Church, to offer worthy incense as a sweet-smelling odor. Benjamin too, the son of the right hand, must offer gold—that is, the substance of this world—so that the faithful people, placed on the right hand, may deserve to hear from the Judge: “For I was hungry and you gave me to eat” (Matt. 25:35), and so forth.

But Manasseh—if indeed he wishes to be the one to whom God appears—must offer the myrrh of mortification, which I think is especially required of our own profession. These things have been said lest we belong to that part [Col. 0114A] of the tribe of Manasseh which remained on this side of the Jordan, but may rather forget the things that are behind and, stretched out and intent toward what lies before, press on.

10. But now let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this word which has come to pass, which the Lord has made and shown to us. It is the house of bread, as we have already said; it is good for us to be there. For where the Word of the Lord is, bread that strengthens the heart is certainly not lacking, as the prophet says: “Strengthen me in your words” (Ps. 118:28). Surely man lives by the word that proceeds from the mouth of God; he lives in Christ, and Christ lives in him. There he rises; there he appears. He does not at all love a wavering or vacillating heart, but one stable and established.

If anyone murmurs, hesitates, wavers, thinks of rolling back into the mud, returning to his vomit, abandoning his vow, or changing his purpose, that person is not Bethlehem, not a house of bread. For hunger alone—fierce hunger—compels him to go down into Egypt, feed swine, and hunger for husks, because he remains far from the house of bread, from the Father’s house, in which even hired servants are known to have bread in abundance. Thus Christ is not born in a heart of this sort, which lacks the strength of faith—that is, the bread of life—for Scripture testifies: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. 2:4). The true life of the soul, which is Christ himself, dwells for the present in our hearts only through faith.

Otherwise, how is Jesus born in such a person? How does salvation arise for him, since it is an altogether true and certain saying that only the one who perseveres to the end shall be saved? (Matt. 10:22). That Christ is scarcely found in him, and that he does not belong to those of whom it is said, “You have an anointing from the Holy One” (1 John 2:20), is especially evident from the fact that his heart has undoubtedly withered as soon as he forgot to eat his bread.

Still less does such a person belong to the Son of God, because his Spirit rests only upon one who is quiet, humble, and trembles at his words (Isa. 66:2); nor can there be any fellowship between eternity and such great changeableness, between him who is and one who never remains in the same condition. Yet however firm, strong in faith, prepared, and abundant in bread we may be—through the generosity of him to whom we daily pray, “Give us this day our daily bread”—we must immediately add: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:11–12). Otherwise, “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). For Truth himself is the one who is born not simply in Bethlehem but in Bethlehem of Judah: Jesus Christ, Son of God.

11. Let us therefore go before the face of the Lord in confession, so that we too may be found sanctified and ready in Bethlehem of Judah, and may thus deserve to behold the Lord being born within us. But if any soul has advanced so far—which indeed is a great deal for us—as to be a fruitful virgin, a star of the sea, full of grace, and having the Holy Spirit coming upon her, I think that he will not disdain to be born not only in her but also, [Col. 0115A] from her. Certainly let no one presume to claim this for himself, except those whom he himself has pointed out by a special designation, as it were with his finger, saying: “Behold my mother and my brethren” (Matt. 12:49). Indeed, hear one of these: “My little children,” he says, “whom I am again bringing to birth, until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). For if he seemed to be born in them when Christ was being formed in them, how should anyone not likewise dare to say that he was born from the one who in some manner was bringing him to birth in them?

And you, impious Synagogue, bore this son for us: you performed a mother’s office, but not with a mother’s affection. You shook him from your bosom, casting him outside the city and raising him above the earth, as though saying to the Church of the Gentiles and at the same time to the Church of the firstborn, which is in heaven: “Let him belong neither to me nor to you, but be divided.” [Col. 0116A] “Divided,” I say: not between the two, but away from both. For when he had been expelled, raised up, and lifted high—indeed, only a little, yet enough that he was neither within your walls nor upon the ground—you hemmed him in with iron on every side, lest perhaps he should escape either this way or that: so that, separated from you, he might arrive at neither of those two. Cruel mother, you meant thus to make him an abortion, while there was no one able to receive him when he had been cast out.

Come now, then: see what you have accomplished—or rather, how you have accomplished nothing. For from every side the daughters of Zion go forth to behold King Solomon in the diadem with which you crowned him. Leaving his mother, he clings to his wife, that the two may be one flesh; and, driven from the city and raised [otherwise: lifted] from the earth, he draws all things to himself, since he is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0115]

## ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

### SERMON I. On the fountains of the Saviour

[Col. 0115B]

1. Great indeed, beloved, is today’s solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity; but the shortness of the day compels us to shorten our discourse. Nor is it surprising if we make our word brief, when God the Father too made the Word abbreviated. Do you wish to know how long, how short he made it? “I,” says this Word, “fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24). Now, having become flesh, he is placed in the narrow confines of a manger. “From age to age,” says the Prophet, “you are God” (Ps. 89:2); and behold, he has become an infant one day old.

Why, brethren, was this done? Or what necessity was there that the Lord of majesty should so empty, humble, and abbreviate himself, unless that you might do likewise? Already by example he cries out what later he will preach in words: “Learn of me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29), so that he who says, “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1), may be found true. Therefore I entreat and earnestly beg you, brethren: do not allow so precious an example to have been displayed to you in vain; but be conformed to it and be renewed in the spirit of your mind. Strive after humility, which is the foundation and guardian of virtues; pursue that which alone can save your souls. For what is more unworthy, more detestable, or more deserving of severe punishment, than that, while he sees the God of heaven made little, man should still set himself to magnify himself upon earth? It is intolerable impudence that, where majesty emptied itself, a little worm should swell and puff itself up.

[Col. 0115D]

2. This, then, is why he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, though in the form of God he was equal to the Father. Yet he emptied himself of majesty and power, not of goodness and mercy. For what does the Apostle say? “The goodness and loving-kindness of God our Saviour appeared” (Titus 3:4). Power had appeared before in the creation of things; wisdom appeared in their governance; but the goodness of mercy has now appeared especially in his human nature.

To the Jews, power had become known through signs and wonders; hence in that Law you will often find: “I am the Lord, I am the Lord.” To philosophers also, abounding in their own understanding, majesty became known, because, according to the Apostle’s words, “what may be known of God is manifest in them” (Rom. 1:19). Yet the Jews were oppressed by that very power, and philosophers, searchers into majesty, were overwhelmed by glory. Power demands subjection; majesty demands admiration; neither demands imitation. Let goodness appear, Lord, to which man, created in your image, may be conformed. For majesty, power, and wisdom we can neither imitate nor ought to emulate.

How long will your mercy be confined to the angelic portion alone, while judgment occupies the rest together with the whole human race? “Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches unto the clouds” (Ps. 35:6), [Col. 0116C] condemning the whole earth and the powers of the air. Let mercy enlarge its borders, stretch out its cords, expand its bosom; let it reach mightily from end to end, ordering all things sweetly. Your bosom is constricted by judgment, Lord; loosen your girdle, and come abounding in compassion and overflowing in charity.

3. Why are you afraid, O man? Why do you tremble before the Lord’s face because he comes? He comes not to judge, but to save the earth. Long ago a certain faithless servant persuaded you to steal secretly and put the royal diadem upon your own head. Caught in theft, why should you not fear? Why should you not flee from his face? Perhaps he was already brandishing a flaming sword. Now, set in exile, you eat your bread in the sweat of your face; and behold, a voice has been heard in the earth that the Ruler has come. Where will you go from his Spirit? Or where will you flee from his face?

Do not flee; do not fear. He comes not with arms; he seeks you not to punish but to save. And lest perhaps you should say even now, “I heard your voice, and I hid myself” (Gen. 3:10), behold, he is an infant and without speech. For the voice of one crying is more pitiable than terrible; or if it is terrible to anyone, it is not terrible to you. He has become a little child; his virgin mother binds his tender limbs in swaddling-clothes. Do you still tremble in fear? Even in this you will know that he has come not to destroy you but to save you; to rescue, not [Col. 0117A] to bind. Already he fights against your enemies; already, as God’s power and God’s wisdom, he treads down the necks of the proud and lofty.

4. Let there be two enemies for you: sin and death—that is, death of body and soul. He comes to defeat both, and from both he will save you: do not be afraid. Already, indeed, he conquered sin in his own person when he assumed human nature without any contagion. A great violence was done to sin; and it is truly known to have been vanquished when the nature which it boasted that it had wholly infected and occupied was found in Christ utterly foreign to it.

Then he pursues your enemies and overtakes them; nor does he turn back until they fail. Fighting against sin in his manner of life, he attacks it alike with words and examples; but in his passion he binds it—yes, binds the strong man—and plunders his goods. In the same order he also overcomes death: first in himself, when he rises as the first fruits of those who sleep and the firstborn from the dead; afterward he will defeat it likewise in all of us, when he raises our mortal bodies and death, the last enemy, is destroyed.

For this reason, when he rose, he was clothed in splendour, not—as when he was born before—in swaddling-clothes. For this reason, he who previously overflowed from the bosom of mercy, judging no one, upon rising girded himself and seems in some manner to have gathered his overflowing bosom of mercy with the girdle of justice: for from then on he is prepared for the judgment which will take place at our resurrection. For he came as a little child in order to grant mercy beforehand; and by anticipating the judgment to come at the end, he tempered it with mercy.

[Col. 0117C]

5. Although he came to us as a little child, he nevertheless brought no small gift and conferred no small benefit upon us. If you ask what he brought: first of all, he brought mercy, by which, as the Apostle testifies, he saved us (Titus 3:5). Nor did he benefit only those whom he found present at that time; he is a fountain that can never be exhausted. Christ the Lord is a fountain for us, from which we may be washed, as it is written: “He loved us and washed us from our sins” (Rev. 1:5).

Yet washing is not the only use of water: waters not only wash away filth, but also quench thirst. “Blessed,” says the Wise Man, “is he who continues in wisdom and meditates upon justice” (Sir. 14:22); and shortly afterward: “He will give him to drink the water of saving wisdom” (Sir. 15:3). Rightly, the water of saving wisdom; for the wisdom of the flesh is death, and the wisdom of the world is itself hostile to God. Only the wisdom which is from God is saving: according to the definition of blessed James, it is “first chaste, then peaceable” (Jas. 3:17). For the wisdom of the flesh is sensual, not chaste; the wisdom of the world is tumultuous, not peaceable. But the wisdom which is from God is first chaste, seeking not its own things but those of Jesus Christ, so that each person may not do his own will, [Col. 0118A] but consider what is the will of God; then peaceable, not abounding in its own opinion, but rather acquiescing in another’s counsel or judgment.

6. A third use of water is irrigation, which new plantings especially need; otherwise they will either make too little progress or perish altogether through dryness. Therefore let whoever has sown seeds of good works seek waters of devotion, so that, irrigated by the fountain of grace, the garden of good conduct may not wither but may grow in perpetual greenness. For the Prophet prays for such a one, saying: “May your burnt offering become rich” (Ps. 19:4). So also, in the praises of Aaron, you read that his sacrifice was received by the daily fire. In all these things nothing else seems to be meant than that good works should be seasoned with the ardour of devotion and the sweetness of spiritual grace.

Do you suppose that a fourth fountain may be found, so that we may recover Paradise, most delightful through the irrigation of four fountains? For if we do not hope that the earthly Paradise will be restored to us, how shall we hope for the kingdom of heaven? “If I have told you earthly things,” he says, “and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John 3:12). But now, so that the expectation of future things may be made firm by the bestowal of present things, we possess a Paradise far better and more delightful than that which our first parents had: our Paradise is Christ the Lord. In him we have already found three fountains; let us seek the fourth.

From the fountain of mercy we have waters of forgiveness for washing away sins; from the fountain of wisdom we have waters of discernment for drinking to satisfy our thirst; from the fountain of grace we have waters of devotion for irrigating the plants of good works. Let us seek boiling waters—waters of zeal—for cooking food. These season and cook our affections, and bubble up from the fountain of charity. Hence the Prophet says: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire will blaze” (Ps. 38:4); elsewhere also: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68:10). For from the sweetness of devotion he loves justice; from the ardour of zeal he hates iniquity.

And see whether Isaiah perhaps foretold these fountains: “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour.” For that you may know this promise concerns the present life, not the future, observe what follows: “You shall say on that day: Confess to the Lord and call upon his name” (Isa. 12:3–4). Invocation belongs to the present time, as it is written: “Call upon me in the day of tribulation” (Ps. 49:15).

7. Of these four fountains, however, three seem properly suited to the three orders of the Church, each to its respective order. [Note: [Col. 0117] Compare Sermon 96 on Various Subjects, where he explains these fountains differently.] The first is common to all. “For in many things we all offend”; and we need the fountain of mercy to wash away the filth of offences. “All,” I say, “have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23): prelates, continent persons, and married persons alike; “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8).

Since, therefore, no one is clean from defilement, the fountain of mercy is necessary to all; and Noah, Daniel, and Job ought to hasten to this fountain with equal desire. But beyond this, Job should seek especially the fountain of wisdom, because he walks amid snares, so that it seems a great thing if he turns aside from evil. Daniel, however, must run to the fountain of grace, since the works of penitence and labours of abstinence especially need to be enriched by the grace of devotion. For above all we ought to do everything cheerfully, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). For our land is by no means fertile for such seed—that is, for good conduct—and therefore it will easily wither unless aided by frequent irrigations. Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we ask for grace of this kind under the name of daily bread. Rightly indeed, lest that terrible curse of prophetic imprecation should fall upon us: “Let them become like the grass upon the housetops, which withered before it was plucked up” (Ps. 128:6). The fountain of zeal, however, is particularly suited to Noah, because this zeal especially befits prelates.

[Col. 0119B]

8. Thus Christ displays these four fountains in himself while we still live in the flesh; but after this age he promises the fifth, the fountain of life, for which the Prophet thirsted when he said: “My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain” (Ps. 41:2). And perhaps it was also because of these four fountains that Christ, while still living upon the cross, was wounded in four places; because of the fifth, after he had already yielded up his spirit, he was pierced in the side. He was still living when they pierced his hands and feet, so that he might bring forth from himself four fountains for us who are still living; he suffered the fifth wound after he had expired, so that after death he might nevertheless open in himself for us the fifth fountain.

But behold, while we speak of the mysteries of the Nativity, we have suddenly come to examine the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion. Yet it is not surprising if we seek in the Passion what Christ brought in his Nativity. For then, tearing open the purse, he poured out the money hidden within it as the price of our redemption.

### SERMON II. On the three principal works of God and the threefold mixture

[Col. 0119D]

1. “Great are the works of the Lord,” says the prophet David (Ps. 110:2). All his works are indeed great, brethren, since he himself is great; but those which seem greatest among them especially concern us. Hence the same prophet sings: “The Lord has magnified his dealing with us” (Ps. 125:3). Finally, three of his works in particular proclaim how magnificently he deals with us: the work of our first creation, of our present redemption, and of our future glorification. How greatly magnified are your works, Lord, in each of these! It is yours to declare the power of your works to your people; we at least shall not be silent about the works themselves.

In these three, brethren, one may observe a threefold mixture: truly a heavenly work and a work of divine power. [Col. 0120A] For in the first work, our creation, God formed man from the mud of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life. What an artisan, what a uniter of things, at whose command the mud of earth and the breath of life are so joined together! The mud had indeed already been created when, in the beginning, God created heaven and earth; but the spirit has not a common but a proper mode of creation. It is not created in a mass, but is breathed in with a certain singular excellence.

Recognize, O man, your dignity; recognize the glory of human creation. You have a body in common with the world; for it is fitting that one set over the whole mass of this bodily creation should in some respect be like it. But you also have something more sublime, and you are not altogether comparable with the other creatures. In you flesh and soul are compacted and allied: the one formed, the other breathed in.

2. But whose interest does this mixture serve? To whom is benefit given by this union? For according to the wisdom of the children of this age, where lower things are joined to higher, those who have power prevail and use the humbler at their pleasure. The stronger tramples the weaker; the wise mocks the unlearned; the cunning deceives the simple; the powerful despises the feeble. It is not so in your work, O God; it is not so in your mixture. You did not join spirit to mud, the sublime to the lowly, a worthy and excellent creature to an abject and useless mass, for this purpose.

Who does not see, brethren, how much the soul gives to the body? Would not lifeless flesh be an insensible trunk? From the soul come beauty, growth, the brightness of sight, and the sound of the voice; indeed every sense comes from the soul. This union commends charity to me; in this very page of my own creation I read charity; in the very beginning the most gracious hand of the Creator not only proclaims but impresses charity upon me.

[Col. 0120C]

3. This union, beloved, was indeed great—but only if it had remained stable. Now, although it had been fortified with a divine seal—for God created man in his own image and likeness—alas, the seal was broken and the unity scattered. That most wicked thief approached and broke the still-new seal; thus the divine likeness was altered, and wretched man “was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). For God made man upright; and this is the likeness of him of whom it is written: “The Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him” (Ps. 91:16). He also made man true and just, as he himself is truth and justice; nor could that unity be broken apart while the integrity of this seal endured.

But the counterfeiter came, promising the unlearned a better seal; alas, alas! he broke what had been impressed by the hand of divinity. “You shall be as gods,” he said, “knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5). O ill-wisher! O malicious one! What need had they of this likeness in knowledge? Let them indeed be as gods: upright and just; let them be true like God, in whom sin cannot fall. For while this seal stands, that unity will stand. Now, wretched as we are, we experience what the cunning of diabolical deceit persuaded us to accept. For when the seal was broken, bitter division and sorrowful divorce followed. Where is what you said, wicked one: “You shall not die at all”? Behold, we all die, and there is no man who lives and shall not see death.

[Col. 0121A]

4. But what will happen, Lord God? Shall your work never be restored? Shall one who has fallen never rise again? None can restore it except the one who made it. Therefore: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise,” says the Lord; “I will place him in salvation; I will act confidently in him” (Ps. 11:6). For the enemy will accomplish nothing against him, and the son of iniquity will not continue to harm him (Ps. 88:23).

“I make,” he says, “a new mixture, in which I set the seal more distinctly and more strongly: him who was not made in my image, but who is the Image itself, the brightness of glory and the figure of substance—not made, but begotten before the ages.” And lest perhaps you fear that it can be broken, hear the Prophet: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21:16)—but such a potsherd that not even the hammer of the whole earth can in any way harm it.

Now, since the first union was made of two, the second union is made of three, so that you may learn from this very fact to approach the sacrament of the Trinity: the Word, who was in the beginning with God and was God; the soul, created from nothing and not existing before; and flesh, separated without any corruption by divine workmanship from the mass of corruption—flesh such as had never existed before. These come together in the unity of one person by an indissoluble bond. In these you have a threefold kind of power: what was not, created; what had perished, repaired; what was above all things, made a little lower than the angels.

These are the evangelical measures of flour which are leavened together (Matt. 13:33), so that there may be bread of angels for man to eat, bread strengthening the heart of man. Blessed is the woman, blessed among women, in whose chaste womb, when the fire of the Holy Spirit came upon her, this bread was baked [variant: “of life”]. Blessed, I say, is the woman who put the leaven of her faith into these three measures. For by faith she conceived, and by faith she gave birth; and, as Elizabeth says, “Blessed is she who believed, because those things which were spoken to her by the Lord have been fulfilled in her” (Luke 1:45). Nor should you wonder that I said the Word was united to flesh through the mediation of her faith, since he also took that very flesh from her flesh. Certainly this interpretation is not opposed by the fact that the comparison is spoken concerning the kingdom of heaven. For it does not seem unworthy that the kingdom of heaven should be compared with Mary’s faith, by which it is also restored.

[Col. 0121D]

5. No creature whatever will be able to loose the bond of this union; for neither the prince of this world has anything in him, nor is John himself worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal. Yet what then? It must certainly be loosed to some extent; otherwise what has been dissolved is not made whole again. What use is there in a whole loaf, a hidden treasure, or concealed wisdom? Rightly did John weep that no one was found to open the book and loose its seals (Rev. 5:4), for while it remained closed none of us could attain that divine wisdom.

Open the book, Lamb of God, true gentleness. Expose your hands and feet to be pierced by the Jew, so that the treasure of salvation hidden in them may come forth, together with abundant redemption. Finally, break your bread for the hungry. You alone can break it, because you alone can stand, so that you may make whole what has been broken; and in the very breaking you alone have power to lay down your soul and, when you will, to take it up again.

Therefore by your compassion let this temple be loosed to some extent, but not utterly dissolved. Let the flesh be separated from the soul; but let the Word preserve the flesh from corruption and grant the soul full liberty, so that, alone among the dead, it may act freely, bringing out captives from the prison-house, those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. Let the holy soul lay down the spotless flesh, to take it up again on the third day, so that by dying it may destroy death and the life of men may rise with the one who rises. Thus it was done, beloved, and we rejoice that it was done thus. By that death death died, and we have been regenerated into the hope of life through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.

[Col. 0122B]

6. Who can speak of what will take place in the third union? “Eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). That will be the consummation, when Christ has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father; and the two will be no longer one flesh, but one spirit. For if the Word, cleaving to flesh, became flesh, how much more will the one who cleaves to God be one spirit with him.

In this middle union, indeed, humility is displayed—humility exceedingly great; but in that union which we await and for which we long, perfect glorification is laid up for us—if indeed it is for us. If we remember that charity was commended in the first union, by which man was compacted of soul and flesh, humility rightly stands out in the second, because the virtue of humility alone repairs wounded charity. But that a rational soul-creature is united to an earthly body is not at all to be attributed to humility, since it is not mixed with flesh through its own deliberation, but is created by being sent into it and sent into it by being created. Not so, certainly, that highest Spirit, who, being more good, came to an uncorrupted body by the free choice of his own good pleasure. Finally, glorification rightly follows charity and humility, because without charity nothing can profit, and no one except the person who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11).

### SERMON III. On the place, time, and other circumstances of the Nativity

1. I consider, brethren, two [Note: [Col. 0121] In the French manuscript of the Feuillants, “three” is read, and more correctly.] kinds of things in this Nativity of the Lord, not merely different but very unlike. For the child who is born is God; the mother from whom he is born is a virgin; and the birth itself is without pain. A new light from heaven shines in the darkness; an angel announces great joy; a multitude of the heavenly host gives praise; glory is given to God and peace to people of good will. The shepherds run, [Col. 0123A] find the word that was spoken to them, and announce it to others; all who hear marvel.

These and similar things, beloved, belong to divine power, not human frailty. They are golden and silver vessels, from which, on account of so great a solemnity, food is served today at the Lord’s table even to the poor. It is not for us to take these vessels; no golden platter or cup is given to us, but the food and drink contained in them. “Consider carefully,” says the Wise Man, “what is set before you” (Prov. 23:1). I acknowledge that the time and place of this Nativity, the tenderness of an infant body, the crying and tears of the little child, and likewise the poverty and watchfulness of the shepherds to whom the Saviour’s Nativity was first announced, are mine. These are for me; they serve my benefit; they are set before me and proposed to me for imitation.

Christ was born in winter; he was born at night. Do we believe it happened by chance that he, to whom belong winter and summer, day and night, should be born amid such harsh weather and darkness? Other little children do not choose when they shall be born, since, when they scarcely begin to live, they have as yet no use of reason, no freedom of choice, and no power of deliberation. But Christ, brethren, although he was not yet man, [Note: [Col. 0123] In other copies the particle “not” is absent, but it must certainly be retained, so that the meaning is that Christ was not a man before this Nativity, but God only.] was nevertheless in the beginning with God and was God, possessing the same wisdom and power that he now possesses, as God’s power and God’s wisdom. Therefore, when the Son of God was about to be born, having the choice to select whatever time he wished, he chose what is more burdensome, especially for a little child and the son of a poor mother, who scarcely had swaddling-clothes in which to wrap him or a manger on which to lay him.

[Col. 0123C]

And certainly, although there was such need, I hear no mention of skins being provided. The first Adam is clothed in tunics of skins; the second is wrapped in swaddling-clothes. The world does not judge thus: either this one is mistaken or the world errs. But divine wisdom cannot be mistaken. Hence the prudence of the flesh—for it is itself death—is rightly hostile to God (Rom. 8:7), and the prudence of the age is also called folly (1 Cor. 3:19). For Christ surely, who is not deceived, chose what is more burdensome to the flesh. Therefore that is better, more useful, and more to be chosen; and whoever teaches or advises otherwise must be guarded against as a deceiver.

2. Moreover, he also chose to be born at night. Where are those who so shamelessly delight in displaying themselves? Christ chooses what he judges healthier; you choose what he rejects. Which of the two is wiser? Whose judgment is more just? Whose verdict is sounder? Christ, in short, is silent: he does not exalt, magnify, or proclaim himself; and behold, an angel announces him and a multitude of the heavenly host praises him. You too, then, who follow Christ, hide the treasure you have found. Love to be unknown; let another’s mouth praise you, and let your own be silent.

Moreover, Christ is born in a stable and laid in a manger. Is he not the one who says: “The world is mine and its fullness” (Ps. 49:12)? Why, then, did he choose a stable? Clearly, in order to reject worldly glory and condemn the vanity of the age. His tongue does not yet speak, and yet all that belongs to him cries out, preaches, and proclaims the Gospel; even his infant limbs are not silent. In everything the judgment of the world is indicted, overturned, and refuted. For what person, if given the choice, would not prefer a strong body and an age capable of understanding to infancy? O Wisdom, drawn from hidden things! O Wisdom truly incarnate and veiled! Yet he is, brethren, that little child long promised through Isaiah, knowing to reject evil and choose good (Isa. 7:15). Bodily pleasure, therefore, is evil; affliction is good: for the wise child, the infant Word, chooses the latter and rejects the former. For the Word became flesh: weak flesh, infant flesh, tender flesh, powerless flesh, incapable of every work and every labour.

[Col. 0124B]

3. Truly, brethren, the Word became flesh and so dwelt among us. While he was in the beginning with God (John 1:14), he dwelt in inaccessible light (1 Tim. 6:16), and there was no one who could comprehend him. For “who has investigated the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Isa. 40:13). “The carnal man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). But now even the carnal person may comprehend him, because the Word became flesh. If he knows how to hear nothing except flesh, behold, the Word became flesh: let him hear it even in the flesh.

O man, Wisdom is presented to you in flesh. That Wisdom once hidden, behold, is now drawn from hiddenness and offers itself even to the senses of your flesh. It is preached to you, so to speak, carnally: “Flee pleasure, because death is placed beside the entrance of delight; repent, because through this the kingdom of God draws near” (Matt. 3:2). This stable preaches this to you; this manger cries it out; those infant limbs speak it plainly; these tears and cries proclaim the Gospel.

For Christ weeps, but not as others do—or, at least, not for the reason others usually do. In others sensation prevails; in Christ affection prevails. They suffer; they do not act, since they do not yet have the use even of their own will. [Col. 0124C] They mourn from suffering; Christ from compassion. They bear the heavy yoke which rests upon all the children of Adam; Christ weeps over the sins of the children of Adam. And certainly, for those for whom he now sheds tears, he will later shed blood. O hardness of my heart! Would that, Lord, as the Word became flesh, so my heart might become fleshly; for through the Prophet you have also promised this: “I will take from you the heart of stone, and I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11:19).

4. Brethren, Christ’s tears produce in me both shame and sorrow. I was playing outside in the street, while in the secrecy of the royal chamber a sentence of death was being pronounced against me. His Only-Begotten heard this; laying aside his diadem, clothed in sackcloth, sprinkling his head with ashes, barefoot, weeping and wailing because his little servant had been condemned to death, he went forth. I suddenly see him coming out, marvel at the novelty, ask the reason, [Col. 0125A] and hear it. What shall I do? Shall I still play, and make light of his tears? Surely, if I am mad and bereft of reason, I shall not follow him or mourn together with the mourner.

What, then, produces shame? Whence come sorrow and fear? Certainly because, from consideration of the remedy, I estimate the magnitude of my danger. I did not know; I seemed sound to myself. Yet behold, the Virgin’s Son, the Son of the Most High God, is sent and commanded to be killed, that with the precious balm of his blood he may heal my wounds. Recognize, O man, how grave are the wounds for which the Lord Christ had to be wounded. If these were not unto death, and eternal death, the Son of God would never die for their remedy. Therefore, beloved, it is shameful carelessly to ignore one’s own suffering, when I see so great a compassion shown for it by so great a majesty. The Son of God has compassion and weeps; shall man suffer and laugh? Thus it is both an estimation of the medicine and an intensification for me of sorrow and fear.

[Col. 0125B]

5. But if I carefully observe the physician’s commands, there will also be an occasion for consolation. For as I recognize the disease to be grave, for which such medicine is applied, so from this very fact I infer that it is not incurable. A wise physician—indeed, Wisdom itself—would not employ such most precious remedies in vain. Now it is evident that they are employed in vain not only if a cure would be easy without them, but much more if it would be impossible even with them. Therefore hope, once conceived, encourages repentance and inflames desire more vehemently.

The visitation and address of angels shown to the watchful shepherds likewise contributes to consolation. “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation,” so that you no longer deserve to have heavenly consolation! For how many noble according to the flesh, how many powerful, how many wise in this age, were resting at that hour on soft beds; and none of them was deemed worthy to see the new light, know that great joy, or hear the angels singing: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 11:14). Let people therefore recognize that those who are not in the labour of humankind do not deserve to be visited by angels. Let them recognize how pleasing to the citizens above is labour directed toward spiritual ends, since they deem worthy of their address—and such a blessed address—even those who labour for bodily sustenance under the compulsion of bodily necessity. [Col. 0125D] Surely they recognize in them the human order [otherwise: ordinance] established by God: that Adam should eat his bread in the sweat of his face (Gen. 3:19).

6. I beseech you, beloved, consider more carefully how much God has done for your exhortation and salvation, lest so living and effective a word—a faithful word, worthy of all acceptance, a word not so much of speech as of deed—be found fruitless in you. Do you think, brethren, that it would grieve me but little if I knew that this very word which I now speak to you were perishing empty and without any benefit in your hearts? And who am I, or what is this word of mine? If a small man—indeed, a man of no account—would grieve that this slight labor of his voice were useless, how much more justly will the Lord of majesty be indignant if so great a work of his should be rendered void by our hardness or negligence? May he avert this from his servants: he who, for their salvation, deigned to assume the form of a servant—the Only-begotten of God the Father, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On the fact that the shepherds found Mary and Joseph and the infant lying in a manger.

1. Recognize, most beloved brethren, how great is today’s solemnity, for which both the day is too short and the earth’s breadth too narrow. It is extended alike in place and time. It takes possession of the night and fills heaven before earth. For night was made bright as day when, at the untimely hour of night, a new light from heaven shone round the shepherds. [Col. 0126B] And that you may know in what place the joys of this solemnity began to be celebrated: the joy already possessed by the angels, and destined for all the people, is proclaimed in good news; and immediately there is present a multitude of the heavenly host resounding with divine praises. Hence this night is celebrated more solemnly than the others, in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; and especially in these vigils we should without hesitation believe that those heavenly princes anticipate those united in singing psalms, “in the midst of maidens playing tambourines.”

But how many altars shine today with jewels and gold! How many walls everywhere are adorned with hangings! Do you suppose that the angels will turn aside to these things and pass by men in rags? If so, why did they appear rather to shepherds of sheep than to kings of the earth, [Col. 0126C] or to priests of the Temple? Why too did the Savior himself, to whom belong alike gold and silver, consecrate holy poverty in his own body? Or rather, why is poverty itself so carefully described by the angel? For not without the reason of a sure mystery is the Savior wrapped in swaddling-cloths and laid in a manger, when this is expressly commended to us by the angel as a sign. “This,” he says, “shall be a sign to you: you shall find an infant wrapped in swaddling-cloths” (Luke 2:12). Your swaddling-cloths, Lord Jesus, were set as a sign—but as a sign still contradicted by many even to this day. For many are called, but not many chosen, and therefore not marked.

Certainly I recognize, I recognize Jesus the great priest, clothed in filthy garments, while he disputed with the devil. I speak to those who know the Scriptures and to whom [Col. 0126D] the prophetic vision of Zechariah is not unknown (Zech. 3). But once our head was exalted above our enemies, he plainly changed his clothing, put on beauty, being clothed with light as with a garment. He gave us an example, that we too should do the same. For in conflict an iron breastplate is more useful than a linen robe, although the former is a burden and the latter an honor. The time will come when the members also shall follow the head, so that the whole body may now sing with one spirit and say: “You have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Ps. 29:12).

2. “You shall find,” he says, “an infant wrapped in swaddling-cloths and laid in a manger.” And shortly afterward: “They came,” says the Evangelist, “in haste, and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in a manger” (Luke 2:16). Why is humility alone apparently commended by the angel, [Col. 0127A] yet not alone found by the shepherds? Perhaps the angel commends humility more especially because, when the others fell through pride, he himself had stood in humility. Or perhaps humility is announced from heaven because it is, as it were, the special virtue to be shown to the divine majesty. Yet it could not be found alone, because grace is always given to the humble.

They found, therefore, Mary and Joseph and the infant lying in a manger. For as the infancy of the Savior displays evident humility, so continence is fittingly signified through the Virgin, and justice through Joseph, the righteous man whose praise is in the Gospel. Surely, who does not know that continence is owed to the flesh? Justice, however, is the virtue that gives to each person what is his own, and it is necessary toward one’s neighbors. But humility [Col. 0127B] reconciles us to God, makes us subject to God, and pleases God in us, as the blessed Virgin says: “He has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48).

Thus, the fornicator sins against his own body; the unjust person sins against his neighbor; the one who exalts and inflates himself sins against God. The fornicator dishonors himself; the unjust person harms his neighbor; the proud person, so far as lies in him, dishonors God. “My glory,” the Lord says, “I will not give to another” (Isa. 42:8). And the proud man says: “I will appropriate it to myself, even if you have not given it.” For the angelic distribution does not please him: giving glory to God and peace to men (Luke 2:14). Therefore he does not worship God, but exalts himself against him—plainly impious and unbelieving. For what is piety if not the worship of God? And who worships God except one who is voluntarily subject to him, [Col. 0127C] and whose heart’s eyes are toward the Lord his God, as the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters?

3. Therefore, that Mary and Joseph and the infant laid in the manger may always be found in us, let us live soberly, justly, and piously in this world. For this reason the grace of God appeared, instructing us; and through this his glory also shall appear. For thus you have it: “The grace of God has appeared to all men, instructing us, that, denying impiety and worldly desires, we may live soberly, justly, and piously in this world, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God” (Titus 2:11–13). Grace appeared in the little child for instruction; but he shall be great, as Gabriel spoke concerning him (Luke 1:32). And those whom he as a little child has instructed in humility of heart and gentleness, he shall afterward magnify [Col. 0127D] and glorify when the great and glorious Jesus Christ our Lord comes—he who is blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON V. On the words of the Apostle: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation” (2 Cor. 1:3–4).

1. Blessed is he who, because of his exceeding love with which he loved us, sent us his beloved Son, in whom he was well pleased, through whom, being reconciled, we may have peace with him; and this same Son may be in us both mediator and pledge of this reconciliation. There is no reason, my brethren, to fear under so merciful a mediator; there is no reason to doubt so faithful a pledge. [Col. 0128A] “But what sort of mediator,” you may say, “is one who is born in a stable, laid in a manger, wrapped in swaddling-cloths like the rest, weeps like the rest, and finally lies as an infant, as others commonly do?” He is indeed a great mediator, seeking peace effectively rather than superficially even in all these things. He is an infant indeed, but the Word as an infant; even his infancy is not silent.

“Comfort, comfort,” says the Lord your God (Isa. 40:1). Emmanuel says this: God with us. The stable cries it out, the manger cries it out, the tears cry it out, the swaddling-cloths cry it out. The stable cries that it is being prepared to tend the man who fell among robbers (Luke 10:30); the manger cries that food is being supplied to the same man, who had been compared with beasts (Ps. 48:13); the tears [Col. 0128B] and swaddling-cloths cry that the same man’s bloody wounds are now being washed and cleansed. For Christ had need of none of these things; none of them was for his own sake, but all for the sake of the elect. “They will reverence my Son,” says the Father of mercies (Matt. 21:37). Indeed, Lord, they reverence him—but who? Certainly not the Jews, to whom he was sent, but the elect, for whose sake he was sent.

2. For we reverence him in the manger, we reverence him on the cross, we reverence him in the tomb. Devoutly we receive him tender for our sake; for our sake bloodied; for our sake pale; for our sake buried, we reverence him. With the Magi we worship the Savior’s infancy devoutly; with holy Simeon we devoutly embrace it, receiving your mercy in the midst of your temple. For he is the one of whom we read: “The mercy [Col. 0128C] of the Lord is from eternity” (Ps. 102:17). Otherwise, what is coeternal with the Father except the Son and the Holy Spirit? Each of the two is not so much merciful as mercy itself in truth. Nevertheless, the Father too is mercy; yet these three are only one mercy, just as they are one essence, one wisdom, one divinity, one majesty.

Yet when God is called the Father of mercies, who does not see that the Son is signified as though by his proper name? And he is rightly called the Father of mercies, whose proper characteristic is always to have mercy and to spare.

3. But perhaps someone will say: How is it his proper characteristic to have mercy, when “his judgments are a great deep” (Ps. 35:7)? For it is not said: “All his ways are mercy alone,” but “mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). He is no less just than merciful, he to whom mercy and judgment are sung (Ps. 100:1). Yet it is true: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18); but having mercy is proper to him. For he takes the material—and, as it were, the seedbed—of mercy from himself. But when he judges and condemns, we in a certain manner compel him to it, so that compassion seems to proceed from his heart very differently from punishment. Hear him himself saying: “Is the death of the wicked my will, says the Lord, and not rather that he should turn and live?” (Ezek. 18:23). Therefore he is rightly called not the Father of judgments or punishments, but the Father of mercies: not only because a father seems more inclined to pity than anger, and because a father has compassion on his children who fear him; but still more because he takes the cause and origin of mercy from what is his own, while the cause of judging or punishing comes rather from what is ours.

4. But if for this reason he is Father of mercy, why “Father of mercies”? “God has spoken once,” says the Prophet, “these two things have I heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, mercy” (Ps. 61:12–13). Yet the Apostle commends to us in the one Word, the one Son, a double mercy as well. He calls God Father not of one mercy only but of mercies; and God not of one consolation but of all consolation, who consoles us not merely in this or that but in all our tribulation. “The mercies of the Lord are many,” says someone (Lam. 3:32), namely because “many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from them all the Lord will deliver them.” The Son of God is one, the Word is one; but our misery is manifold and requires not merely great mercy but a multitude of acts of compassion.

Perhaps, however, because of the twofold substance in which the human condition subsists, and since each is so miserable, human misery may not unfittingly be called twofold, though manifold in each part. For the tribulations of both our body and our heart have multiplied; but he rescues us from both necessities, he who made the whole human being sound. Since, then, the one and only Son of God has now come for souls, namely to take away the sins of the world, and will come a second time for bodies, to raise them and conform them to the body of his glory, [Col. 0129C] it may perhaps not seem unfitting that, when we rightly call him Father of mercies, we confess this twofold mercy. For, taking upon himself a body and soul of human nature, he says not merely once, “Comfort,” but—as we have also recalled above—“Comfort, comfort, says the Lord your God,” so that we may be certain that he will save both, since he did not disdain to assume either. [Col. 0130A]

5. But in whom, do you suppose? Plainly, in his people. For even now he will save—not just anyone, but his people—from their sins (Matt. 1:21); and afterward he will conform not every body, but “the body of humility,” to the body of his glory (Phil. 3:21). In short, he consoles his people, namely the humble people whom he will save, for he will humble the eyes of the proud. Do you wish to know his people? “The poor is left to you,” says the man after God’s own heart (Ps. 9:14). And he himself says in the Gospel: “Woe to you rich, who have your consolation!” (Luke 6:24).

Would that we, beloved, might always desire to be found among that people—not that people to whom he says, “Woe,” but that people whom the Lord their God consoles. What could he console in those who have their own consolation? Christ’s infancy does not console the chatterers; Christ’s tears do not console those who laugh loudly; his swaddling-cloths do not console those who walk in robes; the manger and stable do not console those who love the first seats in the synagogues. Rather, to those who patiently await this whole consolation in silence, mourning and poor in rags, these things will seem to yield place.

But let them hear that even the angels themselves console no others. For to shepherds keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night the joy of the new light is proclaimed, and to them the Savior is said to have been born. To the poor and laboring—not to you rich, who have your consolation and the divine woe—amid the very watches of the night the hallowed day shone forth; and night was illumined as day, indeed changed into day, as the angel said: “For to you a Savior has been born today” (Luke 2:11), certainly today, not “this night.” For “the night has passed, and the day has drawn near”: the true Day from Day, the salvation of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0129]

## ON THE NATIVITY OF THE HOLY INNOCENTS.

### ONLY SERMON. On the four consecutive solemnities: the Nativity of the Lord, and of Saints Stephen, John, and the Innocents.

[Col. 0129C]

1. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord: the Lord is God, and he has shone upon us” (Ps. 117:26–27). “Blessed is the name of his glory, which is holy” (Dan. 3:52). For that Holy One born of Mary did not come idly; rather, he abundantly pours out both the name and the grace of holiness. From him Stephen is holy; from him John is holy; from him the Innocents too are holy. Thus, by a useful arrangement [variant: dispensation], this threefold solemnity accompanies the Nativity of the Lord, so that not only may continual devotion endure amid consecutive solemnities, but also that the fruit of the Lord’s Nativity may thereby become more evidently known to us, as by a kind of continuation.

For in these three solemnities one may observe a threefold form of holiness; nor do I think that, beyond these three, any fourth kind of saints can easily be found among human beings. In blessed [Col. 0130C] Stephen we have both the deed and the will of martyrdom; in blessed John, the will alone; in the blessed Innocents, the deed alone. All these drank the cup of salvation: either in body and spirit together, or in spirit alone, or in body alone. “You shall indeed drink my cup,” the Lord said to James and John (Matt. [Col. 0130D] 20:23); and there is no doubt that he spoke of the cup of suffering. Finally, when he said to Peter, “Follow me,” evidently summoning him to imitate his passion, Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following—not so much with bodily footsteps as with the affection of ready devotion. John therefore drank the cup of salvation and followed the Lord like Peter, although not in every respect as Peter did. For the fact that he remained thus, so as not to follow the Lord also in bodily suffering, was by divine counsel, as the Lord himself said: “Thus I will him to remain until I come” (John 21:19–22)—as if to say: “He too wishes to follow, but I will him to remain thus.”

2. But who could doubt concerning the crowns of the Innocents? Let him doubt that infants slain for Christ are crowned among the martyrs who does not believe that those regenerated in Christ are numbered among the children of adoption. Otherwise, why would the child who was born for us, not against us, permit children of his own age to be killed for his sake—something which he could certainly have forbidden by a mere nod—unless he provided something better for them? Thus, just as circumcision then, and baptism now, suffices for the salvation of other infants without any exercise of their own will, so martyrdom undergone for him might likewise suffice for their holiness.

If you seek their merits before God, by which they were crowned, seek also their crimes before Herod, by which they were slaughtered. Or is Christ’s mercy less than Herod’s impiety—that Herod could hand innocent persons over to death, while Christ could not crown those slain for his sake? Let Stephen therefore be a martyr among human beings, whose voluntary suffering was clearly displayed especially in this: that at the very point of death he showed greater concern for his persecutors than for himself, and the affection of inward compassion overcame in him the sensation of bodily suffering, so that he mourned their crimes more than his own wounds.

Let John be a martyr among the angels, to whom, as spiritual creatures, the spiritual signs of his devotion were more certainly known. But these are plainly your martyrs, O God: in them, where neither human nor angel finds merit, the prerogative of your singular grace is more clearly commended. “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Ps. 8:3). “Glory to God in the highest,” say the angels, “and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke 2:14). Great indeed, but—I dare say—not yet perfect praise, until he comes who says: “Allow the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:14); and peace to human beings even without the exercise of will, in the sacrament of piety.

3. Let those who are accustomed to quarrel in contentious debates over deed and will consider these things; let them consider and observe that neither ought to be neglected wherever the ability does not seem lacking, especially since either without the other—where ability is lacking—may confer not only salvation but even holiness. But let them also firmly maintain this: that a deed without will may indeed benefit, but not against the will [variant: nevertheless]; so that that by which infants are saved may all the more condemn those who approach falsely. Likewise, in some cases will without deed is sufficient, but not, conversely, deed without will.

For example, someone is taken away while possessing a good will indeed, but one not yet perfect or fit to endure martyrdom: who would dare deny him salvation because of that imperfection? Perhaps he is not permitted to enter that severe temptation precisely lest he fail and be condemned. Certainly, if, with such a weak will, he were brought into a temptation [Col. 0132B] above his strength, and his will were not strengthened, who could doubt that he would fail, deny Christ, and, should it happen that he died in that state, even perish? “Whoever has been ashamed of me before men, I also will be ashamed of him,” says the Lord, “before the angels of God” (Luke 9:26). Therefore, with that imperfect will, in which a person is saved when opportunity for a deed is absent, he could no longer be saved because of the lack of a deed—or because of a deed of failure.

The same could happen through ignorance. Let us therefore emulate love and pursue good works, my brethren, and by no means make light of sins of weakness or ignorance. Rather, with care and fear, let us give thanks to the most kind and generous Savior, who seeks occasions for human salvation with such abundant love that he rejoices to find salvation in some through will and deed, in others through will without deed, and in still others through the deed even without will. He wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of himself. For this is eternal life: that we may know the Father, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom he sent (John 17:3), who with him alone is true God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0131]

## ON THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE LORD.

### SERMON I. On the Gospel reading: “After eight days were completed for the Child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus” (Luke 2:21).

[Col. 0131D]

1. We have heard the great sacrament of piety expressed in few words; we have heard a fitting reading concerning the Word whom the Lord made shortened upon the earth. For, shortened in the flesh, he is further shortened by undergoing even the circumcision of the flesh. The Son of God, made a little lower than the angels, put on human nature; but now, not rejecting even the remedy of human corruption, he is plainly made much lower than they.

Here, then, you have a great proof of faith and a manifest example of humility. For what need had you of circumcision, you who neither committed sin nor contracted it? Your age proves that you did not commit it; the Father’s divinity and the mother’s integrity prove much more certainly that you did not contract it. You are the high priest concerning whom it was prophesied in the Law (Lev. 21:11), rather than commanded, that he was not to be defiled over father or mother. For you have a Father from eternity, but he is God, in whom sin cannot fall. You also have a mother in time, but a virgin; incorruption could not give birth to corruption.

Beyond all this, the Child is circumcised, the Lamb without stain. Although he did not need it, he nevertheless chose to be circumcised. Having not even the slightest trace of a wound, he did not refuse the binding for a wound. Not so the ungodly, not so; this is not how the perversity of human pride acts. We are ashamed of the binding of wounds, though at times we even glory in our wounds. He whom no one can convict of sin himself undertook, without any necessity, the remedy for sin—at once shameful and severe; nor did he reject the stone knife, though in him alone there was none of that ancient rust to be scraped away. [Col. 0133A]

We, by contrast, shameless even to the obscenity of guilt, are ashamed to do penance. This is the height of madness: too readily inclined toward wounds, and still more shamefully embarrassed by remedies. He who committed no sin did not disdain to be reckoned a sinner; we both wish to be sinners and do not wish to be thought so. Does a healthy person need medicine, rather than those who are ill? Or rather, does the physician, not the patient, need treatment? What person, conscious of such—not merely glory, but even innocence—would calmly admit the hand of one circumcising? Yet Christ patiently paid what he did not seize [variant: was paying], having come to cleanse sins, not to take them upon himself.

But you say: “Why should not a little child undergo it?” Rather, why should not one humble and gentle undergo it? Why should he not be silent before one circumcising him, when he was silent before the shearer and silent before the crucifier? Besides, it would not have been difficult for him to preserve his flesh intact, so that it might not be cut, he who had caused the gate of the virgin womb not to be opened at his birth. It would not have been difficult for the little child to prevent that flesh from being circumcised, when neither was it difficult for him, when dead, to prevent it from decaying.

2. “Therefore, after eight days were completed for the Child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus.” A great and wonderful mystery! The Child is circumcised and is called Jesus. What does this connection mean? Circumcision seems to belong rather to one who must be saved than to the Savior; and it is fitting that the Savior should circumcise rather than be circumcised. But recognize the mediator of God and humankind, who from the beginning of his birth joins divine things to human, things lowly to things highest. He is born of a woman, but the fruit of fertility comes to her in such a way that the flower of virginity does not fall away; he is wrapped in swaddling-cloths, but the very cloths are honored by angelic praises; he is hidden in a manger, but disclosed by a star shining from heaven.

So too circumcision proves the reality of the humanity he assumed, while the name that is above every name indicates the glory of his majesty. He is circumcised as a true son of Abraham; he is called Jesus as the true Son of God. For this Jesus of mine does not, like those before him, bear an empty or vain name. In him there is no shadow of a great name, but reality. The Evangelist testifies that the name was given from heaven, called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. And attend to the depth of the expression: after Jesus was born, he is called Jesus by human beings—the name by which he was called [variant: who was called] by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. For he is Savior both of angel and of human: of human beings from the incarnation, of angels from the beginning of creation.

3. “His name was called Jesus,” he says, “which was called by the angel.” Thus, by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word stands; and what was abbreviated in the prophet is read more clearly in the Gospel as “made flesh.” This parable concerns us, my brethren. Christ needed neither angelic nor human testimony; but, as it is written, all things are for the sake of the elect (2 Tim. 2:10). Therefore we must seek a threefold testimony concerning our own salvation, lest we seem to have taken the name of our God in vain.

We too, brethren, must be circumcised, and thus receive the name of salvation: circumcised not in letter but in spirit and truth; circumcised not in one member but in the entire body together. Although the appendage of Leviathan—that is, the poison of lust and the attraction of immoderate and disordered pleasure, which is from evil and must be cut off—rules especially in that part in which circumcision was commanded to the Jews, it nevertheless occupies the whole flesh. “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in us,” nor is there any part not diseased by this poison.

Therefore, just as the people, still little in faith and love, received the limited command suitable to it of a small circumcision, so, when it has grown into a more mature man, it is commanded to be baptized in the whole body, baptism being the complete circumcision of the whole person. Hence our Savior deigned both to be circumcised on the eighth day and to be crucified after his thirtieth year, when his entire body was stretched out for punishment. We too are planted in the likeness of his death, as the Apostle writes (Rom. 6:5), observing, indeed, that which was handed down last.

4. What, then, is our moral circumcision, except that which the same Apostle commends: “Having food and clothing,” he says, “let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8)? This voluntary poverty, labor of penance, and disciplined regular observance most excellently circumcise us and cut away every superfluity. Yet in this circumcision we must seek a threefold testimony to our salvation: from the angel, [Col. 0134C] and Mary, and Joseph.

First of all, I say, the angel of great counsel must impose upon us the name of salvation. Then the testimony of the congregation itself is necessary, for it is like the mother of individuals: a mother, I say, who is a virgin, like her whom the Apostle betrothed to one husband in order to present a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Cor. 11:2). Nor should the testimony of the minister himself be despised by one who seeks to imitate the Savior’s example. This is Joseph, holding indeed the place of a bridegroom, but in reality a servant and steward; he is called a father, but is rather a foster-father.

5. But I shall state the same things more plainly. Brethren, one must have a good testimony both from those outside and from the one who is within. For one whose conduct is pleasing to all and burdensome to no one is undoubtedly commended as sound in all respects by the congregation of the brethren itself.
