In vain does that most wicked accuser of the brethren bring charges [variant: brings charges] concerning only matters that are public against someone whom the whole body of brethren excuses.

He also has testimony from his superiors who humbly and with pure confession always lays open for judgment both the sins of secular life and the negligences of this present time—for “we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3:2), unless perhaps we think ourselves holier than the disciple whom Jesus loved [1 John 1:8]—and endeavors to make satisfaction according to their judgment. Even in these matters there is no need to fear that wicked one’s accusation, because the Lord will not judge twice in the same matter.

But perhaps he will wish to accuse the intention and contrive calumny in that area where neither the testimony of the brethren nor that of the father himself seems sufficiently effective. Therefore the inward witness must aid us in this respect: he who looks more upon the heart than the face. Indeed, we must begin with him, so that nothing may first be conceived in the mind until it has received from him the name of salvation. But once it has proceeded into a manifest deed, it is expedient to secure outward testimonies as well, as the Apostle says: “Providing what is good not only before God but also before men” (2 Cor. 8:21).

## SERMON II. On the various names of Christ.

1. “After eight days were completed for the Child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus” (Luke 2:21). From the beginning God approves measure, and nothing immoderate has ever pleased his equity. Hence it was that he created all things not only in weight, measure, and number, but immediately prescribed a limit to humankind itself and gave a command, saying: “From every tree of Paradise you shall eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat” (Gen. 2:16–17). A very light command, certainly, and an altogether generous measure! But the human being transgressed the limit prescribed to him and passed beyond the boundary set for him.

Therefore God turned his face away from him, and only at length, in the days of Abraham his friend, began to be placable again. He established a measure anew and promulgated the Law, though not altogether like the former command. [Col. 0135C] For the first was for precaution; this was for healing. There was a prohibition, made lest excess should enter in; here a cutting-away was now enjoined, so that what had entered might be removed by the remedy of the sacrament. Finally, the former law was given concerning a tree, lest its fruit be eaten; this one concerned the body itself, that the flesh of the foreskin might be cut.

Nor is there any doubt that the same appendage of Leviathan occupied the other members of the human body also: namely the poison of concupiscence and the enticement of immoderate and disordered pleasure. Thus some general cutting-away seemed necessary for all.

2. But because the fragility of human flesh and the weakness of infancy could in no way bear the cutting off of every individual bodily member, divine providence in merciful moderation arranged that concupiscence should be chastened especially in that part in which it was known to rage more violently and exercise more forcefully its malice. For amid every rebellion of the bodily members against the spirit, that member alone is found so utterly rebellious that, contrary to every deliberation of the will, it rises to shameful and unlawful movements.

The fact that this circumcision took place on the eighth day commended the hope of the heavenly kingdom, since the cycle of days returning to the first seemed to display a certain likeness of a crown. Hence the eighth day is especially celebrated after the principal solemnities; and in the Lord’s discourse the eighth beatitude is joined to the first (Matt. 5:3, 10), so that the repeated promise at last of the heavenly kingdom might plainly fashion [variant: fashions] a crown for us.

3. Rightly indeed, when the Child born for us is circumcised, he is called Savior, since he has already begun from this point to work our salvation by shedding for us that spotless blood. Christians need no longer ask why the Lord Christ chose to be circumcised. For he was circumcised for the same reason that he was born and that he suffered. None of these things was for his own sake, but all for the sake of the elect. He was neither born in sin, nor circumcised because of sin, nor did he die for his own sin, but rather for our offenses.

“It was called,” he says, “by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.” It was called, certainly, not imposed; for this has been his name from eternity. By his own nature he possesses the fact that he is Savior; this name is innate to him, not given by human or angelic creation.

4. But what are we to say when that outstanding prophet, foretelling that this very Child would be called by many names, appears to have passed over this one alone—which alone, as the angel foretold and the Evangelist testifies, was “called his name”? Isaiah rejoiced to see this day; he saw it and was glad. Finally, he spoke rejoicing and praising God: “A child has been born to us, a son has been given to us, and dominion has been placed upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Strong, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9:6). Great names indeed; but where is the name that is above every name, the name of Jesus, at which every knee bends? Perhaps in all these you will find that one name, but expressed and, as it were, poured out. For he is the one of whom the bride says in the Song of Love: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1:2).

5. Therefore, in all these appellations you have the one name Jesus; nor indeed could he either be called or be a Savior if any one of these things were lacking. Have not each of us truly experienced him as Wonderful, namely in the change of our wills? This indeed is the beginning of our salvation: when we begin to reject what we loved, to grieve over what once made us glad, to embrace what we feared, to pursue what we fled, to desire what we despised. Wonderful indeed is he who works these wonders. Yet it is no less necessary [Col. 0136D] that he show himself Counsellor in the choice of repentance and the ordering of life, lest perhaps our zeal be without knowledge and prudence be lacking to a good will. We must also, certainly, experience him as God, namely in the remission of former offences: for salvation cannot stand for us without this, and no one can forgive sins except God alone. But even this does not suffice for salvation unless we also experience him as Mighty in overthrowing those who attack us, lest we again be overcome by the same desires and our last state become worse than the former.

Does anything now seem lacking to the Savior? Certainly that greatest thing would be lacking, unless he were also Father of the age to come, so that through him we might rise to immortality [Col. 0137A]—we who through the father of the present age are begotten unto death. Nor is this enough unless, as Prince of Peace, he should reconcile us to the Father, to whom he will hand over the kingdom; lest perhaps, like sons of perdition and certainly not of salvation, we should seem destined to rise again for punishment. His dominion will indeed be multiplied, so that he may rightly be called Savior also because of the multitude to be saved; and there will be no end of peace, so that you may know that this salvation is true, since it cannot fear failure.

## SERMON III. On the Eighth Day [otherwise, On the Eight Days]

1. In the Circumcision of the Lord, brothers, we have something to love and admire, and we also have something to imitate. In it there is plainly a great benefit of condescension, for which we should give thanks; something hidden lies enclosed within it [Col. 0137B], which we ought to fulfill in ourselves. For the Lord came for our sake not only to redeem us by the shedding of his blood, but also to teach us by words and likewise instruct us by examples. For just as it would be utterly useless to know the way if we were held in prison, so redemption would not help if the first person to find those ignorant of the way brought them back first in order to shut them again in prison. Thus, in his more mature age the Savior gave clear examples of patience, humility, and above all charity, as well as of the other virtues; but in infancy he gave them veiled in figures.

2. But before we come to examine these matters, it is pleasing first to say something about so great and so manifest a condescension. The angels possess pure and perfect glory; but neither shall we be without glory. We behold [Col. 0137C] his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father: the glory of mercy and of truly paternal affection, glory proceeding from the Father’s heart and plainly displaying a father’s very bowels. “For all have sinned,” says the Apostle, “and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23). And elsewhere: “Far be it from me,” he says, “to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). For what is more glorious for us than that God has valued us so highly? And what greater glory is there for him than such condescension and such kindness—most sweet precisely because so gratuitous? For he died for the ungodly. You see how much he did, and for what sort of people: for what sort, that we may not be proud; how much, that we may not despair.

Therefore, that you may be found to have not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God, and may know what has been given you by God [Col. 0137D], I beg you: do not become like horse and mule, but like the devout beast of burden that says, “I became like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. 72:23). Such beasts know their owner and their master’s manger, in which the most compassionate fodder has been placed for them: he himself who is the bread of angels. For he is the living bread by which man ought to live; but because man became a beast of burden, the bread also became fodder, so that even thus man might live by him.

3. The mystery of this change was celebrated on the day of the Nativity, when the Word became flesh, though all flesh is grass. On that very day, therefore, he was made a little lower than the angels and was found in outward appearance as a man [Col. 0138A]; but today I hear something more wondrous. He has now been made much lower than the angels—he who has not only the form of a man, but the form of a sinner, and is branded as it were with a criminal’s branding-iron. For what is circumcision except a sign of superfluity and sin? In you, Lord Jesus, what is superfluous that should be cut away? Are you not true God from God the Father, true man from the Virgin Mother without any sin? What are you doing, you who circumcise him? Do you suppose that this sentence can fall upon him: “The male whose foreskin has not been circumcised—that soul shall perish from among his people” (Gen. 17:14)?

Can the Father forget the Son of his womb? Or would he not recognize him unless he bore the sign of circumcision? Indeed, if he could in any way fail to recognize the Son in whom he was well pleased, he could most especially fail to recognize him from this sign—finding in him a circumcision that he himself had appointed for sinners, for the cleansing, certainly, of offences. But what wonder if the Head received for the members a remedy that he had no need of in himself? Do we not often in our own bodies apply treatment to one member because of another’s illness? The head aches, and a cautery is applied to the arm; the kidneys hurt, and it is applied to the leg. Thus today, for the rottenness of the whole body, a kind of cautery has been applied to the Head.

4. Finally, what wonder if he deigned to be circumcised for us, for whom he deigned to die? For he was given wholly to me and expended wholly for my benefit. Hearing that the son of the great King was passing by the prison, I began to groan more deeply and cry out more pitifully [Col. 0138C], saying: “Son of God, have mercy on me.” But he, being most kindly, said: “What is this weeping and wailing that I hear?” And they said to him: “It is Adam, that traitor, whom your Father caused to be thrust into prison until he should consider by what punishments he might make him perish.” What was he to do, whose nature is goodness, whose proper characteristic is always to show mercy and spare? He descended into the prison; he came to bring the captive out of the prison-house.

But the Jews, not forgetting the hatred by which they hated the Father, exercised it upon the Son. Hence he himself says: “They hated both me and my Father” (John 15:24). What then did the ungodly do, to whom he was burdensome even to behold? “This is the heir,” they say; “come, let us kill him” (Matt. 21:38). Thus they killed the Lamb of God—to their own destruction indeed, but to our salvation [Col. 0138D]. For they shed the Lamb’s blood; we came near and drank it. “We received the cup of salvation”: and “how splendid is the cup that intoxicates” [otherwise, “our cup”]!

Behold why we should give thanks. For a few days ago we celebrated his coming into the prison of this world, that is, the day of his Nativity; but today we celebrate that he took upon himself our chains and bonds. For today he who committed no sin, in order to acquit the guilty, placed his innocent hands in their chains; today he was made under the law, he who gave the law.

5. But we must now say what this circumcision spiritually signifies that we ought to do. For it was neither commanded in the Law without reason nor fulfilled in the Lord without reason, that circumcision should take place on the eighth day [Col. 0139A] (Gen. 17:12). “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11:34). May the Advocate Spirit, who searches the depths of God, now be present to your desires and explain to us [otherwise, to you] the mystery of this eighth day.

We already know that a human being must be born anew; for this reason the Son of God was born a second time. For we are all born in sins, and we need to be reborn in grace—a grace which we certainly received in Baptism, but, alas, which was wholly lost in secular life. Now, by God’s mercy, the power of grace first works in us, so that we may walk in newness of life. A person is therefore born when the Sun of righteousness, rising in the mind, illumines the darkness of sins and sets before the inward gaze the dreadful judgment of God, adding to the bond of terror the short number of days and an uncertain end. This is indeed the evening in which weeping will lodge; and the joy of morning must be added, so that he may make us hear his mercy. Thus evening and morning make one day.

This is the day of righteousness, rendering to each what is his own: misery to us, mercy to God. On this day the Child is born, when, from what we have said, the mind is stirred to love of repentance and hatred of sin.

6. But it is dangerous if perhaps he wishes to practice repentance amid the crowds of the world, where some undoubtedly entice him to sin by poisonous persuasions, others by worse examples on every side, others cast down his mind into vain glory through flattery, and others into impatience through detraction. The ray of prudence must now come forth [Col. 0139C]. Let it show how many and how pressing opportunities and occasions of sin the world offers and thrusts upon us, especially in this wicked generation; and how weak the human mind is against them, especially a mind nurtured in the habit of sin. On this day of prudence, therefore, let him choose to flee from the present wicked world, saying with the prophet: “I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the ungodly” (Ps. 25:5).

But this is not yet sufficient. Perhaps he wishes to choose solitude, not paying enough attention to his own weakness and to the dangerous struggle with the devil. For what is more dangerous than to wrestle alone against the wiles of the ancient enemy—by whom one is seen, while one cannot see him? Therefore he now needs the day of fortitude [Col. 0139D], so that he may know that his strength must be kept for the Lord and sought in the battle-line of many fighting together, where there are as many helpers as companions—such men as can say with the Apostle: “We are not ignorant of the enemy’s devices” (2 Cor. 2:11). For a congregation is formidable by its strength, like an army drawn up in battle array. “But woe to him who is alone! For if he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Eccl. 4:10).

If we have heard that this grace was granted to any of the ancient Fathers, it is not fitting rashly to expose oneself to this danger; nor ought one to tempt God, as our master also says when speaking of anchorites: “Those who,” he says, “in the fresh fervor of conversion” (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 1), etc. Therefore on this day of fortitude he adds to what he had already begun—namely, “I have hated the assembly of evildoers”—the following [Col. 0140A]: “I will wash my hands among the innocent.”

7. But when he chooses to be in the congregation of many [Col. 0140A], will he choose to be a master, though he has not yet been a disciple, and to teach what he has never learned? And how will he be able to regulate irrational impulses either in himself or in others? “No one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5:29). How then do you suppose that, if this man is already his own master, he will not easily indulge himself sometimes, all the more because he is so familiar with himself?

Let the day of temperance therefore shine, so that he may seek how the unrestrained impulses of pleasure, the beastly impulses of curiosity, and the stiff-necked impulses of self-exaltation may be moderated and restrained. Let him choose to be lowly in the house of his God and subject to a master, under whom his will may be broken [Col. 0140B] and desire repressed by the bridle of obedience; and let there be fulfilled what the prophet says: “You have set men over our heads” (Ps. 65:12).

The servant should not disdain what came first in the Lord, for “the servant is not greater than his lord” (John 13:16). For when he had already grown in age, wisdom, and grace before God and men; when he was already twelve years old and, having remained in Jerusalem, was found by the Blessed Virgin and Joseph, whose son he was thought to be, amid the teachers, listening to them and questioning them—nevertheless, “he went down with them and was subject to them” (Luke 2:42–51). You too, then, be subject for his sake.

8. But now, on the very path of obedience, perhaps some hard and rough things may occur to you [Col. 0140C], so that you sometimes receive certain commands which, although wholesome, nevertheless seem less pleasant. If you begin to endure these grudgingly, to judge your superior, or to murmur in your heart—even if outwardly you perform what is commanded—this is not the virtue of patience [perhaps, obedience], but a covering of malice. The day of patience must therefore shine, by which you silently embrace in your conscience all hard and rough things, judging yourself more severely and rebuking yourself more harshly, since those things that conduce to salvation displease you; and always in your thoughts, so far as you can, supporting your master’s side against yourself: striving to accuse yourself in all things and to excuse him rather.

9. Moreover, at this point I think you must now beware of pride [Col. 0140D]. For it is altogether a great thing thus to conquer oneself. Solomon says, “The patient person is better than a strong man; and he who rules his spirit than one who captures cities” (Prov. 16:32). Consider, finally, how plainly the prophet teaches that humility is necessary after patience, saying: “Yet be subject to God, my soul, for from him is my patience” (Ps. 61:6). Does he not seem here to have perceived, through the occasion of patience, the temptation of pride? Therefore the ray of humility must enlighten your heart and declare what is from you and what is from God, so that you may not think proudly; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6).

10. But when you have been exercised for a long time in these things, ask that the light of devotion may be given you: a most serene day and a sabbath of the mind. In it, like a soldier discharged from service, you may live amid all labors without labor, running with your heart enlarged in the way of God’s commandments; so that what you previously did with bitterness and coercion of your spirit, you may thereafter accomplish with supreme sweetness and delight.

I think that he was asking for this grace when he said: “Release me, that I may be refreshed” (Ps. 38:14), as if to say: “How long shall I be tortured in this sweat and pain, and be afflicted with death all day long? Release me, that I may be refreshed.” Yet few, I think, attain this perfection in this life. Nor, if someone seems at some time to possess it, ought he immediately believe that he possesses it, especially if he is a novice and has not [otherwise, but has not yet] ascended through the stages mentioned above. For our merciful Lord Jesus Christ often draws little ones in heart by such consolations.

But let those who are such know that this grace has been lent to them, not given to them, so that on the day of good things they may remember evil things, and on the day of evil things may not be forgetful of good things. Very differently, those whose senses are exercised enjoy the happy delight of this devotion. Yet many strive for this all their life and never reach it; nevertheless, if they have striven devoutly and perseveringly, as soon as they depart from the body they receive what was in this life denied them as a matter of divine dispensation. Grace alone brings them there, whither they had formerly tended with grace; so that, “perfected in a short time,” they may fulfill long periods.

[Col. 0142A]

11. But for those who attain the grace of this devotion, one danger seems to remain, and they must altogether fear the noonday demon: “For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14). Therefore the person who does all things with such delight must fear lest, while following his inclination, he ruin his body through immoderate ascetic practice and then be obliged, not without great detriment to spiritual exercise, to occupy himself with the care of a weakened body.

Therefore, lest the runner stumble, he must be enlightened by the light of discretion, which is the mother of virtues and the completion of perfection. This indeed teaches, “Nothing in excess”; and this is the eighth day on which the child is circumcised, because discretion truly circumcises, so that neither more nor less is done. For the excessive person cuts off, rather than circumcises, the fruit of a good work [Col. 0142B], just as the lukewarm person does if he does too little.

On this day a name is given—the name of salvation; and I would not hesitate to say of one who thus conducts himself that he works out his own salvation. For up to this day the angels, who know the heavenly secrets, may speak; but I now for the first time confidently give him the name of salvation. But since this is altogether a rare bird on earth (Juvenal, *Satires* VI), brothers, let the virtue of obedience among you supply the place of this discretion, so that you do nothing more, nothing less, and nothing otherwise than has been commanded.

[Col. 0141]

## ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

### SERMON I. On the Apostle’s words, “The kindness and love for humankind of God our Savior appeared” (Titus 3:4), and on the three manifestations of Christ

[Col. 0141C]

1. “The kindness and love for humankind of God our Savior appeared.” Thanks be to God, through whom our consolation thus abounds in this pilgrimage, in this exile, in this misery. For we often take care to remind you of these things, so that it may never slip from your minds that we are pilgrims, far from our homeland and driven from our inheritance. For whoever does not know desolation cannot recognize consolation. Whoever does not know that consolation is necessary will consequently not possess the grace of God.

> **Note [Col. 0141D].** That is, it follows that such a person does not have God’s grace, which is given only to those who ask and acknowledge their own misery; nor is it preserved except in those who fear losing it. See below, Sermon 1 after the Octave of Epiphany, no. 5; and Sermon 2, no. 8. Add Sermon 1 on Psalm 90, no. 1. Hence in Sermon 5 on the Dedication of a Church, no. 8: “The dissembling of misery excludes compassion, and condescension has no place where there has been presumption of worthiness.” Compare *The Life of Bernard*, nos. 36 and 37.

Hence it is that worldly people, entangled in business and vices, do not perceive mercy because they do not feel their misery [Col. 0141D]. But you, to whom it has not been said in vain, “Be still, and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 45:11); and of whom the same prophet says, “He has declared to his people the power of his works” (Ps. 110:6)—you, I say, whom secular occupation does not hold captive, consider [Col. 0142C] what spiritual consolation is. You who are not ignorant of exile, hear that help has come from heaven.

For the kindness and love for humankind of God our Savior appeared. Before his love for humankind appeared, his kindness lay hidden; for it existed before, since “the mercy of the Lord is from eternity.” But how could so great a kindness be recognized? It was promised, but not felt; hence many did not believe it. For the Lord spoke in the prophets in many portions and in many ways (Heb. 1:1), saying: “I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction” (Jer. 29:11). But what did a human being answer, experiencing affliction and knowing no peace? “How long do you say, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace?” (Ezek. 13:10). Therefore the angels of peace wept bitterly (Isa. 33:7), saying: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. 53:1). But now let people believe even their own sight, because “the testimonies of God have become exceedingly credible” (Ps. 92:5). For, so that it might not escape even a troubled eye, “he has set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18:6).

2. Behold: peace not promised but sent; not deferred [Col. 0143A] but given; not prophesied but presented. Behold, God the Father has sent to earth, as it were, a sack full of his mercy—a sack, I say, to be cut open in the Passion, so that our price, hidden within it, may be poured out; a sack indeed, although small, yet full. For a little child has been given to us, but in him “all the fullness of divinity dwells.” For when the fullness of time came, the fullness of divinity also came. It came in flesh, that it might thus be displayed even to carnal people, and that, as the love for humankind appeared [Col. 0143C], kindness might be recognized.

For where God’s love for humankind is made known, kindness can no longer remain hidden. In what could he more greatly commend his kindness than by taking on my flesh? Mine, I say—not Adam’s flesh, that is, not flesh such as he possessed before his fault [Col. 0143B]. What more greatly declares his mercy than that he took on misery itself? What is so full of compassion as that the Word of God became grass for our sake? “Lord, what is man, that you regard him? Or why do you set your heart upon him?” (Job 7:17). From this let man consider how great is God’s care for him; from this let him know what God thinks and feels concerning him. Do not ask, O man, what you suffer, but what he suffered. Learn how highly he valued you from what he became for you, so that his kindness may appear to you through his love for humankind. For the lower he made himself in his humanity, the greater he showed himself in goodness; and the more lowly he became for me, the dearer he is to me.

“The kindness and love for humankind of God our Savior appeared,” says the Apostle. Great indeed and manifest are God’s kindness and love for humankind; and he who took care to add the name of God to his humanity declared a great proof of kindness.

3. Gabriel the angel, sent to Mary, speaks of the Son of God, but does not call him God. Blessed be God, who gave us from among ourselves such an angel, that our own angel might supply what that one did not say. For he too had the Spirit of God and spoke by his Spirit—a matter most necessary to us. For what so instructs faith, strengthens hope, and kindles charity as the humanity of God? But what the others left unspoken was reserved for our Angel. For it was not fitting that all should say everything, so that we might rejoice to gather different things from different witnesses and return due [Col. 0143D] thanks to each.

Yet there is one thing in which the Apostle and the angels who speak of Christ’s birth agree: namely, the name Savior. Speaking to Mary, as one more fully taught by the Spirit, Gabriel indicates the name alone: “You shall call his name Jesus” (Luke 1:31). When the angel comes to Joseph, he not only gives the name but also interprets and explains its reason: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21). Great joy is also announced to the shepherds: a Savior, Christ the Lord, has been born to them (Luke 2:10–11). Paul says something similar: “The kindness and love for humankind of God our Savior appeared.”

Rightly did none of them leave unspoken that sweet name [Col. 0144A], which was most necessary for me. Otherwise, what would I do on hearing that the Lord was coming? Would I not flee, like Adam, who fled from his face but did not escape? Would I not despair on hearing that he was coming whose law I had so transgressed, whose patience I had so abused, whose benefit had found me so ungrateful? What greater consolation could there be than in a sweet title, in a consoling name? Therefore he himself says that the Son did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17). Now I approach confidently; now I pray in trust. For what should I fear when the Savior comes into my house? I have sinned against him alone; whatever he forgives will be forgiven, for it is certainly lawful for him to do what he wills. “It is God who justifies [Col. 0144B]; who is he that condemns? Or who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect?” (Rom. 8:33–34). Therefore we ought to rejoice that he has come into what belongs to us; for now he will be ready to pardon.

4. Finally, he is a little child; he can be appeased easily. For who does not know that a child readily forgives? Behold, if it is not too little for us, we can be reconciled for something very little. For something very little, I say, though not without repentance; but our repentance itself is something small. We are poor and can give little; nevertheless, we can be reconciled for that small thing, if we will. All that I can give is this wretched body; if I give it, it is enough. If it falls short, I add his body also: for it is from [Col. 0144C] what is mine, and it is mine. “For a little child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6). From you, Lord, I make up what I lack in myself.

O sweetest reconciliation! O most delightful satisfaction! O reconciliation truly easy, yet most beneficial! A satisfaction small, but not to be despised! For as easy as it is now, so difficult will it be later; and as now there is no one who cannot be reconciled, so shortly there will be no one who can be. For as kindness has appeared beyond all hope, beyond all human estimation, so we may expect a corresponding severity of judgment. Therefore do not despise God’s mercy if you do not wish to feel justice—but wrath, indignation, jealousy, fury. “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.” For, so that you might know how great a severity follows, so great a gentleness has gone before it [Col. 0144D]. From the greatness of forgiveness, consider the greatness of vengeance.

For God is boundless and infinite in justice as in mercy: abundant in forgiving, abundant in avenging. But mercy claims priority for itself, so that, if we will, severity may find no one upon whom to rage. For this reason he first extended kindness, so that, reconciled through it, we might look upon severity without fear. Therefore he willed not only to descend to earth, but also to be made known; not only to be born, but also to be recognized.

5. Finally, for the sake of this recognition, this day is held in honor and is the renowned day of manifestation. For today the Magi came from the East, seeking the rising Sun of righteousness, of whom it is written: “Behold the man—Rising is his name” [Latin *Oriens*, “the East/Rising”] (Zech. 6:12). Today they worshiped the Virgin’s new-born child, following the guidance of a new star. Is this not also a great consolation to us, like that word of the Apostle of which we have spoken? He called him God; these men say it not with their voice [Col. 0145A], but by their act.

What are you doing, O Magi? What are you doing? You worship a nursing child, in a lowly hut, in shabby wrappings! Is this man then God? Certainly “God is in his holy temple; the Lord has his throne in heaven”; yet you seek him in a lowly stable, in his mother’s lap. What are you doing, when you also offer gold? Is he then a king? And where is the royal palace, where the throne, where the throng of the royal court? Is a stable a palace, a manger a throne, Joseph and Mary a crowded court? How have men who are wise become so foolish that they worship a little child, contemptible [Col. 0145B] both because of his age and because of his family’s poverty?

They became foolish in order that they might become wise; and the Spirit taught them beforehand what the Apostle afterward preached: “Let him who wishes to be wise become foolish, that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3:18). For since the world in its wisdom could not know God through wisdom, it pleased God to save believers through the foolishness of preaching (1 Cor. 1:21). Was it not to be feared, brothers, that these men might be scandalized and think themselves deceived when they saw things so unworthy? From the royal city, where they supposed that the king was to be sought, they are directed to the small village of Bethlehem; they enter a stable and find an infant wrapped in swaddling cloths. The stable does not disgust them, they are not offended by the cloths, they are not scandalized by the infancy of the nursing child; they fall down, honor him as king, and worship him as God [Col. 0145C]. But surely he who brought them also instructed them; and he who warned them outwardly by the star taught them inwardly in the secret place of the heart. This manifestation of the Lord therefore made this day illustrious, and the Magi’s devout veneration made it devout and venerable.

6. Nor is this the only manifestation: another also, as we have received from our Fathers, is celebrated today—though it is believed to have occurred much later, on this same day. For when Christ had spent thirty years in the flesh—he who according to his divinity is himself the same, and whose years do not fail—he came amid the crowds of ordinary people to John’s baptism. He came as one of the people, though he alone was without sin [Col. 0145D]. Who then would have believed him to be the Son of God? Who would have thought him the Lord of majesty?

You are greatly humbled, Lord; you are hidden in lowliness, but you cannot remain hidden from John. Is he not the one who, while you were not yet born, recognized you while he himself was still unborn through the maternal womb? Is he not the one who recognized you through the walls of both mothers’ wombs and, because he could not cry aloud to the crowds, at least informed his mother by a motion of exultation? (Luke 2:41). But what now? John saw him coming to him, says the Evangelist, and said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Truly a lamb, truly humble, truly gentle. “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” Behold him who brings cleansing from offences; behold, he comes to cleanse our bilge-water of filth. Yet after this testimony [Col. 0146A] he wishes to be baptized by John.

John trembles. What wonder? What wonder, I say, if a man trembles and does not dare touch the holy head of God—the head adored by angels, revered by Powers, feared by Principalities? Do you wish to be baptized, Lord Jesus? But why, or what need had you of baptism? Does a healthy person need medicine, or the clean need cleansing? Whence could sin come to you, so that baptism should be necessary? From your Father? Yet you have a Father, but he is God; and you are equal to him—God from God, light from light. For who does not know that sin cannot befall God? Or from your Mother? For you also have a Mother, but she is a virgin. What sin, then, could you contract from her who conceived you without iniquity and gave birth while preserving her integrity? What stain can [Col. 0146B] the spotless Lamb possess? “I ought to be baptized by you,” says John, “and do you come to me?” (Matt. 3:14).

There is great humility on both sides, but no comparison. For how could a human being fail to humble himself before the humbled God? “Allow it for now,” says the Lord, “for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:14–15). John consented and obeyed: he baptized the Lamb of God and washed the waters. We were washed, not he; for the waters are understood to have been washed so that we might be washed.

7. But perhaps you put too little faith in John’s testimony [Col. 0146C], because he too is a human being and you may regard him with suspicion: he is a kinsman of the one for whom he bears witness. Behold testimony greater than John’s: the testimony of the descending dove. Nor was it incongruous that, in order to identify the Lamb of God, a dove should come, because nothing suits the lamb [Col. 0146C] better than the dove. What the lamb is among animals, the dove is among birds: supreme innocence, supreme gentleness, supreme simplicity in each. For what is so far removed from every malice as a lamb and a dove? They do not know how to harm anyone; they have not learned to injure.

But lest you ascribe this to a chance occurrence, behold the testimony of God the Father. “Behold, the God of majesty thundered; the Lord was upon many waters” (Ps. 28:3), and the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). Truly this is he in whom there is nothing displeasing to the Father, nothing to offend the eyes of majesty. Hence he himself says: “I always do the things that please him” (John 8:29). “Hear him,” he says.

Behold, Lord Jesus [Col. 0146D], now at last speak. How long are you silent? How long do you conceal yourself? You have been silent long, exceedingly long; but now you have permission from the Father to speak. How long, power of God and wisdom of God, do you remain hidden among the people as if someone weak and foolish? How long, noble King and King of heaven, do you allow yourself both to be called and thought the son of a craftsman? For the Evangelist Luke testifies that he was still thought to be the son of Joseph (Luke 3:23).

O humility, strength of Christ! O sublimity of humility! How greatly you put to shame the pride of our vanity! I know a little—or rather, I seem to myself to know—and already I cannot be silent, thrusting myself forward and displaying myself rashly and foolishly: ready to speak, quick to teach, slow to listen. Yet while Christ was silent for so long and hid himself [Col. 0147A], was he afraid of vain glory? What could he fear from vain glory, he who is the true glory of the Father? He was indeed afraid, but not for himself. He was afraid of it for us, for whom he knew it must be feared; he guarded us and instructed us. He was silent in speech, but instructed by deed; and what he later taught in words he already proclaimed by example: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

For I hear very little about the Lord’s infancy; from that point until this thirtieth year I find nothing. But now he can no longer remain hidden, he who is so plainly revealed by the Father. For even in his first manifestation he wished to appear with the Virgin Mother, so that a certain modesty might be marked in virginity.

8. A third manifestation of him is also found in the Gospel [Col. 0147B], and this likewise is celebrated today. For the Lord, invited to a wedding, had compassion on their embarrassment when wine failed and changed water into wine. This too, as the Evangelist says, was the beginning of his signs (John 2:11). Thus, in the first manifestation he was made known as true man, when he appeared as an infant at his mother’s breast; in the second, the Father’s testimony declares him to be truly the Son of God; in the third, he is shown to be truly God, at whose command nature is changed. By so many testimonies our faith is confirmed today, by so many signs our hope is strengthened, by so many incentives our charity is inflamed.

## SERMON II. On the Magi, explaining the passage from the Song of Songs 3:11: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon.”

[Col. 0147C]

1. We read of three manifestations of the Lord: all accomplished on one day, though not at one time. The second is wondrous, and the third wondrous; but the first manifestation is still more wonderfully to be admired. Wondrous is the transformation of the waters; wondrous the testimony together of John, the dove, and the Father’s voice; but more wondrous is this: that He was recognized by the Magi. For their adoration shows that they recognize God; their offering of incense shows it. Nor do they recognize Him only as God, but also as king, as is signified by the gold. Nor in these things is the great mystery of godliness hidden from them: 800 thus by the myrrh they indicate that He will die. The Magi adore Him and offer gifts [Col. 0147D] while He is still sucking at His mother’s breasts. But where, O Magi, where is the purple of this king? Are these cheap cloths in which He is wrapped? If He is king, where is His diadem? Yet you truly behold Him in the diadem with which His Mother crowned Him: in the sackcloth of mortality, concerning which, when risen, He said: “For you have torn my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness” (Ps. XXIX [30]:12). “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him,” etc. Go forth, angelic powers, inhabitants of the heavenly city. Behold your king—but in our crown, in the diadem with which His Mother crowned Him. Yet until now you have lacked these delights; hitherto you have not tasted this sweetness. You possess His loftiness, but you have not seen His humility. Go forth, therefore, and behold [Col. 0148A] King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.

2. Yet they have no need of our exhortation, since they themselves desire to look upon Him. For the better His loftiness is known to them, the more precious and lovable His humility is. Therefore, although we have a greater reason for joy—for He was born for us and given to us—nevertheless they go before us; they exhort us. This is proved by the angel who announces great joy to the shepherds, and by the multitude of the heavenly host that came to be with him (Luke II:10, 13). Therefore we say to you, daughters of Zion: worldly souls, weak and delicate daughters rather than sons, in whom there is no strength, no manly spirit: “Go forth, daughters of Zion.” Go forth from the mind of the flesh to [Col. 0148B] the understanding of the mind; from slavery to fleshly desire to the freedom of spiritual understanding. “Go forth from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house,” and behold King Solomon; otherwise it will not be safe for you to see Him as Ecclesiastes. For He who is Solomon—that is, “peaceful”—is in exile; [Note: [Col. 0147] What follows from this point to the end of the section is found, word for word, in Sermon 50 on Various Subjects.] He will be Ecclesiastes—that is, “Preacher”—at the judgment; and Jedidiah—that is, “beloved of the Lord”—in the kingdom. In exile He is gentle and lovable; in judgment, just and terrible; in the kingdom, glorious and wonderful. Go forth, therefore, and behold King Solomon, for He is king everywhere. Although His kingdom is not of this world, yet He is king also in this world. For when He was asked, “Then are you a king?” He said: “I was born for this, and for this I came into the world” [Col. 0148C] (John XVIII:37). Here, then, He is the governor of morals; in judgment, the discerner of merits; in the kingdom, the distributor of rewards.

3. Go forth therefore, daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him: in the crown of poverty, in the crown of misery. For He was also crowned by His stepmother with a crown of thorns, a crown of misery; and He will be crowned by His household with a crown of righteousness, when the angels go forth and remove from His kingdom every scandal, when He comes to judgment with the elders of His people, when the world fights on His behalf against the senseless. The Father too crowns Him with a crown of glory, as the Psalmist says: “You have crowned him, Lord, with glory and honor” (Ps. VIII [9]:6). Behold [Col. 0148D] Him, daughters of Zion, in the diadem with which His Mother crowned Him. Receive the crown of your king, who became a little child for your sake, and together with the Magi adore His humility; the devotion of whose faith is proposed to you today as an example. To whom shall we compare these men, or whom shall we judge like them? If I consider the faith of the thief and the confession of the centurion, these men seem to surpass them in this: that by then He had already worked many miracles, had already been proclaimed by many, and worshipped by many. Yet let us consider what those men said. The thief cried from the cross: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII:42). Then does He go to His kingdom by way of punishment? Who showed you that the Christ had to suffer and so enter into His glory? You also, [Col. 0149A] centurion, how did you know Him? Seeing that He had expired crying out in this manner, he said: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark XV:39). A wondrous thing, worthy of every admiration!

801 4. Therefore, I beg you, look and see how clear-sighted faith is; consider more carefully what lynx-like eyes it has. It recognizes the Son of God while nursing; it recognizes Him hanging on the wood; it recognizes Him dying. Thus the thief recognizes Him on the gibbet, the Magi in the stable: the one fastened with nails, the others wrapped in swaddling-clothes; while the centurion recognized life in death. The Magi recognized God’s power in the weakness of a tender body; the thief, the supreme Spirit in His last breath. The Magi recognized the Word of God in infancy, for what the thief confesses in words, the Magi confess by gifts. [Col. 0149B] The thief proclaims Him king; the centurion, both Son of God and man. And what do these three gifts of the Magi themselves signify, except that in the incense they showed not so much the Son of God as God? Therefore we beseech you, dearest brethren: may such great love as the God of majesty has shown us profit you; such great humility as He accepted; such great kindness as appeared to us through Christ’s humility. Let us give thanks to our Redeemer and Mediator, through whom such good will toward us of God the Father has been made known to us. For we now know His disposition to be such that we may not unworthily say: “Thus we run, not as though uncertainly” (I Cor. IX:26). Surely the heart of God the Father toward us is such as He expressed to us who proceeded from His heart.

## SERMON III. On the Gospel reading, “Where is he that is born King of the Jews?” (Matt. II:1–11)

[Col. 0149C]

1. Brethren, it seems necessary to us, according to the custom observed on the other solemnities, to explain to you also the meaning of today’s solemnity. At times we speak against vices, and that kind of discourse is very useful; but it seems more fitting for ordinary days. On feast days, and especially on the principal solemnities, it seems better to dwell upon what belongs to the feast, so that both the mind may be instructed and the affections stirred. For how will you celebrate what you do not know? Or how will you know unless it is proclaimed to you? Therefore let it not trouble those [Col. 0149D] who are learned in the law that we accommodate ourselves to the less educated, as the law of charity requires. For I believe that even they ought not to be deprived of their own banquet if, for those less instructed, as for the common crowds, they first set before them coarser food. Indeed, they will set it before them if, out of regard for brotherly charity, the things necessary to those who do not sufficiently understand are pleasing to them, even if these perhaps seem less necessary. Afterwards they will gather up the fragments for themselves, if, pondering more carefully the subtler matters, they ruminate like clean animals upon those things which, by their subtlety, escaped minds less able to understand.

2. The solemnity of this day, then, has taken its name from manifestation. For *Epiphany* means manifestation. Today, therefore, the manifestation of the Lord is celebrated—not merely [Col. 0150A] one, but threefold, as we have received from our fathers. For today our little King, when only a few days had passed since His Nativity, was manifested to the firstfruits of the Gentiles, the star declaring Him. Today also, when He had spent nearly thirty years in the dispensation of the flesh—He who, according to His divinity, is the same, and whose years do not fail—He came, hidden among the common crowds, to be baptized at the Jordan; but He was made known by the testimony of God the Father (Matt. III:13–17). Today likewise, invited with His disciples to a wedding, when the wine failed, by a wonderful sign of His power He changed water into wine (John II:1–11). But it delights us to contemplate more closely that manifestation accomplished in the Savior’s infancy, because it is most sweet and is celebrated today in a more particular way.

[Col. 0150B] 3. Today, then, as we heard in the Gospel reading, the Magi came to Jerusalem from the East. They rightly come from the East, for they announce to us the new rising of the Sun of righteousness; by their joyful report they enlighten the whole world—except that unhappy Judaea, 802 because she hated the light, is darkened by the splendor of this new brightness, and her clouded eyes are blinded all the more by the flashing ray of the eternal Sun. Let us hear, then, what the Magi arriving from the East said: “Where is he that is born King of the Jews?” How certain a faith, and wholly without hesitation! They do not ask whether He has been born; rather, they speak confidently and ask without doubt where He is who has been born King of the Jews. But King Herod, hearing the name of king, feared, suspecting a successor. It is no wonder that Herod is troubled; but who would not marvel that Jerusalem, the city of God, which is the vision of peace, is troubled with Herod? See, brethren, how much wicked power harms; how an impious head also shapes its subjects to its own impiety. Truly wretched is a city in which Herod reigns, for beyond doubt it will share in Herodian malice, and at the rising of the new salvation it will be shaken by Herodian disturbance. I trust in the Lord that he will by no means reign among us, even if it should happen that he is present—may God avert even that! For Herodian malice is Babylonian cruelty: to wish to extinguish religion at its birth and dash the little ones of Israel to pieces. For if anything pertaining to salvation, if anything of religion, arises, whoever resists, whoever [Col. 0150D] opposes it, plainly attempts with the Egyptians to kill the little ones of Israel’s stock; indeed, with Herod he persecutes the Savior at His birth. But let us now continue the history we have begun. I believe that if anyone is conscious of this matter, he will take more careful heed of himself hereafter and will abhor the Herodian disposition, lest he receive a like end.

4. Therefore, when the Magi were seeking the King of the Jews, and Herod inquired of the scribes concerning the place of the Lord’s Nativity, they declared the name of the city in accordance with the prophet. When the Magi had departed and left the Jews, behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them. From this it is plainly understood that, seeking human counsel, they lost divine guidance; and, turning to earthly instruction, the heavenly sign left them. Therefore, when they had left Herod, immediately they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. For the star went before them until it came and stood over the place where the child was. And entering the house, they found the child with Mary His mother; and falling down, they worshipped Him. How came this to you, O foreigners? For we do not find such great faith in Israel. Were you not offended by the humble dwelling of a stable, by the poor cradle of a manger? Did the presence of a poor mother, did nursing infancy, not cause you to stumble?

5. Finally, the Evangelist says, opening their treasures, they offered Him gifts: gold, incense, and myrrh. Had they offered gold alone, perhaps they could seem to have wished to provide for the mother’s poverty, so that she might have means to raise her little son. But now, [Col. 0151B] offering gold, incense, and myrrh together, they unquestionably suggest the kind of spiritual offering. For gold seems to excel among worldly riches; and through His grace we all offered it devoutly to the Savior when, for His name’s sake, we wholly abandoned the possessions of this world. But it is now necessary that we who have perfectly despised earthly things should seek heavenly things with ardent desire. Thus we offer also the fragrant incense, by which, as you read in the Apocalypse of blessed John, the prayers of the saints are signified (Rev. V:8). Hence also the Prophet says in the psalm: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight” (Ps. CXL [141]:2). Thus you read also elsewhere that the prayer of the righteous penetrates the heavens (Ecclus. XXXV [Sirach 35]:21). The prayer, I say, not of just anyone, but of the righteous. For “he who turns away his ear lest he hear the law, his prayer shall be abominable.”

6. But if you would be righteous and not turn your ear away from the Lord’s commandments, lest He also turn His from your prayers, it is necessary not only to despise the present age, but also to chastise the flesh itself and subject it to slavery. For He who said, “Unless a man renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV:33), and elsewhere, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX:21), He Himself says in another place: “Whoever wishes to come after me, 803 let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX:23). Explaining this, the Apostle says: “All who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V:24). Therefore let our prayer have two wings: contempt for the world and affliction of the flesh. Then without doubt it will penetrate the heavens and be directed like incense before God. For our sacrifice will be pleasing and our offering acceptable when, together with gold and incense, there is also myrrh. Though bitter, it is very useful, and preserves the body which is dead because of sin, lest it decay and rot away into corruption. Let this brief statement suffice concerning the Magi’s offering, which we are to imitate.

7. But since we have said that this is a manifestation, it is fitting to ask what appears in it. Surely, according to the Apostle’s words: “The kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared” (Titus III:4). For behold, in the Gospel reading we heard that, entering the house, the Magi found the child with Mary His mother. In the infant body which His virgin mother cherished in her lap, what appeared except the reality of the flesh He had assumed? What is declared by His being found as a little child with His mother, except that He is truly man and truly the son of man? Further, in the second manifestation, see whether He is not plainly confirmed as the Son of God by the testimony of the Father’s voice. For the heavens were opened over Him, the Holy Spirit descended upon Him in bodily form like a dove, and the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III:17). It is surely sufficiently clear, sufficiently evident and beyond doubt, that the Son of God must be God. [Col. 0152B] For no one doubts that the sons of men are human beings and that the offspring even of animals are of the same kind as they. Yet, lest any place remain for sacrilegious error, He who in the first manifestation was declared true man and son of man, and in the second likewise true Son of God, is in the third shown to be true God and the Author of nature, at whose command nature is changed. Therefore, most beloved, let us love Christ Jesus as true man and our brother; let us honor Him as the Son of God; let us worship Him as God. Let us safely believe in Him; let us safely entrust ourselves to Him, my brethren: to Him who lacks neither power to save us, since He is true God and Son of God, nor good will, since, as one of us, He is true man and son of man. For how can He be inexorable toward us, for whose sake He was made like us and capable of suffering?

8. Now, if you desire to hear something for the edification of conduct concerning these manifestations, consider this: first of all Christ appears as a child with His virgin mother, to teach us that simplicity and modesty must above all be sought. For simplicity is natural to children, and modesty is akin to virgins. Therefore, at the beginning of our conversion, no virtue is more necessary to us all than humble simplicity and modest seriousness. But in the second manifestation the Savior comes to the waters of baptism, not indeed to be washed, but rather to receive testimony from the Father. These are the tears of devotion, [Col. 0152D] in which forgiveness of sins is not sought, but the good pleasure of God the Father, when the Spirit of adoption as sons descends into us, bearing witness to our spirit that we are children of God, so that we seem to hear the honey-sweet voice from heaven declaring that God the Father is truly well pleased with Himself in us. And there is no small difference between these tears of devotion, belonging of course to the now mature age, and those which early age poured forth amid the cries of infancy: namely, tears of repentance and confession. Yet far more excellent than both are certain other tears, into which the flavor of wine is poured. For I would say that those tears are truly changed into wine which issue in the ardor of charity through the affection of brotherly compassion; for the sake of which you seem, in a certain sober intoxication, even for a time to forget yourself.

[Col. 0153]

## ON THE OCTAVE OF EPIPHANY. 804 SERMON. On circumcision, baptism, and the Lord’s word to John: “Thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” (Matt. III:15)

[Col. 0153A]

1. For a stiff-necked people a knife was necessary, and for hearts of stone stone knives were deservedly due—such as those with which the circumcision performed by Joshua son of Nun is recalled (Josh. V:2–3). But our Jesus, like a gentle lamb, took away every harshness. Lord, you are a lamb coming with wool and milk: take from me, I beseech you, this knife. For it seems harsh and cruel to apply a stone knife to a newborn little child. Thus the merciful One acts. He changed hardness, well suited to hard servants, into gentleness for sons, so that the rust of original sin, which the knife could scarcely eradicate, might henceforth be easily washed away by water together with the anointing of grace. Therefore it is no wonder [Col. 0153B] that the sacraments were changed according to the diversity of the times, so that each received what was fitting for it. Christ Himself, however, received both, so that, as the cornerstone, He might unite both walls, as though joining the ends of two straps by sewing them together; just as He fulfilled the prefigured Passover and immediately instituted the true one.

2. He also wished to be circumcised in order to show that He was the author of the old law as well as of the Gospel. For He who Himself said, “Unless a man is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John III:5), had earlier said through His servant: “Every soul whose foreskin is not circumcised shall perish from his people” [Col. 0153C] (Gen. XVII:14). If He had received baptism alone, He could seem to have rejected circumcision as having nothing to do with Him. But if He had been circumcised and not baptized, when could I be persuaded to receive baptism, abandoning circumcision? Now, therefore, receiving baptism after circumcision, He handed down to me that which He received last, as what I must observe.

3. Finally, He who loves and commends community, who “makes those of one manner of life dwell in a house” (Ps. LXVII [68]:7), how could He abandon community and scandalize others? For they would have been scandalized to see Him uncircumcised, just as the Church today would be scandalized if she saw an infant not baptized. He wished not only to commend the good of community and unity, [Col. 0153D] but also to display humility, so that He who alone was without a wound might receive the binding of the wounded. Thus the Apostle says: “God sent his Son into the world, born of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. IV:4).

4. But lest anyone perhaps say, “His parents did what was done when He was circumcised, for He was a little child,” at thirty years of age He Himself went to baptism. Under the Baptist’s hands bows the head terrible to powers and principalities, worthy of adoration. What [Col. 0154A] wonder if the Baptist trembled? Who would not tremble even at the thought? O how exalted in judgment will be the head which now bows so low! And how lofty and sublime then will be the crown of that head which now appears so humble! “Allow it now,” He says, “for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” For He who came in the fullness of time, and in whom the fullness of divinity dwells, knows nothing but fullness. For He came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matt. V:17). There is a certain righteousness that is strict and very narrow, such that as soon as you turn your foot, you fall into the pit of sin: neither to set oneself above an equal nor to make oneself equal to a superior. Its definition is to render to each what is his due. There is another righteousness, broader and more ample: neither to make oneself equal to an equal nor to set oneself above an inferior. For just as it is great and grave pride to prefer oneself to an equal or to make oneself equal to a superior, so it is great humility to show oneself inferior to an equal or equal to an inferior. The highest and fullest righteousness is to show oneself inferior even to one who is inferior. For just as it is supreme and intolerable pride to set oneself above a superior, so to place oneself below [variant: submit oneself to] an inferior is supreme and full righteousness. What 805 John said, “I ought to be baptized by you” (Matt. III:14), belonged to the first kind, because he subjected himself to his superior. But what Christ did belonged to full righteousness, since He bowed Himself beneath the hands of His little servant.

[Col. 0154C] 5. Let each now see whom he imitates: this One, or him “who exalts himself above every being that is believed to be God or is worshipped” (II Thess. II:4). Let us also strive, I beseech you, brethren, to fulfill all righteousness. For it is the very path by which joy is reached. Joy is the reward; righteousness, however, is its merit and material. For our joy will arise from righteousness itself, when Christ, who is our life, appears and we appear with Him in glory, because He is the one made righteousness for us by God the Father. Blessed, moreover, are those who even now rejoice in righteousness and are gladdened in their consciences, sucking honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone. For righteousness now [variant: however] appears laborious; but the time will come when, in sweetness and delight, [Col. 0154D] without any labor, it will be desired and possessed, loved and received, when we shall enjoy righteousness itself. But woe to those who leave the path, who, abandoning righteousness, seek vain and passing joy. For when they seek joy in passing things, it cannot fail to pass away with the passing of those things from which it arose. For as fire fails when wood fails, so the world passes away, and its desire; and without doubt its joy also.

[Col. 0155]

## FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EPIPHANY

### SERMON I. On the miracle performed at the wedding (John II:1–11), and on the Lord’s saying: “And you yourselves [be] like men awaiting their master when he returns from the wedding.” (Luke XII:36)

[Col. 0155A]

1. In the reading of the holy Gospel, brethren, we heard today that our Lord went to a wedding. Let us therefore do what He commands elsewhere, and strive to become like men awaiting their master when he returns from the wedding. For to a man holding a plow in a field, or selling or buying something in the market, we do not say, “What are you waiting for?” They are not like those who wait. But when we see someone standing before a door, knocking repeatedly, looking frequently toward the windows, it is no wonder if we say, “What are you waiting for?” Therefore they are like those who wait who have not heard with a deaf ear: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Ps. XLV [46]:11). The Lord will come to those who truly await Him, as did the man who says: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord” (Ps. XXXIX [40]:1). He will come as one returning from a wedding, intoxicated with the wine of charity and forgetful of our iniquities. He will come to those who do not wait as one returning from a wedding, as a strong man overcome with wine. Truly [variant: He will come] drunk, and forgetful of His mercies. Then, as far as they are concerned, God will forget to have mercy. He will come in wrath and indignation, as though furious; but, O Lord, “rebuke me not in your fury.” Let these remarks for now have been made, not so much about the present wedding as on its occasion.

[Col. 0155C] 2. Now let us follow with the disciples the Lord as He goes to the wedding, so that, seeing what He will do, we may believe together with them. When the wine failed, the Mother of Jesus said to Him: “They have no wine.” For, being merciful and most kind, she had compassion on their embarrassment. What could proceed from the fountain of mercy except mercy? What wonder, I say, if bowels of mercy show mercy? Does not one who has held an apple in his hand for half a day retain the apple’s scent for the remainder of the day? How greatly, then, did the power of mercy affect those bowels in which He rested for nine months? For He filled the mind before He filled the womb; and when He came forth from the womb, He did not depart from the soul. The Lord’s response might perhaps seem rather hard and stern; but He knew to whom He spoke, and she did not fail to know who spoke. Finally, that you may know how she received the response, or how much she trusted in the kindness of her Son, she said 806 to the servants: “Whatever He commands you, observe and do.”

3. Now there were set there six stone water-jars. We must now set forth—or rather, show as already set forth—these jars for the purification of true Jews, not by the letter but by the Spirit. Since the Church has not yet reached the perfect purification in which Christ will present her to Himself glorious, without spot or wrinkle or anything of that sort, [Col. 0156A] she meanwhile needs many purifications, so that as sins abound, forgiveness may abound; as misery is multiplied, so mercy may be multiplied—except that the gift is not like the offence. For grace not only washes away sins, but also bestows merits. The six jars, then, are set for those who fall into sin after baptism. For we speak of them because we are among them. We put off the old tunic; but alas, we put it on again more grievously. We washed our feet; but more grievously we soiled them. Therefore, as one person washed what another had defiled, so we must be washed by ourselves when we have become defiled. Water not our own washed those whom another’s fault had defiled. Yet I would not call it so foreign as to deny that it is ours; otherwise it would not defile us. But it is foreign because in Adam we all sinned without knowing it; it is ours because, although in another, we nevertheless sinned, and it was imputed to us by God’s just judgment, though hidden. Yet, so that you may now have no ground for complaint, O man, against Adam’s disobedience Christ’s obedience is given you, so that, if you were sold for nothing, you may also be redeemed for nothing; if you perished unknowingly in Adam, you may be made alive unknowingly in Christ. You did not know when old Adam stretched his guilty hands toward the forbidden tree; likewise you did not know when Christ stretched His guiltless hands upon the saving tree. From the first man the stain by which you were defiled flowed into you; from Christ’s side came the water by which you were cleansed. But now, defiled by your own fault, you will likewise be cleansed by water that is your own—yet by Him and through Him who alone accomplishes the cleansing of sins.

[Col. 0156C] 4. The first jar, then, and the first purification, is contrition, concerning which we read: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, I will remember none of all his iniquities” (Ezek. XVIII:21–22). The second is confession, for everything is washed in confession. The third is the generous giving of alms. Thus you have in the Gospel: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean to you” (Luke XI:41). The fourth is forgiveness of injuries, according to what we say in prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI:12). The fifth is affliction of the body; hence we pray that, made clean by abstinence, we may sing glory to God (*Church Hymn at Prime*). The sixth is obedience to the commandments, as the disciples heard—which would that we too might deserve to hear!—“You are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John XV:3). Surely because they were not like those to whom it is said, “My word has no place in you” (ibid. VIII:37), but in hearing the word they obeyed Him. These are the six jars set for our purification. They are empty and full of wind if they are observed for vain glory. They are filled with water if they are kept in the fear of God, because the fear of the Lord is a fountain of life. Water, I say, is the fear of the Lord: though not very tasty, it excellently cools the soul burning with harmful desires. It is water that can quench [Col. 0157A] the enemy’s fiery darts. Nor is this at odds with the fact that water always seeks the lowest place, and fear draws thought downward, dwells upon lower things, and surveys dreadful places with a fearful mind, according to the saying: “Let them go to the gates of hell” (Isa. XXXVIII:10). But by divine power water is changed into wine when perfect charity casts out fear.

5. The jars are called stone, not so much because of hardness as because of stability. Each held two or three measures. Two measures: a twofold fear—lest one perhaps be cast into Gehenna; lest one perhaps be excluded from eternal life. But because these concern a future that may happen, and the soul can flatter itself, saying, “After you have lived for some time in your pleasures, you will repent; you will neither lose these things now nor perish in those things hereafter,” it is good to add a third measure. This is known, indeed, to spiritual persons; and it is the more useful because it concerns the present. For those who know spiritual food fear lest they should perhaps be deprived of it. Those who have set their hand to mighty things need strong food. Let those who serve in works of mud and brick live on the straw of Egypt; stronger food is necessary for us, because a great journey remains for us, that we may walk in the strength of that food. It is the bread of angels, the living bread, daily bread. This is that of which we are promised that we shall receive a hundredfold in this age (Matt. XIX:29). For as laborers are given daily food while they work and their payment is reserved for the end, so the Lord will render eternal life at the end, while in the meantime He promises and gives a hundredfold. [Note: [Col. 0157D] Gaufridus, no. 68, reports the same words in the *Declamations* hitherto ascribed to Bernard. There, at no. 70, he says that this hundredfold, which Bernard affirms to be proper to religious, is the grace of devotion, the delights of charity, the glory of a good conscience, and joy even in [Col. 0158D] tribulation. Bernard says much the same in Sermon 4 on Psalm XC, nos. 1 and 2. Compare the following Sermon 3 after the Octave of Epiphany, no. 8.] What wonder, then, if one who has already attained this grace fears to lose it? This is the third measure, which he significantly places as an alternative, because it is not for everyone; for the hundredfold was promised not to all, but only to those who have left everything.

## SERMON II. On the spiritual wedding signified in the Gospel history [Alternatively: On the transformation of water into wine]. (John II:1–11)

1. In the Lord’s works, brethren, the outward consideration nourishes even minds less capable; while those whose senses are more exercised find within a more substantial and sweeter food, like the richness and marrow of wheat. For these works are delightful in outward appearance and much more delightful in inward power, just as He Himself was outwardly “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,” but inwardly like the brightness of eternal light, surpassing even the countenances of angels. For outwardly there appeared a man without fault, flesh without sin, a lamb without blemish. “How beautiful are the feet of him who announces peace, who announces good things!” (Isa. LII:7). But much more beautiful [Col. 0158A] and precious is His head, for the head of Christ is God. Delightful is the sight of a man into whom sin does not fall, and blessed are the eyes that saw Him; but far more blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt. V:8). Finally, when the Apostle had reached the kernel, he no longer valued the shell, however very beautiful, saying: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know Him no longer thus” (II Cor. V:16). Surely because the Lord Himself had foretold: “The flesh profits nothing; it is the Spirit who gives life” (John VI:64). But this is the wisdom which Paul speaks among the perfect, not among those concerning whom we read that he said: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II:6, 2). He is wholly sweet, wholly health-giving, wholly delightful, wholly, indeed, desirable according to the bride’s words (Cant. V:16). And as this has been shown in Him, so you will find it also in His works. For their very surface, as considered outwardly, is very beautiful; and if anyone breaks the nut, he will find inside what is more pleasant and much more delightful. You will not find this so among the Fathers of the Old Testament. For in their deeds the mystical signification is beautiful and delightful; yet the deeds themselves, considered in themselves, are sometimes found less worthy, as are Jacob’s actions, David’s adultery, and many like things. The dishes are indeed precious, but the vessels are not equally precious. Perhaps for this reason it was said: “Dark water in the clouds of the air,” because those clouds were dark; and it is added concerning the Lord: “At the brightness before him the clouds passed” (Ps. XVII [18]:12–13).

2. I believe you have now perceived what I mean by saying these things. For today you heard of the miracle performed at the wedding, indeed the beginning of the Lord’s signs; its narrative is sufficiently wondrous, but its meaning is more delightful still. For it was a great indication of divine majesty that, at the Lord’s command, water was changed into wine; but far better is that change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, which he prefigured in this event. For we have all been called to spiritual nuptials, in which the bridegroom is Christ the Lord; hence we sing in the Psalm: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth [Col. 0158D] from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18:6). We ourselves are the bride—if this does not seem incredible to you—both all together one bride, and the individual souls, as it were, individual brides. But when will our frailty be able to conceive this concerning its God: that he loves it with the affection by which a bride is loved by her bridegroom? For this bride is far beneath her bridegroom in birth, in beauty, and in dignity. Yet for the sake of this Ethiopian woman, from far away the Son of the eternal King came; and, in order to betroth her to himself, he did not fear even to die for her. Moses indeed took an Ethiopian woman [Col. 0159A] as his wife, but he could not change the Ethiopian woman’s color; Christ, however, having loved her while she was still lowly and ugly, will present the Church to himself as glorious, without spot or wrinkle. Let Aaron murmur, and Mary too—not the new Mary, but the old; not the Mother of the Lord, but Moses’ sister (Num. 12); not our Mary, I mean. For she is concerned if perhaps something is lacking at the wedding. But you, as is fitting, while priests murmur and the Synagogue murmurs, devote yourselves with all affection to giving thanks.

3. For whence comes this to you, O human soul? Whence comes to you such inestimable glory, that you should deserve to be the bride of him upon whom the angels themselves desire to look? Whence comes this to you: that he should be your bridegroom, [Col. 0159B] whose beauty sun and moon admire, at whose nod all things are changed? What will you render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to you: that you should be companion of his table, companion of his kingdom, finally companion of his bridal chamber, so that the King may bring you into his chamber? Consider now what you should think of your God; consider how much you should dare to hope from him; consider with what arms of reciprocal love he should be loved again and embraced, he who valued you so highly—indeed, who made you of such value. For he refashioned you from his own side when he fell asleep upon the cross for your sake and [variant addition: “for this reason”] accepted the sleep of death. For your sake he went forth from God the Father and left his mother, the Synagogue, so that, cleaving to him, you might become one spirit with him.
