Therefore hear, O daughter, and see, and consider how great is the condescension of your God toward you; forget your people and [Col. 0159C] your father’s house. Abandon fleshly affections; unlearn worldly habits; refrain from former vices; forget harmful customs. For what do you suppose? Does not the angel of the Lord stand ready to cut you in two if perhaps—may he himself avert it!—you admit another lover?

4. For you are already betrothed to him; the wedding feast is already being celebrated, though the supper is being prepared in heaven and in the eternal court. But will wine fail there? Far from it! “We shall be filled with the abundance of God’s house, and shall drink from the torrent of his delight” (Ps. 35:9). A river of wine is certainly prepared for that wedding—wine, I say, which gladdens the heart; for “the rush of the river gladdens the city of God” (Ps. 45:5). But now, because a great journey remains for us, we receive a midday meal here, though not in [Col. 0159D] such abundance; the fullness and satisfaction of the supper are reserved for eternity. Here, therefore, wine sometimes fails: namely, the grace of devotion and the fervor of charity. How often, brothers, after your tearful complaints, must I entreat the Mother of mercy to tell her most gracious Son that you have no wine? And she, I tell you, beloved, if devoutly appealed to by us, will not fail our need; for she is merciful, and the Mother of mercy. For if she had compassion on the embarrassment of those by whom she had been invited, much more will she have compassion on us if devoutly invoked. For our wedding pleases her, and concerns [Col. 0160A] her far more than that one; for from her womb, as from his bridal chamber, the heavenly Bridegroom came forth.

5. Yet who would not be troubled that, at that wedding, the Lord answered his most gracious and most holy mother, saying: “What is there between me and you, woman?” What is there between you and her, Lord? Is it not that of son and mother? Do you ask what she has to do with you [variant: “what you have to do with her”], when you are the blessed fruit of her immaculate womb? Is she not the one who conceived you with her modesty unharmed and bore you without corruption? Is she not the one in whose womb you remained nine months, from whose virgin breasts you were nourished, with whom, when you had become twelve years old, you came down from Jerusalem and were subject to her? Why then, Lord, are you troublesome to her now, saying, “What is there between me and you?” You have very much to do with her in every respect. But I now clearly see that you said, “What is there between me and you?” not as one indignant, nor wishing to put the tender modesty of your virgin Mother to shame; for when the servants came to you at your Mother’s direction, you did without hesitation what she suggested. Why then, brothers, why did he first answer thus? Surely for our sake: so that, once converted to the Lord, we may no longer be troubled by concern for fleshly parents, and so that those family ties may not hinder spiritual exercise. For as long as we are of the world, we are plainly debtors to our parents. But after we have left ourselves, we are much more free from concern for them. Thus we read of a certain brother dwelling in the desert: when his fleshly brother [Col. 0160C] came to him seeking assistance, he replied that he should go to their other brother, who had already died. When the visitor, astonished, replied that he was dead, the hermit answered that he too had likewise died.

> [Note: [Col. 0159D] This was Abbot Apollo. See the *Lives of the Fathers*.]

The Lord therefore taught us very well not to be concerned for the relatives of our flesh beyond what religion requires, when he replied even to his Mother—and such a Mother—“What is there between me and you, woman?” Likewise, elsewhere, when someone told him that his mother was standing outside with the Lord’s brothers and seeking to speak to him, he answered: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” (Matt. 12:48). Where now are those who are accustomed to be so fleshly and vainly concerned about their fleshly relatives, as though they themselves still lived with them?

6. But let us now see what follows. “There were,” says [Col. 0160D] the Evangelist, “six stone water jars set there, according to the purification of the Jews.” Even from this you can more plainly perceive that this is not the fullness but the preparation of the wedding, since purification is still needed. These are therefore the nuptials of betrothal, not of consummation. Far be it from us to believe that there will be vessels of purification at that wedding when Christ presents to himself the Church as glorious, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind! For where [variant: “but where”] there will be no spot, what purification will be necessary? Now indeed is the time for washing; now purification is plainly necessary, when no one [Col. 0161A] is clean from defilement—not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day. Now the bride is washed; now she is purified, so that at those heavenly nuptials she may be presented to her bridegroom without any stain. Let us therefore seek the six water jars in which this washing of the Jews—that is, of those who confess—this purification, may take place. For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us: that truth which alone frees, alone saves, alone washes. But if we confess our sins, water jars of purification will not be lacking to true Jews; for God is faithful to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity (1 John 1:8–9).

7. I consider the six water jars to be six observances which the holy Fathers instituted for cleansing the hearts of those who confess; and all of them, unless I am mistaken, we shall be able to find here. The first water jar, then, is the restraint of chastity, by which whatever lust previously defiled is washed away. The second is fasting, so that abstinence may now cleanse what gluttony stained. Through sloth and idleness also, which is the enemy of the soul, we have contracted many defilements, contrary to God’s sentence, eating bread “in the sweat of another’s face, not our own” (cf. Gen. 3:19). For this reason too the third water jar is set before us, so that those stains may be washed away in the labor of our hands. Thus [Col. 0161B] also through sleepiness and the other works of night and darkness we have sinned much; therefore the fourth water jar, the observance of vigils, is appointed, so that, rising by night to confess the Lord, we may redeem the unprofitable nights of past time. Further, who does not know how greatly the tongue has defiled us by empty talk and lies, by detractions and flatteries, by malicious words and boastful words? For all these, the fifth water jar is necessary: namely, silence, the guardian of religious life, in which our strength lies. The sixth water jar is discipline, by which we live not according to our own judgment but another’s, so that whatever we sinned by living without discipline may be blotted out. These jars are of stone: they are hard, but we need to be washed in them, unless perhaps we wish [variant: “shall wish”] to receive from the Lord a writ of divorce because of our foulness. Yet in their being called stone, not only hardness but, much better, firmness may be understood; for these do not wash unless they endure with steadfast stability.

[Col. 0161D] 8. Therefore the Lord said to the servants: “Fill the water jars with water.” What does this mean, Lord? The servants are concerned about the lack of wine, and you say, “Fill the water jars with water.” They are thinking of cups, and you command that vessels of purification be filled. Exactly so: just as, when Jacob longed for Rachel’s embrace, Leah was substituted by the father (Gen. 29:22–24). To us, brothers, who are your ministers and servants, Christ commands that we fill the water jars with water whenever wine is lacking. It is as though he said: They desire devotion, seek wine, demand fervor; but my hour has not yet come: fill the water jars with water. For what is the water of saving wisdom, though not so sweet, except the fountain of life and “the fear of the Lord,” the beginning of wisdom? Therefore the servants are told: Instill fear, and fill with the spirit of fear not so much the vessels as the hearts, because, in order to attain charity, they must be initiated by fear, so that they too may say: “From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived and have brought forth the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26:18). But how will the water jars be filled? For the Evangelist had said: [Col. 0162B] “Each holding two or three measures.” What are the two measures, and what the third? Certainly the twofold fear common and known to all; while the third is less common and less well known. The first fear is that we may be tortured in Gehenna; the second, that, excluded from the vision of God, we may be deprived of such inestimable glory; the third fills the soul with anxious fear lest perhaps it be abandoned by grace.

9. Indeed every fear of the Lord, just as water extinguishes fire, extinguishes the desire for sin; but especially that fear which immediately confronts every temptation, lest one happen to lose grace, so that a person, left to himself, may slide daily from bad to worse, from a lesser sin into a graver fault—such persons as we plainly see, when they are in filth, still becoming filthier. For against this fear the soul has no ground on which to flatter itself, whether because the quantity of sin is perhaps smaller or because amendment is to come later. For the first two kinds of fear are to some extent hindered by such flatteries. The Lord therefore commands us to fill the water jars with this water. For sometimes they are empty and full of wind, if anyone is so mad as, through the pursuit of vanity, to deprive the observances we mentioned of their eternal reward—like the foolish virgins, in whose vessels there is no oil (Matt. 25:3). Sometimes, however—and this is worse—they are indeed full, but full of poison: envy, murmuring, bitterness of spirit, and detraction. Therefore, lest these things enter while [Col. 0162D] wine is lacking, we are commanded to fill the water jars with water, so that the commandments of the Lord may be kept in fear. This water is changed into wine when fear is cast out by charity and all things are filled with fervor of spirit and joyful devotion.

> [Note: [Col. 0161] Compare Sermon 55 *On Various Subjects*, where these water jars are explained morally in almost the same manner, and Sermon 57 concerning the measures.]

[Col. 0161]

## IN SEPTUAGESIMA

### SERMON I

[Col. 0161D]

1. My brothers, I find great consolation in that saying of the Lord: “He who is of God hears the words of God” (John [Col. 0162D] 8:47). For you gladly listen because you are of God. Nor am I unaware that Scripture says elsewhere: “From him, and through him, and in him are [Col. 0163A] all things” (Rom. 11:36). But those who, according to the Gospel of blessed John, “were born not of the will of the flesh, but of God” (John 1:13), are from him in a far different manner. Thus you will find John himself writing in his Epistle: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin; but the heavenly generation preserves him” (1 John 5:18). “Does not sin,” he says—that is, does not remain in sin—because that heavenly generation, which cannot be deceived, preserves him so that he cannot perish. Or “does not sin” means as much as “does not sin at all,” namely because sin is not imputed to him; for the heavenly generation preserves him in this respect also.

> [Note: [Col. 0163D] This passage, and any similar passages in Bernard, do not at all support the threefold error of heretics. First, that of Jovinian and Pelagius, who maintained that the righteous live without any sins. Second, that of Calvin and his followers, who deny that one who has been justified can fall away from charity. Third, that of the same persons, who assert that believers are justified by the mere non-imputation of sins.  
>
> As regards the first: the holy Doctor explains his thought in Sermon 23 on the *Song of Songs*, no. 15; but more clearly in *On Grace and Free Will*, ch. 9, explaining John’s statement, “Everyone who is born of God,” etc.: “This,” he says, “is said of those predestined to life: not that they do not sin at all, but that sin is not imputed to them, because it is either punished by fitting penance or hidden in charity.” See also Sermon 4 *On Various Subjects*.  
>
> Regarding the second point—that charity once possessed can be lost—he declares in Epistle 42, to Henry of Sens, ch. 4, while discussing feigned faith: “Therefore some depart from faith, because Truth affirms it; consequently also from salvation, because the Savior rebukes it. From this we infer that they also depart from charity, without which salvation cannot exist,” etc. See Melchior Cano, Book IV of *On Theological Commonplaces*, final chapter, in the response to the eighth argument, and William Estius on the aforementioned passage of John, where they assess St. Bernard’s view.  
>
> Regarding the third point—that justification does not consist in God’s non-imputation alone but in a certain supernatural quality—the holy Doctor teaches this clearly in various places, and expressly in Epistle 11 to the Carthusians; and, drawing from it, in the final chapter of the *Treatise on Loving God*, he writes: “Thus charity gives charity: the substantial gives the accidental. Where the giver is signified, the noun is one of substance; where the gift is signified, it is one of quality.” See Sermon 27 on the *Song of Songs*.]

But who shall recount this generation? Who can say: “I am among the elect; I am predestined to life; I am among the number of the children”? Who, [Col. 0163B] I say, can say these things? Scripture itself protests: “A man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Eccl. 9:1). We certainly do not have certainty; but the confidence of hope consoles us, lest we be utterly tormented by the anxiety of this doubt. For this reason certain signs and manifest indications of salvation have been given, so that it may be beyond doubt that one in whom these signs endure belongs to the number of the elect. For this reason, I say, God foreknew and predestined some to be conformed to the image of his Son: so that, while he denies them certainty as a cause for watchfulness, grace may nevertheless afford them confidence as a consolation. This is why we must always be watchful and, in fear and trembling, humble ourselves beneath the mighty hand of God: for we can know, at least in part, what we are; but it is altogether impossible for us to know what we shall be. Therefore let him who stands take heed lest he fall; and let him persevere and make progress in that form which is an indication of salvation and evidence of predestination.

2. Now among the things that afford confidence and furnish matter for hope, there is one especially great thing, of which we have now begun to speak: “He who is of God hears the words of God.” For you will sometimes find certain people listening as though what is said did not concern them at all: as though it did not enter their hearts, examine their conduct, or lead them to consider whether perhaps what they hear said is directed at them. But especially if perhaps the word of God—living and effective, proceeding wherever it wills by its own judgment and not by that of the speaker—should plainly [Col. 0164A] advance against those vices to which they feel themselves bound, they dissemble, turn away the eyes of their heart, or by some contrivance cover over the vices [variant: “the things heard”], and so miserable people deceive themselves. In such persons, therefore, I see no signs of salvation; rather I fear that perhaps they do not hear the word of God because they themselves are not of God. But in you, brothers—thanks be to God—I truly find ears for hearing, since the fruit of the word appears without delay in your amendment; indeed, while I speak, I confess that I sometimes seem to sense the fervor of your zeal. For the more abundantly you draw in, the more the condescension of the Holy Spirit fills my breasts; and the more copiously I am given what to offer you to drink, the more quickly you drink [variant: “have drunk”] what is offered. Therefore I speak to you more often, [Col. 0164B] even beyond the custom of our Order. For I know who said: “Whatever you spend beyond this, when I return, I will repay you” (Luke 10:35).

3. Today, brothers, we celebrate the beginning of Septuagesima, whose name is sufficiently famous throughout the whole Church. But, beloved, I tell you that in this name I have very great compassion for myself. For my spirit is stirred within me, sighing for that homeland in which there is neither number nor measure nor weight. How long shall I receive every good of body and soul by weight, measure, and number? “How many hired servants in my Father’s house have bread in abundance, while I perish here with hunger!” For concerning bodily food it was said to Adam, and it has reached even to me: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” [Col. 0164C] (Gen. 3:19). Yet even when I have labored, bread is given to me by weight, drink by measure, and dishes by number. Such is bodily food. But what of spiritual food? Before I eat, I sigh; and would that, after sighing and weeping, I might deserve even a tiny fragment from the heavenly feast and, like a little dog, eat from the crumbs falling from the table of my masters! O Jerusalem, city of the great King, whom he satisfies with the fat of wheat and whom the rush of the river gladdens! In you there is neither weight nor measure, but fullness and supreme abundance. Nor do you have number, for your participation is “in the same.” But I, who am wholly in change and number, when shall I come to that one thing which I seek? When shall I be filled when your glory appears, O Lord? When shall I be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and when will you give me to drink from the torrent of your delight? For now the droplets falling upon the earth are so scanty that I cannot even swallow my saliva.

4. Exactly so, brothers, it is true: now all things are given by weight, measure, and number; but a day will come when all these shall cease. For concerning number we read that “there is no number of his wisdom” (Ps. 146:5). And elsewhere in the same prophet: “Delights are at your right hand unto the end” (Ps. 15:11). Hear also from the Apostle of weight without measure: “Beyond measure,” he says, “an eternal weight of glory in the heights” (2 Cor. [Col. 0165B] 4:17). Hear “an eternal weight”; but observe that he first said, “beyond measure.” So too I hear Christ promising measure without measure: “A measure,” he says, “pressed down, shaken together, running over” (Luke 6:38). But when will these things come? Certainly at the end of the present Septuagesima, which is the time of our captivity. For we read that the children of Israel, carried captive to Babylon, received a term of seventy years; when these had passed, they returned to their own land, the temple was restored, and the city rebuilt (Jer. 25, 29; 1 Ezra, etc.). But when, brothers, will our captivity end, stretched out through so many years from the very beginning of the world? When shall we be freed from this servitude? When shall Jerusalem, the holy city, be restored? Surely when this Septuagesima is completed, which consists of ten and seven, because of the ten commandments we have received and the seven hindrances by which we are delayed from obedience to the commandments.

5. Our first hindrance and burdensome occupation is the very necessity of this wretched body, which, while it seeks now sleep, now food, now clothing, and the like, unquestionably often hinders us from spiritual exercise. In second place, the vices of the heart hinder us: frivolity, suspicion, movements of impatience or envy, the desire for praise, and similar things which we experience daily in ourselves. Take prosperity in this world and adversity as the third and fourth hindrances. For just as “the corruptible body weighs down the soul,” so “the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks upon many things” (Wis. 9:15). Therefore beware of the snare of temptation from either side, and seek the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left. The fifth hindrance, most serious and dangerous, is our ignorance. In many matters we are wholly uncertain what we ought to do, so that we do not know what we ought to pray for. The sixth hindrance is our adversary, who [Col. 0166A] “goes about as a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). Would that we were delivered from these six tribulations, so that in the seventh evil might not touch us, nor danger overtake us through false brothers. Would that evil spirits alone attacked us with their suggestions, and that human beings did us no harm by pernicious examples, importunate persuasions, words of flattery or detraction, and a thousand other means. You surely see how necessary it is that, against these seven dangers which hinder us, we should be supported by the sevenfold help of the Holy Spirit. For the sake of these seven things by which we are delayed from keeping the Decalogue, the present Septuagesima is observed in the mourning of penitence. Hence the solemn Alleluia is temporarily omitted,

> [Note: [Col. 0165D] Such was indeed the Church’s practice from about the age of Gregory the Great onward, except among the Cistercians. They did not omit the Alleluia before Lent—as Abelard reproaches Bernard in his fifth letter—by the prescription of the Benedictine Rule, chapter 15. Yet long before Bernard, the abbots at the Synod of Aachen in 817 had preferred the Roman practice, ch. 30. It had not yet prevailed in St. Benedict’s time; indeed, neither had the institution of Septuagesima. The Fourth Council of Toledo in 633 insists on the older practice.]

and the mournful history of human transgression is recounted from its beginning [Col. 0166B].

## SERMON II. On the text, “The Lord cast a deep sleep upon Adam” (Gen. 2:21–24)

1. “The Lord cast a deep sleep upon Adam.” He also cast one upon himself, when he became the second Adam; but perhaps there is no small difference. For Adam seems to have fallen asleep through an excess of contemplation; Christ through an affection of compassion: so that Truth cast the former into that sleep, and Charity the latter—though each is the Lord. For John the Evangelist says: “God is charity” (1 John 4:16); and the Lord himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Certainly no one Christian even in name can doubt that Christ’s sleep was wholly charity. For “he lay down”

> [Note: [Col. 0166D] This should be read *accubuit* (“he lay down”), not *occubuit* (“he died”), so that the reclining refers to sleep.]

like a lion: plainly not conquered, but conqueror, laying down his life by his own power and accepting the sleep of death by his own will. But what sort of sleep ought that to be called or believed to have been which the Lord cast upon Adam, during which, with no awareness at all of pain, a rib was taken from the sleeping man’s side to be fashioned into a woman? It seems to me that he fell asleep only by passing beyond bodily senses in contemplation of unchangeable truth and the abyss of divine wisdom. This may especially be inferred from his words. For when he returned, he showed where he had gone, as though coming drunk from the wine-cellar and uttering that great mystery which, much later, the Apostle commended concerning Christ and the Church: “This now is bone of my bones”; and: [Col. 0166D] “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Eph. 5:31–32). Does he seem to you to have slept completely, he who, awakened, burst forth into this utterance? Could he not rather have said: “I sleep, but my heart keeps watch” (Song 5:2)?

2. Yet I say this without prejudice, should anyone perhaps think otherwise, especially if something else is found in the writings of the saints. For I do not think that his sleep was common, or like our dreams, which are brought on neither by excess of contemplation nor by affection of compassion, but by the failing of weakness; which are produced neither by truth nor charity, but by necessity. For “a heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam” (Ecclus. 40:1)—not, however, upon Adam in the beginning, but now upon his children. What is not burdensome to the wretched, for whom even living is labor? For whom—even, what few seem to notice and no one fully feels—the very exercise of the senses is found burdensome, so that it cannot be endured unless we are restored by alternating rest? What is not toil, pain, and affliction of spirit among all things under the sun, when even that by which one takes greatest delight is most burdensome: namely, the animation [Col. 0167B] and sensation of the flesh? Indeed, how sweet its companionship is becomes evident from the sadness of its separation, since it can scarcely at last be torn away, since the very corruption of the body is wholly intolerable to the living being. Certainly it is not the body simply, but “the corruptible body,” that weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15); so you may know that the soul of the first parent was free from this burden so long as it still possessed [variant: “dwelt in”] an incorruptible body. God placed him in freedom, so that, moving between the highest things and the lowest, he might ascend to the former without difficulty and descend to the latter without attraction or necessity: penetrating the former by the natural vigor and purity of his mind, and judging the latter by the authority of one presiding. Finally, the animals were brought [Col. 0167C] to Adam “to see what he would call them” (Gen. 2:19); he was not himself led by curiosity to see them.

3. Reason is not free in this way in us; rather, it must struggle on every side. For it is held captive by the lower things in a kind of entangling glue, and repelled as unworthy from the higher; so that it can neither be torn away from the former without pain nor be admitted to the latter [Col. 0168A] except rarely and with great groaning. Hence those who seek my soul exert force, so that I must cry: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24). And before I eat I sigh, because “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). Nevertheless, there must be unity there and division here, just as Adam fell asleep in contemplation and distinguished the animals by giving them names. Thus Abraham too, in the sacrifice, is read to have divided not the birds but the animals (Gen. 15:9–10). And Martha is troubled about many things, though one thing is necessary—necessary indeed, and most necessary, because this is the better part which shall not be taken away (Luke 10:41–42). Division will cease when fullness comes, and the participation of the whole holy city Jerusalem will be “in the same.” Meanwhile, the Spirit of wisdom is not only one, but manifold: making the inner things firm in unity, but distinguishing outward things under judgment. Both are commended to you in the primitive Church, when “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul,” lest the birds be divided; but distribution was made “to each as anyone had need” (Acts 4:32, 35), so that the animals might be cut apart. Therefore let there also be unity of souls among us, beloved: let hearts be united by loving one, seeking one, cleaving to one, and mutually thinking the same thing. Thus the outward division itself both escapes danger and incurs no scandal, since, although each may have his own endurance and at times his own judgment in managing earthly affairs, and although there are sometimes different gifts of grace and not all members appear to have the same function, inward unity and unanimity gather and bind even this multiplicity with the glue of charity and the bond of peace.

[Col. 0167]

## AT THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST

### SERMON I. What it means to anoint the head and wash the face (Matt. 6:16–17)

[Col. 0167C]

1. Today, most beloved, we enter the sacred season of Lent, the season of Christian warfare. This observance is not peculiar to us; it is one for all who come together in the same unity of faith. Why should Christ’s fast not be common to all Christians? Why should the members not follow their head? If we have received good things from this head, why should we not also endure evil things? Do we wish to reject sorrows and share in joys? If so, we show ourselves unworthy of participation in this head. For everything that he suffers, he suffers for us. But if we are reluctant to cooperate with him in the work of our salvation, in what thereafter shall we show ourselves his fellow workers? It is no great thing for one to fast with Christ who is to sit at the Father’s table with him. It is no great thing for a member to suffer with the head with which it is also to be glorified. [Col. 0168C] Blessed is the member that adheres in every respect to this head and follows it wherever it goes. Otherwise, if it should happen to be cut off and separated, it must immediately also be deprived of the spirit of life. For what portion does not adhere to the head—whence then could it have sensation or life? Nor will there be lacking one who seizes it when cast out, so that even then it may not be without a head. The root of bitterness will sprout again; the poisonous head will again put forth shoots—that head, I mean, which the strong woman, Mother Church, had earlier crushed in that person when he was reborn through her into hope of life, though his fleshly mother had brought him forth by nature as a child of wrath.

2. Therefore whoever has the eyes of his heart unveiled, and sees spiritually, will behold a wholly dreadful monster: a human body indeed, but bearing a demon’s head. Not only so, but surely “the latter state of that man will be worse than the former,” when that viperous head which had previously been cut off returns with no fewer than seven more wicked ones [Col. 0169A] in company. Who would not tremble at the hearing alone? Shall I take a member of Christ and make it a member of demons? Cut off from Christ’s body, shall I, wretched man, be joined to Satan? May that accursed exchange [variant: “communion”] always be far from us, my brothers. For me, it is altogether good to cling to you, O glorious head, blessed forever, into which angels too desire to look. I shall follow you wherever you go: if you pass through fire, I shall not be torn away from you; I shall fear no evils, because you are with me. You bear my pains and suffer for me; you first pass through the narrow opening of suffering, that you may provide a broad entrance for the members who follow. “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ?” (Rom. 8:35). For it is through this charity that the whole body grows through bonds [Col. 0169B] and joints. This is the good glue mentioned by Isaiah (Isa. 41:7). This is that through which it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in one. This is the ointment that descends from the head to the beard, descends from the head even to the hem of the garment (Ps. 132:2), so that not even the smallest fringe lacks anointing. For in the head is the fullness of graces, from which we all receive; in the head is the totality of compassion; in the head is the inexhaustible fountain of divine mercy; in the head is the entire abundance of spiritual ointment, as it is written: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8). Yet Mary too did not fear to anoint that head which the Father had anointed so abundantly. The disciples indeed criticize her; but Truth answers on her behalf that she has performed [Col. 0169C] a good work (Matt. 26:7–10).

3. Finally, what does he command us today in the Gospel? “But you, when you fast,” he says, “anoint your head.” A wondrous condescension! “The Spirit of the Lord is upon him, because he has anointed him”; and yet, preaching the Gospel to the poor, he says: “Anoint your head!” The Father is well pleased in the Son, and while the voice resounds in the heavens, the Spirit descends in the form of a dove. Do you suppose, brethren, that chrism was lacking at Christ’s baptism? The Spirit of the Lord remains upon him; and who can doubt that he was anointed by him? “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). This indeed is the fragrance of spiritual ointment. The Father anointed the Son above his companions, in whom he is uniquely well pleased above all others. [Col. 0169D] For the Father loves the Son with a love truly divine and unknown to every creature. The Father, I say, anointed the Son above his companions, heaping upon him all the gifts of kindness, gentleness, and sweetness, filling him more abundantly with the depths of mercy and compassion. Finally, he sent him to us as the Anointed One, whom he showed us as “full of grace and compassion” [alternatively, “loving-kindness”]. Thus our Head was anointed by the Father, and yet he asks also to be anointed by us. “When you fast,” he says, “anoint your head.” Does the inexhaustible fountain ask water from the stream? Without doubt it asks—or rather, it reclaims it. For rivers return to the source from which they flow, that they may flow again (Eccl. 1:7).

4. Christ does not reclaim what he gave because he has less of it [Col. 0170A], but lest whatever you wish to refer back to him should perish for you. For even the water of a river, if it begins to stand still, itself grows putrid; and when an overflowing flood comes upon it, it is driven back. So indeed, so the flow of graces ceases where there is no return-flow. Not only is nothing increased for the ungrateful person, but even what he had received is turned to his ruin. But one faithful in little is judged worthy of a greater gift.

Anoint your head, therefore, pouring back upon him who is above you whatever devotion, whatever delight, whatever affection is in you. Anoint your head, therefore, so that whatever grace is in you may be referred to him; and seek not your own glory, but his. For he anoints Christ who is his good fragrance in every place. Remember indeed that this saying was directed against hypocrites. “Do not,” he says, [Col. 0170B] “become gloomy like the hypocrites.” He does not forbid us every kind of sadness, but that which appears in the face before human beings. Otherwise, “the heart of the wise is where there is sadness” (Eccl. 7:5); and Paul too does not regret having made the disciples sorrowful, because they were made sorrowful unto salvation (2 Cor. 7:8). The sadness of hypocrites is not of this kind: it is not in the heart but in the face. For they disfigure their faces.

5. Note accordingly that he did not say, “Do not be gloomy like the hypocrites,” but “Do not become”—that is, do not feign yourselves to be so. For common speech says, “He makes himself gloomy,” or “He magnifies himself”; and, “He who pronounces you blessed leads you into error” (Isa. 9:16), and similar expressions, which concern pretence rather than truth. “But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face.” They disfigure [Col. 0170C] their face, but you are commanded to wash yours.

Now there is a face which consists in one’s outward conduct. The faithful servant of Christ washes this, lest he offer any stumbling-block to one who observes him; the hypocrite rather disfigures it, while pursuing things more exceptional and unusual. Nor does he anoint his head, whose affection is estranged from Christ and delights in empty favour. Rather, he anoints himself, that he may diffuse the fragrance of his own reputation. Or certainly, since it is evident that Christ is not the hypocrite’s head, neither can he anoint whatever head of his own he may have, for his mind is soothed not by the witness of his own conscience but by flatteries. “Give us some of your oil,” say the foolish virgins (Matt. 25:8). Why? Because they have no oil in their own vessels. But it is not for the prudent to give oil of this sort. For what they would not wish done to themselves, when would they do it to others?

But hear the Prophet, to whom God had revealed the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom: “Let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Ps. 140:5). Hypocrites buy this oil, as the Lord says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.” For they disfigure their faces in order to appear to be fasting. You see how, in a brief saying, he both marks hypocrites as seekers of singularity and rebukes them for vanity. See also how briefly he urges good things before God and prudent conduct before human beings. “Anoint your head and wash your face”: that is, show yourself outwardly irreproachable in such a way that you strive to win divine grace for yourself; and before human eyes seek not your own glory, but that of your Author.

[Col. 0171A] 6. Yet the washed face may also be understood in another way as a pure conscience, and the anointed head as a devout mind. If you approve this interpretation, these two words, washing and anointing, seem to have been spoken against the twofold vice especially sought by those who fast. One person fasts from a desire for vanity, and to him it is said, “Wash your face.” Another fasts with impatience and resentment, and he needs to anoint his head. This head is the inner mind, which is anointed in fasting when it takes spiritual delight therein.

Or does it seem novel to you for us to say that the head is anointed by fasting? I say more: it is even made fat. Have you never read what is written: “That he may feed them in famine?” (Ps. 32:19). Bodily fasting, then, is an anointing of the head; and the hunger of the flesh is a refreshment of the heart. Why should I not call it an anointing, when it both heals wounds and soothes exasperated consciences? Let the hypocrite, then, buy the sinner’s oil with his fasting. As for me, I do not sell my fasting; it itself is the oil with which I am anointed. “Anoint,” he says, “your head,” lest perhaps some murmur or impatience arise within you. And not only so, but “glory in tribulation” as the Apostle says (Rom. 5:3). Glory, I say, but without any pursuit of vanity, so that your face too may be clean from the oil of the sinner.

## SERMON II. How we ought to turn to the Lord

1. “Turn to me with your whole heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning; and rend your hearts, [Col. 0171C] and not your garments,” says the Lord Almighty (Joel 2:12–13). What does the Lord mean, most beloved, when he commands us to turn to him? For he is everywhere, filling all things, and yet encompassing all things. Where shall I turn, that I may turn to you, Lord my God? “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138:8). What do you command? Where shall I turn to you—to what is above or below, to the right or to the left?

This is counsel, my brethren; it is a secret entrusted only to friends. It is a mystery of the kingdom of God; it is revealed in the ear to the Apostles, for nothing is said to the crowds except in parables. “Unless you are converted,” he says, “and become like this little child, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). I clearly recognize [Col. 0171D] where he wishes us to turn. We must turn to the Little One, that we may learn from him, because he is gentle and humble of heart; for to this end a little child has been given to us.

Certainly, he is also great—but in the city of the Lord, to which it is said: “Rejoice and give praise, dwelling-place of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel” (Isa. 12:6). Why are you puffed up, O man? Why are you exalted without cause? Why do you think lofty thoughts, and let your eyes behold every high thing, which will not turn to your good? The Lord is indeed sublime, but he is not set before you in that way. His greatness is praiseworthy, but not imitable. [Col. 0172A] His magnificence is exalted, and you cannot attain to it; even if you burst yourself, you will not grasp it. “Man shall approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63:7–8). For the Lord is high and looks upon lowly things, and knows lofty things from afar (Ps. 137:6). Humble yourself, and you have grasped him. This indeed is the law of godliness, and because of this law I have waited for you, O Lord.

If perchance the path of loftiness had been set before us, and the way by which the salvation of God might be shown lay there, what would people do to be exalted! How cruelly they would cast one another down and trample one another! How shamelessly they would crawl and strive upward with hands and feet, that men might place themselves above the heads of others! And surely, one who strives to surpass [alternatively, exceed] his neighbours will find many difficulties, have many rivals, and suffer many opponents climbing up against him. Yet nothing is easier for one who wills it than to humble oneself. This, beloved, is the saying that leaves us altogether without excuse, so that we may not even put forward the slightest veil of defence.

2. But let us now see how we must turn to this Little One, the teacher of gentleness and humility. “Turn,” he says, “to me with your whole heart.” Brethren, if he had said merely, “Turn,” adding nothing, perhaps we would be free to answer: “It is done; now set before us another command.” But now he warns us, as I understand it, of a spiritual conversion, which is not accomplished in one day. Would that it could be completed even in the whole life that we spend in this body! For a bodily conversion, if it stands alone, is nothing. It is merely the form of conversion, not its truth, bearing the empty appearance of piety without its power.

Wretched is the person who proceeds wholly into outward things and is ignorant of his inner self, supposing himself to be something when he is nothing, and so deceiving himself. “I am poured out like water,” says the Psalmist in the person of such a man, “and all my bones are scattered” (Ps. 21:15). And another prophet says: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it” (Hos. 7:9). For, looking at his outward surface, he supposes that all is safe with him, unaware of the hidden worm that gnaws away his inner parts. The tonsure remains, the garment has not yet been changed, the rule of fasts is kept, psalms are sung at the appointed [Col. 0172D] hours; “but their heart is far from me,” says the Lord (Mark 7:6).

3. Attend carefully to what you love, what you fear, what makes you rejoice or grieve.

> [Note: [Col. 0171D] The ancients, including Bernard, commonly identify these four as the principal passions, as though they alone were such, because the others depend on them. Compare Sermon 14 on Psalm 90, no. 9; Sermon 50 *On Various Subjects*, [Col. 0172D] nos. 2 and 3; Sermon 85 on the *Song of Songs*, no. 5; Book V of *On Consideration*, no. 9; and also the treatise *On Loving God*, no. 23.]

Under the habit of religion you will find a worldly mind; under the rags of conversion, a perverse heart. For the whole heart is contained in these four affections; and I think that the command to turn to the Lord with your whole heart must be understood in reference to them.

Let your love, therefore, be turned, so that you love absolutely nothing except him, or at least for his sake. Let your fear also be turned to him; [Col. 0173A] for every fear by which you fear anything apart from him, or not for his sake, is perverse. So likewise let your joy and your sorrow be turned equally to him. This will happen if you grieve or rejoice only according to him. For what is more perverse than to rejoice when you have done evil and to exult in the worst things? But sorrow according to the flesh also works death. If you grieve for your own sin or your neighbour’s, you do well, and this sorrow is unto salvation (2 Cor. 7:10). If you rejoice in gifts of grace, this joy is holy and secure joy in the Holy Spirit. In Christ’s love, you ought to rejoice with your brethren in their prosperity and grieve with them in adversity, as it is written: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15).

[Col. 0173B] 4. Yet even bodily conversion is not to be despised, since it is known to be no small aid to this spiritual conversion. This is why, when the Lord had said here, “With your whole heart,” he immediately added, “In fasting,” which plainly belongs to the body. Nevertheless, my brethren, I want you to be warned that this must be observed not only in abstaining from food, but from all enticements of the flesh and every bodily pleasure. Indeed, we must fast much more from vices than from food.

But there is a bread from which I do not want you to fast, lest perhaps you faint on the way. If you do not know it, I mean the bread of tears. For it follows: “In fasting and weeping and mourning.” Repentance for one’s former way of life demands mourning from us; desire for future blessedness demands weeping. “My tears became my bread day [Col. 0173C] and night,” says the Prophet, “while I am told daily, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. 41:4). The newness of this life gives too little pleasure to one who does not yet mourn the old things, does not yet mourn sins committed, does not yet mourn time squandered. If you do not mourn, you plainly do not feel the wounds of the soul and the injury to conscience. Nor do you desire future joys sufficiently if you do not daily ask for them with tears. They are too little known to you if your soul does not refuse to be comforted until they come.

5. Then the Prophet adds: “Rend your hearts, and not your garments.” By these words the earlier people of the Jews are plainly reproved both for hardness of heart and empty superstition. For among them the rending of garments was customary and frequent, but not the rending of hearts. [Col. 0173D] For when would their stony hearts be rent, since they could not even be circumcised? “Rend,” he says, “your hearts, and not your garments.”

Who among you has a will that is habitually found too obstinate about some one thing? Let him rend his heart with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; let him rend it and hasten to distribute it into many small pieces. Otherwise, one does not turn to the Lord with one’s whole heart unless the heart has been rent. For until you receive that one thing in Jerusalem, “whose participation is in the same,” many things are commanded you in the meantime; and “if you offend in one point, you have become guilty of all.” “The Spirit of the Lord is manifold,” says the Wise Man (Wis. 7:22), and one cannot follow the manifold Spirit without manifold rending.

Finally, hear the man whom God had found according to his own heart: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 56:8). Ready for adversity, ready for prosperity; ready for lowly things, ready for lofty things; ready for whatever you command. Do you wish to make me a shepherd of sheep? Do you wish to appoint me king of peoples? “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.” Who entered and went out, and proceeded at the king’s command, as faithfully as David? And he said of sinners: “Their heart is curdled like milk; but I have meditated on your law” (Ps. 118:70). For hence comes hardness of heart, hence obstinacy of mind: someone meditates not on the law of the Lord, but on his own will.

6. Let us therefore rend our hearts, beloved, that we may consequently keep our garments whole. For our garments are virtues. Love is a good garment; obedience is a good garment. Blessed is one who keeps these garments, lest he walk naked. Thus: “Blessed are those whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31:1); and, “Love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). Let us rend our hearts, as has been said, that we may keep these garments whole, just as [Col. 0174C] the Saviour’s tunic was preserved whole. And the rending of the heart not only preserves the garment whole, but also makes it full-length and many-coloured, like the garment received from the holy patriarch Jacob by the son whom he loved above the others (Gen. 37:3). Hence comes perseverance in virtues; hence the variegated unity of a beautiful manner of life. Hence comes that glory of the king’s daughter “in golden fringes, clothed round about with varieties” (Ps. 44:14–15).

Yet this rending of the heart may be understood in another way: if it is perverse, let it be rent unto compunction [alternatively, confession]; if hard, unto compassion. Why should a sore not be lanced, that pus may flow out? Why should the heart not be rent, that the inward parts of compassion may flow forth? Both rendings are altogether beneficial: so that the poison of sin may not lie hidden, shut up in the heart, and that we may not shut the bowels of mercy against a neighbour in need; so that we ourselves too may obtain mercy from our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0173]

## IN LENT

## SERMON III. On the Fast of Lent

[Col. 0173D]

1. I beseech you, beloved, receive the Lenten fast with whole-hearted devotion. It is commended not by abstinence alone, but much more by its sacramental meaning. For if we have fasted devoutly until now, certainly we ought to fast far more devoutly in this holy [Col. 0174D] season. If anything is added to the customary measure of abstinence, is it not very unworthy that what the whole Church bears together with us should weigh upon us as a burden? Until now we alone have fasted until the ninth hour; now all alike will fast with us until evening—[Col. 0175A] kings and princes, clergy and people, noble and lowly, rich and poor together as one.

I say this, brethren, lest anyone perhaps be disturbed by faintheartedness of spirit and receive the present fast with less devotion, recalling perhaps that he found even the burden of the earlier fast quite hard to bear. For our adversary labours as much as he can to strip our burnt offering of the fatness of devotion, so that it may be less acceptable to God and our conscience may rejoice less in spiritual joy; and so, from faintheartedness in endurance, faintheartedness of conscience may also arise. Since we are not ignorant of his devices, I beseech you to keep watch against him with all vigilance. And because God loves a cheerful giver, and our conscience itself is thereby raised with greater confidence, let us diligently set before ourselves the examples of the whole Church, so that our fasts may be more devout.

2. But why do I speak of those whom we have as companions in this observance of fasting, as though we did not have leaders in it far more excellent—indeed, consecrators of it? With what devotion ought we to receive what was handed down by holy Moses as by hereditary right (Exod. 34:28), he to whom the Lord spoke face to face by a privilege special above the other prophets? (Exod. 33:11). With what fervour ought we to embrace what that Elijah commends (3 Kings 19:8), who was carried into heaven in a fiery chariot? (4 Kings 2:11). For behold how many thousands from those days onward have been overtaken by the universal condition of death; yet Elijah, preserved by the Lord, has until now escaped its grasp.

But if Moses and Elijah, though great, are nonetheless our fellow servants and commend this present fast, how greatly does Jesus our Lord commend it, who himself fasted the same number of days? (Matt. 4:2). What sort of man is he—not to say monk, but Christian—who receives with less devotion the fast handed down to him by Christ himself? Finally, beloved, we ought to imitate Christ’s example in fasting with so much greater devotion as it is more certain that he fasted for us, not for himself.

3. Therefore, dearest brethren, let us fast; and let us fast devoutly in this holy time of Lent. Yet let us understand that our Lent does not consist of forty days alone. For we must continue this Lent throughout all the days of this miserable life, while by the help of grace—which is commended in the four Gospels—we must fulfil the Decalogue of the Law. Those are plainly mistaken who think these very few days sufficient for repentance, since it is certain that the entire span of this life has been appointed for repentance alone. “Seek the Lord,” says the prophet, not merely for forty days, but “while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55:6).

For the time for calling upon him will not then be when God is near to no one, but when he will be present to some and exceedingly far off from others. Yet in the meantime, from his being called near it is clear that he is not yet possessed; but he can nevertheless easily be possessed and found. Who seems to you to have been neighbour to the man who fell among robbers? Surely, the one who showed him mercy (Luke 10:36–37). Therefore, because throughout this whole time he is near through mercy, seek the Lord, dearest brethren, while he may be found; call upon him while he is near.

4. Nevertheless, we must seek him with greater fervour during the present Lent, which is not only a part but also a sacrament of this entire period. Therefore, if perhaps our efforts had grown somewhat lukewarm on other days, it is fitting that they now grow warm again in fervour of spirit. If gluttony alone has sinned, then let it alone fast, and that is enough. But if the other members too have sinned, why should they not also fast? Let the eye fast, then, which has plundered the soul; let [Col. 0176B] the ear fast, let the tongue fast, let the hand fast, and let the soul itself fast as well.

Let the eye fast from curious looks and all wantonness, so that it may be suitably humbled and restrained in repentance after wandering badly and freely in guilt. Let the wickedly itching ear fast from tales and rumours, and from whatever is idle and in no way relevant to salvation. Let the tongue fast from detraction and murmuring, from useless, empty, and buffoonish words; and sometimes, for the gravity of silence, even from things that might seem necessary. Let the hand fast from idle gestures and every action not commanded. But far more should the soul itself fast from vices and from its own will. For without this fasting the other things are rejected by the Lord, as it is written: “In the days of your fasts your own wills are found” (Isa. 58:3).

## SERMON IV. On Prayer and Fasting

1. Since the time of the Lenten fast has come, which I urge your love to receive with whole-hearted devotion, I think it fitting to explain somewhat what benefit fasting has and how one ought to fast. First, brethren, because we abstain even from things lawful in themselves, the unlawful deeds previously committed by us are forgiven us. And what is forgiveness of deeds committed except that everlasting fasts are redeemed by a brief fast? For we have deserved Gehenna, where there is never any food, no consolation, and no end; where the rich man asks for a drop of water and does not deserve to receive it (Luke [Col. 0176D] 16:24–26). Therefore fasting is good and salutary: by it everlasting fasts and punishments are redeemed, while sins are thereby redeemed [alternatively, remitted].

Moreover, it is not only an abolishing of sins but an uprooting of vices; it not only obtains pardon but also merits grace; it not only deletes past sins that we have committed but also repels future sins that we could have committed.

2. I shall mention one further thing which, I think, you have often experienced and can readily understand. Fasting gives devotion and confidence to prayer. See how fasting and prayer are joined to each other, as it is written: “A brother helping a brother, both shall be comforted” (Prov. 18:19). Prayer obtains the power to fast, and fasting merits the grace to pray. [Col. 0177A] Fasting strengthens prayer; prayer sanctifies fasting and presents it to the Lord. For what profit would fasting bring us if it were left on earth? Far be that from us. Let fasting, then, be raised up by a certain wing of prayer. Yet lest this wing perhaps prove insufficient, it must be joined by another. “The prayer of the righteous,” says Scripture, “pierces the heavens” (Ecclus. 35:20–21).

Let our fasting therefore have two wings by which easily to pierce the heavens: prayer and justice. And what is justice except that which renders to each person what is his due? Therefore do not regard God alone, as though he were the only concern. For you are a debtor also to your superiors and to your brethren; and God does not wish you to despise those whom he himself does not despise. The Apostle does not without reason say: “Providing good things not only before God, but also before human beings” (Rom. [Col. 0177B] 12:17). Perhaps you said: “It is enough for me if God alone approves what I do; what concern have I with human judgment?” But be certain that whatever you do with scandal to his children and contrary to the will of him whom you ought to obey as his vicar is altogether displeasing to God.

“Sanctify the fast,” he says; “call an assembly” (Joel 3:15). What is it to call an assembly? To preserve unity, love peace, and cherish fraternity. That proud Pharisee fasted; he sanctified the fast, for he fasted twice on the Sabbath and gave thanks to God. But he did not call an assembly, saying: “I am not like the rest of humankind” (Luke 18:11). Therefore, supported by only one wing, his fasting did not reach heaven.

You therefore, dearest brethren, wash your hands in the blood of the sinner, and be altogether careful that your fasting have two wings: holiness and peace, without which no one shall see God. Sanctify the fast, so that pure intention and devout prayer may offer it to the divine majesty. Call an assembly, so that it may accord with unity. “Praise the Lord with tambourine and choir” (Ps. 150:4), so that the mortification of the flesh may be harmonious.

3. Since we have said something about fasting and justice, it is fitting to say a few words about prayer as well. The more effective it is when made as it ought, the more cunningly the adversary is accustomed to obstruct it. Sometimes prayer is gravely hindered by faintheartedness of spirit and excessive fear. This usually happens when a person so reflects on his own unworthiness [Col. 0177D] that he does not turn his eyes to divine goodness. For “deep calls to deep” (Ps. 41:8): the luminous deep calls to the dark deep; the deep of mercy calls to the deep of misery. The human heart is indeed deep and unsearchable. But if my iniquity is great, Lord, your loving-kindness is far greater. Therefore, when my soul is troubled within me because of myself, I remember the multitude of your mercies and take breath in it; and when I enter into my weaknesses, I do not wish to remember your righteousness alone.

> [Note: [Col. 0177D] Here manuscripts and printed editions vary. Some read, “Into my powers, I do not wish,” etc. Horstius reads “your powers.” [Col. 0178D] But our reading is better, so that “weaknesses” may refer to faintheartedness.]

4. Yet just as prayer that is too timid is dangerous, so on the opposite side there is no less—indeed, greater—danger if it is rash. Hear what the Lord says to the prophet concerning those who pray in this way: “Cry aloud,” he says, “do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1), and so forth. “Like a trumpet,” he says, because rash persons must be rebuked with a vehement spirit. “For they seek me,” though they have not yet found themselves.

I say this not to take away sinners’ confidence in prayer. Rather, I want them to pray as a people that have committed sin, not righteousness. Let them pray for pardon of their sins in a contrite heart and humble spirit, like that publican: “God,” he said, “be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). For by rashness I mean when someone in whose conscience sin or some vice still reigns walks in things too great and wonderful for him, being insufficiently concerned [Col. 0178B] for the danger to his soul.

A third danger arises if prayer is lukewarm and does not proceed from living affection. Timid prayer indeed does not pierce heaven, because excessive fear constrains the mind, so that prayer cannot, I will not say ascend, but cannot even go forth. Lukewarm prayer, however, languishes and fails in its ascent because it has no strength. Rash prayer ascends, but rebounds; for it is resisted. Not only does it fail to obtain grace, but it even merits offence. But prayer that is faithful, humble, and fervent will without doubt pierce heaven; and therefore it is certain that it cannot return empty.

## SERMON V. On the Threefold Mode of Prayer

1. The love by which I am concerned for you, my brethren, compels me to speak to you; and under its pressure I would speak much more often, were I not hindered by so many occupations. Nor is it surprising that I am concerned for you, since I find in myself much matter and occasion for concern. For whenever I consider my own misery and manifold dangers, there is no doubt that my soul is troubled within me. Nor is my concern for each one of you any less, if indeed I love you as myself. He who searches hearts knows how often concern for you outweighs concern for myself in my heart.

Nor is it surprising that I have much concern and great fear troubles me for all of you, whom I see placed in such misery and in such great [Col. 0178D] dangers. For we ourselves, as is plain, carry our snare; everywhere we carry about our own enemy. I mean this flesh, born from sin and nourished in sin, corrupted greatly by its very origin and much more deeply depraved by evil habit. Hence the flesh so keenly desires against the spirit; hence it constantly murmurs and is impatient of discipline, suggests unlawful things, and neither obeys reason nor is restrained by any fear.

2. To it is added, it is aided by, and it is used against us by the most cunning serpent, whose sole desire, pursuit, and business is to shed the blood of souls. He is the one who continually devises evil, stirs up the desires of the flesh, as it were fans the natural fire of concupiscence with poisonous suggestions, inflames unlawful impulses, prepares occasions for sin, and does not cease to tempt human hearts by a thousand arts of harm. He is the one who binds our hands with our own belt and, as the saying goes, beats us with our own stick, so that the flesh given as an aid may become our ruin and snare.

3. But what profit is there in pointing out dangers if no consolation and no remedies are supplied? The danger is great indeed, and the struggle hard against a household enemy—especially since we are strangers and he a citizen; he inhabits his own country, while we are exiles and pilgrims. It is also a great peril to have such frequent, indeed continuous, conflicts against the stratagems of diabolical deceit—an enemy whom we cannot even see, and whom both a subtle nature and long practice in malice have made exceedingly crafty.

Nevertheless, it lies within us, if we do not wish to be conquered; and none of us is defeated in this contest against his will. “Your desire is under you, and you shall rule over it” (Gen. 4:7). The enemy can arouse the impulse of temptation; but it is within your power, if you will, to give or refuse consent. It is within your power, if you will, to make your enemy your servant, so that all things may work together for your good. Behold: the enemy inflames desire for food, suggests thoughts of vanity or impatience, or stirs a movement of lust. Only do not consent; and as often as you resist, so often you will be crowned.

4. Nevertheless, brethren, we cannot deny that these things are troublesome and dangerous. But even in the contest itself, if we resist manfully, a certain holy tranquillity is born from a good conscience. I believe also that if, as soon as we notice these thoughts within us, we do not allow them to linger, but the mind is aroused against them in vehement spirit, the enemy will depart from us in confusion and will not so readily return at once.

But who are we, or what is our strength, that we should be able to withstand so many [Col. 0179D] temptations? This was surely what God sought; this was what he laboured to bring us to: that, seeing our weakness and that we have no other help, we might run with all humility to his mercy. Therefore, brethren, I ask you always to keep at hand the safest refuge of prayer, about which I remember having spoken a little earlier at the end of the sermon.

3. Yet whenever I speak about prayer, I seem to hear in your hearts certain words of human thought, which I have often heard from others and sometimes experienced in my own heart. For why is it that, although we never cease from prayer, scarcely any of us seems ever to experience what the fruit of prayer is? As we come to prayer, so we seem to return: no one answers us a word, no one gives us anything, and we seem to have laboured in vain.

But what does the Lord say in the Gospel? “Do not judge according to appearance,” he says, “but judge righteous judgment” (John 7:24). And what is righteous judgment except the judgment of faith? For “the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4). Therefore follow the judgment of faith and not your experience, because faith is true but experience deceptive. What then is the truth of faith except what the Son of God himself promises: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you shall receive it, and it shall be done for you”? (Matt. 21:22).

Let none of you, brethren, make light of his prayer. For I tell you that he to whom we pray does not make light of it. Before it has gone forth from our mouth, he commands it to be written in his book. And we may confidently hope for one of two things: either he will give what we ask, or what he knows to be more useful for us. For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought; but he has compassion on our ignorance. Kindly receiving our prayer, he does not grant what is either of no use to us at all, or not yet necessary to be given so quickly. Yet prayer will not be fruitless.

6. Yes indeed—if we do what the psalm exhorts us to do, that is, if we delight in the Lord. For holy David says: “Delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the petitions of your heart” (Ps. 36:4 [Vulgate]). But what is it, O Prophet, that you so unconditionally exhort us to delight in the Lord, as though such delight lay ready to our hand? We know the pleasures of food, sleep, rest, and the other things that are on earth; but what delight does God possess, that we should delight in him? My brothers, secular people may say this; you cannot. For which of you is there who has not often experienced the delight of a good conscience? Who has not tasted the savor of chastity, humility, and charity? This is not the delight of drink or food, nor of any similar thing; yet it is delight, and greater than all those. For it is divine, not carnal, delight; and when we delight in these things, we plainly delight in the Lord.

7. Yet perhaps many complain that they experience this pleasant affection, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, too seldom—doubtless because meanwhile they are exercised by temptations. And they act much more courageously if they pursue the virtues themselves, not for the pleasure they experience, but for the virtues themselves and for God’s good pleasure alone, with their whole intention, even if not with their whole affection. Nor is there doubt that one of this kind most fully fulfills the Prophet’s exhortation when he says: “Delight in the Lord”; for he speaks not of affection but of practice. That affection belongs to blessedness; practice belongs to virtue. “Delight,” he says, “in the Lord”: direct yourself to this, strive for this—that you may delight in the Lord—and he will grant you the petitions of your heart. But observe that he said *petitions of the heart*: petitions approved by the judgment of reason. You have no ground for complaint, but rather for being wholly occupied in thanksgiving with all your affection; since your God has such care for you that, whenever in ignorance you ask for what is useless to you, he does not grant you this, but exchanges it for a more useful gift. Thus a fleshly father gladly gives bread to a little child who asks for it; but when the child asks for a knife, which he judges unnecessary, he does not consent, but rather breaks the bread he had given him, or orders one of the servants to break it, so that the child may have neither danger nor labor.

8. Now I believe that the petitions of the heart consist in three things, nor do I see what besides these any elect person ought to ask for himself. Two belong to this present time—namely, the goods of body and soul; the third is the blessedness of eternal life. Nor should you be surprised that I have said bodily goods are to be sought from God, since all bodily things, just as all spiritual goods, are his. Therefore we must ask and hope from him for the means by which we may be sustained in his service. Nevertheless, we must pray more frequently and more fervently for the needs of the soul—that is, to obtain the grace of God and the virtues of the soul. Likewise, we must pray for eternal life with all piety and all desire, where there will doubtless be full and perfect blessedness of body and soul.

9. In these three requests, if they are to be petitions of the heart, we must observe three things. For excess commonly creeps into the first, impurity into the second, and at times pride into the third. Temporal things are sometimes sought for pleasure, virtues for display; and perhaps some seek eternal life not in humility, but as though trusting in their own merits. I do not say this to deny that grace received gives confidence in prayer; but no one ought to place in it his confidence of obtaining. These first [elsewhere: preceding] gifts accomplish only this: that still greater gifts may be hoped for from that mercy which gives these. Therefore let prayer for temporal things be restricted to necessities alone; let prayer for the virtues of the soul be free from every impurity and directed only to God’s good pleasure; and let prayer for eternal life be made in every humility, presuming upon the divine compassion alone—as is fitting.

## SERMON VI. On the Lord’s Prayer. (Matt. 6:9–13.)

1. The will of the Lord, brothers, which first created the angels by making them what they are, afterward, when accomplished in them, made them blessed. For just as the Word which was in the beginning, taking flesh, is said—and truly said—to have “become flesh” (John 1:1, 14), so that eternal will was made in the angel when it wholly absorbed the angelic will into itself. Why should it not be said to have been made in the angel, when it became angelic? For this is the summit of their happiness, this the torrent of heavenly delight: that the divine will itself has become the will even of angels, so that, just as the whole ordering of creation pleases God, so they too rejoice in all things and delight in everything.

This, therefore, is what we pray: that this will, as it has been accomplished in heavenly creatures, may also be accomplished in earthly ones; that, as the angel, so the human being, cleaving to God, may be one spirit with him. But alas for me! How many obstacles separate us, how many hindrances prevent it! Malice interposes itself between us; weakness interposes itself; our concupiscence and ignorance interpose themselves. For there is in us, as though by nature—rather, by the destruction of nature—a most evil disposition and a lust for doing harm, so that an inextinguishable delight in malice is found in our wretched souls. And what is farther from the divine will? Truly a great chaos has been fixed between us and it in this respect: for while it always delights God to confer benefits, in us, ungrateful as we are, there arises instead a most cruel disposition, wishing to harm even the innocent. From this springs every root of bitterness; from this grow envy, detractions, dissensions; from this enmities run wild. These poisonous shoots, indeed, must always be cut off with the sickle of justice, by which we root out from ourselves the impulse to do to anyone what we do not wish done to ourselves; and by which we do to others what we wish people to do to us. Yet malice cannot be wholly uprooted or extirpated from our hearts while we remain in this world, which lies wholly in the evil one. The serpent’s head is indeed crushed, but it is often found lying in wait for the heel.

2. In the second place, we are also hindered by the weakness of this corruptible body, lest our will be able to cleave to the divine will. What we feel to be painful cannot but displease us; and in these matters our will frequently disagrees with the divine will. In order that it may not wholly oppose it, we need fortitude, which is the second kind of virtue.

3. Nor is bodily affliction the only hindrance: concupiscence also hinders us, by which we are drawn apart by manifold and insatiable desires. But when can a will full of windings and corners be united to that which is utterly straight and in every respect without distortion? Alas for me, Lord God! Everywhere there are wars for me, everywhere weapons fly, everywhere dangers, everywhere impediments! Wherever I turn, there is nowhere any security. I fear both what soothes and what troubles: hunger and refreshment, sleep and vigils, labor and rest, all wage war against me. “Give me neither riches nor poverty,” prays the wise man (Prov. 30:8), doubtless because on either side there is a snare, on either side danger. If temperance restrains concupiscence—for this is the one remedy in such a case—there will indeed then be some union, but it will not be complete. Hence the Apostle also confesses concerning himself: “I myself with my mind consent to the law of God, but with my flesh to the law of sin, which is in my members” (Rom. 7:25, 23). Thus he cleaves in part and disagrees in part, until that which is perfect comes and that which is in part is abolished.

4. The fourth hindrance is ignorance, which, as you too know, harms us greatly. For how can I follow God’s will when it goes before me, if I do not know it? Yet I know only in part, and not yet as I am known. Therefore we must seek with all desire an increase of prudence, so that God may make his will more and more known to us, and we may know at every time what is pleasing to him. Thus the perfection of the virtues—justice, fortitude, temperance, and prudence—will complete that union, so happy and so desirable, so that we may have one will with God, and whatever pleases him may please us too. And this will be for us—as was said above concerning the angels—utterly perfect joy.

5. We pray that the kingdom of the Lord may come, so that we may have full security through the power of the kingdom. When we ask that his name be sanctified, we are altogether desiring already to advance in knowledge of him above ourselves. When in ourselves we have both happy security and secure happiness, we shall then be carried with the whole force of the spirit toward him who is above us. “Hallowed be thy name.” His name is his glory. And when is that glory not holy? Yet his glory is said to become holy when it is glorified by us in holiness; just as we ask that his will, which is eternal, may be accomplished in us, so that it may become ours. Therefore the first thing we ask to be accomplished—the greatest thing—is that the undefiled holiness of his glory may become known to us. Thereafter we desire what concerns ourselves: the power of the kingdom for security, and the perfection of his will in us for joy.

But because, not yet enjoying that perfection, we cannot obey the divine will without great labor, we need food lest we fail—we need, I say, daily bread. Since we also stray from it often and sin—that is, forsake it—we necessarily beg forgiveness, saying: “Forgive us our debts,” etc. And lest, after receiving forgiveness of sins, we perhaps fall again into the same things, we must pray to that same one not to lead us into temptation, but rather to bring us out and deliver us from evil. Amen.

## SERMON VII. On the Stranger, the Dead Man, and the Crucified Man

1. Blessed are those who show themselves strangers and pilgrims to this evil present age, keeping themselves unstained from it. For “we have here no lasting city, but seek the city that is to come” (Heb. 13:14). Therefore let us abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul, as strangers and pilgrims. For the pilgrim walks along the royal road; he turns neither to the right nor to the left. If he happens to see people quarrelling, he pays no attention; if people marrying, dancing in choruses, or doing anything else whatever, he nevertheless goes on, because he is a pilgrim and such matters do not concern him. He sighs for his homeland and makes his way toward it; having clothing and food, he does not wish to burden himself with other things. Blessed indeed is the person who thus recognizes and laments his state of exile, saying to the Lord: “For I am a stranger with thee and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 38:13 [Vulgate]).

This is great indeed, but perhaps there is some higher degree. For although the pilgrim does not mingle with the citizens, he may nevertheless sometimes delight in seeing what is done, hearing about it from others, or himself recounting what he has seen. By these and similar things, even if he is not wholly held fast, he is nevertheless detained and delayed, as he remembers his homeland less and hastens toward it with less desire. Indeed, he may delight in them so greatly [elsewhere: for so long] that he is no longer merely delayed and arrives less quickly, but, remaining altogether, does not arrive even late.

2. Who, then, is more alien to the activities of the world than a pilgrim? Surely those to whom the Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3). A pilgrim can, by reason of provisions for the journey, easily be delayed by seeking more than is fitting and burdened by carrying it; a dead man does not feel it even if burial itself is lacking. Thus he hears those who blame him as those who praise him, flatterers as detractors—indeed, he does not hear at all, because he is dead. Entirely blessed is the death that keeps one so unstained; indeed, that makes one wholly alien to this world. Yet it is necessary that Christ live in one who does not live in himself. For this is what the Apostle says: “Yet I live—no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). It is as if he said: “To all other things I am dead; I do not perceive them, attend to them, or care for them. But whatever belongs to Christ finds me alive and ready. If I can do nothing else, at least I perceive it: I am pleased by what I see done for his honor, and displeased by what is done otherwise.” This is altogether a great degree.

3. But perhaps something still higher can be found. In whom, then, shall we seek it? In whom, do you suppose, but in the one of whom I was just speaking, who was caught up to the third heaven? For who forbids us to call it the third heaven if you can find some degree above these?
