Hear him, then, from that great height, glorying not in himself but saying: “But far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). Not merely, he says, dead to the world, but crucified: which is an ignominious kind of death. I am crucified to it, and it likewise to me. Everything the world loves is a cross to me: delight of the flesh, honors, riches, empty human praise. But I am fastened to those things which the world regards as a cross; I cleave to them, I embrace them with my whole affection.

Is not this person greater than the second and first degree? The pilgrim, if prudent and not forgetful of his pilgrimage, passes through, albeit with effort, and is not greatly entangled in worldly matters. The dead man equally despises the pleasant and the harsh things of this age. But for one caught up to the third heaven, everything to which the world cleaves is a cross; and he cleaves to those things which appear to be a cross to the world. Yet in these words of the Apostle it may also suitably be understood that the world was crucified to him by his judgment of it, while he himself was crucified to the world by compassion. For he saw the world crucified by the bonds of vices, and he was crucified to it by an affection of compassion.

4. Let each of us now weigh the degree in which he stands, and let us strive to advance day by day, because “they shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83:8 [Vulgate]). Above all, I beseech you, let us strive during this holy season to live in every purity, since a fixed and brief number of days has been appointed, lest human weakness despair. For if we were told, “At all times be wholly vigilant to preserve the purity of your manner of life,” who would not despair? But now we are admonished to amend, within a brief number of days, all the negligences of other times, so that at least in this way we may taste the sweetness of perfect purity, and thereafter, at every time, bright traces of this holy Lent may shine forth in our way of life.

Let us therefore, brothers, undertake this holy season with entire devotion, and now more especially repair our spiritual arms. For now the Savior engages the devil with a certain general army of the whole world; blessed are those who have fought valiantly under such a leader. Throughout the whole year the household of the king fights, and is continually in readiness for battle [elsewhere added: struggle]; but once, at a fixed season, the whole empire is assembled in a general army. Blessed are you who have deserved to be members of the household, to whom the Apostle says: “Now you are no longer strangers and pilgrims, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. 2:19). What, then, ought those to do who have undertaken to fight all year, when even those who were previously untrained and idle take up spiritual arms? Surely they must press on in their customary struggle more than usual, so that some great victory may accrue to the glory of our King and to our salvation.

## ON PSALM 90 [Vulgate], “HE WHO DWELLS”: SEVENTEEN SERMONS, DELIVERED IN LENT

[Note: In Vatican manuscript no. 663 it is called *Book on the Psalm “He Who Dwells”*, and consists not of sermons but of eighteen chapters. In certain manuscripts only fifteen sermons are counted, the first three having been combined into one. They were delivered after the year 1138, as is clear below from Sermon 6.]

### PREFACE

1. I consider your labors, brothers, not without a great feeling of compassion. I seek some consolation that I may offer; a bodily one presents itself, but it is of no benefit and may even do very great harm. For a small reduction in seed produces no small loss of harvest; and if your penitence is diminished through cruel compassion, little by little your crown is deprived of its jewels. What then are we to do? Where is the prophet’s meal? (2 Kgs. 4:41 [Vulgate]). For “there is death in the pot,” and you are “being put to death all day long” in many fasts, frequent labors, excessive vigils, besides the inward contrition of hearts and the multitude of temptations. You are being put to death, but for him who died for you. And if your tribulation abounds for him, your consolation will abound through him, so that the soul which refuses consolation in other things may delight in him. For in him even tribulation itself may find a certain great consolation.

Is it not certain that what you endure is beyond human strength, beyond nature, contrary to habit? Another, therefore, bears these things: without doubt, he who, according to the Apostle, “upholds all things by the word of his power” (Heb. 1:3). Is not the enemy now slain by his own sword, and does not the greatness of tribulation—by which he was accustomed to tempt—overcome temptations all the more, as the surest proof of the divine presence? For what need we fear if he is present who bears all things? “The Lord is the protector of my life; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. 26:1 [Vulgate]). “For if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, for thou art with me” (Ps. 22:4 [Vulgate]). What sustains the entire mass of the earth? And upon what does the whole world rest? For if there is something that supports all else, by what is it itself supported? Nothing is found except the Word of power upholding all things. “For by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6 [Vulgate]).

2. Therefore, so that you may have consolation in the word of the Lord, especially in these days, when—as is altogether fitting—your labor is somewhat greater, it will, I trust, not be useless to discuss with you something from the holy Scriptures, as some of you have also requested. We should choose for ourselves the very psalm from which the enemy took an occasion of temptation [Note: For the devil, in tempting Christ, misused the words of Psalm 90, namely verse 11.], so that the weapons of the evil one may be shattered from the very source from which he presumed to seize them for his own use.

Therefore, brothers, I do not want you to be unaware that all who make an unholy use of something from the holy Scriptures and hold the truth of God in falsehood, as some sometimes do, are plainly imitators of the enemy. Beware of this, beloved, because it is utterly devilish; those who do it prove themselves to belong to his party, attempting, to their own destruction, to pervert writings that bring salvation. But I shall delay no longer on this point: I think it sufficient to have touched on it briefly. Let us now attempt, with the Lord’s help, to discuss and explain something concerning the psalm itself that we have chosen.

## SERMON I. On the First Verse: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven.”

1. Who is an inhabitant of divine help can be better recognized from those who do not dwell in it. You will find three kinds of such persons: one class does not hope; another despairs; a third hopes in vain. For he does not dwell in God’s help who has not made God his helper, but trusts in his own strength and in the multitude of his riches. He is deaf to the voice of the prophet saying: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55:6). Seeking only temporal things, he envies evildoers when he sees the prosperity of sinners; and he removes himself far from the help of the Most High, because he does not judge that he needs it for such things.

But what business have we to judge those outside? I fear, brothers, lest perhaps there be even among us someone who does not dwell in the help of the Most High, but trusts in his own strength and in the multitude of his riches. For perhaps someone has fervor, being strong in vigils, fasts, labor, and similar things; or has also, as he thinks, acquired over a long time the riches of many merits. Trusting in these, he is more slack in the fear of God and now easily turns, with a ruinous kind of security, toward idleness and curiosities; he murmurs, detracts, and judges others. If he dwelt in the help of God, surely he would attend to himself and fear to offend one whom he knew to remain so necessary to him. For he ought to have feared God more and been more solicitous in proportion as he had already received greater gifts from him. We cannot keep or retain without him what we have received from him.

Yet now—what we say and see not without sorrow—there are some who are sufficiently fearful and vigilant at the beginning of conversion, until they have received some beginning of religious life [elsewhere: conversion]; and when they ought to desire all the more, according to the saying, “Those who eat me shall still hunger” (Sir. 24:29), they begin to act as though saying: “Why should we serve him any longer, since we now have what he was going to give?” Oh, if you knew how little you have, and how quickly you would lose even that, unless he who gave it preserved it! These are the two things that can make us very watchful and subject to God, so that we may not belong to those who do not dwell in the help of the Most High because they do not consider it necessary to them. These are the persons who do not hope in the Lord.

2. There are also others who despair: those, namely, who, considering their own weakness, fail and are overwhelmed by faintheartedness of spirit. They dwell in their own flesh and are always intent upon their own weakness, ready to enumerate at once everything they suffer. For wherever you direct your attention, ingenuity is effective. But they do not dwell in God’s help, nor do they know it; nor are they able to rise up so as ever to think of it. There are others who do indeed hope in the Lord, but in vain, because they flatter themselves so concerning his mercy that they do not amend their sins. This hope is wholly empty and brings shame, because charity is lacking. Against such persons the prophet says: “Cursed is he who sins in hope” [Note: It is uncertain who this prophet is, unless it is Jeremiah, who has something similar in chapter 17, verse 5.]; and another says: “The Lord is well pleased with those who fear him, and with those who hope in his mercy” (Ps. 146:11 [Vulgate]). About to say, “those who hope,” he significantly first added, “those who fear him.” For one hopes in vain who, by his contempt, drives grace away from himself and wholly empties his hope.

3. Therefore none of these three dwells in the help of the Most High. The first dwells in his merits, the second in punishments, the third in vices. The dwelling of the third is unclean; that of the second is anxious; that of the first foolish and dangerous. For what is more foolish than to dwell in a house scarcely begun? Do you think that you have completed it? Yet “when a human being has finished, then he begins” (Sir. 18:6). In short, this dwelling is altogether ruinous, and needs support and propping up more than inhabitation. Is not the present life fragile and uncertain? Whatever is founded upon it must necessarily be similar. For who could believe a building stable when it is built upon a fragile foundation? The dwelling of those who hope in their own merits is dangerous because it is ruinous.

The dwelling of those who are cast down into despair by considering their own weakness is anxious, and we have said that they dwell in torments. For while they endure punishments in which they are worn down night and day, they are tortured still more by punishments they do not yet feel. Thus the evil of the day does not suffice for them; they are oppressed even by things they may perhaps never experience. What torments—what hell more unbearable—can be imagined? Especially since they are burdened with such labor and are not sustained by the nourishment of heavenly bread. These are those who do not dwell in the help of the Most High because they despair. The first group does not seek it because they do not at all feel that they need it. The last group is far from it because it seeks God’s help in a way in which it cannot obtain it.

Only those dwell in the help of the Most High who desire only to obtain this help and fear only to lose it, continually and anxiously occupied with thought concerning it—which is surely the piety of God’s worship. Blessed indeed is the one who thus dwells in the help of the Most High, because he “shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven.” What among the things beneath heaven can harm one whom the God of heaven wills to protect and preserve? Now beneath heaven are all things that can harm: beneath heaven are the powers of the air, beneath heaven this present evil world, and the flesh that lusts against the spirit.

4. It is therefore excellently said: “He shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven,” so that whoever has deserved to possess his protection may fear none of the things beneath heaven. Or perhaps the sentence depends on the following verse: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven; he shall say to the Lord: Thou art my protector.” In that case, “he shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven” explains the preceding clause, “He who dwells in the help of the Most High.” Or it may rather appear to add that we must seek not only help for doing good, but also protection for deliverance from evil.

But carefully observe that he says “in protection,” not “in presence.” The angel rejoices in his presence; would that I might abide in his protection. The angel is blessed in his presence; would that I might be secure in his protection. “Of the God of heaven,” he says. Though it is not doubted that he is everywhere, he is nevertheless in heaven in such a way that, by comparison with his presence there, he scarcely seems to be on earth. This is why we say in prayer: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). For just as the soul, though it is in the whole body, is more excellently and distinctively in the head, in which all the senses are—for in all the other members it exercises scarcely one sense only, namely touch, so that, in comparison with the manner in which it is in the head, it seems in a sense not so much to inhabit as to govern the other members—so, if we consider that presence which the blessed angels enjoy, we may seem scarcely to possess even the protection and name of God. Yet blessed is the soul that deserves even this protection. For it will say to the Lord: “Thou art my protector.” But let us reserve this for another sermon.

## SERMON II. On the Second Verse: “He shall say to the Lord, Thou art my protector,” etc.

1. “He who dwells in the help of the Most High,” says the Prophet, “shall say to the Lord: Thou art my protector and my refuge; my God, I will hope in him.” He will say this in thanksgiving, confessing to the Lord and to his mercy for his twofold help. For everyone who still dwells in help, not in the kingdom, frequently needs to flee and sometimes falls. While we are in this body, we must flee, I say, from the face of pursuing temptation. If we flee less quickly, we are sometimes—as often happens—driven forward and overthrown; but the Lord receives us.

Therefore he is a refuge, so that we may swiftly flee the stoner who comes with the dung of sluggish oxen, and may escape that exceedingly foul stoning (Sir. 22:1). He is also a receiver, so that even when we have fallen we may not be dashed to pieces, because he puts his hand beneath us. Therefore, when we sense the assault of temptation in our thought, let us immediately flee to him and humbly seek help. But if it perhaps overtakes us, as sometimes happens when we flee to him more slowly than we ought, let us be anxious that the hand of the Lord may receive us. For human beings must sometimes fall while they are detained in this age; but some are dashed down and others are not, because God puts his hand beneath them. But how can we distinguish them, so as, following the Lord’s example, to separate the sheep from the goats, the righteous from the unrighteous? (Matt. 25:32). For “the righteous falls seven times a day” (Prov. 24:16).

2. Yet this is the difference between their falls: the righteous person is received by the Lord and therefore rises stronger; but when the unrighteous person falls, he does not add anything further by which to rise. Indeed, he falls either into harmful shame or into shamelessness. Either he excuses what he has done—and this is shame that brings about sin—or he acquires the forehead of a prostitute and no longer fears God or respects man, but proclaims his sin like Sodom. The righteous person, however, falls upon the hand of the Lord, and in a wonderful way even the sin itself cooperates with him toward righteousness. For “we know that all things cooperate for good to those who love God” (Rom. 8:28). Does not that fall cooperate for our good, by which we become both humbler and more cautious? Does not the Lord receive the one who falls and is sustained by humility? “I was pushed and overthrown so that I might fall,” says the Prophet; but the one who pushed me gains nothing, because “the Lord received me” (Ps. 117:13 [Vulgate]).

Thus the faithful soul will say to the Lord: “Thou art my receiver.” All can say, “Thou art my Creator”; animals too can say, “Thou art my Shepherd”; all human beings can say, “Thou art my Redeemer.” But “Thou art my receiver” can be said only by one who dwells in the help of the Most High. Therefore he added: “And my God.” Why not “our God”? Because in creation, redemption, and the other common benefits, he is God of all; but in their temptations each of the elect has him as his own. For he is so ready to receive the one who falls and to rescue the one who flees that, having left all others, he may seem to devote himself to that person alone.

3. Therefore it is profitable for every soul always to attend to God as its own, not merely as helper but also as observer. For how can one become negligent who never ceases to behold God beholding him? Or how does one not seem to have him as one’s own, when he sees him so intent upon him that he never ceases at every hour to observe all his inward and outward matters, and to search out and judge not only all actions but even the most subtle motions of the soul? Such a person may rightly say: “My God, I will hope in him.” Observe that he did not say, “I have hoped,” or “I hope,” but “I will hope.” “This,” he says, “is my vow, this my purpose, this the intention of my heart. This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom, and in it I will persevere. I will hope in him. I will not despair, nor will I hope in vain, because cursed is he who sins in hope, and likewise he who sins in despair. Nor do I wish to be among those who do not hope in the Lord.”

“I will hope in him,” he says. But now tell us: with what fruit, what reward, what gain? “For he has delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word.” Let us defer this snare and this word until another day and, if you please, another sermon.

## SERMON III. On the Third Verse: “My God, I will hope in him. For he has delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word.”

1. Brothers, in these words I am indeed pierced by great compassion for myself, and I greatly pity my own soul. “He has delivered me from the snare of hunters.” Are we, then, beasts? Beasts indeed. For “man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13 [Vulgate]). Human beings are certainly beasts: wandering sheep without a shepherd. Why are you proud, O human being? Why do you boast of being clever? See that you have become a beast, for whom snares are prepared to be hunted.

But who are these hunters? Hunters utterly evil and wicked, most cunning and cruel; hunters who do not sound the horn, lest they be heard, but “shoot at the blameless in secret.” They are the rulers of these darknesses, most skillful in the wickedness and cunning of diabolical fraud, so that, as a beast is before a hunter, so even the cleverest of human beings is in comparison with them—except only those who, with the Apostle, “are not ignorant of their designs” (2 Cor. 2:11), those to whom it has been granted in God’s wisdom to detect the deceits of evil beings.

I beseech you, new plantings of God, you whose senses have not yet been trained to distinguish good from evil: do not follow the judgment of your own heart; do not abound in your own understanding, lest that crafty hunter deceive you while you are still untrained. For against those wild and utterly beastlike beasts—I mean secular people—he spreads sufficiently open snares, since he does not doubt that they are easily caught. But for you, who, like wiser stags, kill serpents [Note: See St Augustine, *Expositions on the Psalms*, on Psalm 41.] and thirst for the living fountain, he hides subtler snares and seeks more cunning devices of his deceit. Therefore, I beseech you, humble yourselves beneath the mighty hand of God, your shepherd, and submit to the counsels of those who know that hunter’s cunning better, taught by the prolonged exercise of a long time and by frequent experience, both in themselves and in many others.

2. But now that we know the hunters and the beasts, we must ask what this snare is. I do not wish to devise it from myself or to hand on to you anything uncertain. Let the Apostle show us this snare; for he does not fail to understand the devices of those hunters. Tell us, blessed Paul, what this snare of the devil is, from which the faithful soul rejoices to have been freed. “Those who desire to become rich in this world,” he says, “fall into temptations and into the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. 6:9). Are, then, the riches of this world the devil’s snare? Alas, how few we find who rejoice to be freed from this snare; how many who grieve because they think themselves too little entangled in it, and still labour, as far as they can, to wrap and entangle themselves in it! [Col. 0191C] You who have left all things and followed the Son of Man, who had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58), rejoice and say: “For he has delivered me from the snare of the hunters.” Confess to him with your whole heart, your whole soul, and all your strength; from the very marrow of your hearts give him thanks, saying: “For he has delivered me from the snare of the hunters.” And, that you may know how great this benefit is, and may know the things granted to you by God, hear what follows: “And from the harsh word.”

O man—or rather, beast—did you not fear the snare? Fear at least the hammer. “From the harsh word,” he says. What is this word except that of insatiable Gehenna: “Bring! Bring! Strike! Tear apart! Kill quickly! Strip off the spoil at once!” What is the harsh word except, “Let the wicked man be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10)? How hunters rejoice when the beast is caught, and cry: “Take it away! Take it away! Pierce it with spits, put it on the coals, and set it upon the violently boiling cauldrons!” The harsh word uttered by the exasperating house, the Jewish people, was: “Take him away, take him away, crucify him” (John 19:15). How horrible a word, how harsh, how cruel! Truly, “their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.” You endured this harsh word, Lord. Why, unless to free us from the harsh word? May it now be an act of your mercy that we do not endure what you deigned to endure for us.

3. When we urge worldly people [Col. 0192A] to repent, they answer and say: “This saying is hard.” Indeed, this is what we read in the Gospel. The Lord was speaking of repentance itself, but figuratively, as to those to whom it had not been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God. And when they heard him saying, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,” they said, “This saying is hard,” and they went back (John 6:61). But what is eating his flesh and drinking his blood, except sharing in his sufferings and imitating the manner of life which he maintained in the flesh? This too is signified by that undefiled sacrament of the altar, where we receive the Lord’s body: so that, just as the form of bread is seen to enter into us, we may know that through the manner of life which he had on earth, he himself enters [Col. 0192B] into us, to dwell in our hearts through faith. For when righteousness enters, he enters who was made righteousness for us by God the Father. And “he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16).

Yet many still say to us: “This saying is hard.” Is, then, this momentary and light tribulation hard, which works in us, beyond all measure in sublimity, an eternal weight of glory? Is it hard, by the briefest and lightest labour, to redeem oneself from those torments and punishments which no end will finish and no mind suffice to conceive? Does it seem hard to you when it is said, “Repent” (Matt. 3:2)? You are mistaken; but one day you will hear a harsh word, a hard saying, an evil hearing: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire.” [Col. 0192C] Therefore I say to you: fear this; regard this as hard. Then you will find that the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light. If you cannot yet believe that it is sweet in itself, at least you know that in comparison with this it is most sweet.

4. But you, my brothers—you who are winged, before whose eyes the net is spread in vain; you who have utterly forsaken the riches of this world—what have you to fear from the harsh word, now that you have been delivered from the snare? Blessed are you, Idithun, for whom certain psalms are inscribed (Pss. 38, 61, 76), who have leapt over the snare, so as to be altogether far from the harsh word. For to whom is it said, “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire; for I was hungry and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25:41–42)? To whom, I say, will this be said, except to those who possessed the substance [Col. 0192D] of this world? Are not your hearts greatly cheered by this word and filled with spiritual joy? Do you not esteem your poverty more precious than the treasures of the age? For it is poverty itself that frees you from the harsh word. How, indeed, could God demand from us what has been left behind for love of him? Yet you do even this: by the labour of your hands Christ is fed and clothed, so that nothing is lacking. Therefore give thanks, rejoice, and say: “For he has delivered me from the snare of the hunters, and from the harsh word.”

Rejoice, I say—but meanwhile still with trembling. I want you to be glad, but not yet secure; rejoicing in the Holy Spirit [Col. 0193A], yet still fearful and guarding against relapse.

5. For what remains for you to fear? Surely one thing, and that most grave: the sin of Judas, the sin of apostasy. It was well done that you received wings like a dove and flew to rest. For on earth there was no rest, but labour, sorrow, and affliction of spirit. What, then, is to be feared by one flying thus, except perhaps that he may see a corpse or something similar upon the ground, be drawn by desire for it, be seen by those most wicked hunters, caught in their prepared snares, and so the last state of that man become worse than the first? This, I say, is altogether to be feared: lest anyone return to his vomit, whether in heart alone or even in body. For we read of the children of Israel that in heart [Col. 0193B] they returned to Egypt (Num. 14:3). In body they were prevented from returning by the Red Sea, closed behind their heels.

This is what every person must especially fear: lest at some time they offend God so far as to be openly rejected and vomited out by him; or, if shame prevents apostasy of the body, lukewarmness itself gradually introduces apostasy of the heart, so that under a religious habit they bear a worldly heart and embrace whatever worldly consolation they can find. For we are not holier than the Apostle, who nevertheless feared lest, after preaching to others, he himself should become reprobate (1 Cor. 9:27). But this must be feared until the snare is broken, until the soul lays down this body. [Col. 0193C] For the body itself is a kind of snare; hence the eye is said to prey upon the soul (Lam. 3:51). It is therefore by no means fitting that the person who carries his snare with him should be secure. Rather, it is good to dwell in the help of the Most High, so that through him the snare may be avoided.

## SERMON IV. On the fourth verse, “He will overshadow you with his shoulders,” etc.

1. To one who humbly confesses and devoutly renders thanks, greater benefits are deservedly promised. For one found faithful in little will rightly be set over much; whereas, conversely, one who is ungrateful for benefits received is unworthy to receive further ones. Thus the Spirit answers that devout thanksgiving: [Col. 0193D] “He will not merely do this,” he says, “but he will also overshadow you with his shoulders.” By these shoulders I believe that the twofold promise of God is to be understood: namely, of the life that now is and of that which is to come. For if he promised only the kingdom but lacked provisions for the journey, people would certainly complain and reply: “What is promised is indeed great, but no means of arriving there is given.” Therefore he who promised eternal life after this age, in his most provident mercy promised also to give a hundredfold even in this age (Matt. 19:29).

What excuse have you now, O man? Surely the mouth of those speaking iniquity is stopped. What further argument can the enemy bring in order to tempt you, except that your life will be long? And if a great journey remains for you, why should you fear this, when strong food is given to you lest you fail on the way? Food was indeed brought to Elijah by an angel—food than which none is considered more lowly in ordinary human use, namely bread and water—yet such strength was imparted in it that, walking for forty days, he was neither wearied nor hungry (3 Kings 19:5–8). Do you wish this food to be ministered to you by angels? It would be very strange if you did not.

2. But if you desire this food and seek angelic ministrations, not with proud but rather with humble ambition, hear what is written of the Lord: when the devil tempted him and urged him to make [Col. 0194A] bread from stones, he resisted and said: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” Then, after the temptations had been overcome and the tempter put to flight, angels came and ministered to him (Matt. 4:3–11). Therefore, if you wish to have the ministry of angels, flee worldly consolations and resist the devil’s temptations. Let your soul refuse to be comforted by other things, if you wish to delight in the remembrance of God.

When you are hungry, it urges you to run to bread; but you should rather hear the one who says, “Man does not live by bread alone.” Why are you distracted by such variety, seeking now food, now drink, now clothing or a bed, except for the body’s necessary support, when in the one thing—that is, in the word of God—you can find all these things? For it is manna, possessing every flavour and delight of fragrance; it is true and sincere rest, sweet and health-giving, pleasant and holy.

[Col. 0194C] 3. This is the promise of the present life. But who can explain the promise of the future? If “the expectation of the righteous is joy” (Prov. 10:28), and such joy that everything desired in this world cannot be compared with it, what will that which is expected itself be? “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. 64:4).

Under these shoulders, then, four benefits are bestowed upon us. Under them we are hidden; under them we are protected from the assault [variant: encounter] of hawks and kites, which are the powers of the air; under them a health-giving shade refreshes us and repels the excessive heat of the sun; under them likewise we are fed and cherished. For the Prophet says in another psalm: “He has hidden me in his tabernacle in the day of evils” (Ps. 26:5): that is, while [Col. 0194D] the days are still evil and we are in a foreign land, which has been given into the hand of the wicked, where the kingdom of peace is not found and the God of peace does not reign in it. For if he reigns, why is it that we say in prayer: “May your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10)?

It is therefore necessary for the present to hide whatever good we have, because the man who finds the treasure of the kingdom of heaven hides it (Matt. 13:44). For this reason we too hide ourselves bodily in cloisters and forests. And if you wish to know how much we gain by this concealment, I believe there is no one here who, if he performed in the world a fourth part of the things he does here, would not be adored as a saint and regarded as an angel; whereas now he is daily reproved and rebuked as negligent. Do you reckon it a small gain that you are not considered saints [Col. 0195A] before you are saints? Or do you not fear lest, having received here a cheap reward, you may have no reward in the future?

This concealment is therefore necessary not only from the eyes of others, but much more from your own eyes. For this is the meaning of that saying of the Lord: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done’” (Luke 17:10). Woe to us indeed if we had not done it! And this is surely great virtue and the highest security: when you live devoutly, yet attend more to what is lacking in you than to what you seem to have attained, forgetting what lies behind and stretching yourself toward what lies ahead. This, then, is the concealment which we said is granted beneath the Lord’s shoulders—perhaps like the concealment or overshadowing wrought in Mary by the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0195B] in order to conceal so incomprehensible a sacrament.

4. Concerning protection the same prophet also says: “You overshadowed my head in the day of battle” (Ps. 139:8). For just as a mother, seeing a hawk coming, spreads her wings so that her chicks may enter beneath them and have a safe refuge, so the supreme and ineffable mercy of our Lord has been prepared for us and, as it were, extended in a spread and broadened bosom. Thus he also said above: “For you are my refuge.”

Now beneath these same shoulders we have both health-giving shade and protection. Just as this bodily sun, though good and very necessary, can nevertheless harm a weak head by its heat if it is not moderated, and weak eyes by its brightness—and this is not the sun’s fault, but the fault of weakness—so too there is the Sun of righteousness. Hence it is said: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccl. 7:17). Not because righteousness is not good, but because, while we are still weak, even good grace itself must be moderated, lest perhaps we fall into the fault of pride or indiscretion.

Why is it that, though we pray and entreat unceasingly, we cannot attain the abundance of grace that we desire? Do you suppose that God has become miserly or poor, powerless or inexorable? Far be it—utterly far be it! Rather, he has known our frailty and overshadows us with his shoulders. Yet we must not therefore cease from asking: for, although he does not give to satiety, he nevertheless gives to sustain us; although he guards us from [Col. 0195D] excessive heat, he nonetheless cherishes us as a mother with her warmth. This is the fourth thing which we said is supplied to us beneath his shoulders: that, like chicks, we may be warmed by the heat of the maternal body, lest, wandering outside, we die as charity grows cold—for charity is not poured forth in us except through the Spirit who is given to us. Beneath his wings, therefore, you will hope securely, so that the expectation of future gifts may be firm through the bestowal of present gifts.

## SERMON V. On the fifth verse, “His truth will surround you with a shield.”

1. “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Mark 14:38). You know who said this, and you know the time: it is the Lord’s word as his passion was now approaching. Notice that he himself was about to suffer, not the disciples; yet he did not say that prayer should be made for himself, but for them. Thus he said to Peter: “Behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have once turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:31–32). If they had so much cause for fear in the Lord’s passion, how much must we fear, brothers, in our own passion? Therefore watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation, because you are surrounded by temptations on every side. Thus you have also read that “the life of man upon earth is temptation” (Job 7:1). If, then, our life is so full of temptations that the whole of it may rightly be called temptation, there is need of sleepless vigilance and prayer, lest we be led into it; hence also that petition in the Lord’s Prayer: [Col. 0196B] “And lead us not into temptation.” Since, therefore, you are thus surrounded by temptations on every side, his truth will surround you with a shield, so that, just as wars are on every side, so defences may also be on every side. From this it is altogether clear that the shield which can surround must be spiritual. Truth surrounds us because he who promises is true and fulfils his promises as he makes them. “God is faithful,” says the Apostle, “who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” (1 Cor. 10:13).

2. The grace of divine protection is aptly compared to a shield, since in its upper part it is broad and wide in order to protect the head and shoulders, but narrower below so as to weigh less heavily; especially since the lower legs are more slender, less easily wounded, and less dangerously wounded in those parts. Thus, precisely thus, Christ grants his soldiers, for guarding the lower things—that is, the flesh—a great, so to speak, narrowness and scarcity of temporal goods. He does not wish them to be weighed down by an abundance of such things, but, “having food and clothing,” as the Apostle says, wishes us to be content with these (1 Tim. 10:13). In higher things, however, he gives a more ample breadth and abundance of spiritual grace. For you have: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). He spoke, of course, of food and clothing, concerning which he had said that they should not be anxious. For our heavenly Father too, in his most kindly mercy, supplies these things for a twofold reason: lest [Col. 0196D] we should think him altogether hostile if he denied them, and thus despair; or lest excessive anxiety about them should impair spiritual exercise. For without them it is impossible either to live or to serve God. Besides, the stricter the provision, the better.

3. Therefore “his truth will surround you with a shield; you will not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the business that walks in darkness, the assault and the noon-day demon.” These are the four temptations by which we are surrounded on every side; and thus we need also to be surrounded by the Lord’s shield, so that it may be at our right and left, before and behind. [Col. 0197A] I want you to be forewarned of this: no one on earth will live without temptation. Thus, when one temptation is perhaps removed, he should expect another—not securely, perhaps, but rather fearfully—and so ask to be delivered from it, never daring to promise himself perfect freedom or rest while he remains in this body of death.

In this matter we must consider the very kindly dispensation of divine mercy toward us: he permits us to remain occupied for a longer time with certain temptations lest more dangerous ones occur; but from others he frees us sooner, so that we may be exercised in those which he foresees will be more useful for us. We must consider, however, not only this, but what these four temptations are which he sets forth here. For I believe that they rise against those who are converted in the very order in which they are here enumerated and are, as it were, the chief temptations of all.

## SERMON VI. On the second part of the fifth verse, “You will not fear the terror by night”; and on the sixth verse, “The arrow flying by day,” etc.

[Col. 0197B]

1. In the divine Scriptures adversity is customarily denoted by night; and we know that the first conflict against those who are converted is usually over bodily discomforts. For the flesh, hitherto undisciplined, does not patiently endure being chastised and reduced to servitude. Still freshly mindful of its lost freedom, it lusts more vehemently against the spirit—especially amid those penalties in which you are daily dying, or rather have been given over to death all day long, penalties beyond your strength, beyond nature, and contrary to your accustomed way of life. What wonder, then, if these things disturb people—especially those not yet accustomed, who do not yet have ready recourse to prayer and flight to holy meditations, so that the burden and heat of the day may thus be relieved? At the very beginnings of our conversion, the Lord’s shield is plainly necessary, that we may not fear the terror by night. It is rightly said that the terror by night, not the night itself, is not to be feared; for the affliction itself is not temptation, but rather the fear of it. For all of us suffer, though not all are thereby tempted; and those who are tempted are harmed much more by fear of future punishment than by present pain.

2. Since fear itself, therefore, is temptation, it is fittingly said of the one surrounded by the Lord’s shield that he will not fear this temptation. Perhaps he will be attacked, perhaps tempted, perhaps fear the night; but this fear will not harm him. Rather, if it has not gained dominion, [Col. 0197D] then he will be without stain and will be cleansed, as it is written: “Those who have been terrified will be purified” (Job 41:16). This fear is a furnace; but truth makes it a furnace for testing, not for burning up. It is certainly a nocturnal and dark fear; but the ray of truth easily overcomes it. For truth sets before the eyes of the heart, now the sins we have committed, so that, as the prophet says of himself, we too may be ready for scourges, declaring our iniquity and thinking upon our sin (Ps. 37:18–19); now the eternal punishments which we have deserved, so that in comparison with those which we escape, we may reckon every suffering we endure as delights; now also the heavenly rewards toward which we strive, frequently remembering that “the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which will be revealed [Col. 0198A] in us” (Rom. 8:18); and now also what Christ suffered for us, so that frequently considering how much that Majesty endured for useless servants, we may be ashamed not to endure even small things for ourselves.

3. But perhaps truth has prevailed, especially truth so manifold and encompassing on every side, not merely to repel but even utterly to drive out this fear. The night has passed: as one who walks honourably as a child of light and of the day, fear the arrow. It flies lightly and penetrates lightly; but I tell you, it inflicts no light wound and kills swiftly. This arrow is, beyond doubt, vain glory. It does not attack the faint-hearted and lax. Those who seem more fervent should fear; they should guard themselves in this respect, and still anxiously not abandon the invincible shield of truth. For what is more opposed to vanity? We do not need to set against this arrow those hidden and, as it were, innermost depths of truth: let the soul know itself and hold the truth concerning itself.

It is very difficult, I think, for anyone to be led by the words of people praising him in his lifetime into high-mindedness if he examines himself inwardly in the light of truth by anxious reflection. For if he reflects on his own condition, will he not say to himself: “Why are you proud, dust and ashes?” (Sir. 10:9). If he considers his own corruption, must he not confess that there is no good in him? Even if he seems to possess something, I think he will find no answer to the Apostle saying: “What have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7); and elsewhere: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12). Finally, if he reckons faithfully, he will readily perceive that he cannot meet one who comes against him with twenty thousand even with ten thousand, and that all his righteousnesses are reckoned as a menstrual cloth.

4. The same truth must likewise be set against the temptations which follow. For the ancient enemy does not desist even thus, but perhaps turns to more cunning devices. He has found the tower firm on either side: there is nothing by which he may shake it, whether from the left through the faint-heartedness of fear or from the right through human praises, having been frustrated in both attempts. “But if,” he says, “I cannot cast it down by force, perhaps I can deceive it by the ingenuity of some traitor.” [Col. 0198D] Who, do you think, will this traitor be? Plainly, covetousness: the root of iniquity; ambition, a subtle evil, secret poison, hidden pestilence, artificer of deceit, mother of hypocrisy, parent of envy, source of vices, tinder of crimes, rust of virtues, moth of holiness, blinder of hearts—creating diseases from remedies and generating languor from medicine.

“He has despised vain glory,” he says, “because it is vain. Perhaps he will desire something more substantial—perhaps honours, perhaps riches.” How many has this business walking in darkness caused to be thrust into outer darkness, stripping them of the wedding garment and emptying the exercises of virtue of the fruit of piety? How many has this pestilence wickedly undermined and shamefully cast down, so that all the rest, by whom the hidden underminer had gone unnoticed, might suddenly tremble at the fall? What nourishes this worm except alienation of mind and forgetfulness of truth? Or what but truth tracks down and exposes this traitor, and convicts the business of darkness? It is truth, surely, that says: “What does it profit a man if he gain the whole world but lose himself and suffer loss of himself?” (Matt. 16:26); and likewise: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6:7). By diligent suggestion truth recalls to mind how trifling is consolation in ambition, how grave the judgment, how brief the enjoyment, and how unknown the end.

5. Thus far were the Lord’s temptations; the enemy did not presume to bring the fourth. [Note: [Col. 0199D] Yet he does bring the fourth below, in Sermon 14, no. 4.] For that one concerns ignorance; and he did not doubt the wisdom of one who so controlled his answers that the devil could never discover what he was seeking. In the first temptation he urged the hungry man to make bread from stones; but Christ answered neither that he could nor that he could not, setting forth another food and saying: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” In the second temptation he urged him to throw himself down, promising that he would not be injured if he were the Son of God, and that thus the whole city would see him and praise and magnify him; and he answered neither that he was nor that he was not. The third concerned ambition, when the devil promised him all the kingdoms of the world if he fell down and worshipped him (Matt. 4:3–9). Do you see that the way of ambition is worship of the devil, by which he promises his worshippers they will attain the world’s honours and glory? As I said, he refrained from the fourth temptation in the case of one whose great prudence he had learned from his answers.

[Col. 0199C] 6. But what does he do against others, whom he sees altogether to love righteousness and hate iniquity? What except to disguise iniquity beneath the likeness of virtue? Those whom he knows to be perfect lovers of good, he tries to persuade toward evil under the appearance, not of ordinary good, but of perfect good; so that one who loves good intensely may quickly consent, and one who runs may easily stumble. This, then, is the demon not only of the day but also of noon. Did not Mary fear this when she was troubled at the angel’s new greeting? (Luke 1:29). Did not the Apostle indicate this when he said: “For we are not ignorant of his devices” (2 Cor. 2:11)? For Satan himself transforms [Col. 0199D] himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14). Finally, did not the disciples themselves fear this when, seeing the Lord walking on the sea, they cried out, supposing it to be a phantom? And observe how aptly it agrees that it is said to have been the fourth watch of the night (Matt. 16:26, 25), when the disciples are reported to have kept watch against the fourth temptation. In so plain a matter, I do not think our own explanation is necessary: truth alone exposes falsity that is thus disguised.

7. A careful observer will not find it difficult to discover these four temptations also in the general condition of the [Col. 0200A] Church. Did not the terror by night test the still newly planted Church, when everyone who killed God’s servants thought that he was rendering service to God? Then, after persecution ceased and day was restored, the flying arrow disturbed and afflicted it more grievously, when certain persons went out from the Church, puffed up by the spirit of their flesh, desiring empty and volatile glory; and, wishing to make a name for themselves by magnifying their tongues, fashioned diverse and perverse doctrines.

But now there is peace from pagans, peace from heretics, yet no peace from false sons. “You have multiplied the nation, Lord Jesus, but have not increased its joy,” because many are called but few are chosen. All are Christians, and nearly all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. The very offices of ecclesiastical dignity have passed over into shameful gain and the business of darkness; in them the salvation of souls is not sought, but the luxury of riches. For this they are tonsured; for this they frequent churches, celebrate masses, and chant psalms. Men today contend shamelessly for bishoprics and archdeaconries [Note: [Col. 0199D] Horstius adds “abbeys and other dignities.” But these words are absent from other printed editions and from the manuscripts.], so that the revenues of churches may be squandered on superfluity and vanity.

It remains, then, for the man of sin, the son of perdition, to be revealed: the demon not only of day but also of noon, which not only transforms itself into an angel of light but exalts itself above everything called God or worshipped (2 Thess. 2:4). Surely it lies in wait more cruelly for the heel of Mother Church, whose head it grieves to have been crushed by her. This assault will indeed be most grievous; but Truth will free the Church of the elect even from this, shortening the days for their sake (Matt. 24:22) and destroying the noon-day demon by the brightness of his coming.

Let these remarks suffice concerning these temptations. For I remember that in a sermon on the Song of Songs I treated the same matters similarly [Note: [Col. 0200D] Namely, in Sermon 33 on the Song of Songs. From this it is clear that these sermons were delivered around the year 1140, since Sermon 33 on the Song of Songs was preached after 1138.], when mention arose of this noon-day demon on the occasion of the bride’s noon-day repose, which she had asked to be shown to her.

## SERMON VII. On the seventh verse, “A thousand shall fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand; but it shall not come near you.”

[Col. 0200D] 1. We live in hope, brothers, and do not fail amid present tribulation, because we await joys that cannot fail. For this expectation does not appear vain to us, nor our hope uncertain, since it rests upon the promises of eternal truth. Moreover, our expectation of future things is made firm by our reception of present gifts; and the power of present grace bears most credible witness that the happiness of promised glory will without doubt follow. For the Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory; and in the hymn we also call him—or, according to the variant, sing of him as—the Father of everlasting [Col. 0201A] glory, the Father of mighty grace (*Breviary*, Monday, at Lauds). To him we sing in the psalm: “For God loves mercy and truth; the Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 83:12).

Let piety, therefore, endure the struggle manfully in this world and bear any persecution with equanimity. Why should it not endure all things, when it has promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come, which is profitable for all things? Let it resist its assailant strongly, for an unfailing defender will be present to one who resists, and a most generous rewarder will not be absent from one who triumphs. “His truth,” he says, “will surround you with a shield.”

2. The invincible protection of truth is plainly necessary not only while one dwells meanwhile in the flesh, but also afterward when one departs: now because of dangerous conflicts, then because of the monstrous encounters of evil spirits. Indeed, the hostile party wished to harm even that most holy soul of glorious Martin; and the bloody beast, knowing that only a little time remained to it, in the whole madness of its untiring malice did not hesitate to stand near even one in whom it had nothing. Indeed, that most shameless audacity presumed to approach even the King of glory himself, as he testifies: “For the prince of this world comes, and finds nothing in me” (John 14:30).

Blessed is the soul which has so repelled the darts of temptations with the shield of truth that, allowing nothing poisonous whatever to take root in it, it is not at all put to shame when it speaks with its enemies in the gate. “You will find nothing in me, deadly one” [variant: “deadly thing”]. Blessed is the one whom the shield of truth so surrounds that it guards both his going out and his coming in: his going out from this life and his coming into the future one, so that the enemy may attempt no evil either from behind or from before. For there will certainly be need there of a guardian, a faithful guide, and a great comforter because of those dreadful visions, no less than here there is need of a helper and defender against invisible tempters.

3. Therefore, beloved, glorify Christ and bear him meanwhile in your body: a delightful burden, a sweet weight, a saving load—even if he sometimes seems to press upon you, even if at times he beats your sides and lashes you when you kick against him, even if he sometimes constrains and restrains your jaws with bit and bridle. All this is entirely blessed. Be like a beast of burden, you who bear the Saviour; but do not be altogether like a beast of burden. “Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48:13). Why does the Prophet so greatly lament or rebuke in man this likeness to beasts, especially when elsewhere he seems to speak of himself and say to God, not without a certain joy: “I have become like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. 72:23)?

I think—or rather, I do not think, but know—that a certain likeness to beasts is commended to a human being; but certainly not that likeness which consists in lack of understanding and folly, but in imitation of patience. For it would seem the voice, not merely of one who was angry, but not even of one who was lamenting, if he had said: “Man, when under God’s burden, did not kick against it; he became like a beast of burden before him.” For who would not greatly envy that beast upon whose lowly back the Saviour deigned to sit, in commending his ineffable meekness, if with the bearing of so precious a burden it had also possessed understanding of so singular an honour? Be like a beast of burden, therefore, but by no means a beast of burden: patiently bearing the load, indeed, but understanding the honour; wisely and delightfully considering both the quality of the burden itself [Col. 0202B] and your own benefit.

4. That great Ignatius, hearer of the disciple whom Jesus loved, our martyr, by whose precious relics our poverty has been enriched, greets a certain Mary as “Christ-bearer” in several letters which he wrote to her. [Note: [Col. 0201D] The printed editions, including the older ones, have simply “Mary”; manuscripts add “a certain,” and rightly so, since the present passage does not concern Mary the most holy Mother of God, but another Mary—namely, the Cassabolitan or Castabolite—to whom two letters ascribed to the holy martyr Ignatius survive, and in which she is greeted as “Christ-bearer” [Col. 0202D]. Although the same greeting also appears in another widely circulated letter, bearing the name of the same Ignatius, addressed to Mary the Mother of God. But the present discourse concerns that Mary to whom several letters were then circulating as Ignatian.] A splendid title of dignity indeed, and a commendation of immeasurable honour. For to serve him is to reign; to bear him is not to be burdened, but to be honoured [variant: adorned].

But could the Saviour’s little ass, of which I was just speaking, have had any cause to fear [variant: whence] that it might fail on the road beneath such a burden? Or ought it to fear an attack by wolves, an encounter with robbers, a precipice, or any danger under so great a guide? Blessed is the one who has thus borne Christ, so as to deserve to be led by the Holy of holies into the holy city. There is absolutely no reason for it to fear either an obstacle on the way or rejection at the gate. For faithful peoples prepared the way for that beast of burden (Matt. 21:7–9); for this one, holy angels do so: “For he has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.” But these matters ought not yet to be anticipated; rather, the sequence of the exposition of Scripture itself must be followed in order.

5. “A thousand shall fall at your side,” he says, “and ten thousand at your right hand; but it shall not come near you.” This is the verse that must be treated today, as you know. In the preceding chapter, which was most recently expounded, it was said, if you recall, how the protection of truth frees one from four very great and grievous temptations of this life: from terror by night, from the arrow flying by day, from the business that walks about in darkness, and from assault and the noonday demon. What follows, therefore—“A thousand shall fall at your side,” and so forth—I judge should be assigned rather to the life to come.

Thus, at the beginning of this discourse, you still remember, unless I am mistaken, the apostolic saying by which he commends godliness as profitable for all things, having the promise both of the present life and of that which is to come [Col. 0203A] (1 Tim. 4:8). Hear, then, and hear with gladness of heart, what appears to pertain to the promise of the future life and to your expectation. “Where your treasure is, there let your heart be also.” You listened attentively to present things, and I do not forget it; but it is fitting to listen still more attentively to things to come.

Indeed, even the false prophet—Balaam, I mean; recall it, you who know the histories—even he, wicked as he was, desired the death of the righteous and prayed that his own last things might become like theirs (Num. 23:10). So great is the fruit of godliness, so great the reward of righteousness, that it cannot fail to be desired even by the ungodly and unjust themselves. Yet the willows of Babylon take little delight in the song of Zion. Therefore instruments must be hung up among them; rather, one must lament by the rivers of Babylon, if perhaps they may be persuaded [Col. 0203B] to weep.

Here, indeed, singing is proper, where there will not be lacking those who leap with all the gladness of the spirit at the sound of the psaltery, at the song of Zion, and who, with a certain intensity of holy longing, yearn to fly before it, saying: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and be at rest?” (Ps. 54:7). For what else is to exult than to leap out of oneself? News of the peace or pleasantness of a distant shore, already almost despaired of, however favourable it may be, has less savour for those still endangered in the midst of the sea, tossed by waves and driven by billows.

But what is proposed to us today does not concern such a soul; for one of that sort does not yet deserve to hear: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” Remember to whom this promise was made: namely, to one “who dwells in the aid of the Most High and shall abide under the protection of the God of heaven” [Col. 0203C].

6. Therefore let the one hear it who already approaches the harbour of salvation in thought and longing; who, having cast before him, as it were, an anchor of hope, appears to cling immovably to that desirable land; who, throughout all the days in which he now serves as a soldier, awaits until his change comes. Certainly the surest and chief approach to this harbour is this very manner of life in which you have been placed: the preparation for departure, namely, through divine calling and justification.

For in these two there is established a faithful connection, as it were, from one eternity to another—that is, from predestination to glorification. As predestination is cut off by no beginning, so glorification likewise is to be enclosed by no end. But lest you suppose that the middle link in this twofold eternity is an invention of ours, listen to the Apostle and see whether he himself does not set it before you more plainly: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.” But how, do you suppose, or in what order will he glorify them? For the things that are from God are ordered. Will you arrive from predestination at glorification by some sudden leap? Find for yourself a bridge between; or rather, enter upon the one already prepared. “Those whom he predestined,” he says, “he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” [Col. 0203D] (Rom. 8:29–30).

[Col. 0204A]

7. This way indeed seems good to some people—and it is good: nothing need be feared concerning its end. Let not the final stages of this way seem doubtful to you; go on securely, and all the more vigorously as they now seem more certainly near. For you possess the middle stages: how could the final ones not be drawing near? “Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2).

“But,” you say, “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). No access to it lies open to me except through the ranks of enemies. Giants stand in the middle of the way; they fly in the air, besiege the passage, and watch those who pass. Yet act confidently; do not be afraid. They are great, they are many; but “a thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” They shall fall on every side, never afterwards to harm you for all eternity; indeed, more than this: they shall not come near you.

Certainly the sinner will see and be angry, but he will come from the side: that is, the mercy of your God will go before you, and that same mercy will likewise follow you, guarding both your entrance, as we recalled above, and your going out [Col. 0204B]. Otherwise, in that most terrible encounter with spiritual wickedness, what human faculty could stand without being shaken by intolerable terror?

8. What do you think, brothers? If even one of those many princes of darkness were allowed to rush into your midst and to appear in all his ferocity and the dark monstrosity of his body, who could endure him either with bodily sense or with the heart? Indeed, a few days ago—as you yourselves know—one among you, first while sleeping and then after being awakened, was permitted to be so gravely disturbed by a nocturnal apparition that he could scarcely retain his reason that day, scarcely be secure. All of you likewise were terrified together when that frightened man cried out in a most terrible voice.

It is indeed shameful that faith in you appeared to have fallen asleep so completely, even while you slept. But this undoubtedly happened as a warning to us, that with all vigilance we may remember against whom our struggle is, lest we be found either ignorant of the enemy’s malice or ungrateful for divine protection. For, from the most violent torment of its own envious spite, inveterate malice has broken out into such fury, especially in these holy days, showing more sharply that it is tormented by your devotion [Col. 0204C–D]. With the same zeal of wasting madness, though with fuller licence, it is present when the saints depart—but only from the side. For it will no longer be permitted either to confront them face to face as if to use force, or to creep up from behind in order to deceive.

9. Nor will it henceforth set a stumbling-block even beside your path: “it shall not come near you.” Not only will it not touch you in order to strike, but it will not even approach in order to terrify. For I think you feared that horror might perhaps seize you at those monstrous forms and that great multitude of ghostly faces. But the excellent Paraclete, the most effective Comforter, will be with you—he, namely, of whom you have read: “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down, and his enemies shall lick the earth” [Col. 0205A] (Ps. 71:9). Indeed, the wicked one shall be reduced to nothing in his sight; he shall glorify those who fear him.

In your presence, Lord Jesus, let enemies rush in as much as they may—indeed, let them not rush in, but fall. Let them gather from every quarter, yet only in order to melt away and perish from the presence of the Lord, as wax melts before fire. Why should I fear those who fail? Why should I dread those who tremble? Why should I be afraid of those who fall? “Though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, provided that you are with me, Lord my God” (Ps. 22:4). For day will immediately breathe forth, and the shadows will decline; the princes of darkness will fall here and there.

Those whom even now, while we still walk by faith and not by sight amid their wicked and hidden suggestions, victorious faith triumphs over—how much more easily will the evident knowledge of truth, then revealed, blow them away together with all those dark and rust-coloured images of theirs [Col. 0205B]. Nor should you complain perhaps about their number, or fear even their multitude. Remember that, at a single command of the Saviour, an entire legion of demons departed from the body of one man who had long been possessed; nor did it dare even to touch the swine unless commanded by him (Mark 5:1–16). How much more, with him as leader, however many they may be, will they fall from every side in great amazement and confusion, saying: “Who is she that rises like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army set in array?” (Song 6:9).

Therefore, fearless and wholly undaunted—rather, rejoicing and praising—you shall look with your eyes; you shall no longer endure attack or dread fury, but shall instead see the recompense of sinners [Col. 0205C].

10. What has been said seems sufficient for today; yet I think that some of you are still held in suspense by a certain expectation. For the more diligent among you are troubled, unless I am mistaken, by what it means that ten thousand are said to fall at the right hand, but only a thousand at the left. For “side,” when used without qualification, can, I think, only be understood here as the left side, especially because the right is immediately designated by its own name.

And not without the rationale of a certain mystery does he seem to have foretold that many would fall at the left, but far more at the right. Unless perhaps someone is so dull and foolish as to suppose that, when “a thousand and ten thousand” are said [Col. 0205D] (Song 6:9), a precise numerical calculation is being expressed rather than an overflowing comparison. We do not understand the divine Scriptures in that way, nor does the Church of God.

Therefore a thousand shall fall at the left, but ten thousand at the right: because with more abundant malice and, as it were, a more numerous force, they are accustomed to press upon the right side and to seek the right flank. If we consider that great body of the Church, we readily see that the spiritual men of the Church itself are attacked far more fiercely than the carnal; and these two, I think, are not inappropriately understood as its right and left sides.

Proud and envious malice always acts in this way, attacking each of the more perfect more violently, according to the words: “Its food is choice”; and again: “It will swallow the river and not marvel, and has confidence that Jordan may flow into its mouth” [Col. 0206A] (Job 40:18). It acts thus, I say, yet not without the definite ordering of divine counsel. For God permits neither the less perfect to be tempted beyond what they can bear, making with the temptation a way of escape; and for the more perfect he prepares from the enemy triumphs not only more glorious but also more numerous.

Thus the whole Church of the elect shall be crowned, because it has fought lawfully on both sides—using both horns, as it were, to scatter enemies so powerfully that shortly it may be seen more openly that “a thousand fall at its side and ten thousand at its right hand.” Thus long ago, when David’s more perfect virtue had been proved, though Saul’s rejection had not yet been made public in Israel, they sang in chorus: “Saul has struck down his thousand, and David his ten thousand” [Col. 0206B] (1 Sam. 18:7).

11. But if you prefer to refer this rather to each individual, you do not lack even in this matter a path of spiritual understanding, provided that you consult your own experience. For with much greater watchfulness and manifold cunning, the opposing party strives to wound [variant: wounds] the right side in us than the left; and it labours to take away not so much the substance of the body as that of the heart.

They are known to begrudge humankind both kinds of prosperity; they strive to deprive us [variant: them] of both kinds of happiness, heavenly and earthly, but far more of the dew of heaven than of the fatness of the earth [Col. 0206C]. Judge whether we have improperly called these the two sides upon which the twofold substance of man is known to rest. For in assigning spiritual goods to the right and carnal goods to the left, I do not at all fear correction—especially from you, whose constant study it is never to reckon the right hand as the left or the left as the right.

Nor does true Wisdom teach otherwise: “In her left hand are riches and glory, and in her right hand length of days” (Prov. 3:16). It is likewise by no means advantageous for you to be ignorant where the persistent multitude of enemies presses most fiercely against you. There one must resist more earnestly: where the heavier necessity bears down, where the whole weight of the war threatens, where the entire business of the struggle lies—whence either shameful captivity is prepared for you if conquered, or triumphant glory if victorious [Col. 0206D].

12. Finally, for this reason—not through folly, indeed—you seem to have freely exposed your left side for the adversary to strike, so that you may preserve your right with all watchfulness. This is the prudence of the serpent commended by Christ and to be imitated by all Christians: if necessary, it exposes the whole body in order to protect the head alone. This is true philosophy; this is the counsel of the Wise One: that the heart be guarded with all vigilance, because life proceeds from it (Prov. 4:23).

This, finally, is the grace and mercy of God toward his servants, and his regard for his elect: that, as though overlooking their left side for the time being, he stands always as the diligent protector of their right. Hence the prophet testifies concerning himself: “I kept the Lord always before my sight, because he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved” [Col. 0207A] (Ps. 15:8). Do you not think that he held the right hand—and that alone—the right hand of the one to whose possessions and flesh he permitted the enemy to do whatever he pleased? “Yet spare his soul,” he says (Job 2:6).

Would that you were always at my right hand, good Jesus! Would that you always held my right hand! For I know and am certain that no adversity will harm me if no iniquity rules over me. Let my left side meanwhile be shorn and beaten; let it be struck by injuries and pinched by reproaches. I gladly expose it, so long as I am guarded by you, provided that you yourself are my protection over my right hand.

[Col. 0207B]

13. Perhaps also the thousand who are to fall on the left should be understood as human beings rather than demons. For they oppose us only because of whatever temporal and transitory goods they either desire to possess themselves through envious malice, or grieve through unjust covetousness not to possess. Perhaps they try to take away the goods of this world, perhaps human favour, perhaps life itself in the body. Human persecution can rage no further; it has nothing it can do to the soul.

Demons, however, are known rather to begrudge us heavenly and eternal goods—not that what they irreparably lost might come to them, but that the poor person raised from the dust might not arrive where they themselves, created in glory, irreparably fell. Obstinate malice is indignant and wastes away with envy that human frailty should obtain what it did not deserve to retain [Col. 0207C].

But even if at times they try to inflict temporal losses on someone, or rejoice that such losses have been inflicted, their whole contrivance is this: that the outward loss may become an inward occasion either for that person or for another. Conversely, whenever human beings try to persuade us to do, or in any way bring about, something by which our right hand is harmed, they do not principally do this; rather, they seem to wish either to gain or avert some temporal loss or advantage that may result for themselves, for us, or perhaps for some other person. Unless perhaps someone has passed so far from being a human being into being a demon that he can in any manner wish any person, however hostile to himself, to be punished with eternal damnation.

[Col. 0207D]

14. Why do we wretches sleep in regard to spiritual devotion, when spiritual wickedness attacks us in so many ways? It is shameful to say it, and the force of grief forbids silence. For how many, brothers, are to be found even among those who live under the religious habit and profess perfection, whom that terrible saying of the prophet appears to have seized: “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be given over to forgetfulness!” (Ps. 136:5).

For, wholly absorbed in guarding the left side, they are exceedingly skilled—but in the wisdom of this age, which they ought to have renounced; and likewise in that wisdom which flesh and blood reveal, though, according to the Apostle, they appeared unwilling to yield to these (Gal. 1:16). You may see them so avidly seeking present gains, rejoicing so worldly over transient advantages, so faint-heartedly disturbed by even the slightest loss of earthly possessions, so carnally contending over them, running about so shamelessly, and entangling themselves so irreligiously in secular affairs, as if this were their entire portion and all their wealth [Col. 0208A].

A poor farmer cultivates his small plot more carefully, perhaps because he possesses no other possession larger or more precious. A beggar hides a morsel of bread in his breast because this is the only kind of metal that rusts in his purses. Why do you devote yourself to this extreme poverty, and indeed squander your own labour so badly? You have another possession, though perhaps remote. You are mistaken: nothing is so near us as what is within us.

But perhaps you complain that it is not farther away but useless, and therefore think that sufficiency must rather be sought here. You are deceived: there you will find it more; indeed, you will find it nowhere except there. Or do you think that it either requires no labour from you or yields less to the labourer? Or do you believe that it has been placed in safety and no longer needs any watchfulness from its guardian? Whichever of these you think, know that you think very foolishly [Col. 0208B].

For there especially “whatsoever a man sows, that shall he also reap.” And “he who sows sparingly shall reap sparingly; but he who sows in blessings shall also reap from blessings” (2 Cor. 9:6), so as to produce one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one hundredfold. Yet you have this treasure in earthen vessels—if indeed you still have it. For I think you have already lost it; I think it has already been taken away; I think strangers have already consumed your strength and you did not know it. Nor can you set your heart upon your treasure, since you do not have the treasure itself.

Otherwise, I ask you: if you are so watchful, if you despise not even the smallest things, if you guard your chaff so prudently, remember also to guard and protect your granary. Indeed, do not expose your treasure while you brood so over your dungheap. For perhaps a thousand envy you that heap, but ten thousand besiege this treasure, no less exceeding in cunning and cruelty than in number. “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” Turn the eyes of faith there. Perhaps they have already burst through the entrances; perhaps they are already freely plundering everything; perhaps they are already dividing the spoils themselves.

Why do you, so disastrously diligent a guardian of the left side, cling to it—unless because things on the left no longer seem to you to be at your side but before your face, because you set these things always before your eyes, and whoever touches them is thought to have touched not your side but the pupil of your eye? [Col. 0208C–D]

15. But now take heed, whoever you are: neglectful of the right and a cultivator of the left side, lest you receive a place with the goats at the left which you chose (Matt. 25:33). It is a harsh saying, brothers: you were frightened, and not without reason. Yet it is no less necessary to beware than to be afraid.

My Lord Jesus, after the other benefits of his immeasurable mercy toward me, also suffered his right side to be pierced for my sake: because he wished to give me drink only from the right side and to prepare a place of refuge only on the right. Would that I might deserve to be such a dove as dwells in the cleft of the rock and in the opening of the right side [Col. 0209A].

Yet consider that he did not feel this wound at all. For he did not choose to receive it until he had already fallen asleep in death: thereby warning you, while you live, always to keep watch in guarding this side; and that the soul which, through destructive insensibility, ignores a wound inflicted in its right side ought to be regarded as dead.
