With good reason the human heart is said to be situated on the left side, because its inclination is always downward and prone toward earth. Nor was he ignorant of this who lamented miserably: “My soul cleaves to the pavement; give me life according to your word” (Ps. 118:25).

But he who spoke this admonition did not will that we should remain under this weight of human condition and heaviness of heart: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God” [Col. 0209B] (Lam. 3:41). He plainly counselled that they should be raised from the left side to the right. Secular soldiery, brothers, carries its shield only on the left side. Let us not imitate it, if we do not wish to be counted among those who are known to serve this world rather than Christ. “No one serving as a soldier for God,” he says, “entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4): that is, he applies his shield not so much to the right as to the left.

16. Nevertheless, brothers, we must cover both sides, if you remember. “His truth shall surround you with a shield,” he says; and the Apostle himself says, “through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left” (2 Cor. 6:7). But hear righteousness itself. Perhaps the same form of conduct is not prescribed for both sides.

For on the one hand it is commanded: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” (Rom. 12:19); and: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). On the other, it is commanded: “Do not give place to the devil” (Eph. 4:27); and again: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4:7).

Hear further how you should cover both sides. “Providing good things,” says the same Apostle, “not only before God, but also before men” [Col. 0209C] (Rom. 12:17). For this is the will of God: that by doing good you may cause not merely the envious spite of malicious demons to waste away, but also the ignorance of foolish men to be silenced (1 Pet. 2:15).

Will this protection, however, be necessary for us forever? Or will a hostile host always press upon us from both sides? The time will come when they will not merely cease to press upon us, but will not even stand. “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” For then human malice will no longer have anything it can do; nor shall we fear thousands of demons any more than equal ranks of worms or flies. We shall look upon them no otherwise than the children of Israel, after they had crossed the Red Sea, looked in every direction upon their Egyptians dead and saw the wheels of their chariots sink into the deep; so that we too, though far more securely and joyfully, may sing to the Lord that he has been gloriously honoured, casting horse and rider into the abyss [Col. 0209D] (Exod. 14–15).

## SERMON VIII

### On the Eighth Verse: “Nevertheless, you shall look with your eyes, and shall see the recompense of sinners.”

[Col. 0210A]

1. At times, beloved, we would speak to you more briefly if this were permitted more often; and we believe you may sometimes have noticed this. But whenever, through the pressing evil of the day itself, we have perhaps endured for several days the most burdensome silence from your exhortation and consolation, none of you, I think, ought to wonder if, while we seek to redeem the time itself, a discourse delivered less often sometimes seems more extended.

Let this brief preface therefore accomplish this much for us: that the length of yesterday’s discourse and the brevity of today’s may alike be excused in your eyes. For I fear that some may find—or may have found—the former less agreeable, or the latter; or rather, both more than either one separately.

“His truth shall surround you with a shield: you shall not fear the terror of the night, the arrow flying by day, the business walking about in darkness, assault, and the noonday demon. A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; but it shall not come near you.” In the preceding discourses we said, insofar as Truth itself deigned to grant, how it protects the faithful soul for the present from temptations and afterwards from difficulties.

The same prophet, briefly commending both in another psalm, says: “In you I shall be delivered from temptation, and in my God I shall pass over a wall” [Col. 0210B] (Ps. 17:30): so that, with God himself as guide, he suffers neither a stumbling-block while walking here nor an obstacle when departing from here. Thus, in the one phrase frequent deliverance is signified; in the other, full and secure liberation.

But in this third statement which he adds—“Nevertheless, you shall look with your eyes”—I judge that a promise of no small blessedness is also contained. “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; but it shall not come near you. Nevertheless, you shall look with your eyes.” So I pray, Lord; so may it be. Let them fall, and let me not fall; let them be afraid, and let me not be afraid; let them be confounded, and let me not be confounded.

2. For in these few words the immortality of the soul is more clearly commended to me, and the truth of bodily resurrection itself is established. When they fall, I shall remain to see; and these eyes too, with which I behold their final recompense, shall not fail. For he does not say merely “with eyes,” but “with your eyes you shall look”: with those very eyes which now grow weak through want and fail while you hope in your God.

And indeed, brothers, the eyes fail while we hope. For “what a man sees, why does he hope for it?” “Hope that is seen,” he says, “is not hope” (Rom. 8:24). Therefore you shall then look with those same eyes which you now do not dare to lift to heaven; with those very eyes which meanwhile so often flow with tears and are worn down by frequent compunctions. Do not suppose that new eyes must be created for you; your own eyes are to be restored.

But why should I speak of the eye, though it is the smallest yet most eminent and excellent portion of the human body? Blessed hope lies stored in our bosom, by the promise of Truth itself: not even a hair of the head shall perish [Col. 0210C–0211A] (Luke 21:18).

3. Perhaps, however, the sight of the eyes is expressly promised because this seems at present to be the supreme desire of the soul: to see good things. “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13). It longs for the highest windows of its body to be opened to heavenly truth, yearning to walk rather by sight than by faith. Certainly faith comes by hearing, not by seeing. Finally, it is “the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing” (Heb. 11:1). Thus in faith, as in hope, the eye fails, while the ear alone advances.

“The Lord God has opened my ear,” says the prophet (Isa. 50:5); but one day he will also uncover the eye. The time will come when it shall no longer be said, “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear” (Ps. 44:11), but rather: Lift up your eyes and contemplate. What? Clearly the joy and exultation which your God stores up for you. What? Clearly not merely those things which, although you cannot yet see them, you can nevertheless hear and believe; but also that which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” [Col. 0211B] (Isa. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9).

The eye of resurrection will receive things so great as neither hearing nor the mind itself can now receive. Because of this intense desire of the soul to see what it hears and believes, I think that another most evident herald of the future resurrection also made express mention of his own eyes: “Again,” he says, “I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God my Saviour; whom I myself, and not another, shall see, and my eyes shall behold.” And he added: “This hope has been laid up in my bosom” (Job 19:26–27).

Perhaps, however, one should consider more carefully what he says: “My eyes,” just as in the Psalm: “You shall look with your eyes.” For do my eyes now appear to be mine? Certainly not mine. At one time they did appear to be mine, because they too are known to belong to that portion of paternal substance which I received, only to guard so badly. For it was swiftly squandered; I dispersed the whole of it all too quickly. The law of sin occupied all my members; death entered freely through my windows, and I myself had become its slave [Col. 0211C–D].

A wretched slave indeed—not serving even a human being, but an unclean and filthy beast. Nor did I serve even on the condition of a hired labourer, but wholly as a slave. Unless perhaps one thinks a reward is given to someone who is denied even food—and food more ruinous than hunger itself. For no one gave the pods to one who desired them, so that I might live as the swine do, not live together with the swine. Finally [variant: then], was my eye mine when it was plundering my soul? Under this necessity I was at last compelled to surrender [variant: renounce] the benefit into the hand of its Lord, so that he himself might rescue for himself from hostile tyranny what I was altogether unable to rescue [Col. 0212A].

5. Consider carefully, beloved, and observe from whose power you escaped the intolerable yoke of Pharaoh, so that your members may no longer be weapons of iniquity for sin, nor sin reign any longer in your mortal bodies. This is not your own work, brothers: “The right hand of the Lord works mightily”; only he can do this who cannot do nothing at all. Do not say, “Our hand is exalted” (Deut. 32:27); but confess, as healthfully as truthfully, that the Lord does all these things.

Finally, let no one doubt that he must take every possible care lest, while the days are still evil and there is nowhere any security for a human being, he should presume to wish to reclaim this possession of his from the hand of so merciful and provident a guardian into a liberty presently dangerous and destructive. For what the Father guards jealously, he guards jealously for you; and it is not envy but providence that makes him command the whole estate to remain his, lest it perish to you.

Finally, when you have arrived at that great and holy city whose boundaries he has made peace, where no hostile attack is any longer feared, he will not only restore you to yourself, but will give you himself besides [Col. 0212B]. Meanwhile turn away from your own wills, and do not rashly claim for yourself the members consecrated to God, knowing that things sanctified to godliness are assumed for the uses of vanity, curiosity, pleasure, or such secular business only at the cost of grave sacrilege.

“Do you not know,” says the Apostle, “that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own?” And again: “The body is not for fornication.” But for whom? Is it for you? Certainly, let it be free to you—but only if you can rescue it, or after rescuing it can thereafter preserve it from the onslaught of fornication by your own strength. But if perhaps you cannot—indeed, because you truly cannot—let the body be not for fornication but for the Lord (1 Cor. 6:19, 13); and let it meanwhile serve sanctification, lest it happen that it serves corruption again, and more grievously.

“I speak in human terms,” says the Apostle, “because of the weakness of your flesh. As you presented your members to serve iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” [Col. 0212C] (Rom. 6:19). Yet this is because of weakness, as he himself also prefaced it. But when that which was sown in weakness has risen in power, there will no longer be any necessity of serving. When security is free and freedom secure, why should he not all the more restore a person to himself? Rather, why should that great householder not grant freedom to his faithful servant, since he will appoint him over all his goods? [Col. 0212D]

6. Therefore, then, with your own eyes you shall behold—provided that meanwhile you have faithfully acknowledged that they are his, not yours. For apart from the reason we have mentioned, namely that necessary vow by which, renouncing your own wills, you consigned to divine service those very members which you could not at all rescue from the tyranny of sin—do they even now seem to be yours, in which the contrary law, though it does not reign, nevertheless dwells; in which the penalty of sin, [Col. 0213A] indeed your second enemy, not only remains, but even prevails and rules freely? Will you call your body your own when it is dead because of sin, or that belonging to the soul which never ceases to burden the soul? Certainly, if anyone wishes to call it his own, he will seem appropriately to have called it nothing other than his burden, his prison. Otherwise, how will you call your eyes your own, when meanwhile, whether you will it or not, sleep so often overtakes them, smoke disturbs them, a tiny speck of dust wounds them, harmful moisture clouds them, sharp pain torments them, and finally death itself, the last death, blinds them? But then indeed they will be yours, when none of these things shall exist: so that truly to behold with your own eyes will mean that thereafter you may use them for all things as freely as securely, at your pleasure. For your eyes will no longer need to be turned away [Col. 0213B] lest they see vanity, since they shall behold the purest truth; much less will death enter through the windows, since that last enemy itself shall also be destroyed. Or do you fear that, amid so great an abundance of light, where every righteous person shines as a separate sun, they will at some time grow dim? This would indeed be to be feared if the resurrection did not glorify the eyes themselves, as it glorifies the other members of the human body.

7. And you shall see the recompense of sinners. This indeed will be a grievous torment for them, and a great accumulation of evils. For perhaps it might seem some consolation if, amid their torments, either the awareness of those whom they had so maliciously attacked could remain hidden from them, or if at least they themselves could avoid their sight. Yet, although [Col. 0213C] from our beholding there will accrue to them an immeasurable weight of misery, what necessity, what usefulness, what delight will there be for us? For what could now appear so irreligious—indeed, so inhuman and execrable—as to wish to feed one’s eyes on the blood of enemies, however great their enmity, however wicked they may be, and to delight one’s gaze in the sufferings of the miserable? Nevertheless, just as “the sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away”—for the blessed will be called into the kingdom before the accursed are cast into the furnace of eternal fire, so that they may grieve more keenly when they see what they have lost—so also the righteous shall see and rejoice, considering what they have escaped. Therefore, in that great separation, just as the sight of the lambs will become an occasion of most grievous envy to the goats, so, conversely, the contemplation of the reprobate will provide the elect with an immeasurable matter for thanksgiving and praise. For how could the righteous give thanks so magnificently unless, together with the inconceivable happiness which they enjoy, they also beheld the recompense of the unjust, from whom they remember, most faithfully and devoutly, that they have been separated solely by the mercy of the Redeemer? And how would the impious waste away in such fury of mind unless they saw others admitted before their eyes into the kingdom of highest blessedness, while they themselves then at last groaned that they were condemned to those stenches, those horrors, those torments of everlasting fire, those, finally, miseries of immortal death? “There,” he says, “shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 13:50). Weeping [Col. 0214A] indeed because of the fire that is not quenched; gnashing because of the worm that does not die. Certainly, weeping arises from pain, gnashing of teeth from fury. The enormity of the torments will extort the weeping, while the very violence of wasting envy and obstinate malice will extort the gnashing of teeth. Thus you shall see the recompense of sinners, lest, being ignorant of so great a danger, you might appear at some time ungrateful to your deliverer.

8. Moreover, the visible recompense of sinners will also be the perfect security of the righteous, so that they can fear neither human nor diabolical malice any longer: they who, with a thousand falling at their side and ten thousand at their right hand, shall not merely see them fall, but see them fall into Gehenna. Do you suppose they could still be afraid, [Col. 0214B] or regard with suspicion the serpent more cunning than all living creatures—especially as they remember the woman once deceived in Paradise—unless they saw him already delivered, together with his whole body, to avenging flames, and a great chasm firmly established between themselves and him?

9. This contemplation of sinners will also provide you with a third benefit: that, by comparison with their deformity, you may shine forth more conspicuously and gloriously. For opposites set beside one another seem each to receive some increase of their own quality: if you compare white with black, the former will appear whiter and the latter darker. But hear a more certain testimony on this matter, the prophetic word: “The righteous man shall rejoice when he sees vengeance.” Why so? “He shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Ps. 57:11). Certainly, he will not defile them in blood, but wash them: so that where the other appears more bloodstained, this one may appear cleaner; where the other is more defiled, this one may shine more beautifully.

10. Perhaps no human affection can now be found that would recoil from any of these three reasons; but Wisdom will laugh at their destruction not because of any one of them—though she will without doubt do so. For Wisdom itself, which cannot possibly lie, foretells: “Because I called and you refused, I stretched out my hand and there was no one who looked.” And shortly afterward: “I too will laugh at your destruction and mock when that which you feared comes upon you, when sudden calamity rushes upon you and destruction comes like a storm” (Prov. 1:24, 26–27). What, then, do we think will please Wisdom in the destruction of fools, except its own most just ordering and the irreproachable order of things? Certainly, whatever will then please Wisdom must please all the wise as well. Therefore do not think it harsh that it is said, “With your own eyes you shall behold,” when you too shall laugh at their destruction: not because cruelty, as though by a certain savage inhumanity, takes delight in vengeance itself, but because the most beautiful order of divine governance, beyond what can be believed, delights an admirer of justice and lover of equity. When, truth illuminating more fully and perfectly, you recognize that all things are excellently ordered and that each has attained its own place—indeed, that each has passed into its own proper place—[Col. 0215A] how could you not delight to behold all things and to magnify in all things the ruler of all?

The apostle Peter aptly attested that the son of perdition “went to his own place,” because he burst asunder in the midst in the air (Acts 1:25, 18), a companion of the aerial powers: since neither heaven would receive nor earth sustain the betrayer of the true God and true man, who had come down from heaven to work salvation in the midst of the earth.

11. Thus with your own eyes you shall behold, and you shall see the recompense of sinners: first, because of your own escape; second, because of complete security; third, because of comparison; fourth, because of a perfect emulation of justice itself. For then it will be a time not of mercy but of judgment; and no pity whatsoever toward the impious is to be expected there, where no correction at all is to be hoped for. Far away will be that softness of human weakness which, nevertheless, for the present uses charity for salvation, gathering both good and bad fish—that is, pleasant and troublesome affections alike—into the broad bosom, as it were, of the outspread net [variant: namely]. But this is in the sea. On the shore it will select only the good, so rejoicing with those who rejoice that from then on it cannot weep with those who weep. Otherwise, how will this world be judged in us unless we forget this tender affection and are introduced into the wine-cellar, according to him who said: “I will enter into the powers of the Lord; O Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone” (Ps. [Col. 0215C] 70:16)?

Even now we are not permitted to regard the person of the poor man or to pity him in judgment; rather, even though with pain, such a feeling of compassion must be restrained, and the sentence of equity pronounced. How much more, where there can be no struggle of mind and no distress can enter, must what was said be fulfilled: “Their judges were swallowed up, joined to the rock” (Ps. 140:6). They are swallowed up indeed into the affection of justice, imitating the firmness of the Rock to which they are joined. “Joined to the rock,” he says—a Rock which, in order to follow it alone, they undoubtedly left all else behind. For this is what the Rock itself answered to Peter when he asked what they would receive: “When the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Foretelling this, the prophet likewise said: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3:14). Do you suppose that anything pliable will be found in judges joined to the Rock? “He who is joined to God,” says the Apostle, “is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17); and he who is joined to the Rock is one stone. It was to this, rightly enough, that the prophet sighed: “For me, to cling to God is good” (Ps. 72:28). Thus their judges were swallowed up, joined to the Rock. O grace of intimacy! O height of honor! O privilege of confidence! O prerogative of perfect security!

12. For what can be conceived so fearful, so full of anxiety and most vehement concern, as to stand to be judged before that so terrifying [Col. 0216A] tribunal and still await an uncertain sentence under so exacting a Judge? “It is dreadful,” says the Apostle, “to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). Let us be judged meanwhile, brothers, and let us strive by present judgment to avoid that terrible expectation. “God will not judge twice for the same thing.” Certainly, just as the sins of some, so also the good efforts of some are manifest beforehand, going before them to judgment: so that the former, not awaiting sentence, may immediately be cast down into Tartarus by the very weight of their crimes, while the latter, on the contrary, may ascend with complete freedom of spirit and without any hesitation to the seats prepared for them.

Blessed is the poverty of those who voluntarily leave all things and follow you, Lord Jesus! Blessed indeed, because it makes them so secure—indeed, so glorious—in that unique crashing of the elements, in that dreadful examination of merits, in that great crisis of judgments! But now let us hear what the devout and faithful soul answers to such great promises, lest perhaps it seem either to distrust or to trust otherwise than it ought. “For you are,” it says, “O Lord, my hope.” What could be said more soberly, what more piously? Nor does anything seem able to answer this phrase more fittingly than what follows: “You have made the Most High your refuge.” But forgive us, brothers: today again we seem to have exceeded, though only slightly, the limits of the brevity promised.

## SERMON IX

On the ninth verse: “For you are, O Lord, my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.”

[Col. 0216C]

1. Yes, brothers, today let us hear something concerning the Father’s promise, the children’s expectation, the end of this our pilgrimage, the reward of labor, the fruit of captivity. And indeed it is a hard captivity—not only that common one which we endure from the very condition of the human race, but also this one by which, hastening to mortify our own wills and even to lose our own souls in this world, we have committed ourselves to these chains of such strict discipline, to this prison of such grievous penitence. A wretched slavery indeed—if it seemed forced, if it did not seem voluntary. But now, since you voluntarily sacrifice yourselves to God, and no violence is imposed upon the will except through the will itself, certainly there is something at issue [Col. 0216D] here. I think it is that something greater than which nothing can exist. Or does anything, however great, however laborious, that is done for God seem lamentable? Even if the magnitude of the labor sometimes perhaps draws forth compassion, the consideration of its cause demands much more rejoicing. Moreover, all good things are known to be done not only for him, but through him. For “it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13). Thus he is the author, he the rewarder of the work, he the whole reward: so that the highest Good, whose simplicity in itself is so perfect, seems in us in a certain manner to be the twofold cause of good things, namely efficient and final. Rightly therefore, beloved, in all these many labors of yours [Col. 0217A] you not only stand firm but even overcome through him who loved you. Or is it not through him? It is manifestly so. “For as our tribulations abound for Christ,” says the Apostle, “so also our consolations abound through him” (2 Cor. 1:5).

2. “For God’s sake” is a customary phrase, a common phrase; but where it is not spoken emptily, it is a most profound phrase. It often sounds on the lips even of those whose hearts are proved to be far from it. Everyone asks that favors be done for them for God’s sake. Everyone demands assistance for themselves for God’s sake. Even things not according to God are readily requested for God’s sake; and one entreats that God do for him what he does not desire for God’s sake, but perhaps rather against God. Yet the phrase is living indeed and effective where it proceeds not perfunctorily, not presumptuously, not as a mere convention of speech or an art of persuasion, but, as is fitting, from the richness of devotion and purity of intention. For the world passes away, and its desire; and things done for it will not seem either profitably established or firmly secured when it falls. [Col. 0217B] For when the cause itself fails, how will not all things that appeared to rest upon it be emptied together? Therefore [variant: finally] those also who sow in the flesh reap corruption from the flesh, because all flesh is grass, and its glory like the flower of grass; and when the grass withers, the flower must likewise fall. He alone who is, is an unfailing cause; and the word of the Lord, not the flower of grass, abides forever (Isa. 40:6–8). Finally, he says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24:35).

3. Wisely therefore, beloved, and profitably, for the words of his lips you have chosen to keep hard ways, sowing there where not even the smallest portion of your seed can perish. Certainly, “he who sows sparingly shall not fail to reap, but shall reap sparingly” (2 Cor. 9:6). For he who reaps receives wages; and we know who promised that even he who gives a cup of cold water to one who thirsts in his name shall not lack his own reward (Matt. 10:42). Yet will he not be repaid in the same measure in which he measured, or be equal in recompense [Col. 0217D] to one who, not offering water but shedding blood, drank the cup of the Savior that was given to him? This is not a cup of cold water, but “an intoxicating cup, how splendid!” (Ps. 22:5), a cup of pure wine, indeed full of mixture (Ps. 74:9).

For my Lord Jesus alone had unmixed wine: he alone was perfectly pure, and can always make pure what was conceived from impure seed. He alone indeed had unmixed wine: since according to his divinity he is Wisdom, reaching everywhere because of her purity, and nothing defiled falls into her; and according to his humanity “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” He alone tasted death not by the debt of his condition, but by the good pleasure of his own will—not indeed for his own advantage, for he has no need of our goods; nor as repaying us grace for grace, since he died for friends only in order to acquire them, namely, to make friends from enemies. “For while we were still enemies, we were reconciled to God through the blood of his Son.” Or rather, he died for those already his friends, though not yet loving him, but already loved by him. For herein is grace: not that we loved God, but that he himself first loved us. Would you know how much earlier? “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” says the Apostle, “who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world”; and shortly afterward: “He bestowed grace upon [Col. 0218B] us,” he says, “in his beloved Son” (Eph. 1:3, 4, 6). How were we not already beloved in him when we were chosen in him? How were we not pleasing to him in whom grace was bestowed upon us? Thus Christ, according to time, died for the ungodly; but according to predestination, for brothers and friends.

4. In all these things, therefore, his wine alone is unmixed, so that none of the rest may dare presume that the prophetic saying does not apply to him: “Your wine is mixed with water” (Isa. 1:22). First, because meanwhile no one is clean from defilement; no one can at all boast that he has a pure heart. Second, because they must sometime pay the debt of death. Third, because, in laying down their lives for Christ, they purchase eternal life by this advantage for themselves [Note: [Col. 0217D] Tiraquellus and Horstius: “they earn eternal life.”]; yet woe to them if they should be ashamed of his testimony. Fourth, because they render a return far too unequal and scanty for such love freely shown to them beforehand. Yet he who is without mixture does not disdain even this mixed wine, so much so that the Apostle confidently says that he fills up in his own body what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ (Col. 1:24).

Therefore, although one and the same denarius of eternal life is to be paid to all the elect alike, nevertheless, just as “star differs from star in glory,” and there is one glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars, so also will be the resurrection of the dead; and although the house is one, there are nevertheless different dwelling places within it. Thus, with respect to eternity and sufficiency, neither is the one who has little diminished [Col. 0218D] nor the one who has much made to abound; but with respect to eminence and the distinction of merits, each shall receive according to his labor, so that nothing at all which has been sown in Christ may perish.

5. These things, brothers, have been said so that the significance of that highly spiritual answer which we are to consider today may be commended: “For you are, O Lord, my hope.” Whatever must be done, whatever avoided, whatever endured, whatever desired—you, O Lord, are my hope. This is the ground of all my promises; this is the whole reason for my expectation. Let another put forward merit; let him boast that he bears the burden of the day and the heat; let him say that he fasts twice on the Sabbath; finally, let him glory that he is not like other people. But for me, it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God. Let others hope in other things: perhaps one trusts in literary learning, another in worldly cunning, one in nobility, another in rank, another in some other vanity. “For your sake I have counted all things loss and regard them as dung,” because you are, O Lord, my hope. Let whoever wishes hope in the uncertainty of riches; but I do not even hope for the necessities of life except from you, trusting in your word, for which I have cast aside all things: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). For “the poor man is left to you; you will be a helper to the orphan” (Ps. 9:14). If rewards are promised to me, I shall hope to obtain them through you; if battles rise up [Col. 0219B] against me, if the world rages, if the evil one roars, if the flesh itself desires against the spirit—in you I shall hope.

6. Brothers, to think thus is to live by faith; nor can anyone rightly say, “For you are, O Lord, my hope,” unless he is inwardly persuaded by the Spirit that, as the prophet counsels, he should cast his thought upon the Lord, knowing that he will be nourished by him (Ps. 54:23), in accordance also with the saying of the apostle Peter: “Casting all your care upon him, for he cares for you” (1 Pet. 5:7). For if we think this way, why do we hesitate utterly to cast aside miserable, vain, useless, deceptive hopes, and to cling to this one hope, so solid, so perfect, so blessed, with the whole devotion of the soul and the whole fervor of the spirit? [Col. 0219C] If anything is impossible or even difficult for him, seek another in whom to hope. But he can do all things by a word. What is easier to say? Yet I wish you to understand such a saying [variant: “do not neglect it”]. If he has decreed to save us, we shall immediately be delivered; if he is pleased to give life, life is in his will; if he wills to bestow eternal rewards, he is permitted to do what he wills. Or perhaps you do not now doubt his ability, but his will itself is suspect to you? Certainly, the testimonies of his will have been made altogether credible. “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Finally, when does that majesty, which so earnestly urges us to hope in itself, fail one who hopes in it? Certainly, it does not abandon those who hope in it. “He will help them,” he says, “and deliver them; he will snatch them from sinners and save them” (Ps. 36:40). Why? By what merits? Hear what follows: “Because they hoped in him.” A sweet cause, yet effective, yet unanswerable. This indeed is righteousness from faith, not from the law.

“From whatever tribulation they cry out to me, I will hear them.” Behold, count the tribulations. In proportion to their multitude, his consolations will gladden your soul—provided you do not turn to another, provided you cry out to him, provided you hope in him, and make your refuge not something lowly or earthly, but the Most High. Who has hoped in him and been put to shame? Heaven and earth will pass away more readily than his word can be made void.

7. “You have made the Most High your refuge.” There the tempter will not approach, the slanderer will not ascend, that most evil accuser of the brethren will not reach. For this is said to him—recall the beginning of the psalm—to him who dwells in the protection of the Most High, fleeing there from faintness of spirit and tempest. There is indeed a twofold necessity of fleeing: because there are battles without and fears within. We would need to flee less if either inward greatness of soul could courageously endure outward tumults, or inward faintness were cherished by outward tranquility. “You have made the Most High,” he says, [Col. 0220A] “your refuge.” Let us flee there often, brothers: the place is fortified; no enemy is feared there. Would that we might rather be permitted always to remain there! But this does not belong to the present time. What is now a refuge will someday be a dwelling place, and an everlasting dwelling place. Meanwhile, although we are not permitted to remain there continually, we must nevertheless return there frequently. For in every temptation, every tribulation, and finally every necessity of whatever kind, the city of refuge is open to us; the bosom of our mother is outspread; the clefts of the rock are ready; the bowels of the mercy of our God stand open. Whoever turns away from this refuge, it is no wonder if he does not deserve to escape.

8. Now indeed, brothers, what has been said might seem sufficient for expounding this verse if the prophet had said, “Because I have hoped in you,” as is found in certain other psalms (Ps. 15:1). But when he says, “You are, O Lord, my hope,” perhaps he means something more and higher: namely, that he not only hopes in him, but hopes for him. For our hope is more fittingly called that which we hope for than that in which we hope. There may be some who desire to obtain from the Lord whatever temporal or spiritual things; but perfect charity thirsts only for what is highest, crying out with the whole intensity of its desire: “What have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth? God of my heart, and God is my portion forever” (Ps. 72:25–26). Today’s reading from the prophet Jeremiah aptly commended both things to us in a few words: “The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him” (Lam. 3:25). Here carefully observe also the distinction of number: he says “those who hope in him” in the plural, since this seems common to many; but “the soul that seeks him” in the singular, because it belongs to singular purity, singular grace, singular perfection, not merely to hope for nothing except from him, but to seek nothing except him. If he is good to the former, how much more to the latter?

9. Accordingly, the soul that seeks him is rightly answered: “You have made the Most High your refuge.” For the soul that thirsts for God in this manner neither wishes, with Peter, to make him a tabernacle on an earthly mountain (Matt. 17:4), nor thereafter, with Mary, to touch him on earth (John 20:17); but cries aloud: “Flee, my beloved; be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of Bethel” (Song 8:14). For it has heard him say: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). It has heard him say: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” [Col. 0221A] (John 20:17). And, no longer ignorant of the heavenly counsel, it cries with the Apostle: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus” (2 Cor. 5:16).

“Upon the mountains of Bethel,” that is, above every power and principality, above angels and archangels, cherubim and seraphim also—for these are none other than the mountains of the house of God, which is what Bethel means—indeed, at the right hand of the Father, where the Father is no longer greater than he, longing to grasp the co-highest at the right hand of the Most High. For this is eternal life, brothers: that we know the Father, the true God; and also Jesus Christ, whom he sent, no less truly God and one with him, God above all, blessed for ages. Amen.

## SERMON X

On the tenth verse: “No evil shall approach you, and no scourge shall come near your tent.”

[Col. 0221B]

1. It is neither our own opinion nor one new to you, but a thoroughly familiar proposition: in each of the principal parts of our faith, it is easier to know what something is not than what it is, and more dangerous to be ignorant of the former. The same may fittingly be attributed also to hope. For the human mind, having experienced such great evils, understands much more readily the things of which it will be deprived than those which it will enjoy. There is indeed a close kinship between faith and hope: what the former believes will be, the latter begins to hope will be for itself. Accordingly, the Apostle defines faith as “the substance of things hoped for” (Heb. 11:1), since no one can hope for what he has not believed, any more than he can paint upon emptiness.

Faith says: Great and inconceivable goods have been prepared by God for his faithful ones. Hope says: They are kept for me. But charity, the third, says: “I run toward them for myself.” Yet, as I have already mentioned, it is altogether difficult, even impossible, to investigate the quality of those goods, unless perhaps God himself has revealed it through his Spirit to someone, according to the Apostle’s words: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). Certainly, however perfect one may be while still dwelling in mortal flesh—unless there were here some, so to speak, imperfect perfection, the Apostle would not say, “As many of us as are perfect, let us think the same”; namely, precisely what he had previously said: “Not as though I had already received or were already perfect” (Phil. 3:12)—even Paul himself must confess: “Now I know in part”; and again: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). Therefore that which can meanwhile be more readily known by humanity is commended more fully through devout and provident repetition. For it is characteristic of the afflicted to regard deliverance from troubles as the height of happiness, and freedom from misery as the highest blessedness. Hence the prophet says in the psalm: “Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you”; yet he does not enumerate any of the gifts of happiness conferred, but adds: “For he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling” (Ps. 114:7–8). In these words [Col. 0222A] he clearly indicates how great a rest and how great benefits of the Lord he judges deliverance from tribulations and dangers to be.

2. The passage from the ninetieth psalm which we must discuss today is found to be like this proposition: “No evil shall approach you, and no scourge shall come near your tent.” The meaning of this verse, as far as we understand it, is easy; perhaps some among you have already anticipated it. For you are neither so untrained nor so inexperienced in spiritual study that you cannot most readily distinguish between yourselves and your tents, and likewise between that which is called evil and that which is called a scourge. You have certainly heard the Apostle say, when he had already fought the good fight, that the laying aside of his tent would come swiftly (2 Tim. 4:6). But why do I mention the Apostle’s words? As though a soldier could fail to know his own tent, or needed instruction from another’s example.

We certainly see some who have turned their tents into dwellings of the most shameful captivity and who do not serve as soldiers in them, but endure a wretched slavery. Indeed—and this is wholly ridiculous—some err so greatly, and have arrived at such forgetfulness and spiritual madness, that they seem to think themselves nothing other than this outward tent of theirs. For what else is it but ignorance not only of God but even of themselves, when, as though dead in heart, they expend all their effort upon the flesh, attending to their tent as though they thought it would never fall? Yet it must fall, and that soon. Do not those who are so given over to flesh and blood appear not to know themselves, as though they judged themselves to be nothing at all but flesh alone, thus taking their souls in vain as though they were altogether ignorant that they possess souls? “If you separate the precious from the vile,” says the Lord, “you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. 15:19): that is, if you carefully distinguish between the outward and inward substance, so that you fear no more for your tent from the scourge than for yourself from evil. For this is the evil of which it is said: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27). This is the evil that deprives the soul of its own soul, that separates between you and God; so that, when it reigns, the soul is without God as the body is without soul—plainly dead in itself, like one of those whom the Apostle recalled as having been without God in this world [Col. 0222D] (Eph. 2:12).

3. Nor would I say that you should hate even your own flesh. Love it as given to you for help and prepared for participation in eternal blessedness. Yet let the soul love the flesh in such a way that it is not thought to have passed over into flesh, nor said to it by the Lord: “My spirit shall not remain in man, because he is flesh” (Gen. 6:3). Let the soul love its flesh, but preserve its own soul much more. Let Adam love his Eve, but not so as to obey her voice more than the divine voice. Finally, it is not even good for the flesh itself to be loved in such a way that, by guarding it meanwhile from the scourge of paternal correction, [Col. 0223A] you store up wrath for it in eternal condemnation.

“Brood of vipers,” says John, “who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come? Produce worthy fruits of repentance” (Matt. 3:7–8). It is as though he spoke more plainly: Embrace discipline, lest at some time the Lord grow angry; endure the correcting rod, lest you feel the crushing hammer. How do carnal people say to us: “Your life is cruel; you do not spare your flesh”? Very well: we do not spare the seed. In what way could we spare it better? Is it not better for it to be renewed and multiplied in the field than to rot in the granary? “Alas! the beasts have rotted in their dung!” (Joel 1:17). Is this how you spare your flesh? Let us for the present be cruel by not sparing it; but you are certainly more cruel by sparing it. For even now our flesh rests in hope. You yourselves must see what disgrace yours now endures, what misery awaits it in the future.

“No evil shall approach you, and no scourge shall come near your tent.” Here a twofold robe and a twofold immortality are commended. For from what does death arise except from the separation of soul and body? That is why a dead body is called lifeless. And whence comes this separation except from present scourges, from every intensity of pain, from the corruption of the body itself, from the punishment of sin? Accordingly our flesh rightly fears and hates the scourge, because through it it suffers a most bitter divorce from the soul’s so delightful and honorable companionship. Yet meanwhile, until it is recalled [variant: renewed], whether it wishes or not, it must endure [Col. 0223C] it. But it is expedient to endure it in such a way that you escape utterly, and thereafter no scourge comes near your tent.

4. Now, as we have recalled above—and as it is fitting to recall unceasingly—God is the true life of the soul; and among these things he also separates evil, but the evil of the soul, which is nothing other than sin. Come then, brothers: let us be free to trifle, let us delight in indulging idleness—while this pair of serpents is nearby, depriving us of a double life, one of the body and the other of the heart. Why should we sleep securely, except that negligence amid graver danger is an indication not so much of security as of despair? Indeed, we ought to desire deliverance from both; but meanwhile we must certainly guard against sin more than against sin’s punishment, and turn away from evil more zealously than from the scourge, inasmuch as it is more destructive and altogether more unhappy for a soul to be separated from God than from its body.

Certainly, when every sin has been wholly removed, its cause having entirely been taken away, neither will its effect thereafter remain. Thus, just as evil will no longer be able at all to come near you, so neither will the scourge be able to approach your tent: that is, any punishment will be as far from the outward person as guilt has been from the inward person. For he does not say, “Evil will not be in you,” or, “The scourge will not be in your tent,” but: “It will not come near; it will not approach.”

5. For one may observe people in whom sin not only dwells but also reigns; nor does anything seem capable of being nearer or more inward—unless perhaps it comes to rule them in such a way that it can thereafter no longer fail to rule. But others too may be found in whom sin still remains, yet no longer rules or prevails: in a sense uprooted, though not yet expelled; cast down, but not wholly cast out. Certainly, this was not so in the beginning. In our first parents, before that first transgression of the command, sin not only did not reign, but was not even present. Yet it seems in some sense already then to have been near them, since it was so easily persuaded and entered so swiftly.

What else was he warning than that even the punishment of sin, although it had not yet entered their bodies, was already, as it were, at the door, when he said: “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17)? Happy, therefore, is our expectation, and blessed our hope, for whose sake the resurrection to come will be so much more glorious than the first creation: so that neither guilt nor punishment—neither evil nor scourge—may either reign or dwell, or ever again be capable of reigning or dwelling, in our souls or bodies. “Evil shall not come near you,” he says, “and the scourge shall not approach your tent.” Surely nothing is so remote as that which can no longer be present.

6. But what are we doing, brothers? I fear that I have been caught out. For that great and common abbot of mine and yours is known to have assigned this hour not for leisure in speaking, but for manual work (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 48). Yet I think he will readily forgive it, especially since he is not forgetful of that devout stratagem by which Romanus formerly ministered piously for three years to Benedict while he was lodged in a cave. For, as we read, “he devoutly stole hours from his father’s eyes and, on appointed days, brought bread to Benedict, whom he could secretly supply with food” (Gregory, *Dialogues*, book II, ch. 1).

And I do not doubt, brothers, that many among you have at hand a more abundant supply of spiritual delights. Yet what I share with you, I do not steal from myself. Rather, whatever the Lord grants, I receive more securely and more sweetly with you; for this nourishment is not diminished by being distributed, but is rather increased in ministry. Nevertheless, when we occasionally [variant: at some time] speak to you outside the custom of our order, we do not do so through our own presumption, but by the will of our venerable brothers and fellow abbots, who even impose this upon us, though they by no means wish such permission to be generally allowed to themselves. For they know that I have a different situation and a particular necessity. I would not be speaking to you now if I could work with you. That perhaps would be a more effective word for you, and more acceptable to my conscience.

But since this is denied me—through my sins demanding it, through this burdensome and, as you yourselves know, manifold bodily weakness, and also through the necessity of the time—may I, though speaking and not doing, deserve to be found at least the least in the kingdom of God. Amen.

## SERMON XI. On the eleventh verse: “For he has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may guard you in all your ways.”

[Col. 0225A]

1. It is written—and truly written—that “it is through the mercies of the Lord that we have not been consumed,” that he has not delivered us into the hands of our enemies (Lam. 3:22). That tireless and ever-watchful eye of singular mercy watches over us: “he who guards Israel neither sleeps nor slumbers.” This indeed is necessary. For he who attacks Israel neither sleeps nor slumbers. And just as God is solicitous for us and we are his concern, so the enemy is solicitous to slaughter and destroy us; and his single concern is that perhaps one who has turned away might return.

But we either pay no heed, or pay too little heed, to the reverence due to him who presides, to the protection of him who guards us, and to the benefits of him who bestows them—ungrateful for grace, indeed for the many graces by which he anticipates and helps us. Now he himself fills our souls with brightness; now he visits through angels; now he instructs through human beings; now too he consoles and teaches through the Scriptures. “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15:4). Well does it say “for instruction,” so that through patience we may hope; for, as has been said elsewhere, “a man’s teaching is known through patience” (Prov. 19:11). And patience produces tested character, while tested character produces hope (Rom. 5:4).

Why are we alone not attentive to ourselves? Why are we alone negligent of ourselves? Are we to disregard our duty because help comes to us from every side? On the contrary, we must for that very reason watch more diligently. Such great concern for us would not be exercised both in heaven and on earth if no great necessity seemed to press upon us; nor would such manifold guardianship be provided for us except because of manifold snares.

2. Happy, therefore, are our brothers who have already been delivered from the hunters’ snare, who have passed from the tents of those at war into the courts of those at rest, with fear of evils removed and established in a singular hope. To one of these—indeed, to the whole company—is said: “Evil shall not come near you, and the scourge shall not approach your tent.”

Consider carefully: this promise is made not to the person who lives according to the flesh, but to one who, dwelling in the flesh, walks according to the Spirit. For in the former it is impossible to distinguish between the person and his tent. Everything in him is confused, as in a son of Babylon. Indeed, such a person is himself flesh, and the Spirit does not remain in him. But where the good Spirit is absent, when will evil be lacking? Moreover, where evil is, the scourge too must necessarily draw near. Punishment always accompanies evil. “Evil shall not come near you, and the scourge shall not approach your tent.” It is a great promise; but on what grounds may one hope for it? How shall I escape evil and scourge? How shall I flee or keep them at a distance, so that they do not approach me? By what merit, what wisdom, what power? “For he has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may guard you in all your ways.”

In all what ways? In those by which you turn away from evil and flee the wrath to come. Many are the ways, and many are the kinds of ways: truly great is the traveler’s danger. How easily will one who lacks discernment of ways go astray at the meeting of many paths! For he has not commanded the angels to guard us “in all ways,” but “in all our ways.” There are ways from which we ought to be guarded, not ways in which [variant: and in which] we ought to be guarded.

3. Let us therefore search out our ways, brothers; let us investigate also the ways of demons, the ways of the blessed spirits, and the ways of the Lord. What I am undertaking is above me; but you will help by your prayers, that God may open for me the treasury of his understanding and make the freewill offerings of my mouth pleasing to himself.

The ways of the children of Adam lie in necessity and desire. We are led by both and drawn by both, except that we seem to be pressed more by necessity and drawn more by desire. Necessity seems properly attributable to the body. Nor is it simple, but has many windings and many losses; for shortcuts are extremely few, if there are any at all. Who does not know how manifold human necessity really is? Who could explain how manifold it is? Experience itself teaches us; affliction itself gives understanding. In these things everyone is taught how necessary it is to cry out to the Lord, not, “Deliver me from necessity,” but, “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. 24:17).

Nor will anyone who has not received with a deaf ear the warnings of Wisdom fail to wish deliverance not only from this way of necessity but also from that of desire. For what does Wisdom say? “Turn away from your own desires”; and again, “Do not go after your lusts” (Sir. 18:30). Of two evils, it is far better to walk in necessity than in desire. Necessity is manifold; but desire is in every way, indeed beyond all measure, more manifold still. Desire is a matter of the heart; therefore it is greater by as much as the soul is greater than the body.

These, indeed, are the ways that seem good to human beings, but they have no end except when they plunge into the depths of hell. If you have found the ways of human beings, consider also whether it may be said of them: “Destruction and misery are in their ways” (Ps. 13:3)—so that destruction is in necessity, and misery in desire. How is misery in desire—that is, not happiness, as it is thought to be? What if someone imagines happiness smiling upon him in the desired abundance of earthly things? He is thereby the more miserable, in proportion as he more eagerly embraces misery itself as happiness, or sinks more deeply into it and is swallowed by it. Woe to the children of men because of this false and deceitful happiness! Woe to the one who says, “I am rich and need nothing,” while he is poor, naked, wretched, and pitiable! Necessity proceeds from the weakness of the flesh; desire, from the hunger and forgetfulness of the heart. The soul begs for what belongs to another because it has forgotten to eat its own bread; it hungers after earthly things because it does not meditate on heavenly things.

[Col. 0227A]

4. Let us also look at the ways of demons; let us look at them and beware, look at them and flee from them. For their ways are presumption and obstinacy. Do you wish to know how I know this? Consider their prince: such as he is, such are his household. Consider the beginnings of his ways: did he not immediately leap forth into the most monstrous presumption, saying, “I shall sit upon the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13)? What reckless and dreadful presumption! Were not all workers of iniquity cast down there, expelled and unable to stand? Through presumption they could not stand; through obstinacy, one who has fallen will not add that he may rise again. From the former comes the spirit that goes forth; from the latter, the spirit that does not return. [Variant: “indeed” for “from the former.”]

The demons’ presumption is astonishing, but no less astonishing is their obstinacy: their pride always rises, and therefore there is no change in them. Because they were unwilling to turn from the way of presumption, they fell into the way of obstinacy. How perverse and overturned in heart are the children of men who follow the footsteps of demons and enter the ways of demons! For the entire struggle of the spiritual forces of wickedness against us is to deceive us, to lead us into their ways, to guide us along them, and bring us to the destined end prepared for them. Flee presumption, O human being, lest your enemy rejoice over you. For he especially delights in these vices, having learned in himself how difficult it is to recover one’s breath from so great an abyss.

5. I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of how one descends—indeed, falls—into those ways. The first step of this descent, as it now occurs to me, is the concealment of one’s own weakness, wickedness, and uselessness: while sparing himself, flattering himself, and persuading himself that he is something when he is nothing, a person already deceives himself. The second step is ignorance of oneself. For once, at the first step, he has sewn himself useless girdles of leaves, what remains except that he does not see the wounds he has covered—especially since he made the covering for this sole purpose, that he might not see them?

From this it finally comes about that, even when another uncovers them, he insists that the wounds do not exist, “turning to words of malice, to make excuses for sins.” This is the third step, now very near—indeed adjoining—presumption. For what evil will one already hesitate to do who presumes even to defend it? Yet he will scarcely remain here amid darkness and slippery ground, especially when there is also at hand an evil angel of the Lord to pursue and drive him on. Thus the fourth step—or rather, the fourth precipice—is contempt, so that, as Scripture says, “When the wicked person comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3).

Thereafter the pit presses its mouth more and more heavily upon him, since contempt hands such a soul over to impenitence, and impenitence is strengthened by obstinacy. This is now the sin forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come, because a hard and hardened heart neither fears God nor respects any human being. Whoever thus clings to the devil in all his ways has manifestly become one spirit with him.

The ways of human beings which we have shown above are those of which it is said: “No temptation has seized you except what is human” (1 Cor. 10:13); and because it is human to sin. But who does not know that diabolical ways are foreign to human nature? Except that in some persons habit itself seems to have put on the character of nature. Yet, although such conduct may be found in certain human beings, persevering in evil is not human but diabolical.

6. What, then, are the ways of the holy angels? Surely those which the Only-Begotten described when he said: “You shall see angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:51). Their ways, then, are ascent and descent: ascent for their own sake; descent—or rather condescension—for ours. Thus those blessed spirits ascend through the contemplation of God and descend through compassion for you, so that they may guard you in all your ways. They ascend at his face; they descend at his command, “for he has commanded his angels concerning you.” Yet even in descending they are not deprived of the vision of glory, because they always see the Father’s face.

7. I think you also want to hear of the Lord’s ways. I seem to presume greatly if I promise to show them. Yet it is written of him that “he will teach us his ways” (Ps. 24:9; Mic. 4:2). To whom else could they be entrusted? He taught his ways when he opened the lips of the prophet to say: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). Thus he comes to each person, and to all together, in mercy and truth.

Where there has already been much presumptuous reliance on mercy, but forgetfulness of truth, God is not thereby present. Nor is he present where there is much terror from remembrance of truth but no consoling recollection of mercy. For one does not possess truth who does not recognize mercy where mercy truly exists; nor can mercy be true without truth. Thus, where mercy and truth have met one another, justice and peace also kiss; and he cannot be absent whose dwelling is made in peace.

How much we have heard and learned—since our fathers have declared it to us—concerning this most happy union of mercy and truth! “Your mercy and your truth have upheld me,” says the Prophet (Ps. 39:12); and elsewhere, “Your mercy,” he says, “is before my eyes, and I have been well-pleasing in your truth” (Ps. 25:3). The Lord himself also says of him: “My truth and my mercy are with him” (Ps. 88:25).

8. Consider also the manifest comings of the Lord: in the one already undertaken, hold him as the merciful Savior; in the one promised at the end, await him as the truthful Requiter. Perhaps this too is why it is said: “Because God loves mercy and truth, the Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 83:12). Although in the former coming he remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel, and in the latter, though he will judge the world in equity and peoples in his truth, the coming judgment will nevertheless not occur without mercy—except perhaps for one who has not shown mercy.

These are the paths of eternity, of which you find this in the prophet: “The hills of the world were bowed down by his eternal paths” (Hab. 3:6). The proof is readily at hand: “The mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity” (Ps. 102:17), and “the truth of the Lord remains forever” (Ps. 116:2). The hills of the world—the proud demons, the rulers of this world and of these darknesses—were bowed down by these paths. They did not know the way of truth and mercy, nor did they remember his paths. What has he to do with truth who is a liar and its father? Indeed, it is plainly written of him: “He did not stand in the truth.” How far he was from mercy is also testified by the misery he inflicted upon us. When was he ever merciful, who “was a murderer from the beginning” (John 8:44)?

Finally, one wicked toward himself—to whom can he be good? How utterly wicked toward himself is he who never grieves for his own iniquity and is never pierced with sorrow over his own condemnation! Clearly, false presumption drove him from the way of truth; cruel obstinacy barred the way of mercy. Thus he can never attain mercy within himself or receive mercy from the Lord. In this manner those swollen hills were bowed down by the paths of eternity: they fell away from the ways of the Lord—which are straight—through their own windings and crooked courses, which are not so much paths as precipices.

How much more wisely and beneficially other hills have been bowed down and humbled by these paths unto salvation! For they are not bowed down by them as though dissenting from their rectitude, but because the paths of eternity themselves have bent them. Do we not see the hills of the world already bowed down when every exalted and powerful person inclines in devout submission to the Lord and worships his footsteps? Are they not bowed down when they turn from their own destructive heights of vanity and cruelty to the humble paths of mercy and truth?

9. To these ways of the Lord the ways not only of good spirits but also of chosen human beings are directed. The first step for a miserable person emerging from the depth of vices is that mercy by which he has compassion on his mother’s son, has compassion on his own soul, and thereby pleases God. For such a person imitates that great work of divine compassion: pierced with contrition together with him who was first pierced for him, he too dies in some fashion for his own salvation and does not spare himself.

This compassion first receives one who returns to his heart, and it is exercised within the hidden recesses of the inward parts. It remains for him to proceed upon the royal road and go forward as far as truth; and, as we most frequently urge upon you, let confession of the mouth accompany contrition of the heart. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” One who has returned to the heart must become little in his own eyes, as Truth says: “Unless you are converted and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). Therefore, he should not wish to conceal what he cannot fail to know: how utterly he has been brought to nothing. Let him not be ashamed to bring into the light of truth what he has seen secretly, not without an affection of compassion. Thus a person enters the ways of mercy and truth—indeed, the ways of the Lord, the ways of life; and the fruit of these ways is the traveler’s salvation.

10. It is equally clear that the ways of angels tend toward the same ends. When they ascend in contemplation, they seek truth; desiring it, they are satisfied, and being satisfied, they desire it. But when they descend, they exercise mercy toward us, in order that they may guard us in all our ways. For they are ministering spirits, sent into service on our account (Heb. 1:14). Clearly, they are our ministers, not our lords. In this they imitate the form of the Only-Begotten, who came not to be served but to serve (Matt. 20:28), and who stood among the disciples as one who serves.

The fruit of angelic ways, so far as angels themselves are concerned, is their own blessedness and the obedience of charity; but so far as we are concerned, it is, on the one hand, the obtaining of divine grace, and, on the other, the guarding of our way. For he has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may guard you in all your necessities and in all your desires. Otherwise it is easy for you to run into the ways of death: namely, to break out from necessity into obstinacy, or from desire into presumption—ways now not of human beings but of demons. For in what are people so readily found obstinate as in that which they either pretend or suppose to concern necessity? “Whatever you advise,” says such a person, “I can do what I can do, and I cannot do more.” “If you were here, you would think differently” (Terence, *Andria*, act 2, scene 1). And from what do we leap into presumption except some rush of more vehement desire?

11. Meanwhile, therefore, God has commanded his angels not to remove you from your ways, but to guard you in those very ways and, as it were, through their own ways to direct your ways into his. “How?” you ask. In this way: what an angel does more purely through charity alone, you too, at least compelled and instructed by your own necessity, should do—namely, descend and condescend to show mercy to your neighbor. And again, raising your desires with the same angel, you should strive with the whole longing of your soul to ascend to the supreme and everlasting truth.

For this reason we are urged to lift up our hearts with our hands (Lam. 3:41); for this reason we hear daily, “Lift up your hearts.” For this reason also we are rebuked when negligent, and it is said to us: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3). A heart relieved of its burden and made light is lifted higher, to seek and love truth. Do not wonder that they do not disdain to admit us—indeed, to bring us—into the ways of the Lord, when they deign to guard us in ours. Yet how much more happily and securely they themselves walk in those ways! Still, they too move in mercy and truth, though far beneath him who is Truth itself and Mercy itself.

12. How fittingly God has arranged each being in its own rank and according to what befits it! He who is highest holds the highest place: he above whom there is nothing, beyond whom there is nothing. He has placed his angels not in the highest place, but in safety; for, cleaving nearer to him who stands on high, they are strengthened by power from above. Human beings, however, are neither in the highest place nor in safety, but in watchfulness. Indeed, they are also on solid ground—that is, on earth—occupying the lowest place, yet not the uttermost lowest, from which they both can and must take care for themselves. But demons wander in the suspended air, roaming, fickle [variant: empty] and windy. For, unworthy to ascend to heaven, they nevertheless disdain to descend to earth.

Let these things suffice for today. And may we, by the gift of him from whom our sufficiency comes, be able sufficiently to render him thanks. For we are not sufficient even to think anything of ourselves as from ourselves (2 Cor. 3:5), unless he gives it to us—the one who gives abundantly to all and is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XII. On the eleventh verse, “For he has commanded his angels concerning you,” etc., and on the twelfth verse, “They shall bear you in their hands,” etc.

1. If you remember, in yesterday’s sermon we said that the ways of demons are presumption and obstinacy, and we did not conceal why we said so. Yet, if you judge it necessary, we may investigate still another way of theirs. For although they labor by every means to hide them, the Holy Spirit betrays them in many ways and in many ways makes known in the holy Scriptures the paths of the wicked.

We read concerning them all: “The wicked walk in a circle” (Ps. 11:9). We read concerning their prince that he “goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). He himself is compelled to confess this in the presence of Majesty, when, standing among the sons of God and asked from where he comes, he says: “I have gone around the earth and walked through it” (Job 1:7). Let us therefore name his ways: circling and circumvention. He employs the former upon himself, the latter upon us. He is always exalted, yet always cast down; his pride always rises and is always humbled. Is this not a circling? For one who walks in a circle moves indeed, but makes no progress.

Woe to the person who follows this circling and never departs from his own will. If you try to pull him away, he may seem to follow a little, but deceitfully. It is circling: he prepares a return by another route and will not be entirely led away from it. He struggles on every side and flees in every direction, yet always remains attached to his own will.

2. Yet, if one’s own circling is evil, another’s circumvention is far worse. This especially makes the devil what he is. But how, brothers, does that supremely proud being descend in order to circumvent a miserable human being? Observe the circling of the wicked even in this. His eyes behold everything lofty; yet he also curiously traces the very lowest things, in order to rise higher, swell more violently, and, having trampled down the humble, seem loftier to himself—as it is written: “While the wicked is proud, the poor is set on fire” (Ps. 9:2).

How perversely the evil angel imitates the ascending and descending good angels! He ascends through zeal for vanity; he descends through the envy of malice. His ascent is deceitful and his descent cruel; he is devoid, as we said yesterday, of mercy and truth. Yet if malignant spirits descend to circumvent us, let us give thanks to him at whose command good angels descend to assist us and guard us in all our ways. And not only this: “They shall bear you,” he says, “in their hands, lest you ever strike your foot against a stone.”

3. How much instruction, admonition, and consolation is offered us, brothers, in the words of this Scripture! In all the Psalms, what passage more magnificently consoles the fainthearted, admonishes the negligent, and instructs the ignorant? Divine providence wished to grant this very benefit to its faithful people: that the verses of this psalm should be especially on their lips during this Lenten season. The occasion seems to have arisen from nothing other than the devil’s own misuse of it, so that the wicked servant might serve the Son even unwillingly. For what could be more vexing to him, or more delightful to us, than that his very evil should cooperate for our good?

“He has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may guard you in all your ways.” Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men. Let them confess and say among the nations that the Lord has magnified his work with them. “Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him? Or why do you set your heart upon him?” You set your heart upon him: you exercise solicitude for him and take care of him. Thus you send your Only-Begotten Son to him, pour your Spirit into him, and promise him even your own face. And lest anything in heaven should remain unoccupied by the work of our care, you send those blessed spirits into service for our sake, appoint them to our guardianship, and command them to become our guardians and instructors.

For it is not enough that you make your angels spirits; you also make them angels of little ones. Indeed, “their angels always see the face of the Father” (Matt. 18:10). You make those spirits, so blessed, both your angels toward us and our angels toward you.

4. “He has commanded his angels concerning you.” Wondrous condescension, and truly great love of charity! Who commanded whom, concerning whom, and what did he command? Let us consider carefully, brothers; let us diligently commit to memory this so great command. Who commanded? Whose angels are they? Whose commands do they obey? Whose will do they fulfill? Surely: “He has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may guard you in all your ways”; and they do not delay, but even lift you in their hands.

The highest Majesty, therefore, has commanded angels—and commanded his own angels: those lofty, blessed spirits, so closely united to him, so intimately attached to him, truly members of God’s household. But he commanded concerning you. Who are you? “Lord, what is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you regard him?” As if man were not corruption, and the son of man a worm. But what do you think he commanded concerning you? Did he write bitter judgments against you? Did he command them to display their power against a leaf driven by the wind and to pursue dry straw? Did he command them to remove the wicked person so that he might not see the glory of God?

That is something to be commanded *against* a person, not a command made *concerning* a person. “Do not depart from the help of the Most High; dwell in the protection of the God of heaven,” lest that command should sometime be issued against you. For concerning one protected by the God of heaven, it will not be commanded against him, but for him. And what is not at present commanded against him is deferred for his benefit, so that all things may be for the elect. Thus, when the servants were preparing to go and wished immediately to gather up the weeds sown among the crop, the provident householder said: “Let them remain until the harvest, lest perhaps you uproot the wheat together with them” (Matt. 13:30, 29). How then will it be preserved meanwhile? Precisely this: this is the present work; this is the command for the present time.

5. Therefore, he has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may guard you. O wheat among weeds! O grain among chaff! O lily among thorns! Give thanks to him, brothers; give thanks to him both for us and for you. He had entrusted to us a precious deposit, the fruit of his cross, the price of his blood. He is not content with a guardianship so little secure, so little effective, so fragile, so inadequate. “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, he has set guards.” Even those who seem to be walls, or pillars within the wall itself, need these guardians—and most of all.

6. “He has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may guard you in all your ways.” How much reverence this word ought to instill in you, devotion to bring you, and confidence to confer upon you! Walk cautiously, so that, wherever angels are present—as they have been commanded—in all your ways, you may show reverence to your angel in every lodging and every corner. Would you dare to do in his presence what you would not dare to do while I was watching? Or do you doubt that one is present whom you do not see? What if you heard him? What if you touched him? What if you smelled him? Observe that the presence of things is not established by sight alone. Not all things are subject to sight, not even bodily things; how much more are spiritual things far removed from every bodily sense and to be traced rather spiritually?

If you consult faith, it proves to you that angelic presence is not lacking. And I do not hesitate to say that faith proves it, since the Apostle defines faith as “the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). They are present, then, and present for you: not merely with you, but also for you. They are present to protect you; they are present to benefit you.
