What will you render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to you? For honor and glory belong to him alone. Why to him alone? Because he commanded; and every good gift is from no one but him (Jas. 1:17).

7. Yet although he commanded it, we may not be ungrateful to those who both obey him out of such great charity and assist us in such great need. Therefore let us be devoted; let us be grateful to such great guardians. Let us return their love; let us honour them as much as we can, [Col. 0234A] as much as we ought. Nevertheless, let all our love and honour be rendered to him, from whom both they and we have everything by which we can honour or love, and by which we deserve to be loved or honoured.

For when the Apostle says, “To God alone be honour and glory” (1 Tim. 1:17), he is not to be thought to contradict the prophetic utterance which testifies that God’s friends too are exceedingly honoured (Ps. 138:17). I think the Apostle’s saying is like that other statement: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another.” For he did not mean that all other obligations were to be denied, especially when he himself says, “To whom honour, honour” (Rom. 13:8, 7), and the rest in the same manner.

So that you may understand more fully what he meant or advised in each case, consider how, amid the rays [Col. 0234B] of the sun, lesser lights cannot be seen. Do we suppose that the stars have thereby been removed? Have they been extinguished? By no means; rather, being in a manner covered by a greater brightness, they cannot for the time appear. Thus love, surpassing every other obligation, ought as though alone to reign within us, so that it claims for itself whatever is owed to others, and we do everything out of love. Thus divine honour ought to prevail and in a manner take precedence over all things, so that it alone is honoured not only above all else, but in all things. You may reasonably think the same said also about love. For what did he leave to others outside it, who gave his whole heart, his whole soul, and his whole strength in love to the Lord his God?

Therefore, brothers, let us lovingly love his angels in him, as those who will someday be our fellow-heirs, [Col. 0234C] but who meanwhile have been appointed and set over us by the Father as agents and guardians. For now we are children of God, although it has not yet appeared what we shall be, because we are still little children under guardians and stewards, being meanwhile no different from slaves.

8. But although we are so little, and so great a path remains for us—and not merely so great, but also so perilous—what have we to fear under such great guardians? Those who guard us in all our ways cannot be conquered, cannot be deceived, and still less can they deceive. They are faithful, prudent, powerful: why do we tremble? Let us only follow them, cling to them, and dwell under the protection of the God of heaven.

See how necessary this protection, [Col. 0234D] this guardianship in all your ways is for you. “They shall bear you in their hands, lest at any time you dash your foot against a stone.” Does it seem a small thing to you that there is a stone of stumbling in the way? Consider what follows: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.” How necessary is a pedagogue—indeed, even a bearer—especially for a little child walking among these things! “They shall bear you,” he says, “in their hands.” In your ways indeed they shall guard you and lead the little child wherever a little child can walk. But they will not permit you to be tested beyond what you can bear; rather, they will lift you in their hands so that you may pass over the stumbling-block. How easily one passes who is borne in their hands! How pleasantly, according to the common proverb, does he swim whose chin another supports!

[Col. 0235A] 9. Therefore, whenever some most grievous temptation is seen to press upon you, or a violent tribulation to threaten, call upon your guardian, your guide, your helper in times of need, in tribulation. Cry out to him and say: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” He neither sleeps nor slumbers, even though for a time he may sometimes appear to disregard you, lest perhaps you should yourself rashly cast yourself more dangerously from his hands, if you failed to recognize that you were sustained by them.

For these are spiritual hands, and assuredly spiritual aids, which are spiritually and variously furnished by the angels appointed to them, to each of the elect according to the nature of his danger and the difficulty set before him, as it were according to the magnitude of a stony mass. Yet I shall mention some such aids which I judge more common, and unfamiliar to only a few [Col. 0235B] among you.

Is someone severely troubled, either by some bodily affliction, or by some worldly distress, or growing weak through spiritual listlessness and a certain failure of heart? He is already beginning to be tested beyond what he can bear; he will soon strike and stumble against the stone unless there is one to help him. But what is this stone? I understand it to be the stone of stumbling and rock of offence, against which, if anyone strikes, he is shattered; but upon whom it falls, it crushes him: namely, the chosen and precious cornerstone, who is the Lord Christ (Isa. 8:14; 1 Pet. 2:6–8). To strike against this stone is to murmur against him, to take offence through faintness of spirit and storm. Therefore one who has already failed, [Col. 0235C] who has almost stumbled against the stone, needs angelic consolation and angelic hands. And indeed he strikes against the stone who murmurs and blasphemes, shattering himself, not him against whom he furiously rushes.

10. I think that such persons are sometimes supported by angels as if by two hands, so that, in a manner without perceiving it, they pass through what they so greatly feared, and afterward are not a little amazed both at the ease of their later passage and at the previous difficulty. Do you wish to know what I understand these two hands to be? Certainly, a twofold showing: namely, that on the one hand the brevity of tribulation and, on the other, the eternity of recompense are shown—or rather painted or impressed—upon the heart, so that with an inward affection we may feel that “this momentary and light tribulation of ours [Col. 0235D] works in us, beyond measure in sublimity, an eternal weight of glory.”

Who would not believe that these good effects are wrought through good beings, when it is certain that, conversely, evil promptings are indeed made through evil angels? Keep angels, my brothers, as familiar companions; frequent them with diligent thought and devout prayer, for they are always present to guard and console you.

## SERMON XIII. On the twelfth verse, “They shall bear you in their hands,” etc.

1. We may understand this verse at hand—namely, “They shall bear you in their hands,” etc.—as spoken not only of present consolation, but also of future consolation. Holy angels indeed guard us in our ways; but when the way is ended—that is, when life is ended—they lift us in their hands. Nor do faithful witnesses fail us. You have recently heard read concerning our most blessed father Benedict, truly blessed in every respect, how, while he appeared to hold his eyes fixed upon the splendour of flashing light, he saw the soul of Germanus, bishop of Capua, carried to heaven by angels in a fiery sphere.

> **Note:** [Col. 0235D] Hence it is evident that this sermon was delivered shortly after the feast of St Benedict, concerning whom this is read [Col. 0236D] in Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 35.

But why seek testimonies of this kind? Truth itself in the Gospel says of the beggar covered with sores that he “was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom” (Luke 16:22). For we could not walk by ourselves in that region, so new and so unknown to us, especially since so great a stone lies in the way. What stone? He who formerly used to be worshipped in stones; he who offered stones to the Lord, saying, “Command that [Col. 0236B] these stones become bread” (Matt. 4:3).

Moreover, your foot is your affection; the foot of the soul, which angels bear in their hands lest you dash your foot against a stone. For how would the soul not be most violently disturbed if it departed hence alone, if it entered those paths without consolation, if it walked with its own feet among those stones?

2. Indeed, hear more plainly how necessary it is for you to be borne in hands not your own, yet in no hands but angelic ones: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.” What could a human foot do among such things? What could the affection of a human being endure among such horrible [variant: terrible] monsters? They are certainly spiritual wickednesses, and they are designated by fitting names.

For it was said also of these, as I think has by no means escaped you: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” But who can know whether the operations of malice and ministries of iniquity are divided among them, so that from their different offices—or rather [variant: *quin potius*], misdeeds—they have received different names: one is called an asp, another a basilisk, another a lion, and another a dragon, because in their own invisible fashion they harm in various ways, as though one by a bite, another by sight, another by roar or blow, another by breath?

I have also read of a certain kind of demons which is not cast out except by prayer and fasting; for the word of apostolic rebuke had no power against it (Matt. 17:14–20). How could it not have been an asp—[Col. 0236D] that asp, assuredly, of the Psalm, deaf and stopping its ears lest it hear the voice of the charmer? (Ps. 57:5.) Do you wish not to be terrified by so terrifying a monster? Do you wish to walk securely upon this asp after death? Take care meanwhile that you do not walk after it; take care that you do not imitate it, and there will be nothing for you to fear in the future.

3. Indeed, it is a vice over which, I think, such a spirit rules; and if you wish to know, it is self-will, against which we warned you to be on guard in yesterday’s sermon; it is obstinacy, against which we spoke the day before. For whenever an opportunity is given, I do not regret fortifying you against this most grave pestilence, that you may flee it in every way; since it is a certain complete [Col. 0237A] overthrow of religion and truly, according to the testimony of the Lawgiver, “the incurable poison of asps” (Deut. 32:33).

The asp is said to press one ear as closely as it can to the ground, and likewise to stop the other by thrusting in its tail, lest it hear. What can the voice of the charmer do against this? What can the speech of the preacher accomplish? I shall pray for him; I shall humble my soul with fasting; I shall be baptized for the dead with a most copious flow of tears, when I see in him that no human incantation, however wise, and no diligence of admonition, however great, prevails.

Yet let the obstinate man know that he fixes his head not in heaven but in the earth, for the wisdom that is from above is not only chaste but also peaceable; whereas this wisdom, if one may so call it, cannot be other than asp-like, unless it is earthly. Nor would he become so deaf unless the tail too [Col. 0237B] stopped his hearing. What is this tail? The end of human intention. This is desperate deafness: on the one hand, as if fixed in the earth, each person clings to his own will; on the other, as if bending back the tail, he devises some end and fixes in his heart what he desires to attain.

I beg you, brothers, do not stop your ears; do not ever harden your hearts. For this is why speech so biting and bitter is found in the mouth of the obstinate person: no goodwill of an admonisher can penetrate to him. This is why the asp’s poison persists in the sting of his tongue: he has stopped himself with such zeal against the tongue of the charmer.

4. But the basilisk, they say, carries poison in its eye: a most evil creature and more detestable than all others. Do you wish to know [Col. 0237C] the poisoned eye, the evil eye, the bewitching eye? Think of envy. For what is envy but “seeing evil” (*invidere*)? If that basilisk had not existed, death would never have entered the world through its envy. Woe to the wretched man because he did not foresee the envious one! Let us overcome this vice while we are still alive, if after death we wish not to fear the minister of such great wickedness.

Let no one look upon another’s good with an envious eye. For this itself, so far as it lies within its power, is to infect that good with its corruption and in some fashion to kill it. Truth itself testifies that one who hates a human being is a murderer (1 John 3:15). And what of one who hates the good in a human being? 866 Can he not be called a murderer? The person still lives, yet that man is already guilty of his death. The fire which the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth still burns (Luke 12:49), yet the envious man, as though he had extinguished the Spirit, is already condemned.

5. [Col. 0237D] Woe to you because of the dragon! It is a savage beast; with fiery breath it kills whatever it touches, not only beasts of the earth but also birds of heaven. I consider this dragon to be none other than the spirit of anger. How many people of elevated life, as it seemed, miserably scorched by this dragon’s breath, have we lamented as falling shamefully into its mouth! How much better they might have been angry with themselves, so as not to sin!

Certainly anger is a natural human affection; but when the good of nature is abused, it becomes grave ruin and lamentable destruction. Let us employ it, brothers, where it is useful, lest it break out into useless and unlawful things. Thus love is accustomed to drive out love, and fear to drive out fear. [Col. 0238A] “Do not fear those who kill the body,” says the Lord, “and after that have nothing they can do to the soul.” And immediately: “But I will show you,” he says, “whom you should fear. Fear him who has power to cast body and soul into Gehenna. Yes, I say to you, fear him” (Luke 12:4–5). It is as if he said more plainly: Fear him, so that you may not fear them. Let the spirit of the fear of the Lord fill you, and alien fear will have no place in you.

And I say to you—not I, but Truth; not I, but the Lord: Do not be angry with those who take transitory things from you, who heap insults upon you, who perhaps inflict punishments, and beyond these [variant: after these] do nothing. But I will show you with whom you ought to be angry. Be angry with that which alone can harm you, which alone can make all those things [Col. 0238B] of no benefit to you. Do you wish to know what it is? Your own iniquity. Yes, I say to you, be angry with this. For no adversity will harm you if no iniquity rules you.

One who is perfectly angry with this is not moved by other things, but rather embraces them. “I am ready for scourges,” he says (Ps. 27:18). Let there be loss, insult, bodily injury: I am ready, and I am not troubled, because my pain is always before me. Why should I not regard all outward things as little in comparison with the estimation of this pain? “The son of my womb persecutes me, and shall I be angry with an insulting little servant?” (2 Kings 16:11.) “My heart has forsaken me; my strength has forsaken me, and the light of my eyes”: and shall I lament temporal losses or reckon bodily discomforts?

[Col. 0238C] 6. From this there arises not only gentleness, which the dragon’s breath cannot injure, but also greatness of soul, which the lion’s roar cannot terrify. “Your adversary,” says Peter, “like a roaring lion” (1 Pet. 5:8). Thanks be to that great Lion of the tribe of Judah: this one can roar, but cannot strike. Let him roar as much as he wishes; only let Christ’s sheep not flee. How much he threatens! How much he exaggerates! How much he menaces! Let us not be beasts, so that this empty roar may throw us down.

For those who have investigated such matters more curiously report that at the lion’s roar no beast can stand, not even one which resists its attack with all courage and often overcomes it when it strikes, yet does not endure it when it roars. Truly a beast, truly devoid of reason, is one so faint-hearted that he yields through fear alone, who, overcome only by the exaggeration of future toil, is thrown down before the conflict—not by a weapon, but by a trumpet. “You have not yet resisted unto blood” (Heb. 12:4), says that vigorous leader who knew this lion’s roar to be empty. And another says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4:7).

## SERMON XIV. On the thirteenth verse, “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk,” etc.

1. Let us give thanks, brothers, to our maker, our benefactor, our redeemer, our rewarder—or rather, to our hope. For he is both our rewarder and our reward; and we now expect nothing other than himself from himself. The first thing he bestowed upon us [Col. 0239A] is ourselves: for “he made us, and not we ourselves.” Is it too little in your eyes that he made you? Consider what kind of being he made you: certainly, even in body an excellent creature, but still more in soul, as one marked by the image of the Creator, a participant in reason, capable of everlasting blessedness; and further, in both together, more admirable than other creatures, joined to itself by the Creator’s incomprehensible craftsmanship and unsearchable wisdom.

Thus, as great a gift as man is a great thing. But how gratuitous do you suppose it was? It is clear that he merited nothing beforehand who was utterly nothing. Or was he afterward expected to return grace to his Maker? “I said to the Lord: You are my God, because you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2). Therefore he was expected not to return a necessary [Col. 0239B] favour to one who so completely suffices for himself in every respect, but to render devout thanks to one who so deserved it. Why should he not give thanks?

If someone seemed at some time to have restored for you the obstructed function of your eyes, ears, nostrils, hands, or feet; if someone by some means awakened reason in you when it had fallen asleep: who would not be most deeply angry with you if he found you at any time forgetful of such a benefit or ungrateful to the benefactor? Yet the Lord your God, having bestowed upon you even these instruments, made all these things from nothing. Nor did he merely make them: he also joined and formed them, and endowed each with its own function. How can he not rightly demand from you greater thanks for these things?

2. [Col. 0239C] Nor, content with this gift, great though it was, did he who gave you being when you had not existed before fail also to add that by which you might be sustained now that you existed. And he accomplished this no less generously than he had done the former thing wonderfully. “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” he says. But what follows? “And let him rule over the fish of the sea, the beasts of the earth, and the birds of heaven.” For he had previously taught that he also created the elements of heaven for your use. They are said to have been made “for signs, and seasons, and days and years” (Gen. 1:26, 14). For whom, do you suppose? Certainly for no one but you. For all other creatures either have no need of all these things or do not understand them.

How abundant was he in this second benefit, how liberal! How much did he bestow on you for sustenance, for instruction, [Col. 0239D] for consolation, now also through these things for correction, and even for delight! Yet he did these two things freely, and freely in a twofold sense. What do I mean by “freely in a twofold sense”? Without your merit, without his labour. For “he spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32:9). Are you therefore less devoted, less indebted, less grateful because he made them, as it were for nothing, out of nothing? It belongs to a perverse heart to seek occasions for ingratitude. No one does so except one who is ungrateful even for a free gift.

For I think neither benefit is less useful to you because it was by no means difficult for the giver. Otherwise, if you consider what cost him labour to be more advantageous to you, you derive this judgment from yourself; and I think you learned it nowhere but from yourself. For you yourself would more willingly give something to your brother if it involved no inconvenience to you. Yet even if you wished to give freely, you would not wish him to put forward this as a reason for ingratitude toward you.

[Col. 0240A] 3. But now consider the third work: your redemption. Here there is no covering for excuse; labour was certainly expended upon it. This too was bestowed freely, but freely as regards you. As regards him, however, by no means freely. You were saved for nothing, yet not out of nothing. Why does your affection still sleep? Indeed it is dead, not sleeping, if it does not answer this benefit, if it does not pour itself wholly out in thanksgiving and a voice of praise.

For the other two benefits most clearly commend this third also, so that true love may be proved in them as well: he bestowed easily, not because he would not have acted otherwise, but because there was no other way fitting for him to act. Thus your God made you; he made so many things for you; for you he made even himself. [Col. 0240B] “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). What remains? He has made himself one flesh with you; he will also make you one spirit with himself.

Let these four things not depart from your heart, your mouth, your memory, or your affection. Think of them always; delight in them continually. Press your anxious soul as it were with these spurs; take care to set it aflame with these torches, to return the love of him who in so many ways commends to you his love toward you. Remember also what he himself says: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15). Therefore keep the commandments of your Creator, of your benefactor, of your redeemer, of your rewarder.

4. But if these are four, how many commandments are there? We all know that there are ten. Therefore, by multiplying this [Col. 0240C] Decalogue of the law by the number four, you have a true forty, you possess a spiritual Lent. Only stand in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation. Beware of the serpent’s cunning; watch for the enemy’s snares. For by a fourfold temptation he attempts in four ways to hinder the action of thanksgiving which you owe.

Christ was tempted in all these things, so that the Apostle could truly write [variant: writes], “Tempted in every respect according to likeness, without sin” (Heb. 4:15). Perhaps someone will wonder and say that he has not read of the Lord’s fourth temptation. Yet, in my judgment, he would not say this if he remembered having read that “the life of man upon earth is temptation” (Job 7:1). One who remembers this does not suppose [Col. 0240D] that the Lord was tempted only by the three temptations which occurred in the fasting of the desert, on the pinnacle of the temple, and on the summit of the mountain (Matt. 4).

Certainly, in all these there was manifest temptation. But that which from then onward did not leave him until the death of the cross, though more hidden, was nevertheless more vehement. Nor will this seem inconsistent with the analogy proposed. For the three benefits already mentioned are known to be most evident and placed in the light. But with respect to the hope of eternal life, it has not yet been bestowed or revealed to us. It is therefore no wonder if the temptation is less open where the cause of temptation is also hidden. But it is itself both more lasting and stronger, because the enemy brings forth against our hope whatever malice he possesses.

[Col. 0241A] 5. Thus, first, in order to make us ungrateful to the Author of nature, he brings upon us an excessive anxiety about nature, just as he dared to say to Christ himself when hungry: “Command that these stones become bread,” as though he who formed us did not know his own creature, or did not care for human beings when he feeds the birds of heaven.

How ungrateful, then, to him who created this whole world for humankind is anyone who, in order to obtain the wealth he covets, does not fear to fall down and worship the evil one! “All these things,” he says, “I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.” Did you make them, wretch? How will you give what he created? Or how can things which he created and placed under his own dominion be hoped for from you or sought by your worship?

And when he says, “Cast yourself down,” beware, whoever you are who have climbed the pinnacle of the temple; beware, watchman of the house of the Lord; beware, you who seem to hold an exalted place in Christ’s Church. For how ungrateful—indeed, how injurious—you are [Col. 0241B] to that great mystery of godliness if you suppose godliness to be gain! How unfaithful you are to him who consecrated this ministry with his own blood, if you seek in it your own glory, which is nothing, if you seek your own things and not those of Jesus Christ! How unworthily you answer his condescension, who in the dispensation of his humility made you exalted, entrusted heavenly mysteries to you, and gave you a heavenly authority, perhaps even greater than that granted to the heavenly spirits themselves, if you cast yourself down, thinking not of things above but of things upon the earth!

[Col. 0241C] And everyone who lowers and casts himself down from the excellence of virtues to the desire for empty glory undoubtedly repays with insult the Lord of virtues, who endured so much among us in order to impress upon us the pattern of this holiness.

6. Let us consider more carefully, brothers, whether that first temptation, which disturbs the mind on the occasion of bodily necessity, ought perhaps to be compared with the asp. For this animal harms in a certain manner by a violent bite [variant: Latin *violentum* for *violento*], and stops its ear lest it hear the charmer’s voice. What does the tempter seek to do in this respect except to shut and stop the ear of the heart against faith’s consolation? But the enemy did not succeed in him; he did not shut the hearing of him who said: [Col. 0241D] “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God.”

But in the saying, “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:3–9), observe the dragon’s persuasive hiss for evil. They report that, hiding in the sand, it draws even flying birds by its poisonous breath. How poisonous was this breath: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me!” Yet that was no ordinary bird: the dragon’s breath could accomplish nothing against it.

7. What shall we say of the basilisk? It is said, more monstrous than the others, to infect and kill a person by its sight alone. If I am not mistaken, it is empty glory. “Take heed,” he says, “not to perform your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6:1). It is as though he said: Beware of the basilisk’s eyes.

But whom is the basilisk said to harm? [Col. 0242A] The one who does not see the basilisk. For if you see it first, then, as they say, it does you no harm; rather, it itself dies. Thus it is, brothers. Empty glory kills those who do not see it: the blind and careless, who display themselves to it and expose themselves, instead of themselves looking upon it, attending to it, examining it; instead of finally seeing how frivolous, how fleeting, how vain, how useless it is.

For if anyone looks at it in this way, the basilisk dies. Glory no longer kills him; rather, it is killed, and in some manner he kills it—turned to dust, indeed reduced to nothing. I think, moreover, that there is no need to ask how that temptation in which it was said, “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down,” seemed to pertain to empty glory. For what purpose was this, except that he might be seen and praised by the basilisk?

[Col. 0242B] 8. And see how the basilisk concealed itself, as though so that it could not be seen beforehand. “It is written,” he says, “that he commanded his angels concerning you, and they shall lift you in their hands.” What is written, malicious one? What is written? “He commanded his angels concerning you.” What did he command? Attend and see: the evil and deceitful one passed over in silence what would undo the devices of his malice.

For what did he command? Certainly what follows in the Psalm: “That they may guard you in all your ways.” Does this mean in precipices? What kind of way is it to cast oneself down from the pinnacle of the temple? This is not a way but a fall; and if it is a way, it is yours, not his. In vain you have twisted into a temptation of the head what was written for the consolation of the body. For that one must be guarded who has reason to fear lest he dash his foot against a stone. There is no need to guard one who has nothing [Col. 0242C] to fear.

Why, moreover, do you suppress what follows: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon”? This parable concerns you. Monstrous malice is marked out for trampling under monstrous names, not only by the Head himself but also by the whole body. For after this threefold humiliation, the enemy no longer employed serpent-like cunning against the Lord, but leonine cruelty—reaching insults, scourges, blows, death, even death on a cross. But the Lion of the tribe of Judah also openly trampled you, lion that you are.

So also against us, brothers, when he sees himself frustrated in all other things, he now [Col. 0242D] raises persecution in all his fury, such as has not been from the beginning, in order to bar the kingdom of heaven to those who hope for it by the violence of tribulation. Blessed is the soul which, trampling even this lion by mighty power, shall be able to seize that kingdom by force!

9. Therefore, beloved, let us walk more cautiously and carefully, as it were, upon the asp and basilisk. Let us beware every root of bitterness, so that none of us may be found biting, none rash or fiery, none implacable or rebellious. Nor let us cast ourselves down, but let us rise above and leap across [variant: pass across] the deadly gaze of temporal glory, so that, as it is written, “In vain is the net cast before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. 1:17). Let us likewise trample both lion and dragon, so that neither the lion’s roar may terrify nor the dragon’s breath [Col. 0243A] infect us.

These four monsters seem to press upon four corresponding affections, each upon its own. Against which affection, then, does the dragon especially lie in wait? I think it is desire, because he knows this to be the root of all evils and that which most readily overturns the heart. Thus, as though giving advice, he said: “All these things I will give you.” With the lion it is manifest that he gives terrifying roars only at the doorway of fear. The asp, moreover, watches at the gates of sadness, because it judges them especially open to its bites. Thus it did not approach Christ the Lord until it saw him already hungry. Conversely, joy must beware of the basilisk, for it is chiefly through that entrance that it customarily shoots in the poisonous rays of its eyes; and empty glory harms only by the vanity of joy.

[Col. 0243B] 10. Consider also whether we may perhaps oppose four virtues to these four temptations. “The lion shall roar; who will not fear?” If there is anyone who does not fear, he will be strong. But when the lion has been frustrated, the dragon hides in the sand in order to draw the soul with poisonous breaths, breathing into it, as it were, the desire for earthly things. Who, do you think, will escape his snares? Certainly no one but the prudent person.

But perhaps, while you take care not to descend to these things, some affliction presses you; and behold, at once the asp is present, for it seems to have found a favourable time. Who will not be exasperated by this asp? Certainly the temperate and self-controlled person, who knows how to abound and how to endure want. I think that on this occasion the flattering evil eye will seek to bewitch you. Who will turn away his face? Certainly the just person, who not only [Col. 0243C] does not take for himself the glory which belongs to God, but does not even wish to receive it when another offers it—provided that he is the just person who performs what is just justly, who does not do his righteousness before people, and who, finally, even if he is righteous, does not lift up his head. For this virtue consists especially in humility; this purifies intention; and it obtains all merit all the more truly and effectively because it claims less for itself.

## SERMON XV. On the fourteenth verse, “Because he hoped in me, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he has known my name.”

1. “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you,” says the Lord. “Take [Col. 0243D] my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light” (Matt. 11:28–30). He invites those who labour to refreshment and calls those who are burdened to rest. Yet he does not meanwhile take away burden or labour; rather, he exchanges them for another burden and another labour—but for a light burden and a sweet yoke, in which rest and refreshment, though less visible, are nevertheless found.

Iniquity is a heavy burden, sitting upon a talent of lead (Zech. 5:7). Under this load groaned the one who said: “My iniquities have passed over my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed me down” (Ps. 37:5). What, then, is Christ’s burden—the light burden? As I understand it, it is the burden of benefits. A sweet burden, but only for one who feels it, one who experiences it. Otherwise, if you do not discover or notice it, it is altogether [Col. 0244A] heavy and dangerous.

During the time of his mortality, a human being is a burden-bearing animal. If he still bears his sins, the burden is heavy. If perhaps he has already been relieved of sins, it is indeed less heavy; but, if he has sound judgment, he will find no less great a burden in that very relief of which we have spoken. God burdens us when he relieves us: he burdens us with a benefit when he relieves us from sin.

The voice of one burdened: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115:12). The voice of one burdened: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord” (Luke 5:8). The voice of one burdened: “For I always feared God, as waves swelling over me” (Job 31:23). “Always,” he says: he feared both before and after receiving forgiveness of sins. Blessed is the person who is thus always fearful and is troubled with no lesser [Col. 0244B] anxiety lest he be overwhelmed by benefits as well as by sins.

2. For this reason divine beneficence, so diligent toward us and so lavish, is commended to us: that we may be stirred to gratitude and invited to love. “He commanded his angels concerning you, that they may guard you in all your ways.” What more could he do for you that he has not done? I know what you are thinking, noble creature. You are grateful to the Lord’s angels, but you seek the Lord of angels himself. You pray and desire that, not content with messengers, he himself who spoke may also be present, and may kiss you not, as it were, through an intermediary, but with the kiss of his own mouth.

You have heard that you must walk over the asp and basilisk, lion and dragon alike; nor are you ignorant of Michael’s and his angels’ victory over the dragon itself. Yet your desires cry not to Michael but to the Lord: “Deliver me, and set me beside you; then let any hand fight against me” (Job 17:3). This indeed is to seek refuge not merely higher than other refuges, but higher even than the highest, so that to one who declares, “For you are, Lord, my hope,” it may rightly be answered: “You have made the Most High your refuge.”

3. For the compassionate and merciful Lord does not disdain to be the hope of the wretched; nor does he refuse to show himself at once Deliverer and Protector to those who hope in him. “Because he hoped in me,” he says, “I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he has known my name.” Indeed, unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain (Ps. 126:1), whether that one be a human being or even an angel. “Mountains surround Jerusalem”; but this would be little—indeed, nothing—unless the Lord also surrounded his people. Rightly, therefore, in the Song the bride is described as, though she had found the watchmen—or rather, had been found by them, for she herself was not seeking them—not having stopped, nor having been content with the watchmen, but having briefly asked them concerning her beloved and then hastened swiftly onward to him (Song 3:3–4). For her heart placed its confidence not in the watchmen but in the Lord; and to those who perhaps advised otherwise she said: “In the Lord I trust: how do you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Ps. 10:2).

The Corinthians had observed this less vigilantly when, as though offended by the watchmen, they withdrew to them and did not at all pass beyond them. “I indeed am of Cephas; I, however, of Paul; and I of Apollos,” they say (1 Cor. 1:12). But what did the sober watchmen, the watchmen who kept careful watch, do? They could not take the bride for themselves, since they rightly loved her with jealousy, with God’s jealousy; they had betrothed a chaste virgin to one husband, to present her to Christ. “They struck me and wounded me,” she says. Why so? Unless I am mistaken, they urged her to pass on, as though she would thereby find her beloved. Finally, “they even took away my cloak” (Song 5:7), she says—doubtless so that, freed of encumbrance, she might run. Observe how forcefully the Apostle strikes, with what arrows he wounds those who appeared to have turned aside among the watchmen: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:13). And again: “For when one says, ‘I am of Paul,’ and another, ‘I am of Apollos,’ are you not merely human? What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers through whom you believed” (1 Cor. 3:4–5).

“Because he hoped in me, I will deliver him.” Not in the watchmen, not in a human being, not in an angel, but “in me,” he says, “he has hoped,” expecting no good except from me—not even through them. For “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17). From me come the useful watchings of human beings, concerning works that are manifest; to them, indeed, I have assigned human guardians. From me come the vigils of angels, who observe more hidden movements, take special care, and drive away wicked instigators. But the inward guarding of the most secret intention must certainly be effected not merely from me but through me; for neither a human eye nor even an angelic eye can penetrate there.

4. Let us recognize this threefold guardianship, brothers, and present ourselves to each as it is fitting to be presented. Let us provide what is good before human beings, before angels, and before God. Let us strive to please all in everything, but especially him who is greatest over all. Let us sing psalms to him in the sight of angels, so that in them may be fulfilled what is written: “Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice, because I have hoped exceedingly in your words” (Ps. 118:74). Let us obey our superiors, who keep watch as those who will render an account for our souls, so that they may not do this with sorrow (Heb. 13:17).

And indeed—thanks be to God, from whose gift alone this comes—I need not admonish you much, nor need I fear much for you in this respect. For what is my joy and my glory if not your ready obedience and irreproachable conduct? What if I knew with certainty that not even the angels could discover anything further in you that were unbecoming; that among none of you was anything from the accursed spoil of Jericho concealed; that no one murmured, none spoke ill in secret, none acted hypocritically or negligently, none turned over in mind disgraceful thoughts, by which, alas, even the bodily member itself is sometimes disturbed? This would be a great increase of joy for me, but certainly not yet its fullness. For we are not so great that it can matter so little to us not to be judged by a human being, and that we should be conscious of nothing against ourselves. Yet if even the great fear the most hidden Judge, how greatly ought we to tremble at the remembrance of that examination! Oh, if it were granted me to know with certainty that in all of us there is nothing offending that eye which alone perfectly knows what is in a human being, seeing in him even what he himself does not see in himself! Let us above all seek out this judgment, brothers, and all the more frequently engage in its consideration with fear and trembling, the less we can comprehend the unsearchable abyss of God’s judgments and his irresistible ordering. With this fear hope has merit; with this dread one hopes fruitfully.

5. This fear itself is, if one considers wisely, a most firm and effective ground of hope. For this fear is a great gift of God, and from the reception of present gifts comes firm expectation of those to come. Finally, “the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him” (Ps. 146:11); and surely life is in his will, and eternal salvation in his good pleasure. “Because he hoped in me, I will deliver him.” Sweet generosity: not to fail those who hope in him. For this is the whole merit of a human being: to place all his hope in him who makes the whole human being safe. “Our fathers hoped in you; they hoped, and you delivered them. They cried to you, and were saved; they hoped in you and were not put to shame” (Ps. 21:5–6). For who has hoped in him and been put to shame? “Hope in him, all the assembly of the people.” For whatever place the sole of your foot treads shall be yours. Your foot, surely, is your hope. However far it advances, it will possess, provided that it is wholly fixed upon God, so that it may be firm and not waver. What need it fear from the asp or basilisk? Why should it dread the lion’s roar or the dragon’s hissing?

6. “Because he hoped in me, I will deliver him.” Moreover, once delivered, lest he be attacked again and need deliverance again, “I will protect him and preserve him”—provided that he has known my name and does not attribute his deliverance to himself, but gives glory to my name. “I will protect him, because he has known my name.” For glorification is bestowed in the presence of the face, protection in knowledge of the name. Hope lies in the name; possession lies in the face. “For who hopes for what he sees?” (Rom. 8:24). Faith, certainly, is from hearing (Rom. 10:17), and according to the same Apostle it is the substance of things hoped for (Heb. 11:1).

“I will protect him, because he has known my name.” He does not know his name who takes it in vain; who says to him, “Lord, Lord,” and does not do what he himself says. He does not know his name who neither honors him as Father nor fears him as Lord. He does not know his name who turns toward vanities and false madnesses. “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked to vanities and false madnesses” (Ps. 39:5). He knew this name who said: “There is no other name given to human beings in which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). If we too know the holy name invoked over us, we must desire that it may always be sanctified in us; and so we must pray, according to the Savior’s teaching: “Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name” (Matt. 6:9).

Finally, hear what follows in the Psalm: “He cried to me, and I will hear him.” This is the fruit of knowledge of the name: the cry of prayer; and the fruit of the cry is the hearing of the Savior. For how could one who does not call upon him be heard, or one who does not know the Lord’s name call upon him? Thanks be to him who made known to human beings the Father’s name, establishing the fruit of salvation in its invocation, as it is written: “Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel 2:32).

## SERMON XVI. On the sixteenth verse, “He cried to me, and I will hear him,” etc.

1. “He cried to me, and I will hear him.” This is truly the covenant of peace, the pact of loving-kindness, the agreement of mercy and compassion. “He hoped in me,” he says, “I will deliver him. He knew my name; I will protect him. He invoked me, and I will hear him.” He does not say: “He was worthy, just, upright, innocent in hands and clean in heart; therefore I will deliver, protect, and hear him.”

> [Note: [Col. 0247D] Here there was a notable gap, wholly destroying the sense. These words, “He does not say,” etc., up to “For if,” etc., are absent from other editions; they are restored [Col. 0248D] from the Cistercian manuscript and other manuscripts.]

For if he said this or anything similar, who would not despair? “Who shall boast that he has a chaste heart?” But now “with you is propitiation,” and because of this I have waited for your law, Lord. Sweet is the law which places the merit of being heard in the cry of petition. “He cried to me,” he says, “and I will hear him.” Rightly is he not heard who neglects to cry out, whether by not asking at all or by asking coldly and sluggishly. For in God’s ears vehement desire is a great cry; conversely, a slack intention is a low voice. When will that penetrate the clouds? When will it be heard in heaven? Indeed, so that a human being may know that he must cry out, at the very beginning of his prayer he is immediately reminded that the Father to whom he is about to pray is in heaven, so that he may remember to launch his prayer toward him with a certain force of spirit. God is spirit, and whoever desires his cry to reach him must cry in spirit.

> [Note: [Col. 0248D] Compare Sermon 9, no. 2, “On Right Intention.”]

For just as he does not look upon a person’s face as a human being does, but rather beholds the heart, so his ears attend rather to the voice of the heart than to that of the body; and he is rightly called “the God of my heart” (Ps. 72:26). Thus Moses, though silent outwardly, is heard inwardly, the Lord saying: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14:15).

2. “He cried to me, and I will hear him.” Not without reason. Great necessity wrung from him a great cry. For what did he ask in crying out, except consolation, deliverance, and glorification? Otherwise, how is he heard concerning these things if he cries for others? “I will hear him,” he says. In what, Lord, or in what matters will you hear him? “I am with him in tribulation; I will rescue him and glorify him.” I think this threefold saying should be referred to the great three days which we are soon to celebrate. For he himself also found tribulation and sorrow for our sake, when, for the joy set before him, he endured the cross, despising shame. Yet the things concerning him, as he foretold before his death, came to their end; and as he said in death, “It is finished,” and thereafter he rested on the Sabbath. Nor was the glory of the resurrection delayed: on the third day, at earliest dawn, the Sun of righteousness rose for us from the tomb. Thus both the fruit of tribulation and the truth of deliverance appeared in the manifestation of glorification.

Likewise, a kind of similar three days may be assigned in us. “I am with him,” he says, “in tribulation.” When is this, except on the day of our tribulation, on the day of our cross?—while what he himself said is fulfilled: “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16:33); and what his Apostle says: “All who desire to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12). For full and perfect deliverance cannot come before the day of burial, because “a heavy yoke remains upon the children of Adam from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40:1). “Therefore, on that day I will rescue him,” he says, when the world will have nothing further that it can do either to body or soul. Certainly glorification awaits the last day, the day of resurrection, when that which is now sown in dishonor shall rise in glory.

3. How do we know that he is with us in tribulation? Surely from the fact that we are in tribulation itself. For who could endure, who could stand firm, who could persevere without him? “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations”—or, in another reading, “tribulations” (Jas. 1:2)—not only because “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21), but because “the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. 33:19). “If I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death,” says one, “I will fear no evils, because you are with me” (Ps. 22:4). Thus he is with us all days, even to the consummation of the age.

But when shall we be with him? Certainly when we are caught up to meet Christ in the air, and so shall always be with the Lord. When shall we appear with him in glory? Surely when Christ, our life, appears. Meanwhile it is necessary that we remain hidden, so that tribulation may precede deliverance, and deliverance glorification. The voice of one delivered is: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you; because he has rescued my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from falling” (Ps. 114:7–8). “I will rescue him and glorify him.” Blessed is the person who meanwhile has you as comforter and helper, a helper in timely need, in tribulation. But how much happier is one whom you have already rescued and removed from such great evils; happier still one already removed from the snare of hunters, already taken away lest wickedness change his understanding or deceit deceive his soul! Yet beyond all these, happiest by far will be the one whom you have taken to yourself, whom you have filled with the good things of your house, and whom you have conformed to your brightness.

4. And now, little children, let us cry to heaven, and our God will have mercy on us. Let us cry to heaven, because beneath heaven all is labor and pain, vanity and affliction of spirit. For “the heart of a human being is crooked and unsearchable” (Jer. 17:9), and his senses incline toward evil. “There is no good in me,” that is, in my flesh. The law of sin dwells in it and lusts against the spirit. Finally, even my heart has forsaken me, and the body is dead because of sin. “Sufficient for the day is its own evil,” and the world itself lies in wickedness. How evil in all respects is this present age! How wickedly worldly desires are known to wage war against the soul! There are also the rulers of this world, of these darknesses, spiritual forces of wickedness, powers of the air, and among them the serpent more cunning than all living creatures.

All these are beneath the sun; all these are beneath heaven. To which of them do you flee for refuge? In which of them do you hope to find any consolation or help? If you look within yourself, your heart has dried up, and you will find yourself consigned to oblivion, as one dead in heart. If beneath yourself, “the corruptible body weighs down the soul.” If around yourself, even “the earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). Seek therefore above yourself, but take care to pass beyond the windy hosts. For because they know that every good gift and every perfect gift is only from above, brigands have occupied the middle way. Pass on, then; pass through those ever-watchful wicked powers, which so tirelessly guard and observe lest anyone escape into that city. If they strike you, if they wound you, leave them your cloak, which Joseph once left to the adulteress in Egypt (Gen. 39:12); leave them your linen cloth, so that, like that young man in the Gospel, you may flee from them naked (Mark 14:52). Did not God give only his cloak and linen cloth into the hands of the wicked one, into whose power he gave flesh, saying: “Nevertheless, preserve his soul” (Job 2:6)? Therefore let your heart be above, your cry above, your desires above, your manner of life above, your intention above; and let all your expectation be from above. Cry to heaven so that you may be heard, and may the Father who is in heaven send you help from the sanctuary and defend you from Zion. May he now send help in tribulation, rescue from tribulation, and glorify in the resurrection. These things are great; but you, great Lord, have promised them. We hope from your promise; hence we dare to say: “If we cry with a devout heart, certainly you must, by your promise…”

> [Note: [Col. 0249D] In the hymn for Lent.]

Amen.

## SERMON XVII. On the seventeenth verse, “With length of days I will fill him,” etc.

1. It goes well with us, brothers; the Psalm verse is quite suited to this season. Since we shall soon celebrate the Sunday of the Resurrection, what is promised in the Resurrection is already promised to each of us, so that the members may recall more festively in their Head what they await to be accomplished in themselves one day. The Psalm ends fittingly where so blessed an end is promised to the singer. It is pleasantly fulfilled when so delightful a fullness is promised in it. “With length of days,” he says, “I will fill him, and I will show him my salvation.”

I often remind you, brothers, that according to Paul’s teaching godliness has the promise both of the life that now is and of that which is to come (1 Tim. 4:8). Hence he also says: “You now have your fruit unto sanctification, but the end is eternal life” (Rom. 6:22). This is the fullness promised here; this is the length of days. For what is as long as what is eternal? What is as long as what is cut off by no end? A good end is eternal life; a good end is that which has no end. And surely that whose end is good is itself also good. Let us therefore embrace sanctification, because it is good, because its end is life without end. Let us pursue holiness and peace, without which no one shall see God (Heb. 12:14).

“With length of days I will fill him, and I will show him my salvation.” This is a promise of God’s right hand; it is the gift of that right hand, which the holy man of old desired to be extended to him: “You will stretch forth your right hand to the work of your hands” (Job 14:15). “Delights are at this right hand unto the end.” This is the right hand which he desired to be extended to him, and which he obtained—the one of whom the Psalmist says: “He asked life of you, and you gave him length of days for age upon age” (Ps. 20:5). Finally, the Wise Man said it more clearly: “In her left hand are riches and glory, but in her right hand length of life” (Prov. 3:16).

“Who is the person who desires life, who loves to see good days?” For this life that we live is rather death; nor is it simply life, but mortal life. We say that a person is dying when he has certainly already approached death. But what do we do from the first moment that we begin to live, except approach death and begin to die? Moreover, whatever the days of this life may be, they are few and evil, as the holy patriarch testifies (Gen. 47:9). There is true life where life is lively and life-giving; there are good days where there is unending length of days. Thanks be to him who orders all things not only powerfully but sweetly. The fewness of days will shortly end for those for whom each day’s own evil is enough; but where days possess goodness, eternity also will not be lacking.

2. “With length of days I will fill him.” What he had previously said, “I will glorify him,” he has explained more plainly in this verse. Yet whom would it not suffice to be glorified by him whose works are perfect? For no such immensity can glorify anyone except unto immensity. Great must be the glorification which descends from magnificent glory. Peter says, “a voice came down from magnificent glory” (2 Pet. 1:17). Rightly is it magnificent glory, glorifying so magnificently in length, abundance, and fullness of brightness.

Deceptive is glory, and vain is splendor; the day of human beings is short. The wise man did not desire such a day; rather, he speaks from his heart to him who sees the heart: “I have not desired the day of man; you know it” (Jer. 17:16). Yet I desire something more than not desiring it: I desire not even to receive it. For I know whose voice this is: “I do not receive glory from a human being” (John 5:41). How wretched we are, who seek glory from one another and refuse that which comes from God alone! Only that glory, which alone we neglect, has length; only it has fullness. The days of a human being are brief, and “his days shall flourish like the flower of the field. The grass has withered,” he says, “and the flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:8). The true day, therefore, is that which knows no setting: eternal truth, true eternity, and consequently true and eternal satiety. Otherwise, how could that glory fill us which is deceptive and vain? It is even called empty, so that you may know that you can be emptied rather than filled by it. Therefore, for the present, lowliness is better than exaltation; necessity better than pleasure, because, although both pass quickly, one brings punishment and the other will bring a crown.

3. Tribulation is useful: it produces proven character and leads to glory. “I am with him in tribulation,” he says; “I will rescue him and glorify him.” Let us give thanks to the Father of mercies, who is with us in tribulation and consoles us in all our tribulation. For tribulation is, as I have said, a necessary thing, which is turned into glory; sorrow which is changed into joy—indeed, joy that is long, which no one takes from us, manifold joy, full joy. This necessity that brings forth a crown is necessary. Let us not despise it, brothers: the seed is small, but great fruit rises from it. Perhaps it is tasteless, perhaps bitter, perhaps it is a grain of mustard. Let us not consider the things seen, but the unseen things in it; “for the things seen are temporal, but the things not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18). Let us taste beforehand the first fruits of glory; let us glory in hope of the glory of the great God. And not only so, but, to say it more plainly, let us glory in tribulation, for in it is hope of glory. See whether the Apostle did not wish to teach you this very thing when he added: “Because tribulation produces patience, patience proven character, and proven character hope.” It is plain from these words that, having first spoken of glorying in hope, the Apostle added not something different, but something further, when he said: “Not only so, but we glory also in tribulations” (Rom. 5:3–4). For a different glorying is not commended; rather, it is added where hope of glory exists, where glorying in hope itself is required. For in tribulation is hope of glory; indeed, glory itself is contained in tribulation, as hope of fruit is in seed, and the fruit itself is in the seed.

In this manner the kingdom of God is even now within us: a vast treasure in an earthen vessel, in a lowly field. It is, I say, but it is hidden. Blessed is the person who finds it there. Who is that? Surely the one who thinks more of the harvest than of the sowing. The eye of faith finds this treasure, not judging according to outward appearance, but seeing what does not appear and beholding what is not seen. How truly that person had found this treasure—who wished it to be found by others also—when he said: “This momentary and light tribulation of ours works in us beyond measure an eternal weight of glory in the heights” (2 Cor. 4:17). He did not say, “It will be rewarded,” but “it works in us an eternal weight of glory.” Glory is hidden, my brothers; it is hidden from us in tribulation. In this momentary thing eternity lies hidden; in this light thing, a lofty and immeasurable weight. Let us therefore hasten meanwhile to buy this field for ourselves, to buy this treasure hidden in the field. Let us count it all joy when we fall into various tribulations. Let us say sincerely, let us say with conviction: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7:3).

4. “I am with him in tribulation,” says God; and shall I meanwhile seek something other than tribulation? “It is good for me to cling to God,” not only this, “but also to place my hope in the Lord” (Ps. 72:28), because, he says, “I will rescue him and glorify him.” “I am with him in tribulation.” “My delights,” he says, “are to be with the children of human beings” (Prov. 8:31). Emmanuel: God with us. “Hail, full of grace,” the angel says to Mary, “the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28). In fullness of grace he is with us; in fullness of glory we shall be with him. He descended in order to be near those troubled in heart, in order to be with us in our tribulation. But that will be when we are caught up in clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so shall always be with the Lord—provided we take care meanwhile to have him with us, that he may be companion on the way who will be the one restoring us to our homeland; indeed, he who will then be homeland may now be the way.

It is good for me, Lord, to suffer tribulation, provided you yourself are with me, rather than to reign without you, feast without you, or glory without you. It is good for me, Lord, to embrace you more in tribulation, to have you with me in the furnace, rather than to be without you even in heaven. “For what have I in heaven, and apart from you what have I desired upon earth?” “The furnace tests gold, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous persons” (Ecclus. 27:6). There, there you are with them, Lord; there you stand in the midst of those gathered in your name, just as you once deigned to appear even to a pagan with the three young men, so that he said: “The appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God” (Dan. 3:92). Why do we tremble, hesitate, or flee this furnace? The fire rages, but the Lord is with us in tribulation. If God is with us, who is against us? Likewise, if he snatches away, who can take from his hand? Or who is there that can rescue from his hand? Finally, if he glorifies, who else will make dishonorable? If he glorifies, who will humble?

5. Hear, finally, with what glory he glorifies. “With length of days,” he says, “I will fill him.” First, by putting “days” in the plural, he meant to emphasize not succession but abundance. Otherwise, if you suppose succession, “one day in the courts of the Lord is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11). We read that even holy and perfect men departed this life “full of days”; and we understand this to mean nothing other than full of virtues, full of graces. Surely into this fullness they are transformed, as it were from day to day, from glory to glory, not by their own spirit but by the Spirit of the Lord.

If, therefore, grace is called “day”; if, as we noted above, “the day of man” is the glory that comes from a human being, and the ill-shining glory which we seek from one another: how much more is the fullness of true glory the true day, indeed the full noon? And if by many days we mean the divisions of graces, how is their multitude not understood in the manifold glory of days? Finally, hear more plainly of many days without any succession: “The light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun sevenfold, like the light of seven days” (Isa. 30:26). The faithful king wished to sing his psalms in the Lord’s house throughout all the days of his life, I think, in all these days. For it will be to be devout toward God for each of the gifts of such great and manifold glory, and always to give thanks in all things, as though singing psalms to his name on all days.

6. “With length of days I will fill him.” As though he said more plainly: I know what he desires, I know what he thirsts for, what is savory to him. Gold and silver are not savory to him; neither pleasure, nor curiosity, nor any worldly dignity. He counts all things loss; he spurns all things and judges them as dung. He has completely emptied himself, nor does he allow himself to be occupied with things by which he knows that he cannot be filled. He is not ignorant in whose image he was created, nor of how great a capacity he is capable; nor can he bear to grow from what is small so as to be diminished from what is greatest. Therefore, “with length of days I will fill him,” whom only true light can refresh, whom only eternity can fill; for that length has no termination, that brightness no setting, that satiety no disgust. For there will be security from eternity, glorying from truth, exultation from satiety.

“And I will show him my salvation.” Surely from then on he will merit to see what he desired, when the King of glory presents to himself the Church as glorious, having neither spot because of the brilliance of the day nor wrinkle because of the utter fullness of herself. Otherwise, at the brilliance of that light, no mind rises which is either impure or troubled in any respect or restless. Hence even now, as I mentioned above, we are commanded to pursue both holiness and peace, because without these no one sees God (Heb. 12:14). Therefore, when he has filled your desire with good things, so that there is nothing else you seek, your mind having been wholly made serene by this fullness itself, you will then be able to see that serenity, that fullness of majesty, made like God because you see him as he is. Or perhaps, because already full of all glory in himself, he will also look abroad upon salvation, which God has wrought, and upon the whole earth, full everywhere of his majesty, as an inhabitant of the most delightful age. This too may seem to be the reference of what he added: “And I will show him my salvation.”

7. Or, if it pleases more, let us understand this also in this way: that in this showing of salvation he explains the very days which he had promised. “With length of days,” he says, “I will fill him.” And as though you asked whence there will be day in the city of which we read that “the sun shall not shine there by day, for there shall be no night in it”: “I will show him my salvation,” he says, so that, as Scripture also says, “its lamp may be the Lamb” (Rev. 21:23). “I will show him my salvation.” No longer will I instruct him in faith; no longer will I exercise him in hope; but I will fulfill him in sight. “I will show him my salvation; I will show him my Jesus,” so that he may now see forever him in whom he believed, whom he loved, whom he always desired.

“Show us, Lord, your mercy, and give us your salvation” (Ps. 84:8). Show us, Lord, your salvation, and it is enough for us. For whoever sees it sees you also, because it is in you and you are in it. “And this is eternal life: that we may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Therefore, then you will dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace, when my eyes have seen your salvation—your Jesus, our Lord, who is God over all, blessed unto the ages. Amen.

[Col. 0253]

## ON PALM SUNDAY

## SERMON I. On the three ranks of those rendering service to Christ

[Col. 0253D]

1. Not without reason has the Church, possessing alike the Spirit of the Bridegroom and of her God, today joined procession to passion in a new and wonderful conjunction. For the procession has applause; the passion, lamentation. Therefore, since we are debtors to the wise and to the foolish, let us see what this conjunction offers to each. First, what it indicates to worldly people: “for not first the spiritual, but the natural.” Let the worldly soul therefore see and understand that sorrow occupies the farthest end of joy. For this reason he who also began to do and to teach everything else, preaching not only by words but also by examples, wished, when appearing in flesh, plainly to demonstrate in himself what he had foretold through the prophet: “Because all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6). Therefore he wished the glory of the procession to be exalted, though he knew that the day of most shameful passion would soon be upon him.

Who, then, ought now to hope in the uncertainty of temporal glory, when he sees that even in him who committed no sin—the Creator of times and Maker of the universe—so great a humiliation follows so great an exaltation? For in the same city, by the same people, and at the same time, he is now honored with the glory of a procession and divine praises; afterward, he is questioned with insults and torture, and reckoned among criminals. This is the end of passing joy; this is the fruit of temporal glory. Therefore the prophet wisely prays that his glory may sing to the Lord and that he may not be pierced with sorrow (Ps. 29:13); that is, that he may have a procession which the passion does not follow.

2. But for you, beloved, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, in the procession we represent the glory of the heavenly homeland; in the passion we show the way. For if the future joy and exceedingly abundant exultation come to your mind in the procession—when we shall be caught up in clouds to meet Christ in the air; if with all longing you desire to see that day when Christ the Lord, the Head together with all the members, will be received into the heavenly Jerusalem, bearing the triumph of victory, amid applause not now from popular crowds but from angelic powers, while the peoples of both Testaments cry out on every side, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21:9)—if, I say, you have considered in the procession the destination toward which you must hasten, learn in the passion the way by which you must go.

For this is the way of life: present tribulation; the way of glory, the way to the city of habitation, the way to the kingdom—as the thief cries from the cross: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). He saw him going into the kingdom and asked him, when he arrived there, to remember him. And he too arrived; but if you wish to know how short the route was, on that same day he deserved to be with the Lord in paradise. Thus the glory of the procession makes the labor of the passion bearable, because nothing is difficult to one who loves.

3. Nor should you wonder that I have said a heavenly procession is represented by the present one, since one and the same person is received in both, though in a very different way and by different persons. For in this procession Christ rides upon an irrational animal; but in that one the animal will indeed be present, yet rational: “You will save men and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. 35:7). Similar is this: “I became like a beast before you, yet I am always with you” (Ps. 72:23). And see whether he is not speaking of the procession when he goes on: “You held my right hand; you led me according to your will, and received me with glory.” There certainly not even the colt itself will be absent. For although the heretic murmurs, not allowing little children to come, and disparaging the baptism of infants [Note: [Col. 0255] He means the Henricians, concerning whom see Epistle 241. They were followed by the people of Cologne, whose doctrines are refuted in Sermons 65 and 66 on the Song of Songs], he who was born a little child and chose the first company of little children—I mean the Innocents—does not even today exclude little children from grace. For it is neither inconsistent with his mercy nor difficult for his majesty to supply, by the gift of grace, what nature has made less possible in them. There no crowd of common people will spread branches of trees or cheap garments; rather, the holy living creatures will lower their wings, the twenty-four elders will lay down their crowns before the throne of the Lamb, and all the angelic powers will ascribe and attribute wholly to him whatever glory or beauty they possess [Col. 0256A] (Rev. 4).

4. Now, since mention has been made of the animal, the garments, and the branches of trees, I wish to consider more carefully the threefold service which I see rendered to the Savior in this procession: first, by the animal upon which he rides; second, by those who spread their own garments for him; third, by those who are said to cut branches from the trees. Yet do not all the others send from their abundance and serve the Lord, as it were, without burden, while the animal alone offers itself for his service? Should I be silent, so that you may avoid self-exaltation? Or should I rather speak, that you may have consolation? Surely you are the animal upon which Christ rides, according to the Apostle’s command [Col. 0256B] to glorify and bear God in your bodies (1 Cor. 6:20). Secular people spend in the Lord’s service not their bodies, indeed, but the things at hand and necessary to their bodies, when they bestow alms from earthly possessions. Prelates also cut branches from trees, for example when they preach from Abraham’s faith and obedience, Joseph’s chastity, Moses’ gentleness, and the virtues of the other saints. Yet they too give from full storehouses; and these are likewise commanded to give freely what they have freely received. Nevertheless, if each faithfully attends to his own ministry, all are in the Savior’s procession and enter the holy city with him [Col. 0256C]. For the prophet foresaw three who would be saved: Noah, cutting branches for the building of the ark; Daniel, through scant food and the labor of abstinence made like a beast, bearing the Savior; and a third, Job, administering the goods of this world well and warming the sides of the poor with the fleeces of his sheep (Ezek. 14:14). But who is nearer to Jesus in that procession, and to whom salvation is nearer among the three ranks, I think you can readily perceive.

## SERMON II. On the Passion, the Procession, and the Four Ranks in the Procession

1. We must speak more briefly today because of the narrowness of time. The procession which we are about to celebrate furnishes us with much material, yet it itself prevents [Col. 0256D] us from saying more. Today we shall celebrate the procession, and shortly afterward hear the Passion. What does this remarkable conjunction mean? What did our fathers intend in adding the Passion to the procession? For the procession is rightly represented today, since it took place today; but why is the Passion added, which is known to have followed on Friday? The Passion is fittingly joined to the procession, so that we may learn to place confidence in no joy of this world, knowing that sorrow occupies the end of joy. Therefore let us not be foolish, so that our prosperity may kill us [Col. 0257A]; rather, on the day of good things let us not forget evil things, and conversely.

For the present age is mixed with these things, not only for worldly people but also for spiritual persons. For we see that worldly people sometimes meet with what pleases them and sometimes with what displeases them; and likewise, for spiritual persons, sorrowful things do not always follow, nor joyful things always, but “evening and morning [make] one day”; and: “You visit him at daybreak, and suddenly test him” (Job 7:18). This is so meanwhile, as long as the present age remains—or rather, runs and flows away.

2. But after this age there will be two ages, very sharply divided and different: so that in one there will be nothing but weeping and gnashing of teeth, while in the other there will be only thanksgiving and the voice of praise. For God “will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints; and death shall be no more, neither mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” [Col. 0257B] (Rev. 21:4). Meanwhile, just as lovers of the world suffer many adversities, so not every desired thing comes to God’s servants in this world. Therefore, on evil days they remember good things, lest they become faint-hearted and impatient, like the man of whom we read in the Psalm: “He will praise you when you have done him good” (Ps. 48:19). And on good days they do not forget evil things, lest they be exalted and say in their abundance: “We shall never be moved.”

For just as the prosperity of worldly things kills the foolish worldly person, so abundance of spiritual prosperity can kill the untaught spiritual person—and therefore one who is not spiritual. For the spiritual person judges all things. And why prosperity kills the fool [Col. 0257C], but not the wise, we have elsewhere: “The heart of the wise is where there is sorrow, and the heart of fools where there is joy.” Therefore he rightly says: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7:3). For although adversity breaks many, prosperity exalts far more, as it is written: “A thousand shall fall at your side”—that is, the left side, by which adversity is signified—“and ten thousand,” that is, far more, “at your right hand” (Ps. 90:7), in which prosperity is signified. Finally, because danger lies on both sides, the Wise Man prays and says: “Give me neither riches nor poverty” (Prov. 30:8), lest [Col. 0257D] riches perhaps exalt him into pride, or poverty cast him down into impatience.

3. Thus the Lord took care to display humility in the procession, just as he displayed patience in the Passion. In the latter he was led “as a sheep to the slaughter,” and “like a lamb before its shearer he was silent and did not open his mouth”; when struck, he did not threaten, but rather prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). But what in the procession? The people were preparing themselves to go out to meet him, and this was not hidden from him who knew what was in man. Therefore he too was prepared, not with chariots and horses, nor with silver bridles or gold-covered saddles, but seated humbly on the back of a donkey, upon garments of the apostles spread beneath him [Col. 0258A]—garments which I do not think were among the costlier things of that region.

4. But why did he wish to have a procession when he knew that the Passion would shortly follow? Perhaps in order that the Passion might be more bitter because the procession had preceded it. For by the same people, in the same place, at that very time, with very few days intervening, he was first received in so great a triumph and afterward crucified. O how unlike: “Away with him, away with him, crucify him” (John 19:15), and “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest!” (Matt. 21:9). How unlike: “King of Israel” (John 12:13), and “We have no king but Caesar!” (John 19:15). How unlike are green branches and the cross, flowers and thorns! He for whom others’ garments were first spread [Col. 0258B] is now stripped of his own, and lots are cast for them. Woe to you, bitterness of our sins, for whose payment such bitterness was necessary.

5. Now, as I approach the procession, I seem to behold four ranks in it; and perhaps they may all be found in our own procession today. Some went ahead and prepared the way. These are those who prepare the Lord’s way into your hearts: those who govern you and direct your steps into the way of peace.
