Others followed; these are those who, conscious of their own ignorance, follow devoutly and always cling to the footsteps of those who go before. There were also disciples, like members of his household, close at his side. These are those who have chosen the better part [Col. 0258C], who live in the cloister for God alone, always cleaving to God and considering what pleases him. Nor was the animal upon which he rode absent; it signifies those hard of heart and, in some sense, beastlike in disposition.

But there was not a more numerous multitude of animals of this sort there, nor ought there to have been. Such people are more a burden than an honor, and the procession is not greatly more glorious on their account. For people of this kind do not know how to sing, but utter harsh-sounding brays. They are those who always need a rod and spurs. Yet the Lord will not abandon even them, if they are willing to bear discipline. For to them it is said: “Serve the Lord in fear,” and: “Embrace discipline, lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the right way” [Col. 0258D] (Ps. 2:11–12). Once this animal is unwilling to bear discipline, what remains except that the Lord cast it away with a certain indignation? It immediately leaves the path, running toward thorns and briars, by which the word of God is choked: namely, the riches of this world and pleasures of the flesh.

6. But if there are any here of such a kind, to whom the rule is burdensome and everything onerous, whom it is often necessary to prick and urge, we beg them to strive, if perhaps they can, to be changed from beasts into human beings and to be reckoned among some of the others: whether among those going before, those who cling close beside him, or those who follow. But if they do not do this, I beg that they at least remain what they are and meanwhile bear patiently things that are salutary, though less pleasant, until it pleases the Lord to regard their humility [Col. 0259A] and advance them to something better.

Do you wish us to offer some consolation to our animal? We know indeed that it does not know how to sing. For it is not among those who can say: “Your statutes were my songs in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118:54). Yet there is one thing: the Lord is closer to it than to any of the others. For not even those who cling to him on either side have him as close as the animal upon which he rides. Hear this also from the Prophet: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. 33:19). A mother too cherishes and embraces more often the son whom she knows to be ill. Therefore let no one be indignant or contemptuous if he wishes to be Christ’s animal. For whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble gravely offends him who cherishes them, like a mother, in the lap of his mercy until they are strengthened [Col. 0259B]. Thus blessed Benedict also warned that infirmities of character must be borne with the greatest patience (Rule, ch. 72).

7. Therefore there are four kinds in the Lord’s procession: good prudent persons and good simple persons; these are those who go before and those who follow. I added “good,” because prudent people who are not good are wicked, according to the saying: “They are wise to do evil” (Jer. 4:22); and simple people who are not good are fools. But in the Lord’s procession neither the wicked nor the fool has a place. Moreover, those who cleave to him are contemplatives. Those who bear him and are burdened by him are hard of heart and little devoted.

Yet see: all are in the Lord’s procession, and none of them sees his face [Col. 0259C]. For those who go before are occupied in preparing the way, anxious about the sins and temptations of others. Those who follow cannot at all see his face; rather, as Moses was told, they see his back. The animal on which he rides never raises its eyes to see, but always bends toward the ground. Those, however, who cleave to him can sometimes see, but fleetingly and not continuously, nor fully while they are still on the way. Yet in comparison with the others, they see him more face to face, according to what is likewise written [variant: affectuosus, “affectionate”] of Moses: that God spoke to the other prophets through visions and dreams, but to Moses face to face.

As for the full vision, not even Moses himself, while living in this world, could obtain the vision of his face [Col. 0259D], because, as God himself says: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:23, 11, 20). “I shall not be seen,” he says, “in this life; no one shall see my face on this way and in this procession.” May he therefore, in his great mercy, grant us so to persevere in his procession while we live that, in that great procession in which he is to be received by the Father with all his own, and to hand over the kingdom to God the Father, we may deserve to enter the holy city with him, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. On the Five Days: of the Procession, Refreshment, Passion, Rest, and Resurrection

1. Since God has made all things “in number, weight [Col. 0260A], and measure” (Wis. 11:21), he nevertheless arranged with particular care those times in which he was seen on earth and lived among human beings, and all that he did, said, or suffered in them, so that not even the smallest moment, not one iota, lacked sacramental significance or passed without mystery. Yet he more plainly illuminated the four nearest days and the very day which we celebrate today: the day of his procession, the day of refreshment, of passion, of rest, and of resurrection. These are exceedingly notable days, more distinguished than the others.

On the first day he deigned to receive human glory and, amid a certain immense rejoicing and the exultation of the whole earth, to enter Jerusalem not on his own feet, as had been his custom until then, but carried upon an animal. This was indeed a preparation for the Passion, chiefly because it aroused the envy of the priests [Col. 0260B]. Certainly, when crowds were at one time going to seize him and make him king, he is recorded as fleeing and withdrawing (John 6:15). But now he was present even though not sought, that he might be received and proclaimed by them as King of Israel; indeed, he undoubtedly stirred their minds to these very acclamations.

So too may we observe concerning the Passion. At one time he went out and hid himself from them, that is, from the Jews; nor did he wish any longer to walk openly in Judea, because they sought to kill him (John 7:1). But knowing that his hour had come, he voluntarily offered himself to the Passion as one having authority. For it was fitting that our High Priest should be tested in all things in likeness to us, yet without sin (Heb. 4:15), so that, as a true human being, he might fittingly avoid and fittingly accept both human prosperity [Col. 0260C] and adversity, and in himself furnish us a salutary example of both. For just as it belongs to temperance to avoid the acclamations of the people and the prosperity of this age, so it sometimes belongs to justice, by a definite dispensation, to admit them. Persecution also, and every temporal adversity, should sometimes prudently be fled according to place and time; but when necessary, it should be borne courageously.

2. All human life is occupied with these two things—prosperity and adversity. Yet all virtue consists in those four well-known kinds [of virtue]. Therefore it was fitting that he should fulfill every virtue, in whom the whole fullness of virtue dwelt most fully [Col. 0260D], so that it might be known to all that he knew especially how to abound and also how to suffer want. For the Wisdom of God was not among those whom their prosperity kills; nor was the Power of God among those whom turning away could destroy. For it is written of both that prosperity kills—not everyone, but fools—and that turning away destroys—not just anyone, but little ones (Prov. 1:31–32).

Yet how modestly he appears to have received this glory, coming to the triumphal reception on a donkey, not in chariots or on horses! And he said: “If anyone says anything to you, say: ‘The Lord has need of them’” (Matt. 21:31, 3). A great need, a need of salvation. For God had come, multiplying his mercy, to save men and beasts [Col. 0261A]. This gracious condescension would be the beginning of our conversion: that we should first beget a son from the slave woman. At the Lord’s command, one formerly bound is loosed—either unable or unwilling to do good, or bound more strongly by both bonds, neither willing nor able. Meanwhile, he does not know how to rejoice more purely in the Lord. He is convinced that what he does pleases God, and he takes comfort in this: he thinks that he somehow makes God his debtor, often recalling that “the Lord has need of them.”

But as time goes on, he will be moved rather by concern about his own debt, and fear lest he be found ungrateful for such great benefits, saying: “I am an unprofitable servant, and you have no need of my goods.” This is, however, a true and faithful disposition: this is the son of the free woman, with whom the son of the slave woman cannot be heir. Thus, then, in this procession.

3. But before the Passion, the most loving (affectuosissimus) householder [variant: affectuosius, “more lovingly”] took care to set refreshment before his household; and in this too the kindness and humanity of the Savior appeared. For since he had loved his own, he loved them to the end, and said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” [Col. 0261B] (Luke 22:15). For it was necessary. Satan had demanded them, to sift them like wheat; refreshment had to come first. Indeed, those who had been refreshed scarcely failed; what would they have done fasting? Accordingly, he refreshed not only their bodies, but also their hearts—and especially their hearts. For not bodily suffering but spiritual temptation was imminent, since he alone was to suffer until it had passed. That sacrifice alone, just as it alone could avail, so it alone sufficed; nor was it fitting that Christ should suffer for humanity’s salvation together with Peter, James, or John. Two others indeed were crucified with him, but they were two evildoers, so that absolutely no suspicion could arise that the less effective sacrifice needed to be supplemented by theirs.

4. With what loaves, then, did he refresh the apostles at supper? In my judgment, with five. “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34). It is food indeed, but food for the heart. For what equally strengthens and fortifies the human heart, what so encourages and sustains it in every necessity, as the fulfillment of the divine will, received into a kind of stomach of the soul—that is, into its conscience? [Col. 0261D] Likewise, only one whose heart has already dried up because he has forgotten to eat his own bread does not know that the word of divine exhortation, the consolation of God’s promises, and the tears of those praying (orantium) [variant: orationum, “of prayers”] are breads for the heart. Above all, however, the Lord’s flesh is truly food, food of life, the living bread from heaven (John 6:56, 48, 51).

If you attend carefully, you will find that none of these was absent from this most solemn supper of the Lord. While the disciples were still reclining, he rose from supper, girded himself with a towel, put water into a basin, washed and dried the disciples’ feet [Col. 0262A]. This is not the will of flesh and blood, but the will of the Father and our sanctification. Finally, when Peter resisted most insistently, the Lord said to him: “If I do not wash you, you shall have no part with me” (John 13:8). And we know who said: “Whoever comes to me I shall not cast out; because I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:37–38).

Appropriately, and in his usual manner, he joined an exhortation of words after the example of his deed. While speaking—for his discourse was very abundant—he took care to cheer and strengthen them with many promises, especially because of the approaching Passion: promises about his resurrection, the coming of the Paraclete, their strengthening, and at length their being taken to himself. Not long afterward they came to prayer [Col. 0262B], and in his agony he prayed even a third time. There he seems to have wept not with his eyes alone but, as it were, with all his limbs, so that his whole body, which is the Church, might be cleansed by the tears of the whole body. As for the sacrament of his body and blood, no one fails to know that this food, both entire and so unique, was first given on that day (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 13–18), commended on that day, and commanded thenceforth to be frequently received.

5. From this follows the day of the Passion, in which, just as he made the whole human being whole, so he made his whole self a saving sacrifice: exposing his body to so many torments and insults, and his soul to a twofold most human compassion—on the one hand, for the inconsolable grief of the holy women; on the other, for the despair and scattering of the disciples [Col. 0262C]. In these four things was the Lord’s cross; and he suffered all these things for us, he who felt compassion for us with such great love. Yet the things concerning himself came to an end, as he himself said to the mourning women (Luke 23:28): an end indeed most swift and most glorious—first rest, then resurrection.

We too, if we hasten to enter that rest, should remember that we must pass through many tribulations. And at first, while we are in tribulation, it seems to us [videtur; variant: videretur, “would seem”] a great thing to aspire to rest, as though we should desire nothing further. Yet we shall not be at rest—not even in rest itself—from desire for glory, from desire for resurrection. “Henceforth,” says the Spirit, “let them rest from their labors” [Col. 0262D] (Rev. 14:13). Therefore those who die in the Lord rest from labor; but meanwhile they do not rest from crying out. For the souls of the slain cry out beneath God’s throne, because, although they have nothing to afflict them, they do not yet have everything that delights them—until resurrection follows rest, and Easter follows the Sabbath. Amen.

[Col. 0263]

## ON WEDNESDAY OF HOLY WEEK. SERMON ON THE PASSION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0263A] 1. Be vigilant in spirit, brothers, lest the mysteries of this season pass over you without fruit. The blessing is abundant: provide clean receptacles; offer devout souls, watchful senses, sober affections, and pure consciences for such gifts of grace. You are certainly urged to this diligence not only by the particular manner of life which you have professed, but also by the general observance of the Church, whose children you are. For all Christians in this holy week cultivate piety more than usual, or beyond their customary measure; they display modesty, pursue humility, and put on seriousness, so that they may seem in some way to suffer with Christ in his Passion. For who is so irreligious as not to be pierced with compunction? Who so insolent as not to be humbled? Who so angry as not to forgive? [Col. 0263B] Who so self-indulgent as not to abstain? Who so shameful as not to restrain himself? Who so malicious as not to repent in these days?

And rightly so. For the Lord’s Passion is present, even (usque) today [variant: utique, “certainly today”], shaking the earth, splitting rocks, and opening tombs. His resurrection also is near, in which you will celebrate the feast for the most high Lord—if only you may enter with eagerness and ardor of spirit into the highest things which he has wrought! Nothing better could have been done in the world than what the Lord did in these days. Nothing better or more useful could have been commended to the world than that, by a perpetual rite, it should celebrate every year his memorial in the desire of the soul and pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of his (ejus) sweetness [variant: suae, “its own”] [Col. 0263C]. Both are for our sake, because in both is the fruit of salvation for us, in both the life of our spirit.

Wonderful is your Passion, Lord Jesus: it has driven away all our sufferings, made propitiation for all our iniquities, and is found ineffective against none of our plagues. For what is so bound to death that it is not loosed by your death?

2. Therefore, brothers, in this Passion three things especially should be considered: the deed, its manner, and its cause. For in the deed patience is commended; in the manner, humility; in the cause, love. The patience is unique because, when sinners built upon his back; when he was stretched out on the wood so that all his bones could be counted; when that most mighty stronghold which guards Israel [Col. 0263D] was pierced on every side; when his hands and feet were dug through—he was led like a lamb to slaughter and, like a sheep before its shearer, did not open his mouth. He did not murmur against the Father who had sent him; nor against the human race, for which he paid what he had not stolen; nor, finally, even against the people especially belonging to him, from whom he received such evils in return for such great benefits.

Some are punished for their sins and bear it humbly; this itself is nevertheless reckoned to them as patience. Others are scourged not so much to be cleansed as to be tested and crowned [Col. 0264A]; and their patience is proved and commended as greater. How should patience not be judged greatest in Christ, who, in the allotted territory of his inheritance, was punished with a most cruel death like a thief by those to whom he had come especially as Savior, while he possessed absolutely no sin—not by his own act, not by inherited taint, nor even any in which he could grow?

For in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells, not shadowily but bodily; in him God reconciles the world to himself, not figuratively but substantially; finally, he is full of grace and truth, not cooperatively (cooperative) [variant: comparative, “comparatively”] but personally, in order to accomplish his work. “His work is alien from him,” Isaiah says (Isa. 28:21), because the work which the Father gave him to do was his own, yet it was alien to him that one such as he should suffer such things [Col. 0264B]. Thus in the deed you have patience.

3. If you attend carefully to the manner itself, you will recognize him as not only gentle but humble in heart. For “his judgment was taken away in humility,” since he gave no answer either to such great blasphemies or to the utterly false charges brought against him. “We saw him, and he had no appearance, nor beauty above the sons of men, but [was] the reproach of men and as a leper; the last of men, truly a man of sorrows, stricken by God and humbled: so that he had neither form nor comeliness” (Isa. 53:2–4). O lowest and highest! O humble and exalted! O reproach of men and glory of angels! No one is more exalted than he, nor more humble [Col. 0264C]. Finally, he was smeared with spittle, filled with reproaches, condemned to a most shameful death, and counted among criminals. Shall not even this humility merit something—a humility of this measure, indeed one so far beyond measure? As his patience is unique, so his humility is admirable; both are without example.

4. Yet the cause itself splendidly commends both: namely, love. For because of his exceedingly great love, with which God loved us, in order to redeem the slave neither did the Father spare the Son, nor did the Son spare himself. Truly it was exceedingly great, since this too exceeds measure and surpasses all bounds, plainly transcending everything. “No one,” he says, “has greater love than that one should lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). You had greater love, Lord, laying it down even for enemies. For while we were still enemies, through your death we were reconciled both to you and to the Father [Col. 0264D]. What other love, then, will seem to be, to have been, or to be hereafter comparable to this?

Scarcely does anyone die for a just person; you suffered for the unjust, dying for our offenses—you who came freely to justify sinners, to make slaves brothers, captives co-heirs, and exiles kings. And surely nothing illustrates this patience and humility equally with the fact that he gave his life over to death, bore the sins of many, and even prayed for transgressors [Col. 0265A] that they might not perish. “Faithful is the saying and worthy of all acceptance!” For because he willed it, he was offered. Not only did he will it and was offered, but he was offered because he willed it. He alone had authority to lay down his life; no one took it from him; he offered it voluntarily. When he had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished.” Nothing remains to be fulfilled; there is nothing now for which I should wait. And, bowing his head, having become obedient unto death, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30).

Who sleeps so easily whenever he wishes? To die is indeed great weakness; but to die in this way is plainly immense power. For what is weak in God is stronger than human beings. Human madness may lay criminal hands upon itself for death; but this is not to lay down one’s life—it is rather to force it and violently break it off than to lay it down at one’s will [Col. 0265B]. To you, impious Judas, there was the pitiable ability not to lay down your life, but to hang yourself; and it was not by your surrendering it but by the noose dragging you that your most wicked spirit departed—not released by you but lost by you. He alone gave his life over to death who alone by his own power returned to life. He alone had authority to lay it down who equally had the free power to take it up again, possessing dominion over life and death.

5. Worthy, then, is love so immeasurable, humility so admirable, patience so invincible. Worthy indeed is a sacrifice so holy, so unstained, so acceptable. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain [Col. 0265C] to receive strength, to accomplish that for which he came, to take away the sin of the world. But I speak of a threefold sin that has prevailed over the earth. Do you think I mean the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life? A threefold cord is not easily broken; therefore many draw—indeed, are drawn—by this cord of vanity. Yet that former triad rightly prevails in the elect. For how can remembrance of that patience not restrain every pleasure? How can consideration of that humility not utterly crush pride of life? And that love is surely worthy for meditation upon it to occupy the mind and claim the whole soul for itself, so as altogether to blow away the vice of curiosity. Therefore the Savior’s Passion is strong against these things.

[Col. 0265D] 6. But I had intended to say how the power of the cross equally blots out another threefold sin, and perhaps this will be more useful to hear. The first I call original, the second personal, the third singular. Original sin is that greatest offense which we inherit from the first Adam, in whom we all sinned and on whose account we all die. It is indeed greatest, because it so possesses not only the entire human race but every individual in that race that there is no one who escapes, no one at all. It extends from the first human being to the last; and in each individual this poison is spread from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head. It also extends in another way throughout the whole span of life: namely, from the day on which one’s own mother conceives each person until the day on which the common mother receives him [Col. 0266A].

Otherwise, whence comes the heavy yoke upon all the children of Adam without exception, from the day when they come out of their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all? We are conceived in filth, nourished in darkness, and born in pain. Before our birth we burden our unhappy mothers; at birth we tear them like vipers. It is astonishing that we ourselves are not torn apart as well. We give forth our first cry in weeping—and deservedly, since we have entered the valley of weeping—so that the saying of holy Job may be fittingly applied to us in every respect: “A human being born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job 14:1).

That this is true [variant adds: verbum, “saying”] has been taught us not by words but by blows. “A human being,” he says, “born of woman”: nothing is more lowly. And lest perhaps he flatter himself in the very pleasure of bodily senses, which he draws from sensible things, he is immediately and terribly warned at his entrance also about his departure, when it is said: “living for a short time.” And lest he think the little interval left between entrance and exit is free to him, it says: “filled with many miseries” [Col. 0266B]. With many and manifold miseries, I say: miseries of the body, miseries of the heart; miseries while asleep, miseries while awake, miseries wherever he turns.

Yet he too who was born of a Virgin—indeed, made of a woman, but of her who is blessed among women, he who says to his mother, “Woman, behold your son” (John 19:26)—also lived for a short time on earth and was nonetheless filled with many miseries: in that brief time beset by snares, challenged with insults, struck with injuries, harassed by punishments, assailed with abuse [Col. 0266C].

7. Do you then doubt that this obedience is sufficient to absolve every guilt of the first transgression? Indeed, the gift is not like the offence. For sin, from one man, led to condemnation; but grace, from many offences, to justification. That original offence was certainly altogether grievous: it infected not only the person but also nature. Yet each person’s personal sin is more grievous when, with the reins now loosened, we offer our members on every side as weapons of iniquity to sin, bound not merely by another’s [variant: a second’s] crime, but by our own as well. Most grievous of all, however, is the singular offence committed against the Lord of majesty, [Col. 0266D] when wicked men unjustly killed the just man and, most cruel murderers, laid sacrilegious hands upon the very Son of God—indeed, if it be permitted to say so, even deicides. What are the two preceding offences in comparison with the third? At this the whole fabric of the world grew pale and shuddered, and almost all things were turned back into their ancient chaos.

Let us suppose that one of the princes of a kingdom had devastated the royal land by hostile destruction; let us suppose another who, though admitted to the king’s table and counsel, had strangled his only son with treacherous hands. Would not the first, in comparison with the second, seem innocent and guiltless? Such is every sin in relation to this sin. Yet he bore this sin in himself, who made himself sin, in order that by sin he might condemn sin. For through this every [Col. 0267A] sin, both original and personal, has been wiped away; and that singular sin itself has been abolished through himself.

8. I argue from the greater: the two lesser matters have been refuted. And behold the argument. He bore the sin of many and prayed for transgressors, that they might not perish: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Your irrevocable word flies forth, Lord, and shall not return to you empty, but shall accomplish that for which you sent it. See now the works of the Lord, the wonders which he has set upon the earth. He was scourged with whips, crowned with thorns, pierced with nails, fastened to the cross, sated with reproaches—yet forgetful of all pains: “Forgive them,” he says. Here are the many miseries of the body; here the mercies of the heart; here pains, [Col. 0267B] here compassions; here the oil of gladness, here drops of blood running down to the earth. Many are the Lord’s mercies, but many too are the Lord’s miseries. Will miseries overcome mercies, or will mercies surpass miseries? Let your ancient mercies prevail, Lord; let wisdom conquer malice. For great is their iniquity; but is not your mercy greater, Lord? Great indeed, in every way.

“Is evil returned for good,” he says, “because they have dug a pit for my soul?” (Jer. 18:20). Certainly they dug a pit of impatience, furnishing very many and very great occasions for indignation. But what is their pit beside the abyss of your meekness? In returning evils for good, they dug a pit; [Col. 0267C] but love is not provoked, does not rush headlong, never fails; it does not fall into the pit, and in return for evils it heaps up good things. Far be it that dying flies should destroy the sweetness of the ointment (Eccl. 10:1) which flows from your body! For with you is mercy, and with him plentiful redemption. Dying flies are miseries; dying flies are blasphemies; dying flies are insults, which a perverse and exasperating generation returns to you.

9. But what do you do? At the very raising up of your hands, when the morning sacrifice was already passing into the evening burnt offering; at the very power, I say, of the incense which ascended to heaven, covered the earth, and sprinkled the lower regions, crying out to be heard because of your reverence, [Col. 0267D] you say: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” O how abundant are you in forgiving! O how great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord! O how far are your thoughts from our thoughts! O how firmly is your mercy established even over the ungodly! A wondrous thing! He cries, “Forgive”; the Jews cry, “Crucify” (John 19:15). His words are softer than oil, but these are arrows. O love that is patient and also compassionate! Love is patient: that is enough; love is kind (1 Cor. 13:4): that is an overflowing measure. “Do not be overcome by evil” is abundant love; “but overcome evil with good” (Rom. 12:21) is superabundant. For not patience alone, but also God’s kindness, led the Jews to repentance; because kind love loves even those whom it endures, and [Col. 0268A] loves them so ardently. Patient love overlooks, waits, and bears with the offender; but kind love draws, leads, causes him to turn from the error of his way, and finally covers a multitude of sins.

O Jews, you are stones, yet you strike a stone softer than yourselves: from it resounds the ringing of mercy, and boils forth the oil of love! How, Lord, will you give those who desire you drink from the torrent of your delight, when you so bathe those crucifying you in the oil of your mercy?

10. It is therefore clear that this passion is most powerful for exhausting every kind of sin. But who knows whether it has been given to me? It has been given to me, because it could not be given to another. To an angel? But he had no need of it. To the devil? But he does not rise again. Finally, he was made not in the likeness of angels—far be it that he was made in [Col. 0268B] the likeness of demons!—but in the likeness of men; and, found in outward appearance as a man, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7). He was a Son, and became as a servant. He took not only the form of a servant, to be subject, but even that of a bad servant, to be beaten; and that of a servant of sin, to pay its penalty when he had no guilt.

“In the likeness,” he says, “of men,” not of man; because the first man was created neither in the flesh of sin nor in the likeness of sinful flesh. For Christ plunged himself more closely and deeply into the universal misery of humankind, lest that subtle eye of the devil should detect this great sacrament of mercy. Therefore he was found in outward appearance, and in every outward respect, as a man; nor, [Col. 0268C] so far as nature’s due was concerned, did any mark of singularity appear in him. Because he was thus hidden, he was therefore crucified. Yet he revealed himself to a few, that there might be those who believed; while to the rest he was concealed: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). To that singular sin he also joined ignorance, so that those acting in ignorance might be forgiven under some shadow of justice.

11. That ancient Adam, who fled from the face of God, left us two things as an inheritance: labour and pain—labour in action, pain in suffering. Did he not himself hear this in paradise, which he had received to work and to keep: to work it delightfully and keep it faithfully, for himself and his descendants? Christ the Lord looked upon labour and [Col. 0268D] pain, that he might deliver them into his hands—or rather, deliver himself into theirs—fixed in the mire of the deep, while those waters entered even to his soul. “Look,” he says, “upon my humility and my labour” (Ps. 24:18); “for I am poor, and in labours from my youth” (Ps. 87:16). He laboured by enduring; his hands served in labours. Concerning pain, see what he said: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any pain like my pain” (Lam. 1:12). Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our weaknesses and pains (Isa. 53:4): a man of sorrows, poor and suffering, tempted in all things without sin.

In life he had a passive activity, and in death he bore an active passion, while he worked salvation [Col. 0269A] in the midst of the earth. Therefore, as long as I live, I shall remember those labours which he endured in preaching, his weariness in journeying about, his temptations in fasting, his vigils in prayer, and his tears in compassion. I shall remember also his pains: insults, spittings, blows, mockeries, reproaches, nails, and things of this kind, which passed over him and upon him more abundantly.

> [Note: Bernard repeats the same words in *Sermon 22 On Various Subjects*, no. 5, and in *Sermon 43 on the Song of Songs*, no. 3. Nicholas of Clairvaux likewise used them for his own purposes in Letter 6. [Cols. 0269D, 0270D]]

Thus his strength benefits me, and his likeness benefits me—but only if imitation is added, so that I follow his footsteps. Otherwise the righteous blood which was shed upon the earth will be required even of me, and I shall not be innocent of that most singular crime of the Jews: namely, that I was ungrateful for so great a love, that I insulted the Spirit of grace, that I considered the blood of the [Col. 0269B] covenant unclean, and that I trampled underfoot the Son of God.

12. There are many who suffer labour and pain, but necessity is the cause, not will; and these are not conformed to the image of the Son of God. There are those who endure voluntarily, but they have neither lot nor share in this saying. The lustful man stays awake all night, not only patiently but willingly, to satisfy his pleasure; the robber, armed with iron, stays awake to seize his prey; the thief stays awake to break into another’s house. But all these, and those like them, are far from the labour and pain upon which the Lord looks.

But people of good will, who by Christian resolve have exchanged riches for poverty—or who, even without possessing riches, have despised them as though possessed—leaving all things for his sake, just as he left all things for theirs, [Col. 0269C] follow him wherever he goes. Such imitation is to me a most compelling proof that the Saviour’s passion and the likeness of his humanity pass over to my benefit. For here is the savour, here the fruit, of both labour and pain.

13. See, then, how greatly that majesty has magnified his dealings with you. Of all things in heaven and beneath heaven, he spoke, and they were made (Ps. 148:5). And what is easier to say? But was it accomplished by a word alone when he remade you whom he had made? For thirty-three years he was seen upon earth and lived among men; he had calumniators of his deeds and mockers of his words, and had nowhere to lay his head. Why was this? Because the Word had descended from his subtlety and taken on a grosser garment. For he had become flesh, and therefore employed a more laborious and slower work.

But as thought clothes itself in a bodily voice without any diminution of itself, whether before or after the voice, so the Son of God assumed flesh, suffering neither mixture nor diminution, neither before the flesh nor after it. With the Father he was invisible; but here our hands handled the Word of life, and we saw with our eyes that which was from the beginning. Because this Word [Col. 0270A] had united to himself a most pure flesh and a most holy soul, he freely governed the actions of his body—both because he was wisdom and righteousness, and because he had absolutely no law in his members opposing the law of his mind.

My word is neither wisdom nor righteousness, yet it is capable of both; and these may be absent from it or present in it, though more readily absent. For it has now become more natural to us to serve the vices of our flesh than to order its actions and passions, because every age is inclined toward evil from adolescence onward, seeking its pleasures even amid scourges and swords, even under the threat of death.

14. Blessed is the person whose thought—that is, our word—directs all its actions toward righteousness, so that the intention is sound and the operation upright. Blessed is the person who orders the passions of his body for righteousness, so that whatever he suffers, he suffers for the Son of God; so that murmuring may be removed from the heart, while thanksgiving and the voice of praise are upon the lips. He who has thus raised himself takes up his bed and goes to his house. Our bed is the body, in which we formerly lay weak, serving our own desires and lusts. But now we carry it, when it is compelled to obey the spirit; and we carry our dead thing, because the body is dead because of sin.

Yet we walk; we do not run. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). We also walk into our house. Into what [Col. 0270C] house? Into the mother of all, because “their tombs are their houses for ever” (Ps. 48:12). Or rather, into our house, which we have from God, not made with hands, eternal in the heavens (2 Cor. 5:1). We who walk beneath this burden—when it is laid down, how, do you think, shall we run? How shall we fly? Truly, upon the wings of the winds.

The Lord Jesus embraced us through our labour and pain; let us in turn embrace him with certain reciprocal embraces, for and toward his righteousness, directing our actions toward righteousness and sustaining sufferings for righteousness. Let us say with the bride: “I held him, and I will not let him go” (Song 3:4). Let us also say with the patriarch: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. 32:26). [Col. 0270D] For what remains now except blessing? What remains after an embrace except a kiss? If I thus clung to God, how could I fail joyfully to cry: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1)?

Meanwhile feed us, Lord, with the bread of tears, and give us tears to drink in measure, until you bring us to the good measure, pressed down and shaken together, which you will give into our bosoms—you who are God, blessed above all, in the bosom of the Father for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0271]

## ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

### Sermon on Baptism, the Sacrament of the Altar, and the Washing of Feet

[Col. 0271A] 1. These are days which we ought to observe, days full of mercy and grace, by which even the minds of wicked people are stirred to repentance. So great, indeed, is the power of the sacraments commemorated on these days that they can split even hearts of stone and suffice to soften every breast, though made of iron. For even to this day we see that, at Christ’s passion, not only did the heavens share in suffering, but the earth shook, rocks were split, and tombs were opened in the confession of sinners.

But since spiritual foods resemble bodily foods in this respect—that in some their flavour is immediately present, while in others one must labour—things which are manifest need no ministry of ours, whereas things which are hidden demand careful consideration [variant: a careful examiner]. A mother does not give a small child a whole nut, but breaks it and offers the kernel. So I too, dearest brothers, ought, if I could, to open for you the hidden sacraments. But because my ability is slight, let us pray that the mother Wisdom may break these nuts for you and for me alike: those nuts, I say, produced by the priestly rod, the rod of strength which the Lord sent forth from Zion.

There are many sacraments, and an hour is not enough for searching them all out. Perhaps some of you are also too weak to grasp so much at once. Therefore, concerning three sacraments [Col. 0271B] quite fitting for this season, we must say what the Lord himself grants.

> [Note: Here the name “sacrament” is used in a broader sense, embracing not only true sacraments of the New Law, such as baptism and the sacrament of the altar, but also sacramentals, such as the washing of feet. Arnald, abbot of Bonneval, likewise calls it a sacrament in his sermon on the washing of feet, the sole sermon in the book *On the Chief Works of Christ*. Hugh of Saint Victor, an author of that period, elsewhere gives the customary number of sacraments. [Cols. 0271D, 0272D]]

[Col. 0271C] 2. A sacrament is called a sacred sign or a sacred secret. Many things are done solely for their own sake; others are done to signify something else, and these are called signs—and are signs. To take an ordinary example: a ring may be given simply for the ring itself, with no significance; it may be given to invest someone with an inheritance, and then it is a sign, so that the recipient may say: “The ring is worth nothing; it is the inheritance that I sought.”

Accordingly, when the Lord drew near to his passion, he took care to invest his own with his grace, so that invisible grace might be bestowed through some visible sign. For this purpose all the sacraments were instituted: for this purpose participation in the Eucharist, for this purpose the washing of feet, and finally baptism itself, the beginning of all sacraments, in which we are planted together in the likeness of his death. Hence the threefold immersion bears the form of the three days now to be celebrated.

For as outward signs are various and—as we may continue the example begun—investitures differ according to the things in which we are invested: for example, a canon is invested by a book, an abbot by a staff, a bishop by staff and ring together; so, I say, in matters of this sort, various distributions of grace are bestowed through different sacraments. [Col. 0272A] What, then, is the grace with which we are invested through baptism? Surely, the cleansing of sins. For who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed, except he alone who is clean and into whom sin does not fall—God?

Circumcision was formerly the sacrament of this grace, so that the knife might cut away the rusty stain of original guilt which had flowed down from our first parents. But when the Lord came, the Lamb wholly gentle and mild, whose yoke is sweet and whose burden light, it was most suitably changed: water, with the anointing of the Holy Spirit, washed away the long-standing rust, and that harshness ceased.

3. But perhaps someone asks: “If what we contracted from our parents has been erased in baptism, why does the fuel of desire still remain, like a certain incitement to sin?” For there is no doubt that this law of sin was transmitted to us from our first parents. We are all generated by sinful will, and thence our will is corrupted, as though full of ulcers.

> [Note: In some manuscripts this phrase is absent: “and thence … full of ulcers.” Yet these words fit properly with what follows, where the matter is the discharge of an old ulcer. [Col. 0272D]]

Thus, though unwilling, we feel certain itching urges of concupiscence and movements like those of beasts. I have often told you, and it must not pass from your mind, that in the fall of the first man we all fell. We fell upon a heap [Col. 0272C] of stones and into mud; hence we were not merely defiled but also wounded and grievously shattered. We can indeed be washed quickly; but to be healed requires much treatment.

We are therefore washed in baptism because the bond of our condemnation is erased; and this grace is bestowed upon us, that concupiscence may no longer harm us, provided that we refrain from consent. Thus, as though the discharge of an old ulcer were being removed, condemnation is taken away, together with the sentence of death which formerly issued from it. But who can break such savage impulses? Who can bear the itching of this ulcer? Take courage: grace comes to our aid in this also; and, that you may be secure, you have the investiture of the sacrament [variant: of the sacrament] of the Lord’s body and precious blood. [Col. 0272D]

For that sacrament accomplishes two things in us: it lessens the sensation in minor matters, and in graver sins removes consent altogether. If any of you now feels less often, and less sharply, impulses of anger, envy, lust, or the other things of this sort, let him give thanks to the body and blood of the Lord, since the power of the sacrament is at work in him; and let him rejoice that the most grievous ulcer is moving toward health.

4. Yet what are we to do, since in this body of sin and in this evil age we cannot be without sin? Shall we despair? Far from it! “If we say,” says blessed John, “that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, God is faithful to forgive sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John 1:8–9). So that we may not doubt at all concerning the remission of daily sins, we have its sacrament: the washing of feet.

Perhaps you ask how I know that it is a sacrament of this remission, [Col. 0273B] especially when the Lord himself promised Peter, saying: “What I do, you do not know now, but you shall know afterwards”; and said nothing about a sacrament, but only, “I have given you an example, that you also should do likewise.” Yet he had many things to say to them, but they could not then bear them. Therefore he wished neither to leave them wholly anxious and doubtful nor to say what they could not then understand.

Do you wish to know that this was done as a sacrament, and not merely as an example? Consider what was said to Peter: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me.” Something necessary to salvation therefore lies hidden here, since without it not even Peter himself would have a share in the kingdom of Christ and God. See whether Peter did not tremble at the terrifying word of so great a threat, and whether he did not recognize the mystery as saving, when he replied: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and head.” And how do we know that this washing pertains to the cleansing of sins not unto death, sins from which we plainly cannot wholly guard ourselves before death? Clearly from the answer given when he offered hands and head together to be washed: “He who has been washed does not need [Col. 0273C] anything except to wash his feet” (John 13:7–10, 15).

For one is washed who, by grace, has no sins: whose head—that is, intention—and hands—that is, action and manner of life—are clean. But the feet, which are the soul’s affections, cannot be wholly clean while we walk in this dust, without the mind at some time yielding, even for an hour, more than it ought to vanity, pleasure, or curiosity. “For in many things we all offend” (James 3:2).

5. Nevertheless, let no one despise or make light of these sins. For it is impossible to be saved with them; impossible for them to be cleansed except through Christ Jesus and by Christ. Let no one, I say, slumber in ruinous security, turning aside to words of wickedness to make excuses for sins. For, as Peter heard from Christ himself, unless Christ washes them, we shall have no part with him. Yet it is not necessary to be too anxious concerning them: he will readily—indeed willingly—forgive, if only we acknowledge them.

For in matters of this kind, as though unavoidable, both culpable negligence and excessive fear are present. This is why, in the prayer which he himself instituted, he willed that we should pray daily concerning those sins (Luke 11:4). For, as we said of concupiscence, although he has taken away condemnation—because, according to the Apostle, “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:1)—yet he still permits it to live within us, humbling us and grievously afflicting us, so that we may feel what grace bestows upon us and always have recourse to its help. So too, by a merciful dispensation, [Col. 0274C] these lesser sins are not entirely removed; rather, God instructs us through them, so that, when we cannot avoid the least faults, we may be certain that we do not overcome greater ones by our own strength, and may always be fearful and wholly concerned not to lose his grace, which we recognize as necessary to us in so many ways.

[Col. 0273]

## ON THE HOLY DAY OF EASTER

### Sermon on the Seven Seals Opened by the Lamb

[Col. 0273D] 1. “The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. 5:5). He has indeed conquered malice by wisdom, reaching from end to end mightily and ordering all things sweetly: mightily for me, sweetly to me. He conquered the Jews’ blasphemies upon the cross, bound the strong man armed in his courtyard, and triumphed over the very dominion of death. Where are your reproaches now, Jew? Where are your vessels of captives, Zebulun? Where is your victory, O death? The slanderer is confounded; the plunderer has been despoiled. A new kind of power! Death, hitherto victorious, stands astonished.

What of you, Jew, who the day before shook your sacrilegious head before the cross? Why did you assail with reproaches Christ, the true head of humankind?

> [Note: Variant: “Why did you assail with reproaches the sacred head of the man Christ?” [Col. 0273]]

“Let Christ, the king of Israel, come down from the cross” (Mark [Col. 0274D] 15:32). O poisoned tongue, utterance of malice, wicked speech! This is not what you said a little before, Caiaphas: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11:50). But that statement, because it was not a lie, you did not speak from yourself; you did not say it of your own accord: “If he is king of Israel, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:42)—this truly is yours, or rather his who was a liar from the beginning.

For what consequence is there in saying that he should come down if he is king, rather than that he should ascend? So you do not remember, ancient serpent, how you departed in confusion of old, when you presumed to say: “Throw yourself down,” and “All these things I will give you if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:6, 9). So, Jew, have you forgotten what you heard: that the Lord reigned from the wood, [Col. 0275A] so that you deny him to be king because he remains upon the wood? But perhaps you did not even hear [variant: read] it, because this proclamation was due not to the Jews but to the nations. “Say among the nations,” he says, “that the Lord has reigned from the wood.”

> [Note: Ps. 95:10. This reading is still found in the Roman or Italian version, as also in our Psalter of Saint-Germain. See Saint Justin’s *Dialogue with Trypho*. [Col. 0275]]

2. Accordingly, the Gentile governor rightly inscribed the title of kingship on the wood; and the Jew could not, as he wished, corrupt the title’s inscription, much less hinder the Lord’s passion and our redemption. “Let him come down,” they say, “if he is king of Israel.” On the contrary: precisely because he is king of Israel, let him not abandon the title of kingship or lay aside the sceptre of empire, for “his dominion is upon his shoulder,” as Isaiah foretells (Isa. 9:6).

The Jews say to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but, ‘He said, I am king of the Jews.’” And Pilate says: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19:19–22). If Pilate stands by what he wrote, will Christ not complete what he began? For he began it, and he will save us. But they say: “He saved others; himself he cannot save” (Matt. 27:42). On the contrary, if he comes down, he will save no one. For since no one can be saved unless he perseveres to the end, how much less can he be the Saviour? He saves [variant: saved] others; for, being salvation, he himself has no need of salvation. He works our salvation and does not permit the saving victim’s evening sacrifice to lack its tail. Wicked one, he knows what you are devising. He will not give you an opportunity to steal from us perseverance, which alone is crowned. [Col. 0275C] He will not silence the tongues of preachers who comfort the fainthearted and say to each one: “Do not leave your place”; which would undoubtedly follow if men could reply that Christ leaves his own.

For human senses and thoughts are inclined to evil. In vain, malicious one, have you prepared your arrows in the quiver and added the Jews’ reproaches to the disciples’ sighs. The latter despair; the former mock. But neither weapon will harm Christ. He chose one time for strengthening his disciples, another for confuting his adversaries.

3. Meanwhile he displays patience more fully, commends humility, fulfils obedience, and perfects love. [Col. 0275D] The four horns of the cross are adorned with these four gems of virtue: love is foremost; obedience is on the right; patience on the left; and humility, the root of virtues, is below in the depth. With these gifts the completion of the Lord’s passion enriched the trophy of the cross: humble in response to the Jews’ blasphemies, patient in response to wounds, wounded within by tongues and outwardly by nails. For love was perfected in him in that he laid down his life for his friends; and obedience was consummated when, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit, becoming obedient unto death.

Those who said, “If he is king of Israel, let him come down from the cross,” strove to despoil the Church of these gifts and deprive her of this glory: so that there might no longer be [Col. 0276A] a model of obedience, an incentive to love, or an example of patience and humility; so that those sweetest words, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, might be blotted out of the Gospel: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13); and, to the Father, “I have completed the work which you gave me to do” (John 17:4); and likewise, to the disciples, “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29); and, “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

For this is what grieves the cunning of the venomous serpent: that the bronze serpent has been raised up in the wilderness, by the sight of which the wounds it inflicted are healed (Num. 21:8). Otherwise, by what other instigator are we to believe Pilate’s wife was sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that just man; for I have suffered much today in a dream because of him” (Matt. 27:19)? The enemy feared even then; but now, above all, feeling himself weakened by the power of the cross, he is led to late repentance. Those whom he incited to crucify, he incites to urge Christ to come down from the cross. Finally, they say: “If he is king of Israel, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him.” This indeed is the serpent’s cunning, this the invention of spiritual wickedness.

The impious one had heard the Saviour’s voice saying, “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24), and knew how great a zeal he seemed to bear for the salvation of that people. Therefore, by most maliciously instructing the tongues of blasphemers, he suggested that they should say: “Let him come down, and we will believe,” as though nothing could now prevent [Col. 0276C] him from coming down, since he so greatly desired their faith.

4. But what is the deceiver contriving, or for whom does he prepare his snares? Surely, for him in whom the enemy will accomplish nothing, and against whom the son of iniquity will add no harm. He is not moved by an empty promise, for he knows all hearts; nor is the meekest of all moved by blasphemous reproach. For the malicious persuasion aimed not at making them believe, but at causing even whatever faith in him we might possess to perish utterly. For when we read, “The works of God are perfect” (Deut. 32:4), how could we confess as God one who had left the work of salvation incomplete?

But let us hear how Christ answers these things through the prophet: “You seek signs, Jew? Wait for me on the day of my resurrection” (Zeph. [Col. 0276D] 3:8). If you wish to believe, I have already shown you greater works. I multiplied signs; yesterday and the day before I performed healings; today I have a greater work to complete. Was it not greater that you saw evil spirits depart from possessed bodies and paralytics leap from their beds than that the nails you drove through my hands and feet should spring loose? But this is a time for suffering, not for acting; and just as you tried in vain to anticipate the hour of my passion, so you will not be able to hinder it.

5. But if the perverse and adulterous generation still seeks a sign, no sign shall be given it except the sign of Jonah the prophet (Matt. 12:39): not the sign of descent, but of resurrection. [Col. 0277A] But if the Jew does not seek it, let the Christian embrace it and rejoice. For the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered. The lion’s cub was raised by the Father’s voice; he came forth from the sealed tomb, who did not come down from the cross.

Whether this is greater, let our enemies be judges, since they had so carefully secured the tomb, sealing the stone with guards. That very great stone, about which those devout women had asked one another, after the Lord’s resurrection had occurred, the angel rolled away and, as Scripture says, sat upon it (Matt. 28:2; Mark 16:3). It is therefore established that the revived body came forth from the sealed tomb—the body which, born through the sealed womb of the Virgin, came forth into life, and entered the disciples’ room through closed doors.

But there was one place from which he did not wish to come forth through closed doors: namely, the prison of Gehenna. For he broke the iron bars and shattered every fastening, so that he might freely lead out his own, whom he had redeemed from the enemy’s hand; and that through open gates there might go forth companies [variant adds: of saints] of those made white, who had washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb—white indeed in blood, because with him and in him there also came forth water which makes white; and he who saw bears witness to it. Or certainly they were white in blood, but in the blood of the young Lamb, milk-white, white and ruddy, as you find in the Song of Songs: “My beloved,” says the bride, “is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands” (Song 5:10). Hence the witness of the resurrection also appears in a white robe and with a shining countenance.

[Col. 0277C] 6. Now, if this alone seems sufficient to refute the Jews’ slanders—that he came forth from the sealed tomb, though in mockery they said, “If he is king of Israel, let him come down from the cross”—for they took greater care to close and seal the tomb than to drive in the nails; if, therefore, the Lion of the tribe of Judah conquered in this very emergence and displayed a greater work than they demanded, to what can the miracle of his resurrection itself be compared?

We do indeed read that certain resurrections—or rather revivifications—preceded it, as its forerunners; yet it is known to surpass them by a twofold privilege. For the others who had risen were to die again; but Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more: death shall no longer have dominion over him. Those others, dead anew, need to be raised again; Christ, in that he died, died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God (Rom. 6:9–10), and lives in eternity. Christ is therefore rightly the first fruits of those rising: he rose so as never again to fall, he who alone attained immortality.

7. There is another respect in which the singular glory of this resurrection becomes known. For who, among all the rest, ever raised himself? It is ineffable that he who sleeps should himself awaken from death; it is unique: “there is none that does it, no, not one.” The prophet Elisha raised a dead man (4 Kings 4:35), but another, not himself. For behold, after how many years he lies in the tomb, unable of himself [Col. 0278A] to do anything, hoping to be raised by another—namely, by him who triumphed over death’s dominion in himself. Hence we say that the others were raised, but that Christ rose again: he alone came forth from the sepulchre victorious by his own power. For in this also the Lion of the tribe of Judah conquered. How great must be his power—or rather, what will not seem possible to him—living and saying to the Father: “I have risen, and I am still with thee” (Ps. 138:18); he who was so mighty, though “reckoned among the dead,” yet “free among the dead”?

8. Nor did he delay the resurrection beyond the third day, that he might be shown a faithful prophet who said: “After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. 6:3). It is fitting, surely, that as the head has gone before, so the members should follow. On the sixth day he redeemed humankind upon the cross, on the very day on which he had made humankind [Col. 0278B] in the beginning. On the following day he kept sabbath in the tomb, having completed the work he had undertaken. But on the third day—which is the first of days—he appeared as the firstfruits of those who sleep, the conqueror of death, the new man.

So too let us, all who follow our Head, throughout this day on which we were fashioned and redeemed, never cease to do penance; never cease to take up our cross, persevering upon it as he persevered, until the Spirit bids us rest from our labours. Let us listen to no one, brothers—not to flesh and blood, nor to any spirit whatsoever urging us to come down from the cross. Let us remain on the cross; let us die on the cross; let us be taken down by the hands of others, not through our own fickleness. Righteous men took down our Head; but may holy angels, by his gracious favour, take us down, [Col. 0278C] so that, having manfully completed the day of the cross, we may rest sweetly on the second day, which comes after death; may sleep happily in our tombs, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God, who will raise our bodies at last on the third day, conformed to the body of his glory. Those who have been dead four days stink, as is written of Lazarus: “Lord, by this time he stinketh, for he hath been dead four days” (John 11:39).

9. The invention of Adam’s children fashioned a fourth day, which they did not receive from the Lord. Therefore they were corrupted and made abominable, like beasts that have rotted in their own dung. For the three-day order which we have described belongs to divine ordinance: labour, rest, resurrection. These things do not please the children of men; rather, they prefer their own day, [Col. 0278D] postponing repentance in order to indulge pleasure. This is not the day which the Lord has made: they have become four-day dead, and already stink.

That which was born of Mary, the Holy One, did not know this fourth day: he rose on the third day, lest he should see corruption. Thus the Lion of the tribe of Judah conquered. The Lamb was slain, but the Lion conquered. “The lion will roar: who will not fear?” The Lion, I say—the strongest of beasts, who will fear no encounter whatsoever—namely, the Lion of the tribe of Judah. Let those fear who denied him, who said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). Let those fear who said: “We will not have this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14). For he returns after receiving the kingdom, and will miserably destroy the wicked. Do you wish to know that he returns after receiving the kingdom? “All power,” he says, [Col. 0279A] “is given unto me in heaven and in earth” (Matt. 28:18). And the Father likewise says in the Psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance, and the ends of the earth for thy possession. Thou shalt rule them with a rod of iron, and shalt break them in pieces like a potter’s vessel” (Ps. 2:8–9). For he is a mighty Lion, not a cruel one; yet his indignation is weighty, and the wrath of the Dove unbearable. But the Lion will roar for his own, not against his own. Let strangers fear; let the tribe of Judah rather rejoice.

10. Let those rejoice who are hardened by confession, whose every bone says: “Lord, who is like unto thee?” (Ps. 34:10). The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David. For David is said to mean “desirable in appearance” or “strong in hand”; and he himself says: “All my desire is before thee” (Ps. 37:10), and: “I will keep my strength unto thee” (Ps. 58:10). [Col. 0279B] “The root,” he says, “of David.” David is not his root; rather, he is David’s root, because he bears and is not borne. Rightly, holy David, you call your son your Lord, because you do not bear the root, but the root bears you: the root of your strength and of your desire, the desirable root, the strong root.

“The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, to open the book and loose its seven seals.” These are words of the Apocalypse. Let those learn who have not read it; let those recall it who know it. John says: “I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book sealed with seven seals, and there was none who could read or open it. And I,” he says, “wept greatly because no one was found worthy to open the book. And one of the elders said to me: ‘Do not weep; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered.’ And I saw, and behold, in the midst [Col. 0279C] of the throne a Lamb standing, as though slain; and, coming, he took the book from the right hand of him who sat upon the throne, and opened the book.” Then great joy and thanksgiving came about.

John had heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb. The Lamb was slain; the Lamb received the book; the Lamb opened it—and the Lion appeared. Finally, the elders say: “Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power” (Rev. 5:12): not to lose meekness, but to receive strength, so that he may remain a Lamb and yet be a Lion. I say more: it seems to me that he himself is also the book that could not be opened. For who could be found worthy to open this book? John the Baptist himself declares that he is unworthy—he than whom none greater has arisen among those born of women: “I am not worthy,” he says, “to loose the strap of his sandal” (Mark 1:7). For shod Majesty had come [Col. 0279D] to us, divinity incarnate; the Wisdom of God had come, but in a book closed and sealed. What the strap of the sandal bound, the seals of the book enclosed.

11. But what are we to say concerning these seven? Perhaps the threefold power of the soul—reason, memory, and will—and the fourfold composition of the body, namely from the four elements, are to be understood in these seven, so that we may know that nothing belonging to the truth of humanity was lacking in the Saviour? Or rather, is his humanity itself the book, and must the seven seals be sought? For I think that seven things may be found by which the presence of Majesty was especially concealed in the flesh, so that the book could not be opened and the Wisdom hidden within it recognized.

[Col. 0280A] The first things that occur are these: the betrothal of his Mother, by which the virgin’s childbirth and the purity of her conception were veiled, so that the Maker of humankind was thought to be the son of a human craftsman. Then also bodily weakness: in that he wept and cried, nursed and slept, and was subject to the other necessities of the flesh, the power of divinity lay hidden among these things. So too, receiving the sign of circumcision—the remedy for sin, the medicine for sickness—he who had come to remove every sickness and sin. Likewise, fleeing into Egypt from the face of petty King Herod, he could not be recognized either as the Son of God or as the King of heaven.

What of that threefold temptation by the enemy—in the wilderness, upon the pinnacle, above the mountain? “If thou art the Son of God,” he says, “command that these stones become bread”; and again: “Cast thyself down.” Christ did neither, so that the book might remain sealed and the crafty one be deceived. [Col. 0280B] Finally, he was deceived so completely that he now held it certain that Christ was a mere human being, and blind pride broke forth into such madness that he no longer said, “If thou art the Son of God,” but: “All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:3–9).

The sixth seal is that of the cross, where the Lord of Majesty hung between thieves and was reckoned with the wicked. Burial also closed this book; and no seal at all so bound it, so concealed the great mystery of godliness. For when the Lord had been buried, despair alone seemed to remain, so much so that the disciples themselves said: “But we had hoped” (Luke 24:21). Who would not at that time have wept that the book was more tightly shut, and that there was none to open it?

12. But weep no longer, holy John; neither do you weep, Mary. Let mourning be far away; let the cloud of sorrow be scattered. “Rejoice in the Lord, and exult, ye righteous; and glory, all ye upright in heart” (Ps. 31:11). Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, the Lion who rose again; finally, the book itself is worthy to open itself. For in rising from the dead, [Col. 0280C] rising by his own power, after three days as he himself foretold, with his enemies bearing witness; and rising in such majesty and glory, he plainly shows that all the seals or coverings we have mentioned were voluntary, not necessary—not matters of condition, but of gracious condescension.

Why, Jew, did you recently seal the stone of the tomb? Because “that deceiver” had said while still alive: “After three days I will rise again” (Matt. [Col. 0280D] 27:63). Truly a deceiver, but benevolent, not malicious. Indeed, your prophet says in your person: “Thou hast deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived; thou wast stronger than I, and hast prevailed” (Jer. 20:7). He deceived you, O Jews, in the Passion; for in the resurrection he prevailed and triumphed, the Lion of the tribe of Judah conquering. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

What, then, will you do? He foretold it, and now he has returned to life. Examine carefully the seal of the burial: it has been opened. The sign of the prophet Jonah is given you, because he himself also foretold it. Jonah comes out of the belly of the whale; Christ comes forth from the heart of the earth on the third day. Except that here is manifestly more than Jonah (Matt. 12:39–41), for he courageously brought himself out even from the very womb of death. Therefore the men of Nineveh [Col. 0281A] will rise against you in judgment; therefore they will be your judges, because they obeyed the prophet, while you obey neither the Lord of the prophets.

13. Where is what you said: “Let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 27:42)? You wanted the seal of the cross to be broken, promising that you would enter into faith. Behold, it has been opened, not broken: enter. Otherwise, if you do not believe him risen, surely you would not have believed him descending. If Christ’s cross so scandalized you—for, as the Apostle says, “the word of the cross is a stumbling-block to the Jews” (1 Cor. 1:23)—let at least the newness of the resurrection stir you.

We find glory in the cross. For us who are being saved, it is God’s power and, as we have shown, the fullness of every virtue. Let there be for you at least a share in the resurrection. Yet perhaps even that—indeed, [Col. 0281B] far more than that—scandalizes you, and what is for us “an odour of life unto life” is for you “an odour of death unto death.” Why then do we persist? The elder brother cannot bear to hear the music and the dancing; he is indignant that the fatted calf has been killed for us. He stands outside and wholly refuses to enter (Luke 15:28). Let us enter, brothers, and feast on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth; for “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7). Let us embrace the virtues commended to us on the cross: humility, patience, obedience, and charity.

14. Let us carefully consider what is commended to us in this most eminent solemnity. Surely: resurrection, passage, and migration. For Christ, brothers, did not fall back today, but rose again; [Col. 0281C] he did not return, but passed over; he migrated, he did not come back. Indeed, the very Pascha which we celebrate is interpreted as “passage,” not “return”; and Galilee, where he who rose again promises to be seen by us, does not signify return but migration. I believe that some minds are already flying ahead and suspect the direction in which these observations tend. Yet let us speak briefly, especially lest the length of the discourse should seem to burden your devotion amid so great a solemnity.

If, after completing the cross, Christ the Lord had returned to this our mortality and to the miseries of the present life, I would not say, brothers, that he had passed over, but that he had returned; not that he had migrated to something higher, but that he had gone back to his former state. [Col. 0281D] But now, because he passed over into newness of life, he invites us also to passage and calls us into Galilee. Therefore, “in that he died, he died to sin once”; because now that he lives, he lives not to the flesh but to God.

15. What are we to say of ourselves, who deprive the Lord’s holy resurrection of the name Pascha, making it for us a return rather than a passage? During these days we have mourned, giving ourselves to compunction and prayer, seriousness and abstinence, desiring to redeem and wash away by this sacred forty-day period the negligences of other times. We have shared Christ’s sufferings; through a kind of baptism of tears, repentance, and confession, we have again been planted together with him. If, then, we have died to sin, how shall we still live [Col. 0282A] in it? If we have lamented our negligences, what reason is there for us now to relapse into the same things? Shall we now again be curious as before, talkative as before, slothful and negligent as before, vain, suspicious, detracting, angry, and entangled in the other vices which we have so anxiously bewailed during these days? “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them again? I have put off my garment; how shall I put it on?” (Song 5:3). This is not migration, brothers; Christ will not thus be seen, nor is this the way by which God will show us his salvation. For “he who looks back is not fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

16. Thus lovers of the world, enemies of Christ’s cross—who are called Christians because they have received his name in vain—throughout this whole forty-day season eagerly long for the approaching days of the Resurrection, alas, so that they may indulge pleasure more freely. A sadder subject darkens, brothers, the joy of the solemnity; but we lament an affront to the solemnity itself, which we cannot pass over even during it—indeed, least of all during it. Alas for sorrow! The resurrection of the Saviour has become a time for sinning, an end-point for relapsing! From this time feasts and drunkenness return, beds and acts of uncleanness are sought again, and the reins are loosed for desires—as though Christ had risen for this purpose and not rather for our justification.

Is this how you honour, wretches, the Christ whom you have received? You prepared lodging for one who was coming, confessing sins with groaning, chastising your bodies, and giving alms; and behold, once received, you betray him to his enemies—or rather, compel him to depart—by admitting your former wickednesses. [Col. 0282C] For there can be no dwelling together of light with darkness, of Christ with pride, avarice, ambition, brotherly hatred, lust, or fornication. What is owed less to one who is present than to one who is coming? What does the time of resurrection demand less of reverence than the time of the Passion? But you evidently honour neither. For if you suffered with him, you would reign with him; if you died with him, you would rise with him.

17. But now that humiliation proceeded merely from seasonal custom and a kind of pretence; spiritual exultation does not follow it. For this reason, as the Apostle says, “many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep” (1 Cor. 11:30). For this reason there is frequent mortality among people in different regions, especially during these days. What is this? You have been caught in straits as transgressors—not those who have transgressed, but those who persist in sin, adding transgression to transgression; either wholly unrepentant or lukewarm in repentance, and not fleeing dangerous [variant: “dangers”] incentives to sin even after wretched experience. The enemy has ensnared you in “the twisted sinews of his testicles,” as Scripture says (Job 40:12).

If with this conscience you avoid Christ’s sacraments, you have nothing in common with Christ; you do not have life in yourselves. Hear him himself saying: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). If you receive unworthily, you eat judgment upon yourselves, not discerning the holy body of the Lord. [Col. 0283A] Therefore return to your heart, transgressors, and seek the Lord with your whole heart; hate evil; repent not merely in word and tongue, but in spirit and truth. For it seems that a person is not sufficiently sorry to have fallen if he still intends to remain on slippery ground; nor sufficiently sorry to have gone astray if he does not seek a guide. Let flight from opportunity, the removal of occasion, be an indication of true compunction. Otherwise there is grave cause to fear lest this day—which itself has been set for the fall and resurrection of many—reject you, either as persons manifestly alien to Christ, not communicating with Christ, or as companions of Judas, into whom Satan entered after the morsel (John 13:27).

18. But what is it to us, brothers, to judge those who are outside? Except that we lament having been in the same snare, rejoice that we have been delivered from it through mercy alone, and, in brotherly charity, grieve that they are miserably held fast in the same thing. Would that we ourselves might now be found sanctified and wholly alien to this wretched and sacrilegious custom, and that nothing in us might perish [Col. 0283B] or be diminished from our spiritual exercise at the coming of the sacred resurrection, but that we might rather strive to pass onward and to increase!
