[Col. 0284A] For whoever, after the mourning of repentance, does not return to carnal consolations, but advances into confidence in divine mercy, enters into a certain new devotion and joy in the Holy Spirit; and is less pierced by the remembrance of past sins than delighted by the memory and inflamed by the desire of eternal rewards—such a person plainly rises with Christ, celebrates Pascha, and hastens into Galilee. Therefore, dearest brethren, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth (Col. 3:1–2), so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, you too may walk in newness of life (Rom. 6:4); so that you may rejoice to pass from worldly joy and the consolation of the world, through compunction [Col. 0284B] and godly sorrow, into holy devotion and spiritual exultation, by the help of him who passed from this world to the Father and deigns to draw us also after himself and call us into Galilee, that he may show himself to us—he who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0283]

## AT THE TIME OF THE RESURRECTION, TO THE ABBOTS

### SERMON II

[Note: [Col. 0283D] Thus we have restored from the manuscripts and the early printed editions the old order of the Paschal sermons, omitting here Sermon 44, *On Various Subjects*, which was formerly known to have been placed after the following third sermon [Col. 0284D]. Compare Sermon 58, *On Various Subjects*.]

On the Gospel reading, “Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome,” etc. (Mark 16:1).

[Col. 0283C]

1. We have received from the Apostle that Christ dwells through faith in our hearts (Eph. 3:17). Hence it seems not unfitting to understand that Christ lives in us so long as faith lives. But after our faith has died, Christ in some sense has died in us. The works, moreover, bear witness to the life of faith, as it is written: “The works which the Father has given me, they themselves bear witness concerning me” (John 5:36). Nor does he seem to differ from this judgment who declares faith without works to be dead in itself (Jas. 2:20). For just as we recognize the life of this body from its movement, so we recognize the life of faith from good works.

[Col. 0283D] Thus the life of the body is the soul, by which it moves and senses; but the life of faith is charity, because faith acts through charity, as you read in the Apostle: “Faith which works through love” (Gal. 5:6). Accordingly, when charity grows cold, faith dies, as the body does when the soul departs. Therefore, if you see someone vigorous in good works and cheerful in the ardour of religious life, do not doubt that faith lives in that person, holding unquestionable proofs of that life. But there are some who, though they began in the Spirit, alas, are afterward perfected in the flesh. We know that then the Spirit of life no longer remains in them, because it is written: “My Spirit shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh” (Gen. 6:3). And if the Spirit does not remain, then charity undoubtedly falls away, which indeed has been [Col. 0284C] poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit given to us (Rom. 5:5).

2. Now he who stated that faith works through love placed the life of faith, as we have said, in charity. Thus it follows that, when the Spirit departs, faith dies, because “it is the Spirit that gives life” (John 6:64). Finally, if “to have the mind set on the flesh is death” (Rom. 8:6), there is no doubt that those whom we rejoiced to see alive, so long as they put to death the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, must be mourned as dead when they live according to the flesh. Hence you also read in the same Apostle: “If you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you shall live” (ibid., v. 13). Woe to you, whoever you are, dog returned to its vomit and washed sow to wallowing in the mire (2 Pet. [Col. 0284D] 2:22)! I speak not only to those who return to Egypt in body, but also to those who return there in heart, pursuing the delights of this world and consequently lacking the life of faith, which is charity. For “if anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15). Who is more dead than the person who warms fire in his bosom, sin in his conscience, and neither feels it, fears it, nor shakes it off?

3. Behold then: Christ is in the tomb; faith is dead in the soul. What shall we do for it? What did the holy women do, who alone among all his followers were held by a fuller affection? They bought spices, that, coming, they might anoint Jesus. Was it in order to raise him? We too know, brothers, that raising is not ours to do, but anointing is our charge. Why this? Surely, lest one of this sort should stink [Col. 0285A] and become for others an odour of death; lest he decay and wholly dissolve. Therefore let the three women—the mind, tongue, and hand—buy their spices. For, I think, it is concerning these that Peter received the threefold command to feed the Lord’s flock (John 21:17). “Feed,” he says, “with mind, feed with mouth, feed with work; feed by the prayer of the soul, the exhortation of speech, the display of example.”

4. Let my mind, then, seek its spices: first of all, an affection of compassion; next, zeal for uprightness; and amid these, let it not omit the spirit of discernment. For whenever you see a brother sinning, the affection of compassion ought at once to go forth, as something akin to humanity, since you conceive it from yourself. “You who are spiritual,” says the Apostle, “instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering [Col. 0285B] yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1). And when the Lord went out carrying his cross and they wept over him—not yet, indeed, all the tribes of the earth, but a few women—he turned to them and said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children” (Luke 23:28). Attend carefully to the order: “Over yourselves,” he says, first; then, “over your children.” Attend to yourself, that you may know how to have compassion on another, and may rebuke in a spirit of gentleness. Consider yourself, lest you too be tempted.

But because example persuades more effectively and impresses itself more deeply upon the mind, I send you to that holy old man who, when he heard that one of the brothers had sinned, wept most bitterly, saying: “He today, and I tomorrow” (*Lives of the Fathers*). Do you think that he who so wept over himself did not have compassion on his brother? This affection of compassion, therefore, benefits many, because a generous spirit is ashamed to distress one whom it sees anxious on his behalf.

5. But what are we to do when some are so stiff-necked and their brow so hardened that the more we have compassion on them, the more they abuse both our compassion and our patience? Must we not, just as we have compassion on a brother, also have compassion on justice itself, which we see so shamelessly rejected and so rashly provoked? I know that, if there is any charity in us, we cannot bear this contempt of God with equanimity. This is zeal for justice, by which we are inflamed against offenders, as though led by devotion toward that justice of God which we see despised. Yet the affection of compassion ought to claim precedence for itself. Otherwise, in a violent spirit, we smash the ships of Tarshish, crush the bruised reed, and quench the smoking flax.

6. But when both are present, namely the affection of compassion and zeal for justice, the spirit of discernment must also be present, lest perhaps, when the one should be displayed, the other go forth, and indiscretion itself throw everything into confusion. Let our mind therefore possess this third thing, the spirit of discernment, so that, fitting times to times, it may know how opportunely both to be zealous and nevertheless to forgive. Let it be a Samaritan, guarding and observing when to apply the oil of mercy and when the wine of fervour. And lest you think this my own invention, hear the prophet asking for these very things, and in the same order, in the Psalm: “Teach me goodness, and discipline, and knowledge” (Ps. 118:66).

7. But where are these things to come from for us? The soil of our heart produces no such shoots of virtue; rather, it produces thorns and briars for us. We must therefore buy them. But from whom are they to be bought? Surely from him who says: “Come, buy without money and without any exchange, wine and milk” (Isa. 55:1). You know what the sweetness of milk and the severity of wine signify. But what is it to buy without money and without exchange? Purchase is not such among lovers of this world; but with the Creator of the world it cannot be otherwise. For the prophet said to the Lord: “Thou art my God, for thou hast no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2). What exchange, then, can a human being give him [Col. 0286B] for his grace, he who needs nothing and to whom all things belong? Grace is given freely; even when it is bought, it is bought freely, because what is given for it is retained to our greater good.

8. Therefore the three spices of the mind are to be bought with the coin of one’s own will. In abandoning it, we lose nothing; indeed, we gain very much, exchanging it for something better, so that what was private becomes common. Now a common will is charity. Therefore we buy without exchange, receiving what we had not and retaining in a better way what we had. When will someone have compassion on a brother who, in his own will, knows how to have compassion only on himself? Or when will one who loves himself love justice and hate iniquity? He can indeed pretend before people’s eyes, and even deceive himself, so that when he is driven by private love or hatred, he may suppose it to be an affection of compassion or zeal for justice. Yet it is easy to recognize how foreign to self-will are those things that belong to charity, against which self-will sets itself in open opposition. For charity is kind; charity does not rejoice in iniquity (1 Cor. 13:4, 6). And we already know concerning the spirit of discernment that nothing so extinguishes it as self-will, which overturns human hearts and closes the eyes of reason. Therefore the three spices of the mind must be bought, as stated, with the coin of self-will: the affection of compassion, zeal for uprightness, and the spirit of discernment.

9. Likewise, the tongue has three spices: moderation in rebuking, abundance in exhorting, and effectiveness in persuading. Do you wish to possess these spices? Buy them from the Lord your God. Buy them, I say, and, as with the former spices, without any exchange: so that you receive something yet lose nothing. Buy from the Lord measured correction, for it is altogether a great good and an excellent gift, and few possess it. For, as blessed James says, no one can tame the tongue (Jas. 3:8). You may see many who approach with sincere intention and kindly disposition, yet say lightly what is heard gravely. “The irrevocable word flies forth” (Horace, *Epistles* 1.18.71); and what ought to have healed, because it seems perhaps too biting, instead irritates and wounds more deeply. When impudence is added to negligence, impatience too accumulates, so that one who was in filth becomes filthier still, turning aside into evil words to make excuses for sins, and, like a madman, not only repelling but even attempting to bite the physician’s hand.

Many also lack abundance of speech, and through poverty of expression feel their tongue cleave to their palate; and this too can sometimes harm hearers considerably. Others, however, have abundant speech readily at hand, but what they say has little savour and little acceptance; and because they lack grace, their words are less effective. You see, then, how necessary it is to buy from him from whom every good thing comes, from whom all knowledge comes, moderation in rebuking, abundance in exhorting, and effectiveness in persuading.

10. Therefore buy these with the coin of confession, so that you confess your own sins before undertaking to cleanse those of others. The raising of a soul is indeed a great and wondrous mystery: see that you do not approach it unclean. But if perhaps you cannot be innocent—indeed, because you cannot—wash your hands among the innocent before you surround the Lord’s tomb. For all things are washed in confession. And this washing will be reckoned to you as a kind of innocence, so that you may stand among the innocent. No one approaches the service of the altar in ordinary clothing; whoever is to approach is clothed in white. Therefore, when you hasten to the Lord’s tomb, wash, make yourself white, clothe yourself in garments of glory, that it may be said to you: “Thou hast put on confession and beauty” (Ps. 103:1). For where there is confession, there is beauty in the sight of the Lord. [Col. 0287C] These things have been said for this reason: that the spices of the tongue—measured rebuke, copious exhortation, effective persuasion—may be bought with the coin of confession.

11. Nevertheless, we read (in Gregory the Great’s *Pastoral Rule*), and have also learned from daily experience, that where a person’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is held in contempt. Therefore let the hand also prepare its spices, lest the Wise Man mock us as that sluggard for whom it is labour to bring his hand to his mouth (Prov. 19:24); lest the person whom you rebuke be able to say: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself?” (Rom. 2:21). For you bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders, unwilling to move them with your finger (Matt. 23:4).

I tell you: a living and effective word is the example of a deed, readily persuading us of what we intend, because it proves that what we urge is practicable. For this purpose, the hand too must have its spices: continence in relation to the flesh, mercy toward one’s brother, patience in godliness. Thus the Apostle says: “Let us live soberly, justly, and godly” (Titus 2:12). These three are especially necessary to our way of life, because the first we owe to ourselves, the second to our neighbour, and the third to God. For the fornicator sins against his own body, depriving it of great honour, enslaving it to shameful gratification and disgrace; taking a member of Christ and making it a member of a prostitute. But I say that we should abstain not only from her who is so abominable, but from every pleasure of the flesh. First of all, then, seek this perfect continence [Col. 0288A] which you owe to yourself, for no one is nearer to you. Then add the mercy which you owe to your neighbour, because you are to be saved with him. Then also add the patience which you owe to God, because you are to be saved by him. For “all who wish to live godly in Christ shall suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12); and “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14:21). Take care, then, lest you perish through impatience; instead, endure everything for him who first endured greater things for you, and with whom patience will not be fruitless, as the prophet says: “The patience of the poor shall not perish for ever” (Ps. 9:19).

12. Now these spices of the hand are bought with the coin of submission. For submission directs our steps and merits the grace of holy conduct. If a contrary law has been found in our members through disobedience, who does not know that continence is given through obedience? Submission also knows how to order mercy; it both teaches and gives patience. With these spices, therefore, approach one in whom faith is dead.

Yet if we consider how great a thing it is for us to raise such a person, and how difficult it is even to approach his heart, which a certain stony obstinacy and shamelessness have closed, I think that we too must say: “Who will roll away for us the stone from the door of the tomb?” But while we tremble thus and fear to approach, hesitating before so great a miracle, it sometimes happens that, in his customary mercy, the divine ear hears the preparation of our heart; and at the voice of his power, the one who was dead rises. And behold, the angel of the Lord—a certain cheerfulness in that person’s countenance—appears to us as if at the tomb’s entrance; and a radiance, an indication of resurrection, so that his face is plainly seen to have changed, granting us access to his heart—indeed, even inviting us in. He rolls away the very stone of his obstinacy and sits upon it, [Col. 0288C] so that, with faith raised, he himself also displays the grave-clothes in which it had been wrapped. And as he lays open all that formerly went on in his heart and confesses how he had buried himself within, revealing his very lukewarmness and negligence, he says: “Come and see the place where the Lord was laid” (Matt. 28:6).

### SERMON III

On Naaman’s sevenfold immersion in the Jordan and the cleansing of sevenfold leprosy; and on the seven appearances of the risen Lord, by which the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified.

[Col. 0288D]

1. Just as, in treating bodies, purgations are applied first and restoratives afterwards—so that the body may first 903 be emptied of harmful humours and then strengthened by healthier food—so Christ the Lord, physician of souls, whose entire dispensation which he fulfilled in the flesh is medicine for salvation, gave seven purifications before his Passion and, after his Resurrection, an equal number of wholesome and delightful foods.

Our Elisha commanded the leprous Naaman to immerse himself seven times in the Jordan (4 Kings [2 Kings] 5:10), which is interpreted as “descent.” For in the descent of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, in the humility of his manner of life [Col. 0289A], which he displayed before the Passion—we are cleansed and purified; but in the Resurrection and the life which he manifested for forty days, we are refreshed and fed with delightful nourishment.

For the leprosy of pride has seized us sevenfold: in possessiveness concerning property, in the glory of clothing, in bodily pleasure, twice in the mouth, and likewise in the heart. The first is the leprosy of the house, by which we wish to be rich in this age. But we are cleansed from it if we are immersed in the Jordan, that is, in Christ’s descent. For we find that, though he was rich, he became poor for our sake. He descended from the inexpressible riches of heaven; and, coming into the world, he did not even wish to possess such modest riches as these, but came in such poverty that, when born, he was immediately laid in a manger, because there was no room for him in the inn [Col. 0289B] (Luke 2:7). Finally, who does not know that the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head? Whoever is well immersed here—when will he seek the riches of this world? It is indeed a great, an utterly great perversity, that a worthless little worm should wish to be rich, for whose sake the God of majesty and Lord of Sabaoth chose to become poor.

2. Further, understand by the leprosy of clothing all the ostentatious vanity of this age. For you will likewise be cleansed from it in immersion in the Jordan, where you find the Christ of the Lord wrapped in poor rags, made the reproach of men and the outcast of the people. We are also cleansed of bodily leprosy in that same Jordan if, properly considering the Lord’s Passion, we blush to follow bodily pleasure.

But in the mouth, as we said, [Col. 0289C] there is a double leprosy. When some adversity occurs, we murmur, and a word of impatience flows out like the discharge of leprosy. But we are cleansed from this if we attend to him who was led as a sheep to slaughter and did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7), who, when reviled, did not revile in return; when suffering, did not threaten (1 Peter 2:23).

In prosperity, too, contrary to him who said, “It is not the one who commends himself who is approved” (2 Corinthians 10:18), we commend ourselves—not in much patience, but in arrogance—and the other leprosy, the word of boasting, defiles us. Therefore, that we may be cleansed from it, let us immerse ourselves in the Jordan and imitate him who did not seek his own glory. Hence he commanded the demons, who cried out [Col. 0289D] that he was the Son of God, to be silent (Luke 4:34–35); and he forbade the blind men whom he had enlightened to speak of it (Matthew 9:30).

3. In the heart there is a double leprosy: one’s own will and one’s own counsel. Both leprosies are exceedingly bad, and the more destructive because more inward. By one’s own will I mean a will not shared with God and human beings, but merely our own: when what we will, we do not for God’s honour or our brothers’ benefit, but for ourselves; when we aim not to please God and benefit our brothers, but to satisfy the movements of our own minds. Opposed to this is charity, upright of countenance, which is God. For this will wages enmity against God and a most cruel war. What does God hate or punish [Col. 0290A] except one’s own will? Let one’s own will cease, and hell will not exist. Against what, indeed, does that fire rage except one’s own will? Even now, when we suffer cold, hunger, or something of that kind, what is injured except one’s own will? But if we endure it willingly, the will itself has now become shared; yet a certain weakness, as it were an itch of the will, still belongs to what is one’s own, and in that we suffer every punishment until it is entirely consumed. For that is properly called one’s own will to which we assent and toward which free choice inclines itself.

904 But those desires and lusts which hold us against our will are not will but corruption of the will. Let the servants of their own will hear and fear with what frenzy it attacks the Lord of majesty. First, indeed, it withdraws and removes itself from the dominion of him whom it ought by right to serve as its author, when it becomes its own. But will it be content with this injury? By no means. It goes further and, so far as lies within it, takes away and plunders [Col. 0290B] everything that belongs to God. For what limit does human greed set for itself? Would not one who acquires a little money through usury likewise endeavour to gain the entire world, if possibility were not lacking and the means available to his will? I say confidently: the entire world could not suffice for anyone who remains in his own will. Yet would that it were content even with these things, so that it might not rage against the Author himself—horrible to say! But now one’s own will, so far as lies within it, even kills God himself. For it would wholly wish God either to be unable [Col. 0290C] to punish its sins, or unwilling to do so, or ignorant of them. It therefore wishes him not to be God, since, so far as lies within it, it wishes him to be either powerless, unjust, or unwise. This is plainly a cruel and altogether accursed wickedness, which desires God’s power, justice, and wisdom to perish. This is the cruel beast, the most savage wild creature, the most rapacious she-wolf, and the fiercest lioness. This is the most unclean leprosy of the soul, for which one must be immersed in the Jordan and imitate him who did not come to do his own will; hence, in the Passion, he says: “Not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 22:42).

4. But the leprosy of one’s own counsel is more destructive inasmuch as it is more hidden; and the more it abounds, the healthier each person appears to himself. It belongs to those [Col. 0290D] who have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, following their own error and obstinate in it, so that they are unwilling to yield to any counsel. These are dividers of unity, enemies of peace, strangers to charity, swollen with vanity, self-pleasing and great in their own eyes, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own. And what pride is greater than that one person should prefer his own judgment to that of the whole congregation, as if he alone possessed the Spirit of God? It is the crime of idolatry not to submit, and the sin of divination to resist (1 Samuel 15:23). Let those now go, who make themselves more religious than others, who are not like the rest of humankind. Behold, they have become diviners and idolaters—if, at least, they judge that greater credence is to be given even to him who said this than to themselves.

Nor does the saying of Truth disagree with this: “If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector” (Matthew 18:17). But where can this leprosy be cleansed except in the Jordan? Immerse yourself there, whoever you are of this sort, and attend to what the angel of great counsel did: how he set aside his own counsel in favour of the counsel—or rather, the will—of a single woman, the blessed Virgin, and of a poor craftsman, Joseph. For, when he was found in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them, he was in some sense rebuked by his mother: “Son, why have you done this to us?” But he said: “Why was it that you sought me? Did you not know that I must be occupied with my Father’s affairs?” But they did not understand the word. And what did the Word do? He did not remain contained within himself: he descended, so that he was even subject to them (Luke 2:46–51). Who now will not blush [Col. 0291B] to be obstinate in his own counsel, when Wisdom itself abandoned its own? He so changed his counsel that what he had then already begun, from that time until the thirtieth year of his age he wholly set aside. For from his twelfth year until the age of thirty you find nothing concerning his teaching or deeds.

5. But perhaps we should ask him himself how he abandoned his will or counsel. O Lord, the will of which you said that it should not be done—if it was not good, how was it yours? If it was good, why was it abandoned? Likewise, if the counsel was not good, how was it yours? If it was good, how was it to be relinquished? Both were good, and both were his; yet they were nevertheless to be relinquished, precisely so that better things might be done. For what is private ought not to take precedence over what is shared. 905 [Col. 0291C]

Therefore Christ’s will was good when he said, “If it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). But the will of which he said, “May your will be done” (Luke 22:42), was better, because it was shared not only by the Father but also by Christ himself—for he was offered because he himself willed it—and by us. For unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground had died, it would have remained alone; but dying, it brought forth much fruit. And this was the Father’s will: that he might have those whom he could adopt as sons; Christ’s will: that he himself might be firstborn among many brothers; and our will: because he acted for us, that we might be redeemed.

We say the same about counsel. For that counsel of Christ was his and was good, when he said, “I must be occupied with my Father’s affairs.” But because they did not [Col. 0291D] understand, he changed that counsel so as to cleanse us [Col. 0292A] from the leprosy that is one’s own counsel. For he gave us an example, that we too might do likewise. From the beginning, indeed, he knew what he was going to do; but he wished to display to us the pattern of this humility and to prepare in himself a divine Jordan for washing away this most pernicious leprosy. Therefore let both alike hear—those defiled by the leprosy of their own will and those defiled by that of their own counsel—let them hear what the Spirit says to the churches, condemning both leprosies in one brief verse: “The wisdom that is from above,” he says, “is first pure,” against the impurity of one’s own will; “then peaceable” (James 3:17), against the obstinate rebellion of one’s own counsel.

6. When the sick person has been cleansed of these seven things, let him, as it were, seek seven dishes after seven cells: [Col. 0292B] the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. And just as we find seven purifications in the Lord’s life before his Passion, so in the seven appearances which are read as having occurred after the Resurrection we may find those seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

In the first, receive the spirit of fear: when the holy women came, an angel descended from heaven, and there was an earthquake, so that they, terrified by fear, had to be comforted by the angel (Matthew 28:2–10). In the spirit of piety he appeared to Simon (Luke 24:34), because it was altogether a great and truly Lord-Jesus-worthy condescension of piety that he deigned to appear, as it were specially and before the others, to him whose guilty conscience was more confounded than the rest by his denial of him, so that where the offence abounded, grace might superabound.

In the spirit of knowledge [Col. 0292C] he expounded the Scriptures to the two travelling to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and the prophets (ibid., v. 27). In the spirit of fortitude he entered through closed doors, showing his hands and side (John 20:19–20), just as holes in shields are customarily displayed as a sign of bravery. In the spirit of counsel he advised those labouring fruitlessly at fishing to cast the net on the right side (John 21:6). In the spirit of understanding he opened their minds so that they understood the Scriptures (Luke 24:45). In the spirit of wisdom he appeared to them on the fortieth day, when, as they watched, he was lifted up (Acts 1:9), and they saw the Son of Man ascending where he had been before. For until that day he was, as it were, saving believers through the foolishness of preaching; but after he ascended before them to the Father, wisdom began to be made manifest.

[Col. 0291]

## ON THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

### SERMON I. On faith that conquers, and the three testimonies in heaven and on earth. (1 John 5:4–11)

1. “Everything that is born of God conquers the world.” After the Only-begotten of God did not consider equality with God something to be seized, and yet deigned also to become the Son of man, being found in outward appearance as a man, human lowliness may rightly now presume upon heavenly birth. For it is not unworthy of God to become the father of those whose brother Christ made himself. This is why blessed John—who more frequently and more earnestly commends to us this adoption as children of God—says even at the beginning of his Gospel: “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12). Similar, therefore, is the word that we heard today recited from [Col. 0292D] his Epistle: “Everything that is born of God conquers the world.” For all who belong to Christ are hated by the world together with Christ; but together with Christ the world is also conquered [Col. 0293A] by them. [Col. 0293B] “Do not wonder,” he says, “if the world hates you; know that it hated me before you” (John 15:18). And again: “Take courage, for I have conquered the world” (John 16:33). Thus the truth of the Apostle’s saying is plainly shown, when he says: “Those whom he foreknew”—that is, without doubt, God the Father—“he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). Observe the conformity. After him they are adopted, so that he may be firstborn among many brothers; after him the world hates them; and after him the world is conquered by them.

2. Thus what is born of God rightly conquers the world, so that victory over temptation may be a testimony of heavenly birth. And just as he who is Son by nature triumphed over the world with its prince, so may we all who are children by adoption be found conquerors. Conquerors indeed, but in him who strengthens us, in whom we can do all things, because “this is the victory which conquers the world: our faith.” For by faith we are adopted as God’s children; the world, lying in the Evil One, hates and persecutes faith in us; and by faith it is also conquered, as it is written: “By faith the saints conquered kingdoms” (Hebrews 11:33). Why should victory not be attributed to faith, when life also belongs to it? “The righteous,” he says, “lives by faith” (Romans 1:17).

Whenever, therefore, you resist temptation, whenever you conquer the Evil One, do not attribute it to your own strength; do not glory in yourself, but rather in the Lord. For when would that armed strong man yield to your weakness? Hear, finally, what the appointed shepherd of the Lord’s flock warns: [Col. 0293C] “Your adversary the devil,” he says, “goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Resist him, steadfast in faith” (1 Peter 5:8–9). You see how the testimonies of truth agree with one another: Paul says that the saints conquered kingdoms by faith; Peter, that the prince of the world must be resisted in faith; John also says, “This is the victory which conquers the world: our faith.”

3. It follows: “Who is it that conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” Certainly, brothers, everyone who does not believe in the Son of God is by that very fact not merely conquered but already judged. For without faith it is impossible to please God (Hebrews 11:6). Yet perhaps it may trouble us that we see so many people believing that Jesus is the Son of God and nevertheless still entangled in the desires of the world [Col. 0293D]. What then does he mean: “Who conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God,” when the world itself now believes this? Do not even the demons believe and tremble? But I say: Do you think that any person considers Jesus the Son of God if he is neither frightened by his threats nor drawn by his promises, neither obeys his commands nor yields to his counsels? Does not such a person, even if he professes to know God, nevertheless deny him by his deeds? For faith without works is dead in itself (James 2:20). Nor can it seem strange if one does not conquer who does not even live.

4. Do you ask what living and victorious faith is? Without doubt, it is that by which Christ dwells in our hearts. [Col. 0294A] For Christ is both power and our life. “When Christ, your life, appears,” says the Apostle, “then you too will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:4). Whence comes glory, except from victory? Or why shall we appear with him, unless because in him we also conquer? Finally, if authority to become children of God was given only to those who receive Christ, then the saying, “Everyone born of God conquers the world,” must likewise be understood only of them.

Hence, too, after saying, “Who conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” John immediately added concerning his coming, so as to make clearer the faith he commends, through which—as was said—Christ dwells in our hearts: “This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ.” But, showing a way still more excellent, he says: “And it is the Spirit who testifies that Jesus is the Son of God.” Now his emphatic repetition, “Not in water only, but in water and blood,” should, 907 I think, be understood as distinguishing him from Moses. [Col. 0294B] For Moses came in water, from which he received the name Moses.

5. Let those to whom the history of the Old Testament is known recall how, in Egypt, while all the male infants of Israelite stock were being killed, Pharaoh’s daughter took up Moses, exposed in the waters (Exodus 2:3). And see whether, even in this, a figure of Christ is not plainly seen to have preceded him. Herod too, suffering from suspicion like Pharaoh, resorted to the same devices of cruelty, but was deceived in the same way [Col. 0294C] (Matthew 2:16). In both cases, a multitude of children is slaughtered because of one suspected person; in both, the one sought escapes. And just as Pharaoh’s daughter received Moses, so Egypt also—which is not inappropriately understood as Pharaoh’s daughter—received Christ to preserve him.

Yet this one is plainly greater than Moses, since he came not in water alone but in water and blood. “Many waters” are “many peoples” (Revelation 17:15). Therefore he came in water only who indeed gathered a people but did not redeem that people. For even liberation from Egyptian slavery was accomplished not by Moses but by the blood of the Lamb, prefiguring our liberation from the vain manner of life of this age by the blood of Christ Jesus, the spotless Lamb. [Col. 0294D] This is our true lawgiver, with whom redemption is abundant. For he died not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.

Remember, moreover, that this is John, who saw and bore witness—and we know that his testimony is true—that blood and water together came forth from the side of the Lord sleeping upon the cross; so that from the side of the new Adam, as he slept, the new Church might together be brought forth and redeemed.

6. Thus today also he comes to us through water and blood, so that water and blood may be the testimony of his coming and of victorious faith. Nor only this: there is a greater testimony than these, borne by the Spirit of truth. The testimony of these three is true and certain, and happy is the soul that merits to receive it.

[Col. 0295A] For there are three who give testimony on earth: Spirit, water, and blood. By water understand baptism; by blood, martyrdom; by Spirit, charity. For the Spirit is what gives life, and love is the life of faith. Finally, if you ask what Spirit has to do with charity, let Paul answer: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). The Spirit is necessarily added to water and blood because, as the same Apostle testifies, without charity whatever you have profits nothing (1 Corinthians 13:1–3).

7. Now, since we have said that water signifies baptism and blood martyrdom, remember that baptism is both unique and daily, and similarly martyrdom. For there is a kind of martyrdom, a certain shedding of blood, [Col. 0295B] in the daily affliction of the body. There is also a kind of baptism in compunction of heart and continual tears. It is necessary for the weak and faint-hearted, who are not able to lay down their blood for Christ once and for all, at least to shed blood in a certain milder but more enduring martyrdom. So too, since the sacrament of baptism may not be repeated, it must be supplied by frequent washing in those who frequently offend in many things. Hence the Prophet says: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will drench my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6:7).

Do you therefore wish to know who conquers the world? Examine more carefully what there is in him to be conquered. For blessed John himself also indicates this, saying: [Col. 0295C] “Beloved, do not love the world or the things that are in the world. For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition” (1 John 2:15–16). These are the three bands which the Chaldeans formed (Job 1:17). But I also remember that holy Jacob made three bands when, returning from Mesopotamia, he feared the face of Esau (Genesis 32:7).

Thus you too need a threefold defence against a threefold kind of temptation: let the desire of the flesh be conquered by its own mortification, which, if you remember, we said is understood in the testimony of blood; let the discipline of compunction and constant tears overcome the desire of the eyes; and let the power of charity exclude the vanity of ambition—charity which alone makes the soul chaste, alone purifies the intention. For it is a certain testimony that the world has been triumphed over [Col. 0295D] if you chastise the body and bring it into servitude, lest by destructive liberty it become enslaved to pleasure; if you give your eyes more to weeping than to wantonness or curiosity; if, finally, burning with spiritual love, you give your heart to no vanity.

8. The Spirit rightly is the one who bears testimony both on earth and in heaven, because bodily affliction will cease, and the fountain of tears will dry up; but charity never fails. [Col. 0296A] Here it is a kind of foretaste; its completion and fullness remain for the future. Yet although the Spirit remains after water and blood—for water and blood will not possess the kingdom of God—nevertheless, for the present, the Spirit is scarcely or not at all found without them, because, he says, “these three are one”: so that, if any one of these three is absent, you should not presume the others to be present.

But when these testimonies are joined together, they become exceedingly credible; and one in whom these are present on earth cannot lack testimony also in heaven. He confesses the Son of God before men not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth; and the Son too will confess him before the angels of God. Can the Father fail him in testimony when he sees the Son bearing witness for him? Without doubt, he too will confess what he has seen in secret. Nor will the Spirit dissent from Father and Son, being the Spirit of Father and Son. Finally, how can one lack his testimony in heaven who has merited to possess it on earth?

Therefore there are three who give testimony in heaven: Father, [Col. 0296B] Son, and Holy Spirit. And lest you suspect any discord, these three are one. Those will indeed have a great testimony whom the Father receives in heaven as sons and heirs, whom the Son admits as brothers and co-heirs, and whom the Holy Spirit makes, as they cling to God, to be one spirit with him. For the Spirit himself is the indissoluble bond of the Trinity, through whom, just as Father and Son are one, so may we be one in them, by the mercy of him who deigned to pray this very thing for his disciples, Jesus Christ our Lord.

### SERMON II. On the three testimonies. (1 John 5:4–11)

1. Today a reading from the Epistle of blessed John has been recited to us, in which we learn that a threefold testimony is given in heaven and a threefold testimony on earth. In my understanding, the former is a sign of stability and the latter of restoration; the former pertains to angels and the latter to human beings; the former distinguishes the blessed from the wretched, the latter the just from the ungodly. [Col. 0296C] For the vision of the Trinity rightly bears testimony to the angels who, in that first transgression, when Lucifer was growing proud, stood fast in truth; while for human beings whom divine mercy saves, there are Spirit, water, and blood.

Why should the Father not bear testimony to those by whom he is honoured as Father? But to you, evil one, he speaks thus: “If I am Father, where is my honour?” (Malachi 1:6). You must altogether lack the Father’s testimony, since you attempt to usurp his glory for yourself, desiring not to honour him but to equal him. “I shall sit,” he says, [Col. 0296D] “upon the mountain of the covenant; and I shall be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13). Will you, newly created as you are, sit beside the Father of spirits? And surely he has not yet said to you: “Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109 [110]:1). If you do not know, shameless one, it is that Only-begotten One to whom equality with the Father and sitting beside him have been granted by eternal generation. You, thinking equality with God something to be seized, begrudge the Son his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, so that you may not even deserve to receive testimony from him. But can the Spirit of both bear witness to one rejected by Father and Son? He who rests upon the quiet and humble, the lover of peace and consecrator of unity, certainly abhors the proud and restless; he is zealous against you for peace and unity.

2. Why should we wonder, brothers, if we fear that this little vineyard of the Lord may perhaps begin to be ravaged by the solitary beast [Col. 0297A]? For how many shoots of the heavenly vine did that first singularity trample down? But perhaps you readily observed pride in him, though not singularity. I say, then: where the whole host of angels stood, did not he who presumed to desire to sit have the vice of singularity? But perhaps you ask how I know of this standing of the angels. I have two suitable witnesses, each of whom testifies to what he saw. “I saw the Lord sitting,” says Isaiah, “but the seraphim stood” (Isaiah 6:1–2). And Daniel: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Daniel 7:10). Do you desire a third witness too, that every word may stand by the mouth of three witnesses? I bring forward the Apostle, who was caught up to the third heaven and, upon returning, said: [Col. 0297B] “Are they not all ministering spirits?” (Hebrews 1:14). Is it so? Where all stand and all minister, you, enemy of peace, will sit?

Clearly you grieve the Spirit, who makes those of one disposition dwell in a house; you offend charity, because you divide unity and break the bond of peace. Therefore the Spirit rightly bears testimony to the charity, unity, and peace of the angels, who did not abandon either their order or their dwelling; by that Spirit your envy, singularity, and restlessness are indeed condemned. This, then, concerns the testimony given in heaven.

3. There is also another testimony given on earth, [Col. 0297C] to distinguish those who are exiles upon it from its natives—that is, citizens of heaven from citizens of Babylon. For when does God leave his elect without testimony? Or what consolation could they have, tossed by anxious concern between hope and fear, if they did not merit to possess any testimony at all of their election? The Lord knows who are his, and he alone knows whom he has chosen from the beginning. But what human being knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred? And if, as is certain, certainty is altogether denied us, would it not be all the more delightful if we could perhaps find some signs of this election? For what rest can our spirit have while it still possesses no testimony of its predestination?

Therefore the saying by which the testimonies of salvation are commended is faithful and worthy of all acceptance. By this word consolation is supplied to the elect, and excuse is removed from the reprobate. For once the signs of life are known, whoever neglects them is plainly convicted [Col. 0298A] of receiving his soul in vain and is shown to account the desirable land as nothing.

4. “There are three,” he says, “who give testimony on earth: Spirit, water, and blood.” You know, brothers, that in the first human being we all sinned, and in him we all fell. We fell indeed into a prison full alike of mud and stones. There we lay captive, defiled, shattered, until the Desired of the nations came to redeem, wash, and help us. For he gave his own blood for redemption, brought forth water as well from his side for washing, and then sent down from on high his Spirit, to help our weakness.

Do you therefore wish to know whether these things work anything in you, lest perhaps you be guilty of the Lord’s blood, which you render ineffectual so far as lies within you; and lest that water itself, which ought to have cleansed you, add a judgment of condemnation while you remain in filth; and lest the Spirit, whom you resist, fail to free the evil-speaker from his own lips? [Col. 0298B] For care must be taken lest these things be fruitless for you, since they would necessarily be harmful as well.

5. But who possesses testimony that Christ’s blood was not shed without cause, except the one who restrains himself from sins? For the one who commits sin is a slave of sin. Thus, if from that point onward he is able to restrain himself and cast off the yoke of miserable slavery, this is the surest testimony of redemption, which Christ’s blood undoubtedly accomplishes. But restraint does not suffice for a sinner unless repentance is also present. He therefore also has testimony from water who labours in his groaning, washing [Col. 0298C] his bed every night. For as that blood redeemed us so that sin might not reign in our mortal body, so that water washes away those sins which we committed 910 before.

But what is to become of us, broken by long use of chains and by dwelling in a cruel prison, crushed and exhausted on the way of life? Let us call upon the life-giving and helping Spirit, trusting that the Father who is in heaven will give the good Spirit to those who ask him. Certainly, a new way of life gives the surest testimony that a new Spirit has come upon us. To repeat briefly, then: one has testimony from blood, water, and Spirit if one restrains oneself from sins, produces fruits worthy of repentance, and performs works of life.

[Col. 0297]

## IN THE ROGATION DAYS

### SERMON ON THE THREE LOAVES. (Luke 11:5–10)

[Col. 0297D] 1. “Which of you will have a friend,” and so forth. Why does he say that one friend has arrived, yet is not content to ask for one loaf? Do you suppose he considered his friend so ravenous that one loaf could not suffice for one person? For to set three loaves before one person seems wholly incongruous. Suppose, therefore, that the man arrived with his wife and servant, so that his friend wishes to set a loaf before each of them.

For my part, I understand the friend coming to me as no one other than myself. No one is dearer to me; no one is more closely related. Therefore a friend comes to me from the road when, abandoning transitory things, I return to my heart, as it is written: “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isaiah 46:8). Moreover, each person is then truly a friend to himself when he returns from the road, since “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul.” From the day of my conversion, therefore, the friend has come to me [Col. 0299A] from the road. He has come from a far country, where he used to feed pigs and hunger insatiably for their husks. He comes suffering hunger, worn out by lack of food, emaciated by fasting. He comes needing to find a friend; but alas for me, he has chosen a poor host and enters an empty dwelling.

What shall I do for this wretched and pitiable friend? I have absolutely nothing to set before him. I admit he is a friend, but I am a beggar. Why have you come to me, friend, in such great need? I am a beggar, and there is no bread in my house. “Hurry,” he says, “run about; rouse that great friend of yours, than whom no one has greater love, nor more abundant resources. Seek, ask, knock; for everyone who seeks finds, the one who asks receives, and to the one who knocks it shall be opened. Cry out and say: ‘Friend, lend me three loaves.’”

2. Who are these loaves, brothers? Would that we might merit to receive them! Perhaps no one knows even them except the one who receives them. Yet I believe that we ought to ask for [Col. 0300A] three loaves: of truth, charity, and strength. I confess that I need these three when the friend comes to me from the road—coming, as I said, with wife and servant. For my reason—this is the husband—fails through ignorance of truth; the will languishes through starvation of affection; the flesh is weakened through lack of strength. For reason insufficiently understands what must be done, the will insufficiently loves what has been understood, and moreover the corruptible body weighs down the soul, so that we do not do the things we wish.

“My heart has withered, and my body also, because I forgot to eat my bread.” For I would not suffer this failure if reason were continually exercised in the search for truth, the will in the desire for charity, and the flesh in the practice of virtue. Therefore, friend, lend me three [Col. 0300B] loaves, that I may understand, love, and do your will. For thus one lives, and in such things is the life of my spirit, as Scripture says: “For life is in his will” (Psalm 29 [30]:6).

[Col. 0299]

## ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

### SERMON I. On the Gospel reading. (Mark 16:14–20)

[The supplied source ends here; the sermon continues beyond this point.]

1. Jesus appeared to the eleven disciples as they were reclining at table (Mark 16:14). Truly the kindness and humanity of the Savior appeared. For it gives great confidence that he is more willing to be present with those intent upon prayer, since he does not even disdain to be present with those reclining. His kindness appeared, I say—he who knew our frame and does not disdain our necessities, but has compassion on them, provided that we do not make provision for the flesh in its desires, but in its need. Considering this, the same Apostle says: “Whether we eat or drink, or do anything else, let us do all to the glory of the Lord” (1 Cor. 10:31).

Yet the fact that he appeared to them while they were reclining may also be referred to what he said elsewhere when the Jews accused the disciples of not fasting: “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them” (Matt. 9:15). It follows: “And he reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen.” You hear Christ rebuking his disciples—indeed, and, what sounds harsher, even reproaching them—and not at just any time, but at the very hour when he was about to withdraw his bodily presence from them.

[Note: [Col. 0299D] Gregory the Great expresses the same view in Homily 29 on the Gospels, although, from Luke chapter 24, the rebuke preceded the Ascension by several days [Col. 0300D]. Consult the interpreters.]

Therefore do not henceforth be angry if Christ’s vicar should at some time rebuke you as well. For Christ is read to have done for his disciples precisely this, as he was about to ascend from them into heaven. But what is this, brothers, that he says: “They did not believe those who had seen him risen”? Who, then, were those blessed eyes that deserved to see the glorious miracle of the Lord’s resurrection? For no mortal is recorded—or believed—to have seen him rising. It remains, therefore, that this must be understood of the angels, whose testimony to the resurrection was met with hesitation by the faint-hearted apostles.

2. Now, in order to do what is written—“Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge” (Ps. 118:66)—let the grace of visitation, the correction of reproach, and also the instruction of preaching follow; and let him say: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved.” But what shall we say to this, brothers? In this saying, an exceedingly great assurance appears to be granted to worldly people; and I fear that they may begin to turn it into an occasion for the flesh, flattering themselves beyond what is proper concerning baptism and belief without works.

Nevertheless, let us consider what follows: “And these signs shall follow those who believe.” From this saying perhaps no less despair will appear to arise even among religious people than the earlier saying seemed to offer worldly people an occasion for vain hope. For who appears to possess those signs of belief that are written in the present passage—belief without which no one can be saved, since “he who does not believe shall be condemned,” and “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6)? Who, I say, casts out demons, speaks with new tongues, picks up serpents?

What then? If nobody has these things—or if very few in our time seem to have them—either no one will be saved, or only those who boast in these gifts, which are not so much merits as indications of merits. So much so that many who say, “Have we not cast out demons in your name, and done many mighty works in your name?” will hear at the judgment: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:22–23). Where, then, is what the Apostle says when speaking of the just Judge: “Who will render to every man according to his works” (Rom. 2:6), if—God forbid!—signs rather than merits are to be sought at judgment?

3. Yet merits themselves are certain signs, indeed more reliable and more salutary ones. Nor do I think it difficult to recognize how these present signs may be understood so that they become undoubted signs of belief and therefore of salvation.

For the first work of faith working through love is compunction of heart, in which demons are undoubtedly cast out when sins are uprooted from the heart. Then those who believe in Christ speak with new tongues, when old things depart from their mouths and they no longer speak the ancient tongue of our first parents, who turn aside into words of malice in order to make excuses for their sins.

But when former sins have been erased by compunction of heart and confession of mouth, and they do not suffer a relapse, so that later things are not worse than the former, then they must take up serpents: that is, they must extinguish poisonous suggestions. But what is to be done if perhaps some root sprouts which cannot be uprooted so swiftly, while the desire of the flesh still stings the mind? Certainly, if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them; for, following the Savior’s example, when they taste it, they will not wish to drink—that is, when they perceive it, they will not consent to it. Thus the sensation of desire without consent will not harm them, “because there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” [Col. 0301C].

But what then? Such a struggle with a corrupt and infirm affection is certainly burdensome and perilous. Yet those who believe “shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover”: that is, they shall cover sick affections with good works, and by this remedy they shall be healed.

## SERMON II. How he ascended above all heavens, that he might fill all things.

1. This feast, dearest brothers, is glorious and, if I may say so, joyful, in which singular glory is displayed for Christ and a special joy for us. For it is the consummation and fulfillment of the other feasts, and the happy conclusion of the whole journey of the Son of God. For he who descended is the same who today ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things [Col. 0301D] (Eph. 4:10).

Having already proved himself Lord of all things on earth, in the sea, and in hell, it remained only for him to demonstrate by similar, or rather greater, proofs that he was Lord of the air and of the heavens. The earth recognized its Lord, because at the word of his power, when he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11:43–44), it gave back the dead man. The sea recognized him because it made itself firm beneath his feet, so that the apostles thought him a phantom (Matt. 14:25–26). Hell recognized him, for he shattered its bronze gates and iron bars (Ps. 106:16), and there bound that insatiable murderer called the devil and Satan (Rev. 12:9; 20:2).

Certainly, he who raised the dead, cleansed lepers, gave sight to the blind, strengthened the lame, and drove out every infirmity, was Lord of all; and with the same hand by which he had made them, he restored what had failed. Likewise, he who foretold that in the mouth of a fish he would find a coin together with the fish itself (Matt. 17:26) is plainly, beyond doubt, Lord of the sea and of all that moves in it. And he who stripped the powers of the air and fastened them to his cross clearly received power over the infernal workshops. For he is the one “who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil” (Acts 10:38), who stood in a level place to teach the crowds; before the governor, to endure blows; throughout the time he was seen upon earth and conversed with men, standing amid many labors and working salvation in the midst of the earth.

2. Therefore, to close your seamless tunic, Lord Jesus—to perfect the wholeness of our faith—it remains that, while the disciples look on, you should ascend through the midst of the air, as Lord of the air, above all the heavens. Then it will be proved that you are Lord of all things, that you have filled all things in all; and then it will surely be due to you that at your name every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that you are in glory and at the right hand of the Father (Phil. 2:10–11).

At this right hand are delights unto the end. Therefore the Apostle exhorts us to seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God (Col. 3:1), because there indeed is our treasure, Jesus Christ [Col. 0302C], in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and in whom the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Col. 2:3, 9).

3. But what do you think, brothers: how great a grief and fear seized the hearts of the apostles when they saw him taken from them and lifted into the air—not aided by ladders, not raised by ropes; though accompanied by angelic service, yet not supported by assistance, but advancing in the multitude of his strength? What he had said to them was fulfilled: “Where I go, you cannot come” (John 13:33). Wherever on earth he went, they would follow him inseparably; they would even enter the sea with him, as Peter once did (Matt. 14:29), though to sink with him. But they could not follow him this way, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks upon many things” (Wis. 9:15).

Their grief, therefore, was immense, because they saw him for whom they had left everything taken away from their perceptions and sight. Since the bridegroom had been taken from them, could the children of the bridegroom fail to mourn? Their fear arose because they were left orphaned among the Jews, not yet strengthened by power from on high. Blessing them, therefore, he was borne into heaven, perhaps because the bowels of his singular mercy were moved when he left behind his poor and wretched school—except that he was going to prepare a place for them, and it was expedient that he withdraw his bodily presence from them.

How happy and worthy was that procession! The apostles themselves were not yet worthy to be admitted to it. Escorted in triumphal pomp by holy souls and heavenly powers to the Father, he sits at the right hand of God. Now he has truly filled all things: he was born among men, conversed with men, suffered and died by men and for men, rose again, ascended, and sits at the right hand of God. I recognize the tunic woven from above throughout its whole extent, which that heavenly dwelling completes: there the Lord Jesus Christ has been fulfilled and has filled all things.

4. Yet what are these feasts to me? Who will console me, Lord Jesus, because I did not see you hanging upon the cross, bruised by wounds, pale in death; because I did not suffer with you crucified or attend you dead, so that I might at least soothe those places of your wounds with my tears? How did you leave me without a farewell when, beautiful in your robe, O King of glory, you received yourself into the heights of heaven [Col. 0303B]?

My soul would utterly refuse consolation, unless the angels had anticipated me with their voice of exultation, saying: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same manner as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11). “In the same manner,” they say, “he will come.” Then will he come to seek us in that procession at once so singular and so universal, when all the angels go before and all humanity follows, and he descends to judge the living and the dead?

Without doubt he will come, but as he ascended, not as he formerly descended. First he came humble, to save souls; but he will come exalted, to raise this corpse and conform it to the body of his glory, so that he may seem to bestow more abundant honor upon this weaker vessel. Then he will appear with great power and majesty, he who formerly lay hidden in the weakness of the flesh. I too shall behold him, but not now; I shall see him, but not near—so that this second glorification will manifestly outshine the first glorification because of its surpassing glory.

5. Meanwhile Christ, the sheaf of our first fruits, has been offered, taken up to the right hand of the Father, and now stands before the face of God for us. He sits, holding mercy in his right hand and judgment in his left—mercy exceeding great, and judgment exceeding great; water in his right hand, fire in his left, holding both immovably.

Indeed, he has strengthened mercy upon those who fear him according to the height of heaven above the earth (Ps. 102:8, 11), so that they may feel greater heaps of the Lord’s compassion than there is distance between heaven and earth. For God’s purpose concerning them remains immovable; and this mercy [variant: “of the Lord”] is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him: from eternity through predestination, unto eternity through glorification. Likewise, concerning the reprobate he is terrible toward the children of men; and on either side the sentence of eternity stands fixed—both in those who are saved and in those who perish.

Who knows whether the names of all of you whom I see here are written in heaven and recorded in the book of predestination? For I seem to discern certain signs of your calling and justification in the manner of life of this humility [variant addition: “so great”] [Col. 0304A]. With how great joy, do you think, would all my bones be filled if I were granted to know this? But “man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Eccl. 9:1).

6. Therefore, beloved, persevere in the discipline that you have undertaken, so that through humility you may ascend to exaltation. This is the way, and there is no other besides it. He who goes otherwise falls rather than ascends. For humility alone exalts; humility alone leads to life.

Since Christ, by the nature of his divinity, had nowhere to grow or ascend—for beyond God there is nothing—he found by descent how he might grow: he came to be incarnate, to suffer, and to die, so that we might not die eternally. Therefore God exalted him, because he rose again, ascended, and sits at the right hand of God [Col. 0304B]. Go, and do likewise. For you cannot ascend unless you descend, because it is fixed by an eternal law: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

O perversity! O abuse by the sons of Adam! For although ascent is most difficult and descent most easy, they readily ascend and descend with greater difficulty: prepared for honors and lofty ecclesiastical ranks, fearful even to angelic shoulders. Yet those who will follow you, Lord Jesus, are scarcely found—even those willing to allow themselves to be drawn, willing to be led along the way of your commandments.

Some are drawn, who can say, “Draw me after you.” Others are led, who say, “The king has brought me into his storehouses” (Song 1:3). Others are carried away, as the Apostle was carried away to the third heaven. The first are happy indeed, who possess their souls in patience; the second happier, because they confess him by their own will; the third most happy, who in the deepest mercy of God, with the power of their own choice, as it were, now buried, are carried away into the riches of glory in a spirit of fervor, not knowing whether in the body or outside the body (2 Cor. 12:2), knowing only that they have been carried away.

Blessed is the one who has you as guide everywhere, Lord Jesus—not that fugitive spirit who at once wished to ascend and was struck down by the whole right hand of divinity. But we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, let us follow you, through you, unto you; for you are “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6): the way in example, the truth in promise, the life in reward. For you have the words of eternal life, and we know and believe that you are Christ, the Son of the living God (John 6:69–70), who are God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON III. On understanding and affection.

1. Today the Lord of the heavens penetrated the heights of heaven by heavenly power; shaking off the infirmities of the flesh as though they were clouds, he put on the robe of glory. The Sun was lifted up at his rising; he grew warm and strong; he spread and multiplied his rays over the earth, and there is none who can hide from his heat.

The Wisdom of God returned to the region of wisdom, where all both understand and seek the good: most penetrating in understanding, most ready in affection to hear the voice of his words [Col. 0305A]. But we are in this region, where there is much wickedness and little wisdom, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks upon many things” (Wis. 9:15).

By “mind” here, I think, understanding is indicated. It is truly weighed down when it thinks upon many things, when it does not gather itself around that one and only meditation conceived from that city “whose participation is in the same.” Such an understanding must be weighed down and scattered among many things, in many and manifold ways. By “soul,” however, I think the affections are meant: they are affected by various passions in the corrupt body, and can never be softened—much less healed—until the will seeks one thing and tends toward one thing.

2. Therefore there are two things in us that must be purified: understanding and affection—understanding, that it may know; affection, that it may will. Happy, and truly happy, were those two men, Elijah and Enoch, from whom every material and occasion was removed that could hinder either their understanding or their affection, because, living for God alone, they knew nothing but God and desired nothing but God.

Thus it is written of Enoch:

[Note: [Col. 0305D] This is by appropriation; for these words are stated generally in Wisdom, chapter 4, verse 11. But Enoch is expressly mentioned in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 44, verse 16: “Enoch pleased God and was translated into paradise” [Col. 0306D]. The same occurs in Bernard below, Sermon 5, no. 9.]

“…that he was taken away, lest malice should change his understanding or deceit deceive his soul” (Wis. 4:11). Our understanding was troubled, not to say blinded; our affection was defiled, and greatly defiled. But Christ enlightens the understanding; the Holy Spirit purifies the affection.

For the Son of God came and performed so many and such great wonders in the world that he rightly summoned our understanding away from all worldly matters, so that we may always think—and never be able to think enough—because he has done wonderful things. Truly he left us very broad fields in which understanding may range; and the torrent of these thoughts is most deep, which, according to the prophet, cannot be crossed on foot (Ezek. 47:5). For who can sufficiently consider how the Lord of all things anticipated us, came to us, aided us; how that singular Majesty willed to die that we might live, to serve that we might reign, to go into exile that we might return to our homeland, and to stoop even to the lowliest slave’s works, that he might set us over all his works?

3. The Lord of apostles showed himself such to the apostles that they no longer beheld “the invisible things of God, understood through the things that are made,” but saw face to face him who made all things. Because the disciples were carnal, and God is spirit, and spirit and flesh do not fit well together, he tempered himself to them by the shadow of his body, so that through the object before them of his life-giving flesh they might see the Word in flesh, the sun in a cloud, light in a vessel, a candle in a lantern.

For Christ the Lord is “the breath of our nostrils,” to whom we said: “In your shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lam. 4:20). “In your shadow,” he says, “among the nations,” not among the angels, where we shall behold the most pure light with most pure eyes. Thus also the power of the Most High overshadowed the Virgin, lest even that singular eagle, dazzled by excessive splendor, should be unable to bear the lightning-flash of divinity [Col. 0306A].

He presented his flesh to them for this purpose: that he might draw together all their thought away from human matters and toward his flesh—by which he both spoke wonders and performed wonders—and thus transfer them from flesh to spirit. For “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). Does it not seem to you that he enlightened their understanding when he opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures, showing that Christ had to suffer these things, rise from the dead (Luke 24:45), and thus enter into his glory?

4. But being accustomed to his most holy flesh, they could not bear to hear the word of his departure: that he should leave those for whom they had left everything. Why was this? Because their understanding had been enlightened, but their affection had not yet been purified. Therefore the gracious master gently and sweetly addressed [variant: “consoled”] them, saying: “It is expedient for you that I go away. For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you. But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart” (John 16:6–7).

Why could the Holy Spirit not come to them while Christ remained upon earth? Did he shrink from fellowship with that flesh which had been conceived and born in the Virgin, of the Virgin Mother, from him and through him? Far be it! Rather, he did so in order to show us the way by which we should walk, and to set before us the pattern into which we should be formed.

He was indeed lifted into heaven while they wept; and he sent the Holy Spirit, who cleansed their affection—that is, their will—or rather changed it, so that they might now desire more that the Lord should have ascended, whom they had formerly wished to keep. What he foretold them was fulfilled: “You will indeed be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16:20). Thus their understanding was enlightened through Christ and their will cleansed through the Spirit, so that, as they knew the good, so they might also will it. This alone is perfect religion, or religious perfection.

5. I now recall the holy Elisha. When Elijah told him to ask, at his departure or ascent, whatever he wished, he answered: “I pray that your spirit may be doubled in me.” But Elijah said: “You have asked a difficult thing. Nevertheless, if you see me when I am taken from you, what you have asked shall be yours” (4 Kings 2:9–10).

Does it not seem to you that Elijah prefigures the person of the ascending Lord, and Elisha the apostolic company anxiously longing at Christ’s Ascension? For as Elisha could by no means be torn from Elijah, so neither could the apostles be separated from Christ’s presence. At last he scarcely persuaded them that without faith it would be impossible to please God.

What, then, is this double spirit that is sought, except the illumination of understanding and the purification of affection? It is a difficult thing, because rare upon earth is one who deserves to possess it. “Nevertheless,” he says, “if you see me when I am taken from you, what you have asked shall be yours.” There is nothing that your disciples, Lord Jesus, have or ought to lose because you were lifted into heaven while they looked on, and they followed you with longing eyes as you advanced in the multitude of your strength.

Or we may call the double spirit that of which the Savior said to his disciples: “He who believes in me will do the works that I do; and he will do greater works than these” (John 14:12). Did not Peter do greater things than Christ—though through Christ? Of him it is written that the sick were placed on beds in the streets, so that, as Peter came by, at least his shadow might overshadow one of them and they might be freed from their infirmities (Acts 5:15). For nowhere is the Lord found to have healed infirmities by his shadow.

6. I do not doubt that the understanding of all of you who are here has been enlightened; but that your affection has not been purified in equal measure I shall demonstrate by evident indications. All of you know what is good, the way in which you ought to walk, and how you ought to walk in it; but your wills are not one.

Some not only walk, but run—indeed, rather, fly—in every exercise of this way and life, so that short vigils, sweet food, soft garments, and labors seem to them not merely bearable but desirable. Others, however, are not so. With dry heart and a resisting affection, they are scarcely drawn to these things by shame:

[Note: [Col. 0307D] In some copies “scarcely by shame” is absent, as in Colbertinus 3632; in that manuscript, after “are compelled,” one reads “wretched and pitiable,” six lines having been omitted. Yet “by shame” seems to be retained, as in Sermon 5, no. 7: “Whom, finally, the fear of hell scarcely restrains, shame scarcely holds back.”]

They are scarcely compelled by fear of hell. Some we do not compel even at all: their brow has become that of a harlot, and they refuse to blush. There are, I say, many among us who eat one bread with us, sleep with us, sing with us, work with us—wretched and pitiable, sharing in every respect [variant: “in every respect” absent] in tribulation, but not in consolation to the same degree.

Has the hand of the Lord been shortened, so that he cannot grant to all, he who opens his hand and fills every living thing with blessing? What, then, is the cause? Exactly this: they do not see Christ when he is taken from them. That is, they do not consider how he has left them orphaned; that they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth; that for so long they are held in the dreadful prison of a foul body and are not with Christ.

If such people remain long under this burden, they are either crushed and fall beneath it, or are in some sense in hell, since they never fully breathe in the light of the Lord’s mercies [Col. 0307D], nor in the freedom of the Spirit, which alone makes the yoke sweet and the burden light.

7. From this comes that most destructive lukewarmness: their affection—that is, their will—has not yet been purified, and they do not will the good as they know it, being grievously drawn away and enticed by their own desire. For in their flesh they love little earthly consolations, whether in word, sign, action, or anything else; and although they sometimes interrupt these things, they do not utterly break with them.

Thus they seldom direct their affections toward God; their compunction is not continuous but hourly, or, to speak more truly, momentary. The soul subject to these distractions cannot be filled with the visitations of the Lord. And the more it is emptied of those things, the more it will be filled with these: much, if it is emptied much; little, if little [Col. 0308A].

Or, if you prefer, these things can never be mixed with those eternally. For where oil finds no empty vessels, it must stop; nor do they put new wine except into new wineskins, so that both may be preserved. For spirit and flesh, fire and lukewarmness, do not dwell in one habitation—especially since lukewarmness commonly provokes the Lord himself to vomit (Rev. 3:16).

8. For if the apostles, while still clinging to the Lord’s flesh—which alone was holy, because it belonged to the Holy of Holies—could not be filled with the Holy Spirit until it was taken from them, do you, bound and glued to your own flesh, which is utterly filthy and filled with the phantasms of various impurities, think that you can receive that most pure Spirit unless you attempt utterly to renounce these fleshly consolations?
