Truly, when you begin, sorrow will fill your heart; but if you persevere, your sorrow will be turned into joy. Then affection will be purified and the will renewed—or rather, created anew—so that all things that formerly appeared difficult, indeed impossible, may be pursued with great sweetness and eagerness. “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created; and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:30).

As the outward person is recognized by the face, so the inward person is shown by the will. Therefore, when the Spirit is sent forth, the face of the earth is created and renewed: that is, the earthly will becomes heavenly, ready to obey at a nod more quickly than the nod itself [Col. 0308C]. Blessed are those who are such, who not only do not feel evil but dwell in a certain wondrous enlargement of heart.

But God says terrifyingly of those mentioned above: “My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3)—that is, carnal; and whatever spirit there had been in them has vanished into flesh.

9. Since, therefore, beloved, today is the day on which the bridegroom is taken from us—and not without some tumult in our souls—yet for the purpose of sending us the Spirit of truth, let us weep and pray that he may find us worthy, or rather make us worthy, and fill this house where we sit, so that not vexation but his anointing may teach us concerning all things. Thus, with understanding made clear and affection made pure, may he come to us and make his dwelling among us.

And as Moses’ serpent devoured all the serpents of the magicians (Exod. 7:12), so when this Spirit comes he will swallow up all our carnal affections and pleasures and pour in [variant: “pour in” absent] consolations, so that we may have rest from labor, joy from tribulation, glory from reproach—like those whom he had filled, who went rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been judged worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41).

For the Spirit of Jesus—the good Spirit, the Holy Spirit, the upright Spirit, the sweet Spirit, the sovereign Spirit—makes light and broad whatever in this world seems evil, difficult, and narrow. He judges reproach to be joy and persuades us that contempt is exaltation. Let us therefore, according to the prophet, search our ways and our pursuits; let us lift up our hearts with our hands (Lam. 3:40), that we may rejoice in the feast of the Holy Spirit and rejoice more abundantly, he who, as the Son of God promised, may lead us into all truth (John 16:13).

## SERMON IV. On the two evil ascents, of the devil and the first man; and the six good ascents, of Christ and of ourselves.

1. If we celebrate with fitting devotion the feasts of the Lord’s Nativity and Resurrection, it is fitting that we celebrate today’s day of the Ascension with no less devotion. For this feast in no way falls short of those feasts; rather, it is their end and fulfillment. The day is rightly observed with solemnity and joy, when that super-heavenly sun, the Sun of righteousness, showed himself to our sight, moderating his splendor and inaccessible light with the cloud of flesh and the sackcloth of mortality.

There is also great joy and exceedingly abundant exultation when, the sackcloth being torn, he is clothed with gladness; and when, from the midst of that sackcloth, not its substance but its oldness, corruption, misery, and vileness having been removed, he consecrated the first-fruits of our resurrection.

Yet what are these feasts to me if my manner of life is still detained upon the earth? Who, indeed, would dare even to desire ascent into heaven, unless he who had descended first ascended? Therefore I say to you: this dwelling in exile would seem to me scarcely more tolerable than hell, unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed of confidence and expectation when he was lifted up in the clouds and made hope for believers. For he says: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John 16:7).

Who is this Paraclete? Surely he through whom love is poured out and hope no longer confounds; that Paraclete through whom our citizenship is in heaven; the power from on high, through whom our hearts are above.

[Note: [Col. 0309D] Some copies read, “and made hope for believers.” I think, however, that this may refer to the one who said, “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell,” and therefore said, “My life drew near to hell” [Col. 0310D]. But now we have been saved in hope, into whose height Christ’s Ascension has raised us. “I go,” etc.]

“I go,” he says, “to prepare a place for you; and if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself” (John 14:2–3). “For where the body is, there also the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. 24:28). Do you see how the feast we celebrate today both contains the consummation of the other feasts, reveals their fruit, and increases grace?

2. For as all the other acts of him who was born for us and given to us were for us, so his Ascension itself was accomplished for us and works for us. In our own life we seem, so far as we are concerned, to do many things by chance and many by necessity. But Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, could be subject to neither. What necessity could compel God’s power? Or what could God’s wisdom do by chance?

Therefore do not doubt that whatever he said, did, or suffered was voluntary, full of mysteries, full of salvation. Knowing this, if at any time some matter concerning Christ comes to our knowledge, we should not hear it as though we were presenting some newly invented discovery, but as something which, even before its reason was known, was certain not to have been without a reason.

For just as a writer arranges everything according to definite plans, so things that come from God are ordered—especially those things which the Majesty present in the flesh performed. Yet woe to the narrowness of our knowledge [variant: “thought”]; woe to the poverty of our understanding, for we know only in part, and that a small part! Hardly a few little sparks shine forth for us from such an abundance of light, from the lamp set upon the lampstand.

Certainly, the less each individual receives, the more faithfully what is revealed to individuals must be shared with the rest. And I, brothers, neither wish nor ought to withhold from you what he himself deigns to grant me for your edification concerning his Ascension—or rather, concerning his ascents. Especially since this is the prerogative of spiritual gifts: when shared, they are not diminished.

Perhaps these matters are already known to some, to whom they have likewise been revealed. But for those who perhaps have not noticed them because they were intent upon loftier matters or occupied with others; or also for those whose understanding has less capacity, it is incumbent upon me to speak what I think.

3. “He who descended is the same also who ascended” [Col. 0310C] (Eph. 4:10). These are the Apostle’s words. Yet I believe that in descending he also ascended. For Christ had to descend in such a way [variant: ascend] that we might be taught to ascend. We are indeed eager for ascent; all of us desire exaltation. For we are creatures of noble birth and of a certain greatness of spirit, and therefore by a natural longing we seek height.

But woe to us if we wish to follow him who says: “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. 14:13). Alas, miserable one—on the sides of the north! [919] That mountain is cold; we do not follow you. You desire power; you presume upon eminence of authority. Yet how many still today follow those foul and unhappy tracks! Indeed [Col. 0310D], how few escape whom the lust of ruling does not itself rule! Hence those who hold power are called beneficent; hence the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul. For all flatter the powerful, and all envy them.

Whom do you follow, miserable human beings? Whom do you follow? Do you not see Satan falling like lightning? Is this not the mountain upon which an angel ascended and became a devil? Or at least consider this: after his fall, tormented by envy and wickedly intent upon overthrowing man, he nevertheless did not dare persuade him to ascend that mountain [Col. 0311A], upon which he had learned by experience that so terrible a precipice followed upon a vain ascent.

4. Yet the crafty enemy was not at a loss what to do. He pointed out another mountain resembling it: “You shall be like gods,” he says, “knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5). This ascent too is ruinous—or rather it is a descent from Jerusalem to Jericho. Knowledge that puffs up is a most evil mountain. Yet even today you may see very many sons of Adam climbing it with such desire, as though they did not know how far their father descended in mounting that mountain—or rather, how grievously he fell, and how greatly all his poster­ity was cast down and shattered.

The wounds inflicted upon you in climbing that mountain have not yet been healed, although you were still in your father’s loins; and now, in your own person [Col. 0311B], do you again attempt to climb, so that the latter error may be worse than the former? What dreadful desire is this among wretched people? “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3). Do you not know that “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Cor. 1:27)? Neither the terror of God’s threat—that he will destroy the wisdom of the wise and reject the prudence of the prudent—nor our father’s example, nor finally our own understanding and the hard experience of the necessity to which we are bound by the foolish appetite for knowledge, calls us back!

5. Behold, brothers, we have shown you another mountain—not one to climb, but one to flee. It is that upon which he ascended who wished to be like [Col. 0311C] God, knowing good and evil. It is the mountain that his children still heap up and raise, finding nothing so base from which they do not wish to increase the mountain of knowledge. You may see one passionately pursuing learning, another worldly business, this one the knowledge of lawsuits displeasing to God, that one some servile craft—so ardently that he counts no labour excessive, provided only that he may be thought more learned than certain others.

Thus they build Babel; thus they suppose that they will attain likeness to God. Thus they desire what is not expedient, while omitting what is expedient. What have you to do with these mountains, whose ascent involves such difficulty and such great danger? Or why do you desert that mountain whose ascent is easy and highly beneficial? Ambition for power deprived an angel of angelic blessedness [Col. 0311D]; appetite for knowledge stripped man of the glory of immortality.

Let someone try to climb the mountain of power: how many opponents do you think he will have, how many repulsers he will find, what obstacles, what a difficult way? And if at last he should attain what he sought: “The mighty,” Scripture says, “shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6:7)—to say nothing of the present cares and anxieties which power itself produces. Another desires knowledge that puffs up: how much will he labour, how greatly will his spirit be troubled? Yet he will hear: “Even if you burst yourself, you will not grasp it.” His eye will dwell in bitterness whenever he sees someone whom he judges inferior to himself, or whom he thinks is judged by others to be so. And what when he has become greatly swollen? “I will destroy,” says the Lord, “the wisdom [Col. 0312A] of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent” (1 Cor. 1:19).

6. But, not to linger over many matters: you have seen, I think, how both mountains must be fled, if we dread the angel’s precipice and man’s fall. “Mountains [920] of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you” (2 Sam. 1:21). Yet what are we to do? It is not expedient to ascend in this fashion, and nevertheless we are held by the desire to ascend. Who will teach us a wholesome ascent? Who, except him of whom we read that “he who descended is the same also who ascended” (Eph. 4:10)? The way of ascent had to be shown us by him, lest we follow either the track or counsel of an evil guide—indeed, seducer.

Therefore, because there was nowhere for the Most High to ascend, he descended; and by his descent he consecrated for us a gentle and [Col. 0312B] health-giving ascent. He descended from the mountain of power, clothed in the weakness of flesh; he descended from the mountain of knowledge, because “it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.” What appears weaker than a tender body and infant limbs? What appears more untaught than a little child who has known only its mother’s breasts? Who is more powerless than he whose every limb was fastened with nails, whose every bone was counted? Who more foolish than he who handed over his soul to death and paid then what he had not taken by robbery? You see how far he descended, how greatly he emptied himself of his power and his wisdom.

But he could not ascend higher upon the mountain of goodness, nor could he commend his love more plainly. Nor is it surprising that Christ ascended by descending, when each of the former two fell by ascending. And it seems to me that he sought a climber of this mountain who said: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place?” (Ps. 23:3). Perhaps Isaiah too, seeing people fall through desire of ascent, called them back to this mountain, crying: “Come, let us ascend the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. 2:3). Does he not plainly rebuke them for ascending the former mountains and proclaim the abundance of this mountain when he says: “Why do you look with envy upon the curdled mountains? The curdled mountain, the rich mountain” (Ps. 67:16–17)?

This, therefore, is the mountain of the house of the Lord, prepared upon the summit of the mountains; upon the mountains she had seen the Bridegroom leaping who said: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains” (Song 2:8). [Col. 0312D] For he taught one ignorant of the way, drew the little child, led the infant; and therefore he went, as it were, by certain steps, so that “the God of gods might be seen in Zion from strength to strength” (Ps. 83:8). For “his righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35:7).

7. But now, if you please, let us consider also the leaps themselves by which he rejoiced “like a giant to run his course,” and whose going forth is from the highest heaven, returning by certain stages even to its highest point (Ps. 18:6–7). First, then, set before yourself that mountain upon which he ascended with Peter, James, and John, and where he was transfigured before them. “His face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as snow” (Matt. 17:1–2). This is the glory of the resurrection, which we contemplate upon the mountain of hope.

For why did he ascend to be transfigured, except to teach us to ascend in thought to that future glory which shall be revealed in us? Blessed is the person whose meditation is always before the Lord, who diligently turns over in thought within his heart the delights at the Lord’s right hand for evermore. What can seem burdensome to one who continually reflects that the sufferings of this present time are not comparable to the glory to come? What can one desire in this wicked world whose eye always sees the Lord’s good things in the land of the living, always sees eternal rewards?

“My heart said to you”—the Prophet speaks to the Lord—“my face has sought you; your face, Lord, I will seek” (Ps. 26:8). Who will grant me that you may all rise and stand on high and [Col. 0313B] see the exultation that will come to you from the Lord?

8. I beg you, do not be troubled that we linger somewhat longer upon this mountain; for we may pass more swiftly over the others. Yet on this one, who would not be detained by that saying of Saint Peter which he uttered upon it and concerning it: “Lord,” he says, “it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:4)? For what is so good—or rather, what else appears good—than for the soul to linger amid good things, when the body cannot yet do so?

I think that the sound of one feasting was this utterance: “It is good for us to be here,” spoken by him who entered “into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and confession” [921] (Ps. 41:5). For which of you, reflecting within himself upon that future life—upon its joy, delight, blessedness, and the glory of the children of God—which of you, I say, turning such things over within himself with a tranquil conscience, does not immediately cry out from the abundance of inward sweetness: “Lord, it is good for us to be here”?

Certainly not in this wretched pilgrimage, where he is held by the body, but in that sweet and health-giving meditation in which he moves in heart: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly and be at rest?” (Ps. 54:7). But you, children of men—children of the man who descended from Jerusalem to Jericho—children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? “Ascend to the lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63:7–8). For this is the mind in which Christ is transfigured. Ascend, and you shall know that the Lord has made his [Col. 0313D] Holy One wonderful.

9. I beg you, my brothers, let not your hearts be burdened with worldly cares; for concerning gluttony and drunkenness, thank God, I do not greatly need to admonish you. I beg you, unburden your hearts of the heavy mass of earthly thoughts, so that you may know that the Lord has made his Holy One wonderful. Raise your hearts with, as it were, the hands of your thoughts, so that you may see the Lord transfigured.

Fashion in your hearts not only the tabernacles of patriarchs and prophets, but all the many mansions of that heavenly house, according to the example of him who went about sacrificing in the tabernacle of the Lord a sacrifice of jubilation, singing and speaking that psalm to the Lord: “How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” [Col. 0314A] (Ps. 83:2–3). You too, beloved, make your circuit with the offering of piety and devotion: visit in spirit the heavenly dwellings and the many mansions in the Father’s house; humbly prostrate your hearts before the throne of God and of the Lamb; reverently make supplication to each order of angels; salute the company of patriarchs, the ranks of prophets, and the apostolic senate; behold the crowns of martyrs gleaming with purple flowers; admire the choirs of virgins fragrant with lilies; and, as far as the weakness of the heart can prevail, raise your hearing to the honey-sweet sound of the new song.

“I remembered these things”—the Prophet speaks [variant: “to the Lord” is added]—“and poured out my soul within me.” What things? “For I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Ps. 41:5). And again: “I remembered God,” he says, “and was delighted” (Ps. 76:4). What the apostles saw, this man also saw, and, I think, by no unlike vision—except that his vision was wholly spiritual, with nothing bodily in it. Certainly he did not see him as did the one who said: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53:2). Without doubt he saw him transfigured and “beautiful in form above the sons of men,” he who declares himself delighted, just as the apostles did: “Lord,” they say, “it is good for us to be here.” And, lest anything be lacking from the proposed likeness, they are indeed read to have fallen face downward (Matt. 17:6), while he confesses that his spirit failed (Ps. 76:4).

“How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” Therefore, ascending this mountain and beholding the Lord’s glory with unveiled face, you too will doubtless have to cry out: “Draw us after you.” For what advantage is it to know where one ought to go, if one does not know the way by which one ought to go?

10. Therefore you must ascend another mountain, upon which you hear him preaching and raising a ladder marked out by eight rungs, whose summit touches heaven: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Now, if you have ascended the first mountain through continual meditation upon heavenly glory, you will not find it burdensome to ascend this mountain likewise, so that you may meditate on his law day [Col. 0314D] and night—as the same Prophet meditated not only upon rewards, but also upon the commandments of the Lord which he loved (Ps. 118:47).

Thus you too will hear: “You know where I am going,” by reason of the first ascent; “and you know the way” (John 14:4), by reason of the second. Therefore set it in your heart to seek the way of truth, lest perhaps you belong to the number of those who “did not find the way to a city of habitation.” Rather, be concerned to ascend not only by contemplation of heavenly glory [922], but also by a manner of life deserving heavenly glory.

11. I read likewise of a third mountain, upon which he ascended alone to pray (Matt. 14:23). You see, then, how rightly the Bride says in the Song: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains” [Col. 0315A] (Song 2:8). On the first he was transfigured, that you might know where to tend; on the second he spoke words of life, that you might know by what way to arrive; on the third he prayed, that you might strive to obtain the good will both to go and to arrive. For “to one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (Jas. 4:17).

Therefore, knowing that good will is given in prayer, when you see what must be done, ascend to prayer so that you may be strengthened to do what you see. Pray urgently, pray perseveringly, as he spent the night in prayer, and the good Father will give a good spirit to one who asks him. And see how fittingly we seek bodily seclusion too at the time of prayer, since he taught this not only by his word—“Enter,” he says, “into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” [Col. 0315B] (Matt. 6:6)—but also commended it by his example, admitting none even of his household, but ascending alone to pray.

12. Do you think that we can discover anything further concerning his ascents? We certainly can. For I do not want you to forget even the animal upon which he is read to have mounted. Nor do I want you to omit the ascent of the cross itself. For upon it too the Son of Man had to be lifted up: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

Thus, when understanding is now available and willingness is present, what will you do because you do not find how to accomplish the good, while certain asinine and bestial impulses have a contrary law and seek to take you captive? What, I say, will you do with the irrational desires [Col. 0315C] that are in your members? Even when you agree to fast, the enticement of appetite presses you; when you resolve to keep vigil, sleepiness weighs you down. What shall we do with this donkey? For this is donkey-like, common to donkeys, because “man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13).

Mount, Lord, upon this donkey; trample down these bestial impulses, because they must be tamed lest they prevail to rule. For unless they are trampled, they will trample us; unless they are pressed down, they will oppress us. Therefore, my soul, follow Christ the Lord also in this ascent, so that your desire may be subject to you and you may rule it. For if you are to ascend to heaven, you must first lift yourself above yourself, trampling the fleshly desires that fight within you against [Col. 0315D] you.

13. Follow also him ascending the cross and lifted up from the earth, so that you may be established by the height of the mind not only above yourself, but also above the whole world, looking down upon and despising all things upon the earth, as it is written: “They shall see the land from afar” (Isa. 33:17). Let no delights of the world bend you down; let no adversities cast you down. Far be it from you to glory except in the cross of your Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to you: thus count as a cross what the world desires; and, yourself crucified to the world, cling with your whole love to those things which the world counts a cross.

14. And now what remains from this, except that you ascend to him [Col. 0316A] who is God above all, blessed for ever? “To be dissolved and to be with Christ is far better.” “Blessed is the man whose help is from you,” says the Prophet to the Lord; “he has set ascents in his heart; he shall go from strength to strength, until he sees the God of gods in Zion” (Ps. 83:6, 8). This is the final ascent, in which all things are fulfilled, as the Apostle says: “Christ, who descended, is the same also who ascended, that he might fill all things” (Eph. 4:10).

But what can I say about that ascent? Where shall we ascend, so that we too may be where Christ is? What shall be there? “Eye, O God, has not seen apart from you what you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9). Let us desire this, my brothers; let us continually sigh for it. And let our affection grow stronger in proportion as understanding fails.

[923] **SERMON V. On Understanding and Affection**

[Col. 0316B]

1. Today the Son of Man has been presented, to sit together with the Ancient of Days upon his throne (Dan. 7:13); and henceforth he shall be not only “the Branch of the Lord in magnificence and glory,” but also “the exalted fruit of the earth” (Isa. 4:2). Blessed union, and a mystery to be embraced with ineffable joys! For he is both the Branch of the Lord and the fruit of the earth; he is both the Son of God and the fruit of Mary’s womb; the same is David’s son and David’s Lord, whose joy has today been fulfilled, concerning whom David long ago sang: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1).

For how is the Lord not the Branch of the Lord? Yet he is also his son, as the exalted fruit of the earth, the fruit of the rod that came forth from the root of Jesse. Today, therefore, the Father glorifies with himself this Son who is both his own and man’s, with the glory which he had with him before the world was made (John 17:5). Today heaven glories that Truth, which sprang up from the earth, has been restored to it. Today the Bridegroom is taken away from the bridegroom’s sons, and they must mourn, as he himself foretold. For the sons of the bridegroom could not mourn while the Bridegroom was with them; but the day came when he would be taken away from them, so that thereafter they might mourn and fast (Matt. 9:15).

Where now, Peter, is what you said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here; let us make three tabernacles here” (Matt. 17:4)? For behold, he has entered a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands—that is, not of this [Col. 0316D] creation.

2. How then is it now good for us to be here? Rather, it is troublesome, burdensome, dangerous. Surely this is where wickedness is very great and wisdom scant—if even a little is found; where all things are sticky, all slippery, covered in darkness, beset by snares of sins; where souls are endangered, where spirits are afflicted under the sun—yet all is vanity and affliction of spirit.

Therefore, my brothers, let us raise our hearts to heaven with our hands, and let us strive to follow the ascending Lord by, as it were, certain steps of devotion and faith. For the time will come when, without delay and without difficulty, we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet him; and spiritual bodies will then be able to do what natural spirits cannot now do. For now, with how great exertions it is necessary to raise our hearts, which, as we read with sorrow enough in the book of our own experience, are both weighed down by the corruptible body and depressed by earthly habitation [Col. 0317A].

3. Perhaps, however, we should explain what it is to raise the heart, or how it ought to be raised; but this should surely be taught by the Apostle rather than by us. “If you have risen with Christ,” he says, “seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God; set your minds on things above, not on things on earth” (Col. 3:1–2). It is as though he said more plainly: If you have risen, ascend with him also; if you live with him, reign with him also.

Let us follow, brothers, let us follow the Lamb wherever he goes. Let us follow him suffering; let us follow him rising; let us follow him, with far greater readiness, ascending [Col. 0317B]. Let our old man be crucified with him, so that the body of sin may be destroyed, and we may no longer serve sin—our members which are upon the earth having been put to death. And just as he rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so let us also walk in newness of life. For he died and rose for this purpose: that, dead to sins, we might live to righteousness.

4. But because newness of life requires a safer place and the dignity of resurrection seeks a higher station, let us also follow him ascending: that is, let us seek and set our minds on the things above, where he is, rather than on the things upon earth. Do you ask what that place is? Hear the Apostle: “The Jerusalem above,” he says, “is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4:26). Do you wish to know what is there? It is the vision of peace. “Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion, who has made your borders peace” (Ps. 147:12, 14).

O peace surpassing every understanding! O peace even above peace! O measure beyond measure—pressed down, shaken together, and [924] overflowing! Therefore, Christian soul, suffer with Christ; rise with him; ascend with him. That is: “Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. 33:15). Thus Paul, in the Acts of the Apostles, is remembered to have taught disciples concerning continence, righteousness, and the hope of eternal life (Acts 24:25). Thus Truth itself admonishes in the Gospel that loins be girded, lamps be kindled, and that thereafter people be found like those awaiting their lord (Luke 12:35–36).

[Col. 0317D] 5. But, if you have observed carefully, a certain twofold ascent is commended to us by the Apostle in his admonition both to seek and to set our minds upon—not low, but heavenly—things. Perhaps the Prophet himself too may appear not to have passed over this distinction entirely when he says: “Seek peace and pursue it.” To seek the peace that is to be pursued, and to pursue it once sought, is to seek the things above that are to be relished, and to relish those once sought—not the things upon earth.

For as long as our hearts are divided and are found meanwhile to possess many recesses, and do not appear wholly united with themselves, they must be raised somehow in portions and members, so that they may be gathered into that heavenly Jerusalem, “whose participation is in the same”; where not only each individual, but all together, begin to dwell as one—not merely undivided within themselves, but also undivided from one another.

For, to distinguish what may be called the principal members of the heart itself, there is in us understanding and there is affection; and these frequently oppose one another, so that the one seems to seek what is highest while the other desires what is lowest [Col. 0318A]. How great a pain, how grievous a torment of soul, when it is thus torn apart, thus mangled, thus broken away from itself! Let anyone infer this at least from the rending of the body, which all can readily experience, if he has not neglected to observe it in his own spirit through a ruinous and dangerous insensibility. A person’s legs are pulled apart, and his feet separated from one another by the obstacle of a long piece of wood; and although the skin remains intact, what torment that is!

6. Thus, yes, thus we lament miserable people who live bodily among us, perhaps equally enlightened, but found to have unequal affections. They equally understand the good things they ought to do, but they do not equally love what they understand. For what excuse, brothers, can ignorance offer us, for whom heavenly teaching, divine reading, and spiritual instruction are never absent? “Whatever things are true, whatever things are chaste, whatever things are just, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, if there be any praise of discipline”—these things you learn and receive; these things you alike hear and see in the examples and words of those among you who are perfect, by whose exhortation and manner of life everyone is more fully instructed.

Would that these things, as they admonish understanding [Col. 0318C], might also move affection, lest there be within a most bitter contradiction and a most painful division, while we are drawn upward from one side but pulled downward from the other.

7. Indeed, in nearly all religious communities you can observe people filled with consolation, abounding in joy, always cheerful and glad, fervent in spirit, meditating day and night upon the law of God, often looking up to heaven and lifting pure hands in prayer; scrupulous guardians of conscience and devoted followers of good works. To them discipline is pleasant, fasting sweet, vigils brief, manual labour delightful, and, finally, all the austerity of this manner of life seems refreshment.

Conversely, one finds people faint-hearted [Col. 0318D] and lax, failing under the burden, needing rod and spur; whose joy is weak and whose sadness faint-hearted; whose compunction is brief and rare, whose thought is animal, whose manner of life lukewarm; whose obedience lacks devotion, whose speech lacks circumspection, whose prayer lacks attention of heart, whose reading lacks edification. As we see, scarcely fear of hell restrains them, scarcely shame contains them, scarcely reason checks them, scarcely discipline curbs them. Does not their life seem to you to approach hell completely, since, with understanding resisting affection and affection understanding, they must set their hands [925] to the works of the strong, though they are not sustained by the food of the strong—companions indeed in tribulation but not in consolation?

Let us rise up, I beg, whoever we are that are such; let us repair our souls and recollect our spirit, casting off destructive lukewarmness. If not because it is dangerous and often, as we sometimes lament sorrowfully, provokes God even to vomiting, then at least because it is most burdensome, full of misery and pain, plainly near to hell, and rightly reckoned the shadow of death.

8. If we seek the things above, let us also strive meanwhile to taste and anticipate them. For perhaps the admonition both to seek the things above and to taste them may suitably be applied to understanding and affection, so that by the hands, as it were, of pious effort and spiritual exercise we may strive to raise to God our hearts in their principal members, as was said above.

All of us, unless I am mistaken, seek the things above by the understanding of faith and the judgment of reason [Col. 0319B]; but perhaps we do not all equally taste the things above, being enticed by the things upon earth through a certain violent bias of affection. For whence comes the diversity of dispositions that we showed a little earlier, such disparity of pursuits, such dissimilarity of ways of life? Whence such want of spiritual grace in some, while in others such abundance overflows?

Certainly the distributor of grace is neither miserly nor impoverished; but where empty vessels are lacking, the oil must remain standing. Love of the world presses in from every side. With its consolations—or rather, desolations—it watches for entrances; it rushes in through windows and occupies the mind. But it does not occupy the mind of him who said: “My soul refused to be consoled; I remembered God and was delighted” (Ps. 76:3–4). For holy delight turns aside from a mind already occupied by worldly desires; nor can true things be mingled with vain, eternal things with perishable, spiritual things with bodily, things highest with lowest, so that you might at once taste the things above and the things upon earth.

9. Blessed indeed are those men by whom the Lord’s ascent is read to have been prefigured: Enoch, who was taken up (Sir. 44:16), and Elijah, who was translated (2 Kgs. 2:11). Blessed indeed are those who now live for God alone, are free for him alone in understanding, loving, and enjoying. For corruptible bodies do not weigh down those souls, nor does earthly habitation depress their thoughts as they consider many things; they are known to have walked with God. Every hindrance has been removed, every occasion taken away; no material remains that might weigh down their affection or depress their understanding [Col. 0319D]. For this reason Scripture records that the former was taken up [Note: [Col. 0319D] See above, Sermon 3, no. 2.], “lest wickedness overcome his wisdom, and his understanding or soul be deceived or changed further” (Wis. 4:11).

10. But for us, whence comes truth amid these darknesses, whence love in this wicked age, in this world which lies wholly in the evil one? Do you think there will be one to enlighten understanding and kindle affection? There certainly will be, if we turn to Christ, so that the veil may be removed from our hearts. For this is he of whom it is written: “To those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isa. 9:2).

For God, overlooking the times of former ignorance, announced to human beings that all everywhere should repent, according to Paul’s teaching to the Athenians [Col. 0320A] (Acts 17:30). Remember the Word of God and Wisdom made incarnate. For throughout all the time during which that ineffable power, glory, and majesty deigned to be seen on earth and to live among human beings, its work was to illumine the eyes of the heart and to persuade people to faith by preaching and by the showing of signs alike. Finally, he says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor” (Isa. 61:1). And he said to the apostles: “Yet a little while the light is among you; walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:35).

Nor was it only before his passion, but also after his resurrection, appearing to them over forty days with many proofs and speaking of the kingdom of God [Col. 0320B] (Acts 1:3), that he is read to have opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45). He was shaping their understanding rather than purifying their affection.

11. For how could those who were natural be disposed toward spiritual things? Indeed, they could not even [926] endure the pure light itself to any extent; rather, the Word had to be offered to them in flesh, the sun in a cloud, light in an earthen vessel, honey in wax, a taper in a lantern. Christ the Lord was “the spirit before their face,” yet certainly not without a shadow, in which they might meanwhile live among the nations. Hence he is read also to have overshadowed the Virgin (Luke 1:35), lest, dazzled by a more intense radiance, even the sight of that eagle should be blunted before that most brilliant light and most pure splendour of divinity.

Yet not even the cloud itself could be light and idle [Col. 0320C], but he also used it for salvation. And because the minds of the disciples could neither advance to an understanding of faith without some change of affection nor yet rise to spiritual things, he directed them toward affection for his flesh: so that, with a certain human love, they might cling to the man performing wonders and speaking wonders—still indeed with carnal love, but one so strong that it prevailed over all else.

This was surely Moses’ serpent, which devoured all the serpents of Egypt’s magicians together (Exod. 7:12). Finally, they say: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). Blessed indeed were the eyes that saw the Lord of majesty present in flesh, the author of the universe living among human beings, shining with miracles, healing the sick, walking on the seas [Col. 0320D], raising the dead, commanding demons, and conferring similar power upon human beings; gentle and humble of heart, kind, approachable, abounding in bowels of mercy, the Lamb of God without sin and bearing the sins of all.

Blessed were the ears that were worthy to receive words of life from the mouth of the incarnate Word himself. To them the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, declared and made known whatever he had heard from the Father, so that they might draw streams of heavenly doctrine from the most pure fountain of Truth itself, to be given to drink—indeed, poured forth—to all nations thereafter.

12. What wonder, brethren, if sorrow filled their hearts [Col. 0321A] when he again foretold his departure from them and added: “Where I am going, you cannot come now” (John 8:21)? Why should their inmost feelings not be shaken, their affection disturbed, their minds hesitate, their faces grow fixed, their hearing be alarmed? How could the announcement of his departure be received with any equanimity—that he would leave those who had left everything for him? Yet their whole affection had been gathered to him, not so that it might remain in the flesh, but that it might be transferred to the spirit; so that they might one day say: “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). Therefore that most gracious Master, refreshing them with gentle consolations, said: “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, who may remain with you for ever” [Col. 0321B] (John 14:16); and again: “I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go. For unless I go, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John 16:7).

A great mystery, my brethren. For what does this mean: “Unless I go, the Paraclete will not come”? Was Christ’s presence unwelcome to the Paraclete? Or did the Holy Spirit recoil from fellowship with the Lord’s flesh—flesh which, as we learned from the angel’s announcement, could not even be conceived unless he came upon it? (Luke 1:35.) What, then, does it mean: “Unless I go, the Paraclete will not come”? Unless the presence of the flesh is withdrawn from your sight, a mind already occupied cannot admit the fullness of spiritual grace; the soul does not receive it, the affection cannot contain it.

13. What do you think, brethren? If this is so—indeed, because it is so—will anyone henceforth, given over to certain fantastical allurements, pursuing the seductions of his own flesh—flesh, certainly, that is sinful, born in sins, accustomed to sins, and in which, finally, there is no good—nevertheless dare to expect that Paraclete as well? Will one, I say, who always clings to this dung-heap, who cherishes the flesh, sows in the flesh, savours the flesh, nevertheless dare to hope for that consolation of heavenly visitation, that torrent of delight, that grace of the mighty Spirit which, as Truth itself testifies, not even the apostles could in any way receive while the flesh of the Word itself was present?

He is altogether mistaken if he imagines that heavenly sweetness can be mingled with this ash, that divine balm with this poison, those gifts of the Spirit with such allurements. You are mistaken, holy Thomas, you are mistaken if you hope to see the Lord [Col. 0321D] while separated from the fellowship of the apostles. Truth does not love corners; secluded lodgings do not please her. She stands in the midst; that is, she delights in common discipline and life, in shared pursuits. How long, wretched man, will you seek byways and seek the consolations of your own will with such labour, begging them with such shame? “And what am I to do?” you ask. “Cast out the slave-woman and her son; for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Gen. 21:10). As has been said, there is no fellowship between truth and vanity, light and darkness, spirit and flesh, fire and lukewarmness.

14. “But while he delays,” you will say, “I cannot be without some consolation.” On the contrary, if he delays, wait for him; for he will come and will not be late [Col. 0322A] (Hab. 2:3). The apostles spent ten days in this expectation, persevering with one accord in prayer with the women and Mary, the mother of Jesus (Acts 1:14). You too, therefore, learn to pray; learn to seek, ask, and knock, until you find, until you receive, until it is opened to you. The Lord knows your frame; he is faithful and will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear. I trust in him that, if you wait faithfully, he will not even wait for the tenth day. He will surely anticipate the desolate and praying soul with blessings of sweetness, so that, though he refuses to console you, you may happily—and not foolishly—delight in his remembrance, be made drunk with the abundance of God’s house, and drink from the torrent of his delight.

Thus Elisha too is recorded once to have prayed when he lamented that the exceedingly sweet consolation, the presence of Elijah, was to be withdrawn from him. But consider more carefully what he prayed and what answer was given to his request. “I pray, lord,” he says, “let your spirit be doubled in me.” Clearly, the spirit needed to be doubled in him, so that doubled grace might supply the absence of his departing master. Therefore Elijah said to him: “If you see me when I am taken from you, what you have asked will be done” (4 Kings 2:9–10). The sight of the departing one doubled his spirit, when Elijah, visibly caught up into heaven, carried away all Elisha’s desires with him, so that he too might now begin to savour the things above, not the things upon earth. The sight of the departing one doubled his spirit, so that spiritual affection might be joined to understanding, when the very flesh to which he was chiefly attached was caught up into heaven.

15. This is found more evidently fulfilled in the apostles. [Col. 0322C] For when that Jesus of theirs was so manifestly lifted up before their eyes and borne into heaven that none of them needed to ask, “Where are you going?”, they were taught, as it were, by a faith that had seen with its own eyes, to raise their eyes suppliantly to heaven, stretch out pure hands, and ask for the promised gifts of grace, until there came suddenly from heaven the sound of the coming mighty Spirit—the coming fire which the Lord Jesus was sending upon earth and ardently desiring to be kindled.

Certainly they had received the Spirit earlier, when he breathed upon them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22); but they received plainly the Spirit of faith and understanding, not of fervour: by it reason was more enlightened than affection inflamed. That was the work, indeed, of the doubled Spirit. For the Word of the Father had formerly taught them discipline and wisdom [variant: knowledge], and had filled their hearts with understanding; then the divine fire came, found vessels already cleansed, poured out the gifts of grace more abundantly, and wholly transformed them into spiritual love. Thus charity, kindled in them and strong as death, no longer thought it worthy to shut not merely doors but even their own mouths for fear of the Jews. As we prepare ourselves for this grace according to the measure of our smallness, let us, dearly beloved, endeavour to empty ourselves in every way and to clear our hearts of miserable pleasures and passing consolations; and, especially now as the feast-day approaches, let us persevere more fervently, more confidently, and with one accord in [Col. 0323A] prayer, that the gracious Spirit—the sweet Spirit, the strong Spirit, strengthening the weak, making rough things smooth, purifying hearts—may deign to visit, console, and strengthen us. With the Father and the Son he is the same thing, yet is not the same person: so that the Catholic Church, adopted by the Father, espoused by the Son, and confirmed by the Holy Spirit, may confess most truly and most faithfully that the Three are One and the One is Three [Col. 0324A]; to whom belongs one substance and likewise the same glory for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0323]

## ON THE FEAST OF PENTECOST

### SERMON I. How the Holy Spirit works three things in us

1. Today, dearly beloved, we celebrate the solemnity of the Holy Spirit, to be celebrated with every joy [Col. 0323B] and worthy of every devotion. For the Holy Spirit is something most sweet in God: the goodness of God, and himself God. Therefore, if we celebrate the solemnities of the saints, how much more should we celebrate him from whom all who have been saints received the power to be saints? If we venerate those who have been sanctified, how much more fittingly ought we to honour the Sanctifier himself?

Today, then, is the feast of the Holy Spirit, on which the Invisible One appeared visibly. So too the Son, though he is likewise invisible in himself, deigned to show himself visibly in the flesh. Today the Holy Spirit reveals to us something concerning himself, just as formerly we knew something concerning the Father and the Son; for perfect knowledge of the Trinity is eternal life. But now we know in part; the rest we believe, which we are far from able to comprehend.

Concerning the Father, indeed, I know creation, as the creatures cry: “He made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. 99:3). “For the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are understood through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20). Yet it is beyond me to comprehend his eternity and immutability: he dwells in inaccessible light. Of the Son, however, by his grace I know something great, namely the Incarnation. “For who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8.) Who can comprehend one begotten equal to the begetter? Of the Holy Spirit too, if I do not know the procession by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son—for “this knowledge is wonderful to me; it is strengthened, and I shall not attain to it” (Ps. 138:6)—nevertheless I know something: namely, his inspiration. For there are two matters: whence he proceeds, and whither. His procession from the Father and the Son “has made darkness his hiding-place”; but his procession to human beings began to become known today and is now manifest to believers.

2. At first, indeed—as was fitting—the invisible Spirit declared his coming by visible signs. Now, the more spiritual his signs are, the more fitting they are, and the more worthy they appear of the Holy Spirit. Then he came upon the disciples in tongues of fire, so that they might speak fiery words in the languages of all nations and preach a fiery law with fiery tongues. Let no one complain that this manifestation of the Spirit is not made to us; for “to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness” (1 Cor. 12:7). Indeed, if it must be said, this manifestation was made more for us than for the apostles. For what need had they of the languages of the nations except for the conversion of the nations? There was in them another manifestation more directly relevant to themselves; and this is still made in us today.

It was manifest that those who had come from such faintheartedness of spirit to such constancy had been clothed with power from on high. They no longer fled or hid for fear of the Jews; now they preach more steadfastly than they had formerly hidden in timidity. In short, the fear of the chief of the apostles amid the words of a servant-girl, and later his courage amid the blows of rulers, clearly demonstrates that transformation by the right hand of the Most High. Scripture says: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41). Yet earlier, when he was being led before the council, they had abandoned him and fled. Who can doubt that the mighty Spirit had come, illuminating their minds with invisible power? In this same way, what the Spirit now works in us bears witness [variant added: in us] concerning him.

3. Since, therefore, we have received the command that, turning away from evil, we should do what is good (Ps. 33:13), observe how the Spirit helps our weakness in both respects: “there are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:4). Thus, for turning away from evil, he works three things in us: contrition, supplication, and forgiveness. For repentance is the beginning of returning to God; and without doubt repentance is worked not by our spirit but by God’s Spirit. Both sound reasoning teaches this and authority confirms it.

For who, coming cold to a fire and becoming warmed, would doubt that the warmth which he could not possess without the fire came to him from the fire? Thus, if one formerly cold in iniquity is later kindled with a certain fervour of repentance, let him not doubt that another Spirit has come to him, one that rebukes and judges his own spirit. You have this also in the Gospel, where, speaking of the Spirit whom believers in him would receive, he says: “He will convict the world concerning sin” (John 16:8).

4. But what good is it to repent of guilt and not to pray for pardon? It is necessary that the Spirit also work this, filling the soul with a certain sweetness of hope through which you may ask confidently and without hesitation. Would you have me show you that this too is the work of the Holy Spirit? Certainly, while he is absent, you will not find anything of this kind in your spirit. For he himself is the one in whom we cry, “Abba, Father”; he is the one who intercedes for the saints with unutterable groanings (Rom. 8:15, 26). And these things occur [Col. 0325A] in our heart.

But what does he do in the Father’s heart? As in us he intercedes for us, so in the Father he forgives sins together with the Father: our advocate with the Father in our hearts, our Lord in the Father’s heart. Thus the very one whom we ask grants what we ask, and grants that we may ask. As he raises us by a kind of devout confidence, so by his still more devout mercy he inclines God toward us. Therefore, that you may know fully that the Holy Spirit works forgiveness of sins, hear what the apostles once heard: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20:22). This, then, regarding turning away from evil.

5. But, for doing good, what does the good Spirit work in us? He warns, moves, and teaches [Col. 0325B]. He warns memory, teaches reason, and moves the will. For in these three our whole soul consists. He suggests good things to memory by holy thoughts, and thus drives away our sluggishness and lethargy. Therefore, whenever you perceive in your heart such a suggestion of good, give honour to God and reverence the Holy Spirit, whose voice sounds in your ears. For he is the one who speaks righteousness. And in the Gospel you have that “he will bring to your mind all things whatsoever I have said to you.” Notice what he said beforehand: “He will teach you all things” (John 14:26).

For I said that he teaches reason. Many are indeed admonished to do good, but do not at all know what ought to be done unless the grace of the Holy Spirit is again present, so that he may teach them to bring into action the thought which he inspires, lest the grace of God be empty in us. But what then? “To one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” [variant added: grace] “to him” (Jas. 4:17). Therefore it is necessary not only to be warned and taught, but also to be moved and affected toward good by that Spirit who helps our weakness and through whom charity, which is good will, is poured into our hearts.

6. Therefore, when the Spirit comes in this way and possesses the whole soul—suggesting, instructing, affecting, always speaking in our thoughts, so that we too may hear what the Lord God speaks within us—enlightening reason and inflaming will: does it not seem to you that the divided tongues as of fire have filled the entire house? For above it was said that the whole soul consists in these three things. Let the tongues be divided because thoughts are manifold; but let their multiplicity be, as it were, fire through the one light of truth and the one ardour of charity.

Or rather, let the filling of the house be reserved for the end, when they shall give into our bosoms a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing. But when shall these things be? Certainly, when the days of Pentecost have been fulfilled. Blessed are you who have already entered the fiftieth year of rest and the jubilee year. I speak of our brethren to whom the Spirit has already said that they should rest from their labours. For we find this also among his works.

We celebrate two seasons, brethren: one of Lent, the other of Pentecost. The former is before the Passion; the latter after the Resurrection [Col. 0326A]. The former is in contrition of heart and the lamentations of repentance; the latter in devotion of spirit and the solemn Alleluia. The first season signifies this present life; the latter signifies the rest of the saints after death. But when the end of that Pentecost shall come—namely, at judgment and the resurrection—when the days of Pentecost have been fulfilled, the fullness of the Spirit will be present and will fill the whole house. For the whole earth will be full of his majesty when not only the soul but the very body also rises spiritual, provided that, according to the Apostle’s admonition, while it is still natural it has been sown (1 Cor. 15:44).

### SERMON II. On the works of the Trinity upon us, and on the threefold grace of the Holy Spirit

1. Today, dearly beloved, “the heavens dropped before the God of Sinai, before the God of Israel, and a voluntary rain was set apart for Christ’s inheritance” (Ps. 67:9–10). [Col. 0326B] For the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father, came upon the apostles with a more abundant gift of his majesty and bestowed upon them gifts of grace. After the magnificence of his resurrection, the glory of his ascension, and the sublimity of his enthronement, nothing remained except that the awaited joy [variant: for the expectation] of the righteous should arrive, and heavenly men should be filled with the gifts of heaven.

See whether Isaiah did not long before predict all this both in the weight of his statements and in the sequence of his words. “In that day,” he says, “the Branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth lofty, and an exultation for those who have been saved from Israel” (Isa. 4:2). The Branch of the Lord is Jesus Christ [variant: not the branch of Adam], alone conceived from seed most pure: for though he was in the likeness of sinful flesh, he was not in sinful flesh. Though the son of Adam’s flesh, he was not the son of Adam’s transgression; for he was not by nature a child of wrath like all the rest, who are conceived in iniquities.

This Branch, which sprang from the rod of Jesse in virginal freshness, was in magnificence when he rose from the dead; for then: “O Lord my God, you have been greatly magnified, clothed with confession and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment” (Ps. 103:1–2). But how great was the glory of his ascent, when, in the midst of angels and holy souls, you were led to the Father; when, carried into heaven with the palm of triumph, you enclosed assumed humanity within the very identity of divinity? Who can conceive—much less speak—how lofty is the fruit of the earth in its session at the Father’s right hand: that fruit which overwhelms the eyes of heavenly natures, which the angelic gaze trembles before and cannot attain? Let exultation come, then, Lord Jesus, to those saved from Israel: to your apostles, whom you chose before the foundation of the world. Let your good Spirit come, to wash away filth and pour in virtues, in the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning [variant added: of God].

2. Come then, brethren, let us reflect upon the works of the Trinity over us and within us from the beginning of the world to its end, and see how solicitous that Majesty has been—he upon whom alike rests the administration and governance of the ages [Col. 0327A]—that we should not perish eternally. He had made all things with power and governed all things with wisdom; and most evident signs of both power and wisdom were displayed in the creation and preservation of the structure of the world.

Goodness too was in God—goodness exceedingly abundant—but it lay hidden in the Father’s heart, to be heaped at the fitting time upon the race of Adam’s children. Yet the Lord said: “I think thoughts of peace” (Jer. 29:11), intending to send us him who is our peace, who made the two one, that he might now give “peace upon peace” to those far off, and peace to those near (Eph. 2:14, 17). Therefore the Word of God, established on high, was invited to descend to us by his own kindness, drawn by mercy, compelled by the truth by which he had promised to come, received by the purity of a virgin’s womb without injury to the Virgin’s integrity, brought forth by power, guided in all things by obedience, armed by patience, and manifested by charity in words and miracles.

3. Truly, I now have exceedingly ample material both from my evils and from my Lord’s goods, so that when I have considered my ways I may turn my feet toward his testimonies. Those goods are ineffable because, to sum everything up in one brief statement, the Wisdom of God in all his wisdom could find nothing better by which to redeem us. Yet evils without number had surrounded us, for “I have sinned,” the righteous man says, “beyond the number of the sand of the sea”; and: “For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be merciful to my sin, for it is great” (Ps. 24:11).

The twisting serpent was sent by the devil, to pour venom through the woman’s ear into her mind and thus pour it back into the origin of all her posterity. Meanwhile the angel Gabriel was sent by God, to utter the Word of the Father through the Virgin’s ear into her womb and mind, so that the antidote might enter by the same way through which the poison had entered. Truly we have seen his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, because everything Christ brought to us from the Father’s heart is paternal, so that the trembling human race may suspect nothing in the Son of God except sweetness, except what is paternal. From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there was no health in us. We had gone astray from the womb; condemned in the womb before we were born, because conceived from sin and in sin.

4. Therefore Christ first applied the remedy where the first opening to the wound lay: entering substantially into the Virgin’s womb, he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, so that he might cleanse our conception, which the evil spirit, if he had not made it, had nevertheless infected. Thus even his life in the womb was not idle, while during nine months he cleansed the ancient wound, probing, as it is said, the virulent corruption down to its depths, so that everlasting health might follow. Then he was already working our salvation in the midst of the earth—that is, in the womb of the Virgin Mary, which by a wondrous property is called the middle of the earth [Col. 0328A].

For to her, as to a centre, as to the ark of God, as to the cause of things, as to the business of the ages, look those who dwell in heaven and those in hell, those who preceded us, we who now are, those who shall follow, the children of those children, and those who shall be born from them. Those in heaven look to her that they may be restored; those in hell, that they may be delivered; those who went before, that they may be found to have been faithful prophets; those who follow, that they may be glorified. Therefore all generations shall call you blessed (Luke 1:48), Mother of God, lady of the world, queen of heaven. All generations, I say. For there are generations of heaven and of earth. “The Father of spirits,” says the Apostle, “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. 3:15). Thus all generations shall call you blessed, you who have borne life and glory for all generations. For in you angels find joy, the righteous grace, and sinners pardon [variant: have found] for ever. Rightly do the eyes of all creation look to you, because in you, through you, and from you the gracious hand of the Almighty recreated whatever it had created.

5. “Will it please you, Lord Jesus, to give me your life, as you gave [me] your conception? For not only is my conception unclean, but my death is perverse, my life perilous, and after death a more grievous death remains: the second death.” “Not only my conception,” he says, “but also my life; and this through every stage of age—infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth—I will give to you, adding my death, resurrection, ascension, and sending of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0328C]. This I do so that my conception may cleanse yours, my life instruct yours, my death destroy yours, my resurrection go before yours, my ascension prepare yours, and, moreover, the Spirit help your weakness.

“For thus you will clearly see both the way by which you are to walk, the caution with which you are to walk, and the dwelling toward which you are to walk. In my life you will know your way: just as I kept the undeviating paths of poverty and obedience, humility and patience, charity and mercy, so you too may walk in the same footsteps, turning neither to the right nor to the left. But in my death I will give you my righteousness, breaking the yoke of your captivity and defeating the enemies who are in the way or beside the way, that they may no longer be able to harm you. When these things are completed, I shall return to my house from which I came forth, and to those sheep which remained on the mountains, and which I had left for your sake—not to lead you back, but to carry you back—I shall restore my presence.”

6. “And lest you either complain or grow sorrowful at my absence, I shall send you the Paraclete Spirit, who will give you the pledge of salvation, strength for life, and the light of knowledge. The pledge of salvation: that the Spirit himself may bear witness to your spirit that you are a child of God; that he may impress and show to your heart the most certain signs of your predestination.

> **Note:** [Col. 0327D] He calls the signs “most certain” in the sense in which he speaks in Sermon 2 in the Octave of Easter, no. 3, where “certainty is altogether denied to us.” Compare Sermon 1 in Septuagesima, no. 1: “Certainly we do not possess certainty; [Col. 0328D] but the confidence of hope consoles us … For this reason certain signs and manifest indications of salvation have been given … so that, to those for whom the cause of anxiety denies certainty, the grace of consolation may nevertheless provide confidence.”

“He will give joy in your heart and, from the dew of heaven, if not continually, yet very often enrich your mind [Col. 0329A]. Strength for life: so that what is impossible to you by nature may become through his grace not only possible but even easy; so that amid labours, vigils, hunger and thirst, and all these observances—which, unless this little flour were to sweeten them, would make ‘death in the pot’ plainly appear (4 Kings 4:41)—you may proceed with delight, as amid every abundance. The light of knowledge: so that, when you have done all things well, you may regard yourself as an unprofitable servant; and whatever good you find in yourself, you may attribute it to him from whom comes every good and without whom you can begin—not merely accomplish—nothing at all.”

Thus this Spirit will teach you all things in these three, but all things pertaining to your salvation; for in them lies full and complete perfection.

7. This is what the same Spirit says through the prophet: “Sow for yourselves unto righteousness,” where the pledge of salvation is shown; “reap the hope of life,” where vital strength is received; “make light for yourselves with the light of knowledge” (Hos. 10:12), which he immediately adds in his own words. Therefore this Spirit appeared over the apostles in fire, for both light and ardour. Those whom he fills he causes both to burn in spirit and to know in truth that mercy alone both goes before them and brings them onward.

The servant of the Lord had derived much from this mercy on every side [variant: had made an agreement], when he said: “His mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58:11); “Your mercy is before my eyes” (Ps. 25:3); “Your mercy will follow me all the days of my life” (Ps. 22:6); “Who crowns me in mercy and compassions” (Ps. 102:4); and “My God, my mercy” (Ps. 58:18). How sweetly, Lord Jesus, you lived among human beings! How abundantly you bestowed many and great goods upon them! How resolutely you endured for them things both unworthy and harsh! Thus we may suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone: hard toward words, harder toward blows, hardest toward the horrors of the cross; for in all these things, “as a lamb before one who shears it, he was silent and did not open his mouth.”

You see, then, how truly the one who said, “The Lord is solicitous for me” (Ps. 39:18), spoke. The Father does not spare the Son in order to redeem a servant; the Son most willingly gives himself; both send the Holy Spirit; and the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings.

8. O hard, hardened, and obdurate children of Adam, whom so great a kindness does not soften—such a flame, such immense ardour of love, such a vehement lover, who spends such precious merchandise for worthless little burdens! For he redeemed us not with corruptible gold or silver, but with his precious blood, which he poured out abundantly; for copious streams of blood flowed from the body of Jesus through five parts. What more ought he to have done and did not do? He enlightened the blind, brought back the wandering, reconciled the guilty, justified the ungodly; for thirty-three years he was seen upon earth and lived among human beings; he died for human beings—he who spoke concerning cherubim and seraphim and all angelic powers, “and they were made,” and to whom, whenever he wills, all power is subject [Col. 0330A].

What, then, does he seek from you, he who sought you with such solicitude, except that you should walk solicitously with your God? Only the Holy Spirit produces this solicitude: he searches the depths of our hearts, discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart, and suffers not even the smallest straw to remain within the dwelling-place of the heart that he possesses, but immediately burns it away with the fire of most subtle watchfulness. He is the sweet and gracious Spirit, who bends—indeed, raises—and more truly directs our will toward his own, so that we may understand it truly, love it fervently, and fulfil it effectively.

### SERMON III. On the manifold working of the Holy Spirit in us

1. The Spirit himself knows how willingly I would share with you whatever I perceive has been inspired in me by heavenly condescension—the Spirit whose solemnity, and a most eminent solemnity, we celebrate today, if only with most eminent devotion. For he is, dearly beloved, the one who causes you to sit not only in one city but also in one house, so that he may sit upon those who sit and rest upon the humble and those who tremble at his words [Col. 0330B]. He is the one who overshadowed the Virgin and strengthened the apostles, both tempering the access of divinity to the virginal body and clothing the apostles with power from on high—namely, most fervent charity.

That apostolic choir put on this charity as a breastplate, like a giant, “to execute vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples; to bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron manacles” (Ps. 149:7–8). Since they were sent to bind the strong man in his house and plunder his goods, a greater strength was necessary. Otherwise, how could they triumph over death, and how could not even the gates of hell prevail against them, unless there flourished in them a love strong as death, an ardour hard as hell, which would conquer within them? They had drunk in this zeal when they were thought drunk with wine (Acts 2:13). And truly they were drunk with wine, but not with the wine by which unbelievers thought them drunk. Yes, they were drunk—but with new wine, which old wineskins neither deserved to receive nor could contain.

For that true Vine had poured down this wine from on high: wine gladdening the heart, not overthrowing the mind’s composure; wine producing virgins, not causing even the wise to apostatize. New wine—but for those dwelling upon earth. For in heaven it had long overflowed most abundantly, not in wineskins or earthen vessels, but in the wine-cellar, in spiritual storehouses. Wine flowed through all the streets and lanes of that city: wine in which there is joy of heart, not the luxury of the flesh. For earthborn people and children of humankind did not possess such wine.

2. Thus heaven enjoyed its own wine, which earth meanwhile did not know; yet earth itself was not wholly impoverished, for it gloried in Christ’s flesh, whose presence heaven likewise longed for. Why should there not be a most faithful and welcome exchange between heaven and earth, between angels and apostles—so that Christ’s flesh might be given to the former and heaven’s wine to the latter, the Spirit might be upon earth and the flesh in heaven, and thereafter all things be shared by all for ever? “Unless I go,” he says, “the Paraclete will not come to you.” This is to say: If you do not give up what you love, you will not have what you desire. Therefore “it is expedient for you that I go” (John 16:7), so as to transfer you also from earth to heaven, from flesh to spirit.

For the Son is spirit, the Father is spirit, and the Holy Spirit is spirit. Indeed, “Christ the Lord is spirit before our face.” The Father too, because he is spirit, seeks such worshippers as worship him in spirit and truth. Yet the Holy Spirit is called Spirit in a special manner because he proceeds from both, the most firm and indissoluble bond of the Trinity; and properly Holy because he is the gift of the Father and the Son, sanctifying every creature. Nevertheless the Father too is both spirit and holy; and likewise the Son is both spirit and holy: “From whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things,” says the Apostle (Rom. 11:36).

3. In the great work of this world we should consider three things: what it is, how it is, and for what end it has been established. The inestimable power inherent in things is displayed in the fact that so many, so great, and so manifold things have been created so magnificently. Certainly, singular wisdom shines out in the very manner of it: that some things are set above, others below, others in the middle, in the most orderly arrangement. But if you reflect upon the end for which it was made, there comes to mind such useful goodness, such gracious utility, as can overwhelm even the most ungrateful people by the multitude and magnitude of its benefits [Col. 0331C]. For all things have been created most powerfully from nothing, most wisely beautiful, and most graciously useful.

Nevertheless, we know that from the beginning there were, and still see that among the children of humankind there are many, who, wholly weighed down by their sensuality in the lower goods of this sensible world, have given themselves wholly to created things, neglecting how they were made or for what end they were made. What should we call these but carnal people? I suppose that they are now very few. Yet we read that there were at times some whose chief study and sole concern was to investigate the mode and order of created things, so much so that many of them not only neglected to seek the usefulness of things, but even magnanimously despised the things themselves, content with food most scanty and cheap. They call themselves philosophers; but we more rightly call them curious and vain.

4. There then succeeded to both kinds of men others wiser than either: men who, passing beyond both what had been made and how it had been made, fixed the eye of the mind upon seeing for what purpose it had been made. Nor was it hidden from them that God made all things for himself, all things for his own. Yet in one way for himself, in another for his own. For in the saying, “The Lord has made all things for himself” (Prov. 16:4), the originating cause, which comes first, is commended; whereas in the saying, “All things for his own,” the resulting fruit is more clearly expressed. He made all things for himself, that is, out of gratuitous goodness; all things for his elect, namely for their benefit: so that the former is the efficient cause, the latter [Col. 0332A] the end. These are spiritual men: they use this world as though not using it, but seek God in simplicity of heart, without greatly investigating even the manner in which this worldly mechanism is turned. The first kind are filled with pleasure, the second with vanity, the third with truth.

5. I rejoice that you belong to this school—the school, that is, of the Spirit—where you learn goodness, discipline, and knowledge, and say with the saint: “I have understood more than all who teach me.” Why, I ask? Is it because I clothed myself in purple and fine linen, or because I abounded in more sumptuous feasts? Is it because I understood Plato’s subtleties and Aristotle’s sophistries, or laboured to understand them? Far from it, I say; rather, because “I have sought out thy testimonies” (Ps. 118:99). Blessed is the person who dwells in this bridal chamber of the Holy [Col. 0332B] Spirit, so as to understand that threefold spirit of which the same servant of God, understanding more than the elders, cried aloud and sang:

> “Cast me not away from thy presence,  
> and take not thy holy spirit from me.  
> Create in me a clean heart, O God,  
> and renew a right spirit within me.  
> Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation,  
> and strengthen me with a principal spirit”  
> (Ps. 50:12–14).

Understand “the Holy Spirit” as designated by his proper name. He therefore asks that he not be cast from God’s presence as something unclean, because this Spirit hates filth and cannot dwell in a body subject to sins. For he whose special work it is to repel sins has also the special characteristic of hating sins; such purity and such impurity will not dwell together in one habitation. Having therefore received [Col. 0332C] the Holy Spirit through holiness, without which no one shall see God, a person dares to appear before his face as washed and clean—if only he keeps himself from every evil and restrains his actions, even though not his thoughts.

6. But because perverse and unclean thoughts separate us from God (Wis. 1:3), we must pray that a clean heart may be created in us. This will surely happen if a right spirit has been renewed within us.
