The “right spirit” of which he speaks may fittingly be applied to the Son, who strips us of the old man and clothes us with the new; who has renewed us in the spirit of our mind, as it were in our inward parts, so that we may think what is right, walk in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter. For he brought from heaven the pattern of uprightness [Col. 0332D] and left it on earth, indeed mingling and imparting sweetness to uprightness in all his works, as the same Psalmist had foretold of him: “The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he will give a law to those who stray in the way” (Ps. 24:8). Therefore, once the body has been chastened through holiness of works, and the heart cleansed—or rather renewed—through the uprightness of thoughts, the joy of salvation is restored, so that you now walk in the light of God’s countenance and exult in his name all the day.

7. What then remains except that you be strengthened by a principal spirit? Understand the Father as the principal spirit: not because he is greater, but because he alone is from no one; whereas the Son is from him, and the Holy Spirit from both. And in what does this strengthening consist, if not in charity? Or what other gift is so worthy of the Father? What other present is so fatherly? [Col. 0333A] “Who,” says the Apostle, “shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or peril? Or persecution? Or the sword?” Be assured that neither death nor life, nor any of the other things which the Apostle so copiously and boldly enumerates, will be able to separate us from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:35, 38–39). Does this not demonstrate strengthening in every part of the sentence?

Do you know how to possess your vessel in sanctification and honour, and not in the passion of desire? You have received the Holy Spirit for yourself. Do you wish to do to others whatever you wish people to do to you, and not to do to another what you do not wish done to you? You have received the right spirit for your neighbour’s benefit. For this is the uprightness commended by both laws: the law implanted in nature and that handed down through Scripture. But if you persevere firmly in both goods, and in what belongs to each of them, you have received the principal spirit, which God alone approves. Otherwise, he who truly is does not accept things which now are and now are not; nor can eternity find delight for itself in these perishable things. Therefore, if you desire that God may choose in you a portion for himself, take care, as you render the Holy Spirit to yourself and the right spirit to your neighbour, to render also to him—the true ruler and Father of spirits—the principal spirit.

8. Truly manifold is the Spirit, who is breathed into the children of men in so many ways, so that there is none who can hide from his heat. For he is granted for use, for miracle, for salvation, for help, for consolation, [Col. 0333C] and for fervour.

For the use of life, he most abundantly grants common goods to good and evil alike, worthy and unworthy alike, [Col. 0334A] so that here he seems not to observe the bounds of discrimination. Ungrateful is the person who does not acknowledge the Spirit’s benefit even in these things. He is given for miracle in signs and wonders, in diverse powers, which he works through the hands of any persons whatsoever. He is the one who raises up ancient miracles, in order to establish faith in past events from present ones. But because he grants even this grace to some without their own benefit, he is imparted thirdly for salvation, when we return to the Lord our God with our whole heart.

Further, he is given for help when, in every struggle, he assists our weakness. For when the Spirit bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God, that inspiration is for consolation. He is also given for fervour when, breathing more forcefully in the hearts of the perfect, he kindles the mighty [Col. 0334B] fire of charity: so that they glory not only in the hope of being children of God, but also in tribulations, reckoning insult as glory, reproach as joy, and contempt as exaltation.

The Spirit has been given to all of us, I think, for salvation; not so for fervour. For few are those who are filled with this Spirit; few who strive to emulate it. We are content with our distresses and do not attempt to breathe freely in that liberty, or even at least to aspire toward it. Let us pray, brothers, that in us may be fulfilled the days of Pentecost: days of remission, days of exultation, days of the truest jubilee; and that the Holy Spirit may always find us all in one place, both through bodily presence and through unity of hearts, by our promised steadfastness, to the praise and glory of Jesus Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0333]

## FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST. SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0333D] This sermon is appended in certain manuscripts to the nineteen sermons of Nicholas of Clairvaux, dedicated to Henry, Count of Troyes; but in no fewer manuscripts, nor in manuscripts of inferior authority, is it attributed to Bernard [Col. 0334D]. It also appears in the Flowers from Bernard collected four hundred years ago by William, monk of Tournai, as we said in the Preface to this volume.]

On David and Goliath, and the five stones. (1 Kings 17:40.)

[Col. 0333C]

1. We have heard from the book of Kings that Goliath, a man of towering stature, presuming upon his great strength and bodily size, shouted against the ranks of Israel and challenged them to single combat. We have heard likewise that God stirred the spirit of a younger boy, so that he could not bear that a spurious and uncircumcised man should reproach the camp of Israel and the armies of the most high God. We watched [Col. 0333D] the young man advance with sling and stone against a man of monstrous size, armoured and protected by shield and helmet, and made terrible by his other military weapons. If there was any compassion within us, we could not help fearing for one who entered upon so unequal a contest, nor rejoicing with the victor. We praised the courage of the little one, because zeal for the house of God consumed his soul, and he did not regard as alien to himself the reproaches of those who reproached God; rather, he was moved as if by a personal injury and grieved over [Col. 0334C] the crushing of Joseph. We marvelled at such confidence in an adolescent, confidence not found in all Israel. Finally, we received with as much gladness the victory granted from heaven and manifestly wrought by divine power as we had watched with anxiety the contest between the child armed with faith and the giant glorying in his own strength.

2. Now, if we do not fail to know, on the Apostle’s testimony, that the law is spiritual [Col. 0334D] (Rom. 7:14), and was written for us not merely that we might be delighted by the sight of its outward surface, but also that our inward senses might be fed by its taste, like the kernel of wheat, we must consider who this Goliath may be. He alone presumes to reproach the people of God, now entered into the land of promise and already triumphant over many enemies, being lifted up and puffed up by the spirit of his flesh. I believe that, not inappropriately, the vice of pride is signified in this proud man. For it is the greatest sin, which most insults the people of God and rises especially against those who seem already to have conquered their other sins. Hence he challenges them to single combat, as though the others had already been subdued. For at that time the Philistines altogether feared to enter into conflict with Israel, except that all their confidence depended on Goliath, a man of enormous size.

For why should pride tempt a soul such as has been brought under the yoke of envy, or of that lukewarmness which is accustomed to provoke God to vomit (Rev. 3:16), or of sloth, which causes one to be stoned with ox-dung? (Ecclus. 22:2). Why, I say, should pride tempt such a person? Why should haughtiness of eyes tempt one so ruled by other vices that, conscious of evil within himself, he thinks himself judged by all? Finally, who but one strong of hand, who has already subdued the other vices through mighty strength, should come forward to fight against the most wicked vice of pride? Let David, strong of hand, come forward; for so mighty an enemy cannot be conquered except by a strong hand. Let him who has conquered both bear and lion arm himself against Goliath.

3. Let him see whether Saul’s armour can help him; whether by secular wisdom and philosophical traditions, [Col. 0335B] or even by the outward surface of the divine Scriptures—which the Apostle calls the killing letter (2 Cor. 3:6)—he can defeat pride or attain humility. Let him feel himself burdened rather than strengthened by these arms, cast aside such weapons and encumbrances, cast all his thought upon the Lord, despair utterly of his own ability, and, armed with faith alone, not take account of Goliath’s stature, lest he be crushed beneath the weight of that great size. Rather, let him sing with the spirit and sing also with the mind: “The Lord is the defender of my life; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. 26:1).

For Peter too, while he considered neither the violence of the winds, nor the depths of the sea, nor the weight of his body, but cast himself upon the Lord’s word, could neither perish nor fear. But when he saw the strong wind coming, he was afraid, and through that very fear immediately began to sink (Matt. 14:28–30). Even now King Saul seeks to suggest something similar to our athlete: “You cannot,” he says, “resist this Philistine or fight against him, because you are a boy, whereas he has been a warrior from his youth.” Yet David does not consent to entertain such a thought. Rather, trusting in the power of him by whose help he had already conquered earlier contests, he approaches without fear.

Therefore, having cast off Saul’s armour, he gathers five stones from the torrent. The torrent could polish them, since it carried off whatever was light, but could not carry the stones away with it. For the torrent—which may our soul pass beyond!—is the present age, Scripture bearing witness: “One generation comes and another passes away” (Eccl. 1:4), like a swelling wave filling another wave. Since all flesh is grass and all its glory like the flower of the field, this flooding torrent readily carries away such light things. But the word of the Lord, yielding to no waves, remains for ever (Isa. 40:6, 8).

4. Therefore I think that these five stones may not unfittingly be understood as the fivefold word: of threat, promise, love, imitation, and prayer. A widely extended abundance of these five words is found throughout the sequence of the divine Scriptures. Perhaps these are the very five words of which Paul speaks, when he prefers to speak five words with understanding rather than ten thousand in a tongue (1 Cor. 14:19). For “the fashion of this world passes away” (1 Cor. 7:31); and according to another testimony, “the world passes away, and its desire” (1 John 2:17). Yet these words not only remain while the world passes away, but are even more polished [Col. 0336B] as more people pass through, and knowledge becomes manifold.

David, preparing to fight against the spirit of pride, should place these gathered stones in the vessel of his memory, considering how great are God’s threats to us, how great his promises, how great the charity he shows us, how many examples of holiness he sets before us, and finally how everywhere he commends to us persistence in prayer. Whoever hastens to defeat the vice of pride should take these stones with him. Whenever it dares to raise its poisonous head, let whichever of these stones first comes to hand—the hand of thought—strike it; then Goliath, struck in the forehead, will fall, covered with shame. In this conflict the sling also is necessary: it bears the form of long-suffering, which by no means can be lacking especially in this contest.

5. Therefore, whenever a thought of vanity strikes the mind, if from an inward affection of heart you begin to fear God’s threats or desire his promises, Goliath cannot endure the blow [alternate reading: cast] of either stone, but all swelling is immediately repressed. But if that ineffable love which the God of majesty has shown you comes to mind, do you not immediately, inflamed toward charity, begin utterly to abhor and reject vanity? Likewise, if you set before yourself the examples of the saints with diligent reflection, this thought will without doubt be very useful for repressing exaltation. But if, when sudden self-exaltation rises, your hand cannot grasp any of the things we have said, turn with all fervour to the one remedy that remains—prayer. Immediately the wicked man whom you had seen lifted up and exalted like the cedars of Lebanon will be overthrown and be no more.

6. But perhaps you ask how you can cut off Goliath’s head with his own sword; for this is all the more pleasing to you, as it is distressing to the enemy. I shall say it briefly, because I speak to those who have experienced it and who can readily grasp and observe without delay what they frequently feel at work in themselves. Whenever, prompted by vanity, you begin to be confounded and ashamed through remembering the divine threats, promises, or the other matters mentioned above, [Col. 0337A] Goliath has indeed been conquered [alternate reading: cast down], but perhaps he still lives. Come nearer, therefore, lest he rise again; stand over him and cut off his head with his own blade, killing vanity by the very vanity that attacks you. For if, assailed by an exalted thought, [Col. 0338A] you draw from that very thought material and occasion for humility, so that henceforth you think of yourself more humbly and lowly, as of a proud person, you have surely slain Goliath with Goliath’s sword.

[Col. 0337]

## SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

### SERMON I. On the Gospel reading in which the crowd, having remained with the Lord for three days, is fed with seven loaves (Mark 8:19).

[Col. 0337A]

1. “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now remained with [Col. 0337B] me for three days and have nothing to eat.” Brothers, the Gospel was written so that it might be read; and it is read for no other reason than that we may receive from it rational consolation or desolation. Worldly people have a vain consolation in the abundance of earthly things and an equally vain desolation in their scarcity. But the Gospel, the mirror of truth, flatters no one and deceives no one. Each person will find himself in it exactly as he is: he will neither tremble in fear where there is no fear nor rejoice when he has acted wrongly.

But what does Scripture say? “If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man considering the face of his birth in a mirror. For he considered himself, went away, and immediately forgot what sort of person he was” (Jas. 1:23–24). But we, brothers—let it not be so, I beseech you, let it not be so! Let us consider ourselves in the reading of the holy Gospel which we have heard, so that we may profit by it and amend, in accordance with it, anything we discover in ourselves that needs amendment. For this reason the Prophet desires that his ways be directed to keep the Lord’s ordinances: “Then,” he says, “I shall not be confounded, when I look upon all thy commandments” (Ps. 118:5–6).

For my part, I am not confounded, but glory on your behalf, my brothers, because, having followed the Saviour into the wilderness, you confidently go out to him beyond the camp. Yet I fear lest someone perhaps be found faint-hearted during the three-day waiting, and return to the Egypt of this wicked world either in heart or even in body. Divine Scripture therefore rightly cries aloud and says: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let thy heart be strengthened; and wait for the Lord” (Ps. 26:14). But how long must one wait? Precisely until he has compassion on you. Do you ask when? “I have compassion on the crowd,” he says, “because they have now remained with me for three days.”

2. For you must travel a three-day journey in the wilderness if you wish to offer an acceptable sacrifice to your God; and you must remain with the Saviour for three days if you desire to be satisfied with the loaves of miracle. The first is the day of fear: the day, I say, which reveals and illuminates your inner darkness and displays the dreadful punishment of Gehenna, where outer darkness is found. Such reflection, as you yourselves know, is accustomed to exercise the beginnings of our conversion.

The second is the day of devotion, in which we breathe again in the light of God’s mercies. The third is the day of reason, in which truth becomes known, so that the creature may be subject to the Creator, as by a certain debt of nature and without any contradiction, and the servant may serve the Redeemer. Thereafter we are commanded to recline, so that charity may be ordered within us; thereafter the Lord opens his hand and fills every living thing with blessing.

But because the apostles are told, “Make the people recline,” and you have us as their representatives, however unworthy we are—to our shame—we urge you, dearest brothers, to recline, so that, refreshed by the bread of blessing, you may be able to continue on the way. Otherwise, compelled by wretched necessity, you too may descend into Egypt, and those who have not yet followed the Saviour with you into the wilderness may begin to mock you. Wretched indeed are those who did not go out with those who went out; but plainly more wretched than all people are those who set out with others but are not refreshed with them.

3. Further, if there were any who, while the others reclined, lay hidden behind thickets or in whatever shelters, who does not know that such persons remained hungry and empty? So too those who, led by frivolity and curiosity, wandered about in every direction and did not sit down; or those who did sit down, but not in order or among the number of the others. We therefore exhort your charity and warn you with pastoral concern that none of you may be found loving corners, pursuing hiding places, or seeking side paths. For “he who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved” (John 3:20).

Nor let there be among you persons carried about by every wind of doctrine, unstable and restless, having no solidity and no gravity in themselves, like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth. For what shall I say of those whose hand is against everyone and everyone’s hand against them? These are those who separate themselves, animal persons, not having the Spirit; for no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Jesus be accursed” (1 Cor. 12:3). This is an utterly wicked and most destructive plague: the obstinacy of one person disturbs all, becoming for all a source of discord and material for scandals. Hear, finally, the Prophet speaking of the Lord’s vineyard: “The solitary wild beast has devoured it” (Ps. 79:14).

For such conduct I ask and beseech you, my brothers: flee every pretense and the corners of self-will; flee restlessness and the spirit of frivolity; flee obstinacy and the most wicked vice of singularity—unless, God forbid, you wish to deprive your souls of the food of the blessed bread.

4. Now, not to detain you longer, these are the seven loaves by which you are refreshed. The first loaf is the word of God, in which is human life, as he himself testifies (Luke 4:4). The second loaf is obedience, for “my food,” he says, “is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34). The third loaf is holy meditation, concerning which it is written: “Holy thought will preserve you” (Prov. 4:6); and elsewhere it seems likewise to be called the bread of life and understanding (Ecclus. 15:3). The fourth loaf is the tears of those who pray. The fifth is the labour of repentance. Nor should you wonder that I have called labour or tears bread, unless perhaps you have forgotten what you read in the Prophet: “Thou wilt feed us with the bread of tears” (Ps. 79:6); and likewise in another psalm: “Because thou shalt eat the labours of thy hands, thou art blessed, and it shall be well with thee” (Ps. 127:2).

The sixth loaf is the pleasant unanimity of fellowship: bread, I say, made from diverse grains and leavened by the grace of God [alternate reading: indeed, the wisdom of God]. The seventh loaf is the Eucharist, for “the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52).

[Note: [Col. 0339D] Here the thirty-sixth sermon and the following three sermons *On Various Subjects* are inserted in the manuscripts, except in the Cistercian codex, where it is noted that they should be transferred among the *Various Subjects*. The following two sermons on the seven mercies vary considerably in old books; but this variation does not alter the sense.]

### SERMON II. On the seven mercies.

1. “I shall sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord” (Ps. 88:2). Why does some foolish thought, I know not what, murmur to me about the burden of this repentance [Col. 0339C], to make it heavy upon my neck? I feel another burden, indeed gentler but everywhere much greater. For God so burdens me with his mercies, so encloses me, so overwhelms me with his benefits, that I cannot feel any other burden. “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” He gives so much, and renders so much; and you speak to me of another burden? My spirit fails—utterly fails—under the consideration of such great benefits. Although I am unable to offer adequate thanks, my soul utterly hates ingratitude.

For ingratitude is a deadly thing: an enemy of grace and a foe of salvation. I tell you, beloved, that in my judgment nothing displeases God so much, especially in children of grace and people of conversion, as ingratitude. For it blocks the paths of grace; where it is present, grace finds no entrance and has no place. Hence, brothers, I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart because I see some so prone to frivolity, so readily given to laughter, idle words, and buffoonery, that I greatly fear lest, perhaps, remembering the divine mercy less than is fitting and being ungrateful for so many benefits, they may one day be abandoned [Col. 0340A] by the grace which they do not revere [alternate reading: possess] as grace.

2. What, then, shall I say of one who persists in grumbling and impatience with an obstinate mind; or who regrets having adhered to God, and whose good action, contrary to custom and reason, is attended by repentance? Such a person undoubtedly not only fails to give thanks for God’s mercies, but returns insult. For, so far as he can, anyone who remains in sadness and resentment in God’s service dishonours the one who called him. I mean that sadness which is according to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0340D] In other copies: “He little honours … whoever serves him in sadness and resentment,” if indeed one can serve in that sadness which is according to the flesh.], and works death. Do you think, then, that greater grace will be given to him? Will not even what he seems to have rather be taken away? Is not what has been given to an ungrateful person rightly reckoned as lost? Or does one not regret having given what seems to have perished?

A person must therefore be grateful and devout if he desires that the gifts of grace received may not only remain with him but also be multiplied. Certainly, no one who seeks will fail easily to find grounds for being greatly indebted to God, since there is none who hides from his heat. But especially we, whom he has set apart for himself and taken up to serve himself alone, if, in accordance with the Apostle, we receive not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things given to us by God (1 Cor. 2:12), shall surely find very many grounds for giving him continual thanks. For who among us cannot confess: “Thy mercy is great upon me”? Therefore, from so great a multitude of the Lord’s mercies, I wish briefly to set some before you, so that one who is wise may, on receiving the occasion, become wiser.

3. I see seven mercies of the Lord in myself, which I believe you yourselves will readily find in yourselves. The first is that, while I was still in the world, he preserved me from many sins. First, I say, not among all the mercies he has bestowed on me, but first among these seven. For who does not see that, as I fell into many sins, so I would have fallen into other sins also unless the compassion of the Almighty had preserved me? I confess, and shall confess, that unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have fallen into every sin. And how great was this condescension of compassion: that grace preserved one who was ungrateful and disdainful, and, although in many things opposed and contemptuous, most graciously protected him from other sins! But, O Lord, by what words can your second mercy toward me be explained—how kindly, how generously, and how gratuitously it was bestowed? I sinned, and you overlooked it; I did not refrain from crimes, and you refrained from punishment. I prolonged my iniquity for a long time, and you, O Lord, prolonged your mercy. But what would waiting avail unless repentance followed? It would be an accumulation of condemnation, the Lord saying: “You did these things, and I was silent” (Ps. 49:21).

4. Therefore the third mercy was that he visited and changed my heart, so that things once wickedly sweet became bitter; and I, who rejoiced when I did evil and exulted in most evil things, began at last to recall my years to him in the bitterness of my soul. And now, Lord, you have shaken the earth of my heart and troubled it; heal its breaches, for it has been shaken. For many have been led to repentance, but fruitlessly, because even their repentance was rejected, just as their former fault was. Thus the fourth mercy was this: that you mercifully received me as I repented, so that I might be found among those of whom [Col. 0341B] the Psalmist says: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31:1).

5. The fifth mercy follows, through which you granted me thereafter the power of continence and of living more rightly, lest I suffer relapse and the last error be worse than the first. For it is manifestly, O Lord God, a work of your power and not human strength to shake from one’s neck the yoke of sin once assumed; because “everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34), and one cannot be freed except by a strong hand.

But after you have delivered us from evil through these five mercies, that what is written may come about, “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. [Col. 0341C] 33:15), you grant good things in two others. These two are: the grace of meriting, by which you grant the practice of a good manner of life; and the hope of attaining, by which you give to an unworthy and sinful person, from your goodness so often experienced, the boldness to hope even for heavenly things.

### SERMON III. On the fragments of the seven mercies.

1. Do you know what I have done in setting the seven mercies before you today? I have distributed seven loaves. For if my tears became bread to me day and night, how much more the divine mercies? These have a far sweeter taste, refresh much better, and strengthen the human heart more abundantly. Yet many fragments, I think, fell for us today from these loaves. For I myself felt, while breaking them, that many crumbs escaped from my hands and slipped between the fingers of one hurrying. Whether you yourselves collected any, you must see. But I, if you are not yet weary of them, shall without envy share the fragments that I had gathered, lest perhaps I incur the curse pronounced upon one who hides grain from the people (Prov. 11:26).

The first loaf, if I remember correctly, was the preserving grace that, although I was unworthy and still living in the world, kept me altogether from many sins. Of this loaf I retain three fragments, possessing a great delight of taste and nourishment of life. For I remember that I was preserved from sin in three ways: by the removal of opportunity, by strength given to resist, and by soundness of affection. I would easily have fallen into many sins if opportunity had been given; but, through God’s mercy, such an occasion did not overtake me. I would also almost have fallen into many sins, violently impelled by the force of temptation; but the Lord, the King of powers, gave strength, so that my desire was subject to me and I did not consent to the concupiscence I felt. But from some sins your mercy, O Lord, removed me so far that I utterly abhorred them, and no temptation from them troubled me at all.

2. The second loaf also was waiting, by which he delayed punishment because he intended forgiveness. Receive then three fragments of this loaf, reflecting on the long-suffering he displayed, the election of his predestination which he willed to fulfil, and the exceeding charity with which he loved me. For this reason the Lord waited and waited for me; he did not look upon me, but turned his eyes from my sins, as though unwilling to notice how greatly I offended. For this reason, I say, he overlooked them: that he might commend his patience, fulfil his election, and confirm his charity.

3. From the third loaf also—that mercy, namely, by which he turns us to repentance—I set before you three portions rather than fragments. For then, as I remember well, he shook my heart, rousing it to notice the wounds [Col. 0342C] of its sins and to feel the pain of its wounds. He also terrified it, leading it to the gates of hell and showing the punishments prepared for the wicked. And so that no harmful pleasure might remain, he breathed into me a better consolation and gave hope of forgiveness. In these three ways, therefore, I was converted; I believe that you were also.

4. Now, as to the fourth bread—indulgence itself—I beg you to gather up its fragments carefully, lest they perish. For they are exceedingly wholesome, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Thus indeed he forgave wholly, and remitted every injury so generously that he neither condemns by punishing, nor shames by reproaching, nor loves less by imputing it. For some forgive an injury in such a way as not to avenge it, yet they reproach it repeatedly. Others too, although they remain silent, nevertheless keep it stored deep in their mind and retain resentment in their heart: neither of these is full forgiveness. Far removed from all such things is the most gracious nature of the Godhead [Col. 0342D]. It acts generously and forgives completely, so that, because of the confidence of sinners who repent, where transgression has abounded, grace is accustomed to abound still more.

Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, is a witness—he who laboured more than all others, yet with divine grace. Matthew is a witness, chosen from the tax-office to be an apostle, and to whom was also granted the distinction of being the first writer of the New Testament. Peter too is a witness: after his threefold denial, the pastoral care of the whole Church was entrusted to him. Finally, that most renowned sinful woman is also a witness: at the very beginning of her conversion so great an abundance of love was granted her, and afterwards so great a grace of intimacy bestowed. Who accused Mary, so that she herself needed to answer? If the Pharisee murmurs, if Martha complains, if the apostles are scandalized, Mary is silent; Christ [Col. 0343A] defends her and even praises her silence. Finally, what a privilege, what an excellence it was, that she deserved to be the first to see, and the first to touch, him risen from the dead!

[Note: [Col. 0343] Here Magdalene is confused with Mary, Lazarus’s sister, and with the sinful woman, as in Sermon 2 on the Assumption. Bernard’s authorship is doubtful in Sermon 12 on the Song of Songs.]

5. But now let us pass on to other things. It is indeed good for us to be here, where confidence is given to sinners; yet the remaining matters must not be passed over in silence. Thus even in continence itself, which is the fifth bread, I nevertheless find three things from which I may rightly cry out: “For he who is mighty has done great things for me” (Luke 1:49). Perhaps you regard your continence as something slight; but I do not. For I know what assailants it has, and how great the strength must be by which it can withstand such enemies.

The first enemy of our continence is the flesh, which lusts against the spirit. What a domestic enemy! What a dangerous struggle! What an inward war! This most cruel enemy, O my soul, we can neither flee nor drive away. We must carry it about with us, because it is bound to us; for, what is more dangerous and more pitiable, we are compelled ourselves to sustain our enemy, though we are not permitted to kill it. See, therefore, how watchfully you must guard yourself against her who sleeps in your bosom.

Yet this is not my only adversary; I still have another, which has surrounded and besieged me on every side. And, if you do not know it, that enemy is this present evil age. The enemy has shut up my ways, and through five gates—that is, the five bodily senses—wounds me with his darts [alternate reading: “attacks me”]; and death enters through my windows. These two could more than suffice; but, [Col. 0343C] alas for me, behold, I see a mighty wind coming from the north, from which every evil is opened up. And what remains now but this: “Lord, save us; we are perishing” (Matthew 8:25)?

For behold the hammer of the whole earth; behold the serpent, more cunning than every living creature; behold that enemy whom I cannot even see—how much less can I beware of him! For those who wish to preserve continence do not wrestle merely against flesh and blood. By continence I mean continence not only from lust, but also, as is necessary, from other vices and sins. Their wrestling is not against flesh and blood alone, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Ephesians 6:12). And who can extinguish their fiery darts [Col. 0343D]? For they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart (Psalm 10:3); they have also spoken in order to hide snares, and have said, “Who will see them?” (Psalm 64:6).

At one time openly and violently, at another secretly and deceitfully, but always maliciously and cruelly, they [Col. 0344A] attack and persecute us. And who is fit to endure these things—much less to overcome them? I believe that the difficulty of continence is now becoming somewhat known to you, so that, in the Apostle’s words, you may know the things given to you by God (1 Corinthians 2:12). For we perform this virtue wholly in the Lord, and he brings to nothing those who afflict us. He is the one who crushes beneath our feet not only our flesh with its desires, but also this present evil age with its curiosities and vanities, and even Satan himself with his temptations. Was I not right to say that in continence there is something from which I might cry: “For he who is mighty has done great things for me”?

6. Now receive the fragments of the sixth bread. This bread is the grace of meriting, namely, the good things [Col. 0344B] of eternal life. I judge that this grace consists chiefly in three things: hatred of past evils, contempt for present honours, and desire for future goods.

The seventh bread also is hope of obtaining; and I likewise retain three fragments of it, whose taste is exceedingly sweet to my throat. I say three things strengthen and confirm my heart in such a way that neither lack of merits, nor reflection on my own worthlessness, nor estimation of heavenly blessedness can cast me down from the height of hope in which I am firmly rooted. Do you desire them, or should they be reserved because of him who said: “Have you found honey? Eat only as much as is sufficient for you” (Proverbs 25:16)? Thus is daily fulfilled what Wisdom herself prophesied of herself; and now I see the same thing: “Those who eat me,” she says, “will still [Col. 0344C] hunger” (Sirach 24:29).

Accordingly, I shall not draw you out further, but neither shall I defraud your hunger; for I see you so ready, as though you had not yet received anything. I consider three things in which all my hope consists: the love of adoption, the truth of the promise, and the power of fulfilment. Let my foolish thought murmur as much as it wishes, saying: “For who are you? How great is that glory? By what merits do you hope to obtain it?” And I shall answer confidently: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that in his surpassing love he has adopted me, that he is true in promise, and powerful in fulfilment; for it is lawful for him to do whatever he wills.”

This is the threefold cord that is not easily broken; I beg that we hold firmly to it, cast down to us from [Col. 0344D] our homeland as far as this prison, so that it may itself raise us up, itself draw us and draw us through to the sight of the glory of the great God, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0343]

## FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY OF NOVEMBER

### SERMON I. On the words of Isaiah 6:1: “I saw the Lord sitting,” etc.

[Col. 0343D]

1. “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and the whole earth was full of his majesty” [Col. 0344D]. A certain sublime vision is described to us in the prophet’s discourse. “I saw,” he says, “the Lord sitting.” [Col. 0345A] A great spectacle, brethren, and blessed are the eyes that saw it. Who would not desire with his whole longing to contemplate the glory of so great a majesty? This indeed was always the one desire of all the saints. For he is the one into whom angels desire to look, and to see him is eternal life.

But, brethren, I hear another vision of the same prophet and of the same Lord, far unlike this one. For this Isaiah is he who says elsewhere: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty; and we considered him as though a leper” (Isaiah 53:2), etc. Here the first point to consider is that the former vision seems common, whereas this one is peculiar to prophetic prerogative. Not without reason, surely, is it written there, “we saw,” and here, “I saw”: so that you may understand the former to be common, but this [Col. 0345B] one to be a singular excellence. For Herod saw him without form and beauty, and despised him; the Jews also saw him, those who even counted all his bones. But concerning this blessed vision the prophet plainly declares: “Let the wicked man be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26:10).

2. Therefore in many and various ways he was not only spoken in the prophets, but also seen by the prophets. David recognized him as made lower than the angels; Jeremiah too saw him living among human beings on earth; Isaiah testifies that he saw him now upon a high throne, now not only below the angels or among human beings, but as though a leper—that is, not merely in flesh, but in the likeness of sinful flesh [Col. 0345C].

You too, if you desire to see Jesus exalted, take care first to see him humble. First look upon the serpent lifted up in the wilderness, if you desire to see the King seated upon his throne. Let this vision humble you, that the other may exalt you once humbled. Let this restrain and heal your swelling pride, that the other may fill and satisfy your desire. Do you see him emptied? Let not the vision be idle, for you will not be able idly to see him exalted. You shall be like him when you see him as he is; be now also like him, seeing him as he was made for your sake. For if you do not refuse likeness to him even in humility, a sure likeness in exaltation is owed to you as well. He will never permit a companion in tribulation to be shut out from sharing in glory.

Indeed, so far is he from disdaining to admit a companion in his suffering into the kingdom with him, that the thief who confessed him on the cross was with him that same day in paradise. Hence he also says to the apostles: “You are those who have remained with me in my trials, and I appoint for you a kingdom” (Luke 22:28–29). Therefore, because if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him, let our meditation for the present, brethren, be Christ—and him crucified. Let us place him as a seal upon our heart, as a seal upon our arm. Let us embrace him with the arms, as it were, of responsive love; let us follow him by zeal for devout conduct. For this is the way by which he who is [Col. 0346A] God’s salvation may be shown also to us—not now without form or beauty, but in such radiance that his majesty fills the whole earth.

3. Fittingly, then, in the first vision, as though it were still winter, he is seen not upon the throne, but in a lower and humbler dwelling. Every great house commonly has a double residence: the summer dwelling above, the winter dwelling below. Therefore, while even the hearts of the disciples were still constricted by wintry ice, and Peter too warmed himself at the coals with a heart no less cold than his body, it was altogether not the time to dwell upon a throne—or rather, to appear there. But when the new song shall be sung, “Winter has passed and gone away; flowers have appeared in our land” (Song of Songs 2:11–12), then it will fittingly be time to ascend the throne, and the Lord will dwell on high [Col. 0346B].

4. Suppose then that Isaiah, when he spoke these things, foresaw with prophetic eye the glory of that time: “I saw,” he says, “the Lord sitting upon a high throne,” etc. But what do we think, brethren? What sort of throne is this? For the Most High does not dwell in things visible or made by hands. No bodily material appears suitable for so great a throne, fitting for so great a structure, or worthy of so great an inhabitant. The structure must be built of living stones, a spiritual edifice, which the true and eternal Life may deign to inhabit by his indwelling.

But if angelic creation is insufficient for so great an edifice, diminished as it was by the fall of transgressors, let him surely raise the needy from the earth and lift the poor from the dust, [Col. 0346C] that he may set him with princes and fill the throne of glory. Perhaps this is why he who saw it describes the throne as not merely high, but also exalted: so that the steadfast height of angels and the merciful elevation of human beings may be indicated. What follows seems also to require more careful consideration; therefore for today let it suffice even to have begun.

945 **SERMON II.**  
[Note: [Col. 0345D] In most manuscripts the following three sermons are joined in one continuous series, and the fifth sermon—which is a new exposition of the words of Isaiah—is nearly absent; nevertheless it is found in the Colbert and Albo-Mantellorum codices [Col. 0346D]. These five sermons are cited in the books of *Flores*. See Book X, chapters 9 and 10. Observe that in old books the words *seraphim* and *cherubim* are written in the singular with the letter *m*, in the plural with *n*.]  
On the words of the prophet Isaiah, 6:1, 3.

1. “The whole earth,” says our contemplator concerning him whom he had seen upon the throne, “was full of his majesty.” “May your kingdom come, Lord,” so that as heaven is filled with your majesty, earth too may be filled. For why does the prince of this world rage everywhere with such fury, except because the earth has been given into the hands of the wicked? But this is his hour and the power of darkness. Surely the time will come when he who had no place in heaven will be driven, miserable creature, even from the earth’s surface, to be confined in subterranean caverns.

Thus the prophet David, after setting forth the prosperity of the saints, added concerning the evil one and his angels or members: “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Psalm 1:4). Then there will be no power to tempt, [Col. 0347A] no freedom to disturb, no possibility of doing harm. The whole earth will be filled with the majesty of the Lord when there will no longer be any transgression of his will; or rather, when creation itself shall be freed from this bondage of corruption, because of which it groans and labours in childbirth even now. For there will be a new heaven and a new earth, so that wherever you turn your eyes, in the very appearance of things divine majesty may in some manner be seen shining forth.

2. But you have another earth nearer to you, and over it a greater and more just concern. For no one has ever hated his own flesh (Ephesians 5:29). Console it, therefore, that it too may rest in hope, hearing indeed that the whole earth will be filled with the majesty of the Lord. For how, beloved, can divine majesty now fill our flesh, when even that great Paul, possessing only the firstfruits of the Spirit, groans most miserably and says: “I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, no good dwells” (Romans 7:18)? Yet sin certainly no longer ruled in his mortal body (Romans 6:12). Notice nevertheless that his body is still called mortal, and that only sin’s dominion is denied. For even then there was in his members the law of sin (Romans 7:23), which the fullness of majesty, when it comes, will utterly exclude. And not only this: the last enemy, death, also will be destroyed.

Therefore our earth will be filled with the majesty of the Lord when every sense of sin and the debt of death have utterly disappeared from its midst. I say, all our earth will be filled with the Lord’s majesty [Col. 0347C] when it is clothed with the glory of resurrection, puts on the robe of immortality, and is finally conformed to the brightness of Christ’s body. For we await the Saviour, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, made conformable to the body of his glory (Philippians 3:20).

Why do you still murmur, wretched flesh? Why do you still kick back and lust against the spirit? If he humbles you, chastens you, reduces you to slavery, that is surely in your own interest, no less than in his, according to your kind. Why do you envy those who are not ashamed to beg for utterly inglorious glory from the work of worms and from the skins of mice, in clothing unworthy of men and forbidden even to women, dishonouring themselves rather than adorning themselves? Let them refashion—or rather, certainly disfigure—their bodies. But if you are the body of lowliness, the same craftsman who formed you will refashion you. If you are not foolish, await that hand which may restore what it made [Col. 0347D].

3. Now attend to what follows in the prophetic vision itself: “And those things,” he says, “which were beneath him filled the temple.” This is why it is said: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation” (1 Peter 5:6). See that you are found beneath him; otherwise you will not be able to be with him. Do you suppose that he will admit human beings indiscriminately into that temple of such great blessedness, when he did not even leave the angels there indiscriminately? Or will he not distinguish among clods of earth, he who distinguished among the stars? He will surely assay the silver, he who tested and rejected even gold itself.

What kind of person, then, do you suppose must be found worthy to receive the place of the rejected angel? Clearly one free from every iniquity, but especially from that which was found even in the angel himself—not for a slight offence, not for a momentary wrath, but for everlasting hatred. Pride once disturbed that kingdom, shook its walls, and even cast down a part—and no small part. What then? Does it seem easily admissible thereafter? Does not that city hate and vehemently abhor such a pestilence? Be assured, brethren: he who did not spare the proud angels will not spare human beings. He is not contrary to himself; he shows no partiality. His judgments are alike. Humility alone pleases him, whether in angel or human being; and he who sits upon the throne chooses only subjects from among whom to fill the temple. For it is written: “Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth?” (Psalm 113:5–6).

But see whether perhaps Michael’s name is a word addressed in resistance to that proud one who said, “I shall be like the Most High.” For Michael is said to mean, “Who is like God?”

4. Therefore, when the prophet had said well that he saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne, lest perhaps you should understand “high” to be said of him who declared, “I shall ascend above the height of the clouds” (Isaiah 14:14), or refer “exalted” to those human beings who rise into pride, he added: “And those things which were beneath him filled the temple.” Thus you may plainly understand that he does not commend the height which exalts itself against him, but that those who are beneath him will be in the temple or on the throne: some high in steadfast stability, others raised from the depths by divine mercy.

And lest you perhaps object that all things are subject to his dominion, and that the phrase “which were beneath him” therefore expresses no distinction, he added also concerning the seraphim—of whom we shall speak in their place—that this had been granted by him, so as to approve and commend only that subjection to God which is voluntary and proceeds from the fervour of love.

5. “And those things,” he says, “which were beneath him filled the temple.” From the beginning God had created angels, in whom the fullness of that blessed temple might consist; yet not all pleased him, because, as it is written, he found perversity even in his angels (Job 4:18). For among them there was one who said, “I shall set my throne in the north” (Isaiah 14:13), and he had a people who trusted him. Miserable he, who preferred to be without God rather than under God; miserable too were those who, seeing a thief, ran with him. They went out unhappily, and the place left empty is to be received by another.

“Will you not be subject to God, O my soul?” Otherwise you too will have no place in the temple, because “those things which were beneath him filled the temple.” The foolish virgins will knock in vain; they will cry out to no purpose when the wedding feast has been filled with those reclining at table and the door has been shut. Unhappy the soul that is excluded from that wedding feast! Unhappy the one concerning whom it shall be cried: “Let the wicked man be taken away, lest he see the glory [Col. 0349A] of God” (Isaiah 26:10). For why does that wretch see this temporal light, who will not deserve to behold that glory? Would that my eye had never seen anything, if it is to be deprived—as God avert it—of that vision!

Let the proud go on; let them grow more insolent; let them exalt and puff themselves up; let them always seek to appear upon a height, so that, when the measuring line of righteousness comes, they may be cast out from the fullness. But you, O my soul, not so: be subject to God—subject from your heart indeed, subject with fervour of devotion. For the seraphim stood above it. Let us stand with them today, brethren, and not be moved from this temple, in which all declare glory because they contemplate the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

### SERMON III. On the words of the prophet Isaiah 6:2

[Col. 0349B]

1. I do not think that you have forgotten that today we are to have a discourse about the two seraphim, because Isaiah, after testifying that he had seen the Lord seated upon the throne, added that seraphim stood above it. Seraphim, beloved, as you have often heard, is the name of the heavenly spirits, one of the nine orders, and that order the highest and supreme. Yet in this place, as I judge, the word is not used in that sense, especially since those hosts are innumerable, whereas only two seraphim are described here.

And I, brethren, if in this matter each may abound in his own understanding, judge that in the two seraphim a twofold rational creation is meant: the angelic and the human. Do not wonder that a human being is made a seraph; remember that the Creator and Lord of the seraphim was made human. To your disgrace, O proud one—you who were created among angels and did not deserve to stand among angels—behold, our King has come to fashion new angels upon earth. And, that you may waste away yet more and be tortured by your own envy, not angels of any sort, nor those of some lower order, but seraphim.

Hear what he himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will, except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49). Therefore he wills seraphim to be fashioned, that they may stand where you fell. “Seraphim stood above it.” Why then, O Lucifer, you who rose in the morning, did you not stand in the truth, except because you were not a seraph? For *seraphim* is interpreted “burning” or “kindling.” But you, miserable one, had light, yet you did not have burning. It would have been good for you had you been a bearer of fire rather than a bearer of light; nor, cold as you were yourself, would you have chosen a cold region through so immoderate a desire to shine. For you said: “I shall ascend above the height of the clouds; I shall sit upon the sides of the north” (Isaiah 14:13–14).

Why do you hasten to rise in the morning, Lucifer? Why do you glory above the stars, among which at one time you seemed to glow more brightly? Your glorying will be altogether brief. The Sun of righteousness follows you, whom in vain pretence you boasted yourself to be; by whose heat and brightness alike you will be reduced to nothing and wholly disappear. In vain also do you prepare to forestall, in that condemned human being whom you will assume, the Lord who is to come at the end of the ages, as though you were the rising of the true sun; and to exalt yourself above everything called or worshipped as God. For even then you will be utterly destroyed by the brightness of his coming [Col. 0350A].

2. How much better—and certainly not to his own folly—was John the Baptist, who was also a light-bearer, sent before the Lord not by his own presumption, lest he too should be a thief and robber, but by the authority of God the Father! “Behold,” he says, “I send my angel before your face” (Luke 7:27), etc. You have also in the Psalm, concerning the same man: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Psalm 132:17). For he was a burning and shining lamp; and the Jews wished to rejoice for a while in his light—but he did not. Whence then? Ask him himself; let him speak concerning himself: “The friend of the bridegroom stands and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29).

John therefore stands, for he is not a reed shaken by the wind. He stands because he is a friend; he stands because he burns; and seraphim are described as standing. Truly he is the bridegroom’s friend, who does not envy the glory of him coming forth from his bridal chamber, but prepares the way and proclaims grace, so that he himself may deserve to receive from his fullness. John shines, then, the more brightly in proportion as he burns more intensely; he shines the more truly in proportion as he desires to shine less. He is a faithful light-bearer, who came not to usurp but to announce the splendour of the Sun of righteousness.

“I am not the Christ,” he says. “One mightier than I comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie”; and: “I baptize you with water; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (John 1:20, 26, 27, 33). As though the light-bearer were plainly saying: “Why do you marvel as you behold my brightness? I am not the sun. You shall see another, in comparison with whom I am darkness and not light. I, like a star before dawn, sprinkle you with morning dew; he will send forth his rays in heat, melt the ice, dry the marshes, warm those who are cold, and be clothing for the poor.” Nor indeed does the voice of the forerunner disagree with the saying of the Judge; rather, Christ visibly supplied the fire promised by John when he said: “I came to cast fire upon the earth.”

3. Perhaps you will say that fire has brightness as well as heat. I do not dispute it, although heat seems in some manner more substantial to it. Let us rather hear him himself, to learn what he chiefly commends in fire. “I came,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will, except that it burn?” You know surely what he wills. Yet you do not fail to know that “life is in his will” (Psalm 30:6), and that the servant who knows and does not do his master’s will shall be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47).

Why do you hasten to shine? The time has not yet come when the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. In the meantime, this desire to shine is pernicious; for it is far better to burn. Finally, if you desire brightness so vehemently because you wish to be seen, take care to be what you wish to seem; and first seek fervour, and without doubt brightness too will be added to you. Otherwise you labour in vain, because brightness without fervour is empty. The light that does not proceed from fire is borrowed—or, rather, counterfeit—light [Col. 0351A]. What is another’s you may usurp only for a little while. It will be a greater shame to have wished what was not yours to appear yours.

The moon, they say, has brightness without heat, but borrows even that from the sun; and therefore it changes so often—or rather always—and never remains in the same state. Thus indeed the fool changes like the moon, while the wise person remains like the sun (Sirach 27:12): that fool, I mean, who lost wisdom in his beauty, that is, who grew cold amid splendour.

4. Therefore Lucifer fell from heaven like lightning, but the seraphim stand above it. The seraphim truly stand, because love never fails (1 Corinthians 13:8). They stand astonished and intent in contemplation of him sitting upon the throne; they stand in eternal unchangeableness and unchangeable eternity. You attempted to sit, O impious one; therefore your feet were moved and your steps poured out. It is the Son who sits upon the throne, the Lord of hosts, judging all things in tranquillity. The Trinity alone sits, which alone possesses immortality [alternate reading: “immutability”]; it alone is that in which there is no change or shadow of alteration.

The seraphim, however, stand unchangeable in their own manner, but not in comparison with him. They stand, stretching and directing themselves toward him into whom they desire to look. He who presumed to sit wished to be satisfied with himself; therefore even now he hungers only for wickedness, because that alone he possesses from himself. “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own,” because he is a liar and its father (John 8:44). What you hear concerning the word of falsehood, understand also concerning the work of wickedness. Although he takes evil pleasure in evil, he can nevertheless never be sufficient to himself even in it.

The supreme Trinity alone therefore sits, for it alone has being in itself: it is in itself, and thus alone truly is; it alone enjoys itself, alone needs nothing, and alone is sufficient to itself.

### SERMON IV. On the words of the prophet Isaiah 6:2

1. When the prophet had said that the seraphim stood, he then added: “Six wings to the one, and six wings to the other.” What do these wings mean, brethren? Then, even when winter has passed and the King sits upon the throne, will the seraphim still have to fly, so that they may meet the various needs of different persons, rescue from imminent dangers, bring aid to those in distress, and comfort those placed in tribulation? Far be it that in that kingdom of eternal blessedness there should be need, danger, toil, or tribulation requiring assistance.

What then are the wings for? I like that standing still; I want altogether to remain so, and I admit nothing whatever by which that stability might be lost to me. Yet I know, blessed Isaiah, that you are a prophet and possess the Spirit of him whose abundance of compassion surpasses not only human merits but even human wishes. Let that stability, so dear to me, remain secure; but if these wings add anything to blessedness, I do not refuse them. I believe that, as standing promises immutability, so flight promises alacrity, lest an insensible and, as it were, stony stability be imagined. But you may say: even if wings are necessary, why so many? What is the meaning of this multiplicity [Col. 0352A] of feathers? Hear what follows: “With two wings they covered the head, with two the feet, and with two they flew.” In these words I seem to see that what was said concerning standing is more plainly explained by flight. For where do the seraphim fly except toward him whom they love ardently? See a flame as though flying and standing at once; then you will no longer wonder that seraphim, standing, fly, and flying, stand.

2. But since we have said where they fly, your devout curiosity seems to require also the wings by which they fly. One to whom it was given both to see and to testify could offer a more certain and credible witness. Yet I think it not unfitting to understand these wings as knowledge and devotion, by which the seraphim are carried upward toward him who is above them. For the wing of knowledge lifts, but it is not sufficient by itself. He who attempts to fly with one wing alone falls more quickly; and the higher he is raised, the worse he is dashed down.

The philosophers of the Gentiles experienced this: although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Finally, being handed over to a reprobate mind, they fell even into dishonourable passions (Romans 1:21, 26, 28). Thus the saying is proved true: “For one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (James 4:17). In the same way zeal without knowledge, the more violently it rushes forward, falls the more grievously, striking and recoiling. But where love accompanies understanding and devotion accompanies knowledge, whoever is such will fly securely, will fly without end, because he flies into eternity.

3. Concerning the covering of the head and feet mentioned earlier, there is an interpretation approved by the Fathers: that God’s head and feet are covered because what was before the world and what will be after its consummation are hidden. This is based upon the fact that Latin manuscripts distinctly write: “his head and his feet.” Yet our translator [Note: [Col. 0351D] Blessed Jerome.] testifies that in Hebrew there is a word common to “his” and “their own,” so that according to the ambiguity of the Hebrew language the seraphim may be said either to cover God’s face and feet, or their own face and feet [Col. 0352D]. It may therefore seem remarkable why, of the two senses, he chose in translation the one which the sequence of the vision itself seems less to allow: namely, that they should fly and at the same time cover the head and feet of the one seated—unless it is because in this respect he followed Origen’s exposition.

4. But if the passage may also be understood of the seraphim themselves, picture them thus: with head and feet covered, only the middle of the body appears, and even that not wholly, on account of the wings by which they are said to fly. For I consider that I have, as it were, a head, a body, and feet in the Apostle’s words: “For those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son; and those whom he predestined, these he also called; those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also glorified” (Romans 8:29–30).

Thus my beginning is grace alone, and I have nothing to attribute to myself in predestination or calling. Yet I am not in the same way excluded from the work of justification. Grace works that too, but plainly with me. Do you see how the seraph appears in some measure in the middle? Moreover, the consummation too is grace alone; in this respect I have no ground to glory, either with it or in it, as though I appeared its helper or fellow-worker.

Therefore the seraph covers its head with two wings if it both truly recognizes and humbly confesses that mercy alone has gone before it. It covers its feet likewise with two wings if it is neither ignorant nor ungrateful concerning the mercy that is to follow. We ought not neglect this covering of head and feet even now, though it is chiefly to be perfected then, when the Judge sits upon the throne and more subtly enlightens the seraphim standing before him with knowledge of truth and more vehemently enkindles them with the ardour of love.

May that mercy of which we have spoken deign to establish us, unworthy servants of his name, in their number—a mercy which is from eternity and unto eternity over the elect, showing free choice to some degree in the middle, for the sake of merit, but claiming wholly for itself the beginning and the end: so that the Lord our God may be alpha and omega to us [Col. 0353C], and that for each right we may cry: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Psalm 113:1). Amen.

### SERMON V. On the words of the prophet Isaiah 6:1, 3.

1. Holy Scripture commends to us Christ the Lord as from the Father, in the Father, with the Father, from the Father, for the Father, and also under the Father. “From the Father” signifies his ineffable birth; “in the Father,” the unity of consubstantiality; “with the Father,” equality of majesty. For these three are indeed eternal. But if he is born from the Father, what does it mean that he is in the Father or with the Father? He may not unfittingly be said to recline in the Father and to sit with the Father. Hear the meaning of this sitting-with and this reclining.

For as sitting expresses majesty, so sitting-with expresses equality of majesty—especially since his seat is at the right hand of the Father, certainly not beneath his feet or, as it were, behind him. To sit is already to rest; but to recline is still more so. What, then, will seem more delightful and, in a sense, sweeter to the Son: that which is in the Father, or that by which he presides over all things with the Father? In which of these, do you think, should that supreme peace of God which surpasses all understanding, and the Lord’s unique repose, more fittingly be placed? Though this cannot be adequately expressed by speech, perhaps it may be devoutly conceived in the heart: that, while preserving in every respect the indivisible simplicity of that essence, a distinction may be thought possible between equality of glory and unity of substance, somewhat analogous to the distinction between sitting-with and reclining. [Col. 0353D–0354A]

2. Finally, it seems too little for the bride merely to see him sitting; she asks that he be shown to her reclining. “Tell me,” she says, “you whom my soul loves, where you recline at noon” (Cant. 1:6). And to every soul that has sound understanding, what the Apostle says is altogether sweeter: “He who is joined to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17), than what is said to the apostles: “When the King shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, you too shall sit, judging” (Matt. 19:28). Reclining is unquestionably more pleasant than sitting.

“I am in the Father,” says the Son, “and the Father is in me” (John 10:38). The unity of substance could not have been more expressly commended. For where each is in the other, nothing may be thought of as external, nothing as internal; rather, in both one must believe the most simple unity of substance. Yet there is some likeness to this in the saying, “He who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16), except that here there is a certain spiritual union, according to what we recalled above: “He who is joined to God” is not one thing—that is, not one substance—but “one spirit”; whereas there a natural and substantial unity is rather signified. Hence in the Gospel you have: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Accordingly, according to the likeness already stated, that is as it were the bedchamber of the Only-begotten, and a kind of supreme repose of the Lord. Through this union of wills and adherence of spirit—which charity produces in us according to our measure—the First-born likewise introduces us into this his bedchamber and his repose. [Col. 0354A–C]

3. Now the expression “from the Father” signifies his walking forth, and concerns the coming of his Incarnation, which we shall shortly celebrate through his own gift. Thus he himself says: “For I proceeded from God and came” (John 8:42). Seen upon earth and conversing with men, he stood in our midst—he whom we did not know—true Emmanuel, “God with us”: standing with us, yet for the Father. That he stood with us signifies help; that he stood for the Father signifies zeal. For in all things he sought the Father’s glory, whose will he had come to do.

But if you consider him hanging—if you attend to Christ, and him crucified—there you find him most plainly and evidently under the Father. For this belonged properly and especially to the humility of his human nature, according to which he himself says, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). Shall we dare say that he was ever even without the Father? No one would presume it, had he not first said himself: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). For there was, as it were, a certain abandonment there, where in such necessity no exercise of power was displayed, no manifestation of majesty. [Col. 0354C–D]

4. Thus we have Christ: born from the Father, reclining in the Father, sitting with the Father, walking forth from the Father, standing for the Father, hanging under the Father, and in some sense dying without the Father. How then shall we believe that Isaiah saw him in any of these ways when he said: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up”? For that vision was wholly unlike the one of which the same prophet elsewhere says: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor comeliness; and we accounted him as a leper, struck by God, and humbled.” In both places he saw the same one, but he did not see him in the same way; and in this sense, he somehow did not see the same one.

There he saw him bruised by blows, filled with reproaches, afflicted with punishments, assailed by injuries. In short, he saw him contemptible; he saw him hanging; he saw him dying for us; and he said: “He was crushed because of our crimes; by whose bruise we were healed” (Isa. 53:2–5). There, I say, he appeared as the last and despised among men; but here the whole earth was full of his majesty. There, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness; here, the Lord sitting.

That former vision is designated by the plural expression: “We saw”; this one is as singular as it is sublime. There, therefore, as one among a multitude: “We saw,” he says; but here as alone and solitary, raising himself above himself: “I saw,” he says, “the Lord sitting,” and so forth. The one seen sitting is fittingly called Lord. For sitting belongs to one who presides; sitting belongs to one who exercises dominion and reigns. Above all, sitting upon a throne signifies dominion; for simply sitting may sometimes signify humility also. But, as we said before, he who reclines in the Father in delight sits with the Father in rule: there he is the beloved Bridegroom; here, the wonderful Lord; in short, God glorious in his saints, wonderful in his majesty. [Col. 0355A–C]

5. “I saw,” he says, “the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and the whole earth was full of his majesty; and those things which were beneath him filled the temple.” What were those things beneath him? Was it the throne itself which he had mentioned? However high and lifted up it might be, it was nevertheless beneath him. For if he himself sat upon the throne, then the throne was plainly beneath him. And how did it fill the temple? Moreover, when the whole earth is already full of his majesty, how, or from what source, is the temple still filled?

Learn, then, from what you hear not to imagine a material contrivance as the throne, but to understand an angelic creature. For if the soul of the righteous is a seat of wisdom, what seat is worthier than a holy angel? This indeed is the throne of his glory, lofty by nature but raised far more by grace. Nature made them lofty by their creation; grace elevated them by their confirmation, of which it is said: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32:6).

Therefore those ranks of angels in which God sits, and which are beneath him, fill the temple, though the whole earth is already full of his majesty. For he reigns everywhere, rules everywhere, and his majesty is everywhere; but perhaps his grace is not so everywhere. No: his good, pleasing, and perfect will is not everywhere as his power is. Otherwise, why do we say, “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” (Matt. 6:10)? His will is done concerning all things and through all persons, but not in all persons. In the elect spirits the will of God is done when one will with him is brought about in them. This spiritual adherence makes one spirit, just as the multitude of believers is also recorded to have been “one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

“And those things which were beneath him filled the temple.” They filled it with every spiritual blessing; they filled it with divine consolation; they filled it with distributions of graces; they filled it, finally, with the fruit of sanctification: “for holiness befits thy house, O Lord.” They filled it with the varied gifts of charisms: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety; and they filled it with the spirit of the fear of the Lord. [Col. 0355C–0356A]

6. “Seraphim stood above it.” This is the name of the highest and supreme order of angels, and they are rightly described as standing above the rest. Yet, although they excel the others, they nevertheless stand beside the Lord who presides, rendering devoted service and reverent attendance. For the standing of the Lord, of an angel, and of a human being must be understood differently.

Christ stands for the Father in zeal, seeking the Father’s glory; and, as the Father’s faithful Only-begotten—indeed, also First-born—he assists his adopted brethren by the Father’s zeal. Thus Stephen saw him standing (Acts 7:55), him whom he had as his helper; thus the Prophet prayed that he might rise to help: “Rise up, O Lord,” he says, “help us” (Ps. 43:26). Angelic standing, however, is ministry, as the prophet says: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10). Human standing is perseverance in strength of soul and in keeping one’s resolution. Thus Moses “stood in the breach” before the Lord, to turn away his wrath; thus Phinehas “stood and made atonement” (Ps. 105:26, 30).

“Seraphim stood above it.” What is the meaning of the prophet’s reporting that he saw not one standing, nor many, but two? That two appeared to him is clear from what follows: “Six wings to one, and six wings to the other.” And fittingly two stood: “Woe to him who is alone, for if he falls, he has none to raise him” (Eccl. 4:10). Woe to you, spirit of pride, lover of solitude and solitary presumption: you did not stand in the truth; you were cast out; the foot of pride could not stand. Wishing to sit alone, you fell like lightning from heaven, never to have anyone to raise you. [Col. 0356A–D]

7. “Six wings to one, and six wings to the other.” Why this multitude of wings? “With two,” he says, “they covered his head, and with two his feet; and with two they flew.” Great is the mystery, and deep indeed the sacrament! These words demand attentive ears in you, but far more an eloquent tongue in us, and above all a spiritual mind. I say, then, in whatever manner I can, what I think; and I say it not as an assertion, but rather as a conjecture and opinion.

What prevents us from thinking that, after Lucifer’s fall, seraphim were appointed to unwearied watch, just as, after man’s expulsion, Scripture testifies that God set cherubim as guardians? Perhaps the cherubim’s flaming sword is not unfittingly described in this way (Gen. 3:24), so that cutting and burning from the tree of life—than which nothing is more terrible to flesh—might restrain the bodily hand. But the seraphim receive only wings, whose covering bars the spiritual eye. “With two,” he says, “they covered his head, and with two his feet,” so that that wicked one may be unable to contemplate either God’s heights or his depths.

It shall be so when the glory of the Lord is revealed; but this shall not happen until what is written has first occurred: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10). Meanwhile the head is veiled and the feet are veiled, so that something intermediate may remain for the impious one to see—but indeed only to envy. And they are veiled by wings which restrain him in such a way as to support and lift up the others. [Col. 0356D–0357A]

8. Yet we must first ask by which wings they are said to fly, for “with two,” he says, “they flew.” Perhaps we may not unfittingly call these two nature and grace, especially since we previously assigned to these same things the loftiness and elevation of the throne. For by a keen intellect through nature, and by a fervent affection through grace, continually stretched and directed toward him who is above them, they are said both to stand, as we have said, through ministry, and to fly through zeal.

Though they veil the Lord’s head and veil his feet, they do not veil these things from themselves. Rather, they diligently fly and flutter among them, searching out both the heights of his power and the depths of his wisdom. They are not, however, searchers of majesty so as to be crushed by glory; for they love no less than they understand, since they are ruled and moved by that Spirit who searches even the deep things of God.

That proud Lucifer, bearing light but not possessing fire, leaning upon only one wing, was able to fall, not to fly. For he exulted in being bright, not fervent, not burning—which is what seraphim means. Therefore he did not stand, because he despised; nor was he able to fly, because he presumed. Nature’s keenness lifted him up, but altogether to his own ruin, since the loss of grace immediately cast him down.

Nor is the fall unlike that of those who, although they knew God, did not glorify him or give thanks; and therefore were finally given over to a reprobate mind, and their foolish heart was darkened (Rom. 1:21, 28). Indeed, a veil has also been placed before their prince, which he can no longer pass through by any keenness of nature, so as to behold the head or feet of him who sits upon the throne. For the seraphim, standing and attending, veil the head with two wings and the feet with two. [Col. 0357B–D]

9. The divine substance is not bodily, nor is it divided into bodily limbs after the form of human beings. God is spirit, and what is said concerning him must be sought spiritually.
