Otherwise, who will reveal to us this head and these feet, which the seraphim veil with two pairs of wings, except the Spirit himself, who knows all that is in him and searches even the deep things of God?

I think that the things designated in this passage by the name of head are these very things: his majesty, his power, his everlasting might and divinity. His head, according to that prophetic saying: “Thy righteousness is like the mountains of God.” What follows—“Thy judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7)—may perhaps not unfittingly be marked by the designation of feet. For his feet are, as it were, his unsearchable ways, his inscrutable judgments, the depth of his wisdom, and a certain irreproachable but incomprehensible ordering of his.

The mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation also belongs especially to these feet, as does every work of our salvation. It is to see how lofty that righteousness is which the prophet marvels is like the mountains of God. For our righteousness, if any is ours, is lowly: perhaps upright, but not pure. Unless perhaps we think ourselves better than our fathers, who said no less truly than humbly: “All our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruous woman” (Isa. 64:6). For how can righteousness be pure where guilt cannot yet be absent?

Accordingly, the righteousness of human beings may meanwhile seem upright, provided that they do not consent to sin, so that it may not reign in their mortal body. The first man’s righteousness, however, was at the beginning not only upright but also pure, as long as it was granted him not even to experience sin. Yet, because this righteousness itself was not firm, it both easily lost purity and did not retain even its uprightness.

Among the angels, righteousness is upright, pure, and firm; it is lofty indeed, but still far inferior to the divine. For it is not innate in them, but bestowed by God; so that nature itself is found capable, in what is from itself, not only of righteousness but also of unrighteousness. Is this not a certain perversity which that true Righteousness is said to have found in his angels? (Job 4:18). “No living being shall be justified in thy sight,” says one who was by no means ignorant of God’s righteousness (Ps. 142:2). He does not say, “No human being,” but “no living being,” perhaps so that you may know that he did not except even angelic spirits. For they also live, and all the more truly because they stand nearer to him with whom is the fountain of life.

Nevertheless, they too are righteous—but from him, not before him; by his gift, not in comparison with him. For he is righteousness to himself, whose will is not so much equitable as equity itself; and both are nothing other than his very substance. Therefore that righteousness is most truly like a mountain which is upright, pure, firm, and, so to speak, substance itself. What height lies hidden in this head! What glory, and what sublimity, is laid up in this shadowy and thick mountain! [Col. 0357D–0358D]

10. Yet with what wings do we suppose that the seraphim veil this head, so that no loftiness of nature and no sharpness of reason may allow a wicked eye to break into that brightness of true light? With two wings, I think: their own glory and blessedness. For they delight ineffably in the admiring contemplation of it; nor do they glory less in its veneration.

That wicked one possessed admiration indeed, but not veneration; because he was unwilling to submit through veneration, he could not remain fixed through admiration. Indeed, he turned admiration itself into rivalry; he did not deign to venerate, but attempted to imitate. How much better the seraphim become blessed through their own admiration and venerable through veneration, having true glory in him for whom to serve is to reign, and with whom everyone who humbles himself is exalted.

Now hear how, by these two wings, the seraphim seem to veil the Lord’s head of which we have spoken, lest that wicked one see it. Whenever the malicious one directs his gaze upward, he immediately stumbles upon angelic blessedness and glory; and his own most evil humor—envy—injures his eye, so that he cannot penetrate farther. Thus, as if by a twofold veil, the envious one is hindered from looking upon higher things, wasting away as his gaze is turned back by the blessedness, at one moment, or the glory, at another, or both together, of those whom he grieves to have above him. For what itch of the eye is so grievous as envy? The envious man is tormented by nothing but another’s glory and blessedness. “Misery,” as they say, “is without envy.” [Col. 0358D–0359B]

11. The seraphim also veil the Lord’s feet—which, as we said, signify the impenetrable abyss of his judgments and the unsearchable ways of his ordering—with two wings likewise. I say: prudence and fidelity. For since they are at once faithful and prudent ministers, they administer divine affairs and provide for the salvation of the elect in such a manner that the malicious one can detect nothing at all.

I think it was through this veiling of the feet that, not knowing the Lord of glory, he brought about his crucifixion. And through it he is daily made to serve, ignorantly and unwillingly, the work of our salvation; afterwards he laments too late that, while he wished to harm, he was found to have helped. Thus, through ministering spirits, his cunning is mocked: they are faithful and therefore unwilling to reveal, and prudent and therefore able to conceal, the secrets of God’s providence and ordering toward us. [Col. 0359B–C]

12. But just as that utterly wicked one had admiration from the two upper wings, but not veneration, as we have said, so from the middle wings nature gave him spiritual understanding, but grace did not give him affection. Yet from these two lowest wings it may readily be seen how he was found lacking fidelity, while not similarly lacking prudence. Unless perhaps you suppose that someone else is meant who was called “more cunning than all living creatures,” the serpent (Gen. 3:1).

Perhaps we may also not unfittingly say that his fall was so irrevocable and his ruin irreparable precisely because, among the wings we have mentioned, just as none was present on the right side, so none was lacking on the left. Not so the two whom the prophetic vision commended to us as standing and attending the Lord of majesty. With two wings, as was said, they veil his head: namely, by their own admiration, in which they delight blessedly, and their veneration, in which they glory sublimely. With two they also veil his feet: that is, with fidelity and prudence. With two they fly: with the keenness of nature and the efficacy of grace, as we said.

They leave visible and uncovered, as it were, a certain middle span of long-suffering: I mean the length and kindness of God, inviting human beings to repentance. For everyone can see how he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the righteous alike and the unrighteous. With this charity the true Solomon, as it were, paved his middle space “for the daughters of Jerusalem” (Cant. 3:10), so that those who are not permitted to seek things higher than themselves or to trace out the depths may at least exercise themselves in these intermediate things, and may one day deserve to advance from them to contemplation of things subtle and sublime.

But that most wicked one is more sharply tormented by this vision in the present, and will be more grievously tortured in the future: first, because he envies us this very long-suffering kindness; then because he does not even provide for himself by this opportunity so as to be brought to repentance. [Col. 0360A–C]

# Sermons of Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, on the Saints

[Col. 0359]

## On the Conversion of Saint Paul

### Sermon I. How We Ought to Be Converted after His Example

[Col. 0359D]

1. Beloved, it is fitting that the conversion of the Doctor of the Gentiles is today celebrated by all the nations with festal rejoicing. For we see that many branches have sprung from this root. Paul, having been converted, became a minister of conversion to the whole world. While still in the flesh, though no longer walking according to the flesh, he converted many to God through the office of preaching. Now too, living more blessedly in him and with him, he has not yet ceased from the conversion of human beings: I mean by example, prayer, and teaching.

Therefore the memory of his conversion is frequently observed, because it too is found useful to those who remember it. In this remembrance the sinner conceives hope of forgiveness and is stirred to repentance; and one who has already repented receives a pattern of perfect conversion. Who can despair any longer because of the greatness of any crime, when he hears that Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, suddenly became a vessel of election? Who, crushed beneath the weight of iniquity, can say, “I am no longer able to rise toward better pursuits,” when, on the very journey on which, thirsting for Christian blood, he breathed out with his whole heart a dreadful poison, the most cruel persecutor was suddenly changed into a most faithful preacher? In this single conversion, therefore, both the greatness of mercy and the efficacy of grace are wonderfully commended. [Col. 0360D–0361A]

2. “Suddenly,” says Luke, “a light from heaven shone around him” (Acts 9:1–8). O truly inestimable condescension of divine mercy! He illumines with heavenly brightness one still incapable of light within; since the light could not yet be poured into him, divine brightness is at least poured around him. “And there was a voice.” The testimonies of light and voice became utterly credible, and there can be no doubt of the truth that makes itself known through both windows, namely those of the eyes and ears.

Thus, at the Jordan too, a dove appeared above the Lord’s head and a voice sounded (Matt. 3:16–17); thus also on the mountain, when he was transfigured before the disciples, brightness was seen and the Father’s voice was likewise heard (Matt. 17:2, 5): “Saul, Saul, why dost thou persecute me?” Saul was truly caught: there was no room for evasion, no possibility of denial. In his hands were letters for a most cruel mission, of execrable authority and unjust power.

“Why dost thou persecute me?” he says. Did not he persecute Christ who slaughtered Christ’s members on earth? Or did those persecute Christ who fastened that most sacred body to the gibbet of the cross, whereas he did not persecute him who raged with wicked hatred against his body, which is the Church—for the Church too is his body? Finally, if he gave his own blood as the price of redemption for souls, do you not think that he suffers a more grievous persecution from one who, by evil persuasion, harmful example, or an occasion of scandal, turns away from him the souls whom he redeemed, than from the Jew who shed that blood? [Col. 0361A–C]

3. Recognize, beloved, and shudder at the fellowship of those who obstruct the salvation of souls. It is a wholly dreadful sacrilege, seeming even to surpass the crime of those who laid sacrilegious hands upon the Lord of majesty. The time of persecution seemed already to have ceased; but, as has become plain, persecution is never absent from the Christian, nor from Christ. And now, what is more grievous, those persecute Christ who are called Christians from him.

“Thy friends, O God, and thy neighbors have drawn near and stood against thee.” The whole body of the Christian people, from the least to the greatest, seems to have conspired against you. “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness”: iniquity has gone forth from the elders, the judges, your vicars, who seem to govern your people. It can no longer be said, “As the people, so the priest” (Isa. 24:2), because the people are not even as the priest.

Alas, alas, Lord God! For those who seem in your Church to love preeminence and exercise authority are foremost in persecuting you. They have occupied the citadel of Zion, seized the fortifications, and thereafter freely and authoritatively hand over the whole city to the flames. Their wretched conduct is the miserable overthrow of your people.

Would that they harmed only in this respect! Perhaps someone, warned and fortified by the Lord’s exhortation, would take care not to imitate their examples but to observe their commands, according to the saying: “Do what they say, but do not look to their deeds” (Matt. 23:3). But now sacred ranks have been made an opportunity for shameful profit, and they consider godliness a means of gain. For there are indeed abundant means of godliness in undertaking—or rather accepting—the care of souls; but with them this care is of minor importance, and the salvation of souls their last thought.

Could any persecution be more grievous for the Savior of souls? Others too act unjustly against Christ, and in our times many are antichrists. Yet he rightly judges more cruel, because of benefits received, and feels more grievously, because of their power, the persecution he suffers from his own ministers, although many others also appear in many ways, by many methods, and on various occasions to act against the salvation of their neighbors.

Christ sees these things and is silent; the Savior endures them and conceals them. Therefore we too must conceal them and be silent for the present, especially concerning our prelates, the masters of the churches. Thus it pleases them that they should now escape human judgments, and that at last a severe judgment should come upon those who rule, and the powerful should suffer powerful torments. [Col. 0361C–0362C]

4. I fear, beloved, that perhaps someone even among us may be a persecutor of the Lord, because clear reasoning has taught that to obstruct salvation is to persecute the Savior. What thanks for the salvation of my soul can I offer to that brother who serves me the poison of fraternal detraction? Detractors are rightly described as hateful to God (Rom. 1:30), as persecutors.

And what of one who by his example incites others to more lax conduct; or who disturbs by singularity, vexes by curiosity, troubles by impatience and murmuring; or in whatever way grieves the Spirit of God who is in them, scandalizing one of these little ones who believe in him? Does he not plainly persecute Christ as well?

Therefore, that both the name and the crime of persecutors may always be far from us, I beseech you, beloved: always show yourselves kind and gentle, bearing one another in all patience and stirring one another toward what is better and more perfect. What servant thinks it enough not to persecute the Lord, while not even serving the Lord? What favor will he have if, as he does not oppose, so he does not even assist? Finally, if anyone is so faint-hearted that he counts it enough neither to be a persecutor nor a fellow-worker of God, let him hear what the Lord himself says: “He who is not with me is against me; and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12:30). [Col. 0362C–D]

5. “Saul, Saul, why dost thou persecute me?” And he said, “Who art thou, Lord?” From this it is clearly understood that brightness was truly poured around him, not poured into him. Paul heard the Lord’s voice but did not see the Lord’s face, because he was being trained for faith; and, as he himself later taught, “Faith is from hearing” (Rom. 10:17).

“Who art thou?” he says. For he persecuted one unknown to him, and therefore obtained mercy, because he did this ignorantly in unbelief. Learn from this, brothers, that God the righteous judge considers not only what is done but also with what intention it is done. Henceforth beware lest anyone count it a small matter to be convicted [variant: to appear] of knowingly committing even small sins. Let no one say in his heart, “These are light matters; I do not care to correct them. It is not serious if I remain in these venial and very small sins.”

For this, beloved, is impenitence; this is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, blasphemy that cannot be forgiven. Paul indeed was a blasphemer, but not against the Holy Spirit, because he acted ignorantly in unbelief. He did not utter blasphemy against the Holy Spirit; therefore he obtained mercy. [Col. 0363A–B]

6. “Who art thou, Lord?” And the Lord said to him: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom thou persecutest.” I am the Savior whom you seek by persecuting. I am he of whom you read in your law that it was foretold, though you do not know that it has been fulfilled: “For he shall be called a Nazarene” (Matt. 2:23).

And he said: “Lord, what dost thou wish me to do?” This, brothers, is indeed the pattern of perfect conversion. “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” (Ps. 107:2). “I am ready, and am not troubled, that I may keep thy commandments” (Ps. 118:60). “Lord, what dost thou wish me to do?” O brief word, yet full; living and effectual; worthy of all acceptance! How few are found in this pattern of perfect obedience—those who have so cast aside their own will that they do not even possess a heart of their own, and who seek at every hour not what they themselves wish, but what the Lord wishes, saying without ceasing, “Lord, what dost thou wish me to do?” And likewise Samuel’s words: “Speak, Lord, for thy servant hears” (1 Sam. 3:10).

Alas! We have more imitators of that blind man in the Gospel than imitators of the new apostle. “What dost thou wish?” the Lord says to that blind man, “that I should do for thee?” (Luke 18:41). How great is thy compassion, Lord; how great thy condescension! Does the Lord thus ask in order to do the will of servants? The blind man was truly blind, because he did not consider, did not fear, did not cry out: “Far be this from thee, Lord! Rather, say what thou wishest me to do.” For this is fitting; this is wholly worthy: not that my will should be sought from thee and done, but that thy will should be sought from me and done.

You see, brothers, that conversion was truly necessary in this place. Indeed, even today the faint-heartedness and perversity of many require that they must be asked, “What dost thou wish that I should do for thee?” rather than themselves asking, “Lord, what dost thou wish me to do?” The ministers and vicars of Christ must consider what he wishes to command them; they themselves do not consider what is their master’s will. Their obedience is not complete; they are not ready to obey in all things; they have not resolved to follow in every respect him who came not to do his own will but the Father’s.

They distinguish and judge, choosing the matters in which they will obey the one commanding them—or rather, the matters in which their teacher must obey their own will. Such persons, therefore, even though they see that they are tolerated, that allowance is made and compliance given to their weakness, should make progress, I beseech them; and let them be ashamed always to be found children, lest perhaps one day they hear: “What ought I to have done for you that I have not done?” And for those abusing the patience and kindness of their prelate, the abundance of mercy shown may finally become the accumulation of a just condemnation. [Col. 0363B–0364A]

7. “Lord, what dost thou wish me to do?” And the Lord said to him: “Rise, and enter the city; there it will be told thee what thou must do.” O Wisdom, truly ordering all things sweetly! The one to whom you speak, you send to a human being to be taught your will, so that the usefulness of social life may be commended; and, having been taught through a human being, he may himself learn to assist human beings according to the grace given to him.

“Enter the city.” You see, brothers, that it was not without divine counsel that you entered this city of the Lord of hosts, in order to learn the divine will. The one who beneficially terrified you and turned your heart to desire his will, he himself said to you: “Rise, and enter the city.” But hear how clearly voluntary simplicity and Christian gentleness are commended in what follows. “Though his eyes were open, he saw nothing; but he was led by the hand by those accompanying him.”

Blessed blindness, by which eyes once ill-illumined in transgression are at last beneficially blinded in conversion. Paul’s remaining for three days without food, persevering in prayer, especially concerns those who, newly renouncing the world, have not yet found refreshment in heavenly consolation. Let them too wait for the Lord in all patience; let them pray without ceasing, seeking, asking, knocking, because the heavenly Father will hear them at the appropriate time. He will not forget them forever; he will come and will not delay. If for three days you wait for him without having anything to eat, trust that the Lord, compassionate and merciful, will not leave you fasting. [Col. 0364A–C]

8. Thereupon Ananias is commanded to lay his hands upon Saul; but, as one well instructed, he does not immediately comply. [Col. 0364D] For see whether Paul himself did not afterward impart this teaching to his disciple: “Lay hands hastily on no man” (1 Tim. 5:22). “He saw,” says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0363] These words, enclosed in parentheses in Acts, are to be attributed to Luke as narrator, not to Christ.], “a man laying hands upon him, that he might receive his sight.” Brothers, though Paul had seen this, he was not immediately enlightened. Did he not wait for Ananias’s hand because he had perhaps foreseen in dreams that he would come? (Acts 9). I say these things to you, dearly beloved, because I fear that perhaps there may be among you someone who, on the basis of a dream alone, presumes himself to have been enlightened, and no longer bears patiently to be led by the hand, but declares himself a guide of others. For one upon whom the care of administration has not yet been laid, to whom stewardship has not yet been entrusted, to whom it has not yet been commanded that he should see and provide for those who, having open eyes, see nothing—what does he attempt by such presumption except to devise vain things and pursue empty dreams? Let us beware of this vice, brothers. So far as lies in us, let us always choose to be lowly and to be led by the hand, learning gentleness and humility from Christ the Lord, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II

1. Paul has been converted today—or rather Saul, being converted, has been turned into Paul. For he has become like that evangelical little child of whom the Lord says: “Unless you are converted and become like this little child, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). Perhaps he was speaking of himself. Indeed, he himself is [Col. 0365B] the great Lord, greatly to be praised; he himself is the little child given to us. Yet for the present he is displayed not as great, but as little, that he may make himself an attractive and effective example of the necessary littleness. Therefore let your conversion be toward the little child, that you may learn to be little; you too, when converted, become little. Hear, moreover, how plainly he reveals himself to you as little—the very one in whom he has established the pattern of conversion—setting before you, for imitation in himself, those qualities that belong to a little child. “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). A twofold littleness: humility and gentleness. The former is inward, the latter outward, littleness. Yet neither is a small virtue; for that little one who is so great professes them as his sole teaching. Therefore Paul has been converted today; today he has ceased to be Saul. Today he has become humble and meek of heart. The confession of his mouth proves the humiliation of his heart [Col. 0366A] when he cries, “Lord, what would you have me do?” Yet even more does the very greatness of the grace bestowed prove it—a grace which was not given in such abundance except to one greatly humbled.

2. But gentleness, since, as we have said, it is a certain outward littleness, and for that reason more evident, is commended to us threefold in this conversion. Our gentleness is assaulted, as it were, by a threefold battering ram: injuries of words, loss of possessions, and bodily harm. In these three consists every display of patience and every exercise of gentleness. That virtue has been tested which none of these seems able to shake. It is worth considering how Paul, tested in all these things immediately upon his conversion, was truly found already to be Paul—truly already meek and patient in this respect. “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.” Truly a hard saying: a rebuking word, full of threat. As regards his body, he was shaken and thrown to the ground. But was he tested also by loss? Very much so: for the very light of his eyes was taken from him, and, as it is written, “with his eyes open he saw nothing” (Acts 9:1–8). Job’s patience too was tried and exercised in these three things; God gave him as a most renowned example in this virtue. But we leave it to your diligence to investigate this. It is enough for us to remind you that the pattern of true conversion consists in large part in this gentleness, so that those who ought to have been converted may be ashamed if, in bodily injury, in loss of possessions, or—what is more disgraceful—in verbal injuries, they are found utterly perverse and turned away. [Col. 0366C]

[Col. 0365]

## ON THE PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED MARY

### SERMON I. On the threefold mercy

1. Today the Virgin Mother brings the Lord of the temple into the temple of the Lord; Joseph too presents to the Lord not his own son, but his beloved Son, in whom he is well pleased. The righteous Simeon recognizes the one whom he awaited; Anna also, the widow, confesses him. By these four the present-day procession was first celebrated, a procession afterward to be celebrated in every place and by every people amid the exultation of the whole earth. Nor is it surprising that it was then small, since he who was received was small. No sinner had a place there: all were righteous, all holy, all perfect. But will you save only these, O Lord? Let the body grow, and let mercy grow also. “You will save men and beasts, O Lord, when you have multiplied your mercy, O God” (Ps. 35:7–8). In the second procession crowds go before and crowds follow; no virgin carries him, but a little ass. Therefore he disdains no one, not even those who have rotted like beasts in their own dung. He does not disdain them, I say, provided that apostolic garments are not lacking—provided that the teaching of the apostles, righteousness of conduct, obedience, and charity cover a multitude of sins. From that point he will not judge them unworthy of the glory of his procession. Indeed, it remains for us also to discover from him that mercy itself, which seems to have been bestowed on so few. Why should he not reserve it for those who came after, when he granted it beforehand to those of old? [Col. 0366C]

2. David, king and prophet, rejoiced to see this day; he saw it and was glad. Otherwise, if he had not seen it, how could he have sung: “We have received, O God, your mercy in the midst of your temple” (Ps. 47:10)? David received this mercy of the Lord; Simeon received it; we too have received it, and all who are foreordained to life—for Christ is yesterday, today, and forever. Mercy is in the midst of the temple, not in a corner or side-room, because with God there is no respect of persons. It is placed in common, offered to all; and no one is without it except one who refuses it. “Your waters flow forth abroad, O Lord God”; nevertheless, your fountain is your own, and no stranger drinks from it. He who is yours shall not see death until he sees the Christ of the Lord, so that he may be dismissed in peace without fear. Why should he not be dismissed in peace who has the Christ of the Lord in his breast? For he himself is our peace, who dwells by faith in our hearts. How will you depart from here, wretched soul, who do not know Jesus as guide of the way? For some have ignorance of God. [Col. 0367A] How is this? Clearly because light came into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light. “And the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5). As though he said: Waters also flow through the streets, and the stranger does not drink from them; mercy too is in the midst of the temple; yet none of those whom eternal condemnation awaits approaches it [variant: “yet they do not approach”]. “One stands in your midst, O wretched ones, whom you do not know,” so that, dying before you have seen the Christ of the Lord, you may not be dismissed in peace, but rather be carried off by roaring ones ready to devour.

3. “We have received, O God, your mercy in the midst of your temple.” This thanksgiving is far removed from that voice of one groaning: “O Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches unto the clouds” (Ps. 35:6). What then? Does mercy seem to you to have been in the midst when it was possessed only among the spirits born of heaven? But when Christ was made a little lower than the angels, and became the mediator of God and men, and, as a cornerstone, made peace through his blood between the things in heaven and those upon earth, then indeed we have received, O God, your mercy in the midst of your temple. For we too were by nature children of wrath, but we obtained mercy. Children of what wrath, and what mercy did we obtain? Clearly, children of ignorance, weakness, and captivity; and we obtained wisdom, strength, and redemption. The ignorance of the deceived woman had blinded us; the softness of the man, drawn away and enticed by his own desire, had enfeebled us; the malice of the devil had, by God’s just judgment, taken us captive when we were exposed to him. Thus we are all born: first, wholly ignorant of the road, the city, and the dwelling-place; then weak and feeble, so that, even if the way of life were known to us, we would nevertheless be hindered and held fast by our own inertia; finally, captives under the worst and cruellest tyrant, so that, even if we were prudent and strong, we would still be oppressed by the very condition of wretched slavery. Does not such misery need mercy and abundant compassion? Or certainly, if now we have been saved from this threefold wrath through Christ, who has become for us wisdom from God the Father, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption (1 Cor. 1:30), how watchful we must be, beloved, lest—God forbid!—our latter state be found worse than the former, if we should again kindle wrath, since we are now children of wrath not by nature but by our own will. [Col. 0367D]

4. Let us therefore embrace the mercy which we have received in the midst of the temple, and, with blessed Anna, let us not depart from the temple. “For the temple of God is holy, which temple you are,” says the Apostle (1 Cor. 3:17). This mercy is near; the word is near, in your mouth and in your heart. Finally, Christ dwells through faith in your hearts. This is his temple [Col. 0368A] and this his dwelling-place—unless perhaps it has escaped you that “the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” [Note: [Col. 0367D] This passage is frequently cited by the holy Fathers as though from Scripture—Augustine, Gregory the Great, and others—and also by Bernard, as in Sermon 27 on the Song of Songs, where see the notes.] Therefore, what I frequently—indeed always—desire to urge upon my brothers, I now entreat: let us not walk according to the flesh while in the flesh, lest we displease God. Let us not be friends of this world, lest we be made enemies of God. Let us also resist the devil [variant: “therefore”], and he will flee from us, so that we may now walk freely in the Spirit and have our manner of life in the heart. For the body which is corruptible weighs down, weakens, and feminizes the soul; and an earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks on many things (Wis. 9:15), so that it does not rise toward heavenly things. Hence the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God (1 Cor. 3:19); and whoever is overcome by the evil one is also made his slave. But mercy is received in the heart; Christ dwells in the heart; in the heart he speaks peace to his people, to his saints, and to those who turn to the heart. [Col. 0368B]

### SERMON II. On the order and manner of Christ’s procession into the temple

1. Thanks be to our Redeemer, who has so abundantly gone before us with blessings of sweetness, multiplying our joys by the mysteries of his infancy. For, having celebrated a little while ago his Nativity, Circumcision, and Manifestation, today the festal day of his offering has dawned upon us. Today the lofty fruit of the earth is presented to the Creator of the earth; today the propitiatory and God-pleasing victim is offered in the temple by virginal hands, borne by parents, awaited by elders. Joseph and Mary offer a sacrifice of praise, a morning sacrifice; Simeon and Anna receive it. By these four the procession was celebrated, which today is recalled through the four regions of the world with solemn joys. Since therefore we ourselves, beyond the custom of the other solemnities, are today to make a festive procession [Note: [Col. 0368D] To this relates Abelard’s objection in Letter 5 to Bernard: “You have excluded from among yourselves almost the whole veneration of processions.”], I think it not useless to examine its manner and order more carefully. We shall proceed two by two, carrying candles in our hands, and those candles lit—not with just any fire, but with one first consecrated in the church by priestly blessing. Moreover, in our procession the last shall be first and the first last; and we shall sing in the ways of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord.

2. We rightly proceed two by two; for the holy Gospels testify that the Savior sent his disciples so, to commend brotherly charity and life in fellowship (Luke 10:1). A person disturbs the procession if he seeks to walk alone; he harms not only himself but is troublesome to others also. These are they who separate themselves, being animal men without the Spirit, and who are not careful to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Now, just as it is not good for a man to be alone, so it is forbidden to appear empty before the Lord (Exod. 23:15). For if even those whom no one hired are rebuked for idleness [Col. 0369A] (Matt. 20:6), what do those deserve who have already been hired if they are found idle? Faith without works is dead (Jas. 2:26). Our works themselves must be done with fervor and with desire of heart, that they may be burning lamps in our hands. Otherwise we must fear lest he who speaks in the Gospel begin to vomit us out as lukewarm, saying: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it should burn?” (Luke 12:49). This is indeed the sacred and blessed fire which the Father sanctified and sent into the world, and which is blessed in the churches, as it is written: “Bless God the Lord in the churches” (Ps. 67:27). For our adversary too, being a perverse imitator of divine works, has his own fire: the fire of carnal desire, the fire of envy and ambition, which the Savior came not to kindle in us but to extinguish. Finally, if anyone presumes to offer this alien fire in divine sacrifice, even if he has Aaron for his father, he shall die in his iniquity. [Col. 0369B]

3. Beyond what has been said concerning communal life and brotherly love, good works, and holy fervor, the virtue of humility is greatest and most necessary: that we may outdo one another in showing honor, and that each person may place not only those who are before him, but even those younger than himself, above himself. This is the perfection of humility and the fullness of righteousness. And because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7), and joy in the Holy Spirit is the fruit of charity, let us sing, as it is said, “in the ways of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord” (Ps. 137:5); let us “sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things” (Ps. 97:1). In all these matters, if anyone perhaps neglects to make progress and to proceed from virtue to virtue, let such a person know that he is at a standstill, not in procession—indeed, that he is in retreat; for not to advance on the way of life is to go backward, since nothing remains in the same state. But our progress consists in this, as I remember having often said: that we should never imagine ourselves to have laid hold of it, but should always stretch out toward the things before us, continually strive for what is better, and constantly place our imperfection before the gaze of divine mercy. [Col. 0369C]

### SERMON III. On the Child, Mary, and Joseph

1. Today we celebrate the Purification of the blessed Virgin Mary, which took place according to the law of Moses forty days after the Nativity of the Lord. For it was written in the law that a woman who had conceived seed and borne a son should be unclean for seven days, and that on the eighth day the child should be circumcised; then, intent upon washing and purification, she should refrain from entering the temple for thirty-three days; when these were completed, she should offer the son to the Lord with gifts (Lev. 12). But who does not perceive, at the very beginning of this ordinance, that the Mother of the Lord is entirely free from this command? Do you think that Moses, when about to say that a woman who bore a son was unclean, did not fear incurring the charge of blasphemy against the Mother of the Lord [Col. 0370A] and for that reason prefaced it with “having conceived seed”? Otherwise, unless he had foreseen that the Virgin would bear without seed, what necessity was there to mention conceived seed? It is evident, therefore, that this law does not include the Mother of the Lord, who bore a son without having conceived seed, as was foretold through Jeremiah, because the Lord would create a new thing upon the earth. What new thing, do you ask? “A woman,” he says, “shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). She shall not receive a man from another man, nor conceive a human being by human law; but within untouched and inviolate womb she shall enclose a man. Thus, indeed, when the Lord enters and departs, according to another prophet, the eastern gate remains continually shut (Ezek. 44:2).

2. Do you think, then, that her mind could not have been stirred to say: “What need have I of purification? Why should I refrain from entering the temple, when my womb, knowing no man, has become a temple of the Holy Spirit? Why should I not enter the temple, when I have borne the Lord of the temple? Nothing in this conception, nothing in this birth, was unclean, unlawful, or in need of purification, since this offspring is the fountain of purity and came to accomplish the cleansing of sins. What can legal observance purify in me, who have been made most pure by the very immaculate birth?” Truly, O blessed Virgin, truly you have no cause and no need of purification. But did your Son need circumcision? Be among women as one of them, for your Son also is numbered among boys. He was willing to be circumcised; and should he not much more be willing to be offered? Offer your Son, consecrated Virgin, and present to the Lord the blessed fruit of your womb. Offer, for the reconciliation of us all, the holy victim pleasing to God. God the Father will certainly accept the new offering and most precious victim, concerning whom he himself says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). But this offering, brothers, seems rather slight, when he is merely presented to the Lord, redeemed with birds, and immediately carried home. The time will come when he will be offered not in the temple, nor in Simeon’s arms, but outside the city in the arms of the cross. The time will come when he will not be redeemed by another, but will redeem others with his own blood, because God the Father has sent redemption to his people. That will be the evening sacrifice; this is the morning sacrifice. This is indeed more pleasing, but that more complete. This is at the time of birth; that at the fullness of age. Yet of both you may understand what the prophet foretold: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53:7). For he is offered now not because he had need, not because he was under the command of the law, but because he himself willed it; and likewise he was offered on the cross not because he deserved it, not because the Jew was able to do it, but because he himself willed it. “I will sacrifice willingly to you, O Lord,” because you were willingly offered for my salvation, not for your own necessity. [Col. 0370D]

3. But what, brothers, do we offer, or what do we render to him for all that he has rendered to us? He offered for us the most precious victim that he had—indeed, one than which none could be more precious. Therefore let us do what we can, offering to him the best that we have: namely, ourselves. He offered himself; who are you that you hesitate to offer yourself? Who will grant me that so great a Majesty may deign to receive my offering? I have two small coins, Lord—my body and my soul; would that I might be able to offer these perfectly to you in a sacrifice of praise! For it is good for me, and far more glorious and beneficial, that I should be offered to you rather than left to myself. For my soul is troubled within me when it is turned toward myself, but my spirit will rejoice in you if it is truly offered to you. Brothers, when the Lord was dying, the Jew offered dead victims; but now the Lord says: “As I live, I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33:11). The Lord does not will my death, and shall I not gladly offer him my life? For this is an acceptable victim, a victim pleasing to God, a living victim. But three persons are said to have been present at the Lord’s offering, and three things are likewise required by the Lord in our offering. There was at that offering Joseph, the husband of the Mother of the Lord, whose son he was thought to be; there was the Virgin Mother herself; and there was the child Jesus, who was offered. Therefore let there be in our offering manly constancy, bodily continence, and humble conscience. Let there be, I say, a manly resolve to persevere; in continence, virginal chastity; and in conscience, the simplicity and humility of a child. Amen. [Col. 0372A]

[Col. 0371]

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT VICTOR, CONFESSOR

[Note: [Col. 0371D] His body is preserved in the monastery of Arremar, commonly called Montier-Ramey, in the diocese of Troyes; his deposition is celebrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of March [26 February]. The office for the same saint is found near the end of this volume. See Letter 398.]

### SERMON I

1. Victor’s life [variant: “virtue”] and particular glory summons all who are upright in heart not so much to glory as to virtue. It is clearly the disposition not of an upright but of a perverse mind to seek glory before practicing virtue, and to wish to be crowned without having contended lawfully. “It is vain for you,” he says, “to rise before the light” (Ps. 126:2). So it is. In vain does one strive for the height of glory who has not first shone in virtue. In vain do the foolish virgins rise to meet the bridegroom, their lamps going out; and they are foolish because they glory in empty lamps, having no oil of virtue. Far be it from me to glory except in the glory of those to whom the Prophet, rejoicing with them, says: “O Lord, in the light of your countenance they shall walk; and in your name they shall rejoice all the day, and in your righteousness they shall be exalted.” And he adds: “For you are the glory of their virtue” (Ps. 88:16–18). It is beautifully said that glory belongs not to them but to their virtue. For glory without virtue is surely gained without right, pursued prematurely, and sought dangerously. Virtue is the step to glory; virtue is the mother of glory. Glory is deceptive and beauty vain when virtue has not brought it forth. Virtue alone is that to which glory is rightly due and safely given. [Col. 0371C]

2. Saint Victor lacks neither virtue nor glory; but it is worthwhile to consider how both came about in the man, and in what order. He fought bravely, overcame manfully, and only then was crowned with glory and honor. How, indeed, could a strong warrior and humble victor have remained without glory? Yet even on the day of his prowess he was not without glory, being wondrous in signs and miracles. In Victor’s life, beloved, we have both what we may rightly admire and what we may profitably imitate. I marvel that he gave wine in the wilderness, not from a vine but from a spring. I marvel and am astonished that, while still an infant in the womb, he was a terror to the fearful demons, being foreknown by them and even then designated by name. Nor was the name empty when the flight of enemies and their extorted confession granted victory to the little infant. Who likewise would not marvel at a thief detected by a demon, and then at a man shortly afterward freed by a demon? Who would not judge altogether astonishing that a man surrounded by flesh, while heaven stood open, fixed the eyes of flesh upon the heavenly light, saw visions of God, was additionally soothed by angelic song, and instructed by an oracle? We venerate such things and similar things in the holy man; we do not imitate them. Rightly so, because they may fail to occur without danger to salvation, but they cannot be assumed without danger to salvation. More solid things than sublime things are certainly safer to imitate: those which smell more of virtue and less of glory. [Col. 0372B]

3. Let us therefore strive to be conformed in conduct to him whom, in marvelous deeds, we cannot imitate even if we wish to do so. Let us imitate in this man a sober manner of life and devout affection; let us imitate gentleness of spirit, chastity of body, restraint of speech, purity of mind; putting a bridle upon anger and a measure upon the tongue; sleeping less, praying more often, admonishing ourselves with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; joining days to nights and occupying them with divine praises. Let us imitate the better gifts. Let us learn from him that he was meek and humble of heart. Let us imitate, I say, his generosity toward the poor, his graciousness toward guests, his patience with sinners, and his kindness toward all. This is better. In these things is the pattern by which we are to be formed; in miracles is the glory from which we should restrain ourselves. Let those things gladden us; let these build us up. Let those move us; let these advance us. Let us feast, beloved, called to the table of a rich man—a table abundant in bread and heaped with delights. Is he not rich who refreshes us with examples, protects us with merits, and gladdens us with signs? Truly rich, at whose solemn feast today angels and human beings gather together: the latter to be refreshed, the former to delight; these to make progress, those to rejoice. What is a life filled with good things but a table heaped with food? Yet not everything is set before everyone; each person should take what he sees will be useful and suitable to himself. [Col. 0372D]

4. For my part, with more salutary judgment, I carefully consider what is set before me. I am instructed to choose what is mine and not touch what belongs to another. I shall not stretch out my hand toward the glory of miracles, lest, if I attempt what I have not received from above, I deservedly lose even what I seem to have received. I do not raise my eyes with him to investigate the secret things of heaven, lest, overwhelmed and confounded by glory, I recoil, fleeing too late to the counsel of the Wise Man, who says: “Do not seek things too high for you, nor search into things stronger than you” (Ecclus. 3:22). New wine from reddened waters is brought to the table; I do not touch it, because I know it has not been set before me, since I am unable similarly to change elements and renew natures. I see likewise upon Victor’s table that he heard angels singing. Shall I too see heavenly singers displayed to me? Or shall those harpists from the Apocalypse play their harps before me on their harps? (Rev. 14:2). While still living in the body, he commands demons; once released from the body, he frees one bound in a body. These are foods, but not mine—indeed pleasant and savory, but my soul does not touch them, since I, being poor, have nothing with which I can render such things in return. But if I consider carefully, behold: before my eyes upon the saint’s table are the rigor of judgment, the strength of discipline, the mirror of holiness, the pattern of life, the badge of virtue. These I take without presumption and take to my salvation; and if I neglect them, they will be strictly required of me. [Col. 0373B]

5. Hear further what I judge has rightly been set before me. If you offer from the rich man’s table the bread of sorrow and wine of compunction, I, being poor and needy, take it without fear. “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. 41:4), and “I shall mingle my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101:10). This is my portion, for I have committed deeds to be mourned. Yet, I think, I shall not be weary of this food, because he who has added knowledge has also added sorrow. And if examples of temperance, justice, prudence, or fortitude appear, I take them without hesitation, knowing that I ought to prepare such things. I do not doubt that these are set before me and that these will be required from me. Are signs and miracles to be demanded of us, so that we may in return prepare them for the rich man? Brothers, they are vessels of honor for him who has invited us, not food for the poor. Therefore you who have been invited, carefully consider what he has set before you and what he has set before himself. For not everything placed upon the table is placed before you. What if a drink is served in a golden cup? The cup is not set before you, but the drink: take the drink and set down the gold. Thus the householder shares examples of good works and rectitude of conduct with his household, while retaining for himself the prerogative of miracles. Yet in both these and those, he must be glorified to whom belongs the gift of living holily, whose power it is to work signs, who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity for ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 0373D]

### SERMON II

1. Rejoice in the Lord, beloved, who, among the continual benefits of his mercy, granted to the world a man by whose example many might be saved. Again I say, rejoice that, having been taken from our midst, he has drawn near to God, so that many more may be saved through his intercession. The merciful and compassionate Lord has one drawn from humankind through whom he may forgive human sins; the devout and merciful advocate has time and place for interceding—indeed, a quiet place and a time of leisure. He was seen on earth that he might be an example; he was raised to heaven that he might be an advocate. Here he forms us for life; there he calls us to glory. He who was an encourager to work has become a mediator to the kingdom. A good mediator: now asking nothing for himself, he desires to transfer wholly to us both the affection of the suppliant and the fruit of supplication. For what can one seek for himself who lacks nothing? “The Lord preserves him, gives him life, and makes him blessed in glory”; nothing will be lacking to him, set in a place of pasture. This is the day of his glorious departure, the day of his heart’s joy; let us exult and rejoice in it. He has entered into the powers of the Lord; let us rejoice, because he is now more powerful to save. [Col. 0374B]

2. Today Victor, having laid aside the body by which alone he seemed hindered from entering into glory, entered the holy places with all the more alacrity because he was more unencumbered, made like the saints in glory. Today, from the last and lowly place which he had chosen for himself at the Savior’s counsel, summoned by the supreme householder himself, the true friend went up higher, and he has glory before those dining with him. Today, having despised the world and triumphed over the prince of the world, Victor truly ascended above the world, receiving from the Lord’s hand the crown of victory. He ascended with an immense store of merits, illustrious in triumphs and glorious in miracles. The veteran soldier rests; after the labors and sweat of his completed sacred service, he is happily established and sublimely crowned. “His soul shall dwell among good things.” Where, you ask? With Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. Thus he sits with such companions and in such a place: he sits lofty and radiant; he sits rejoicing and praising; he sits in delight, adorned with her jewels, surrounded with apples, supported by flowers; he sits, I say, at ease, free from anxieties, abounding in delights, rich in leisure and rest for devotion to wisdom. She who sat and wept by the rivers of Babylon now sits beside the fountain of life, and her dwelling is beside the torrent of delight whose rush makes glad the city of God. She has found for herself a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters; and with the Samaritan woman she drinks the water of saving wisdom, that she may never thirst. The fruit of her hands is given to her, her works praise her in the gates, and she glories in the testimony of conscience—her own conscience, I mean, not another’s. He sits amid angels, plainly worthy of their companionship: he burns with longing for them, shines with purity, and is adorned with chastity. He sits among the apostles, a man of apostolic grace; nor has he any reason to hide from the company of prophets, since he glorified and bore in his body the one whom they foretold. Nor does our Victor think himself to be excluded from the victorious choirs of martyrs, since by a harsh and prolonged martyrdom he offered the living sacrifice of his own body. [Col. 0374D]

3. The veteran soldier sits, now at rest in the sweetness and security due to him—secure indeed concerning himself, yet solicitous for us. For he did not lay aside with the body’s decay the feelings of compassion; nor did he put on the robe of glory in such a way as also to put on forgetfulness of our misery and of his own mercy. The dwelling inhabited by Victor’s soul is not a land of forgetfulness; it is not a land of toil, in which he might be occupied; it is not, indeed, land at all, but heaven. Does the heavenly dwelling harden the souls it receives, rob them of memory, or strip them of compassion? Brothers, the breadth of heaven enlarges hearts; it does not constrict them. It gladdens minds; it does not estrange them. It does not contract affections, but extends them. In God’s light memory is made clear, not obscured; in God’s light one learns what one does not know, not unlearns what one knows. Do those heavenly spirits, who have inhabited heaven from the beginning, disdain the earth because they dwell in heaven, rather than visiting and frequenting it all the more? Does their continual vision of the Father’s face render the service of compassion void? “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who shall inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14). What then? Angels hasten about and assist human beings; and those who are from among us do not know us, nor do they now know how to suffer with us, though they too suffered in the same condition? Those who do not know sufferings nevertheless feel ours; and those who came out of great tribulation no longer recognize the state in which they themselves were? I know one who said: “The righteous await me until you repay me” (Ps. 141:8). Victor is righteous, undoubtedly awaiting our recompense also. He is not Pharaoh’s cupbearer, who kept found favor to himself and did not remember his prophet and fellow captive (Gen. 40). He is a minister of Christ and follows Christ. Christ did not forget his promise, nor deny the fellowship of the kingdom to his companion in suffering. The disciple is not above the master; Victor can do nothing except what he sees the master doing. The works which he did, this man also did likewise.

4. Now that he has entered heaven—which even before he had beheld open to his blessed eyes—he truly contemplates the glory of God with unveiled face, absorbed indeed, yet not forgetful of the cry of the poor. Blessed vision, by which he is transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. A little one for battle, great for victory, not yet emerging from his mother’s womb and already casting out demons, Victor was translated alive among sinners, with an increase of virtues and merits. O man of singular [Col. 0375D] holiness, holy before he was born, Victor in deed before he was Victor in name! While still enclosed in the womb, he already triumphed over the enemy. O holiness venerable even to the angels, which, with equal eagerness though unequal intention, evil spirits flee and good spirits frequent. Nor could I easily say what establishes the man as holier: the favor of these, or the terror of those. Dwelling on earth in body but in heaven in mind, he would sometimes hear more intimate communications, at other times the pleasing voices of the heavenly spirits, with an ineffable sweetness of song. Truly, Victor, your soul was one of the jewels that appeared to you on the cross. Truly fastened to the cross, when grafted into divine glory it put on for itself the same image of brightness that it found there. He who had given his spirit to the combatant opened his bosom to the conqueror. O victorious soul, which, like a flying sparrow, escaped the snares of the world: look upon heedless souls entangled and endangered in them, that through your patronage we may be delivered.

[Col. 0376B] 5. O veteran soldier, who exchanged the hard labors of Christian warfare for the repose of angelic blessedness: look upon your unwarlike and weak fellow-soldiers, who amid hostile swords and spiritual wickedness are occupied with your praises. O illustrious Victor, who triumphed most gloriously both from earth and from heaven, nobly scorning the glory of the former and piously seizing by force the kingdoms of the latter: look down from heaven upon those bound to earth, so that this may be the completion of your triumphs—that at last we too may know that you have conquered. For if your name comes from the thing itself, the perfect truth of the name will be reckoned from our deliverance. Indeed, its interpretation remains deficient so long as we, who are yours, are by no means set free. How devout, how sweet, how delightful, O Victor, it is in this place of affliction and in this body of death to [Col. 0376C] sing of you, honor you, and pray to you! Your name and your memorial are dripping honeycomb on the lips of captives; honey and milk are beneath the tongue of those delighted by remembrance of you. Come then, strong athlete, gentle patron, faithful advocate: rise to our aid, so that we too may rejoice in our rescue and you may glory in your full victory. O almighty Father, we have sinned against you, becoming alien children; but we have drawn near in Victor, who, as he conquered his own desire, may also conquer your wrath and mightily restore us likewise to favor. O victorious Jesus, we praise you in our Victor, because we acknowledge that you conquered in him. Grant him, most merciful Jesus, so to glory in his victory in you that forgetfulness of us may not come over him. Son of God, cause him always to remember us before your sight, [Col. 0376D] to undertake and plead our cause at your fearful judgment—you who live and reign as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0375]

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BENEDICT THE ABBOT. SERMON.

[Col. 0375D] 1. As you gather together to hear the word of salvation, my brothers, I greatly fear that someone may perhaps receive it less worthily, and not receive it as the word of God ought to be received. For I know that the land which has often received rain falling upon it, if it does not bear fruit, will be rejected and near to a curse (Heb. 6:7–8). And I certainly, if I could, would rather give you [Col. 0376D] blessings than curses. Indeed, I desire that the very blessing of our heavenly Father—not my own, though by his gracious favor you receive it through my mouth—may always remain a blessing to you and never be capable of being changed into a curse.

2. Today we celebrate the birth-feast of our glorious master Benedict; therefore, as custom requires, a solemn sermon is owed to you both for him and about him. [Note: [Col. 0377] In the manuscript of Marmoutier there is much variation in the wording that follows, though the sense is the same; the familiar reading is preferable.] His most sweet name you should embrace and honor with every joy, since he is our leader, our teacher, and our lawgiver. I too take delight in his remembrance, though I do not dare to mention the name of this blessed father without shame of my own. For I share with you the renunciation of the world in imitation of him and the profession of monastic discipline; yet, apart from you, I share with him alone the title of abbot. He was an abbot, and so am I. O abbot—and abbot! One name, but in the one only the shadow of a great name; one ministry, but alas for me, how unlike the ministers, how unlike the ministry itself! Woe to me if in the future I shall be as far from you, blessed Benedict, [Col. 0377B] as I am found in the present to be far from the footsteps of your holiness. But there is no need for me to expound this among you. I know that I speak to those who know; I ask only that you lighten this shame and fear of mine by brotherly compassion.

3. Yet since a stewardship has altogether been entrusted to me, although I have nothing with me to set before you, I shall seek from blessed Benedict three loaves with which to feed you. Let his holiness, his righteousness, and his piety refresh you. Remember, beloved, that not all who were in the Lord’s procession spread their own garments before him. In that procession, I mean, which, with the Lord’s assent, we are shortly to celebrate: when the people came out to meet the Lord as he approached his Passion, seated upon an ass, not all spread their garments in the road; rather, some cut branches from the trees (Matt. 21:1–9). It was no great thing that they gave freely what they had freely received. Yet neither were they altogether idle, nor are they said to have been excluded from the procession. My brothers, the Lord Christ’s gentle beast of burden, who can say with the Prophet, “I became like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. 72:23): you upon whom Christ sits, since “the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom”; and the Apostle proclaims [Col. 0377C] Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24)—if I do not have garments to spread beneath your feet, I shall at least try to cut branches from trees, so that my ministry may not be wholly lacking some small service for so great a procession.

[Col. 0377D] 4. Blessed Benedict was a tree, great and fruitful, like the tree planted beside streams of water (Ps. 1:3). Where are the streams of water? Surely in the valleys, because “waters pass through the midst of the mountains.” For who does not see that even mountain torrents avoid the heights and always turn toward the low-lying middle of the valley? Thus indeed, thus God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4:6). Here plant your foot securely, whoever you are, beast of Christ; lean upon this branch; walk the path of the valley. Certainly the ancient serpent has established his seat on the mountain, biting [Col. 0378A] the horse’s hoofs so that its rider falls backward. Therefore choose the valley rather for walking; choose the valley for planting. Nor indeed do we ordinarily choose mountainous places for planting trees, because they are frequently dry and stony. In the valleys is richness: there plants thrive; there the ear is full; there a hundredfold fruit springs up, according to the saying, “The valleys shall abound in grain” (Ps. 64:14). You hear that everywhere the valley is praised, everywhere humility is preached. Therefore plant where there are streams of water, because there is abundance of spiritual grace; and “the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord,” that is, heavenly blessings cause him to be praised. Let us stand in this valley, beloved, and stand planted, so that we may not wither. Let us not be moved by every wind, as it is written: “If the spirit of one having authority rises up against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. 10:4). For no temptation will prevail against you if you do not walk in things great and wonderful beyond you, but remain rooted and founded with firm roots in humility. Thus this holy confessor of the Lord, planted beside streams of water, gave his fruit in its season.

5. For there are those who bear no fruit; there are those who bear fruit, but not their own; and there are those who bear their own fruit, but not in its season. There are, I say, fruitless trees, such as oak and elm and other wild trees; but no one plants such trees in his garden, because they bear no fruit, and whatever fruit they bear is not fit for human food but for swine. Such are the children of this age, acting in revelry and drunkenness, [Col. 0378C] in gluttonous feasting and voracity, in beds and shameless acts. For these are food for swine, which the true Jew is forbidden to eat (Deut. 14:8)—that is, the Christian, who ought not to cling to such things. For just as swine’s flesh, when eaten, adheres to our flesh so that it becomes one flesh with us, so the transgressor of the Lord’s command associates with himself foul spirits and, clinging to them, becomes one demon with them. For this reason too that animal is forbidden as an offering in sacrifices: it signifies foul and unclean spirits who, abandoning all purity, delight only in their own filth and ever take pleasure in being enveloped in the mire of vices and crimes. Thus in the Gospel, when that accursed legion was cast out of a human being, it asks for swine as animals like itself, and is not refused (Mark 5:1–13). Fruitless trees bear fruit for these, and the axe already seems laid to their roots.

6. But the trees which bear fruit, yet not their own, are hypocrites, who, like Simon of Cyrene, carry a cross not their own: lacking religious intention, they are compelled into service, and are compelled by love of the glory they desire to do what they do not love. Moreover, in the phrase “in its season” (Ps. 1:3), some are rebuked who wish to bear fruit before its time. Do we not fear untimely blossoms even in our own trees when they bud sooner than they should? So there are some whose fruits arise less successfully because they arise too hastily. These are those who, at the beginning of their conversion, presumptuously wish immediately to bear fruit for others, contrary to the decrees of the law plowing with a firstborn ox and hastening to shear the firstborn of a sheep. Do you wish to know how carefully this holy master of ours avoided that? I offer you this branch also: for three years he remained known to God alone and unknown to human beings. He indeed bore much fruit, as you see, but in its season. For he did not believe it was the time to bear fruit while he was oppressed by such a severe temptation of the flesh that he almost yielded, almost withdrew. Nor shall I pass over even this branch, because, although it is in some manner shaggy with the prickly thorns [Col. 0379B] into which Benedict cast himself for the Lord, it is nevertheless wholly useful—useful to the Lord’s beast of burden because of the pits of temptation, lest it fall into them by consenting, but instead resist, act manfully, endure the Lord, and not despair. Therefore set your foot here, beast of Christ, and learn, however fiercely bitter temptation may rage, neither to yield nor to believe that you are for that reason abandoned by the Lord; rather remember what is written: “Call upon me in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. 49:15).

7. Therefore, as I began to say, blessed Benedict did not believe it was then the time to bear fruit while he was still oppressed by such great temptations; but the time came, and in its season he gave his fruit. Of his fruit are the three things I touched upon above: his holiness, [Col. 0379C] his righteousness, and his piety. Miracles prove his holiness, teaching his piety, and life his righteousness. You see, beast of Christ, branches green with leaves, blooming with flowers, laden with fruit. Lean on these, so that you may make straight paths for your feet. But how do I set his miracles before you? Is it so that you may wish to work miracles? By no means, but so that you may lean upon his miracles: namely, that you may trust and rejoice because you are placed under such a shepherd, because you have deserved to have so great a patron. For he is altogether very powerful in heaven who proved so powerful on earth, exalted in greatness of glory according to the greatness of grace. For branches are known to emerge according to the size of the roots; and by however many roots a tree is supported, by so many branches, as they say, it is adorned. Thus, although we do not have miracles of our own, our patrons’ miracles ought to be a great consolation to us. Teaching, moreover, instructs us and directs our steps in the way of peace. The righteousness of his life altogether strengthens and encourages us, so that we are stirred all the more to do what he taught because we are certain that he taught nothing other than what he did. The living and effective word is the example of a deed, making what is said highly persuasive by showing that what is urged is possible.

8. Thus holiness strengthens, piety forms, and righteousness confirms. For how great was his piety, in that he benefited not only those present but was also concerned for those to come? This tree bore fruit not only for those who then existed; its fruit remains and increases even to this day. Clearly beloved by God and by human beings: not merely one whose presence was a blessing, as are many beloved by God alone because they are now known to God alone; but his memory too is still in blessing. For even to this day, in a threefold confession of love for the Lord, he feeds the Lord’s flock with this threefold fruit. His life feeds, his teaching feeds, and his intercession feeds. Helped continually through this, bear fruit also, beloved, because you have been established for this purpose: that you may go and bear fruit. Go out from where? Certainly from yourselves, as it is written: “Turn away from your desires” (Ecclus. 18:30). For we read of the Lord too that he went out to sow his seed (Matt. 13:3). Behold, here also we have his seed, just as earlier we had his fruit. Let us imitate him also, brothers, [Col. 0380B] because he came for this purpose: to give us a pattern and show us the way.

9. Perhaps the Lord himself is also a tree, and we ought to receive from him too branches to place beneath your feet. Indeed, not perhaps: rather, he truly is a tree and a heavenly plant, but planted on earth, as it is written: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84:12). From him, therefore, I place this branch before you: that, as he emptied himself, you may have this same mind in yourselves. Yet it is not so much I who place it before you as the Apostle, in whom you have read: “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness [Col. 0380C] of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2:5–7). Therefore, dearest brothers, empty yourselves, humble yourselves, sow yourselves, lose yourselves. Sow the natural body, and it shall rise a spiritual body. Lose your souls, and you shall preserve them unto eternal life. Do you wish to know how the Apostle himself who taught this did it? “Whether,” he says, “we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5:13). What then about you? “I,” he says, “became like a lost vessel” (Ps. 30:13). One rightly loses himself who never does anything for himself; rather, all his intention and every desire tend toward God’s pleasure and the benefit of his brothers. For unhappy is the one who sows in the flesh, because from the flesh he shall reap corruption (Gal. [Col. 0380D] 6:8). Elsewhere it is written: “Blessed are those who sow beside all waters” (Isa. 32:20). But how beside all waters? Perhaps also beside the waters of which we read: “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:4): these are the angelic powers and heavenly peoples. Precisely so: “For we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Cor. 4:9).

10. Therefore let us sow among human beings a good example through visible works; let us sow among angels great joy through hidden sighs and other such things known to them alone. For there is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance. Hence the Apostle said: “Providing what is good not only before God, but also before human beings” (2 Cor. 8: [Col. 0381A] 21). For we are altogether known to God; but he said “before God,” that is, before those who always stand before his face. They especially are pleased when they see you praying secretly, or pondering some psalm, or doing something of that kind. Sow in this way, then; bear fruit in this way, beloved. Sow also, because so many before you have sown; bear fruit, because they have sown for you. O race of Adam, how many have sown in you, and how precious is the seed! How wretchedly you will perish, and how deservedly, if so great a seed—and with it the labor of those who sowed—perishes in you. To what destruction will you be handed over by the husbandman if all these things perish in you? The whole Trinity sowed in our earth; angels and apostles likewise sowed; martyrs, confessors, and virgins sowed. God [Col. 0381B] the Father sowed, because his heart poured forth the good Word. For “the Lord gave goodness, and our land gave its fruit.” The Son also sowed: for he is the one who went out to sow his seed. The Father did not go out, but the Son proceeded from the Father and came into the world, so that he who had first been the thought of peace in the Father’s heart might himself become our peace in his mother’s womb. The Holy Spirit also sowed, because he too came, and divided tongues as of fire appeared to the disciples. Thus the whole Trinity sowed: the Father, namely, peace from heaven; the Son, truth; and the Holy Spirit, charity.

11. The angels too sowed when, while others fell, they themselves stood. For that Lucifer said—now no longer light-bearer (*lucifer*), but darkness-bearer and evening star: “I shall sit on the mountain of the covenant; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14). [Col. 0381C] O shameless and foolish one! “Thousands of thousands minister to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stand before him” (Dan. 7:10), and you will sit? “The cherubim,” says the prophet, “stood” (Isa. 6:2; Ezek. 10:3); they did not sit. What labor have you undertaken that you should now sit? “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?” And you will sit? What have you sown, that you should now reap? This is not yours, not yours, but belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by the Father. Why do you envy them? Surely they shall sit—those worms of the earth shall sit in judgment, while you shall not merely fail to stand, but shall stand to be judged. “Do you not know,” says the Apostle, “that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3). They, certainly, who went forth weeping, casting their seeds, shall come again [Col. 0381D] with exultation, carrying their sheaves (Ps. 125:6). There are two sheaves that you seek: honor and rest. You desire a seat and exaltation; but not so, impious one, not so. You shall not gather, because you did not sow. Those who sowed labor and lowliness shall reap honor and rest alike. For “instead of their double shame and reproach [variant: labor], they shall possess double in their land.” Hence one said: “See my lowliness and my labor” (Ps. 24:18). Today you have certainly heard in the Gospel the Lord promising and saying to the disciples: “You shall sit upon seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Behold the rest of sitting and the honor of judgment. For the Lord himself did not wish to attain these except through lowliness [Col. 0382A] and labor. Thus he was condemned to a most shameful death, questioned under tortures, and filled with reproaches, so that the enemy, together with all who imitate him and depart from the way, might be clothed with shame. He is the one, wicked one—he is the one who shall sit on the throne of his majesty, like the Most High and co-equal in height with him. Holy angels considered this when, as the evil one fell, they did not consent to that apostasy, leaving us an example so that, as they chose to minister, we too may do likewise. Those also who flee labor and seize at honor should know that they imitate him who sought a seat and exaltation; and if his fault does not sufficiently terrify them, let at least his punishment terrify them. For all things have turned to the opposite, so that he was made to be mocked and eternal fire prepared for him. The holy angels sowed prudence for us to avoid these things, having themselves retained it when others fell.

12. The apostles too sowed this same prudence for us when, while those who followed the wisdom of this world—which is foolishness with God—and the prudence of the flesh—which works death and is hostile to God—withdrew, they themselves clung to the Lord. For those others, scandalized on hearing of the mystery of flesh and blood, no longer walked with him. But when the disciples were asked whether they too wished to depart, they answered: “To whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.” We must imitate this prudence, brothers, because many still walk with Jesus until it comes to eating [Col. 0382C] his flesh and drinking his blood—that is, to sharing in his sufferings, for both that saying and the sacrament itself signify this. From that point they are scandalized and go back, saying that this is a hard saying (John 6:67, 68, 69, 61). Let us be prudent with the apostles and say: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. We do not depart from you; you will give us life. A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4). The world does not alone possess delight; rather, delight is much greater in your words. Thus the Prophet says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103). To whom, therefore, shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, Lord, and they are beyond all that the world can possess.
