Not life itself alone, but also the promise of eternal life and the expectation of the righteous is joy—such great joy that nothing which is desired can be compared to it. Thus the holy apostles sowed this prudence for us. The martyrs, moreover, plainly sowed fortitude. The confessors sowed righteousness, which they pursued throughout all their life. For this is the difference between martyrs and confessors: it is like the difference between Peter, leaving everything at once, and Abraham, expending worldly substance in good uses. For the former, made perfect in a short time, fulfilled many ages; but the latter endured long and manifold martyrdoms. Holy virgins plainly sowed temperance, since they so trampled lust underfoot.

[Col. 0383]

## ON THE FEAST OF THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY.

### SERMON I

[Note: [Col. 0383] In the Fuldensis manuscript this is third, while the sermon that is third here is second there; but our third sermon is first in that manuscript.]

On the words of Psalm 84:10–11: “That glory may dwell in our land.”

[Col. 0383A]

1. “That glory may dwell in our land, mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed.” “This is our glory,” says the Apostle, “the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). Not, indeed, the sort of testimony possessed by that proud Pharisee, who, through a deceived and deceiving thought, bore testimony about himself (Luke 18:11–12), and whose testimony was not true; but when the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit. I believe that this testimony consists of three things. First of all it is necessary to believe that you cannot have forgiveness of sins except through [Col. 0383B] God’s pardon; next, that you can possess no good work whatsoever unless he himself has also given it; lastly, that by no works can you merit eternal life unless it too is freely given you. For who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed, except the one who alone is clean? (Job 14:4). Certainly, what has been done cannot become undone; yet, if he does not impute it, it shall be as though it had not been. Considering this, the Prophet also says: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 31:2). As for good works, it is entirely certain that no one possesses them from himself. For if human nature, even while still whole, could not stand, how much less can it rise again of itself now that it has been corrupted? It is certain that all things, insofar as they are concerned, tend toward their origin and are always more inclined toward it. Thus we too, created from nothing, plainly fall continually into sin—which is nothing—if we are left to ourselves.

2. As for eternal life, we know that the sufferings of this present time are not proportionate to the glory to come, even if one person endured them all. Human merits are not such that eternal life should therefore be owed by right, or that God would commit any injustice if he did not give it. For, not to mention that all merits are gifts of God and that a human being is therefore more indebted to God for them than God is to a human being, what are all merits in comparison with such glory? Indeed, who is a better prophet than the one to whom the Lord himself bears such remarkable testimony, saying: “I have found a man after my own heart” (1 Sam. 13:14; Acts 13:22)? Yet even he had to say to God: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord” (Ps. 142:2). Therefore let no one deceive himself: for if he wishes to reckon carefully [variant: calculate], he will undoubtedly find that he cannot meet one who comes against him with twenty thousand even with ten thousand (Luke 14:31).

3. Yet the things we have just said do not altogether suffice; rather, they are to be regarded as a kind of beginning and foundation of faith. Therefore, if you believe that your sins cannot be blotted out except by him against whom alone you have sinned and in whom sin cannot fall, you do well; but add this also: believe that your sins are forgiven you through him. This is the testimony which the Holy Spirit bears in your heart, saying: “Your sins are forgiven you.” For thus the Apostle judges that a human being is justified freely by faith (Rom. 3:28). Likewise, if regarding merits you believe that they cannot be possessed except through him, it is insufficient until the Spirit of truth bears witness to you that you possess them through him. So also you must have the Spirit’s testimony regarding eternal life: that by the divine gift you shall attain it. For he himself forgives sins, he himself gives merits, and he likewise himself bestows rewards.

[Col. 0384B] 4. These testimonies, moreover, have become exceedingly credible to me. For concerning forgiveness of sins I hold the Lord’s Passion as an utterly powerful proof. The voice of his blood has indeed prevailed far more than the voice of Abel’s blood, crying in the hearts of the elect for the forgiveness of all sins. For he was delivered up for our sins; and there is no doubt that his death is more powerful and effective for good than our sins are for evil. Likewise, the resurrection is an effective proof to me regarding good works, because “he rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4:25). Concerning hope of rewards, moreover, his Ascension is its testimony, because he ascended for our glorification. You have these three in the Psalms, where the Prophet says: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 31:2); elsewhere, “Blessed is the man whose help is from you” (Ps. 83:6); and again elsewhere, “Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken up; he shall dwell in your courts” (Ps. 64:5). This is true glory, indwelling glory, because it comes from him who dwells in our hearts through faith. But the children of Adam, seeking glory from one another, did not desire the glory which comes from God alone; and so, pursuing glory that flowed in from outside, they had glory not in themselves but rather in others.

5. Do you wish to know whence comes to a human being this indwelling glory? I shall say briefly, because my purpose hastens toward the mysteries. For I had proposed only to investigate more diligently the mystical sense in those prophetic words [Col. 0384D]; but the apostolic saying about inward glory and the testimony of conscience, meeting me at the outset, turned me back toward moral matters. Thus this glory dwells even here in our land if mercy and truth meet one another, and righteousness and peace kiss each other. For our truth of confession [variant: conversion] must meet the mercy that goes before; and thereafter we must pursue holiness and peace, without which no one shall see God. For when someone is pierced with compunction, mercy has already gone before that person; [Col. 0385A] but it will by no means enter until the truth of confession meets it. “I have sinned against the Lord,” David himself said to Nathan the prophet when he was rebuked for adultery and murder. And the prophet said, “The Lord has taken away your sin from you” (2 Sam. 12:13). Clearly mercy and truth met one another. And this is so that you may turn away from evil. But that you may do good, you must sing praise with tambourine and dance, so that the mortification of your flesh, the fruits of penitence, and works of righteousness may be performed in unity and harmony—for unity of spirit is the bond of perfection—and so that you may turn neither to the right nor to the left. For some have a right hand that is a right hand of iniquity. That Pharisee whom we mentioned above was not like other people (Luke 18:11); but, as we said, he bore testimony concerning himself, and it was not true. Certainly, whoever he may be in whom mercy and truth have met one another, and righteousness and peace have kissed, may glory securely; but let that person glory in him who bears witness to him, namely, in the Spirit of truth.

6. “That glory may dwell in our land, mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed.” If a wise son is his father’s glory, and since none is wiser than Wisdom itself, it is surely clear that Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, is the Father’s glory. Since it had been foretold concerning him “at many times and in many ways” through the prophets (Heb. 1:1), that he would be seen on earth and dwell among human beings, the Psalmist indicates by these words how this came about, and how, once those things foretold concerning him through the mouth of all the prophets had been fulfilled, glory dwelt in our land. It is as though he said more plainly: In order that the Word might become flesh and dwell among us, mercy and truth met one another, righteousness and peace kissed. This is a great mystery, brothers, and ought to be examined more diligently, were words not lacking both for the understanding of the mystery and for understanding itself. Yet I shall say, however imperfectly, a little of what I think, in case I may seem to have given an occasion to someone wise. I seem to see, beloved, the first human being clothed from the beginning of creation in these four virtues and, as the prophet recalls, dressed in the garment of salvation (Isa. 61:10). For in these four lies the wholeness of salvation, and salvation cannot stand without all of them, especially since they could not be virtues if they were separated from one another. Thus the human being received mercy as a guardian and attendant, so that it might go before, follow after, protect, and preserve him everywhere. You see what a nurse God gave his little child, what an attendant he gave to the newly born human being. But he also needed an instructor, as a noble and rational creature, so that he might not be guarded like some beast of burden, but educated like a child. No teacher could have been found more suitable for this office than Truth itself, which would eventually lead him into knowledge of the highest Truth. Meanwhile, lest he should be found wise for doing evil, and sin should be counted against him as one who knows the good [Col. 0386A] and does not do it, he also received righteousness to govern him. Moreover, the most kindly hand of the Creator added peace, by which he might be cherished and delighted: a twofold peace, namely, so that there might be neither battles within nor fears without—that is, neither should the flesh desire against the spirit nor should any creature be a terror to him. For he freely gave names to all the beasts, and the serpent itself, since it did not venture violence, attacked him rather by deceit. What could be lacking to one whom mercy guarded, truth instructed, righteousness governed, and peace cherished?

7. But alas! this man, to his great ruin and folly, went down from Jerusalem to Jericho; for he fell among robbers, by whom he is said first of all to have been stripped [Col. 0386B] (Luke 10:30). Was he not stripped, when, at the Lord’s coming, he complained that he was naked? Nor could he be reclothed, or receive back the garments taken from him, unless Christ lost his own. For just as he could not be brought to life in his soul except through Christ’s bodily death, so neither could he be reclothed without Christ’s being stripped. And see whether it was not on account of these four parts of the garment, which the first and old man had lost, that the garments of the second and new man were likewise divided into four parts.

Or perhaps you ask also about the seamless tunic, which was not divided but fell by lot? I judge this to be the divine image, which, certainly, is not sewn on but implanted and impressed upon nature itself, and cannot be divided or torn. For man was made in the image and likeness of God: he has freedom of choice in the image [Col. 0386C], and virtues in the likeness. The likeness indeed was lost; nevertheless, man passes on in the image. For the image can be burned even in Gehenna, but not consumed; it can burn, but not be erased. Therefore this is not torn, but falls by lot. And wherever the soul arrives, this image will be there with it. The likeness is not so: either it remains in goodness, or, if the soul sins, it is miserably changed, made like the senseless beasts.

8. But since we have said that man was despoiled of four virtues, it is fitting to say how he was despoiled of each. Man lost justice when Eve obeyed the serpent’s voice, and Adam the woman’s, rather than God’s. Yet something remained [Col. 0386D] that they could grasp, and the Lord indicated this in his examination; but they rejected even that, turning to words of wickedness, to make excuses for sins. For the first portion of justice is not to sin; the second is, through repentance, to condemn sin.

He also lost mercy when Eve was so inflamed by her desire that she spared neither herself nor her husband nor her children yet to be born, binding them all together under a terrible curse and to the necessity of death. Adam too exposed to God’s indignation the woman for whom he had sinned, as though wishing to turn aside the arrow behind her back. For the woman saw that the tree was beautiful to look upon and pleasant for eating, and had heard from the serpent that they would be like gods. A threefold cord is not easily broken: curiosity, pleasure, and vanity. These alone the world has [Col. 0387A]: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life. Drawn away and enticed by these, the cruel mother cast off all mercy. Adam likewise, who had wrongly shown mercy to the woman by sinning with her, was unwilling rightly to show mercy by enduring punishment for her [variant: “or to endure punishment”].

The woman was also deprived of truth: first, by perversely twisting what she had heard, “You shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17), and saying, “Lest perhaps we die”; finally, by believing the serpent, who utterly denied it and said, “You shall certainly not die.” Adam too was deprived of truth when he was ashamed to confess it, putting forward leaves—that is, coverings of excuses. For Truth itself says: “Whoever is ashamed of me before men, I too will be ashamed of him before my Father” (Luke 9:26).

They immediately lost peace as well, because “there is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord (Isa. 48:22). Had they not found a contrary law in their members, when they began anew to be ashamed of their nakedness? “I was afraid,” he says, “because I was naked” (Gen. 3). Not so, poor man, not so did you fear a little before: you did not seek leaves, though naked in body, as you are now.

9. From this point indeed—to pursue the parable of the Prophet himself, who recalled that they met and were reconciled in a kiss—a grave contention seems to have arisen among the virtues. Truth and Justice afflicted the wretched man; Peace and Mercy, strangers to this zeal, judged that he should rather be spared. For these two are foster-sisters to one another, just as the former two are. Thus it happened that, while Truth and Justice persisted [Col. 0387C] in vengeance, striking the transgressor from either side and adding present troubles to the threat of future punishment, Peace and Mercy withdrew into the Father’s heart, returning to the Lord who had given them. For he alone was thinking thoughts of peace when all things seemed full of affliction. Peace did not cease, nor did Mercy allow him silence; but, beating upon his fatherly heart with a certain pious whisper, they said:

“Will God cast off forever? Or will he no longer add that he may again be well pleased? Will God forget to have mercy? Or will he restrain his mercies in his anger?” (Ps. 76:8, 10).

And although the Father of mercies seemed long and greatly to dissemble, in order meanwhile to satisfy the zeal of Justice and Truth, yet the importunity of the petitioners was not fruitless, but was heard at the fitting time.

10. Perhaps he gave this response to their intercession: “How long will your prayers continue? I am indebted also to your sisters, whom you see girded for executing vengeance among the nations—Justice and Truth. Let them be called; let them come, and let us deliberate together concerning this matter.”

The heavenly messengers hastened; and when they saw the misery of humankind and the cruel wound, as the prophet says, “the angels of peace wept bitterly” (Isa. 33:7). For who would more faithfully seek or request the things belonging to peace than the angels of peace? Indeed, by common deliberation Truth ascended on the appointed day; but she ascended only as far as the clouds: not yet entirely bright, but still somewhat darkened and overcast [Col. 0388A] by the zeal of indignation. Thus came to pass what we read in the Prophet: “Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches unto the clouds” (Ps. 35:6).

The Father of lights sat between them, and each side spoke more profitably what it had to say. Who, do you suppose, was worthy to be present at that conversation and will tell us? Who heard it and will recount it? Perhaps these things are inexpressible, and it is not permitted for a human being to speak them. Yet the sum of the whole controversy seems to have been this.

“Rational creation needs compassion,” says Mercy, “because it has become miserable, and exceedingly pitiable. The time has come to have mercy on it, because the time has now passed.”

Truth, on the other hand, says: “The word that you spoke, Lord, must be fulfilled. Adam must wholly die, with all who were in him, on the day when he tasted the forbidden fruit in transgression.”

“Why then,” says Mercy, “why did you beget me, Father, only to perish so soon?” For Truth herself knows that your mercy has perished and is nothing, if you never at any time show mercy.

Likewise, conversely, Truth spoke thus: “For who does not know that, if the transgressor escapes the sentence of death pronounced against him, your truth, Lord, has perished and will no longer remain forever?”

11. Then, behold, one of the cherubim [added elsewhere: that is, the Angel of great counsel] suggests that they should be sent to King Solomon; “for,” he says, “all judgment has been given to the Son” (John 5:22). Therefore Mercy and Truth met one another also in his presence, repeating the words of complaint mentioned above.

“I confess,” says Truth, “that Mercy has good zeal [Col. 0388C], but I wish it were according to knowledge. For now why does she judge that the transgressor should be spared rather than her sister?”

“But you,” says Mercy, “spare neither one: you rage against the transgressor with such indignation that you involve the sister along with him. What evil have I deserved? If you have anything against me, tell me; but if not, why do you persecute me?”

A great controversy, brothers, and an exceedingly intricate dispute. Who would not there have said: “It would have been good for us had this man not been born”? So it was, beloved; altogether so it was. It did not appear how Mercy and Truth could both be preserved in relation to man. And when Truth added that an injury to her cause was being turned even against the Judge himself [variant: “to turn merits back”], saying [Col. 0388D] that every care must be taken lest the Father’s word become void, lest the living and effective Word be emptied on any pretext: “Spare us, I beg you,” says Peace, “spare such words. Such contention does not befit us; shameful contention among virtues it is.”

12. Now the Judge bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground. These were the words of Scripture, which Peace herself read in the hearing of all—for she sat nearest:

“This one says: ‘I perish if Adam does not die’; and this one says: ‘I perish unless he obtains mercy.’ Let death become good, and each will have what she seeks.”

All were astonished alike at the word of wisdom and at the form of reconciliation and judgment. For it was evident that no occasion for complaint remained to them, since both requests could be fulfilled: that he should both [Col. 0389A] die and obtain mercy.

“But how will this happen?” they ask. “Death is most cruel and most bitter, terrible, dreadful even to hear of. By what means can it become good?”

He says: “The death of sinners is very evil, but the death of the saints can become precious. Will it not be precious if it becomes the doorway of life, the gate of glory?”

“Precious,” they say. “But how will this happen?”

“It can happen,” he says, “if someone dies from love—someone who owes nothing to death. For death will not be able to hold one who is innocent; rather, as it is written, the jaw of Leviathan will be pierced (Job 40:19), the middle wall will be destroyed, and the great gulf that has been fixed between death and life will be dissolved. Assuredly love is strong as death—indeed stronger than death. If it enters the court of that strong one, it will bind him and plunder his goods; and by its very passage it will make the depths of the sea a way, that the delivered may pass through.”

13. The saying seemed good, as being faithful and worthy of all acceptance. But where could that innocent man be found who would be willing to die, not by obligation but voluntarily; not through evil desert, but by his own good pleasure? Truth traverses the circle of the earth, and no one is clean from defilement—not even an infant whose life on earth is but one day old (Job 14:4–5, according to the Septuagint). Mercy too searches all heaven; and even among the angels she finds, if not perversity, at least a lesser love. Surely this victory was owed to another, one than whom no one had greater love: that he should lay down his life for useless and unworthy servants. For although he no longer calls us servants, this itself is an act of immeasurable love and exceptional condescension. Yet even if we had done all that was commanded us, what else ought we to say except that we are useless servants? (Luke 17:10). But who would dare summon him to account for this? Truth and Mercy return, exceedingly anxious, on the appointed day, having not found what they sought.

14. Then Peace, consoling them privately, says: “You know nothing and consider nothing. There is none who does good—no, not one. Let him who gave the counsel provide the help.”

The King understood what she meant and said: “I repent that I made man” (Gen. 6:7). “Punishment holds me; it rests upon me to bear the punishment, to do penance for the man [Col. 0389D] whom I created.”

Then he said: “Behold, I come. For this cup cannot pass unless I drink it.”

And immediately calling Gabriel, he said: “Go, tell the daughter of Zion: ‘Behold, your king comes’” (Zech. 9:9).

Gabriel hastened and said: “Prepare your bridal chamber, Zion, and receive the king.”

Mercy and Truth went before the coming king, as it is written: “Mercy and truth shall go before your face.” Justice prepares the throne, according to the words: “Justice and judgment are the preparation of your seat” (Ps. 88:15). Peace came with the king, so that the faithful prophet might be found true who had said: “There will be peace in our land when he comes.” Hence, at the Lord’s birth, the choir of angels sang: “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Then too Justice and Peace kissed, though until then they had seemed far from concord. For the justice that came through the Law, insofar as there was any, had not a kiss but rather a sting, urging more by fear than inviting by love. Nor did it possess that reconciliation which is possessed now by the justice known to come through faith. Otherwise, why could neither Abraham nor Moses nor the other righteous persons of that time, at their death, attain that peace of eternal blessedness or enter the kingdom of peace, except because Justice and Peace had not yet kissed one another? Therefore, beloved, we must pursue justice with more ardent zeal, since Justice and Peace have kissed and entered into an indissoluble covenant of friendship: so that whoever bears with him the testimony of justice may now be received by Peace with a cheerful countenance [Col. 0390B] and joyful embraces, sleeping and resting henceforth in unity.

977  
## SERMON II. On the Sevenfold Spirit in Christ

1. Brothers, in today’s solemnity of the Lord’s Annunciation, one may contemplate, as it were, a most delightful plain: the simple history of our restoration. A new embassy is entrusted to the angel Gabriel; and the Virgin, having professed a new virtue, is honored by the service of a new greeting. The old curse of women is cast out; a new mother receives a new blessing. She who knows no concupiscence is filled by grace, so that, when the Spirit of the Most High comes upon her, she may bear a son while disdaining the admission of a man.

Through the same gate by which the serpent’s poison entered and seized the whole human race, the antidote of salvation enters to us [Col. 0390C]. It is easy to gather countless flowers of this kind from these meadows; but I behold in the midst an abyss of fearful depth. Truly an unsearchable abyss: the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation; an impenetrable abyss. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). For who can investigate it, who attain it, who grasp it? The well is deep, and I have nothing with which to draw. Yet vapor rising from wells often moistens cloths spread over them.

Therefore, although I fear to break in, conscious of my own weakness, yet I frequently stretch out my hands to you, Lord, as it were over the mouth of this well, because my soul is like land without water before you [Col. 0390D]. And now, if, as mist rises from below, some slender thought has absorbed anything, I shall endeavor, brothers, to share that little with you without envy, as though squeezing out the cloth and pouring forth a small sprinkling of heavenly dew.

2. I ask, therefore, why the Son was incarnate rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit, since the glory of the whole Trinity is not merely equal, but is one and the same substance. But who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? The mystery is exceedingly high, and we ought not rashly to rush into an opinion concerning such things.

Yet it seems that the incarnation of neither the Father nor the Spirit would have escaped confusion amid a plurality of sons, since one would be called Son of God and another son of man. It also seems fitting that he who was Son should become Son in these particular respects, lest there be any ambiguity in the name. Finally, this is the singular glory and excellent prerogative of our Virgin Mary: that she deserved to have one and the same Son in common with God the Father. This privilege, certainly, would have been lost if the Son had not been incarnate.

Nor could any like occasion of hoped-for salvation and inheritance be given to us. For he who was the only-begotten became the firstborn among many brothers; and without doubt he admitted into inheritance those whom he called to adoption. For if brothers, then co-heirs. Thus Christ Jesus, the faithful mediator, just as in one person he joined the substance of God and man by an ineffable mystery, so also in that reconciliation, employing the highest counsel, did not abandon the middle course of justice [Col. 0391B], granting to each what was due: honor to God, compassion to man. For this is the best form of reconciliation between the offended Lord and the guilty servant: that the servant should not be crushed by an excessively severe sentence out of zeal to honor the Lord, nor, conversely, should the Lord be defrauded of due honor by immoderate indulgence toward the servant.

3. Hear then, and carefully observe, the angelic distribution at the birth of this mediator. “Glory,” they say, “to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). Accordingly, for the sake of this observance, the faithful reconciler Christ lacked neither the spirit of fear, through which he always showed reverence to the Father, always deferred to him, always sought his glory; nor the spirit of piety, through which he compassionately suffered with humankind. Hence he also required the spirit of knowledge, through which the distribution of fear and piety might be made without confusion.

And note that in the first sin of our parents there were indeed three agents, but three things were plainly lacking to the three. I mean Eve, the devil, and Adam. Eve did not have knowledge, for, as the Apostle says, she was deceived in transgression (1 Tim. 2:14). The serpent, indeed, did not lack this, for he is described as more cunning than the other animals; but the malignant one did not have piety, for from the beginning he was a murderer. Adam perhaps appears pious, in not grieving the woman; but he abandoned fear of the Lord, obeying her voice rather than the divine voice [Col. 0391D]. Would that the fear of the Lord had prevailed more in him! As is notably read of Christ: “He filled him”—not with the spirit of piety, but—“with the spirit of fear” (Isa. 11:3).

In all things and through all things, the fear of the Lord must be preferred to piety toward one’s neighbors; and it alone ought to claim the whole person for itself. In these three, therefore—fear, piety, and knowledge—our mediator reconciled humankind to God; for by counsel and strength he delivered us from the hand of the adversary. By counsel, indeed, he deprived the enemy of his former right by granting him power to lay hands on the innocent one; by strength he prevailed, so that the enemy could not forcibly hold the redeemed, when the victor returned from the lower world and the life of all rose with him [Col. 0392A].

4. Thereafter he feeds us with the bread of life and understanding, and gives us to drink the water of saving wisdom. For understanding of spiritual and invisible things is the true bread of the soul, strengthening our heart and fortifying it for every good work in every spiritual exercise. But the carnal person, who does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, but considers them foolishness, should groan and mourn, saying: “My heart has dried up, because I have forgotten to eat my bread” (Ps. 101:5).

For behold, it is pure and perfect truth that it profits a person nothing if he gains the whole world but suffers loss to his soul. But when can the greedy person grasp this? Whoever tries to persuade him of it labors in vain. Why is this? Because it seems foolishness to him. What is truer than that Christ’s yoke is sweet? Set it before a worldly person and see whether he does not consider it a stone rather than bread. Yet by this understanding of inward truth the soul lives, and this is spiritual food. “For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8:3).

Nevertheless, until truth becomes sweet to you, it does not pass into the inner person without difficulty. But when you begin to delight in it, it is no longer food but drink; and it enters the soul without difficulty, so that spiritual food, namely understanding, may be digested by the drink of wisdom, lest it be a burden rather than a benefit to the faculties—that is, the affections—of the inward person when they suffer from dryness.

[Col. 0392C] 3. Therefore, of all things necessary for the salvation of peoples, absolutely nothing was lacking to the Savior. For he is the one of whom Isaiah prophesied: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:1–3).

Observe carefully, indeed, that he said this flower would rise from the root, not from the rod. For if Christ’s new flesh had been created in the Virgin from nothing—as some have thought—the flower might perhaps have been said to rise from the rod, not from the root. But now, since he came forth from the root, he is undoubtedly shown to have had matter in common from the beginning [Col. 0392D]. And the fact that the Spirit rested upon him declares that there was no contradiction in him. For in us, because the spirit is not altogether dominant, it does not rest: the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. May the new man and true man, in whom there was nothing like that, free us from this conflict: he who received the true origin of our flesh, but did not receive the old leaven of concupiscence.

979  
## SERMON III

[Note: Delivered in the year 1150, when the Annunciation was celebrated on the Saturday after the Third Sunday of Lent: [Col. 0392D] on which day the history of Susanna is read, and the Gospel of the adulterous woman.] On the adulterous woman (John 8:3–11); on Susanna (Dan. 13); on Blessed Mary (Luke 1:26–38).

1. How rich you are in mercy, how magnificent [Col. 0393A] in justice, how generous in grace, Lord our God! There is none like you, most abundant giver, most equitable rewarder, most loving deliverer! You freely regard the humble, justly judge the innocent, and mercifully save even sinners. These, beloved, are the things which, from the table of this rich householder, are set before us today in the holy testimonies of Scripture more abundantly than usual, if we attend carefully. This abundance is provided because the holy season of Lent and the most sacred day of the Lord’s Annunciation have coincided.

For today, in our hearing, the Redeemer’s forgiveness absolves the woman caught in adultery; today it delivered the innocent blood of Susanna; today also it filled the blessed Virgin with the singular gift of gratuitous blessing. A great banquet, at which mercy, justice, and grace are together set before us! Is not mercy food for human beings? It is wholly salutary and effective for healing. Is not justice also bread for the heart? Indeed, it strengthens that heart excellently, as solid food for nourishment. Thus, “Blessed are those who hunger for it, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6). Is not the grace of God food for the soul? It is indeed most sweet, containing in itself every sweetness and delight of taste; rather, it claims all these things together for itself, not merely delighting, but also refreshing and healing.

2. Let us come to this table, my brothers, and taste at least a little from each dish. “Moses commanded that such women be stoned in the Law,” sinners say of the sinful woman, Pharisees of the adulteress. But he spoke thus because of the hardness of your stony hearts. Jesus, however, bent down. “Lord, bend your heavens and come down” (Ps. 143:5). Bending down and inclining toward mercy—for he did not possess a Jewish heart—he wrote with his finger, no longer on stone but on earth. Nor was this done only once: here too there is a double writing, as there were two tablets with Moses. Perhaps he was writing truth and grace, and, writing again, seems to have impressed them upon the earth, according to what the apostle John says: “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

Consider, finally, whether he can be thought to have read from the tablet of truth the words by which he refuted the Pharisees: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.” The saying is brief, but living and effective, sharper than a two-edged sword. How grievously the stony hearts were pierced by this saying, how violently the stony foreheads were broken by this one little stone, their blush of shame and stealthy departure proved. The adulteress deserved to be stoned; but let that person hasten to punish her who does not himself deserve punishment. Let that person presume to exact vengeance from a sinner who does not deserve to suffer the same. Otherwise, being nearer to himself, let him begin with himself; let him first pass sentence upon himself and carry out vengeance upon himself. This is Truth.

3. But still this is not enough: Truth refutes the accusers, yet does not absolve the guilty woman [Col. 0394A]. Let him write again; let him write grace. Let him read, and let us hear: “Has no one condemned you, woman?” “No one, Lord.” “Neither will I condemn you; go, and sin no more.”

O voice of mercy, O hearing of saving joy! “Cause me to hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you, Lord” (Ps. 142:8). For hope alone has a place with you in receiving compassion; nor do you place the oil of mercy except in the vessel of confidence. But there is a faithless confidence, capable only of a curse: namely, when we sin in hope. Yet it should not be called confidence, but rather a kind of insensibility and destructive disregard. What confidence is there for someone who does not notice danger? Or what remedy of fear is there where neither fear itself nor even the cause of fear is felt? Confidence is consolation; and the person who rejoices when he has done evil, and exults especially in the worst things, has no need of consolation.

Let us therefore ask, brothers, that we be told how many iniquities and sins we have; let us desire that our crimes and offences be shown to us. Let us search our ways and our pursuits, and weigh every danger with watchful attention. Let each person say in his dread: “I shall go to the gates of hell,” so that we may breathe again only in the mercy of God alone. This is the true confidence of a person who has failed in himself and rests upon his Lord. This, I say, is the true confidence to which mercy is not denied, the Prophet testifying that “the Lord is pleased with those who fear him, and with those who hope in his mercy” (Ps. 146:11). And certainly no small assistance is available to us: in ourselves, the cause of fear; but in him, the cause of confidence. He is gracious and gentle, abundant in mercy, superior to wickedness, and generous in forgiving.

Let us indeed believe even his enemies, who found in him nothing else from which they could construct an occasion for calumny. “He will have compassion on the sinful woman,” they say, “and will by no means permit her, when brought before him, to be put to death. Thus he will be held to be an open adversary of the Law when he has absolved one condemned by the Law.” The entire device of your malice, O Pharisees, is turned back upon your own heads. You mistrust your case, since you evade judgment. For she is indeed absolved without injury to the Law, because she is not left to an accuser [variant: “because she is left without an accuser”].

4. But let us consider, brothers, where the Pharisees go from here. Do you see the two elders—for they began to leave from the eldest—how they hide in Joachim’s garden? They seek Susanna, his wife. Let us follow them, for they are full of wicked intent against her. “Consent to us,” say the elders; say the Pharisees; say the wolves, who a little earlier had been frustrated in devouring another little sheep, though she had gone astray. “Consent to us, and have intercourse with us.” You who have grown old in evil days, just now accused adultery, and now urge adultery. But this is the whole of your justice: what you denounce openly, you do secretly. This is why you went out one after another when he who knew all hidden things struck your consciences so powerfully by saying: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.”

Rightly, therefore, Truth says to the disciples: “Unless your justice exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20). “Otherwise,” they say, “we shall testify against you.” Seed of Canaan and not of Judah! Nor did Moses command this in the Law. Did he who decreed that an adulteress be stoned command that a chaste woman be accused? Or did he who ordered an adulteress to be crushed with stones also order testimony to be borne against an innocent woman? On the contrary, he commanded that, just as the adulteress, so also the false witness should not go unpunished (Deut. 19:16–21; Prov. 19:9). But you who glory in the Law dishonor God through transgression of the Law.

5. Susanna groaned and said: “I am hemmed in on every side.” For death was on every side: bodily death on one side, spiritual death on the other. “If I do this,” she says, “it is death to me; but if I do not do it, I shall not escape your hands.” Your hands, O Pharisees, neither the adulteress nor the chaste woman escapes; neither saint nor sinner evades your accusations. You conceal your own sins when you find those of others; otherwise, if someone happens to have none of his own, you fasten your crime upon him.

But what does Susanna do, hemmed in on every side between death and death—of soul, that is, and body? “It is better for me,” she says, “without doing the deed, to fall into the hands of men than to abandon the law of my God.” Certainly she knew how terrible it is to fall into the hands of the living God. For men, when they have killed the body, have nothing more that they can do to the soul; but he is to be feared who has power to cast both body and soul into Gehenna (Matt. 10:28).

Why does Joachim’s household delay? Let it rush in through the back way, for a cry is heard in the garden—the cry of fierce wolves and of a bleating little sheep among them. But he who so graciously rescued even one who did not deserve rescue from their very jaws does not allow the innocent woman to be devoured by them. Thus, when she was led to death, her heart rightly had confidence in the Lord, whom she had feared so greatly that she set aside every human fear and placed his law above both life and reputation. For no such report had ever been made of Susanna. Moreover, her parents were righteous, and her husband was more honorable than all the Jews. Rightly, therefore, she obtained from the just Judge righteous vengeance upon the unjust, since she hungered so intensely for justice that for its sake she despised bodily death, disgrace to her family, and the inconsolable grief of her friends.

6. And if we, brothers, have heard from Christ, “Neither do I condemn you,” then, if we no longer wish to sin against him, if we wish to live piously in Christ, we must endure persecution, so that we may not return evil for evil or curse for curse. Otherwise, whoever does not preserve patience will lose justice; that is, will lose life; that is, will lose his soul. “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,” says the Lord (Rom. 12:19). It is precisely so. He himself will repay—but if you reserve vengeance for him, if you do not take judgment away from him, if you do not repay those who repay you with evil. He will execute judgment, but for the one suffering injury; he will judge in equity, but for the meek of the earth.

By now, unless I am mistaken, you are troubled that these delights delay. Do not wonder: they are delights. They will not burden even those thoroughly satisfied, nor can they be loathed even by those who are belching.

7. “The angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth.” Do you wonder that Nazareth, a small city, is made illustrious by the messenger of so great a king—and by so great a messenger? But a great treasure lies hidden in this small city; hidden, I say, from men, not from God. Is Mary not God’s treasure? Wherever she is, there too is his heart. His eyes are upon her; everywhere he regards the humility of his handmaid. Does the only-begotten Son of God the Father know heaven? If he knows heaven, he knows Nazareth as well. Why should he not know his own country? Why should he not know his inheritance? He claims heaven from his Father and Nazareth from his mother [Col. 0396B], just as he himself testifies that he is both Son and Lord of David (Matt. 22:42–45). “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men” (Ps. 113:16). Therefore both must yield to him as a possession, because he is not only Lord but also Son of man.

Hear also how, as Son of man, he claims the earth for himself and shares it as bridegroom: “Flowers have appeared in our land” (Song 2:12). Nor does the fact that Nazareth is interpreted “flower” conflict with this. The flower from the root of Jesse loves a flower-bearing homeland, and the flower of the field and lily of the valleys gladly feeds among lilies. Flowers are commended by beauty, sweet fragrance, and the hope of fruit: a threefold grace. God also reckons you a flower, and you rightly please him if you lack neither the beauty of honorable conduct, nor the fragrance of a good reputation, nor an aim toward future recompense. For the fruit of the Spirit is eternal life.

8. “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with the Lord.” How great a grace? Grace full, grace singular. Singular or general? Both, without doubt: full, and singular precisely because general. For you alone received the general grace in a singular manner. Singular, I say, because general: for you alone, before all others, found grace. Singular, because you alone found this fullness; general, because all receive from that fullness. “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.”

The fruit of your womb is indeed singular; yet through you it comes to the minds of all. Thus, indeed, long ago the whole dew was in the fleece, the whole dew was on the threshing floor; but in no part of the threshing floor was it all together as it was in the fleece (Judg. 6:37–40). In you alone that rich and exceeding-rich King was emptied; the exalted one was humbled; the immeasurable one was made small; and he was made lower than the angels: in short, the true God and Son of God was incarnate.

But for what fruit? Surely so that all of us may be enriched by his poverty, raised up by his humility, magnified by his abasement, and, by his incarnation, cleaving to God, may begin to be one spirit with him.

9. But what are we to say, brothers? Into what vessel, above all, will grace be poured? If, as we recalled above, confidence is capable of receiving mercy, while patience is capable of receiving justice [Col. 0397A], what receptacle shall we now be able to offer that is fit for grace? Balsam is most pure, and it requires a very sound vessel. And what is so pure, or what so sound, as humility of heart? Rightly, therefore, does God give grace to the humble; rightly did he look upon the humility of his handmaid. By what merit, you ask? Precisely by this: that no human merit occupied the humble mind, preventing the fullness of divine grace from flowing freely into it. Yet we must ascend to this humility by certain steps.

First, the heart of a person who still delights in sin and has not changed a wretched habit by a better resolve is hindered by its own vices from being capable of grace. Secondly, when one has now resolved to reform one’s conduct and no longer repeat former wickedness, the sins themselves [Col. 0397B] that have gone before, although they seem already in some manner cut away, do not admit grace while they remain in that person. They remain until they are washed away by confession, until, through the worthy fruits of repentance that follow, they are removed from the midst. But woe to you if ingratitude, more ruinous than vices and sins, should perhaps succeed them. For what is more plainly opposed to grace? As time passes, we grow lukewarm from the fervor of our religious life; charity gradually grows cold, iniquity abounds, so that we who began in the Spirit may be brought to completion in the flesh. Hence we know less of the things bestowed on us by God, being at once undevout and ungrateful. We abandon the fear of the Lord; we neglect devout solitude; we become talkative, inquisitive, witty, even slanderers and murmurers, occupied with trifles, avoiding labor [Col. 0397C] and discipline whenever this may be done without reproach—as though it were therefore immediately without harm. Why, then, do we wonder that grace is absent from us when so many obstacles repel it?

But if anyone, according to the Apostle, is grateful so that the word of Christ, the word of grace, may dwell in him (Col. 3:16, 15); if anyone is devout, attentive [Col. 0398A], fervent in spirit, let such a one beware of trusting in personal merits or relying upon personal works. Otherwise grace does not enter even such a mind: it is plainly full, and grace finds no room there.

10. Have you considered that Pharisee at prayer? He was not a robber, unjust, or an adulterer. Was he without fruits of repentance? He fasted twice in the Sabbath-week; he gave tithes of all that he possessed. Perhaps you suppose him ungrateful. Listen to what he says: “God, I give you thanks.” Yet he was not empty, not self-emptied, not humble, but exalted. He did not endeavor to know what he lacked; instead, he magnified his own merit. Nor was that a solid fullness, but a swelling. Therefore he returned empty, because he simulated fullness. But that publican, who emptied himself, because he took care to present an empty vessel, carried away greater grace (Luke 18:10, 14).

Therefore, brothers, if we desire to find grace, let us henceforth refrain from vices in such a way that we also worthily repent of past sins. Let us likewise be attentive, and show ourselves devout toward God and truly humble. Such souls he graciously regards with that merciful regard of which the Wise Man says: “For the grace and mercy of God are upon his saints, and his regard upon his chosen ones” (Wisdom 4:15). Perhaps for this reason he calls back four times the soul upon which he looks, saying: “Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may behold you” (Song 6:12). This is so that it may persist neither in the habit of sinning nor in the consciousness of sins; nor again in the lukewarmness and torpor of ingratitude, or in the blindness of self-exaltation. May he deign to recall and deliver us from this fourfold danger—Jesus Christ our Lord, who was made for us by God the Father wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption; who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through unending ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0397]

## ON THE NATIVITY OF ST JOHN THE BAPTIST. 983  
### SERMON: On the lamp burning in a threefold manner and shining in a threefold manner.

[Col. 0397C] Let that rebuke of the prophet be far from these assemblies, brothers—the rebuke by which he condemns the Jewish gatherings and says: “Your assemblies are wicked” (Isa. 1:13). These assemblies, indeed, are not wicked, but plainly holy, devout, full of grace, and worthy of blessing. For you gather to hear God; you gather to praise, pray to, and worship him. Each gathering is sacred, pleasing to God, familiar to angels. Stand therefore in reverence, brothers; stand with watchfulness and devotion of mind—especially in the place of prayer, in this school of Christ and spiritual lecture-hall. Do not consider, beloved, the things that are seen and temporal, but rather those that are unseen and eternal. Judge according to faith, not according to appearance.

For each place is terribly to be feared; nor should the number of human beings present be thought greater than that of angels. In both places, without doubt, the gate of heaven stands open; that ladder is set up, and angels ascend and descend upon the Son of Man [Col. 0398C]. For this Son of Man is a giant: heaven is his seat, and earth his footstool. His magnificence is raised above the heavens [Col. 0398D]; yet he remains with us until the consummation of the age. Therefore holy angels ascend and descend to God, because Christ is one—head and body.

2. Yet wherever the body is, not merely where the head is, there the eagles also will gather—although the head cannot be separated from the body. Indeed, he himself says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am in their midst” (Matt. 18:20). But perhaps someone may say: Where is Christ now? Show us Christ, and that is enough for us. Why do you cast your curious eyes about? Have you gathered to see, rather than to hear? “The Lord God has opened my ear,” says the prophet (Isa. 50:5). He opened my ear, that I might hear what he says; he did not enlighten my eye that I might see his face [Col. 0399A]. Or rather, he opened his ear to me; he did not reveal his face. He stands behind the wall; he hears and is heard, but does not yet appear. He hears those praying; he instructs those hearing. Do you seek proof of him—of Christ who speaks in me? (2 Cor. 13:3). “I am he,” he says, “who speaks righteousness” (Isa. 63:1). Why should he not speak through the mouth that he himself formed? Why should the craftsman not use his own instrument as he pleases? “Open not only their ears but also my lips, O Lord; for I will not restrain my lips, Lord—you have known.” For you do all things well: you make the deaf hear and the mute speak.

3. Hear, then, brothers, what he says of John, whose solemn nativity is celebrated today: “He was,” he says, “a lamp burning and shining” (John 5:35) [Col. 0399B]. A great testimony, my brothers: great is he to whom it is borne, but greater is he who bears it. “He was a lamp burning and shining.” To shine alone is vain; to burn alone is insufficient; to burn and shine is perfect. Hear what Scripture says: “The wise man remains as the sun, but the fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27:12). For the moon shines without heat: now it seems full, now small, now absent. Borrowed light never remains in the same condition; it grows, wanes, diminishes, is annihilated, and disappears altogether. So those who have placed their consciences in the lips of others are now great, now small, now nothing, according as flattering tongues choose to blame or praise them.

But the splendor of the sun is fiery [Col. 0399C], and the more intensely it burns, the brighter it appears even to the eyes. So the inward ardor of the wise shines outwardly. And if both are not granted him, he always takes care rather to burn, so that his Father, who sees in secret, may reward him. Woe to us, brothers, if we merely shine. We do shine, indeed, and are magnified by people; but it is a very small thing to me to be judged by a human day. For the one who judges me is the Lord 984, who requires fervor from all, but not splendor in the same way. “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49). This, indeed, is the common command; this is required of all, and no excuse is accepted if it should be lacking.

[Col. 0399D] 4. But to apostles and apostolic men in particular it is said: “Let your light shine before people” (Matt. 5:16): namely, as persons kindled and intensely kindled, whom no mere breath or gust of wind need be feared to extinguish. It was also said to John; but they hear it in the ear, whereas John is instructed in spirit as an angel. He is so much nearer to God as the Voice is near to the Word, and need not be informed by an intervening outward sound. For preaching did not teach John, but inspiration—the Spirit who filled him in his mother’s womb. Truly burning and intensely kindled was he whom the heavenly flame so forestalled that he already perceived Christ’s coming when he could not yet perceive even himself.

For that new fire, recently sent down from heaven [Col. 0400A], had entered the Virgin’s ear through Gabriel’s mouth; then, through the Virgin’s mouth and the mother’s ear, it passed to the little child, so that from that hour the Holy Spirit might fill the vessel of his choice and prepare a lamp for Christ the Lord. Thus he was already then a burning lamp, but still beneath the bushel, until he should be placed upon the lampstand and shine for all who were in the house of the Lord. At that time he could still illumine only his own bushel; meanwhile, he shone only for his mother, revealing to her the great mystery of godliness by the very movement of a new exultation. “Whence is this to me,” she says, “that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” Who told you, holy woman, that she was the mother of the Lord? How did you know me? “As soon,” she says, “as the voice of your greeting was made in my ears, the child in my womb leaped for joy” (Luke 1:43–44).

[Col. 0400B] 5. Thus he already illumined the bushel beneath which he lay hidden. But the burning lamp beneath the bushel did not remain hidden; shortly afterward it was to illumine the whole world with new radiance. “He was,” he says, “a lamp burning and shining.” He did not say, “shining and burning,” because John’s brightness proceeded from his fervor, not his fervor from his brightness. For there are some who do not shine because they burn, but rather burn in order to shine; yet such persons plainly do not burn with the spirit of charity, but with zeal for vanity.

Do you wish to know how John burned and shone? I think that in him both may be found in a threefold manner: both ardor and brightness. He burned in himself through the intense austerity of his way of life; toward Christ through a certain inward and complete fervor of devotion; toward sinful neighbors through the steadfastness of free rebuke. He likewise shone, to speak briefly, by example, by his finger, and by word: showing himself for imitation; pointing out the greater luminary that lay hidden, for the remission of sins; and illuminating even our own darkness, as it is written: “For you light my lamp, O Lord; my God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. 17:29)—that is, for correction.

6. Consider, then, the man promised by an angelic oracle, conceived by miracle, sanctified in the womb; and marvel at [variant: imitate] the new fervor of repentance in the new man. “Having food and clothing,” says the Apostle, “let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8). This is apostolic perfection; yet John even despised these. For hear the Lord in the Gospel: “John the Baptist came,” he says, “neither eating nor drinking” (Matt. 11:18) [Col. 0400D]—plainly, neither dressing. For just as a locust is not food except perhaps for certain irrational animals, so camel hair is not human clothing. Why have you, camel, shed your hair? Would that you had rather shed your hump. Why do you, irrational beasts and reptiles of the wilderness, seek delicate foods? John, a holy man sent by God—indeed, an angel of God, as the Father says: “Behold, I send my angel before you” (Luke 12:27)—this John, than whom none born of women is greater, chastises, emaciates, and afflicts that most innocent body in this way; while you hasten to clothe yourselves in fine linen and purple, and to feast splendidly?

Alas! Is this the entire honor of the present day? Is this the whole reverence shown to the Baptist? Is this the joy at his nativity [Col. 0401A], prophesied long ago? Whose memorial are you observing, O excessively delicate worshippers? Whose birthday are you celebrating? Is it not his who was in the wilderness, rough in clothing and worn out by hunger? What did you go out into the wilderness to see, children of Babylon? A reed shaken by the wind? What then? A man clothed in soft garments? One reared in luxury? Indeed, your entire celebration consists in these things: pursuing the breeze of popular favor, the glory of clothing, and the pleasure of food. But what have these to do with John? For John did not act in this way, nor could he ever delight in such things.

7. “Many,” says the angel, “will rejoice at his birth” (Luke 1:14). This is indeed true: many rejoice at his birth; and, as we have heard, it is a glad and solemn feast even among pagans. They celebrate what they do not know; but Christians ought not to do so. Yet now they too rejoice at this nativity of blessed John the Baptist—but would that it were over the nativity, rather than over vanity. For what is everything under the sun except vanity of vanities? Or what more does a person gain from all the labor by which he toils under the sun? Brothers, everything seen by the eyes, everything that seems subject to this bodily light, is under the sun [Col. 0401B]. But what is that, except “a vapor appearing for a little while”? (Jas. 4:45.) What is it except grass and the flower of grass? “All flesh is grass,” says the Lord, “and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withered and the flower fell; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:6, 8).

Let us labor in this word, brothers, in which we can both live and rejoice forever. Let us work not for food that perishes [Col. 0401C], but for that which endures unto eternal life. What is it? “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4). Let us sow in this word, beloved; let us sow in the Spirit, since those who sow in the flesh reap only corruption. Let us rejoice inwardly, and not under the sun; but, according to the Apostle, “as sorrowful,” because of humility and seriousness, “yet always rejoicing” (2 Cor. 6:10), because of inward consolation. Let us rejoice, beloved, at the birth of blessed John, and rejoice in the birth itself.

8. For in remembrance of him we have abundant cause for joy, a manifold subject for rejoicing. He was a lamp burning and shining, and the Jews wished to rejoice in his light [Col. 0401D]; but he himself rather rejoiced in the fervor of devotion, rejoicing at the Bridegroom’s voice as the Bridegroom’s friend. We ought to rejoice in both: in the one, rejoicing with him; in the other, for ourselves. For he burned for himself, but shone for us. Let us rejoice in his fervor, for imitation; and rejoice also in his light—yet not remaining there, but so that in his light we may see the light: the true light, which is not himself, but he to whom John bears witness.

“John came,” says the Lord, “neither eating nor drinking” (Matt. 11:18). This is for me an incentive to fervor and a matter for humility. For who among us, brothers, looking upon John’s repentance, would presume to magnify his own, or even regard it as of any value whatsoever? Who would dare murmur amid personal labors [Col. 0402A] and say, “What I suffer is enough—indeed, more than enough”? For what murders, sacrileges, or shameful deeds was John so punishing in himself? Let us be kindled to repentance, brothers; let us question our consciences and stir ourselves to exact vengeance upon ourselves, so that we may escape the dreadful judgment of the living God. Yet whatever is lacking in fervor, let the humility of pure confession supply. For God is faithful: if we confess our iniquities, expose our miseries, and do not excuse our weaknesses, he will forgive us our sins.

9. From this, moreover, observe John’s fervor toward the faults of neighbors. For this is a worthy and reasonable order: remember that you must begin with yourself. “Cleanse me from my hidden faults,” he says, “and spare your servant from those of others” [Col. 0402B] (Ps. 18:13–14). “Brood of vipers,” says John, “who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” What sparks—indeed, what devastating coals—do you think proceeded from such fervor of mind? Thus he did not spare even the Pharisees: “Do not say,” he says, “‘We have Abraham as our father’; for God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones” (Luke 3:7–8).

But this might seem too little if he were to fear even the face of a powerful man, and not rebuke a sinful king—cruel and proud—with complete freedom of spirit; if, although he came out of the wilderness in a kind of sacred vehemence for this very purpose, he were moved either by Herod’s flatteries or by the terror of death itself. “Herod feared John,” it says, “and when he heard him, did many things and heard him gladly.” Yet John spared him nothing: “It is not lawful,” he said, “for you to have her” [Col. 0402C]. Even when bound and thrown into prison, he nevertheless stood firmly in the truth and happily died for the truth (Mark 6:17–28).

May this zeal likewise burn in us, beloved; may love of righteousness and hatred of iniquity burn. Let no one, brothers, flatter vices; let no one conceal sins. Let no one say, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” Let no one, so far as lies in him, bear it complacently when he sees order perishing and discipline diminished. For to be silent when you can rebuke is to consent; and we know that a like punishment awaits those who commit such things and those who consent to them.

10. But what shall we say of John’s humble and altogether most fervent devotion toward the Lord? From this he leaped in the womb (Luke 1:44); from this he trembled when about to baptize him in the Jordan [Col. 0402D] (Matt. 3:14); from this he denied that he was the Christ, as people supposed, and even denied that he was worthy to loosen the strap of Christ’s sandal (Mark 1:7); from this the Bridegroom’s friend rejoiced at the Bridegroom’s voice (Luke 1:44); from this he confessed that he had received grace for grace, while he proclaimed that Christ had the Spirit not by measure but in a fullness from which all might receive (John 1:16).

“Will you not be subject to God, my soul?” (Ps. 61:1.) Otherwise I shall not be a burning lamp unless I love the Lord my God with all my heart, all my mind, and all my strength. For charity alone kindles unto salvation; it alone is poured in and inflamed by the Spirit, whom we are forbidden to quench (1 Thess. 5:19). You have seen how John burned; and in this very fact [Col. 0403A], if you noticed, it has been shown how he shone. For you could not have known his ardor unless he had shone.

11. Therefore, as I recalled above, he shone by example, finger, and word: by his works showing himself; by his finger declaring Christ; by speech declaring ourselves to ourselves. “You, child,” says his father, “shall be called prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people.” “To give,” he says, “not salvation.” For John is not the light, but gives knowledge of salvation, in order that he might bear witness to the light. “Knowledge,” he says, “of salvation, unto remission of sins” (Luke 1:76–77).

Can a wise person make light of knowledge of salvation? Yet let us suppose that John had not yet come, had not yet indicated Christ to us. Where shall we seek salvation? I have committed a great sin, one that cannot be wiped away by the blood of calves or goats, because the Most High does not delight in burnt offerings. My memory is stained by the dregs of this bitter oil [*amurca*]; no razor can scrape this parchment clean, because it has wholly absorbed the dregs throughout [Col. 0403B]. If I forget my sin, I am foolish and ungrateful; if it remains in my memory, it will accuse me forever. What then shall I do? I shall go to John and hear the voice of joy, the voice of mercy, the discourse of grace, the word of remission and peace. “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29); and elsewhere: “He who has the bride,” he says, “is the bridegroom” (John 3:29).

He thus shows that God has come, that the Bridegroom has come, that the Lamb has come. Since he is God, it is certain that he can forgive sins; but whether he is willing is still in question. He certainly is willing, because he is the Bridegroom, because he is lovable [Col. 0403C]. And John is the Bridegroom’s friend, because the Bridegroom does not know how to have anything but friends. Although he wishes to have a glorious bride without spot, wrinkle, or anything of that kind [Col. 0404A], he does not seek her already such—for where would he find her? Rather, he himself makes her such and presents her to himself as such. Hear, finally, what he says through the prophet: “It is commonly said: ‘If a woman sleeps with another man, will she return to her former husband?’ But you have committed fornication with many lovers. Yet return to me, and I will receive you” (Jer. 3:1). Behold what he asks; behold what he wills.

12. But perhaps you fear the cleansing from sins which he has come to accomplish, lest through burning and cutting he crush bones and the marrow of bones, lest he inflict pain more grievous than death. Hear: he is a Lamb; in gentleness he comes with wool and milk, justifying the ungodly by word alone. For what, according to the comic poet, is easier to say? [Col. 0404B] (Terence, *Phormio* 2.1.70.) “Only say the word,” he says, “and my servant shall be healed” (Matt. 8:8). Why, then, should we henceforth hesitate, brothers, and not approach with every confidence the throne of glory? [Variant: “ascend.”]

Let us give thanks to John and, through his mediation, pass on to Christ, because, as John himself says: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:36). How must I decrease? In brightness, certainly, not in fervor. He withdrew his rays and drew himself together [variant: “gathered himself again”], lest he become like one who pours out his whole spirit. “He must increase,” he says—he who cannot be exhausted, from whose fullness all receive—“but I must decrease,” to whom the Spirit was given by measure; and I must take care rather that I may always be able to burn [Col. 0404C] than to shine. I went before the sun like the morning star; now that the sun has risen, I must be hidden. I possess only a little oil with which I may be anointed; I wish to possess it more safely in the vessel than in the lamp.

[Col. 0403]

## ON THE VIGIL OF THE HOLY APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL.  
### SERMON: On the threefold help that we receive from the saints.

[Col. 0403C] 1. At the vigils of the saints, the spiritual person who desires to celebrate their solemnities in spirit and truth must keep watch. For the vigils of the carnal are one thing, those of the spiritual another. The former prepare more splendid attire and more lavish banquets; perhaps even during the vigils themselves they perform works of darkness, rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst deeds. But you have not learned Christ in this way—you who have followed Christ, left all things, and ought to heed with watchful eye the name of the vigils.

For vigils are appointed so that we may awake if we are asleep in some sin or negligence, and may go beforehand before the saints in confession. Not so the children of this age; not so those mighty at drinking wine and strong at mixing drunkenness, who have fallen asleep in their shameful acts and crimes. Let this not escape you: those who are drunk are drunk at night, and those who sleep sleep at night. The name of holy Vigils sounds in vain to them, since they strive more to sleep than to watch. But you are not children of night or darkness, but of light and day [Col. 0404C] (1 Thess. 5:5–8), so that the saints’ feast-days may not overtake you and find you unprepared.

2. Therefore there are three things which we ought attentively to consider in the feasts of saints: the saint’s help, the saint’s example, and our own shame. The saint’s help: for one who was powerful on earth is more powerful in heaven before the face of the Lord his God [Col. 0404D]. If, while living here, he had compassion on sinners and prayed for them, now he prays all the more for us, because he knows our miseries more truly; for that blessed country has not changed his charity but increased it. Nor has he become devoid of compassion merely because he is wholly incapable of suffering; rather, now that he stands before the fountain of mercy, he has clothed himself with bowels of mercy [variant: “stands”].

There is another reason that more urgently moves the saints to be concerned for us: according to the Apostle’s words, God provides for us so that they may not be made perfect without us (Heb. 11:40), as holy David says: “The righteous await me, until you repay me” (Ps. 141:8). We should also consider his example, because as long as he was seen on earth and lived among human beings [Col. 0405A], he turned neither to the right nor to the left, but held to the royal road until he came to him who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Look upon the humility of his works and the authority of his words; then you will see how he shone among people both in word and example, what kind of footsteps he left us, 988 so that we might walk in them and not wander from them. Truly, according to the prophet: “The path of the righteous is straight; the track of the righteous is straight for walking” (Isa. 26:7).

3. Let us also inspect our own shame with more diligent attention. That man was like us: capable of suffering, formed from the same clay as ourselves. What then is the reason that we believe it not merely difficult but impossible to do the works he did and follow his footsteps [Col. 0405B]? Let us be ashamed, brothers, and tremble at this thought, if perhaps this shame may bring us glory, if perhaps this fear may generate grace in us. These were people who went before us, who advanced so wonderfully along the paths of life that we can scarcely believe they were human. Thus at the feasts of saints we ought both to rejoice and to be ashamed: rejoice because we have sent patrons ahead; be ashamed because we cannot imitate them.

Thus our joy in this valley of tears must always be seasoned with the bread of tears, so that mourning may always occupy not only the end but also the beginning of joy. For although the matter for rejoicing is great, the matter for sorrow is greater [Col. 0406A]. “I remembered God,” the righteous man cries, “and was delighted”; but immediately he adds: “My spirit failed; I was troubled, and I did not speak” (Ps. 76:4–5).

4. But if we ought to consider these things at the vigil of every saint, what shall we do on the solemnity of the holy and chief Apostles—Peter and Paul? The feast of one alone would suffice to pour exultation into the whole earth; yet the feasts of both are joined together to increase our joy, so that, as they loved one another in life, they might not be separated in death. What men were more powerful while on earth? To one are entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven; to the other, the teaching office for the Gentiles. One kills Ananias and Sapphira by the words of his mouth; the other gives whatever he gives in the person of Christ, and when he is weak, then is stronger and powerful [Col. 0406B]. How much more powerful are they in heaven, who were so powerful on earth! And who have left us greater examples than those who were continually afflicted in hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and in all the things Paul enumerates (2 Cor. 11:23–33; Heb. 11:36–38), and at last ascended to the kingdoms of heaven through blessed martyrdom? Truly they are a blush of shame to us, men whom we scarcely dare to look upon, much less imitate. Let us therefore pray to them that they may make their friend, our judge, favorable to us—he who is God blessed forever. Amen.

[Col. 0405]

## ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL.  
### SERMON I: On the threefold guardianship the apostles exercise over us, and on the three stages of our conduct.

[Col. 0405C]

1. A glorious solemnity has dawned upon us, consecrated by the most glorious death of the illustrious martyrs, leaders of martyrs and princes of the apostles. These are Peter and Paul, two great luminaries whom God established in the body of his Church as the twin light of its eyes. They have been given to me as teachers and mediators, to whom I may safely entrust myself, because they have made known to me the paths of life, and through their mediation I shall be able to ascend to that Mediator who came to reconcile through his blood both the things in heaven and those on earth.

For he is most pure in both natures—he who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found [Col. 0405D]. How, then, shall I dare approach him, I who am a sinner sinful beyond measure, who have sinned beyond the number of the sand of the sea, when he cannot be more pure and I more impure? I must fear lest I fall into the hands of the living God if I presume to approach or cling to him from whom so great a difference separates me as lies between good and evil. Therefore God gave me these men, who were human beings, sinners, and very great sinners, so that in themselves and from themselves they might learn how they ought to have mercy on others. For those guilty of great crimes readily grant pardon for great crimes; and in the measure in which it has been measured to them, it shall be measured back to us.

The apostle Peter committed a great sin [Col. 0406C]—perhaps none greater exists—and obtained pardon as swiftly as it was easily; and in such a way that he lost nothing of the singularity of his primacy. Paul too, who raged so uniquely and incomparably against the very inward parts of the Church at its birth, was brought to faith by the voice of the very Son of God; and for such great evils he was filled with such great goods that he became a vessel of election to bear God’s name before Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel (Acts 9:15): a worthy vessel, filled with heavenly delicacies, from which both the healthy may receive food and the sick medicine.

2. Such pastors and teachers ought to have been appointed for humankind—gentle, powerful, and no less wise [Col. 0406D]. Gentle, that they might receive me kindly and mercifully; powerful, that they might protect me strongly; wise, that they might lead me to, and along, the road which leads to the city. What is gentler than Peter, who so sweetly calls all sinners to himself, as both the Acts of the Apostles and the sequence of his Epistles attest? What is more powerful than he, whom earth obeyed when he restored the dead, and whom the sea gave itself under his feet to be trodden (Matt. 14:29); who struck Simon Magus in the air with the spirit of his mouth; who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven so singularly that Peter’s sentence precedes heaven’s sentence? “Whatever you bind,” he says, “on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:19).

And what is wiser than he to whom not flesh and blood, but the Father who is in heaven, revealed with lavish bounty that wisdom which is from heaven [Col. 0407A]?  

> **Note:** [Col. 0407D] Other editions read thus: “to whom flesh and blood did not reveal,” omitting the rest.

I follow Paul most gladly, who through excessive gentleness mourns for those who have sinned and have not repented (2 Cor. 12:21); who is stronger than every principality and power (Rom. 8:38); who brought back in abundance the wisdom and marrow of sacred meanings, not from the first or second but from the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:21).

3. These are our teachers, who learned the paths of life more fully from the teacher of all and teach us to this present day. What, then, have the holy apostles taught, or what do they teach us? Not the fisherman’s craft, not tentmaking, or anything of that kind; not to read Plato, not to overturn Aristotle’s subtleties [Col. 0407B], not always to learn and never to arrive at the knowledge of truth. They have taught me to live. Do you think it a small thing to know how to live? It is something great—indeed, the greatest thing.

One does not live who is puffed up by pride, defiled by luxury, or infected with the other plagues; for this is not to live, but to confound life and draw near even to the gates of death. But I consider the good life to be suffering evil, doing good, and thus persevering until death. It is commonly said that one who feeds oneself well lives well. But iniquity has lied to itself: no one lives well unless one does good.

4. I judge, however, that you who are in the community live well, if you live in an orderly, sociable, and humble manner: orderly with regard to yourself, sociably with regard to your neighbour, humbly before God.
