Orderly, so that in all your conduct you are careful to observe your ways, both in the sight of the Lord and in the sight of your neighbour, guarding yourself against sin and him against scandal. Sociably, so that you strive both to be loved and to love; to show yourself gentle and approachable; to bear, not only patiently but gladly, the infirmities of your brethren, both of character and of body. Humbly, so that, when you have done all these things, you strive to blow away the spirit of vanity which is wont to arise from such things; and, however much you feel it, utterly refuse it your consent. So too in suffering evil, since it is threefold, you must employ a threefold prudence. For there is that which you suffer from yourself, that which you suffer from your neighbour, and that which you suffer from God. The first is the austerity of penance; the second, the affliction caused by another’s malice; the third, the scourge of divine correction. In what you suffer from yourself, you ought willingly to make sacrifice; what comes from your neighbour, patiently to bear; what comes from God, to endure without murmuring and with thanksgiving. Not thus do many of Adam’s children, who “wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place” (Ps. 106:4). They certainly wandered, and wander from the way of truth, who, withdrawing into the wilderness of pride, refuse to live a social life, whose singularity cannot be joined in fellowship. And they are in a waterless place also: for, untouched by any shower of tears, they remain in a barren and parched land, in perpetual dryness. Therefore they “found no way to a city of habitation,” because, grown old in a foreign land, they have been defiled among the dead and reckoned with those who are in hell.

5. Not so solitary was that man of whom Saint Jeremiah says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He shall sit solitary and keep silence, because he has lifted himself above himself” (Lam. 3:27–28). They wandered, but he shall sit. For they always err in heart; but he does not sit now, but shall sit solitary when he has received the honour of singularity—that is, the insignia of judicial power—which the saints shall possess in their own land, when everlasting joy shall be theirs. He shall also keep silence, that is, he shall judge in tranquillity, just as the Lord of hosts judges all things in tranquillity.  
[Note: [Col. 0408D] This period, “He shall keep silence . . . all things,” is absent from other editions and from certain manuscripts.]

Why? Because “he has lifted himself above himself”: that is, when he was young and felt the ardours of slippery age, he put on the old man, leaving what he was and assuming what he was not. “He lifted himself above himself,” it says, because he looks not to himself, but to him who is above himself. For he shall sit, and even now keep silence from the tumult of diabolical suggestions, from the tumult of carnal desires, from the tumult of the world. Happy the soul which does not heed these tongues, even though it hears them; far happier still, if indeed there is any such, is the soul to which they speak not at all. This is the wisdom which the Apostle speaks among the perfect, hidden in mystery, which none of the rulers of this age has known (1 Cor. 2:6–7). Thus the apostles taught me both to live and to ascend [or: believe]. I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus, who “have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to these little ones” who followed you and left all things for your name’s sake.

## SERMON II

1. These saints, whose solemn passion is celebrated today, have supplied us with much occasion and material for speaking about them. Yet I fear one thing: that words of salvation, heard so often, may begin to seem cheap to us merely as words. For the word of man is indeed a cheap and fleeting thing: of no substance [or: duration], no weight, no value, no solidity. It strikes the air—whence it is called a *verbum*, “word”—and, like a leaf carried away by the wind, it passes away, and there is none to regard it. Let none of you, brethren, receive the word of God thus; indeed, let no one despise it thus. For I tell you: it would have been better for that man had he not heard it. The words of God are fruits of life, not leaves; and if leaves, they are golden. Therefore let them not be lightly esteemed, let them not pass by, let them not fly past. Gather up even the fragments, lest they perish. For “the earth which has received the rain falling upon it often, and has not produced fruit, is reprobate land, near to a curse” (Heb. 6:7–8). So too the barren fig tree mentioned in the Gospel: if, after the vine-dresser has dug about it and put manure upon it, it is nevertheless found barren (Luke 13:6–9), is not the axe now to be laid to the root of that tree?

2. And I tell you: if the Lord finds less good among secular people, he will exercise greater patience toward them than toward us, for whom he has set apart a voluntary rain of heavenly consolations; for whom neither the hoe of discipline nor the manure of poverty and lowliness has been lacking. Are not “the abominations of the Egyptians,” which we sacrifice to our God, manure? Manure is indeed lowly to look upon, but useful for fruitfulness. Let him who desires fertility not shrink from this foulness. For from the unsightly heap of manure carried into the field there will rise a beautiful heap of sheaves, carried back from the field. Therefore let not precious lowliness become cheap to you; rather, esteem the reproach of Christ more precious than all the treasures of Egypt. Yet for those who have an earthly dung-heap, the heavenly rain itself is not lacking: namely, the devotion of prayers, the pleasant rumination of psalmody, sweet meditation, and the consolation of the Scriptures. Indeed, this very rain too is what you receive through my mouth, whenever some drops may happen to trickle upon you, as we speak of them, from the river “whose rush makes glad the city of God,” and from the torrent of his delight.

3. But I must sometimes dig around you, since they have appointed me guardian and cultivator in the vineyards. Alas, I who have neither cultivated nor guarded my own vineyard must nevertheless, while I occupy this place, sometimes dig around and apply manure. It is burdensome indeed, but I dare not conceal it, knowing that the axe will harm far more than the hoe, and fire more than manure. Thus it is sometimes necessary to rebuke and reprove. Nor am I unaware that a word of rebuke is manure,  
[Note: [Col. 0409] Some manuscripts add, “a bitter word,” which is absent from other editions and manuscripts.]

a word of reproach, and one which, unless necessity excuses it, is scarcely fitting even for its speaker to utter. But what are we to do, since we see that by this manure some are indeed fattened, while others plainly become stoned and hardened? For it is written: “The sluggard shall be stoned with ox-dung” (Ecclus. 22:2). Is not he fattened who, when reproved, receives it kindly, answers meekly, and gladly endeavours to amend? This is indeed wholesome and fruitful fattening: “Let the righteous correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.” For from the fatness generated by the sinner’s oil, thorns and briars spring up more abundantly, and every root of bitterness sprouts more copiously. Therefore, he who calls the rebuke of the righteous “mercy” sufficiently indicates how it ought to be received: with what kindly spirit, what devoted mind, and what gratitude. Thus, if we receive it in this way, it will be a wholesome fattening, not one fertile in vices like the sinner’s oil, but productive of that fruit which, according to the Apostle, we have in sanctification (Rom. 6:22). But what are we to do with you, O sluggard? Why are you the more provoked and embittered by this mercy? Did I not scatter good manure in your field? Whence then has it stones? But you, O enemy-man—for “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6)—you, I say, enemy-man, have done this. Persisting not in shaking off but in excusing your sloth, you turn manure into stones for yourself; and from that by which you ought to have been fattened, you are stoned. These things, brethren, have been said so that you may know how kindly everything pertaining to the salvation of souls ought to be heard, how devoutly received, how carefully preserved—not as the word of men, but as, what it truly is, the word of God, whether it be heard [or: seen] as consoling, admonitory, or even reproving. I have gone beyond my subject, I confess, almost forgetting the feast itself; yet, I think, not to your disadvantage, if what you have heard remains firmly fixed in your minds.

4. And now let us try to say something briefly about the solemnity itself. The festal day of Christ’s apostles is being celebrated. I know certainly that very great honour is owed them by us; yet I am greatly uncertain whether any honour can be rendered to them adequately. For “your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured; their rule has been greatly strengthened” (Ps. 138:17). For if, while still placed upon earth, they could do all things—not indeed in themselves, but in Christ—what will they not be able to do today, living with him in eternal blessedness? Still mortal and destined to die, they seemed to have authority over life and death, killing the living and raising the dead, to be sure, by word alone. How much more now, when they have been exceedingly honoured and their rule has been greatly strengthened? But what is this, brethren? Since the blessed memory of the apostles is celebrated today, is there perhaps a solemn commemoration of their birth, conversion, life, or miracles? No, brethren: this is not a feast of human birth, as a little while ago you celebrated the birthday of blessed John. He is honoured at his birth because he was born sanctified. Indeed, in John alone his birth is more celebrated than his passion; for although he suffered for Christ when he died for justice and truth, he was more plainly born for him—being, of course, “a man sent from God,” who was born and came into the world for this purpose, to bear witness to the truth (John 1:7). Nor do we today recount the conversion of the apostles or their miracles, as on other appointed days the conversion of one apostle or another’s liberation from prison by an angel is recalled with the Church’s festal joy. We venerate especially the death which, by human judgment, nothing among human things is more dreadful.

5. Consider, brethren, the judgment of holy Church: according to faith, not according to the outward appearance of the judge. For in the chief solemnity of the apostles she commemorates their death. Today Peter was crucified; today Paul was beheaded. This is the reason for today’s feast; this is the substance of the present rejoicing. Therefore, in keeping a feast-day and rejoicing over these things, the Church undoubtedly has the spirit of the Bridegroom, the spirit of the Lord, in whose sight, as you have in the Psalm, “precious is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). For how many do we believe were present when the apostles suffered, who did not at all envy their precious deaths? For “they seemed in the eyes of fools to die, and their departure was judged an affliction”; and thus indeed they seemed in the eyes of fools to die. “But to me,” says the Prophet, “your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured; their rule has been greatly strengthened.” Brethren, the friends of God seem to die in the eyes of fools; but in the eyes of the wise they are judged rather to fall asleep. Thus Lazarus too was sleeping, because he was a friend (John 11:11); and “when he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126:2–3).

6. Let us strive, brethren, to live the life of the righteous; but let us desire much more to die their death. For the wisdom of the righteous prefers the last things, judging us there where it finds us. It is altogether necessary that the end of the present life adhere to the beginning of the life to come; and there can be no tolerable dissimilarity there. For just as, if someone wished, so to speak, to sew or bind together two girdles for himself, caring less about the remaining parts, he prepares uniformly the ends which are to be joined together, lest they disagree with one another; so I say to you: however spiritual our manner of life may have been, if our end is carnal, it does not adhere at all to that spiritual life, nor can flesh and blood possess the kingdom of God. “Son,” says the Wise Man, “remember your last things, and you will not sin” (Ecclus. 7:40). Clearly, this remembrance especially makes one fearful; fear drives out sin and admits no negligence.

7. Hence Moses says of certain persons: “Would that they were wise, and understood, and foresaw their last things!” (Deut. 32:29). In these words I see three things commended to us: wisdom, understanding, and foresight. I judge that they may be assigned to three times, so that a certain image of eternity may appear renewed in us: regulating the present by wisdom, judging the past by understanding, and foreseeing the last things for caution. This is indeed the sum of spiritual exercise, this the aim of spiritual study: that we wisely order our present affairs, reconsider our past in the bitterness of our soul, and diligently provide for the future. “Let us live soberly, justly, and godly in this world,” says the Apostle (Titus 2:12): so that sobriety may be observed in the present; so that by just satisfaction the times past, which passed for us without the fruit of salvation, may be redeemed; and so that we may set the shield of piety against the dangers that threaten from the future. For piety alone avails for all things: that is, humble and devout worship of God. Nor can we otherwise provide for our last things than by diligently turning over in thought all dangers which seem to threaten us, learning to distrust wholly our own efforts—indeed, rather our own merits—and to commit ourselves to divine protection alone, with a certain pious affection of mind and the affection [variant: “and effect” is absent] of a devout intention toward him, whose good gift and perfect donation are a happy consummation and a precious death.

8. In the Gospel you have these same three things commended to you by the Lord’s saying: “Blessed are the poor; blessed are the meek; blessed are those who mourn” (Matt. 5:3–5). Blessed are those who are wise concerning future things, who, from desire for heavenly things, reject present things with a certain inward savour of mind. Blessed are those who foresee their last things, receiving in meekness the implanted word which can save their souls, and through piety of heart pressing toward the inheritance to come. Blessed are those who understand their former error and often wash their bed with tears. Do you see what the holy man desires, what he wishes to obtain for those for whom he prays? “Would that,” he says, “they were wise, and understood, and foresaw their last things!” As though he were saying more plainly: Would that there were in them a spirit of wisdom, understanding, and counsel! Would that these things might be found in us, brethren: that we may sweetly order all that is ours through wisdom; that by understanding we may condemn past sins; that by counsel we may provide for future things. Would that we may be wise for the regulation of our present life; understand for the correction of the past; and provide in devout faith toward God, so that, through his mercy, we may have a happy end. For this is the threefold cord by which we are drawn to salvation: ordered conduct, right judgment, and devout faith.

## SERMON III. On the Reading from the Book of Wisdom: “These Are Men of Mercy” (Ecclus. 44:10–11)

1. Rightly, brethren, does Mother Church apply to the holy apostles what is read in the books of Wisdom: “These are men of mercy, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten; good things remain with their seed.” For these are truly men of mercy: whether because they obtained mercy, or because they were full of mercy, or because they were mercifully given to us by God. And see what mercy they obtained. Ask Paul about himself, or rather listen to him willingly confessing: “I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an injurious man; but I obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1:13). Who has not heard how great evils he did to the saints in Jerusalem? And not in Jerusalem only: throughout all Judaea he was driven by the reins of madness, to tear apart Christ’s members on earth. Indeed, carried onward by this fury he was going; but he was forestalled by grace. He went “breathing threats and slaughter” against the Lord’s disciples, and became a disciple of the Lord, to whom it might be shown how great things he must suffer for that name. He went, exhaling a dreadful poison from his whole body, and suddenly was changed into a vessel of election, so that his heart now poured forth “a good word,” a pious word, and he said: “Lord, what do you wish me to do?” (Acts 4). This indeed, this is “the change of the right hand of the Most High.” Rightly, therefore, did he say: “Faithful is the saying, and worthy of all acceptance, that the Lord Jesus came to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Tim. 1:15). Receive this, then, brethren, as grounds of confidence and consolation in blessed Paul: that, once converted to the Lord, you may not be too severely tormented by consciousness of past offences; but let it only humble you, as it humbled him. “I,” he says, “am the least of the apostles, and am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9). So let us also be humbled under the mighty hand of God and have confidence, because we too have obtained mercy; we have been washed, we have been sanctified. And this applies indeed to us all, because all have sinned and need this glory of God.

2. Yet in blessed Peter I have something else to add—so much the dearer as it is rarer, and so much the more sublime as it is more singular. Paul sinned, but he acted ignorantly in his unbelief; when Peter fell, he had his eyes open. Yet where the offence abounded, grace superabounded. For those who sin before they know God, before they have experienced his mercies, before they have borne the sweet yoke and light burden, before they have received the grace of devotion and the consolations of the Holy Spirit—for such persons, I say, redemption is abundant. And all of us were such. But among those who, after conversion, become entangled in sins and vices, ungrateful for received grace, and, after putting hand to plough, look back—having become lukewarm and carnal—or who, after knowing the way of truth, turn back as manifest apostates: among these you find very few who thereafter return to their former state. Rather, being in filth, they become filthier still. Over them the prophet laments: “How the gold has grown dim, how the finest colour has changed!” and, “Those who were nourished in saffron have embraced dung-heaps” (Lam. 4:1, 5).

3. Yet if anyone is such a person, we do not despair of him, provided only that he wishes to rise quickly. For the longer he remains, the more difficult he will become to rescue. Blessed, however, is he who “shall seize and dash the little ones of Babylon against the rock”; for if they grow, they can scarcely be overcome. “Little children, I say these things so that you may not sin. But if anyone sins, we have an Advocate with the Father,” who can do what we most certainly cannot. Only let him who has fallen not add evil upon evil so as to fall more deeply; but rather let him rise, trusting that pardon will not be denied him if he confesses his sins from the heart. For if Peter, of whom we speak, after so grave a fall returned to such an eminence of holiness, who thereafter should despair, if only he wishes to emerge from sins? Attend to what is written: “He went out and wept bitterly” (Matt. 26:75). In his going out, understand confession of the mouth; in his bitter weeping, compunction of heart. And observe that only then did he first remember the word which Jesus had spoken: only then did the word by which his weakness had been foretold enter his heart, when his presumptuous rashness had vanished. Woe to you who, after a fall, present yourself to us as stronger. Why are you so unyielding to your own ruin? Bend rather, that you may be raised up the better; and do not prevent what is distorted from being broken, so that it may be made sound more effectively. Why are you angry with the reproving cock? Be angry with yourself instead. “You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance, and it was weakened,” says the Psalmist. Good is the weakness set apart for the inheritance, which does not reject the physician. For he “will break the hardened like a potter’s vessel with an iron rod”; and “the inheritance was weakened,” it says, “but you have perfected it” (Ps. 67:10).

4. You have surely heard what mercy our apostles obtained, so that none of you may henceforth be ashamed beyond what is necessary over past sins, while pierced with compunction in the chamber of your conscience. What then? Perhaps you sinned in the world; did you sin more than Paul? Or even in the religious life; did you sin more than Peter? Yet they, repenting with their whole heart, obtained not only salvation but holiness, and received also the ministry of salvation and the office of teaching holiness. You therefore do likewise, since Scripture says that those men were men of mercy for your sake—assuredly on account of the great mercy which they deserved to obtain.

5. Yet in this expression you may also rightly understand that the apostles were men of mercy—that is, full of mercy—or men of mercy, that is, mercifully given to the universal Church. For we know that these men neither lived for themselves nor died for themselves, but for him who died for them; or rather, for all of us because of him. For how much shall their righteousness benefit us, when, as has been shown, even their sins benefited us so greatly? Their life, their teaching, and even their death itself work for us. In their conversion the blessed apostles bestowed continence upon us; in their preaching, wisdom; in their passion, patience. Full of mercy, they do not cease even to this day to bestow a fourth gift: the fruit of holy prayers. And in their earthly life itself you may find something further to add: namely, the confidence which they supplied us through the performance of miracles. And who can enumerate how many benefits have come to us through them? Scripture speaks rightly, then, concerning them: “For these are men of mercy”; and adds, “whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten” (Ecclus. 44).

6. Do you wish that your righteousness too may not be forgotten? Guard against a threefold danger, and it shall flourish eternally before the Lord. For you read: “Because you are lukewarm, I will begin to remove you from my mouth” (Rev. 3:16); you read: “If the righteous turns away from his righteousness,” and so forth, “I will not remember any of his righteous deeds” (Ezek. 18:24); you read that some will be told at judgment: “I never knew you” (Matt. 7:23)—those, without doubt, who have received their reward. Therefore every lukewarm righteousness, every transitory righteousness, every righteousness sold for payment, shall be forgotten before God. But the righteousness of the apostles is not so. This is sufficiently evident from what follows: “Good things remain with their seed.” For the apostles’ footprints remain among us to this day; and their religion, because it is from God, cannot be dissolved. The garments of the Israelite people remained whole in the wilderness for forty years (Deut. 8:4); much more the garments of the apostles, laid upon the Saviour’s beast. “With their seed,” it says. What is this seed? For it goes on to add: “Their descendants are a holy inheritance.” Clearly, seed and descendants are the same. You remember, I believe—for I speak to those who know the law—you remember, I say, the legal command that the surviving brother should raise up seed for a brother who died without seed (Gen. 38:8; Deut. 25:5). Who is without seed? “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140:10). Therefore, after rising, he says: “Go, tell my brethren” (John 20:17). As though he said: They are brethren; let them do what brethren do. Therefore through the Gospel they begot us—yet not for themselves, but for Christ, because it was through Christ’s Gospel. Hence Paul was displeased that some were called after those through whom they had been begotten by the Gospel, and protested against those who said, “I am of Paul; I am of Cephas; I am of Apollos” (1 Cor. 1:12; 3:4), wishing all rather to become and to be called Christ’s. Thus we are the apostles’ seed through preaching; but through adoption and inheritance, Christ’s seed and the apostles’ descendants.

[Col. 0415]

## ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

### SERMON I. On the Twofold Reception, Namely of Christ and of Mary

[Col. 0415A]

1. Today the glorious Virgin ascends to heaven, and undoubtedly has increased the joys of the citizens above with abundant additions. For she is the one whose voice in greeting causes even those to leap for joy whom their mothers’ wombs still enclose (Luke 1:41). If the soul of an as yet unborn little child melted when Mary spoke, what, then, do we suppose was that exultation of heaven when they deserved both to hear her voice, to see her face, and to enjoy her blessed presence? But for us, dearly beloved, what occasion of solemnity, what cause of gladness, what matter for rejoicing is there in her Assumption? Mary’s presence illumines the whole world, so that even the heavenly country itself now gleams more brightly, irradiated by the splendour of the virginal lamp. Therefore thanksgiving and the voice of praise rightly resound on high; but for us it seems more fitting to mourn than to applaud. For as much as heaven rejoices in her presence, does it not consequently follow that this lower world of ours mourns her absence by the same measure? Yet let our complaint cease, because here too “we have no abiding city,” but seek that city to which blessed Mary came today. If we are citizens enrolled there, it is fitting indeed that even in exile, even beside the rivers of Babylon, we remember her, share in her joys, and participate in her gladness—especially in that joy which today makes glad the city of God with so abundant a rush that we too may feel drops trickling down upon the earth. Our queen has gone before us; she has gone before us and has been received so gloriously that her servants may confidently follow their Lady, crying: “Draw us after you; we will run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3). Our pilgrimage has sent ahead its advocate, who, as the Judge’s mother and the mother of mercy, will humbly and effectively transact the business of our salvation.

2. Today our earth has sent a precious gift to heaven, so that, in giving and receiving, human things may be joined with divine, earthly with heavenly, and lowly with highest things by a happy covenant of friendship. For the sublime fruit of the earth has ascended to that place from which “good gifts and perfect donations” descend. Therefore, ascending on high, the blessed Virgin will herself also give gifts to human beings. Why should she not give? For neither power nor will can be lacking to her. She is Queen of Heaven; she is merciful; indeed, she is the mother of the only-begotten Son of God. Nothing can more greatly commend either the greatness of her power or her compassion—unless perhaps one does not believe that the Son of God honours his mother, or can anyone at all doubt that Mary’s womb has passed into the affection of love, when that charity which is from God itself rested bodily in it for nine months?

3. I have said these things for our sake, brethren, knowing how difficult it is in such great poverty to find that perfect charity which does not seek its own. Yet, to say nothing for the moment of the benefits which we obtain through her glorification: if we love her, we shall certainly rejoice because she goes to her Son. Indeed, I say, we shall congratulate her—unless, God forbid, we are found altogether ungrateful toward her who found grace. For she had first received into herself him who entered the little fortress of this world; today, entering the holy city, she is received by him. But with what honour, think you; with what exultation; with what glory? On earth no place was more worthy than the temple of the virginal womb, in which Mary received the Son of God; nor in heaven was there a place more worthy than the royal throne, on which Mary’s Son today exalted Mary. Happy indeed is each reception; each is ineffable, because each is beyond thought. Why then is that Gospel reading recited today in Christ’s churches, in which a woman blessed among women is understood to have received the Saviour? I believe it is so that this reception which we celebrate may be estimated in some measure from that one; indeed, so that, in accordance with the inestimable glory of that reception, this one too may be known as inestimable. For who, even if speaking with the tongues of men and angels, can explain how, when the Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, the Word of God through whom all things were made became flesh, and the Lord of Majesty, whom the whole creation cannot contain, enclosed himself within virginal entrails, becoming man?

4. And who can even adequately conceive how gloriously the Queen of the world proceeded today, with what affection of devotion the entire multitude of heavenly legions came forth to meet her; with what songs she was led to the throne of glory; with what gracious countenance, serene face, and joyful [variant: divine] embraces she was received by her Son; and how, exalted above every creature, she was received with that honour which so great a mother deserved and that glory which so great a Son befitted? Truly happy were the kisses impressed upon the lips of the nursing child, whom the mother joyfully held in her virginal lap. Yet shall we not judge happier those which she received today in blessed greeting from the mouth of him sitting at the right hand of the Father, when she ascended to the throne of glory, singing the bridal song and saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1)? Who shall recount Christ’s generation and Mary’s assumption? For as much grace as she obtained above all others on earth, so much singular glory does she possess in heaven. And if “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” what God has prepared for those who love him: who can speak of what he has prepared for her who bore him and—what is certain to all—loved him above all? Blessed indeed is Mary, and blessed in many ways, whether when she receives the Saviour or when she is received by the Saviour. In either case, marvellous is the dignity of the Virgin Mother; in either case, the condescension of Majesty is to be embraced. “Jesus entered into a certain little fortress, and a certain woman received him into her house” (Luke 10:38). But we must rather devote ourselves to praise, since this day is owed festal proclamations. Yet because the words of this reading provide us abundant material, tomorrow also, when we assemble together, we must share without envy what has been given from above, so that in remembering so great a Virgin not only may the affection of devotion be awakened, but morals may also be built up for progress in conduct, to the praise and glory of her Son, our Lord, who is God blessed above all for ever. Amen.

### SERMON II. On a House to Be Cleansed, Adorned, and Filled

1. “Jesus entered into a certain little fortress, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house” (Luke 10:38). At this point the prophetic exclamation seems especially fitting for me to adopt: “O Israel, how great is the house of the Lord, and how immense the place of his possession!” (Baruch 3:24). Is it not immense, when the spacious expanse of this earth is called a little fortress by comparison with it? Is not that homeland and country inestimable, when the Saviour, coming from it, is said, upon entering the world, to enter a little fortress? Unless perhaps someone thinks that “the little fortress” should be understood otherwise than as the court of the strong armed man, the prince of this world, whose goods one stronger who comes upon him came to plunder (Luke 11:21–22). Let us hasten, brethren, to enter that spaciousness of blessedness where no one confines another, so that with all the saints we may comprehend “what is the length and breadth, height and depth” (Eph. 3:18). Nor should we despair of this, since the heavenly inhabitant and Creator of that country did not shun the narrowness of this little fortress of ours.

2. But what do we mean when we say that he entered a little fortress? He entered even the most narrow lodging of a virgin’s womb. Indeed, “a certain woman received him into her house.” Happy woman, who deserved to receive not now the spies of Jericho, but rather the mighty plunderer of that foolish one who truly “changes like the moon”; not envoys of Jesus son of Nave, but the true Jesus, Son of God himself. Happy, I say, the woman whose house, when it received the Saviour, was found clean indeed, but certainly not empty. For who would call empty her whom the angel greets as “full of grace”? Nor is this all: he also declares that the Holy Spirit is yet to come upon her. For what purpose, think you, except that he may fill her even more? For what purpose, except that, already full for herself through the Spirit’s coming, she might through that same Spirit’s coming become overfull and overflowing even for us? May those perfumes—namely, the charisms of graces—flow into us, so that we may all receive from so great a fullness! She herself is indeed our mediatrix; she is the one through whom we have received your mercy, O God; she is the one through whom we too receive the Lord Jesus into our houses. For each of us has his own little fortress and his own house; and Wisdom knocks at each person’s door. If anyone opens to her, she will enter and dine with him. There is a common proverb, which is often on people’s lips but more often in their hearts: “He keeps a fortress well,” they say, “who guards his body.” But the Wise Man does not say this; rather, he says: “With all vigilance guard your heart, because life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4:23).

3. Yet let it be so: let us yield to the multitude; let him who guards his body guard a good fortress. But we must certainly ask what guard ought to be set over this fortress. Does that soul seem to you rightly to have guarded the fortress of its body, whose members, as though they had formed a conspiracy, delivered dominion over it to its enemy? For there are those who have made a covenant with death and struck a bargain with hell (Isa. 28:15). “The beloved,” he says, “grew fat and kicked; he grew fat, stout, and bloated” (Deut. 32:15). This is precisely the kind of guarding praised by sinners in the desires of their flesh. What do you think, brothers? Must we yield to the multitude even in this matter? Far from it! Let us rather ask Paul, the vigorous leader of the spiritual warfare. Tell us, Apostle: what is the guard of your fortress? “I so run,” he says, “not as though toward an uncertainty; I so fight, not as one beating the air. Rather, I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” [Col. 0418B–C] (1 Cor. 9:26–27). And elsewhere: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Rom. 6:12). This is indeed a useful guard; and blessed is the soul which so guards its body that the enemy may never lay claim to it.

For there was once a time when that impious one had subjected this fortress of mine to his tyranny, imperiously commanding all its members. How much harm he did in that time, the desolation and poverty still present bear witness. Alas! He left in it neither the wall of continence nor the outer rampart of patience. He devastated the vineyards, reaped the crops, uprooted the trees; indeed, “this eye of mine was plundering my soul.” Finally, unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell [Col. 0418D]. And by hell I mean the lower hell, where there is no confession, and from which no one is permitted to depart.

4. Yet even then it lacked neither prison nor hell. For, having been detected at the very beginning of that most wicked conspiracy and betrayal, it was consigned to prison custody nowhere other than in its own house, and handed over to torturers who were none other than members of its own household. Conscience was its prison; reason and memory were its torturers—cruel, harsh, and merciless indeed, yet far less so than those roaring creatures prepared for their prey, to whom it was on the very point of being delivered. But blessed be God, who did not give me as prey to their teeth. Blessed, I say, be the Lord, who visited us and wrought redemption.

For while the malignant one was hastening to hand it over to the lower prison [elsewhere added: “and to the torturers”], and also to burn the fortress itself with everlasting fires, so that its perjured members might receive their due recompense, a stronger one came upon him. Jesus entered the little fortress; binding the strong man, he plundered his goods, in order to make what had formerly been for dishonour into vessels for honour. He shattered the bronze gates and broke the iron bars, bringing the captive forth from the prison-house and the shadow of death [Col. 0419A]. Moreover, its going forth is in confession. For confession is the broom by which the prison, cleansed and adorned, returns from being a prison to being a house, beautifully strewn with certain green reeds of regular observances. The woman therefore now has her house; she has somewhere to receive him to whom she is indebted for such great benefits. Otherwise, woe to her if she refuses to receive him, if she does not hold him fast, if she does not compel him to remain with her, “because evening is drawing on.” For when he who was first cast out returns, he finds the house cleansed and adorned indeed, but empty [Col. 0419B].

5. Thus the woman is left with her house deserted, because [elsewhere: “since”] she neglected to make it worthy of the Saviour’s hospitality. “How?” you ask. Can a house cleansed by confession of former sins and adorned by the observance of regular practices still be judged unworthy of the dwelling of grace, of the Saviour’s entrance? Undoubtedly it can, if it has been cleansed only on the surface and strewn, as was said, with green reeds, while inwardly it is full of mire. For who would think the Lord should be received in whitewashed tombs of the dead, which appear beautiful outwardly but within are filled with every uncleanness and corruption?

Suppose, indeed, that at some time, as if pleased by the surface itself, he begins, as it were, first to set his foot there, granting such a person some initial grace of his visitation. Will he not immediately recoil in indignation? Will he not flee away, crying, “I am sunk in deep mire, and there is no firm ground” [Col. 0419C] (Ps. 68:3)? For the appearance of virtue without its reality is, as it were, a quality, not a substance. Nor can the thin surface of outward conduct sustain his entrance, for he penetrates all things, and his dwelling is in the innermost heart. And if the spirit of discipline does not dwell in a body manifestly subject to sins, it certainly not only avoids what is false, but flees from it and withdraws far away (Wis. 1:5).

Or is it anything other than detestable pretence if you scrape sin away only from the surface and do not root it out inwardly? Be sure that it will sprout more luxuriantly; and the malignant guest [elsewhere: “enemy”] who had been cast out will enter the cleansed but empty house with seven others more wicked than himself [Col. 0419D]. For the dog returning to its vomit will be much more hateful than before; and he who, after forgiveness of his sins, falls again into the same filth will become a son of Gehenna many times over, like a washed sow in a wallowing-place of mud.

6. Do you wish to see a house cleansed, adorned, and empty? Look at the person who has confessed and abandoned the manifest sins that go beforehand to judgment, and who now merely moves his hands in the works of the commandments [Col. 0420A], with a heart utterly dry, led by a certain habit, just like Ephraim’s heifer, trained to love threshing. Of outward observances, which are of little worth, he omits not one iota or one tittle; yet he swallows the camel while straining out the gnat. For in his heart he is a servant of his own will, a worshipper of greed, eager for glory, a lover of ambition; either cherishing all these vices within, or each one separately. And iniquity lies to itself, but God is not mocked.

At times you may see such a person so disguised that he deceives even himself, paying no attention at all to the worm that devours his inward parts. The surface remains, and he thinks everything is safe for him. “Strangers,” says the prophet, “have consumed his strength, and he did not know it” (Hos. 7:9). He says, “Because I am rich and need nothing,” while he is poor, wretched, and pitiable [Col. 0420B] (Rev. 3:17). For, when occasion is found, you may see the corruption which lay hidden in the ulcer boil forth; and the tree that was cut down, not uprooted, sprout into a denser forest. If we wish to avoid this danger, we must lay the axe to the roots of the trees, not to the branches. Let there not be found in us bodily exercise alone, which is of little profit; but let godliness, profitable for all things, and spiritual exercise be found.

7. “A woman named Martha,” he says, “received him into her house; and she had a sister named Mary.” They are sisters and ought to live together. Martha is occupied with much serving; Mary is intent upon the Lord’s words. Adornment belongs to Martha, but fullness to Mary. For she is free for the Lord, so that the house may not be empty. But to whom can we attribute cleansing [Col. 0420C]? For if we also find this, there will be a house in which the Saviour is received, cleansed, adorned, and not empty. Let us assign it to Lazarus, if this seems right to you. For by the right of brotherhood this house is shared by him with his sisters. I mean Lazarus, whom the voice of power raised from the dead after four days, when he was already beginning to stink, so that he seems quite fittingly to represent the penitent.

Let the Saviour therefore enter the house and frequently visit it: Lazarus the penitent cleanses it, Martha adorns it, and Mary fills it, devoted to inward contemplation.

8. But perhaps someone will inquire too curiously why in the present Gospel reading absolutely no mention is made of Lazarus. I think this too accords with the proposed comparison. For the Spirit, wishing the house to be understood as virginal, appropriately kept silence concerning penitence, which surely accompanies evil [Col. 0420D]. Far be it that this house should ever be said to have had any defilement of its own, so that Lazarus’s broom would be sought in it. But if she contracted from her parents the original stain, Christian piety forbids us to believe that she was less sanctified in the womb than Jeremiah, or not more fully filled with the Holy Spirit than John; for she would not be honoured at her birth with festal praises if she were not born holy.

> [Note: [Col. 0419] Incorrectly in Horstius: “For this one is honoured at her birth with festal praises.” Finally.]

Finally, since it is in every respect certain that Mary alone was cleansed from original contagion by grace—inasmuch as even now in baptism grace alone washes away this stain, and formerly the rock of circumcision alone scraped it away—if, as it is altogether pious to believe, Mary had no personal sin, penitence was likewise far removed from that most innocent heart. Let Lazarus therefore be among those whose consciences must be cleansed from dead works. Let him withdraw among the wounded who sleep in tombs, so that in the virginal chamber Martha and Mary alone may be found. For she it was who humbly served Elizabeth, pregnant and advanced in years, for about three months [Col. 0421A] (Luke 1:56); she it was who kept in her heart, pondering, the words spoken concerning her Son (Luke 2:19).

9. Let no one, then, be troubled because the woman who receives the Lord is called not Mary but Martha; for in this one and supreme woman are found both Martha’s work and Mary’s non-idle leisure. “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within,” yet she is “clothed round about with variety in golden fringes.” She is not among the foolish virgins: she is a prudent virgin; she has a lamp, but carries oil in her vessel. Or have you forgotten that Gospel parable which recounts that the foolish virgins were forbidden entrance to the wedding feast? [Col. 0421B] (Matt. 25:1–13). Their house was indeed clean, for they were virgins; it was adorned, because all alike—that is, foolish as well as prudent—adorned their lamps; but it was empty, because they did not take oil in their vessels. Hence the heavenly Bridegroom neither deigns to be received by them into their houses nor admits them to the wedding feast [Col. 0421C].

Not so that valiant woman who crushed the serpent’s head. For among the many things said in her praise, you have this: “Her lamp shall not be extinguished in the night” (Prov. 31:18). This is said as a reproach to the foolish virgins, who, when the bridegroom comes at midnight, complain too late and say: “Our lamps are going out.” The glorious Virgin therefore went forth, whose most burning lamp was a miracle of light even to the angels themselves, so that they said: “Who is this that goes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” (Cant. 6:9). For she shone more brightly than all others, whom Christ Jesus, her Son and our Lord, filled with the oil of grace above her companions.

## SERMON III. On Mary, Martha, and Lazarus. (Luke 10:38–42.)

[Col. 0421D] 1. Jesus entered into a certain little fortress, and a woman named Martha received him into her house. What is this, brothers, that of the two sisters only one is said to have received the Lord—and she the one who seems inferior? For Mary chose the best part, according to the testimony of him whom Martha received. Yet Martha appears to have been the elder, and action rather than contemplation is known to claim for itself the beginning of salvation. Christ praises Mary, yet is received by Martha. Jacob loves Rachel, but Leah is substituted for her without his knowing. If he complains of the deception, he will hear that it is not the custom for younger daughters to be given first in marriage [Col. 0422A] (Gen. 29:23–26).

But if you understand this house as one of clay, it will be easy to see how Martha rather than Mary receives the Lord in it. For the Apostle’s saying, “Glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20), is addressed to Martha, not Mary. Martha, of course, uses the instrument of the body, whereas for Mary it is rather an impediment. “For the corruptible body,” he says, “weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). Does it also burden the mind that works? Martha therefore receives the Saviour into her house on earth; Mary rather considers how she may be received by him into the house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. Perhaps she too seems to have received the Lord, but in spirit; for “the Lord is spirit.”

[Col. 0422B] 2. “She had,” he says—undoubtedly Martha—“a sister named Mary, who also, sitting at Jesus’ feet, heard his word.” You see that both received the Word: Martha in the flesh, Mary in the voice. But Martha was troubled about much serving. She stood and said: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?” Do you suppose that, in a house in which Christ is received, the voice of grumbling will be heard? Blessed is the house, and ever blessed the congregation, in which Martha complains of Mary. For Mary’s envying Martha is wholly unworthy, wholly unlawful. Where else do you read Mary complaining, “My sister has left me to be free for God alone”? Far, far be it that one who is free for God should aspire to the tumultuous life of the brothers’ offices! Martha should always seem insufficient for herself and less fit for the task, and should wish others to be set over the work she administers [Col. 0422C].

Jesus answered her: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things.” See Mary’s prerogative: in every case, what an advocate she has. The Pharisee is indignant (Luke 7:39), the sister complains, and even the disciples murmur (Matt. 26:8); everywhere Mary is silent, and Christ speaks for her.

> [Note: [Col. 0421D] Here Bernard recognizes one Mary, as above in Sermon 3 for the sixth Sunday after Pentecost, and in Sermon 4 on the Dedication of a Church, no. 3. Compare Sermons 12 and 13 on the Song of Songs, where he remains uncertain and hesitant on this question.]

“Mary has chosen for herself the best part,” he says, “which shall not be taken from her for ever.” This is that one thing necessary; this is the one thing which the Prophet sought so earnestly: “One thing,” he says, “have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek” (Ps. 26:4).

3. Yet what does it mean, brothers, that Mary is said to have chosen the best part [Col. 0422D]? Where then will be what we are accustomed to cite against her, whenever perhaps one wishes to judge the anxiety of Martha’s service unequal to Mary’s: “The iniquity of a man is better than a beneficent woman” (Ecclus. 42:14)? Where will also be this: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honour him” (John 12:26)? And this: “He who is greatest among you shall be your servant” (Matt. 20:26)? Finally, what consolation is there for one who labours if, as though to reproach her, her sister’s part is exalted?

I therefore think one of two things: either Mary is praised for her choice, because that part itself, so far as lies in us, ought to be chosen by all; or else neither is said to have been lacking in her, nor did she precipitately incline her judgment toward either part, but she was ready for either at the command of her superior [Col. 0423A]. For who is faithful like David, entering and going out, and proceeding at the king’s command? (1 Sam. 22:14). “My heart is ready,” he says, “my heart is ready” (Ps. 56:8)—not merely once, but twice: both to be free for you and to serve one’s neighbours. This indeed is the best part, which shall not be taken away: this is the best mind, which will not be changed wherever you call it.

“He who has ministered well,” he says, “acquires a good degree” (1 Tim. 3:13). Perhaps better is he who has been free well for God; but best is he who is perfect in both. I say one thing further, if it is permissible to conjecture this about Martha. Does she not seem to have regarded Mary as idle, when she asked that Mary be given to her as a helper? But he is carnal and wholly does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, whoever rebukes an unoccupied soul for its repose. Let such a person therefore hear that this part, which remains for ever, is the best. Does not a soul seem in some sense untrained which, entirely bereft of divine contemplation, enters that region where this alone is the work of all, the one pursuit, the same life? [Col. 0423B]

4. But let us consider, brothers, how the order of charity has distributed these three things in this house of ours: Martha’s service, Mary’s contemplation, and Lazarus’s penitence. Every perfect soul possesses all these together; nevertheless, particular things seem to belong to particular persons: some may be free for holy contemplation, others devoted to fraternal service, and others may recall their years in the bitterness of their soul, like wounded persons sleeping in tombs [Col. 0423C]. Thus indeed, thus it must be: Mary should think piously and sublimely of her God; Martha kindly and mercifully of her neighbour; Lazarus miserably and humbly of himself.

Let each consider his own rank. “If Noah, Daniel, and Job are found in this city, they shall be delivered by their own righteousness,” says the Lord; “but they shall not deliver son or daughter” (Ezek. 14:14–16). We flatter no one; would that none of you might deceive himself! For those to whom no stewardship has been entrusted and no administration committed must wholly either sit at Jesus’ feet with Mary, or else remain with Lazarus within the enclosure of the tomb. Why should not Martha be troubled about many things, when she is anxious for many? But for you [Col. 0423D], upon whom this necessity does not lie, one of two things is necessary: either not to be troubled at all, but rather to delight in the Lord; or, if you cannot yet do this, to be troubled not about many things but, as the prophet says of himself, concerning yourself (Ps. 41:7).

5. Again I say this, lest anyone excuse himself through ignorance: you, brother, for whom nothing is involved in Noah’s task of constructing or governing the ark amid the floodwaters, must either be a man of desires, as Daniel was, or, with blessed Job, a man of sorrows and one who knows infirmity. Otherwise I fear that he who wishes to find you either warm through consideration of yourself and burning with the fire of charity, or cold through knowledge of him alone and extinguishing the devil’s fiery darts with the water of compunction, may vomit you from his mouth as lukewarm and provoking nausea [Col. 0424A].

But Martha herself too must be admonished that among stewards this is especially required: that a person be found faithful. And he will be faithful if he seeks not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ, so that his intention may be pure; and if he makes not his own will but the Lord’s, so that his action may be ordered. For there are those whose eye is not single, and they receive their reward. There are those who are carried along by the motions of their own minds, and everything they offer is defiled, because their own wills are found in them.

Come now with me to the nuptial song, and consider how the bridegroom, when he calls the bride, omits none of these three and adds nothing to them: “Arise,” he says, “make haste, my beloved, my beautiful one, my dove, and come” (Cant. 2:10). Is not she beloved who, intent on the Lord’s gains, faithfully lays down even her own life for him? For as often as she interrupts [elsewhere: “interposes”] her spiritual study for one of his least ones, so often she spiritually lays down her life for him [Col. 0424B]. Is not she beautiful who, beholding with unveiled face the glory of the Lord, is transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord? (2 Cor. 3:18). Is not she a dove who weeps and groans in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding places of the wall (Cant. 2:14), as though buried beneath a stone?

6. “A woman named Martha,” he says, “received him into her house.” It is certain, brothers, that this woman holds the place of the officials whom regard for fraternal charity has assigned to various ministries. Would that I myself might deserve to be found faithful among the stewards! For to whom does what the Lord says—“Martha, Martha, you are anxious”—seem more suitably applied than to prelates, provided that they preside worthily in their anxiety? Or who is troubled about many things except one upon whom rests all concern both for Mary in her repose and Lazarus in his penitence, and also for those to whom he distributes their burdens? [Col. 0424C]

See Martha anxious; see Martha troubled about many things. I speak of the Apostle, who, while admonishing prelates regarding care, himself bears the care of all the Churches. “Who is weak,” he says, “and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29). Let Martha, therefore, receive the Lord into her house, to whom the stewardship of the house has been entrusted. She is a mediatrix, that she may obtain salvation both for herself and for those subject to her; let her receive grace, as it is written: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness” [Col. 0424D] (Ps. 71:3). Let each of her other helpers receive him according to the character of his ministry: let them receive Christ, serve Christ, minister to him in his members—one in sick brothers, another in the poor, another in guests and strangers.

7. While these are thus anxious about much serving, let Mary see how she may be free, and see that the Lord is sweet. Let her see, I say, with what devoted mind and tranquil spirit she sits at Jesus’ feet, setting him always before her sight and receiving words from his mouth—he whose look is delightful and whose speech is sweet. For “grace is poured out upon his lips,” and he is beautiful in form above the sons of men, indeed even above all the glory of angels [Col. 0425A].

Rejoice and give thanks, Mary, who have chosen the best part. For blessed are the eyes that see what you see, and the ears that deserve to hear what you hear. Blessed indeed are you who perceive the veins of divine whispering in silence, in which it is surely good for a person to wait for the Lord. Be simple, not only without deceit and pretence, but also free from the multiplicity of occupations, so that you may have converse with him whose voice is sweet and whose face is beautiful. Beware of one thing: do not begin to abound in your own understanding and wish “to be wise above what is fitting”; lest perhaps, while pursuing light, you stumble into darkness, deceived by the noonday demon—a subject not for discussion at this time.

But where has Lazarus gone? “Where have you laid him?” I address the sisters who buried their brother by preaching and service, example and prayer. Where, then, have you placed him? He is hidden in a pit in the earth, he lies beneath a stone, he is not easily found. Therefore it will not be unsuitable to reserve a fourth sermon for the man dead four days, so that, following the Saviour’s example and hearing, “Behold, he whom you love is ill” [Col. 0425B] (John 11:3), we too may remain here on this day.

## SERMON IV. On Lazarus’s Four Days and the Virgin’s Praise

1. It is a time to speak for all flesh when the Mother of the incarnate Word is assumed into heaven; and mortal humanity ought not to cease from praise when, in the Virgin, human nature alone is exalted above immortal spirits. Yet devotion does not permit silence about her glory; barren thought cannot conceive anything worthy, nor can unlearned speech bring it forth. Thus the princes of the heavenly court themselves, considering so great a novelty, cry out not without wonder: “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights?” [Col. 0425C] (Cant. 8:5). It is as though they said more plainly: How great is she? Or whence, as she ascends from the wilderness, comes to her so great an abundance of delights?

For no delights equal to these are found even among us, whom the rushing of the river makes glad in the city of God, and who drink from the torrent of delight from the countenance of glory [elsewhere: “glory”]. Who is this who ascends, from beneath the sun—where there is nothing but labour, sorrow, and affliction of spirit—abounding in spiritual delights? Why should I not call delights the honour of virginity joined with the gift of fruitfulness, the distinction of humility, the dripping honeycomb of charity, the bowels of mercy, fullness of grace, and the prerogative of singular glory? Therefore, as the Queen of the world ascends from the wilderness, she becomes, even to the holy angels, as the Church sings, beautiful and sweet in her delights [Col. 0425D].

Yet let them cease to marvel at the delights of this wilderness, because “the Lord has given goodness, and our land has yielded its fruit” (Ps. 84:13). Why marvel that Mary rises from a desolate land abounding in delights? Rather let them marvel that poor Christ descends from the fullness of the heavenly kingdom. For it seems worthy of a far greater miracle that the Son of God should be made a little lower than the angels than that the Mother of God should be exalted above angels. His emptying became our fullness; his miseries are the delights of the world. Finally, “though he was rich, for our sake he became poor, that we might be made rich through his poverty” [Col. 0426A] (2 Cor. 8:9). And the ignominy of the cross became the glory of believers.

2. Yet our life hastens also to the tomb, to bring back from the tomb the man dead four days; and it seeks Lazarus—the Lazarus concerning whom, if your charity remembers well, a discourse is owed to you today—so that it may be sought and found by Lazarus. For “in this is charity: not as though we loved God, but because he first loved us.” Therefore act, Lord: seek him whom you love, that you may make him both a lover and a seeker. Seek where they have laid him, for he lies shut in, bound, burdened. He lies in the workhouse of conscience, held by the bonds of discipline, and pressed down and oppressed, as though by a stone laid upon him, by the weight of penitence [Col. 0426B]—especially because, for the moment, strong love as death and charity that endures all things are lacking. And in all these things he already stinks, Lord, for he has been dead four days.

I believe the minds of many already run ahead to understand whom I mean by Lazarus: undoubtedly, the one who has recently died through sin, “dug through the wall” in order to see “many abominations” (Ezek. 8:8–9), the evil things of his perverse and inscrutable heart; and who, according to another prophet, “entered into the rock,” hidden in a pit in the earth, from the face of the Lord’s wrath (Isa. 2:10).

3. But what is meant by, “Lord, he already stinks, for he has been dead four days”? Perhaps not everyone immediately understands this stench and these four days. I think the first day is that of fear, by whose shining upon our hearts we die to sin and are in some manner buried in our consciences. The second, unless I am mistaken, is passed in the labour of struggle. For at the beginning of conversion, the temptation of evil habit is accustomed to rise more fiercely, and the devil’s fiery darts can scarcely be extinguished [Col. 0426C]. The third seems likewise to be one of sorrow, while a person recalls his years in the bitterness of his soul, and labours less to avoid future things than he mourns and laments the past.

Do you wonder that I call these days? But such are the days owed to burial: days of cloud and darkness, days of mourning and bitterness. The day of shame follows, not unlike the other three, when the wretched soul is now covered in dreadful confusion, as it considers intensely what and how great its sins have been, and turns over in the eyes of the heart the foul images of its sins [Col. 0426D]. Such a mind conceals nothing, but judges, burdens, and exaggerates all things; a harsh judge toward itself, it spares itself nothing. This sharpening of pain is useful indeed, and such mercilessness worthy of mercy; it easily gains divine grace for itself, since the mind is zealous for him even against itself.

Nevertheless, Lazarus, come forth, lest you remain longer in so great a stench. Putrid flesh is near to corruption; and one who is overwhelmed by shame and wastes away is near to despair. Therefore, Lazarus, come forth. Deep calls to deep: the deep of light and mercy calls to the deep of misery and darkness. His goodness is greater than your iniquity; and where sin abounds, he makes grace superabound. “Lazarus,” he says, “come forth” [Col. 0427A] (John 11:39, 43). It is as though he said more plainly: How long will the darkness of your conscience hold you? How long will you be pierced with compunction in your bed, heavy of heart? Come forth; step out; breathe in the light of my mercies. For this is what you read in the prophet: “I will bridle your mouth with my praise, lest you perish” (Isa. 48:9). Another prophet speaks even more plainly of himself: “My soul was troubled within me; therefore I remember you in prayer” (Ps. 41:7).

4. But what is meant by his saying, “Take away the stone,” and a little later, “Loose him”? (John 11:39, 44). Will he cease to do penance after the visitation of consoling grace because the kingdom of heaven has drawn near? Or will he cast aside discipline, lest perhaps the Lord become angry and he perish from the righteous way? Far be it! Let the stone be removed, but let penitence remain—not now pressing and burdening him, but rather strengthening and confirming a living and vigorous mind; a mind whose food is to do the Lord’s will, something it did not previously know [Col. 0427B]. Thus discipline no longer binds the free person, according to the saying, “The law is not laid down for the just” (1 Tim. 1:9); rather, it governs the willing person and directs him in the way of peace.

Concerning this raising of Lazarus the prophet sings more plainly: “You will not abandon my soul in hell”; for, as I remember having said on the second day of this festival, a guilty conscience is a kind of hell and prison of the soul. “Nor will you give your holy one”—not his own holy one, but yours, certainly, whom you yourself sanctify—“to see corruption.” For the man dead four days, who had already begun to stink, was near to corruption [Col. 0427C]. He was near to being wholly dissolved and, coming into the depth of evils, to despising them as an impious man. But, forestalled by the voice of power and given life by it, he gives thanks and says: “You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with joy through your countenance” (Ps. 15:10–11). For you summoned me to its contemplation and brought my soul up from hell, while my spirit was distressed within me as it looked upon the utterly abominable face of its own conscience.

“He cried,” it says, “with a loud voice: ‘Lazarus, come forth’”—with a loud voice, surely, loud not so much in clamorous sound as magnificent in pity and power.

5. But where have we gone? Were we not above following the Virgin as she went beyond the heavens? And behold, with Lazarus we have descended into the abyss. The discourse runs swiftly down from the splendour of virtue to the stench of the man dead four days. Why is this, except because we were borne by our own weight and drawn by matter so much more abundant because it was more familiar? I confess my lack of skill; I do not conceal my own faint-heartedness. There is indeed nothing that delights me more, but neither is there anything that frightens me more, than to speak of the glory of the Virgin Mother [Col. 0427D].

For, not to mention for the moment the ineffable privilege of her merits and her altogether singular prerogative, all fittingly embrace, honour, and receive her with such devoted affection, and all eagerly desire, insofar as they can, to speak of her. Yet whatever is said of the unspeakable, simply because it can be said, is less pleasing, less welcome, less acceptable. Why should whatever the human mind can comprehend concerning incomprehensible glory not have less savour? If I praise in her virginity, many virgins after her seem to present themselves to me. If I preach humility, perhaps a few will be found who, taught by her Son, became meek and humble of heart [Col. 0428A] (Matt. 11:29). If I wish to magnify the multitude of her mercies, there are certain merciful men, and women also.

There is one thing in which she seems neither to have had an equal before her nor a successor after her: she possesses a mother’s joys together with the honour of virginity. “Mary has chosen for herself the best part” (Luke 10:42). The best indeed: for marital fruitfulness is good, virginal chastity better, but virginal fruitfulness—or fruitful virginity—is altogether best. This is Mary’s privilege; it shall not be given to another, because it shall not be taken away from her. It is singular, and immediately proves ineffable: no one can attain it, and therefore no one can express it.

What if you add this too: whose mother she is? What tongue, even an angelic one, could extol in worthy praises the Virgin Mother—the mother not of merely anyone, but of God? A double novelty, a double prerogative, a double miracle, yet one altogether worthy and most fitting. For neither did any other son befit a virgin, nor any other birth befit God [Col. 0428B].

6. Yet if you attend carefully, you will find not only this but also Mary’s other virtues to be altogether singular, although they seemed common. What angelic purity would dare compare itself with that virginity which was worthy to become the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit and the dwelling of the Son of God? If we estimate the worth of things by their rarity, she who first proposed on earth to live an angelic life stands above all. “How shall this be,” she says, “since I know not a man?” An immovable purpose of virginity, which did not waver in the least even when an angel promised her a son. “How shall this be?” Not, surely, in the manner in which it usually occurs in others. “I know no man at all,” neither for desire of a son nor for hope of offspring [Col. 0428C].

7. But how great and precious was the virtue of humility joined with so great purity, so great innocence, a conscience utterly without sin—indeed, with so great a fullness of grace! Whence came your humility, and such humility, O blessed one? Truly you were worthy for the Lord to look upon you, worthy for the King to desire your beauty, worthy to draw him from the eternal repose of the Father’s bosom by your most sweet fragrance. Observe how plainly the song of our Virgin and the nuptial song harmonize with one another; for her womb was the bridegroom’s chamber.

Hear Mary in the Gospel: “He has looked,” she says, “upon the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:34, 48). Hear the same woman in the bridal song: “While the king was at his repose, my nard gave forth its fragrance” [Col. 0428D] (Cant. 1:11). Nard is indeed a lowly herb and cleanses the breast, so that it is clear that humility is signified by the name of nard: its fragrance and beauty found favour with God.

8. Let anyone be silent about your mercy, blessed Virgin, if there is anyone who recalls that, when you were invoked in his necessities, you failed him. We indeed, your little servants, rejoice with you in your other virtues; but in this one we rejoice rather for ourselves. We praise your virginity, we admire your humility; but to the wretched mercy tastes sweeter; we embrace mercy more dearly, remember it more often, and invoke it more frequently. For this is what obtained the restoration of the whole world and secured the salvation of all. For it is certain that she to whom it was said, “Do not fear, Mary; you have found grace” (Luke 1:30), was solicitous for the entire human race—namely, the grace that you sought.

Who, then, O blessed one, can trace the length and breadth, the height and depth of your mercy? For its length assists all who invoke it unto the last day. Its breadth fills the earth, so that the whole earth also is full of your mercy. [Col. 0429B] Thus its height found restoration for the heavenly city, and its depth obtained redemption for those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. For through you heaven has been filled, hell emptied, and the fallen places of [Col. 0430A] the heavenly Jerusalem restored; through you lost life has been given to the wretched who awaited it. Thus your most powerful and most merciful love abounds both in the affection of compassion and in the effect of assistance, equally rich in both.

9. Therefore let our thirsty soul hasten to this fountain; let all our misery flee, with every solicitude, to this abundance of mercy. Behold, with such prayers as we could, we have escorted you as you ascended to your Son and have followed you, at least from afar, blessed Virgin. Henceforth let it be the work of your loving kindness to make known to the world the grace which you have found with God: by your holy prayers obtain pardon for the guilty, healing for the sick, strength for the faint-hearted, consolation for the afflicted, assistance and deliverance for those in peril. On this day also of solemnity and joy, may Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord—who is God above all, blessed for ever—through you, merciful Queen, bestow the gifts of his grace upon his servants who invoke with praise the most sweet name of Mary. Amen.

[Col. 0429]

## SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

**Sermon on the twelve prerogatives of the Blessed Virgin Mary, from the words of Revelation 12:1:** “A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars.”

[Col. 0429C]

1. Most grievously indeed, beloved, one man and one woman injured us; but, thanks be to God, by one man nevertheless and one woman all things are restored—and not without a great increase of graces. For the gift is not as the offence; rather, the greatness of the benefit exceeds the estimate of the loss. Thus the most wise and merciful craftsman did not break what had been shaken, but restored it in a wholly more useful fashion: namely, that he might form for us a new Adam from the old, and transform Eve into Mary.

Indeed Christ could have sufficed, since even now all our sufficiency is from him; but it was not good for us that man should be alone. It was more fitting that both sexes should be present in our restoration, since neither had been absent from their corruption. Christ Jesus, the man who is the faithful and all-powerful mediator between God and men, is indeed such a mediator; but in him human beings stand in awe of the divine majesty. His humanity seems swallowed up in divinity—not because its substance has been changed, but because the affections are deified. Mercy alone is not sung of him; judgment is sung together with it (Psalm 100:1). For although he learned compassion from the things he suffered, that he might become merciful, he nevertheless possesses judicial authority. For “our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24; Heb. 12:29). Why should not the sinner fear to approach, lest, as wax melts before fire, so he himself perish before the face of God?

2. Therefore even that woman, blessed among women, will not appear idle in this reconciliation: her place will certainly be found in it. For there is need of a mediatrix to this Mediator, and none is more useful to us than Mary. Eve was an exceedingly cruel mediatrix, through whom the ancient serpent poured its deadly venom even into the man himself; but Mary is faithful, who administered the antidote of salvation [Col. 0430C] to men and women alike. The former was the minister of seduction; this one, of propitiation. The former suggested transgression; this one brought in redemption.

Why should human frailty tremble to approach Mary? There is nothing harsh in her, nothing dreadful: she is wholly gentle, offering milk and wool to all. Review more carefully the whole sequence of the Gospel narrative; and if you encounter in Mary anything reproachful, anything severe, or indeed any sign even of slight indignation, then thereafter regard her with suspicion and fear to approach her. But if, as is truly the case, you find that everything concerning her is instead full of loving kindness and grace, full of gentleness and mercy, then give thanks to him who in his most gracious compassion has provided you with such a mediatrix, in whom nothing can be suspect. For she has become all things to all; in her most abundant charity she has made herself debtor to the wise and the foolish alike. She opens the bosom of mercy to all, that all may receive from her fullness: the captive redemption, the sick healing, the sorrowful consolation, the sinner pardon, the righteous grace, the angel joy; finally, the whole Trinity glory, and the person of the Son the substance of human flesh—so that there is no one who hides himself from her warmth.

3. Do you suppose that she is the woman clothed with the sun? Granted that the sequence of the prophetic vision itself shows that this is to be understood of the present Church; yet it seems by no means unfitting that it should be attributed to Mary. She, indeed, is the one who has put on, as it were, another sun. For as he rises indiscriminately upon the good and the evil, so she too does not examine past merits, but shows herself ready to be entreated by all, most merciful toward all, and compassionates the necessities of all with a certain most ample [Col. 0431A] affection.

For every defect is beneath her; and whatever there is of frailty or corruption she surpasses and transcends, by a certain most excellent loftiness, beyond all other creatures, so that the moon is deservedly said to be beneath her feet. Otherwise we should seem to have said nothing great in declaring that this moon is beneath her feet, whereas it is impious to doubt that she has been exalted above all the choirs of angels, even above cherubim and seraphim. Now the moon is accustomed to signify not only the defect of corruption but also folly of mind, and sometimes the Church of this present age: the former because of its changeability, the latter because of the brightness received from another. Both moons, if I may so speak, are fittingly placed beneath Mary’s feet, though in different ways; for “the fool changes like the moon, but the wise man remains like the sun” (Ecclus. 27:12).

For in the sun there are both heat and stable brightness; in the moon brightness alone, and that wholly mutable and uncertain, never remaining in the same state. Mary, therefore, is rightly said to be clothed with the sun, since she penetrated the most profound abyss of divine wisdom beyond what can be believed; so that, as far as the condition of a creature permits without personal union, she seems immersed in that inaccessible light. By that fire the prophet’s lips are purified (Isa. 6:7); by that fire the seraphim are kindled. But Mary deserved something far different: not merely to be touched, as it were, in passing, but rather to be covered on every side, surrounded, and enclosed as though by the very fire itself. Most radiant indeed, yet also most warm, is the garment of [Col. 0431C] this woman: all things in her are known to be so excellently illumined that one may suspect in her nothing—not merely dark, but even somewhat shadowy or less bright; nor anything lukewarm, or not most fervent.

4. Every kind of folly, then, is far beneath her feet, so that she is wholly removed from the number of foolish women and from the company of foolish virgins. Indeed, that one fool—the prince of all folly—who, truly changed like the moon, lost wisdom in his splendor, lies trampled and crushed beneath Mary’s feet and endures miserable servitude. She is assuredly the woman once promised by God, who would crush with the foot of her power the head of the ancient serpent; though it lay in wait for her heel with many stratagems (Gen. 3:15), it did so in vain.

She alone crushed every heretical perversity.
