One dogmatized that Christ did not derive from the substance of her flesh; another hissed that she had not borne an infant but had found one; another blasphemed that after childbirth she had known a man; another, refusing to hear her called Mother of God, most impiously assailed that great name *Theotokos*, “God-bearer.” But the plotters were crushed, the usurpers trampled down, the detractors refuted; and all generations call her blessed. Finally, the dragon immediately lay in wait through Herod for the woman giving birth, that he might receive and devour her newborn Son, because there was enmity between the seed of the woman and the dragon.

5. But if by the name of the moon the Church is thought rather to be meant—because it does not shine from itself [Col. 0432A] but from him who says, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5)—then you have the mediatrix whom we commended to you a little earlier, clearly portrayed: “A woman,” he says, “clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet.” Let us embrace Mary’s footsteps, my brothers, and with most devout supplication cast ourselves before those blessed feet. Let us hold her and not let her go until she blesses us, for she is powerful.

For the fleece stands between the dew and the threshing-floor; the woman between the sun and the moon; Mary between Christ and the Church. But perhaps you wonder, not so much at the fleece covered with dew, as at the woman clothed with the sun. Great indeed is the intimacy, but altogether marvelous is the nearness, of sun and woman. How can so fragile a nature subsist in such vehement heat? You rightly wonder, holy Moses, and desire to look more closely. Yet remove the sandals from your feet and lay aside the wrappings of carnal thoughts, if you desire to approach. “I will go,” he says, “and see this great vision” (Exod. 3:3). Great indeed is the vision: a bush burning without being consumed; a great sign: the woman remaining unharmed while clothed with the sun. It is not in the nature of a bush, when covered on every side with flames, nevertheless to remain unburned; nor is it in a woman’s power to endure the sun’s garment. It is not the power of human beings, nor even of angels: something higher is necessary. “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you.” And as if she had replied, “Because God is spirit, and our God is a consuming fire,” he says: “The power—not mine, not yours, but of the Most High—will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). Therefore it is no wonder that under such a shadow such a garment is sustained.

6. “A woman,” he says, “clothed with the sun.” Truly, “clothed with light as with a garment.” Perhaps the carnal person does not grasp this: it is spiritual and seems folly to him. It did not so seem to the Apostle, who said, “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:14). How familiar you became to him, Lady! How near—indeed, how inwardly united—you deserved to become; what grace you found with him! He remains in you, and you in him; you clothe him, and you are clothed by him. You clothe him with the substance of flesh, and he clothes you with the glory of his majesty. You clothe the sun with a cloud, and are yourself clothed with the sun.

For the Lord made something new upon the earth: “a woman shall encompass a man” [Col. 0432D] (Jer. 31:22)—and none other than Christ, of whom it is said, “Behold the man: Rising is his name” (Zech. 6:12). He made something new also in heaven: a woman appeared clothed with the sun. Finally, she crowned him, and in return deserved to be crowned by him. “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Song 3:11). But this elsewhere. Meanwhile, rather go in and see the Queen in the diadem with which her Son crowned her.

7. “Upon her head,” he says, “a crown of twelve stars.” A head which shines far more brightly even than the stars is surely worthy to be crowned with stars, and rather adorns them than is adorned by them. Why should not the stars crown her whom the sun clothes? “As on spring days, rose blossoms and lilies of the valleys surrounded her” (Ecclus. 50:8). Surely the bridegroom’s left hand is beneath her head, and now his right hand embraces her (Song 2:6). Who could appraise those jewels? Who could name the stars of which Mary’s royal diadem is composed? It exceeds human capacity to explain the meaning of this crown or to describe its arrangement.

Yet, in proportion to our smallness, abstaining from a perilous scrutiny of mysteries, perhaps we may not unfittingly understand these twelve stars as twelve prerogatives of graces [variant: “may be able to understand”] with which Mary is singularly adorned. For in Mary one finds prerogatives of heaven, prerogatives of flesh, and prerogatives of heart; and if this threefold division is multiplied by four, perhaps we have the twelve stars through which the diadem of our Queen shines before all others. To me there shines a singular radiance: first, in Mary’s birth; second, in the angelic salutation; third, in the coming of the Spirit; fourth, in the ineffable conception of the Son of God. Likewise, in these things too a truly starry splendor shines forth: that she was foremost among virgins; fruitful without corruption; pregnant without burden; a mother in childbirth without [Col. 0433B] pain. No less does a special brightness gleam in Mary through the gentleness of modesty, the devotion of humility, the magnanimity of faith, and the martyrdom of her heart. It will be your diligent task to examine each of these more carefully. We, meanwhile, shall seem to have done enough if we can briefly indicate them.

8. What, then, shines with a starry brightness in Mary’s birth? Surely this: that she sprang from kings; that she was of Abraham’s seed; that she was noble from David’s line. If this seems too little, add that she is known to have been divinely granted to that lineage by a singular privilege of holiness; that it was promised from heaven long beforehand to those same fathers; foreshadowed by mystical miracles; and foretold by prophetic oracles. For the priestly rod, when it flowered without a root (Num. 17:8), foreshadowed her; Gideon’s fleece, when it was wet amid a dry threshing-floor (Judg. 6:37–38), foreshadowed her; and the eastern gate in Ezekiel’s vision, which never opened for anyone (Ezek. 44:1–2), foreshadowed her.

Finally, Isaiah above all the others now promised that a rod would arise from the root of Jesse (Isa. 11:1), now more plainly that a virgin would give birth. This great sign is rightly written to have appeared in heaven, since it is known to have been promised from heaven so long before. The Lord says, “He himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive” (Isa. 7:14). He indeed gave a great sign, because he himself who gave it is great. Whose sight is not powerfully dazzled by the brilliance of this prerogative?

Again, in the fact that she was greeted by the archangel with such reverence and service that even then she seemed to be seen exalted on a royal throne above all orders of the heavenly legions—and he who had hitherto been calmly adored by men seemed almost about to adore a woman—the most excellent merit and singular grace of our Virgin are commended to us.

9. Likewise, that new manner of conception shines forth: unlike all other women, she conceived not in iniquity but, the Holy Spirit coming upon her, alone and from sanctification alone. For the fact that she bore the true God and Son of God, so that from Mary himself, Son alike of God and of man, should come forth one and the same God and man—this is an abyss of light. I could scarcely say that even the angelic eye is not dazzled by the force of this splendor.

Furthermore, the virginity of her body and her purpose of virginity are clearly illuminated, especially the novelty of that very purpose: namely, that in the freedom of the spirit, transcending the decrees of the Mosaic law, she vowed to God the unimpaired holiness of body and spirit together. The inviolable foundation of this purpose is demonstrated by her reply with such constancy to the angel promising a son: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” [Col. 0434B] (Luke 1:34).

Perhaps she was first troubled at his words and considered what sort of greeting this might be because she had heard herself called blessed among women, whereas she had always desired to be blessed among virgins. From that point she considered what sort of greeting [variant: “blessing”] it might be, because it already seemed suspicious. But when, in the promise of a son, the danger to virginity appeared manifest, she could no longer conceal herself from saying, “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?”

She therefore deservedly received that blessing and did not lose this one: so that virginity is made far more glorious by fruitfulness, and fruitfulness by virginity, and these two stars seem to illuminate one another with reciprocal rays. For it is great to be a virgin, but to be a virgin mother is in every respect much greater. Likewise, she alone did not experience that most troublesome weariness which all other pregnant women are known to suffer, because she alone conceived without lustful pleasure. Thus, at the very beginning of her conception, when other women are especially more grievously afflicted, Mary ascended the hill country in complete joy to minister to Elizabeth. She also went up to Bethlehem when childbirth was already imminent, carrying that most precious deposit, carrying a light burden, carrying him by whom she herself was carried.

Likewise, how radiant is her childbirth: with a new exultation she brought forth a new offspring, alone among women free from the common curse and pain of those who give birth. If we assess the value of things by their rarity, nothing rarer than these can be found. In all these things she appears neither to have had a predecessor like herself nor to have a successor. From them, if we contemplate them faithfully, we undoubtedly conceive admiration, veneration, devotion, and consolation.

10. But those things which remain still require imitation. It is not ours to be so variously and in so many ways divinely promised before our birth, or announced from heaven; nor are we to be honored by the archangel Gabriel with the services of so novel a greeting. The remaining two communicate still less to us: she keeps her secret to herself. For she alone is the one of whom it is said, “That which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20); she alone is the one to whom it is said, “That holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Virgins are offered to the King [Col. 0435A] after her, for she alone claims the first place. Still more, she alone conceived without corruption, bore without burden, and gave birth to a son without pain.

Therefore none of these things is required of us; yet surely something is required. For if we lack even modest gentleness, humility of heart, magnanimity of faith, or compassion of mind, will the singularity of her gifts excuse our negligence? A blush upon the face of a modest person is a most pleasing jewel in a diadem, a star shining upon the head. Or does anyone think that she who was full of grace lacked this grace? Mary was modest: we prove it from the Gospel. Where does she ever appear talkative or presumptuous? “She stood outside, seeking to speak with her Son” (Matt. 12:46); nor did she, by maternal authority, interrupt his discourse or force her way into the dwelling where the Son was speaking.

Indeed, in the whole text of the four Gospels, if we remember correctly, Mary is heard speaking only four times. First to the angel, but only after he had addressed her once and again; second, to Elizabeth, when the voice of her greeting caused John to leap in the womb, and, although Elizabeth magnified Mary, she took care rather to magnify the Lord (Luke 1:34–55); third, to her Son, when he was already twelve years old, saying that she and his father had sought him in sorrow (Luke 2:48); fourth, at the wedding, to her Son and the servants (John 2:3, 5).

And that speech was a very certain indication of her inborn gentleness and virginal modesty. Considering the shame of others as her own, she could not endure—could not conceal—the lack of wine. When she was rebuked by her Son, as one gentle and humble of heart she neither answered him nor lost hope, but instructed the servants to do what he should tell them.

11. Do we not read that the shepherds came from the beginning and found Mary first of all? “They found,” says the Evangelist, “Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in a manger” (Luke 2:16). Likewise the Magi too, if you recall, found the child not without Mary his mother (Matt. 2:11). And when she brought into the temple of the Lord the Lord of the temple, she heard much indeed from Simeon both concerning him and concerning herself (Luke 2:34–35): slow to speak, quick to listen. “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them [Col. 0435D] in her heart” (Luke 19:51); yet in all these things you will not find that she uttered any word whatever even about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

Woe to us, who have breath in our nostrils! Woe to those who pour forth their whole spirit, who, in the comic poet’s phrase, “being full of cracks, flow out everywhere” (Terence, *Eunuchus*, I.ii.25). Mary heard her Son so often, not only speaking in parables to the crowds, but also privately revealing to the disciples the mysteries of the kingdom of God; she saw him working miracles; then she saw him hanging on the cross, saw him breathe his last, saw him rise again, and saw him ascend. Yet in all these things, how often is the voice of the most modest virgin, how often the voice of the most chaste turtledove, recorded as having been heard?

Finally, you read in the Acts of the Apostles that, after returning from the Mount of Olives, they persevered unanimously in prayer. Who? If Mary was present, let her be named first, she who is above all others both by the prerogative of her Son and by the privilege of her own holiness. “Peter and Andrew,” it says, “James and John,” and the others who follow. “All these persevered unanimously with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus.” Did she so present herself as the last even among the women that she was placed last of all? Truly the disciples were still carnal, to whom the Spirit had not yet been given because Jesus had not yet been glorified (John 7:39), when contention arose among them concerning precedence (Luke 22:24); whereas Mary, the greater she was, humbled herself not only among all but before all.

She deservedly became last and first, because, though first of all, she made herself last. She deservedly became mistress of all, because she presented herself as the servant of all. Finally, she deservedly was exalted above the angels, because with ineffable gentleness she lowered herself even beneath widows and penitents, beneath her from whom seven demons had been cast out. I beseech you, little children, emulate this virtue if you love Mary; if you strive to please her, emulate her modesty. For nothing is so fitting for a human being, nothing so suitable for a Christian, and especially nothing so becomes a monk.

12. And from this very gentleness the virtue of humility shines forth quite clearly in the Virgin. Humility and gentleness are surely milk-sisters, more closely joined in him who said, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). For as pride is the mother of presumption, so true gentleness proceeds only from true humility. Yet humility is commended not only in Mary’s silence; it resounds more clearly in her speech.

She had heard, “That holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God”; and she replied nothing except that she was his handmaid. Then she came to Elizabeth, and at once the Virgin’s singular glory was revealed to Elizabeth by the Spirit. Elizabeth marveled at the person who had come, saying, “Whence is this to me, that the Mother of my Lord should come to me?” She praised also the voice of her greeting, adding: “When the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb”; and she pronounced the believer’s faith blessed: “Blessed,” she said, “is she who believed, for the things spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled in you.”

Great praises indeed; but her devout humility allowed herself to retain nothing, and instead referred everything back to him whose benefits in her were being praised. “You magnify,” she says, “the Mother of the Lord; but my soul magnifies the Lord. You report that, at my voice, your son leaped for joy; but my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior; and he also, like the friend of the bridegroom, rejoices with joy at the bridegroom’s voice. You say that she who believed is blessed; but the cause of faith and blessedness is the regard of heavenly loving kindness, so that from this all generations may rather call me blessed” (Luke 1:35–48), because God looked upon his humble and lowly handmaid.

13. Yet do we suppose, brothers, that holy Elizabeth erred in this, when she was certainly speaking through the Spirit? Far be it! Blessed indeed is she upon whom God looked, and blessed is she who believed. For this was a great fruit of the divine regard. By the ineffable workmanship of the Spirit who came upon her, such magnanimity entered the inner chamber of the virgin heart together with such humility that, as we said before of integrity and fruitfulness, these too are nevertheless made brighter stars by their mutual regard: namely, that neither does such humility lessen magnanimity, nor such magnanimity lessen humility. Rather, though she was so humble in her own estimation, she was nevertheless magnanimous in believing the promise: she who regarded herself as nothing but a lowly handmaid did not in the least doubt that she had been chosen for this incomprehensible mystery, this wonderful exchange, this unsearchable sacrament, and believed that she would soon become the true mother of God and man.

For the prerogative of divine grace accomplishes this in the hearts of the elect: it ensures that humility does not make them faint-hearted, nor magnanimity arrogant. Rather, these cooperate, so that not only does no pride enter through magnanimity, but humility is especially advanced through it: so that people are found more reverent and not ungrateful to the giver of gifts. Conversely, no faint-heartedness slips in through the occasion of humility; rather, the less each person is accustomed to presume upon himself even in small things, the more he trusts in divine power even in the greatest matters.

14. The Virgin’s martyrdom—which, if you remember, we named the twelfth among the stars of her diadem—is commended both in Simeon’s prophecy and in the history of the Lord’s Passion itself. “This child,” says the holy old man concerning the infant Jesus, “is set for a sign that shall be contradicted”; and “a sword shall pierce your own soul also”—and he said this to Mary (Luke 2:34–35). Truly a sword pierced your soul, O blessed Mother. Otherwise, it could not pierce your Son’s flesh except by passing through it.

And indeed, after that Jesus of yours—of all men, certainly, but especially yours—had yielded up his spirit, the cruel lance did not touch his soul, though it opened his side (spared not even the dead, whom it could not harm); it pierced your soul, certainly. For his soul was no longer there; but yours could not be torn away from there. The force of grief therefore pierced [Col. 0438A] your soul, so that we not undeservedly proclaim you more than a martyr, since in you the effect of compassion exceeded the experience of bodily suffering.

15. Was not that saying more than a sword to you, truly piercing the soul and reaching even to the division of soul and spirit: “Woman, behold your son” (John 19:26)? O exchange! John is given to you in place of Jesus; the servant for the Lord, the disciple for the master, the son of Zebedee for the Son of God, a mere human being for the true God. How could this hearing fail to pierce your most loving soul, when its mere remembrance rends even our hearts, though they be stone or iron?

Do not wonder, brothers, that Mary is said to have been a martyr in soul. Let him wonder who does not remember hearing Paul list among the greatest crimes of the Gentiles that they were “without natural affection” (Rom. 1:31). This was far from Mary’s heart; let it be far also from the hearts of her servants. But perhaps someone may say: Did she not know beforehand that he would die? Certainly. Did she not hope confidently that he would rise again immediately? Certainly. Did she nevertheless grieve intensely that he had been crucified? Most intensely. Otherwise, who are you, brother, or whence comes this wisdom of yours, that you should wonder more that Mary sympathized than that Mary’s Son suffered? He could die in body; could she not die with him in heart? That was done by the love than which no one had greater; this also was done by a love after which there was none other like it.

And now the moon lying prostrate at your feet, Mother of Mercy—that is, the Church [Note: [Col. 0437D] That is, the Church. See above, sections 3 and 5.]—addresses you, established as its mediatrix with the Sun of righteousness, with devout supplications through the affection of your most sincere heart: that in your light it may see light, and through your intercession may deserve the grace of the sun, who truly loved you above all and adorned you, clothing you with a robe of glory and placing a crown of beauty upon your head. You are full of graces, full of heavenly dew, leaning upon your beloved, abounding in delights. Feed your poor today, Lady; let even the little dogs eat of the crumbs; and grant drink from your overflowing jar not only to Abraham’s servant but also to the camels (Gen. 24:15–20), because you are truly the maiden chosen beforehand and prepared for the Son of the Most High, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0437]

## ON THE NATIVITY OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY: SERMON ON THE AQUEDUCT

[Note: [Col. 0438] This note appears at the foot of columns 437 and 438, but the callout number has not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0437D] On this feast, see Letters 86, 152, 174, and 410. Likewise, concerning the Octaves of the same feast, read Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, Book IV, Letter 41, to Ernulf, Prior of Canterbury.]

[Col. 0437D]

1. Heaven embraces the presence of the fruitful Virgin; earth venerates her memory. Thus there is there the possession of every good, and here its recollection; there satiety, here a slight tasting of firstfruits; there the reality, and here the name. “Lord,” he says, “your name is for ever, and your memorial from generation to generation” [Col. 0438D] (Psalm 101:13). “Generation and generation” belongs, certainly, not to angels but to human beings. Do you wish to know that her name and memorial are among us, while her presence is on high? “Thus shall you pray,” he says: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matt. 6:9).

A faithful prayer, whose very opening reminds us both of divine adoption and of earthly pilgrimage: so that, knowing that as long as we are not in heaven we are pilgrims from the Lord, we may groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption as sons—namely, the presence of the Father. Therefore the prophet speaks pointedly also of Christ, saying: “Christ the Lord, the breath before our face; in his shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lam. 4:20). For among the heavenly blessednesses life is lived not in shadow but rather in splendor. “In the splendors of the saints, from the womb before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109:3). Yet this is the Father’s work.

2. But the Mother did not bear that same one in splendor, but in shadow—though only in the shadow with which the Most High overshadowed her. Therefore the Church sings deservedly—not that Church of saints which is in the heights and in splendor, but that which meanwhile journeys upon earth—“Under his shadow whom I desired I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2:3). For she had asked that the noonday light, where the bridegroom feeds his flock, be shown to her; but she was checked, and instead of fullness of light received shadow, instead of satiety a taste for the present.

Finally, she does not say, “Under his shadow which I desired,” but, “Under his shadow whom I desired I sat.” For she had not sought his shadow, but indeed the noonday itself, full light from full light. “And his fruit,” she says, “is sweet to my throat”—as though she said, “to my taste.” “How long will you not spare me, nor let me alone until I swallow my spittle?” How long does that saying remain: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” [Col. 0439C] (Ps. 33:9)? And indeed he is pleasant to the taste and sweet to the throat, so that the bride deservedly burst forth even over this into a voice of thanksgiving and praise.

3. But when will it be said: “Eat, friends, and drink; and be intoxicated, dearest ones” (Song 5:1)? “Let the righteous feast,” says the Prophet, “but in the presence of God” (Ps. 67:4)—certainly not in shadow. And of himself he says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15). The Lord likewise said to the apostles: “You are those who have remained with me in my trials; and I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table” (Luke 22:28–30). But where? “In my kingdom,” he says. Blessed indeed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God.

Therefore may your name be hallowed, [Col. 0439D] Lord: by it you are, meanwhile and in whatever measure, within us, dwelling through faith in our hearts, because your name has already been invoked over us. May your kingdom come. Let that which is perfect come, indeed, and let that which is partial be done away with. “You have your fruit,” says the Apostle, “unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6:22). Eternal life is an unfailing fountain, watering the whole surface of paradise. Nor does it merely water, but it gives intoxication: “a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing impetuously from Lebanon”; and “the rush of the river makes glad the city of God.” But what is the fountain of life, except Christ the Lord? “When Christ, your life, shall appear,” he says, “then you also shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4). Truly, Fullness itself emptied itself, that it might become for us righteousness, [Col. 0440A] sanctification, and remission; not yet appearing as life, or glory, or blessedness. The fountain has been led down even to us; “the waters have been distributed in the streets,” though “no stranger drinks from them” (Prov. 5:16–17). That heavenly vein has descended through an aqueduct, not displaying the abundance of the fountain, but pouring drops of grace into our parched hearts—more to some, less to others. The aqueduct is indeed full, so that others may receive from its fullness, but not the Fullness itself.

4. You have already perceived, unless I am mistaken, what aqueduct I mean: the one which, receiving from the Father’s heart the fullness of that very fountain, brought it forth for us—not as it is in itself, but at least as we were able to receive it. For you know to whom it was said: “Hail, full of grace.” Or should we wonder that there could be found the source from which such a great and such a mighty aqueduct might be made—one whose summit, [Col. 0440B] truly like that ladder seen by the patriarch Jacob, would touch heaven (Gen. 28:12), indeed would transcend the heavens, and could reach that most living fountain of the waters above the heavens?

Solomon too wondered, and, like one in despair, said: “Who shall find a valiant woman?” (Prov. 31:10). Doubtless for this reason the streams of grace were lacking to the human race for so long a time: the aqueduct of which we speak, so desirable, had not yet intervened. Nor will you wonder that she was awaited so long if you remember how many years Noah, a righteous man, labored in building the ark, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved, and that only for a brief time.

5. But how did this our aqueduct reach that fountain [Col. 0440C] so sublime? How do you suppose, unless by the force of desire, by the fervor of devotion, by the purity of prayer? As it is written: “The prayer of the righteous penetrates the heavens” (Ecclus. 35:21). And who is righteous, if not righteous Mary, from whom the Sun of righteousness has arisen for us? How, then, did she reach inaccessible Majesty unless by knocking, asking, and seeking? Finally, she found what she sought, she to whom it was said: “You have found grace with God” (Luke 1:30).

What? Is she full of grace, and does she still find grace? She is indeed worthy to find what she seeks, whose own fullness does not suffice, and who cannot be content with her own good; rather, as it is written, “He who drinks me shall still thirst” (Ecclus. 24:29), she asks for an overflowing abundance for the salvation [Col. 0440D] of all. “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “shall come upon you” (Luke 1:35), and that precious balm shall flow into you with such abundance and fullness that it will flow forth most copiously all around.

So it is: now we feel it; now our faces are made glad with oil. Now we cry out: “Your name is oil poured forth, and your memorial is from generation to generation.” Yet this is not in vain: although the oil is poured out, it is not lost. For this reason the young maidens—that is, little souls—love the bridegroom (Song 1:2), and not a little; and the ointment descending from the head has been received not only by the beard, but even by the hem of the garment itself.

6. Consider, O man, the counsel of God; recognize the counsel of wisdom, the counsel of mercy. When he was about to water the threshing-floor [Col. 0441A] with heavenly dew, he first drenched the whole fleece (Judg. 6:37–40); when he was about to redeem the human race, he placed the entire price in Mary. Why did he do this? Perhaps so that Eve might be excused through her daughter, and the complaint of the man against the woman might thereafter be silenced. Do not say any longer, O Adam: “The woman whom you gave me gave me from the forbidden tree” (Gen. 3:12); say rather: “The woman whom you gave me has fed me with blessed fruit.”

This is indeed a most merciful counsel; but perhaps another meaning lies hidden, and this is not the whole of it. It is true, but it is too little, I think, for your desires. There is sweetness in the milk; perhaps, if we press more strongly, the richness of butter will be drawn out. Look, then, more deeply: with what an affection of devotion he wished her to be honored by us, he who placed in Mary the fullness of every good; so that, consequently, whatever hope, [Col. 0441B] grace, or salvation there is in us, we may know it overflows from her who “comes up abounding in delights.” She is plainly a garden of delights, upon which not only did that divine south wind breathe as it came, but through which it blew as it descended, so that her spices—that is, the charisms of graces—might flow and overflow on every side.

Take away this solar body which illumines the world: where is the day? Take away Mary, this star of the sea—of the great and spacious sea, certainly—and what remains but enveloping darkness, the shadow of death, and densest gloom?

7. Therefore let us venerate this Mary with all the marrow of our hearts, with every affection of our inmost being, and with all our vows; for such is the will of him who willed that we should have everything through Mary. This, I say, is his will, but it is for our sake. For in all things and through [Col. 0441C] all things providing for the wretched, he comforts our trembling, arouses faith, strengthens hope, drives away distrust, and raises faintheartedness.

You were afraid to approach the Father: terrified by hearing of him alone, you fled to the leaves; he gave you Jesus as mediator. What would such a Son not obtain from such a Father? He will surely be heard because of his reverence; for the Father loves the Son. But do you tremble even before him? He is your brother and your flesh, tried in every respect without sin, that he might become merciful. Mary gave you this brother.

But perhaps even in him you fear the divine majesty, because, though made man, he nevertheless remained God. Do you wish to have an advocate even with him? Have recourse to Mary. For in Mary there is pure humanity—not merely pure from [Col. 0441D] every defilement, but pure in the singularity of her nature. Nor would I hesitate to say that she too will be heard because of her reverence. The Son will surely hear the Mother, and the Father will hear the Son.

Little children, this is the ladder of sinners; this is my greatest confidence; this is the whole ground of my hope. What then? Can the Son either reject or endure rejection? Can the Son fail to hear or fail to be heard? Certainly neither. “You have found grace with God,” says the angel. Happily so. She will always find grace, and grace alone is what we need. The prudent Virgin sought neither wisdom, as Solomon did, nor riches, nor honors, nor power, but grace. Assuredly, grace alone is that by which we are saved.

8. Why do we desire other things, brothers? Let us seek [Col. 0442A] grace, and seek it through Mary; for she finds what she seeks and cannot be frustrated. Let us seek grace—but grace with God; for favor with human beings is deceptive. Let others seek merit; let us strive to find grace. What then? Is it by grace that we are here? Certainly, it is through the mercy of the Lord that we have not been consumed. Who are “we”? We who are perjurers, adulterers, murderers, robbers—indeed, the refuse of this world. Examine your consciences, brothers, and see that where sin has abounded, grace has abounded still more.

Mary does not put forward merit, but seeks grace. Finally, she so trusts in grace and does not think highly of herself that she is afraid at the angel’s greeting. “Mary,” he says, “considered what manner of greeting this might be” (Luke 1:29). Doubtless she judged herself unworthy of an angelic greeting. And perhaps she was pondering such things as these: “Whence is this to me, that the angel of my Lord should come to me?” Do not fear, Mary; do not wonder at the angel coming: one greater than an angel comes. Do not wonder at the angel of the Lord: the Lord of the angel is with you. Finally, why should you not see an angel when you already live angelically? Why should an angel not visit one who shares his life? Why should he not greet a fellow-citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household? Virginity is plainly an angelic life; and “those who neither marry nor are given in marriage shall be like the angels of God.”

9. Do you see that in this way also our aqueduct ascended to the fountain? It penetrates the heavens now not by prayer alone, but also by incorruption, which, as the Wise Man says, makes one near to God (Wis. 6:20). [Col. 0442C] For she was a holy virgin in body and spirit, to whom it was especially fitting to say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Holy, I say, in body and spirit, lest you perhaps have any doubt concerning this aqueduct. It is indeed exceedingly lofty, but nevertheless remains wholly intact: a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, the temple of the Lord, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit. For she is not a foolish virgin, possessing not oil only, but a fullness of oil stored in her vessel.

“She has arranged ascents in her heart,” ascending both by her manner of life and by prayer, as we have already said. Finally, she went with haste into the hill country and greeted Elizabeth; and she was in her service for about three months, so that even then mother might say to mother what, much later, the Son said to his mother: “Allow it now; for thus it is fitting for us [Col. 0442D] to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15). She plainly ascended the hill country, she whose righteousness is like the mountains of God.

This was the Virgin’s third ascent, so that the threefold cord might not easily be broken. For love burned in seeking grace, virginity shone in her flesh, and humility stood out in service. Indeed, if everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted, what is loftier than this humility? Elizabeth wondered that she had come, saying: “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43). Yet she should marvel still more that, in the likeness of her Son, Mary too came not to be served but to serve.

Therefore that divine singer, singing beforehand in wonder at her, said: “Who is she that comes up like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed in battle?” (Song 6:9). She plainly rose above the human race, rose as far as the angels, and even transcended them; she surpasses every heavenly creature. Surely she must draw living water from above the angels, she who pours it back upon human beings.

10. “How shall this be,” she says, “since I do not know a man?” Truly she is holy in body and spirit, possessing both integrity of flesh and the purpose of integrity. But the angel answered and said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:34–35). Do not question me, he says; this is above me, and I cannot attain to it. The Holy Spirit, not an angelic spirit, shall come upon you; and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you, not I. Do not remain even [Col. 0443B] within the company of angels, holy Virgin; the thirsty earth awaits something loftier to be bestowed through your ministry.

When you have passed them by a little, you will find him whom your soul loves. “A little,” I say, not because he does not incomparably surpass them, but because you will find nothing intermediate between him and them. Pass, then, beyond the powers and dominions, even beyond the cherubim and seraphim, that you may come to him concerning whom they cry to one another: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3). “For that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

The fountain of wisdom, the Word of the Father, is on high. Through you this Word shall become flesh, so that he who says, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:10), may nevertheless say, “I proceeded from God and came” (John 8:42). “In the beginning,” he says, [Col. 0443C] “was the Word.” The fountain already bubbles forth, but for the time being only within itself. Finally, “the Word was with God” (John 1:1), dwelling, certainly, in inaccessible light; and the Lord said from the beginning: “I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction” (Jer. 29:11). But your thought is within you, and we do not know what you think. “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?”

The thought of peace, therefore, descended into a work of peace: “the Word was made flesh” and now dwells among us. He dwells through faith in our hearts, he dwells in our memory, he dwells in our thought, and descends even into our imagination itself. For what could a human being formerly think of God, except perhaps that he fashioned an idol in his heart?

[Col. 0443D] 11. He was incomprehensible and inaccessible, invisible and altogether unthinkable. But now he willed to be grasped, willed to be seen, willed to be thought of. In what way, you ask? Surely as lying in a manger, resting in a virgin’s lap, preaching on a mountain, spending the night in prayer, or hanging on the cross; pale in death, free among the dead, and ruling in hell; or likewise rising on the third day, showing the apostles the places of the nails, signs of victory, and finally ascending before them into the secrets of heaven.

What among these things cannot be thought of truly, devoutly, and holily? Whatever of these things I think upon, I think upon God; and through them all he is my God. I have called this meditation wisdom, and have judged it prudence to utter from memory the recollection of sweetness which the priestly rod [Col. 0444A] has abundantly produced in such kernels; which Mary, drawing it from things above, poured back upon us more abundantly. From things above indeed, and beyond the angels, she received the Word from the very heart of the Father, as it is written: “Day unto day utters the word” (Ps. 18:3). Certainly the Father is day, since the saving help of God is “day from day” (Ps. 95:2). Is not the Virgin also day? And a glorious one: a radiant day, coming forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun.

12. Consider, therefore, how she reached as far as the angels through fullness of grace, and above the angels through the coming of the Holy Spirit. In angels there is love, purity, and humility. Which of these did not shine in Mary? But this superiority has been shown above, as far as we were able to show it; let us continue with her preeminence.

For to which of the angels was it ever said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God”? [Col. 0444B] Finally, Truth sprang from the earth, not from angelic nature; and he took hold not of angels, but of the seed of Abraham. It is a great thing for an angel to be a servant of the Lord; but Mary merited something loftier, to be a mother. Thus the Virgin’s fruitfulness is surpassing glory; and she has been made superior to the angels by so singular a gift, inasmuch as she received the name of mother, so different from that of servants. She found this grace though already full of grace: by ardent love, unbroken virginity, and devoted humility, she became pregnant without knowledge of a man and a mother in childbirth without womanly pain. This is too little: what was born of her is called Holy, and is the Son of God.

13. For the rest, brothers, we must take the greatest care lest the Word which has gone out from the Father’s mouth to us through the Virgin return empty; rather, through that same Virgin let us render grace for grace. Let us utter the recollection until we sigh for the presence, and let the streams of grace be restored to their source, that they may flow more abundantly. Otherwise, unless they return to the fountain, they dry up; and, unfaithful in a little, we do not deserve to receive what is great.

Memory is indeed little in comparison with presence; little in comparison with what we desire; great in comparison with what we deserve: far below desire, yet nevertheless above merit. Therefore the bride wisely rejoices not a little even in this little thing [variant: “glories”]. [Col. 0444D] For when she had said, “Tell me where you feed, where you rest at noon” (Song 1:6), receiving a small thing in place of immeasurable things and, instead of noon-day pasture, tasting the evening sacrifice, she nevertheless does not murmur or grieve, as often happens, but gives thanks and shows herself more devoted in all things. For she knows that if she is faithful in the shadow of remembrance, she will without doubt obtain the light of presence.

Therefore, you who remember the Lord, do not be silent and give him no silence. Certainly those who have the Lord present do not need exhortation; and what another prophet says, “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion” (Ps. 147:1), is an expression of congratulation rather than admonition. Those who walk by faith need to be reminded not to be silent [Col. 0445A] and not to give him silence. For he speaks, and speaks peace to his people, to his saints, and to those who turn to the heart. Moreover, “with the holy you shall be holy, and with the innocent man you shall be innocent” (Ps. 17:26): he will hear the one who hears him, and speak to the one who speaks to him. Otherwise, if you are silent, you have given him silence. But whence should you be silent? From praise. “Do not be silent,” he says, “and give him no silence, until he establishes and makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth” (Isa. 62:6–7). The praise of Jerusalem is pleasant and fitting praise. Unless perhaps we imagine that the angels, citizens of Jerusalem, delight in mutually praising one another and deceive one another with vanity.

14. “May your will be done, Father, as in heaven, so also on earth,” so that Jerusalem’s praise may be established on earth. For what is the case now? Do angels not refrain from seeking glory from angels in Jerusalem, while man desires to be praised by man on earth? Detestable perversity! But let this belong to those who have ignorance of God, who have forgotten the Lord their God. You who remember the Lord, do not be silent from his praise until it is established and perfected on earth.

For there is a silence beyond reproach—indeed, more praiseworthy still. There is also speech that is not good. Otherwise the prophet would not say that it is good for a man to await the saving help of God in silence (Lam. 3:26). Silence from boasting is good; silence from blasphemy is good; silence from murmuring and detraction is good. One man, embittered by the greatness of his labor and the burden of the day, murmurs inwardly and judges those who keep watch for his soul, as those who must certainly render an account. It is an outcry; yet this outcry of a hardened mind, more than any silence, makes one silent, because it does not allow him to hear [Col. 0445C] the voice of the Word.

Another fails through faintness of spirit while waiting; and this is the worst word of blasphemy, which is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come. A third walks in great things and in wonders above himself, saying, “Our hand is high,” thinking himself to be something when he is nothing. What would he say to one who speaks peace? For he says: “I am rich and need nothing.” But the judgment of Truth is: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation here” (Luke 6:24). On the other hand: “Blessed,” he says, “are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

Let the evil-speaking tongue, the blaspheming tongue, the boastful tongue, therefore be silent within us; for it is good, in this threefold silence, to await the saving help of the Lord, so that you may say: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears” (1 Sam. 3:10). For voices of this kind are not directed to him, but against him, as the lawgiver said to the murmurers: “Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord” (Exod. 16:8).

15. Yet be silent from these things in such a way that you are not altogether silent, and do not give him silence. Speak to him against boasting in confession, that you may obtain forgiveness for the past. Speak in thanksgiving against murmuring, [Col. 0446A] that you may find fuller grace in the present. Speak in prayer against distrust, that you may obtain glory in the future. Confess, I say, the past; give thanks for present things; and then pray more earnestly for future things, so that he too may not be silent—from remission, from imparting, from promise.

Do not be silent, I say, and do not give him silence. Speak, that he too may speak, and that you may be able to say: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song 2:16). A pleasant voice and sweet speech! Certainly this is not the voice of murmuring but the voice of the turtledove. And do not say: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?” (Ps. 136:4). It will no longer be reckoned strange, of which the bridegroom says: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” For she had heard him saying: “Catch for us the little foxes” (Song 2:12, 15); and perhaps from this she broke forth into a voice of exultation, saying: “My beloved is mine, and I am his.”

It is plainly the voice of the turtledove, which remains with its mate in singular chastity, both while he lives and after he dies, so that neither death nor life separates it from the love of Christ. Consider, then, whether anything could have turned this beloved away from the beloved so that he would not remain faithful to her even when she sinned and turned away. Massed clouds strove to cast a shadow over the rays, so that our iniquities might separate us from God; but the sun grew hot [variant: “grew strong”] and dissolved them all. Otherwise, when would you have returned to him, unless he had remained faithful to you, unless he had cried: “Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon you” (Song 6:12)? Be, therefore, yourself also faithful to him, that you may not be turned away from him by any punishments or labors.

16. Wrestle with the angel; do not yield, because “the kingdom [Col. 0446C] of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). Is not “My beloved is mine, and I am his” a wrestling match? He has made his love known; let him experience yours too. For “the Lord your God tests you in many things.” He often turns aside and turns away his face, but not in anger. It is for testing, not for rejection. Your beloved has endured you; endure your beloved, endure the Lord, act manfully. Your sins did not overcome him; let his scourges likewise not overcome you, and you will obtain the blessing.

But when? When dawn has come, when day has now breathed forth, when he has established Jerusalem as a praise in the earth. “Behold,” he says, “a man wrestled with Jacob until morning” (Gen. 32:24). “Make me hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you, Lord.” I will not be silent, nor give you silence until morning; would that I might not even fast. For you deign to be fed—yet among lilies. “My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies.” Surely, as you remember, it was clearly expressed above in the same Song that the appearance of flowers accompanies the hearing of the turtledove’s voice.

But observe that this seems to indicate a place, not food; it does not state what he feeds upon, but among what things he feeds. Perhaps he is fed not by the food but by the fellowship of lilies; he does not eat lilies, but dwells among them. Lilies please rather by their fragrance than by their taste; they are more suited to sight than to eating.

17. Thus, therefore, he feeds among the lilies until the day breathes forth and abundance of fruits succeeds the beauty of flowers. Meanwhile [variant: “thus”], this is a time of flowers, not fruits, while we are more in hope than in possession; [Col. 0447A] while we walk by faith, not by sight; and rejoice more in expectation than experience. Consider, finally, the tenderness of a flower, and remember the Apostle’s saying that “we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). How many dangers seem to threaten flowers! How easily the lily is pierced by the thorns’ points! Therefore the beloved fittingly sings: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song 2:2).

Was he not a lily among thorns who said: “I was peaceable with those who hate peace” (Ps. 119:7)? Moreover, although “the righteous man springs up like a lily,” the bridegroom is not fed on a single lily, nor does he delight in isolation. Hear him, finally, dwelling among lilies: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:2). Jesus always loves what is in the middle; the Son of Man, mediator of God and human beings, always rejects secluded retreats and couches. “My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies.” Let us take care to have lilies, brothers; let us root out thorns and briars and hasten to plant lilies, in case perhaps the beloved may deign to descend even to us to be fed.

18. He was surely fed with Mary, and more abundantly because of the multitude of lilies. Are not the glory of virginity, the distinction of humility, and surpassing love lilies? Yet we too shall have lilies, though very much inferior ones; but the bridegroom will not disdain to feed even among these, provided that the cheerfulness of devotion adorns the acts of thanksgiving mentioned above, the purity of attention makes prayer white, and forgiveness whitens confession, as it is written: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and though they be red as crimson, they shall be white as wool” (Isa. 1:18).

But whatever it is that you are preparing to offer, remember to entrust it to Mary, so that by the same channel through which grace flowed in, grace may return to the giver of grace. God was not unable to pour out grace as he wished without this aqueduct; but he willed to provide you with a vehicle. [Col. 0448B] Perhaps your hands are either full of blood or contaminated by gifts, because you have not shaken them free from every gift. Therefore [variant: “and so”] take care to hand over this small thing which you desire to offer, to be offered by those most welcome hands of Mary, hands worthy of all acceptance, if you do not wish to suffer rejection. They are certainly lilies of a most brilliant whiteness; nor will that lover of lilies complain that whatever he finds in Mary’s hands was not found among lilies. Amen.

[Col. 0447]

## On the Feast of Saint Michael

### Sermon I. On the offices of angels toward us, and our reverence toward them  
[Variant: “on the threefold reason why angels are solicitous for us.”]

[Col. 0447C]

1. Today the commemoration of the angels is celebrated, and you demand the sermon due to so great a solemnity. But what can lowly worms say about angelic spirits? We certainly believe, and hold with unhesitating faith, that they rejoice without end in the blessedness of the divine presence and vision, in the good things of the Lord “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man.” What, then, can a human being say to human beings concerning things which he himself cannot even think, and which they cannot adequately hear? Indeed, if “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart,” the tongue must nevertheless be silent because thought is impoverished.

[Col. 0447D] Yet if it is too great a matter to speak to us of that brightness and glory in which the holy angels utterly surpass our hearts in themselves—indeed, in their God—let us speak of the grace and love which they show toward us. For in the heavenly spirits there is found not only an admirable dignity, but also a lovable condescension. It is fitting, therefore, brothers, that since we cannot comprehend their glory, we should embrace all the more their mercy, in which, nevertheless, the household of God, the citizens of heaven, the princes of paradise, are known to abound. Finally, the Apostle himself bears witness—he who, caught up to the third heaven, deserved to enter that blessed court and know its secrets—that they are all ministering spirits, sent to serve those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb. 1:14).

[Col. 0448C] 2. Nor should this seem incredible to anyone, since the Creator and King of the angels himself came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life for many (Matt. 20:28). Why, then, should anyone disdain that ministry of angels in which he goes before them, whom they serve on high with all eagerness and blessedness? And if you doubt even this, he who saw it has certainly given testimony: “Thousands of thousands served him,” he says, “and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10). Another prophet also, speaking to the Father concerning the Son, says: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6).

Thus indeed, thus it was fitting that he who conquered in sublimity should also conquer in humility; and that he should be so much lower than the angels as he devoted himself to a humbler ministry—he who is so much more excellent [Col. 0448D] than they as he inherited a name differing more greatly from theirs. But perhaps you ask in what respect he appears to have been made lower than the angels when he came to serve, since, as we recalled above, they too are sent for ministry. It was in this, certainly: he not only ministered, but was also ministered to; and one and the same person both ministered and was ministered to.

Therefore the bride fittingly says in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills” (Song 2:8). In ministering he leapt among the angels, yet in being ministered to he leapt over even them. For the angels minister, but with what belongs to another: they offer to God good works not their own but ours, and bring back his grace to us. Thus Scripture, saying, “The smoke of the incense went up before the Lord from the hand of the angel,” carefully first states that “much incense had been given to him” [Col. 0449A] (Rev. 8:4, 3). For they offer God our labors, not their own; our tears, not theirs; and they bring back to us his gifts, not their own.

3. Not so that minister who is loftier than all and humbler than all, who offered himself as a sacrifice of praise, who, offering his life to the Father, ministers his flesh to us even to this day. By the grace of so great a minister, it is no wonder if the holy angels minister to us willingly—indeed, gladly. They themselves love us because Christ loved us. A common proverb says: “He who loves me loves my dog also.” But we, O blessed angels, are the little dogs of that Lord whom you love with so great an affection—little dogs, I say, desiring to be filled with the crumbs which fall from the table of our masters, who are yourselves.

I have said this, brothers, so that henceforth you may have greater confidence toward the blessed angels and accordingly invoke their assistance more familiarly in every necessity; and so that you may endeavor to live more worthily in their presence, to conciliate their favor toward you ever more and more, to win their goodwill, and to entreat their clemency. For this purpose I consider it necessary to set before your love also the reasons which make the blessed angels solicitous for our weakness—without anxiety on their part, certainly, but not without benefit to us; not to the detriment of their blessedness, but for the increase of our salvation.

4. There is no doubt that human souls, endowed with reason and capable of blessedness, are, if we dare say it, kindred in nature to angelic beings. Nor does it befit you, O blessed spirits, contrary to the precept of the law, to disdain to visit your own likeness, although, as you see, it has been brought low into great vileness. Nor do we suppose, citizens of heaven, that you delight in the destruction of your city and in the ruin of its walls, which you yourselves see half-collapsed. If you desire its restoration, as is fitting, repeatedly, I pray you, renew before the throne of glory this word of prayer: “Deal favorably, O Lord, in your good pleasure with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built up” (Ps. 50:20).

If you love the beauty of the house of God—indeed, because you truly love it—let the living and rational stones experience your zeal, for they alone can be built up with you into its restoration. This, beloved, is the threefold cord [Col. 0449D] by which the surpassing love of the angels is drawn down from the lofty dwelling-place of heaven to console, visit, and help us: for God’s sake, for our sake, and for their own sake. For God’s sake, certainly, whose great compassion toward us they too imitate, as is fitting. For our sake, because they pity in us their own likeness. For their own sake, because they await with all desire the restoration of their ranks from among us. For in the mouths of little ones, who now feed on milk and not yet on solid food, that praise of the divine majesty must be perfected, the firstfruits of which the angelic spirits enjoy with blessed delight; but they await us all the more eagerly because they are solicitous in expectation and desire for its completion.

[Col. 0450A] **5.** Since these things are so, consider, beloved, how great our own vigilance must be, that we may show ourselves worthy of their company and conduct ourselves in the sight of the angels in such a way that we do not perhaps offend their holy gaze. For woe to us if, provoked by our sins and negligences, they should judge us unworthy of their presence and visitation, so that we too must lament and say with the Prophet: “My friends and my neighbours drew near and stood against me; and those who were near me stood afar off, and those who sought my life used violence” (Ps. 37:12–13). That is, those whose presence could protect us and drive away the enemy have withdrawn.

If, then, we have such need of the intimate condescension of angels, we must guard against offending them and must especially devote ourselves to those things in which we know they delight. There are many things pleasing to them, things which they delight to find in us: sobriety, chastity, voluntary poverty, frequent groans directed toward heaven, prayer with tears, and concentration of heart. Yet above all these, the angels of peace require from us unity and peace. Why should they not especially delight in things which display in us a certain image of their own city, so that they may behold the new Jerusalem upon earth? I mean that, just as the fellowship of that city is in unity (Ps. 121:3), so we too may think the same thing, all say the same thing, and have no schisms among us; but rather may all together be one body in Christ, each individually members of one another.

[Col. 0450C] **6.** Conversely, nothing offends and provokes them to indignation as much as dissensions and scandals, should they be found among us. Let us hear what Paul says to the Corinthians: “For while there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal and walking according to man?” (1 Cor. 3:3). We likewise read in the Epistle of the Apostle Jude: “These are they who separate themselves, animal persons, not having the Spirit” (Jude 19).

One may observe how the soul of a human being gives life to all the members of the body which cohere with it. Separate any member from the union of the rest, and see whether it thereafter gives it life. Such is everyone who says, “Anathema to Jesus” (1 Cor. 12:3), [Col. 0450D] which no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, because *anathema* means separation. Such, I say, is everyone divided from unity; do not doubt that the spirit of life has departed from him. Therefore the apostles rightly call contentious persons, and those who separate themselves, carnal and animal persons, not having the Spirit.

When those holy and blessed spirits find scandals and dissensions, they say: “What have we to do with this generation that has not the Spirit? For if the Spirit were present, charity would surely be poured forth through him, and unity would not be torn apart.” And they say: “We shall not remain with these human beings forever, because they are flesh.” For what fellowship has light with darkness? We belong to the kingdom of unity and peace, and we had hoped that these people would come into the same unity and peace. But [Col. 0451A] how can those who disagree with themselves adhere to us?

You see how fitting to this feast is the Gospel reading which so frightens us away from scandalizing the little ones, since scandals are so vehemently displeasing to the angels: “Whoever shall scandalize one of these little ones” (Matt. 18:6). What follows is severe. But the hour is now passing, and we must go to Mass. I ask that the postponement not be burdensome to you; it may prove not useless if we pursue the present chapter more carefully in another sermon.

## SERMON II. On the words, “Whoever shall scandalize one of these little ones who believe in me,” etc. (Matt. 18:6–9)

**1.** You have heard, brothers, the Gospel reading thunder terribly enough against those who scandalize the little ones. Truth flatters no one, strokes no one, deceives no one; it openly declares: “Woe to that man through whom scandal comes.” “It would have been good for that man if he had not been born” (Matt. 26:24)—he who is indeed born again, born unto life, born of the Spirit, and afterward is brought to completion in the flesh.

It is expedient for anyone who stirs up scandals in this house, in this holy congregation pleasing to God and exceedingly dear and familiar to his angels, [Col. 0451B] that a millstone be hung about his neck; and that, with the heavy mass of earthly desire laid upon his shoulders instead of the Savior’s sweet yoke and light burden, he be plunged into the depths of this great and wide sea, which is undoubtedly this evil age. For it would have been less blameworthy for him to perish in the world than in the monastery. For a person who does not have charity must perish, even if he should give up his body to be burned.

And I say this, brothers, not because I think less well of you, or because this most wicked vice seems to reign among you, but so that you may be diligent to persevere—and to abound yet more—in the charity, unanimity, and peace in which you stand in the Lord. For what is our hope, our joy, and our crown of glory? Is it not your unity and unanimity, in which I rejoice to find you lovers of brotherhood, having above all mutual charity among yourselves, which is the bond of perfection? Therefore I beseech you: stand thus in the Lord, most dearly beloved. For by this all, [Col. 0451C] even the holy angels, know that you are Christ’s disciples: if you have love for one another.

**2.** Finally, if you remember the threefold cause of angelic charity and concern for us which we set before you in the preceding sermon, the usefulness of brotherly love may be powerfully commended from this also. For it is easy to see that, in a person who does not love his neighbour, none of the reasons we then mentioned is available. Will we be loved by the angels through Christ’s grace, if they learn from our lack of mutual love that we are not at all his disciples? Will they love us for our own sake—that is, because of the likeness of our spiritual nature [variant: “by likeness”]—if we are found not to love those who share our human nature? Indeed, if from the contentions [Col. 0452A] among us it becomes clear that we are more carnal than spiritual?

Finally, will they love us for their own sake and for the future restoration of their city from among us, if—God forbid—the one glue by which alone we can be united and built together with them, the glue of charity, should be lacking? How will they hope that the everlasting walls of that city will be rebuilt from us, if they know and see that we are not living stones able to cleave to one another, but rather dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth, which the breath of a single word stirs into a whirlwind, and which the slightest breeze of any suspicion scatters?

And let this be enough to have said concerning the Lord’s words: “If anyone shall scandalize one of these little ones.” For I believe that henceforth you will guard with greater vigilance against this most wicked plague.

[Col. 0452B] **3.** But who is not moved by what follows in the Gospel: “If your eye scandalizes you, pluck it out”? Are we really warned to pluck out this bodily eye, or likewise to cut off one of these hands or one foot? Far be from us such an altogether carnal and excessively ridiculous thought! Rather, after the divine discourse has sternly deterred us, as you heard, from external scandals, it gives counsel about what we should do concerning that scandal which we suffer inwardly, when we find a contrary law in our members. For he knows our frame: such a scandal cannot so easily be avoided by us.

Now daily experience teaches us that this scandal occurs in three ways. [Col. 0452C] Sometimes there is in us the single eye of spiritual intention, which ought rather to be called the eye of grace than ours; yet our own eye—truly our own—scandalizes us when our will importunately introduces another, less chaste intention. But we already have the Savior’s wholesome counsel concerning this: “Pluck it out,” he says, “and cast it away from you.” This will occur if you do not consent, if you reject it, if you resist it.

The same must be understood concerning the hand and foot. When we are intent on good works, and our own will tries to draw us to other works, it is our hand that scandalizes us; but it must be cut off and cast away from us, so that we do not consent to it.

**4.** Likewise, when we desire to advance in holy conduct, to ascend the rungs of the ladder which appeared to Jacob, and, as the Psalmist says, to go “from strength to strength” (Ps. 83:8), we often suffer scandal from a certain foot of our own faint-heartedness and negligence. It seeks rather to go down and to walk more slackly; but it must be cut off, so that the foot of grace, which stands upright, may run without stumbling, scandal, or hindrance.

[Col. 0452D] When he says that it is good for us to enter life with one eye, hand, or foot, rather than, having two, to go into the hell of fire, he refers to those who follow their own will equally, whether it be good or evil, and walk by two ways—now pursuing good, now evil—according as their desires vary. It would rightly be more advantageous for them to cleave to grace in all things and, wherever their own will opposes it, to cut that will off and cast it away from themselves.

But sometimes, after being exercised for a long time in cutting off our own will, we tame it to some extent, so that it learns no longer to be proud but instead our soul is subject to God without any scandal or contradiction. Then it is no longer necessary to cast away our eye, since, cleaving to the single eye, it too has become single; or rather, the eye is no longer another eye, but one with it, as the Apostle testifies: “He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit with him” [Col. 0454A] (1 Cor. 6:17). What was said about the eye must be understood in the same manner about the hand and foot. For the person whose will cleaves with affection and desire to grace, so that he neither desires to do evil nor to do lesser goods, nor to do good less well than grace suggests, is truly a perfect man. Yet this peace belongs rather to blessedness; the cutting off of scandals and victory over temptations belong to fortitude. The former belongs to glory; the latter to virtue.

[Col. 0453]

## ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS

### SERMON I. On the Gospel reading, “Seeing the crowds, Jesus,” etc. (Matt. 5:1–12)

[Col. 0453B]

**1.** The present feast of All Saints ought to be celebrated with every devotion. For if the solemnity of blessed Peter, or blessed Stephen, or any of the others seems great—and is great—how great is this feast, which belongs not to one alone but to all of them? Yet you know, brothers, that it is the custom of worldly people to prepare festive banquets for themselves on feast days; and the more splendid the solemnity, the more splendidly they feast.

What then? Must not those who turn inward seek the delights of the heart and provide spiritual things for spiritual persons? Therefore our banquet is now prepared, brothers; all things are now cooked, and the time for feasting has come. For it is fitting that the soul first be satisfied, since this portion is undoubtedly and incomparably the better one—especially because it is evident that the feasts of the saints concern souls more than bodies, and that souls more readily receive what belongs to souls, joined to such things as they are by a certain natural kinship.

For this reason also these saints have greater compassion for us; for this reason they desire the good of souls more, and take greater delight in their refreshment: because they themselves too were like us, capable of suffering; they too bewailed the hardships of this pilgrimage and miserable exile; they too experienced the heavy burden of this body, the tumult of the world, and the temptations of the enemy. Therefore there is no doubt that the feast [Col. 0453D] which attends to the nourishment of souls is more pleasing and far more acceptable to them than that celebrated by worldly persons, who make provision for the flesh in its desires of pleasure.

**2.** Yet from where shall we obtain bread for souls in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude? From where shall we obtain spiritual food under the sun, where there is nothing but labour, pain, and affliction of spirit? But I know who said, “Ask and you shall receive”; and again: “If you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give a good spirit to those who ask him?” (Matt. 7:7, 11; Luke 11:9, 13).

Nor do I fail to know how earnestly, throughout this night and day, you have begged that living bread from heaven might be given to you—not the bread that strengthens the body, but that confirms the human heart. Indeed, I would not dare call us guests; rather, we are beggars, living on God’s allowance. [Col. 0454B] Beggars, I say, lying before the door of the exceedingly rich king, covered with sores, and desiring to be filled—or rather, even sustained—with the crumbs falling from the table of our lords, whose solemnity we celebrate today. They abound in delights and receive a good measure, pressed down and overflowing. But we trust that there will be one who gives to us, for there is an immense gulf and a very great distance between the liberality and kindness of God and the cruelty of the greedy rich man.

Therefore our Father has today given bread; for the Father of mercies must be the father also of the miserable. He has given us bread from heaven and provisions in abundance. Would that I might be a faithful cook for these things; would that my soul might seem a useful kitchen!

[Col. 0454C] **3.** For in preparing your dishes, throughout this whole night my heart grew warm within me, and in my meditation a fire blazed up: undoubtedly that fire which the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth and intensely desired to be kindled (Luke 12:49). For spiritual food requires a spiritual kitchen and spiritual fire.

It remains now for me to distribute what I have prepared; but you should consider rather the Lord who gives than the minister who distributes. For, so far as I am concerned, I am nothing other than your fellow-servant, who together with you begs from heaven, for myself and for you, as the Lord himself knows, bread and the sustenance of life. Therefore I do not give to you; your Father himself gives you the living bread from heaven. He feeds you by the deeds and words, and even by the flesh, of his Son, which is truly food.

For I read concerning deeds: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34); and concerning words: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8:3). Thus we now have nourishment in his deeds and words; afterward, God willing, we shall also receive at the most holy table of the altar the undefiled sacrament of the Lord’s body.

[Col. 0454D] **4.** Today we read in the Gospel that, seeing the crowds, Jesus went up the mountain. For the people followed the Lord as he preached through cities and villages: he saved their souls and healed their bodies; and they clung to him, delighted alike by his speech and his appearance. For his voice was sweet and his face beautiful, as it is written: “You are fairer in form than the children of men; grace is poured out upon your lips” (Ps. 44:3).

Such is he whom we follow and to whom we cling: wholly desirable, the one upon whom not only peoples but even the holy angels desire to gaze. What sweeter thing shall we set before you? These indeed are the delights of angels. Therefore taste and see that the Lord is sweet. And to this sweetness, this savour, this wisdom—which is truly drawn forth from hidden things—nothing that can be desired is able to compare. What then? Do you marvel at brightness in the sun, beauty in a flower, flavour in bread, fruitfulness in the earth? Yet all these things have been given by God; and there is no doubt that he has reserved for himself far more than he has given to creatures.

[Col. 0455A] **5.** Nor should we think idle even the fact that he went up the mountain, especially since it was so long before foretold, as though by a prophet crying from afar: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; raise your voice with strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem” (Isa. 40:9).

If you have no better interpretation, I think that in this ascent we should understand what blessed Luke mentions at the beginning of the Acts of the Apostles: “The first account, O Theophilus, I made concerning all the things which Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). Certainly this was not according to the practice of the Pharisees, who “bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them upon people’s shoulders, but are unwilling to move them with their own finger” (Matt. 23:4).

Is this not good bread for the soul, exceedingly strengthening the human heart? Confidently I follow you, Lord, wherever you go, and safely walk the way [Col. 0455C] of your commandments, knowing that you yourself have gone ahead by it. Safely, I say, I run the way of your commandments, since I know that “your going forth is from the height of heaven” to run this way, and “your circuit is to its height” by this way.

I cannot now, brothers, chew over every particular in this fashion. Be clean animals and ruminants, so that what is written may come to pass: “Desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21:20). For both the brevity of the hour and the greatness of the matter perhaps compel me to gird up and cut short my discourse.

**6.** Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up the mountain. He saw them with a gaze of compassion, because they were like wandering sheep without a shepherd. What does it mean that, before beginning to teach, he went up the mountain, except that in this very action he taught that preachers of God’s word must tend toward lofty things in the desires of their soul and in holy conduct, and climb the mountain of virtues?

“And when he had sat down, his disciples came to him.” “When he had sat down,” it says. Otherwise, who could approach that lofty giant? Most graciously indeed he bent himself down and emptied himself as far as sitting, so that he says to the Father: “You have known my sitting down and my rising up” (Ps. 138:2). He sat down so that even tax collectors and sinners might approach him whom not even the angels themselves, while standing, could attain; that Mary Magdalene might approach, and the thief from the cross might approach.

“And when he had sat down, his disciples came to him.” They came not so much by the movement [Col. 0456A] of their feet as by the affection of their hearts and imitation of his virtues. It is well that not the crowds, not just any persons from the people, but the disciples are said to have come: so that, just as the Old Testament is read as having been given on Mount Sinai, with Moses alone ascending and the people waiting below (Exod. 24:12–18), so now “the mountains might receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness”; and as though in certain darkness and secrecy, that might be said to the apostles which they would later speak in the light, and heard in the ear which they would afterward preach upon the rooftops. Hence it follows:

**7.** “And opening his mouth, he taught them.” He opened his mouth now, he who had previously opened the mouths of the prophets.
