Thus we read in the psalm, the Prophet saying: “Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” [Col. 0456B] (Ps. 50:17). But now he who formerly spoke in many portions and in many ways through the prophets finally spoke with his own mouth, as though saying: “I who was speaking, behold, I am present” (Isa. 52:6).

Blessed are those who heard Wisdom speaking in the flesh; blessed are those who heard the words of the Word of God which proceeded from his own mouth. Yet what they heard is still reserved for us, because we too can hear it, though not from him in person. “Opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

Truly his mouth is open, for in it are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. And this teaching is truly his who says in the Apocalypse: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5), and who had earlier foretold through the Prophet: “I will open my mouth; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world” (Ps. 77:2; Matt. 13:35). For what is so hidden as that poverty should be blessed? Yet Truth speaks, which can neither be deceived nor deceive; and it is Truth itself that says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

Thus you, senseless children of Adam, still seek riches and desire riches, although the blessedness of the poor has already been commended by God, proclaimed to the world, and believed by human beings. Let the pagan seek them, who lives without God; let the Jew seek them, who received earthly promises. But with what face—or rather, with what mind—does a Christian seek riches after Christ has proclaimed the poor blessed? How long, children of strangers, how long will your mouth speak vanity, calling blessed the people who possess these things—these visible, present things—when the Son of God, opening his mouth, has spoken the truth: that the poor are blessed, and woe belongs to the rich?

[Col. 0456D] **8.** But attend carefully: he does not simply call the poor blessed, on account of common people made poor by a misery imposed through necessity rather than by a praiseworthy will. I do hope that this very misery of their affliction will benefit them with the mercy of divine goodness; yet I know that the Lord was not speaking here of such persons, but of those who can say with the Prophet: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. 53:8).

Yet not every voluntary poverty has praise before God. For philosophers too are said to have abandoned all their possessions in order, freed from worldly cares, to devote themselves more freely to the pursuit of vanity; and they did not wish to abound in earthly wealth, so that they might abound more in their own understanding. The word “in spirit” distinguishes these persons—that is, by spiritual will. Blessed therefore are the poor in spirit: poor by spiritual intention and spiritual desire, for the sole good pleasure of God and the salvation of souls, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

But who is this who speaks thus, who thus blesses the poor and enriches them? Do you suppose it can be true? It certainly will be true, since the one who promises is truthful and powerful. If the enemy murmurs, the answer will be given him: “Is it not lawful for me to do what I will? Or is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. 20:15). If you were justly humbled because you sought to exalt yourself against me, are not those who humble themselves for me rightly to be exalted?

And truly, brothers, if that most miserable being was cast down from heaven because he coveted height, desired loftiness, and presumed sublimity, does it not follow that those are blessed who freely lower themselves into the humility of poverty, and of whom, according to the Lord’s promise, is the kingdom of heaven which he lost? Observe how wisely Wisdom has set the first remedy against the first sin. It is as though he said more openly: “Do you wish to obtain the heaven which the proud angel lost, who trusted in his own strength and in the multitude of his riches? Embrace the lowliness of poverty, and it shall be yours.” It follows:

[Col. 0457B] **9.** “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” Well—exceedingly well. For after poverty had been commended, meekness also had to be proclaimed, because for those who leave all things the first temptation commonly arises from bodily discomforts and the unfamiliar affliction of the flesh. What benefit will poverty bring if, God forbid, the poor person falls into murmuring, becoming bitter and impatient of discipline?

It is also most fitting that, after the promise of the kingdom, another lesser kingdom is given as a pledge, so that, according to Scripture, we may have “the promise of the life which now is, and also of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4:8), and that the bestowal of present things may make expectation of future things secure. “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.”

I understand this earth to be our body. If the soul wishes to possess it, if it desires to reign over its members, it must itself be meek and subject to its superior; for it will find its inferior to be such as it has shown itself toward its superior. For creation is armed to avenge the injury done to its Creator. Therefore let the soul that finds its flesh rebellious toward it know that it too is less subject than it should be to the higher powers. Let it become meek and humble itself beneath the mighty hand of the Most High; let it be subject to God, and likewise to those prelates whom it must obey in God’s stead. Then it will immediately find its body obedient and subject.

For Truth is the one who speaks: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” And see whether the second medicine has not gone forth against the wound of the second sin. For after the ruin of the angelic transgression, Eve first sinned, agitated by unrest of spirit and casting off the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden of prohibition, because [Col. 0458A] she would not wait to merit from the Lord’s hand—from which she had already received all else—even the perfection of blessedness, but attempted by the serpent’s counsel to seize it beforehand. On this account she lost paradise, the land of delights; on this account she found in her very body a contrary law.

But perhaps now, at this word of the Lord, you burn with desire for meekness and complain about the harshness of your heart, certain bestial impulses, and untamed fierceness. Attend, then, to what follows:

**10.** “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” Whips tame an unbroken horse; contrition of spirit and constancy in tears tame an unyielding soul. Therefore, in all your works remember your last things: do not permit the horror of death, the fearful ordeal of judgment, and the dread of burning Gehenna ever to be removed from the eyes of your heart. Consider the misery of your pilgrimage; reconsider your years in the bitterness of your soul; consider the dangers of human life; consider your own frailty. If you persevere in such reflection, I tell you, you will scarcely feel whatever outward thing seems troublesome, while you are occupied with your whole heart upon inward trouble.

But the Lord will not permit you to be without consolation, because he is the Father of mercies and God of all consolation; and what Truth promises will wholly be fulfilled: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” This saying also agrees with what you read in Solomon: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7:3).

[Col. 0458C] Therefore, Eve, you would have been blessed if after your fault you had sought the consolation of tears and, turning to repentance, had obtained pardon more quickly. But instead you sought a most miserable consolation in the like fall of your husband; and with the worst poison—the most wicked vice—you infected your whole posterity, so that to this day one person regards another’s destruction as consolation for his own. Most wretched indeed was Eve’s consolation, and that of those who imitate this misery! But “blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.”

What else, however, is this consolation than the grace of devotion proceeding from hope of pardon, the sweetest delight in good, and a taste of wisdom, however slight, with which in the meantime the kindly Lord refreshes the afflicted soul? Yet that taste is nothing other than a stimulus of desire and an incentive to love, as it is written: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Ecclus. 24:29). Therefore there immediately follows:

[Col. 0458D] **11.** “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.” Let the one who hungers hunger more; let the one who desires desire still more abundantly. For however much one can desire, so much one will receive. Indeed, one will not receive according to the imperfection or measure of one’s desire, since until one has perfectly one cannot desire perfectly; nor can one have perfectly until one desires perfectly. But one will receive a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.” To the weaker palate of the heart and to the still sickly soul, righteousness seems a hard and tasteless thing; but those who have tasted know how blessed are those who hunger for it, because they shall be filled.

[Col. 0459A] O truly happy and glorious fullness! O holy banquet! O desirable feast! There, certainly, no anxiety and no weariness can exist, because there will be the highest fullness and the highest desire. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.”

I believe that this saying goes forth against Adam, who seems to have maintained some share of righteousness in having compassion on the woman; but if he had hungered for righteousness, he would undoubtedly have taken care to render what he owed, not only to his wife but much more to his Creator. He owed his wife compassion, certainly, and discipline, as one inferior to himself; “for the husband is the head of the wife” (Eph. 5:23). But he owed God obedience and subjection.

Yet, brothers, what do we think? Very many people to this day judge that deed severely, and yet imitate it foolishly. They are indignant with Adam because he obeyed the voice of his wife more than God’s; yet they themselves daily obey their own Eve—that is, the flesh—more than God. Brothers, if we could now see Adam placed at that critical moment, with thoughts rising in his heart and pressing him between his wife’s request and his Creator’s command, would we not cry out against him, saying: “Take care, miserable man; see that you do not do it! The woman has been deceived; do not consent to her!” Why, then, whenever a similar temptation overtakes us, do we not similarly persuade ourselves?

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.” But what can all our righteousness be before God? Is it not, according to the Prophet, reckoned “like the cloth of a menstruous woman” (Isa. 64:6)? And if it is judged strictly, all our righteousness will be found unrighteous and deficient. What, then, will become of sins, when righteousness itself will not even be able to answer on its own behalf? Therefore, crying earnestly with the Prophet, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord” (Ps. 142:2), let us flee in all humility to mercy, which alone can save our souls; and let us carefully consider what follows:

[Col. 0459D] **12.** “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” Observe how Zacchaeus briefly embraces both things in one statement: “Behold, I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). You see how greatly this man hungers for righteousness: an equal repayment does not satisfy him unless he restores fourfold. His mercy also is great, in giving half his goods to the poor.

Yet I will not remain silent about what I think. “My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord”—the Lord’s, plainly, not yours. For I give glory not to you but to his name. Zacchaeus, certainly, whose praise is in the Gospel, gave half his goods to the poor; but here I see many Zacchaeuses who have left nothing for themselves out of all they possessed. Who will write this Gospel for me concerning these Zacchaeuses—or rather, concerning these Peters—who can confidently say to the Lord: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27)?

[Col. 0460A] But it is already written in the eternal Gospel, written and sealed in the book of life: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” This saying, moreover, touches Adam’s cruelty, he who had first seemed to sin from love for his wife. For we know, Adam, that she is bone of your bones and flesh of your flesh, and that you sinned out of love for her. Let us now see how much you love her.

The Lord comes holding a fiery sword to avenge the transgression. Put yourself forward for peril on her behalf and say: “Lord, the woman is weaker; the woman was deceived. Mine is the iniquity; mine is the sin; let vengeance proceed against me alone.” But he does not speak thus. “The woman,” he says, “whom you gave me, gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12).

[Col. 0460B] O perversity! You refuse to undergo punishment for her, yet you did not refuse to incur guilt! Alas, how you have confounded everything! You were disastrously merciful where you ought to have been strict, and still more disastrously cruel where you ought to have shown mercy. For you should in no way have sinned on her account; but you should have been willing in spirit to make satisfaction on her behalf.

For this is how it ought to be, brothers: a person should never sin on another’s account—that is righteousness; and should willingly bear another’s sins—that is mercy. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” It follows:

13. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. [Col. 0460C] Blessed indeed, and altogether blessed, are those who shall see him upon whom the angels desire to look, whom to see is eternal life. “My heart has said to you: My face has sought you; your face, O Lord, will I seek” (Ps. 26:8). “For what have I in heaven? And apart from you what have I desired upon earth? My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever” (Ps. 72:25–26). When will you fill me with joy in your countenance? Woe to me because of the impurity of my heart! While it obstructs me, I am not yet worthy to be admitted to that blessed vision. With what anxiety, brothers, with what earnestness must we strive for the cleansing of the eye by which God is to be seen! For I perceive myself to be defiled by a threefold stain: the concupiscence of the flesh, [Col. 0460D] the desire for temporal glory, and consciousness of past offences. There are in the soul certain movements of both kinds of desire which I can extinguish neither by reason nor by strength, so long as I remain in this wicked world and am held bound in this body of death. Yet against these stains I set the remedy of prayer; and therefore, “as the eyes of servants are in the hands of their masters, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God, until he have mercy upon us” [Ps. 122:2], who alone is pure and can make pure that which was conceived from impure seed. Likewise, against consciousness of sin the remedy of confession has been appointed, and all things are washed in confession. Behold, these are what cleanse the eye of the heart: prayer and confession. But blessed are the pure in heart, because [Col. 0461A] they shall see God. They shall indeed see him at the end, face to face; they see him even now, but through a mirror in an enigma; and now they know in part, but afterwards they shall know perfectly.

For everyone in whose conscience a concealed sin still lives either sins in hope, and thus thinks of God as though sins displeased him less; or sins in despair, thinking God without mercy. To both it is rightly said: “You wickedly supposed that I should be like you” (Ps. 49:21), because neither sees God; rather, iniquity lies to itself, fashioning for itself an idol instead of God as he is. But the pure in heart are blessed, because they alone see God; they alone think of him in goodness—as he is truly good, so that none is good except he alone. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. [Col. 0461B] Miserable, therefore, are Adam and Eve, who, turning to words of malice to excuse their excuses in sins, flee the cleansing of confession, remain impure in heart, and are driven from the presence of the Lord. It follows:

14. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. They will rightly be called by the name of children, since they have fulfilled the work of the Son. For he is the one through whom, having been reconciled, we have peace with God; he who made peace by his blood between the things in heaven and those upon earth, the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. Observe how in the first three [beatitudes] the soul is reconciled to itself; in the following two, to its neighbour; in the sixth, to God; and in the seventh it reconciles others also, as one received into the Lord’s favour and endowed with a blessed intimacy.

For through poverty, meekness, [Col. 0461C] and mourning there is renewed in the soul a certain likeness and image of eternity that embraces all times: through poverty it gains the future; through meekness it claims the present for itself; through penitential grief it recovers even the past, as it is written: “I will recount to you all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. 38:15). Moreover, by justice and mercy we are perfectly joined to our neighbour: through justice, by doing to no one what we do not wish done to ourselves; and through mercy, by doing to others whatever we wish people to do to us. Reconciled now to ourselves and also to our neighbour, we are confidently reconciled to God through purity of heart. Blessed, however, are those who, not ungrateful for their own reconciliation and piously concerned for their brothers, labour, insofar as they are able, to reconcile them also both to themselves and to God.

With what praises, how warmly, do you think that brother ought to be embraced who lives among his brothers without complaint, takes every care that there be nothing in himself which others must bear, and bears with the greatest patience whatever is burdensome in others? He who counts every person’s scandals as his own; who speaks with the Apostle: “Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed? Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29). Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. For God is not a God of dissension but of peace; therefore it is fitting that children of peace should also be called children of God.

15. The eighth beatitude that follows is the prerogative of martyrs; for us, neither the time nor the strength for such endurance seems present. Justice is now honoured, at least insofar as it appears openly; either no one, or few, suffer persecution for it. Yet happy are any such persons, if there are any, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven, so that [variant: where] no one persecutes them. If tribulation should become manifold, then exultation should become still more abundant—not looking at visible hardships, but at rewards which are unseen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but those which are unseen are eternal. “Blessed,” he says, “shall you be when people hate you, when they separate you, cast you out, and, lying, say every evil thing against you on my account. Rejoice on that day and exult: for behold, your reward is abundant in heaven,” far more abundant than the labour upon earth.

Yet [Col. 0462B] what does it mean that the same promise is made to the poor and to martyrs, unless voluntary poverty is truly a kind of martyrdom? “Blessed,” says the Prophet, “is the man who has not gone after gold and has not placed his hope in money-treasures. Who is he? And we shall praise him. For he has done wonders in his life” (Ecclus. 31:8–9). What is more wonderful, or what martyrdom more grievous, than to hunger amid feasts, to be cold amid many costly garments, to be oppressed by poverty amid the riches which the world offers, which the Evil One displays, and which our own appetite desires? Is not he rightly crowned who has contended in this manner: rejecting the world that promises, mocking the enemy that tempts, and—more gloriously—triumphing over himself and crucifying his itching concupiscence? Finally, [Col. 0462C] the kingdom of heaven is promised alike to the poor and to martyrs because it is purchased by poverty, but in suffering for Christ it is received without any delay.

## SERMON II. On the Condition of the Saints before the Resurrection

1. Since today, beloved, we celebrate the festal memory of All Saints, most worthy of every devotion, I think it worthwhile, with the help of the Holy Spirit, to speak to your charity concerning their shared blessedness, in which they already enjoy blessed rest, and the future consummation which they await. I shall do so, indeed, by following not the conjectures of my own opinion but the authority of the divine books, [Col. 0462D] so that I may not seem to prophesy from my own heart, but may rely, as far as I can, upon the testimonies of Scripture.

With the Lord’s assistance, this discourse will have a threefold benefit: that, once we have come to know, at least in some measure, the happy recompense of the saints, we may thereafter strive with more abundant care to follow in their footsteps, with more fervent longing to sigh for fellowship with them, and with more devoted reverence to commend ourselves to their patronage. For it is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance: that those whom we honour with solemn veneration we should also follow by a similar manner of life; that toward the blessedness of those whom we proclaim most blessed we should run with all eagerness; and that, delighted by their praises, we should be supported by their patronage. Nor is the saints’ festal commemoration found unfruitful in any small degree: it drives away our weakness, lukewarmness, and error. For through their intercession our frailty is helped; through consideration of their blessedness our negligence is stirred; and through their examples our ignorance is instructed.

Therefore, since I do not doubt that by today’s reading from the holy Gospel and by the Lord’s own discourse you have been perfectly instructed to imitate the saints’ footsteps—since the ladder by which the whole choir of saints whom we venerate today ascended has plainly been raised before your eyes—and since I know that almost the whole time of this night and day has been spent in religious devotion seeking their aid, I shall now venture to speak some small thing about their blessedness: whatever he may grant, who already magnifies and glorifies those whom he first called [Col. 0463B] and justified.

2. We read in the Prophet: “Return, my soul, unto your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you; because he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from falling” (Ps. 114:7–8); and in another psalm: “Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of hunters” (Ps. 123:7). I seem also to have found in the sequence of the divine Scriptures many similar utterances of people who rejoice, not without great wonder, that they have been set free—words of perfect security and immense happiness, a voice of thanksgiving and gladness—which, to my understanding, do not at all suit those who still inhabit houses of clay and eat their bread in the sweat of their faces.

For who among them will boast that he has a pure heart? Who would dare to boast that the snare has been broken or that his feet have been delivered from falling, when the Apostle plainly objects and says: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12)? Thus he says also of himself: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24). And elsewhere: “Brothers, I do not reckon that I have attained. But one thing: forgetting those things which are behind, and stretching forward to those which are before me, I pursue the prize” (Phil. 3:13–14), and so forth. Again: “Thus I run, not as though uncertain; thus I fight, not as one beating the air. Rather, I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9:26–27). These surely are the trumpet-call of warfare, the words of a vigorous leader [Col. 0463D] fighting bravely. The former passages, however, seem rather to be those of one triumphing; or at least of one not yet triumphing, but already returning from battle with victory and awaiting with joyful, confident conscience the future day of a great triumph.

3. For what does the brave soldier, the faithful servant, say upon returning from battle? “Return now,” he says, “my soul, unto your rest.” For while you served the Lord in the body of death, there was no rest: both because of the labour of combat and because of the danger of an outcome still uncertain. On one side the tumult of temptations stirred you; on the other, fear of falling more grievously troubled you. Yet even then, brothers, Christ’s soldier had glory, though he had no rest. For that vigorous and most valiant soldier, whom we mentioned a little earlier, says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12).

I do not think that this testimony of conscience should be understood as though conscience itself bore testimony to itself. “For he who commends himself is not approved, but he whom God commends” (2 Cor. 10:18). Therefore the testimony of conscience in which the Apostle glories is not what conscience bears, but what the Spirit of truth speaks within it, bearing witness to our spirit that we are children of God (Rom. 8:16). It is the testimony of a conscience that receives testimony, not one that gives it. For when truth applauds, when justice bears witness, it is without doubt the voice of God commending, and the testimony of the Holy Spirit bearing witness—as if a king, standing nearby, should joyfully applaud a soldier fighting bravely for his king’s love and honour, praise his courageous deeds, proclaim that victory is near, that rewards are ready, and promise an eternal crown. In this testimony the approved and vigorous soldier indeed glories; nevertheless, he does not rest, but fights all the more eagerly and courageously.

Thus, while they still serve in warfare, God’s elect certainly rejoice, but only in the firstfruits of the Spirit, who both aids their weakness with his power and consoles their faint-heartedness by his attestation. Hence the Apostle of whom I was speaking says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but justice, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 14:17).

[Col. 0464C] 4. But once the time of warfare has been completed, the saints have joy also in their own spirit, until that day comes when they deserve to enter into the joy of their Lord, having joy also in their own bodies. Thus we have in the Psalm: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been sealed upon us; you have given joy in my heart.” Whence? Plainly from what follows: “From the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil” (Ps. 4:7–8). For such a soul has heard the voice saying: “Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates” (Prov. 31:31).

Thus John is commanded to write in the Apocalypse that blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. Why blessed? “Henceforth,” says the Spirit, “let them rest from their labours” (Rev. 14:13). Therefore in the very psalm of which we spoke a little [Col. 0464D] earlier, the words quoted above are joined with this: “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the same place” (Ps. 4:9). And concerning works we have in the Apocalypse: “For their works follow them” (Rev. 14:13). But why do they follow, except that their works may praise them in the gates? Why do they follow, except that they may be multiplied from their fruit, and, receiving the fruit of their hands, the calves may be fattened which, when the walls of Jerusalem are rebuilt, we know from prophetic testimony are to be offered upon the altar of the Lord? (Ps. 50:20–21).

Meanwhile, that they are beneath the altar, and not above it, let him himself teach us whose testimony has become exceedingly trustworthy—he who, as he writes in the Apocalypse, heard even their voices [Col. 0465A] beneath the altar itself (Rev. 6:9–10). The light of the Lord’s countenance is therefore still sealed upon them.

> **Note:** That is, sealed up, not yet unsealed and revealed. This appears both from what follows and from Sermon 4, §2, where he says that the souls of the blessed now see only Christ’s humanity, not his divinity itself. Many similar passages occur in Bernard, in which he seems to approach the opinion of those who teach that the souls of the righteous after this life, before the general resurrection of bodies and the Last Judgment, are not admitted to that blessedness which consists in the vision of God; but meanwhile exist in a certain imperfect happiness, which excludes all pain and provides refreshment, rest, light, and joy, but does not yet fulfil their desire.

> Pope John XXII is reported to have taught this and to have instructed the theologians of Paris to teach the same. Bernard seems to favour this opinion in several passages, and it will not be irrelevant to apply here, once and for all, an antidote to them. For, besides the cited words, in Sermon 3 on All Saints he again establishes three states of holy souls: first, in a corruptible body; second, without a body; third, in consummated blessedness. The first is in tents; the second in courts; the third in the house of God, into which house he denies that they will enter without bodies. And in Sermon 4 he says that the souls of martyrs are beneath the altar because they see Christ’s humanity alone, but that after the resurrection of their bodies they will be raised above the altar in order to see his divinity. There is a similar passage in Sermon 4 on the Dedication of a Church, and elsewhere.

> Yet the common opinion of the holy Fathers and Doctors of the Church is that the souls of the devout, released from their bodies, have not merely already been received into heaven and reign with Christ, but are simply blessed and enjoy the sight of God. Augustine’s opinion on this question is judged variously. Some think that he remained uncertain concerning the place of righteous souls—whether they are already in heaven or elsewhere. In *On Care to Be Had for the Dead*, chapter 3; *Enchiridion*, chapter 108; book 12 of *The City of God*, chapter 9; and elsewhere, he places righteous souls in hidden seats, in secret and concealed receptacles. In Tractate 49 on John, he counts eternal life with angels among things promised to them but not yet bestowed; and in book 1 of the *Retractations*, chapter 14, he says that one may rightly ask concerning holy persons already dead whether they themselves should at least now be said to stand in that possession in which holy angels are known without doubt to be. See similar passages in the same author, book 12 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 35. Likewise, on Psalm 36: “After this life,” he says, “you will not yet be where the saints will be, to whom it shall be said, ‘Come, blessed ones,’” etc. See Letter 111 to Fortunatus; Tractates 53 and 111 on John; *Exposition on Psalm 85*; Sermon 1 on Psalm 48; *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 21. In these passages he indicates that the devout are not to be admitted to the beatific vision before the Last Judgment.

> Yet the diligent reader of Augustine will observe that he is doubtful not concerning the place but rather the state of souls. For he held that the souls of saints do indeed see God face to face, but not so perfectly as they will see him after the resurrection; and this because their natural appetite, by which they are borne toward the body in order to be reunited to it and govern it again, delays them from being carried toward God with their whole attention, and thus they have not yet attained equality with the angels, whom no hindrance delays from being borne wholly toward God. Augustine himself, however, did not hold this so certainly as to regard it as established fact. For although in book 22 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* he seems to affirm it, nevertheless afterwards, in book 1 of the *Retractations*, chapter 14, he indicates that he still doubts.

> The question, namely whether the souls of the blessed now see God as perfectly as after the resurrection, has not altogether been determined, except that the Council of Florence, when it says that the souls of saints enjoy perfect happiness but will enjoy it more perfectly with their bodies after they rise, may appear to some to incline toward Augustine’s opinion. Others, however, more rightly think this should be understood not of a more intense but of a more extensive blessedness, because of the blessedness of the body which will be added to the former blessedness of the soul. The words of St Bernard should be understood in the same way. For he denies only that the souls of saints now see God as perfectly as they will when they have received their bodies.

> That this is his meaning is proved by these words in Sermon 3 on All Saints, in which he addresses the flesh: “Holy souls desire you: without you their joy cannot be completed, their glory perfected, their blessedness consummated. For this natural desire is so vigorous in them that their whole affection does not yet move freely toward God, but is in some manner contracted and forms a wrinkle while they incline toward desire for you.” And in Sermon 87 on Various Subjects: “They are in some manner delayed from perfect contemplation of the divinity while they still await the resurrection of their body at the end of the world.” Thus Bernard followed Augustine’s opinion in this matter, as also did St Thomas, Bonaventure, Richard, and Marsilius, writing on *Sentences*, distinction 49, question 4—although St Thomas later changed his opinion. For in I–II, question 4, article 5, he expressly teaches that, when the body is resumed, the blessedness of the soul will increase not intensively but extensively.

> Moreover, concerning the state of holy souls after this life, Bernard holds, first, that they are in heaven, as he clearly testifies in various places, especially in Sermon 4 on All Saints, where, distinguishing Abraham’s bosom from that of blessed souls, he says: “The former was in darkness, the latter in great light; the former in hell, the latter in heaven.” Secondly, he holds that they “have already received their single robes, but not yet double ones,” in Sermon 3 on All Saints, where he explains both robes: “The first robe,” he says, “is the happiness and rest of souls of which we have spoken; the second is the immortality and glory of bodies.” Thirdly and finally, he expresses quite clearly in various places his opinion that they also enjoy the divine vision. For near the end of *On Loving God* he says that martyrs “are immersed in the immense sea of eternal light and luminous eternity.” In the letter to the brothers in Ireland he says that “the soul of Malachy walks no longer by faith but reigns by sight.” And in the sermon on the same saint he says that Malachy reigns with the angels in equal glory and happiness. In Sermon 3 on Palm Sunday, §5; Sermon 1 on Pentecost; Sermon 2 on the Ascension; likewise Sermon 6 on the *Song of Songs*, he says that some have already deserved to be introduced into the Holy of Holies, where they see the face of the One standing—that is, the brightness of the unchangeable God. He offers some similar general testimony concerning the souls of saints in Sermons 4 and 5 on All Saints, *On the Death of Humbert*, Letter 98, §8, again Letter 266, and elsewhere more frequently.

> This opinion was defined at the Council of Florence, where the Fathers decreed that “purified souls are immediately received into heaven and clearly behold the triune and one God himself as he is.” To this was added the decree of the Council of Trent, session 25, asserting that “the saints reign with Christ and enjoy eternal happiness in heaven.” See Benedictus Justinianus on the Epistle to the Philippians, chapter 1, verse 21, on the words, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain,” where he observes from Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others that death cannot truly be considered gain unless the souls of the righteous are immediately raised to the sight of God.

They have, though not complete, yet great joy in their heart, until that day comes when he shall fill them with joy [Col. 0466A] in his countenance. Meanwhile, I say, those souls return to their rest until the day comes when they deserve to enter into the Lord’s rest. Their works still praise them in the gates, until the time comes [Col. 0467A] when each shall have praise from God. You see, brothers, how great is the unity of the Scriptures: with one sense and almost the same words they speak of the blessedness of souls.

5. Let none of you suppose, then, that the rest or joy of those who, wholly free from every distress, recall their years in the sweetness of their soul is in any way small. They rejoice for the days in which they were humbled, for the years in which they saw evils. With delightful wonder and marvellous gladness they consider the dangers they escaped, the labours they endured, and the conflicts they conquered. For all these things they await, with certain and undoubting faith, the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of their great God and Saviour, who will raise and transform [Col. 0467B] their bodies so that they are conformed to the brightness of his own body.

6. How great is their happiness, how immeasurable their joy! They exult in a threefold joy: in recollection of virtue already accomplished, in possession of their present rest, and in certain expectation of future consummation. For concerning that future consummation we have their voice at the end of the psalm of which we spoke above. Each soul which has already been granted arrival at this rest says: “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the same place, because you, O Lord, have established me singularly in hope.” Singularly in hope, I say—not now between hope and fear, where before I fluctuated amid much anxiety and distress.

Likewise, concerning the saints’ present rest we find it written in another psalm: “Return, my soul, unto your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you.” He has dealt well with me, I say, though not yet most excellently. Finally, hear how well: “Because he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from falling” (Ps. 114:7–8); that is, he has entirely set me free from every sin and punishment for sin, and also from fear and from the danger of falling again. This is the soul’s most sweet bed, which tears neither wash nor moisten any longer, when God wipes every tear from its eyes. This is the couch in which it is no longer pierced or turned in its misery while it is transfixed by the thorn. For it has departed from that land which brought forth thorns and thistles for it. This indeed is the soul’s bed, which no longer turns in its weakness, because all that belonged to weakness has together passed away. This, I say, is the soul’s most sweet and health-giving rest: a conscience clean, tranquil, secure. Let purity of conscience, then, be the blessed soul’s mattress; tranquillity its pillow; security its covering—so that on this bed it may meanwhile sleep delightfully and rest happily.

7. Concerning the recollection of virtue already accomplished, you have plainly in Psalm 123 the words which I also mentioned above. For they consider and recall with much wonder from what snares and how great dangers they deserved to be delivered by divine aid; and exulting in the Lord, they say: “Unless the Lord had been in us, let Israel now say: unless the Lord had been in us when people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. Our soul passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul would have passed through unbearable water.” And they add: “Blessed be the Lord, who has not given us as prey to their teeth” (Ps. 123:1–6).

The words which the Apostle spoke when the time of his departure was at hand, uttered in confidence concerning the condition in which he now happily rests, seem now to suit him far better. For now he speaks securely: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. For the rest, there is laid up for me a crown of justice, which the Lord, the just judge, will render to me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:7–8). These, I tell you, brothers, are now all the occupations of the saints; this is their food, this their sleep. For this reason the Holy Spirit willed that the words we have set forth, and other similar ones, should be written, so that from them their condition might become known to us in some measure.

8. Yet in such meditations they are affected far differently and delight far more abundantly than either our thought can grasp or our speech express. Hear how the Prophet labours, piling up and multiplying words, yet unable thereby worthily to magnify what he intends: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” Yet what does he add? “You have perfected it,” he says, “for those who hope in you, in the sight of the children of men” (Ps. 30:20). There is therefore a multitude of sweetness, hidden indeed and very great, but not yet perfect, because it will be perfected openly, not in concealment, when the saints shall not rest beneath the altar but sit upon thrones as judges.

For holy souls, once stripped of their bodies, are immediately admitted to rest, but not so to the full glory of the kingdom. “The righteous await me,” says the Prophet, while he was still held in the prison of this body, “until you recompense me” (Ps. 141:8). And the divine voice speaks to the souls [lacuna; surviving letters: ctas], demanding the resurrection of their bodies: “Wait a little while, until the number of your brothers is fulfilled” (Rev. 6:11). But now the sermon must be concluded, for the solemnities of the Masses still to be celebrated call us. What remains to be said on this same subject, then, let us reserve for another sermon.

## SERMON III. How Holy Souls Shall Be without Spot and Wrinkle

[Col. 0468D]

1. You have observed, unless I am mistaken, from what was said in the preceding sermon, that there are three states of holy souls: the first in a corruptible body; the second without a body; the third in a body already glorified. The first is in warfare, the second in rest, the third in consummated blessedness; finally, the first is in tents, the second in courts, the third in the house of God. “How lovely are your tents, O Lord of hosts!” Yet the courts are much more desirable, according to what is added: “My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:1–2). But since even in the courts, as you hear, there is some deficiency, they are altogether blessed who dwell [Col. 0469A] in your house, O Lord.

Indeed, brothers, I rejoiced in what was said to me: “We shall go into the house of the Lord.” If you ask from where I presume this so confidently, it is without doubt from this: many of us already stand in the courts, waiting until they receive their bodies, until the number of the brothers is fulfilled. For into that most blessed house they do not enter without us or without their bodies: that is, neither the saints without the people, nor spirits without flesh. For entire blessedness ought not to be bestowed until the whole human being exists to receive it, nor should the Church be endowed with perfection while imperfect. Therefore, when they sought the resurrection of their bodies, as we have already said in the preceding sermon, they received the divine reply: “Wait a little while, until the number of your brothers is completed” (Rev. 6:11). Yet they have already received their single robes; but they shall not be clothed in double robes until we also are clothed, as the Apostle says concerning the patriarchs and prophets: “God having provided something better for us, that they should not be made perfect without us” (Heb. 11:40).

For the first robe is, as we have said, the happiness and rest of souls; the second, the immortality and glory of bodies. Thus they say: “Avenge, O Lord, the blood of your saints which has been shed” (Rev. 6:10), not as persons eager for vengeance nor from zeal for their own retaliation, but from desire for the resurrection and glorification of their bodies, which they do not doubt must be deferred until the day of judgment.

2. But whence is this for you, O wretched flesh, O foul, [Col. 0469C] O fetid flesh—whence is this for you? Holy souls, whom God has marked with his own image, desire you; those whom he redeemed with his own blood await you; and without you their joy cannot be completed, their glory perfected, their blessedness consummated. So powerful indeed is this natural desire in them that their whole affection does not yet freely proceed toward God, but is in some manner contracted and forms a wrinkle while they bend toward desire for you.

Hence blessed John, who through the Spirit disclosed to us many things concerning that state in which blessed souls happily rest, says: “They are without spot before the throne of God” (Rev. 14:5). Without spot, I say, but not yet without wrinkle, until the day comes when Christ presents to himself [Col. 0469D] a glorious Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle. For among those who are still engaged in warfare the Church is not even without spot, because no one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon earth is one day—and blessed Job testifies that this life is warfare (Job 7:1). But among those who rest beneath the Lord’s altar the Church is now without spot, as you have in the Psalm: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tent? Or who shall rest upon your holy mountain? He who walks,” it says, “without spot” (Ps. 14:1–2). Therefore he who walks without spot shall rest upon the Lord’s mountain; but he who is without wrinkle shall be exalted above the mountain.

But if you wish to know when holy souls shall be without wrinkle—when the heavens shall be stretched out like a skin, which is wholly extended [Col. 0470A] and expanded, so that not even the slightest wrinkle is found in it—then certainly this will be when they follow the Lamb wherever he goes. For the souls which must follow the Lamb must indeed be stretched and expanded. For where does he go? He reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly.

3. Do you wish further to know where the Lamb goes, and where blessed souls must follow him? “I have sought rest in all things” (Ecclus. 24:11). This is indeed the Lord’s rest, uninterrupted and confined to no specific object: for he rejoices in all things, delights in all things, seeks and finds rest in all things. For good things please him in themselves, and he is likewise delighted by the good ordering of evils. He loves mercy and judgment; he takes pleasure not only in the glory of the good, but also in the punishments of the wicked themselves, since these are just.

What then? Do you think that the human soul can enter into this joy of its Lord and into this rest of his, so that it too may delight in all things and no longer be contracted into a wrinkle by any private affection, but may pass into a certain general and divine affection? It certainly can, if it is found faithful over the few things which it received during the time of its warfare—that is, over its members, senses, and appetites, which it undertook to govern, so that in these it might be proved how faithful it is to its Lord.

Let Christ’s servant, therefore, know how to possess his vessel in sanctification; let him glorify and bear God in his body. There is no doubt that the generous and rich Lord will appoint the servant faithful in little over [Col. 0470C] many things—indeed, over many things, because he will appoint him ruler of his household and prince over all his possession. Nor should this seem incredible to you, brothers, as though I spoke it from myself, because Truth itself plainly promises it, and his promise cannot possibly be doubted. “Blessed,” he says, “is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, shall find so doing. Amen, I say to you: he shall appoint him over all his goods” (Matt. 24:46–47).

For then the faithful servant is appointed over all his Lord’s goods, when he deserves to enter into his joy and thereafter rejoice with him in the universe, delight in all things, and find pleasure in everything. For one who clings to God, according to the Apostle’s testimony, becomes one spirit with him (1 Cor. [Col. 0470D] 6:17); and his will, wholly adhering to the divine will, becomes one with it, so that nothing contrary to that will is found in all creatures, but all things come to be—or rather, remain—according to his good pleasure.

4. This, then, is the blessed hope for which holy souls wait. And although they are occupied in giving thanks for that happiness in which they now rest, yet they still pray and cry out to God for that consummation which they await. Therefore, just as we said that they are without the blemish of old age, yet not without the wrinkle of contraction, so they seem already to have attained thanksgiving, but not yet the voice of praise; for it befits the Perfect One to praise the perfected, so that he may be praised together with his inheritance, when they too will praise him, and each will have praise from God. [Col. 0471A] Hence the Prophet also seems deliberately to have used a future tense: “Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5).

For blessed John too, in the Apocalypse, heard not a voice of praise but rather a voice of prayer. Thus you have it: “Under the altar of God I heard the voices of the slain.” What voices? “Avenge, O Lord, the blood of your saints which has been shed” (Apoc. 6:10). This is a voice of petition, not of praise. But how long shall we stand at a distance around this altar, and be afraid to approach? Your charity, unless I am mistaken, desires to hear the sacrament of this altar and to know its sacred and hidden mystery. But who am I, rash investigator, that I should dare easily to burst into the chamber of the saints? As though I had not read that the investigator of majesty [Col. 0471B] shall be overwhelmed by glory (Prov. 25:27). Nevertheless, let us pause here today, if you please, in the hope that, when we knock, the holy souls who dwell there may deign to open to us the mystery of that altar—not indeed through our merit, but because of him who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood—recognizing us also among the citizens and household of God, and not judging that we, like strangers and foreigners, should be driven away from that hidden dwelling.

## SERMON IV. On Abraham’s Bosom, the Altar beneath Which Blessed John Heard the Souls of the Saints, and the Seven Loaves from Which an Equal Number of Baskets Are Read to Have Remained

1. When the subject arose of that heavenly altar beneath which blessed John heard the voices of the saints (Apoc. 6:9–10), [Col. 0471C] we postponed discussion, as I believe your charity remembers, so that, prayer having first been offered, a safer access might be opened to us into so sacred and hidden a chamber. It is time now to say what has been given us to think concerning it—without prejudice, of course, should it perhaps have been revealed otherwise to someone else.

The first thing that may perplex us is what blessed John means when he declares that he heard the voices of holy souls beneath God’s altar, whereas the Savior, speaking in the Gospel of Lazarus’s soul, says that it was carried by angels not beneath God’s altar but into Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:22). Saint Job too, it seems, did not dare at all to aspire to God’s altar when he said: “Who will grant me this: that you protect [Col. 0471D] me in hell, and hide me until your wrath passes away, and appoint me a time when you will remember me?” (Job 14:13).

But, brethren, the time had now come for which blessed Job asked: the time of remembrance had come, the time of mercy had come, when blessed John heard the voices of the saints beneath God’s altar. For until that Desired One should come, who by his blood would blot out the bond of our condemnation and, extinguishing the flaming sword, open the kingdoms of heaven to believers, no access at all to them was open to any of the saints. [Col. 0472A] But the Lord had provided for them, in hell itself, a place of rest and refreshment, establishing a great chasm between those holy souls and the souls of the wicked.

> [Note: [Col. 0471D] Augustine opposes this opinion in *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XII, chapter 33, no. 63, where he holds that the ancient righteous were never detained in hell, and that in Scripture the name “hell” properly belongs only to the place of punishments.]

For although both were in darkness, both were not in punishments: the wicked were tormented, while the righteous were comforted. That they were in darkness we learn from the testimony of blessed Job, who declared that he too would go to a dark place covered with the gloom of death (Job 10:21). This place, therefore—dark indeed, but tranquil—the Lord calls Abraham’s bosom, as I think, because it rested in faith and expectation of the Savior. For Abraham’s faith was so manifestly tested and approved that he himself was the first to deserve to receive the promise of Christ’s future incarnation.

Descending into this place, the Savior [Col. 0472B] shattered the brazen gates and broke the iron bars; and, having led the bound ones forth from the prison-house—sitting, that is, resting, yet in darkness and the shadow of death—he then placed them beneath God’s altar, hiding them in his tabernacle in the day of evils and protecting them in the secrecy of his tabernacle, until the time comes when, the number of their brethren now completed, they may come forth and receive the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

If, indeed, the present rest of the saints is ever also called Abraham’s bosom—

> [Note: [Col. 0471D] Bernard himself uses this term in *On Consideration*, book V, [Col. 0472D] no. 9.]

—it is certain that this usage has become established from the Gospel. Yet no one ought to doubt that this bosom is far different from that one: for that was in darkness, this in abundant light; that was in hell, this in heaven. Nevertheless, it does not seem inappropriate even now to say that the children of the patriarchs are received into their father’s bosom when they deserve to pass from this world into their fellowship [variant: “have deserved”].

2. Now the altar itself of which we must speak, so far as I understand, I judge to be nothing other than the very body of the Lord Savior.

> [Note: [Col. 0472D] This is not Bernard’s absolute definition but an opinion, as is clear from no. 1, where he wishes this statement to be understood without prejudice, should it perhaps have been revealed otherwise to someone else. See the preface to this volume, nos. 20 and 21.]

And I believe that I too have his meaning on this point, especially when I hear him promise in the Gospel: “Wherever the body shall be, there the eagles also shall be gathered” (Luke 17:37). Therefore, for the present the saints [variant: “the blessed souls”] rest happily beneath Christ’s humanity, into which even the angels themselves greatly desire to look, until the time comes when they are no longer placed beneath the altar but are exalted above the altar.

[Col. 0472D] But what have I said? Can anyone—not merely a human being, but even an angel—attain, much less surpass, the glory of Christ’s humanity? In what sense, then, have I said that those who now rest beneath the altar will be exalted above the altar? In vision and contemplation, certainly, not in precedence. For the Son, as he promised, will show himself to us (John 14:21), not in the form of a servant but in the form of God. He will also show us the Father and the Holy Spirit, without whose vision nothing could possibly suffice for us; for this is [Col. 0473A] eternal life: that we may know the Father, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom he sent (John 17:3), and, in them—as cannot be doubted—the Spirit of both.

For, passing by, he will minister to us the new delights of his manifest contemplation, delights wholly untried by us until that time. Hence blessed John says in his Epistle: “Now we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be”; and he adds: “But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Finally, hear the bride in the Song of Songs speaking confidently and already, in hope, placed above the altar: “His left hand,” undoubtedly the Bridegroom’s, “is beneath my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6). For the blessed soul transcends Christ’s [Col. 0473B] incarnation and humanity, which is rightly called his left hand, in order that it may contemplate more sublimely his divinity and majesty, which it not inappropriately calls his right hand.

3. For, brethren, in that eternal and perfect blessedness we shall enjoy God in three ways: seeing him in all creatures; possessing him in ourselves; and—what is unspeakably more delightful and blessed than all these—knowing also the Trinity itself in itself, and contemplating with the pure eye of the heart that glory without any enigma. For eternal and perfect life will consist in this: that we may know the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit, and see God as he is—that is, not merely as he is present in us or in other creatures, but as he is in himself.

[Col. 0473C] Hence the two things already mentioned seem to surround this knowledge, as it were, and to be like the husk of wheat; while this knowledge, the summit of blessedness, is the kernel of the wheat, the fat of grain with which the holy city Jerusalem is satisfied (Ps. 147:14). Yet as great as that blessedness is, so hidden is it from our eyes; for neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what brightness, sweetness, and delight await us in that knowledge. It is that peace of God which surpasses all understanding; how much more, then, all our speech? Therefore, let no one attempt to utter what has been granted to no one to experience.

“The measure,” says the Lord, “full, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, they shall give into [Col. 0473D] your bosoms” (Luke 6:38): full through the totality of creatures; pressed down in our inner person; shaken together in the outer person; overflowing in God himself. There is the fullness of happiness; there surpassing glory; there overflowing blessedness.

4. For how he is to be seen in creatures and possessed in ourselves, we can partly conjecture from the firstfruits of the Spirit which we have already received. But that knowledge is still altogether unknown to us: it has become wonderful; it has been strengthened so that we cannot attain to it. Yet we can understand to some extent how he is to be seen in creatures, since even now he is seen in them; and thus, as the Apostle testifies, philosophers beheld God’s invisible things through the things that were made (Rom. 1:20).

But [Col. 0474A] however greatly someone may advance in understanding how mightily, wisely, and benignly eternal Majesty has made all things, governs all things, and orders the universe, he grasps very little of what God is. But the time will come when, as we said in the preceding sermon, we shall follow the Lamb wherever he goes and attain him in all creatures, so that we may rejoice in all things—which is the joy of the Lord our God. Let us indeed rejoice in all things, but from nothing other than him, just as he himself enjoys not other things but himself.

5. We may likewise think, at least in part, how he is to be possessed in ourselves. For it is agreed that souls have a threefold nature. Thus the wise men of this world have taught that the human soul is rational, irascible, and concupiscible; and nature itself, along with daily experience, teaches us this threefold power of the soul. Now, as knowledge and ignorance exist in relation to our rational faculty, like possession and privation, so desire and contempt concern the concupiscible faculty; and joy together with anger pertains to what is called the irascible faculty.

[Col. 0474B] Therefore God will fill our rational faculty with the light of wisdom, so that we shall lack absolutely nothing in any knowledge. He will fill our concupiscible faculty with the fountain of righteousness, so that we may desire righteousness altogether and be wholly filled by it, as it is written: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6). For no other thing can fill the soul’s desire; no other thing besides righteousness can make the soul blessed.

When, therefore, God has filled our concupiscible faculty with righteousness, the soul will reject whatever it ought to reject, desire whatever it ought to desire, and among all things will desire more what ought more to be desired. Rightly, then, we assign righteousness to our concupiscible faculty, since it is from this that we are reckoned either righteous or unrighteous.

And when God has filled what is called the irascible faculty in us, perfect tranquility will exist in us, and we shall be filled with divine peace unto supreme delight and joy. See, then, whether perfect blessedness, at least insofar as the soul is concerned, does not consist even in these three things: when knowledge will no longer inflate because of righteousness, nor grieve because of joy, so that the proverb may cease, [Col. 0474D] “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccles. 1:18); when righteousness will be neither undiscerning because of knowledge nor burdensome because of joy; when joy will be neither foolish [variant: “suspect”] because of knowledge nor impure because of righteousness.

6. But in all these things our outer person has as yet received nothing. Therefore, in order that glory may dwell also in our land (Ps. 84:10), and, according to another prophet, the whole earth may be filled with the majesty of the Lord (Isa. 6:3), four things must be sought for it, since it is known to be composed of four elements. Nor should you wonder that one who is more miserable seems to need more, since you also read in the Psalm the Prophet saying: “My soul thirsted for you; how manifoldly has my flesh [thirsted] for you!” (Ps. 62:2).

Let our land, then, have immortality, [Col. 0475A] so that it need no longer fear being reduced again to dust. For our body, once risen, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over it. But what benefit would it be if one should perhaps live forever amid the miseries and afflictions of this capacity for suffering, by which this corruptible body is continually afflicted, and if it dies not once but always? Let it, then, also at last possess complete impassibility. For they say that the causes of sufferings arise from disordered humors.

But our body now desires lightness too, according to that portion which it has from air, so that it may not be burdensome even by its own weight. Therefore such lightness and agility of the blessed bodies must be believed to be forthcoming that, if they wish, they can follow without any delay or difficulty even the very swiftness of our thoughts [Col. 0475B] wherever they go. What further is lacking for the body’s perfect blessedness? Beauty alone. Since we shall possess this in its highest perfection, we may not unreasonably assign it to the part which we have from fire.

For we await the Savior, as the Apostle says, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory (Phil. 3:20–21), fulfilling what he promised: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43). Thus God will fill our souls when there is perfect knowledge in them, perfect righteousness, and perfect joy. Thus the whole earth will be filled with his majesty when the body is incorruptible, impassible, agile, and finally conformed to the body of his glory.

And perhaps these are the seven [Col. 0475C] loaves with which the Savior is read to have satisfied four thousand men, from which the apostles took up baskets full in the same number to be kept (Matt. 15:32, 38). For now we are refreshed by these loaves when, in joyful meditation, we chew over the blessed hope, until the time comes when, rejoicing no longer in hope but in the reality itself and its manifestation, we may deserve, as it were, to receive full baskets in return for each loaf.

## SERMON V

1. This is a festival day for us, and today’s solemnity is counted among the chief solemnities. What, then, shall we say? Whose apostle, whose martyr, whose saint is it? Not that of any one person alone, but equally of all. For we all know that the feast which we celebrate today is called, and is, the Feast of All Saints. [Col. 0475D] Of all, I say, whether heavenly or earthly. For there are saints of heaven and saints of earth; and among those who are of earth, some are still on earth, while others are already in heaven.

The feast of all these, therefore, is celebrated together, though perhaps not in one uniform manner. Nor is this surprising, since even the holiness of all is not uniform; there is a considerable difference among saints and saints. Nor do I mean merely that one is holier than another—for that is a difference of degree rather than kind—but that we find saints called saints not only more or less so, but in different ways, and rightly so. Perhaps this diversity of holiness and celebration may be assigned respectively to angels and human beings.

[Col. 0476A] For those who are known never to have fought do not seem capable of being honored as triumphants. Yet they too must be honored, but in another manner: as your friends, O God, who have always clung to your will, with as much felicity as readiness. Unless perhaps they are believed to have fought in this: that when others sinned, they steadfastly remained, not walking in the counsel of the wicked, but each saying, “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 72:28). Therefore, in them is to be celebrated grace that went before in the blessing of sweetness; God’s goodness is to be honored, a goodness which does not lead to repentance but leads away from all things for which repentance would be owed; which does not rescue from temptation but preserves from temptation.

2. There is surely another kind of holiness among those who “have come out of great tribulation and have made their robes white in the blood [Col. 0476B] of the Lamb” (Apoc. 7:14): those who, after many contests, now triumph crowned in heaven because they have fought lawfully. Is there still a third class of saints? There is, but it is hidden. For there are saints still engaged in warfare, still fighting; they are still running and have not yet attained.

Perhaps I may seem rash in calling such persons saints; yet I know one of them who did not fear to say to God: “Guard my soul, for I am holy” (Ps. 85:2). So too the Apostle, conscious of the divine mysteries, says more plainly: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. 8:28). This, then, is the diversity of application in the name “holiness”: some are called saints already according to consummation; others only according to predestination as yet.

Such holiness, therefore, is hidden with God; it is enclosed and, in a manner, celebrated in secret. For a human being does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things are reserved uncertain for the future (Eccles. 9:1–2). Let the celebration of these saints, then, be in the heart of God, for the Lord knows who are his and he himself knows whom he chose from the beginning. Let it also be among those ministering spirits sent to minister for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation. We are forbidden to praise a person during his lifetime. For how can praise be secure where life itself is not secure?

[Col. 0476D] “He shall not be crowned unless he has fought lawfully,” says that heavenly trumpet (2 Tim. 2:5). And hear the law of the contest from the mouth of the Lawgiver himself: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). You do not know who will persevere, you do not know who will fight lawfully, you do not know who will receive the crown.

3. Praise the virtue of those whose victory is now certain; extol with devout praises those whose crowns you can safely share in rejoicing. We sang to the saints this night, saying: “Fear the Lord, all his saints” (Ps. 33:10); but not to these. No, I say, we were not exhorting those who have persevered to the end to fear, for it is written: “There shall no longer be fear within our borders.” Rather, we spoke to those saints [Col. 0477A] for whom manifold guarding is necessary because of the multitude of dangers. For their struggle is not against flesh and blood only, but also against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. 6:12).

They certainly need guarding who are attacked in so many ways, not only at close quarters but also from afar. And where there are so many battles outside, fears must not be lacking within; thus it is fittingly said to them: “Fear the Lord, all his saints.” Meanwhile, our whole blessedness is to fear God, as Scripture says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. 28:14). And again the Psalmist says: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways” (Ps. 127:1).

But blessed in a far different way are those in whom perfect charity has cast out fear: they no longer fear while walking in the ways, but rather praise while dwelling in the house, as the same Psalmist says: “Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). Therefore our happiness, our present festival, consists in the fear of God; theirs rather consists in exultation and praise.

4. This is why people are safely praised who no longer live their own life but God’s, for human life is indeed temptation. Yet there is a twofold security in this praise—unless perhaps, on careful consideration, one security appears to be contained within the other. For there is no reason to fear praising those who are most truly and certainly praiseworthy; there is no reason to hesitate to glorify those so absorbed in glory [Col. 0477C] that they cannot at all be moved by our praise. For there is no entrance for vanity where truth has already occupied everything.

“But,” you ask, “what glory do the saints have?” For individual saints do not glorify themselves, since it is written: “Let not your own mouth praise you” (Prov. 27:2). Nor does one praise another in return, because intent and stretched forth toward the praise of the Creator—in whom all their blessedness is laid up—they can never be free for mutual praises. The Prophet says, as we have already recalled above: “Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you.”

Nevertheless, I cannot agree that the saints are without glory, especially because of what the Apostle says: “The momentary and light affliction of our present tribulation [Col. 0477D] works in us, beyond measure unto sublimity, an eternal weight of glory” (2 Cor. 4:17). And the Prophet says: “Visit us with your salvation, that we may see the goodness of your elect, rejoice in the joy of your nation, and be praised together with your inheritance” (Ps. 105:4–5). He does not say, “That you may be praised by your inheritance,” but “together with your inheritance,” so that the praise may be understood to be shared.

If the inheritance itself praises the Lord, who shall praise the inheritance? Let us hear from the Apostle: “Then,” he says, “each shall have praise.” From whom? “From God” (1 Cor. 4:5). Great is the one who gives the praise, and greatly to be desired is that praise. Happy exchange of praise, where both to praise and to be praised are blessed.

5. What need, then, have the saints of our praise? What need have they of our glorification or of this solemnity of ours? [Col. 0478A] What are earthly honors to those whom the heavenly Father honors according to the true promise of his Son? What are our proclamations to them? They are full. It is entirely so, beloved: the saints do not need our honors, nor is anything bestowed upon them by our devotion. Surely, it is our concern, not theirs, that we venerate their memory.

Would you know how much it concerns us? I confess that, in myself, from this remembrance I feel a vehement desire kindled—a threefold desire. It is commonly said: “What the eye does not see, the heart does not grieve for.” My eye is my memory; and to think of the saints is, in a manner, to see them. Thus our portion is in the land of the living—and indeed no small portion—provided that affection, as is fitting, accompanies remembrance. Thus, I say, our citizenship is in heaven; yet not in the same way as theirs. For their substance is there, but our desires; they are there by presence, we by memory.

When shall we too be added to our fathers? When shall we be presented to them in our very being? This is the first desire which the memory of the saints awakens in us—or rather urges—that we may enjoy their most desirable fellowship and deserve to be fellow citizens and fellow lodgers with the blessed spirits: to be mingled with the assembly of patriarchs, the ranks of prophets, the senate of apostles, the numerous armies of martyrs, the colleges of confessors, the choirs of virgins; in short, to be gathered and rejoice together in the communion of all the saints.

6. For the remembrances of individuals are like individual sparks, [Col. 0478C] indeed like most burning torches, setting devout minds aflame so that they thirst for the sight [variant: “sense”] and embrace of those saints. Thus they often count themselves even to be among them, darting their hearts with all eagerness and force, now toward all together, now toward these or those. Otherwise, what negligence, what sloth—indeed, what madness—is it that we do not endeavor, with frequent sighs and most fervent affection, to break away from here and cast our souls into those so blessed companies?

Woe to us for the hardness of our heart! Woe for the sin of the nations, which the Apostle says were without affection! (Rom. 1:31). That Church of the firstborn awaits us, and we neglect her; the saints desire us, and we make little of it; the righteous await us, and we disregard it. Let us at last be stirred up, brethren; let us rise with Christ, seek the things above, and set our minds on the things above. Let us desire those who desire us; let us hasten to those who await us; let us forestall with the desires of our souls those who await us.

For behold, in this communion of ours there is no security, no perfection, no rest; and yet even here, “how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!” Whatever trouble occurs, inward or outward, is made more tolerable by the fellowship itself of brothers so closely akin, with whom we have one heart and one soul toward God. How much sweeter, more delightful, and more blessed will be that unity where no suspicion can exist and no occasion for discord; where perfect charity will bind all together by an indissoluble bond, so that, as the Father and [Col. 0479A] Son are one, so we too may be one in them!

7. Not only the fellowship but also the happiness of the saints is to be desired by us, so that we may seek with most fervent zeal the glory also of those whose presence we desire. For this ambition is not harmful, nor is the pursuit of that glory in any way dangerous. For when we say, “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113:1), this is the voice of the present time, when even the angels cry: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

“Do not touch me,” he says, “for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17). It is a word concerning glory. Certainly the wise Son is the glory of the Father. Therefore glory says: “Do not touch me. Do not seek glory for the present; flee it instead. And take great care that you do not touch me until we come to the Father, where every glorying will at last be secure.” There “my soul shall be praised in the Lord; let the meek hear and rejoice.”

Does not she seem to have heard him say, “Do not touch me; for I have not yet ascended to my Father,” who cries in the Song: “Flee, my beloved, flee” (Song 8:14)? This is what we recalled above: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name.” Thus in the hymn we sing today: “Grant peace to your servants, and to us also glory through all ages,” according, of course, to the angelic distribution.

8. Since human life upon earth is temptation, it is right that on earth a human being should seek not glory but peace: peace with God, peace with the neighbor, peace within oneself. “O Guardian of human beings, why have you set me against you, so that I have become burdensome to myself?” (Job 7:20). For the struggle is close at hand, and the rebellion is internal: a war not civil but domestic, the spirit desiring against the flesh and the flesh against the spirit.

Why is this, unless because you have set me against you? For you are true freedom, life, glory, sufficiency, blessedness; I am poor, wretched, and miserable, confused and humiliated in every way, dead because of sin, sold under sin. Finally, you are perfect and holy delight, and the rest of blessed spirits; from the beginning you placed me opposite Eden—which signifies delight—that is, in labor and misery. Yet you say: “Turn to me with your whole [Col. 0479D] heart.” It is clear that we have turned away, whom you exhort to return; it is clear that we are contrary, whom you call back in order that we may turn.

But how? “In fasting,” he says, “and weeping and mourning” (Joel 2:12). A marvelous thing! Is it in fasting that you dwell, in weeping that you live, in mourning that you abide? All these are far from you; you yourself are very far from them. Your kingdom, assuredly, is in Jerusalem, which you satisfy with the fat of wheat; and there is no mourning or crying there, nor any pain, but rather thanksgiving and the voice of praise. “Let the righteous feast in the presence of God,” he says, “and delight in joy and exultation” (Ps. 67:3).

How, then, shall we turn to him in fasting, weeping, and mourning?
