Or is it that the righteous person finds him in joy and exultation, while one who is not yet righteous finds him only in fastings, weeping, and [Col. 0480A] mourning? Precisely so—but the righteous person who has already deserved the vision, not one who still lives by faith. Certainly the Lord’s words, “I am with him in tribulation” (Ps. 90:15), apply to one who walks by faith, not to one who has now attained to face-to-face vision.

Indeed, both have one head, but it is not displayed to all the members in one and the same way. To some the head is shown shaggy with thorns and bent upon the cross, so that they may alike be humbled and pierced with compunction. To others it appears glorious, so that they may be glorified by it and glory in it, made like him [variant: “that which”] whom they see as he is.

9. This, therefore, is the second desire which the commemoration of the saints kindles in us: that, as Christ appears to them, so he may also appear to us as our life, and that we too may appear with him in glory. Meanwhile our head is represented to us not as he is, but as he was made for us: not crowned with glory but surrounded by the thorns of our sins. Scripture says: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Song 3:11).

[Col. 0480B] O King! O diadem! For his mother, the Synagogue—showing herself not a mother but a stepmother—crowned our king with a crown of thorns. Let the members be ashamed to pursue glory when their head is shown to them so inglorious, having neither form nor beauty nor anything of that kind. Certainly he is Solomon, which means “peaceful”—a term appropriate to the present state—not, indeed, “beatifying” or “glorifying”; so that in all things that angelic pronouncement may be commended, by which they assigned peace to earth and glory to heaven.

Let a member under a thorn-crowned head be ashamed to become delicate, when every purple garment is for it, meanwhile, less an honor than a mockery. Yet today one may see the present day honored in many places with much display and feasting. Shall I say honored, or dishonored? Let those who do these things judge for themselves. Such a celebration belongs to them, not to the saints: they do what pleases themselves, not what pleases the saints.

The time will come when Christ comes and his death will no longer be proclaimed, so that we may know that we too have died and that our life is hidden with him. The glorious head will appear, and with it the glorified members will shine, [Col. 0480D] when he refashions the body of our lowliness, conformed to the glory of the head, which is himself. Therefore let us desire this glory with complete and secure ambition, lest we too hear: “Because you seek glory from one another and do not desire the glory that is from God alone” (John 5:44).

10. Moreover, so that we may be permitted to hope for this glory and aspire to so great a blessedness, we must most earnestly desire the aid of the saints as well, so that what our own capacity does not obtain may be granted us through their intercession. “Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, at least you, my friends” (Job 19:21). You yourselves know our danger; you know our fashioning; you know our ignorance and the deceits of our adversaries; you know their assaults and our [Col. 0481A] frailty. For I speak to you who have been in the same temptation; who overcame the same conflicts and escaped the same snares; who learned compassion from the things you suffered.

Indeed, I trust also concerning the angels that they do not disdain to visit their own likeness, especially since it is written: “You shall visit your likeness, and you shall not sin” (Job 5:24). But although I think I may presume upon them because of the likeness of spiritual substance and rational form, I nevertheless believe that I should turn with greater confidence [variant: “make use”] to those whom I know to be my companions in humanity itself, since they ought to have a more familiar and particular compassion on bone of their bones and flesh of their flesh.

11. Finally, as they passed from this world to the Father, they left us holy pledges. Their bodies, indeed, lie buried among us in peace; their names will live for ever—that is, their glory is never buried. Far be from you, holy souls, that Egyptian cruelty of Pharaoh’s cupbearer, who, restored to his former rank, immediately forgot holy Joseph, held in prison! (Gen. 40). For they were not members of one head, nor was there any partnership of believer with unbeliever, or any fellowship of Israelite with Egyptian, any more than of light with darkness.

[Col. 0482A] For “Egypt” is interpreted “darkness,” but “Israel,” “One who sees God”; and therefore wherever Israel was, there was light. Not so could our Jesus forget the thief crucified with him: what was promised indeed came to pass; on the very day on which he suffered with him, he also reigned with him (Luke 20). And if we too are not members of that same head, of which the saints are members, why do we rejoice for them today with such solemn vows and such great affection? Moreover, he who said, “If one member is glorified, all the members rejoice together,” also said likewise, “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12:26). Thus this is the bond between us and them: we rejoice with them; they suffer with us. We reign in them by devout meditation; they fight in us and for [Col. 0482B] us by their pious intercession. Nor should we doubt their charitable concern for us, since, as we recalled above, they await us, not to be made perfect without us, until recompense is rendered to us; so that, on the last great day of the feast, all the members may together attain to a perfect man with their most exalted head, and Jesus Christ our Lord may be praised with his inheritance—he who is above all, blessed, praiseworthy, and glorious for ages. Amen.

[Col. 0481]

## On the Passing of Saint Malachy, Bishop

[Note: [Col. 0481D] He died in the year 1148. His Life is found in volume II.]

### Sermon I

[Col. 0481C]

1. Today, dearly beloved, a certain abundant blessing has been sent to you from heaven. To fail faithfully to distribute it would be harmful to you, and dangerous to me, to whom this stewardship seems to have been entrusted. Therefore I fear for your loss; I fear for my condemnation, lest it be said: “The little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it to them” (Lam. 4:4). For I know how necessary to you is consolation coming from heaven, since you are known to have stoutly renounced the enticements of the flesh and worldly pleasures.

Let no one doubt that it was a heavenly benefit and fixed by divine counsel that Bishop Malachy should fall asleep among you today and receive among you the burial he desired. Since not even a leaf [Col. 0481D] of a tree falls to the ground without the divine will, who is so dull as not to perceive plainly, in the coming and passing of this blessed man, an altogether great purpose of heavenly mercy? From the ends of the earth he came, to lay his body here in the earth, hastening indeed for another reason, though he is known to have greatly desired this because of his special affection for us. On the journey itself he endured many hindrances, nor was he permitted to cross the sea until the time of his consummation and the term that could not be passed drew near.

We received him, coming to us after many labours, like an angel of God, out of reverence for his holiness. Yet he himself, through his deeply rooted gentleness and humility, received us with devout affection far beyond what we deserved. He then remained with us a few days in health, while awaiting companions who had been scattered through England when the vain suspicion of that king hindered the man of God. Once they had all gathered to him, he was preparing to journey to the Roman curia for which he had come, when he was suddenly overtaken by illness and immediately perceived that he was being summoned rather to the heavenly palace—God providing something better for us, lest, after leaving us, he should reach his end elsewhere.

2. Physicians could perceive in him no sign, not merely of death, but even of grave illness. Yet he, rejoicing in spirit, said that Malachy must by all means depart this life in that year. On the other hand, efforts were made through devout prayers to God and by every means within our power; but [Col. 0482D] his merits prevailed, so that the desire of his heart was granted him and he was not deprived of the wish of his lips. Thus everything concurred according to his prayers: under divine inspiration he had chosen this very place above all, and he had long wished also to have for the day of his burial the day on which the general commemoration of all the faithful is celebrated.

And this also rightly increased our joy: by God’s ordering, the same day had been chosen for us to bring here and reinter the bones of our brethren from the former cemetery.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] At Clairvaux the bones of those first holy monks were once to be seen in an underground chapel, arranged throughout with fitting devotion.]

As we carried them and sang psalms according to custom, that same holy man said that he took great delight in the chant; and not long afterwards he himself followed them, lulled into the sweetest and happiest sleep. Therefore we give thanks to God for all [Col. 0483A] his dispositions: that he willed to honour us unworthy people with the presence of his blessed death; to enrich his poor people with the most precious treasure of his body; and to support us weak people with so great a pillar of his Church. This sign made for our good persuades us of one of two things: either that the place is pleasing to God, or that he wishes to make it pleasing to himself, since he brought a man of such holiness from the ends of the earth to die and be buried here.

3. Yet the very love of this blessed father compels us to grieve more warmly with that people, and to abhor more vehemently the cruelty of death, which did not refrain from inflicting this dreadful wound upon so pitiable a Church. Truly dreadful and inexorable is death, which by one blow has bereaved so great a multitude of people; blind and thoughtless, which bound Malachy’s tongue, hindered his steps, relaxed his hands, and closed his eyes.

Those devoted eyes, I say, which were accustomed by most compassionate tears to reconcile divine grace to sinners; those most pure hands, which had always loved to be occupied in laborious and humble works, which so often offered the saving sacrifice of the Lord’s body for sinners, and were lifted to heaven in prayer without anger or dispute; hands known to have bestowed many benefits upon the sick and shone forth in diverse signs. Those beautiful feet of one proclaiming peace, proclaiming good things; those feet so often wearied in zeal for mercy; those footsteps worthy always to be pressed with devout kisses. Finally, those holy lips of the priest, which [Col. 0483C] kept knowledge; the mouth of the righteous man, which meditated wisdom; and his tongue, which spoke judgment—indeed mercy also—and was accustomed to heal such great wounds of souls.

Nor is it surprising, brothers, that death should be unjust, since iniquity begot it; or thoughtless, since deceit is known to have produced it. It is no surprise, I say, if it strikes without discrimination, since it came from transgression; if it is cruel and foolish, since it proceeded from the deception of the ancient serpent and the folly of the woman. Why, however, do we complain that it dared to assail Malachy, a faithful member of Christ, when it likewise violently assailed Malachy’s head, the head of all the elect? It assailed one who was immune, but did not itself emerge immune. Death struck life, and life enclosed death within itself; death was swallowed up by life. By swallowing its own hook, it began to be held precisely where it seemed to have held.

4. But perhaps someone will say: “How does death appear conquered by the head, when it still rages with such freedom against the members? If death is dead, how did it kill Malachy? If it is defeated, how does it still prevail over all, and why is there no human being who lives and does not see death?” Death—the devil’s work and sin’s penalty—has certainly been conquered; sin, the cause of death, has been conquered; the Evil One himself, author of sin and death, has been conquered. And these things have not merely been conquered: they have already been judged and condemned. The sentence has indeed been determined, but not yet promulgated. Fire is already prepared for the devil, although he has not yet been cast into the fire; for a little while he is still permitted [Col. 0484A] to work evil.

He has been made like the hammer of the heavenly craftsman, “the hammer of the whole earth”: he crushes the elect for their benefit and crushes the reprobate for their condemnation. Such as the master of the household is, such are his servants: namely sin and death. For sin too, although it is not doubted that it was nailed with Christ to his cross, was nevertheless allowed still, for the time being, not to reign but to dwell even in the Apostle while he lived. I lie if he himself did not say: “It is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Rom. 7:17). Thus death itself is by no means compelled yet to be absent, but it is compelled not to harm. Yet the time will come when it shall be said: “Where, O death, is your victory?” (1 Cor. 15:55). For it too, the last enemy, shall be destroyed.

But now, under the governance of him who has power over life and death and restrains even the sea within the fixed bounds of its shores, death itself is a sleep of refreshment for the Lord’s beloved, as the Prophet testifies: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126:2–3). The death of sinners is indeed most evil, for their birth is evil and their life worse; but “precious is the death of the saints” (Ps. 115:15). Precious indeed: as the end of labours, the completion of victory, the gateway of life, and the entrance into perfect security.

5. Let us therefore rejoice, brothers; let us rejoice, as is fitting, for our father. For it is devout to lament Malachy dead, but more devout to rejoice with Malachy living. Does he not live? And blessedly so. To the eyes of the foolish he appeared to die, [Col. 0484C] but he is in peace. Now at last a fellow citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household, he sings psalms and gives thanks, saying: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment” (Ps. 65:12). He passed indeed manfully, and he passed through happily.

A true Hebrew, he celebrated Passover in spirit, and as he passed he spoke to us: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover among you.” He passed through fire and water: neither hardships could break him nor comforts detain him. Beneath us is a place which fire wholly claims for itself, so that the miserable rich man there could not obtain even the smallest drop of water from Lazarus’s finger. Above is the city of God, which is gladdened by the rush of a river, the torrent of delight, the exceedingly splendid cup that intoxicates. Between these, indeed, lies the knowledge of good and evil; here one experiences both pleasure and tribulation. Unhappy Eve brought us into these alternations. Here indeed are day and night; in hell there is only night, and in heaven only day. Blessed, therefore, is the soul that passes through both, neither clinging to pleasure nor failing in tribulation.

6. I think I should briefly recount to you one of this man’s many great deeds, in which he is known to have passed bravely through both fire and water. The tyrannical offspring of a family had claimed for itself the metropolitan see of the great Patrick, apostle of the Irish, making itself archbishops by hereditary succession and possessing the sanctuary of God as an inheritance. Asked therefore by the faithful to oppose such great evils, our Malachy, placing his soul in his hands, came forward without fear and assumed the archbishopric, exposing himself to manifest danger in order to end so great a crime. Amid dangers he governed the Church; after those dangers he immediately canonically ordained another as his successor.

For he had accepted it on this condition: that, when the frenzy of persecution had ceased and another could safely be appointed, he would be permitted to return to his own see. There, without ecclesiastical or secular revenues, dwelling in the religious communities which he himself had founded, living among them as one of them, he lived until this time without any private property. Thus the fire of tribulation tested the man of God but did not consume him, for he was gold; nor did enticement hold or weaken him. Nor did he, a curious onlooker, halt upon the road, forgetful of his own pilgrimage.

7. Which of you, brothers, would not ardently desire to imitate his holiness, if one dared even hope for it? I believe, therefore, that you will listen more gladly if we can perhaps say what made Malachy holy. Yet lest our testimony perhaps seem less acceptable, hear Scripture saying: “In his faith and gentleness he made him holy” (Ecclus. 45:4). By faith he trod down the world, as John testifies when he says: “This is the victory that conquers the world: our faith” (1 John 5:4). In a spirit of gentleness he bore every harsh and adverse thing with an even mind. Thus, after Christ, by faith he trod upon the seas, lest he be caught by their allurements; and in patience he possessed his soul, lest he be broken by troubles.

Of these two things you have in the psalm: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand” (Ps. 90:7): for the deceptions of prosperity cast down many more than the scourges of adversity. Therefore, dearly beloved, let none of us, delighted by the smooth surface of the gentler path [variant: “wave”], judge that sea-route [variant: “greatest”] more convenient for himself. This plain has great mountains, invisible indeed, but for that very reason more dangerous. Perhaps the way through the steepness of hills and ruggedness of rocks seems more laborious; but those who have experienced it find it far safer and more desirable.

Yet he knew that there is labour and danger on both sides, who said: “Through the weapons of righteousness, on the right hand and on the left” (2 Cor. 6:7). Rightly, therefore, do we rejoice for those who have passed through fire and water and have been brought into refreshment. Do you wish to hear of refreshment? Would that another might speak of it to you! For I cannot pour forth what I have not tasted.

8. Yet today I seem to hear Malachy speaking of this refreshment: “Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you; for he has delivered my soul from death” (Ps. 114:7–8), and so forth. Hear briefly what I understand by these words. The day has already declined, and the sermon has gone on longer than I had hoped. I am unwilling to be torn away from the sweetness of a father’s name, and my tongue fears to be silent concerning Malachy and shrinks from bringing itself to an end.

The death of the soul, my brothers, is sin—unless perhaps you have forgotten what you read in the prophet: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:[Col. 0486A]4). There is, therefore, a threefold cause for rejoicing in one liberated from every sin, labour, and danger. Henceforth sin is not said to dwell in him; no mourning of repentance is imposed upon him; nor is he told that he must thereafter beware of any fall. Elijah laid aside his cloak: there is nothing for him to fear, nothing by which he fears he may be touched, much less held, by the adulteress. He mounted the chariot: he need no longer tremble lest he fall. He ascends pleasantly, flying not by his own labour but seated in a swift vehicle.

To this refreshment, dearly beloved, let us run with the whole eagerness of our souls, in the fragrance of the ointments of this blessed father of ours, who today seems to have stirred our sluggishness into most fervent desire. Let us run after him, crying to him more often: “Draw us after you”; and let us give devout thanks, both in affection of heart and in progress of life, to almighty mercy, because he has willed that his unworthy servants, who lack merits of their own, should at least not lack the aid of another’s merits.

### Sermon II

1. It is clear, dearly beloved, that while we are held in the body we are away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6); and therefore our pitiable exile and consciousness of sins impose mourning upon us rather than joy. Yet because the apostolic voice exhorts us to rejoice with those who rejoice (Rom. 12:15), the time and the occasion require us to be stirred to every joy. For if, as the Prophet perceived, “the righteous rejoice in the presence of God” (Ps. 67:4), then Malachy undoubtedly rejoices, he who pleased God in his days and was found righteous. In holiness and righteousness he ministered before him: his ministry was pleasing, and the minister also was pleasing.

Why should he not have pleased God? Without cost to others he set forth the Gospel; he filled his country with the Gospel; he especially subdued the deadly barbarism of his fellow-countrymen, the Irish; by the light yoke of Christ, wielding the sword of the Spirit, he subjected foreign nations, restoring God’s inheritance to him even to the ends of the earth. O fruitful ministry! O faithful minister! Was not the Father’s promise fulfilled to the Son through him? Was this not the man whom the Father long ago regarded when he said to the Son: “I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. 2:8)? How gladly the Saviour received what he had purchased—and had purchased at the price of his blood, the shame of the cross, and the horror of his Passion! [Col. 0486D] How gladly he received it from the hands of Malachy, because he ministered without charge! Thus, in the minister, the gratuitous gift was pleasing; in the ministry, the conversion of sinners was pleasing. In the minister, I say, simplicity of eye was grateful and pleasing; in the ministry, the salvation of the people.

2. Even if the ministry had produced less effect, nevertheless God would rightly have looked upon Malachy and his works—he for whom purity is beloved and simplicity familiar; whose justice it is to weigh the work by the intention and to judge the whole state of the body from the quality of the eye. But now great are the works of the Lord, wrought in accordance with every will and effort of Malachy: great, many, and very good, though better still because they sprang from the good source of a chaste intention. What work of piety passed Malachy by? Poor for himself, he was rich for the poor. He was father of orphans, husband to widows, and protector of the oppressed. A cheerful giver, rarely a petitioner, a modest recipient. He took the greatest care, and showed great effectiveness, in restoring peace among the discordant.

Who was equally compassionate in feeling with others, prompt in bringing aid, and free in rebuking? For he was zealous, yet knowledge, the moderator of zeal itself, was not lacking. He became weak with the weak, but was nonetheless powerful with the powerful; he resisted the proud, scourged tyrants, and was teacher of kings and princes. It was he who, by prayer, took sight from a king acting wickedly and restored it when he had been humbled. It was he who frustrated the violators of a peace he had made—those handed over to a spirit of error—in the evil they intended to do, [Col. 0487B] and again compelled them to peace, ashamed and astonished at what had happened to them.

It was he for whom, against other equally covenant-breaking men, a stream most dutifully appeared, marvellously thwarting the designs of the wicked by placing itself in their way. There had been no rains, no flood of waters, no gathering of clouds, no melting snow; when suddenly the little stream became a great river. The stream flowed, swelled into a flood, and wholly denied passage to those wishing to work evil.

3. How much have we heard and learned concerning the man’s zeal and the punishment of his enemies, though he was gentle, mild, and full of mercy toward all who suffered need! Like the one parent of all, he lived for all; as a hen cherishes her chicks, so he cherished everyone and protected them beneath the covering of his wings. Neither sex, age, condition, nor person was distinguished: no one was neglected, for the bosom of his compassion was opened to all. Whatever tribulation brought an appeal to him, he regarded as his own—except that he was patient in his own sufferings, compassionate in those of others, and often even impatient.

For at times, filled with zeal, he was moved against some on behalf of others, so that by rescuing the poor and restraining the powerful he might thus provide for everyone’s salvation. Therefore he was angry, but lest he sin by not being angry [variant: “lest he sin by being angry”], according to the psalm: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5), anger did not rule him; he ruled his own mind. He possessed mastery of himself. Truly victorious over himself, he could not be overcome by anger. His anger was in his hand. Called, it came; departing, it did not burst forth; it was directed by a nod, not by an impulse. He was not burned by it, but used it.

Great was his careful discipline and circumspection, both in this matter and in governing or restraining all the movements of his inner and outer person. For he did not attend to everyone else in such a way as to expose himself alone, or alone to except himself from the common care. He was attentive also to himself. He guarded himself. Thus he was wholly his own and wholly everyone’s, so that neither charity hindered or delayed his self-guardianship, nor personal concern hindered or delayed his service of the common good in anything. If you saw him immersed amid crowds and entangled in cares, you would say that he had been born for his country, not for himself. If you saw him alone and dwelling with himself, you would suppose that he lived for God alone and for himself.

[Col. 0488A] 4. He moved amid crowds without disturbance; he spent without idleness the time that he had given to leisure. How was he idle when he was exercised in the Lord’s ordinances? Even if he had time free from the necessities of the people, it was not vacant from holy meditations, the labour of prayer, or the leisure of contemplation. In time of leisure his speech was either serious or absent altogether. His gaze was either serviceable, or lowered and restrained within himself. For, as is counted no slight praise among the wise, “his eye was in his head” (Eccles. 2:14), never wandering except when it obeyed virtue.

His laughter either showed charity or invited it, though it was itself rare. It was occasionally drawn forth, never shaken out; it announced the joy of his heart in such a way as not to diminish the grace of his countenance, but to increase it. It was so modest that it could not be suspected of frivolity, yet so slight that it sufficed to preserve a cheerful face from every mark or cloud of sadness. O perfect offering! O rich burnt-offering! O service pleasing in mind and hand! How sweet a fragrance to God are the prayers of one at leisure; how sweet to human beings are the labours of one occupied!

5. Therefore, beloved by God and human beings for such qualities, Malachy is deservedly received today into the fellowship of angels, attaining in reality what he was called by name. Even before, he was an angel no less in purity than in name; but now the interpretation of his glorious name is fulfilled in him more happily, since he rejoices in equal glory and blessedness with the angels. Let us therefore rejoice, brothers, let us rejoice as is fitting, for our father. For it is devout to lament Malachy dead, [Col. 0488C] but more devout to rejoice with Malachy living. Does he not live? And blessedly so. To the eyes of the foolish he appeared to die, but he is in peace. Now at last a fellow citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household, he sings psalms and gives thanks, saying: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. 65:12). He passed indeed manfully, and he passed through happily.

A true Hebrew, he celebrated Passover in spirit, and as he passed he spoke to us: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover among you.” He passed through fire and water, whom neither hardships could break nor comforts detain. Let us rejoice that our angel has ascended to his fellow citizens, acting as ambassador for the children of captivity, conciliating the hearts of the blessed toward us and conveying to them the prayers of the miserable. Let us rejoice, I say, and exult, because that heavenly court has one from among us who cares for us, protects us by his merits, formed us by his examples, and confirmed us by miracles.

6. The holy bishop, who in a spirit of humility had frequently carried peace-offerings into heaven, entered today through himself to the altar of God, himself both sacrifice and priest. As the priest departed, the rite of sacrifice was changed for the better: the fountain of tears was dried up, and the whole burnt-offering is seasoned with joy and exultation. Blessed be the Lord, the God of Malachy, who through the ministry of so great a bishop visited his people and now, having taken him into the holy city, does not cease to console our captivity by the remembrance of such great sweetness.

Let the spirit of Malachy rejoice in the Lord, because, freed from the weight of bodily mass, he is no longer weighed down by any foul or earthly matter, and may therefore, with all liveliness and vigour, pass beyond every bodily and incorporeal creature, proceed wholly into God, and, cleaving to him, be one spirit with him for ever.

7. Holiness befits this house, in which the memory of such great holiness is celebrated. Holy Malachy, preserve it in holiness and righteousness; have mercy on us, who amid so many and such great miseries pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness. Great is the dispensation of divine mercy concerning you: he who made you little in your own eyes made you great in his; he who did great things through [Col. 0489B] you, saving your country, did great things for you, bringing you into his glory. May your feast, which is rightly offered in votive observance of your virtues, become saving for us through your merits and prayers. The glory of your holiness, which is celebrated by us and continued by angels, will then fittingly delight us if it is also fruitful for us. As you depart, allow us to retain some relics from the fruits of the Spirit with which you ascend; we are gathered today at your so delightful banquet.

8. We ask you, holy Malachy, be for us another Moses or another Elijah, imparting to us also from your spirit; for you came in their spirit and power. Your life is a law and discipline of life; your death, a harbour from death and a gate of life; your remembrance, the sweetness of grace and delight; your presence, a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord your God. O fruitful olive tree in the house of God! O oil of gladness, anointing and shining, cherishing through benefits and flashing through miracles! Make us participants in that light and sweetness which you enjoy.

O fragrant lily, sprouting and flowering eternally before the Lord, spreading everywhere the life-giving fragrance of sweetness—your memory among us is in blessing, your presence among those above is in honour—grant that those who sing of you may not be deprived of a share in so great a fullness. O great luminary and light shining in darkness, illuminating the prison by the rays of signs and merits, gladdening the city: [Col. 0490B] drive from our hearts, by the splendours of virtues, the darkness of vices. O morning star, brighter than the rest because nearer to the Day [variant: “God”], more like the sun! Deign to go before us, that we too may walk in the light as children of light and not children of darkness. O dawn breaking over the earth, yet illuminating the higher regions of heaven with midday light! Receive us into the fellowship of the light by which, illumined, you shine widely without and burn sweetly within; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0489]

## On the Feast of Saint Martin, Bishop: Sermon on Examples of Obedience

[Col. 0489C]

1. I think that both this assembly of yours and the arrival of these honourable persons, whose presence from afar we rejoice to welcome, demand a sermon from us. Indeed, I myself would more gladly listen to them; but since they choose—indeed rather require—that I speak, if I am not permitted to hear them, they must necessarily obey me. Their great gentleness itself is a living sermon for us: holier by merits, higher by rank, richer in wisdom, they have deigned to come down not only to visit us, but even to hear us. This is effective instruction and teaching worthy of all acceptance. For they admonish us, not in word and tongue but in deed and truth, to be imitators of them as they are of Christ, and to learn what they themselves surely learned from him: to be gentle and humble of heart.

Thus Mary sought Elizabeth (Luke 1:39–40): a virgin sought a married woman; the mistress, a handmaid; the mother of the Judge, the mother of his forerunner; the Mother of God, the mother of a servant. Thus later Jesus himself also came to John, and came to be baptized, because it was fitting for him to fulfil all righteousness (Matt. 3:13, 15). You also, reverend fathers, do not make your own part inferior to yourselves [variant: “you make our part inferior to us”]: for you are swifter to hear than to speak, even among those who stood in greater need of your instruction. As for us, because we cannot fulfil all righteousness, we take care at least to render you some measure of it, knowing well that it is just for an inferior to obey superiors.

[Col. 0490C]

2. But of what shall we speak? “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth,” says that voice of one crying out (John 3:31). Therefore let us speak of the earth, because we subsist from the earth and upon the earth. Listen, all you earthborn and children of men: we speak to you and about you. In the earth we are born, upon the earth we remain, into the earth we die, returning to that from which we were taken. Here our entrance is narrow, our stay brief, and death alone certain. All Adam is compelled to bear the judgment he deserved. He has spread exceedingly, multiplied, and filled the earth. Yet whether he will or not, however greatly he rebels, he still bears universally the sentence he received: “You are earth,” it says, “and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

A heavy sentence indeed, but not without the moderation of great mercy; exceedingly harsh, yet, if you consider the deserts, full of indulgence. For the sinner might no less justly have been told: “You are earth, but henceforth you shall go beneath the earth.” Even then the Lord would be righteous indeed and exceedingly praiseworthy. Worthy certainly to be praised—but I would not be fit to praise him. Otherwise, even then I would nonetheless truly say, if only I could say it: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Ps. 118:137). But hell will not confess you, nor will death praise you; rather, we who live bless the Lord.

You therefore spared your creature and spared the glory of your name, so that you did not permit the man descending from Jerusalem to be carried all the way to Jericho. Left half-alive on the road, I can still give you half-praise (Luke 10:30); when I shall live wholly, there I shall wholly burst forth into praise, and all my bones shall say: “O Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. 34:10). For this reason, when you had been angry, you remembered mercy: not condemning humanity in the place of perdition, but humbling it in the place of affliction. Why do you complain, O human being? Why do you protest that the sentence is too harsh? You are assigned to earth, made from earth, so that it may be your homeland—the very material from which you were made.

3. “But,” you say, “I would rather hear: ‘You are spirit, and to spirit you shall go.’” For I too am spirit, insofar as the soul is concerned; and I would not doubt that this part of me is the better. I have heard indeed from the Apostle that “the Lord is Spirit” (2 Cor. 3:17), and from the Lord himself that “God is spirit” (John 4:24). Nor is he only Spirit, but also Father of spirits. Why then does the mother of flesh hold me, because I am in part flesh, while the Father of spirits does not receive me, though I am in part spirit?

I know, I know: this is caused not so much by substance itself as by guilt. For just as sinful spirits occupy this windy middle region between heaven and earth, whence they are called “powers of the air” (Eph. 2:2), so our sins separate us from God—between the Creator and Father of spirits and his spiritual creature. The body has drawn the soul into its own region; and behold, prevailing, it oppresses the exile. It has become a talent of lead, but only because iniquity sits upon it. For the body weighs down the soul—but the body which is corruptible (Wis. 9:15); and it is corruptible, indeed, as the Apostle testifies, even dead because of sin (Rom. 8:10).

Thus, although in some sense a human being is heaven, undoubtedly similar to heavenly spirits both in form and in substance—substance, because spiritual; form, because rational—these two features are now by no means sufficient to raise the human being so that he deserves to hear: “You are heaven, and into heaven you shall go.” In vain does one boast of freedom of choice, which is in the mind: one is led captive into the law of sin, which is in the flesh. For even if perhaps a double cord might seem able to prevail over another equally double cord—so that the one whom earth claims for itself by a kind of twofold right, as both homeland and material, might nevertheless be received by heaven as heavenly because of the aforementioned twofold likeness, namely of substance and form—yet the lower cord, drawing downward, has now become threefold by the addition of sin. Unless grace also comes to meet it from the other side, it will not be broken. But when grace is present, there is no doubt that this heavy cord of iniquity by which we are drawn—indeed, which we ourselves draw—will easily be loosened. For grace does not intervene between us and God to separate, but to restore and unite.

4. Therefore I will go to the mountain of grace and the hills of mercies, all whose treasures, I hear, are laid up with Christ. I will go to him who is full of grace and truth, if perhaps I may receive something from that fullness—or rather, if perhaps I may be received into that fullness—so that I may one day, together with the other members, attain to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. For no one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven [Col. 0492A] (John 3:13). Truly he is a most faithful and most gracious mediator, who did not divide but made both one, breaking down the middle wall of partition (Eph. 2:14), forgiving us all our offenses, blotting out the handwriting of the decree that stood against us and was contrary to us; he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross; stripping principalities and powers, he made a public display of them, triumphing over them openly (Col. 2:13–15), and through his blood making peace for things in heaven and things upon earth (Col. 1:20).

For the sake, indeed, of this salvation which he was to work in the midst of the earth, he did not immediately place man beneath the earth, as man had deserved by sinning, but upon the earth. For we must be given breathing-space and must in no way despair, while we are still placed upon earth [Col. 0492B] and can look up to heaven and receive every good gift and every perfect gift from above, from the Father of lights, the Father of spirits, the Father of mercies. For this reason too he made man upright, even in his very body, and gave man a face raised on high, while all other living creatures look downward upon the earth: so that, lifting his countenance toward the stars, he might sigh for that place where he beholds so blessed and enduring a dwelling.

5. For surely, to us who look with piety and faith, is not the very sight of so radiant a region a most powerful incentive to love and a summons to most ardent desire? The stars of heaven are not like clods of earth. There is no slight distance between the splendor of the sun and the darkness of this soil. Perhaps, however, even here [Col. 0492C] some things appear beautiful, though beautiful only in their own kind; and these themselves are everywhere mixed with what is not beautiful, like gold in mud, a jewel in dung, a lily among thorns. “You are wholly beautiful, my country, and there is no stain in you”: wholly beautiful, apart from that which lies hidden within. What is that? Namely, those blessed angelic spirits and the souls of the saints themselves, who have already deserved to enter into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God.

For just as there are earthly bodies and heavenly bodies, though the glory of heavenly bodies is far different from that of earthly ones, so too there are heavenly spirits and earthly spirits, and the distance between them is no less: angels, archangels, virtues, principalities, powers, dominations, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. I know the names well. Perhaps that is the whole of it [Col. 0492D]. For what more can an earthborn person grasp of heavenly things, a fleshly human being of spiritual and divine things? Yet even if I do not know what lies hidden under these great titles, I know with utter certainty that something great and wonderful is enclosed and sealed beneath this lofty majesty of words. Not without reason is this called heaven: something altogether extraordinary, I know not what, is concealed in it. It is concealed, I say, but it is by no means denied to faith. For while we are on earth we are granted to see the outward beauty of heaven, though not to enter it; and concerning the inward glory of its mysteries, although I cannot comprehend it, I am nevertheless granted to hear. We see our homeland, but greet it from afar; we smell those delights, but do not taste them.

6. Indeed, not without reason does the Only-Begotten, who is [Col. 0493A] in the bosom of the Father, himself declare to us, in this region of the shadow of death which we inhabit, the glory of the heavenly spirits by faith, but display that of bodies to sight. “Hear, O daughter,” he says, “and see.” And it came to pass. To what end is this? “Incline,” he says, “your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44:11). He wishes us to lay aside stubbornness, learn obedience, and lay hold of discipline. He also wishes us to forget what lies behind, despise what is below, abandon earthly habits and native vices [or, corrupted offspring], to savor heavenly things, seek what is above, and yearn for what lies before us. He wishes the free-born creature to desire intensely that beauty of his house, so that she may be transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord; and [Col. 0493B] consequently that the king too may desire her beauty—spiritual beauty, assuredly.

“But in what,” you ask, “does that sight or hearing instruct and urge me to incline my ear and obey?” For that it produces desire is evident.

7. Consider, then, how all this glory of the heavenly bodies obeys the divine laws unceasingly, never exceeding the limits of time appointed for them amid such constant movements, nor transgressing the established bounds of place. Hear also that the spirits themselves, so exalted, are all ministering spirits, sent forth for ministry—a ministry most worthy, lest I call it unworthy. Yet I think you will never find in the Scriptures that any one of them either contradicted the one sending him or was even slightly troubled toward those so far beneath himself, for whose service he was sent [Col. 0493C]. If you attend carefully, these are examples of obedience, all the more acceptable because they belong to a more worthy subject.

But I know what human feeling murmurs against these things, and what the thought ever prone to evil says: “Why do you set before me the obedience of the heavenly elements? As though they possessed any perception or any active deliberation of reason, rather than seeming to be acted upon instead of acting. And why do you so commend the obedience of the angels themselves? Angels do indeed perceive, but only delightful things; they obey their Creator, certainly, but with a will as happy as it is easy. Why should they not obey? For they always behold the face of the Father, whom to behold is perfect blessedness, eternal glory, and supreme delight.”

[Col. 0493D] 8. Bring forth for us, Lord, patriarchs and prophets, men obedient to your commands: obedient willingly, obedient against their own will. It is done. Abraham is presented to us—passing over the others for brevity’s sake—Abraham, I say, is presented to us: at the Lord’s command leaving his land, casting out the handmaid and her son, and ready even to sacrifice his dearest son Isaac. What can human cleverness cavil at here?

Perhaps it will answer that God appeared to him in many and various ways, was received as a guest, shared his meal, strengthened him by conversation, instructed him with counsel, granted him children, illumined him with victories, and heaped riches upon him. What will you say when Christ comes, made obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross? [Col. 0494A] “Much,” it replies, “in every respect. For when should I presume to emulate Christ, the Only-Begotten of God the Father, the power of God and the wisdom of God? He was offered because he himself willed it; he suffered when and as much as he willed, being truly man indeed, but nonetheless truly God.”

Indeed, I would prefer that you not bring forward even the obedience of the apostles. For in accordance with the prophetic promise, they are known to have seen their teacher with their own eyes and heard with their own ears his admonishing voice (Isa. 30:20–21). Thus one of them writes more explicitly: “What we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon, and what our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). Why should they not leave everything? Why should they not follow in all things the presence of such great majesty? What would I not do if the same abundance were granted me? [Col. 0494B] But he has not dealt thus with every nation—not, to be sure, with one that went before him, nor with one that followed him. For just as many kings desired to see and did not see, so days have now come when we shall long to see one day of the Son of Man and yet shall not deserve it.

9. Martin therefore now comes suitably into the midst, that the occasion of sins may be removed from the midst. For today he is in every respect like us, plainly perceptible and capable of suffering; far removed too from those times of patriarchal and prophetic visions; a mere man, possessing nothing of the divine nature, yet believing in him whom he did not see; full of the fruit of obedience and rich in virtues. He left the soil and entered heaven, entrusting to earth what he had from earth; directing his spirit to the Father of spirits, whom he faithfully served in the spirit of adoption [Col. 0494C]. He was not a heavenly body, nor even a heavenly spirit: a rational animal, mortal too, earthborn, a son of man. He was born on earth, brought up on earth, exercised and tested on earth, and on earth also brought to perfection. Nor was he a patriarch or one of the prophets, concerning whom Truth itself says in the Gospel: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Matt. 11:13). Much less was he Christ; yet Christ was in him, assuredly in no other way than through faith.

10. Indeed, in this manner the word is even now near you, in your heart and in your mouth (Deut. 30:14), provided only that you seek it with an upright heart. For, as the Apostle interprets it, this is the word of faith of which Moses speaks (Rom. [Col. 0494D] 10:8). Thus the same apostle says elsewhere: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Heb. 13:8). “Yesterday” means from the beginning of the world until the Lord’s Ascension; “today,” from then until the consummation of the age; and “forever,” after the common resurrection of all. Christ is absent from none of these; Jesus is absent from none; anointing is absent from none; salvation is absent from none. He was shown to patriarchs and prophets in vision, to the apostles in humanity, to Martin in faith, and to the angels already in sight.

He promised that he would show this sight also to all the elect—not indeed today, but forever. Finally, “yesterday” had already passed and our “today” had already dawned when the Apostles said: “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus” (2 Cor. 5:16). Yet it seems that even in this morning something of the flesh of the Lamb has been kept over; but what remains is now given to the fire: namely, that this same flesh is still offered to us today, yet spiritually and not carnally [Col. 0495A].

11. Nor should we complain that our age has been denied either the manifestation made to the fathers of the Old Testament or the bodily presence shown to the apostles. For those who consider faithfully will clearly see that neither is absent from us. Even now the true substance of his flesh is present to us, undoubtedly in the sacrament. Revelations too are present, but in spirit and power, so that it may be proved that no grace is lacking in any respect to this present age of grace. For “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him”; yet to us he has revealed them through his Spirit [Col. 0495B].

Nor should you wonder that he gave bodily manifestations to those who awaited his bodily coming. For a grace more effective and a revelation more worthy are necessary for us, inasmuch as what we await is known to be more excellent.

12. Thus, as we said above, Martin was not Christ, but he possessed Christ: not as angels possess him in the presence of majesty; not as the apostles possessed him in the sight of his humanity; not as he formerly spoke in vision to his saints; but as the Church possesses him even now, in faith and sacraments. “He was not the light” (John 1:8), but plainly a burning [Col. 0495C] and shining lamp (John 5:35)—said concerning John. But if I bring him forward, I think you will say: “He is the greatest of men, more than a prophet; he is even an angel of God the Father, as he himself testifies: ‘Behold, I send my angel’” (Luke 7:27), and so forth.

Martin too was a burning and shining lamp. At least do not shrink from imitating him; but imitate in him what is imitable, not what is presented as wonderful. Today you sit at a rich man’s table: carefully consider what is set before you. Distinguish between the foods and the vessels containing the foods. You are commanded to take the former, not the latter. This Martin is rich: rich in merits, rich in miracles, rich in virtues, rich in signs. Therefore carefully consider what is set before you: namely, what is for admiration and what for imitation. Or rather, since the Scripture continues, “for you ought to prepare such things” (Prov. 23:1–2, according to the Septuagint), carefully consider what is set before you and in what manner.

Martin raised three dead persons, as many as he had read that the Savior raised. He restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, movement to the lame, health to those whose limbs were withered. By divine power he escaped dangers; with the protection of his own body he repelled flames; with a column likewise descending from heaven he cast down the immense mass of a sacrilegious engine; with a kiss he cleansed a leper; with oil he healed a paralytic; he conquered demons, saw angels, and foresaw the future [Col. 0495D].

13. But these and the rest of his sublime deeds—why should I not call them splendid vessels of this rich man, heavy with gold, gleaming with gems, precious alike in material and workmanship? Do not seek flavor in them, but admire their brilliance [Col. 0496A]. Let our light shine in such a lamp, so that in its light we may see the light which, pure as it is in itself, you are not yet able to behold. For he is not that light, but bears witness to the light; and meanwhile God may appear glorious to you in his saint, while you cannot attain to his glory as it is in himself.

Yet do not suppose that Martin’s lamps are adorned but found empty: he is not a foolish virgin; he has oil in his vessels. He has wine in his bowls; within these dishes he has an abundance of food—spiritual delights—so that not only may people see and marvel, but the poor may eat and be satisfied; that in the former they may praise the Lord, and in the latter their hearts may live. Otherwise, how shall the dead praise you, O Lord? Therefore, that praise may be delightful and beautiful in admiration, let them also live through imitation; and that they may take the delights more eagerly, let them contemplate the riches themselves more attentively.

Thus we must move back and forth between the splendor and the heat of this lamp with a kind of alternating affections, so that each may commend the other to us and each become more pleasing through their mutual comparison [Col. 0496B]. For this Martin was humble and poor in spirit, as the very effect of divine grace, which certainly would not have been given in such abundance except to one exceedingly humble, most clearly proves.

14. Yet, to set forth a few indications of his virtues: blessed Hilary knew him poor in spirit when, attempting to impose upon him the office of deacon and failing because Martin declared himself unworthy, he ordered him to be an exorcist [Col. 0496C]. This might seem in some respect an affront, since he knew that Martin would by no means reject the humbler ordination. He was poor, shabbily clothed, unkempt in hair, and unattractive in appearance. Although some ill-disposed persons raised these very things against him at his election, yet, as it is written, he changed them not at all even in his episcopate (Sulpicius, *Life of Martin*, ch. 7). Finally, because Martin was truly poor in spirit, he deserved to be called poor and lowly.

Hear now of his meekness, as his Sulpicius writes:

> “He had assumed such patience toward every injury that, though he was the chief priest, he could be injured with impunity even by the lowliest clerics; yet he never removed them from their office because of this, nor, so far as lay within him, repelled them from his charity” (Id., *Dialogues* III, ch. 20).

[Col. 0496D] I think you all remember how this was clearly demonstrated in Brictio. For from among them all Martin chose him as his successor and forewarned him of the great hostility that was to come. Finally, he made that man holy in his faith and levity—the man to whose words he had lent his ear when, in reply to someone asking about Martin, he said: “If you seek that madman, look into the distance; behold, like a madman he is looking toward heaven as usual.”

For the man of God, despising earth, frequently looked up to heaven. He knew that, as we have recalled above, he had received for this very purpose an upright stature even in his body. He knew that his treasure was there; he knew that his Christ sat there at the Father’s right hand; he knew that he would never attain what he desired until he reached that place. Hence he rightly paid no attention to being called mad on earth, since his citizenship was in heaven and his eyes were in his head [Col. 0497A]. Indeed, his tears too were accustomed to rise from his cheeks thither; he abounded in them so greatly that he would even weep for the sins of those who seemed to be his detractors.

15. How greatly he hungered for righteousness was shown both in his other deeds and especially in his persecution of idolatry: in the destruction of temples, the casting down of statues, and the cutting down of sacred groves. On one occasion he did not fear to expose himself to danger, so that the occasion of so great a crime might be removed. For the Savior himself gloried before the angels that he had found Martin merciful in a poor man, displaying the half of the cloak that had been given to him.

Would that he might deign to show that mercy also to us wretches before the supreme Judge, into whose wonderful tabernacle he has entered—the mercy by which he rescued those once destined for death and assigned to various tortures, for whom he is recorded to have lain at midnight before the door of an earthly judge [Col. 0497B]. For how will he not hear him now, when he caused him to be heard then also?

Moreover, this especially indicates the purity of his heart: he was not ashamed when speaking to the enemy in the gate: “You will find nothing in me, destroyer; Abraham’s bosom will receive me.” For, happily completing his labors in the work of peacemaking, although he did not fail to know the end of his days, he went to clerics who were in disagreement; once peace had been restored among them, he himself rested in peace.

16. But it would take long to enumerate the persecutions he endured for [Col. 0497C] righteousness’ sake: how under the Emperor Julian, in the city of the Wangiones, he was fearless—indeed, made still more steadfast by the terror inflicted—and was committed to custody so that, unarmed, he might on the following day be exposed to barbarians; how in the Alps he remained entirely secure beneath the axe which a robber was brandishing over his head; how Auxentius the Arian grievously persecuted him at Milan and, after assailing him with many injuries, finally expelled him from the city; how elsewhere, after first fighting most fiercely against the faithlessness of priests, he was subjected to punishments, publicly beaten with rods, and then forced to depart from that place also; how, in the destruction of a certain shrine, when a pagan attacked him with drawn sword, he offered his bare neck to be struck, until the man, raising his right hand for the blow, fell backward [Col. 0497D]; and how another wished to strike him with a knife, but the blade slipped from his hands and suddenly disappeared.

For all these things there is no doubt that he is crowned in manifold ways: though he was not a martyr more than once in the actual completion of suffering, he was a martyr as often in the disposition of a most devoted will. “Eat now, friends, and drink; and be intoxicated, beloved.” For thus one lives, and in such things is the life of your spirit. Unless perhaps the divine discourse pronounces blessed those who raise the dead, give sight to the blind, heal the sick, cleanse lepers, cure paralytics, command demons, foretell the future, and shine with miracles—and not rather the poor in spirit, the meek, those who mourn, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, peacemakers, and those who endure persecution for righteousness’ sake [Col. 0498A].

17. Forgive me, brothers: I nearly passed over an example of obedience which, even by itself, should in accordance with the intended order be presented to us in Martin also. We are indeed lingering, but, I think, it is good for us to be here; for today we came late to Martin.

> “Lord,” he said, “if I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labor; let your will be done.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0497D] (Sulpicius, *Epistle* 3, to Bassula).]

O truly most holy soul! O immeasurable charity! O singular obedience! You have fought the good fight, finished the course, and kept the faith; henceforth there remains for you the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to you today; and still you say: “I do not refuse the labor; let your will be done!” Truly you offered Isaac; as far as lay in you, you slew that only one whom you love [Col. 0498B]; with pious devotion you sacrificed your unique joy, ready to return again to dangers, renew the conflicts, undergo labor once more, endure tribulation, prolong temptation, and then be delayed still further from that great happiness and long-desired fellowship of blessed spirits; to be recalled from the very entrance of glory into the miseries of this mortality; and finally, what is greatest of all, to remain longer in exile from your Christ, if he himself should so will.

And indeed there is no doubt that one merits a greater grace who shows himself ready even before a command than one who strives to obey after a command. Great indeed is your obedience, holy angels; but, if I may say so with your leave, I do not know whether there is found among you anyone ready to be sent at some time upon such a ministry as would require him not to see the face of the Father. It is a great thing, Peter, that, intending to follow the Lord, you left everything; but I heard you saying on the mountain, where he was transfigured before you: “Lord, it is good for us to be here; let us make three tabernacles here” (Matt. 17:4). This is not: “If I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labor.” Your heart was ready, Martin, your heart was ready, whether to remain in the body or to be dissolved and to be with Christ [Col. 0498C].

18. Great indeed is the security found in facing a dreadful death; great is the perfection found in desiring the vision of Christ, and [Col. 0498D] desiring it so fervently and singularly. But in every respect far greater is this: that you who do not fear to die—indeed, who long with such desire for the Lord’s presence—do not refuse to live also, and to be wearied by the most burdensome waiting. In what other matter could one have failed to obey who, at this decisive point, cried out so devoutly: “Let your will be done”?

Therefore, brothers, let this be our portion at today’s banquet. Let us carefully consider this obedience set before us at the table of this poor man—or rather, now rich man—knowing that it is what is required of us, what we ought to prepare, so that each of us may say: “I am ready and am not troubled, that I may keep your commandments” (Ps. 118:60). Not merely once or in part, but: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 56:8); ready for either outcome, prescribing nothing to your disposition in any matter [Col. 0499A]. Perhaps I desire this, particularly and intensely; but I do not refuse that either: [Col. 0500A] “As the will has been in heaven, so let it be done.” I desire rest, but I do not refuse labor: let your will be done.

[Col. 0499]

# SERMON ON SAINT CLEMENT, POPE AND MARTYR

## On the Three Waters

[Col. 0499A] 1. “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). Let the sinner hear and be angry; let him gnash his teeth and waste away. He has been caught in his own cunning; he has fallen into the pit that he made; he has fallen into the snare that he set. For through the envy of the devil death entered into the world; but behold, the death of the saints has become precious. Hear, therefore, enemy of life; author of death, attend. What [Col. 0499B] now does your deception avail? What harm does your craftiness do?

Indeed, to make you grieve more, all things work together for good even to those saints who are called according to his purpose (Rom. 8:28). For the blessed martyr whose feast we celebrate today triumphed over you by the death of the body itself—which is your work. He made necessity into virtue and transformed the penalty of sin into the merit of glory; he proved faithful in little, that he might be found worthy to be set over much. For whatever that blessed soul had previously received was little indeed, utterly little, compared with the glory that he merited through his present suffering. For every delight of this world, all its glory, and whatever is desired in it, are altogether little in comparison with that happiness and blessedness—if they should even be called little, rather than nothing, a vapor appearing for a little while [Col. 0499C].

Blessed Clement had received noble birth, extensive possessions, a great inheritance, and very abundant learning, so that he was regarded as one of the foremost philosophers of his time. He had received all these things from the Lord; for these too are God’s gifts. He therefore proved faithful to the one who gave them when, for love of him, he despised all things, counted everything as loss, and considered them as dung, that he might gain Christ.

2. But perhaps even now the enemy murmurs: “Skin for skin,” he says, “and all that a man has he will give for his life” (Job 2:4). What then? Do you think that in the very life of his body, which he received from the Lord, [Col. 0499D] he will be found unfaithful, so as to prefer even that life to him? Behold, you have authority: rush upon him through your agents, so that he may be forced to choose between separation from the Lord and separation from his body. Seek out varied and terrible kinds of torture; but know that you are fashioning crowns for our martyr.

For as he despised the ornaments and supports of this life, so he despises life itself. He exposes his whole body to death; he curses you to your face and blasphemes your idols with his sacred mouth; even amid your tortures he freely preaches the Lord his God and openly [or, in the fire] confesses him. Therefore he shall be crowned, because he has contended lawfully, conquered faithfully, and refused to be separated from the love of Christ either by the enticements of this life or by the horror of death.

Tell us, I pray, holy soul, who so exposed your body to tortures: I ask you, did you love it or not? “Certainly I loved it,” he says. “For no one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5:29). “Therefore I loved it; but I loved it little, as a handmaid, and I loved the Lord God far more. And so that the proof of love might be the display of a deed, I gladly embraced even bodily death for his glory” [Col. 0500A].

[Col. 0500B] 3. What shall we say to these things, brothers? We congratulate the martyr, but now his glory is not without our shame. For behold, blessed Clement was a human being like us, capable of suffering, encompassed by the same weakness, and joined to his own flesh by the same bond of natural affection. If, then, he so glorified Christ in his body and received the cup of salvation, what do we render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to us? Certainly he marked us with the same image, redeemed us with the same blood, and called us to the same inheritance: incorruptible, undefiled, eternal, reserved in heaven.

Why then are we unable to drink Christ’s cup freely with blessed Clement? But perhaps some answer: “We could, if opportunity were not lacking; but the time of persecution [Col. 0500C] has ceased.” Yet I confess I do not sufficiently believe those who say this. What then? Every day you yield to the prick of a single needle, and do you think that you could withstand the point of a sword? Test yourselves in small conflicts, to see how manfully you could stand in the greater contest. For you are not told: “Sacrifice to idols and live; or, if you refuse, you must perish under various tortures.” The Lord knows our frailty and does not give us such a severe contest. He gave blessed Clement a severe contest, that he might conquer and learn that wisdom is stronger than all things.

4. But what is your contest, my brothers? Every day suggestions are put into your hearts: “Break your rule, murmur, slander, act more laxly, feign weakness, answer the one who perhaps spoke rather [Col. 0500D] harshly to you, so that you may satisfy your desire.” And no one is told: “Unless you do these things, you will die”; rather, at most you resist your inclination with difficulty and effort. “And who could endure so much?” This is what we are accustomed to hear within and to answer those who exhort us—whether a human being outwardly or the Holy Spirit inwardly.

If, then, we are endangered in such a contest, if we scarcely resist, if sometimes we even give way, what would we do in that so grave a contest? If our weakness yields to fragile reeds, how would it withstand spears? You see how we have been reduced to nothing: like women or little children, we praise those who fight, but cannot fight ourselves. What, then, shall we do? Certainly we are all called to the wedding feast of the Lamb, and it is not permitted for us to appear empty in his presence [Col. 0501A]. Therefore let us carefully consider what is set before us, because we ought to prepare such things.

Blessed Clement considered that wine had been set before him by the Lord, and, being rich himself, he likewise brought to that wedding feast wine through the shedding of his own blood. But we are poor, and, Lord, we have no wine. Yet he says, “Fill the jars with water” (John 2:7). Shall water too be accepted, then, if we bring it? Certainly it shall be accepted. For the person who, following the counsel of the Wise Man, carefully considers what is set before him (Prov. 23:1), will find that it too has been set before us with the wine by him who came not by water only, but by water and blood. For he who saw bore witness that, when the side of the Lord sleeping on the cross was opened, blood and water came forth (John 19:34–35) [Col. 0501B].

5. Therefore, brothers, that we may at least prove ourselves faithful to our God: if we do not have the martyrdom of blood—for martyrdom means testimony—let us seek at least the testimony of water, and God will not despise even that. For there are three who bear testimony on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood (John 5:8). Blessed are those who possess the threefold testimony, because a threefold cord is not easily broken (Eccl. 4:12). If we do not have the testimony of blood, let us have spirit and water; for without the spirit neither blood nor water will suffice. Indeed, if the spirit itself is found without water or blood, its testimony suffices, since it is the Spirit of truth. Neither blood nor water is of any use by itself; it is the Spirit who bears testimony in them [Col. 0501C].

Yet I think that the spirit is found either rarely or never without water or blood. Therefore, beloved, let us seek water, since we do not have blood. And because we have mentioned the water jars above, let us seek the measures of two or three which the jars contained. For Christ too sets before us a threefold water, and everyone who is perfect among us is like him—that is, whoever can have three measures. Therefore it is said with this distinction, “two or three,” so that at least two may clearly be necessary, while the third is not required of everyone.

[Col. 0502A] 6. Receive, then, the threefold water which the Savior sets before you. He weeps over Lazarus (John 11:35) and over the city of Jerusalem (Luke 19:41): this is the first water. He sweats when the hour of his Passion is already at hand: this is the second water, flowing not merely from his eyes but from his whole body. It is red and the color of blood, as it is written: “His sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground” (Luke 22:44). The third water, however, is that which, as we have already said, flowed from his side together with blood [Col. 0502B].

You too have the first water if you moisten the bed of your conscience with your tears and, through the sorrow of compunction for past sins, wash away the stains of sin. You have the second water if you eat your bread in the sweat of your face, chastise your body with the labor of penitence, and restrain the flame of desire. It is blood-colored, either because of the labor or because of the very fire of desire that it extinguishes. But if you can advance as far as the grace of devotion, you will drink the water of saving wisdom; and the Spirit of Christ, sweeter than honey, will become in you a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. Remember that this is the water which proceeds from the side of the one sleeping, and flows without any distress [Col. 0502C]. For one must already be dead to the world who wishes to delight in this grace.

Therefore, to summarize briefly: the first washes the conscience from past offenses; the second extinguishes desire, so that you may guard against future sins; the third, if you deserve to attain it, gives drink to the thirsty soul.

[Col. 0501]

# SERMON ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE

## How We Ought to Anticipate the Solemnities of the Saints by Fasting
[Col. 0501C] 1. The authority of the Fathers has ordained that the principal feasts of the saints should be anticipated by voluntary fasts—usefully indeed, and not to our folly, if there is someone to take heed. For every day we incur many sins, [Col. 0501D] and in many things we all stumble; nor is it at all safe to undertake the celebration of sacred feasts, especially those of the highest rank, unless first the purification of abstinence has been applied, so that we may be found both worthier of and more capable of spiritual joys. Thus the righteous person at the beginning of his speech is his own accuser, nor does he begin the praises of another except from self-reproach. But if even the righteous person trembles, anxiously seeking to forestall him who is ready to judge even righteous deeds themselves, what are we to do, whose sins have meanwhile neither been judged nor uncovered? It is greatly to be feared that perhaps those things which go before unto judgment may be found manifest. If not even the righteous man presumes to approach the praises of the saints without modesty and a certain reverence, how much more must the sinner—since “praise is not seemly in the mouth” [Col. 0502C] of such a one—always fear that saying: “Why do you recount my ordinances?” (Ps. 49:16); or this: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. 22:12). Blessed, therefore, [Col. 0502D] are those who are careful at all times to preserve their robe—that is, the glory of their conscience—unstained, always presenting it splendid. But because few are those who thus guard their heart with all vigilance, and fewer still, if indeed there can be fewer, who preserve it in all holiness, it is necessary by frequent abstinence to wash away the stains which creep in, especially when any principal feast approaches to be celebrated.

2. Yet fasting observed beforehand is not merely a preparation for the approaching celebration; it is also a kind of admonition and no small instruction. From this very thing we learn what is the true path to the eternal feast. For what does it mean that we anticipate solemnities with fasts, except that “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God”? For one who does not observe the appointed abstinence of the vigil is unworthy of solemn [Col. 0503A] joy. Certainly, I say: if you refuse to afflict your soul in the vigil, you are rightly judged unworthy of festal rest and exultation. Indeed, the whole time of present repentance is a kind of vigil for the great solemnity and eternal Sabbath-rest for which we wait. Nor may you complain that the vigil is too long, if you consider the eternity of the feast. For daytime solemnities are customarily preceded by a daytime preparation; but that feast, though eternal, does not demand an eternal preparation. But where is the more delightful remembrance of that happiness carrying us? For that feast is more often, and perhaps more fittingly, called by this name. We must return to the matter at hand.

1059 3. The occasion, then, of today’s fast, and of the solemnity and joy for which we wait, is the blessed passion of the apostle Andrew. For it is fitting that, if we cannot hang with him, we should at least fast with him. And when he hung on the cross for two days, who can doubt that he also fasted? Let us therefore be found to share, however slightly, in his passion: if not fastened with him to the gibbet, then afflicted with him by fasting; so that, through God’s mercy, we too may share his crown, and even now be companions in spiritual joys. For how should we not exult in memory of his triumph, when we know that he exulted so vehemently in the very presence of his punishment? Will not the feast be joyful where even the cross itself is full of joy? For we customarily call that “festive” which is joyful; and the cross is surely named from torment, or at least torment from the cross. [Col. 0503C] With what exultation, therefore, ought all the earth to celebrate the miracle of so great a novelty, so magnificent a work of divine power? Andrew was a man like us, capable of suffering; yet with so burning an ardour of spirit he thirsted for the cross, and with joy unheard of through the ages he danced for delight when he saw from afar the gibbet prepared for him.

> “O cross,” he said, “long desired and now prepared for my longing soul! Secure and rejoicing I come to you, so that you too may receive me exultantly.”

[Note: [Col. 0503D] These words are reported from the Acts of Saint Andrew, attributed to the presbyters of Achaia. The Blessed Spanish abbot mentioned them near the end of Book I against Elipandus nine hundred years ago; I do not know whether anyone mentioned them before him.]

You see that he cannot contain himself for the greatness of his joy. “So that you too,” he says, “may exult.” Is the exultation then so great that the cross itself exults and contains nothing merely joyful, but is wholly joy? Or who would say something less contrary to custom, beyond reason, and beyond nature: that the cross should exult, or that the crucified man should exult more than the cross [variant: “that the crucified man should exult than the cross”]? [Col. 0504A] Nature denied the cross a capacity for joy; but in the crucified man, whatever strength it has, it banishes all joy and brings in pain. “I have always been your lover,” he says, “and I have desired to embrace you.” Brothers, this is a flashing fire, not a speaking tongue; and if it is a tongue, it is surely a fiery one. These are coals from that fire which Christ had sent down from on high into his bones. Would that they might be desolating to us, consuming and burning up whatever carnal affection is in us! For what sparks are these, and from what inward conflagration do they shine forth?

4. Truly, blessed Andrew, your faith is a grain of mustard seed, which, when it began to be crushed, began to produce from itself so unexpected a heat. What if it had been crushed a little more? What mind could endure that fervour, what ear those words? While Aegeas threatened him less severely, [Col. 0504B] the mustard seed still seemed contemptible. It was whole; we did not know what lay hidden within. “The Lord,” he says, “sent me to this province, in which I have acquired for him no small people.” Let the pestle of threat draw near: it will now taste far more pungently, and speak more steadfastly.
