Aegeas thinks to terrify him by threatening the punishment of the cross—but it is not so. He is rather inflamed by this word, and cries freely: “If I feared the gibbet of the cross, I would not preach the glory of the cross.” But when he caught sight of the timber prepared for him, now wholly kindled, he applauded and addressed endearments to his beloved: he greeted it with the greatest devotion, received it most reverently [variant: “looked upon it”], exalted it magnificently, and gloried in its praise, crying out more with affection than with voice: “Hail, precious cross, which received comeliness and beauty from the limbs of the Lord! Hail, cross, consecrated in the body of Christ and adorned from his limbs as with pearls!” Those who are servants of the cross rightly honour the lover of the cross; but he rightly demands a fuller devotion from those who have more particularly resolved to take up their own cross. I say this to you and of you, my brothers, who did not hear with a deaf ear that evangelical trumpet: “Whoever does not carry his own cross and follow me cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:27). Be ready to devote all the diligence of your heart to this solemnity and to celebrate it with a great heart; for in it there is laid up for you a great treasury both of consolation and exhortation, if there is one to dig and search it out.

[Col. 0503]

## ON THE FEAST OF ST ANDREW THE APOSTLE

1060 **SERMON I. On the three kinds of fish: those in the sea, the river, and the pond** [variant: *On clean fish*].

[Col. 0503D]

1. As we celebrate today the glorious triumph of blessed Andrew, we have exulted and delighted in the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth. For there could be no place for sadness where he himself rejoiced so vehemently. None of us felt compassion for one suffering thus; none dared lament one who was exulting. Otherwise he might fittingly have said to us what the Saviour, carrying the cross, said to those who followed and mourned for him: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves” (Luke 23:28). Finally, when blessed Andrew himself was led to the cross, the people, grieving that the holy and righteous man was unjustly condemned, wished to prevent his punishment; but he himself, with most urgent prayer, rather prevented them—lest he not be crowned, indeed lest he not suffer. For he desired “to depart and be with Christ,” but upon the cross which he had always loved; he desired to enter the kingdom, but [Col. 0505A] through the gibbet. For what does he say to his beloved? “Through you,” he says, “may he receive me who through you redeemed me.” Therefore, if we love him, let us rejoice with him—not only because he was crowned, but because he was crucified: because the Lord granted him the desire of his soul and placed upon his head a crown of precious stone. Yet while we congratulate him because he is granted the embrace of the cross so long desired, it would be very strange if we did not also marvel at the wonderful joy of him with whom we rejoice.

2. As we celebrated the vigils of this night and delighted in singing words of such great exultation, perhaps there was someone among us who thought to himself and said: What does this mean? Or whence comes such new joy? Is the cross indeed precious; can the cross be loved; does the cross possess exultation? It does, my brothers. If there is one to gather it, the wood of the cross always puts forth life, bears the fruit of delight, drips the oil of gladness, and sweats the balm of spiritual gifts. It is not a wild tree; it is “a tree of life to those who lay hold of it.” It is a fruitful tree, a saving tree; otherwise, how would it occupy the Lord’s land? I mean that most precious soil into which it is fixed by the roots that are its nails. If it were not more precious than all things and more fruitful than all, it would never have been planted in that garden, nor allowed to occupy that vineyard. Finally, why should we wonder if he gave sweetness to the cross, who gave it also to fire? Or how is the cross judged tasteless where even flame tastes sweet? What taste had that fire for Lawrence when he laughed at his executioners and mocked the judge? What shall we say to this, brothers? Why does the tribulation endured for Christ not taste sweet to us also? Why do we not taste this hidden manna? Thus the devil would be utterly conquered and would have nothing at all to bring forward [variant: “take away”]. This one thing would suffice us against the enemy’s double malice.

3. For that most wicked one has snares and darts, being the most cunning hunter of human beings, thirsting only for the blood of souls. Some he attacks with the arrows of whatever malicious suggestion, and by these he wounds many whose patience is slight. Others he labours to entangle in pleasures, and in these he certainly encloses a great multitude of those who creep upon the earth or flutter close to it. Let there then be joy in tribulation; and the evil one no longer has anything with which to entice or [Col. 0505D] cast down: we have been delivered from the snare of hunters and likewise from the harsh word. For the enemy will gain nothing against one whom Christ’s cross delights, if he suggests carnal pleasure; and “the son of iniquity shall not continue to harm him” if he attempts to introduce any bitterness whatever in order to embitter his mind. 1061 He who feeds upon fasting does not care for luxuries; much less can one complain about that in which he even delights. Truly he has set his refuge on high, where neither the enemy’s trap nor arrow need be feared; indeed, he is a clean fish, having both scales and fins. For as a net is cast in vain before the eyes of birds, so a weapon is cast in vain at the scales of those clothed in armour. The legal ordinance judged such fish clean: those lifted by fins and protected by scales, whether [Col. 0506A] they are in the sea, the river, or the pond (Lev. 11:9; Deut. 14:2). For this great and wide sea also has clean fish, worthy of the Lord’s table: from those who live amid the breadth, habit, and activity of the world, he has reserved for himself many thousands, whom the apostolic net draws, so that, once it is brought ashore, they may be separated from the wicked. There our fisher of human beings will also sit, he who now draws all Achaia after him. The river too has clean fish: all who are found among faithful stewards. For the order of preachers is a river, not remaining in one place but stretching forth and running in order to water different lands. There are also clean fish in ponds: those who serve God in cloisters in spirit and truth. Monasteries are rightly compared with ponds, where fish are in a manner imprisoned and have no freedom to wander, so that they may always be ready for spiritual feasts, each saying inwardly: “When will he come who shall carry me away? All the days during which I now serve as a soldier I wait until my change comes.”

4. Moreover, as we mentioned above from the law, whether in sea, river, or pond, those fish are clean which have scales and fins. The scales are many, but from them a single breastplate is in a manner woven: for patience is one virtue, although we seem to exercise it separately in each tribulation. And as scales may fittingly be referred to patience, so I think fins may likewise appropriately be referred to cheerfulness. For cheerfulness lifts and raises up, so that whoever is made cheerful seems to make certain leaps on high. To have two fins, then, we must seek a twofold cheerfulness. And perhaps for this reason the Apostle teaches—for he truly had wings, by which he was caught up even to the third heaven and flew even into paradise—not only to glory in hope, but also to glory in tribulations (Rom. 5:2–3). He flies truly on high who is delighted not only by the expectation of future goods, but by the very presentation of present evils, so that he even glories in them. We find this quality in this blessed Apostle; such he is that we admire him, such that we rightly praise him.

5. Hence we may consider here a threefold grade: of beginners, of those making progress, and of the perfect. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning [Col. 0506D] of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1:16); hope is the middle; love the fullness. Hear the Apostle, then: “Love is the fulfillment of the law” (Rom. 13:10). One initiated by fear endures the cross of Christ patiently; one advancing in hope bears it willingly; but one made perfect in love embraces it ardently. For only this person can say: “I have always been your lover and have desired to embrace you.” This utterance is far from that of one who does endure, but would wholly wish, if possible, not to have come to this hour. Finally, if I do not seem rash, it is far from the utterance: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39). What then? Surely he had mounted the colt so that not even this might be left to his enemies. I recognize, indeed, in the leader of the battle the trembling of the faint-hearted; I recognize in the physician the voice of the sick man; I recognize the hen becoming weak with her chicks. I consider the love, I am astounded at the compassion, I stand in awe of the condescension. The merciful Lord did not take to himself the robust disposition of blessed Andrew, because “those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12). If anyone perhaps is offended by this condescension, he surely deserves to hear: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. 20:15). To such a one this is “an aroma of life unto death.”

6. What great thing would it have been, Lord Jesus, if, when the hour for which you had come approached, you had stood fearless, as one who had power to lay down his life and from whom no one took it? Or was it not far more glorious, since all was done for our sake, that not only the suffering of your body but [Col. 0507A] also the feeling of your heart should work for us; and that those whom your death gave life might likewise be made strong by your trembling, joyful by your sadness, eager by your weariness, tranquil by your disturbance, and consoled by your desolation? I indeed read in the raising of Lazarus that he groaned in spirit and troubled himself (John 11:33, 38). But let it stand, for the moment, that he troubled himself—not by the necessity of his condition, but by the choice of his benevolent will. Now, however, I hear something greater still. For love, “strong as death,” prevailed to such an extent that an angel of God strengthened Christ. Who strengthened whom? Hear the Evangelist: “An angel appeared,” he says, “strengthening him” (Luke 22:43). Whom did he strengthen? Truly him at whose birth the closed womb of the Virgin was opened; at whose command water was changed into wine; at whose touch leprosy fled; [Col. 0507C] beneath whose feet the solid sea stood; at whose voice the dead arose; finally, him “who upholds all things by the word of his power,” through whom all things were made, and through whom all things—including the angel himself—subsist. And what can I say? Whom did he strengthen? I would delay less if he were not utterly ineffable. He therefore strengthened him whose majesty not even his own strengthener could comprehend.

7. I ask you, angel: whom are you consoling? Did you not know who he was whom you came to console? Surely he is the Consoler; surely he is the Paraclete. Otherwise he would not say that another Paraclete would be sent by the Father to the apostles (John 14:16), unless he himself were also a Paraclete. Finally, I recognize in this very matter the greatest Paraclete, the most gracious Paraclete, who [Col. 0507D] is near to those who are troubled in heart. I no longer despair, Lord, even if the tribulation I suffer seems burdensome to me, even if I am faint-hearted, even if I desire that the cup be removed from me. I do not despair, I say, provided that I too add: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26:39). From this very thing I have also learned not to resort to carnal or passing consolation, but to angelic, to heavenly consolation. Certainly—provided I do not murmur, for that would utterly separate me from you unless I quickly came to my senses—I do not refuse, even if I need consolation. For what then? I recognize my own voice in the Saviour, and should I despair of salvation? Surely, [Col. 0508A] in my patience I shall possess my soul.

8. Yet I wish to make progress, if I can, and not be content merely with salvation once attained. “He who fears God,” says the Wise Man, “will do good” (Ecclus. 15:1). But that is too little; [Col. 0508B] for it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. 36:27). Do not be content with salvation: seek peace, lest even salvation itself be in danger for you. Hear, therefore, the angel rejoicing and singing at the birth of him who became our peace: “Peace on earth to men of good will” (Luke 2:14). And what good will is this, unless it is a well-ordered will? What is it, you ask? Surely, the will that accords with reason, which says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). If you have begun to feel this, there can be no doubt that you will bear the cross of the Lord willingly and say: “I am ready and am not troubled, that I may keep your commandments” (Ps. 118:60).

9. But if you wish to be perfect, one thing is still necessary for you. What is it, you ask? Surely joy in the Holy Spirit. For one restrained by fear is patient, and one led by the reasoning of hope is well-disposed; but unless he is also fervent in spirit, he can easily fall. But the love poured forth through the Spirit is patient and kind; and, what is more, it never fails. In the first command given to our first parents, if you consider carefully, Eve seems to have been patient and Adam well-disposed. Yet because both fell, it is clear that neither he nor she stood on a stable footing. “The woman saw,” Scripture says, “that the tree was beautiful to behold and pleasant for eating.” Does she not seem to you scarcely to restrain her hand? Likewise, when questioned by the serpent, see whether her words do not plainly indicate that the command was burdensome to her. “From every tree [Col. 0508C] of paradise,” she says, “we eat; but concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, he said to us: ‘Let us not eat’” (Gen. 3:2–3). She does not say: “Such is the Creator’s will; why it is so, he himself knows; it is enough for us to obey, because our life is in his will.” Thus the woman was easily deceived, both to believe the promise and to yield to persuasion. The man, however, “was not deceived” (1 Tim. 2:14), but was overthrown by love for the woman. For he would have wished always to keep the command, which he knew was useful to him, had not the woman persuaded him otherwise. Nor did he seem to suffer any difficulty in keeping the command; but his good [Col. 0508D] will had no strength because it had no fervour.

10. For it is not patience or hope but love that is “strong as death” (Song 8:6); not fear or reason but the spirit of strength. Patience says: “This must be done,” because it is pressed by fear. Good will says: “This is expedient, and this must be done,” because it is drawn by the reasoning of hope. But love, inflamed by the Spirit, says neither, “This must be done,” nor, “This is expedient”; rather it says: “This I will; this I desire; this I long for intensely.” You see how great is love’s sublimity, how great its security, and how great its sweetness. Blessed is the soul that has attained this state of love! Nor should we despair, since the memory of the one who attained this degree is celebrated especially for this purpose: that we may invoke his help and be stirred by his example. [Col. 0509A] I say more: I seem to see some among us at this degree. If you say that Andrew the Apostle is blessed and that you, being insignificant, cannot follow his footsteps, at least be ashamed not to imitate those who are with you. No one becomes supreme at once; the top of the ladder is reached by climbing, not by flying. Let us climb, then, as with two feet: meditation and prayer. Meditation teaches what is lacking; prayer obtains that it may not be lacking. The former shows the way; the latter leads us along it. By meditation we recognize dangers threatening us; by prayer we escape them, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON II. On the Four Horns of the Cross

[Col. 0509B]

1. Today the feast of blessed Andrew the Apostle is celebrated. If we search it with devout attentiveness, we find in it many things that build up our souls. For at the very beginning of his conversion he affords us a great example of perfect obedience. This is necessary indeed for all Christians, but is to be embraced more dearly by us, who by our very profession are especially bound as debtors to obedience. The wise money-changer [variant: merchant] is Wisdom itself, to whom we must render this coin of obedience; and he will not accept it unless it is found both whole and free from any falsity. For if we weigh matters up, if we make distinctions, and obey in this command but not in that, the coin is broken. Christ will not accept it, since we are debtors to him for a coin not broken but whole. For we have all promised obedience simply and without any exception. But if anyone obeys indeed, yet hypocritically and for appearance, while murmuring in secret, his coin is false: it contains lead, not silver, and “wickedness sits upon the talent of lead.” He acts deceitfully, but before the sight of God, because God is not mocked.

2. Do you wish to hear the form of perfect obedience? “The Lord,” says the Evangelist, “saw Peter and Andrew casting a net into the sea; and he said to them: ‘Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.’” “I will make,” he says, “fishers out of fishers”—indeed, preachers. But they immediately, weighing nothing up or hesitating, not anxious about how they would live, not considering how uneducated and illiterate men could become preachers, asking nothing at all, left their nets and boat without any delay and followed him (Matt. 4:18–20). Recognize, brothers, that these words are recited every year in the Church for your sake: so that, learning the form of true obedience, you may discipline your hearts in the obedience of love. This, indeed, alone commends the coin of obedience; this is its tested and refined silver. For love alone makes obedience pleasing and acceptable to God. “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). And again: “Though I give my body to be burned, but have not love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

3. Do you wish us also to say something about the passion of this blessed apostle, which we celebrate today, to the praise of Christ and for your edification? [Col. 0510A] You have surely heard how, when blessed Andrew reached the place where the cross was prepared, he was strengthened in the Lord and, through the Spirit whom he had received with the other apostles in tongues of fire, spoke words truly fiery. For when he saw the cross prepared for him at a distance, his face did not grow pale, as mortal weakness might seem to demand; his blood did not freeze; his hair did not stand on end, nor did his voice stick in his throat; his body did not tremble, his mind was not troubled, and his understanding did not depart, as it usually does. [Col. 0510B] Out of the abundance of the heart his mouth spoke, and the love burning in his heart sent forth, as it were, certain most blazing sparks in his voice. For what did blessed Andrew say when he saw from afar, as I said, the cross prepared for him?

> “O cross, long desired and now prepared for my longing soul! Secure and rejoicing I come to you, so that you too may receive me exultantly, as the disciple of him who hung upon you; for I have always been your lover and have desired to embrace you.”

I ask you, brothers, is it a human being who says these things? Or is he not a human being, but an angel or some new creature? He is indeed a human being like us, capable of suffering. For his very passion bears witness that he is capable of suffering, since he exults so joyfully as it approaches. Whence, then, this new exultation in a human being, and joy unheard of until now? Whence such constancy in such frailty? Whence such a spiritual mind, such fervent love, such a robust spirit in a human being? Far be it from us to believe that so great a power resides in him from himself! It is a perfect gift, descending from the Father of lights—from him, indeed, “who alone does great wonders.”

4. Truly, beloved, it was the Spirit who helped his weakness, through whom love, strong as death—indeed, stronger than death—was poured forth in his heart. Oh, that we too may be found sharers in it! For the labour of repentance is burdensome to us, bodily affliction grievous, abstinence oppressive. During vigils our soul nods with sleepiness through weariness, and for no other reason, certainly, than lack of the Spirit. For if he were present, he would without doubt help our weakness; and as he made the cross and death itself not merely tolerable but desirable and altogether delightful to blessed Andrew, so he would make our labour and repentance not merely moderate, but desirable and altogether delightful to us. For “my spirit is sweeter than honey,” says the Lord (Ecclus. 24:27); so that even the bitterness of death, however bitter, cannot prevail against its sweetness. What will not that sweetness temper, which makes even death most sweet? What harshness can resist that anointing, which makes death itself most pleasant? “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 127:2–3). What burden will not that joy banish, which makes death itself most glad? Let us seek this Spirit, brothers. Let us labour with all diligence to deserve to have this Spirit—or rather, to have yet more abundantly the Spirit whom we already have. “For whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). But “we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12). The works themselves of salvation and life provide testimony to his presence—works which we could in no way perform unless the Spirit of the Saviour were present, giving life to our souls. Let us seek, therefore, that God may multiply his gifts in us and increase his Spirit, who has already given the firstfruits. For there is no surer testimony whatever to his presence than a desire for greater grace, since he says: “Those who eat me will still hunger, and those who drink me will still thirst” (Ecclus. 24:56).

5. But perhaps the consciences of many among us now answer: “We desire this Spirit, who may thus help our weakness; but we cannot find him.” And I say: You do not find because you do not seek; you do not receive because you do not ask. You ask and do not receive because you ask negligently.

[Note: [Col. 0511] In Sermon 27 *On Various Subjects*, he says that ingratitude is the cause.]

For God awaits nothing else, seeks nothing else, except that he be sought diligently and with desire. For when will he deny those who ask, he who even urges and exhorts those who do not ask to ask? “If you,” he says, “though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father [Col. 0511C] from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke 11:13). Ask, therefore, beloved; ask without ceasing; ask without hesitation; and in all your works invoke the presence and assistance of this ever most sweet and pleasant Spirit. For we too, brothers, must take up our cross with blessed Andrew—indeed, with the Lord and Saviour whom Andrew himself followed. For this was the source of his joy and exultation: he seemed to die not only for Christ but with Christ, and to be conformed to the likeness of his death, so that by suffering with him he might also reign with him. That we too may be crucified with him, let us hear with attentive ears of the heart the voice that says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9: [Col. 0511D] 23). As though he said: Whoever desires me, let him despise himself; whoever wishes to do my will, let him learn to break his own.

6. But immediately wars arise, and enemies at once arm themselves against them. Let us also arm ourselves in opposition. Let us imitate the arms of our King, that we too may take up our cross, in which we may triumph over all enemies. Hear what the Psalmist promised—or rather, what the Holy Spirit promised through his mouth: “His truth,” he says, doubtless the truth of the Most High, “will surround you with a shield”; for he was speaking of him, as the preceding words of the psalm clearly show. Why, brothers, are we surrounded with a shield, except because wars surround us on every side? Finally, consider why he surrounds you with a shield. “His truth will surround you with a shield.” [Col. 0512A] For what purpose? “You will not fear,” he says, “the terror of the night; the arrow flying by day; the thing that walks in darkness; the assault and the noonday demon” (Ps. 90:5–6). Do you see how necessary it is that truth should surround you with a shield, when the weapons of enemies thus surround you? For from below the terror of the night rises up; from the left the arrow flies by day; from the right the dark thing walks; and, lest anything be empty, from above the noonday demon rises [variant: “comes upon you”]. Yet we, wretched and pitiable, with so many serpents close by, fiery arrows flying on every side, and enemies attacking from every side, nevertheless sleep in ruinous security and negligence; we grow sluggish in idleness; we indulge in vanities and buffooneries; we are so slow in spiritual exercises [Col. 0512B] as though peace and security already existed, and human life upon earth were not warfare. This, beloved, I tell you, is what frightens me more violently, what pierces my soul altogether with the sword of most bitter fear: that amid such great dangers we seem less fearful, less exercised [variant: “less awakened”], less watchful than is necessary. For this negligence of ours proves one of two things: either that we have been wholly handed over to our enemies and do not know it; or else that, if we are preserved amid these things, we are found exceedingly ungrateful to him who guards us. How dangerous each of these is is sufficiently clear. Therefore, I beseech you, beloved, let the sleepless malice of our enemies itself awaken us; and let their evil persistence, by which they are so diligent and so anxious for our destruction [variant: [Col. 0512C] “persecution”], make us also diligent and watchful, so that we may work out our own salvation in fear and trembling.

7. For behold, our salvation is on the cross—provided only that we cling to it manfully. “The word of the cross,” says the Apostle, “is indeed foolishness to those who are perishing; but to those who are being saved, that is, to us, it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:18). It is the shield with which we are surrounded, so that its four horns may repel the enemies’ missiles in four directions. Let the lower horn, then, stand against “the terror by night,” that is, against faint-heartedness arising from the affliction of the flesh, so that we may strive manfully to chastise that which is beneath us—our body—and reduce it to servitude. But if someone reviles us to our face, if someone openly [Col. 0512D] attempts to persuade us to evil, then the arrow flies by day and is from the left; nevertheless it must be received upon the left horn of the cross. If, however, he flatters, if, under the appearance of a counsellor’s goodwill, he offers the poison of detraction against a brother and attempts to sow hatred; if, finally, he tries to persuade us that something unjust is just—then he is at my right hand. Yet he is Judas: he betrays me with a kiss; and the “business that walks in darkness” must be repelled by the right horn of the cross. But behold the noonday demon: namely, the spirit of pride, which is wont to rise up more fiercely amid the greater brightness of virtues. We have often endeavoured to impress upon you how ruinous this is. For pride is the beginning of every sin and the cause of all destruction. Therefore, whoever you are who strive to work out your salvation, remember to hold the horn of the cross above your head against this enemy, lest you be lifted up in pride, lest your heart be exalted, lest you walk in things too great or too wonderful for you; but let the horn of the cross, rising above your head, receive those missiles which come from on high. Indeed, this alone bears the inscription both of salvation and of kingship, because only one who humbles himself deserves to be saved and exalted.

8. To recapitulate briefly: these four horns are continence, patience, prudence, and humility. Happy is the soul that glories in this cross, that triumphs upon this cross—provided only that it perseveres upon it and cannot be cast down by any temptations.

Let whoever is upon this cross pray, then; let him pray with blessed Andrew to his Lord and Master that he may not permit him to be taken down from the cross. For what would that malignant one not dare? What would the impious one not presume to attempt? What he had planned to do through the hands of Aegeas to the disciple, he had planned to do through the tongues of the Jews to the Master. Yet in both cases, led by tardy repentance, defeated and confounded, he withdrew. May he likewise depart from us, conquered by him who triumphed both in himself and in his disciple! May he grant that we too may deserve to be happily brought to completion upon this poor cross of penitence of ours, which we have borne for his name’s sake—he who is God above all, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0513]

## ON THE DEATH OF LORD HUMBERT

[Note: [Col. 0513D] In the royal manuscript this sermon occurs after the sermons on the Dedication, under this title: “On the death of the most reverend father Humbert,” namely the abbot of Igny, to whom Epistle 141 is addressed, in which Bernard reproves him for having relinquished his office without consultation. It is remarkable that no mention is made here of Humbert’s abbatial dignity. There was also another Humbert, likewise of Clairvaux, concerning whom Nicholas, Bernard’s secretary, writes in Epistle 15: “That Humbert who has put off the old man is not that common father about whom you are uncertain.” Moreover, the holy man had similar funeral orations upon the deaths of his own: concerning his brother Gerard, Sermon 26 on the Song of Songs; likewise concerning a certain lay brother, in Book 7 of the *Life*, chapter 26. For Abbot Humbert see Book 1 of the *Life*, no. 48, and the *Great Cistercian Exordium* in various places, especially Book 3, chapter 4, where this sermon is mentioned.]

### A SERMON OF THE MONK OF CLAIRVAUX

[Col. 0513B]

Humbert, the servant of the Lord, has died: a devoted servant, a faithful slave. You yourselves saw how, on the night just past, he breathed his last in our hands, like one of the little worms of the earth. During these three days death exhausted him and broke him down within its jaws, that it might be sated with the blood for which it thirsted. Come then: it has done what it could; it has killed the flesh, and behold, it is laid away in the heart of the earth. It has separated from us a sweet friend, a prudent counsellor, a strong helper. That insatiable murderer spared neither me nor you—though me less than you.

Is this how you separate us, bitter death? O cruel beast! O bitterness most bitter! O terror [variant: stench] and horror of the children of Adam! What have you done? You have killed. But what? The flesh alone, certainly; for you have nothing that you can do to the soul. It flies to its Creator, whom it had so ardently desired and so steadfastly followed throughout all the days of its life.

[Col. 0513C] Yet even that body which you seem to possess will be taken away from you, when you, the last enemy, are destroyed and swallowed up in victory. You shall indeed give back—yes, someday give back—this body which yesterday, at the sign of your approach, you had filled with such torrents of spittle, curses, and manifold filthiness, rejoicing and praising yourself because you had entangled this man also in your snares. The Only-begotten of the Father will come in great power and majesty to seek Humbert and to conform that same corpse-like body to the body of his glory. And what of you? Surely, as it is written in Jeremiah, “in the latter days you shall remain foolish” (Jer. [Col. 0513D] 17:11); and while Humbert lives eternally, you shall die for ever. The sea-beast vomited forth the prophet whom it had swallowed (Jonah 2:11); and you shall restore Humbert, whom you see enclosed within your most vast belly.

[Col. 0514B]

2. Moreover, brothers, this servant of God displayed before you a sermon made of deeds, in every form of holiness—a sermon both long and great.

[Note: [Col. 0514D] That is, a sermon consisting of the deeds or examples which Humbert displayed.]

Long in respect of the length of its journey [variant: of life]; great in respect of the loftiness of his life. I need not open my mouth further if you have retained his sermon well, if you have impressed it upon your hearts. For fifty years and more he lived in the service of him whose service is kingship, because in his boyhood he was placed in God’s sanctuary.

[Note: [Col. 0514D] Namely, in the monastery of La Chaise-Dieu, where he lived as a monk for twenty years from his early youth before withdrawing to Clairvaux; this occurred about the year 1118.]

For thirty years he lived among us, almost from the very beginning of this monastery, not merely without reproach but with grace.

[Note: [Col. 0514D] The *Great Cistercian Exordium*, Book 3, chapter 4, gives the same number of years.]

Accordingly, his memory will be blessed among us [Col. 0514C] and among the generation to come. As a stranger and pilgrim, he passed through this path and this life, taking as little as he could from worldly things, knowing that he was not of this world. He had no abiding city here, any more than his fathers had; but stretching forth toward what lay before, he followed after the prize of the heavenly calling. The world has nothing that it can rightfully claim in him or concerning him, for neither did the world please him nor he the world. He took from its substance as sparingly as possible; and he would have taken less, had obedience not compelled him. Having food and clothing, he was content with these—not for excess, but for necessity; except that he often declared even necessity itself to be excess.

[Col. 0514D] A few days ago, if I remember rightly, while we were speaking together, he said that he was a recipient of this monastery’s daily allowance,

[Note: [Col. 0514D] The term *praebendarii* was also used of poor persons who received their daily provisions from others. Thus Bernard, Sermon 1 on the Feast of All Saints, no. 2: “We are beggars, living upon God’s allowance.”]

and was fed in the house of God as a man of no usefulness.

[Col. 0515A] For he was truly meek and humble of heart; and although he flourished in other virtues, he possessed in a special manner the grace of gentleness. Therefore he showed himself lovable and approachable to all, as indeed he was exceedingly lovable.

3. Yet in all these things, how restrained his mouth and tongue were, all of you most fully knew who for so long saw his manner of life and heard his speech. Who ever heard from his mouth a sound of detraction, a word of buffoonery, talk of self-glory, the voice of envy? Who ever caught him either judging others or assenting to one who judged? Who could hear him speak empty things? Rather, who did not fear being overheard by him if he happened to speak such things? Clearly he carefully guarded [Col. 0515B] his ways so that he might not sin with his tongue, knowing that “the man who does not offend in word is a perfect man” (Jas. 3:2).

Far from you, Humbert, be that evangelical woe: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn” (Luke 6:25). Did any one of you find him laughing, even among many who laughed? He did indeed brighten his countenance for the sake of those sitting with him, so as not to become burdensome; but, if you remember well, he did not permit himself full laughter.

Moreover, how great his fervour in God’s work was by day and night, you not only saw but admired, even to the day of his death. For although he had nearly reached decrepit old age, and, besides the inconveniences of old age, was wearied and broken by so many and such great infirmities—of which many of you [Col. 0515C] are not ignorant—nevertheless, as the saying goes, his spirit conquered his years and did not know how to yield to infirmity. In cold and heat, climbing and descending hills and valleys, he kept pace with the labour of the young, so that he was an object of wonder and astonishment to all.

Whenever, because of the multitude of business matters, I kept him back for counsel, he remained sad and clouded until he was restored to your company. Very rarely was he ever found absent from the choir of those chanting at the solemn vigils—which he nonetheless often anticipated—or from the other Hours; and then only because, when an immediate summons of death had come, infirmity followed.

4. In the refectory he scarcely used even the common foods; if anything else happened to be set before him—

[Note: [Col. 0515D] Thus the holy Father sometimes arranged for the sick to receive something in the refectory besides the common foods, as in Sermon 36 on Various Subjects, no. 2. For the use of wine, see the notes on Epistle 1.]

—he either did not accept it [Col. 0515D] or accepted it so reluctantly that he often troubled our whole community over the matter. He had resolved always to drink water, had I not resisted with all my strength. If at any time he was compelled to drink wine, it was wine more in colour than in taste, so excessively did he drown it with water. Hardly ever did he enter the infirmary except when obedience compelled him; hardly, once he had entered, could he be kept there.

I confess it: in this respect he was insufficiently obedient, because he oppressed me with the weight of his authority. I praise him; in this I do not praise him, because, as you know, he persisted in such things with no little obstinacy. I believe that if he felt anything grievous, he felt it because [Col. 0516A] he agreed with us too little concerning the necessity of his body.

[Note: [Col. 0516D] The same is said of him in the already cited *Exordium*. Compare Bernard’s Sermon 19 on the Song of Songs, no. 7, where he reproves religious who are too much attached to their own will in such austerities.]

But what was he like in counsel? Pure indeed, and discerning. I know this all the better because I more often sounded his heart. Yet I do not alone know it; the whole of your community knows it also. For who, struck by the multitude or magnitude of temptations, did not hear from his mouth both the root of the temptation and the remedy for its cure? Thus he traversed every corner of the sick person’s conscience, so that one making confession could believe that he had seen everything, had been present at everything.

5. And how great was his charity? He had so clothed himself with bowels of mercy that he excused everyone and interceded for all, even without the knowledge of those for whom he spoke; he did not respect persons, but needs.

[Col. 0516B] Therefore he was humble in heart, sweet in speech, energetic in work, fervent in charity, faithful in what was entrusted to him, circumspect and prudent in counsel. He was more self-possessed than all the men whom I have seen in these days: one and the same man, steadfast at every time and every hour. Truly, he set his footsteps in the paths of the Lord Jesus and did not draw back his foot until he had completed the course of his journey.

He was poor, and this man also was poor. He lived amid labours, and this man amid many labours. He was crucified, and this man, fastened to many and great crosses, bore the marks of the Lord Jesus in his body, completing in his flesh what was lacking of Christ’s sufferings. He rose again, and this man shall rise again. He ascended into heaven, and this man is believed to be about to ascend.

[Col. 0516C] He shall indeed ascend when the King of glory descends for our sake, as he had previously ascended, in order to make his power known; for it is an excellence no less great to descend through the air than to have ascended through the air. For thus the angels once foretold: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from us into heaven, shall so come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

“Do not praise a man during his lifetime,” says Scripture (Sir. 11:30), because praise is not secure except after death. I carefully observed this principle with him: while he lived, I did not open my mouth on such matters, lest perhaps I might incur the charge of flattery, or he the fault of vanity. Now, certainly, neither is feared; for I do not see him, and perhaps he does not hear me. Yet even if he hears, he is not moved [Col. 0516D] by human words, cleaving more strongly and more happily to the Word of God. The enemy shall gain no advantage over him, and the suggester of vanity shall not add harm to him.

6. Behold now before you, sweetest Father, is that fountain of purity for which you thirsted with such ardour of soul. Behold, you are immersed in that abyss of divine mercy, the memory of whose abundant sweetness you were wont so devoutly to pour forth. For who was so devout a preacher of divine mercy, so zealous a commender of human purity, so affectionate a lover of both? Or to whom did you ever speak five words [Col. 0517A] in which true purity did not resound, in which the holy mercy of God was not heard?

Therefore I do not grieve for you, to whom God has granted the desire of your soul. Rather, I grieve that faithful counsel, great assistance, a man of one heart with me, a man after my own heart, has been taken from me. All these evils have fallen back upon me. “Your wrath, O Lord Jesus, has passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me.” You have removed friend and neighbour far from me; and, delivering my acquaintances from misery, you have left me in miseries. You have taken from me brothers in the flesh, brothers still closer in the spirit, men wise according to you both in your affairs and in secular concerns. You have taken away, one after another, those who bore my burden—a great burden which you imposed upon me.

Of so many persons necessary to me, Humbert alone, or nearly alone, remained; [Col. 0517B] the sweeter friend because the older—and you have taken him, because he was yours. I, I alone am left for blows; I die in every one of them, and you have brought all your waves over me. Would that you who scourge would kill once for all, and not preserve a miserable man for so many and such great deaths! Yet I do not contradict the words of the Holy One; but may he who has begun himself crush me, and let this be my consolation: that, while afflicting me with pain, he does not spare me. I am ready for scourges, if perhaps the merciful Father may change scourges into benefits.

Thus my words are not full of murmuring, but of sorrow. I do not weep for Humbert; for one summoned to the rich man’s table is not to be wept for. But I weep for myself and for you, for this house and for our other brothers, all of whom awaited counsel from his mouth.

[Col. 0517C] Thus too the Saviour, bearing his cross as a thief bears his noose, when he saw the women who had followed him from Galilee lamenting over him, turned to them and said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me; but weep over yourselves and over your children” (Luke 23:28). “For those things that concern me have an end” (Luke 22:37). The things you see prepared for me are temporal; the things you do not see are eternal. If they are temporal, they are transitory; if transitory, they are also mortal. And this alone is proof that a thing is passing or mortal: it can be seen. The things we beheld in Humbert’s death were temporal; but now he possesses joy and gladness through everlasting ages.

7. Therefore we ought not to mourn for one for whom there is neither mourning [Col. 0518A] nor sorrow. Nor ought we murmur on our own account, from whom he has been taken away; rather, let us give thanks that he was granted to us for so long. For, as I judge, a decade has now elapsed during which he lived only for us and on our behalf.

[Note: [Col. 0517D] Abbot Humbert withdrew to Clairvaux in the year 1138. If he survived there for a decade, his death must be dated not to 1145, as Manrique holds, but to 1140. Manrique assigns Humbert’s final day to 7 December, Chalemot to 7 September.]

And this is my fear: lest he was transferred because we were no longer worthy of his companionship. Yet who knows whether he was perhaps taken away in order that he might protect us by his intercessions before the Father? May it be so! For if he possessed such charity while he was with us that he more willingly yielded to me than to himself everything pertaining to bodily need, how much more now, when he cleaves to that supreme charity which is God, does he have greater favour and charity toward me?

But perhaps he now knows more fully [Col. 0518B] the truth about me and my manner of life; and he does not sympathize as he used to, but, as I fear, is indignant. And if God has taken him away even because of our sins, may he himself obtain that this very thing be mercifully remitted to us, lest we bear punishment upon punishment!

8. For the rest, brothers, I tell you: if you followed his footsteps, you would not so easily fall into vain thoughts and idle speech, jokes and buffoonery; for in these you lose much both of your life and of your time. Irrevocable time flies; and while you think you are avoiding that least punishment, you incur a greater one. Know this: after this life, in places of purification, things neglected here will be repaid a hundredfold, even to the last farthing.

[Col. 0518C] I know that it is hard for the undisciplined person to embrace discipline, for the talkative person to endure silence, for one accustomed to wandering to remain stable. But it will be harder—much harder—to endure those future sufferings. This man who is buried here endured much at the beginning, as I myself knew, in struggles of this kind; but he fought with much effort and conquered. And just as it was then hard for him to endure conflict amid temptations, so it would now be harder for him to return to those follies, because good habit had become second nature.

Exercise yourselves in this discipline, and attend to that pattern which you saw and heard in him, so that you may attain to him whom he attained, who is God blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0517]

## ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Note: [Col. 0517D] Chalemot records the dedication of the basilica of Clairvaux on the third day before the Ides of October; but it was later than the dedication referred to here by Bernard—namely, that of the new basilica, which was not yet completed when Bernard departed this life. If the Dedication sermons are correctly arranged in the old books, the dedication of the old basilica was celebrated after the feast of St Andrew.]

### SERMON I. On the five sacraments of dedication

[Col. 0517D]

1. Today’s feast, brothers, ought to be more devout for us in proportion as it is more familiar. The other solemnities of the saints we share with other churches; this one, however, belongs so specifically to us that [Col. 0518D] it must be celebrated either by us or by no one. It is ours because it concerns our church; but it is more truly ours because it concerns ourselves.

Perhaps you are surprised and ashamed that feasts should be celebrated concerning yourselves. But do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding. For what holiness could these stones have possessed [Col. 0519A] that we should celebrate their solemnities? They do indeed possess holiness, but on account of your bodies. Or can anyone doubt that your bodies are holy—bodies which are the temple of the Holy Spirit—so that each person may know how to possess his vessel in sanctification? Therefore souls are holy because of God’s Spirit dwelling in you; bodies are holy because of souls; and the house too is holy because of bodies.

Certainly, that soul was still held in corruptible flesh and in a body of sin, and yet committed the grave crime of adultery—the soul of him who said: “Guard my soul, for I am holy” (Ps. 85:2). God is indeed wonderful in his saints, not only in those who are heavenly but also in those who are earthly. In both places he has saints, and in both he is wonderful: making the former blessed, the latter holy.

[Col. 0519B]

2. Do you seek proof of the holiness of which we speak, and desire that miracles of these saints be shown to you? Surely many of you have courageously emerged from sins and vices in which you rotted like beasts in their own dung; and daily, as these things assail you, you powerfully resist them, according to the Apostle, who certainly speaks of saints: “They were strengthened,” he says, “out of weakness; they became strong in battle” (Heb. 11:34).

What could be more wonderful than when one who formerly could scarcely abstain for two days from lust, gluttony and revelry, drunkenness, chambers and indecencies, and other vices both like and unlike these, now abstains from them for many years—indeed, for his whole life? What greater miracle is there than when [Col. 0519C] so many young men, so many adolescents, so many nobles—in short, all whom I see here—are held as though in an open prison without chains, bound only by the fear of God; when they persevere in so great an affliction of penitence, beyond human capacity, above nature, against custom?

You yourselves, I think, see how many miracles we could now discover if it were permitted to investigate individually each person’s exodus from Egypt and journey through the desert—that is, his renunciation of the world, entrance into the monastery, and conduct within the monastery. And what are these but manifest proofs of the Holy Spirit dwelling in you? For the vital motions of the body prove that the soul dwells in a body; spiritual life proves that the Spirit dwells in a soul. The former is discerned by sight [Col. 0519D] and hearing; the latter by charity and humility and the other virtues.

3. Therefore today’s feast is yours, dearest brothers; it is yours. You have been dedicated to the Lord; he has chosen and taken you as his own. “To you,” says the Prophet, “the poor man is abandoned; you will be a helper to the orphan” (Ps. 9:14). How well, beloved, you have exchanged whatever you might have possessed in the world, since now, by leaving it, you have deserved to belong to the Maker of the world as his own, and to have as your own possession him who is without doubt the portion and inheritance of his own.

For not as the children of iniquity said—“Happy is the people for whom these things are,” namely the temporal things previously mentioned: storehouses pouring forth one kind into another, fruitful sheep, and the like—not, I say, is happy the people for whom these things are; [Col. 0520A] “but happy is the people whose Lord is their God” (Ps. 143:13, 15).

See then whether it is not fitting that we should keep feast on the day when he took us as his own and took possession of us through his ministers and vicars, so that what he himself promised long ago may come to pass: “I will be their God in the midst of them” (Zech. 2:11), and we shall be his people and the sheep of his pasture. For when this house was dedicated to the Lord through the hands of bishops, it was done for our sake without doubt—not only for those of us who were then present, but also for all who until the end of the age are to serve the Lord in this place.

4. Accordingly, what visibly took place in the walls must be fulfilled spiritually in us. And, if you wish to know, these things are: sprinkling, inscription, [Col. 0520B] anointing, illumination, and blessing. Bishops performed these things in this visible house; Christ, present as high priest of good things to come, works them invisibly in us every day.

First, indeed, he sprinkles us with hyssop, that we may be cleansed, washed, and made white, and that it may be said of us: “Who is this that comes up made white?” (Song 8:5). He washes us, I say, in confession; he washes us with the rain of tears; he washes us with the sweat of penitence; but most of all he washes us with that most precious water which flowed from the fountain of mercy, that is, from his side.

He sprinkles us with hyssop, a low-growing herb and a cleanser of the breast, with the water of saving wisdom—which is the fear of the Lord, the beginning of wisdom and the fountain of life—adding also the seasoning of salt, lest fear without hope and devotion be tasteless.

[Col. 0520C] Nor does he only sprinkle us: he also inscribes us with the finger of God, by which he cast out demons, undoubtedly in the Holy Spirit. He inscribes his law, I say, no longer upon stone but upon fleshy tablets of the heart, fulfilling the prophetic promise by which he pledged to take away the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh (Ezek. 11:19): that is, a heart not hard, not obstinate, not Jewish, but pious, gentle, tractable, and devout.

“Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach out of your law” (Ps. 93:12). Blessed, I say, are those taught and mindful of his commandments, but so as to do them (Ps. 102:18). Otherwise, “to one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (Jas. 4:17); and the servant who knows [Col. 0520D] his master’s will and does not do it “shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12:47).

5. Hence it is necessary that the anointing of spiritual grace should help our weakness, applying the grace of its devotion to the crosses of these observances and of manifold penitence. For one cannot follow Christ without a cross; and without the anointing of the cross, who could endure its harshness? This is why many abhor and flee penitence: they see the cross, indeed, but not the anointing as well.

But you who have experienced it know yourselves that our cross is truly anointed, and that, through the grace of the assisting Spirit, our penitence is sweet and delightful; indeed, if I may say so, our bitterness is most sweet. Yet after the anointing of this grace has gone before, Christ no longer places his lamp [Col. 0521A] under a bushel, but upon a lampstand; for it is time that our light should shine before people, that they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16).

6. But we await the blessing at the end, when he opens his hand and fills every living creature with blessing. For in the four things previously mentioned merits consist; in blessing are the rewards. In blessing the whole grace of sanctification will be completed, when we pass into the house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. It is the house built from living stones—namely, angels and human beings. For both the building and the dedication itself will be completed together.

Separated timbers and stones do not make a house, nor can anyone dwell in them; only their joining together makes a house. Thus the perfect unity of the heavenly spirits, joined together without any division among themselves, makes a whole and fitting dwelling-place for God, which the indwelling glory of his majesty makes blessed beyond speech.

[Col. 0521B] Who could know all the counsels of kings, or know all their words and deeds, as the timbers and stones of a palace would know them—if they lacked no faculty of understanding? Thus the living and rational stones of that heavenly court are present at divine counsels, know the mysteries of the Trinity, and hear ineffable words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). For the more they see, understand, and know, the more they love, the more they praise, and the more deeply they marvel.

7. But because we have said that that house is coherent and perfectly joined together, it remains for us to express in some measure the joint and connection itself. We read in Isaiah: “It is good for glue” (Isa. 41:7). Therefore those stones adhere to one another by a double glue: full knowledge and perfect love. For they are united to one another in proportion as they stand nearer to charity itself, which is God. Nor can any suspicion separate them from one another, where the ray of truth, penetrating all things, allows nothing whatever in one to remain hidden from another.

Since even now “the one who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6:17), there can be no doubt that the blessed spirits who cleave perfectly to him likewise penetrate all things together with him and in him.

[Col. 0521C] If you desire to reach this house, let your soul long and faint for the courts of the Lord, as the Prophet cries: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4). Imitate, nonetheless, the Prophet himself, who, as he swore to the Lord, made a vow to the God of Jacob: “If I enter into the tabernacle of my house,” and so forth (Ps. 131:2–3). But this must be treated by us in another sermon, should the Lord himself grant it.

### SERMON II. How we ought to cleave both to ourselves and to others

1. Long ago the glorious king and prophet of the Lord, holy David, began to be moved by a certain devout reflection, judging it unworthy that the Lord of hosts should as yet have no house on earth, while he himself dwelt in a house of royal dignity (2 Sam. 7:2; 1 Chron. 17:1). [Col. 0522A]

Brothers, it is fitting that we too should faithfully consider this same matter and vigorously bring it into effect. Why, although God was pleased by that thought of the Prophet, the work was nevertheless reserved for Solomon, is another question, perhaps requiring a longer discussion.

Now, soul, you indeed dwell in a lofty house constructed for you by God: I mean this body, which he has so joined together, fitted, adorned, and ordered that you might dwell within it gloriously and delightfully. But he has also made for the body itself a lofty house, most suitable and beautiful: I mean this sensible and inhabitable world. Do you not then judge it unworthy [Col. 0522B] that he should have made a house for you, while you neglect to build a temple for him?

You still have a house, but be assured that your house will shortly fall; and unless you first provide another, you will be exposed to rain, wind, and cold. Alas! “Who can stand before his cold?” How happy, therefore—exceedingly happy—is the soul that can say: “We know that, if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1).

Therefore, soul, do not now give sleep to your eyes or slumber to your eyelids, until you find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob (Ps. 131:4–5).

2. But what do we suppose, brothers? Where is the site of this building found, or who can be its architect? For this visible temple was certainly made for us, for our habitation; “the Most High does not dwell in things made with hands.” What temple, then, shall we build for him who says—and says truly—“I fill heaven and earth”? (Jer. 23:24).

[Col. 0522C] I should be greatly troubled, and my spirit would be distressed within me, were it not that I hear him say of someone: “I and the Father will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Therefore I now know where a house must be prepared for him, since nothing can contain him except his own image. The soul is capable of him, since it was created in his image.

Therefore make haste now, Zion; adorn your bridal chamber, for the Lord has delighted in you and your land shall be inhabited. Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion; your God shall dwell within you. Say with Mary: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to your word.” Say in the words of blessed Elizabeth: “And whence is this to me, that the majesty of the Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:38, 43).

[Col. 0522D] For how great is God’s kindness, how great his condescension, how great the dignity, how great the glory of souls: that the Lord of all, who has no need of anything, commands that a temple be made for him in them!

Therefore, brothers, with whole-hearted desire and fitting thanksgiving let us strive to build him a temple within ourselves: first taking care that he may dwell in each individual, then that he may dwell in all together; for he does not disdain either individuals or the whole body. First, then, [Col. 0523A] let each person take care not to be at variance with himself; for “every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and house will fall upon house” (Matt. 12:25). Nor will Christ enter where the walls are leaning and the partitions broken down. Does not the soul itself wish to possess the house of its body intact? And must it not leave if the members are scattered from one another? Let it therefore see to this also: if it desires Christ to dwell through faith in its heart—that is, in itself—let it carefully beware lest its members be at variance with one another: reason, will, and memory.

Let reason be free from error, so that it may agree well with the will; for the will loves such reason. Let the will likewise be free from wickedness, since reason approves such a will. Otherwise, if the soul judges itself, on account of [Col. 0523B] the perversity of its will, in the very matter which it approves through reason, there is civil war and dangerous discord; for reason continually reproves such a will—accuses it, judges it, condemns it. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be reconciled with your adversary while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps the adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the torturers, and you be thrown into prison” (Matt. 5:25).

Let memory also be free from stain, so that no sin may remain in it which is not erased by pure confession and worthy fruits of repentance. Otherwise, the conscience in which sin lies hidden is hated by the will and abhorred by reason. Thus he prepares a good dwelling for God whose reason has not been deceived, whose will has not been perverted, and whose memory has not been defiled.

[Col. 0523C]

### 4.

Now, when individuals are thus disposed, it is necessary that we too should all be joined and bound together by mutual charity, which is the bond of perfection. For perfect knowledge cannot be possessed in this life; perhaps it ought not to be. In the heavenly house, knowledge is the nourishment of love. For who will boast that he has a pure heart? Therefore what is known could easily cause confusion, and the knower could be offended. There knowledge will be delightful, where there is no longer any stain.

That house, therefore, is more firmly joined together, as though destined to remain forever; this one, like the encampment of soldiers, coheres less perfectly within itself. That indeed is the house of joy; this [Col. 0523D] is the house of warfare. That is the house of praise; this, of prayer. This, I say, is the city of our strength; that is the city of our rest. Therefore, if we are victorious here, there we shall be glorious: having a diadem instead of a helmet; a sceptre and palm instead of a sword; a golden cloak instead of a shield; and a robe of joy instead of a breastplate.

Meanwhile it seems more useful to be pressed down than to be destroyed; and to bear the weight of shield and breastplate rather than to be wounded by the fiery darts of the Evil One. May he who is blessed for ages preserve us from these by his heavenly protection. Amen.

## SERMON III. On the Threefold Equipment We Have for Guarding God

### 1.

This house, brothers, is the stronghold of the eternal King, [Col. 0524A] but it is besieged by enemies. Therefore, all of us who have sworn allegiance to his arms and enlisted in his service ought to know that we need three kinds of equipment for guarding this fortress: namely, fortification, weapons, and provisions.

What, then, is the fortification? “Zion, the city of our strength,” says the prophet: “A Savior will be placed in it as wall and outer wall” (Isa. 26:1). The wall is self-restraint; the outer wall is patience. Good is the wall of self-restraint, which so surrounds and encircles us on every side that death is granted no entrance through the windows of the eyes or through the other senses. Good is the outer wall of patience, which withstands the first assaults of the enemy, so that amid many temptations we may stand bravely and persevere continually without being shaken.

For the one remedy, when self-restraint is struck and in some way begins to totter, is to oppose patience, and, however fiercely the inclination to sin may burn, to refuse consent in every way. “In your patience,” he says, “you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). Thus the Savior himself is placed in his city as wall and outer wall, made for us by God the Father righteousness, and by the prophet patience, as the same prophet says: “For you are my patience, O Lord” (Ps. 70:5). A wall, I say, is set in one’s manner of life; an outer wall in suffering: abstaining from all enticements of the flesh and of this present world, and bravely enduring every adversity.

### 2.

Weapons also must be prepared—but spiritual weapons, mighty through God—not only for resistance, but also for attacking and courageously conquering the enemy. “Put on the armor of God,” says the Apostle [Col. 0524C] (Eph. 6:11), and so forth.

For what do we suppose, brothers? The enemy’s temptation is indeed grievous to us; but our prayer is far more grievous to him. His wickedness and cunning harm us; but our simplicity and mercy torment him much more. He cannot endure our humility; he burns at our charity and is tortured by gentleness and obedience.

Nor can we even be brought under the pressure of famine so as to be compelled to surrender the fortress to our enemies; for, thanks be to God, that dreadful threat of the prophet—indeed, of the Lord through the prophet—has not come upon us: the famine and thirst, not of bread and water, but of the word [variant: of hearing the word] of God (Amos 8:11). For thus we have it: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God” [Col. 0524D] (Deut. 8:3; Matt. 4:4).

Thus provisions do not fail us, since we often hear sermons, and still more frequently sacred readings; and at times we taste the delights of spiritual devotion, as though little dogs were eating of the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table. I mean those heavenly guests who are filled from the abundance of God’s house. We also have the bread of tears, which, though less sweet, nevertheless strengthens the human heart exceedingly well. We have also the bread of obedience, of which the Lord speaks to his disciples: “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34). Above all, we have the living bread from heaven, the body of the Lord and Savior, by whose strength as food every strength of the adverse party is cast down.

[Col. 0525A]

### 3.

Thus the strength of the Lord’s fortress is fortified in such a way that we need fear nothing, provided we are willing to act faithfully and courageously—that is, provided we are found neither traitors nor cowards nor sluggards. For traitors are all those who attempt to introduce Christ’s enemies into this fortress of the Lord: such, certainly, are detractors, hateful to God, who sow discord and foster scandals among brothers. For just as the Lord’s dwelling was made in peace, so it is evident that in discord a place is made for the devil.

Do not be surprised, brothers, if I seem to speak rather harshly, because truth flatters no one. Let anyone know himself altogether to be a traitor if, heaven forbid, he attempts to introduce any vices into this house and to make the temple of God a den of demons. Thanks be to God, we do not [Col. 0525B] find many such persons here. Yet we sometimes discover certain people who converse with the enemy and make a pact with death: that is, who endeavor, as far as they can, to weaken the discipline of the order, cool its fervor, disturb peace, and injure charity.

But let us beware of them as much as we can, as it is written of some: “But Jesus did not entrust himself to them” (John 2:24). I tell you that, although they are tolerated for the present, they will soon bear a heavy judgment unless they reform themselves more quickly, just as they endeavor to inflict serious harm. For why, brother, do you prove faithful by your deeds to vanity, lukewarmness, or any other vice, while by your tonsure you lie to God? You have indeed delivered Christ an excellent fortress if you hand Clairvaux over to his enemies. Each year he receives from it the choicest and most precious revenues in his sight; and he is accustomed to bring into this place of his defense much spoil which he tears from enemies, and he has great confidence in its strength.

For behold, those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, he gathered from the regions, from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea. To what punishments, then, do you suppose the traitor of this fortress ought to be exposed after he has been detected and seized? For he can neither hide nor flee. He will certainly not be condemned to the common death of others, but must perish by refined torments. But I shall not dwell longer on these matters. I trust that henceforth we shall more carefully guard against so detestable a betrayal, striving with greater vigilance not to draw vices in, but to repel them—whatever they may be, whether carnal or worldly—lest we deserve to incur the mark or punishment of traitors.

[Col. 0525D]

### 4.

In the second place, this too must be guarded against: lest anyone, cast down by faint-heartedness, flee from the fortification, trembling in fear where there is no fear, while, where the greatest danger lies, he is secure with insane recklessness. For whoever flees exposes himself to hostile hands and hostile swords, as though he did not know that those enemies are utterly without mercy—cruel indeed toward outsiders, but far more cruel toward their own, since they are most cruel toward themselves.

### 5.

Now I shall briefly mention the third danger also, because the hour has passed while, being—as is fitting—most eager for your salvation, I seek diverse remedies for diverse infirmities of conduct. What good is it if you will neither betray the fortress nor abandon it, but remain within it sluggish and idle?

Therefore, beloved, let us labor with our whole soul and all our strength to hold in our hands the fortress entrusted to us by the Lord and our King: watchful against every cunning device of the enemy and prepared against all his stratagems, as it is written: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). But since we know by whom it was said, “Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. 126:1), let us humble ourselves under the mighty hand of the Most High, committing both ourselves and this house with all devotion to his mercy, that he himself may guard us from all the snares of all enemies [Col. 0526B], to the praise and glory of his name, which is blessed for ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On the Threefold Dwelling

### 1.

We celebrate this day with vowed praises and honor it with festal joys. But since it neither befits religious persons nor becomes wise persons to be ignorant of what they venerate or to celebrate what they do not know, we must inquire in whose—or in commemoration of which saints—this is done. Yet I do not think that I should presume to determine this from myself: let another speak first, whose testimony may seem greater and more credible.

Perhaps you wonder why we say these things beforehand, when the present church itself, whose annual dedication is celebrated, more clearly presents itself to your sight. For why should we hesitate to call its walls holy, when the consecrated hands of bishops have sanctified them by such great mysteries? From that time onward, the frequent sound of holy readings has resounded there, the devout murmurs of holy prayers have whispered, the blessed presence of holy relics has been honored, and the tireless watch of holy spirits is known to keep guard.

Perhaps you say: “The rest is indeed evident; but who boasts that he has seen angelic watches?” Even if you perhaps do not see them, there is one who sees them—the very one who sends them. Who is he? Surely he who speaks through the prophet: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have set watchmen” (Isa. 62:6). There is indeed the Jerusalem above, which is free, our mother; but I could never believe that watchmen have been set upon her walls, of whom the Prophet sings in praise: “He has made your borders peace” (Ps. 147:14). But if you judge that insufficient, go on and hear what follows in the preceding testimony: “All day,” he says, “and all night, forever they shall not be silent” (Isa. 62:6). For even this shows that this is not the Jerusalem of which you read: “Its gates shall not be shut by day; for there shall be no night there” (Rev. 21:25). That Jerusalem, therefore, suffers no alternation and needs no watchmen; rather, watchmen must be assigned to ours both by day and by night: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have set watchmen.”

### 2.

You are gracious, Lord: you cannot be content with the frail protection of our walls, but over the human prelates set over human beings you also place angelic guardianship, that they may defend both the walls and those enclosed by their circuit. Yes, Father, because thus it has pleased you, and thus it is necessary for us. For our administration is insufficient unless you send those ministering spirits both with us and for us into service, so that we may inherit salvation.

For what if we do not see their service, when we experience their help? What if we do not deserve the sight, when we feel the effect? From this very fact we certainly learn that invisible things are to be preferred to visible. “For the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18). Indeed, in invisible things lies the cause of visible things, so that, according to the Apostle, “the invisible things of God are understood and perceived through the things that have been made, from the visible creation” (Rom. 1:20). Thus he formerly refuted the Jews, who blasphemed the Holy One of God concerning the invisible forgiveness of sins, by the visible sign of bodily healing: “That you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins”—then he says to the paralytic—“Arise, take up your bed, and go into your house” (Mark 2:10).

### 3.

Likewise, he overcame by manifest proofs that Pharisee who murmured against the physician working salvation and was angered at the infirm woman being saved, recounting the woman’s services. For he erred in recoiling from her as though she were still a sinner, though, clinging to the divine feet, she watered them with tears, wiped them with her hair, pressed them with kisses, and anointed them with ointment. For who would recount crimes now erased? Who would be angry with her for touching him? Who would deem her a sinner, when, as she laments her sins, she hates iniquity; as she kisses the Lord’s feet, she loves righteousness; again, as she wipes them with her hair, she displays humility; and as she anoints them with ointment, she shows gentleness? Is it possible for sin to reign in a contrite mind and a groaning spirit? Or does not great love cover a multitude of sins? “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:38–47). Rightly, therefore, she will now be called, not a sinner according to your judgment, Pharisee, but a holy disciple of Christ, from whom she also learned in so short a time to be meek and humble of heart.

Surely this is what you read in the prophet, but perhaps neglected: “Overthrow the wicked, and they shall be no more” (Prov. 12:7). So, beloved, if that ancient accuser of the brethren reproaches you with your past sins, sins of which you too are ashamed, hear the Apostle nobly consoling you and saying: “Such indeed you were, but you have been washed, you have been sanctified” (1 Cor. 6:11); and: “You now have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6:22); and, expressing it more plainly: “The temple of God,” he says, “is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17).

### 4.

Surely he is the one whose first word, out of reverence for him, we reserved for the beginning of this sermon, when we were asking which saints’ holiness we joyfully celebrate with solemn devotion. For although the consecration of bishops, the frequent use of Scripture, the diligence of prayers, the relics of saints, and the visitation of angels make these walls both called holy and actually holy, yet their holiness must by no means be believed to be honored for their own sake, since it is not certain that they are sanctified for their own sake. Rather, houses are holy for the sake of bodies, bodies for the sake of souls, and souls for the sake of the indwelling Spirit.

Nor should anyone doubt this, since a visible sign of his invisible grace is given us for good. I mean in this: that you yourselves rise like that Gospel paralytic; that you so easily take up this bodily bed on which you lay sick; and, finally, that you walk into your house—indeed, that house of which you rejoice, saying with the Prophet, “We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121:1). O wonderful house, to be preferred to beloved tabernacles and desirable courts! “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord.” But much more: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:2, 5). For glorious things have been said of you, city of God. In the tabernacles there is the groaning of penitence; in the courts, a foretaste of joy; in you, fullness of glory. This is the lowest house, of prayer; that is the middle house, of expectation; you are the house of thanksgiving and praise. Happy, therefore, is the one who here turns away from evil, which is guilt, and does good, so that there he may be freed from evil, which is punishment, and in you receive good.

Here are the firstfruits of the Spirit; there, riches; in you, fullness: where that good measure, packed down, shaken together, and overflowing, will be given into our bosoms. Here, finally, people become holy; there, secure; in you, blessed. For these are the firstfruits of the Spirit granted meanwhile to those who are fighting: holiness in conduct, piety in intention, strength in struggle.
