By holiness of conduct understand the fruits of repentance and every bodily exercise of the divine commandments. And because these cannot be simple unless the eye is simple, piety of intention and purity of heart are necessarily required, lest either ambition for honor or desire for praise creep in; but that he alone may be desired who alone fills desire, and that every grace we have received may return to the source of its own fountain. Remember, however, that perseverance alone is crowned, and that amid so many dangers it cannot easily be preserved unless, in so manifold a struggle, you attain manifold strength. These things are in the tabernacles.

### 5.

But in the courts, which receive those departing after troublesome conflicts in order to refresh them with pleasant joy [Note: [Col. 0527D] The statement concerning the courts which now receive the souls of the righteous as they depart seems less satisfactory. But we have spoken sufficiently of this matter a little earlier, at sermon [Col. 0528D] 2 on All Saints. See Cornelius on Rev. 6:9; and there Pererius, Disputations; Bellarmine, book I, On the Beatitude of the Saints, chap. 3.], the riches of the Spirit are now bestowed: rest from labors, security from anxieties, peace from enemies. For the Spirit himself now says that they may rest from their labors—the same Spirit who hitherto, with such fervor, was accustomed to forbid rest and impose labors. He himself will set them apart from cares and separate them from every anxiety—the same Spirit who now lays counsels in the soul and makes it anxiously troubled about many things. Having won the victory, he himself will grant them sweetly to sleep in peace, who, while the roaring lion still rages, both summons them to vigils and girds them for battle.

Yet in these things, as we touched on above, there is rather deliverance from evil than a bestowal of good—except that the harsh experience of our necessity compels us to count the absence of evil as heaps of good, just as conscience counts freedom from graver crimes as fullness of holiness. From this one may perceive how far we are from the highest good, since we judge freedom from guilt to be righteousness and freedom from misery to be blessedness.

### 6.

But far be it from anyone to imagine the abundance of that house, the torrent of delight, and whatever other things “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man,” which God has prepared for those who love him. Therefore, O man, do not wish to hear what no human ear has heard, nor seek from a human being what neither a human eye sees nor a human mind comprehends. Yet, lest we be altogether silent concerning this, as we greet our homeland from afar, we seem to scent a threefold promise: of power, magnificence, and glory.

For he was a man, and a son of this captivity, who said: “I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. 70:16). But we, being surrounded by weakness, can know what it is to be without weakness; what it is to be clothed with strength and to enter into power—not merely power, but great power, perhaps even omnipotence—we cannot yet know. The faithful witness also cries out that “those whom he justified, them he also magnified” (Rom. 8:30). But magnificence, especially such as befits one to proceed from greatness that has neither end nor number—would that our present smallness may be permitted to expect it; for it is not permitted to assess it.

Nor need anyone fear or distrust the promise of glory itself: then you will happily and confidently drink in the glory whose desire now is deterred by such great threats. For then there will be for each one praise from God, surely secure and everlasting, free alike from end and discrimination; and, as it is written, “Pleasant and fitting is praise” (Ps. 146:1). Come then, brothers: let us meanwhile fight manfully in the tabernacles, that afterward we may rest sweetly in the courts, and at last glory sublimely in the house, when this momentary and light tribulation of ours works in us, beyond all measure unto heights, an eternal weight of glory; when we shall praise in the Lord all day, in truth indeed, not in vanity.

## SERMON V. On the Twofold Consideration of Oneself

### 1.

We celebrate this day with vows of praise and honor it with festal joys. Now it is easy enough for me to say this; but if you go on to ask in whose commemoration it is observed, that may perhaps not be so easy. Whenever the memorial of an apostle, martyr, or confessor is celebrated, it is not difficult to say whose it is—for instance, that of Saint Peter, glorious Stephen, our holy father Benedict, or one of the other great princes of the great court of heaven.

But now no one of these has a solemnity observed; yet some solemnity is being observed. And not merely some solemnity, but no small one. And, if you now wish to hear: it is the feast of the house of the Lord, the temple of God, the city of the eternal King, the bride of Christ. Certainly no one doubts that the bride of the Holy of Holies is holy and most worthy of every honor of celebration. Or who can doubt that the house of God is holy, of which it is written: “Holiness befits your house” (Ps. 92:5)? So too his temple is holy, wonderful in righteousness (Ps. 64:5–6); and John testifies that he saw the holy city: “I saw,” he says, “the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” [Col. 0530B] (Rev. 21:2).

In these words, indeed, I have begun to reveal what I confess I had still wished to conceal. I mean that the same bride is a city, and also a temple, and no less a house. Nor is this surprising, especially since there is one who deigns to show himself to her alike as bridegroom, king, God, and householder.

Yet I do not think you have been satisfied until you learn more clearly what this house of the householder is, what this temple of God is, what city of this king, and finally what bride of this so glorious bridegroom has deserved both to be called and to be these things [variant: “hear”]. But concerning this I greatly fear to say what I think, lest any one of you—God forbid—happen to hear less faithfully or less humbly; lest perhaps someone leave this assembly either puffed up by the greatness of the glory or unbelieving because of the smallness of his own spirit.

For I always desire to find you both faithful and humble, since each is supremely necessary for salvation. For he gives grace only to the humble, and without faith it is impossible to please him. Therefore I desire and earnestly wish by every means that you should take care to present yourselves to him as both little and great; indeed, that you should present yourselves as both nothing and something, even [Col. 0530D] something great [variant: “nothing other than something great”]. For without a great heart you cannot receive those so great goods or do violence to the kingdom of heaven, any more than you can enter that same kingdom of heaven unless you are converted and become as little children (Matt. 18:3).

I am not a man of deep insight, nor can I pour forth to you what I have not tasted. Yet I shall say what I sometimes feel taking place within me, so that, if anyone perhaps judges it useful for himself, he may imitate it. Since long ago I was persuaded to have mercy on my own soul, in order thereafter to please my God (Sir. 30:24), I frequently reflect upon it. Would that it were permitted me once and for always [variant: rather, always]! There was a time when I did not at all wish to do this, because I loved it less—if indeed less, and not rather not at all. For how does anyone love that whose death he loves? But if, as is true and indubitable, the death of the soul is wickedness, then it is plainly an absolute judgment that “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6). Therefore I hated it, and would still hate it, unless he who first loved it had granted me this whatever-beginning of love for it.

[Col. 0531A]

### 3.

By his benefit, therefore, when I think of it, I sometimes seem to find in it, I confess, two contrary things. If I consider it as it is in itself and from itself, according to the truth of the matter, I can think nothing more truly of it than that it has been reduced to nothing. Why is it now necessary to enumerate its individual miseries: how burdened it is by sins, darkened by shadows, entangled in enticements, itching with desires, subject to passions, filled with illusions, always inclined to evil, prone to every vice, and finally full of all confusion and disgrace?

Indeed, if even all our acts of righteousness, when examined in the light of truth, are found like a menstrual cloth (Isa. 64:6), what then will our acts of unrighteousness be judged to be? If the light that is in us is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be? It is easy for each of us, if he examines all that is his more fully [variant: better] and without dissembling, and judges without partiality, to bear witness in every respect to apostolic truth and freely proclaim: “He who thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3).

“What is man, that you magnify him?” says the faithful and devout confession; “or why do you set your heart upon him?” [Col. 0531C] (Job 7:17). What indeed? Without doubt, man has become like vanity; man has been reduced to nothing; man is nothing. Yet how is he wholly nothing whom God magnifies? How is he nothing upon whom the divine heart is set?

### 4.

Let us take breath, brothers; and if we are nothing in our own hearts, perhaps something else concerning us lies hidden in the heart of God. O Father of mercies! O Father of the miserable! Why do you set your heart upon them? I know, I know: where your treasure is, there is your heart. How, then, are we nothing, if we are your treasure? “All nations are as though they were not before you; they are counted as nothing and emptiness.” Indeed, before you—but not so within you. Thus they are in the judgment of your truth, but not so in the affection of your mercy.

For you call the things that are not as though they were. Thus they are not, because you call things that are not; and they are, because you call them. For although they are not in relation to themselves, yet with you they are—indeed, according to the Apostle, not from works of righteousness but from him who calls (Rom. 9:12). Thus, indeed, you console in your mercy the person whom you have humbled in your truth, so that he who is rightly constricted in his own inward parts may be magnificently enlarged in yours. For all your ways are mercy and truth to those who seek your covenant and your testimonies (Ps. 24:10): the covenant, surely, of mercy, and the testimonies of truth.

### 5.

Read, O man, in your own heart; read within yourself the testimonies of truth concerning yourself. Even by this common light you will judge yourself unworthy. Read in the heart of God the covenant established in the blood of the Mediator, and you will find how far different it seems to possess by hope from possessing in reality.

“What is man,” he says, “that you magnify him?” Great, indeed, but in him; for he has been magnified [Col. 0532A] by him. Or how is he not great in the sight of the one who has such great care for him? “For he cares for us,” says the Apostle Peter (1 Pet. 5:7). And the Prophet: “But I am needy and poor; the Lord is mindful of me” (Ps. 39:18). Clearly this is an artful conjunction of the two considerations: by which, as though in one moment descending and ascending together, he saw both himself poor and needy and God solicitous for him.

This is angelic: to ascend and descend at once. “You shall see,” he says, “angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:51). For there is no such alternation in their ascents and descents. They are at once sent into ministry for those who shall inherit salvation, and stand before the face of majesty: God mercifully providing that we may have consolation and that they may suffer no disturbance. Otherwise, how could they endure with equanimity to be separated, even for a little while, for our sake from that countenance of glory upon which they always desire to look?

Finally, hear Truth himself in the Gospel: “Their angels”—that is, doubtless, the angels of the little ones—“always see the face of my Father in heaven” (Matt. 18:10); so assigned to the guardianship of little ones that they are in no way deprived of their own blessedness.

[Col. 0532C]

Hence Saint John saw the city Jerusalem descending; he could not behold it standing. And observe that he said “descending,” not “falling.” For once no small part of that city fell; but that part was by no means holy, since its grievous fall was that it became the enemy of all holiness.

### 6.

But John could not see this ruin and terrible fall, because it had not yet occurred; rather, the Word who was in the beginning saw it—the Beginning who spoke to the Apostles: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). Therefore that part which fell is to be restored by God when he fills up the ruins and rebuilds the walls of Jerusalem [Col. 0532D], though not from among those who fell.

But this city which appeared descending was already prepared, as the following words add: “Prepared by God” (Rev. 21:2). For it is divine preparation that causes the holy angels to descend without falling: by it both the will and the ability for this are prepared for them. Hence the Apostle also testifies that they are not only ministering spirits but are sent for ministry (Heb. 1:14). Why should he not send angels, for whose sake he himself willed to be sent by the Father? Why should he not bend down the heavens for those for whom the King of heaven himself also bent down, so that he wrote on the ground with his finger? (John 8:6). “O Lord, bend down your heavens”—that is too little—“and descend” (Ps. 143:5). What more? That he may also cause those to whom he condescended to ascend with him.

But, as we have already said, angelic ascent and descent lack alternation. We, however, must turn now in this direction, now in that, since it is neither permitted us to remain above for long nor expedient to linger below too long. “They rise up to the heavens and descend to the depths; their soul wasted away in evils” [Col. 0533A] (Ps. 106:26). Why is this? Clearly because their soul meanwhile wastes away in evils more than it delights in goods, since the former seem possessed in reality, but the latter only in hope. “Who then can be saved?” the disciples say to the Savior. And he: “With men this is impossible, but not with God” (Matt. 19:25–26). This is the whole of our confidence, this our one consolation, this the whole ground of our hope.

7. But now that we are certain of the possibility, what are we to do about the will? Who knows whether he is worthy of love or of hatred? [Col. 0533B] Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? (Rom. 11:34.) Here faith must plainly come to our aid; here truth [or: piety] must bring help: so that what concerning us lies hidden in the Father’s heart may be revealed to us through his own Spirit, and that his Spirit, bearing witness, may persuade our spirit that we are children of God. Let it persuade us by calling and freely justifying through faith; in these, indeed, there is as it were a middle passage from eternal predestination to future glorification. Therefore we believe that this twofold consideration is rightly called, on the one hand, that of judgment and truth, and, on the other, that of faith and piety.

Nor will you wonder that qualities so unlike are found in human beings, if you carefully observe how great a diversity of natures seems to have come together in man’s very substance. [Col. 0533C] For what is more exalted than the spirit of life? What lower than the clay of the earth? I think that even the wise men of this world were not unaware of this conjunction in man of things so discordant, when they defined man as “a rational mortal animal.” Marvelous indeed is the union of reason and mortality, the strange fellowship of discernment and corruption. So too, assuredly, in human habits, affections, and pursuits there is found no lesser—perhaps even a greater—contrariety; so that, if you look separately upon all depravity as it is, and then consider one by one whatever good appears to be present, you would judge it a full miracle that such opposites have met together.

Hence a man now deserves to hear “Bar-Jonah,” and now “Satan.” [Col. 0533D] Do not be surprised at this. Recall from the Gospel to whom it was said—and both truly, for both were spoken by Truth itself—first, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah”; and not long afterward, “Get behind me, Satan.” One person, then, was both, though not both from one source. The former was from the Father, the latter from the man; yet he himself was both. Whence “Bar-Jonah”? Because not flesh and blood, but the Father revealed to him what he had spoken. Whence “Satan”? Because he savoured the things that were of men, not those of God (Matt. 16:17, 23).

Now, if by both considerations we diligently examine what we are—indeed, in one, how nothing we are; in the other, how greatly exalted: since so great a Majesty even takes thought for us and has set his heart upon [Col. 0534A] us—I think our boasting appears moderated, though perhaps it is rather increased; yet it is made firm, so that we may boast not in ourselves but in the Lord. For in this alone is our relief: that we may say, “If he has decreed to save us, we shall immediately be delivered.”

8. From this higher watchtower, then, lingering a little, let us seek the house of God; let us seek the temple; let us seek the city; let us seek also the bride. For I have not forgotten, but I say it with fear and reverence: we are these. We, I say, are these—but in the heart of God; we are these by his condescension, not by our own worthiness. Let not man appropriate what belongs to God, nor add to it by magnifying himself; otherwise God, doing what belongs to him, will humble the man who exalts himself. And if, with childish presumption, we wish to be saved freely, we are deservedly not saved. The denial of misery excludes compassion; and condescension has no place where there has been a presumption of worthiness. But a humble confession of suffering calls forth compassion.

Indeed, this alone causes him, like a rich householder, to feed us in famine, and causes us to be found under him abounding in bread. Therefore we are his house, which never lacks the nourishment of life. And remember that he declared his house to be “a house of prayer” (Matt. 21:13), since this also seems sufficiently to accord with the prophetic testimony which asserts that we are to be fed by him—in prayers, certainly—with the bread of tears, and are to receive drink in tears (Ps. 79:6). But according to the same Prophet, as we also recalled above, holiness befits this house (Ps. 92:5), so that [Col. 0534C] the tears of repentance may be accompanied by the purity of continence, and the house which already exists may subsequently also become the temple of God. “Be holy,” he says, “for I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. 11:44). And the Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit, and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you? If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:16–17).

9. Yet is holiness itself now sufficient? Peace also is necessary, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Pursue peace with all men, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12:14). This is what causes brothers to dwell together in unity of disposition, building for our king—truly the Prince of Peace—a new city, which itself is called Jerusalem, that is, “vision of peace.” [Col. 0534D] For where a headless multitude is gathered without the covenant of peace, without observance of law, without discipline and government, it is called not a people but a mob; it is not a city but confusion; it displays Babylon and has nothing of Jerusalem.

But how can so great a king be thought able to become a bridegroom, and a city be advanced into a bride? Love alone can do this—love strong as death, which can do all things. How could it fail easily to lift her up, when it has already inclined him? Yet here you must by no means consult that earlier consideration of yourself which we mentioned; here is the chief exercise of the magnanimity of faith. For he himself says: “I have espoused you to myself in faith; I have espoused you in judgment and righteousness”—understand, his righteousness, not yours—“I have espoused you in mercy and compassions” [Col. 0535A] (Hos. 2:20, 19). If he has not acted as a bridegroom, if he has not loved as a bridegroom, if he has not been jealous as a bridegroom, do not consent to think yourself a bride.

10. Therefore, my brothers, if by the abundant refreshment of the great householder we are proved to be a house; if by sanctification, the temple of God; if by the fellowship of social life, the city of the supreme King; if by love, the bride of the immortal Bridegroom—I think I need no longer hesitate to say that the feast is ours. Nor should you wonder that this celebration is held on earth, since it is also held in heaven. For if—as Truth says, and it cannot fail to be true—there is joy in heaven, even among the angels of God, over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15:10), there is no doubt that today they have manifold joy over so great a sinner doing penance. [Col. 0535B] Would you hear something further? Even “the joy of the Lord is our strength” (2 Esdr. 8:10). Let us therefore rejoice with the angels of God, rejoice together with God, and let the present solemnity be celebrated in thanksgiving; for the more it belongs to our household, the more devout it ought to be.

## SERMON VI. On the reverence due to sacred places

1. The dedication of our house is a celebration belonging to our household; but more intimate still is the dedication of ourselves. For that sprinkling was ours, that blessing was ours, that consecration was ours, which was performed through the hands of holy bishops and which, even today, is recalled in votive praises at its annual return. [Col. 0535C] Does God care about stones? It is not walls but human beings that speak: “For he has care for us” (1 Pet. 5:7).

Jacob was one man, and while asleep he saw angels descending and ascending. This is too little: he also testified that the Lord of angels was present, saying, “Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it” (Gen. 28:12, 16). For he marvels at grace and trembles at the greatness of the condescension. How much more awe-inspiring is this place; how much more evidently and certainly is the Lord in this place, where not merely two or three but so many persevere, gathered in his name! Let no one now fail to know it; let none of you be ignorant. For we have received not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God, [Col. 0535D] that we may know the things given to us by God (1 Cor. 2:12). Truly this is an awe-inspiring place, worthy of all reverence: a place inhabited by faithful men, frequented by holy angels, and one which the Lord himself also deigns to honor by his presence.

> **Note:** [Col. 0535D] This appears to be the passage intended by John the Hermit in Book 2 of *The Life of St Bernard*, no. 7, where he reports Bernard’s words from a sermon delivered at the dedication of a church: [Col. 0536D] “Now the holy angels have attended your solemn celebration,” etc., vol. 6.

2. For how could so great a patriarch have failed to know that there was no place where God was not? But perhaps he marveled at something else when he said, “Truly the Lord is in this place.” He is truly there, and is truly Lord, where angels and human beings are gathered together in his name. [Col. 0536A] For although he is in every place, since he is enclosed by no place, we nevertheless say specifically: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9), because there he manifests himself present in another and distinctive manner—not that he himself is different, but that he distinguishes different things.

Thus he is in every place, universally containing and ordering all things; yet in very different ways. Among evil people he bestows and overlooks; among chosen people he works and preserves; among those above he feeds and rests; among those below he reproves and condemns. “He makes his sun rise even upon the evil”; but where evil people are for the time being overlooked, in a sense truth is not there. Therefore, if it may be said, he is among the impious in forbearance; among the righteous in truth; among angels in blessedness; [Col. 0536B] among those below in his fierceness.

Does what I said about fierceness sound harsh to you? Yet I fear both wrath and fury: “Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury” (Ps. 6:2), and so forth. “Truly,” he says, “the Lord is in this place.” Where he rains upon the just and unjust, he is Father, the Father of mercies, awaiting human beings’ repentance. Where he condemns the obstinate, he is Judge, and “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). Where he rests, he is Bridegroom; and blessed is the soul whom he brings into his chamber.

3. Yet in this place the Lord is truly present, provided that we serve him in spirit and truth. For he was not truly Lord among those to whom he said: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46). Holy Scripture testifies that the first Adam was once placed in paradise [Col. 0536C] “to cultivate it and guard it” (Gen. 2:15). Thus the second Adam is in the Church of the saints, in the assembly of his own people, in the garden of delights; for his delights are to be with the children of men. Thus, I say, the Lord himself is in this place in order to work and guard it. Otherwise, just as “unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain,” so likewise “unless he guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Ps. 126:1).

Moreover, the patriarchal vision itself makes clear that angels are ascending and descending in this place: ascending to see the face of the Father, descending to provide for us. What then? How ought we to be here? [Col. 0536D] With what reverence ought we to stand in this place, where God is at work and guarding, and angels are ascending and descending? Clearly, it is fitting for us to be penitent and expectant. For this is to forget the things behind: to disregard them, reject them, reconsider those years in the bitterness of our soul, and thereafter to stretch ourselves forward at once by thought and longing. For this we have come; in this we are placed. These are what are required of us: repentance for past sins and expectation of future rewards.

[Col. 0537]

# SERMONS OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS (G)*

1084

## SERMON I. On the deceitfulness and brevity of the present life

[Col. 0537A]

1. It is altogether a true saying, brothers, that “the life of man upon earth is a temptation” (Job 7:1), since it is deceitful and is not accustomed to deceive in merely one way. For in order to mock human beings in many ways, it changes face and changes voice: now it says yes, now it says no, and is not ashamed. Regarding its very duration it says different things to different people; indeed, at different times it suggests contrary and opposing things even to the same person.

For when sinning is still pleasant, life groans deeply at its own brevity. Its brevity is not false, but its groaning is deceitful: it recalls with sorrow what it ought rather to rejoice in. For it is good for a person, if he persists in acting thus, that necessity should at least put an end to the disgraceful acts to which his will sets no limit. It is expedient for one who is always dying to die in body sooner; yet it would have been better for that man had he not been born. Finally, even the remembrance of life’s brevity ought to have been a remedy rather than an incentive to sin, as it is written: “Remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7:40).

But if sin so reigns in you—indeed, if serving sin so pleases you—that you grieve that you have only a little time in which to serve it; if you so love the broad way that you wish by every means, if you could, to make it long as well: willing or unwilling, its end is not far away. But you, I confess, are far from the kingdom of God and seem to have entered into a most binding covenant with death, a pact with hell.

[Col. 0537C]

2. “They wandered,” says the Prophet, “in the wilderness, in a waterless place; they found not the way to a city of habitation” (Ps. 106:4). This wilderness is that of the proud, because they consider themselves alone and desire to be considered alone. A man is learned: he hates a companion. A man is shrewd in worldly affairs: he would wish no one to be found like himself. A man is wealthy: if he sees another becoming rich, he is tormented. A man is strong or handsome: give him an equal, and he wastes away. He is solitary, but wandering. He wanders in his solitude, for he cannot dwell alone upon the earth.

Nor is it surprising that “waterless” is added to this wilderness, so that it is said: “in the wilderness, in a waterless place.” For as water is usually lacking in wildernesses, and deserted places are commonly barren and dry, so impenitence accompanies pride. For the exalted heart is hard and devoid of piety, ignorant of compunction, dry of every dew of spiritual grace, because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). “He sends forth springs in the valleys; the waters shall pass through the midst of the mountains,” says the Prophet (Ps. 103:10). Hence he says, lamenting miserably concerning himself: “My soul is before thee as land without water” (Ps. 142:6).

For lack of water makes one not only dry but also dirty, since there is nothing with which to wash; and the human heart that knows no tears must be not only hard but impure. “Every night,” he says, “I shall wash my bed,” that I may cleanse the stains of conscience. “With my tears I shall drench my couch” [Col. 0538B] (Ps. 6:7), lest in me also occur what is written of the seed that fell upon the rock and, once sprung up, withered because it had no moisture (Luke 8:6).

3. “They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place; they found not the way to a city of habitation.” They plainly wandered in a trackless place, and not on a way. For the broad way is not a way. Straightness belongs to a way; breadth belongs rather to an open plain than to a way. Solitude on the broad way is itself a way; and where there is no way, everything is way. Such is a life exposed to vices, having the broadest boundaries on either side because it has no boundaries. Nor indeed should it be called life, since it is plainly lived for death alone, as the Apostle testifies: “If you live according to the flesh, you shall die” [Col. 0538C] (Rom. 8:13). Nor is it a circuit of a way; yet it is the way of the ungodly, as is written: “The ungodly walk in a circle” (Ps. 11:9).

This is the spacious way, the expanse of whose breadth is enclosed by no limits, where there is neither law nor transgression. Therefore, to such children of unbelief, who have wholly surrendered themselves to bodily pleasures and their own wills, deceitful life confidently confesses that it is short, so that they may grieve carnally because they know that, like their prince—

> **Note:** [Col. 0537] That is, the devil, concerning whom Revelation 12 says: “The devil has come down to you with great wrath, knowing that he has little time.”

—they have little time; and so may burn all the more fiercely for every shameful act, as some are reported to say: “Let not the flower of time pass us by; let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither. Let there be no meadow through which our lust does not pass; let none be without [Col. 0539A] our sensual indulgence. Everywhere let us leave signs of merriment, for this is our portion and this our lot.” And more plainly: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (Wis. 2:6–9; Isa. 22:13).

But tomorrow their own injustice will answer them: indeed, even they have no abiding city here, they who have not found the way to the city of habitation. But in hastening to sin for that reason, they are utterly mad. Yet if these same persons should at some time begin to dread the remembrance of their impending death and tremble at the dreadful expectation of judgment, the deceitfulness of this life immediately lies that it is long. Thus, whereas a little before they had lamented a life short for sin, they suddenly find that same life so greatly prolonged that they think they can safely spend a considerable portion of it still in sins, because what remains is long and will suffice for doing penance for sins.

Yet, just as upon the former, unless they come to their senses, the fear they dread shall come—indeed, something more grievous than what they fear shall happen to them, so that not only will the time for shameful acts pass swiftly, but a time, or rather an eternity, of punishments will follow—so too upon these, when they say, “Peace and security,” sudden destruction shall come (1 Thess. 5:3), so that they will not be able even to halve the days in which they imagine they are still to live, nor complete that division of their days which they meanwhile promise themselves.

4. As for you, brothers, I fear neither the empty sadness arising from true brevity nor the deceitful consolation arising from pretended length, because you have most certainly already begun to go [Col. 0539C] toward the city of habitation, and walk not in a trackless place but in the way. Yet I fear lest life itself may wish also to mock you, though differently, by the pretense of length—not bringing consolation from this, but rather bringing desolation. I fear, I say, lest someone who thinks a longer life remains to him, and judges that a great journey still lies ahead, may be overwhelmed by faintness of spirit and despair of being able to endure labors so great and so long-lasting.

As though divine consolations do not gladden the souls of the elect according to the multitude of their sorrows in their hearts. And now indeed they do so according to the multitude of sorrows, while they are still given as it were in measure. But after this there will be delights, no longer consolations, at his right hand for evermore. Let us desire that right hand, brothers, which will embrace us wholly; let us sigh for those delights, so that, since the time is altogether short, even a few days may appear few to us in comparison with the greatness of love. “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

A pleasant promise, and one to be embraced with every desire. For we shall not stand as empty and vacant spectators, nor will that glory be revealed to us as though from outside; rather, it will be revealed in us. For we shall see God face to face, yet not outside ourselves, because he will be in us—namely, all things in all. Surely that glory will fill even the whole earth; how much more will the soul itself be filled! “We shall be filled,” he says, “with the good things of thy house” (Ps. 64:5). And why do I say that glory will not merely be present to us, but within us? It is now also within us, but then it shall be revealed. For now we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be.

[Col. 0540A]

5. My brothers, if we have received not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God, let us know the things given to us by God. For I say: everything. And if you do not believe me, believe the Apostle: “He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how has he not also given us all things with him?” (Rom. 8:32). This is the power of the children of God, which he gave to those who received him. This is the glory of every believer: glory as of one adopted by the Father, through him whose glory we saw, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father. Hear, finally, of this power: “All things,” he says, “are possible to the believer” (Mark 9:22).

[Col. 0540B]

6. “But,” you will say, “many things still grievously trouble us; many things more openly oppose us.” And I wonder how those who remember that all things have been given them can say this, when scarcely anything serves them according to their desire. Some things seem to serve us, but only with our labor, and only if we have first served them. Even beasts of burden, unless they have been fed, tamed, and sustained by fodder from us, do not help. The earth itself, which ought to have been more kin to us, will not furnish us bread except by the sweat of our face; indeed, even when we have cultivated it, it brings forth thorns and thistles for us. And, finally, if we consider all other things carefully, they demand service from us more than they render it to us—not to mention for the moment those things ready to harm us: fire for burning, water for drowning, wild beasts for tearing apart.

These things are indeed so; nevertheless, the Apostle does not lie when elsewhere he more plainly declares that he knows “that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. 8:28). Yet carefully observe that he says not that they serve according to our pleasure, but that they cooperate for good. For they serve not our will but our advantage; not pleasure but salvation; not our wish but our benefit. Indeed, all things cooperate for our good in such a way that among all these things are numbered even things which are nothing: trouble, sickness, death itself, and even sin—things which are evidently not natures but corruptions [Col. 0540D] of nature. Or do sins themselves not cooperate for good for the person who is found by them to be more humble, more fervent, more watchful, more fearful, and more cautious?

7. These, therefore, are the firstfruits of the Spirit, the firstfruits of the kingdom, a foretaste of glory, the beginning of power, and a kind of earnest of the paternal inheritance. But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away, so that henceforth all things may be arranged according to desire, since usefulness and delight, joined together by an indissoluble bond, can no longer be separated. This indeed will be that eternal weight of glory of which the Apostle repeatedly says: “This momentary and light affliction of ours works in us, beyond measure in sublimity, an eternal weight [Col. 0541A] of glory” (2 Cor. 4:17).

Go on, then, murmur and say: “It is long, it is heavy; I cannot bear things so immense and so lasting!” The Apostle declares that what he endures is momentary and light. And certainly you have not yet received from the Jews five times forty lashes less one; you have not yet been a night and a day in the depths of the sea (2 Cor. 11:24–25); you have not yet labored more than all others (1 Cor. 15:10); finally, you have not yet resisted unto blood (Heb. 12:4). See, then, how sufferings are not worthy to be compared with glory. What belongs to affliction is momentary and light; what belongs to glory is eternal, and a weight even beyond measure in sublimity.

Why do you count days and years uncertainly for yourself? The hour passes, and the punishment passes too; they do not accumulate but rather yield and succeed one another. Glory is not so, nor recompense, nor the wage of labor itself. It knows no alternation, knows no end; it remains whole at once and remains forever. “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126:2–3). For the evil of the day suffices for each day now, and one cannot reserve one’s labor for the following day; but the reward of all labors will be rendered on that one day to which no other succeeds. “There is laid up for me,” says the Apostle, “a crown of righteousness, which the just Judge will render to me—not on those days, but on that day” (2 Tim. 4:8). For “one day in those courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11).

Punishment is drunk drop by drop, taken gradually, passing away in small portions; but in recompense there is a torrent [Col. 0541C] of delight and the rush of a river: a torrent overflowing with joy, a river of glory [or: grace], and a river of peace. It is indeed a river, but one that flows toward us, not one that flows away or out. It is called a river not because it passes or flows past, but because it abounds.

8. “An eternal weight of glory.” For not a glorious garment, not a glorious house, but glory itself is promised to us. If such things, or things like them, are ever mentioned, they are figures. For in truth the expectation of the righteous is not something joyful, but joy itself (Prov. 10:28). Human beings rejoice in food, rejoicing in pageants, rejoicing in riches, and even rejoicing in vices; but sorrow takes possession of the end of joys of this sort, because joy in a changeable matter must change when the thing changes.

A candle is lit: it is not pure light but a lamp, [Col. 0541D] since the fire itself consumes its own fuel and is sustained only by that very consumption. When the material fails, it too will fail; and when you see the material wholly burned up, you will likewise find that the flame has been extinguished. Therefore, just as smoke and darkness take possession at the end of that flame, so the joy arising from a pleasant thing is changed into sorrow.

But God has laid up for us not a honeycomb, but honey most pure and most liquid: joy itself, life, glory, peace, delight, loveliness, happiness, pleasantness, and exultation. The Lord our God has stored up all these things for us; and all these are one, so that Jerusalem may be “participation in the same.” And this one and same thing is none other than God himself, as we recalled above, according to the Apostle’s saying that “God will be all in all” (1 [Col. 0542A] Cor. 15:28). This is our reward, this our crown, this our prize. May we run toward it in such a way as to attain it!

Brothers, a prudent farmer who desires the abundance of the future harvest never judges the opportunity for sowing too long. But your days, no less certainly than your hairs, are all numbered (Luke 12:7); and as not a hair from the body, so not a moment from time shall perish (Luke 21:18). Therefore, having such a promise, beloved, let us not fail or grow weary at any time. Let us not complain that Christ’s burden is heavy, though by his own testimony it is light, nor that his yoke is burdensome, though it is truly sweet (Matt. 11:30). Rather, amid every burden of the day that we seem to bear, let us think upon the eternal weight of glory. May the Lord of virtues and King of glory lead us to it by his mercy; to him meanwhile let us cry in devout humility: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to thy name” (Ps. 113:9).

## SERMON II. On obedience, patience, and wisdom; or, on knowing oneself, that we are human beings

1. I beg you, brothers, by our common salvation, diligently embrace the opportunity given you to work out salvation. I beg you, by the mercy for which you have labored to make yourselves so miserable, do that for which you have come, for which you have ascended from the rivers of Babylon. “By the rivers of Babylon,” says the Prophet, “there we sat and wept, when we remembered thee, Zion” (Ps. 136:1). Here you have no care for rearing children, no concern over how you may please wives; [Col. 0542C] you need not think about markets, secular business, or even food and clothing. To a great extent, the evil of the day and life’s anxiety are far from you. Thus God has hidden you in the hiding-place of his tabernacle. Therefore, beloved, be still and see that he is God (Ps. 45:11).

But if you are ever to be able to do this, you must first take care to see what you yourselves are; and, in the words of the same Prophet, “Let the nations know that they are human beings” (Ps. 9:21). Let this entire vocation of yours be assigned to this twofold consideration, as the saint prayed: “O God, may I know myself; may I know thee” (Augustine, in the books of the *Confessions*). For how does a person who flees labor and pain appear to know himself? Or how does one know himself to be human who is not ready for that for which he was born? “Man is born to labor” (Job 5:7). A person doubts that he was born for pain if he was not born in pain. Yet the cry of the woman in labor indicates pain, and the crying and wailing of the child indicates labor.

“You consider labor and pain,” says the Prophet (Ps. 9:14). Labor is in actions; pain is in sufferings. Therefore one who knew himself to be human said, in humble confession, ready for both: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 56:8). Expressing this twofold readiness more plainly, he said concerning action: “I am ready and am not troubled, to keep thy commandments” (Ps. 118:60); and concerning suffering: “I am ready for scourges, and my pain is always before me” (Ps. 37:18).

[Col. 0543A]

2. Let no one boast that he escapes this twofold affliction in this miserable life. For among all the children of Adam no one lives here without labor, and no one without pain. There is one who avoids some afflictions, but he undoubtedly falls into graver ones. “They are not in the labor of men, nor shall they be scourged with men.” Yet they are not therefore immediately without labor or unscourged. “Therefore,” he says, “pride has taken hold of them.” Truly a grievous labor: “They are covered with their iniquity and impiety” (Ps. 72:5–6). Surely they are afflicted with grievous scourges, for the Lord says, “There is no joy for the ungodly” (Isa. 57:21). The very insensibility by which they feel neither the anxiety of labor nor the wound of the scourge indicates the intensity of their suffering.

The poor person sweats outwardly at work; but does the rich person labor any less anxiously inwardly in his own thought? One opens his mouth in yawning; another opens his in belching; and at times the latter is tormented more grievously by disgust than the former by hunger. Finally, willing or unwilling, not only human beings but even demons both do and suffer what supreme providence has ordained.

3. But neither leprous obedience nor canine patience is commended. Hence we do not simply ask that the Lord’s will be done, although it is certain that it is done in all things and through all things: for who resists his will? Rather, we ask that it be done “as in heaven, so on earth.” I think this addition should likewise be applied to the two preceding petitions: that we pray to our Father who is in heaven that his name may be hallowed, his kingdom may come, and his will be done (Matt. 6:9–10)—all these things as in heaven, so on earth.

For where is his name not hallowed? Where has his kingdom not already come, when at the name of Jesus every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2:10)? “I know that you are the Holy One of God,” even the evil one says (Mark 1:24). But that name is hallowed in heaven in a far different and wholly unlike disposition, where with inexpressible joy they cry: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3). Likewise, he reigns not only on earth but also in hell, holding dominion over life and death. Yet he reigns altogether differently in those who serve unwillingly and in those who minister willingly.

[Col. 0543D]

4. Obedience is good food, concerning which the Lord himself says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34). And the Prophet says: “Because you shall eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127:2). The patience of the poor, which shall not perish forever, is good food: bread of tears, bread of sorrow. Yet both require seasoning, without which each is so tasteless that it not only fails to refresh but, when tasted, brings death. Each food, brothers, is indeed very hard; and unless some third savory element be added, there is surely death in the pot. What could be as savory as wisdom? It is the tree of life which, through Moses, sweetened the waters of Marah (Exod. 15:25). It is the little flour which, through Elisha, made the prophets’ stew savory [Col. 0544A] (4 Kings 4:41). It is the fire which is commanded always to burn upon the altar (Lev. 6:12). It is the oil for lack of which the door of the wedding-feast is shut against the foolish virgins (Matt. 25:12). It is the salt which is commanded to be lacking from no sacrifice (Lev. 2:13). Hence we call people “insipid” when we mean that they are not wise at all. And the Lord commands us to have salt in ourselves (Mark 9:49). The Apostle also teaches that all our speech should be seasoned with salt (Col. 4:6).

5. Yet I think that this wisdom itself, which we wish to add as a third element to obedience and patience, is likewise found to be threefold, so that this seasoning of ours may be compounded, as it were, of three herbs. For justice must be present in the intention, cheerfulness [Col. 0544B] in the performance, humility in one’s estimation of oneself. For our obedience, and likewise our patience, is tasteless and in a certain sense insipid to God unless he himself is the cause of all that we either do or suffer; since whatever we do, we are commanded to do for the glory of God; and we are blessed, not if we suffer anything, but if we suffer something for righteousness’ sake. Moreover, faint-heartedness and sadness must be guarded against in everything that is to be done or endured, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). Indeed, cheerfulness itself and willing devotion are particularly known to belong to the preparation mentioned above. Pride, furthermore, must above all be shunned. For whoever thinks lofty thoughts, both his work and his patience have a vain flavor; and no flavor is more unpleasant or more contrary [Col. 0544C] to truth. 1089

Do you see how useful it is for a human being to know that he is human, and therefore to be ready for obedience to the commandments and endurance of chastisements, and thereafter to strive, since for the present he can escape neither toil nor pain, at least to labor and suffer in such a way that these may become for him wholesome foods? For “obedience is better than sacrifices” (1 Sam. 15:22); and: “The patient man is better than a strong man” (Prov. 16:32). Disobedience is the cause of death: we all experience it; we all die because of it. Impatience is the ruin of the soul, as the Lord says: “By your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). Nevertheless, the wisdom of which we have spoken is also necessary for salvation. For not only did those perish through disobedience [Col. 0544D] who lacked obedience, or through impatience who lacked patience; but those also who lacked wisdom perished through their own folly.

6. These things are so that people may know that they are human, now assigned to actions and sufferings. There was a time when man was placed in action and meditation, having action without suffering and meditation also without labor. I mean when he was placed in paradise, “to cultivate it and to keep it.” Yet even from there, had he not fallen, he was at some time to be advanced, so as then to enjoy contemplation alone. Likewise, from this lower degree which he now occupies, unless he strives to rise again, he will at some time fall into the lowest degree: namely, so as then to be occupied with suffering alone, since among [Col. 0545A] those below there is neither work nor reason, but suffering only.

Happy indeed was he whose soul was not weighed down by the body, because it was not corruptible. But far happier would he have been, had he attained this: that, diminished as to activity, he might receive wisdom more fully and perfectly, loving the body freely, as though in no respect needing the body. For this would be a most beautiful order, and will yet be so when it comes to be. Nor should this in any way be despaired of: namely, that, just as the soul might seem to say to God, so the flesh might seem to say to the soul: “You have no need of my goods; you will fill me,” he says, “with gladness in the presence of your countenance” (Ps. 15:2, 11). There is fullness there; there is satisfaction, when your glory appears. For what we await concerning the re-formation of bodies and their conformity to the brightness of his body will be, in a certain way, an excess and overflow beyond measure: so that we may indeed rejoice happily in its glorification, [Col. 0545B] but not principally.

“Your wife,” he says, “shall be like a fruitful vine, within the sides of your house.” The flesh will be honored, but according to its measure: dwelling not in the middle of the house, but apart; placed not in an easy position for us, but at the side. “Your children [shall be] like young olive trees around your table” (Ps. 127:3). Surely works themselves also will not be lacking, but those which are done now, not those which will then be done; as it is written: “Their works follow them” (Rev. 14:13). Yet, although we rejoice and give thanks to God for those things which we have accomplished with his help, we shall not give them the first place; rather, they shall be placed around it.

7. But now, dwelling in the region of bodies, we are subject to bodies; and ever since our first parents broke [Col. 0545C] the law, it is not only a time for doing, but also for suffering, and our lot is pre-eminently toil and pain. Barley bread is indeed hard food; but when a king has been offended and a soldier, however refined, has been driven from the palace, he may be obliged to turn aside to one servant, perhaps the only one he possesses. There he must shelter in hiding and take unfamiliar meals at the servant’s house; exchange royal delicacies for rustic porridge, and noble beds for his servant’s dung-heap, in accordance with that saying of prophetic lamentation: “Those who were fed on saffron embraced dung” (Lam. 4:5).

There above all the prophet laments that noble creatures, forgetful of their own condition, should conceal from themselves so great a misery: not merely failing to reckon what they endure, but embracing as great goods things which are scarcely less than the utmost evils. [Col. 0545D] Therefore he says also of himself: “I am the man who sees my poverty under the rod of his indignation” (Lam. 3:1).

8. Let us groan beneath this burden, brothers, and lament our present miseries. Let each of us often break forth into the words of a devout complaint and cry: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). Let us also strive sometimes to steal ourselves away, and withdraw ourselves, even for an hour, from these most wretched occupations: to hurl forth our minds, to send our hearts darting toward that which is their own, and which is the sweeter precisely because it is more natural. For this is what is said: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. 45:11). This is not vision by the eyes, [Col. 0546A] but by the heart, when the Lord says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

This is the heart’s own good, and it needs no servile instrument for this purpose. For this is the soul’s proper food, of which the Prophet says: “My heart has withered, because I have forgotten to eat my bread” (Ps. 101:5). Certainly, when we say that nothing is easier to say, we mean in comparison with works: the tongue is far more mobile than the right hand, and it is moved more easily to speech than the other is to action. Otherwise, thought is easier both to speak and to do, since in thought the soul speaks, as it were, with its own mouth, sees with its own eyes, and acts with its own hands. Though even here it is sometimes necessary for it to labor in its groaning, and to be pierced even within its own chamber.

For our life has drawn so near to hell, which is surely the place of suffering alone, that suffering has taken possession even of action, indeed action and suffering alike have taken possession of thought itself. Are not even our actions in some sense passive [Note: [Col. 0545D] Elsewhere Bernard says that Christ had passive action in life and endured active [Col. 0546D] suffering in death: sermon for the Greater Wednesday, no. 11.], and pain and labor present also in our thoughts? Alas for Ephraim, the heifer taught to love threshing (Hos. 10:11), accustomed to the yoke and ignorant of rest! When shall I come and appear before the face of God? When will all these things cease, and there be no more mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, nor any labor? When will the abundance of God’s house inebriate the soul, and that unfailing torrent of divine delight? When will the contemplation of the most serene light claim the whole soul for itself?

Little children, let us long [Col. 0546C] for the courts of the Lord; let us sigh frequently for that place. It is our very homeland: let us at least breathe in its fragrance and greet it from afar. Amen.

## SERMON III. On the canticle of King Hezekiah, “I said, in the midst of my days,” etc. (Isa. 38:10–20)

1. “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Ps. 54:24), persisting in their old condition unto death; and this is because they do not fear the Lord. But one who is initiated into wisdom by the fear of God immediately halves his days, crying out in fear: “I shall go to the gates of hell.” When, through fear of that hell, he begins to cease from evil deeds, he begins to seek consolation in good things, because he must find consolation in one of the two. There is good consolation in the hope of eternal salvation [Col. 0546D], by which, after the sins that separated him from God have been removed, he is revived and gladdened through God’s grace.

When he begins to make progress in this—for this is to live devoutly in Christ—he must, as Scripture testifies, suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12). Thus recent joy is changed into sorrow, and the sweetness of good, scarcely touched, as one might say, by the very edges of the lips, is transformed into bitterness, so that he is pleased to say: “My harp is turned into mourning, and my song into lamentation” (Job 30:31). Thus he weeps more bitterly for sweetness lost than he had previously wept for the bitterness of sins committed. And he does this until, by God’s mercy, consolation returns. When it returns anew, [Col. 0547A] he recognizes that the temptation he suffered was a trial, not a desolation; moreover, that the trial was for instruction, not destruction, as it is written: “You visit him in the morning and suddenly test him” (Job 7:18).

Therefore, having recognized his progress through temptation, he not only does not flee it, but even desires to be tested: “Test me,” he says, “and try me” (Ps. 25:2). By frequent alternations of this kind between the visitation of grace and the testing of temptation, he advances in the school of virtues—the visitation ensuring that he does not fail, the temptation ensuring that he does not grow proud. At last, when the inner eye has been cleansed by such exercise, the light is immediately present. Desiring faithfully to cleave to it, but unable because he is weighed down by the body, he recoils upon himself, unwillingly and sorrowfully. Yet, having in some measure tasted [Col. 0547B] how sweet the Lord is, even when he returns to his own concerns he retains the flavor of him upon the palate of his heart. Hence it comes about that he now desires not merely any goods belonging to him, but himself. And this is charity that “does not seek its own”; this makes a son, who does not seek his own interests but loves the Father. Fear, indeed, would make a slave, turning aside to his own advantages; hope would make a hireling, pursuing his own gains.

2. Hezekiah undoubtedly passed through these stages and made them known to those who would pass through them: “I said, in the midst of my days: I shall go to the gates of hell.” As though he said: When, having put off the image of the earthly man, I began to desire to bear the image of the heavenly, conceiving through fear, as it is written (Isa. 26:17–18), I cried out: “I shall go to the gates of hell.” Yet, not [Col. 0547C] despairing through that fear, I sought the remainder of my years, so that I who had until then lived contrary to myself might begin to live for myself. I sought it, moreover, from him who said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). For without him I could not return to him—indeed, I could not even turn toward him—as a spirit that goes and does not return. Therefore I sought the remainder of my years.

Having received it—for he does not refuse to give, who urges us to seek—I immediately experience the true saying of the Wise Man: “Son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir. 2:1). Thus, when I was pressed by temptations and the newly conceived hope of salvation seemed on the point of being shut off from me, I said: “I shall not see [Col. 0547D] my Lord in the land of the living,” which I had presumptuously expected in prosperity. For I said in my abundance: “I shall never be moved,” not observing that it was by your favor, not by my own power, that you had bestowed strength upon my beauty. Therefore you turned your face away from me, and I was troubled (Ps. 29:7–8), no longer to see the Lord God—that is, the Father—in the land of the living. “I shall look upon man no more,” namely the Son, of whom it is said: “And he is a man; and who has known him?” (Jer. 17). Nor shall I behold “the inhabitant of rest,” that is, the Holy Spirit, of whom it is written: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, unless upon the humble and quiet?” (Isa. 66:2).

3. He also adds: “My generation has been taken away and rolled up [Col. 0548A] from me.” That is, the offspring of good works, which I had begun to bring forth through fear, so that it might be said of our soul: “She who had many children has become weak.” This devout offspring was taken away and rolled up from me like a shepherds’ tent: entrusted for a time, certainly, not handed over forever. He further added: “My life has been cut off as by a weaver,” so that I might learn that the progress of my life lies not in my own hand but in the hand of the Almighty, like cloth in the hand of a weaver. For while I was still weaving the warp—that is, immediately at the beginning—he cut me off, so that at nearly one and the same time he both gave and took away what he had given.

But though my strength failed, he did not forsake me, lest he who had begun might seem unable to complete. Why say more? I at once learned in truth that “strength is perfected in weakness” [Col. 0548B] (2 Cor. 12:9), and I say: “It is good for me that you have humbled me” (Ps. 118:71). For I recognized that “from morning until evening you will finish me,” that is, perfect me. My perfection will not be in the morning of visitation alone or in the evening of temptation alone, but in both together. Fool that I was, who hoped only until morning, when David says: “Let Israel hope in the Lord from the morning watch until night” (Ps. 129:6). And because I was little in hope, “like a lion he crushed all my bones”: that is, all the strength in which, still under the protection of grace and heedless of what was to come, I had trusted. But who crushed them except our adversary the devil, who “goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8)? Therefore you, O Lord, will from morning until evening [Col. 0548C] 1092 perfect me, humbled and tested by this crushing, because “there was morning and evening, one day.”

4. Therefore, as I have learned, I shall bless the Lord at every time, that is, morning and evening; not like the one “who will praise you when you have done him good” (Ps. 48:19); not like those who “believe for a time and in the time of temptation fall away” (Luke 8:13); but I shall say with the saints: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10). In the morning I shall cry out like a young swallow; but in the evening I shall meditate like a dove, so that, when the morning of grace smiles upon me, rejoicing and crying out in the manner of a swallow, I may give thanks for the visitation; and when evening falls [Col. 0548D], the evening sacrifice will not be lacking, as, groaning like a dove, I pour out tears in tribulation. Thus each time will serve God: weeping will last until evening, and joy will come in the morning. I shall mourn mournfully in the evening, in order to enjoy the morning joyfully.

Both are pleasing to God: the contrite sinner and the devout righteous person. By contrast, the ungrateful righteous person displeases him as much as the self-assured sinner. Or, like a young swallow darting here and there, I shall devote myself to Martha’s services, showing myself a cheerful giver to everyone who suffers need; and I shall meditate like a dove, groaning, of course, over what stands in the way while I look toward what remains. I shall do this morning and evening, that is, first and afterward, according to what was said in the type of the two lives by Laban: [Col. 0549A] “It is not our custom to give the younger in marriage before the elder” (Gen. 29:26), although one may pass indifferently from one to the other. I think Job signifies this when he says: “If I lie down, I say: When shall I rise? And again I await the evening” (Job 7:4). Resting in the evening of contemplation, he desired the morning, when he might rise for action; and again, wearied by business, he awaited evening, gladly returning to the leisure of contemplation.

5. The chattering bird may also signify the song of those chanting psalms together in the Church, and the groaning dove the private sighs of prayers. But the following verse seems to favor the middle interpretation: “My eyes are weakened, looking upward.” Whether this is said to mean weakened, that is, made subtle [Col. 0549B] through constantly looking upward, namely, contemplating sublime and lofty things; or whether it is understood to mean weakened, that is, dazed and in some fashion diminished from their sharpness, according to the saying, “My eyes have failed for your word” (Ps. 118:82), and again, “I remembered God and was delighted; I was exercised, and my spirit failed” (Ps. 76:4): whether it is taken in the one way or the other, nothing but contemplation is indicated. Yet the latter exposition seems more suitable to what follows.

For he says: “Lord, I suffer violence.” As though he said: Lord, not willingly but against my will I am drawn back and barred from contemplation of you, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). Therefore answer for me [Col. 0549C], O Creator, you who know the condition of nature. Or if my sins do this, and the fault lies not in nature but in my own most evil habit, even so answer for me nonetheless: fastening sins to the cross and blotting them out with your blood, so that there may be nothing to hinder me in contemplation. For what shall I say, or what will he answer me, when he himself has done it? To whom else, indeed, shall I turn, or who else will answer for me, when he himself, and no other, has imposed this difficulty—indeed impossibility—upon me, pronouncing over me that sentence: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3:19)?

[Col. 0549D]

6. But if the reading is not “he has done,” but “I have done,” he reproaches himself for having, as it were, cast blame back upon the author when he complained of nature. He imputes everything to himself and to his sins, saying: “What shall I say, or what will he answer me, when I have done it?” That is, I have deserved by sinning the thing that I suffer. Therefore there is one thing I can do: “I shall review for you all my years in the bitterness of my soul.” Surely I am not worthy to be able to contemplate you with sweetness; I shall do what I can: I shall think upon myself in the bitterness of my soul. 1093 You dwell in inaccessible light, and I cannot long fix the weak gaze of my mind upon the ray of your splendor; and therefore, confounded, I return to the familiar and customary shadows of my former life—not to lie down in them anew with deadly delight, but to punish them and review them in the bitterness of my soul.

It would indeed be necessary, if it were possible [Col. 0550A], for me to live again, so to speak, the life I have lived badly. But because I cannot do this, at least “I shall review for you all my years in the bitterness of my soul”; by reviewing I shall do what I cannot do by living it over. I shall review them for you because “against you alone have I sinned,” so that, in condemning myself, you may be justified and may prevail in mercy when you judge me. I had indeed thought upon these things before; but because matters which can still hinder me have not been punished enough, I return again to reviewing them in the bitterness of my soul, until they are so completely uprooted that they can no longer hinder me.

7. Nor, I think, will this endeavor be fruitless [Col. 0550B]. For if one lives thus—indeed, because one lives thus—not according to the flesh but according to the spirit, and if the life of my spirit lies in such things, that is, both in considering myself and in contemplating you, you will increasingly correct me and give me life. For I am corrected when, by thinking of myself, I am pierced with compunction; I come to life when, raised up in whatever measure, I behold you. Thus, by showing me to myself, you will correct me; by showing yourself, you will give me life.

And indeed you must give me life, for behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter. I suffered bitter bitterness for sins at the beginning of conversion, when I cried: “I shall go to the gates of hell”; a more bitter one through terrors in the progress of my manner of life, when I said: “I shall not see the Lord God in the land of the living.” But behold, now that sins have been punished by repentance and the terrors which used to assail me have been lulled, I nonetheless endure in this peace a most bitter bitterness because contemplation fails me. Yet [Col. 0550C] you, O Lord, who mercifully forgave my sins and, by helping me, overcame temptations, will now also restore to me the joy of your salvation. For this is what he says: “But you have rescued my soul that it should not perish,” namely, in the conflict of vices or the assault of temptations; “you have cast all my sins behind your back,” according to the multitude of your mercies.

8. And not without reason. For hell will not confess you, into which I had almost descended when assailing temptations battered me; since, unless God had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell (Ps. 93:17). Nor will death praise you, by which I was at one time held, while I still lay dead in sins. Nor will those who descend [Col. 0550D] into the pit await your truth: namely, those who, after tasting the sweetness of contemplation, descend into the pit of despair.

For death belongs to one lying in sin before conversion; hell to one overcome by temptations after receiving remission; but the pit to one despairing after experiencing contemplation. For the higher someone has advanced, the more grievously, if he falls, is he shattered in his fall. Therefore hell will not confess you—that is, those who are indeed converted but are overcome by temptations; nor will death praise you—that is, those not yet converted or confessed, who rather “rejoice when they have done evil and exult in most wicked things” (Prov. 2:14). For confession perishes from the dead person, as from one who does not exist (Sir. 17:26). Nor will those who descend into the pit [Col. 0551A] await your truth: those who may happen to fall from the summit of divine contemplation into the pit of their own distrust. This undoubtedly happens when someone is swallowed up by excessive sadness after receiving so great a joy.

But “the living, the living, he shall confess you.” One person lives in the flesh but is dead in spirit; another is dead in the flesh and yet dead in spirit; but neither of these will praise you or confess you. Rather, “the living, the living, he shall confess you”: the one who lives not only in flesh but also in spirit shall confess you, as I do 1094 today. By your gift I trust that I live this double life. It follows:

9. [Col. 0551B] “The father will make known your truth to the children.” Truth is not revealed to a slave, because “the slave does not know what his lord does” (John 15:15). Nor is the hireling lifted up to contemplate truth, since he seeks his own advantage. But the Father will make his truth known to the son whom he hears saying: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will, Father” (Matt. 26:39). Thus power is revealed to God’s slave, blessedness to the hireling, truth to the son. Not that these are distinct in God, for in him the ability to act, to be blessed, and to be true are one and the same; but the Creator is perceived by the creature under diverse aspects according to the diverse dispositions of that same creature. “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverse” (Ps. 17:26).

Hear, finally, the voice of the son: “Lord, save me.” Why? Perhaps lest he burn in hell, perhaps lest he be deprived of reward? No, he says: “But we shall sing our psalms all the days [Col. 0551C] of our life in the house of the Lord.” No, he says, I do not seek salvation in order to escape punishments or reign in heaven, but that I may praise you eternally with those of whom it is written: “Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). The slave says, “I shall go to the gates of hell.” The hireling says, “I shall not see the Lord God in the land of the living.” The son says, “We shall sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house of the Lord.” Like this is the saying: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; entering through them, I shall confess the Lord” (Ps. 117:19).

Both the one who fears going to the gates of hell and the one who desires to see God for his own repose undoubtedly seek their own interests. But the one who desires to sing psalms in the house [Col. 0551D] of the Lord neither flees his own dangers nor pursues his own gains; he undoubtedly loves him whom he longs to praise all the days of his life. Rightly is he praised forever who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On seeking God and on the threefold bond by which we cleave to God  
*Alternatively: On the threefold coherence of cords, nails, and glues.*

1. We do not stand here idle all day. For we know both what we seek and who has hired us. We seek God; we await God. It is no small matter, nor is it for a small spirit, when she who glories in the unique name of piety so often complains that she is disappointed, saying: “I sought him and did not find him” (Song [Col. 0552A] 3:1). For as he is lovable, so too is he wonderful: he is found when he is not sought, and is not found when he is sought. Even if we had been born when man was made upon the earth and our life were extended to a hundred thousand years, this temporal seeking would still not be commensurate with the future glory that shall be revealed in us.

Behold, now is the time of seeking; behold, now the days of finding are at hand. “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55:6). A time will come when there will be no opportunity, when that fountain of mercy will be dried up by an unending drought. “You shall seek me,” he says, “and shall not find me” (John 7:34). You are good, O Lord, to the soul that seeks you. If you are good to one who seeks, how much more to one who finds? If remembrance is so sweet, what will presence [Col. 0552B] be like? If honey and milk are sweet under the tongue, what will they be above the tongue?

2. Therefore test yourselves in this, brothers: whether you are on the way, whether you do not stray. “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice” (Ps. 104:3). If you rejoice in labors, if you run the way of God’s commandments with an unoffended and untiring foot, if every day the condition of both the inner and outer person is fresher for making progress than for beginning, then you surely seek his face always. Where, then, has the beloved gone from the beloved, that we should seek him? Where is he? What have I said, wretch that I am! Where is he not? He is higher than heaven, deeper than hell, broader than earth, more widespread than sea. He is nowhere and everywhere, because he is absent from none and is contained by no place. He is here, but I am not [Col. 0552C] here. How much more likely it would seem that you were not here and I were here, O Lord! But I am neither here nor elsewhere, because “I have been reduced to nothing and knew it not” (Ps. 72:22). Truly to nothing—that is, to sin—and I did not know it 1095, because I was not there when death devoured my first parent with its most bitter bite. Hence, broken in heart and body, I dissolve into pleasures and bitterness, bearing an innate fault, a kindred punishment, wholly fluid and feeble. But he who is himself the same, who said, “I am who am” (Exod. 3:14), truly is; for his being is what he is.

3. What participation, then, what agreement can there be between one who is not and him who is? How can things so different be joined? “It is good for me,” says the saint, “to cleave to God” (Ps. 72:28). We cannot be joined to him immediately; but perhaps through some intermediary [Col. 0552D] this union can be effected. And, not to delay you longer, there are three bonds by which we are bound to him—and precisely three, so that by these alone, or things like them, everything that is bound is bound. First, take cords; second, wooden or iron nails; third, glue. The first binds strongly and harshly; the second more strongly and more harshly; the third sweetly and securely.

A person is in some sense bound to the Redeemer by a cord if, when troubled by a particularly violent temptation, he sets before himself regard for honor, remembrance of the promise, and for the time being restrains himself by this cord, lest his resolution be altogether broken. This is certainly a hard and troublesome bond, but also exceedingly dangerous, and one that cannot hold for long; for cords rot, and [Col. 0553A] we either forget the bond of shame or quickly break it. But another is fastened by nails to the Lord of majesty: one whom fear of God binds, who does not shrink before human faces but at the thought of infernal torments. Such a person does not fear to sin, but to burn. Yet he is impressed more harshly and strongly than the first, because whereas the other wavers in his resolution, this one does not lose his resolution.

But the third is glued fast to him by glue—that is, by charity. Bound as sweetly as securely, cleaving to God, he is one spirit with him. He is the one who turns and directs to his own good whatever happens, from wherever it comes, whether things done by him or things done to him.
