Blessed is such a person, suffused with the majesty of an abundant spirit, who bears everyone sweetly and gently and himself burdens no one; who judges it more terrible and dreadful than [Col. 0553B] hell itself knowingly to offend, even in the slightest matter, the countenance of the Almighty. This is the lover of the brethren and of the people of Israel. This is the one who prays much for the people and for the holy city Jerusalem (2 Macc. 15:14). “It is good with glue,” says Isaiah (Isa. 41:7). Truly it is good and pleasant, because the other two—lest I call them evil—are, in comparison with this one, burdensome and unbearable.

4. But that merciful eye, which knows our frame, leaves none of those to be saved in the first state, but advances them to the second; nor does it desert them there, but leads them from the second to the third. For in the first state, because we are ashamed to abandon those in distress, we scarcely endure for an hour; in the second, now fearing and hoping, we make progress; in the third, loving, we are perfected. Thus, when fear and shame, the two preceding bonds, have been cast out [Col. 0553C], we abide in the resting-place of love alone.

Thus Christ too was first bound, secondly crucified, thirdly anointed with the adhesive unction of spices. This was not because that body needed to be strengthened by such spices, for it could not be dissolved or see corruption; but he who for our sake endured the spittle of the Jews did not for our sake disdain the ointments of believers. Note also that, having remained in cords and nails scarcely for the space of a single day, he rose victorious with the anointing, and destined to conquer forever. So too he does not allow the elect to remain long in the two aforesaid states, but anoints them with the anointing of his mercy, so that, crucified to the world and the world to them, they may now rise in newness of spirit and say: “Who shall separate us from the charity of God?” (Rom. 8:35).

5. [Col. 0553D] By this glue that divine regard bound us fast to himself from the foundation of the world, that we might be holy and immaculate before him in charity. For we know that one born of God does not sin, because heavenly generation preserves him (1 John 5:18). Heavenly generation is eternal predestination, by which God foresaw that we should be made conformable to the image 1096 of his Son. Of these no one sins—that is, persists in sin [Note: [Col. 0553] Compare Sermon 23 on the Song of Songs, no. 15, and *On Grace and Free Choice*, no. 29, with Sermon 1 for Septuagesima.]—because “the Lord knows those who are his,” and God’s purpose remains unshaken.

Although David is branded with the mark of dreadful crimes, although Mary Magdalene is laden with seven demons, although the chief of the apostles [Col. 0554A] is submerged in the depth of denial, nevertheless none can snatch them from the hand of God. “For those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified” (Rom. 8:30). Is it not good to cleave to him? Seek, brothers, seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always (Ps. 104:4). “Seek the Lord, and your soul shall live” (Ps. 68:13). “And my soul,” he says, “shall live for him” (Ps. 21:31)—the soul that is dead to the world. For the soul that lives to the world does not live for him. Let us therefore seek him in such a way that we always seek him, and that, when he comes to seek us, he may say of us: “This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob” (Ps. 23:6). Thus may the eternal gates be opened, and may the King of glory enter, and we with him, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON V. On the words of Habakkuk 2:1, “I will stand upon my watch”

[Col. 0554B]

1. We read in the Gospel that, when the Savior was once preaching and, under the mystery of eating his body, was exhorting his disciples to share in his sufferings, some said: “This saying is hard,” and from that time were no longer with him. But when the disciples were asked whether they too wished to depart, they said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:61, 67–69). So I say to you, brothers: even to this day it is plain to some that the words Jesus speaks are spirit and life, and therefore they follow him; to others they seem hard, and they seek miserable consolation elsewhere.

[Col. 0554C]

For Wisdom cries aloud in the streets, namely, in the broad and spacious way that leads to death, in order to call back those walking upon it. Thus: “For forty years,” he says, “I was near this generation, and I said: These always err in heart” (Ps. 94:10). You also have in another psalm: “God has spoken once” (Ps. 61:12). Once, indeed, because always. For his utterance is one: not interrupted, but continuous and perpetual.

2. He calls sinners back to their heart; he rebukes them for the error of the heart, because he himself dwells and speaks there, doing indeed what he taught through the prophet when he said: “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem” (Isa. 40:2). But Babylon, because it is earth, cannot bear all his words; it withdraws from the heart and walks rather in the flesh, as though dead to the heart [Col. 0554D]—indeed, like a deceived dove without a heart. For it wishes to rejoice when it has done evil and to exult in the worst things; and, hearing the voice of the Lord approving no such joys, but detesting, reproving, and condemning them, it flees and hides itself after the manner of transgressing Adam. But alas for me! What a worthless covering you seek, wretched soul! What a useless covering you seek! For the leaves you weave together are leaves—leaves, I say, which give you no warmth and possess no firmness. When the sun rises, they will wither, and the burning wind will scatter them; but you will remain naked and miserable. Then there will be nothing covered that shall not be revealed, for the Lord will come, [Col. 0555A] who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts. There will no longer be anywhere for you to hide, wretch. In vain you will say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us” (Hos. 10:8); for you must stand naked and exposed before Christ’s tribunal, to hear the voice of judgment—you who despised the voice of counsel. For behold what God says: “Repent” (Matt. 3:2). Yet many disregard it, stop their ears, and say, “This saying is hard.” Not so, ungodly ones: you will not be able thus to disregard it when that harsh word and dreadful hearing shall sound: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41).

3. You see, brothers, how salutarily the Prophet admonishes us: if we hear his voice today, let us not harden our hearts. For you read almost the same [Col. 0555B] words in the [1097] Gospel and in the prophet. The Lord says in the Gospel: “My sheep hear my voice” (John 10:27). And holy David says in the psalm: “His people”—without doubt, the Lord’s—“and the sheep of his pasture: today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. 94:7–8). For it is more useful and far more salutary to hear him today as one counselling, consoling, warning, teaching, and, at the most, rebuking, reproaching, correcting, than on that day, so bitter, so mournful, so dark, to hear him judging, angry, taking vengeance, raging, condemning. It is good for me, I say, to be humbled; good that the righteous man should correct me in mercy and rebuke me, rather than [Col. 0555C] that the oil of the sinner should make my head fat—lest perhaps I be found to be earth, struck by the rod of his mouth, when the vessels of the potter shall be shattered with an iron rod. It is good for me, because of the words of his lips, to keep the hard paths with the Prophet (Ps. 16:4), rather than to be slain together with the ungodly by the breath of his lips.

4. Now, if I feel any bitterness in his voice, it is not without sweetness; for when he is angry, he will remember mercy. Indeed, even that indignation itself proceeds from nothing other than mercy. For “whom he loves he rebukes and chastens, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6), visiting his iniquities with a rod and his sins with blows; yet he does not disperse his mercy from him. Therefore those who are wise do not [Col. 0555D] cover their wounds, but uncover them and confess to the Lord, “for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever”; and thus he pours in the wine of reproof so that the oil of consolation is not lacking. Therefore, I say, the wise person embraces correction, lest the Lord become angry and, according to the multitude of his wrath, no longer inquire, but his zeal depart from him. Hence the heart of the wise is where there is sorrow, but the heart of fools where there is merriment (Eccl. 7:5); yet that wise person’s sorrow shall be turned into joy, while mourning will seize the end of those others’ joy. Hear, finally, the prophet Habakkuk, how he does not disregard the Lord’s rebuke [Col. 0556A] but turns it over with diligent and anxious thought. For he says: “I will stand upon my watch, and set my foot upon the stronghold, that I may see what he will say to me and what I shall answer to him who rebukes me.” Therefore, brothers, I beseech you, let us stand upon our watch, because it is a time of warfare. Let our dwelling be not upon the dung-heap of this miserable body, but in the heart where Christ dwells, in the judgment and counsel of reason. Yet let us not place our confidence in reason itself, nor lean upon a fragile watch; rather, let us set our foot upon the stronghold, relying with all our strength upon Christ, the most firm rock, as it is written: “He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Ps. 39:3). Thus established and made firm, let us now contemplate, that we may see what [Col. 0556B] he says to us and what we shall answer to him who rebukes us.

5. For this, beloved, is the first degree of contemplation [Col. 0556B]: continually to consider what the Lord wills, what pleases him, what is acceptable before him. Since we all offend in many things, and our strength conflicts with the rectitude of his will and cannot be joined or fitted to it, let us humble ourselves under the mighty hand of the most high God. Let us be altogether anxious not to appear pitiable in the eyes of his mercy, saying: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved” (Jer. 17:14); and: “Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5). Once the eye of the heart has been cleansed through thoughts of this kind, [Col. 0556C] we then move no longer in our own spirit with bitterness, but rather in the divine Spirit with great delight. Nor do we then consider what God’s will is in us, but what it is in itself. For life is in his will, so that we must not doubt that in all things what accords with his will is more useful and altogether more beneficial to us. Therefore, as carefully as we wish to preserve the life of our soul, so carefully must we endeavour, insofar as we can, not to depart from that will.

Then, once we have made some progress in spiritual exercise, following the guiding Spirit who searches even the depths of God, let us consider how sweet the Lord is, how good in himself; praying with the Prophet, [1098] that we may behold the will of the Lord and visit no longer our own heart, but his temple [Col. 0556D] (Ps. 26:4); and saying nevertheless with the same Prophet: “My soul has been troubled within me; therefore I shall remember you” (Ps. 41:7). For the whole sum of spiritual life lies in these two things: that, in considering ourselves, we be troubled and saddened unto salvation; and that in considering God we breathe again, receiving consolation from the joy of the Holy Spirit—thereby conceiving fear and humility, and thence hope and charity.

## SERMON VI

[Note: [Col. 0555D] This sermon is appended to the sermons of Nicholas of Clairvaux, but is not unworthy of Bernard, although some matters approach those read in Sermon 32 *On Various Subjects*, no. 3 [Col. 0566D]. It is cited in Book VIII of the *Flores*, chapter 68. It was first published at Rouen, without indication of the year, under Bernard’s name.]

### On the skin, flesh, and bones of the soul

1. Blessed David speaks in the psalm concerning the righteous, saying: [Col. 0557A] “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, but from all these the Lord will deliver them. The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them shall be broken” (Ps. 33:20–21). Let no one suppose this to have been said of bodily bones, especially since the bones of so many blessed martyrs have been broken by the hands of wicked men and crushed by the teeth of beasts.

Yet the condition of human souls is altogether wonderful and pitiable: although they perceive so many things externally with lively intelligence, they are nevertheless unable, by any keenness, to know or consider themselves as they are. They utterly require certain figures and riddles of bodily likenesses, in order that from things visible and external they may infer, at least in some degree, things invisible and internal. Let us therefore suppose thought to be, as it were, the [Col. 0557B] skin of the soul; affection, its flesh; and consequently we may understand intention as its bone. Thus, in the soundness of its bone will be the soul’s life; in the incorruption of its flesh, its health; and in the beauty of its skin, its loveliness.

What, then, are the tribulations of the righteous, except that the skin is sometimes discoloured when an unprofitable thought turns about in the heart? At times, moreover, the flesh [Col. 0557C] too is wounded, when the harmful thought advances so far that affection is corrupted by delight. But the bones of the righteous are kept wholly sound and unharmed by the Lord: the purpose of their heart is never broken, and their intention toward salvation is never crushed, so that assent is given even to the solicitation of concupiscence. For just as sinful thought discolours and affection wounds, so consent utterly kills the soul.

2. Therefore, beloved, [Col. 0557C] let us beware of useless thoughts, that the face of our souls may remain beautiful; so that, forgetting the things behind—our people and our father’s house—the King may desire our beauty. Let us depart from our land, lest a thought directed toward fleshly pleasure overtake us. Let us depart also from our kindred, that is, from thoughts of curiosity, which, because they dwell in bodily senses, are certainly kindred to fleshly pleasure. Let us depart likewise from our father’s house, that we may flee thoughts of pride and vanity. We too were once, like the rest, children of wrath; we too were of the devil our father, who is king over [Col. 0557D] all sons of pride and has prepared for himself a seat and most unhappy dwelling-place upon the mountains of exaltation.

If perhaps any such thought enters the mind at some time, let us labour with every care to wash away and eradicate quickly the defilement by which we see ourselves stained, crying with the Prophet: “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50:9). But if through our carelessness and negligence a useless thought should pass into the heart’s affection, knowing that it is no longer a stain but a wound, let us flee with all haste to the help of the Spirit who aids our infirmity, crying out [Col. 0558A] the words of the psalm: “Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5).

For these are human temptations, and they cannot wholly be avoided while, in this body of death, we are away from the Lord. Yet let no one make light of them or disregard them: although they are not deadly, they are certainly dangerous.

3. But, brothers, let us guard [Col. 0558B] the intention and purpose of the mind with the same care with which we desire to guard the life of our souls. For this is indeed sin unto death: when we sin by consent and deliberation, condemned by our own judgment. I do not say this in order that anyone conscious of this offence might despair, but that he may dread the precipice and, having fallen, hasten to rise again. Whoever is such a person should know that he has departed from righteousness. He whose bone has been broken and shattered should know that he has been cut off from Christ’s body, concerning which it is written: “You shall not break a bone of it” (Exod. 12:46; John 19:36).

Thus, in Christ’s passion, although the skin was discoloured with the bruises of scourges, so that by his bruise we might be healed; although the flesh was wounded by nails and his side opened by a lance, so that we might be redeemed by his blood—yet no bone of him was broken. Hence holy David also says: “My bone, which you made in secret, was not hidden from you” (Ps. 138:15). And in another psalm: “My bones have withered like a hearth” (Ps. 101:4). This happens when the soul seems to have wholly lost every delight in good [Col. 0558C] and to have retained for itself only the strength of a dry intention. Consider whether perhaps blessed Job suffered something of this kind when he said: “My bone has clung to my skin, my flesh having been consumed” (Job 19:20), so that, with affection corrupted, spiritual thought could scarcely claim for itself the bare intention alone.

## SERMON VII

[Note: [Col. 0557D] This sermon too has been appended to Nicholas’s sermons; yet it wholly bears Bernard’s genius, and appears [Col. 0558D] among these sermons of Bernard in all printed and manuscript editions, as does the preceding sermon.]

### On the threefold glory, concerning the Apostle’s words: “Let him who glories glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17–18)

1. “Let him who glories glory in the Lord.” The Apostle knew that glory belongs properly to the Creator, not to the creature, according to the words: “I will not give my glory to another” (Isa. 42:8); and: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14); likewise [Col. 0558D]: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113:9).

But he considered that the rational creature so desires glory that it can scarcely, if ever, be restrained from this desire, since it was made in the image of its Creator. Therefore, according to the wisdom given him by God, he found a most salutary counsel, saying: Since we cannot be persuaded not to glory at all, at least let him who glories glory in the Lord.

Consider how greatly Paul’s philosophy surpasses that of the wise of this world, which is foolishness before God (1 Cor. 3:19). For when philosophers saw some people delighting in the praises of others [Col. 0559A] and seeking glory from one another, those among them who were foremost wisely perceived that such glory was vain and altogether to be despised. But then, considering and more diligently investigating what glory ought to be sought by the wise person, here they altogether vanished in their reasonings, supposing each person’s own glory sufficient—as though the soul, which cannot exist from itself, could be blessed through itself. Thus, just as those greedy for others’ praise devoted every effort to doing what people might admire and praise, so these thinkers judged that only those things should be pursued which the inner judge, the mind, approved.

2. Such is the highest philosophy of the wise of this world; even this falls short, though it is nearer to the truth. Therefore the Apostle, transcending both glories by the lofty contemplation of truth, says: “Let him who glories glory neither in another nor in himself, but in the Lord.” And he rebukes with greater care the glory that seemed nearer to truth, condemning it by the certain judgment of truth: “For it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends” [Col. 0559B] (2 Cor. 10:18).

For why should I be concerned with the judgment either of another human being or of myself, when I shall be found neither rejected by that person’s blame nor approved by that person’s praise? Brothers, if I had to stand before your tribunal, I might rightly glory in your praises. If I were to be judged by my own examination, I might justly be content with my own testimony and delight in my own praise. But now, since I must be presented for judgment not before yours or mine, but before God’s [Col. 0559C], how great is the folly—indeed, the madness—of glorying either in your testimony or in my own, especially since he is the one before whose eyes all things are naked and exposed, and who has no need for anyone to bear witness to him concerning a human being?

Rightly, therefore, the Apostle himself, reprover of vain and deceitful glory, says: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day; but I do not even judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified; he who judges me is the Lord” (1 Cor. 4:3–4). In these words we should carefully observe also that, though he regarded another’s judgment as very slight, he was nevertheless unwilling to follow even his own judgment, though he did not consider it quite so slight. For “no one knows what is in a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him” (1 Cor. 2:11), so that in comparison with inner testimony external testimony must be regarded as utterly nothing. What have I to do with the praises of people to whom I am unknown? [Col. 0559D]

If even the spirit that is in a human being could know all that belongs to that person, its testimony would surely suffice. But now the human heart is perverse and inscrutable even to itself (Jer. 17:9), so that it is ignorant in large measure even of present things and cannot know its future at all. Yet, because it knows present things to some extent, if our conscience does not rebuke us, we have not glory indeed, but confidence toward him, as blessed John says (John 3:21). But when we have deserved to receive the judgment concerning us of Truth itself, from which nothing is hidden, [Col. 0560A] then we may safely glory in that judgment.

3. “Therefore,” says the Apostle, “judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness” (1 Cor. 4:5). For then glorying will be wholly perfect and secure, when each person’s praise comes from God. Even now, though not fully, and not without fear and much anxiety, nevertheless we glory to some degree in the Lord, while the Holy Spirit bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God. For in this we can truly glory: that we have so great a Father, and that we are an object of concern to ineffable Majesty. Hence the prophet says: “Lord, what is man, that you magnify him? Or why do you set your heart upon him?” (Job 7:17).

Therefore let him who glories no longer glory in his own merits. For what does he have that he has not received? And if he received it, why does he glory as though he had not received it? Let him glory in the one from whom he received it—not as though he himself were great, but because God magnifies him: that is, let him glory in the things he has received, not as though he had not received them, but as one who has received them. For the Apostle does not say, “If you have received, why do you glory?” but, “Why do you glory as though you had not received?” [Col. 0560B] (1 Cor. 4:7): thus he does not forbid glorying, but teaches how to glory.

4. But what does he mean when he says: “For it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends”? For whom does God commend in this world? How can Truth commend one who is still found blameworthy? “For I,” he says, “rebuke and chasten those whom I love” (Rev. 3:19). Is this all commendation? [Col. 0560C] Indeed, as it seems to me, it is precisely that. For what commendation is better or more effective than the divine attestation of his love toward us?

No testimony of his love in this life is more credible or more certain than that which the prophet desires when he says: “Let the righteous man correct me in mercy and rebuke me” (Ps. 140:5). For this rebuke, by which the Spirit of truth continually suggests to us inwardly what we lack, repels pride, negligence, and ingratitude. Nearly every class of religious people suffers dangerously from these three vices because they do not hear with sufficiently attentive inner ears what he says within—the Spirit of truth, who flatters no one.

From this, unless I am mistaken, it results for some that, being eager for their own glory, [Col. 0560D] they cannot by any means rest when they find absolutely nothing in themselves by which they may glory even a little. But perfect and secure glorying consists in fearing all our works, as blessed Job testifies of himself (Job 9:28), and in recognizing with the prophet Isaiah that all our righteousnesses are to be considered nothing but a menstrual cloth (Isa. 64:6). Nevertheless, we still trust and glory in the Lord, whose mercy toward us is so great that he keeps us from graver sins, those which are unto death; and graciously deigns both to make known to us the very offences of our imperfection and the impurity of our manner of life, and, once they are known, to pardon them. Thus, rooted firmly in humility, carefulness, and thanksgiving, [Col. 0561A] we glory no longer in ourselves but in the Lord.

## SERMON VIII

[Note: [Col. 0561D] This sermon is attributed to Guerric, abbot of Igny, in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*; but it is not found among Guerric’s sermons in the Cologne manuscript. Rather, it occurs among Bernard’s sermons *On Various Subjects* in all printed and manuscript editions, and is cited in the *Flores*.]

### On the various affections or states in which the soul is under God

1. The reason why we call God by different names—now Father, now Teacher, or Lord—is not any diversity in his most simple and wholly unchangeable nature, but the manifold variation of our affections according to the different advances or failings of the soul. For some souls appear to act under a householder, some under a Lord, some under a teacher, some also under a father, and some with a bridegroom; so that he himself seems to advance with those advancing and change with those changed—he who, according to the Prophet, changes creatures and they shall be changed, though he remains the same and his years do not fail (Ps. 101:27–28).

Observe, finally, what the same Prophet says to him in another psalm: “With the holy you will be holy; with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the chosen you will be chosen; and, more wonderfully still, with the perverse,” he says, “you will be perverse.” And how he is thus changed—or rather, how he thus changes while remaining himself unchangeable—he adds in explanation: “For you will save the humble people and humble the eyes of the proud” (Ps. 17:26–28).

2. But since “that which is spiritual” does not come first, “but that which is natural; afterward that which is spiritual,” it seems to me that four states sometimes precede our conversion: one under ourselves, three under the prince of this world. The soul is under itself when it follows its own [Col. 0561C] will, rejoicing in a harmful freedom. This is the prodigal son who received the portion of his father’s substance falling to him: namely, intelligence, memory, bodily powers, and other similar goods of nature. He used these not for the divine will but for his own will, and was as though without God in this world.

A person remains under himself while satisfying his own will, yet is not possessed by vices and sins; for one who commits sin is no longer servant of himself but of sin. From this point he goes into a far country: he had indeed separated himself, but had not yet gone far from his father. Having received his share of the substance, he became his own master; and although he withdrew from his author [Col. 0561D], he remained near so long as he had not withdrawn in deed. This lasts while he follows, according to his own will, things that are lawful indeed but not expedient. But once he departs even from himself, that is, turns aside into sin, then he truly goes into a far country; for from him who is supremely and uniquely Being, nothing is farther than that which is in no way; and nothing is more remote from him from whom, through whom, and in whom all things are than sin [1102], which is nothing among all things.

3. Moreover, it is a just judgment of divine vengeance [Col. 0562A] that another should usurp as a slave the father’s fugitive son. Thus the one who went into a far country is said to have attached himself to one of the citizens there. I understand this to be none other than one of the evil spirits, who, because they sin with irreparable obstinacy and have passed into an affection for malice and wickedness, are no longer strangers and sojourners, but as it were citizens and inhabitants of sin.

What does it mean that the poor young man and stranger is said to have attached himself to a citizen, except that he became subject to him? The following words show how he attached himself: “He attached himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his field to feed swine.” Notice that he is said to have attached himself to that evil citizen through the necessity of hunger, just as Israel is said to have gone down into Egypt in a time of famine (Gen. 46:6). A dangerous and destructive [Col. 0562B] hunger indeed: it consigns free persons to wretched slavery, subjects them to works of mud and brick, associates them with swine—indeed, makes them slaves of swine.

Whence such want for one who had arrived rich, having gathered all the things that he had received as his portion from his father’s substance? Without doubt, from what was said before: he had squandered his goods, living extravagantly with prostitutes. “Therefore,” it says, “he began to be in want” (Luke 15:11–15).

4. Understand these prostitutes as the lusts of the flesh. Living extravagantly with them, one squanders the goods of nature by misusing them for pleasure. Then, as we have said, destructive want follows, Scripture testifying that “the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing” (Eccl. 1:8). He is therefore sent to feed swine, that is, the bodily senses, which delight in wallowing in mud and filth [Col. 0562C]. Consider whether perhaps these are the swine into which evil spirits, cast out from a human being, enter (Matt. 8:32). For sin, cast out from our rational part—that is, the mind—clings to the bodily senses, as the Apostle testifies when he says that with the mind he assents to God’s law, but with the flesh to the law of sin which is in our members. Hence he says elsewhere: “I know that no good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7:18, 25).

But what is to be done when unclean spirits, thus cast out from a human being, inhabit swine? Remedies of tears must be sought, and we must run to the waters, by whose abundance the harmfully vigorous root of sin may be choked in them. Yet this complete destruction of sin seems rather to be reserved for the end.

5. These things have been said by way of digression [Col. 0562D], in order to show more clearly how the evil one subjects to himself the person whom he finds under himself, like a strong armed man entering and possessing the court in which he finds a poor and feeble inhabitant. Nevertheless, people seem to me to be under the prince of darkness in three ways.

First, neither willingly nor unwillingly: this applies [Col. 0562D] to those who do not yet possess the use of will, yet are vessels of wrath because of original sin, until the stronger one comes through the sacrament and, having bound the strong man, plunders his vessels—the true Moses, who came in water, not in water alone, but in water and blood.

Secondly, willingly: when they sin voluntarily.

Thirdly, unwillingly: when they would indeed already repent [Col. 0563A], except that, wretchedly bound by the habit of sin, by God’s just judgment they who are in filth become yet more defiled. The prodigal son seems to have laboured in this third state—truly excessively prodigal—who had not only squandered his possessions but had subjected himself to wretched slavery, unhappy and sold under sin. Returning to himself, he says: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have bread in abundance, but I am perishing here from hunger!” If anyone has experienced this within himself, I think he will readily recognize in these words the wretched state of mind.

For who, bound by the habit of sin, would not count himself happy if he were permitted to be like one of those whom he sees in the world, lukewarm but living without crime, not at all seeking the things above but those upon the earth? “How many,” he says, [Col. 0563B] “hired servants in my father’s house have bread in abundance!” That is, they are comforted in their innocence and enjoy the good of their own conscience; “but I am perishing here from hunger,” that is, I am tormented by the insatiable desires of sins and the affections of vices.

Yet it may be understood that he declares himself afflicted not by hunger for bread nor thirst for water, but by hunger and thirst for the divine word, with which the prophet threatens Judaea also (Amos 8:11). I say these things not because they are so, but because the wretch humbled beneath sin feels them to be so. For those whose intention is worldly and mercenary do not glory in the testimony of conscience; but the repentant sinner judges another person most holy whenever, for whatever reason, he sees that person innocent. “Make me,” he says, “as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15:17, 19).

6. Behold, this is now the first [Col. 0563C] state under God into which those begin to enter who live under the householder as hired servants. These are the people we see in the world serving God as it were for wages, with no desire, or only a slight desire, for eternal things, and asking from him the earthly things which they desire. But in the second state one begins to be under the Lord, as a servant fears prison and dreads being subjected to punishment. In this state, indeed, are conversion, departure from the world, and entrance into life. Hence you read: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1:16); and another prophet says: “From your fear we have conceived and given birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26:18).

Very near to this degree, and as it were mingled with it, is a third [Col. 0563D]: that of those who, still little children in Christ, desire milk and live as under a teacher and guardian. This especially suits novices, who, if they begin perhaps to find delight in the consolations of holy meditation, tears, psalmody, and other such things, fear in a childlike manner lest they offend their teacher, be beaten, or be deprived of the little gifts by which that most kindly instructor is accustomed to attract them. These are they who set the Lord always before their eyes and are disturbed if he should happen to be absent even for an hour. They no longer fear punishments in a servile way, but, like little children, fear the strokes of the rod. They embrace the discipline of their teacher, lest he become angry and they perish from the right way; lest the grace of devotion be withdrawn, all things become burdensome to them [Col. 0564A], and they labour under a kind of weariness, as though being beaten inwardly in the soul by the bitterness of thoughts.

For these are the blows by which God chastens his little children—blows which we recognize better through experience than through speech. Hence the Lord himself says through the prophet: “If his children forsake my law,” and so forth, “I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with blows” (Ps. 88:31, 33).

7. In these beginnings, therefore, and in this almost infant stage, the fear of the Lord and the discipline of the teacher succeed one another in turn, so that anyone careful to observe this attentively will find himself now in one state, now in the other. Hence, speaking to the still new Church, he mentions both names together: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, [Col. 0564B] for I am” (John 13:13).

Let our novices recognize their place here, that henceforth they may be diligent to occupy themselves more earnestly with these matters. Before all else, fear is necessary to them, so that they may erase past sins and avoid future ones. For, as Scripture says, “the fear of the Lord drives out sin” (Ecclus. 1:27), whether sin already committed or sin attempting to enter. It drives out the former by repentance and the latter by resistance.

But because the way leading to life is narrow and steep, you, O little children, need a guardian and nurse, as little ones in Christ: one who may teach, lead, cherish you, play as it were with little children, and console you with certain endearments, lest your weak age perish. Therefore not I, but rather the [Col. 0564C] prince and shepherd of the Church, admonishes you: “As newborn infants, desire the reasonable milk without deceit”—yet not in order to remain in it, but to grow through it unto salvation (1 Pet. 2:2).

Another Scripture expresses this more clearly: “Rejoice with joy, all you who mourned over her”—undoubtedly [1104] Jerusalem, for it was speaking of her—“that you may drink,” it says, “of the milk and be satisfied from the breasts of her consolation; and when you have been weaned from milk, you may delight in the entrance of her glory” (Isa. 66:10–11).

8. For this is the state of the son already of vigorous age, who lives under the Father and is no longer given milk but fed with solid food. He has indeed forgotten the things behind, in which the servile eye dwelt in bitterness; [Col. 0564D] yet he does not even consider present things or seize upon the little consolations of little children. Rather, he stretches himself toward the things ahead, toward the prize of the heavenly calling and the entrance into future blessedness, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God.

For he has put away the things of a child and no longer occupies himself with consolations of this kind, sweet though they are, yet not enduring. But because he has now advanced to a perfect man, he must be occupied with the things of his Father, sighing after the inheritance and engaging in diligent meditation upon it. Would anyone judge him a hired servant because he longs for the paternal inheritance and seeks and awaits it with all affection? The Prophet testifies that this is the recompense of sons, not of hired servants: “When he gives sleep to his beloved ones, behold, children are the inheritance of the Lord; the fruit of the womb, the reward” [Col. 0565A] (Ps. 126:2–3).

9. Yet there is found another, higher degree, and an affection worthier than this, when, with the heart wholly made chaste, the soul desires nothing else and asks nothing else of God than God himself. For by frequent experience it has learned that the Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him; so that now, from the affection and conviction of its heart, it cries aloud that saying from the psalm: “For what have I in heaven? And what have I desired from you upon earth? My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the God of my heart, and my portion for ever” (Ps. 72:25–26). For a soul of this sort desires nothing of its own—not happiness, not glory, nor anything else—as though from a private self-love; but it goes wholly toward God, and its one perfect desire is that the King may bring it into his chamber, that it may cleave to him and enjoy him. Hence also, with unveiled face, continually contemplating, insofar as it can, the glory of its heavenly Bridegroom, it is transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. It plainly deserves to hear: “You are altogether beautiful, my friend” (Song 4:7). And it too dares to say: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song 2:16). In such most blessed and most delightful converse the glorious soul takes pleasure with the Bridegroom.

## SERMON IX. On the words of the Apostle in Romans 1:20, “The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world,” etc.; and on the words of Psalm 84:9, “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me,” etc.

[Col. 0565C]

1. “The invisible things of God,” as the Apostle testifies, “are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that have been made.” This sensible world is like a common book, bound together as books ordinarily are, so that whoever wishes may read in it the wisdom of God. Yet the time will come when heaven shall be folded up like a book; and then no one will need to read any longer in it, since all shall be taught by God (John 6:45). And just as the creature of heaven, so also the creature of the world, shall now see God, not through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face, and shall contemplate his wisdom clearly in itself.

Meanwhile, the human soul needs the creature as a kind of vehicle by which to rise to knowledge of the Creator; whereas angelic nature, far more blessed and perfect, has knowledge of the creature in the Creator. To that excellence, though only for a little while, that blessed soul seems to have been caught up which beheld the whole universe gathered beneath one ray of the sun.

[Note: [Col. 0565D] Namely, Saint Benedict, whom Bernard believes to have seen God, though only in a momentary rapture, without the “vehicle of creature,” and therefore in God himself, indeed “in the light of God,” as Gregory expresses it. Nevertheless Bernard, in Sermon 31 on the Song of Songs, no. 2, says “that neither a wise man, nor a saint, nor a prophet can, or could, see him as he is in this mortal body.”]

Writing of this miracle, blessed Pope Gregory says in the book of the *Dialogues*: “To one who sees the Creator, every creature is narrow” (*Dialogues*, book II, ch. 35). Blessed therefore are those who are filled with the fatness of wheat and have no need to suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone; that is, those who do not seek out the invisible things of God by investigating visible things, but see them clearly understood in themselves. But this, as we have already said, belongs to angelic blessedness, not to human frailty.

[Col. 0566A]

2. Let us therefore seek, at least through the things that have been made, an understanding of the invisible things of God. If the soul sees these understood in other creatures, it must necessarily see and understand them much more fully and much more subtly in the creature made in the image of the Creator—that is, in itself. For among all creatures dwelling beneath the sun, there is no degree nearer to God than the human soul. Thus the Prophet rightly says to him: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you! He has set ascents in his heart”; and shortly afterward: “They shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83:6, 8).

[Col. 0566B]

Therefore, brothers, we exhort you unceasingly to walk in the ways of the heart and always to hold your soul in your hands, so that you may hear what the Lord God speaks within you; for he will speak peace. To whom will he speak peace? Certainly to his people and to his saints. Who are the people, or who are the saints? Surely those who turn back to the heart. Hence it follows: “And to those who turn to the heart.”

3. Yet in these words we commonly understand three classes of people, to whom alone God speaks peace, just as another prophet foresaw only three who would be saved: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. 14:14). They are named in the reverse order, but the same ranks are expressed: namely, the continent, the prelates, and the married. The continent must turn from carnal enticements to the things of the heart—that is, to spiritual desires; whence Daniel is called by the angel “a man of desires” (Dan. 10:11). Prelates must strive rather to be of benefit than to exercise authority, since holiness especially befits them; hence in the psalm they are specifically called saints. And married persons must not transgress the commandments, so that they may rightly be called the Lord’s people and the sheep of his pasture.

[Col. 0566C]

4. Indeed, within ourselves also—since for us this is a matter of greater concern—we commonly identify these three ranks. By “the people” we mean the working brothers, occupied with outward and, as it were, public affairs. But those who turn to the heart are the cloistered brothers, whom no business obstructs, but who are freely at leisure to see that the Lord is sweet. God speaks peace over each wall, because both tend toward the same end, though not by the same way. The psaltery is pleasant with the harp, and the sound of the harp is no less pleasant than that of the psaltery, although the former produces its sound from above and the latter from below. Nevertheless Mary chose the better part, although perhaps Martha’s humble manner of life is of no lesser merit before God. But Mary is praised for her choice (Luke 10:42), since that way is altogether to be chosen, insofar as we are concerned; whereas Martha’s, if imposed upon one, must be borne patiently.

[Col. 0567A]

5. Now the phrase inserted, “over his saints,” pertains to prelates, for whom both kinds of life are necessary. It belongs to them to provide for both groups and to join together the walls coming from opposite directions, because they have been appointed vicars of the cornerstone, Christ Jesus. Nor is there any doubt that their administration is far more dangerous than that of others. Yet if they minister well, they will acquire for themselves a good rank and receive a greater abundance and overflowing measure of peace, so that it may rightly be said of them: “For God speaks peace over his saints.” Does anyone doubt whom he called saints? Let him hear Isaiah: “You shall be called the saints of the Lord, ministers of our God” (Isa. 61:6).

I had intended to give some example of how the human mind ought to rise from consideration of itself to spiritual understanding; but this must be postponed until another day and another sermon.

## SERMON X. On the life and five senses of the soul.

1. Great, I tell you, beloved, and exceedingly inexcusable is our negligence: we squander time in idle thoughts. Yet we need neither penetrate clouds nor cross seas in order to find wholesome thoughts; rather, as Moses says, “The word is near, in our mouth and in our heart” (Deut. 30:14), and within ourselves we can find countless occasions and seeds of useful thoughts. Finally, if the soul is so unlearned and negligent that it cannot sufficiently search its own interior, let it at least attend to what it openly and manifestly does outwardly; and in these things too, if it seeks carefully, it will find wisdom.

[Col. 0567C]

For behold—for it is written, “Give opportunity to a wise man, and he will become wiser” (Prov. 9:9)—consider, O soul, what you bestow upon your body, and you will undoubtedly find that you give it life and sensation. You will find life uniform throughout the whole body—for the eye, for example, does not live differently from a joint—but sensation is not so. Seek, therefore, that your soul also—which is beyond doubt your God—may grant you like things. For a soul that has no knowledge of truth is not to be said to live, but is still dead within itself; just as a soul without sensation is one that does not yet possess love. Therefore the life of the soul is truth, and its sensation is charity.

Do not wonder that sometimes the souls of the impious have knowledge of truth and yet lack charity, since you find in some bodies life without sensation—as in trees and similar things—which are indeed animated, but by animation rather than by a soul. Likewise the souls of the wicked possess knowledge of truth through natural reason; yet although they are sometimes aided by grace, they are by no means animated by it. But in those into whom the spiritual soul pours both knowledge of truth and love, not in any outward manner but as their very soul—by cleaving to which they become one spirit with it—in these, I say, knowledge of truth is undivided, according to what was said concerning the life of the body.

[Col. 0568A]

For by the same knowledge you comprehend both the least and the greatest things.

2. Love, however, if you observe carefully, can be found various and perhaps divided into five parts according to the five bodily senses. There is dutiful love, by which we love parents; pleasant love, by which we love companions; just love toward all people; strenuous love toward enemies; and holy or devout love toward God. In all these, if you attend closely, you will find a mode proper to each and wholly different from the others.

Indeed, if it pleases you to consider more curiously, perhaps the first love—the love of parents—will not without reason seem suited to touch, because that sense perceives only things near and joined to the body; just as that love is shown only to those nearest to us by flesh. Nor is it inconsistent with the reasoning of the analogy that touch alone of the senses is diffused throughout the whole body, because that natural love belongs to all flesh, so much so that even brute animals both love their offspring and are loved by them.

[Col. 0568B]

Social love also seems very properly suited to taste, because of its greater sweetness and because this is the one sense which human life needs most. Nor can I see how one should be said to live, at least in this common human life, if one does not love those among whom one lives. General love, by which all human beings are loved, resembles smell, because this sense perceives things more remote and because, though it is not wholly devoid of carnal delight, it possesses that delight more faintly in proportion as it is more widely diffused.

Hearing, however, reaches things much more distant; and among human beings no one is more remote from one who loves than one who does not love. Finally, while in the other senses there is some pleasure of the flesh itself, and they seem to belong more to the flesh, hearing almost wholly goes beyond the flesh; and it seems not undeservedly suited to that love whose whole basis is obedience. That obedience pertains to hearing is sufficiently obvious, whereas, as we have said, some occasion is taken from the flesh for the other kinds of love.

[Col. 0568C]

3. Sight claims for itself an analogy with divine love in that it is found superior to all the other senses, of a singular kind of nature, more penetrating than the rest, and able to distinguish things much more distant. Smell and hearing, indeed, seem to perceive things afar off; but they are thought to draw toward themselves more the air which they perceive. Sight does not do this; rather, it seems itself to go out and advance toward distant things.

So it is with loves. In some manner we draw to ourselves those near to us, whom we love as ourselves; we draw enemies too, whom we love in order that they too may become like us—that is, become friends. But if we love God, as is fitting, with all our strength, all our soul, and all our heart, we ourselves go more toward him and hasten with all speed toward him who is ineffably above us.

[Col. 0569A]

4. It is also evident that among the bodily senses sight is superior to all the others, and hearing superior to the remaining three. Smell also seems to surpass taste and touch, if not in usefulness, at least in dignity; and taste excels touch. The very arrangement of the bodily members makes this clear. Who does not know that the eyes are placed at the summit and the ears beneath them? It is likewise clear that the nostrils are below the ears, the throat below the nostrils, and below the throat are the hands together with the remaining parts of the body to which touch belongs.

According to this pattern, therefore, one may also consider one sense of the soul more worthy than another. Since you can now easily perceive this, I pass it over for brevity’s sake. I leave for your diligence also to consider that, just as the bodily members must fall as soon as the soul ceases to animate them, so also the affections we have mentioned, which are like members of the soul, must utterly fall without the soul of the soul itself—which is God. Thus either that which ought to be loved is not loved at all, or it is not loved for the end for which it ought to be loved, or not in the way in which it ought. For some love their parents only carnally; they too acknowledge the Lord when he has done them good. But such a love either ought not to be called love at all, or is perishable and falls to the ground.

## SERMON XI. On the twofold baptism and the abandonment of one’s own will.

[Col. 0569C]

1. You know, brothers—for you hold the Catholic truth most firmly—that in baptism, when we renounce the devil, the heavenly Father adopts us and transfers us from the power of darkness into the kingdom of the Son of his glory. This is indeed the first robe, which the Father’s affection commands his servants to bring forth at once, awaiting neither the request of the lips nor the desire of the heart, but anticipating even understanding itself with blessings of sweetness. For as many as have been baptized into Christ Jesus have put on Christ (Gal. 3:27). Of him another also cries out, a faithful witness likewise, that “to as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

Nor is that power empty or weak, for we too are immediately certain that neither death nor life, nor powers, nor angels, nor height nor depth, can separate us from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:38–39). But observe how many things the Apostle enumerated—for they are his words—yet did not add: “Not even we ourselves.” This is indeed the freedom with which Christ has made us free: no creature whatsoever can tear us away or use force against us. We alone can abandon it, drawn away and enticed by our own will, by our own desire. Beyond this there is nothing that we need fear.

[Col. 0570A]

For until each person who has been reborn receives the use of will and the capacity for deliberation, that person cannot at all be separated from the charity of God. In the meantime such a one lives securely under the protection and advocacy of the Lord his God; there is nothing among all things to fear. But when, upon entering the years of discretion, one is restored to oneself, one need fear not even the violence of other things, but must beware of that which sleeps in one’s bosom—namely, one’s own will. Perhaps sin will be at the door, but its desire is subject to him; let him only refuse to open and decline to consent.

2. Thus the first parents were overthrown not by a bear or a lion, but rather by a serpent—more cunning, indeed, but not stronger than the other living creatures; and it was not the man who overcame the woman, but the woman the man. O Eve, the serpent deceived you: it truly deceived you, but did not drive or compel you. O Adam, the woman gave you fruit from the tree; but she did so by offering it, not by using violence. For it came about not by her power but by your will that you obeyed her voice more than the divine voice.

[Col. 0570B]

But if he failed to protect himself through ignorance, let us at least, forewarned by so many examples, beware for ourselves. Indeed, since we too have suffered miserably in this respect, let us henceforth diligently strive to provide some remedy for such great evils. When did that armed strong man, whom one stronger coming upon him bound, ever gain possession of his former court by any violence? Rather, he found the dwelling empty and foolishly exposed to him; entering with seven others more wicked, not stronger, he freely inhabited it—not breaking in by force (Luke 11:21–26). Who admitted him but one’s own will? It is this which again returned into the power of darkness and once more subjected us to the dominion of death.

3. Come, Lord Jesus; come even now, good Jesus; cast out again with strength him whom we foolishly admitted. Then indeed we shall be free even now, if you set us free. We have made void the first covenant; we have sinned against you, Lord, binding ourselves anew to Satan and his works, voluntarily putting our necks beneath the yoke of iniquity and submitting ourselves to miserable slavery. Therefore, my brothers, we must be rebaptized; we must enter into a second covenant; a second profession is needed. It is no longer enough to renounce the devil and his works: we must also renounce the world and our own will. For he deceived us; it led us astray.

[Note: [Col. 0569D] The common reading, “he betrayed us,” has been corrected from the manuscript of the Celestines of Paris: “it led us astray.”]

In the first baptism, when our own will had not yet harmed us, it was enough to renounce the devil, through whose envy both sin and death entered through one man and passed to all human beings. But after we have plainly experienced the enticements of the deceiving world and the faithlessness of our own will, henceforth in the second baptism, so to speak, of our conversion, we rightly take care—not foolishly merely to repair the first covenant, but also to strengthen it—and together renounce our very affections as well.

[Col. 0570D]

[Note: [Col. 0569D] Not a few ancient writers called religious profession a second baptism, as Bernard himself does in Sermon 37 *On Various Subjects*, no. 3, and in the book *On Precept and Dispensation*. See Jerome, in his letter to Paula on the death of Blaesilla, where he says that she had washed herself in “a second baptism, in a certain manner, of her resolve”—thus he calls monastic profession.]

Let us therefore strive, most beloved, to keep ourselves unstained from this world, knowing that “pure and unstained religion before God” is this (James 1:27). Let us beware of our own will as of a most evil and wicked viper, which alone can henceforth condemn our souls.

## SERMON XII. On beginnings, middles, and ends, upon Ecclesiasticus 7:40, “Remember your last things,” etc.

[Col. 0571A]

1. “My son, remember your last things, and you will never sin.” Recall your beginnings, attend to the middle, remember your last things. The first induce shame, the second bring sorrow, the last strike fear. Consider whence you came, and blush; where you are, and groan; where you are going, and tremble. Take care not to add the further ignorance of yourself, lest perhaps that terrible threat come upon you which the Bridegroom thunders forth, saying: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out and follow after the flocks of your companions” (Song 1:7).

For at first, when you were in honour, O man, you did not understand; hence you were compared to senseless beasts and made like them (Ps. 48:13, 21). And if affliction does not give understanding to hearing, you too will go after the flocks, exposed to every evil while they feel nothing evil. Know therefore your beginnings, and blush that you have been compared to beasts; remember your last things, and fear lest you go even after the beasts.

[Col. 0571B]

Blush, I say, because instead of fellowship with angels you have received fellowship with cattle, not only in the needs of the body but also in the affections of the heart. You share the food of the earth with beasts, because you have despised the bread of angels, heavenly bread. And not only this: what is worse, in an upright body the soul is bent low. In the body there remains the likeness of the human soul; but in the soul the likeness of God has been changed into a beastly likeness.

2. Are you not ashamed to have your head raised upward while you have not your heart raised upward? To stand upright in body while in heart you crawl upon the earth? Is it not to crawl upon the earth to savour the flesh, desire carnal things, and seek carnal things? Yet because you were created in the image and likeness of God, if you have lost the likeness, you have become like the beasts; but you have passed on in the image. Therefore, if placed on high you did not understand that you were mud, do not, fixed in the mud of the deep, fail to know that you are the image of God; and blush that you have placed upon it an alien likeness.

[Col. 0571C]

Remember your nobility, and be ashamed of so great a debasement. Do not be ignorant of your beauty, so that you may be more ashamed of your ugliness. This is, according to Solomon, “shame bringing glory” (Ecclus. 4:25): when you are ashamed that you have fallen from so great a glory. For once you were crowned with glory and honour, set over the works of the Lord’s hands, an inhabitant of paradise, a fellow citizen of angels, and a member of the household of the Lord Sabaoth. From this state you cast yourself down into these inner darknesses; from them you will one day be cast out also into outer and palpable darkness, unless you take care. From that glory of the children of God, I say, you have cast yourself down; from that blessed and sweetest homeland, from the garden of delight, you have made yourself an exile.

3. Behold whence you came. Do you wish to know whither you have come? Certainly, into a place of affliction, for your life has drawn near to hell. For what is here except toil and sorrow and affliction of spirit?

[Col. 0572A]

But now it has happened to you as if a child were born and raised in prison, and, because he has never seen the light, wondered at his mother’s sadness and anguish. For she knows why she grieves; and because she knows good things, evils are more grievous to her, and by the remembrance of peace her bitterness is most bitter. To you great goods seem lesser evils; and, because you are accustomed to heavier fetters, you count lesser chains as rest. You desire to eat because hunger torments you. Both are toil; but because hunger is the greater hardship, you do not know that eating is toil. Finally, once hunger has been driven away, see whether you do not find eating more burdensome than hunger.

So all things under the sun are ordered: nothing in them is truly pleasant, but a person always wishes to pass from one thing to another, and is relieved somehow only by change, as though leaping from water into fire and then springing back from fire into water, since one can bear neither. For every remedy for toil is the beginning of another toil. No wicked person in this world can possess what he wishes, since neither is the righteous person satisfied with righteousness, nor the pleasure-seeker with pleasure, nor the curious person with curiosity, nor the ambitious person with empty glory.

[Col. 0572B]

Here is what should cause you sorrow, if you have not yet become insensible: here is what should cause you sorrow—that you are placed in exile, dwell in a desert, walk in darkness and on slippery ground, and eat your bread in the sweat of your face. Does not your eye dwell in bitterness whenever it considers these things and lament together with the Prophet: “Alas for me, that my sojourn has been prolonged!” (Ps. 119:5).

4. You now have your beginnings and also your middle; but what are your last things? For it is said of them that, if you remember them, you will not sin. They are death, judgment, and hell. What is more dreadful than death? What more terrible than judgment? For nothing more intolerable than hell can be imagined.

[Col. 0572C]

What will anyone fear if such things do not make him tremble, shudder, and quake with fear? O man, if you have lost shame, which belongs to a noble creature; if you have not felt the sorrow of affliction, which belongs even to carnal people; at least do not abandon fear, for that is found even in beasts. We load an ass and weary it with many labours, and it does not care, because it is an ass. But if you wish to drive it into fire or cast it into a pit, it guards itself as much as it can, because it loves life and fears death.

Does it not therefore seem just to you that whoever is now more insensible than beasts should be compelled to go even after the beasts and, placed amid torments, occupy a lower place? Fear, therefore, O man, that in death you will be separated from all the goods of this body, and that the sweet bond of flesh and soul must be cut by a most bitter divorce.

[Col. 0572D]

Fear that at the terrible judgment you must be presented to him into whose hands it is dreadful to fall; and that, when he examines you, from whom nothing is hidden, if iniquity be found in you, you will be excluded from all peace and glory and separated from the number of the blessed. Fear that in hell you will be exposed to eternal and immeasurable torments, in the lot of the devil and his angels, in the eternal fire prepared for them.

Therefore this fear is called the beginning of wisdom (Ps. 110:10), not shame or sorrow, because neither begins wisdom in this way, nor has either such power. Hence it is not said, “Remember your beginnings,” or “your middle,” but “your last things, and you will not sin.” For the spirit of fear is stronger and more forceful in resisting sin than shame or sorrow; because shame takes consolation from the crowd, and sorrow from whatever consolation this world may offer, but fear finds no source of consolation. In death you will carry with you neither much nor little from the goods of this world; in judgment it will be impossible either to deceive or to resist; in hell there is no consolation whatsoever, but perpetual woe, howling, weeping, and gnashing of teeth.

## SERMON XIII. On the threefold mercy and the four acts of compassion.

[Col. 0573B]

1. As there are small sins, middling sins, and great sins, so too there is small, middling, and great mercy. A great sinner therefore needs great mercy, so that where transgression has abounded, grace may abound still more. By small mercy I mean forbearance, by which God does not immediately punish the sinner, but waits for repentance. It is called small not in itself, but in comparison with the others. Otherwise, the Lord’s forbearance is plainly great, altogether great mercy. For he did not wait at all for the angel who sinned, but cast him down from heaven; nor did he delay in the case of man when he sinned, but immediately drove him from paradise. Now, however, he waits, overlooks, and endures for ten years, twenty, even unto old age and advanced years.

[Col. 0573C]

And if we consider how great and how numerous are the sins committed every day, shall we not count slight those sins which nevertheless immediately received a sentence of condemnation? It is no wonder, then, if the feet of the prophet himself were almost moved and his steps almost slipped, because he was envious of the wicked when he saw the peace of sinners; or if sinners themselves say: “How does God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?” (Ps. 72:2–3, 11).

But this is the grace and power of Christ’s cross. “As I live,” says the Lord, “I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live” (Ezek. 33:11). As it seems to me, this is the voice of Christ risen again, as though he said: “Whether the Jew wishes it or not, I live; I do not will the death of the sinner—I who chose to die for sinners. I will that my death may be fruitful and that through it redemption may be abundant.”

[Col. 0573D]

2. This mercy of the Lord, therefore, by which he delays to strike and stands ready to forgive, I have called small, not indeed in itself but in comparison with the others. If it stands alone, it is by no means sufficient for salvation; indeed, it increases the judgment of condemnation, so that it may be said: “You did these things, and I kept silence” (Ps. 49:21). Let us therefore hear the Apostle, thundering terribly in his accustomed manner: “Do you despise,” he says, “the riches of his goodness”—undoubtedly God’s—“and forbearance? Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance? But you, according to your hardness and impenitent heart, store up wrath for yourself in the day of wrath” (Rom. 2:4–5).

[Col. 0574A]

“You store up,” he says, treasures of wrath for yourself in place of the privileged treasures of mercy which you despise, and you empty out in yourself the mercy of God. But according to what? “According to your hardness,” he says, “and impenitent heart.” Who will break this hardness except him who by his passion split rocks? Who will give a repentant heart except him from whom comes every good gift?

3. This is the second mercy, altogether greater than the first: it prevents the first from being fruitless and becoming a judgment of death, by giving repentance, without which forbearance not only does not benefit, but harms greatly. This mercy can suffice in lesser sins, because in those from which we cannot altogether abstain while we bear the body of sin, daily repentance can suffice for salvation.

[Col. 0574B]

But in graver sins—sins unto death—there is need not only of repentance but also of continence. It is altogether difficult, and possible only to divine power, to shake from one’s neck a yoke of sin once assumed; for whoever commits sin is the slave of sin, and can be set free only by a strong hand.

4. This is the great mercy necessary for great sinners, of which it is said: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your compassions” (Ps. 50:1–2), etc. The four daughters of great mercy have been spoken of (*Sermon Three on the Sixth Sunday after Pentecost*): the infliction of bitterness, the removal of opportunity, the strength to resist, and the healing of affection.

[Col. 0574C]

For sometimes, upon one held bound by any sin, the Lord mercifully sends certain bitternesses which occupy the person’s mind and drive out the pernicious delight of sin. Sometimes he removes the opportunity and does not permit weakness to be tempted. Sometimes he grants strength to resist—which is greater—so that, feeling temptation, one acts courageously and does not consent. Sometimes he heals the affection—which is most perfect, and in which temptation is utterly uprooted [or: removed]—so that one not only does not consent to it, but does not even feel it.

## SERMON XIV. [Note: [Col. 0573] There is much variation in this sermon in the Cistercian manuscript; but, as in other cases, this matters little for the sense. It is cited in the *Flores*, book 7, chapter 46.] On the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit against the seven vices.

[Col. 0574D]

1. Wisdom conquers malice, while the power of God and Christ, the wisdom of God, crush Satan. Thus it reaches from end to end mightily: in heaven, casting down the proud one; in the world, overcoming the evil one; in hell, despoiling the greedy one. And it orders all things sweetly (Wis. 7:30; 8:1): in heaven, confirming the standing angels; in the world, redeeming those sold; in hell, freeing captives.

Or, if it seems better, let us take it in this way. The sevenfold Spirit advances in ordered battle-line against the seven degrees of sin. First, fear rises against negligence. It is fear by which the soul is shaken, the conscience examined, deadly sleep driven out, and watchfulness instilled. For “he who fears God neglects nothing” (Eccles. 7:19), but fears all his works.

[Col. 0575A]

2. Yet, in order that the conflict may be more severe, scale is joined to scale, and neglect of oneself and curiosity about others accompany one another in the human heart. For, as the Wise Man says, three evils drive a resident from his house: smoke, dripping water, and a bad wife (Prov. 27:15). But when are these lacking to the negligent person? Whoever neglects his own affairs does not drive away smoke, correct his wife, or repair his roof. Sins smoke, unextinguished by any zeal of mercy or any waters of tears; and that smoke is utterly foul and intolerable. The will grows malignant, becoming daily worse through this very neglect. The indignation of the heavenly Judge drips down because of the lack of charity, which alone covers a multitude of sins.

[Col. 0575B]

Therefore one must go outside and scrutinize exterior things more curiously, when one thus despises inward things, does not look back upon the past, does not examine the present, and does not look ahead to the future. Piety therefore plainly opposes curiosity: what curiosity calls away from the heart, piety calls back. For piety is the worship of God; and he is worshipped in the heart, where he is known to dwell.

Curiosity, however, produces experience of evil, so that one who wanders through many things easily stumbles, easily falls into a snare, and easily finds what gives pernicious delight. Against it contends the spirit of knowledge, teaching one to choose good and reject evil; teaching what is dangerous and what it is advantageous to experience.

[Col. 0575C] 3. Yet in many cases experience now seems to pass over into desire. You have these stages in Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, whom, when she went out to see the women of that foreign people, Hamor the son of Shechem is said to have seized, violated, and afterward, while she was sorrowing, to have won over by caresses, so that his soul clung to her soul (Gen. 34:1–8). I mean that a person has passed into desire and, as the Prophet recalls, into the inclination of the heart when he has despised the law (Ps. 72:7), cast aside honor, bid farewell to shame, wholly leapt over the fear of the Lord, and is carried along by appetite alone, follows desire alone, is drawn by pleasure alone, and has his will in place of reason.

Against this desire for evil, then, fortitude fights; for now there is no liberation except by a strong hand. A person imposes fasts upon himself, chastises his body, and reduces it to servitude, lest perhaps from the serpent’s root there should now come forth a basilisk—from desire, habit. How wretched beyond measure and pitiable is human frailty, which, without the itch of desire or the assault of longing, is drawn to unlawful things by habit itself: would that all might be permitted not to know it! Surely, whoever commits sin is the slave of sin (John 8:34), plainly the slave of the devil, following wherever he is drawn toward wicked things by him who holds him captive to do his will.

4. This habit, moreover, is a certain heavy and ruinous chain, easier indeed to loosen than to break. Here the common proverb seems especially applicable: skill is stronger than force. [Col. 0575D] As force is repelled by force, and the ardor of desires is extinguished by the fervor of the spirit, so you should outwit the craft of the evil one by craft, and oppose counsel to habit. Otherwise, if you perhaps seek violence and hope that bodily mortification will prevail over habit, there is every reason to fear that your labor will be ruinous and that the bodily substance itself will fail before ingrained desire does—especially since habit itself is, as it were, a second nature.

Counsel is therefore necessary, whether imparted by the Angel of Great Counsel himself, or by some spiritual person who is not ignorant of Satan’s devices or of spiritual remedies. The occasion must be withdrawn from us and the opportunity for sin avoided. We read, brothers, that in the desert a certain man, grievously assailed by the spirit of fornication, was cured by a father through a most praiseworthy stratagem. The elder secretly summoned another brother and ordered him to provoke that man with insults; he himself was first to complain as though he had received an injury from him. The man was distressed and deeply confused; in a short time he so forgot his former temptation that, when asked about it, he answered with great astonishment: “Father! One is not allowed to live, yet one feels like fornicating!” (See St. Jerome, *Letter to Rusticus*, about the middle.)

[Col. 0576A] 5. But perhaps the one for whom victory has been stored up has not yet arrived; the one whom triumph awaits, to whom a crown is due. Contempt arises from habit: sinning all the more freely because more hopelessly, he now lets loose all the reins of desire and hurls himself headlong with full force, as it is written: “When the sinner comes into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3).

This contempt, then, must be assailed by the spirit of understanding, which illumines the darkness of the heart and pours in the light of divine mercy and abundant compassion. For understanding must be attributed to divine and most exalted matters, which human reason cannot comprehend at all, and even faith itself can comprehend only with difficulty; as, for example: “Where transgression abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5:20).

[Col. 0576C] 6. If contempt persists, malice must necessarily follow, so that the wretched desperate person may admit whatever consolation he can; and, having no share in good things, may take delight even in evil things; may rejoice when he has done wrong and exult in the worst deeds. The one remedy for these things is that wisdom itself engage against malice and fight with its own right hand—a hand that has never known defeat. For when will one who has descended into Babylon [or, “habitation”] be delivered, unless he is anticipated by the blessings of heavenly sweetness, so that nail may drive out nail and the delight of spiritual anointing may exclude the pestilential sweetness of vices?

[Col. 0576D] 7. Therefore victorious wisdom reaches mightily from end to end, uprooting individual vices and implanting individual virtues. Negligence is shaken off, so that the spirit of fear may fill the mind; curiosity is cast away, so that piety may succeed it; experience of evil is driven out, and knowledge is put in its place. Thus fortitude also prevails over desire; counsel removes habit; vigorous understanding takes away contempt; and, when malice has wholly disappeared, wisdom reigns.

When wisdom thus triumphs, that wretched soul, which negligence had ruinously put to sleep, curiosity had roused still more disastrously, experience had drawn away, desire had held, habit had bound, contempt had thrust into prison, and malice had slain—fear raises it up, piety gently soothes it, knowledge, by showing what has been done, adds sorrow; fortitude restores what belongs to it, counsel loosens its bonds, understanding leads it out of prison, wisdom sets a table, refreshes the hungry one, and restores it with saving food.

## SERMON XV. On Seeking Wisdom

1. What are we doing in this world, brothers? Or what are we making of this world? If we strive to be saved from this present evil age, why do we still make plans concerning this world? If we wish to leave, why do we labor to drag our fetters with us? Grant that they are golden; yet it is far better to be freed without them than to be held because of them. Let us not assess their price, but consider the impediment: lest, in addition to the necessity of our condition—which must itself be considered sufficiently hard—we begin also to cling to them in the glue of covetousness and become entangled in the bonds of vain anxiety.

[Col. 0577B] What someone might do in fetters may perhaps be judged an unsuitable question, since people are customarily fettered more for suffering than for doing anything: fetters hinder action and support suffering. Nevertheless, we have something to do in this world—namely, repentance; yet this seems to concern suffering more than action.
