Still, we have something to do here: not something derived from this world, but something done in this world. For since Adam is read to have been placed from the beginning in the place of delight in order to work (Gen. 2:15), what sensible person would suppose that his children were placed in a place of affliction for idleness?

Let us therefore work, but for food that does not perish; let us work at the work of our salvation. Let us work in the Lord’s vineyard, so that we may deserve to receive the day’s denarius. Let us work in wisdom, which says: “Those who work in me shall not sin” (Ecclus. 24:30). “The field is the world,” says Truth (Matt. 13:38). Let us dig in it; a hidden treasure lies there—let us dig it up. For this is wisdom, which is drawn from hidden places. We all seek it; we all desire it.

[Col. 0577D] 2. But he seeks in vain who seeks upon his bed, for it is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly. Is that your bed, and there you seek the giant? Is it yours, and there you hope to find him who always disregards lodging places? “If you seek,” he says, “seek; turn yourselves, and come” (Isa. 21:12). Do you ask, “From where?” From your bed. Do you ask, “From what should you turn?” “Turn away,” he says, “from your own desires” (Ecclus. 18:30).

“But if I do not find wisdom in my desires,” you ask, “where shall I find it?” For my soul desires it intensely; and, should I happen to find it, merely to have found it will not suffice unless I put into my bosom “a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over.” Rightly so: “Blessed is the person who finds wisdom, and who abounds in prudence” (Prov. 3:13). Seek it, then, while it may be found; and while it is near, call upon it. Do you wish to hear how near it is? “The word is near you, in your heart and in your mouth” (Rom. 10:8)—provided only that you seek it with an upright heart. Raise your heart; rise from your bed, lest you hear in vain the admonition to hold your heart on high. Thus you will find wisdom in your heart and abound in prudence with your mouth; but take care to abound, not to pour it out or vomit it forth.

[Col. 0578A] 3. Surely, if you have found wisdom, you have found honey; only do not eat much of it, lest, when satiated, you vomit it. Eat in such a way that you are always hungry. For Wisdom herself says: “Those who eat me shall still hunger” (Ecclus. 24:29). Do not think much of what you possess; do not become satiated, lest you vomit it and even what you seem to have be taken from you, since you have ceased seeking before the time. For while it may be found, while it is near, one must not cease from seeking or calling upon it.

In another sense also, just as one who eats much honey, as Solomon himself says, does not fare well, so “one who searches into majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25:27). Why, Pilate, do you ask the Lord privately, as though he might whisper in your ear what truth is? It is too much for you: the holy thing will not be given to a dog, nor the pearl to a pig. Seek rather the taste of faith; do not yet seek the satiety of understanding. Rightly, brothers, did he immediately recoil with blunted vision and, unable to wait for an answer, go out to the Jews—he who had begun to walk among things great and wonderful beyond himself, asking what truth was (John 18:38).

[Col. 0578C] 4. Therefore let us seek wisdom in the heart, and wisdom that comes from faith, as the Apostle says: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly” (Rom. 12:3). Sober wisdom consists in repentance for past sins, contempt for present advantages, and desire for future rewards. You have indeed found wisdom if you mourn the sins of your former life, count lightly the desirable things of this age, and desire eternal blessedness with your whole longing. You have found wisdom if each of these things tastes to you as it truly is: if you judge and distinguish them with a certain inward savor of the soul—these as bitter and wholly to be fled, those likewise as fleeting and transitory and therefore to be despised, but the latter as perfect goods to be sought with every desire.

This is sober wisdom, and it does not know vomiting. There the chill of fear, arising from remembrance of sins, and the fervor of love, arising from desire for the divine promises, remove the lukewarmness produced by the very evil occupations that now exist—so that you neither vomit wisdom nor are vomited forth by it. For as blessed is the person who finds wisdom, so also blessed, or even more blessed, is the person who will remain in wisdom (Ecclus. 14:22); perhaps this belongs to abundance.

[Col. 0578D] 5. In these three ways you abound in wisdom or prudence with your mouth: if your mouth contains confession of your own wrongdoing, thanksgiving and the voice of praise, and also speech for edification. For “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). At the beginning of his speech the righteous person is his own accuser (Prov. 18:17); in the middle he ought to magnify the Lord; and thirdly—if wisdom so abounds—he ought to edify his neighbor.

But must one also abound in wisdom in one’s deeds? Most certainly. Let us therefore seek a threefold abundance in deed as well; for long ago a certain Wise Man said that wisdom was described threefold (Prov. 22:20). So, unless you have a better view, I think that, in respect of action, whoever among you lives continently, patiently, and obediently abounds quite copiously in wisdom—provided only that faithful obedience mortifies one’s own will; humble continence cuts off both carnal and worldly pleasure; and cheerful patience manfully endures both bodily and worldly adversity together.

## SERMON XVI. On the Threefold Kind of Goods, and Vigilance over Thoughts

[Col. 0579B]

1. More earnest zeal and more vigilant care [Note: [Col. 0579D] In like manner Nicholas of Clairvaux began a sermon on the feast of Saint Andrew, at which this same sermon was delivered, as may be gathered from section 6, with the words: “Then both study and attentive silence,” etc.; he began the sermon [Col. 0580D].] ought to be given to our thoughts, my brothers—ours, I say, to whom matter for such holy meditations is constantly supplied. For night and day prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic utterances are sung and read to us, utterances that threaten the punishment of hell and promise the glory of the kingdom.

Whence, then, do thoughts so vain, so harmful, so shameful arise in us—thoughts which now impurity and self-exaltation, now pride and ambition and other passions, toss about so that we can scarcely ever breathe freely into the serenity of holy thoughts? Woe to us because of the sluggishness and lukewarmness of our hearts! We allow ourselves to be occupied by these vanities instead of passing at once to the good things of the Lord: whether natural, spiritual, or eternal. Natural goods are indeed great, spiritual goods greater, but eternal goods are greatest. In the first we are restored; in the second we are exercised; in the third we are stretched forth and made blessed.

[Col. 0579C] If you cannot fix the eye of meditation upon that height of eternal goods, because they are remote and surpass every understanding, turn your sight toward the goods of grace, which lie in the exercise of virtues. See how pure the conscience and how free the countenance are in living and conducting oneself in chastity and love, patience and humility, and the other virtues which make one pleasing to God, propitious, and worthy of imitation by human beings. But if these too are too exalted and exceed your weakness, lower your eyes to the goods of nature, which ought to be as familiar to you as you are familiar to yourself.

We do not call them goods of nature as though they were not also gifts of grace; rather, because they were in some manner inborn in and implanted within nature itself before that sin was committed which infected not only the person but nature as well. Since then they are shown not to come so readily to hand because of the wound inflicted, although we often perceive them to be in us and around us both by reason and by affection. And because we consist of soul and body, let us begin, according to the Apostle’s saying, from the animate part—that is, from the goods of the body—“so that what is spiritual is not first, but what is animate” (1 Cor. 15:46).

[Col. 0580A] 2. All the goods of the body—and all that we owe to it alone—are health. Nothing further should be given to or sought for it; it must be bound and restrained by this limit, since it bears no fruit and death is its end. But here is a pitfall which I do not want you to overlook. Pleasure lies in ambush against health and pursues it with such subtle malice that scarcely anyone can either avoid it or recognize it. If pleasure rather than health is served, this is no longer according to nature but beneath nature; it gives its hand to death when it appoints pleasure as mistress.

Hence many have descended—or, more truly, fallen—to such beastly and rebellious impulses that they prefer pleasure to health, most often wallowing in the very things which they know will be followed by difficult and most acute sufferings. As health is the nature of the body, so purity is the nature of the heart; for God will not be seen with a troubled eye, and the human heart was made in order to see its Creator. But if careful guardianship must be provided for bodily health, still more careful diligence must be devoted to purity of heart, insofar as this part is shown to be more worthy than the other.

Here, however, we understand purity simply: that is, that whatever we do, we confess it purely and humbly to the Lord in prayer and to a human being in confession, saying: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31:5).

[Col. 0580C] 3. Since we are social creatures, let us pass from the things that are within us to those around us, so that, if possible, as far as it depends on us, we may have peace with all people. For this is the law of natural fellowship: that we should not do to others whatever we do not wish done to ourselves, and that we should endeavor to render to others what we wish rendered to ourselves. Therefore, as we owe health to the body and purity to the heart, so we owe peace to a brother.

From here we must pass to the souls of the saints, who have flown from the prison of this mortality to the joys of heaven. To them we certainly owe imitation, because they were like us, capable of suffering, and made known to us the paths of life, which they held as tirelessly as they held them unceasingly. But to those who departed without such great sanctity or completed penance, we owe compassion and prayer because of our fellowship in the same nature: that the merciful Father may remove their dross, turn their scourges into benefits, and so at last restore them to the joys of the blessed city.

[Col. 0580D] For if bulls, upon finding a dead bull, weep, bellow, and accompany their brother’s funeral with certain services seemingly owed by humanity, what does one human being owe another, when both reason instructs and affection draws? As, then, we owe imitation to holy souls, so we owe compassion to those less holy, drawing an example from the former and a groan from the latter.

4. From the holy angels we must seek help by hidden sighs and frequent tears, that they may offer our prayers to that surpassing Majesty and bring grace back to us; for they are ministering spirits, sent for our sake, that we may receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb. 1:14). From the Lord of all things, however, we must seek mercy: that he whose nature is goodness, whose proper work is always to have mercy and spare, may not look upon the multitude of our iniquities, but may have mercy upon us according to the multitude of his mercies.

[Col. 0581A] To him we owe both love and submission with all reverence and humility: love, because he made us and has done us good; submission, because he is above us and commands us [or, “excels us”], terrible in counsel above the children of men. Thus we owe health to the body, purity to the heart, peace to a brother, imitation to the saints, and compassion to the dead; from an angel we must seek help, and from God mercy [other witnesses: “let us ask from God”; “from the treasury/chest,” etc.]. From the treasury of natural goods we ought to possess and seek these things, so that we may know that, when we have done the things commanded and granted to nature, we are unprofitable servants: “we have done what we ought to have done.”

For scarcely, if ever, is any command given to human beings that surpasses the limits and capacity of nature. In these goods, as we said before, we are restored and, as it were, returned to our former state when we return to the inborn sweetness of nature and render the due order of things both to ourselves, to those around us, and to those above us. And this is enough concerning natural goods.

[Col. 0581C] 5. The spiritual goods in which we are exercised in order to tend toward eternal goods are these same things, but different because regarded with a different intention—along with many others which would take too long to enumerate. The former are known to be according to nature; the latter, above nature. For in spiritual exercise we owe not health to the body, but servitude, affliction, and labor, according to the saying of that spiritual and supremely spiritual man: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude” (1 Cor. 9:27).

Nor do we owe the heart merely this purity—namely, that we confess our sins purely and humbly—but that in intention, thought, and deed we show such carefulness that our life may be fruitful and our reputation glorious: fruitful not for itself but for God; glorious not for itself but for its Father who is in heaven. Nor do we say merely that peace must be shown to brothers on this path; rather, one must be peaceable with those who hate peace, bear everyone, and wish to be borne by no one.

[Col. 0581D] We also profess that not only compassion and prayer, but even rejoicing in hope, should be directed toward the dead; because, although we ought to grieve that they suffer in purgatorial places, we ought much more to rejoice that the time is near when God will wipe every tear from their eyes and there will be no more mourning or crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away.

To the holy souls we ought no longer merely to give imitation, nor merely to seek help from the holy angels; rather, we should ardently desire their sight, to be with them, and to see what those pillars of heaven are which sustain the orb of the earth, in whom so great and surpassing an emblem of divinity shines and gleams. From the Lord, moreover, we must seek not mercy alone, but direct all our affection toward him, so that we may love ourselves for his sake and contemplate that Majesty which makes all things, sustains all things, and into which rational creatures desire to look.

[Col. 0582A] 6. These are the paths of spiritual exercise in which the religious mind is both expanded and delighted. Forgetting the things behind and stretching itself toward what lies before—that is, eternal goods—it follows toward the prize of the heavenly calling. Did not the blessed Apostle Andrew, whose feast is at hand, pass beyond nature when he said: “O good cross, long desired and now prepared for the longing soul! I come to you secure and rejoicing”? This is the voice of a transformed person, one who had risen from the goods of nature to the goods of grace: so that he not only gloried in hope but also in tribulations, and went rejoicing from the presence of the council because he had been accounted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus. He hastened toward torments not merely patiently but willingly, indeed ardently—as toward ornaments; toward punishments as toward delights.

[Col. 0582B] 7. But those eternal goods are goods which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which never depart from that country which knows nothing but joy and jubilation. There nothing is lacking: behold abundance sufficient to fill human desire. What is this plenty, where nothing that you do not want exists, and everything that you want exists? “Let peace be in your strength,” says the Prophet to Jerusalem, “and abundance in your towers” (Ps. 121:7). In those towers, I say, which, according to another prophet, will be built with gems, where God will satisfy us with the fat of wheat, not with the husk of sacrament.

But if nothing were lacking to us and something nevertheless remained hidden from us, would glory be complete? Therefore nothing will be hidden from us; and behold wisdom, by which human curiosity will be satisfied. O wisdom, by which we shall then know most perfectly all things in heaven and on earth, drinking in the very fountain of wisdom the knowledge of all things! I shall not fear suspicions; I shall not fear schemes, because that city, according to John, will be like the purest glass (Rev. 21:19), so that, as we see most clearly through glass, we shall likewise see others’ consciences with the greatest clarity.

[Col. 0582D] But what if nothing is lacking and nothing is hidden, yet fear and anxiety lest these things be lost remain? Therefore nothing terrifies us; and behold power, by which human weakness is strengthened. “He has made your borders peace,” he says, “and strengthened the bars of your gates” (Ps. 147:14, 13), so that no enemy may enter and no friend may be able to leave. Where, then, there is supreme abundance, supreme wisdom, and supreme power, I think nothing is lacking to the fullness of blessedness insofar as concerns the height of human happiness.

These are the goods of nature, grace, and glory: the goods of humanity, the goods of virtue, the goods of eternity. Let us think upon these, let us ruminate upon these, brothers, and, according to the precept of the law, bring rumination back to mind (Lev. 11:3), because in this way one lives, and in such things is the life of our spirit. For holy thought will preserve us, so that we may say with the saint: “May the meditation of my heart be always in your sight, O Lord, my helper and my redeemer” (Ps. 18:15).

## SERMON XVII. On the Threefold Guarding of Hand, Tongue, and Heart

[Col. 0583A]

1. We all complain that grace is lacking to us; but perhaps grace itself more justly complains that some persons are lacking to it. For this grace of devotion which we seek is a thing of the heart, and the person who neglects to provide it with an inward lodging deprives himself of this gift. Besides, how can one care for the heart when he has not yet subjected even the watchfulness of the mouth or the guarding of the hand? Let no one who has not grasped the beginning wonder that perfection is lacking to him; nor even one who seems already to hold the beginning, if he has not reached the middle.

[Col. 0583B] For a worldly person it is a great thing to have clean hands; for a monk it is not a great thing, but it is plainly proved to be a great evil for him not even to avoid their defilements. Indeed, even concerning the hands themselves, far greater cleanness and more abundant righteousness are required of us than of them. To them it is said: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6:18); and: “Let the one who stole steal no more” (Eph. 4:28), and other such things—those who do them will not inherit the kingdom of God. Must we also fear such defilements of works and so grave a pollution of hands?

Yet the cleaner the hands, the more seriously even a smaller blemish on them offends. Just as any tiny stain more disgracefully discolors a precious garment, so for us any least disobedience is sufficient for uncleanness; it is no longer a blemish but a grave stain if negligence even concerning lesser commands remains in our actions. This diligence in keeping our works exercises the beginnings of our manner of life, while as yet only a little—but still some—light is in us. Unless perhaps those to whom Truth says, “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say, ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done’” (Luke 17:10), consider that they have a great light.

“But,” you say, “he instructed us to say this for humility’s sake.” Certainly, for humility’s sake—but is it contrary to truth? Moreover, if we are found still rather negligent even in guarding our deeds, no wise person should urge someone to strain out a gnat who, if only he might not swallow even a camel.

[Col. 0583D] 2. But even if the hands have already been cleansed, one does not immediately proceed to the heart. Rather, after the first diligence, a middle degree of care must be given to cleansing the lips. If you say, “Rare is the person who seems to set his words in order for judgment,” even from this you will learn how rare perfection is, when you find that not even progress is common to all.

Who could count the many defilements contracted by the small member of the tongue, the manifold uncleanness that thickens on uncircumcised lips, the great destruction caused by an unguarded mouth? There is a loose tongue in idle speech; there is an indecent tongue; there is also a boastful tongue. The first serves wantonness; the next, arrogance. There is also a deceitful tongue, and likewise a slanderous tongue. The former is divided into the lying and the flattering; the latter now inflicts insults to one’s face, now speaks ill in secret.

[Col. 0584A] If people must render an account to God on the day of judgment for every idle word they have spoken (Matt. 12:36), how much more strictly will they be judged for a lying, biting, or insulting word; for a haughty or wanton word; for a flattering or slanderous one?

3. How true is the saying, brothers: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. 10:19). For, to pass over other things, if a word is idle because it has no reasonable cause, what account can we render for what is beyond reason? None of you, brothers, should value lightly the time spent on idle words, for it is an acceptable time and a day of salvation. An irrevocable word flies away; irrecoverable time flies away; and the fool does not notice what he loses.

“They say, ‘We like to converse until the hour has passed.’” [Note: [Col. 0583D] From this some infer that the Cistercians were at one time granted an hour for conversation, as below in section 5: “After long conversations.” The holy man thus censures, above, conversations, jokes, and buffooneries, and elsewhere even slanders. Yet among them the observance of silence was strict, according to Sermon 3 on Advent, section 5, and other passages.] O, until the hour has passed! O, until the time has gone by! Until the hour passes—the hour which the Creator’s mercy has granted you for doing penance, obtaining pardon, acquiring grace, and meriting glory! Until the time passes in which you ought to have made divine mercy favorable toward you, hastened toward the society of angels, sighed for your lost inheritance, aspired to promised happiness, aroused your slackened will, and wept for the wrongdoing you have committed!

[Col. 0584C] Do farmers act thus when the long-awaited opportunity for sowing has come? Do vintners, when the hoped-for season of pruning has arrived, rejoice that they have found occupations and spent the day, as it were irreproachably, without work? Do merchants, when markets are imminent, customarily spin out delays and seek opportunities lest some profit might happen to come to them from those markets? Finally, do poor beggars, when the distributor of alms, summoned with loud cries, has at last appeared, seek byways, try to occupy empty retreats away from their companions who run together, and cherish hiding places in the corners of streets?

4. Would that only the time of life were lost in words! But many are proved to lose life in them as well—not only to lose it themselves, but to take it away from their brothers. Do not slanderers, hateful to God and hateful to life, lose life? Life flees those whom it hates, and those from whom life flees must die. Does not the person himself die who drinks the poison administered to him by the honeyed tongue of a slanderer? For the life of love is secretly taken away from him, and, while he does not know it, brotherly love gradually grows cold within him.

[Col. 0584D] Perhaps the person slandered will hear it too. Words fly everywhere; and when a report has first passed through many mouths, it can scarcely happen that it will not reach each person’s tongue and, as though now grown strong, be carried back to the one whose offense is involved. Accordingly, when he hears it he will be scandalized and waste away; and love will be extinguished in him all the more easily because it had seemed to be living more fully before. “If my enemy had cursed me,” he says, “I would surely have endured it” (Ps. 54:13).

A prudent listener guards himself; and the person who knows that he has been slandered guards himself too, if he is not foolish—the former lest he be infected by poison, the latter lest he be disturbed by scandal. Yet, as far as it lies within it, the slanderous tongue, striking the former’s conscience and wounding the latter’s love, kills them both together with itself. Is not this tongue a viper? Indeed, a most ferocious one: it infects three persons so lethally with a single breath. Is not this tongue a spear? Certainly, a most sharp one, which pierces three persons with one blow. “Their tongue,” he says, “is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5). The tongue of the slanderer is surely a two-edged—indeed, a three-edged—sword.

[Col. 0585B] 5. Do not hesitate to call such a tongue crueller even than the point by which the Lord’s side was pierced. For it too pierces Christ’s body, member from member; and it pierces not now a lifeless body, but makes it lifeless by piercing it. It is also more harmful than the thorns which military fury placed upon that most exalted head, or than the iron nails which the consummated iniquity of the Jewish people drove into those most holy hands and feet. For unless he had preferred the life of this body, now pricked and pierced, to the life of his own body, he would never have handed over that body to the injury of death and the shame of the cross for this body.

And we say, “Speech is a light thing; the tongue of a human being is tender, soft, and little flesh—what wise person would value it highly?” Speech is indeed a light thing because it flies lightly, but it wounds heavily. It passes lightly, but burns heavily; it lightly penetrates the mind, but does not lightly depart; it is uttered lightly, but not lightly recalled. It flies easily and therefore easily violates love. A dead fly is a worthless thing, yet it ruins fragrant oil (Eccl. 10:1).

[Col. 0585C] The tongue is a tender member, yet can scarcely be held; in substance it is weak and small, but in use it is found great and strong. It is a small member; but unless you are careful, it is a great evil. It is thin and broad, a most suitable instrument for emptying hearts, as I think many consciences among you bear witness for me—unless perhaps we are all so perfect that after long conversations our mind has never been found somehow empty, meditation less devout, affection drier, and the sacrifice of prayer less rich because of words, whether the words we ourselves have spoken or those we have heard—yet words all the same.

6. For the tongue slips easily, and no less easily slips into the heart; so that in conversation many have profited less from restraining their own tongue because they did not guard against another’s. The brother speaking to you is useful, wise, devout, and God-fearing; I say more: he is an angel, an angel of light—yet even so, beware lest you hear something by which you are harmed. I would not have you suspect the person, but the tongue, especially in ordinary conversation. The dove’s simplicity is indeed good; [Col. 0586A] but in this respect do not omit the serpent’s prudence as well. Mary did not pass even an angelic word without examination, but considered what manner of greeting this might be (Luke 1:29). You too, who have at least through repeated experience carefully noticed how much harm words do, will not be foolish if—since participation in conversation is necessary—you take care not only over the mouth, but likewise apply caution to the ear. Do not wonder that we linger rather long over this grade of those making progress: for we believe that among us there are more who are progressing than who are perfect.

7. Perhaps, however, we may seem excessive in censuring words. But remember that it is the tongue which speaks against the vices of the tongue; and it should especially be considered excused in this, that it spares not even itself and fortifies its hearers against its own dangers as well. Speech is wind, but it is not always a scorching wind. “Arise, north wind,” he says, “and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4:16). Yet speech also has great usefulness, and a most precious fruit is often found in the tongue. For the righteous person lives by faith, faith comes by hearing, and hearing through the word of God. How indeed shall anyone live unless he believes? How shall he believe unless he hears? How shall he hear unless it is proclaimed to him? Certainly, therefore, it is fitting to bestow upon it greater diligence and more diligent guardianship, because, according to Scripture, death and life are in the power of the tongue (Prov. 18:21). Otherwise, if life alone resided in it, it would not even require circumcision; if death alone, it would require cutting off. [Col. 0586C] But now a guard must be set upon our mouth [variant: is added, “for us”], and a door of restraint upon our lips, so that eternal closure may not condemn life-giving edification, nor deadly ruin obtain free passage outward. Therefore, brothers, let us watch over our deeds, lest we either omit what is commanded or commit what is forbidden. The Prophet urges us to this twofold watchfulness when he says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27 [37:27]). Let us likewise watch over our words, lest through them we happen either to offend God or to harm our neighbour. Happy indeed is the person whom, in every conversation, that double fear keeps alert and reflection upon two hearers spurs on: first, the divine majesty, into whose hands it is utterly dreadful to fall; then, the brother’s weakness, to which it is nonetheless exceedingly easy to give offence.

8. Yet I think that even the person who guards against giving offence in speech should not yet be called perfect—unless perhaps in comparison with the former person, who watched only over deeds. For Truth himself, speaking in the Gospel about servants who keep watch and await the Lord’s coming, says: “If he comes in the third watch and finds them so, blessed are those servants” (Luke 12:38). You will find this said neither of the first nor even of the second watch. This is the watch over the heart, to which the Wise Man urges that every guard now be applied, because life proceeds from it (Prov. 4:23). Yet I judge that this watch consists especially of two things: namely, that the vigilant and concerned mind carefully attend equally to the flocks of its [Col. 0587A] affections and its thoughts. And rightly is every guard given to that from which the other two are known to proceed—unless, heaven forbid, they are carried out for the sake of display and have an appearance of godliness but not its power. For just as a gushing spring, unless it first fills the adjoining ditches, cannot flow back, settle, or rise on high, because it is otherwise occupied; so the human mind, until it diligently fulfils the aforementioned guards of hand and tongue, can neither turn itself to this perfect care of itself, nor enjoy the pleasant tranquillity of devotion, nor advance to the lofty degree of divine contemplation. Come then, brothers: if we seek the grace of heavenly visitation, let us seek it thus; if we desire to receive spiritual consolations, let us ask thus; if we wish heaven to be opened to us, let us knock thus. Finally, let us keep watch in this threefold manner if we wish to enter the wedding feast with the Bridegroom, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. On spiritual joy, or on the Apostle’s words: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink,” etc. (Rom. 14:17)

1. Why do we pass beyond the way, we who hasten toward joy? There is indeed joy in [variant: concerning] the kingdom of God, but it is not the first [variant: reward]. There is joy concerning the kingdom of God, but it is not carnal joy, not worldly joy, not joy whose end is seized by mourning, but rather joy into which sorrow is transformed; nor, finally, the joy of those who rejoice when they have done evil, [Col. 0587C] nor exultation in wicked things, but joy in the Holy Spirit. But from where does this joy meanwhile arise, except from righteousness and peace? Let these, therefore, come forth like cells of honey, so that a more solid substance may easily contain the still-fluid liquor of sweetness. The time will come when we shall enjoy simple honey itself, and our joy will be full and pure, so that we may rejoice not only in the Spirit but also concerning the Spirit himself. The time will come when joy will in every respect be spiritual: no bodily occasions will then arouse it—not works of mercy, not tears of repentance, not the exercise of righteousness, not the testing of patience—but rather the very presence of the Spirit, into whom even the angels desire to look. [Col. 0587D] Meanwhile, wisdom seasons everything else for me as though it were salt, as though it too were not food. Meanwhile, before I eat, I sigh; and even then I am not permitted to swallow my own saliva. For a person is wise when all things taste to him as they are. But one to whom wisdom itself already tastes, in itself and as it is, is not merely wise but blessed. For this is to see God as he is; and this is that river’s rush which gladdens the city of God, this the torrent of delight, this finally the abundance which intoxicates.

2. But now, Lord, “they have no wine”: for in this present wedding feast there is a lack of wine—namely, the wine of carnal allure and worldly desire. “Their wine,” he says, “is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32:33). May this wine always fail us, my brothers, because it is not good wine. Good wine is drawn not from the vineyard of impurity but from the jar of purification. Good wine is not made from the grape of Gomorrah but from the water of Judaea. “You have kept the good wine until now,” he says (John 2:3, 10). The best wine, indeed, is preserved even until now: it is not to be made from water, but rather to be pressed from that great cluster of the promised land, which meanwhile is carried on a pole, while we know Christ according to the flesh—and him crucified. Did not that man lack wine who said, “My soul refused to be comforted”? Yet he seemed to have tasted wine made from water when he added: “I remembered God and was delighted” (Ps. 76:3–4 [77:3–4]). What will he do in the presence of God, who delights in remembrance alone? Thus the apostles too plainly tasted wine made from water when they went away rejoicing from the council’s presence because they had been considered worthy to suffer insult for Jesus’ name (Acts 5:41). How is joy in insult not wine from water? Clearly the promise of Truth made to them was already being fulfilled: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16:20); that is, your water shall be turned into wine. Do you marvel that water is changed into wine? It also becomes bread—unless perhaps you have forgotten to eat your bread, of which you read: “You will feed us with the bread of tears and give us tears to drink in measure” (Ps. 79:6 [80:5]). Finally, hear the measure: “There were,” he says, “six stone jars set there, according to the purification of the Jews” (John 2:6). If you are a true Jew—not in flesh but in spirit—you shall serve six years and go out free in the seventh; you shall be purified in six jars, labour six days, be delivered in six tribulations, and in the seventh evil shall not touch you. [Col. 0588C] Moreover, you shall not only be delivered in them but shall also drink wine from them, when, according to the Apostle, you begin to glory not only in hope but also in tribulations (Rom. 5:2–3).

3. This, then, is the present twofold joy which you have in the Holy Spirit: from remembrance of future good things and from endurance of present evils. For nothing carnal, worldly, or vain tastes in these; rather, they are the Spirit of truth and heavenly wisdom, whose sweetness is tasted beforehand in each. “Rejoice in the Lord always,” says the Apostle; “again I say, rejoice.” And, following the subject of this double [Col. 0588D] joy, he added: “Let your gentleness be known to all people; the Lord is near” (Phil. 4:4–5). What is our gentleness but meekness and patience? Let us then rejoice in what we await, because the Lord is near. Again, let us rejoice in what we endure, so that our gentleness may be known to all. For tribulation produces patience, patience testing, testing hope, and hope does not disappoint (Rom. 5:4–5).

4. Indeed, for the mind to become fit to receive this twofold spiritual gladness, two things for practising righteousness and likewise two for preserving peace must necessarily be set beforehand; Holy Scripture commends both of them to us quite abundantly. For the practice of righteousness seems wholly to rest upon these two commandments: that no one do to another what he does not wish done to himself, as is contained in the letter of the apostles sent to the Gentiles (Acts 15:23); and, as the Lord says to those same apostles: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7:12). But since we all offend in many matters, it is impossible in this place and time of offences—for the angels have not yet come to remove every offence from God’s kingdom, nor are we in that blessed city whose boundaries God has made peace—it is therefore impossible here and now to preserve peace completely among ourselves unless the person who has perhaps offended a neighbour in some respect guards against high-spirited pride, and the offended person likewise guards against unyielding obstinacy.

5. Let us strive, therefore, my brothers, to be humble in making satisfaction to those who have something against us, and ready to forgive those who have offended us. For not only does the preservation of mutual peace among us consist in these two things, but even divine propitiation itself cannot be obtained without them: God neither receives an offering from one who does not first go to be reconciled with his brother (Matt. 5:24), nor does he fail strictly to exact a debt already forgiven from one who does not remit his fellow servant’s debt. Now if these three remain in us—righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit—let us not be secure merely because the kingdom of God is within us; rather, let us all the more work out our own salvation in fear and trembling, knowing that we still possess so great a treasure in earthen vessels.

## SERMON XIX [Note: [Col. 0589D] St Jerome.]. On the same words of the Apostle: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink.” (Rom. 14:17)

[Col. 0589C]

1. The Apostle Paul is usually brief in words, abundant in meanings. This was not unknown to that man, approved for gifts both of eloquence and wisdom, who judged every single word of Paul to be a thunderclap. [Note: [Col. 0589D] Nicholas of Clairvaux mentions this sermon [Col. 0590D] in Letter 24, to the Abbot of Celles, as was said in the Preface to this volume.] For he expresses everything so pointedly, and thunders forth with such spirit and power, that he wonderfully displays order in the sequence, fullness in the meaning, and connection in both. “The kingdom of God,” he says, “is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.” What do you say to this, you gluttons and libertines, whose god is their belly, whose whole occupation is either in the belly or beneath the belly, who, as the Apostle James says, [Col. 0589D] “have fattened your hearts and bodies in luxury” (James 5:5)? Hear, hear: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. 6:13). “Woe to you who sleep on ivory beds and revel on your couches; who eat calves from the herd, drink clarified wine, and anoint yourselves with the finest ointments” (Amos 6:1, 4, 6). Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart because fat of body? Why do you love vanity (Ps. 4:5 [4:2]) and neglect truth? The fatness of flesh, bodily pleasures, and fullness of belly will either desert you before death, or you will leave them at death. “For,” says the holy man, [Col. 0590A] “when he dies, he shall take none of it away, nor shall his glory descend with him. Like sheep they are placed in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Ps. 48:18, 15 [49:17, 14]). How aptly, “like sheep”: because, stripped harshly and closely shorn of the fleece of worldly riches, they shall be assigned naked to everlasting fires. “Death shall feed upon them,” because they shall always die into life and always live into death. Thus here the flesh is assigned to worms, there the soul to fires, until they are again bound together in their unhappy fellowship and joined in penal torments, they who were companions in vices.

2. O delicate one, surrounded—and confused—by delights and riches, awaiting confusion and death: the kingdom of God is not food and drink, not purple and fine linen, because that rich man, overflowing with both, descended to hell in an instant (Luke 16:19, 22). What then? “But righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.” Do you observe and take notice that joy comes at the end? Thus, foolish children of Adam, do you wish, by a headlong leap over righteousness and peace, to turn and pervert the final thing into the beginning? For there is no one who does not wish to rejoice. That joy shall neither stand nor exist; for just as “there is no peace for the wicked,” so too, says the Lord, there is no rejoicing for the wicked (Isa. 48:22; 57:21). “Not so the wicked, not so.” First one must practise righteousness, seek peace, and pursue it; and then at last grasp joy—or rather, be grasped by joy. Thus that angelic assembly first practised righteousness when it stood in truth and abandoned the deserter from truth. After this it was made firm in that peace which surpasses every understanding; for though they are surrounded by diverse ranks of dignities, [Col. 0590C] there is none who murmurs and none who envies.

3. “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion, because he has strengthened the bars of your gates, blessed your children within you, and made your boundaries peace” (Ps. 147:12–14). Praise him, and repeat your praises, because your gates are shut by most secure bars and immovable bolts: no enemy enters, no friend goes out. Your children are blessed in you with every spiritual blessing in heavenly things with Christ. There is now no fear within your boundaries, because he has made your boundaries peace. You have no temptations; no troop of thoughts throws itself into confusion; for that many-faced tormentor is far from your walls and from your children. And he who is the same unites and binds all things together in sameness, “whose participation,” as it is said, “is in the same thing” (Ps. 121:3 [122:3]). There, now as the third blessing, they draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour; and with eyes, as it were, bathed in the waters of divinity, they behold the divine essence, deceived by no image of bodily phantasms. Behold joy at the end, yet without end.

4. Wretched are we, driven from that happy region and descended—indeed fallen—into this vanity. “The children of Zion,” says the prophet, “illustrious and clothed in finest gold, how have they been reckoned as earthen vessels?” (Lam. 4:2). Children of Zion: that is, of the contemplative city which the Lord built, so that he might be seen in his glory; children of the heavenly Jerusalem, which is free and is [Col. 0591A] our mother; illustrious through the dignity of their creation, clothed in finest gold through the image of divinity. How then have we been reckoned from such a state as earthen vessels? How have we degenerated into these clayey and fragile bodies? For angels, dearest brothers, render righteousness to God, peace among themselves, joy to themselves. You too, therefore, human being, do not first seize what is yours and despise the righteousness you owe to God and the peace you owe to your neighbour. Righteousness is the virtue by which each person is rendered what belongs to him. You owe the Creator not merely one righteousness, but many and manifold acts of righteousness. “For the Lord is righteous and loves righteous deeds” (Ps. 10:8 [11:7]). “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35:7 [36:6]). Aptly, like mountains, because he has heaped upon you many masses of his mercies.

5. First, indeed, he created you with all other things and among all other things, not without the great prerogative of dignity. For he said concerning all things, and they were made. Afterwards, that Majesty, inflamed by an exceedingly fervent love for you, redeemed you. Did he do so by the ease of a word? No: for thirty-three years he worked your salvation in the midst of the earth, nailed to a cross, handed over to death, reckoned among objects of mockery. Your God became your brother—not the brother of angels, because “he takes not hold of angels, but takes hold of the seed of Abraham.” That you were made is something you have in common; that you are his brother is special. He added something still more special toward us: from the broad and spacious road leading to death he drew us with his finger and set us in the council and congregation of the righteous. What more ought he to have done that he did not do? What heart of stone would not be softened by so great and such a multitude of benefits conferred by one so great and such as he? Whatever, therefore, you are, whatever you can do, you owe to the one who created, redeemed, and called you.

6. But when you have practised righteousness, practise peace also. For as long as we are in this earthen vessel and in the frailty of the human constitution, we cannot be found wholly free from offences. Therefore, if you remember that your brother has something against you, be humble in seeking forgiveness; if you have something against him, be ready to grant it, and all the members will be in peace. For thus, most ready for these two things, charity and humility, we shall be unable to experience dissension. “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29): meek, which belongs [Col. 0591D] to charity, because charity is patient and kind; humble, which concerns the very meaning of the word. For those who proceed thus, there will be joy in the Holy Spirit. I shall speak of what one who has experienced it knows, and one who has not experienced it does not know: “The natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). Do not all our inmost parts often quake while we pray, at the remembrance of that joy which is in the Jerusalem above, which is our mother, and does not a wave of tears flood the faces of those meditating? O that it might last! “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be forgotten; let my tongue cleave to my jaws if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy” (Ps. 136:5–6 [137:5–6]). Truly at the beginning of joy, because its end is stored up there.

[Col. 0592A] 7. When will you tear apart my sackcloth, Lord Jesus, and gird me with joy, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with sorrow? The beginning of that joy which we sometimes feel here is a drop, a little droplet descending from that river whose rush gladdens the city of God. When will the time come for us to be immersed more deeply, in perpetual joys, in the very fountain of divinity, where wave joins wave without break or interruption? “When shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” When shall I pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God? When, as we have heard, shall we see in the city of the Lord of hosts? Come then, brothers, let us faithfully adhere to this happy triad, and always remember that saying: “Friend, for what have you come?” [Col. 0592B] (Matt. 26:50). For we have not come in order to kill the king under a pretence of friendship, but to serve him who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XX. On the Lord’s words: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and the one who humbles himself shall be exalted.” (Luke 18:14)

1. If we carefully consider, brothers, the stages of humankind, we shall find four: namely, the highest happiness in heaven, for which we sigh; an intermediate happiness in paradise, from which we fell; likewise an intermediate unhappiness in this world, over which we groan; and in hell the extreme unhappiness which we deservedly fear. Yet I can state it more briefly: life and the shadow of life; the shadow of death and death. Thus, placed neither at the summit nor at the bottom, we fear descending and desire to ascend, the more anxious because we seem nearer to the lowest than to the highest. And behold, we are told: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and the one who humbles himself shall be exalted.” What does this barred linkage of exaltation and humiliation mean? Is it not enough, Lord, that in your truth you have humbled us, that you still demand that a human being add the further act of humbling himself? And certainly there remains a lower place to which we may be humbled; but one who falls there will add nothing by which he may rise again, and one who has been humbled so far must vainly hope for exaltation. For “you have humbled us in the place of affliction, and the shadow of death has covered us.” Our life has come so near to hell. Where further shall we humble ourselves? What profit is there in our blood if we descend into corruption? [Col. 0592D] Certainly there is nothing below us except that irreparable corruption. After the shadow of death nothing remains but death; after the place of affliction only the place of death remains.

2. “The one who humbles himself,” he says, “shall be exalted.” If he had said, “The one who is humbled shall be exalted,” I would certainly rejoice as one most certainly, and greatly, humbled. But now, when he says, “The one who humbles himself shall be exalted,” distress surrounds me on every side; I know what I should choose, but not what I should do. I wish to be exalted, because this is supremely necessary: for I have here no lasting city, nor would it be good to remain here even if it were permitted. But to go lower still is to perish. For I already occupy the lower place, which has only the lowest place beneath it, that is, hell. [Col. 0593A] If I humble myself there, there is no hope of exaltation; if I do not humble myself, there is likewise no hope of exaltation, because the one who humbles himself—and only that one—shall be exalted. If I do this, death awaits me; but if I do not do it, rejected from exaltation, I shall not thereby escape the hands of death. But if this seems difficult, let us at least consider what precedes it.

3. “Everyone who exalts himself,” he says, “shall be humbled.” For how does the person whom Truth humbles exalt himself? We do not ask here where he exalts himself, but how; for it seems not that a place is lacking, but that power is lacking. I say, not that there is no place to which a human being may exalt himself, but that there is absolutely no one able to do so. There is indeed abundant will, but no capacity. For, whether people wish it or not, this is the common voice of all Adam, of the whole human race: “In your truth you have humbled me” (Ps. 118:75 [119:75]). Whoever is humbled in truth is humbled truly, and is exalted only falsely. And what is it to be falsely exalted, except truly not to be exalted? Thanks be to him because he did not say, “Everyone who has exalted himself shall be exalted.” For how should we strive in vain to exalt ourselves if we thought that would happen, when not even the present hopelessness of advancement restrains the appetite for exaltation? And perhaps this is what he meant in saying, “The one who exalts himself shall be humbled”: it refers not to an effect, which does not exist, but to an intention, which is foolish.

4. For how many do we see humbled but not humble, struck but not grieving, indeed healed by the Lord but not made sound even by the healing itself? These are those who reckon delights to exist among thorns [Note: [Col. 0593D] 2368 C. “computant” [“they reckon”].—This form of expression occurs in Book III of *The Imitation of Christ*, chapter 20, at the end. It occurs again below in Sermon 28.], [Col. 0593C] concealing the sins they commit, the slippery ground on which they stagger, the darkness by which they are blinded, the snares among which they walk, the place of affliction which they inhabit, the body of death which they bear, the heavy yoke which they endure, the heavier conscience which they hide, and the heaviest sentence which they await. Such was the man to whom John was commanded to write in the Apocalypse: “You say, ‘I am rich and need nothing’; and you do not know that you are poor, wretched, miserable, blind, and naked” (Rev. 3:17). Nor is it surprising if the exaltation of the children of men is vain and deceitful, since they themselves are vain and deceitful. Truth humbles them; vanity exalts them. They have loved darkness rather than light, embracing the vanity which exalts them and seeking falsehood; whereas against the truth which humbles them [Col. 0593D] they rebel, with whatever wishes and efforts they can, with evasions and futile attempts.

5. Have we accomplished anything? I think that we have discovered also how a person may humble himself. I mean that he should adhere [variant: apply his will] to the truth which humbles him, neither concealing nor resisting it, but cooperating with it in a devout disposition of piety. Therefore, henceforth I shall guard, as carefully as I can, against hardness of heart. I shall feel and mourn my pain, lest, if my wound happens to be insensible, it be also incurable. I shall therefore be one who sees my affliction under the rod of his indignation, [Col. 0594A] lest my soul come into the company of those of whom Truth says: “I struck them, and they did not grieve” (Jer. 5:3); and again: “We treated Babylon, and she was not healed” (Jer. 51:9). This humiliation is a severe treatment, but pride is a more severe disease. May it be treated in such a way as to be cured by this treatment! I shall therefore agree with my adversary, acquiesce in my judge, and finally yield to the pressing goad, lest I be pricked twice. For I think this is what the Lord means when he says: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and the one who humbles himself shall be exalted.” It is as though he said: Whoever kicks against the goad shall be pricked twice; but mercy shall be shown to one who agrees and gives place to wrath.

## SERMON XXI [Note: [Col. 0593D] This sermon is elsewhere attributed to Nicholas of Clairvaux [Col. 0594D] on the Octave of Saint Andrew. But since it is not among the nineteen sermons which Nicholas dedicated to Henry, Count of Troyes, I would rather attribute it to Bernard.]. On the words of Wisdom (10:10): “The Lord led the righteous by straight ways,” etc.

[Col. 0594B]

1. There is a righteous person who, at the beginning of his speech, is his own accuser (Prov. 18:17); there is a righteous person who lives by faith (Rom. 1:17); and there is a righteous person who is without fear (Prov. 28:1). The first is good, because he approaches the way; the second better, because he runs along the way; the third best, because he is already nearing the end of the way. Yet here let us take the first, whom we find more quickly. The Lord led him, and no other; because it belongs to him to bring one back from the way of iniquity to the way of truth, to lead him back, and to guide him along it. “By straight ways,” he says. The Lord’s ways are straight ways, beautiful ways, full ways, level ways: straight without error, because they lead to life; beautiful without defilement, because [Col. 0594C] they teach purity; full with a multitude, because the whole world is now within Christ’s net; level without difficulty, because they bestow sweetness. “For his yoke is sweet and his burden light” (Matt. 11:30). “And he showed him the kingdom of God.” The kingdom of God is granted, promised, shown, and received: granted in predestination, promised in calling, shown in justification, received in glorification. Hence: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom of God” (Matt. 25:34). For the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, them he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30). In predestination there is grace, in calling power, in justification joy, and in glorification glory.

[Col. 0594D] 2. “And he gave him knowledge of holy things.” The knowledge of holy people is to be afflicted here temporally and delighted eternally. By contrast, the knowledge of the wicked goes in the opposite direction. One kind is worldly knowledge, which teaches vanity; another is knowledge of the flesh, which teaches pleasure. The former is to us as a father, the latter as a mother. For just as a mother always wishes quiet for her son and excludes every labour whatsoever from him, so flesh, made fat, pampered, and swollen, kicks back and does not allow itself to be touched even by the smallest fingertips. And just as a father wishes his son to run here and there, [Col. 0595A] in order to learn what may someday make him great, so the world wishes a person to become entangled in many labours, so that he may have grounds for pride, for being puffed up, and for becoming foolish in vanity itself. “The leech has two daughters”; that is, self-will, which is as it were the root, has two daughters: vanity and pleasure, crying, “Bring, bring.” These are never satisfied; they never say, “Enough.” If anyone has more fully crushed these within himself, he may deservedly apply to himself that saying: “For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up” (Ps. 26:10 [27:10]).

3. “He honoured him in his labours.” Are we not honoured even in our labours themselves when we unite everything we do to the bond of unity, so that there may not be among us one weight and another weight, one measure and another measure, because both are abominable before God? Are not this lowliness, this ugliness, this half-girded dress also honoured and venerated by the princes of the earth? [Note: [Col. 0595D] These words designate the plain habit of the Cistercians, nevertheless venerable to kings. See the Preface to this volume, no. 45.] Woe to us if we rejoice except in Christ and for Christ! Woe to us if we offer poverty for sale! “And he completed his labours”: either here, through perseverance, so that he does not abandon righteousness even to the end; or there, in glory, so that he may rejoice eternally. Both completions are blessed: here the righteous person dies full of days, and there he rises in fullness [variant: length] of days—full in both places, here with grace and there with glory, because “the Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 83:12 [84:11]). Amen.

## SERMON XXII. On the fourfold debt

[Col. 0595C] 1. You are on the way, brothers—the way which leads to life, a straight and undefiled way, leading to that holy city Jerusalem which is free, which is above, which is our mother. Its ascent is indeed steep, since it is cut through the very summit of the mountain; yet the path’s shortness either moderates or removes the magnitude of the labour. But with a felicity as happy as it is easy, you not only travel this way but run upon it, because you are unburdened and girded, carrying no weight upon your backs. Not so, not so, certain others: dragging four-horse chariots and four-horse loads, they resolve to go around the mountain, and often plunge down its slopes, scarcely finding an end to their lives. Blessed therefore are you who, having left yourselves and all that is yours without any exception, make your way by the mountain’s very summit for him who “ascends above the setting,” whose name is the Lord (Ps. 67:5 [68:4]). But those who, though they have fled Egypt, still long with the tenderest yearning for all things Egyptian, have not found the way to the city of habitation. Weighed down by the heaviest burdens of their own wills, they fall either under the load or with the load, so that they scarcely reach the course set before them.

2. For what is this—thanks be to him whose grace has brought it all about—that your life represents the apostolic life? [Note: [Col. 0596D] Bernard explains this below in Sermon 27 *On Various Subjects*, no. 3, and Sermon 37, no. 7.] They left all things and, gathered in the Saviour’s school in his presence, drew waters with joy from the fountain of the Saviour, drinking the fountain of life itself in that fountain. “Blessed are the eyes that saw.” Have not you too, not in his presence but in his absence, not at the words of his mouth but at the voice of his messengers, done something similar? Maintain for yourselves this prerogative: they believed upon seeing and hearing him; you believed upon hearing and receiving the message. Thus stand firm in the Lord, beloved, so that, just as they held to the royal road amid hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, labours and fasts, vigils and the other observances of righteousness, so you too, though not equal to their merits, yet in some measure equal to their practices, may say to the Lord your God when you come before the throne of his glory: “We rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, for the years in which we saw evils” (Ps. 89:15 [90:15]). In truth I tell you that you are truly on the straight way, on the holy way which leads to the Holy of Holies. I lie—though I say this for your consolation—if souls of monks, novices, and lay brothers have not flown to heavenly joys from the hands of this sinner, as free as they were freed from the prison of our mortality. If you ask how I know this, know that most certain signs of it have been given and shown to me.

1128  
3. Therefore I have no reason to fear, for you or on your behalf, the strength of Satan and his ministers, since I know that his power has been exposed and reduced to nothing through the wounds of the Redeemer. For in the spirit of strength that Stronger One crushed the strong man, [Col. 0596C] breaking gates of bronze and bars of iron. It is his tricks and cunning that make me afraid for you: trained partly by subtlety of nature, partly by the experience of ages through so many thousands of years, he does not fail to know the frailty of human nature, whichever way it may turn.

Thus that insatiable murderer did not choose bears, lions, or the strong animals of the earth for our first parents, but a twisting and crafty serpent, accustomed by its winding coils now to cover its head with its tail, now its tail with its head. Indeed, Scripture says that the serpent was not stronger but craftier than all the living creatures of the earth. And so he began with a question, probing the woman’s mind, knowing that he must work by ingenuity, not by force: [Col. 0596D] “Why has the Lord God commanded you,” he says, “not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?” She replied: “Lest perhaps we die” (Gen. 3:1–3). What God had stated with certainty, saying, “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2:17), she puts forward doubtfully: “Lest perhaps,” she says, “if we eat, we may die.” And listen to the serpent’s ingenuity and malice: “You shall by no means die,” he says (Gen. 3:4). God affirms; the woman doubts; Satan denies. So I too fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ Jesus (2 Cor. 11:3).

[Col. 0597A]  
4. Do you suppose there is anyone among you to whom he says in his thoughts, “Why has God commanded you to keep this Rule?” For according to the disposition of your spirits, he proposes relaxation to one who is lukewarm and a stricter life to another who is fervent, seeking and awaiting this alone: somehow or other to remove him from the council and congregation of the righteous. Certainly the spirit suggesting this to you is a lying spirit, a spirit possessing authority, which begrudges you your place. Hence the Wise Man, not ignorant of this matter, says: “If the spirit of one having authority over you rises up, do not leave your place” (Eccles. 10:4).

Far be it that the Spirit of truth, who led you here, should wish to lead you back; for “Yes and No” are not in his mouth, but in him there is “Yes,” as unassailable authority testifies. “No one,” says [Col. 0597B] the Apostle, “speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus’” (1 Cor. 11:3). Jesus means “Savior” or “salvation”; *anathema* means “separation.” But whoever whispers to you of separation from salvation is neither the Spirit of God nor from God; for the Holy Spirit came not to scatter but to gather, he who always calls scattered Israel back into its own land.

5. What then? Does someone seek a more strenuous life? I tell you: this life is most strenuous, and, in every respect, if you refuse to conceal the matter from yourself, answers according to its capacity to that first school of the Savior. Do you dare even in thought to descend to an easier one? Oh, if you too knew how much you owe, and to how many, you would see how insignificant what you do is, how it is not even to be numbered among the least things in comparison with your debts.

[Col. 0597C] Do you wish to know what and to whom you owe? First, you owe your entire life to Christ Jesus, because he laid down his life for yours and endured bitter torments lest you should endure everlasting ones. What can seem dreadful or hard to you when you remember that he who was in the form of God, in the day of his eternity, begotten before the morning star amid the splendors of the saints, the radiance and image of God’s substance, came into your prison, into your mire, sunk, as it is said, up to his elbows in the deep mud? What will not be sweet to you when you gather together all the bitterness of your Lord and recall first those necessities of infancy; then the labors he endured in preaching, the weariness of his journeys, the temptations of fasting, [Col. 0597D] the vigils of prayer, the tears of compassion, the snares laid in conversation; finally, 1129 the dangers among false brethren, abuse, spitting, blows, scourging, mockery, derision, reproaches, nails, and things like these, which for thirty-three years he wrought and suffered in the midst of the earth for the salvation of our race?

> [Note: [Col. 0597D] Bernard used the same words in Sermon 11 for Wednesday of Holy Week and in Sermon 43 on the Song of Songs, no. 3. Thus he sometimes copies himself, [Col. 0598D] as above in the sermons on St. Malachy, no. 5.]

Oh, what unmerited compassion; what gratuitous and so well-proved love; what unforeseen condescension; what astonishing sweetness; what unconquerable gentleness! The King of glory crucified for a most contemptible servant—indeed, for a little worm! Who has ever heard such a thing? Or [Col. 0598A] who has seen its like? For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; he died for the unrighteous and for enemies, choosing exile from heaven so that he might bring us back to heaven: a sweet friend, a wise counselor, a strong helper.

6. “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid to me?” If all the lives of Adam’s children, all the days of the age, and all the labors of all human beings who have been, are, and shall be, were conferred upon me, would they not be nothing in comparison with that body of his, admirable and astonishing even to the powers above—in its conception by the Holy Spirit, its birth from a Virgin, its innocent life, its abundance [variant: flow] of teaching, its flashing miracles, and its revelations of mysteries?

You see, therefore, that as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so that life was exalted above [Col. 0598B] our life—yet it was laid down for our life. As nothing has no comparison with something, so our life has no proportion to his life, since his could not be worthier, nor ours more wretched. Nor should you think I exaggerate in words; for here every tongue fails, and neither eye [variant: mind] suffices even to contemplate the mystery of so great a condescension.

Therefore, when I have given him whatever I am and whatever I can do, is that not like a star to the sun, a drop to a river, a stone to a tower, dust to a mountain, a grain to a heap? I have only two tiny coins—indeed, the very smallest: body and soul; or rather, one tiny coin, my will. And shall I not give it over to the will of him who, being so great, anticipated so little a thing with such great benefits, who purchased my whole self by giving his whole self? [Col. 0598C]

Otherwise, if I keep it back, with what face, what eyes, what mind, what conscience do I approach the merciful heart of our God? How dare I pierce that most powerful fortress which guards Israel, and divert to my own price not drops but waves of that blood flowing from the five parts of his body? O perverse generation and faithless children! What will you do on the day of calamity coming from afar? To whose help will you flee?

7. But am I indebted to him alone, when I can scarcely repay even some small part? My past sins demand from me my future life: that I should bear fruits worthy of repentance and review all my years in the bitterness of my soul. And [Col. 0598D] who is sufficient for these things? “I have sinned beyond the number of the sands of the sea; my sins have been multiplied; and I am not worthy to see the height of heaven because of the multitude of my iniquity, because I provoked your wrath and did evil before you.” “Evils without number have surrounded me; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I was unable to see” (Ps. 39:13).

How, then, shall I count what is without number? How shall I make satisfaction when I am compelled to repay the debt down to the last farthing? And who understands sins? Ambrose—that heavenly pipe—says:

> [Note: [Col. 0598D] Epistle 56 calls Norbert’s mouth “a heavenly pipe.”]

> “I have found more easily those who preserved innocence [Col. 0599A] than those who performed adequate repentance” (*On Repentance*, book 2, ch. 10).

But however much one repents, however much one afflicts and mortifies oneself, “For your name’s sake, Lord,” says the righteous man, “you will be merciful to my sin, not because of my [variant: repentance’s] merit; for it is great” (Ps. 24:11). Therefore, even if you dedicate all that you live, all that you understand, all that you possess, and all that you can do to this one matter, is it even to be counted among anything? A little earlier you were rendering your life to Christ for his life; now again the recollection of your previous sins requires it all. Have you, as the common saying goes, arranged to make two sons-in-law out of one daughter?

1130  
8. What if I show you a third creditor, who claims it for himself no less urgently than truly? [Col. 0599B] I suppose that you too desire to possess the city of which it is said, “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:3); that glory which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart; the kingdom of all ages; to live forever, unto everlasting eternities. I believe you wish to be equal to God’s angels in heaven, to be an heir of God and a co-heir with Christ, to hear the angelic melody in the streets of the heavenly Zion, and to see whatever that will be when Christ hands over the kingdom to God the Father and God will be all in all. Finally, you wish to be like God and to see him as he is.

Nor do I doubt that you long to receive the receding shadows and the breathing day, when that solemn day dawns and shakes off the clouds of things; when day will no longer decline, [Col. 0599C] but there will be an eternal noon; when there will be fullness of heat and light, the sun standing still, the extermination of darkness, the drying up of marshes, the expulsion of foul odors. Must you not give, to purchase this, your whole self and whatever you can gather from wherever you can gather it? And even when you have fulfilled everything, do not suppose that the sufferings of this present time—or of the body—are worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us. Are you so shameless or so imprudent as to dare count your tiny coin, which both Christ’s life and repentance for sin compete to seize for themselves, also toward acquiring this?

9. What will you say if I bring forward a fourth creditor, who wishes even the preceding three to yield to him by right of his primacy? Behold, at the doors is he who made [Col. 0599D] heaven and earth: he is your Creator, you his creature; you are servant, he Lord; he potter, you the thing fashioned. Therefore you owe him your whole self, from whom you have your whole self—especially to him as Lord, who both made you and has done good to you, who supplies you with the courses of the stars, the temperateness of the air, the fruitfulness of the earth, and the abundance of its fruits.

Truly he must be served with all the marrow of your being, with all your strength, lest he perhaps look upon you with the eye of indignation, reject you, and crush you for ever and ever. I do not think such madness carries you away that you would presume even to name your tiny coin here, much less count it. Explain to me, then, to which of these four you propose to render what you owe, since each is such an exacting creditor

> [Note: [Col. 0599] In the printed editions: “each exactor, both inward and outward.”]

that he can overwhelm you singly.

[Col. 0600A] Ah, Lord, I suffer violence: answer for me. Into your hands, Lord, I commend my tiny coin. Pay all of them; free me from all of them, for you are God and not a human being, and what is impossible to human beings is possible to you. What I could, I have done: Lord, hold me excused, because your eyes have seen my imperfection.

Who then will complain any longer, saying, “We labor too much; we fast too much; we keep vigils too much,” when one cannot answer even for the thousandth—indeed, not even the smallest—part of one’s debts? This, perhaps, brothers, is your true Lent: not external but internal, containing not the husk of the sacrament but the fatness of wheat. For if you owe to each of these four, both for himself and separately, the entire perfection of the Decalogue, surely ten multiplied by four [Col. 0600B] makes your forty, which you ought to keep all the days of your life. And may he who gathered you in this place preserve your life in holy work, so that, when he who is your life appears, you too may appear with him in glory.

## SERMON XXIII. On the Discernment of Spirits  
[Alternative title: On the Seven Spirits.]

1. Paul, teacher of the Gentiles, taking occasion from that spiritual nature by which we live, exhorts his disciples to a spiritual manner of life: “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit” (Gal. 5:25). It is as if he said: If the flesh profits nothing, but it is the spirit that gives life to it, we must separate the precious from the worthless and set the worthier part before the other, so that we may walk according to the spirit, 1131 and not according to the flesh. [Col. 0600C]

For the flesh must be converted to the spirit, so that it may serve and not be served; so that the spirit may say to its servant, “Come,” and it comes; “Do this,” and it does it. Thus our wife will be like a fruitful vine, and she will be saved through the begetting of children—that is, good works—if she herself remains at the sides of our house, in a hidden and humble place, while the soul sits in the center as mistress, as head of the household, as judge; so that what is written may come to pass: “My soul is always in my hands” (Ps. 118:109).

Cursed is that spirit which makes its own worse part predominant. Cursed is the man who feeds the barren woman and does not do good to the widow. Finally, as the same Apostle testifies, if we live according to the flesh, [Col. 0600D] we shall die; for those who walk in the flesh cannot please God (Rom. 8:13, 8), and those who sow in the flesh shall reap corruption from the flesh (Gal. 6:8). But if by the spirit we put to death the deeds of the flesh, we shall live; for those who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God (Rom. 8:13–14), and those who sow in the spirit shall reap eternal life from the spirit (Gal. 6:8).

2. Wisely therefore, brothers—and not foolishly—we have chosen the spiritual life: namely, to chastise the body and subject it to servitude, and to worship God, who is Spirit, in spirit and truth. But because there are different kinds of spirits, we need to discern them, especially since we have learned from the Apostle [Col. 0601A] that not every spirit is to be believed (1 John 4:1).

For those who are less instructed and have senses little trained may think that every thought is the discourse of no other than the human spirit itself. But both the certain truth of faith and the testimonies of the divine Scriptures prove otherwise. “I will hear,” says the Prophet, “not what I shall say, but what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:9). And another prophet says, “The angel who spoke in me” (Zech. 1:9), and so forth. And in the psalm we have learned that visitations can also be made through evil angels (Ps. 77:49).

Hence the Apostle fears lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so the hearts of the disciples to whom he speaks should be deceived (2 Cor. 11:3), namely by him whose devices Paul himself does not fail to recognize. Hence he says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness” (Eph. 6:12). The same Apostle plainly indicates that there is an evil spirit of the flesh when he testifies that some are puffed up by the spirit of their flesh (Col. 2:18). He also declares that there is a spirit of this world when he glories in the Lord, both for himself and for his disciples, not because they received it, but the Spirit who is from God, “that,” he says, “we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12).

3. These, then, are two evil attendants of that prince of darkness: the spirit of wickedness rules over the spirit of the flesh and the spirit of this world. Therefore, whoever among these three spirits speaks to our spirit, [Col. 0601C] let us not believe him; for they thirst not for the blood of bodies but, what is graver, for that of souls.
