But because all have a spiritual nature, we shall recognize them from their speech, and the suggestion itself will show which spirit is speaking. For the spirit of the flesh always speaks soft things; the spirit of the world, empty things; the spirit of malice, always bitter things.

Whenever, therefore, as is its habit, a carnal thought importunately assails the mind—for example, when, thinking of food, drink, sleep, and other such things belonging to care for the flesh, we are inflamed with a certain human desire—let us know with certainty that it is the spirit of the flesh speaking, and let us drive it away as an adversary, saying: “Get behind me, Satan, for you do not savor the things that are of God” (Mark 8:33); rather, your wisdom is hostile to God.

[Col. 0601D] But when an empty thought occupies our hearts, not concerning the enticements of the flesh but worldly ambition, boasting, arrogance, and the like, it is the spirit of the world that speaks: an enemy far more destructive and to be repelled with greater vigilance. At times, however, when these attendants turn their backs, the prince himself, having great wrath, rises against us like a roaring lion; that is, when we are provoked not toward pleasure of the flesh or worldly vanity, but toward anger, impatience, 1132 envy, and bitterness of soul. He presses upon us importunately anything that seems to have been done or said less amicably or less discreetly; anything, finally, in a sign or in any action whatever that appears to afford an occasion for indignation or material for suspicion. Such a thought must be resisted no differently [Col. 0602A] than the devil himself, and guarded against no differently than destruction itself. For it is written: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

4. Yet it sometimes happens that our spirit, frequently overcome by one of these three and made its slave, takes over its role—to its own ruin, alas!—so that now, without any suggestion of another spirit, the soul itself produces from itself either pleasurable, empty, or bitter thoughts. I do not think it easy now to discern when our own spirit speaks and when it hears one of those three others speaking. But what does it matter who speaks, provided that what they say is one and the same? What does it matter to know the speaker’s identity, when what is said is clearly [Col. 0602B] destructive? If it is an enemy, resist the enemy manfully. If it is your own spirit, rebuke it and mourn bitterly that it has fallen into such misery and such wretched slavery.

5. But whenever a salutary thought occupies the mind concerning chastising the body, humbling the heart, preserving unity [variant: the virtue of patience], showing charity to the brethren, or acquiring, preserving, and increasing the other virtues, it is without doubt the divine Spirit that speaks, whether directly or through his angel. And as was said of the human and malignant spirit, so also of the angelic and divine: it is not easy to discern who speaks, nor is it safe to be ignorant; [Col. 0602C] especially since it is certain that a good angel never speaks of himself, but God is the one who speaks in him.

6. Let us therefore henceforth consider more diligently how we ought to hear the suggestions of those malignant spirits—or rather, with how great indignation we ought to reject them—turning our ears away lest we hear blood and the wisdom revealed by flesh and blood. Let us seize the little ones of Babylon—that is, worldly [variant: malicious] thoughts—at their very beginning and dash them against the rock; let us cast the evil one himself, together with his temptations, out of the sight of our heart and reduce him to nothing.

But let us receive with all devotion those thoughts which remind us of justice and truth, and give thanks for the divine condescension. Let us never be found ungrateful for such [Col. 0602D] goodness, knowing that he is the one who speaks justice; he whose speech is truth. For how great a presumption [variant: perversity]—indeed, how great a madness—is it if, while the Lord of majesty addresses us, we senselessly turn away our ear and turn our mind to I know not what trifles? How great is this injury, and how severely deserving of punishment, when a most contemptible worm disdains to listen to the Creator of the universe calling to it?

Yet how great and ineffable is the condescension of divine goodness, which daily sees us wretches turning away our ears, hardening our hearts, and nevertheless calls to us and cries out continually in the streets! Truly in the streets, because in the breadth of charity. For behold, Lord, you have no need of my goods; and [Col. 0603A] yet you say, “Return to me, children of men”; and again you cry out, “Return, return, Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon you” (Song 6:12).

7. Therefore I beseech you, beloved, you who remember the Lord: do not be silent, and give him no silence. Continually hear what the Lord God speaks within you, for he will speak peace. Happy therefore and blessed is the soul that perceives the veins of the divine whisper in silence, often repeating Samuel’s words: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears” (1 Sam. 3:9).

Let today’s sermon then come to an end, so that even as we fall silent, we may hear God speaking within and persuading us concerning his kingdom—more profitably because more subtly, namely through inward inspiration. But if he himself should suggest anything further about hearing this voice of the Lord, [Col. 0603B] we shall treat it in another sermon, lest we burden your minds by the length of our discourse, especially in so useful and spiritual a subject.

## SERMON XXIV. On the Manifold Usefulness of the Word of God

1. You remember, I believe, how in yesterday’s sermon we urged your earnest attention concerning the discernment of spirits, which is greatly necessary for us: so that against the poisoned hissing of the ancient serpent and the deadly songs of the siren, you should endeavor continually to stop up the ears of your heart; so that you may hear neither the spirit of the flesh speaking soft things, nor the spirit of the world suggesting empty things, nor the spirit of wickedness introducing bitterness and sowing scandals.

But it is especially necessary to know that spirit’s tricks, and it is not expedient to be ignorant of its [Col. 0603C] thoughts. For at times that malignant and wicked spirit transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14), so that he may do greater harm by pretending virtue. Yet even then, if we attend carefully, he never scatters anything but seeds of bitterness and discord. For he urges certain persons to particular fasts by which others may be scandalized—not because he loves fasting, but because he delights in scandal.

He is also accustomed to offer many things of this kind, which can nevertheless easily be discerned from divine wisdom if we keep before our eyes that apostolic definition of blessed James, who, describing divine wisdom, says: “The wisdom which is from God is first indeed chaste, then peaceable” (James 3:17). Therefore do not doubt that every thought in which these two do not concur is alien to God’s wisdom. But when a thought appears chaste and does not openly lead toward vices, but holds forth an image of virtue, then only will you know it to be from God if it is peaceable, if it is approved by the judgment of your superior and spiritual brethren; for the Lord God will not do a word which he has not revealed to his servants.

2. With what devotion, humility, and carefulness a salutary thought ought to be received as nothing other than the speech of divine condescension, we have already said in part in yesterday’s sermon; and in today’s sermon we shall nevertheless endeavor to persuade you somewhat more fully. For blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it (Luke 11:28). Do you wish to know how blessed? First, [Col. 0604A] the divine voice sounding in the ears of the soul troubles, terrifies, and judges; but immediately, if you do not turn away your ear, it gives life, melts, warms, illumines, and cleanses.

Indeed, it is our food, our sword, our medicine, our strengthening, our rest, and also our resurrection and consummation. Do not wonder that the word of God is now found to be all things in all things as regards justification, since it shall be all things in all things in glorification. Let the sinner hear it, and his belly will be troubled; at that voice the carnal soul will tremble. For the living and effective word searches out and judges all the secrets of the heart, scrutinizing hearts and thoughts. Hence, although you are dead in sin, if you hear the voice of the Son of God, you shall live. For the word [Col. 0604B] which he speaks is spirit and life.

If your heart is hardened, remember Scripture saying: “He will send forth his word and melt them” (Ps. 147:18); and likewise: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5:6). If you are lukewarm and already fear being vomited out, do not depart from the Lord’s utterance, and it will kindle you; for his utterance is exceedingly fiery. If you mourn the darkness of ignorance, listen carefully to what the Lord God speaks within you; and the word of the Lord will be a lamp to your feet and a light to your paths.

3. But perhaps you grieve all the more because, enlightened more clearly, you recognize even the smallest sins. Yet the Father will sanctify you in truth, which is indeed his word, so that you may deserve to hear among the apostles: “Already you are clean because of the word which I have spoken [Col. 0604C] to you” (John 15:3). And when you have washed your hands among the innocent, behold, he has prepared a table before you, so that you may live not by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God, 1134 and in the strength of that food may run the way of his commandments.

If camps stand against you there and the battle of temptation rises up, seize the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, and in it you will easily triumph. And if perhaps—as commonly happens in combat—you are at some time wounded, he will send forth his word and heal you, and deliver you from your destructions, so that in you too may be seen what the centurion said, whose faith is commended so greatly: “Lord,” he said, “say only the word, and my servant shall be healed” (Matt. 8:8).

And if you still stagger, confess and cry: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had almost slipped” (Ps. 72:2); and he will strengthen you by his words, so that through experience you may learn that the heavens were established by the word of the Lord, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth.

4. Persevere in these and similar things; constantly exercise yourself in such matters until the Spirit says that you should rest from your labors. In this word you shall rest sweetly and sleep pleasantly, until the hour comes when all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice and come forth. But where? Some indeed to judgment, others to eternal life. And who knows whether one is worthy of love or hatred? Then especially remember your word to your servant, Lord, in which you gave me hope, so that I may not fear evil tidings; but rather may that blessed [Col. 0605A] hearing lead to vision when you say, “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34), and so forth. For “whoever confesses me before human beings,” he himself says, “him I too will confess before my Father and the holy angels” (Matt. 10:32; Luke 12:8). May he deign to grant this to us—he who has been appointed judge of the living and the dead. Amen.

> [Note: [Col. 0605C] In the manuscript of Saint-Evroul this sermon ends thus, beginning from no. 4: “Meanwhile exercise yourself in these and similar matters, until that very voice of the Lord, which helps the combatant, summons the victor to rest; [Col. 0605D] and may what is now in strength be in magnificence, the Spirit henceforth saying, ‘Rest from your labors.’ The time will indeed come when the same voice will raise up even the body from the dust, when all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God and come forth. It is necessary also that then he remember his word to his servant, in which he gave you hope, so that you may not fear evil tidings; but the good word: ‘Come,’ he says, ‘blessed of my Father.’ This is the voice that leads to the countenance, so that you too may deserve now to say, ‘I heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.’
>
> “I would not readily believe that one will then regret having heard threats, endured correction, or borne rebukes, in which was the way by which he showed you his salvation. And since all these things are so, and not so much the testimonies of Scripture as the experience of souls bears witness to countless other benefits of hearing the divine voice, why are we wretches distracted by such variety, [Col. 0606C] begging, surely, for fleeting consolation? As though there were not at hand for us, without any difficulty, in the word—which is near, namely in our mouth and heart—whatever salvation, joy, and delight there is to find.
>
> “[Col. 0606D] Therefore blessed indeed are those who hear this word of life and keep it. I say ‘keep it’ in no other sense than as a most precious deposit, so that their heart may be where their treasure is. I shall briefly state for the moment what occurs to me among the things that seem necessary for this keeping. First, set your heart to hear more attentively what he speaks, because it is written: ‘For one who is ignorant shall be ignored.’ Next, fulfill in deed what you have heard, because ‘to one who knows what is good and does not do it, it is sin.’ Finally, patiently endure whatever adversities arise, because this word teaches not only what you ought to do, but also shows how much you must suffer. This truly is *latria*, the worship owed to God alone: that you should be diligent to understand his will wisely and, where necessary, either fulfill it powerfully or endure patiently.”]

## SERMON XXV. On the Apostle’s Words, “I desire first that supplications, prayers,” etc. (1 Tim. 2:1)

1. The Apostle’s words seem to me to express four modes of prayer, when he says: “I desire first that supplications be made, then prayers, petitions, thanksgivings.” For there are some whom the consciousness of sin still terrifies and tortures, before they have received the strength to resist. [Col. 0605B] This is when the Spirit of truth first shines upon them as they lie in the filth of their sins, awakens them, makes them ashamed, and makes them fear God,

> [Note: [Col. 0606D] The manuscripts read: “them.”]

when they see the enormity of their crimes and the scantiness of their merits; and, as though terrified by hell burning before them, since they find nothing good within themselves, they grasp elsewhere for something with which they may be covered. For they know that it is not safe to appear empty before the Lord their God, contrary to the commandment of the Law (Exod. 23:15), and much less do they dare presume to do so with hands full of filth.

Since, then, they fear—and rightly fear—to approach by themselves, they endeavor to make supplication, as it were, through others. Such is that kind of prayer in which we are accustomed to say: “Saint Peter, pray for us,” and similar words. [Col. 0605C] But the most obvious instance of supplication is: “By your cross and passion, deliver us, Lord,” and the rest in this manner. For it seems as though a thief caught and already near hanging, when he utterly despairs and finds nothing in himself by which to beg pardon [variant: mercy], stretches out his arms and says, “Because Christ suffered thus,” in order to move toward pity the hearts of those by whom he is held.

2. I believe it can be said of such persons that “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). That tax collector did violence to the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0606A] when, though he did not dare raise his eyes to heaven, he was able to draw heaven itself down to him (Luke 18:13–14). That woman who had a flow of blood seems to have done something similar: though she feared to approach Christ, she made power go out from him. For she secretly touched the fringe of his garment and was healed of her infirmity. Hence the Lord’s word about her seems, in a certain manner, indignant: “Who touched me?” And he added: “I perceived power to have gone out from me” (Luke 8:43–46).

I do not think there is anyone among us in this condition; but perhaps some, while still in secular dress or manner of life, may at some time have experienced what I mean: suffering unwillingly a flow of blood—namely, that blood which shall not possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 15:50). For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin [Col. 0606B] (John 8:34), and cannot restrain himself by his own strength even when he wishes to do so.

Therefore it is by no means advantageous for such a person to approach Christ by himself. Rather, if he finds one, let him touch Christ’s fringe: that is, let him consider a person whom he sees to be humbler [variant: better] and lowest in the Church, which is Christ’s garment. Let him consider, I say, one who chose to be cast down in the house of God; for this truly is the fringe placed at the edge of the garment, to which the entire abundance of the spiritual ointment descending from the head flows down. If by some acts of kindness, or humble prayer, or pure confession, he touches this person, so as to move that person’s affection toward compassion for himself, let him have faith, and without doubt he will be healed.

Yet let the fringe know that the power has gone forth not from itself but from Christ, who declares that he himself is touched in the fringe. I have now explained to you, as far as I could, what kind of supplication this is and for what sort of soul it is necessary.

3. But once the power of self-restraint has been received, the person who is conscious of it approaches securely, seeking pardon for past offences; and he uses prayer in the proper sense, which is the speech of the mouth, now that with his own mouth he speaks to his God. Hence Mary Magdalene, although no less humble than that woman with the hemorrhage, nevertheless does not fear to approach in the same manner, but wets his feet with tears [Col. 0607A], wipes them with her hair, anoints them with ointment, and kisses them with devout lips (Luke 7:38). From this it is sufficiently clear that she had altogether already resolved in her heart thereafter to abstain from sin; and, as it were, the flow had stopped. If you too have now attained this, it is first necessary that, speaking in prayer to the Lord himself, you should “recall your years in the bitterness of your soul.”

4. Then, after persisting for some time in the lamentations of penitence, when you have conceived a certain cheerfulness and confidence in forgiveness, proceed now to petitions; so that, secure as one restored to the Lord’s favor, you may dare to ask what is fitting for yourself and your fellow servants. But perhaps you ask how or by what means you can know whether you have obtained this forgiveness. Thus, indeed, for the sake of preserving humility, divine mercy is accustomed to order matters so that the more anyone advances, the less he judges himself to have advanced. For even at the highest stage of spiritual exercise, if anyone has reached—or advanced to—that point, something of the imperfection of the first stage remains to him, so that he scarcely seems to himself to have attained even the first.

Yet I know what was read today in the Gospel. [Note: [Col. 0607D] From this it is clear that this sermon was delivered on the eighteenth Sunday after Pentecost.] Jesus had said to the paralytic: “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven you”; and this was reckoned against him as blasphemy. But he—to whom, indeed, “the thought of man will confess”—said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts? You blaspheme me by calling me a blasphemer; and, as though to excuse the power of a visible cure, you say that I claim for myself an invisible power.” [Note: [Col. 0607D] Thus in the Colbertine manuscript and that of Marmoutier; in the printed editions: “to excuse the force of the visible [Col. 0608D] cure, [you say that] I claim for myself an invisible power.” The sense is the same.] “But I rather convict you of being blasphemers, proving invisible power by a visible sign” [Col. 0607C]. “‘That you may know,’ he says, ‘that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins’—then he says to the paralytic—‘Rise, take up your bed, and walk’” (Matthew 9:2–7).

And so, if you now rise by a desire for things above; if you take up your bed—that is, if you lift your body above earthly pleasures, so that the soul is no longer carried along by its desires, but rather itself, as is fitting, governs the body and carries it where it does not wish to go; if, finally, you walk, forgetting what lies behind and stretching yourself toward what lies ahead in the desire and resolve to advance—do not doubt that you have been healed. For you could not rise unless the burden had been relieved to some extent; nor could you take up the bed unless you had been more fully unburdened; since it is impossible to walk [Col. 0607D] in the fervor of religious life while carrying the heavy mass of sins.

5. Therefore one who is such may now petition with confidence. Yet he must take care lest he ask for things that ought not to be asked; or ask too much for things that ought indeed to be asked of God; or seek lukewarmly things that must be sought with one’s whole desire and at all times. “You ask and do not receive,” says James, “because you ask wrongly, in order to spend it on your passions” (James 4:3). So acts everyone who seeks earthly things beyond necessity, who pursues worldly glory or pleasure.

[Col. 0608A] Of this kind also is the practice of worldly people, who ask in their prayers for the death of their enemies, and other similar things that are not fitting. Temporal things, however, if they are lacking, should indeed be requested insofar as human necessity requires; but, according to the judgment of blessed Gregory, they ought not to be sought excessively. Among such things are also those spiritual gifts without which salvation can nevertheless stand firm: for example, the word of knowledge, gifts of healing, and everything concerning which we do not know for certain whether it is expedient for us. Thus, if temptation troubles you, you should certainly pray that it be taken away from you, but not too insistently; for in such matters one must always remember that apostolic saying: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for” (Romans 8:26), and entrust the matter to God rather than rashly determine something for ourselves [Col. 0608B].

But these things are to be sought with one’s whole desire and at all times; for these your desires should cry out to God unceasingly and as earnestly as they can: that you may have his good grace, may be pleasing in the eyes of his mercy, may live in him and die in him, and may deserve to see his glory and enjoy him forever. Of these it was said: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Hence also the Prophet says: “My face has sought you; I shall seek your face, O Lord”; and elsewhere: “One thing,” he says, “have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Psalm 26:8, 4).

6. Further, I believe that very few attain the fourth kind of prayer, which is [Col. 0608C] thanksgiving; [Note: [Col. 0608D] This is explained below, in Sermon 27 on Various Subjects, nos. 5 and 6.] and the rarer it is, the more precious it is. For he will assuredly find great favor with God who, according to God’s promise, is heard before he calls (Isaiah 65:24); and the Spirit whom he has from God will bear witness to his spirit that his desire has been heard, so that he can now be certain not to pray, but to give thanks. Thus you have it in the raising of Lazarus, where the Lord, although he had previously prayed nothing, says: “Father, I thank you because you have heard me” (John 11:41).

The first kind, therefore—that is, supplication—should be made with a reverent disposition. The second, which we have properly called prayer, with a pure disposition: namely, that we do not conceal our sins or flatter ourselves, knowing that each person thus finds mercy with God if he is found [Col. 0608D] a stern judge of himself. The third—that is, petition—requires a generous disposition and the breadth of confidence, as it is written: “But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing” (James 1:6). For I think that this is why it was said: “Every place upon which the sole of your foot shall tread shall be yours” (Joshua 1:3): we shall obtain only so much as we extend the foot of faith. The fourth, which is thanksgiving, should itself be most full of devotion and abundant in delights.

7. Now the authority of the Rule itself has just prompted you, in what was read in the chapter, concerning the reverence due to prayer [Col. 0609A] (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 20); and on that occasion I thought I should say something about prayer. I say this briefly, however: some persons, I suppose, sometimes experience in prayer a dryness and a certain dullness of mind, so that while praying only with their lips, they give insufficient attention either to what they say or to whom they speak, because they have approached almost from habit, with too little reverence and care.

For what else ought a brother to think when he enters into prayer than that prophetic saying: “I shall enter into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God” (Psalm 41:5)? At the time of prayer we ought altogether to enter the heavenly court—that court, certainly, in which the King of kings sits upon his starry throne, surrounded by the innumerable and ineffable [Col. 0609B] host of blessed spirits. Hence even he who had seen it, because he could find no greater number, said: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Daniel 7:10).

With what reverence, then, with what fear, with what humility ought the cheap little frog, crawling forth from its mud-pool, to approach there? How trembling, how suppliant, how humble, and finally how watchful and with the whole mind intent upon the majesty of glory must wretched little man stand in the presence of angels, in the council of the righteous and congregation of the saints?

8. In all our actions, therefore, much vigilance of mind is needed, but especially in prayer. For, as we read in our Rule (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 19), although at every hour and in every place the eyes [Col. 0609C] of the Lord [another reading adds, “and the angels above”; another reading has only, “above”] watch us, nevertheless this is especially so in prayer. For although we are always seen, then we also present and display ourselves, as though speaking face to face with God.

Further, although God is everywhere, he is nevertheless to be prayed to in heaven, and there he is to be considered in time of prayer; so that our mind may not be held back by the roof of the oratory, by the expanse of air, or by the very density of the clouds, according to the form handed down to us by Christ, where he says: “Thus shall you pray: Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matthew 6:9). For heaven, by a certain prerogative, is also called the seat or throne of God; because compared with the way in which the holy angels and the souls of the elect see God in heaven, we wretched exiles [Col. 0609D] upon earth seem scarcely to possess even the name alone.

Let the one who prays, therefore, pray as though taken up and presented before him who sits upon a high throne among the angels who have not fallen, and exalted among human beings whom he has raised up—the needy from the dust and the poor from the dungheap. Let him, I say, consider and attend to himself as one presented before the Lord of majesty, so that he may say with Abraham: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Genesis 18:27). And because, warned by your command and formed by your instruction, I presume this, O Lord, fountain of mercy.

## SERMON XXVI. On Subjecting Our Will to the Divine Will

1. You have now heard from our Rule, brothers, the saying of Christ concerning humility (Rule of St Benedict, [Col. 0610A] ch. 7) [another reading omits “of Christ”]; and whenever it is read, I want you to attend to it with your whole mind. For foolish and mad is whoever trusts in merits of life elsewhere, in another religious observance or wisdom, and not in humility alone.

Before the Lord, brothers, we cannot claim a right, because “in many things we all offend”; nor can we deceive him, for he knows the hidden things of the heart—much more, surely, works that are manifest; nor can we resist him by our strength, because he is almighty. What remains, then, except to flee with all our mind to the remedies of humility, and to supply from it whatever we lack in other respects? Yet—what wonderful vanity! what wonderful folly of our heart!—such an abundance of matter for humility is not enough perfectly to restrain its exaltation [another reading, “elevation”], or wholly to tame its stiff-necked movements [Col. 0610B], yet dust and ashes still grows proud. [Note: [Col. 0609] In the Cistercian manuscript the words “so that . . . ashes” are absent.]

2. Now the sum of all humility seems to consist in this: that our will be subjected, as is fitting, to the divine will, as the Prophet says: “Shall not my soul be subject to God?” (Psalm 61:1). I know indeed that every creature, willing or unwilling, is subject to the Creator; but from the rational creature voluntary subjection is required, so that it may willingly sacrifice to the Lord and confess his name—not because it is terrible and holy, not because it is almighty, but because it is good.

This subjection, however, must be threefold: what it is certain that God wills, we must entirely will; what it is certain that he does not will, we likewise must abhor; but what is uncertain [Col. 0610C], whether he wills it or does not will it, we must neither will altogether nor altogether refuse to will. Here indeed, brothers, in this middle ground, lies the whole danger for religious persons: while we unhappily flatter ourselves and, caressing ourselves, deceive ourselves. Hence it happens that we pretend to seek the Lord’s will while wishing both to do our own will and to have some excuse from ignorance.

For what monk is so wretched that he dares refuse what he is certain God wills, or presumes to will what he is certain God does not will? But the danger lies in the middle for those who have now gone out from the world and dwell in the place of conversion as in a paradise of delight—just as in the middle of paradise stood the tree of transgression, by which our first parents [Col. 0610D] transgressed: the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, not of good alone or evil alone, but of good and evil.

3. Therefore I beg you, brothers, attend carefully, for nothing occurs to me that you could hear more profitably. Where God’s will is certain, let ours wholly follow it: namely, in those matters concerning which we find something certain in the Scriptures, or in which the Spirit himself clearly cries in our hearts what ought to be held—such as charity, humility, chastity, obedience, and the other virtues. Let us approve and desire without hesitation those things that we know beyond doubt please God. Likewise, we must in every way hate those things that it is certain God hates, such as apostasy, fornication, iniquity, and impatience.

But in those matters about which we can find nothing certain [Col. 0611A], let our will determine nothing as certain. Rather, let it hang between the two, or at least not adhere too strongly to either side, always considering that perhaps the other side may please God more; and let us be ready to follow his will, in whichever direction we discover it inclines. Let no one hesitate concerning matters that are certain; let no one admit doubtful things as certain; let no one claim judgment for himself in doubtful matters or rush headlong to a conclusion. Then we shall experience what is written: “Great peace have those who love your law, O Lord, and for them there is no stumbling block” (Psalm 118:165).

For whence come stumbling blocks, whence disturbance [another reading, “tribulation”], except because we follow our own will and rashly determine in our hearts what we desire? If it happens to be forbidden or impeded in any way, we immediately become prone [Col. 0611B] to impatience, murmuring, and stumbling, without attending to the fact that all things work together for good to those saints who are called according to his purpose, and that the very event which seems to us a misfortune is a certain word of God, indicating his will to us. But whoever has established nothing certain in his heart concerning such matters cannot be scandalized whichever way the matter later turns.

Or if anyone intends to do something concerning which he has no certain command, and keeps his will in suspense until he asks his superior and seeks from him the Lord’s will—since he obeys him in the Lord’s place—he will not be disturbed by whatever is commanded him; for truly, “great peace have those who love the law of the Lord, and for them there is no stumbling block.”

[Col. 0611C] 4. Now what I said—that one should keep one’s will in suspense, or subject one’s will to the divine will—I do not say of the desires of concupiscence or of the affections. That is impossible while the soul is still held in this body of sin, this body of death. For what else would it be than eternal life, to follow the divine will in all things with one’s entire affection? But we must subject our consent to the divine will if we desire to have eternal peace, if we desire to have peace now, as it is written: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

The Prophet says: “They shall walk in the light of your countenance, O Lord, and in your name they shall rejoice all the day” (Psalm 88:16–17). One person walks in the light of his own countenance, anxious to do his own will and considering what pleases [Col. 0611D] his own heart. Another walks in the light of the human countenance, always intent upon what pleases people and what the world judges; of him the prophet of God says: “I have not desired the day of man, Lord, you know” (Jeremiah 17:16). “Destruction and unhappiness are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes” (Psalm 13:3). But for the one who always has the fear of God before his eyes, “her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceable” (Proverbs 3:17).

“Come to me,” he says, “all you who labor and are burdened,” whom the harsh slavery of your own will or another’s presses down, “and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matthew 11:28–30). For as much as divine mercy is kinder and sweeter [another reading, “more pleasant”] than any human being [Col. 0612A], so much more pleasant is its yoke plainly than other burdens. Therefore people striving to please themselves or other people have been put to shame. But those who walk in the light of your countenance, Lord, thinking only how to do your will and striving with all their heart to please you, will now indeed rejoice all day in your name and have no stumbling block; but at last they will be exalted in your righteousness, when, leaving their weaknesses and entering into your powers, they remember your righteousness alone, so that they may then possess without labor what they now labor to follow.

## SERMON XXVII. Against the Most Evil Vice of Ingratitude

1. Great is the mercy of our God over us, beloved, exceedingly great [Col. 0612B]: by the ineffable power of his Spirit and the inestimable gift of his grace, he has delivered us from our vain manner of life in this age, in which we once were as though without God, or rather—as is more execrable—even against God: not ignorant of him, but contemptuous of him.

May the grim image of that life—or rather death, for “the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4, 20)—often, if only it would, turn before the eyes of our heart: how great that blindness and perversity was! By diligently considering the weight of our misery, we may, if not as perfectly as it truly is, yet at least in some measure estimate the magnitude of the mercy that delivered us. Moreover, if any one of us does not neglect carefully to consider [Col. 0612C] not only from where he was rescued but also where he has been placed; not only what he escaped but also what he received; not only from where he was called back but also to what he was called: he will undoubtedly find that the fullness of this mercy wholly exceeds the measure of the former mercy.

For God “has not dealt thus with every nation,” so as to make known to them not only his judgments but also his counsels. Indeed, he has magnified his dealings with us, not merely by receiving us as servants but also by choosing us as friends. For we did not choose him, but he chose us and appointed us to go and bear fruit: fruit, I say, not merely “not deadly,” which pertains to judgment and is known even to servants, but even “not perishable,” which belongs to counsel and is revealed to friends.

[Col. 0612D] 2. For we have been placed in this condition: that we may serve neither sin—for that is deadly labor—nor even the world, like those whom we see subject to earthly cares, though not sins; entangled in bodily occupations, though not crimes; and laboring in the passing fashion of this world for the present support of themselves and their households. Their labor, indeed, though it does not lead to damnation, does not in the least pertain to salvation; so that, even if they preserve the foundation, they suffer loss when what they built upon it perishes, while they themselves are saved, yet as through fire.

But what is said to us? What counsel is given to friends? “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (John 6:27). Nor do we cease working for this food [Col. 0613A] even when we may be occupied with earthly work, whether obedience directs it or regard for brotherly charity; for our intention differs from that of those whose labor we have said will perish. Labor that is similar but cleaves to a different root does not perish in the same way, because it is rooted in eternity, which never perishes [another reading, “fails”].

3. Finally, if perhaps, pursuing things not unlawful but nevertheless not expedient, we had, after abandoning our former fornication, remained in the chastity of marriage, not accepting the counsel which we know has been given concerning the unmarried life; or if, abstaining from robbery and fraud, we had lawfully used our own possessions, yet had not reached evangelical perfection, as it is written: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all [Col. 0613B] that you have, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:12, 21)—what great mercy it would itself have been if, delivered from such great crimes, in which many of you had been entangled, crimes that had in themselves only the sentence of death and the judgment of certain damnation, it had been granted us to breathe even at some lower level!

Certainly the prodigal son was afraid to aspire to the number of sons, counting himself happy if perhaps he deserved to be received even among the hired servants. Yet the father’s mercy could not be satisfied unless he showed him such abundant mercy that the elder son, who had never departed from the father, could even envy it (Luke 15:11, 32). So too we, beloved: the mercy of our God, abundantly poured out upon us, has received us, children of wrath and unbelief, not only into the number of the elect but has called us to the fellowship of the perfect.

For even if through the negligence of some persons one does not rise to perfection, let them see what excuse they can offer; for we have all professed the apostolic life, and all of us have given our names to apostolic perfection [another reading, “profession”]. I do not, of course, say this of that glory of holiness which they merited to take upon themselves not for their own sake alone but for that of the whole world, as it is written: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness” (Psalm 81:3); but rather of their profession, of which Peter speaks for all when he says: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matthew 19:27).

4. But now, my brothers, I am altogether moved by what it means that divine mercy seems less generous toward us at present: to us, upon whom it bestowed so much when we did not ask, did not desire, indeed perhaps even refused it, it now seems, when we pray, beseech, and petition most frequently—indeed continually—to deny things far smaller. What are we to think, dearest friends? Has the Lord’s hand been shortened, or have the treasures of grace perhaps failed? What, I ask, are we to think: has his will changed, or has his power diminished [another reading, “changed”]? We may surely think neither of him; it is impious to believe either concerning the almighty and unchangeable Majesty.

What then does it mean that we who pray, beseech, and petition without ceasing are not heard, though he has bestowed upon us such great and gratuitous mercy? [Col. 0614A] For if someone replies that what was answered to the apostle Paul is answered to us—namely, that the grace of God is sufficient for us (2 Corinthians 12:9)—he is wholly mistaken. For all our prayers, supplications, and petitions are made especially for this: that we may not walk in things too great or too wonderful for us; praying that we may be given humility such as is fitting, not, I say, for saints, but for sinful monks; beseeching that patience be granted us, such as was found not, I say, in martyrs, but is necessary to our profession; petitioning for charity, such as we know, on the testimony of the Scriptures, was bestowed by divine gift not, I say, on angels, but on our fathers, who were human beings like ourselves, subject to suffering and even sinners.

5. Woe to this wretched generation because of its imperfection, to which insufficiency seems sufficient—indeed, such great poverty! For who seems even to aspire to that perfection which the Scriptures hand down? Not without cause, certainly: although we have the same beginnings of conversion as the fathers, a very unequal advance in manner of life is found. Thus, whereas we read that they advanced from day to day and completed their course, among us it would be thought a great thing if someone merely preserved the beginnings of his conversion [Col. 0614B], so as to appear no less humble or fearful, no less careful and watchful, no less fervent in spirit, no less patient and gentle in the middle than at the beginning. [Note: [Col. 0613D] From this passage appear to have been taken the words read in *The Imitation of Christ*, book 1, ch. 11: “Now it seems a great thing if someone can retain a portion of his first fervor.”]

For how many do we see as though forgetful of themselves and of their sins, and likewise forgetful of God and his benefits [Col. 0614C], so failing to redeem the time and instead losing it that their conduct and affections scarcely receive even a final mention from them? What else shall I say that these persons do—those who make nothing of buffooneries, detractions, words of boasting and impatience; who easily grieve their neighbors, indeed the Spirit of God who is in them; who think little of the scandals of the weak; who, when others rebuke them, seem either to be asleep in a kind of negligence or to blaze with the torches of anger; and who, like a people that has done righteousness, come freely to church? They sing psalms with the others, but neither in spirit nor in understanding; during prayer they meditate on I know not what foolishnesses; and they do not even fear to partake, with angels, of the dread sacrament of the Lord’s body.

What else, I ask, shall I say that these persons do, except that, now secure concerning the grace of their Lord, they confidently presume upon the familiarity which they have earned over a long time [Col. 0614D]? This is indeed what the common proverb says: “A familiar master breeds a foolish servant.” But where is that, beloved, which you so often sing: “For I am a stranger with you and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Psalm 38:13)? Alas, alas! No one is found who returns and gives thanks to God except this foreigner. “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” You remember, I believe, that these are the words of the Savior, reproving the ingratitude of those nine.

They are indeed read to have prayed, beseeched, and petitioned well, who raised their voices, saying: “Jesus, son of David, have mercy on [Col. 0615A] us” (Luke 17:18, 17, 13). But the fourth element, which the Apostle added—thanksgiving—was lacking to them (1 Timothy 2:1), because they did not return or give thanks to God.

6. To this day also we see many persons asking quite importunately for what they recognize to be lacking to them; but we know very few who seem to give fitting thanks for benefits received. It is not blameworthy that we ask persistently; but what plainly denies effect to petition is that we are found ungrateful. [Note: [Col. 0615D] Another cause is indicated above, in Sermon 2 for the feast of St Andrew, no. 5.] And perhaps it also seems to be an act of mercy to deny ungrateful persons what they ask, lest it happen that we are judged all the more severely for ingratitude the more we are shown to have been ungrateful amid accumulated benefits.

Therefore, in this respect, it is an act of mercy to withhold [Col. 0615B] mercy, just as it is an act of wrath and indignation to show mercy—the mercy of which the Father of mercies himself speaks through the prophet, saying: “Let us have mercy on the wicked man, and he will not learn to do righteousness” (Isaiah 26:10).

For how many brothers do we see and mourn who, provided their habit and tonsure remain, think everything safe for them? The wretches do not consider how the worm of ingratitude, gnawing away the inward parts, deliberately refrains from piercing through the outer bark which they see, lest perhaps they reflect and blush, and are corrected by that very shame. Yet it sometimes presumes that in certain persons all the inward parts have been consumed, so that it does not fear to thrust forth its venomous head even into what outwardly appears—unless perhaps we suppose that those whom we see openly apostatizing from God suddenly become the worst of men, rather than that they have gradually failed, when strangers consumed their strength, and they did not know, [Col. 0615C]

7. You see, then, that it benefits not all to be cleansed from the leprosy of worldly manner of life, whose sins are manifest. Rather, in some there arises secretly a worse ulcer of ingratitude, all the more dangerous because it is more inward. And rightly the Savior asks in the Gospel where those nine are, because “salvation is far from sinners.” Thus he also asks the first man after sin where he is (Genesis 3:9); and at the judgment he will profess not to know the workers of iniquity (Luke 13:27), although we read in the Psalm: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, [Col. 0615D] and the way of the wicked shall perish” (Psalm 1:6).

Nor without reason were those who do not return to the Savior found in the number nine, in which number five is joined to four; and it is an evil mixture of bodily sensuality and Gospel tradition. This usually occurs when we wish to obey the four Gospels in such a way that we also wish to gratify the five bodily senses.

8. But blessed is that Samaritan who recognized that he had nothing which he had not received; and therefore kept the deposit, and returned to the Lord with thanksgiving. Blessed is the one who returns to him, in whom is the fullness of all graces, for each individual gift of grace. When we show ourselves not ungrateful for benefits received [another reading, “after a benefit received”], we make room in ourselves for grace, so that we may deserve still to receive greater things [Col. 0616A]. For our ingratitude alone altogether hinders our advance in religious life: the giver, in a sense judging what an ungrateful person receives to be lost, takes care not to lose so much more as he bestows more upon one who is ungrateful.

Blessed, then, is the one who regards himself as a stranger and gives no slight thanks even for the least benefits, neither doubting nor concealing that what is bestowed upon a foreigner and unknown person is gratuitous. But we wretched and pitiable people, though at the beginning, while we still consider ourselves strangers [Col. 0616B], we are found sufficiently fearful, devout, and humble, afterward so readily forget how gratuitous is everything that we have received. Presuming improperly, as if upon familiarity with God, we do not at all notice that we deserve to hear: “The members of his household shall be his enemies” (Matthew 10:36).

For we offend him more easily then—as though we did not know that the things committed by us are to be judged more severely then [Note: [Col. 0615D] Thus three manuscripts; but in the printed editions: “For we now offend him more easily, the more severely those things which are committed by us,” etc.]—when we read in the Psalm: “For if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it” (Psalm 54:13).

Therefore I beseech you, my brothers, let us humble ourselves more and more beneath the mighty hand of God, and strive to remain far from this greatest and most evil vice of ingratitude; so that, wholly occupied in thanksgiving with all devotion, we may reconcile to ourselves the grace of our God, which alone can save our souls. Let us show ourselves grateful not merely in word or tongue but in deed and truth, because the Lord God who bestows graces requires from us thanksgiving more than thanksgiving speech. He is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0616D] This sermon appears among the sermons of Abbot Guerric in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*; it is absent from the Cologne manuscript containing Guerric’s sermons, according to Horstius. Yet it should not be denied to Bernard, since it is cited in Book 6 of the *Flowers* and has a Bernardine conclusion.] On What Is Read in Job 5:19: “In six tribulations he will deliver you, and in the seventh evil shall not touch you.”

1. It is most fitting, and the principle of equity altogether requires, that those for whom a kingdom is prepared from the foundation of the world should not neglect also to prepare themselves for the kingdom, lest, when the kingdom is prepared, those who were to reign may perhaps be found unprepared. Thus we read of a certain supper, where the Lord says that the supper indeed was prepared, but those who had been invited were not worthy (Matthew 22:8).

We ask, therefore, how future kings ought to prepare themselves when the kingdom is prepared. And if we inquire devoutly with the Prophet of the Lord, we shall surely hear from the Lord with the Prophet: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle? Or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” “He who enters,” he says, “without stain” (Psalm 14:1–2).

“But,” you will say, “this preparation seems to belong to Christ alone.” For no one among all others is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day old [Col. 0617A] (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint). Therefore he alone will enter who alone is the Lamb without stain; he alone could not be convicted of sin, because it was neither done by him nor found in him. He alone, plainly, my high priest, was defiled neither in father nor in mother, as the law says (Leviticus 21:1–2): for he has a father, indeed, but God; and likewise a mother, but a virgin. Hence he alone enters the Holy of Holies, and “no one ascends into heaven except the Son of Man who descended from heaven, who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

2. What then of us? Shall we immediately despair? On the contrary, we shall hope—and especially on this account. For although he alone will enter, yet he will certainly enter whole, and not a bone of him shall be broken. The head will not be found in the kingdom without members, provided that the members are conformed and joined [Col. 0617B] to their head: conformed indeed in conduct, joined in faith. For even the very earliest age has such conformity as it is capable of, and also such union: while by that threefold immersion it is planted together in the likeness of his death, and receives faith in a kind of wrapping, since it is not yet capable of faith unfolded. Surely the Spirit of wisdom is gracious: whom inherited guilt had bound, pardoned righteousness sets free.

But thereafter he will not thus set free the curse from his lips. For to one who sins deliberately after receiving knowledge of grace, no sacrifice for sin remains (Heb. 10:26). Nor will he thus set free from one’s own lips the curse, as he does the curse from alien lips. A curse, brothers, is a grave stain; and we know that it is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth [Col. 0617C] (Matt. 15:11). From there, then, come stain and the curse from one’s lips, though not always from one’s own lips. For original guilt does not proceed in an infant from its own body or heart; it has not only no consent, but for the time being no awareness whatsoever of sin.

How, then, does the Spirit not set free the curse from one’s own lips, or how does no sacrifice remain for those who sin voluntarily, except because Christ is not crucified anew for that person, nor is that person planted again through baptism in the likeness of his death? A person’s own flood of tears is now required; one must carry one’s own cross, mortify one’s own members, and offer one’s own sacrifice. Otherwise he would say “I believe” without cause. The curse of one’s own lips must be expiated by one’s own lips.

For through many [Col. 0617D] tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:21); and no one enters except through tribulations, either one’s own or those of others.

3. Assuredly, the suffering of the second Adam alone cleanses those whom the transgression of the first alone defiled. Not that anyone’s own satisfaction can suffice. For what is all our repentance, except that, if we do not suffer with him, we cannot reign with him at all? What is lacking in us, he himself supplies. Yet he does not allow that small thing—whatever belongs to us—to be withheld. But if union in faith without conformity of conduct cannot save adults, then works without faith can save far less. For a member adhering to the head, if deformed, is more easily re-formed than one torn away, however similar it may be, is joined.

Yet even that which is deformed must either become conformed to the image of his Son and its head, or at last be torn away from him and be anathema from Christ, lest anything unbecoming be found in that fullness of his body.

4. Therefore, where the stain is one’s own, one’s own cleansing is rightly required; and if the defilement is manifold, manifold tribulation is also needed. For whence comes tribulation, except when defilement is resisted and concupiscence opposed? What in a human being can be found pure from this stain, immune from this contagion? From within it flows; the deadly poison comes out from the heart and then seizes the whole body: it afflicts the mind with desires and infects the members with allurements. Hence itching ears, wanton eyes; hence pleasure in smelling; hence such disordered delight in the throat; hence throughout the body the sensation of softness and the ruinous lust of touching; hence within the soul that intoxication of desires, and a kind of furnace fiercely kindled by the passions of ambition, avarice, envy, obstinacy, malice, and finally every vice.

For as many allurements as the body has, as many delights as the world seems to possess, so many tribulations the righteous man suffers, so many temptations he endures. And just as one walking in the flesh delights in the pleasure of the senses and counts it a delight to be among thorns, so everyone who desires to sow in the Spirit strives rather to uproot than to propagate the thorns and briars which his own earth certainly brings forth under the curse; for he is converted [Col. 0618C] in his affliction whenever he is pierced by a thorn.

5. To resist this pest, then, so various in every particular—what manifold tribulation that is! “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in me.” Concupiscence has infected everything; the law of sin is found in all the members. On every side death strives to enter through the windows, while within the tinder of all wickedness rages more dangerously and malignantly more cruelly.

Yet in this struggle, however manifold, one must by no means fail or yield to despair. For although tribulations abound for Christ, consolations also abound through him. Finally, hear consolation. “Sin is at the door”: unless you yourself open, it will not enter. Appetite itches in the heart, but it is under you [Col. 0618D] (Gen. 4:7): unless you willingly yield, it will do no harm. Hear consolation. Restrain consent, lest these prevail; and you will be undefiled, so that you too may enter without stain to dwell in the tabernacle and rest on the holy mountain of the Lord your God. “For if they have not had dominion over you, then you will be undefiled, and you will be cleansed from the greatest transgression” (Ps. 18:14).

Truly the greatest transgression is that which occupies the whole inner and outer person. Hear yet another consolation. “In six tribulations you shall be delivered, and in the seventh evil shall not touch you.” If you are a Hebrew servant, you shall serve six years and go out free in the seventh. You have six tribulations against the desires of the heart and against the fivefold pleasure of bodily sensation; but in these six you shall be delivered from the seventh [Col. 0619A]—not indeed so that it does not come, but so that it does not wound, harm, or touch you with evil.

Death will indeed come: it is the seventh tribulation. But it will be sleep for those beloved of the Lord, and behold, his inheritance. It will be the gate of life, the beginning of refreshment, the ladder of that holy mountain, and entrance into the place of the wonderful tabernacle which God, not man, has pitched. Thus in the seventh evil shall not touch you: that threefold evil which awaits in the seventh those who pretend that in the meantime they have been wholly delivered in the six tribulations and are not thoroughly cleansed in the six jars, so as to be presented at the Bridegroom’s wedding without spot or wrinkle. For horror at departure, pain in passage, and shame before the presence of the glory of the great God await them.

6. Whence comes this pretense in us, my brothers? [Col. 0619B] Whence this so ruinous lukewarmness? Whence this accursed security? Why do we wretches deceive ourselves? Have we perhaps already become rich? Have we perhaps already begun to reign? Do not those horrible spirits besiege the door of our house? Do not those ghostly faces await our departure?

What terror will that be, O my soul, when, leaving behind all those things whose presence is so pleasant to you, whose sight so agreeable, whose very companionship so familiar, you enter alone an utterly unknown region and see those most hideous monsters rushing upon you in troops? Who will come to meet you on a day of such necessity? Who will protect you from those roaring creatures prepared for prey? Who will console you? Who will lead you?

My little children, let us remember these [Col. 0619C] last things of ours, lest we sin. For we too must pass through fire, and fire will test what sort of work each person has done. There our gold will be turned into dross; there all impurity will be revealed; there Truth itself, at the appointed time now given us and despised by us, will judge our righteousnesses. And what will all our righteousnesses be there, except they be reckoned as a menstruous cloth? Whatever we now pass over by making light of it, cover by caressing it, or neglect by pretending not to see it—how great a torment will the avenging flame consume it with there! Would that someone would now give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes: perhaps the consuming fire would not find what a flowing tear had meanwhile washed away.

7. Do you suppose that after that fire anything at all will truly remain in us? Or will there be so much as we might dare to offer to the face of Majesty, or so stand in his presence? What shame will there be, what confusion, when after such benefits we appear lukewarm, so imperfect, so empty before the face of the Lord our God? Adam fled to hide himself from him after tasting only one forbidden fruit (Gen. 3:8): what shall we presume after so many crimes, after so many evil deeds?

When will the eye of the heart be cleansed from this confusion—an eye to which we now neglect to give attention, so that with an undazzled gaze it may be able to behold the rays of that true sun? “As wax melts before fire, so sinners shall perish before the face of God” (Ps. 67:3). Let [Col. 0620A] rottenness therefore enter into my bones and bubble beneath me, “that I may rest in the day of tribulation” (Hab. 3:16), this seventh tribulation, and that in it evil may not touch me: this threefold evil of horror, pain, and shame.

Happy indeed is the soul which shall speak confidently with its enemies at the gate: “Why do you stand here, bloody beast? You will find nothing in me, O deadly one [variant: O deadly thing].” [Note: [Col. 0619] Thus St Martin, when already near death, according to Sulpicius.]

Happier is the person whose work shall not have burned, whom that examination will find to have built with gold, silver, and precious stones. Happiest is the person who, with no cloud at all of shame and with face wholly unveiled, beholding the glory of the Lord, shall be transformed into the same image and shall be like him, seeing him as he is—God blessed, praiseworthy, and glorious above all things for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX. On the threefold love of God [variant title: On loving God].

[Col. 0620B]

1. “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. For all that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and worldly ambition, which are not from the Father” (1 John 2:15–16). What then? Are there things from the Father by which these may be recompensed to us? There certainly are—altogether sweeter and more lovable than these; but they are not entrusted to servants, much less to enemies. Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God. Counsel is entrusted to friends, to whom it is said: “Everything whatsoever that I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you” (John 15:15).

Blessed Gregory explains that love itself is knowledge. Therefore there is a threefold love which excludes those three things that are not from the Father. And for this reason, I think, Peter is asked three times: “Do you love me? Do you love me? Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). Perhaps these are also the things concerning which the Law commands: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. 6:5): that is, you shall love sweetly or affectionately; you shall love wisely; you shall love strongly.

For the love of the heart has something akin to carnal love, since affections are properly said to belong to the heart. The soul, however, has a somewhat higher resonance; hence it is called the seat of wisdom, so that loving God wisely seems rightly to be assigned to it.

2. Certainly the thought of Christ’s Incarnation is greatly effective for that affectionate love of the heart of which we speak, as is the thought of the whole dispensation which he accomplished in the flesh, and especially of his Passion. For God, seeing human beings wholly carnal in their affections, displayed to them such sweetness in the flesh that anyone who does not love him with his whole affection must be very hard of heart.

Wishing indeed to recover the noble creature, man, he said: “If I compel him against his will, I shall have an ass, not a human being; since he will come neither willingly nor voluntarily, so that he can say, ‘I will sacrifice to you willingly’” (Ps. 53:8). Shall I give my kingdom to asses? Or does God care for oxen? “Therefore, that I may have one who comes voluntarily, I shall terrify him, if perhaps he may turn and live.” And he threatened the bitterest things that can be conceived: eternal darkness, immortal worms, unquenchable fire.

But when not even thus was man recalled, he said: “He is not only fearful but also desirous; I shall promise him what seems most desirable.” Human beings desire gold, silver, and things like these; but above all they desire life. This is evident—very evident. “If,” he says, “they so greatly desire this wretched, laborious, momentary life, how much will they love a life that is peaceful, eternal, and blessed?” He therefore promised eternal life; he promised what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart.

3. But seeing that he accomplished nothing: “One thing,” he said, “still remains. There is in human beings not only fear and desire, but also love; and nothing in them is more powerful to draw them.” Therefore he came in the flesh and showed himself so lovable that he bestowed on us that charity than which no one has greater: that he should give his life for us. Whoever should refuse to turn even for this reason rightly hears: “What ought I to have done for you that I have not done?” (Isa. 5:4).

And truly in nothing does God so commend his charity as in the mystery of his Incarnation and Passion; in nothing is his mercy so revealed; in nothing does his kindness so appear as in his humanity, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “The kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared” (Titus 3:4). For his power was hidden, because he came in weakness. Thus Habakkuk says: “There his strength was hidden” [Col. 0621C]—undoubtedly in the cross, whose horns are in his hands (Hab. 3:4). Wisdom too was hidden and made flesh; for it pleased him through the foolishness of the word to save those who believe.

Had he not in some way made himself foolish, he who delivered his life to death, bore the sins of many, and then paid what he had not taken? Was he not drunk with the wine of charity and forgetful of himself, against Peter’s counsel, who said, “Be merciful to yourself” (Matt. 16:22)? Thus strength was hidden, and wisdom was especially veiled and incarnate; but kindness could not be declared more openly [variant: more plainly], expressed more abundantly, or commended more evidently.

4. Now we have said that this belongs to the affectionate love of the heart. For one may see people so affected by such things that they can scarcely either hear or remember them without tears. This love, then, is opposed to concupiscence of the flesh. For what can be sweet to one in the flesh, for whom there is such sweetness in Christ’s Passion?

Yet this sweetness can be deceived if prudence is lacking; and then it will scarcely be possible to guard against poison in honey. Prudence must therefore be present, by which we may diligently investigate the inner mysteries [variant: so that the mysteries of the sacraments may be investigated], so that we may be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks. This prudent love excludes curiosity. For a mind intent on these things cannot be curious about temporal matters, saying with the Prophet: “How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day” (Ps. 118:97).

[Col. 0622A] 5. Thirdly, each person must love strongly, so that, just as he cannot be deceived, so neither can he be compelled, being prepared to suffer everything for righteousness. Who does not know that one who is king of heaven does not seek earthly kingdoms and honors, but rather rejects them? “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10).

Thus Peter is now questioned concerning these three loves, because he had previously been found deficient. On first hearing about the Lord’s Passion, he could not bear it, as one loving sweetly; but he said, “Far be it from you!”—as one loving unwisely. Hence he deserved to hear: “Get behind me, Satan, for you do not understand the things that are of God” (Matt. 16:22–23). Something similar was present in the apostles, to whom it was said: “If you loved me, you would indeed rejoice, because I go to [Col. 0622B] the Father” (John 14:28). Indeed, because they loved, they grieved. They love, and they do not love: they love sweetly, but they do not love wisely.

But on the very night when the Lord was to be betrayed, Peter loved both sweetly and wisely when he said: “I am prepared to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke 22:33); but he did not love strongly, because

> He who fell did not stand with a steady step.  
> —Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book I, verse 1

The power from on high had not yet come; after receiving it, he did not deny, but spoke freely: “You judge whether it is necessary to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Is it not fitting that the question of love should be put to the one set over the flock to feed it? For he ought to preside over others who, drunk with the wine of charity, burns [Col. 0622C] with zeal and forgets himself, so that he seeks not his own interests but rather those of Jesus Christ.

Observe that when Peter was asked whether he loved more than these, he answered only that he loved; he did not dare affirm what he had previously said rashly, for which he was ashamed. And perhaps this was why he was grieved. [Note: [Col. 0621D] The remainder is absent from the Cistercian codex.] For he had previously said: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, yet I will not be” (Matt. 26:33).

## SERMON XXX. On wood, hay, and stubble.

1. There is nowhere security, brothers: neither in heaven nor in paradise, much less in the world. For an angel fell in heaven beneath the presence of divinity; Adam fell in paradise from the place of delight; Judas fell in the world from the school of the Savior. I have said this lest anyone flatter himself on account of this place because it is said, “This place is holy”; for it is not a place that sanctifies people, but people who sanctify a place.

For among us too are three kinds of persons, each quite unsuited both to the order and to one who has entered upon this way. There are those who began well but immediately failed. There are those who never began, but have remained and remain in their softness. And there are those swept away by the spirit of levity: slow to hear, quick to speak, most ready to enumerate hastily what they do—if indeed they do anything. Will God even cast these away [variant: reject them]? No, if they remain on the foundation; but they will be saved, though only as through fire.

Through what fire? The Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. If anyone builds upon this foundation wood, hay, stubble, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:11–12, 15). Christ is the foundation; wood is brittle, hay soft, stubble light. Wood are those who began strongly but, once broken, are not joined together again. Hay are those who, softened by the softness they ought to flee, are unwilling, as the saying goes, to touch arduous labors even with the tip of a finger. Stubble are those blown about by impulses of levity, who never remain in the same state.

2. These persons are indeed to be feared for, but not despaired of; because if they have Christ as their foundation—that is, if they end their life on this way—they will be saved, though only as through fire. Fire has three properties: smoke, light, and heat. Smoke calls forth tears; light illuminates what is near; heat burns. So one who is such a person ought to have smoke, that is, bitterness, in the mind because he is lukewarm, lax, and frivolous, because insofar as he can he undermines and disturbs the order. He should also have light in his mouth, so that in confession he may both acknowledge and lament himself as he is in his mind; thus conscience may sharpen the tongue and the tongue may accuse the conscience. It is also necessary that he feel heat in the body, that is, the tribulation of penance—if not manifold, at least some.

Do you suppose that he who wills all human beings to be saved and wills no one to perish will cast away those who are thus pierced in heart, confess with the mouth, and weary the body? There are also others who build upon this foundation gold, silver, and precious stones: those who begin intensely, advance more intensely, and complete most intensely, looking not to what the flesh can do but to what the spirit wills.

## SERMON XXXI. On careful attention to thoughts.

1. Blessed Benedict admonishes us, brothers, to be watchful concerning our thoughts (*Rule*, chapter 7), following the counsel of the Wise Man, who advises guarding the heart with all vigilance because life proceeds from it (Prov. 4:23). Three kinds of thoughts, then, occur to me, against which those who turn toward the heart and hasten to offer God within themselves a temple worthy of him must be very diligently on guard.

For there are at times certain thoughts wholly idle and irrelevant. The soul can cast them away as easily as receive them, provided that it dwells with itself in the heart and stands in attendance upon the ruler of the whole earth.

2. There are other thoughts which are more violent and cling more firmly: namely, those relating to the necessities of nature, and, as it were, drawn from the same mud from which we too were made. If they settle for even a little while, they cannot be torn away without injury and difficulty. Often, indeed, a carnal thought concerning food, drink, or clothing so affects us that it can scarcely be uprooted from our hearts. This happens for no other reason than that the thought itself, being in a manner muddy and sticky, has found soil that is likewise muddy and glutinous.

For it was not without reason that man was said to have been formed not from any earth whatever, but from mud (Gen. 2:7). See how muddy the body is: it clings so strongly and almost indissolubly even to the spirit itself that it can scarcely at some time be separated except with much affliction. What then must be done when that muddy thought has entered the mind? Clearly we must cry out with holy Jacob and say: “Reuben, my firstborn, do not increase; for you went up to your father’s bed” (Gen. 49:3–4).

For such concupiscence is red, carnal, and bloody. It goes up to our bed when it not only touches memory by thought, but also enters the very bed of the will and defiles it with wicked pleasure. This carnal appetite is rightly called our firstborn, since it springs up in us from the very beginning of our life, whereas the other vices are acquired in the course of time from service in this world and from various occasions. We must therefore restrain the appetite which we cannot extinguish, so that, as soon as it enters our bed, we never allow it to increase, but it may be under us, as Scripture says: “Your appetite shall be under you, and you shall rule over it” (Gen. 4:7).

3. But the third kind of thought is exceedingly unclean and foul-smelling. We must not admit it under any circumstances, but perceive its stench from afar and repel it with all our strength, drive it away with all our mind; and, turning at once to groaning, invoke with tears and sighs the Spirit who helps our weakness. Thus, departing in confusion, the malignant enemy will not thereafter so readily dare to offer or bring us anything similar when we have resisted him manfully.

I mean those thoughts wholly unclean and foul which pertain to lust, envy, and vainglory, and the other detestable vices. For if we wish to preserve our souls clean, we must meet thoughts of this kind while they are still far off with great indignation and blow them away from us, so that no entrance may be given them.

The first kind of thought—idle and irrelevant thought—is mud, but simple mud: that is, not clinging and not foul-smelling, unless perhaps it remains in us too long and, through our carelessness and negligence, changes into the second kind of thought. We experience this daily. For while we despise idle thoughts as insignificant, we slip into shameful and dishonorable ones. The second kind of thought is not simple mud but, as we have already said, sticky and muddy. The third, however, must be guarded against not as mud or mire, but as the most unclean and foul-smelling filth.

## SERMON XXXII. On the threefold judgment: one’s own, human, and divine.

1. “Let a person so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.” A minister of Christ ought to conduct himself in such a way that from the conduct of the visible outward person one may judge the disposition of the unseen inward mind, lest he be judged either by another or by himself; rather, with the same Apostle he should say: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day; indeed, I do not even judge myself. But he who judges me is the Lord” (1 Cor. 4:1, 3–4).

In these words three judgments must be noted: human, each person’s own, and divine. Human judgment can judge external matters perceived by bodily senses, but cannot judge inward matters. For it is written: “Who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the spirit that is in him?” (1 Cor. 2:11). Therefore the human spirit within a person can judge what is in that person; but God judges those same things far more excellently. The Apostle confesses that he has not yet escaped God’s judgment, though he had already transcended human judgment and his own.

Now he despised human judgment when he said: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day.” But neither did he fear his own judgment when he said: “Indeed, I do not even judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself.” Divine judgment alone remained; of it he says: “But he who judges me is the Lord.”

2. Yet everyone ought, as far as possible, to present himself blameless first before God and then also before human beings. This is what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Providing things good not only before God but also before human beings” (Rom. 12:17). For we provide good things before human beings in three ways: in bearing, action, and speech—by bearing, that one may not be conspicuous; by action, that one may not be blameworthy; by speech, that one may not be contemptible.

Before God likewise in three ways: in thought, affection, and intention. For thought should be holy—hence it is written, “A holy thought will preserve [Col. 0625C] you”—affection pure, and intention right.
