These three, namely thought, affection, and intention, are in the soul; yet they seem to have distinct places within it. Thought resides in memory, affection in will, and intention in reason.

3. To see their use and difference more clearly, let us take an example from external things. If any ugly color stains only the skin, the body is indeed made uglier, but it loses none of its health from this. But if some corruption or livid swelling settles in the flesh, then not only the body’s beauty but also its health is disturbed. And if a growing sickness should penetrate deeply even to the bones along with the flesh, then one may rightly despair of life itself.

In the same way, if sin is suggested to memory through thought, but neither the will gives it any affection nor deliberation itself consent, it is indeed a deformity, and that soul does not at the moment deserve to hear: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved” (Song 4:7). Yet, though it is a blemish, it is not a disease. But if the will too is seized by the feeling of pleasure, while the deliberation of reason still resists, the soul is weakened indeed but has not yet died. Yet it must cry: “Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed” (Jer. 17:14).

But it is said to die when reason itself is bent toward sin by intention. For then it consents; and of such a soul it is said: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. [Col. 0626A] 18:4). David lamented this threefold stage in the person of the sinner [variant: Adam], saying to the Lord who drives him from paradise into the wide wandering of this world: “You have strengthened your hand upon me.” And since carnal desires are the punishment of sin: “There is no health in my flesh because of your wrath.” And now there is no strength in reason: “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins” (Ps. 37:3–4).

Again, he sings of the same stages in the person of the righteous, saying: “I remembered God, and was delighted, and was exercised” (Ps. 76:4): delighted through the will, exercised through reason.

4. Therefore, lest the rushing crowd of many thoughts, which are wont to flow out like a worthless populace into a courtyard, expel God from memory, let a gatekeeper be stationed at its door, whose name is remembrance of one’s own profession. When the mind perceives itself weighed down by shameful thoughts, let it rebuke itself and say: “Should you think these things—you who are a priest, a cleric, a monk? Ought a cultivator of righteousness admit anything unrighteous within himself? Is it fitting for a servant of Christ, a lover of God, even to meditate briefly upon anything of this kind?” By saying these things it will exclude the flow of unlawful thought through remembrance of its own profession.

Likewise, at the gate of the will, where carnal desires are accustomed to remain as a household in its domestic dwelling, let a doorkeeper be stationed called remembrance of the heavenly homeland. For this can expel a wicked desire, as wedge drives out wedge, and without delay receive him who says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Rev. 3:20).

Then at the chamber of reason there must be appointed such a fierce guard, who spares no one; whoever the enemy may be, whether he dares to enter secretly or openly, let him keep him far away. And this guard is remembrance of Gehenna. For in the other faculties—memory and will—it is not so intolerable if memory sometimes receives a wandering thought or will an impure affection. But it is most grave and altogether harmful if reason ever loses the rectitude of its intention.

## SERMON XXXIII. On the words of Psalm 23, “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?”

1. It is a word of exhortation, my brothers, that, since we all strive to ascend, all tend upward [Col. 0626D] and aspire above, all endeavor to rise on high, we should strive to ascend there where it is good for us to be, where it is safe for us to be, whence we need not fall, where we can stand. The Prophet asks for the climber of this mountain not only in order to awaken desire, but also in order to teach one who desires to ascend the manner of ascent.

Happy is the one who has set the ascents of this mountain in his heart, longing and failing for the courts of the Lord. For this mountain is a fertile mountain, the sum of all good things, the mountain of eternal delight: it is the house of God. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ages of ages they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). Hear the faithful witness that this house is a mountain: “O Israel, how great is the house of the Lord, and how vast the place of his possession! Great and without end, lofty and immeasurable” (Baruch 3:25, 25). Indeed, it is not only a mountain but the mountain of mountains: there are many dwelling places in it, many mountains. For “its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86:1).

2. Holy Isaiah too did not pass this over in silence: “The mountain of the house of the Lord,” he says, “shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains and shall be raised above the hills” (Isa. 2:2). Why should it not be the mountain of mountains, founded as the joy of the whole earth, where there is so manifold an abundance of every delight, where there is one fullness of all riches? It shall be the mountain of peace, the mountain of joy, the mountain of life, the mountain of glory; and all these mountains are one mountain of perfect happiness.

Is it not a mountain of peace: peace upon peace, peace that surpasses [Col. 0627B] all understanding? Truly great is peace in the heart, peace in the flesh, peace from wicked people, peace with all neighbors, peace from the demons themselves, peace with God; and of peace there shall be no end. There will be joy, but such as the Lord calls full joy, secure joy, which no one will take from us (John 16:24, 22). We shall also have life—and have it more abundantly—since the coming of so great a shepherd cannot be ineffectual, who, as he himself testifies, came to the sheep for this very purpose: that they might have life and have it more abundantly (John 10:10).

Does not the eternal weight of glory beyond measure in the heights also appear to you to be a mountain? Moreover, from all these things, and from whatever similarly desirable things can be imagined, there is one good measure of blessedness, “pressed down, shaken together, running over” (Luke 6:38): as though you gathered into one mountain very many mountains—one of gold, another of silver, another of sapphires and emeralds and the splendor of every jewel; another also of scarlet, purple, fine linen, and all similar riches. For all things shall be restored to us multiplied. And one who has built gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation [Col. 0627C] will marvel that a lowly building has grown into immense mountains; and from a small seed will reap not so much sheaves as heaps of sheaves.

3. Who, then, shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place? He whose hands are innocent and whose heart is clean. Blessed is that man—if indeed such a man exists. But who shall boast [Col. 0627D] of innocent hands, or of possessing a chaste heart? No one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day old (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint). One alone is innocent among the guilty, clean among the unclean; among the dead he alone is free, and no other shall be reckoned apart from him. He is the one of whom you have read: “No one has ascended into heaven except him who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). For his hands were innocent: he committed no sin, but performed many good works; and he freely said to the Jews, “Which of you shall convict me of sin?” (John 8:46). And who can doubt that his heart was most clean, personally united to Wisdom, into which nothing defiled enters, but which reaches everywhere because of its purity? Nor did he receive [Col. 0628A] his soul in vain, he who alone had power to lay down his soul and to take it up again (John 10:18). He did not receive it in vain when he was born; he did not lay it down in vain when he died; he did not receive it again in vain when he rose.

4. But how did he not swear deceitfully to his neighbour? How did he not receive his soul in vain? How did he not accomplish all those things in vain, if he alone receives the blessing? Was it necessary that Christ should suffer, rise again, and thus enter into his glory? (Luke 24:26). That glory was his own. What profit is there in his blood, while we all descend into corruption? What truth is there in the promise if, as we recalled above, no one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven? Let it be granted that he receives the blessing; but why mercy? Yet he will not receive it alone—or rather, if you attend carefully, he will not receive it for himself alone. Continue through the sacred prophetic words and see how, as it were secretly, the multitude is introduced. He spoke of one and said, “This one shall receive”; but immediately he transferred the statement to “this generation,” saying: “This is the generation of those who seek.” Thus in “one” you are not to understand singleness of person, but unity of spirit. Surely this is the bridegroom, and this the bride; and we know who said, “They are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6). Thus this one shall ascend; this one shall receive the blessing. Yet others also shall ascend with him—or rather, in him—because they shall receive the blessing from him. Hear this from the Prophet: “For the lawgiver shall give a blessing; they shall go from strength to strength” (Psalm 83:8). And [Col. 0628C] this is why Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead: that repentance and forgiveness of sins might be preached in his name (Luke 24:46–47); and repentance might be reckoned toward innocence, forgiveness toward purity. For blessed is not he in whom the Lord finds no sin, but he to whom the Lord will not impute sin (Psalm 30:2). “I have found,” he says, “a man after my own heart” (Acts 13:22). Was it so that he could boast of having a chaste heart? No; for “the stars are not clean in his sight” (Job 25:5). But “God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Psalm 50:19). A contrite heart is near to a clean heart; and this is to be near the heart of God, for he is near to those who are troubled in heart. He is the Samaritan, neighbour to the man who fell among robbers (Luke 10:30–36). He will not swear deceitfully [Col. 0628D] to this his neighbour, but will do what he promised: “Amen, I say to you, you shall sit in judgment” (Matthew 19:28).

5. Therefore let us also, most dearly beloved, according to our measure, pursue both innocence of hands and purity of heart. Above all, let us be careful—though, because of human frailty, we cannot wholly avoid it—to turn aside as far as we can from evil, not merely in action but even in thought. Moreover, lest we have received our rational souls in vain, let us exercise ourselves in good works and make use of rational counsel. For how does a human being not receive a human soul in vain, if, like one of the irrational animals, lying immersed in bodily pleasures, he follows only the appetite of the flesh? The Prophet also added: “Nor has he sworn deceitfully to his neighbour.” For as purity must be preserved within ourselves and innocence toward our neighbour, so works of virtue and works of piety must be practised both in ourselves and toward our neighbour. Let us therefore not be useless to ourselves, lest we seem to have received our souls in vain; nor let us be useless to our neighbour, lest we be proved to have sworn to him in vain. The Spirit who spoke through the Prophet knows our formation, and did not wish merely to admonish us concerning our neighbour’s welfare. He reminds us of an oath, so that we may recognize our obligation and fear to render the pledged faith void. For all of us have sworn ourselves to our neighbours, with whom we have entered into the unity of the Church. And this is the profession of Christian faith: that one who lives should no longer live for himself, but for him who died for all.

[Col. 0629B]

6. And let no one say to me, “I shall live for him, but not for you,” since he not only lived for all, but also died for all (2 Corinthians 5:15). For how does one live for him who neglects those so loved by him? How does one live for him who does not fulfil his law, who does not keep his commandment? Do you seek the law? Do you seek the commandment? “This,” he says, “is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34); and the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you shall fulfil the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). Therefore do not suppose that the good you show your neighbour is a gratuitous act, so that you may neglect it if you wish. You are a debtor by the pledge of the sacrament, and are bound by your own profession. “This one,” then, “shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Saviour.” This one, because one receives the prize. But lest you suppose it to mean one human being: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord.” This one shall receive the blessing because head and body are one Christ. But this is a generation because all of us together shall meet in the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4:13).

7. Perhaps the Lord himself is the mountain of the Lord, of whom it is said: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place?” Surely he is the stone cut out without hands, which grew into an immense mountain (Daniel 2:34–35, 45); he who, lifted up from the earth, draws all things to himself (John 12:32): the solid mountain, the rich mountain. “Why do you look with suspicion, you Jews, upon the solid mountain, the mountain in which God has been pleased to dwell?” (Psalm 67:16–17). “By Beelzebub,” they say, “the prince of demons, he casts out demons.” [Col. 0629D] An execrable suspicion and blameworthy blasphemy! Christ is a prince, and a great prince, whose dominion not even the demons themselves can escape. But their kingdom, divided against itself, shall be laid waste (Matthew 12:24–25); his kingdom is whole and perfect, and of his kingdom there shall be no end (Luke 1:33). There is, therefore, a difference between the Prince and princes; nor is there any comparison between the solid and rich mountain and mountains that are merely solid. That Beelzebub of yours is a solid mountain, but not rich; indeed, he is cursed with perpetual barrenness. A mountain, because he is exalted; solid, because scale is joined to scale, and their heart is curdled like milk.

8. Christ the Lord is a mountain: a solid mountain [Col. 0630A] and a rich mountain. He is a mountain by loftiness, solid by the gathering of many, rich by charity. Now see how he draws all things to himself, how all things are united to him in substantial, personal, spiritual, and sacramental unity. He has in himself the Father, with whom he is one substance; he has the assumed manhood, with which he is one person; he has the faithful soul adhering to him, with which he is one spirit; he has as bride the Church, one body of all the elect, with which he is one flesh. Perhaps this union might seem better described as carnal; but I have preferred to call it sacramental, judging that designation more worthy, especially since the Apostle gives occasion for it when he says: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak in Christ and in the Church” (Ephesians 5:32). A most rich and fruitful mountain indeed, in which God has been pleased to dwell; for this reason he anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions. A mountain of heavenly spices, a mountain of spiritual gifts, receiving the Spirit not by measure but possessing every kind of fullness of graces. A great mountain in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden; in which dwells the whole truth of humanity and the whole fullness of divinity; lofty and immense, in which all things in heaven and on earth are restored, so that God may be all in all.

9. Come, brothers, let us ascend this mountain. If the road seems steep to us, let us unburden ourselves; if narrow, let us not spare even to empty ourselves; if long, let us hasten all the more; if laborious, let us cry to him: [Col. 0630C] “Draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song of Songs 1:3). Blessed is the one who runs thus, so as to seize the prize—or rather, so as himself to be seized—and to merit admission into that breadth of the mountain and fullness of the body of Christ. Blessed is the one who ascends that beatifying mountain with such longing and perseverance that, receiving a place of standing in the holy place, he may appear before God the Father in his sanctuary and behold at once his power and glory (Psalm 62:3): truly none other than that same mountain of mountains, the solid and rich mountain, Jesus Christ our Lord. In him, indeed, through predestination from eternity, we appeared before him who loved us and bestowed grace upon us in his beloved Son, in whom he chose us before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). But then we shall know even as we are known, [Col. 0630D] when that most high and most fruitful mountain, more fully and perfectly exalted, shall draw all things to himself—he who is above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIV. On the words of Origen in Leviticus 10:9

1. The words read to you yesterday, I fear, may perhaps harm some if they receive them simply, according to their apparent sound: namely, words from Origen’s homily on that chapter of the Law in which Aaron and his sons are forbidden to drink wine when they are about to approach the altar. “My Saviour,” he says, “still even now mourns my sins, and remains in sorrow as long as we persist in error.” There are also many other statements of this sort, perhaps more copious than circumspect [Col. 0631A], and not so sober as eloquent. What is the meaning of this unfamiliar grunting? Or who among you is muttering something or other? I know that those learned in the divine Law laugh at such words; nevertheless, I confess myself debtor also to the less wise. Nor is the question now merely about Origen’s meaning. Perhaps he spoke hyperbolically; that is his own concern, and it matters nothing to us. Yet I think that this too should not be passed over in silence: the authority of the holy Fathers reports that he wrote certain things plainly contrary to the faith, and therefore advises that he be read only with caution. But at present we are not asking what he himself thought; rather, we wish to ensure that all of you, holding what pertains to sound doctrine, are not disturbed by those words.

[Col. 0631B]

2. Far be it that heaven should be believed to contain a place of sadness, any more than of sin. No one there can sin; no one can mourn: just as there would have been no punishment on earth unless iniquity had first occurred. In heaven there is righteousness alone, and likewise joy alone; in hell there is sin alone and the punishment of sin. Between the two, both are found, and therefore neither is consummated. “We are offended in many things, because we all offend in many things” (James 3:2). Since there could be no place in heaven for suffering or pain, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, who was to redeem humanity by his suffering, assumed flesh in which he might suffer—for he could not suffer in his divinity—and likewise was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings (Baruch 3:38), so that he might humble himself also in the place [Col. 0631C] of affliction. Here, therefore, he deigned to trouble himself, to fear, and to grow weary, “tempted in all things according to our likeness, without sin.” On earth, I say, Jesus truly wept, was truly saddened, truly suffered, truly died, and was truly buried; but where he rose, the old things passed away. Seek your beloved no longer in your bed: he has risen; he is not here. It is the bride’s voice: “On my bed I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him” (Song of Songs 3:1). It was Mary who sought the Lord in the bed, sought him in the tomb, and did not find him. Rather, the watchmen found her and said, “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” (Matthew 28:5; Luke 24:5). He was indeed with the dead, but is no longer there; he was among the dead, yet even then [Col. 0631D] he was free. For he himself troubled himself; he himself laid down his soul; because he was offered of his own will (Isaiah 53:7). Every weakness in him was voluntary, not necessary. Hence “what was weak in God was stronger than men” (1 Corinthians 1:25): even then he was great among little ones, strong among the weak, free among the dead.

3. In our own tribulations, indeed, there sometimes seems to be a certain freedom when, through a free and generous charity, we undergo the labour of penance for the sins of our neighbours: mourning for them, fasting for them, being beaten for them, and paying back what we did not steal. Hence Paul says: “Though I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all” (1 Corinthians 9:19). But this is nothing compared with the freedom [Col. 0632A] of him who had no fault of his own, owed nothing to death, and deserved no tribulation. For from us, even those voluntary tribulations—though perhaps a neighbour cannot lawfully exact them—God nonetheless exacts; and though a person may seem perhaps to repay his neighbour more than he owes, no one has ever repaid God in full what he owed. “But to me,” says the Apostle, “it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by a human day; indeed, I do not even judge myself” (1 Corinthians 4:3). Observe, certainly, that elsewhere he says: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31); and again: “The spiritual person judges all things” (1 Corinthians 2:15). He does not here use *judicare*, “to judge,” but *dijudicare*, “to discriminate or examine,” as he also says: “Blessed is he who does not judge himself in that which he approves” (Romans 14:22). Thus it was a very small thing to him to be judged by those from whom he knew he had withheld nothing of the service due, against whom he had sinned in nothing, but rather had rendered service to all—so much so that, with a secure conscience, he frankly said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Corinthians 11:29). For he became a Jew to the Jews, that he might gain the Jews; and to those without the Law, as though without the Law; finally, he became all things to all people, that he might save all (1 Corinthians 9:22). Rightly, then, it was a very small thing to him to be judged by those among whom he had shown himself so wholly without offence, and among whom he had so honoured his ministry. Yet he did not even examine himself in what he approved, rendering perfectly even to himself what he owed: chastisement to his body, compassion to his soul, and every careful guard to his heart, so that he was not conscious even in himself of sin. But “I am not thereby justified,” he says; “he who judges me is the Lord” (1 Corinthians 4:4). For I cannot at all escape his judgment; and if I were righteous, I should not lift up my head, since all my righteousnesses are before him like a menstrual cloth (Isaiah 64:6). There is no one who may be justified in his sight; there is not one.

4. For, as regards all others, there is no one who ought not to say to God, “Against you have I sinned”; but great is the one who can say truthfully, “Against you alone” (Psalm 50:6). He alone was altogether free even among the dead: he who committed no sin, whose righteousness is like the mountains of God. But now [Col. 0632D] he is no longer among the dead; rather, he has been taken up from them, changed in body and changed also in heart, entered into the powers of the Lord, and stripped of every weakness. He has put off, indeed, those filthy garments in which he first appeared clothed in the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 3:3), and has put on splendid ones, as he says in the Psalm: “You have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Psalm 29:12). For since he assumed the true substance of human flesh and soul, the true nature of each, neither bodily sufferings nor passions of soul were lacking to him; but from this point he has been glorified in both. I think the Prophet comprehends the glorification of both in one brief verse: “The Lord has reigned; he has put on splendour; the Lord has put on strength” (Psalm 92:1). Splendour, certainly, is the radiance of the body; strength, the untroubled state of the mind. Finally, he says, “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matthew 26:38). And, bowing his head, he said, “It is finished” (John 19:30), so that thereafter no weakness may be suspected in him.

5. But this writer says: “If the Apostle himself mourns certain people who previously sinned and did not repent of what they had done” (2 Corinthians 12:21), “what shall I say of him who is called the Son of Charity?” And then: “When, therefore, he has sought the things that are ours, does he now no longer seek us, nor think of the things that are ours, nor grieve over our errors, nor weep over our destruction and ruin—he who wept over Jerusalem?” (Luke 19:41). Again he says: “Now, because the Lord is merciful and compassionate, with greater affection [Col. 0633B] than his Apostle he weeps with those who weep and mourns those who previously sinned. For we must not suppose that Paul mourns and weeps for sinners while my Lord refrains from weeping.” To understand these words in that way—what else is it but still to seek the beloved in the bed? One who does not know how to seek the dead outside the tomb, the sick outside the bed, the little child outside the cradle, does not know how to seek him whom the soul loves. But he, as we recalled above, has been glorified no less in heart than in body—indeed, much more, inasmuch as the soul is greater and more capable of glory than flesh—and therefore, just as he cannot neglect his own, so neither can he mourn for them. But when can human frailty grasp such an affection: one which has compassion without misery, and so loves—even loves vehemently—someone who suffers or is in danger, while itself feels neither pain nor disturbance at all? Yet even though this is far beyond our experience, nothing is impossible to God. He can therefore confer, not only on himself but also on all his own whom, stripped of the weakness of the flesh, he has clothed with power and introduced into the powers of heaven, that love which rejoices with those who rejoice but does not weep with those who weep; and unite most effectively and affectionately those whom he loves, while itself nevertheless remains untroubled. Nor is it doubtful that such love is far more excellent, just as a medicine—if any such exists—is rightly judged more precious when it heals wounds in such a way that neither its power nor its substance is diminished in any respect while healing, than one which [Col. 0633D] heals in such a way as to fail or be corrupted in the act of healing. Therefore, although the Lord wept over Jerusalem, from this point he will not weep at all; just as he died, but having risen from the dead now dies no more (Romans 6:9); just as he was in the bed, but having risen is no longer found in the bed.

6. Yet even now he has an affection unspeakably greater and more effective than that of those who mourn for sinners or lay down their souls for their brothers, although he himself, his work having been completed, will henceforth do neither. This belongs to our weakness, we whose net is still being drawn in the sea and gathers fish of every kind, making no distinction whatever. For he—not he alone, but also the apostles and the other saints with him—has reached the shore; and they have placed in vessels no mixed fish, but only the chosen and good, for they cast the bad outside (Matthew 13:47–48). How many bad fish I am meanwhile compelled to draw! How many anxious and troublesome ones I have gathered within my net, since my soul has become attached to you! I rejoice with those who make progress: a pleasant affection, a good fish. I suffer with those who fail; I weep with those who weep; I am distressed for those in danger; I am weak with the weak; I burn with the scandalized. These things are grievous and bitter: certainly they are bad fish. But I call them bad, not because of guilt, but because of punishment. May God grant that we not be overwhelmed by the multitude of bad fish, by faintness of spirit and tempest, until we reach the resting-place of the desired shore, where we may separate and set apart the bad from the good; so that henceforth there may be no mourning, no crying, no pain, nor even any fear within our borders, but thanksgiving and the voice of exultation.

## SERMON XXXV. On the three orders of the Church, delivered to the fathers in chapter

> **Note:** [Col. 0633D] In the Colbert manuscript, of excellent authority, this sermon is placed before the sermon on the Nativity of Blessed Mary; in the Royal manuscript, after it, under this title: “Sermon to the abbots coming to the chapter at Cîteaux.” In the French manuscript from Feuillants, [Col. 0634D] among the sermons on Lent. Formerly, it was customary for the Chapter of Cîteaux to be held on the Ides of September. This sermon is cited in the *Book of Flowers*, book 8, chapters 26, 37, etc.

1. This great and wide sea—by which, certainly, nothing other than the bitter, surging present age is signified—is passable by three kinds of human beings, each in its own manner, so that they may cross over and be delivered. For there are three: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezekiel 14:14). The first crosses by ship, the second by bridge, the third by ford. Moreover, these three men signify three orders of the Church. Noah indeed governed the ark so that it should not perish in the flood: in him I immediately recognize the image of the rulers of the Church. Daniel, a man of desires devoted to abstinence and chastity, is the order of penitents and continent persons, occupied with God alone. Job, likewise, dispensing well the substance of this world in marriage, signifies the faithful people who lawfully possess earthly goods. We must therefore speak of the first and second orders, since our venerable brothers and fellow abbots, belonging to the number of prelates, are present; and monks also of the order of penitents are present. Yet we abbots ought not to count ourselves strangers to that order, unless perhaps—may it never be!—we have, on account of our office, become forgetful of our profession. I shall pass over the third order, namely that of married persons, more briefly, as less relevant to us. It is this order that crosses the great sea chiefly by ford: a journey altogether laborious, dangerous, and long, since it takes no short cuts. That the journey is dangerous is evident from the fact that we grieve to see so many perish upon it and see so few, as must be the case, [Col. 0635A] cross over. For it is very difficult, especially in these days when wickedness has grown exceedingly strong, to avoid the waves of this age [variant: “world”], the whirlpool of vices, and the pits of grave sins.

2. The order of continent persons, however, crosses by bridge; and no one fails to know that this route is shorter, easier, and safer. But I omit its praises and point out its dangers instead, for that is much better and more useful. Your path, dearly beloved, is straight and safer than that of married persons, yet not wholly safe. For a threefold danger must be feared: that someone may perhaps wish either to make himself equal to another, or to look back, or indeed to stand still or sit down in the middle of the bridge. The narrowness of the bridge and the strait way that leads to life allows none of these three. Against the first danger, therefore, let each of us pray with the Prophet: “Let not the foot of pride come against us, for there the workers of iniquity have fallen” (Psalm 35:12–13). For concerning one who puts his hand to the plough and afterwards turns back, it is certain that he immediately slips, and the sea covers his head. And one who wishes to stand still—not by abandoning the order, indeed, but by neglecting to advance in it—must necessarily fall, thrust down and overthrown by those who follow. For the way is narrow, and he is an impediment to those wishing to advance. Hence they continually rebuke and reprove him: they cannot bear the sluggishness of his lukewarmness; like people using goads, they urge and press upon him with their hands, so that one of two things must happen—either he advances, or he fails utterly. Therefore one must by no means halt one’s step; to look back or to make ourselves equal to others is still less expedient. Rather, we must run and hasten in all humility, lest he who has gone forth as a giant to run his course become far distant from us. If we are wise, keeping him always before our eyes and being drawn by his fragrance, we shall run more easily and swiftly.

3. Nor will the path of the bridge be found excessively narrow by those willing to run upon it. For it is put together out of three timbers, so that the foot of those who desire to lean perfectly upon them will not slip on the way. These are bodily punishment, poverty of worldly substance, and the humility of obedience. For “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14:21); and “those who wish to become rich in this age fall into temptation and the snare of the devil” (1 Timothy 6:9); and whoever was driven away from his God through disobedience undoubtedly returns to him by obedience, along the straight path. These, therefore, must be joined together with one another. For bodily punishment can be neither stable amid riches nor easily regulated without obedience; poverty amid self-indulgence and self-will has no merit and no weight before God; and obedience amid riches and pleasure is neither stable nor glorious.

4. But when these have been rightly arranged, see whether you have not perfectly escaped the three dangers of this sea: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride [Col. 0636A] of life. “Rightly arranged,” I say, so that in bodily punishment you beware the knot of impatience; in poverty, the thorn of covetousness; and in obedience, the blemish of self-will. For “those who murmured perished by serpents” (1 Corinthians 10:9); and those “who wish to become rich”—he does not say, “who are rich,” but “who wish to become rich”—fall into temptations and the snare of the devil. And what difference does it make if, God forbid, you should desire not riches but the very things belonging to poverty with as much affection, or even more ardently, than worldly people desire riches? What difference is there in the substance desired, when the affection is equally corrupted—except that it may seem more tolerable to desire very greatly things that appear, in whatever way, to be of greater value? Moreover, whoever openly or secretly labours to have his spiritual father command him what he himself wants, deceives himself if perhaps he flatters himself that he is acting from obedience. For in that matter it is not he who obeys the superior, but rather the superior who obeys him.

5. Nevertheless, because according to the sentence of the Saviour, “with what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you again” (Mark 4:24), it is good for a person to give this in abundance, so as to belong to the number of those to whom they shall give into their bosom “a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over.” For it is sufficient for salvation patiently to endure bodily hardships; but it is abundance to embrace them gladly in fervour of spirit. It may suffice not to seek superfluities, nor to murmur because necessities are lacking; [Col. 0636C] but it is abundance also to rejoice and gladly seek a way for another to possess necessities more abundantly while oneself suffers want. Likewise, it suffices for salvation neither to seek, through impatience or some pretence, to incline against his will the mind of one’s superior toward what one desires; but it is abundance even to avoid those things in which one perceives one’s own will to take pleasure, insofar, certainly, as this can be done with a good conscience.

6. Prelates, however, are those who “go down to the sea in ships, doing business in great waters.” For they are not constrained by any fixed path of bridge or ford, so that they may freely travel everywhere, meet each person as need requires, direct the path of the bridge or seek out the ford [variant: “seek out the ford”], arrange those who are proceeding, investigate and avoid dangers, rouse the lukewarm, and sustain the faint-hearted. Finally, they ascend up to the heavens and descend down to the depths: now treating spiritual and lofty matters, now discerning infernal and horrible deeds. But what ship can be found that can withstand such enormous waves and remain secure amid such great danger? Surely one with love strong as death and zeal hard as hell, because, as you have elsewhere: “Many waters cannot quench charity” (Song of Songs 8:6–7). This ship is necessary—altogether necessary—for prelates: a ship built of three sides, which is indeed the form of ships, so that it may be, according to Paul’s teaching, “charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5). Let the prelate have purity of heart in this: that he desires to be of benefit, not to exercise authority; that is, that he seeks in his prelation neither his own advantage, worldly honour, nor anything else of his own, except solely God’s good pleasure and the salvation of souls. But together with pure intention, irreproachable conduct is also necessary, so that, made an example to the flock, he may begin to do and to teach; and, according to the Rule of our master [St Benedict, *Rule*, ch. 2], whatever he teaches his disciples to be contrary to, he may show by his own actions not to be done—lest a brother whom he rebukes should perhaps mutter and say, “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23). Such an occasion is the great condemnation of the prelate and the great destruction of those subject to him. I do not say this because I myself guard against it well; but Truth cries out alike to me and to all that one who presides must be irreproachable (1 Timothy 3:2), so that with a secure conscience he may answer the reproaches of others with the Lord’s words: “Which of you shall convict me of sin?” (John 8:46). This does not mean that he can be wholly without sin in this miserable life, but that the master must take the greatest care to avoid those things which he rebukes in his disciples.

7. For this reason, such as he is in conduct, such must he necessarily be also in hidden thought, lest he be humble outwardly but inwardly exalted in his heart, presuming upon his wisdom, strength, or holiness. This is undoubtedly feigned faith, when he does not trust, as the humility of his conduct shows, in the Lord’s mercy alone. And see how aptly three further words of the Apostle seem to correspond to these three—purity of heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith—when he says: “But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by a human day,” and so on. “I do not judge myself,” he says, because I am conscious of no seeking of anything of my own, but only what belongs to Jesus Christ. And “it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you,” because of a good conscience and irreproachable conduct [variant: “life”]. “But he who judges me,” he says, “is the Lord” (1 Corinthians 4:3–4), so that he might teach that he had placed his hope in him alone, humbled under the mighty hand of God. Consider also whether Peter’s threefold question may aptly be applied to these things: “Do you love me? Do you love me? Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). Do you have charity from a pure [Col. 0637D] heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith? Rightly, then, the fisherman is asked concerning the ship whether he has charity, when he is about to be made a fisher of human beings.

## SERMON XXXVI

> **Note:** [Col. 0637D] This sermon, like the three following, is placed in all manuscripts among the sermons for the liturgical seasons, after the sermons for the Sixth Sunday after Pentecost; but [Col. 0638D] in the Cîteaux manuscript it is marked that they should be transferred to after Sermon 39 *On Various Subjects*, although in all printed editions they are placed after Sermon 35.

### On the height and lowliness of the heart

1. Concerning what was said very recently—that some look upward and others downward (*Sermon 12 On Various Subjects*, no. 2)—I have still something that I should not withhold from your charity. For those thoughts which we then set forth, if you remember well, though one is more perfect than the other, are both useful. There are some who have their hearts raised upward in one way, as “God made man upright,” and who confidently answer the priest’s exhorting call: “We have them unto the Lord.” There are others who, bent downward like brute animals, make themselves a laughingstock to unclean spirits, who certainly cry out in mockery: “Bend down, that we may pass over” (Isaiah 51:23). For you know that in a congregation of many it is impossible for all to possess equal strength, whether of body or of character; and the authority of our Rule bids us patiently bear both kinds of weakness [Rule of St Benedict, ch. 72] and charity commands us to accommodate ourselves in some measure to both. Someone sees this, and perhaps begins to envy one whom he ought to pity. Hence it happens that he often counts another blessed in his heart for the very matter on account of which that other regards himself as miserable, bearing his necessity painfully. He therefore proves himself utterly bent over, and carnally minded with a low heart, since even misery itself is not free from envy in him. But he fixes his heart on the dispensations which a prelate grants to another’s necessity out of a sure consideration of charity; he seeks similar concessions and murmurs against him who refuses his unreasonable demand. From this arise suspicions, detractions, and scandals.

2. I do not say this, dearest brethren, as though I had grave complaint against you in this matter. Rather, I have judged it necessary to forewarn and fortify you because many among you are tender and frail, for whom either age or infirmity requires that the strictness of the common rule be moderated somewhat. Give thanks to him from whose gift this comes; for I see here many whose minds, intent upon God, have become so far removed from that base thought that they wholly fail to notice the weaker brethren placed beside them, and complain that they themselves do less than everyone else. Doubtless this is because they always look to those above them, forgetting, with the Apostle, what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead (Phil. 3:13). How greatly, do you suppose, I admire them, how greatly I venerate them in my heart, how greatly I embrace them with the affection of charity: those who, as though unaware of those whom they see daily with them, select from among all perhaps one or two—or even more—whom they have observed to possess greater fervour of spirit; and, though they themselves may perhaps be better, nevertheless always set before and above themselves those persons’ holy endeavours in the Lord and bodily or spiritual exercises.

[Col. 0638D] 3. I remember that I have already said on another occasion—and I shall not be reluctant to repeat it—that a certain lay monk [variant: brother] devoted the whole span of the night watches to a most exalted meditation. Early in the morning he seized me and drew me into the chapter room; then, falling at my feet, he said: “Woe is me, for during the vigils I considered one monk in whom I counted thirty virtues, not one of which I find in myself” (see *Life of St Bernard*, bk. VII, ch. 23). And perhaps that monk possessed no virtue as great as this very humility of religious emulation. Let this, then, be the fruit of our present discourse: always to attend to what is loftier in others, because therein consists the fullness of humility. For even if, in some matter, you seem to have received a grace greater than that of a brother, still, in many things, if you are a good imitator, you may judge yourself inferior.

For what if you are perhaps able to labour or fast more than he, while he surpasses you in patience, goes before you in humility, and excels you in charity? Why do you spend the whole day foolishly turning over in thought that which you think you possess? Be more concerned to know what you lack. This is better. Would that, brothers, we were as eager for spiritual grace as worldly people are for temporal money! Certainly we ought, and greatly ought, to overcome evil with good, and to desire all the more fervently because that which we desire is more precious. Yet would that we might at least be equal to them! [Col. 0639B] For it is a great—indeed a very great—shame that they desire harmful things more ardently than we desire useful things; that they hasten more swiftly toward death than we toward life. Who can explain with what desire of money the miser is tormented, with what craving for glory the ambitious man burns, or with what violence his own pleasure drags each person along? You may certainly see them despise whatever they have acquired, taking no account of the labour and desire through which they could scarcely at last attain it, because everything becomes cheap to them beside the longing for some lesser thing which they have begun to envy in another.

4. Therefore, do not dwell excessively upon what you seem to possess, except perhaps sometimes, so that you may give thanks and recognize yourself as indebted to him who gave it; or by way of consolation when necessary, lest you become too sad for any reason. [Col. 0639C] Otherwise, attend rather always to what another possesses and you do not possess, so that this thought may preserve you in humility, keep you from descending into lukewarmness, and indeed kindle in you a desire to make progress.

But observe how many evils, conversely, are brought forth by that thought through which you continually turn over in your mind what you seem to possess and judge another person not to possess. From this you are lifted up into pride, while you set yourself above another; from this you neglect to advance, while you consider yourself someone great; from this, finally, you even begin to decline, while you think that, by comparison with another, you have done more than enough. Thus you fall into lukewarmness and begin to act more slackly. Yet we know that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4:6), and that cursed is he who performs the work of God negligently (Jer. 48:10). Blessed, however, are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness; for if by the Spirit we mortify the deeds of the flesh, we shall live; but if we live according to the flesh, we shall die (Rom. 8:13).

## SERMON XXXVII

At the harvest labour. [Note: [Col. 0639D] Compare Book I of the *Life of Bernard*, no. 24, and Abbot Guerric’s third sermon on the Assumption of the Blessed Mary, no. 1, where he speaks of harvest labour. From no. 1 [Col. 0640D] it appears that this sermon was delivered on returning from a certain long journey, perhaps to Rome.] On the words of Psalm 23:6: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.”

1. Wearied in spirit by the diverse crowds of people and their diverse pursuits, how eagerly I came today to this company, to refresh my spirit! Thanks [Col. 0640A] be to God: I have not been defrauded of my desire nor disappointed in my hope. I longed to see; I saw, and my soul melted away. I am filled with consolation; I overflow with joy; all that is within me blesses the name of the Lord, and all my bones say: “Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. 34:10). Indeed, as I drew near and looked from afar, I confess that I seemed to see bodily those whom the Prophet had once foreseen in spirit. Immediately there came into my mind what he had uttered with his mouth, so that I might sing the psalm with him, saying: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord.”

2. There are many generations of human beings, and, unless I am mistaken, this is the third generation, which now flourishes and appears among you. The first generation neither yet sought the Lord nor was sought by the Lord, when each person was brought forth by his mother amid forgetfulness of mind and the guilt of iniquity. The second, consequently, immediately—as was necessary—presented us with a swift remedy from water and the Spirit. It was not yet indeed a generation of seekers, but already a generation of those who had been sought; because, though they did not yet know how to seek the Lord or have power to do so, he himself sought them. Therefore, he sought us and acquired us in the second generation, that we might now be a people of possession. If perhaps the elder brother still murmurs and wastes away with envy, he is told that it was fitting to feast and rejoice, because “this brother of yours was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32).

3. Yet the Lord immediately sought us for this purpose: that he might be sought at the proper time, when he could already [Col. 0640C] be sought and found. Woe to us, because for so long we have delayed and neglected to seek life, to seek him who alone is good to those who seek him—to the soul that hopes in him! Woe to you, perverse and provoking generation, evil and adulterous generation, still seeking falsehood today and loving vanity, and not keeping faith with the Truth to whom you were betrothed! Does not such a generation need to be born anew, to be generated again? Most certainly. Having become a brood of vipers, they now need all the more to enter once more into the womb of Mother Grace and be reborn, since their latter state is found worse than their former.

Thanks be to Grace itself, and—to speak if it may be spoken—to mercy more than gratuitous, which overwhelms with benefits not merely the undeserving but those who have deserved very ill and have been ungrateful. [Col. 0640D] Thanks be to him who has regenerated you even this time in the hope of life, that you might receive adoption as sons. For now he has begotten you voluntarily and properly, namely by the word of truth. For although previously he begot you through the sacrament of loving-kindness—and this act was voluntary on the part of the begetter—it could not be voluntary in those begotten, in whom there was as yet no use of will and no exercise of reason, and consequently no awareness of that begetting and no knowledge of so great a begetter. Now at last a voluntary generation offers a voluntary sacrifice, according to the saying: “Freely will I sacrifice to you, and I will confess your name, O Lord, for it is good” (Ps. 53:8).

[Col. 0641A] 4. This is the generation of those who seek the Lord. Shall I say, of those who seek, or of those who possess? Of those who both possess and seek, certainly; otherwise, not possessing, they could not seek. But what do they possess, and what do they seek? Or rather, how do they possess, and how do they seek? Begotten by the Word, they possess the Word. Is not the Word the Lord? Hear John: “And the Word was God” (John 1:1). What more, then, does the generation that seeks [variant: possesses] the Lord now seek? Consider what follows in the psalm: “This,” he says, “is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.” Thus they possess and seek the same one, 1161 because he is one and the same: the Word of the Father and the brightness of the Father’s glory. Perhaps he can be possessed without being sought; but he cannot at all be sought unless he is possessed. [Col. 0641B] Finally, Wisdom herself says of herself: “Those who eat me will still hunger” (Sir. 24:29).

He is able to grant himself even to one who does not seek him, for, as we have shown above, out of the abundance of grace and the blessing of sweetness he seeks and anticipates those still unable to seek. But no one is fit to seek before possessing; for “no one,” he says, “comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6:44). Therefore, he who draws is present, and in a certain way he who is not yet present is present; for he draws by no other means than to himself. For the Father is never and nowhere present through faith without the Son, in order to draw to vision.

How then should my spirit not exult now? How should it not rejoice without measure in this generation of those who seek the Lord? [Col. 0641C] Indeed, the very vehement hunger is an exceedingly trustworthy testimony to wisdom already tasted. To me, you are a most certain proof and an unquestionable argument that you possess him whom you seek in this way, and that he dwells in you who draws you so powerfully to himself. This course is not within human capacity: his right hand works mightily, and you must always cry to him: “Draw us after you; we will run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3). This manner of life, I say, does not come from man; nor do we seek any other proof of Christ dwelling in you than that you seek Christ in this manner.

5. For you see, brothers, what kind of spirit you have received: the Spirit who is from God, that you may know the things given you by God. We have heard of the apostolic, the prophetic, and even the angelic rank, than which, I think, nothing more sublime can be desired by us. Yet I seem to find something from each in you—and something great. Who would hesitate truly to call a celibate life a heavenly and angelic life? Or how are you not already what all the elect will be in the resurrection—like the angels of God in heaven—when you wholly abstain from marriage? [Col. 0641D] Embrace, brothers, this most precious pearl; embrace holiness of life, which makes you like the saints and members of God’s household, Scripture saying: “Incorruption makes one near to God” (Wis. 6:20).

Thus, not indeed by your own merit but by the grace of God, you are what you are: with respect to chastity and holiness, certain earthly angels—or rather, citizens of heaven—yet pilgrims meanwhile on earth. [Col. 0642A] For as long as we are in this body, we are away from the Lord.

6. What shall we say concerning prophecy? “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16). Truth says so. Yet he was not an opponent but indeed a disciple of Truth who said even after John: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.” Prophecy has therefore ceased, because we now know; yet it has not wholly ceased, because we still know only in part. “When,” he says, “that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 13:9–10). For the prophets before John prophesied both comings of the Lord; and, as though neither part of salvation was yet known, both were in prophecy.

This is indeed a great kind of prophesying to which I see you devoted, a great pursuit of prophecy to which I see you committed. What is it? Surely, according to the Apostle, not to consider things seen but things unseen (2 Cor. 4:18) is to prophesy, without doubt. To walk in the Spirit, to live by faith, to seek the things above and not the things upon the earth; to forget what lies behind and stretch forward to what lies ahead: this is, in large measure, to prophesy. Otherwise, how could our citizenship be in heaven except through the spirit of prophecy? Thus the prophets of old were, as it were, not among the people of their own time; but, leaping beyond those days by a certain power and impetus [Col. 0642C] of the Spirit, they rejoiced to see the Lord’s day, and they saw it and rejoiced in it.

7. But let us hear also the apostolic profession: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). If it is permitted to boast, we have a glory; but if we are wise, we shall take care to possess it before God. For this is true boasting: “Let him who boasts, boast in the Lord.” Our hand has not been exalted; rather, the Lord has done all these things. He who is mighty has done great things for us, so that our soul rightly magnifies the Lord. It was by his great gift that we magnificently followed that great purpose in which the apostles gloried so greatly.

Perhaps, even if I wished to boast in this as well, I would not be foolish, for I should speak the truth: there are some here who have left more than a boat and nets. [Note: [Col. 0641D] Certainly people of the highest ranks at that time flocked into the Cistercian Order, especially to Clairvaux, as Bernard himself acknowledges in his first sermon on the Dedication of a Church, no. 2. [Col. 0642D] Read Ernald’s prologue to Book II of the *Life of St Bernard*, and the letter of Peter of Roya, no. 9, above, col. 810.] But what is that? The apostles themselves left everything, but in order to follow the Lord present in the flesh. It is not for us to speak of this; let us more safely hear the Lord himself: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29).

Perhaps also this kind of prophesying will seem more excellent: it fixes attention not on any temporal things which will one day pass away, but on spiritual and eternal things. Nevertheless, the treasure of chastity is more splendid in an earthen vessel, [Col. 0643A] and virtue is in some degree more worthy of approval in frail flesh.

8. Where, then, an angelic manner of life is found in this body, a prophetic expectation in the heart, and apostolic perfection in both, how great is this accumulation of graces! What will you render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to you? The rank is exalted, but the fall from it is correspondingly more dangerous. Have we not ascended three heavens? Therefore, let him who stands take heed lest he fall. “I saw,” he says, “Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). He fell from on high; he was shattered and crushed; his wound became hopeless; he became a spirit that goes and does not return. Do you also wish to depart? Satan fell: do you also fall with him? How much healthier for you to stand in the ways of the Lord, to stand in the grace in which you stand.

For the man who [variant adds: ‘not’] has gone in the way of sinners is not blessed; rather, blessed is he whose help is from you, O Lord. Such persons will go from strength to strength, to see the God of gods in Zion, to behold the goodness of your chosen ones, that you may be praised with your inheritance. For they themselves are the inheritance; they are gods, and all are sons of the Most High.

9. Therefore, my brothers, since this is most truly and certainly the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob, what else shall I say to you except what the same Prophet says: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. 104:3–4). And what another says: “If you seek, seek” [Col. 0643C] (Isa. 21:12). What is “If you seek, seek”? “Seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1:1). Seek not something else as though it were he; seek not something else besides him; seek not something else after him. Seek him in simplicity of heart. The simple nature requires simplicity of heart. Indeed, his conversation is with the simple.

“A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jas. 1:8). He whom you seek cannot be found by those who believe for a time and in the time of temptation fall away. He is Eternity, and cannot be found unless sought perseveringly. Woe also to the sinner who enters the land by two ways (Sir. 2:14). For no one can serve two masters (Luke 16:13). That integrity, that perfection, that fullness does not love even this doubleness. For it is unworthy of him to offer himself to be found unless you seek him [Col. 0643D] with a perfect heart.

Moreover, if a dog returning to its own vomit and a washed sow to wallowing in mire are hateful (2 Pet. 2:22), and if God begins to vomit even the person whom he finds lukewarm out of his mouth (Rev. 3:16), where will the pretender and traitor appear? If cursed is one who does the work of God negligently, what does one deserve who does it deceitfully? Let us flee this doubleness, dearest brethren, and in every way beware the leaven of the Pharisees. God is truth, and he requires seekers who seek him in spirit and truth. If we do not wish to seek the Lord in vain, let us seek him truly, frequently, and perseveringly: so that we seek nothing in place of him, nothing along with him, and do not turn from him to something else. For heaven and earth will more easily pass away [Col. 0644A] than one who seeks thus should fail to find, one who asks thus fail to receive, or one who knocks thus fail to have opened to him.

## SERMON XXXVIII. II

At the harvest labour, on the Apostle’s saying: “All things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. 8:28).

1. We seem poor, and we are poor. But if we have received the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know [variant: “we are, we know, yet we know the things that are from God,” etc.] the things given us by God; great glory [variant: grace] and great power have been granted us by him. “As many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12). Is this not the power of children of God, when all things even serve us? For the Apostle himself knew that all things work together for good to those who love God.

But perhaps one of you may say: “What is this to me?” and in the faint-heartedness of his heart may reflect thus: “Let those certainly boast of the power of children of God in whom filial love for him burns and affection flourishes; let those who truly love God presume that all things work together for their good. But I am needy and poor, lacking filial affection and without worthy devotion.” But attend to what follows. For he who elsewhere speaks thus—“That through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15:4)—left no place in his Scripture for despair. The affection you seek is peace, not patience; it belongs to the homeland, not the road; and those who possess it have no need to be consoled by Scripture.

2. Therefore, through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures, let us have hope, even if we cannot yet [Col. 0644C] attain peace. Thus, after saying that all things work together for good to those who love God, he carefully added: “to those who are called saints according to his purpose.” In this phrase, do not let the name of holiness alarm you. For he calls them saints not according to merit but according to purpose, not according to affection but according to intention, according to the Prophet’s saying: “Preserve my soul, for I am holy” (Ps. 86:2).

Even Paul himself, still weighed down by a corruptible body, did not think that he had attained the holiness which you imagine. “But one thing,” he says: “forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead, I press on toward the prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. 3:13–14). You see that, although he had not yet attained the prize, he already possessed holiness of purpose and the purpose of holiness. Therefore, if you have resolved in your heart to turn from evil and do good, to hold fast to what you have begun and always advance toward what is better; and if, when you have at some time acted less rightly—as human frailty does—you do not persist in it, but repent and correct it as far as you can: then you too will doubtless be holy, though meanwhile you must still cry: “Preserve my soul, for I am holy.”

3. Do you wish, then, to know how saints of this sort have all things work together for their good? I shall not run through each point, because the hour does not permit the sermon to be drawn out at length. We must go: we have already heard the bell, and the time of evening prayer has arrived. Hear, then, a brief word on how all things serve us and work together for good. [Col. 0645A] Let our enemies be our judges. For if they are for us, who is against us? If our enemies act for us, how do not all things together with them do so?

4. Further, as is evident, two kinds of enemies oppose us: the twofold evil which we do and which we suffer. More plainly stated, these are guilt and punishment. Since each is contrary to us, each will, if we are willing, be for us: the latter will free us from the former, and the former in turn will help us against the latter—and not a little. For behold, we are pierced in our hearts and in the bedchamber of conscience over past offences. Yet this repentance—and the voluntary punishment which we undergo—soothes conscience, breaks the teeth of gnawing sins, and restores it [Col. 0645B] to hope of pardon.

It repels not only past sins but also future ones; for it drives back vices that tempt us and destroys some of them so thoroughly that they rarely, or never, dare lift up their venomous head. Thus punishment acts for us against guilt, so that guilt either does not exist at all or is lessened. Guilt likewise acts so that punishment either does not exist or is less; not so that punishment should be altogether absent, or diminished in its amount—which would by no means be expedient—but so that it may not be punishment, or may be a lesser punishment; that is, may either not exist as punishment or be less burdensome.

For whoever has perfectly felt the burden of sin and the wound of the soul will feel bodily punishment outwardly either little or not at all, and will not count as hardship that through which he knows past sins are erased [Col. 0645C] and future sins avoided. Thus holy David did not count the insults of the reviling servant as injuries, mindful of the son pursuing him (2 Sam. 16:11).

## SERMON XXXIX. III

At the harvest labour: On the two tables, or the upper and lower watered ground.

1. This labour, brothers, reminds us of our exile and poverty, and indeed of our iniquity. For why are we afflicted with death all day long, with many fasts, more abundant vigils, labours, and hardships? Were we created for this? Far from it! For although man is born for labour, he was by no means created for labour. Birth is in guilt, and therefore also in punishment. We must all groan with the Prophet, saying: “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” [Col. 0645D] (Ps. 51:7). The first creation was alien to both, because God made neither guilt nor punishment. Scripture clearly testifies this concerning the greatest of all, namely death: “Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world” (Wis. 2:24); and elsewhere: “God did not make death” (Wis. 1:13).

Therefore, just as when the hands labour the eye is not on that account closed, nor does the ear refrain from hearing, so—indeed, much more—the mind itself, while the body labours, should be intent upon its own work and not be idle. Let it ponder the cause of labour while labouring, so that the very punishment which it suffers may set before it the guilt for which it suffers; and while it sees the bandage upon wounds, let it meditate upon the wounds beneath the wrappings. By such thought we are humbled [Col. 0646A] under the mighty hand of God, and the mind, filled with a certain sweet devotion, presents itself as pitiable in his sight. Hence Scripture admonishes us: “Have mercy,” it says, “upon your soul, pleasing God” (Sir. 30:24). Nor is there any doubt that misery pleasing to God can easily obtain his mercy. And we need not ask what there is in our souls requiring mercy. Unless we foolishly conceal it, much may be found in them worthy of compassion.

2. Yet I will mention one thing, so that I may appear to have given you an occasion to notice the rest likewise. Are we not as though placed between two tables, fasting while we watch people feast on either side? This is exactly our condition. Whence then, for those so placed, laughter, jesting, frivolity, pride, or haughty eyes? Or do we perhaps not recognize the tables, not consider the feasts, not see the delights? On this side I have those whom I see living luxuriously amid all the good things of this sensible world; on that side I contemplate others for whom Christ has appointed a kingdom, that they may eat and drink at his table in the kingdom of his Father (Luke 22:29). On both sides I see people like myself, my brothers; and alas for me, I am permitted to extend my hand to neither. I am excluded from both tables: from this one by my profession, from that by the bond of the body. Thus I dare not approach the lower, nor can I attain the upper.

What remains amid these things but to eat the bread of sorrow, so that my tears may be my bread day and night, if perhaps, moved by mercy, one of the heavenly guests lets fall into the mouth of the little dog barking beneath the table even some small fragments [Col. 0646C] of those delights? For the lower consideration, through which we pity ourselves in comparison with those whom we know to live luxuriously in this age, belongs to a soul still weak; nor does such an affection wholly please me in a spiritual soul. For he stands farther from the judgment of truth who calls blessed those whom he ought to mourn as utterly wretched—those who sin and do not repent—and who considers himself miserable, not indeed by agreement with judgment, but by the feeling of affection, because he is not like them, though they ought rather to desire that all might be like him.

3. Yet this alone is praiseworthy in such a thought: if one determines patiently to bear the very misery which one reckons oneself to have, for the love or fear of God, and says to God with a certain devotion: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” [Col. 0646D] (Ps. 17:4). This thought belongs to beginners, like milk for little children. But when the soul has begun to advance and to follow the judgment of reason in its affections, it will undoubtedly regard all things as loss and, considering them as dung, will mourn with the prophet over those who have embraced dung (Lam. 4:5).

The person himself, with a holy and humble pride, will despise all these things; established in great elevation of soul, he will call blessed not the people that have these things but plainly miserable, while blessed is he whose Lord is his God. Yet while here he pities them in comparison with himself, he will surely find persons in comparison with whom he must pity himself as well, if he looks up to the riches of heaven and the delights at the right hand of the Lord forever. [Col. 0647A] Hence it comes about that he who formerly wept, shedding tears over the lower watered ground and saying, “For your sake we are put to death all day long” (Rom. 8:36), now pours forth more abundant tears over the upper, saying, “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 120:5).

## SERMON XL

[Note: [Col. 0647D] This sermon and the following one, in the Lyons edition of 1514, in which they first appeared, were placed outside the class of Bernard’s genuine sermons; nor do they seem fully to attain his style. Nevertheless, we have not considered it important to move them from this place, both because in Vatican manuscript no. 663 they are counted among Bernard’s sermons *On Various Subjects*, and because both are furnished with Bernard’s familiar concluding formula; finally, because the latter, at no. 12, sets forth the same doctrine as the holy Doctor concerning holy souls released from the body. The same judgment should be made concerning the third sermon following, which is likewise attributed to Bernard in the same Vatican manuscript.] On the seven degrees of confession.

1. “You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with joy by your countenance, delights at your right hand forever” (Ps. 15:11). We willingly draw near to you, Lord Jesus: disciples to a teacher, the sick to a physician, servants to their lord. For you are teacher and Lord, whose school is on earth and whose chair is in heaven. You are that eminent physician who restores all things by a word alone. “Show us your ways, O Lord, and teach us your paths” (Ps. 25:4), for “your ways are beautiful ways, and all your paths are peaceful” (Prov. 3:17). Blessed are those who walk in your way, O Lord of hosts; more blessed are those who run in the way of your commandments, who run in the fragrance of your ointments.

For you rejoice like a giant to run your course (Ps. 19:6), and not only run, but also leap upon the mountains and pass over the hills. The giants, the philosophers, rejoiced—not to run your way but to seek vain glory—becoming futile in their thoughts, not in your humility or virtues, but in their own. For they did not know the way of wisdom, nor did they remember her paths. It “has not been heard of in Canaan, nor seen in Teman” (Bar. 3:22). Cursed are those who said to the Lord Jesus: “Depart from us; we do not desire the knowledge of your ways” (Job 21:14). We seek you day by day and desire to know your ways.

2. Your principal ways are two: confession and obedience. In confession all things are washed; in obedience the virtues are made firm. Confession is a good ornament of the soul: it purifies the sinner and makes the righteous purer. If there are sins, they are washed in confession; if there are good deeds, they are commended by confession. When you confess your evils, a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; when you confess God’s benefits, you offer God a sacrifice of praise. Without confession, the righteous person is judged ungrateful and the sinner is considered dead. Confession, therefore, [Col. 0647D] is the sinner’s life and the righteous person’s glory.

I see David saying, “I have sinned,” and hearing, “The Lord has taken away your sin from you, and you shall not die” (2 Sam. 12:13). I consider Mary publicly confessing her crimes, if not in words then by deeds, and the Lord answering on her behalf: “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). I look upon the prince of the apostles denying fearfully, weeping most bitterly, and Christ looking upon him (Luke 22:56–62). I behold the blessed thief [Col. 0648A] accusing himself, excusing Christ, and the Lord promising: “Today you shall be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:40–43).

O how sublime is this confession, through which the condemned and crucified thief ascended from the gallows to the kingdom, from earth to heaven, from the cross to Paradise! Glorious confession, which freed Peter the Apostle from the guilt of threefold denial and did not permit him to fall from the summit of apostleship! Faithful institution, which forgave much to Mary who loved much and joined her, distinguished by the title of great love, to the company of the disciples! Excellent mercy, which cleansed king and prophet from a manifold flood of crimes and restored him by bringing him back to the glory of his former dignity! This is the way which has never deceived its traveller, which has never deserted anyone except one who deserts it.

[Col. 0648B] 3. This way has many roads and manifold paths for finding it, difficult to keep, impossible to enumerate. The first path and first degree on this way is self-knowledge. This maxim fell from heaven: “Know yourself, O man.” See whether the Bridegroom does not say the same to the bride in the Song of Love: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out and depart” (Song 1:7), etc.

Self-knowledge consists in three things: that a person know what he has done, what he has deserved, and what he has lost. What is more degrading, O noble creature, image of God, likeness of the Creator, than to disfigure your flesh with carnal enticements and to lose, for a brief pleasure, the torrent of delight? What is more mad than for the mind to be seized by anger, lifted up by pride, harassed by envy, and tortured by anxiety? You who were nourished in saffron, why do you embrace dung?

Remember also what you have deserved. Let the hellish cauldron come into your memory, the iron furnace of great Babylon, the house of death, the dwelling of anguish, the globe of flames, the bitterness of cold, everlasting darkness. [Col. 0648C] Consider the order of torments, the faces of the torturers, the changes of punishments, the infinity of miseries; run through these things with the eyes of the mind, and you will be able to say: “It would have been better for me if I had not been born.”

Turn back your eyes and observe what you have lost. Remember what the glorious city is like: the heavenly dwelling, the place of life, the palace of sweetness, the splendour of glory, the greatness of grace, infinite brightness. Attend to the order of joys, the faces of those rejoicing, the succession of rewards, the multitude of delights; and you can cry out: “Whoever lost you has lost everything, O Lord God.” If you bind your soul with this threefold cord, you will understand and perceive that knowledge of sin is the beginning of salvation (Seneca, *Letter* 28).

4. The second step is repentance. These two are so joined to one another that a person cannot know himself unless he repents, nor repent unless he knows himself. Let the soul, therefore, wounded by the dart of compunction, repent with a threefold repentance: because it lost innocence, did not seek what it had lost, and neglected the patience of God. [Col. 0649A] I know, Lord Jesus, that in baptism you restored to us the first robe of innocence; yet, clothed in the snow-white garment of the baptized and restored to the throne of righteousness, we quickly departed from the way which you showed us, and with the prodigal son squandered, in the land of unlikeness, the share of substance that fell to us. Most vile spirits and kings of eternal fires came to us: unclean beings to those cleansed, condemned beings to those to be saved, bent beings to those who were upright; and they said to our soul: “Bow down, that we may pass over” (Isa. 51:23). We heard them and were bent down; they passed over us, and we lost innocence. If it is guilt to have lost it, what, do you think, will it be not to have sought what was lost?

Someone loses something in this mortal life: he seeks judges, summons friends, brings an action, leaves nothing untried, [Col. 0649B] until he either finds what was lost or has what was taken restored, and then guards what has been restored. Yet we have lost our incorruptible, unfading, undefiled inheritance in heaven through the wiles of that insatiable murderer, and do not seek it! He bent us down, and do we 1167 not rise again? Let us rise and go to our Father, saying to him: “Father, we have sinned against heaven and before you.” And, rehearsing the whole course of the Gospel reading, let us offer the Father repentance of mind and contrition of heart, in the hope that, while we are still far off, the Father may see us, be moved with compassion, run to us, fall upon our neck, and kiss us with the kiss of his mouth. Perhaps he will order the first robe of innocence brought forth, clothe us in garments of virtues, place on our hand the ring of mysteries, [Col. 0649C] and put shoes upon our feet in readiness for the Gospel of peace.
