Perhaps he will command the fatted calf to be brought and slain as satisfaction for those returning, that there may be feasting and rejoicing, and that we may be restored amid symphony and chorus to the joys of the heavenly city (Luke 15:11–32), where there is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing repentance.

We know, Lord Jesus, that you will not withhold good things from those who walk in innocence (Ps. 83:13), nor from those who walk in repentance. For only one did not commit sin; yet blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin (Ps. 31:2). Whatever he himself has determined not to impute to me is as though it had not been. Consider also how great is the pride with which you have made use—indeed, abused—the patience of God. He saw you sinning and passed it over, [Col. 0649D] as though he did not see; he called and you did not hear; he threatened and you did not fear; he promised and you despised—neither drawn by promises nor struck with terror. Do you not know that the patience of God has led you to repentance? Fear with great fear lest you have stored up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God (Rom. 2:4–5); and remember that it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. 10:31). Bind, therefore, the wound of your soul with this threefold poultice of repentance, and say: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me” (Ps. 6:3), etc.

5. The third step is sorrow; and this likewise is joined by a threefold mission. Truly, after knowledge and repentance, my sorrow was renewed, and in my meditation [Col. 0650A] fire was kindled, because I offended the Creator, did not fear the Lord, and despised my benefactor. “Are you not, like clay in the potter’s hand, also in my hand?” says the Lord (Jer. 18:6). If he made you a vessel for honor, why did you presume to make yourself for dishonor? Does the thing fashioned say to its maker: “Why have you made me thus?” (Rom. 9:20). Have you dared to challenge the Creator, you creature; the maker, you thing made; the craftsman, you work? Remember, most worthless potsherd, that if you fall upon this stone, you will be broken; but if it falls upon you, it will crush you with a dreadful crushing, so that not even the smallest trace will appear.

But you mingled blood with blood, offending the Creator and not fearing the Lord. You were the servant of that Lord whose wrath no one can resist; and in his commandments [Col. 0650B] you had received his will. You refused to understand in order to do good; but, kicking against the command of your ruler, you determined to live by your own law within his commonwealth. Have you heard what sentence awaits the wicked servant who knows his Lord’s will and does not do it, and is reserved for many blows? (Luke 12:47). Angels stand ready to hear the voice of his words (Ps. 102:20); the stars are called and say, “Here we are” (Baruch 3:35); the winds and the sea obey him (Matt. 8:27); and all things keep the law appointed for them with unshaken steadfastness. Are you alone an alien, caring nothing for the decrees of imperial Majesty? Hear that he can send you into the outer darkness, where weeping and gnashing of teeth increase in perpetual misery.

But if offense against the Creator and reverence for his [Col. 0650C] power do not move you, let gratitude at least move you: you have despised so great a benefactor amid such great benefits. Where will you find a like benefactor, who ministers to you the courses of the stars, the temperateness of the air, the fruitfulness of the earth, the abundance of its fruits? Finally, to heap up for you the sum of all life’s benefits, he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us (Rom. 8:32): giving up the Only-begotten for adopted children, the Lord for servants, the just one for the ungodly. What more ought he to have done for you that he did not do? If, therefore, you have grieved with this sorrow, you may say with the Prophet: “My belly aches, my belly aches; the feelings of my heart are troubled” (Jer. 4:19).

1168

6. The fourth step is confession of the mouth. After [Col. 0650D] knowledge of oneself, repentance of mind, and sorrow of heart follows confession of the mouth. In all these matters the heart believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). This too is threefold, if it attains the power of salvation. For it must be true, naked, and personal.

The Most High seeks truth: and where does he wish to be deceived, who has no intention of deceiving? We know many, and have experienced them, who, coming to the grace of confession, returned to their conscience more burdened than freed from sins. Clerics tell what they did in literary pursuits; soldiers, what they did in conflict with the sword: so that beneath the cloak of humility they introduce pride, condemning themselves under that great seal upon which the whole sum of human salvation rests. There are others whom fear drives to confession; [Col. 0651A] others whom pretense leads. For they confess in order at least to appear, outwardly, to have confessed. Do you think that confession true which either fear has extorted or pretense has produced, when the Holy Spirit of discipline flees what is feigned (Wis. 1:5), and the Almighty seeks freely offered satisfaction? That is true confession which descends from contrition of mind, is neither compelled by fear nor covered by fiction, but in a contrite spirit declares what it feels.

It must also be naked, stripped of every covering of concealment. What profit is there in speaking of one part of one’s sins and hiding another; in being cleansed in part and serving uncleanness in part? Can sweet and bitter, savory and tasteless, flow from one and the same vessel? All things are naked and open [Col. 0651B] to the eyes of God (Heb. 4:13); and do you conceal something from him who holds God’s place in so great a sacrament? Display and lay bare whatever tears at your heart; uncover the wound, that you may experience the work of the healer. You ought to seek the Lord in simplicity of heart (Wis. 1:1), not in duplicity; for woe to those who speak with heart and heart, and walk upon the earth by two ways (Sir. 2:14).

It must also be personal. Many, indeed, recount the sins of others with great seriousness and speak of their companions’ transgressions in elaborate declamation. They do not know their own sins, but have committed others’ to everlasting memory. Unhappy and miserable people, to whom it has been granted to lament what belongs to others and to leave aside what is their own! Have you not read that “the just man is the first accuser of himself in his speech”? (Prov. [Col. 0651C] 18:17). Of himself, Scripture says—not of another. Have you forgotten the Apostle James saying: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5:16)? He said “your,” not “others’.” “I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5). The Prophet said “my,” not “your.”

7. The fifth step is mortification of the flesh; and this too is consecrated by the threefold number. It ought to be done secretly, with permission, and discreetly. Break down your tender limbs, reared in refined pleasures, by prolonged martyrdom, so that you may recognize that you should abstain from lawful things in proportion as you remember having committed unlawful ones. This, however, must be done secretly, so that your left hand does not know what your right hand is doing (Matt. 6:3). For the keeping of so great a good is not to be placed in human mouths, [Col. 0651D] but in the hidden place of your heart, so that your glory may be the testimony of your conscience (2 Cor. 1:12). We do not say this in order that your light should not shine before people, so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16), but lest you lodge your intention in the brief span of worthless glory. For nothing is more unhappy than to mortify the flesh here with fasts, afflict it with vigils, receive glory here, and receive hell there.

It must be done with permission, because whatever is done with a pastor’s permission is more pleasing in the sight of God; and the Most High receives in a singular manner that sacrifice which is not offered by the decision of one’s own will, but by the command of the one who orders it. For the exclusion of one’s own will greatly avails to refute pride; and one who loves the vanity of this world cannot root it out. [Col. 0652A] But discretion must be maintained in this austerity, lest, while we desire to scourge ourselves too greatly, we lose health; and while we seek to subdue the enemy, we kill a citizen. Consider your body and its capacity; examine the constitution of your flesh; impose measure upon your austerity.

1169

Keep your body sound for the service of the Creator. We have seen many who so scourged their flesh at the beginning and broke down the barriers of discretion that they were rendered incapable of solemn praises and had to be nursed for long periods with richer provision.

8. The sixth step is amendment of action; and this also is consecrated by the number three: namely, that you do not do evil to yourself, do not harm another, and do not consent [Col. 0652B] to one who harms. You have experienced how fragile is immersion in pleasures, and do you go there again? You observed that pleasure passed away and sin remained. Restrain your foot from the unspeakable paths of most unclean lust. Bow your neck beneath the commandments of the Most High, so that there may be no iniquity in your hands. Cut off from the raging belly festive banquets and empty conversations. Turn away your eyes lest they see vanity (Ps. 118:37); stop up your ears lest they hear blood (Ps. 33:15); and then you will be able to say: “The Lord has chastened me severely” (Ps. 117:18).

But what does it profit to restrain the works of your conduct within the line of uprightness if you desire to harm others? “He who has done no evil to his neighbor and has not accepted reproach against his neighbors shall rest upon God’s holy mountain” (Ps. 14: [Col. 0652C] 3), receiving blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior (Ps. 33:5). Yet do not presume yourself innocent unless, with whatever authority you can, you rebuke the ungodly and those walking contrary to virtue, and set yourself as a wall for the house of Israel: chastising yourself, harming no other, and consenting to no one who harms. For this saying is true: “He who neglects to correct when he can do so undoubtedly makes himself a participant in the offense.” For when the cause of God is brought into public issue and falsehood is preferred to truth, the one who does not resist, in accordance with the position he holds, will be condemned by his own silence.

9. The seventh step is perseverance; and this too is dedicated by the sanctification of the number three. Perseverance is produced by imitation of the saints, the brevity [Col. 0652D] of time, and the frailty of bodies. What indeed could you not endure when you see young men, boys, virgins, old women, old men, and the decrepit not only undergoing but even seeking diverse torments for Christ? Consider the age of boys, the ardor of youths, the tenderness of virgins, the frailty of old women, the weakness of old men, the incapacity of the decrepit; wherever you turn your eyes, you will find in these ages a multitude of examples that have run manfully toward the palm of martyrdom. Were you not formed from the same clay and inspired by the same spirit? Perhaps persecution does not press upon you so that you must suffer martyrdom; nor are you condemned if you serve Christ: indeed, you are praised and proclaimed by all. But if persecution does threaten, [Col. 0653A] it is to be despised on account of its brevity. For nature has well provided for us, showing that no pain is both long and great. If it is great, it cannot be long. The union of body and soul does not sustain severe torments for long; shaken by the greatness of stupefaction, it is dissolved with utmost speed. It is therefore the mark of a great spirit to despise great torments which, in a short time, effect so great a change that they make the sufferer fly from labor to rest, from misery to glory.

The frailty of the body must also be considered; often either some very slight accident or an accumulated mass of burning fever can suffocate it in a brief moment. Give, therefore, to virtue, if necessity requires it, what someday you must give to necessity, gaining an everlasting reward for a brief [Col. 0653B] danger.

10. You see, then, how difficult is the way of confession to run, how manifold the paths to be kept. True is what that great teacher of the Church said: “I have found more easily those who preserved innocence than those who performed suitable repentance” (St Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book II, chap. 10). We have spoken of the way of confession according to our measure, reserving the weightier matters of a higher teaching for those more exalted. We shall, however, attempt to open the way of obedience under another beginning of discourse, lest the words of the Lord Savior—who is blessed for ever—ever become wearisome.

1170

## SERMON XLI. On the virtue of obedience and its seven steps

[Col. 0653C] 1. “We are not able to think anything of ourselves, as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5). For what can the spirit, shut up in prison, corrupted by sin, and weighed down by earthly things, suffice to think in this earthen vessel and amid the frailty of human constitution? “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). Yet the Spirit of wisdom is gracious (Wis. 1:6): he enlightens the imprisoned spirit, heals the corrupted, and raises the depressed. He is the Spirit of mercy, freeing those in chains, enlightening the blind, and raising up the crushed. He is also the Spirit of truth, who teaches us all truth; and he not only teaches but also suggests it (John 14:26). He suggests that we may seek; he teaches that we may understand.

He is the one whom the Lord [Col. 0653D] Jesus, after his obedience to the Father even unto the death of the cross, sent to his apostles, his obedient ones. Do they not seem to you to have ascended the summit of singular obedience—those who, having received permission to remain in the city, shut within the enclosure of a single little house, persevered unanimously in prayer? (Acts 1:14). Have you understood that the apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus? (Acts 5:41). With what great powers of obedience are they supported, who rejoice to be brought before a council for Christ, count it dignity to be beaten for him, and seek glory in dying for him! Blessed souls, overflowing with the abundant majesty of the Spirit: to whom, by a wonderful reversal, lowliness appears exaltation, insults glory, patience victory. [Col. 0654A] “Our soul is greatly filled with the reproach of the prosperous and the contempt of the proud” (Ps. 122:4). You see with what untroubled brow they break upon the face of the high priests, the haughtiness of the Pharisees, and the tumult of the crowd, saying: “It is necessary to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Look upon those two great lights, Peter and Paul, and range through the whole order of the apostolic senate; there you will see the steadfastness of obedience standing bravely amid a multitude of torments.

Was not the very Son of the King, King of that realm which shines with unending joys, made obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross, and did he not learn obedience from the things which he suffered? You have heard of misery: hear also of the crown. You have seen danger: see the reward. You have considered weakness: consider power. “Therefore,” he says, [Col. 0654B] “God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2:8–9).

2. But let us for the present be silent about his obedience, which is enclosed and marked by a singular prerogative. Let that great patriarch come forth into the midst: the light of faith, the model of obedience, the chief of righteousness. He hears from the Almighty: “Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house; and come into the land which I shall show you” (Gen. 12:1). At the sound of one command he flees his country, leaves his parents, abandons his inheritance, and enters as a new stranger the territories of others. A great thing, and consecrated in the father of many nations by the privilege of primordial dignity! First among men, he first renounces his possessions and traverses the way of obedience [Col. 0654C] with tireless speed.

Finally, when he had received in his old age the son in whom the blessing of the whole world was to be gathered, God says to him: “Take your only-begotten son, Isaac, whom you love, and offer him to me as a burnt offering” (Gen. 22:2). O how much bitterness in these words; how much separation of a father’s affection from his heart! He is ordered to kill his son, bone from his bones and flesh from his flesh; the son of great promise, of extreme old age, of his own wife; a son wonderfully promised, happily born, innocently reared. And lest anything should be lacking for the most tender fire of grief to overflow within the father’s breast, the word “only-begotten” is added. For there are many sons, but not only-begotten sons. This one is such a son that he is also only-begotten: unique to his father, only-begotten to his mother, reserved for the inheritance. [Col. 0654D] Do not look to Ishmael, because he who had been born in slavery and from a handmaid did not belong to freedom and inheritance.

Since, moreover, there are many sons who are only-begotten but not beloved, the Lord adds “whom you love,” both to intensify tribulation in the father’s heart and to prove obedience in the mind of the righteous man. And so that the tenderness of the father might be renewed by the remembrance of the beloved name, and inward affection might wholly burn at the sound of the cherished voice, the boy is named by the name which had been called by the Lord before he was conceived in the womb. You see with how many hammers of tribulation Abraham’s affection is struck: he is commanded to take his son, kill his only-begotten, sacrifice the one whom he loves, [Col. 0655A] strike Isaac. He was much tested, much proved, much burned. Sweet is the relation of son to father and father to son; Abraham forgets this sweetness and every bond of affection. He saddles his ass, lays together the wood, kindles the fire, draws the sword. He does not ask the Lord why; he does not murmur, complain, or even show the face of one grieving. Rather, ignorant (variant: knowing) of all that is commanded, he hastens with pious cruelty to the death of his son. Therefore the virtue of highest and admirable obedience in Abraham is to be proclaimed with praises of singular excellence.

3. True obedience is a most strong thing, and it cannot descend into the soul unless that soul has been thoroughly and closely cleansed from the defilement of this world. That its way may shine forth more clearly, let us show, as far as we can, [Col. 0655B] what obedience is special to God, proper to man, and common between God and man.

There are certain highest evils and certain highest goods. The highest goods are: to love God, to love one’s neighbor, to speak truth, not to steal, not to bear false witness, not to commit adultery, and many other things which the brevity of discourse forbids us to enumerate. The highest evils are their opposites and things like them. God commands us to do good and orders us to abstain from evils. The holy and immutable authority of this command cannot in any way be overthrown, because it is sealed with the mark of him who says: “I am the Lord, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6).

If, therefore, that man whom God has placed over our heads should wish to think otherwise—setting darkness for light and light [Col. 0655C] for darkness, so as to command that the aforesaid goods be abandoned or that the aforesaid evils be embraced—the authority of the one commanding must be boldly rejected, and it must be said with a free voice: “It is necessary to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). This is obedience special to God, which must by no means be adjusted to human judgment, but maintained with unchangeable resolve. Hold, therefore, to this sure rule: do not abandon the aforesaid goods at the command of superiors, nor commit evils.

Between the highest evils and highest goods are certain intermediate things which, according to their relation to either side, take the name of good or evil. Intermediate things are walking, sitting, speaking, keeping silence, eating, fasting, keeping vigil, sleeping, and similar things. If these are done with the permission of a pastor, they await the highest recompense. In these intermediate matters, therefore, we ought to be subject and obedient at the nod of those set over us, asking no questions, for conscience’ sake (1 Cor. 10:25); for in these matters God has prescribed no fixed action, but has left them to be arranged by the authority of superiors.

Do not, however, let an unskilled master or indiscreet authority disturb you; remember that “there is no authority except from God, and he who resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:1–2). This is obedience proper to man, which we owe to man, to whom we are subject. It is also common to God and man, because whatever obedience is shown to superiors is shown to him who says: “He who hears you hears me” (Luke 10:16). We must therefore walk on this path with great caution, because many [Col. 0656A] steps lie hidden there, and whoever omits one of them will keep the others without recompense.

4. The first step is to obey willingly. Every age from its youth is inclined toward evil (Gen. 8:21), and each person follows the will of his own perverse heart. For from the strait of that first transgression there has been born in man a love of his own will; abandoning the will of his Creator, it became subject there to slavery where it wished to rule. It is difficult, then, to leave one’s own will and serve the will of another. Yet however grievous it may be, one cannot ascend the first step of obedience who has not made the will of the one commanding his own. The righteous man glories that in his will he confesses himself to the Lord. Hence: “Willingly,” he says, “will I sacrifice [Col. 0656B] to you” (Ps. 53:8). Will alone, therefore, adorns the outcome of the whole work; without it nothing is done well, even if it seems good. The commands of superiors must therefore be accepted willingly, and the very heart must be drawn away from its voluntary turnings, until its own will has been sacrificed and loves the command of the one ordering. This, then, is to obey willingly: voluntarily to fulfill the will of superiors.

5. The second step is to obey simply. “He who walks simply walks confidently” (Prov. 10:9). Solomon joyfully offered all things in the simplicity of his heart; and Scripture teaches beforehand that the Lord is to be sought in simplicity of heart (Wis. 1:1). We see many people, after a superior’s command, raise many questions—continually asking, “Why? For what reason? Wherefore?”—[Col. 0656C] repeating frequent complaints and asking: “Why does he command this? Where does this come from? Who assisted this counsel?” From this comes murmuring; from this, words that sound of murmuring and indignation, and smell of bitterness. From this come constant excuses, a pretense of impossibility, and the calling in of friends.

Not so Abraham. Hear what the Lord declares concerning a simple people: “At the hearing of the ear,” he says, “he obeyed me” (Ps. 17:45), showing that the command of the commander and the service of the obedient proceeded in one and the same moment. “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked” (Gal. 6:7). Do you murmur against a superior in the tabernacle of your body? The right hand of God raises itself to cast you down. Walk, therefore, simply in the commandments of obedience, adding simplicity to willingness [Col. 0656D] and illumination to intention. For “the strength of the simple is the way of the Lord” (Prov. 10:29), which is obedience. Those who are obedient and walk simply thus put on strength.

6. The third step is to obey cheerfully. “God loves a cheerful giver”; “not out of sadness,” says the Apostle, “or out of necessity” (2 Cor. 9:7). Serenity in the face and sweetness in speech greatly color the obedience of the one who obeys. Hence that pagan poet also says: “Above all, a kindly countenance was added” (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book VIII). For what place is there for obedience where the sickness of sadness is seen? Outward signs often reveal the will of the mind, and it is difficult for those who change their will not to change their face. [Col. 0657A] A cloudy bearing of the body and a face darkened by the shadows of sadness indicate that devotion has departed from the soul.

Look at David dancing cheerfully before the ark of the Lord, and at how wisely he checks the indignation of the proud woman. “I shall play,” he says, “and shall be more lowly in the sight of the Lord” (2 Sam. 6:14–22). You see, then, how necessary and fitting cheerfulness is in the execution of obedience. For who willingly commands a person breathing sadness? If, therefore, you wish to be perfect, receive the command of the one ordering cheerfully and with great brightness of countenance, so that to willingness of heart and simplicity of action you may add cheerfulness of face.

7. The fourth step is to comply swiftly. “The word of God runs swiftly” (Ps. 147:15), and it desires one who follows swiftly. You see with how great [Col. 0657B] speed he runs who says: “I ran the way of your commandments” (Ps. 118:32). The faithful obedient person knows no delays, flees tomorrow, is ignorant of slowness, anticipates the one commanding, prepares the eyes for sight, ears for hearing, tongue for speech, hands for work, feet for the journey; he gathers his whole self so as to gather the will of the one commanding.

See the Lord commanding hastily and the man obeying hastily: “Zacchaeus,” he says, “come down quickly, for today I must remain in your house.” And he came down quickly and received him joyfully. You have observed that he both came down quickly and received him gladly.

1173

You have heard obedience; hear also obedience’s reward: “Today salvation has come to this house.” Consider also, from the occasion of this completed obedience, the great mystery and the saying sealed with the seal of mercy: “For,” he says, [Col. 0657C] “the Son of Man came to seek and to save what had perished” (Luke 19:5–6, 9–10). Have you not read that the children of Israel were commanded to eat the lamb hastily? (Exod. 12:11). The eating of the true Lamb is, indeed, signified as to be performed hastily, because those words which he gave through the Law, which he himself presented while present in person, and which he left to be handed down through the superiors of the Church, are to be fulfilled with swift obedience. You also, therefore, when you have joined willingness to the heart, simplicity to action, and cheerfulness to the countenance, add swiftness as well; so that, according to the Apostle James, you may be swift to hear (Jas. 1:19), and swifter to perform.

8. The fifth step is to fulfill manfully. “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope [Col. 0657D] in the Lord” (Ps. 30:25). It is not strength to go toward disobedience, but not to be drawn away from obedience. If tribulation thunders, if persecution resounds, if sinners set a snare for you, if evil men obstruct your way, do not abandon the way of obedience, but say: “I am ready and am not troubled, that I may keep your commandments” (Ps. 118:60). What usefulness do the things enumerated above produce if strength is lacking—the strength that places the virtues upon the citadel of constancy and fortifies them with a rampart against which the assaults of raging foes cannot advance? Have you put your hand to strong things? You must act urgently and obey constantly; amid the harshness either of words or blows, this royal path [Col. 0658A] is not to be abandoned but held with more tenacious zeal. To sum up briefly the endowments of strength: it is the virtue that preserves and fortifies virtues. Join strength, therefore, to swiftness and constancy to urgency; then you will sing securely: “The hand of the sinner shall not move me” (Ps. 35:12).

9. The sixth step is to obey humbly. “In our lowliness he remembered us, who made us” (Ps. 135:23). Humility is a great virtue; without its protection, the virtue of strength is not merely no virtue, but even breaks out into the vice of pride. How strongly Saul ran when he was little in his own eyes! How many ranks of Philistines he overthrew! With what strength he wielded the sword! But after pride seized him and passed into the affection of his heart, he became weak and powerless and fell, easily overthrown by the arms of the uncircumcised.

Look at the king in whom sublime humility and humble sublimity shine with happy harmony. “Lord,” he says, “my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up” (Ps. 130:1). Trace his whole course with diligent attention; wherever you turn your eyes, you will find it sprinkled with the flowers of humility. Hear what he says elsewhere: “I will keep my strength for you” (Ps. 58:10). How truly the righteous executor of righteousness speaks! There are many who reserve their strength not for God but for vain glory; who trust in their own strength; who glory in virtues received, as though they had not received them, doing injury to the Creator, from whom comes every good gift [Col. 0658C] and every perfect donation (Jas. 1:17). Therefore, lest strength pass into pride, it must be seasoned with the salt of humility. For it will profit nothing to obey strongly if one has the misfortune to become proud. Those, then, keep their strength for God who, when they have done what they ought to do, can say: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke 17:10).

10. The seventh step is to obey without ceasing. “Not he who has begun, but he who has persevered, shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). To begin belongs to many; to persevere, to few. Perseverance is the singular daughter of the highest King, the fruit and consummation of virtues, the repository of every good; a virtue without which no one will see God, nor be seen by God. It is the end unto righteousness for everyone who believes; in it the assembly of virtues has consecrated for itself a venerable bridal chamber. What profit is there in running and failing in the course before the finish? “So run,” says the Apostle, “that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9:24).

1174

O with what persevering foot he completed his course who said: “I have finished the course” (2 Tim. 4:7)! O what a long course that blessed thief completed [Note: [Col. 0657D] Some add: “whom perseverance found repentant, made perfect,” etc.], who, “made perfect in a short time, fulfilled many years” (Wis. 4:13)! Finally, the Lord of the prophets speaks through the prophet: “If the righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I shall not remember any of his righteous deeds” (Ezek. 18:24). You see, then, how [Col. 0659A] those virtues are buried in deep oblivion which perseverance has not marked. It alone brings the lover of obedience into the King’s chamber, that he may see him in his beauty—the one upon whom angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1:12).

On this way, therefore, on which we walk, “the proud have hidden a snare for me” (Ps. 139:6). This way is difficult and hard, rough with thorny windings and knotted with the bonds of many fetters. Do you suppose that obedience bears fruit there when the subordinate hears an obedience he had sought with many prayers, when he is commanded what breathes dignity, overflows with joy and gladness, and is sustained by the appearance of power? Or, conversely, do you assign the merit of obedience to that obedience which proceeds amid adversity, terrifies the mind of the hearer, is hard to hear, harder to fulfill, and hardest of all to maintain? It is not so. We must separate our mind from prosperity and embrace adversity in mind, if we wish to follow him who fled kingship (John 6:15) and came willingly to his passion (Isa. 53:7).

11. You observe, therefore, that these ways are ways of life, leading to life. “Blessed are the meek” (Matt. 5:4), because “the Lord will teach the meek his ways” (Ps. 24:9); for what follows will come to pass for them: “You will fill me with gladness by your countenance” (Ps. 15:11). For so long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6), far from the face of God, from the countenance of glory, from the contemplation of majesty—except that the merciful and compassionate Lord often causes his countenance to shine upon us. This occurs when, the cloud having been removed [Col. 0659C] which stood in the way lest prayer should pass through, we draw near to him and are enlightened, beholding with unveiled face the glory of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18).

Yet we should not understand “with unveiled face” in a wholly proper sense, since we still see through a mirror and in an enigma, and are held in a prison-like body. He says “unveiled,” rather with regard to the darkness of bodies. Hence this created spirit sometimes rises up to the Creator-Spirit and, cleaving to him, becomes one spirit with him. But this contemplation is of no duration; for the spirit, surrounded by the confinement of the body, is wounded by frequent contact with the flesh, and, having been set above creation, is immediately found beneath even the most worthless things. Moreover, the Creator-Spirit, whose works are great, “sought out [Col. 0659D] in all his wills” (Ps. 110:2), now draws near while we do not know it, now withdraws while we are unaware; for “we do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3:8). And often, the more frequently he is sought, the more swiftly he withdraws, as he himself says to the Bride: “Turn your eyes away from me, because they have made me fly away” (Cant. 6:4). It also happens that, when he is not sought, he comes; when he is sought, he flees, as the Bride shows herself repeatedly in the Song as having sought and not found him (Cant. 3:2). But whoever finds this countenance has not thereby found the countenance of the Lord’s glory, which is above the cherubim; for it is displayed in utmost purity and clarity to the whole company of angels, whereas to us it is shadowed forth by reflective and obscure images.

12. Since, therefore, we cannot here see the face of God as it is, we do not have fullness of joy until he draws us to himself, the head comes to the body, and God is all in all. There will be fullness there; here there is a taste. For here we taste and see that the Lord is sweet; but this taste does not pass into drinking, because, although we see, we do not penetrate. In tasting he is sweet; in fullness he is wondrous.

The souls of the saints, stripped of earthly bodies and now flown to their heavenly abodes, though they drink, are not yet filled, nor yet made drunk. [Note: [Col. 0659D] See vol. II, *Treatise on Loving God*, ch. 11.] For although they enjoy much blessedness, they nevertheless await the resurrection of their dead bodies, so that, when they have possessed a double portion in [Col. 0660B] their own land, they may be flooded with everlasting joy (Isa. 61:7). For at present a single white robe has been given to each of them, and they have been commanded to wait a little while longer (Rev. 6:11), until the wicked are crushed with a twofold crushing and they themselves are crowned with a twofold blessedness. Therefore, since they do not yet possess what they desire to possess, they cannot be made drunk; but for them that vision is a drink: so that, as they drink without labor, so they may rest without labor, until they are satisfied when his glory appears.

But when we rise again “to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13), and that glorious city is adorned with pearls, and “the dwelling of all who rejoice” is in it, then he will fill us with gladness by his countenance (Ps. 15:11), because we shall see him as he is [Col. 0660C] (1 John 3:2). Then we shall be made drunk with the abundance of his house, and he shall give us drink from the torrent of his delight (Ps. 35:9); and he will say to us: “Drink, and be made drunk, my beloved” (Cant. 5:1), because both the soul’s illumination and the body’s glorification will be possessed by perpetual right.

13. It follows: “Delights at your right hand unto the end” (Ps. 15:10). The left hand of God is the present life. And because we regard as left-handed whatever we do not greatly esteem, the present life is understood by the left hand, in which the Lord permits his elect to be so scourged by the wicked that he even allows them to be killed. Do those who say, “For your sake we are put to death all day; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter”—“why do you turn away your face and forget [Col. 0660D] our poverty?” (Ps. 43:22, 24)—not seem to you to have been given over to forgetfulness?

By the right hand, however, is signified that blessed life which knows only joys, concerning which we can say nothing else except: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:3). There are those delights which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him (1 Cor. 2:9). On the left are tribulations; on the right, delights. But until when? Until the end. What is this end? “Christ, the end unto righteousness for everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). That end of which Wisdom says: “She reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). For to behold God is [Col. 0661A] the consummate end. He is the end at which, when we arrive, we shall thirst for nothing more: Jesus Christ, Bridegroom of the Church, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLII

### On the Five Trades and the Five Regions

1. The Word of the Father, the Only-Begotten of God, the Sun of righteousness, that supreme merchant, brought from the uttermost bounds of heaven the price of our redemption. This is a faithful trade, most worthy of all acceptance, in which the King, the Son of the King, becomes an article of trade; gold is given for lead; the righteous man is given for the sinner. O how unmerited a mercy, how free and so proven a love, how unexpected a condescension, how astounding a sweetness, how unconquered a gentleness, how lowly a trade, in which the Son of God is handed over for a slave, [Col. 0661B] the Creator is slain for the creature, and the Lord is condemned for a bondsman!

These are your works, O Christ: you who descended from heaven’s light to hell’s darkness, from the right hand of majesty to the misery of humanity, from the Father’s glory to the death of the cross—bringing light to hell, redeeming humankind, overcoming death and the author of death. You are one and have no second. Your own kindness invited you to redeem us; mercy drew you; the truth by which you had promised that you would come compelled you; the purity of the virgin womb received you; power brought you forth while the integrity of virginity remained intact; obedience led you through all things; patience armed you; love made you manifest in words and miracles.

Far from me be the merchants of the land of Teman; let the sons of Hagar withdraw, who sought out prudence; let the giants, named from of old, who were from the beginning, great in stature and skilled in war, depart from me [Col. 0661C]. The Lord did not choose these, nor did they deserve the way of discipline; therefore they perished. But he gave it to Jacob his servant and Israel his beloved. For you have hidden these things, Lord, from the wise and prudent—from giants and renowned men, that is, those who have made themselves great in their own eyes—and have revealed them to your little and humble ones (Matt. 11:25).

Gladly I embrace your trade, because it is my business. My soul meditates on these wares with the greatest sweetness. Nor does it merely meditate: it also recalls your meditation, because it understands what it loves and commits to memory what it has chosen. In these trades you command my soul [Col. 0661D] to be engaged, that it may become “the merchant’s ship, bringing its bread from afar.” I shall trade until you come; I shall meet you joyfully at your coming; and would that I might hear: “Well done, good servant” (Matt. 25:21, 23). Yours are the heavens and yours is the earth; in your regions I shall trade securely, having you alone as guide on the journey, protector in dangers, and companion in tribulation.

2. Your regions are five, through which your merchants travel in order to trade; there your beloved seek you and your elect find you.

The first region is the region of dissimilarity. That noble creature, formed in the region of likeness because it was made in the image of God, when it was in honor did not understand, and descended from likeness to dissimilarity. A great dissimilarity indeed: from paradise to hell, from angel [Col. 0662A] to beast, from God to devil! An accursed transformation: to change glory into misery, life into death, peace into warfare, by perpetual captivity! A cursed descent: to descend from riches to poverty, from freedom to slavery, and from rest to labor!

Miserable are we, and miserably born: to whom it has been given to be born in sorrow, to live in labor, and to die in pain. From sinner we are sinners; from debtor, debtors; from corrupt, corrupt; from subdued, subdued: begotten and begetting. A sinful nation, a people burdened with iniquity, a most evil seed, wicked children, adding transgression to transgression. Behold, we are before him as though we were not, counted as nothing and emptiness (Isa. 40:17), thinking ourselves something when we are nothing. We are wounded as we enter the world, [Col. 0662B] while we live in the world, and as we depart from the world: from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in us.

That exalted prophet knew these things, who, lamenting the condition of human misery, broke out in these words: “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40:1).

3. What do we trade in this region of dissimilarity, Lord God? I see the human race, from the rising of the sun to its setting, passing through the markets of this world: some seeking riches, others longing for honors, others carried away by the sweetness of a favorable breeze.

But what of riches? Are they not acquired with labor, possessed with fear, and lost with grief? “You heap up treasure and do not know for whom you will gather it” (Ps. [Col. 0662C] 38:7). See how much labor you have undertaken for perishable riches. You cross seas and, by sailing, open another world for yourself, according to the Wise Man, three fingers’ breadth from death. You flee your homeland, leave your parents, are torn from your wife, know not your children; and, forgetting every family bond, you seek in order to acquire, acquire in order to lose, lose in order to grieve. “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3).

What madness is this, children of Adam: to traverse seas, to travel lands, to be carried beyond the world, amid many labors, many vigils, frequent fasts, and frequent deaths? Behold what riches these are. But what of honors? You are set in a lofty place; they have made you a leader. [Col. 0662D] See whether you are not to be judged by all, watched by all, torn to pieces by all. If you are a soldier, you keep watch before the ruler’s threshold in order to gain office; and, clothed in iron armor, you are nearer to a wound than to honor, to death than to life, to danger than to reward. If you are of the Lord’s portion, does not the bishop fear the Roman pontiff, and the archdeacon or deacon the bishop? See also whether you have shaken your hands free from every gift, lest you hear with Simon: “You have neither part nor lot in this matter, because you wished to possess the gift of the Holy Spirit with money” (Acts 8:21).

It is not for us to judge the rulers of the Church. Let those friends of the Bridegroom see to themselves when he who judges the world in righteousness begins to demand an account from them concerning the Bride. Can anyone be in honor [Col. 0663A] without pain, in prelacy without tribulation, in exaltation without vanity? Behold what honors these are.

But what of glory? Whence comes glory to you, foul dust, mud of the earth, vessel for dishonor? Not to you, not to you, but yield glory to the Lord’s name. Leave his glory to him who is glorious in his saints. Praise him whom the angels praise in the highest. And what of empty glory itself, which is nothing other than a vain swelling of the ears and can scarcely be possessed without envy? Look at those whom you precede, and consider that you have provided seeds of envy for all. Therefore all are kindled against you with hostile eyes; they are tormented by your happiness and burned by your glory. Behold: from the source of your glory comes your hatred; from the source of your exaltation, your humiliation; from that which makes you anxious, that which ought to make you secure. Observe that if you run after [Col. 0663B] glory, you run into envy; if you pursue happiness, you are corrupted by misfortune. You see, therefore, that every human being is vainly troubled (Ps. 38:12).

These are the wares found in the region of dissimilarity. Therefore the prudent merchant, who sees labor in riches, punishment in honors, and envy in glory, makes contempt of the world his baggage and flees.

4. The second region is the cloistered paradise. Truly the cloister is a paradise: a region fortified by the rampart of discipline, in which there is fruitful abundance of precious wares. It is a glorious thing for people of one manner to dwell in a house (Ps. 67:7); it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity (Ps. 132:1). You may see one mourning his sins, another rejoicing in God’s praises, [Col. 0663C] this one ministering to all, that one instructing others; this one praying, that one reading; this one showing mercy, that one punishing sins; this one burning with love, that one excelling in humility; this one humble in prosperity, that one exalted in adversity; this one laboring in the active life, that one resting in the contemplative. And you may say: “These are the camps of God” (Gen. 32:2). “How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28:17).

What, therefore, faithful soul, must you consider in these markets? Survey the virtues of those dwelling in the house of the Lord of hosts, and make from them your baggage, your pattern of life. You who formerly lived in the region of the shadow of death, pass over to the region of life and truth.

[Col. 0663D] 5. The third region is the region of expiation. There are three places allotted to the souls of the dead according to their different merits: hell, purgatory, and heaven. In hell are the wicked; in purgatory, those to be purified; in heaven, the perfect. Those who are in hell cannot be redeemed, because in hell there is no redemption. Those who are in purgatory await redemption, first to be tormented either by the heat of fire, by the severity of cold, or by some grievous pain. Those who are in heaven rejoice in joy at the vision of God: brothers of Christ in nature, co-heirs in glory, alike in delightful eternity.

Therefore, since the first do not merit redemption and the third do not need redemption, it remains for us to pass in compassion to those in the middle, to whom we were joined by humanity. I will go into that region and see this great vision: how the loving Father leaves his children, who are to be glorified, in the hand of the tempter [Col. 0664A]—not for slaughter, but for purification; not for wrath, but for mercy; not for destruction, but for instruction—so that they may no longer be vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, but vessels of mercy prepared for the kingdom.

I shall therefore rise to help them; I shall plead with groanings, entreat with sighs, intercede with prayers, make satisfaction by the singular sacrifice: so that perhaps the Lord may see and judge, and turn labor into rest, misery into glory, blows into a crown. For by these and similar services their penance may be shortened, their labor ended, their punishment destroyed. Run, therefore, whoever you are, faithful soul, through the region of expiation; see what is done in it; and in these markets make compassion your baggage [Col. 0664B].

6. The fourth region is the region of Gehenna. O hard and grievous region, region to be feared, region to be fled! Land of forgetfulness, land of affliction, land of miseries, in which there is no order but everlasting horror dwells! A deadly place, in which there is burning fire, freezing cold, the immortal worm, intolerable stench, striking hammers, palpable darkness, the shame of sinners, the binding fast of chains, horrible faces of demons! I tremble and shudder wholly at the memory of this region, and all my bones are shaken. “How you have fallen, Lucifer, who arose in the morning!” (Isa. 14:12). “Every precious stone was your covering” (Ezek. 28:13); now “the moth is spread beneath you, and the worm is your covering” (Isa. 14: [Col. 0664C] 11). O God, how great the distance between a covering of precious stone and a covering of worms; between the delights of paradise and the gnawing moth of hell!

I know that that fire is prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25:41), and for people like them; there they will be ended without end, die without death, and be tormented without ceasing. Descend, then, alive into hell; survey with the eyes of the mind the workshops of torments. Flee crimes and vices, for which criminal and vicious people have perished. Hate iniquity and love the law of the Lord; and in so dreadful a market make hatred of sin your baggage.

7. The fifth region is the supercelestial paradise. O blessed region of the heavenly powers, where the blessed Trinity [Col. 0664D] is seen face to face by the blessed, where those exalted companies, with the sublime beating of wings, never cease to cry: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3)! It is a place of delight, where the righteous are given drink from the torrent of delight; a place of splendor, where the righteous shine like the brightness of the firmament; a place of joy, where everlasting joy is upon their heads; a place of abundance, where nothing is lacking to those who see him; a place of sweetness, where the Lord appears sweet to all; a place of peace, where his place is made in peace; a place of wonder, where his works are marvelous; a place of fullness, where we shall be satisfied when his glory appears; a place of vision, where the great vision shall be seen.

O exalted region, full of riches! From the valley of tears we sigh for you, where wisdom without ignorance, [Col. 0665A] memory without forgetfulness, understanding without error, and reason without obscurity shall shine. A region in which the Lord, passing by, will minister to his elect—that is, he will show himself such as he is. There God will be all in all, where the universe of things, wondrously ordered, shall give glory to the Creator and joy to the creature.

Run, therefore, spiritual soul, with the eyes of desire through this region; see the King of glory, glorious in his beauty, surrounded by legions of angels, adorned with companies of saints, casting down the proud, exalting the humble, condemning demons, redeeming human beings; and say: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ages of ages they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). When, therefore, you have perceived in mind such precious markets and such splendid wares, fashion [Col. 0665B] your baggage: love of God. You have seen the regions, observed the markets, fashioned your baggage, and you are blessed. Trade, therefore, until the Lord your God comes, so that you may say to him: “Lord, you entrusted five talents to me; behold, I have gained another five”; and may deserve to hear: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:20–21), the Bridegroom of the Church, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLIII

[Note: [Col. 0665D] In the preceding editions this sermon was fifth for the feast of the Ascension.]

### On Great-Souledness, Long-Suffering, and Unity of Mind

1. In a brief statement Saint Luke commends to us a threefold virtue in the primitive Church. After the Lord’s ascension, he describes them as persevering unanimously in prayer (Acts 1:14), awaiting the heavenly consolation whose promise they had received. [Col. 0665C] For with praiseworthy greatness of soul, the little flock, deprived of the comfort of its shepherd, nevertheless did not doubt that he cared for them and bore a fatherly concern for them. With devout petitions they knocked at heaven, certain that the prayers of the righteous would penetrate it, and that the prayers of the poor would not be despised by the Lord or return without abundant blessing.

Nor did they persist without long-suffering, remaining unfailing, according to that prophetic saying: “If he delays, wait for him, because he will surely come and will not be late” (Hab. 2:3). Moreover, their unanimity is plainly stated, because this alone deserves the gifts of the divine Spirit. For God is not a God of dissension [1179], but of peace (1 Cor. 14:33); nor does he cause any to dwell in a house except those of one manner (Ps. 67:7).

[Col. 0665D] 2. Rightly, therefore, the divine ear heard the preparation of their hearts, and did not disappoint them of their expectation, since they were great-souled, long-suffering, and unanimous. For these are most certain testimonies of faith, hope, and love. Clearly hope produces long-suffering, and love unanimity. Does faith also make a person great-souled? Yes, and it alone does so. For whatever is presumed without faith is not solid greatness of mind, but a kind of windy swelling and empty puffing-up. Do you wish to hear a great-souled man? “I can do all things,” he says, “in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4:13).

Let us imitate this threefold preparation, brothers, if we desire to obtain the overflowing measure of the Spirit [Col. 0666A]. For to all except Christ the Spirit is given by measure; but the full measure of what overflows seems in some manner to exceed measure. Greatness of soul was evident in our conversion; let there also be long-suffering in consummation, and unanimity in conduct. For with souls such as these that heavenly Jerusalem desires to be restored: souls in which neither the greatness of faith is lacking for undertaking Christ’s burden, nor the duration of hope for persevering, nor the bond of love, which is the bond of perfection.

## SERMON XLIV

[Note: [Col. 0666D] In the manuscripts this sermon is third for Easter.]

### On Those in Whom the Mysteries of Christ Do Not Yet Appear Fulfilled

1. Everything that we read concerning the Savior is medicine for our souls. Let us see, therefore, lest perhaps it be said of us: “We have treated Babylon, and she has not been healed” (Jer. 51:9). Let each person consider how greatly such healing medicines work within him. For there are some for whom Christ has not yet been born; there are some for whom he has not yet suffered; there are some for whom he has not yet risen. For others he has not yet ascended; for others he has not yet sent the Holy Spirit.

How does his humility work in one who is proud—his humility who, “though he was in the form of God, did not judge equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7)? How, I ask, does God’s humility work in a proud person? What traces of that humility are in those who still, with their whole desire, yearn after earthly riches and honors? Does not your conscience now rejoice, my brothers, because you can say: “A little child has been born to us” [Col. 0666C] (Isa. 9:6)? There are some for whom Christ has not yet suffered: those who flee labor and still fear death, as though he had not overcome both by enduring labors and by dying death.

4. There are some for whom Christ has not yet risen: those who are afflicted all day long by the death of anxious labor and penitential affliction, having not yet received spiritual consolation. But unless those days had been shortened, who could endure? For others Christ has risen, but has not yet ascended; indeed, he still remains with them on earth in gracious sweetness. These are those who are all day long in devotion, weep in prayer, sigh in their meditations, and for whom all things are festive and joyful, while through all those days a continual Alleluia is sung. But milk must be taken from them, so that they may learn to eat solid food; and it is expedient for them that Christ should go away and that this temporal devotion should be withdrawn.

But when will they be able to receive this? They complain that they have been abandoned by the Lord and deprived of grace. Yet let them wait a little while; let them remain in the city until they are clothed with a certain firmer power from on high and receive the greater gifts of the Holy Spirit. Thus the apostles were raised to a higher rank and entered the more excellent way of love, no longer concerned with how they might weep for a little while, but with how they might triumph in a great victory over the common adversary and trample Satan beneath their feet.

[Col. 0667A] There follow the sermons commonly called the *Short Sermons*, which Horstius included among the *Sermons on Diverse Subjects*, though he assigned some to the *Sentences*. Perhaps it was Bernard’s “Flowers of Words” that John of Salisbury sought from Peter of Celle in Letters 96 and 97.

## SERMON XLV

[Note: [Col. 0667D] Otherwise, no. 1 among the Short Sermons.]

### On the Various Trinity—That Is, of God and of Humankind

1. That blessed and everlasting Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, namely one God, supreme power, supreme wisdom, supreme goodness—created a certain trinity in its own image and likeness: namely, the rational soul. It bears a certain trace of that supreme Trinity in that it consists of memory, reason, and will. It was created so that, remaining in God, it might be blessed by participation in him; but, turned away from him, wherever it might betake itself, it would remain miserable.

But this created trinity chose rather to fall through the movement of its own will than to stand in free choice by the grace of its Creator [variant: “of creation”]. It fell, therefore, through suggestion, delight, and consent, from that supreme and beautiful Trinity—power, wisdom, purity—into a contrary and foul trinity: weakness, blindness, and impurity. For memory became powerless and weak; reason, imprudent and dark; will, impure.

Moreover, memory, which while it stood contemplated the power of the simple Godhead, fell from it and, as though crashing upon rocks, burst into three broken parts: affective, burdensome, and idle thoughts. By affective thoughts I mean those by which it is itself affected, such as cares for necessary things—eating, drinking, and the rest of the like kind [variant: “innumerable”]. Burdensome thoughts are those involved in external administration and hard occupations. Idle thoughts are those by which it is neither affected nor burdened and yet distracted from the contemplation of eternal things—for example, if it thinks of a running horse or a flying bird [Col. 0667C].

2. Reason too has a threefold fall. Its function was to distinguish good from evil, true from false, advantageous from disadvantageous; but in distinguishing these it is now so blinded by darkness that judgment often leads in the opposite direction, accepting evil for good, falsehood for truth, what is harmful for what is advantageous, and conversely. Yet it would never be deceived in these matters if it had never been deprived of the light by which it was created. But since it too fell away from that light, it undoubtedly found nothing but the darkness of its own blindness.

Consequently it also lost the instrument by which it administered those distinctions: namely, that threefold way of wisdom—ethics, logic, and physics—which we may call by other names moral, speculative, and natural knowledge. Through ethics, good is chosen and evil rejected; through logic, true and false are known; through physics, advantageous and disadvantageous are known—that is, what should be taken for use and what rejected [Col. 0667D].

3. Next comes the will, whose ruin is likewise threefold. For it ought to cleave to supreme goodness and purity and to love it alone; but, through its own iniquity falling from the heights into these low things, it loved earthly things through the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and worldly ambition. What fall could be judged more unhappy than this, in which, with memory, reason, and will perishing, the entire substance of the soul is destroyed?

4. Nevertheless, that blessed Trinity repaired this fall of our nature, so grave, so dark, so filthy—mindful of its own mercy, forgetful of our fault. Therefore the Son of God came, sent from the Father, and gave faith; after the Son, the Holy Spirit was sent and gave and taught love. Thus through these two, faith and love, hope of returning to [1181] the Father came into being. And this is the trinity: faith, hope, and love. Through it, as by a trident, that immutable and blessed Trinity drew from the mud of the deep to lost blessedness the mutable, fallen, and miserable trinity.

Faith illumined reason; hope raised memory; love purified will. Therefore, when, as has been said, God the Son came and became man—he who was God—he, like a good physician, gave commandments, by whose observance lost health might be restored. In order to inspire faith in the commandments, he showed signs; in order to persuade people of the usefulness of those commandments, he promised blessedness [Col. 0668B].

5. Thus there is one faith of commandments, another of signs, another of promises: that is, the faith by which we believe in God, the faith by which we believe God, and the faith by which we believe God’s word. Through faith in the commandments we believe in God. To believe [Col. 0668C] in God is to hope in him and love him. Through faith in signs we believe God—that he can do such things and can do all things. Through faith in promises we believe God’s word—that he truly fulfils whatever he promises.

Likewise hope is threefold and proceeds from the aforementioned threefold faith. From faith in commandments arises hope of pardon; from faith in signs, hope of grace; from faith in promises, hope of glory.

Love too is gathered under a threefold number: “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5). We owe purity to our neighbor, conscience to ourselves, and faith to God. Purity means that whatever is done is done either for the benefit of one’s neighbor or for God’s honor. It must especially be shown to our neighbor, because we are manifest to God, whereas we cannot be manifest to our neighbor except insofar as [Col. 0668D] we open our heart to that person.

Two things produce a good conscience in us: penitence and continence. By penitence we punish sins already committed; by continence we do not thereafter commit sins needing punishment. We owe this to ourselves. After these remains unfeigned faith, which must be diligently offered to God: so that neither because of our neighbor, to whom we extend love, may we offend God, nor because of conscience, which by penitence and continence we wish to preserve in humility, may we carry out less fully obedience to God’s commandments. This is unfeigned faith.

It is called “unfeigned” in distinction from dead and feigned faith. Dead faith is faith without works; feigned faith is that which believes for a time and in time of temptation falls away. Hence it is called *ficta*, that is, fragile [Col. 0669A].

6. We can gather all this more briefly, so that it may be more easily commended to memory. Let us say, then: There is the creating Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—from which fell the created trinity: memory, reason, and will. There is the trinity through which it fell: suggestion, delight, and consent. There is the trinity into which it fell: weakness, blindness, and impurity.

Again, the trinity that fell is memory, reason, and will. The fall of each was threefold. Memory fell into three kinds of thoughts: affective, burdensome, and idle. Reason fell into a threefold ignorance: of good and evil, true and false, advantageous and disadvantageous. Will fell into the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and worldly ambition.

There is a trinity through which it rises again: faith, hope, and love. These have threefold subdivisions. There is faith of commandments, signs, and promises; hope of pardon, grace, and glory; and love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith.

## SERMON XLVI

[Note: [Col. 0669D] Otherwise, no. 2 among the Short Sermons.]

### On the Connection of Virginity and Humility
Hail, Mary, full of grace. The fullness of grace could not consist in virginity alone, for not all are capable of receiving it. Blessed are those who have not defiled 1182 their garments, and who, together with our Queen, glory in the privilege of virginity. But [Col. 0669C] do you have only one blessing, O Lady? I beseech you, bless me also. That virtue has perished from me [Note: namely, virginity. These words move Bellarmine to judge that the sermon is not Bernard’s, since it is sufficiently established that Bernard preserved the laurel of virginity inviolate to his very last breath. And indeed one of two conclusions seems to follow: either the sermon is not Bernard’s, or Bernard was not a virgin. But what prevents us from maintaining both the sermon and Bernard’s virginity, despite these words, which offer no real obstacle? For it is not unusual for saints and preachers of the divine word to speak from time to time in the person of their hearers, and, as it were, to bring upon and transfer to themselves the sin which they have determined to rebuke. Thus, to return to Bernard, I say that he speaks in the person of his hearers, as though asking what remains for those before the Virgin Mother of God who are not permitted, like her, to glory in preserved virginity. Moreover, among so great a number of religious, who can doubt that there were some who, after suffering the shipwreck of virginity long before in the world, seized in the monastery the plank of penitence? In much the same manner Bernard speaks of himself in Sermon 30 on the Song of Songs, no. 7, where he says that in secular life his faith was dead, being without works; but after his conversion, although he had fared “somewhat better,” he had nevertheless often choked the clusters of good works by anger, borne them away by boastfulness, defiled them by vain glory; nor had sins of gluttony been absent from him—although no one was gentler, humbler, or more temperate than Bernard. Compare likewise what he says of himself in Sermon 54 on the Song, no. 8.], nor is it now possible even to aspire to it. I have rotted away in my dung and have become like a beast; but shall there not be something for me also with you? Shall there be no place where I may be with you, because I can no longer follow wherever you go?

The angel seeks the maiden whom the Lord has prepared for the son of his lord. He himself drinks from your jar, delighted by a virtue akin to himself; but will you not grant drink to the beasts also? The angel drinks because you do not know a man; let the beasts also drink because you glory uniquely in humility. “The Lord,” she says, “has looked upon the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:28, 48). For virginity without humility may perhaps have glory, but not with God. The Most High always looks upon the humble, and knows the lofty from afar [Col. 0669D] (Ps. 137:5). “He gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud” [Col. 0670A] (Jas. 4:6). But perhaps your jar is not even full in these two measures: it is capable of a third, so that not only the angel and the beasts, but now the steward himself may drink. For the angel-minister draws this good wine, “which we have kept until now,” in order to carry it to the steward (John 2:6–10). I mean the Father, who is rightly called the steward as the principle of the Trinity. Indeed, the angel, commending Mary’s fruitfulness—which is the third measure—says: “That holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35); as though saying: In this generation you have fellowship with him alone.

## SERMON XLVII

[Note: [Col. 0670D] Elsewhere, 3 among the Short Sermons.] On fourfold pride.

“Hail, Mary, full of grace.” Well full, because pleasing to God, [Col. 0670B] angels, and human beings: to human beings through fruitfulness, to angels through virginity, to God through humility. In this third respect she testifies that she was regarded by the Lord (Luke 1:28, 48), who looks upon the humble and knows the lofty from afar (Ps. 137:5). For as Satan’s eyes see everything exalted, so the Lord’s eyes behold every humble person. Hence he says in the Song of Songs: “Return, return, Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon you” (Song 6:12). He says “return” four times because of the fourfold pride by which, turned away from the Lord, she was not seen. For there is pride of heart, pride of mouth, pride of deed, and pride of dress.

Pride of heart is when a person is great in his own eyes. Against this the Wise Man prays, saying: “Do not give me the lifting up of my eyes” [Col. 0670C] (Ecclus. 23:5). And elsewhere: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes!” (Isa. 5:21). Pride of mouth or tongue, also called boastfulness, is when a person not only thinks highly of himself, but also speaks highly. Hence the Psalmist: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips, and the tongue that speaks great things” (Ps. 11:4). Pride of deed is when a person acts with a certain outward arrogance in order to appear great. Of this the same Psalmist says: “He who practises pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Ps. 100:7). Pride of dress is when a person adorns himself in costly garments in order to appear glorious. Hence Paul: “Not in costly apparel” (1 Tim. 2:9). And the Lord: “Those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11:8), where pride abounds.

There are five things which the Lord has set before the rational [Col. 0670D] soul [Col. 0671A] as remedies for so deadly a plague: place, body, the devil’s temptation, Christ’s preaching, and his manner of life. Place, because it is exile; body, because it is burdensome; temptation, because it troubles; Christ’s preaching, because it builds up; and his manner of life, because it forms. By these, as it were by five senses, God produces humility in the soul. For as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul; and just as a body not enlivened by the soul through its five senses is dead, so a soul not humbled by the Lord through these things is dead.

## 1183 SERMON XLVIII

[Note: [Col. 0671D] Elsewhere, 4 among the Short Sermons.] On voluntary poverty.

“Jesus entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house” (Luke 10:38). The village into which Christ entered [Col. 0671B] is voluntary poverty, which makes its inhabitants secure against the twofold attack by which lovers of this world are overcome: namely, their own envy and that of others. For poverty, because it is thought wretched, lacks others’ envy; and because it is voluntary, it envies no one anything.

These two sisters signify the two lives of lovers of poverty. Some, with Martha, anxiously prepare two dishes for the Lord Jesus: correction of conduct with the seasoning of contrition, and works of mercy with the condiment of devotion. But those who, with Mary, attend to God alone, considering what God is in the world, in human beings, in angels, in himself, and in the reprobate, contemplate that God is the ruler and governor of the world; the liberator and helper of human beings; the delight and beauty of angels; in himself, beginning and end; and the terror and horror of the reprobate. He is wonderful in creatures, lovable in human beings, desirable in angels, incomprehensible in himself, intolerable in the reprobate.

## SERMON XLIX

[Note: [Col. 0671D] Elsewhere, 5 among the Short Sermons.] On the threefold Word.

“Day utters speech to day.” Day to day: the angel to the Virgin. The angel is day because of blessedness; the Virgin is day because of the virtue of integrity. “And night declares knowledge to night.” The serpent is night because of malice; the woman is night because of ignorance. “Day utters speech to day.” The Godhead to virginity: from the womb of paternal majesty into the womb of maternal integrity.

Alternatively: “Day utters speech to day”: God the Father to the rational soul enlightened by faith. “And night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. [Col. 0671D] 18:3): the rational creature to the rational soul not yet enlightened by faith. Hence the Apostle: “The invisible things of God are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that are made.” Thus we speak of the declared word, the inspired word, and the uttered word. The first produced knowledge; the second, conversion; the third, enlivening. The first harmed; the second did not benefit; the third gave life.

The first harmed, because “when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, nor gave thanks; but they became vain in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened” [Col. 0672A] (Rom. 1:20–21). The second did not benefit, because no law was given that could give life. The third gave life, because through the cross it redeemed. The first was wholly external; the second external and internal; the third wholly internal. Observe that what is uttered is brought forth from the fullness of the utterer, with a certain savor of his very substance. Therefore incarnate Wisdom is said to have in itself all fullness (John 1:16): knowledge in miracles, conversion in teaching, enlivening in passion.

Hence the prophet says: “Come, and let us return to the Lord; for he has seized us, and he will heal us; he will strike, and he will cure us. He will give us life after two days,” namely, those of knowledge and conversion; “on the third day he will raise us up,” by the voice of the incarnate Word through his first resurrection; “and we shall live in his sight,” given life through the Passion, more serenely enlightened by knowledge through miracles; “and we shall follow on in order to know the Lord” (Hos. 6:1–3), instructed through conversion by teaching.

## SERMON L

[Note: [Col. 0671D] Elsewhere, 6 among the Short Sermons.] On rightly ordering the affections.

1. “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon.” He does not say Ecclesiastes or Idida [Note: [Col. 0671D] Solomon was divinely called by Nathan the prophet “Beloved of the Lord”; in Hebrew, Jedidiah. From this, for easier pronunciation, Idida was formed [Col. 0672D]. Thus he bore two names, although this name occurs only at 2 Kings 12:25. Or rather, three names, if you add the name Ecclesiastes.]. For that king was also called by these names, and he signifies Jesus 1184 Christ our true Solomon: Solomon, that is, “peaceful,” in exile; Ecclesiastes, that is, “preacher,” in judgment; Idida, [Col. 0672C] that is, “beloved of the Lord,” in the kingdom; everywhere king. In exile, ruler of morals; in judgment, discerner of merits; in the kingdom, distributor of rewards [Note: [Col. 0672D] Thus far almost from Sermon II on Epiphany, no. 2.]. In exile, gentle; in judgment, just; in the kingdom, glorious. In exile, lovable; in judgment, terrible; in the kingdom, wonderful.

“In the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Song 3:11). This crown is mercy, and in it he is to be imitated. His stepmother also crowned him with a crown of misery, and in it he is contemptible. I mean the Synagogue, which showed herself not his mother but his stepmother. His household will crown him with a crown of justice, and in it he will be terrible; his Father crowns him with a crown of glory, and in it he is desirable. Therefore let sinners see him in the crown of misery—that is, the crown of thorns—and be pierced with compunction; let the daughters of Zion, affectionate souls, [Col. 0672D] see him in the crown of mercy and imitate him; the impious shall see him in the crown of justice and perish; the saints shall see him in the crown of glory and rejoice forever.

2. “Go forth, daughters of Zion,” tender souls, from the sense of the flesh to the understanding of the mind; from slavery to carnal desire to the freedom of spiritual understanding; “and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” Others also, his imitators, are crowned, [Col. 0673A] but only by deliberate effort aided by grace. This one alone was crowned by his mother, because he alone came forth from his mother’s womb with ordered affections, like a bridegroom from his chamber.

These affections are the four best known: love and joy, fear and sorrow [Note: [Col. 0673D] On these affections compare the notes on Sermon 2 at the beginning of Lent, no. 3.]. Without them the human soul cannot subsist; but for some they are a crown, for others confusion. When purified and ordered, they render the soul glorious in the crown of virtues; when disordered, they render it cast down and shameful through confusion. They are purified as follows: if things that ought to be loved are loved; if things more worthy of love are loved more; if things that ought not to be loved are not loved, love will be purified. So too with the rest.

They are ordered as follows: at the beginning, fear; then joy; afterward sorrow; at completion, [Col. 0673B] love. Their combination is such: from fear and joy prudence is born; fear is the cause of prudence, joy its fruit. From joy and sorrow temperance is born; sorrow is its cause, joy its fruit. From sorrow and love fortitude is born; sorrow is the cause of fortitude, love its fruit. The circle of the crown is closed. From love and fear justice is born; fear is the cause of justice, love its fruit.

3. Consider, therefore, how these affections, when ordered, are virtues; when disordered, disturbances. If sorrow follows fear, it produces despair; if joy follows love, it produces dissipation. Let joy, then, follow fear, because fear guards against the future, joy rejoices in the present, and joy possesses the end of prudent caution. Let joy therefore test fear. Tested fear is nothing other than prudence. Let sorrow accompany joy, because one embraces joys moderately who remembers sorrows. Let sorrow therefore moderate joy.
