Moderated joy is nothing other than temperance. Let love be joined to sorrow, because one who desires through love the things that ought to be loved endures sorrows bravely. Let love therefore strengthen sorrow. Strengthened sorrow is nothing other than fortitude. Let love be joined to fear, because one who does not neglect things to be feared clings in orderly fashion to things that ought to be loved. Let love therefore order fear. Ordered fear is nothing other than justice.

The two affections, joy and sorrow, do not extend to others: for we rejoice within ourselves and grieve within ourselves. Love and fear extend to others. [Col. 0673D] For fear is a natural affection which joins us to what is higher through the lower part, and is directed to God alone. Love is an affection which joins us to what is higher, lower, and equal, and is directed both to God and to our neighbor. In these two consists perfect justice: that we fear God because of his power, love him 1185 because of his goodness, and love our neighbor because of our shared nature.

## SERMON LI

[Note: [Col. 0674D] Elsewhere, 7 and 8 among the Short Sermons.] On Mary’s Purification and Christ’s Circumcision.

Why do we say that blessed Mary was purified? And why do we say that Jesus himself was circumcised? [Col. 0674A] Surely she no more needed purification than he needed circumcision. Thus he is circumcised for us and she is purified for us, providing an example for penitents: that, abstaining from vices, we may first be circumcised through abstinence itself and then purified from sins committed through penitence.

But what does it mean that Mary carries Jesus in her womb, Joseph on his shoulder, as he goes into Egypt and returns from it, and Simeon in his arms? These three signify the orders of the elect: Mary, preachers; Joseph, penitents; Simeon, good workers. For one who preaches the Gospel to others carries Jesus, as it were, in the womb, in order that he may give birth to him for others—or rather, give birth to others for him. Among such was blessed Paul, who said: “My little children, for whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

Those who are worn out by labors for Christ, who suffer persecutions, who inflict evil on no one but patiently endure evils inflicted by others, are rightly said to carry him on their shoulders. To them Truth himself also says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9:23), etc. But if anyone gives bread to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, and diligently bestows the other works of mercy upon the needy, does he not rightly seem to carry him in his arms? For the Lord will say to such at judgment: “As long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:40).

## SERMON LII

[Note: [Col. 0674D] Elsewhere, 9 among the Short Sermons.] On the house of divine Wisdom, that is, the Virgin Mary.

1. “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1), etc. Since wisdom is understood in many ways, we must ask [Col. 0674C] what wisdom built itself a house. For there is said to be the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God (Rom. 8:7), and the wisdom of this world, which is folly with God (1 Cor. 3:19). According to the Apostle James, both are earthly, animal, and demonic (Jas. 3:15). According to this wisdom, people are called wise “to do evil,” but “they know not how to do good” (Jer. 4:22); and in their own wisdom they are convicted and destroyed, as it is written: “I shall catch the wise in their craftiness” (1 Cor. 3:19); and: “I shall destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent” (1 Cor. 1:19). Certainly Solomon’s saying seems to me aptly and fittingly applied to such wise people: “There is an evil which I have seen under the sun: a man who seems wise in his own eyes.” [Col. 0674D]

No wisdom of this sort, whether of the flesh or of the world, builds up any house that it inhabits; rather, it destroys it. There is, therefore, another wisdom, which is from above: first chaste, then peaceable (Jas. 3:17). This is Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, of whom the Apostle says: “He was made for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30).

2. This Wisdom, therefore, which was God’s and was God, coming to us from the bosom of the Father, built itself a house: namely, its own mother, the Virgin Mary, in whom it hewed seven columns. What does it mean to hew seven columns in her, except to prepare her by faith and works as a worthy [Col. 0675A] dwelling-place for itself? Certainly the number three pertains to faith because of the holy Trinity; the number four pertains to conduct because of the four principal virtues.

That the holy Trinity was in blessed Mary—I mean by the presence of majesty—where the Son alone was present through assumption of humanity, is attested by the heavenly messenger. Revealing to her the hidden mysteries, he says: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you”; and shortly afterward: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:28, 35). Behold, you have the Lord; you have the power of the Most High; you have the Holy Spirit: you have Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For the Father 1186 cannot be without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, without either of them. The Son himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”; and again: “The Father who abides in me, he does the works” [Col. 0675B] (John 14:10). It is manifest that faith in the holy Trinity was in the Virgin’s heart.

3. But whether she also possessed the four principal virtues as four columns seems worthy of inquiry. Let us first see whether she possessed fortitude. How indeed could that virtue be absent from her, who, casting aside worldly pomp and despising pleasures of the flesh, resolved to live for God alone in virginity? Unless I am mistaken, this is the Virgin of whom one reads in Solomon: “Who shall find a strong woman? Her value is far off and from the uttermost bounds” (Prov. 31:10). She was so strong that she crushed the head of that serpent to whom the Lord said: [Col. 0675C] “I shall put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed: she shall crush your head” (Gen. 3:15).

Further, that she was temperate, prudent, and just we prove more clearly than light from the angel’s conversation and from her own reply. For when she was so reverently greeted by the angel, “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you,” she did not exalt herself as one blessed by a singular privilege of grace, but was silent and reflected within herself what this unusual greeting might mean. In this, what was she but temperate? But when the same angel instructed her concerning heavenly mysteries, she diligently asked how she should conceive and bear a child when she did not know a man. In this she undoubtedly proved prudent. She displays the mark of justice where she confesses herself the handmaid of the Lord [Col. 0675D] (Luke 1:28–38). For that confession belongs to the just is attested by the one who says: “Nevertheless the just shall confess your name, and the upright shall dwell with your countenance” (Ps. 139:14). Elsewhere the just are told: “And you shall say in confession: All the works of the Lord are exceedingly good” (Ecclus. 39:21).

4. Therefore blessed Virgin Mary was strong in resolve, temperate in silence, prudent in inquiry, just in confession. With these four columns of conduct and the three aforesaid columns of faith, heavenly Wisdom built itself a house in her. It so filled her mind that from the fullness of her mind her flesh also became fruitful; and the Virgin, by singular grace, bore in the flesh that same [Col. 0676A] Wisdom veiled in flesh which she had first conceived in her pure mind.

If we too wish to become a house of the same Wisdom, it is necessary that we be built up with the same seven columns: that is, that we be prepared for it by faith and conduct. In conduct, I think that justice alone suffices, yet supported by the other virtues. Thus, lest it be deceived by the error of ignorance, let prudence go before it; and let temperance and fortitude stand on either side, lest it slip by turning either to the right or to the left.

## SERMON LIII

[Note: [Col. 0675D] Elsewhere, 10 among the Short Sermons.] On the names of the Savior.

1. “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9:6). He is Wonderful in birth, Counsellor [Col. 0676B] in preaching, God in working, Mighty in passion, Father of the age to come in resurrection, Prince of Peace in everlasting blessedness. These names can also fittingly be assigned to him in the work of our salvation.

For first he is called Wonderful in the conversion of our will, a change that belongs to the right hand of the Most High alone. Then he is called Counsellor in the revelation of his will, when he reveals to those already converted what they ought to follow. Hence Paul, after his conversion, said: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts 9:6). Those who are converted must then be pierced with compunction for past sins; in their remission he is called God, since it belongs to him alone to forgive sins. Thus, when our Savior forgave sins on earth, the Jews said [Col. 0676C] that he blasphemed (Matt. 9:3), as though he claimed for himself what belonged to God alone. Fourth, he is called Mighty; for, according to the Apostle’s sentence, all who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus must suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12).

1187 2. But who could endure unless he helped? Hence David: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” (Ps. 93:17). Therefore, when he protects us in tribulation, when he keeps and repels from us the powers of the air, what else can he be called in this work except Mighty? Hence it is said: “The Lord mighty and powerful, the Lord powerful in battle” (Ps. 23:8). And because conversion itself and our life must be lived in Christ not in view of temporal things but in hope of future goods, [Col. 0676D] he is placed fifth as Father of the age to come: Father, namely, in the regeneration of our bodies. But since all indeed shall rise, though not all shall be changed (1 Cor. 15:51), to distinguish the transformation of the just from the resurrection of the wicked, he is placed sixth as Prince of Peace. When that peace is attained, all perfection is fulfilled, and nothing further remains to be desired. This is the peace in whose exultation the Psalmist sings: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion: for he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you; he who has made your borders peace” (Ps. 147:12–14).

The angel speaking to Joseph briefly and elegantly comprehends the sequence and power of these six names [Col. 0677A] in one name: “You shall call his name Jesus.” Explaining the meaning of that name, he says: “For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21).

## SERMON LIV

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Elsewhere, 11 among the Short Sermons.] On Christ’s appearing.

The Son of God appeared in order to help and instruct us. He can do so because he is the power and wisdom of the Father: power helps; wisdom instructs and forms. Weakness needs help; blindness needs training and teaching. He instructed us, indeed, “to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live soberly, justly, and devoutly” (Titus 2:12). Ungodliness was unbelief, because we neither believed in nor worshipped God. [Col. 0677B] For as it is godly to worship God, so it is ungodly to deny him.

Worldly desires are the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life; they draw and incline us toward love of the world. When these are denied, a person lives soberly, restraining the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. Once one begins to be sober, he sets a twofold sobriety against a twofold drunkenness. External drunkenness is the unrestrained outpouring of pleasures; internal drunkenness is preoccupation with curiosities. Conversely, external sobriety is restraint of pleasures; internal sobriety is exclusion of curiosities.

Thus a person lives soberly with respect to himself, justly with respect to his neighbor, to whom he gives what is just. Justice consists in two things: innocence and beneficence. Innocence begins justice; beneficence [Col. 0677C] completes it. He lives devoutly with respect to God. Devotion consists in two things: that we do not presume upon ourselves but place perfect confidence in God, so that through him we may overcome every obstacle of the world. We must not distrust God, but act securely and confidently.

Like a kindly and praiseworthy physician, he first drank the medicine which he prepared for his own—that is, he endured passion and death—and thus received the health of immortality and impassibility. He teaches his own confidently to drink the medicine that produces health and life; and he who lives eternal life after the Passion gives us hope, that we too may confidently hope for the same from him.

## SERMON LV

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Elsewhere, 12 among the Short Sermons.] On the six spiritual jars.

[Col. 0677D] 1. “There were set there six stone jars according to the purification of the Jews” (John 2:6). Let us understand these six jars set there to be six observances prescribed to the servants of God, in which they ought, as Jews, to be purified. They are silence, psalmody, vigils, fasting, manual labor, and bodily purity [Note: [Col. 0677D] The same are assigned in Sermon 2 after the octave of [Col. 0678D] Epiphany, from no. 7 onward, but in a slightly altered order.].

In the jar of silence we are purified from sins which we contract through talkativeness. This vice has eight kinds: foolish, 1188 vain, lying, idle, deceitful, malicious, obscene, and self-excusing speech. This plague arises from loquacity and is either utterly overthrown by the discipline of silence or, at least, restrained so that it may not do great harm [Col. 0678A].

In psalmody a twofold confession occurs: the sinner is pierced with compunction for faults, and praises are spoken to God for the judgments of his righteousness. In this jar, therefore, every Jew—that is, every one who rightly confesses [Note: *Judah* in Hebrew means “confession.”]—is purified from the unclean spirit of blasphemy to which he was subject before conversion. For while he praised himself and accused God, what else was he but a blasphemer? Are not those blasphemers who say: “The way of the Lord is not just” (Ezek. 18:25)? Is not that fool a blasphemer who says in his heart: “There is no God” (Ps. 52:1)? But now, converted and confessing and instructed by divine songs, he corrects his words by his corrected life. Accusing himself, he counts evils to his own account; but praising God, he attributes the good [Col. 0678B] which he sees in himself not to himself but to God. All this takes place in psalmody. By “psalmody” understand everything offered to God with the melody of the mind, whether psalms, hymns, or any other songs.

2. Above I placed vigils as the third jar. Perseverance in prayer should always accompany them. Hence the Lord is read in the Gospel to have spent the night in prayer (Luke 6:12); and, exhorting his disciples, he joined both together, saying: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Mark 14:38). Such vigils wash us from the filth that we contracted through slackness in sleep, when through a kind of forgetfulness we grew lukewarm and sluggish upon the way of salvation.

The fourth jar is fasting. Who can doubt whether it too purifies? That maxim is true: opposites are cured by opposites. [Col. 0678C] If, therefore, we have sinned through gluttony and overindulgence, what remains except that we be restored through abstinence? Nor is this vice alone purified by fasting; in addition, power to cast out demons is acquired, as the Lord says: “This kind can come out by no means except by prayer and fasting” (Mark 9:28).

3. The fifth jar follows, called manual labor. If one asks whether it involves any purification, this can readily be shown by many arguments. But, to omit very many, who can worthily assess how greatly to be praised, how gracious it is, for each person to sustain himself by his own labor and desire nothing belonging to anyone else? And lest anyone think that I utter this rhetorically rather than truthfully, let him hear our teacher, the Apostle Paul, “a teacher in faith and truth,” writing to the Thessalonians, teaching and commanding these very things: “We beseech you, brethren, that you abound more and more, and endeavor to be quiet, to mind your own business, and to work with your hands, as we commanded you; that you may walk honestly toward those who are outside, and desire nothing from anyone” [Col. 0678D] (1 Thess. 4:10–11).

Let him hear this same Apostle doing what he taught: “You yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not disorderly among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread for nothing, but worked in labor and weariness night and day, lest we burden any of you” [Col. 0679A]. Again, let him hear him teaching what he did: “When we were with you, we gave you this charge: if anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3:7–8, 10). You see how carefully the Teacher of the Gentiles commanded manual labor to be observed. Why did he care for this so greatly, unless because, as a good and diligent shepherd, he foresaw it to be highly beneficial for the welfare of the sheep?

4. The last remains: bodily purity. In it purification takes place from that fivefold allure of the body: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. The other practices mentioned—silence, psalmody, vigils, fasting, and manual labor—can indeed be exercised without it; but if the loins are not girded, that is, if bodily purity is lacking, what good will burning lamps do? It must therefore be concluded that purification by this jar is necessary, since it alone possesses a power of salvation equal to all the foregoing [Col. 0679B] practices.

It should be noted that in all these observances we owe the first four to ourselves, the fifth to our neighbor, and the sixth to God. Each person should practise silence, psalmody, vigils, and fasting for his own sake—that is, for his own discipline; manual labor for his neighbor’s sake, so as not to burden anyone, but rather to have something from which to give to one who suffers need; bodily purity for God’s sake, in order to please him and do his will. Hence it is written: “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that every one of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor” (1 Thess. 4:3–4).

That the jars are called stone jars signifies [Col. 0679C] that these observances cannot be kept without some difficulty and that the way leading to life is hard and rough. Or they are called stone because of firmness, lest they be easily broken or dissolved and the liquid of grace contained in them be poured out. This could quickly happen if they were earthenware, wooden, or made of any other fragile material. Or again, they are stone—that is, Christian—from Christ the stone, so that they may be performed in faith in Christ.

## SERMON LVI

[Note: [Col. 0679D] Elsewhere, 13 among the Short Sermons.] On the mystical jars to be filled with threefold fear.

1. “Each holding two or three measures.” Here we must first understand that vessels of this kind are sometimes empty and sometimes full. When full, they are sometimes full of poison, sometimes of water, and at times even of wine. They are empty and void, to be sure, when observances are performed for vain glory or some temporal advantage. They are full of poison if they are carried out with murmuring and bitterness of spirit. They are called full of water when they are observed from the fear of God; for fear is understood through water. Thus we also read in Solomon: “The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life” (Prov. 14:27). But they are full of wine when fear is transformed into love; when charity casts out fear; when things formerly observed from fear of punishment are now practiced with delight and love of righteousness.

The Lord does not wish them to be empty or infected with poison; the Lord commands that they be filled with water; but it is the Lord who causes [Col. 0680A] the water to be changed into wine. But whom does the Lord command to fill the vessels with water? Surely the ministers, whom he has also appointed over his household, to give it the measure of wheat in due season; yet Mary first urged them on, saying, “Whatever he tells you, do” [John 2:5]. By this example it is indicated that no one should usurp for himself the office of preaching unless Mary—that is, the mother of grace [Note: [Col. 0679D] Tiraq.: “mother of grace.”]—has first instructed him. Otherwise it will be said to them: “They have reigned, and not by me; they have become princes, and I knew them not” (Hos. 8:4).

Therefore ministers fill the vessels with water: they preach wondrous things concerning the sweetness of the kingdom; they threaten terrible things concerning the terror of punishment. From both arises a great fear in their hearers, lest they be deprived of the former or punished by the latter; and thus the vessels hold two measures. [Col. 0680B] But what does “or three” mean? Let a third fear be added to those two, and the vessels hold three measures. The two aforementioned fears, indeed, concern the future and are very useful; but there is another fear concerning the present, much more fitting: by it a person fears and is always apprehensive lest inward grace be abandoned. Whoever is filled with this fear has certainly increased the two measures to three.

2. It should further be noted that, when the vessels had been made full to the brim, then the water was changed into good wine. For the order of reason plainly requires that, if fear is the beginning of charity, the fullness of love should also follow to perfection. Thus the steward says to the bridegroom: “Every man first sets out the good wine; and when they have become drunk, then that which is inferior. But you have kept the good wine until now” [Col. 0680C] (John 2:6, 10).

It is the custom of worldly people, when they desire to attain some honor, first to win others over by affection. But once they have attained it, puffed up by power, they afterward subject to themselves by fear those very persons to whom, while private persons, they had shown not terror but affection. Such people first set out good wine, that is, love; and when they have become drunk, then that which is worse, that is, fear. Our bridegroom does the opposite. For he always keeps the good wine until the end; but he first gives to drink what is worse by comparison with it, saying: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear” (Ecclus. 2:1). If through fear you make yourself his servant, through charity he will make you his friend. Thus the water of fear will be changed into the wine of love.

[Col. 0680D] For this purpose you are cleansed by the waters of fear in those six vessels; for this purpose you approach him in fear, as a servant approaches a lord: that you may be advanced from servant to son.

## SERMON LVII

[Note: [Col. 0680D] Elsewhere, no. 14 among the *Parvi*.]

On the seven seals loosed by Christ.

1. “Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, to open the book and loose its seven seals” (Rev. 5:5). The seven seals are: temporal birth, legal circumcision, the mother’s purification, flight into Egypt, the necessity of the flesh, baptism, and passion. These are, indeed, certain true marks of humanity, by which the incarnate Wisdom of God willed to be bound and held. For it is the second person of the Trinity; and although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together effected the same incarnation, nevertheless neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit was incarnate, but the Son alone.

[Col. 0681A] The Father and the Holy Spirit did indeed fill the flesh of the Son, from whom neither could be separated; but they filled it by majesty, not by assumption. Therefore the Son displayed in the flesh the power of the Father through works; he showed the goodness of the Holy Spirit by forgiving sins; and he concealed what was his own—indeed, what he himself was, namely Wisdom—under the seals mentioned above.

Thus something marvelous and astonishing came to pass. Supreme power was made weak, and wisdom, if one may say it—and I say it reverently—was made, as it were, foolish. Nor am I ashamed to say what the Teacher of the Gentiles was not ashamed to teach. For he believed thus, taught thus, and left it thus in writing: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God; because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men” [Col. 0681B] (1 Cor. 1:23–25).

2. Yet this power had to be concealed and fulfilled in humility, so that all the oracles of the prophets might be accomplished. Therefore the impassible God suffered on the cross, and the immortal Son of God died and was buried in our mortal flesh. But behold: on the third day he rose from the dead; and he who had been a lamb in his passion became a lion in his resurrection. The lion of the tribe of Judah rose and conquered, because in rising by his own power he trampled down the death which he had endured from our weakness. “Rising from the dead, he now dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9).

By rising and ascending into heaven he opened the book, because from the authority of sacred Scripture it became manifest that he was God. Thus it is written: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” [Col. 0681C] (Ps. 107:6). He also loosed the seven seals of the same book when he opened to the minds of believers the meaning of the sacred utterance; and whatever the Law and the Prophets had foretold allegorically concerning his mysteries—namely, those things which he accomplished temporally as man—he showed more clearly than light to have been foretold of himself and fulfilled in himself and through himself [Col. 0681D].

## SERMON LVIII

[Note: [Col. 0681D] Elsewhere, no. 15 among the *Parvi*.]

On the three women who anoint the dead man: that is, on those who care for their neighbor’s salvation in mind, hand, and tongue.

1. Why is it that, after his death, those three holy women bought spices in order to anoint him as he lay in the tomb? What did they leave us to imitate in their action? For, as blessed Gregory says, a deed performed signifies something that must be done in holy Church (*Homily for Easter*). Therefore, if we perceive Christ dead—that is, the faith of Christ dead—in the heart of some brother, we must take pains to approach the anointing of the dead body with purchased spices.

Those three women signify three faculties within us, which procure spices suited to themselves. What are they? Mind, hand, and tongue. For everyone who buys both gives and receives something; and what he gives, he loses, in order to possess what he receives. Therefore the mind gives the coin of its own will and purchases the affection of compassion, zeal for righteousness, and discernment in counsel. The hand gives obedience and purchases patience in tribulation, perseverance in work, and continence in the flesh. The tongue gives the coin of confession and receives moderation in correction, abundance in exhortation, and effectiveness in persuasion.

2. When spices of this kind have been prepared, and they come together to the tomb, they speak to one another and say: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” [Col. 0682B] (Mark 16:1, 3). This stone is either excessive sadness, sloth, or hardness. While it blocks the entrance of the heart, mind, hand, or tongue comes in vain, with whatever spices, to anoint the dead.

But because it is written, “Your ear has heard the preparation of his heart” (Ps. 9:17), they see the stone rolled away and enter the tomb; and they hear that the one whom they wished to anoint as dead has been raised. Who reports this? Who proclaims it? Surely the angel, witness of the resurrection. For the face of the person in whom Christ has risen is seen to be more joyful, his appearance more lovely, his speech purer, his walk more modest, and his spirit readier for every good work. What are all these things but a kind of glad announcement of inward resurrection?

Moreover, the other things done or said in Christ’s resurrection—for example, concerning the discovered burial cloth, the seeing of the Lord himself in Galilee, and the other matters contained in the Gospel narrative—can doubtless be interpreted according to the moral exposition begun above: so that what historically came first in the head may consequently be believed to occur morally also in his body [Col. 0682C].

## SERMON LIX

[Note: [Col. 0681D] Elsewhere, no. 17 among the *Parvi*. No. 16 is rejected among the *Sentences*.]

On the three loaves of the spiritual person.

“Friend, lend me three loaves” (Luke 11:5). Our friend who comes to us from the road—that is, any neighbor who has been converted—must be refreshed with three loaves. The first loaf is continence, by which the body is restrained, lest from henceforth it dissolve into deadly pleasures. The second is humility, by which the soul is taught not to be proud of its own continence. The third is the fervor of charity, by which the spirit is kindled in order to keep both body and soul perseveringly in chastity and humility.

By these three virtues—chastity, humility, and charity—as by three loaves, the person of God is refreshed and strengthened, so that, according to the Apostle, at the day of the Lord’s coming spirit, soul, and body may be preserved whole [Col. 0682D] (1 Thess. 5:23). By “spirit” I mean the grace which, according to the same Apostle, “helps our weakness” (Rom. 8:26), lest we fail before we reap in due time the good which we have sown (Gal. 6:9).

The first loaf is called carnal or bodily; the second rational; the third spiritual. [Col. 0683A] Whenever these loaves are lacking, they must be sought from God. They are fittingly sought as three, because three come to be refreshed: the soul as the husband, the flesh as the wife, and the spirit as the servant of them both. Note that he does not say, “Give,” but “Lend me three loaves,” as though intending to repay them; for a priest ought indeed to obtain grace from God for a sinner who is being converted, but he ought to ascribe the fruit of that grace not to himself but to God.

## SERMON LX

[Note: [Col. 0683D] Elsewhere, no. 18 among the *Parvi*.]

On Christ’s descent and ascent, and ours likewise.

1. “No one has ascended into heaven except him who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, wishing to teach us how we might ascend into heaven, himself did what he taught: he ascended into heaven. And because he could not ascend unless he first descended, while the simplicity of his divinity did not permit him either to descend or ascend—for it can neither be diminished nor increased nor altered in any way—he assumed into the unity of his person our nature, that is, human nature, in which he might descend and ascend and show us the way by which we too might ascend.

All this is indicated by the words of the holy Gospel set forth. For in the words, “No one ascends into heaven except him who descended,” the assumption of human nature is expressed; but in the added words, “who is in heaven,” the immutability of his divinity is shown. These words also indicate that he himself is the way by which we ascend, and the homeland in which we remain: the way for those traveling, the homeland for those who have arrived [Col. 0683C].

Remaining, therefore, what he was in his own nature, for our sake he descended and ascended in ours: “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). He descended to a depth lower than which it was not fitting to go; he ascended to a height beyond which he could not go. He accomplished the descent mightily, because he was Power; he ordered the ascent sweetly, because he was Wisdom. It is said that he “descended,” not that he “fell”; for one who falls plunges down without a step, whereas one who descends places his foot step by step.

2. Therefore there are steps in descending and steps in ascending. In descending, the first step is from the highest heaven to the flesh; the second, to the cross; the third, to death. Behold how far he descended. Could he have gone farther? Certainly our King might now say, and cry out as if with a certain zeal for his work: “What more ought I to have done, and have not done?” [Col. 0683D] (Isa. 5:4). “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

We have seen the descent; let us also see the ascent. This too is threefold: its first step is the glory of the resurrection; its second, the power of judgment; its third, sitting at the right hand of the Father. From death he deserved resurrection; from the cross, the power of judgment—so that, because on it he was judged unjustly, through it he might receive the just authority of the judge. He himself said after his resurrection: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18).

[Col. 0684A] The very form of a servant—that is, the flesh in which he suffered and died—he raised up after its resurrection above all the heavens and above all the choirs of angels, even to the right hand of the Father. What arrangement could be sweeter, where death is swallowed up in victory and the shame of the cross is transformed into glory? Thus the saints say of it: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!” (Gal. 6:14). Here even the humility of the flesh passes from this world to the Father. Nothing can be said or thought more sublime than this ascent, nothing more glorious than this honor. Thus the Lord descended and ascended through the mystery of his incarnation, leaving us an example that we might follow his footsteps.

3. Let us also take from his mystery an example for our conduct. “For he who says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” [Col. 0684B] (1 John 2:6). Let us descend by the path of humility. Let its first step—that is, its first advance—be unwillingness to rule; the second, willingness to be subject; the third, in that very subjection, the patient endurance of whatever insults and injuries are inflicted.

That Lucifer who said in his heart lacked the first step in heaven: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14). Saying these things, he fell irreparably from heaven; and perhaps this was because the desire to rule is wholly intolerable pride.

The first human beings in paradise lacked the second step: although they preferred to use their own will rather than be subject to the Creator, they nevertheless did not presume to rule others of their own condition. Therefore their guilt and punishment were far different from the pride and downfall of the devil; hence, by divine mercy, they deserved at some time to be restored [Col. 0684C]. Those who believe for a time but withdraw in time of temptation do not possess the third step.

4. We say this so that we may know whose imitation we should avoid. For both devil and human being desired perversely to ascend: the latter toward knowledge, the former toward power; both toward pride. Let us not wish to ascend in this way. Rather, let us hear the Prophet asking how one must ascend: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place? He who is innocent in hands and clean in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor” [Col. 0684D] (Ps. 23:3–4).

Here it should be noted that he establishes a threefold step of ascent. The first step is innocence in action; the second, purity of heart; the third, the fruit of edification. We find these steps in a remarkable way in the earlier steps of ascent. For there the third step had been the endurance of injuries. This is what proves the first step of the present ascent, namely, innocence in action. There the second had been patience in subjection; and purity of heart, which is the second step of ascent, produces this patience. For this reason we have teachers set over us: that we may cleanse the heart, as the Lord says, “You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” [Col. 0685A] (John 15:3). There, too, the first step had been contempt for domination; here the third is the fruit of edification. Whoever does not seek to rule surely presides fruitfully over others who are to be instructed.

## SERMON LXI

[Note: [Col. 0685D] Elsewhere, no. 19 among the *Parvi*.]

On the four mountains to be ascended.

1. “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” (Ps. 23:3). Christ indeed ascended once bodily above the height of the heavens, but now he ascends daily in a spiritual manner in the hearts of the elect. Therefore, if we also wish to ascend with him, we must ascend to the mountains of virtues from the valleys of vices.

There are two kinds of those vices. Some harm ourselves; others harm our neighbors. The former are called *flagitia* (“shameful acts”), the latter *facinora* (“criminal deeds”); and all these are called the valley of tears, because the life of sinners is to be lamented with every stream of weeping. From the valley of shameful acts one ascends to the mountain of chastity by a threefold continence: of bodily members, senses, and thoughts. In the first continence, the act is restrained; in the second, the gaze is avoided; in the third, the desire is cut off.

Likewise, from the valley of criminal deeds one ascends to the mountain of innocence. Here a ladder is raised: “What you do not wish done to you, do not do to another” [Col. 0685B] (Tob. 4:16). Upon it is placed a threefold step of fear: fear of the person suffering, lest he repay in kind; fear of superior authority, lest it inflict punishment; and fear of the inward Judge, who renders to each according to his works. When people have ascended this mountain, they are now righteous and live by faith; but, according to the Apostle, they must suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12).

2. Therefore one must flee from the mountain of innocence to the mountain of patience. Here too a ladder of three steps is raised. The first is the Lord’s passion; the second, the courage of the martyrs; the third, the greatness of the reward. These steps may rightly be called steps of shame, just as in innocence there were steps of fear.

Notice that this mountain of patience, according to these steps, is steep, thorny, and dry: steep because of the difficulty of imitating the Lord’s passion; thorny because of the pricks of manifold temptations—losses of property, insults in words, and tortures of the body, in which holy martyrs are tested; dry because of the recompense of rewards, which is hoped for not in this age but in the future.

After this mountain there remains another mountain to be ascended: the mountain of mountains. When one arrives at it, God already rests there. Thus it is written: “His place has been made in peace” [Col. 0685D] (Ps. 75:3). But on this mountain of peace too a ladder of charity is raised. Hence the Lord says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. 7:12). For we wish recompense to be made to us, we wish to be forgiven, and we wish gifts to be given freely.

## SERMON LXII

[Note: [Col. 0685D] Elsewhere, no. 22 among the *Parvi*. Sermons 20 and 21 are found among the *Sentences*.]

On the various and true following of Christ.

“He who serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26). [Col. 0686A] Some do not follow Christ but flee him; others do not follow but go ahead of him; some follow but do not catch up; others follow and attain him.

Those do not follow but flee who have not yet ceased from sinning. Of them it is written: “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20); and the Prophet says: “Behold, those who distance themselves from you shall perish” (Ps. 72:27). Those do not follow but go ahead who prefer their own judgments to the pronouncements of their teachers. Peter bore their image when he rebuked the Lord, who wished to suffer for our salvation, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you” (Matt. 16:22).

Those follow but do not attain who act sluggishly and half-heartedly, or who fail to persevere to the end and turn back from the middle of the road. To such people the Apostle says: “Lift up the hands which hang down and the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that no one who is lame may go astray, but rather be healed” [Col. 0686B] (Heb. 12:12–13). Those follow and attain who perseveringly imitate the path of his humility with devout affection of mind. Such truly follow the Lord. “He who serves me, let him follow me”: that is, let him imitate me. With what result? “That where I am,” he says, “there also my servant may be” (John 12:26). The fruit of this imitation, therefore, is the dwelling-place of eternal blessedness.

## SERMON LXIII

[Note: [Col. 0686D] Elsewhere, no. 23 among the *Parvi*.]

On the three means prescribed by Christ for recovering blessedness, in the words: “Whoever wishes to come after me,” etc. (Luke 9:23).

“Whoever wishes, let him come after me, through me, to me.” After [Col. 0686C] me, because I am truth; through me, because I am the way; to me, because I am life. “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

Christ, the Power of God and Wisdom of God, the Angel of great counsel, set before the rational soul made in the image of the Trinity three things: servitude, lowliness, and hardship. In self-denial is servitude; in bearing the cross is lowliness; in imitating Christ hardship is marked out. Thus the soul, which through disobedience had fallen from the condition of threefold felicity, may rise through obedience by the humbling affliction of threefold misery.

For it had fallen away from itself, from the society of angels, and from the vision of God: that is, from freedom, dignity, and blessedness. Therefore let it hear the counsel: by denying itself—that is, its own will—it may recover its freedom; by taking up its cross—that is, by crucifying its flesh with its vices and desires—it may through the good of continence recover the society of angels; by following Christ—that is, by imitating his passion—it may recover the vision of his glory. For “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” [Col. 0686D] (Rom. 8:17).

## SERMON LXIV

[Note: [Col. 0686D] Elsewhere, nos. 24 and 25 among the *Parvi*.]

On the precious life and death of the saints.

1. “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). Sometimes life makes the death of his saints precious in the sight of the Lord; sometimes the cause does; sometimes life together with the cause does. In confessors who die in the Lord, life makes it precious. In martyrs who die for the Lord, sometimes the cause alone makes it precious, and sometimes the cause together with life does. That death is precious which life commends; more precious is that which the cause makes so; most precious is that which both life and cause precede.

2. There are three things that make a human life holy: sober nourishment, righteous conduct, and devout understanding. Nourishment will be sober if we live continently, sociably, and obediently—that is, chastely, charitably, and humbly. For through continence chastity is acquired; through sociability, charity; through obedience, humility. This is the virtue that makes the soul, perfectly subjected to God, live securely beneath the shadow of his wings [Col. 0687B].

Conduct will be righteous if it is upright, discerning, and fruitful: upright through good intention; discerning through the measure of one’s ability; fruitful through usefulness to one’s neighbors. Understanding will be devout if our faith perceives God as supremely powerful, supremely wise, and supremely good: so that through his power we believe our weakness is helped; through his wisdom, our ignorance corrected; through his goodness, our iniquity washed away. Three things make the death of saints precious: rest from labor, joy in newness, and security in eternity.

## SERMON LXV

[Note: [Col. 0687D] Elsewhere, no. 26 among the *Parvi*.]

On the connection of the threefold parable in Matthew 13:44–48: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field,” etc.

[Col. 0687C]

1. The threefold parable in a single reading commends to us a threefold step. The field is the body. While the passions of desires still rule it, it lies uncultivated and subject to the curse; it brings forth thorns and thistles, and what lies hidden within it is unknown. Who at that time would judge it capable of bearing fruits worthy of repentance? Why, soul, do you dispose of your body so foolishly? Do you not know what is hidden in it? What but the kingdom of heaven? To find it in the body is to find works of salvation by which you may attain the kingdom of heaven. Therefore buy the field and reclaim your body for yourself from your desires, paying, of course, the price of the fuel and occasions of those very desires [Col. 0687D].

2. But once you have dug up the treasure, become now a merchant and seek precious pearls. If you find one most precious pearl, then sell everything you have and buy it. What, however, is this one thing so precious? It is not surprising that he sold all that he had for the treasure: that is, that for the riches of salvation he abandoned both sins and the incentives to sin. For these alone were what he previously possessed.

But now, after finding this treasure, how does he seek good pearls and sell everything for one? I judge that this one is nothing other than unity. He seeks good pearls who, in the work of his salvation, is not content with lesser goods but seeks out the highest and most excellent things. Finding nothing more precious than unity, therefore, let him spare none of the rest for its sake: let him boldly prefer unity to fasts, vigils, and prayers [Col. 0688A].

3. Yet I wish him to remain in that unity in such a way that he is not one person among all, but one with all. Let him spread wide the bosom of his heart; let him enclose within his inward parts every kind of affection; let him become all things to all, ready both to rejoice with them and to suffer with them: to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep. For when he comes to the shore, he will exclude the bad fish from the net of charity, and whatever is troublesome will be cast out.

## SERMON LXVI

[Note: [Col. 0688D] Elsewhere, no. 27 among the *Parvi*.]

On the eight beatitudes opposed to the same number of sins.

1. In the same order in which guilt came first, the remedy for guilt followed. The first sin was committed in heaven through the pride of the transgressing angel, who said in his heart: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14). He swelled up in himself and, cast out from the company of blessed spirits, lost the kingdom of heaven. Against this sin it was said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0688B] (Matt. 5:3).

The second sin was committed through the disobedience of the woman in paradise (Gen. 3:6). From this sin the flesh was made rebellious against the spirit, so that, because her spirit was not subject to the Creator, neither might her flesh be subject to her spirit. Against this it was said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. [Col. 0688C] 5:4). The Lord includes the remedy for these two sins when he says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

The third sin was that this same woman also drew the man with her into guilt (Gen. 3:6). She ought indeed to have wept for her sin, rather than adding sin to sin; but she thought she would find consolation in having her husband share her sin. In some way it is natural for everyone, whether in vices or virtues, to wish to associate a companion with himself. Against this sin is the remedy: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

2. Adam committed the fourth sin when he consented (Gen. 3:6). For Adam, as the Apostle says, “was not deceived; but the woman, being deceived, was in transgression” [Col. 0688D] (1 Tim. 2:14). She sinned through ignorance; he sinned through weakness. He sinned, however, by loving his wife too much—not because he did her will, but because he preferred her will to the divine will. Thus the Lord said to him: “Because you obeyed the voice of your wife more than mine, the earth is cursed in your work” (Gen. 3:17).

For it was right that he should do the will of the one to whom he owed more. Who, indeed, can doubt that he owed more to his Creator than to his wife? For he was bound to his wife by love alone, but to God by both fear and love. Therefore two bonds ought to have had more force to hold him to God’s command than one alone to hold him to attachment for his wife [Col. 0689A]. Against this fourth sin the remedy was applied: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6).

Adam did indeed possess righteousness, having been created righteous by the righteous God; but because he did not direct it by free choice, he easily slipped away from it by that same free choice. By contrast, the Psalmist says of Christ: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity” (Ps. 44:8). The fifth sin was likewise committed by him who shifted his own guilt onto his wife, when he said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12). First, he was cruel to himself, because he excused his sin; second, to his wife, whom he accused. Indeed, vengeance for sin is sufficiently ample and fitting when he accused her for love of whom he had sinned. [Col. 0689B] Against this sin it was said: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7).

3. Eve committed the sixth sin when, reproved by the Lord for why she had done this, she replied: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (Gen. 3:13). Thus she too turned to malicious words, “to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140:4), casting blame upon the serpent as though free from fault; although the serpent’s suggestion would have harmed her not at all had she refused the consent of her own will. Perhaps some movement of pride had first arisen in her, through which she deserved to be deceived by the serpent. What was said against this? “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

The seventh sin was committed outside paradise, when Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him [Col. 0689C] (Gen. 4:8). From that time onward it has become inveterate for the wicked to rise against the good and oppress them. The remedy for this sin is: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” But if the wicked refuse to cease from hostility, let the righteous endure them patiently, hearing the consolation that follows: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:9–10). See how necessary was Christ’s coming: to subject flesh to spirit, reconcile the human being to himself, and reconcile God to humankind.

## SERMON LXVII

[Note: [Col. 0689D] Elsewhere, no. 28 among the *Parvi*.]

On the two kinds of commandments of the Law: moral and figurative.

[Col. 0689D]

1. “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). In the old Law I find a twofold kind of commandments. Some are moral, such as: “You shall not covet”; “You shall not commit adultery”; “Honor your father” (Exod. 20:17, 14, 12), and things like these. There are also certain figurative and shadowy commandments, such as the sacrifice of bulls and the blood of goats.

Yet that carnal people could neither fulfill the former nor obtain salvation in the latter. Therefore the Savior in the Gospel reproaches the Pharisees concerning the commandments of the Law, because through their traditions they made the commandments of God void (Mark 7:13)—undoubtedly those commandments in which there was moral edification. For concerning the others he himself speaks through the prophet: “I gave them commandments that were not good” [Col. 0690A] (Ezek. 20:25): plainly those in which there was a shadow of things to come.

For what rational consistency is there in a ram being punished when a human being sins, so that he might say with the Prophet: “Then I paid for things which I did not take” (Ps. 68:5)? A people that was not good rightly received commandments that were not good, as the Prophet says: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverse” (Ps. 17:26). For God knew the carnal hearts of the Jews; accordingly, he handed down to them carnal sacraments, which could not make the worshiper perfect in conscience through regulations of the flesh.

Therefore Christ our Lord came full of grace and truth, so that moral commandments might now be fulfilled by grace, while those that had been shadowy and mystical, now that truth has been revealed, might no longer be observed according to the letter but understood spiritually according to the Spirit [Col. 0690B]. Therefore, when a person sins, a ram or bull is no longer slain; rather, a living sacrifice of the body—a rational and acceptable sacrifice—obtains both forgiveness and grace through fasts and labors.

Sermon 68, or no. 29 among the *Parvi*, since it differs in no respect from Sermon 32 *On Various Matters*, is intentionally omitted here.

## SERMON LXIX

[Note: [Col. 0690D] Elsewhere, no. 30 among the *Parvi*.]

On the threefold renewal of threefold oldness.

1. “As we have borne the image of the earthly man, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:49). There are two men, the old and the new: Adam is old, Christ new. The former is earthly, the latter heavenly; the former’s image is oldness, the latter’s image newness. Now there is a threefold oldness, [Col. 0690C] and correspondingly a threefold newness. For there is oldness in the heart, in the mouth, and in the body: the three ways in which we have sinned—by thought, speech, and deed. In the heart are carnal and worldly desires, that is, love of the flesh and love of the world. Likewise, in the mouth there is a double oldness: arrogance and disparagement. There is also a double oldness in the body: shameful acts and crimes. All these are the image of the old man, and all these must be renewed in us. If there were no oldness in the heart, the Apostle would not say: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who according to God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4:23–24). Likewise, if there were no oldness in the mouth, Scripture would not say: “Let old things depart from your mouth” [Col. 0690D] (1 Sam. 2:3). And the Apostle says: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only what is good, for the building up of faith, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. 4:29). He also makes mention of the oldness of the body when he says: “As you have presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity.” And concerning its renewal he adds: “So now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6:19).

2. Let our heart therefore be renewed from carnal and worldly desires, so that, when these have been expelled, love of God and love of the heavenly homeland may be introduced. Let arrogance and disparagement depart from our mouth, and let true confession of our sins and [Col. 0691A] a good estimation of our neighbours take their place. Instead of shameful acts and crimes, which constitute the oldness of the body, let continence and innocence be taken up, so that opposite vices may be driven away by opposite virtues. This aforesaid renewal is wrought by Christ dwelling in us through faith, as he himself says: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5). Hence he says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song 8:6). Thus, dwelling in the heart, he is wisdom; dwelling in the mouth, truth; dwelling in the body, righteousness.

## SERMON LXX

[Note: [Col. 0691D] Elsewhere, 31 among the Short Sermons.] On vigilance and concern for the care of salvation.

“We have become a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men” (1 Cor. 4:9). Indeed, to evil and good alike. For the passion of envy makes the former attentive to us, while the compassion of mercy makes the latter attentive, so that they continually watch us: the former desiring our [Col. 0691B] downfall, the latter our progress. Certainly we are under trial, meanwhile situated midway between paradise and hell, as though placed between the cloister and the world. What we do is carefully observed from both sides; from both sides it is said, “Oh, that he might come over to us!”—with a different intention indeed, but perhaps not with a dissimilar desire. But if the eyes of all are thus upon us, where have our own eyes gone, or why have they alone withdrawn from us? Closely watched with such concern on the right and on the left, we alone neglect to inspect our life; we alone neglect to look upon ourselves, neither fearing deceitful spirits nor at least reverencing ministering spirits. “The righteous await me, until you reward me” (Ps. 141:8). And again: “Sinners awaited me in order to destroy me” (Ps. 118:95). From one side hell is prepared for me, from the other a crown; and between the one and the other do I wish to trifle, do I delight in yawning? So completely am I neither drawn by desire nor frightened by danger—neither eager nor fearful—precisely where these were most necessary: most ruinously insensible to both. Let us arise at last, brothers, and not receive our souls in vain, souls for whose sake others watch with such zeal, whether for good or for evil. It is no small matter which enemies thus pursue and fellow-citizens thus await.

## SERMON LXXI

[Note: [Col. 0691D] Elsewhere, 34 among the Short Sermons; Sermons 32 and 33 having been counted among the Sentences at [Col. 0692D].] A comparison of Egyptian slavery with slavery to the devil.

[Col. 0691D]

1. Complete and perfect morality consists chiefly in two things: avoiding vices and seeking virtues; since it is not enough to abstain from evil unless we also do good. Hence the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27). Let us therefore flee vices and embrace virtues. Thus, sampling the historical narratives briefly, let us gather their moral fruit. Famine compelled Israel to enter Egypt (Gen. 42; 46); immediately it found there a new master, and from free it became enslaved. By dwelling in that land it was reduced under the power of Pharaoh, who commanded the males [Col. 0692A] to be killed and the females preserved. Israel is harshly afflicted with works of clay and brick (Exod. 1); Pharaoh supplies straw to those labouring: famine compelled it.

2. It is not famine of bread or thirst for water, but famine for hearing the word of God, that compels many to enter Egypt. This word of God is the true light, “which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). Hence the Psalmist says: “The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18:9). Whoever follows this light does not walk in darkness, but has the light of life. From the light of the commandments one passes to the light of rewards. Whoever suffers want of this divine word is compelled to enter Egypt, that is, darkness. For he is enveloped in the darkness of ignorance and subjected to the dominion of Pharaoh, that is, the devil, who is prince of Egypt, that [Col. 0692B] is, of darkness, according to the saying of the Apostle: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavens” (Eph. 6:12).

Under Pharaoh’s yoke works of clay are performed, that is, dissolute and filthy works. From him are supplied straws, that is, light thoughts. Straw is easily set alight and consumed in a moment. So also evil thoughts injected by the devil are quickly kindled in our minds, when the softness of the flesh gives consent. But if we strive manfully to resist, with God’s help they are immediately extinguished. With burning straw the clay was baked and hardened into bricks; and wicked thoughts, which are clay, are set alight by the straws of pleasure. When they pass into action, they are then baked; [Col. 0692C] but when they are drawn into habit, they are then hardened.

## SERMON LXXII

[Note: [Col. 0692D] Elsewhere, 35 among the Short Sermons.] On the way of the ungodly and the way of the Lord.

1. “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” (Ps. 1:1). Godly people are those who believe in God and worship him. For godliness is the worship of God (Job 20, according to the Septuagint). This worship consists in three things—faith, hope, and charity—which are invisible. The ungodly lack these three, for they do not worship him; and their counsel is to prefer visible things to invisible, earthly things to heavenly. Their head and prince is the devil, who first departed from godliness and, having become ungodly, by his deceit cast down from that same godliness even human beings placed in paradise, [Col. 0692D] wishing to have them as companions in his error and participants in his iniquity. For he seduced Eve, and she brought her husband under her sway. Likewise, even now the demon makes suggestions to the flesh, the flesh to the spirit, and the counsel of the ungodly comes about. For they say to one another: “Let there be one purse for us all” (Prov. 1:14). Thus each puts his own obol, as it were, into the purse of memory: the demon a suggestion, the flesh pleasure, the spirit consent. Then, as from a common contribution, they purchase for themselves suitable provisions: the flesh purchases burning, namely the fire that is not quenched; the spirit, an evil conscience, that is, the worm that does not [Col. 0693A] die; but the demon purchases the blood of both.

2. The counsel of the ungodly is entered in four ways. Some are dragged there unwillingly; others are drawn there because they are enticed; others are led astray through ignorance; others follow voluntarily. Four virtues are necessary to these, by which, armed, they may resist and not enter into that counsel. Those who are unwilling require fortitude, by which they resist threats, torments, and losses even unto death. Those drawn by enticement need temperance, which restrains unlawful desires, yields neither to promises nor softens under flatteries. Those led astray through ignorance need prudence, which distinguishes useless things from useful and teaches what should be retained and what rejected. Those who follow voluntarily need justice. Justice is rectitude of will, which neither loves to sin nor consents to sin. [Col. 0693B] Justice and fortitude have their seat in the will, because the will ought to be just and strong. Justice is ordered in this way: rejecting evils and preferring better things to good things. Adam does not seem to have possessed it, since by consenting to evil he abandoned what was useful. Prudence and temperance have their seat in reason, because reason ought to be prudent and temperate. Prudence, indeed, is reason taught by grace to avoid the contagions of injustice for the sake of justice. It avoids not only manifest injustice, but also things that are in some way contrary to justice, attending not to what is lawful but rather to what is expedient: avoiding riches and certain other things not because they are unlawful, but because they are accustomed to be hindrances to justice. But because some do this from hypocrisy, the phrase “for the sake of [Col. 0693C] justice” is added.

Justice is the perfection of the rational soul. The other virtues—fortitude, temperance, and prudence—serve its acquisition or preservation; they preserve justice, lest it be lost or diminished. But once justice is perfect and passes into the affection of the heart, it is the same as those three, because it is strong, prudent, and temperate.

3. “Who has not walked.” Walking away belongs to those who are inconstant and can easily be moved. Some, wishing to avoid this, become plainly obstinate: accepting no one’s counsel and holding their purpose immovably. Therefore there is added, “and has not stood”; namely, that he may be neither fickle nor obstinate. The way of sinners is the world, or one’s own will, which is pride; from it come all evils, just as goods come from the common good. “And has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” He sits who, by his example, teaches others to sin. This is the seat, and it rests upon four legs. The first leg is malice; the second, contempt for God; the third, irreverence; the fourth, cunning. Malice is to love evil and take a relish in evil, and to love evil because it is evil, as the devil does and as some wicked people do. But because it sometimes happens that such people fear God—not with a good fear, but lest they incur either loss of possessions or bodily torment—in order to become still more evil they also despise God himself; and thus contempt for God becomes the second leg. Again, it could happen that they love evil and despise God, but are restrained by shame before the people among whom they live. Therefore, for an increase of evil, the third leg follows: irreverence, so that they fear neither God nor reverence human beings. For the completion of malice, moreover, the fourth leg, cunning, is present, so that they know how to make use of the three things mentioned, mixing poison with oil and vinegar with honey. The raised part of the seat, to which its occupant clings, is power. For if one who possesses the things mentioned is powerful, he then does very great harm; or if he can attract to himself a powerful person whom he may seduce by his counsel and drive to evil. [Col. 0694A] Then a cushion is added, that he may sit comfortably. The cushion is made from the light feathers of birds, signifying vain glory and popular favour, by which delighted people are puffed up. A footstool is placed beneath the feet so that they may not touch the ground. For some such people do not perform earthly actions, but feign spiritual ones, [Col. 0694B] in order to deceive more effectively. Their teaching is like a pestilence, occupying and devastating many places.

4. “But his will is in the law of the Lord.” The preceding verse said what must be rejected; this verse says what must be desired. The former said, as it were, “Turn away from evil”; this says, “and do good” (Ps. 36:27), which is certainly to walk in the law. But because this way is travelled not by the step of the body but by the affection of the mind, it is said: “His will is in the law of the Lord.” For, as blessed Gregory testifies, to will is to go with the mind.

Along this way three classes of people proceed and pursue, as it were, a course: the slave, the hireling, and the son. The same chariot is drawn by beasts named threat and promise. The slave sits upon threat; [Col. 0694C] the hireling upon promise. Each draws the chariot, one through fear, the other through desire; and each is driven by his own goads. The son alone, who is neither shaken by fear nor enticed by desire, but is moved by the spirit of love, is borne in the chariot without labour or injury: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8:14).

That chariot also has four wheels, the four well-known affections of the soul: love and joy, fear and sadness. The reprobate love temporal things and rejoice when they have done evil; but this love and this joy are followed by everlasting fear and sadness. But the elect, to whom it is said, “The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; yet your sorrow [Col. 0694D] will be turned into joy” (John 16:20), place fear and sadness as the front wheels, love and joy as the rear wheels. For in them fear is changed into charity, and sadness into everlasting joy.

5. It should be noted that this way of the law of the Lord is completed in six days. The first is called groaning of heart; the second, confession of mouth; the third, the giving away of one’s own possession; the fourth, labour of body; the fifth, denial of one’s own will; the sixth, contempt of death. On the seventh there is rest from all the things mentioned, while one hopes for the eighth, the resurrection. “And in his law he shall meditate day and night.” In whatever state a person may be placed, he must never depart from the law of the Lord, but in the day of good things must not forget evil things, and in the day of evil things must always remember [Col. 0695A] good things. Day and night may also be understood as the contemplative and active life, both of which are contained in the law of the Lord.

## SERMON LXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0695D] Elsewhere, 36 among the Short Sermons.] On the folly of people who neither fear nor love God.

“The fool has said in his heart: There is no God” (Ps. 13:1). Although God is one and is a unity, yet not through any diversity in himself but through the changeability of our minds, he seems, to those who taste him, to have different flavours. To one who fears, he tastes of justice and power; to one who loves, of goodness and mercy. Hence the same prophet says elsewhere: “God has spoken once; these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, O Lord, mercy” (Ps. 61:12–13). To hear this is the same thing as to taste it, because both occur in one and the most simple mind. Thus God spoke once, because he begot one Word. Yet through the one Word we hear or taste these two things: that power belongs to God, and to you, O Lord, mercy. But he is wholly foolish to whom God tastes neither of fear nor of love. Let him learn as much as he wishes; I shall not call him wise so long as he neither fears nor loves God. For how can we call perfected in wisdom one whom I see not even initiated? “For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:9); love is its completion; hope claims the middle place. Therefore he to whom God tastes neither of justice through fear nor of mercy through love plainly says in his heart, “There is no God.” For he does not consider God to be God whom he regards as neither just nor merciful.

## SERMON LXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0695D] Elsewhere, 37 among the Short Sermons.] On the corruption of humankind.

[Col. 0695C]

“They are corrupted and have become abominable in their pursuits; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:1). The soul has its own corruption, and the body has its own. The corruption of the soul is threefold; that of the body fourfold. For the body consists of four elements, while the soul subsists in a threefold power. It is rational, concupiscible, and irascible. The rational power, whose health is knowledge of the truth, is corrupted by pride. Once corrupted, it is deceived in two ways: in knowledge of itself and in knowledge of God. Vain glory corrupts concupiscence, envy anger. Corruption of the body is called abomination; and it occurs in four ways, corresponding to the four elements of which it [Col. 0695D] consists. For four things corrupt the body: curiosity, loquacity, cruelty, and pleasure. There are four parts of the body in each of which one of the elements especially prevails. In the eyes there is fire; in the tongue, which forms speech, air; in the hands, whose proper sense is touch, earth; in the genital members, water. This fourfold plague corrupts these four parts: curiosity the eyes, loquacity the tongue, cruelty the hands, pleasure the genitals. Thus people become corrupt and abominable: corrupt in soul, abominable in body; corrupt [Col. 0696A] before God, abominable before human beings.

“There is none who does good, not even one.” There are four classes of people, and of all of them there is none who does good, except one class. Some neither understand God nor seek him, and these are dead. Others do understand, but do not seek him, and these are ungodly. Others seek, but do not understand, and these are foolish. But others both understand and seek, and these are holy: of these alone can it be said that they are those who do good.

## SERMON LXXV

[Note: [Col. 0695D] Elsewhere, 38 among the Short Sermons.] On repentance not to be postponed until death.

“Their infirmities were multiplied; afterwards they hastened.” Why do people neglect to do repentance during their life and place their hope in a final confession? How do they suppose that, within the space of one hour, all the members of the soul can be recalled, when its concupiscences and desires have been scattered throughout the whole world and cling everywhere in the lands as though by some birdlime? “I do not say,” says the Lord, “that I shall not save some even of such people; for I am able in a moment to recall all things. But I will not gather their assemblies out of blood” [Col. 0696B] (Ps. 15:4), that is, the assemblies of those who persist in blood until, their infirmities having been multiplied, they are abandoned by their sins before they abandon them. I shall not gather great assemblies of such people. If I remember correctly, in the whole canon of Scripture you will find one thief saved in this way. Therefore do not entrust yourself to such a dangerous expectation.

Indeed, the Spirit breathes not only where he wills but when he wills [Col. 0696C] (John 3:8); nor is it difficult for him suddenly to grant perfect contrition of heart, which others scarcely attain over a long time. But how do you know that he will then choose to help you in this way, when meanwhile you repel him so? The spirit of wisdom is indeed gracious; but “he will not acquit a blasphemer because of his lips” (Wis. 1:6). Hear who that person is: “Accursed is he who sins in hope.”

## SERMON LXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0696D] Elsewhere, 39 among the Short Sermons.] On the necessity and excellence of divine grace.

“You have gone before him with blessings of sweetness” (Ps. 20:4). A threefold blessing is necessary for us: prevening, assisting, and completing. The first is of mercy, the second of grace, the third of glory. Mercy precedes conversion; grace assists one’s manner of life; glory perfects completion. Unless God gives this threefold blessing, our land cannot yield the fruit of salvation. For we cannot begin good until we are preceded by mercy, nor do good until we are assisted by grace, nor be completed in good until we are filled with glory.

Yet among these three, that blessing has a more deserved claim to taste sweet which precedes not merely the undeserving [Col. 0696D] but even those who deserve ill: so that, while we are still children of wrath and work the works of death, he thinks thoughts of peace concerning us and bestows the good Spirit, the Spirit of life, the Spirit of adoption, not even upon those who ask—indeed, upon those who assail him.

[Note: [Col. 0696D] Elsewhere: “upon those who repent, indeed, upon those who do not repent.”]

Not upon those who call upon him, [Col. 0697A] but upon those who provoke him; not upon those who intercede, but even upon those who repel him. What can taste sweet to that soul to which such great mercy does not taste sweet? Rightly, therefore, the blessing which precedes is called a blessing of sweetness; that which assists, a blessing of strength; that which completes, a blessing of fullness.

## SERMON LXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0697D] Elsewhere, 40 among the Short Sermons.] On the differing lot of people who know and do not know God, and likewise of those known and not known by God.

“A people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. 17:45). It would not be greatly astonishing if a people known by God served him. But when a people unknown to him serves him and obeys at the hearing of the ear, this must be reckoned as great praise. Among those known and [Col. 0697B] unknown, and those knowing and not knowing, there are four distinctions. Some are known by God and know God; others are neither known nor know; others are known indeed but do not themselves know; still others are not known, yet know. To know on God’s part is to make happy; to know on a human being’s part is to give thanks.

Therefore those who are known by God and know God are the holy angels: made happy by him, they are always occupied with his praises and devoted to his service. Those who are neither known nor know are the poor by necessity: neither abundance of temporal things enriches them, nor does divine service make them happy. Those who are known but do not know are the rich of this [Col. 0697C] world: though they abound in received wealth, pressed down by the carnal desires of this world, they never raise their heart to heavenly things. But those who are not known and do know are voluntary poor: neither tribulation nor distress nor any other dangers whatever can separate them from the charity of God. These, assuredly, are tested in many ways by adversities and wearied by harsh tribulations, as it is written: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. 27:6).

The psalm also speaks in their person: “O God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” Do not those who pray to be looked upon seem to be unknown? Nevertheless, although they seem forsaken, they themselves know God; and immediately in the same [Col. 0697D] psalm, in the person of those who know him, it adds: “My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and it is not folly to me” (Ps. 21:2–3). Therefore the divine voice says of these: “A people whom I did not know served me.” It is as though he openly said to his angels: What if you serve me, whom I make happy, when those serve me whom I leave in their poverty? And what if you obey me, you who see my face, when those too obey who only hear me and do not see? For angels see, human beings hear. They hear, that is, and obey, so that when they have at last been made like angels, they too may deserve to see. Thus hearing is the merit [Col. 0698A] of seeing, and seeing the reward of hearing. Hearing comes first, seeing afterwards, as it is written: “Hear, daughter, and see” (Ps. 44:11). Whoever therefore desires to see God in the future must certainly first hear God in the present and obey at the hearing of the ear.

## SERMON LXXVIII
