[Note: [Col. 0697D] Elsewhere, 42 among the Short Sermons. It appears as no. 51 among the Sentences.] On the distinction between tent, courts, and house.

There are three: tents, courts, and house. In tents are all the righteous who live and labour in the flesh, because tents belong to those who labour and serve as soldiers. A tent has a roof, but lacks a foundation, and is portable, because the righteous are not founded in present things but seek the city above which has foundations. Their faith also, which is the foundation, is not in earthly things [Col. 0698B] but in the Lord. They have a roof, that is, the defence and protection of grace. Courts are spacious places adjacent to the house. In them are holy souls stripped of their bodies, which are in a broad place after laying aside the narrowness of the flesh. Courts have a foundation but no roof, because souls that are in the love of God do not fall—hence, “Our feet were standing” (Ps. 121:2)—but do not yet have a roof, as they await an increase which will come only at the resurrection of their bodies. But after that resurrection they will be with the angels in the house, which has foundation and roof. The foundation is the stability of eternal blessedness; the roof, its consummation and perfection.

## SERMON LXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0698D] Elsewhere, 43 among the Short Sermons.] On the will’s always and in all things being subject to God.

[Col. 0698C]

“My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” (Ps. 56:8). The royal way, brothers, turns neither to the right nor to the left. Yet one finds a person ready once, but not ready a second time. If God says to him, “Cast out the bondwoman and her son” (Gen. 21:10)—by which I mean works of the flesh—he does not hesitate. If he says, “Offer to me your son Isaac, whom you love” (Gen. 22:2), he plainly can no longer bear to hear this patiently: that for the benefit or unity of the brethren he should seem to endure the loss of spiritual devotion. Why should not Christ’s servant easily cast off whatever pertains to bodily pleasure? But to be deprived with equanimity of spiritual delight when either obedience [Col. 0698D] compels it or the claim of brotherly charity requires it—this indeed is to offer a great and God-pleasing holocaust. Remember, however, that in this sacrifice it is not Isaac but the ram of obstinacy that must be slaughtered.

## SERMON LXXX

[Note: [Col. 0698D] Elsewhere, 44 among the Short Sermons.] On manifold unity.

1. “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity” (Ps. 132:1). There is natural unity, carnal unity, virtual unity, moral unity, spiritual unity, social unity, personal unity, and principal unity. Natural unity is between body and soul. Carnal unity is also between man and [Col. 0699A] woman, concerning which it is said: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). Virtual unity is that which joins a person to himself, so that he may not flow out in different directions, but may ask one thing from the Lord with the Prophet (Ps. 26:4). Moral unity is that which joins us to our neighbour. Hence the Psalmist says: “Who makes those of one manner dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:7). Spiritual unity is that which joins us to God. Hence the Apostle: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). Social unity is among the angels, to whom in every respect willing the same thing and refusing the same thing belong. Personal unity is in Christ. Principal unity, which is also substantial unity, is in the Trinity.

2. “Behold, how good and how pleasant.” Some things are good and pleasant; some are neither good nor pleasant; some are good but not pleasant; some are pleasant but not good. From things good but not pleasant one comes to things good and pleasant. From things pleasant but not good one comes to things neither good nor pleasant. Good but not pleasant are continence, patience, and discipline. Pleasant but not good are pleasure, curiosity, and vanity. Neither good nor pleasant are envy, sadness, and acedia. Good and pleasant are honourableness, charity, and purity.

To attain this good and pleasant state, virtual unity and moral unity are necessary. Cowardice and fickleness disturb the first. Cowardice makes one abandon one’s purpose; fickleness makes one change it. Obstinacy, suspicion, and dissimulation disturb the second. Obstinacy does not receive one’s neighbour, suspicion does not trust one’s neighbour, dissimulation does not join itself to one’s neighbour. Hope of eternal things expels cowardice, humble obedience [Col. 0699C] fickleness. Obstinacy is driven away by humility, suspicion and dissimulation by charity.

## SERMON LXXXI

[Note: [Col. 0699D] Elsewhere, 45 among the Short Sermons.] On the praise of God in a sinner’s mouth.

“Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9). Even praise in the mouth of a repentant sinner does not seem beautiful, because he still suffers shame from recollection and remembrance of sin, and is frequently pierced with compunction by it. Yet in him confession is useful and fruitful, even if the praise is not beautiful and comely. But after, progressing from the benefits of God, he cleaves to divine praise and continually delights and progresses in it, so that nothing else pleases him, then beautiful praise of God is in his mouth. This is like a farmer [Col. 0699D] who, while manuring his field, is entirely in mud and dung: his labour is not beautiful, although fruitful; but when he gathers the sheaves of the harvest, then the labour is beautiful and sweet.

## SERMON LXXXII

[Note: [Col. 0699D] Elsewhere, 46 among the Short Sermons.] On the diligent guarding of the heart.

1. “Keep your heart with every guard, because from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4:23). Life proceeds from the heart in two ways: either because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Rom. 10:10), and “the righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), and the heart is purified by faith (Acts 15:9), and God is seen—that is, known—with a pure heart (Matt. 5:8); and this is eternal life, “that they may know you, the one [Col. 0700A] God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3): or because Christ, who is our life and now dwells through faith in our hearts (Eph. 3:17), will be manifested, and we too shall be manifested with him in glory (Col. 3:4). He who now lies hidden in the heart will then proceed, as it were, from the heart to the body, when he transforms the body of our lowliness into conformity with the body of his glory (Phil. 3:21). Hence another Apostle says: “Now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John 3:2).

2. But we must consider how he says, “Keep your heart with every guard.” People of this world are accustomed to say: “He guards a good castle who guards his body.” But we do not say so. Rather, he guards a worthless dung-heap who guards his body, as the Apostle testifies: [Col. 0700B] “He who sows in the flesh shall reap corruption from the flesh; but he who sows in the Spirit shall reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Gal. 6:8). It is as if he said: the fortress of the soul should rather be cultivated and guarded, because eternal life proceeds from it. But this fortress, situated in the land of enemies, is attacked on every side; and therefore it must be fortified with every guard—that is, from every side—with watchful concern: below, above, before and behind, on the right and on the left.

Below, the concupiscence of the flesh attacks, which wars against the soul, because the flesh lusts against the spirit. Above, God’s judgment hangs over us: “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). He had guarded his heart with sufficient care on this side who said: “For I always feared God as waves swelling over me” [Col. 0700C] (Job 31:23). Behind is deadly pleasure, arising from remembrance of past sins; before is the pressure of temptations; on the left is the disturbance of arrogant and murmuring brothers; on the right is the devotion of obedient brothers. For these too, unless care is taken, can harm in two ways: by provoking envy of their good deeds, or by exciting emulation of singular grace.

3. Therefore let the rigour of discipline keep watch against the flesh; against God’s judgment, let there be the judgment of one’s own confession—and let this be twofold, public concerning public sins and secret concerning secret ones. Hence the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31). [Col. 0700D] Against the pleasure that proceeds from remembrance of past sins, let there be frequent reading; against the pressure of temptation, the insistence of suppliant prayer; against the disturbance of brethren, patience and compassion; against the fervour of obedient brethren, rejoicing with them and discernment. For rejoicing with them expels envy, and discernment excessive emulation.

## SERMON LXXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0700D] Elsewhere, 47 among the Short Sermons.] On cautiously receiving human praise.

“Have you found honey? Do not eat much of it, lest perhaps, filled with it, you vomit it up” (Prov. 25:16). The favour of human praise can not inappropriately be understood here by the name of honey; and rightly we are forbidden not every eating of this honey but immoderate [Col. 0701A] eating of it. For sometimes we receive human praises usefully, only for the sake of brotherly charity and for the salvation of those who more readily comply with us on that account. Therefore, if this moderation is preserved, a moderate consumption of this honey will not harm. But whatever exceeds this is from evil and will turn to destruction.

For whoever gives his whole heart to it, puffing himself up, becoming gross and fattened by the favour of human praise, eats too immoderately when he has found honey. The holy Prophet prays to the Lord to be guarded from this, expressing the same favour of which we have spoken, not by the name of honey but by the closely related name of oil, when he says: “But let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Ps. 140:5). Do you wish to know when the immoderate eater [Col. 0701B] vomits up the sweet food of honey, which he took to satiety and thereby exceeded the measure of moderation? Without doubt, when he hears another person praised and wastes away with envy—then, I say, he vomits up with much distress the praises by which he was filled, seeking no other fruit but being content with human favour itself, and which he had eaten with ruinous delight. For a mind given over to vanity and swollen with arrogance considers another’s praise to be its own reproach.

## SERMON LXXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0701D] Elsewhere, 48 among the Short Sermons.] On constancy against the devil who tempts.

1. There are two places belonging to the rational soul: a lower one, which it governs; and a higher one, in which it rests. The lower place which it governs is the body; the higher place in which it rests is God. Of either one may rightly be understood what is written: “If the spirit of one having power rises against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. 10:4): namely, either the lower place, by governing it, or the higher, by resting in it. But what I first said applies to those still untrained and imperfect, to whom the Apostle speaks: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6:19). For the soul has three things to do in the body: to give it life, to give it sensation, and to govern it. But whether life is taken away or sensation disturbed, it is condemned for neither. Yet if, overcome, it yields to the tempter, that is reckoned to it as sin. Therefore it is told, when a spirit rises against it, not to leave its place; that is, when temptation presses upon it, not to present its members to sin as weapons of iniquity.

2. It should be noted, moreover, that it says: “If the spirit of one having power rises against you.” For the malignant spirit can do nothing against us unless sent or permitted. Hence, although his will is always evil, his power is never anything but just. His evil will belongs to himself; but he has power from no source other than God. Yet the Lord always restrains that power, lest through the wickedness of his will he punish more than the merits of those punished require. Let this suffice concerning the lower place. Concerning the higher place, however, this means that, when the devil tempts it, the soul must not abandon the repose of mind which it has in God; rather, wherever he may attack, it should remain steadfastly fixed in God and tranquil. This latter interpretation applies to the perfect, who can say with Elijah: “As the Lord God of Israel lives, in whose presence I stand” (4 Kings 3:14); and also what is said of John the Apostle: “As he is, so also are we in this world” (1 John 4:17). This interpretation, I say, applies to the perfect, who already in their manner of life imitate, in a certain way, the state of eternity.

## SERMON LXXXV

[Note: [Col. 0701D] Elsewhere, no. 49 among the Short Sermons.] On the soul’s irrevocable fall.

“Whether a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, there it shall be” (Eccl. 11:3). In Holy Scripture the warmth and mildness of the south commonly have a good meaning; but “from the north every evil is spread abroad” (Jer. 1:14). Moreover, someone saw human beings “like trees” (Mark 8:24). A tree is cut down in death; and wherever it falls, there it shall be, because God will judge you where he finds you. There, I say, it shall remain immutably and irrevocably. Let it see where it is going to fall before it falls; for after it has fallen, it will neither rise again nor even turn itself about.

But if you wish to know where a tree is going to fall, look to its branches. On whichever side the branches are more numerous and weightier, do not doubt that it will fall in that direction, if it is then cut down. Our branches are our desires: toward the south we stretch them if they are spiritual; toward the north, if they are carnal. Which prevail is shown by the body in the middle. For those desires prevail which draw the body after themselves. Thus our body stands between the spirit which it ought to serve and the carnal desires which wage war against the soul, or the powers of darkness, as though it were a cow placed between a robber and a farmer. Whatever threats the robber may make, whatever he may attempt, if he does not lead the cow away, the farmer has won. So too, however fiercely the malignant one may rage, however grievously corrupt desires may torment: if the soul claims its vessel for itself, it must be considered victorious, so that, as the Apostle says, “Sin may not reign in our mortal body”; but just as we presented our members “as slaves to iniquity unto iniquity,” so may we present them “as slaves to righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6:12, 19).

## SERMON LXXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0702D] Elsewhere, no. 51 among the Short Sermons; no. 50 among the Sentences.] On creation in fixed weight, measure, and number.

[Col. 0702D]

1. “You have made all things in weight, measure, and number” (Wis. 9:21). This is said by contrast with the divine essence itself. Created things were made in weight, measure, and number; the Creator alone is free from all these. Weight is considered in the worth of a thing. Thus that which may be compared with another thing of its kind as greater, lesser, or equal is made in weight. That has weight whose value can be estimated. Measure, however, is considered in place and time. If we understand place as bodily place alone, the measure of incorporeal things will be in time, not in place. For the soul cannot be in a bodily place; nor is the body—which seems more plausibly to be so—the soul’s place. How, indeed, can that which animates external parts just as it does internal parts be enclosed by the body? It is present at the surface of the skin just as it is in the innermost organs.

2. Through carnal affection and familiarity with bodies, the soul errs so greatly that it does not know how to conceive itself except as corporeal. “For where its treasure is, there is its heart also” (Matt. 6:21). It relishes what it loves. Bound and smeared with earthly affections, it cannot behold its own face. It is fixed in the mire of the deep and does not see itself, but thinks its form to be that muddy image which it bears. Yet the matter is altogether otherwise, and the soul’s measure in respect of place is understood differently. For the place of every thing is the boundary of its substance. But the substance of the soul consists in reason, memory, counsel, judgment, and other such faculties; and each of these is enclosed within its own limit. Every spirit, therefore, except the divine Spirit, is made in measure, because its reason, memory, and all else have their proper measure. All things are made in number, either through the composition of parts, as bodies are, or through diversity and mutability, as incorporeal things also are. God alone is one to whom neither weight, measure, nor number applies at all. God is one: he has nothing of his own kind with which he may be compared. He alone is altogether beyond estimation, eternal and immeasurable, indivisible and wholly unchangeable.

## SERMON LXXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0703D] Elsewhere, no. 52 among the Short Sermons.] On the bridegroom’s kiss, or the grace of contemplation.

[Col. 0703C]

1. “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). There are three kisses: the first, of the feet; the second, of the hands; the third, of the mouth. When we first turn back, we kiss the Lord’s feet. Now the Lord has two feet: mercy and truth. God impresses both these feet upon the hearts of those who turn back, and every sinner who truly turns embraces both feet. For if he received mercy alone without truth, he would fall through presumption. Again, if he received truth without mercy, he would likewise perish through despair. But in order that he may be saved, he humbly falls down before both feet: that through truth he may condemn his sins, and through mercy hope for pardon. This is the first kiss.

The second kiss occurs when we first rise to good works. Then we kiss the Lord’s hands, when we offer him our good works or receive from him the gifts of virtues. But the third kiss occurs when, mourning in penitence now spent and gifts of virtues now received, the mind, inspired by heavenly desire, longs in the impatience of love to be brought into the joys of the secret inner chamber; when, with sweet sighs interrupting the voice of the soul, it sings with the devout affection of the heart: “Your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. 26:8). And so, through vehement desire, the Bridegroom whom it thus loves, thus yearns for, and thus sighs after becomes present to it. Therefore the first kiss occurs in the remission of sins and is called propitiatory; the second occurs in the gifts of virtues and is called bestowing; the third occurs in the contemplation of heavenly things and is called contemplative.

2. It should be known, moreover, that there are two kinds of contemplation. Some ascend and fall; others are caught up and descend. Those ascend of whom it is written: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks.” They did not give thanks because they attributed to their own powers and intellect what God had revealed to them. Therefore their fall follows: “They became vain in their thoughts. Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1:21–22). But the elect are caught up, like Paul and those like him. Yet they also descend, in order to speak to little ones of the things which they have seen in an ecstasy of mind, in such a way, indeed, as the little ones can receive them. Paul is caught up when he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God.” He descends when he says: “Whether we are sober-minded, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5:13). By this latter kind of contemplation the perfect soul desires to be caught up into the most chaste embraces of its Bridegroom, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” As though it said: I cannot rise by my own powers, skill, or merits to contemplate the joys of my Lord; rather, let him himself kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. That is, let it come about by his grace: not through instruction, not through nature, but through his grace let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.

In a marvelous manner it elegantly expresses the grace of the agent, the work, and the mode of the work. For when it says “let him kiss,” the grace of the agent is shown; when it adds “with a kiss,” the work itself—that is, contemplation—is indicated; and when it joins “of his mouth,” it clearly expresses the mode of the work, namely, how contemplation comes about. For by “mouth” the Word is understood.

3. Contemplation comes about through the condescension of the Word of God to human nature by grace, and through the elevation of human nature to the Word itself by divine love. Nor should it seem absurd to anyone if we distinguish these elements in the contemplation of the Word of God; for the Gospel testifies that the incarnation of that same Word of God was brought about in the same order. There grace is first set forth when the Virgin is greeted by the angel: “Hail,” he says, “full of grace.” Then he adds whose grace it is and how great it is, saying: “The Lord is with you.” The work of that same grace is then introduced when it is said: “Blessed is the fruit of your womb.” For the fruit of your womb is the incarnation of the Word. The mode of so great a work is taught where it is said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:28, 35). In these works of the Word—whether those cited from the Gospel or those expounded from the Song of Songs—it is plainly established both that this incarnation was brought about from the abundance of divine grace alone, and that the other work, namely contemplation, can never arise from human will but only from a divine gift.

[Col. 0705A] 4. It should also be noted that this contemplation itself is distinguished in three ways according to the different state of the times. First it is called food; second, drink; third, intoxication. Hence, in what follows, the elect are invited by the voice of the Bridegroom, who says: “Eat, friends, and drink, and be intoxicated, dearly beloved” (Song 5:1). First they eat, while they still live in corruptible flesh. Afterwards, stripped of the body and translated to heaven, they are said to drink the same things which they previously ate, because they now contemplate without labor in direct vision what they previously believed by faith while, remaining in the body, they were absent from the Lord and ate their bread in the sweat of their brow. So too we take more easily what we drink than what we chew, because in the latter there is some labor, while in the former there is an easy passage.

Thus, in this state the saints can indeed drink, but cannot be intoxicated, because in some manner they are held back from the most perfect contemplation of the divinity while they still await the resurrection of their body at the end of the age. When that has occurred, body will cleave so to mind, and mind to God, that thereafter there will be nothing capable of recalling it from the inward intoxication of contemplation. Therefore, in the first invitation those who eat are called friends, that is, dear ones; in the second, because they drink, dearer ones; in the third, because they are intoxicated, dearest ones.

5. “For your breasts are better than wine” (Song 1:1). The bride has two breasts: one of rejoicing with others, the other of compassion. Thus the Apostle nurtures little ones with these two when he says: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15). Wine is understood as worldly desire, of which it is written: “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32:33).

6. “Fragrant with the best ointments” (Song 1:2): this suggests that some ointments are good and some better, but that these best ointments surpass them all. Let us say, then, that there are three kinds of ointment. The first is made from the remembrance of sins, when we are pierced with compunction because of them and seek pardon. This ointment is good because “God has not despised a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:19). It is poured out upon the Lord’s feet and there receives its reward, namely the remission of sins, when the Lord says: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47).

The second ointment is made from the remembrance of God’s benefits. This is rightly poured upon the head, because virtues are referred only to God, from whom they come. This ointment is now more precious, because concerning it it is written: “Why was this waste of ointment made? For it could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.” But the Lord approves this waste when he says: “Let her alone. Why do you trouble her? For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.” He not only approves it but also rewards it, saying: “Amen I say to you, wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done shall also be told in remembrance of her” (Matt. 26:8–13; Mark 14:4, 9).

The third ointment is composed of precious spices, as it is written of certain holy women that “they bought spices, so that when they came they might anoint Jesus” (Mark 16:1). But this third ointment is neither poured out nor wasted, because the Lord did not wish it to be poured upon his dead body but preserved for his living body, that is, the holy Church, to which the women who came with the ointments are sent to proclaim the resurrection. Therefore the first ointment is called the ointment of compunction and is consumed by the fire of contrition; the second, the ointment of devotion, and is consumed by the fire of charity; the third is called the ointment of piety, which is not consumed but kept whole.

## SERMON LXXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0705D] Elsewhere, no. 53 among the Short Sermons.] On the right use of God’s gifts.

[Col. 0706B]

1. As there are two things concerning Christ—one unknown to us, namely his divine generation, concerning which it is written, “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8); and another known, such as his human birth or works—so also concerning the Holy Spirit, one thing is hidden from our minds: namely, how he proceeds from the Father and the Son, being equal and coeternal with that same Father and Son; while another is made manifest by his own teaching, namely, the ways in which he works his grace in us.

For the operation of the Holy Spirit is twofold. He works one thing in us for our own sake, another for the sake of our neighbors. For our own sake—that is, for our benefit—he works in us first compunction, consuming sins; second, devotion, anointing and healing wounds; third, creating understanding, by which, as by bread, he strengthens and confirms us; fourth, by increasing these things more abundantly and pouring in love, he intoxicates us as with wine. The remaining charisms—that is, counsels of wisdom and such things—are given to us for the benefit of others. Hence, when the Apostle spoke of the distribution of gifts, he did not simply say, “To one is given wisdom, to another knowledge”; but added, “a word of knowledge, a word of wisdom” (1 Cor. 12:8), in order to show that gifts of this kind are given for the sake of others, namely, that others may be built up.

2. In these operations a twofold danger must be avoided: lest we share with our neighbors the things given for our own sake, or retain for ourselves the things given for the sake of our neighbors. For if we keep only for ourselves what we have received for the benefit of others, we do not have charity; and it is said to us: “Hidden wisdom and unseen treasure: what profit is there in either?” (Ecclus. 20:32). Again, if we wish to become known to human beings through God’s gifts rather than to please God in the hidden places of the heart, we lose humility; and deservedly we are rebuked by that saying: “What have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). Thus we are endangered in both ways: in the one, by losing humility; in the other, charity. And who can be saved without humility and charity?

The right order of our progress, therefore, is that we should first strive to be filled with those gifts—compunction and the others; then, if through the grace of the Holy Spirit further gifts should be added, namely wisdom and knowledge, we should take care to share them with our neighbors. Thus indeed we shall obtain that gift of the Holy Spirit called discernment of spirits, if we reserve for ourselves those things suited to ourselves alone and bestow upon both ourselves and our neighbors those things granted for the benefit of others.

## SERMON LXXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0707D] Elsewhere, no. 54 among the Short Sermons.] On the kiss desired by the bride, that is, the Holy Spirit.

1. “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). The Son is understood as the mouth of the Father. “No one knows the Son except the Father; and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). But this revelation, whether of the Father or of the Son, comes to no one except through the Holy Spirit. Thus, when Peter said to the Lord, “You are Christ, the Son of the living God,” he answered: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona”—which is interpreted “Son of the Dove”—“because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:16–17). And when the Apostle had first said that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard,” and the rest, he immediately added: “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit” (1 Cor. 2:9–10).

The bride, therefore, appears to possess the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which she knows the Son to be equal to the Father. She does not say, “Let him kiss me with his mouth,” which only the Son can say and no creature whatever can say, since no creature can in any way be equal to the Father; rather, she says, “with the kiss of his mouth.” Now a kiss belongs jointly to the one kissing and the one kissed. If, therefore, Father and Son kiss one another, what is their kiss except the Holy Spirit?

2. This, then, is the kiss which the bride ardently longs to receive, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Paul also testifies that she has received this kiss when he says: “Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4:6). The Savior himself promised this kiss when, urging his disciples to persevering prayer, he said: “If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things”—that is, the good Spirit—“to those who ask him” (Matt. 7:11; Luke 11:13).

From the impress of this kiss the rational soul receives from its Bridegroom, the Word of God, knowledge and love of truth; these are like two lips impressed upon it by the power and wisdom of God themselves. For wisdom bestows knowledge, and power love. The soul itself likewise has two lips with which it kisses its Bridegroom: reason and will. It belongs to reason to receive wisdom, and to will to receive virtue. If reason alone receives the knowledge of wisdom and the will does not have love of virtue, the kiss is not full. Or if the will alone obtains love and reason does not receive knowledge, it is likewise half-full. But it is full and perfect when both wisdom illumines reason and power moves the will.

## SERMON XC

[Note: [Col. 0707D] With Sermons 55 and 56 among the Short Sermons rejected among the Sentences, this sermon has here been combined from nos. 57 and 58; and it appears word for word in the treatise *On Love*, year 5, which may be found in volume V.] On the threefold ointment: of compunction, devotion, and piety.

[Col. 0708A]

1. There are two feet of God: mercy and judgment. With these he continually moves about and walks through spiritual minds, “rejoicing as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6), provided they are such that he may rightly say of them: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Cor. 6:16). The sinful soul first anoints these feet with that first ointment which is called compunction. Thus Mary, who was a sinner, anointed Jesus’ feet. Nor should this ointment seem insignificant, for it is written of it: “The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12:3). Nor is this surprising, since the fragrance of such ointment is perceived even in heaven, as Truth testifies when he says: “There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15:10).

Yet however precious this ointment may seem, compared with the other, called devotion and prepared from the memory of divine benefits, by which the Lord’s head is anointed, it is understood to be cheap and of no value. For concerning the former it is said: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50:19); but concerning the latter: “A sacrifice of praise shall honor me” (Ps. 49:23). You anoint the head with it when you give thanks to God for his gifts; for “the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). Therefore, the divinity in Christ is touched whenever we remember his benefits in praise of him, just as humanity rather than divinity must be thought of when we remember not his gifts but our sins.

2. For in assuming flesh he is known to have received those two feet, mercy and judgment, so that the sinner, who had no access to the head—that is, the divinity—might approach the feet—that is, the humanity. For unless that foot which we have called mercy belonged to the assumed humanity, Paul would not have said of him: “Tempted in all things according to our likeness, apart from sin, that he might become merciful” (Heb. 4:15). And unless judgment likewise belonged to the human being, the God-man himself would not have said of himself: “And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:27).

Therefore, approaching these feet of the Man of Sorrows and acquainted with infirmity, the sinner speaks confidently: “Now, therefore, we approach with confidence the throne of grace. For we do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our infirmities” (Heb. 4:16, 15). Thus the sinful woman approaches the feet; the righteous woman approaches to anoint the head. The ointment of the head is to be reckoned more precious than that which is applied to the feet by as much as the spices from which it is prepared are known to be more precious than the latter. For these latter we find easily and without labor in our own region: all of us, indeed, are sinners. But the former we receive with difficulty and from far away, as though brought from the paradise of God. “For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1:17). What is more excellent, finally, than an ointment of this kind, over whose pouring out even the Apostles are said to have murmured, saying: “Why this waste? It could have been sold and given to the poor.”

3. Even now, when someone perhaps seems to devote himself to God with such devotion and grace that he is rightly believed to anoint Christ’s head, remaining constantly in holy quiet, thanksgiving, and the divine delight of devotion, there are not lacking those who call this waste. They complain with what appears to them a just murmur that one able to benefit many should rest for himself—not because they envy holiness, but because they look to charity.

Yet charity itself, which is God, often spares a soul of this kind, seeing that it delights in spiritual pursuits, especially if he knows it to be such that, still like a woman in timidity and weakness, it has not yet advanced to a perfect man. Certainly he who looks upon the heart discerns this better than people who see only the outward appearance and judge according to appearance. For they do not sufficiently attend to the fact that it is not equally easy to rest devoutly and to be usefully occupied; to be humbly subject and to preside beneficially; to be governed without complaint and to govern without fault; to obey willingly and to command with discernment; finally, to be good among the good and good among the wicked—indeed, to be peaceful among the children of peace and to show oneself peaceable to those who hate peace.

Therefore Jesus, knowing who are and who are not fit to be entangled in cares, answers in effect on behalf of such a tender soul. He sees that, because of its still immature condition, it is less able to manage affairs; others think differently and therefore accuse its repose as unfruitful, with good zeal indeed but not according to knowledge. He replies: “Why do you trouble this woman? For although”—as must be admitted—“what you are trying to draw her toward is better, yet she has done a good work to me. Let her meanwhile do the good which she can. For I know that she is still a woman. But when, by the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, a man has been made from the woman”—which will not be able to escape me when it occurs, because she will be advanced at my prompting and maintained by my preservation—“then the iniquity of the man will be better than the beneficent woman” (Ecclus. 42:14). Therefore I hope for that better thing also. Nor do I reckon the pouring out of this ointment a waste, in which both the woman’s devotion is signified and my burial prefigured. Moreover, it spreads its fragrance far and wide; therefore, wherever this Gospel is preached, what she has done shall also be told in remembrance of her” (Matt. 26:8–13).

4. Let us now approach the third ointment. Certainly, by comparing either of the two ointments already mentioned, the latter is recognized without any ambiguity to be better and far more excellent than the former. Yet it seems remarkable if any third ointment can be found which ought rightly to be placed before both, in accordance with the bride’s boast that her breasts are fragrant with the best ointment. Otherwise they are not best if they do not surpass the better ones, just as things are not truly called better unless they exceed good things.

Now the second ointment, with which the head is anointed, has been found of such excellence that scarcely any riches seem capable, not merely of being preferred to it, but even of being compared with it. Yet I would not believe that the bride has lied; for she has as bridegroom Truth itself, whose words she speaks here, and who, just as he does not wish to deceive, cannot be deceived. Otherwise she vainly desires and sighs to be joined in the embraces of truth while lying to truth. For what fellowship has falsehood with truth? Rather, “truth destroys all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5:7).

5. Perhaps if we look in the Gospel, we shall find a figure of this ointment as well. “Mary Magdalene,” it says, “and Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, so that when they came they might anoint Jesus” (Mark 16:1). Do you see, at the very opening of the chapter in question, how highly even this material ointment is to be valued, since one or two women could not suffice to procure its spices? One woman brought the first ointment, and one the second. But to purchase and prepare this ointment, three came together, so that they might buy together what none of them could obtain individually; and so, coming, they anoint Jesus. Not merely his feet, nor merely his head, but, as it says, “so that when they came they might anoint Jesus”—that is, his whole body.

But observe that Christ did not wish so precious an ointment to be wasted. Therefore, not finding the body, they carried it back and were commanded to offer to his living body what they had prepared for his dead body. And they did so when, immediately upon the joyful announcement of the resurrection, they sought to soothe the sorrowful hearts of the disciples, who without doubt were Christ’s members and living members. Unless Christ loved these members more than that crucified body, he would not have handed that body over to be crucified for their redemption. It is therefore clear that this last ointment surpasses the other two by as much as Christ’s own body—namely the Church, to which it is offered—is more beloved to Christ than that body which he wished to be anointed with it and which he also willed to be surrendered for this body’s redemption. [The printed text appears to require: “to Christ” rather than “Christ.”]

## SERMON XCI

[Note: [Col. 0709D] Composed from Short Sermons 60 and 61.] On the three outpourings.

1. “Your outpourings are a paradise” (Song 4:13). This is the voice of that heavenly Jerusalem, rejoicing with this one which is a pilgrim upon earth. There are three outpourings. The first is that of married penitents in the world; the second, of converted continent persons in the cloister or hermitage; the third, of prelates preaching and praying for God’s people.

Concerning the first outpouring, that is, penitence, the angels, who have joy over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15:10), say: “Who is this that comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke?” and so forth. This penitent soul is said to come up through the wilderness—that is, through a trackless and waterless land—by remembering its sins. It comes up like a column, by humbly confessing those same sins. This confession is rightly said to be like a column of smoke, because through many kinds of sins it is drawn forth, like smoke from a censer through many openings.

It should be noted that although smoke never has brightness, it can sometimes have fragrance. That this smoke of confession has a certain fragrance of piety is suggested by what follows: “From the spices of myrrh and incense, and every powder of the perfumer” (Song 3:6). Myrrh and incense—that is, mortification of the flesh and prayer of the heart—must always accompany confession. For without the other, each is of little or no benefit. If anyone mortifies his flesh but neglects prayer, he is proud, and it is said to him: “Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 49:13). Likewise, if he prays but neglects to mortify his flesh, he will hear: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do the things I say?” (Luke 6:46); and also: “The prayer of him who turns away his ear from hearing the law shall be an abomination” (Prov. 28:9). Therefore each supports the other, since it is clear that either is rejected without the other.

2. It follows: “And every powder of the perfumer.” After the remembrance and confession of sins, after mortification and prayer, the fruit of almsgiving must be offered. Alms are rightly called powder because they are made from earthly substance, but “of the perfumer” because they give forth a most sweet fragrance. Hence Cornelius, doing good, was told: “Your prayers and your alms have ascended” (Acts 10:4). Or it says “every powder of the perfumer” because not only great but even the smallest sins must be crushed through confession and washed away through compunction. Let what has been said concerning the first outpouring suffice.

3. The second is the life of continent persons in the cloister or hermitage. In this outpouring there is no mention of wilderness, smoke, or penitence, but of light, splendor, and virtue. Thus in its praise it is sung in the angelic voice: “Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army set in array?” (Song 6:9). These words show its threefold virtue: humility, chastity, and charity.

For dawn is the end of night and the beginning of light. Night signifies the life of the sinner; light, the life of the righteous. Therefore dawn, which drives away darkness and announces light, rightly signifies humility, because just as dawn divides day and night, so humility distinguishes the righteous person from the sinner. For every righteous person begins from humility and advances from it. Hence it is called “the rising dawn,” so that the structure of virtues, rising from humility as from its proper foundation, may be built up. Thus, to show its humility, it is said: “Like the rising dawn.” What follows, “Beautiful as the moon,” demonstrates chastity. Now the moon is said not to have its brightness from itself, but to receive it from the sun; and the more it is set before the gaze of the sun to be seen, the more fully it is illuminated by that same sun’s light. Likewise, if a congregation or any faithful soul is offered to the gaze of the true Sun, it immediately receives from that vision a certain splendor of beauty and loveliness of chastity. Hence, growing and advancing from his light, it is brought even to perfection, so that what follows may rightly be said of it:

4. Chosen as the sun. Why “as the sun”? Is it because “the righteous shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43)? But whence will they shine as the sun there, if not from the splendor of the wedding-garment? (Matt. 22:11). For this is the garment with which, while still placed on earth, those [Col. 0712B] were to be clothed to whom it was said: “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). Whoever has been clothed with this power of charity, which that wedding-garment signifies, and has rightly ordered it within himself, will beyond doubt be terrible to his enemies like an ordered battle-line of camps. For demons take no notice of however many other virtues a person may possess without charity. But when they see charity itself, ordered in battle-array, they are immediately driven headlong into flight. In the words “chosen as the sun,” perseverance may be understood, which belongs only to the elect. But in what follows—“terrible as an ordered battle-line of camps”—is understood discretion, the mother of virtues, through which demons are frightened and driven away, while virtues are acquired and preserved. Many other things also may fittingly be understood and said in this second outpouring [Col. 0712C]; but let it suffice to have said these few things out of many.

5. The third outpouring belongs to holy preachers, concerning whose life and teaching that saying too is uttered in wonder: “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8:5). In the first outpouring it had been said, “Who is this that comes up through the wilderness?”; but here, “Who comes up from the wilderness?” For there penitents are pricked by the thorns through which they walk; but here teachers have trampled beneath an exalted mind whatever they were able to snatch away from the world. Therefore it is said: “from the wilderness, abounding in delights.” But we must ask what those delights are in which they are said to abound; and who that beloved [Col. 0712D] is, or why they are said to lean upon him. For those things which are called delights by the citizens of heaven are not to be accounted trifling. Such delights belong to the mind, not the belly; to the soul, not the body; to the spirit, not the flesh; to reason, not sensuality; to the inward, not the outward person. To describe them briefly in some fashion: they are the abundant infusion of spiritual grace. Blessed is the soul into which such grace is poured, which is anticipated by blessings of heavenly sweetness, so that it becomes a temple of God and an oracle of the Holy Spirit. For such a soul cannot lack the riches of salvation, wisdom and knowledge, and the choicest treasure of that salvation, the fear of the Lord. When it has abounded and been filled with these delights, let it now exalt the Lord in the churches and praise him in the assembly of the elders [Col. 0713A]. Let it preach upon the housetops what it heard in the ear in inner chambers; and thus it will abound in delights. For to abound is said to be steadfast in the word of teaching, to shine by the example of one’s life, and to pursue spiritual work diligently.

6. But it is necessary that in all these things it seek not its own glory, but that of its Author. For he is its beloved, of whom it is written: “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine” (Song 2:16); and of whom the Father said: “This is my beloved Son; hear him” (Luke 9:35). One must lean upon him, so that one’s work may be ascribed to the help of his grace—to him from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and to whom all things are referred. But why one ought to lean upon him, let that beloved himself, who teaches humanity knowledge, teach us more fully [Col. 0713B]. He said to the disciples whom he was filling with such delights: “I am the vine; you are the branches. As the branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me”; and again: “Apart from me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15:4–5). As though he openly said: If you wish to abound in delights, lean upon me.

But now let us see how they abound and lean. Let that outstanding preacher come forward as one for all. Come then, most blessed Paul: abound in your delights. Surely when you had preached the Gospel from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum; when you had set forth the Gospel itself without charge; when, as a prudent and faithful steward, you had distributed heavenly treasures and the mystery of faith to Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish; when you had borne about the mortification of Jesus [Col. 0713C] in your mortal body; and when, among your many admirable virtues—which you were able to perform and we can scarcely recount—you even dared, with every authority and without any arrogance, though in your own judgment the least of the Apostles, to say: “The grace of God in me was not empty, but I labored more abundantly than all of them.” Great, and, so to speak, delightful delights! But lest you lose them, lean upon your beloved. “Yet not I,” he says, “but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). Abound again; for, to tell the truth, such delights are exceedingly pleasing. “I can do all things,” he says. Lean again: “Through him,” he says, “who strengthens me” (Phil. 4:13). Likewise the Apostle says: “Let him who glories, glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17) [Col. 0713D]; that is, let one who abounds in delights lean upon his beloved.

7. With the Lord’s help we have said these things concerning the three outpourings, signifying the three kinds of persons whom holy Church contains in this life, and whom Noah, Daniel, and Job also signify in Ezekiel (Ezek. 14:14); although they may fittingly be assigned also to every individual perfect person. In these persons likewise the first outpouring is repentance; the second, righteousness; the third, teaching. First, they are converted by repenting; second, by living well, they practice righteousness; third, if they have made good progress, they teach by word that very righteousness which they hold in life. [Col. 0714A] But since vices lie in ambush for virtues and are set so close beside them that whoever deviates from the latter falls into the snares of the former, repentance must be without shame, lest one be ashamed to confess sins committed; righteousness must beware of hypocrisy; and prelacy must cast out pride. For where there is greatness of graces, there is also greatness of peril.

## SERMON XCII

[Note: [Col. 0713D] It consists of Sermons 62 and 63 from the *Parvi*.]

On the threefold introduction: into the garden, the cellar, and the chamber.

1. “I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride” (Song 5:1). Elsewhere it is said: “The king brought me into his cellar” (Song 1:3); elsewhere, into “his chamber” (Song 3:4). This threefold introduction is given to the rational soul by its Bridegroom, namely the Word of God [Col. 0714B], according to the threefold sense of Scripture: historical, moral, and mystical. The historical sense is in the garden, the moral in the cellar, the mystical in the chamber.

In the garden—that is, in history—is contained the threefold operation of the Trinity: the creation of heaven and earth, the renewal of heaven and earth, and the confirmation of heaven and earth. The Father created; the Son reconciled; the Holy Spirit confirmed. The time of creation is one thing, that of reconciliation another, and that of confirmation another; just as in a garden the time for planting is one thing, that for gathering fruit another, and that for eating another. Creation and reconciliation belong to the present age; confirmation, to the age to come. At the beginning of time the Father created; in the fullness of time the Son reconciled; after all present time the Holy Spirit will confirm.

The Son said of the Father: “My Father is working until now”; and added of himself: “And I am working” (John 5:17) [Col. 0714C]. Likewise, at the consummation of the age the Holy Spirit may truly say: “The Father and the Son have worked until now; and from this point I am at work”: when, that is, he has made our bodies spiritual, the body has cleaved to the spirit, and the spirit to God; with that same body so confirmed by the Holy Spirit that thereafter, without any intervening moment of time, what is written comes to pass: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). The Old Testament instructs us concerning creation and promises reconciliation. The New Testament displays reconciliation and pledges confirmation.

2. The second introduction is into the cellar. This cellar [Col. 0714D] contains moral knowledge and has three distinct rooms. The first is called the spice-room; the second, the fruit-room; the third, the wine-cellar. In the first are those who conduct themselves well toward superiors; in the second, those who do so toward equals; in the third, those who do so toward subordinates. Thus the first room is that of discipline; the second, of nature; the third, of grace.

For one who strives to attain the summit of perfect conduct first becomes a disciple and enters the room of discipline, where the master composes his character from diverse virtues as perfumers compose spices from various ingredients. Hence this room is also called the spice-room, because those who willingly embrace the labor of discipline diffuse to others, by their example, the excellent fragrance of imitation [Col. 0715A]. Then they proceed into the second room of nature, for those who have learned under a master to break their own will can readily live in harmony with their fellow disciples. This room, where life is held in common with others, is appropriately called the room of nature, because nature brought forth all human beings as equals, though for the sake of merits it has set some above others and subjected some to others.

It is also called the fruit-room because it is highly beneficial if each administers to another the grace which he has received. Hence it is written: “A brother helping a brother shall be exalted like a fortified city” (Prov. 17:19). And the prophet likewise says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1). But when they have been fully perfected in this second room of nature [Col. 0715B], then at last they can enter the third, which is that of grace: so that those who have lived justly and without complaint with others may preside also over the instruction of others. This room too is called the wine-cellar, so that those who preside over others in governance may burn with charity. It is also called the room of grace, a name which can indeed be common to the other two as well. For discipline and social life are gifts of grace. Yet this third room especially claims the name for itself, since it is quite easy to be subject or associated with others, whereas it is rare and difficult for anyone to be transferred usefully to the governance of others.

3. In these three rooms the characters of all people are contained and formed. For all people are either superiors, equals, or subordinates. And just as the more valuable things are selected from gardens and put away in cellars, where they also have separate places in which to be preserved, so the moral sense is taken from history and, as it were, stored in the cellar, from which all human life may be instructed. There superiors read what manner of persons they should show themselves to their subordinates, when they are told: “Not lording it over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock” (1 Pet. 5:3); and: “Not that we lord it over your faith, but that we are helpers of your joy” (2 Cor. 1:23); and the Lord in the Gospel: “The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep” (John 10:11) [Col. 0715C].

Equals likewise find in the same Scripture how they ought to conduct themselves toward one another, when they read: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2); and: “Outdoing one another in showing honor” (Rom. 12:10); and many things of this sort. Subordinates too have there what may order their conduct: namely, how they should be subject to those set over them. To them it is said: “Obey your leaders and submit to them. For they keep watch, as those who will render an account for your souls” (Heb. 13:17).

[Note: [Col. 0715D] On the introduction into the chamber, see Sermon 23 on the Song of Songs, no. 11.]

## SERMON XCIII

[Note: [Col. 0716D] Otherwise, 64 from the *Parvi*.]

On the properties of teeth, applied to the profession of monastic life.

1. “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing; all bearing twins, and none among them is barren” (Song 4:2). The Holy Spirit, from whose more secret fountain the river of the Song of Songs flows, commends to us, as I think, no small mysteries in these teeth [Col. 0716A]. These are not the teeth of which it is said: “God shall break their teeth in their mouth” (Ps. 57:7); nor those concerning which the divine voice cries to the holy man: “Terror is round about his teeth” (Job 41:5). Rather, these teeth are whiter than milk: for they belong to the bride whose beauty the Most High desired, who has neither spot nor wrinkle. Since she is wholly white, she is shown to be whiter in her teeth.

Yet, by a new and unheard-of comparison, he speaks in praise of her, saying: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep.” What, I ask, is worthy in this likeness, so that we should believe it descended from heavenly mysteries? Surely something great, to be understood magnificently with a great mind. For it is the Spirit who speaks; and when he speaks, not one iota can pass by empty. Something is certainly wrapped up in these teeth, which, when unfolded, marks out a mystery of more sacred understanding.

2. Teeth are white and strong; they have no flesh; they lack skin; they can suffer nothing within themselves; there is no pain like their pain; they are enclosed by the lips so as not to be seen; it is unseemly for them to be seen except in laughing; they chew food for the whole body; they derive no taste from it; they are not easily worn away; they are placed in order, some above and some below; and while the lower teeth move, the upper never do. Such teeth, therefore, I judge to be persons of the monastic profession, who, choosing a briefer [variant: straighter] and safer way of life, seem whiter from among the whole body of the Church, which is white [Col. 0716C].

For what is whiter than those who, avoiding the filth of every defilement, bewail the sins of their thoughts as well as of their actions? What is stronger than those for whom tribulation is counted consolation, insult glory, and poverty abundance? They have no flesh because, forgetting flesh while in the flesh, they hear from the Apostle: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit” (Rom. 8:9). They lack skin because, having neither the polish nor the stretching strain of worldly cares, they sleep and rest together in peace. They suffer nothing to linger within themselves, because they judge no stumbling-block, however small, tolerable either within themselves or in the conscience of any individual.

Hence comes your timely importunity, by which you weary us so often that many times you spend much of the day over such matters even when there is no necessity [Col. 0716D]. There is no pain like their pain, because nothing is so dreadful and horrible as murmuring and dissension in a community. They are enclosed by lips lest they be seen: likewise, we are encircled by material ramparts, lest we be exposed to the eyes and approach of secular persons. It is unseemly for them to appear, except perhaps sometimes for laughter; for nothing is more disgraceful than a monk running about through towns and castles, unless charity—“which covers a multitude of sins”—compels this. For charity is laughter, because it is cheerful: joyful indeed, but not undisciplined.

Teeth chew food for the whole body because they are appointed to pray for the whole body of the Church, namely for both the living and the dead [Col. 0717A]. They ought to have no taste from it, because they should ascribe no glory to themselves, but say with the prophet: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 103:1). They are not easily worn away because the older they grow, the more fervent they become; and they run the more swiftly the nearer they draw to the prize. They are placed in order. For where is there anything ordered, if it is not here, where food and drink, watching and sleeping, laboring and resting, walking and sitting, and all other things are established in number, measure, and weight? There are upper and lower teeth because among us there are prelates and subordinates; and the upper are joined to the lower in such a way that the lower do not disagree with the upper [Col. 0717B]. But though the lower teeth move, the upper should never move, because even if subordinates are sometimes disturbed, it belongs to prelates to remain steadfast in a composed mind.

“Like a flock of shorn sheep,” he says. How well monks are compared to shorn sheep! For truly they are shorn, since neither heart, body, nor anything worldly has been left to them as private property. “Which have come up from the washing.” The washing is baptism, from which one ascends who aims at the height of a more perfect life; but one descends who devotes oneself to a dishonorable life. “All bearing twins,” because they give birth both by word and by example. “And none among them is barren,” because none is unfruitful.

## SERMON XCIV

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Otherwise, 65 from the *Parvi*.]

On the progress of Christian or spiritual life, according to the tropological interpretation of Elijah fleeing Jezebel.

[Col. 0717C]

1. Elijah feared Jezebel; and rising, he went wherever his will carried him. He came to Beersheba of Judah, left his servant there, and went on into the wilderness. And when he had come beneath the shade of a juniper tree and sat down, he cast himself down and slept. And an angel of the Lord touched him and said to him: “Arise and eat.” And he looked, and behold, at his head was bread baked under ashes and a vessel of water. Therefore he ate and drank and walked in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights, unto Horeb, the mountain of God (3 Kings 19:3–8).

By Elijah, whose name is interpreted “the Lord,” or “the Lord is strong,” is understood any righteous person who suffers persecution for righteousness’ sake. Hence: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” [Col. 0717D] (Matt. 5:10). Fearing Jezebel—that is, the wickedness of the world or the tyranny of the devil—such a person rises from the temptation of sins and goes wherever the will granted him by the Lord has carried him. He comes to Beersheba of Judah, to holy Church, which is called Beersheba, that is, “the seventh well,” because of the abundant grace of the sevenfold Spirit distributed there among the faithful; or “the well of satiety,” because of the depth of God’s mysteries and the refreshment of the holy Scriptures.

Of this depth we have in the psalm: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17:12); and again: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7) [Col. 0718A]. Contemplating this same depth, the Apostle, terrified and failing through terror, is compelled to cry: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” etc. (Rom. 11:33).

2. Of this satiety you read in the psalm: “He led me beside the water of refreshment” (Ps. 22:2); and likewise: “They shall be inebriated with the abundance of your house” (Ps. 35:9). This kind of intoxication does not induce disgust but stimulates an unfailing appetite with certain desires. In this sea of sacred reading the lamb walks and the elephant swims. At the table of Catholic teaching, meals sufficient for each person are set forth according to the measure of one’s understanding. This is the paradise of delights; this is the garden of every fruit.

Coming, therefore, to Beersheba, to holy Church, as has been said [Col. 0718B], one runs to confession, which is signified by Judah; and leaves there one’s servant, that is, childish understanding or the weakness of former deeds, and goes into the wilderness, that is, into contempt for this world. Having come there, one sits down—that is, rests from secular tumult—singing with the prophet: “This is my rest for ever and ever” (Ps. 131:14). One casts oneself down—that is, accounts oneself worthless—renouncing one’s desires, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9:23). One falls asleep in the shade of the juniper tree because, in the courts of God’s house, according to the senses of the body, one is wholly free from all wickedness, saying with the Psalmist: “In peace together I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4:9).

Then the angelic vision touches one, awakening one to good works [Col. 0718C] and to rising to higher things. One looks at one’s head, that is, to Christ, who is the head of the Church; and behold, bread baked under ashes—that is, the nourishment of divine doctrine, outwardly indeed rough, but inwardly unspeakably strengthening and sweet—and a vessel of water, that is, a fountain of tears with compunction of heart. One eats and drinks—that is, fulfills what one hears—and goes in strength to the mountain of God, namely to the height of blessedness.

## SERMON XCV

[Note: [Col. 0718D] Otherwise, 66 from the *Parvi*.]

On the bitterness of teaching, to be tempered by preachers.

1. There was a famine in the land, and the sons of the prophets dwelt before Elisha; for them he caused a pottage to be set forth. When they tasted the cooking, they cried out: “Death is in the pot, man of God!” And they could not eat [Col. 0718D]. But he said: “Bring meal.” And he put it into the pot and said: “Pour out for the crowd.” And they ate, and there was no more bitterness in the pot (4 Kings 4:38–41).

The famine in the land is scarcity of God’s word in the human mind; the sons of the prophets are the sons of preachers. “Prophet” is interpreted “one who sees.” Holy preachers are not without reason called prophets: they both contemplate the hidden mysteries of God and, according as they perceive human dispositions, apply appropriate remedies. Elisha is interpreted “the salvation of the Lord.” By this name any prelate and teacher of the Church is fittingly designated, since through his health-giving persuasion the Lord’s salvation is announced to the peoples and, in being announced, bestowed.

Such a person, by the obligation of his office, sets before those subject to him a great pot containing wild herbs—that is, an admonition discoursing upon grave matters, filled with bitterness but nevertheless heated by the fire of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0719A]. Therefore those subject to him, shrinking in fear from the austerity of the words, cry: “Death is in the pot!” and cannot taste it.

2. Thus the wise steward does not bring meal—rather, he orders it to be brought—because he does not himself bestow charity but urges that it be possessed. By its seasoning, things that formerly seemed bitter are made sweet. A preacher can indeed sound counsels of salvation in the ears of those standing around, but no one except God alone can pour the taste of charity into the palate of the heart. Hence Gregory: “Unless the Spirit is within to teach, the teacher’s tongue labors outwardly in vain” (*Homily 30 on the Gospels*). The taste of heaven is one thing; the taste of earth another. The taste of heaven cannot possibly please us while we seek the taste of our cook.

In the wilderness quails and manna are given; that is, in the place of discipline, greater and lesser commandments. When the children of Israel saw manna, they said to one another: “Manhu?”—“What is this?” For they did not know what it was. Moses said to them: “This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat” (Exod. 16:15). The mystery of this event is fittingly disclosed in John’s Gospel, where the Lord says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” etc. Therefore many of the disciples, hearing this, said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” From this, many went back (John 6:54, 61, 67) [Col. 0719C].

In this manner, when some simple persons come to conversion, they fear the severity of the Rule. If they are addressed concerning contempt for the world, the conflict of virtues and vices; if the strain of keeping vigil, constancy in prayer, and moderation in fasting are demanded of them, they complain among themselves: “What is this? Who is sufficient to fulfill so many and such great things?” For they do not know how great is the power of the order they have undertaken. But the shepherd must answer them consolingly and urge them to procure the meal.

## SERMON XCVI

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Otherwise, 67 from the *Parvi*.]

On the four fountains of the Savior, and the waters to be drawn from them.

[Col. 0719D]

1. “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior” (Isa. 12:3). In place of the paradise that we lost, Christ the Savior has been restored to us. Therefore, just as four rivers flow from the one fountain of paradise to water paradise, so from the secret place of his breast proceed four fountains, from which four kinds of waters are drawn, by which the Church throughout the whole world is watered. The four fountains are truth, wisdom, power, and charity. From these fountains waters are drawn, one kind from each. From the fountain of truth are taken waters of judgments [Col. 0720A]; from the fountain of wisdom, waters of counsels; from the fountain of power, waters of aids; from the fountain of charity, waters of desires.

In the waters of judgments we know what is permitted and what is not permitted. In the waters of counsels we discern what is expedient and what is not expedient. But because temptations are not lacking to elect persons who rightly advance through these things—and they are tempted in two ways, either by terrors so as to be shaken or by enticements so as to be seduced—they must be armed against terrors with the aids of divine power, and against enticements with desires for heavenly charity. For, as a certain saint says, desires for better things overcome desires for worse things.

Or we may proceed in this way. What good is it to know what is permitted and expedient—which judgments and counsels certainly teach—if there is no ability at all to accomplish it? Therefore, after the waters of judgments and counsels, the waters of aids must be sought. Again, what can ability itself avail if charity is not the end of all these things? Rightly, therefore, after judgments, counsels, and aids, desires are drawn from the fountain of charity, so that whatever we understand or say, whatever we do or suffer, may be concluded by the end of eternal life [Col. 0720B].

2. But that the things said concerning fountains and waters may shine forth more clearly, I think they should be proved by testimonies of Scripture, and that the golden comparisons which we have brought forward should be inlaid with silver. First, I think no one doubts what was said: that those four fountains flow from the breast of Jesus. But how the aforesaid waters are drawn from those fountains must be worked out. Let David then come and say that judgments proceed from the fountain of truth. He certainly seems to have thought this when he said: “Let my judgment come forth from your countenance” (Ps. 16:2). For the holy man would not call that judgment his own which did not come forth from God’s countenance—that is, from truth.

For he knew that God’s elect are ruled by the judgments of truth as by an iron rod; and because he felt himself to be under their rule, he sang exultantly: “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves; more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. 18:10–11) [Col. 0720C]. Lest they perhaps turn aside from them through negligence, let them hear the Father’s threatening voice through the same prophet: “If they do not walk in my judgments,” he says, “and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges” (Ps. 88:31–33).

The key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom disclosed these mysteries of divine judgment when he said: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God. But if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who have not believed the Gospel of God?” (1 Pet. 4:17). And this was said concerning the elect. But there is another judgment concerning the reprobate, which nonetheless proceeds from Truth itself. Thus it is said through Paul: “For we know that judgment is according to truth against those who do such things” (Rom. 2:2). And Truth itself [Col. 0721A] comprehends both judgments, saying: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39) [Col. 0720D]. It distinguishes them both when it likewise says: “And these shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46).

3. Since we have seen how judgments are drawn from the fountain of truth, let us see how counsels are offered from the fountain of wisdom. Who doubts that the apostle Paul is wise, when both Peter, his fellow-apostle, affirms that wisdom was given to him (2 Pet. 3:15), and the whole course of that apostle’s words breathes nothing but wisdom? Let him therefore offer counsels and teach us through them what is expedient for those journeying abroad and hastening toward the heavenly homeland.

“Concerning virgins,” he says, “I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel, as one who has received mercy from the Lord to be faithful. Therefore I judge this to be good because of the present necessity: that it is good for a person to remain thus,” that is, to remain in virginity. Had he possessed a commandment concerning virgins, nothing but what was commanded would have been permitted. But now, when both things are permitted—to marry or not to marry—what could be said more briefly than, “It is good for a person to remain thus”? Especially since the pressure of necessity frequently steals upon us, the very brevity of time urges us to die swiftly, and the form of the whole world passes away [Col. 0721B].

Likewise, when he spoke of a widow, he said: “She will be happier if she remains thus,” that is, unmarried, “according to my counsel.” And lest he seem to have drawn this counsel from his own heart rather than from the fountain of Wisdom, he added: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 7:25, 26, 40). But why should I linger over a few examples, when every sex and every condition can find counsel for salvation in his words, if it seeks diligently?

If anyone wishes to examine more closely whether it is true that counsels flow from wisdom, let him read the books called Wisdom, where the whole course of discourse seems to provide counsels. But if one is eager to choose from there a more prudent and useful life, he will hear Wisdom herself inviting him beneficially: “If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17). Do you ask whose? “Fear God,” she says, “and keep his commandments” (Ecclus. 12:13) [Col. 0721D]. Let him hear her crying out with maternal affection: “Give me your heart” (Prov. 23:26). Oh, how I wish that I too might hang my heart upon her word, from whose wondrous mouth I hear such sweet counsels of life resounding! And would that I might dip the pen of my tongue in her fountain, so that I might be fit to write usefully also what remains concerning the two fountains of power and charity!

4. And because these four fountains so pour their savor into one another that one who drinks from one is invited by a certain ineffable sweetness of love to another, I am pleased now to pass from wisdom to power and, insofar as power itself helps me, to show how waters of aids are drawn from it. As I said above, the judgments of truth are twofold, because they determine what is permitted and what is not permitted; likewise wisdom’s counsels are twofold, determining what is expedient and what is not expedient. So here too let us recognize that double waters of aids must be drawn from the fountain of power: waters which either wash the elect from sins or refresh them amid torments [Col. 0722A]. Let us take an example of each.

Luke the Evangelist reports that a certain woman suffering from an issue of blood, having spent all her substance on physicians and being unable to be cured, came up behind Jesus and touched the hem of the Lord’s garment; immediately her flow of blood stopped. Jesus said: “Who touched me?” When the disciples answered, “The crowds press and afflict you, [Col. 0722B] and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” he repeated: “Someone touched me; for I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8:43–46). See what waters of aid the woman drew from the fountain of power: she was washed from the flow of blood by them, though no medical skill could heal her.

But if anyone objects that the testimony brought forward has nothing to do with the present subject, because that woman does not seem to have been washed from sins but only from bodily illness, let him know that it is the custom of divine power to heal the heart before the body. Thus elsewhere, when a paralytic was brought to him for healing, as a good and merciful physician, wishing first to heal what was of greater importance—the mind rather than the flesh—he said to the paralytic: “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven you” [Col. 0722C]. Therefore, once the conscience has been healed, the body is healed in turn, when he says: “Arise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (Matt. 9:2, 6).

Thus he first washed the heart of this woman inwardly through the gift of faith, as it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9), through which she deserved outwardly to obtain bodily health. The Lord himself indicates this when he says: “Daughter, your faith has made you whole; go in peace” (Luke 8:48).
