That waters of aid amid torments are also drawn from this fountain of power is shown by the three youths set in the blazing fire of the furnace, for whom the very flame grew cool (Dan. 3); and especially by that renowned martyr Vincent, who, while grievously tortured, [Col. 0722D] is said not only to have endured but even steadfastly to have challenged his torturer in these words: “Rise up,” he said, “and rage with the whole spirit of your malice; you will see that by God’s power I am stronger while I am tortured than you yourself are who torture me.”

More could be said at greater length concerning this fountain of power, but I pass over it briefly, because I desire rather to drink from the fountain of power [variant: charity] than to write concerning it.

5. We are invited to this fountain by the voice of our Redeemer, who says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink, and from his belly shall flow streams of living water.” And the Evangelist went on to explain to what fountain he invited us, saying: “Now he said this concerning the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:37–39). What Spirit, if not the Spirit of charity, whom the world cannot receive [Col. 0723A], but whom only those who truly believe in him receive? From this fountain, therefore, let us draw waters of desire for ourselves and divide them into twin streams, so that, as the commandments of charity are two, so also the desires by which those commandments are fulfilled may be twofold. For one desire is that by which God is loved for his own sake; another, that by which one’s neighbor is loved in God, or for God’s sake. In the former there is no measure: God is loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength. In the latter a certain measure is prescribed, when it is said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:37, 39). The prophet burned with the former when he said: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. 41:2); and likewise: “My soul desires and fails for the courts [Col. 0723B] of the Lord” (Ps. 83:3). The Apostle displayed the latter toward the Romans, to whom he wrote: “For I desire to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual grace” (Rom. 1:11); and the Lord in the Gospel toward his disciples: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15).

6. It should be noted that the human mind is especially stirred and advanced toward this by three affections. Hence it is commanded to love God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength. The first is sweet, the second prudent, the third strong. Peter possessed the first when he tried to dissuade the Lord from dying; for from his heart he loved sweetly him whose passion he dreaded. But when he heard, “Get behind me, Satan; you do not understand the things that are of God, but those that are of men” (Mark 8:33), instructed by these words [Col. 0723C] and understanding what good Christ’s death contained, he began prudently to love with his whole soul him whom previously he loved sweetly only with his whole heart; but he did not yet love with his whole strength. Had he done so, he would not have denied him because of the danger of death. Yet after the resurrection and ascension, when the Spirit was given from above, he at last loved with his whole strength; for his sake he afterward did not fear to undergo the dreadful punishment of the cross.

We are likewise exercised in charity toward our neighbor in three ways: either that charity itself may be built up where it is absent; or that it may not perish or diminish where it is present. Whoever practices this toward his neighbor with a pure affection undoubtedly comes to deserve yet more fully that charity which is God.

## SERMON XCVII. On the sweetness of Christ’s word and yoke: outwardly indeed harsh, but inwardly most sweet.

[Col. 0723D]

1. “Honey and milk are under his tongue” (Song 4:11). This is necessary indeed. For what is upon the tongue sounds harsh. “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Eccl. 12:11). Another is he “whose words have been softened above oil” (Ps. 140:5); but “let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head.” Rather, let the righteous rebuke and reprove me, for this is mercy, than let that oil anoint my head, in which there is deceit. For words are fittingly called not soft, but “softened,” whether those of a flattering adviser or of an evil adviser, because in them there is not so much true and solid sweetness as sweetness overlaid and feigned; indeed [Col. 0724A] they are darts (Ps. 54:22).

Finally, what is under his tongue? Hear the Prophet: “Toil and pain” (Ps. 9:7). Yet under his tongue are honey and milk—he who, according to the same prophet, “devises toil in his commandment” (Ps. 93:20). Are you surprised that Truth should devise? You may wonder, but you may not doubt. If you seek another witness, read in the Gospel that “he pretended to go farther” (Luke 24:28). Why should he not offer a contrivance to a creature formed of clay? For he knows our frame: plainly, that it cannot bear toil, cannot endure delay, and is frail with respect to both. Therefore he mercifully provided that godliness should have “the promise of the life which now is, and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4:8); and that he should not impose real toil, but rather devise it in his commandment.

Hear how he himself reveals that he devises toil: “Take my yoke [Col. 0724B] upon you, and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light” (Matt. 11:29–30). How can toil be anything but feigned where not toil but rest is found?

2. Thus toil is on the tongue, honey beneath the tongue. What is above the tongue? “Ineffable things which it is not permitted for a human being to utter” (2 Cor. 12:4). Wretched are those who, attending only to what sounded upon the tongue, could grasp neither what was hidden beneath the tongue nor what was laid up above it! “This saying is hard,” they say (John 6:61). It is hard indeed, but it is nevertheless the same word of life: “Whoever does not carry his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:38). “If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother, and even his own soul, he is not worthy of me” (Luke 14:26–27). What could be said that was harsher [Col. 0724C] than this?

Do not be deceived. It seems a stone; it is bread. Hard in its crust, but most sweet in its marrow. “The Lord your God tests you.” This feigning of toil is an exercise of faith and a testing of love. Yet let it be a stone. Do you believe what even demons believe? “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.” We all know who said this. He does not doubt that, by a word alone—than which nothing is easier—he who believes him to be the Son of God can make bread out of stone. It is lawful to learn even from an enemy.

Let us too say to the Son of God: “Command that these stones become bread.” For he who came for the salvation of human beings, not of demons, so refuted his adversaries as to instruct the little ones. For he said not what that adversary wanted, but what we needed to hear, [Col. 0724D] namely, that this stone of ours might become bread, not his: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:3–4).

3. What do you mutter against these things, enemy of truth? What you yourself confess, and cannot deny at all, is that the Son of God has power to command that stones become bread. Therefore, where he speaks of the words of God, and speaks generally, that life is thus lived, and “in such things is the life of my spirit” (Isa. 38:16), why do you hiss at any one of them, saying, “This saying is hard”? Can you call stones those things which the Son of God spoke and which became food of life—you, who are not the Son of God?

It is not I who judge you to be equal with God—for you yourself have considered that a wholly rash robbery—so that at your word bread should revert [Col. 0725A] to stone. You who are not the Son of God say in vain, “Command that these stones become bread.” No less vainly do you set before us your stone in place of bread, a scorpion in place of an egg, a serpent in place of a fish. Woe to those who call bread stone and stone bread, who make light darkness and darkness light (Isa. 5:20), who deem Christ’s yoke harsh and reckon delight to lie beneath thorns. I do not desire such delights. Rather, I desire “to taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9).

For the very man who urges this had earnestly sought to experience it, not without reason. Thus he says: “How sweet are your words to my palate!” (Ps. 118:103); and again: “How great,” he says, “is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30:20). Where do you suppose it is hidden? Surely beneath his tongue, beneath his head—of whom she says: “His left hand is beneath my head, [Col. 0725B] and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6).

For although in the promise of the life which now is there is sweetness, and an abundance of sweetness—great indeed, and exceedingly great—the perfection belongs only to the promise of the life to come. “You have perfected it,” he says, “for those who hope in you in the sight of the children of men” (Ps. 30:20). What has he perfected? This saying is not on the tongue, but above the tongue. Therefore the ear does not hear, because the tongue has not uttered what God has prepared for those who love him. And that consummation will indeed not be in hiding, but in the sight of the children of men. Aptly, however, he says not that it is still to be perfected, but that he has already perfected it for those who hope: “For by hope we have been saved” (Rom. 8:24).

## SERMON XCVIII. On the children of peace, in whom God dwells.

[Col. 0725C]

“His place has been made in peace” (Ps. 75:3). There is a feigned peace, as in Judah; there is a disordered peace, as in Adam and Eve. Neither of these is God’s dwelling-place. Christian peace alone—the peace which the Lord left and gives to his disciples—is that in which the Lord rests. It is offered through holy preachers to the whole human race; but some reject it and others receive it. As for us, shaking off the dust of our feet against those who hate peace, let us turn to the lover of that same peace.

Of these, some are called recipients of peace, others keepers of peace, others makers of peace. They may also be called by other names: peaceable, patient, peace-making. They bear these names according to the differing states [Col. 0725D] of peace in which they advance. For the peaceable possess, through this peace, the land of their own body, because they are meek (Matt. 5:4). The patient possess their own souls, to whom it is said: “By your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). The peacemakers possess not only their own souls but also those of others, in whom they make peace. Hence they are deservedly called children of God (Matt. 5:9).

Thus those who receive peace are called peaceable, concerning whom it is written: “If a son of peace is there, your peace shall rest upon him” (Luke 10:6). But because they are little ones, disturbed by scandals, they quickly lose the peace which they had received. The patient, however, are those who retain what they have received and do not lose it, however provoked by injury. To these, as stronger persons, the command is given: “Love peace [Col. 0726A] and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12:14). But the peacemakers not only make peace in themselves and in others, but also love those who seek to take it away, as it is written: “With those who hate peace, I was peaceable” (Ps. 119:7). Behold, these are those whom God loves as sons, and of whom Wisdom builds a temple for herself as of living stones.

In order that this building may not be shaken by any assault, while God himself equally dwells and works within it, they are squared like a stone in four ways: above, below, on the right, and on the left. Above, when they humbly and wisely subject their own will to the divine will; below, when they temperately govern the flesh kept subject; on the right, by justly embracing the good; on the left, by bravely enduring the wicked.

## SERMON XCIX. On four kinds of people who obtain heaven.

[Col. 0726B]

There are four kinds of people who possess the kingdom of heaven. Some seize it violently; some purchase it; some steal it; some are compelled into it. Those seize it who have left everything and follow Christ, concerning whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). There are others of a lower rank, from whom temporal things are reaped while spiritual things are sown for them; and to these the Lord says in the Gospel: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). Such people are called merchants, because in the present they give to the poor the temporal things which they [Col. 0726C] possess, in order to receive from them in the future the eternal things which they can deserve to have only through them.

For all who are to be examined in the future judgment must either be friends of the Judge or have friends who intercede with the Judge. Therefore those who intercede hold the first place in blessedness; those for whom they intercede hold the second. There are others who secretly perform certain good works and thereby deserve the kingdom of heaven; yet they are said to steal it because, avoiding human praise, they are content with divine testimony alone. The woman in the Gospel who suffered from a flow of blood represented them. She thought within herself, saying: “If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved” (Mark 5:28). Having said this, she approached secretly, touched it, and was healed.

Others are compelled: for example, needy poor persons, whom the fire of poverty here, by God’s dispensation, purifies, lest the fire of judgment punish them in the future. Of them it is written: “Compel them to enter, that my house may be filled” (Luke 14:23). Many are compelled by various necessities and oppressions: by a marvelous providence of God, while they endure temporal punishment, if not willingly, yet patiently, they obtain eternal life.

## SERMON C. On the difference between the people and the prelate.

As great as the distance between shepherd and flock ought to be, so great ought to be the distance between bishop and people. The one stands [Col. 0727A] lofty and upright; the other bows his head, bent toward the ground. Hence the poet:

> And whereas all other animals look downward upon the earth,  
> He gave the human being an uplifted face.  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book I, verses 84–85

The one governs; the other is governed. The one feeds; the other is fed—so that each may be distinguished by his very form and bearing. The former has in his hand a rod with which to strike, or rather to guide and bring back the sheep. But what is it to have a rod in one’s hand, except to have discipline in one’s conduct, so as to instruct one’s subjects more by example than by word? For the proud are ashamed to be disciples if their teachers have preceded them in humility. Hence it is written of the Lord: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1).

[Col. 0727B] He also has a staff with which to strike the wolf: with the rod, the sheep; with the staff, the wolf. That is, he ought to correct the gentle and obedient more mildly, but rebuke those hard of heart and wicked more sharply; and, when necessary, strike even with a sentence of anathema. He holds a dog on a leash—namely, zeal under discernment—lest he be among those of whom it is written: “They have zeal [alternatively, emulation] for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2). The good shepherd also has bread in his bag: that is, the word of God in his memory.

## SERMON CI. On four modes of loving.

There are two loves, carnal and spiritual; from these are gathered four modes of loving: loving the flesh carnally, loving the spirit carnally, [Col. 0727C] loving the flesh spiritually, and loving the spirit spiritually. In these there is a certain progress and ascent from lower things to higher. For in order that human beings, who knew only how to love flesh carnally, might advance to love God also spiritually, God became flesh; and by speaking and living among human beings, he was at first loved by them carnally.

But when he wished to lay down his life for his friends, they already loved the spirit, though still carnally. Thus Peter replied when he spoke of his passion: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you” (Matt. 16:22). But when they recognized that the mystery of redemption was accomplished through that same passion, in that passion they already loved the flesh spiritually. When he rose again and ascended, they loved the spirit spiritually, and sang joyfully: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16).

We too love our flesh carnally when we love and fulfill its desires. We love the spirit carnally when we wear it down in prayer through weeping, sighing, and groaning. We love the flesh spiritually when, keeping it subject to the spirit and exercising it in spiritual goods, we preserve it with discernment. We love the spirit spiritually when, out of charity, we set even our own spiritual pursuits after the benefit of our brethren.

## SERMON CII. On the manner of returning to God.

1. There is a manner of returning to God opposed to the fall of the first human being. For Adam, placed in paradise [Col. 0728A], first lost his watchfulness toward God. Blessed Augustine testifies (*City of God*, book XIV, ch. 13) that the tempter could by no means have expelled the human being from paradise unless some self-exaltation had first arisen in the human soul, since it is most truly written: “Before ruin the heart is exalted” (Prov. 21:18). Second, he lost justice when he obeyed his wife’s voice more than the divine command. For justice is the virtue that renders to each his due. Third, he lost judgment when, corrected after sinning, he indirectly shifted his own guilt through the woman onto the Creator, saying: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me of the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:6, 12).

Therefore, by the same grades of virtues through which the first human being deserved to be expelled from paradise, the human being placed in exile must return. First, then, judgment must be exercised; second, justice must be practiced; finally, watchfulness must be applied. We owe judgment to ourselves, that we may judge and accuse ourselves; justice to our neighbor; and watchfulness to God.

2. The prophet Micah showed us this path of return, saying: “I will show you, O human being, what is good and what God requires of you: namely, to do judgment, to love mercy, and to walk watchfully with your God” (Mic. 6:8). The Apostle testifies that Christ taught this way of salvation, saying: “The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, instructing us that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously in this age,” etc. Soberly, namely, with regard to ourselves; justly, toward our neighbor; piously, toward God. He also expressed watchfulness toward God more clearly, saying: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:11–13).

And in many other places of Holy Scripture, if this order of the way and rule of life is sought, it may be found, as in this: “Blessed is the man who dwells in wisdom, who meditates upon justice, and who in understanding reflects upon watchfulness toward God” (Ecclus. 14:22). He dwells in wisdom, indeed, and is wise who judges himself here, in order to escape God’s eternal judgment. For, as the Apostle says, “If we judged ourselves, we would not indeed be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31). He is wise, not according to the wisdom of this age, but according to that wisdom which is drawn from hidden things, through which, by God’s marvelous working, [Col. 0728D] each of the elect, worn down here by blows and pressures, is afterward placed in the building of the true Solomon without the sound of a hammer.

## SERMON CIII. On the four stages by which the progress of the elect is distinguished.

1. The progress of all the elect is distinguished by four stages. First, each becomes a friend of his own soul; second, a friend of justice; third, a friend of wisdom; fourth, he becomes wise. In the first progress, he avoids everything that can injure the soul and loves what can soothe it. He therefore dreads hell and desires heaven. Thus he can fulfill that divine commandment which he received at his first conversion: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39).

For while he walks according to the flesh, he cannot do this in any way; but when he is led by the Spirit of God, he can readily do it. For what benefit does a person gain if his neighbor burns in hell? Or what does he lose if that neighbor is with him in paradise? For the inheritance of paradise is not such that it is diminished by the number of those possessing it. He therefore loves his neighbor, whom he does not wish to suffer evil, just as he does not wish it for himself, and whom he wishes, like himself, to possess heaven.

But when could he do this by his own—that is, the human—spirit: namely, dread Gehenna and desire heavenly things? He can do it, however, by that Spirit to whom it is said: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there” (Ps. 138:8), etc. For the Spirit of wisdom, present everywhere, knows what is in heaven and what takes place in hell. When he has filled the human mind [Col. 0729B], he instills fear of the punishments of hell and pours in love of heavenly things; and thus he makes a person love himself, saying to him: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30:24). Therefore the first thing is to love oneself, then one’s neighbor. For it was not said, “You shall love yourself as your neighbor,” but, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” In this manner a person becomes a lover of his own soul through the Holy Spirit, whom he received through faith.

2. Having received this gift, however, he ought not to be content with it alone, but to be carried onward to greater things and make progress for the better. He now lives by the Spirit. But, as the Apostle says, “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit” (Gal. 5:25). And elsewhere he says: “But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of God, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18). The Psalmist also seems to have understood this concerning the saints: “The lawgiver,” he says, “will give a blessing; they will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83:8).

Let this person whom we have in hand also walk; let him go on and advance until he reaches the fourth stage. There, without doubt, having become wise, he will see the God of gods in Zion. Moreover, by the very fact that I said that one who properly loves his own soul must also love justice. Otherwise, if he loves iniquity, he plainly hates, rather than loves, his own soul (Ps. 10:6).

3. By loving justice, he passes to the second stage and hears the command of Wisdom: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. 1:1). If he loves it perfectly, he must for its sake patiently bear every punishment and whatever insult is inflicted upon him. For justice will provide him with two things: first, that he may do what he ought; second, that he may suffer what he ought—namely, that if he has not done the good that he ought to have done, he may suffer the evil that he deserves. Thus, in a marvelous way, even when we abandon justice, we are not abandoned by it, since through it every guilt of transgression is punished. “For there is none who hides himself from its heat.”

The just man, however, not only does not dread this punishment, but even willingly receives it, believing faithfully that through it the sins of his former life are being purified. Hence it is written: “Whatever happens to the just man shall not make him sad” (Prov. 12:21). Therefore he sets against the various pleasures through which he fell the contrary remedies through which he may rise. [Col. 0730A] For example, he fell through disobedience; through the labor of obedience he returns to life. He was slippery and undisciplined; through the pursuit of continence and the rigor of discipline he is restored. He suffers punishment from the very elements of the world, by whose use he had formerly slipped into pleasure.

When he has long been tested by these sufferings as gold in a furnace—so long, namely, as he who feeds us with the bread of tears and gives us drink in tears by measure judges fitting—he begins at last to console him, and he hears that voice of Isaiah saying: “Be comforted, be comforted, my people, says your God. Speak to the heart of Jerusalem and call her; for her evil”—that is, her affliction—“is completed; her iniquity is forgiven. She has received double from the hand of the Lord for all her sins” (Isa. 40:1–2).

[Col. 0730B] After he has received consolation, he is solicitous and seeks how he may please him to whom he has proved himself. Whatever good he does, he does in order to please his Creator alone.

4. He passes to the third stage of his progress: namely, that he may become a friend of Wisdom, which speaks to him with maternal affection, saying: “My son, give me your heart” (Prov. 23:26). When he has reached this stage, nothing remains for him except to ascend to the fourth, where he is said to be wise. This occurs when he now acts not in order that he himself may please God—which he had done in the third stage—but because God pleases him, or because what he does pleases God. Whoever is such can sing with complete confidence and security of conscience that song of the Wise One: “In all things I sought rest,” etc.

For here he rests in all things, since in all things God pleases him; he has learned not to bend God’s will to his own, but to raise his own will to God’s will. “He shall dwell in the inheritance of the Lord” (Ecclus. 24:11), as is promised him by the voice of that same Lord when it is said: “The land on which you sleep I will give to you” (Gen. 28:13). That is: I will make stable and everlasting for you this rest which you have reached through your labor and my gift. And what follows, “and to your seed,” may be understood thus: not only will this tranquility be given to the spirit, both here and in the future, [Col. 0730C] but glorification of your body will also be given to your seed, that is, to your works.

## SERMON CIV. On four impediments to confession.

[Col. 0730D]

1. Four things impede confession: shame, fear, hope, and despair. Some are impeded by shame, because they are ashamed, solely from embarrassment, to declare the sins they have committed. Concerning this it is said through Solomon: “There is a shame that brings sin.” Conversely, concerning those who confess, it is again said: “There is a shame that brings glory” (Ecclus. 4:25). The prophet also commends them, saying: “You have put on confession and beauty” (Ps. 103:1); and elsewhere: “Confession and magnificence are his work” (Ps. 110:3).

Others are impeded by fear. They fear that, if they confess, a severe penance may be imposed upon them; and Job rebukes these, saying: “He who fears frost, snow shall fall upon him” (Job 6:16). There are also some who still desire something in this world and do not think they will obtain what they desire if people learn what they are like. Their confession is impeded by hope—that is, by the covetous desire to obtain what they want. To such persons the Lord threatens in the Gospel: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing” (Matt. 24:19).

There are likewise others who fear none of these things, but fear only this: that after confessing their sins they would be altogether unable to abstain from them. Despair hinders these. To them the following may fittingly be applied: “When the sinner comes into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). It sometimes happens that all these things impede confession at once. But one who is oppressed by these four evils rightly lies already in the tomb and, like that four-days-dead man in the Gospel, stinks (John 11:39). For it is written: “From the dead, as from one who is not, confession perishes” (Ecclus. 17:26). But if one who does not confess is dead, then surely one who confesses will revive. Let Jesus therefore come and say, “Come forth” (John 11:43), and at his voice the dead person will immediately be raised. Let this dead person of ours accept the exhortation and not delay confession.

2. Therefore let it be said to one afflicted by shame: Why are you ashamed to declare your sin, when you were not ashamed to commit it? Or why do you blush to confess to God, from whose eyes you cannot hide? But if perhaps you are ashamed to reveal your sin to one human being, and a sinner, what will you do on the day of judgment, when your conscience, laid open before all, will be manifest? Thus three considerations must be set against shame: consideration of reason, reverence for God who sees, and comparison with the greater shame.

[Col. 0731C] Likewise, three things must be set against fear: one must consider how long the punishment of hell is, how severe, and how fruitless. Conversely, the penance of the present time is brief, light, and fruitful. Three things are likewise set against hope: namely, the goods of the future age, greater, more certain, and more lasting than the goods of the present life. In comparison with them, whatever can be desired in this world is small, uncertain, and, so to speak, momentary. Thus there are three remedies against despair of overcoming sin: first, the vigor itself of a good resolution, which a person assumes through confession; second, the grace of God, which he merits through humility; third, the help which he has from the compassion of the person to whom he confesses.

## SERMON CV. On what is required for justification and salvation.

[Col. 0731D]

1. Our salvation consists in two things: justification and glorification. The one is the beginning; the other, perfection. In the former there is labor; in the latter, the fruit of labor. Justification now comes through faith; glorification will come through sight. Yet the human intellect cannot presently attain to how great the glorification of the saints will be in the future life. For of it it is written that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard” (1 Cor. 2:9), etc.

Leaving this aside for the present, then, because it exceeds our powers, let us say something, for the edification of our brethren, concerning the justification now being accomplished, as seems necessary. For it [Col. 0732A] is the way by which passage is made to glorification, as the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, them he also called; and those whom he called, them he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30). For glorification cannot be obtained unless justification has preceded it, since the latter is the merit and the former the reward. The Lord taught this in the Gospel when, preaching the kingdom of God with his disciples, he first set before them justice, saying: “Unless your justice exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20).

2. It should be noted that, just as in that kingdom of blessedness the Lord will make himself present to his elect for glorification, so he also makes himself present to these same persons on the way of pilgrimage for justification: so that they may first be justified through faith by him through whom they are to be glorified by sight. There are three things from which all who desire to be justified ought to abstain: first, wicked deeds; second, carnal desires; third, worldly cares. Likewise, there are three things upon which they ought to insist, which are also contained in the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5–7): almsgiving, fasting, and prayer.

Thus justification is fulfilled when they abstain from forbidden vices and faithfully perform the good things commanded. Therefore works of mercy should be opposed to wicked deeds; fasts should be employed against carnal desires; and in place of worldly cares there should come love of God and frequent prayer.

## SERMON CVI. On three things necessary for doing penance.

[Col. 0732C]

1. There are three states of the soul: in the body, after the body has been laid aside, and after the body has been received again. The first is given it for doing penance; the other two for receiving rest or punishment, according as it has done good or evil in the body. But three things are necessary for doing penance: time, body, and place. That time is necessary, the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). Likewise he writes concerning the body: “We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, that each may receive recompense for what he has done through the body” (2 Cor. 5:10). Scripture also speaks concerning place, saying: “If the spirit of one having power rises against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. 10:4).

Moreover, [Col. 0732D] time is divided into three: past, present, and future. Whoever rightly performs penance loses none of these. For he restores the past which he had lost when, in the bitterness of his soul, he reviews all his years; he holds the present through the exercise of action; and he possesses the future through constancy in a good resolution. The Apostle speaks of the past when he says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16). He urges us toward present action when he says: “While we have time, let us do good to all, especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. 6:10). The Lord admonishes us concerning the future when he says: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

2. The body is likewise necessary for doing penance. For in the body we can suffer evil and perform good: suffer, namely, for sins committed; act, for the acquisition of eternal rewards. How then can one who lacks a body produce fruits worthy of penance? It should be noted that penance performed through the body is brief and light: brief because it ends with the body’s death; light because it is borne more easily through partnership with the body. For it would be heavy if the soul bore it alone. But when it shares the burden with the body itself, the more heavily the body is burdened thereby, the more fully the soul is relieved.

A place also seems necessary and useful: namely, the Church of the present life. Whoever neglects to do penance rightly in it while living in the body will be unable to obtain any remedy of salvation in the future.

## SERMON CVII. On the affections of those who pray.

[Col. 0733B]

1. As a sick person should be toward a physician, so a sinner should be toward his Creator. Whoever, then, is a sinner ought to pray to God as a sick person to a physician. But a sinner’s prayer is hindered in two ways: by no light, or by excessive light. He is illuminated by no light who neither sees nor confesses his sins. Conversely, he is overwhelmed by excessive light who sees them as so great that he despairs of forgiveness. Neither of these prays. What then? The light must be moderated, so that the sinner may see and confess his sins, and pray for their remission.

First, therefore, his prayer should be made with a modest disposition. This occurs when the sinner does not yet dare approach God by himself, but seeks some holy man—[Col. 0733C] some holy man poor in spirit, who may be like the fringe at the hem of the Lord’s garment, through whom he may gain access. That woman in the Gospel, who suffered from an issue of blood, prefigured this prayer; wishing to be healed, she approached and thought within herself, saying: “If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved” (Matt. IX, 21).

The second prayer is made with a pure disposition; this occurs, namely, when the sinner now approaches by himself and confesses with his own mouth. The sinful woman who watered the Lord’s feet with tears and wiped them with the hair of her head left us an example of such prayer. Of her the Lord said: “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke VII, 47).

The third prayer is poured out with a generous disposition; [Col. 0733D] this occurs when one who had prayed for himself now prays for others. Thus the Apostles prayed for the Canaanite woman who was asking on behalf of her daughter: “Dismiss her,” they said, “for she cries after us” (Matt. XV, 23).

The fourth prayer is sent forth with a devout disposition: it is drawn from purity of heart, without any hesitation, with thanksgiving. The Lord himself made such a prayer when he raised Lazarus, four days dead, from the tomb and said: “Father, I thank you, because you have heard me” (John XI, 41). The Apostle taught us to make such prayers frequently, saying: “Pray without ceasing; in all things give thanks” (I Thess. V, 17–18).

The Apostle gives other names to the four kinds of prayer just mentioned—modest, pure, generous, and devout—and urges us toward them, saying: [Col. 0734A] “I exhort, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made” (I Tim. II, 1). For supplications are made with a modest disposition; prayers with a pure one; petitions with a generous one; thanksgivings with a devout one.

2. We have spoken of the kinds of dispositions and prayers; let us also say with what purity one should pray. Three things, indeed, seem to me necessary here, by which the intention of prayer must be firmly bound: the person praying must consider both what he asks, and him of whom he asks, and himself who asks.

In what he asks, he must consider two things: that what he requests may be according to God, and that he may have that very thing in the highest desire of his heart. For example, if he should ask in prayer for an enemy’s death, or for the injury or downfall of a neighbor, [Col. 0734B] such a prayer is not according to God, since he himself commands and says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. V, 44). But if he seeks forgiveness of sins, the grace of the Holy Spirit, virtue and wisdom, faith, truth, justice, humility, patience, gentleness, and the other spiritual gifts, and ardently desires them in reflection, this is prayer according to God, and this truly deserves to be heard. For God speaks through Isaiah concerning prayers of this kind: “Before they call, I will answer; while they are still speaking, I will hear” (Isa. LXV, 24).

There are other things which, when absent, are given by God and which may be or may not be according to God, insofar as it depends [Col. 0734C] on the end to which they are directed: such as bodily health, money, and abundance of other things. Though they come from God, they should nevertheless not be valued highly or possessed from desire.

Likewise, in him of whom he asks, he should consider two things: goodness, by which he is willing to give freely; and majesty, by which he is plainly able to give whatever is asked. But in himself who asks, he must likewise attend to two things: that he should suppose he will receive nothing on account of his merits, but should hope to obtain from God’s mercy alone whatever he asks. The heart, therefore, is called pure when it thinks these three things, and in the way stated. Whoever prays with this purity and intention of heart should know that he will be heard, [Col. 0734D] because, as the Apostle Peter testifies: “God is no respecter of persons; but in every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X, 34–35).

## SERMON CVIII. On Spiritual Bloodletting

There is a twofold reason for letting blood. Sometimes its quality is harmful; sometimes its quantity. Immoderate abundance is no less dangerous than corruption. The blood of my soul is my will. For blood is called the bodily fluid most akin to nature among the humors, and the life of the soul is in the will. Therefore let the perverse will be bled, for it is the cause of spiritual disease. Let it be bled, I say, since it cannot be entirely drained and dried up. Let the vein be cut and opened by the iron of compunction, [Col. 0735A] so that, if not every awareness of sin, at least consent to it, may flow out and be cast away.

Do you doubt that in the soul, too, there may be a harmful excess of blood that is not itself useless? Listen to the wise physician, who teaches that even the blood of righteousness must be let: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccles. VII, 17). The Apostle says something similar: “Do not think more highly than one ought to think, but think soberly” (Rom. XII, 3). Which vein, do you suppose, should be spared, if both righteousness and wisdom need bloodletting? For what blood is more useful? Yet remember this: neither the excessively righteous person ought to be called righteous, nor, so to speak, wisdom that is drunken ought to be called wisdom. Thus, indeed, one finds that bodily blood, when it has increased excessively, no longer brings nourishment to the body but harm.

Therefore, if it still delights you to sin, your blood is diseased: make haste to let it. If you wish to do penance, you must chastise [or, punish] your members, afflict the body, judge yourself, lest you fall into the hands of the living God. This is indeed just—but nothing to excess. Otherwise an immoderate zeal must be restrained, lest it injure unity and serve indiscretion.

## SERMON CIX. On Guarding against the Empty Splendor of Virtues

Let us beware, brethren, lest we be deceived for a time by the empty brightness of vessels and later have reason to complain that our lamps are going out. For I judge that lamps which then seem to be extinguished were never lit. Thus you have it: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten [Col. 0735C] virgins who took their lamps” (Matt. XXV, 1). He said “took,” not “lit.” For how did they light them, when they did not take oil with them? Or, where fuel for fire was lacking, how was there fire?

Yet chastity shines even by itself. But as a burning lamp is brighter than one without fire, so a chaste life with charity is more beautiful. Likewise, temperance in relation to other pleasures, patience in adversities, honorableness in conduct, circumspection in speech, almsgiving, and such works of piety seem to please by a certain natural grace and to shine with an almost inborn beauty, even among the foolish virgins. But because they shone with a brightness more glass-like than fiery, they judged their lamps to be extinguished precisely when they saw this empty [Col. 0735D] splendor rejected by the eternal light.

## SERMON CX. On a Person’s Address to Himself, or to His Soul

How great is our misery, and how manifold our need! We need even words. And though both conditions are miserable, it is no longer surprising that words are needed between us; more surprising is that they are needed even for ourselves. “No one knows what is in a person except the spirit of the person that is within him” (I Cor. II, 11). A great abyss is fixed between us unless, through words as through an instrument, a certain passage between hearts is made in the communication of thoughts. Words were invented from this necessity; who does not know it?

Nevertheless, we now must address even ourselves with words. “Will you not be subject to God, my soul?,” says the Prophet, “for from him is my salvation” (Ps. LXI, 1). And who does not frequently need to recall his own soul, summon his reason, call together his affections? Who does not need repeatedly to confront himself with words, rebuke himself with threats, stir himself with warnings, press himself with accusations? Indeed, it is useful to persuade oneself by arguments, such as: “For from him is my salvation”; and sometimes to console oneself, according to the saying: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (Ps. XLI, 6); sometimes to rouse oneself, as it were, and say: “Praise the Lord, my soul” (Ps. CXLV, 1); and at other times more carefully to remind oneself of what is fitting, as in: [Col. 0736B] “Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all his benefits” (Ps. CII, 2).

Indeed, my heart has forsaken me, and I must speak to myself—or rather, to another self. This is so much the more necessary for the present, the less I have yet returned to my heart, returned into myself, and finally become united with myself. For even among one another there will no longer be need to use words, when we all meet in the one perfect man. Tongues, therefore, will appropriately fall silent; nor will a mediator-interpreter be needed, where that one Mediator has so filled all that is between with charity that we too have become one in those who are truly and eternally one: God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ himself.

## SERMON CXI. On Bearing Witness to Faith, Life, and Conduct; or, on Rendering Six Testimonies to God

[Col. 0736C]

1. No one who is even nominally faithful doubts that the eternal happiness of the heavenly homeland, toward which our pilgrimage longs, and, conversely, the torments of Gehenna prepared for the ungodly, exceed every perception not only of the human body but even of the heart’s understanding. And would that this faith lived in all, and that belief were followed, as was fitting, by desire on the one hand and fear on the other! For what prevents us, even through drawn swords, or, if necessary, half-burned, from avoiding so great a misery and hastening toward so great a glory, except that our faith is insensible and dead?

Certainly, this is added to the sum of our unhappiness: an impediment to salvation and an occasion of our ruin—that although, in estimating each end, our affection does not agree with our judgment, in considering the ways we do not even sufficiently retain the judgment of truth itself. Nor is it surprising if desire is stirred by no delight in virtues when it is sluggish even about that eternal blessedness; or if one does not fear the present bitterness of sins who does not dread even the eternal punishments prepared for the devil and his angels. Yet in other matters we are accustomed more vehemently to desire pleasant things and fear painful ones, because our experience of them is nearer to us, although they are far less great.

[Col. 0737A]

2. I cannot sufficiently wonder why our faith wavers in present things when it seems so certain about future things. Thus, foolish children of Adam, failing to judge and discern what is true, although you possess “the promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come” (I Tim. IV, 8), you show yourselves altogether unbelieving and unfaithful in that which is immediately to be experienced. Thus it seems plainly apparent that faith in the future promise has been left to you only to increase your condemnation.

The same is to be considered concerning the threat. Is not he who declares that a kingdom is prepared for the elect and fire for the reprobate (Matt. XXV, 34, 41) the very one who, with the same mouth and the same truth, testifies that all who do not come to him labor and are burdened, while those who come will not fail—as is the trembling of human faint-heartedness—but will be refreshed by him? He who promises an indescribably delightful kingdom testifies that his yoke is sweet and his burden light. He who promises eternal blessedness in the homeland also promises present rest and refreshment on the way.

Finally, the Prophet says: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9), and all of us readily believe it. The Lord of the prophets himself says: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest for your souls; for my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. XI, 28–30); yet how many turn away the ear of their heart? Perhaps they no longer dare turn away even the ear of their body. What unbelief is this? Rather, what madness? As though Wisdom could be deceived, or Truth deceive; as though Charity might not will to give what it offers, or Omnipotence might be unable to render what it promises.

3. What person is so given over to pleasure and luxury that he would not choose sobriety and chastity instead, if he were certain that they would be more delightful to him? Who is so ambitious that he would not begin to be content with every form of lowliness and extremity, if he knew—as is truly the case—that charity, which does not seek its own interests, is more lovable than every dignity? Who is so greedy that he would not wholly despise riches if he believed poverty more pleasant?

But now Christ cries out in vain about the lightness of his burden; without cause he proclaims his yoke sweet, since even by those counted by the Christian name [Col. 0737D] the devil’s burden and the yoke of the flesh and of this world are regarded as more delightful. But whence comes to you, Lord my God, such heedlessness as is imposed upon you by these very people? Why do you promise so publicly what you are so easily found not to fulfill? You declare your Spirit sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ecclus. XXIV, 27); and behold, these have found more sweetness in the flesh of game—in the flesh, shame upon them, of a harlot—and in the vanity of the world. Woe to the wretched! They judge from one part, and disdain as bitter your hidden manna, which they have not tasted.

Yet those who have tried both, behold, they know that God is true and every human being a liar (Rom. III, 4). Their testimony, therefore, ought to have been exceedingly credible; but along with your promises, the experience of your own people is despised and ridiculed. For the carnal person does not receive the things of God’s Spirit, but they appear foolish to him (I Cor. II, 14). Nor is it surprising that one who does not believe God promising does not believe a person who has experienced it.

Therefore, we are judged mad when we preach that the Lord’s cross is sweet, extol the delight of poverty, exalt the glory of humility, and pour forth the delights of chastity. Let the Prophet too be judged mad with us, he who says that he delighted in the Lord’s testimonies as in all riches (Ps. CXVIII, 14).

4. You who are wise in your own eyes, prefer not all riches but the few you can somehow beg to divine testimonies, so that your faith may never have any testimony. Let it remain with you in secret, in hiding, where even the Father who is in heaven does not see it (Matt. VI, 4), but may say: “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 12). You firmly believe that God is just, truthful, rewarding, omnipotent, supremely good, and eternal. Show yourselves deaf asps, stopping your ears (Ps. LVII, 5), lest you hear the voice reproaching you and saying: “Show me your faith without works” (Jas. II, 18). What does believing cost you?

But do not enter the way of testimonies, because it is steep, harsh, and impassable. Miserable and unhappy people! You who have not found the way to the city of habitation, and therefore wander in a trackless place and not on a way! (Ps. CVI, 4, 40). For the end of the ways which appear good to you, which you judge delightful—for they possess no true delight—sinks down into the depths of hell; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Awake, you drunkards, and weep, lest that everlasting weeping overtake you unawares. “For when you say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon you, as upon a woman with child, and you shall not escape” (I Thess. V, 3). Justly so, since now you knowingly lose the time for fleeing and refuse the way of escape.

1232

5. “Pray,” says the Lord, “that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. XXIV, 20). Flee while it is an acceptable time and the delightful way is set before you. Flee during the six days in which work is permitted. Flee in the testimonies of those six matters touched upon above: [Col. 0738D] justice, truth, reward, omnipotence, supreme goodness, and eternity—lest perhaps the seventh testimony, namely that of divine zeal, be endured by you unwillingly rather than offered by you. “Brood of vipers, who taught you to flee from the wrath to come?” (Luke III, 7). The way on which you run is the way of death, the way of perdition, a way whose end sinks into the depths of hell.

Yet there is still hope, because the end of the way—that is, of life—has not yet come. Make haste to forestall the end, lest, suddenly overtaken, wherever you fall, there you remain. “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the way of salvation,” the way of God’s testimonies, in which you too may delight as in all riches.

6. Let the first stage be as far as the heart. For there the divine voice calls transgressors (Isa. XLVI, 8), so that the testimony of his justice may produce compunction and fear. From there let one proceed to confession of the mouth, so that we may not delay to bear witness to truth even against ourselves. For whoever is ashamed of it before human beings, it too will be ashamed of him before its Father (Luke IX, 26).

Then let the sale of possessions and distribution of resources follow, as it is written: “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor; his justice remains for ever and ever” (Ps. CXI, 9); and again: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven” (Matt. XIX, 21). For in this generous outpouring of property is a testimony to divine generosity and abundant recompense: one who freely distributes his own goods appears undoubtedly to hope for greater things from the Lord’s hand.

Further, you must also offer the fourth testimony, that of omnipotence: I mean in the affliction of the body. For the natural body must be sown, so that it may rise a spiritual body. Does not one who spares his body appear to doubt the resurrection and transformation? Thus too one who is not pierced with compunction in spirit doubts justice; one who does not confess doubts truth; and one who is greedy doubts future recompense. The same consideration applies also to what follows.

For if you advance so far as to renounce your own will, this is a most certain testimony to divine goodness. For in coming not to do your own will but his, you magnificently commend the will which you so prefer, crying out not in word or speech, [Col. 0739C] but in deed and truth, that “no one is good except God alone” (Luke XVIII, 19).

7. It remains for you to strive after perseverance. For this is the completion of the way, and it bears the testimony of eternity. Perseverance in our conduct is an image of divine eternity, so that, as he is, we too may be in this world, imitating that unchangeableness according to the measure of our capacity. Hence the Wise Man says: “The fool changes like the moon; the wise person remains like the sun” (Ecclus. XXVII, 12). This, therefore, beloved, is the way: walk in it. For by ascending from virtue to virtue, the God of gods shall be seen in Zion (Ps. LXXXIII, 8). May the Lord of hosts and King of glory, who is the way, the truth, and the life—Jesus Christ [Col. 0739D] our Lord (John XIV, 6)—bring us to the glory of that vision.

## SERMON CXII. [Note: [Col. 0739D] From the edition of Pamelius.] On the Fourfold Conscience

“Return, my soul, to your rest.” The soul labors and rests in conscience, because conscience may be good but not tranquil; tranquil but not good; neither tranquil nor good; or both good and tranquil.

Tranquil but not good is the conscience of those who sin in hope and say in their heart that God will not inquire; this is especially the condition of the young. Good but not tranquil is the conscience of those who have already turned to the Lord and recall their years in bitterness. [Col. 0740A] Neither good nor tranquil is that of those who despair because of the multitude of their sins. Good and tranquil is that of those who have subjected the flesh to the spirit, who are peaceable with those who hate peace.

This is the soul’s bed; in it the soul finds rest, though not perfect rest. But for it to provide perfect rest, conscience must be not merely good and tranquil, but secure as well. Hence he adds: “For he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from slipping” (Ps. CXIV, 8). From death, by giving a good conscience; from tears, by giving one that is tranquil and good; from slipping, by giving one that is secure.

## SERMON CXIII. On Avoiding One’s Own and Others’ Sins

“Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. XVIII, 13). There are three hidden things: unlawful action, deceitful intention, and shameless affection. Perverse action defiles memory; deceitful intention defiles reason or mind; shameless affection defiles the will. Memory is cleansed by confession; the mind by reading; affection or will by prayer.

You will be clean from others’ sins if you do not insult, withdraw, consent, or conceal. It belongs to justice not to consent but to resist firmly; to fortitude not to withdraw but patiently to endure a neighbor’s evils; to temperance not to insult but to sympathize with moderation; to prudence not to conceal but carefully to provide that evils may cease.

## SERMON CXIV. On Manifold Peace

[Col. 0740C] The peace of the body is the ordered temperance of its parts. The peace of the irrational soul is the ordered repose of its appetites. The peace of the rational soul is the harmony of thought and action. The peace of body and soul is the ordered life and health of the living creature. The peace of a human being and God is ordered obedience, in faith, under the eternal law. The peace of human beings is ordered concord. The peace of a household is the ordered harmony in commanding and obeying among those who dwell together. The peace of a city is similar. The peace of the heavenly city is the supremely ordered and harmonious fellowship of enjoying God and living in him. The peace of all things is the tranquility of order. Order is an arrangement that assigns to each thing, alike and unlike, its proper place.

## SERMON CXV. On the Threefold Heart

[Col. 0740D] “Let a person approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. LXIII, 7–8). There is a high heart, a humble heart, and a middling heart. The Prophet says: “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. XLVI, 8). The first approach of the transgressing servant is to the humble heart, to which he is drawn by judgment. The second approach of the hired servant is to the middling heart, to which he is called by counsel. The third approach of the son is to the high heart, to which he is lifted by desire. Then God is exalted—that is, raised above the heart—so that, since he cannot be comprehended by reason, he may be desired through affection and love.

Note that these approaches, or ascents, take place in the heart. Hence the Prophet says: “He has set ascents in his heart in the valley of tears” (Ps. LXXXIII, 6–7). But sometimes the inward person exceeds reason and is caught up above himself; this is called an ecstasy of the mind. Thus we say that there are four degrees of ascent: the first, to the heart; the second, in the heart; the third, from the heart; the fourth, above the heart. In the first the Lord is feared; in the second the counsellor is heard; in the third the bridegroom is desired; in the fourth God is seen.

## SERMON CXVI. On Two Deaths and an Equal Number of Resurrections

“If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Col. III, 1). There are two deaths and an equal number of resurrections. The first death is that of the soul; the second, that of the body. The death of the soul is separation from God; the death of the body, [Col. 0741B] separation of the soul from the body. Sin causes the former; punishment for sin, the latter. Likewise, the first resurrection is that of the soul; the second, that of the body. The humble and hidden coming of Christ brought about the resurrection of the soul; his glorious and manifest coming will accomplish the resurrection of the body.

But the invisible soul was created in God’s image. Hence Scripture says: “God made man in his image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26–27). This is fitting. Thus the outward human being—that is, the body—appears upright in form, having life and sensation, so that through this outward and visible person we might understand the inward and invisible one, who was made upright in will, living in knowledge, and capable of sensation in love.

And as the body, that is, the outward person, will receive life and sensation in its resurrection, so the soul, that is, the inward person, receives life and sensation in its resurrection: that is, knowledge and love. That knowledge is life, Truth himself testifies, saying: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3).

And learn from this that love is sensation. Just as the inward person is not differentiated in life, because he lives equally throughout himself, but is differentiated in sensation into the five well-known parts—namely sight, taste, hearing, smell, and touch—because he senses differently in the eye, differently in the mouth, and likewise in the other parts: so the inward person is not differentiated in knowledge, but in love. And as the former is divided into fivefold senses, so the latter is affected in relation to [Col. 0741D] five invisible attributes of God: truth, justice, wisdom, charity, and eternity. For he is affected differently in relation to truth, which he loves for freedom; differently in relation to justice, which he loves for sweetness; differently in relation to charity, which he loves for power; differently in relation to eternity, which he loves for security.

## SERMON CXVII. On Four Spiritual Fountains Healing Four Diseases of the Soul

The faithful soul has its own paradise, spiritual indeed, not earthly, and therefore more delightful and more secluded than the former. In it the soul delights as in all riches. From this paradise come four fountains: truth, charity, virtue, and wisdom. [Col. 0742A] From these fountains salutary waters are drawn for the laboring soul.

For the human soul suffers from a fourfold disease of vices: fear, concupiscence, its own iniquity, and ignorance. Overcome by fear, it is forced into vice; enticed by concupiscence, it is drawn into vice; by its own iniquity, it voluntarily follows vice; deceived by ignorance, it slips into vice. The Prophet consoles souls suffering and groaning under these evils, saying: “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior” (Isa. XII, 3).

Against faint-heartedness arising from the vice of fear comes the water of aids from the fountain of virtue; against desire for temporal pleasure, the water of desires from the fountain of charity; against the malice of voluntary iniquity, the water of judgments from the fountain of truth; against the deception of ignorance, [Col. 0742B] the water of counsels from the fountain of wisdom. And this is done with joy, so that the soul which formerly groaned beneath the weight of vices may now rejoice in attaining virtues: acquiring prudence from the waters of counsels, fortitude from the water of aids, temperance from the water of desires, and justice from the water of judgments. Thus in adversity fortitude expels faint-heartedness; in prosperity temperance restrains wantonness; in action justice excludes iniquity; and in doubts prudence instructs ignorance.

Refreshed by such waters and adorned with virtues, let the soul stretch itself out and comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length, height and depth (Eph. III, 18). These four attributes of God may be comprehended by two arms: true love and true fear. By fear, height and depth—that is, power and wisdom; by love, breadth and length—that is, charity and truth. For God is feared because through power he can do all things; and he is truly feared because through wisdom nothing is hidden from him. God is loved because he is charity; and he is truly loved because he is truth, that is, eternity.

## SERMON CXVIII. On Seven Degrees of Ascent

“Stand in the ways of the Lord, and inquire concerning his paths.” One stands in the way of the Lord who keeps the bodily observances of a good purpose. But because bodily exercise is of little value, as Paul says, he therefore adds: “And inquire concerning his eternal paths” (Jer. VI, 16): [Col. 0742D] that is, desire the lives of the holy fathers, and you will find the way; walk in it. One finds the way who returns to the heart; one walks in it who has set ascents in his heart (Ps. LXXXIII, 6). The first ascent of this way is contrition; the second, confession; the third, affection; the fourth, abandonment of property; the fifth, denial of one’s own will; the sixth, humiliation through voluntary submission; the seventh, perseverance.

## SERMON CXIX. On Three Matters to Be Considered in the Incarnation

The mystery of the Incarnation contains three matters to be considered in itself: the pattern of humility, the proof of love, and the sacrament of redemption. The crying of the infant, the place of lodging, the laying in the manger, and the wrapping in swaddling-clothes demonstrate the pattern of humility. [Col. 0743A] A merciful death demonstrates the proof of love, because “no one has greater charity than that a person should lay down his life for his friends” (John XV, 13). The sacrament of redemption displays the threefold power of the Godhead: it made something from nothing, renewed what had grown old, and made what was temporal everlasting.

## SERMON CXX. On Threefold Ministry

The ministry of Christ’s ministers is threefold: that of servitude, charity, and dignity. The ministry of servitude is chastisement of the body; that of charity, devotion of the mind; that of dignity, consecration of Christ’s body. The first is performed in affliction, the second in cheerfulness, the third in humility. The first is a sacrifice of fear; the second, of love; the third, of praise.

## SERMON CXXI. On the Teaching of Fear and Charity

[Col. 0743B]

We are in Christ’s school, where we are instructed by a twofold teaching: for the one and true master himself teaches one thing directly, and another through ministers. Through ministers, fear; directly, love. Thus, when wine failed, he commanded the servants to fill the jars with water (John II, 7); and even now, as charity daily grows cold, Christ’s ministers fill the jars with water—that is, human minds with fear.

Fear is rightly understood by water: as water extinguishes fire, so fear extinguishes lust; and as water cleanses bodily filth, so fear cleanses the filth of souls. Let us therefore fill our jars—that is, our minds—with this water, because one who fears neglects nothing; and one is well filled where negligence cannot enter. But because water weighs down—that is, fear contains punishment—we must approach him who makes wine from water, who transforms penal fear into love, so that we may hear what he himself teaches concerning love.

For he says: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John XV, 12), as if to say: “I command many things through ministers, but this I especially entrust through myself.” And elsewhere: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII, 35). Therefore, that we may prove ourselves disciples of truth, let us love one another.

In this love let us watch with a threefold care, because God is charity (I John [Col. 0743D] IV, 8), and we owe charity all our care: namely, that it may be born, grow, and be preserved. It is born if you feed your enemy and give him drink, because by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head (Rom. XII, 20). The coals of fire are works of charity, which are heaped upon the devil, who is the head of all the wicked, so that, once he has been removed, God, who is charity, may be born as their head.

Charity grows if you aid one suffering need, lend to one wishing to borrow, and open your heart to a friend. It is preserved if, by speaking or by providing even things that do not appear necessary, you satisfy your friends’ wishes. It is also preserved and increased by a kindly expression, sweet speech, and cheerful action, so that the charity indicated by face and speech may be confirmed by a devout and cheerful action; [Col. 0744A] for the performance of an act is proof of love.

## SERMON CXXII. On Two Vices to Be Feared by Those Fasting

“But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face” (Matt. VI, 17). The Lord said this because of the twofold vice—namely vain glory and impatience—which is accustomed to overthrow those who fast. By commanding the washing of the face, he directs us to preserve purity of intention; for as bodily beauty lies in the face, so the beauty of the whole soul’s action lies in intention. By anointing the head, through which what is harsh is softened, he directs us to maintain gentleness of mind in fasting. Our intention will be pure if in all our action we seek either God’s honor, [Col. 0744B] our neighbor’s benefit, or our own good conscience.

## SERMON CXXIII. On the Life of the Spirit
Walk in the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desires of the flesh (Gal. 5:16). There are people who walk according to the flesh, who devote all their concern to avoiding bodily discomforts. Although they approve of virtues, because they wish altogether to avoid bodily discomforts, they cannot resist its perverse desires. To such persons the Apostle says: “Walk in the Spirit”; that is, lay aside your concern for avoiding the discomforts of the flesh. In this life of the spirit there are two stages, the higher and the lower. At the lower stage a person walks in his own spirit; at the higher, in the Spirit of God. At the lower stage a person walks when, having returned to his heart and being concerned about his affections, he rebukes in himself what he recognizes to be contrary to virtue. At this stage he offers to God, through compunction, the sacrifice of a contrite spirit and humbled heart. Ascending from this stage to the higher, he begins to consider God’s benefits; and, turning to thanksgiving, he offers God through devotion the sacrifice of praise. At both stages he sees Christ: in the first, crucified; in the second, crowned with glory and honour. Isaiah was at the first when he said: “And we saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53:2). He was at the second when he said: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne” (Isa. 6:1). Note that in the first passage he said, “We saw”; in the second, “I saw,” because the former belongs to many, and to sinners; the latter to few, and to the prophet alone. Hence the Apostle says: “We know Christ in part, and him crucified; we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13:9, 12), because we do not yet see him as he is. For we know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). The Prophet saw, but with the prophetic eye, the Lord sitting upon a high throne—that is, above the angelic creature—and exalted—that is, above the human—for he will raise the needy from the dust and lift the poor from the dungheap, that he may seat him with princes and make him hold the throne of glory. “And the whole earth was full of his majesty” (Isa. 6:3). The whole earth—that is, all the bodies of the elect—will be full of his majesty when he refashions the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory (Phil. 3:21). “And those things that were beneath him filled the temple” (Isa. 6:1). When hypocrites, and those who excuse themselves from coming though invited, have been cast into outer darkness, the humble and those subject to God will fill the temple; for he will save the humble people and humble the eyes of the proud (Ps. 17:28).

2. Seraphim stood above it: six wings to the one and six wings to the other. Seraphim—that is, “the burning ones”—signify those who serve God in fervour, whom the Lord finds watching and sets over all his goods. “Six wings to the one and six wings to the other,” because not only prelates but subjects also have wings and are seraphim, if they are fervent. “With two they covered their head, with two their feet, and with two they flew” (Isa. 6:2). Fervent souls have wings by which they fly: hope and fear. For it belongs to one flying sometimes to seek the heights, sometimes the depths. Through hope they seek the heights, because their dwelling is in heaven. Thus some of them say: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Through fear they seek the depths: by condescending to the weak, they instruct them, considering themselves also, lest they too be tempted. With two they covered their feet. Their feet are their affections, by which they are joined to their neighbours. But because offence is committed in these two ways—by casting down the weak through excessive severity, and by consenting to their vices through excessive leniency—the seraphim covered them with two wings: against excessive severity, by consideration of their own frailty; against excessive leniency, by zeal for uprightness. With two they covered their head. The head is the intention of contemplation or spiritual understanding. The seraphim cover this because of enemies—vain glory and hidden pride—with two wings: against vain glory with one wing, namely love of truth; against pride, with the pursuit of humility.

1237 **SERMON CXXIV. On the four stages of good will.**

1. The word of God ought to accomplish two things: to heal vicious souls and to admonish good ones. By “vicious” I mean not all those in whom vice exists, but those who consent voluntarily to vice and do not resist it as much as they can. To such a soul Truth speaks in the Gospel, saying: “Be agreeing with your adversary while you are with him on the way” (Matt. 5:25), etc. He did not say “with vice,” but “with your adversary.” This adversary is the word of God, which is always opposed to vices. The person consents to it who can say with the Prophet: “My sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5). By “good souls” I mean not only the perfect but beginners also: souls which, although they have vice, nevertheless do not consent to it but struggle against it. Such souls, although they often fall through weakness or ignorance, as it is written, “The righteous falls seven times a day” (Prov. 24:16), nevertheless rise again through the good will which they possess. For this is what makes a soul good: although many good things are naturally implanted in souls—such as good natural ability, a capacious memory, alert reason, and the other goods of the soul—yet will alone, if it is good, makes the soul good; if it is vicious, it makes it vicious. But because, as Job says, a human being “never remains in the same state” (Job 14:2), but either declines or advances, one must advance in this will. For it is the way of which the Prophet says: “This is the way; walk in it” (Isa. 30:21); and the Psalm says: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has set ascents in his heart in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83:6–7). “In his heart,” that is, in his will.

2. The first stage of this life is right will; the second, strong will; the third, devout will; the fourth, full will. At the first stage the soul consents in its mind to the law of God; but, with the flesh resisting, it does not find how to accomplish the good which it loves, and often does the evil which it hates through weakness (Rom. 7:16–25). Yet its will is right in this: consenting to its adversary, it hates in itself what he rebukes. At the second stage the soul not only does not commit the evil which it hates, but also courageously accomplishes the good which it loves, though with difficulty, saying with the Prophet: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” (Ps. 16:4). At the third stage, its heart now enlarged, it runs in the way of God’s commandments and delights in them as in all riches. For, anointed with the oil of spiritual grace and knowing that God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7), it stretches itself gladly to every good work and cries with the prophet David: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118:32). At the fourth stage are the angels, who, with the same ease with which they always will, fully accomplish the good. The soul may indeed desire this stage, but cannot ascend to it while in the body, because it is weighed down by the body. Whoever does not yet have right will should know that a carnal intention hinders him. Whoever has right will but not strong will should know that a perverse habit hinders him. Whoever has devout but not yet full will should know that earthly habitation hinders him. Whoever still has a vicious will should pray and say: “May your will be done, as in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 6:10), understanding himself as earth and the one who has right will as heaven; for as far as heaven is from earth, so far is right will from vicious will. In the same way, let one who has right but not strong will pray, understanding himself as earth and the one whose will is already strong as heaven. And so with the rest, so that the soul may always attend to making progress; for just as one who remains in vicious will is condemned, so one who does not strive to advance in the other stages is blameworthy.

**SERMON CXXV. On glorifying the wisdom of God.**

1. “Glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20). Elsewhere Scripture says: “Wisdom has been justified by her children” (Matt. 11:19). And in prayer we say: “May your name be sanctified” (Matt. 6:9). Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, is justified, sanctified, and glorified by his children. Let us first say, then, how wisdom is justified by her children. “God scourges every son whom he loves” (Heb. 12:[6]). But at the beginning of the scourging, while God’s servant is still under the law and does not know how he will become God’s son, he murmurs, declares himself innocent, and pronounces God cruel. Christ, the power of God, appears to such a person, but not yet the wisdom of God; for through the scourge he feels the power of strength, but does not yet grasp through understanding the sweetness of wisdom. Wisdom reaches such a person mightily through the scourge and orders him sweetly through understanding (Wis. 8:1), when it inspires in him the Apostle’s teaching: namely, to rejoice in tribulations, to know that tribulation produces patience, patience tested character, tested character hope, and hope does not disappoint (Rom. 5:3–5). Now he recognizes that he is not punished as a servant but instructed as a son through the scourge, so that he may receive an inheritance. Declaring himself a sinner and God righteous, he justifies Mother Wisdom in himself.

2. But what good is it to confess sins amid scourges, if you do not abstain from those same sins through the holiness of continence?
