As it is written: “Be holy, because I too am holy” (Lev. 19:2), so that as the Father is, so the son may be, and the Father’s name may be sanctified in the holiness of his children. This too we ask daily in prayer: that, just as the Father complains concerning certain wicked and incontinent people, saying, “My name is blasphemed daily among the nations because of you” (Isa. 52:5; Rom. 2:24), so it may be sanctified through the holy. But lest you think it my invention that holiness is continence, hear the Apostle saying to the Thessalonians: “For this is the will of God, your sanctification.” And lest you suppose sanctification to be something other than continence, hear what follows: “That you abstain from fornication, that each one of you may know how to possess his vessel in sanctification” (1 Thess. 4:3–4). Hence we call holy those whom we see steadfast in their purpose of continence, abstaining not only from unlawful actions of this age but even from shameful speech. Hence it is written: “The wise person remains like the sun; the fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27:12).

3. But because a wise son is the glory of his father, Mother Wisdom must be not only sanctified by him through steadfast continence, but also glorified through the fruitfulness of good work. Thus Truth says in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). Hence the Psalmist, describing the son of Wisdom, says: “Pleasant is the man who has mercy and lends” (Ps. 111:5). Truly this is a brief and perfect definition of the wise person. Pleasant, he rejoices in confessing his offence amid scourges, glad that it is being wiped away through present tribulation. He has mercy on his own soul, pleasing God through the beauty of continence; he lends to his neighbour the fruit of good action. This is the righteous person, rendering to each what is his: confession to God, mercy to himself, love to his neighbour. Thus Wisdom is justified by her children through confession of sins; sanctified through the good of continence; glorified through the fruitfulness of good work. The first conflict of the fear of God is against negligence, for fear rouses a person to guard himself. If negligence prevails, it produces curiosity. For when the soil of the heart, neglected, sprouts thorns and thistles, and finds no rest within itself, it is compelled to wander abroad. Thus curiosity goes forth from the heart; against it piety fights. Piety is the worship of God; and he who is known to dwell in the heart is worshipped in the heart. If curiosity is not overcome, it produces experience of evil, because, while the mind wanders through many things, it easily finds where to experience harmful pleasure. Knowledge attacks this, teaching what is safe to experience and what is not. But if experience prevails, it produces desire, so that it may pass into the heart’s affection.

[Col. 0747]

## SENTENCES OF ST BERNARD

1. “There are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Three [give testimony] on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood” (1 John 5:7–8). Likewise in hell, as we read in Isaiah: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24). There are two evils, worm and fire: by the one the conscience is gnawed; by the other bodies are burned. A third is added: despair, which is certainly understood in the words, “shall not die” and “shall not be extinguished.” To those who are in heaven testimony of blessedness is given; to those on earth, testimony of justification; to those in hell, testimony of condemnation. The first testimony is of glory, the second of grace, the third of wrath.

2. Scripture testifies of the Holy Spirit that he proceeds, breathes forth, indwells, fills, and glorifies. He is said to proceed in two respects: from where, and to where? From where? From the Father and the Son. To where? To the creature. In proceeding, he predestines; in breathing forth, he calls those whom he predestined; in indwelling, he justifies those whom he called; in filling, he enriches with merits those whom he justified; in glorifying, he endows with rewards those whom he enriched with merits.

3. The Holy Spirit convicts the world concerning the sin which it conceals; concerning the righteousness which it does not order rightly, while it attributes it to itself rather than to God; and concerning the judgment which it usurps, while it rashly judges both itself and others.

4. To this day, among the citizens of Babylon, the pouring forth of waters—that is, the confusion of thoughts—makes the earth empty and void. For while every thought surges around the flesh, no fruit of salvation can be hoped for from it. Therefore let the waters be divided from the waters (Gen. 1:6), so that the soul too may, as is fitting, claim for itself a share of concern and meditation. Let the lower waters indeed be restrained within fixed limits, confined within fixed channels, and not exceed the bounds of necessity; but let the higher waters be expanded more abundantly. From this the Lord grants blessing, and “our land will yield its fruit” (Ps. 84:13).

5. Since among God’s people some are carnal and others spiritual, neither the former are without desire for eternal things, nor the latter altogether without desire for temporal things. They differ in this: some desire one set of things more than others, and according to what they prefer they are judged spiritual or carnal. Thus in the blessings of Jacob and Esau both the dew of heaven and the fatness of earth are named, but not in the same order for each. Isaac says to Jacob: “May God give you abundance from the dew of heaven and from the fatness of the earth.” But to Esau he says: “In the fatness of the earth, and in the dew of heaven from above, shall your blessing be” (Gen. 27:28, 39–40). What each prefers is made known by their pursuits and concerns.

6. “The death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. 23:22). It is evil in the loss of the world, because they cannot be separated without pain from what they love. It is worse in the dissolution of the flesh, from which their souls are torn away by evil spirits. It is worst in the torments of hell, when body and soul alike are consigned to everlasting fires. Conversely, the death of the good is best, because there is rest from labour, delight in newness, and security in eternity.

7. “The lazy man is stoned with ox-dung” (Ecclus. 22:2). The oxen are those who exert themselves vigorously in God’s work, who sow in tears but reap in joy. These indeed regard whatever belongs to this world as dung. But the lazy person, whose sabbaths enemies see and ridicule, is dishonoured by enemies in his idleness, just as vigorous oxen are honoured by God in their labours. For when evil spirits see someone lazy in spiritual exercises, they importunately cast earthly matters into his thoughts—as though gathering clods from ox-dung—and stone the lazy person as he deserves.

8. “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). There are three kisses: the reconciling, the gift-bestowing, and the contemplative. The first is received at the feet, the second at the hand, the third at the mouth. In the first forgiveness of sins is received; in the second, the gift of virtues; in the third, knowledge of mysteries. Or, alternatively, they are the kiss of teaching, of nature, and of grace.

9. The bride has two breasts: rejoicing with another and compassion. The twofold kind of milk is exhortation and consolation. There are three ointments: compunction, devotion, and piety. Compunction comes from the remembrance of sins; devotion from the remembrance of benefits; piety from consideration of the wretched.

10. “Return, return, O Shunammite; return, return, that we may behold you” (Song 6:12). Return first from foolish joy; return secondly from useless sadness; return thirdly from vain glory; return fourthly from hidden pride. Vain glory comes from the speech of people outwardly; hidden pride arises inwardly. When the soul has left all these vices, her bridegroom will behold her. She ought therefore to abstain from the others, that she may become worthy of his embraces. Hence she is told: “Return, return, that we may behold you.”

11. Shepherds must watch over the flock for three necessary purposes: discipline, protection, and prayers. For discipline, in order to correct manners, lest the flock entrusted to them fail through its own misery. For protection, against diabolical suggestion, lest it be led astray by hostile cunning. For prayers, because of the pressure of temptations, lest it be overcome by faintheartedness. In discipline is the rigour of justice; in protection, the spirit of counsel; in prayer, the affection of compassion.

12. The Author of the universe created two creatures to understand him: human being and angel. Faith and memory justify the human being; understanding and presence make the angel blessed. And because human beings are at some time to be brought to equality with angels, they must meanwhile be justified through faith and advance toward understanding. For it is written: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint). Therefore faith is the way to understanding: for the heart is purified by faith, so that understanding may see God. Likewise, the memory of God is the way to the presence of God. Whoever here remembers his commandments in order to do them will at some time merit also to see his presence. Let God’s angels, then, have understanding and presence in heaven; and let us have his faith and memory in the world.

13. “We are your portion, which you took from the hand of the Amorite by your sword and your bow” (Gen. 48:22). Your sword is the living and effective word (Heb. 4:12); your bow is your incarnation. For there, as though the wood of wisdom were bent and divinity in a certain pious manner bowed, the string of flesh is mightily stretched and humanity is known to be ineffably enlarged. Therefore we are your portion and the people of your acquisition (1 Pet. 2:9), whom you acquired through the word of preaching and the mystery of the incarnation.

14. In the circumcision of the Lord neither sinew is severed nor bone broken, so that all that is stronger and firmer may be preserved unharmed. But the skin is opened, the flesh cut away, and blood shed, so that seductive softness may be chastised. Understand in the flesh the sin which remains in it; in the skin, its covering; and in the blood, its incitement. This, then, is the true circumcision in spirit, not letter: if through compunction of heart and confession of mouth you remove the veil of excuse and dissimulation; if through the correction of conversion you cut off the habit of sin; if finally, as is necessary, you flee also occasions of sin and the fuel of desires.

15. The Magi offered the Lord gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matt. 2:11). Perhaps these appeared necessary for the place and time: the value of gold because of poverty; myrrh as an ointment because of the tenderness, as is usual, of an infant’s body; incense as a fragrance because of the filthy dwelling in the stable. But since all these things have now passed, let us offer him more acceptable gifts: the anointing of myrrh in participation in social life; the form of incense in the sweet fragrance of good repute; the splendour of gold in purity of conscience. Thus we should strive to seek neither familiar favour from dutiful conduct, nor vain glory from praiseworthy reputation, but the honour of God and the benefit of the brethren.

16. Before all things, let the brethren be without murmuring. Perhaps some think murmuring a slight sin; but not the one who warns that it must be avoided before all things (St Benedict, *Rule*, ch. 34). Nor, I think, did he who said to those who murmured consider it slight: “Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord. For what are we?” (Exod. 16:8). Nor did he who said: “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (1 Cor. 10:10). That destroyer, indeed, is appointed for this very purpose: to bar murmurers from the boundaries of that blessed city and remove them far from its borders, to which it is said: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion, who has made your borders peace” (Ps. 147:12, 14). For murmuring and peace, thanksgiving and detraction, bitter zeal and the voice of praise, have nothing in common. Therefore let this saying stand on the testimony of three such witnesses: we must know that this plague of murmuring is to be avoided by us with the utmost care.

17. There are three with whom we must be reconciled: human beings, angels, and God. With human beings, by outward works; with angels, by hidden signs; with God, through purity of heart. For concerning works to be done before people, it is written: “Let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). David says of angels: “In the sight of angels I shall sing psalms to you” (Ps. 137:1). Hidden signs are groanings, sighs, the use of haircloth, and the other marks of penitence which please angels. Hence: “There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15:10). But in order to be reconciled with God, we need neither works nor signs, but purity and simplicity of heart. For it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8); and: “If your eye is single” (Matt. 6:22), etc.

## OTHER SENTENCES OF ST BERNARD

> [Note: [Col. 0751D] From the library of Dunensis.]

18. “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). The temple of God is the cloister of religious persons. The cloister has two walls: active and contemplative, Mary and Martha, inner and outer. The inner wall requires two orders of stones: namely, avoiding the vice of pleasure and that of curiosity. The outer likewise requires two: that they not be deceitful or turbulent. Hence the Lord says: “A faithful and prudent servant” (Matt. 24:45): faithful, lest he be deceitful; prudent, lest he be turbulent. The wall opposite, which joins these two together, consists of prelates and those who faithfully go in and go out, as was said of the Lord: “His going forth is from the height of heaven, and his course unto its height; and there is none who hides himself from his heat” (Ps. 18:7).

19. A person learns for five reasons: to know, to be known as knowing, to sell, to build up, or to be built up. To learn in order to know is curiosity; in order to be known as knowing, vanity; in order to sell, simony; in order to build up, charity; in order to be built up, humility. “Those who had been nourished in saffron embraced dung” (Lam. 4:5), that is, concern for the belly.

20. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). The first fear recalls those going to death; worldly sorrow follows it, and hope of eternity excludes this sorrow.

21. It is commonly doubted whether love of God temporally precedes love of neighbour. It seems so because we cannot love our neighbour for God’s sake unless we first love God. Conversely, love of neighbour seems to precede love of God, because it is written: “He who does not love his brother whom he sees—how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20). But it should be known that the love of God is considered in two ways: as beginning and as nourished. A person begins to love God before loving his neighbour; but because this love cannot be perfected unless it is nourished and increases through love of neighbour, the neighbour must be loved. Thus the love of God precedes as beginning, and is preceded by love of neighbour as needing nourishment. If any persons belong to your governance, correct and restrain them with love and charity, having regard to eternal salvation, lest, while you spare the flesh, the soul perish. Do these things, and you will have to endure many people upon whom you cannot exercise discipline. Bear threats; be secure, for the Lord will perform mercy and judgment for all those who suffer injury.

22. “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 19:19). Each person ought to love his neighbour as himself, so that he may lead any person he can to the worship of God, whether by the consolation of beneficence, the instruction of teaching, or the restraint of discipline. Whoever chooses these things with discrimination alone is prudent; whoever is turned aside from them by no affliction is strong; whoever is turned aside by no other pleasure is temperate; whoever is moved by no self-exaltation is righteous.

23. “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9); in a penitent sinner it is fruitful; in one justified it is beautiful. Just as when fields are manured, it is not beautiful but fruitful; afterwards, in the gathering of crops, it becomes beautiful.

24. Four things impede confession: fear, lest one lose something; shame, lest one become contemptible; hope of honour or of some earthly advantage if one is thought innocent; and despair of those same things if one is not thought innocent.

25. There are eight trinities. The first is that supreme and indivisible Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The second is that which fell. The third is that through which it fell. The fourth is that into which it fell. The fifth is that through which it rises again, which is divided into three trinities. The trinity which fell is memory, reason, and will. Memory was weakened in three ways: by affectionate, burdensome, and idle thoughts. Reason was blinded in three ways, because it often accepts true things for false, and conversely; lawful for unlawful, and conversely.

> [Note: [Col. 0753] It should be added: advantageous for disadvantageous, and conversely, as is inferred from Sermon 15 *On Various Subjects*, no. 2.]

Will was defiled in three ways: through the desire of the flesh, desire of the eyes, and ambition of the world. The trinity through which it fell is suggestion, pleasure, and consent. The trinity into which it fell is weakness, foulness, and blindness. The trinity through which it rises again is faith, hope, and charity. Faith is threefold: faith in commandments, signs, and promises. Hope likewise is threefold: hope of pardon, hope of grace, and hope of glory. Charity too is threefold: with the whole heart, with the whole soul, and with the whole strength.

26. There ought to be two walls in a community: one inner, the other outer. The inner wall consists of those within the cloister; the outer, of those assigned to obediences. The former ought not to be curious or pleasure-seeking; the latter neither turbulent nor deceitful. Because peace between them is rare, there is a third wall coming from the opposite side, joining the divided walls: namely, the abbot, the prior, and the other spiritual brethren. The foundation is the holy purpose.

27. The correspondence of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit to the appearances of the risen Lord. First he appeared to the women, to whom the angel said: “Do not fear” (Matt. 28:9, 5): behold the spirit of fear. He appeared to Peter, who had denied him (Luke 24:34): behold the spirit of piety. He appeared to the woman to whom he said: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17): behold the spirit of knowledge. He appeared to the eleven on the mountain which he had appointed, when he said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18): behold the spirit of fortitude. He appeared to the two going to Emmaus, of whom it is written: “And he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures”: behold the spirit of understanding. Finally he appeared to them reclining at table, when he ascended into heaven (Luke 24:27, 45, 51), because it is said of him: “I, wisdom, dwell in the highest places” (Ecclus. 24:7): behold the spirit of wisdom.

28. Grace is fourfold: creating grace; redeeming, or merciful, grace; giving grace; and rewarding grace. The first: “All things were made through him.” The second: “The Word was made flesh.” The third: “Full of grace.” The fourth: “And truth” (John 1:14).

29. Peace is fourfold: toward God, toward neighbour, in the flesh, and in the spirit. For each peace to be firm, a foundation must be laid beneath it: temperance for peace of the flesh; fortitude for peace of the spirit; prudence for peace with one’s neighbour; justice for peace with God. “Glory in the highest”: behold peace with God; “and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14), peace with one’s neighbour; “Peace to you; see my hands and my feet” (Luke 24:36, 39), peace of the flesh; “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22), peace of the spirit.

30. “Dying flies destroy the sweetness of ointment” (Eccl. 10:1), that is, vanity, curiosity, and pleasure. Because these abound in Egypt and around the sacrifices of the Egyptians, we cannot sacrifice to the Lord our God in Egypt the sacrifice of righteousness and charity. Therefore we set out into the desert—that is, into the solitude of the heart—by a journey of three days (Exod. 8:26–27). Of the first day the bridegroom says to the bride: “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride” (Song 5:1), that is, into the plantings of good virtues. At the second the bride rejoices and says: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar” (Song 1:3), that is, among the delights of the Scriptures. The third day is the bridal chamber, the fullness of love, in which bridegroom and bride delight in one another. Note: against vanity, the solidity of virtues; against curiosity, the varied delight of the Scriptures; against pleasure, the bridal chamber of that highest love.

31. The two breasts of charity are compassion and rejoicing with another. From compassion the milk of consolation is drawn; from rejoicing with another, the milk of exhortation is drawn.

32. There are three things by which unity is preserved: patience, humility, and charity. With these the soldier of Christ must be armed: patience as a shield, to bear and carry around against all adversities; humility as a breastplate, to preserve the inward parts of the heart; charity as a spear, by which, as the Apostle says, urging all people toward the provocation of charity (Heb. 10:24), and making himself all things to all people, he fights the Lord’s battle. He must also have the helmet of salvation, which is hope, guarding and preserving the head—that is, the ruling part of the mind. Let him also have the sword of God’s word and the horse of good desire. Goliath is to be killed by his own sword; vain glory, by consideration of vain glory itself.

33. There are two last things: death and life. Toward them we fly with two wings, fear and hope. With two we cover our feet: penitence of heart and confession of mouth, according to the saying: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). With two we cover our head: love of God and of neighbour. Hence the Apostle says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober-minded, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5:13).

34. Note that from fear comes compunction; from compunction, renunciation of all things; from this, true humility; from this, true confession, in which is the cleansing of all vices. From confession comes the budding forth of virtues; virtues formed together produce purity of heart, in which are true wisdom and perfect charity. It should be understood that the spirit of fear gives fear; the spirit of piety, compunction; the spirit of knowledge, renunciation of present things; the spirit of fortitude, true humility—for humility conquers all things; the spirit of counsel, confession; the spirit of understanding, acquisition of virtues; the spirit of wisdom, perfect purity of heart and love.

35. There are four orders in the house of the Lord. Some fall at Jesus’ feet, like the Ethiopians, like Mary penitent and confessing; some sit at his feet, as the same Mary did while hearing his word; some lie upon his bosom; some sit at his side. The first two orders live for themselves; the third for itself and for its neighbour, like John the Evangelist, receiving and drawing peace from the Lord’s bosom and proclaiming it to the people. The fourth lives for its neighbour, like the Apostle who says: “I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith.” Hence he adds confidently: “There is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4:7–8). “And therefore I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:23–24). Such persons neither fear death nor refuse life.

36. One kind of pride is blind, another vain, another both blind and vain. It is blind when a person thinks that there is in himself what is not there. It is vain when he glories in people’s thinking that he possesses what he does not. It is at once blind and vain when, concerning a good which he does not possess, he both glories in himself and seeks others’ praise.

37. Humility is of one kind sufficient, of another abundant, of another superabundant. It is sufficient to submit to a superior and not prefer oneself to an equal. It is abundant to submit to an equal and not prefer oneself to an inferior. It is superabundant to submit to an inferior. Hence the Lord said to John: “Allow it for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15).

38. Whoever wishes to please God perfectly must shine in both chastity and charity. Chastity is fivefold: namely, in the ears, the eyes, the sense of smell, taste, and touch. Charity is fourfold, which, according to the Apostle, “believes all things,” that is, is not suspicious; “hopes all things,” is not slothful; 1244 “bears all things,” does not complain; “endures all things” (1 Cor. 13:7), is not impatient. Behold nine qualities: whoever possesses them perfectly is perfect, and lives on earth according to the nine orders of angels. Hence the Apostle: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). And, if I may put it so, a human being living in this manner has greater merit than an angel. For in a human being it is a matter of virtue; in an angel, of rank.

[Col. 0756A] 39. The holy soul mortifies its flesh from the corruption of vices when, through self-restraint, it renounces all the pleasures of the world; and then it applies, as it were, myrrh to its mortal body, so that after the judgment it may remain sound, free from eternal corruption. But when it kindles itself toward heavenly things with greater desire, and fervently casts all superfluous thoughts out of the chamber of its heart, it makes its heart before God like a censer. While it gathers virtues in it through love, it arranges them there like coals in a censer, in which the mind may set itself aflame before God with the fire of charity. And while it sends forth fervent and pure prayers to God, it draws out, as it were, the smoke of spices from the censer, so that it may smell sweet before the Beloved and may not cease to stir up all its neighbors to his love through good works.

[Col. 0756B] 40. “You shall not cook a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exod. 34:26). The kid is the sinner; the mother, the first parents from whom we all have been begotten; the milk, the vices that came from original sin. “You shall not cook a kid in its mother’s milk”: that is, the sinner must not be allowed to remain in sins until the day of death, but must be recalled to good works before death, lest he perish.

41. “There are three that bear witness on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood” (1 John 5:8). When the Lord came, he caused circumcision and the other baptisms to cease; but he instituted baptism, in which he willed the aforesaid three to operate as a testimony to Christianity on earth.

[Col. 0756C] Hear how the blood of Christ operates, and is a sign that we should die to sin, according to the Apostle: “Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” The water, which encloses the body as though in a certain tomb, is a sign that we should no longer serve sin: “For we were buried with him through baptism into death.” The Spirit gives life and brings it about that we who are buried in that element of waters may rise again, renewed through that same Spirit, so that, “as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:3–4). And because these three accomplish one thing, they are one, as John says: one in mystery, not in nature. Therefore, the blood is the witness of death, the water of burial, the Spirit of life. The blood pertains to the ransom, the water to the washing;

[Col. 0756D] the Spirit renews the mind. The Lord’s blood redeemed us; the wave of the sacred font washed us; through adoption the Spirit makes us children of God.

42. “In the fourth watch he came to them”—the apostles—“walking upon the sea” (Matt. 14:25). The first sleep is the terror of the night, namely fear concerning adversities; the succeeding watch is prudence. The second sleep is “the arrow flying by day,” that is, temptation through prosperity; its watch is fortitude. The third sleep is “the business that walks about in darkness,” namely vainglory; its watch is justice. The fourth sleep is “the assault and the noonday demon,” that is, intemperance. Then the Lord comes to them, walking above the sea. The Lord is above, but Peter sinks. At first he is thought to be a phantom, but afterward he is recognized. The others, more lukewarm though still faithful, magnify the Lord in such things.

[Col. 0757A] 43. Seven things ought to be present in prayer. Prayer ought first to be faithful, according to the saying: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you shall receive it, and it shall be yours” (Mark 11:24). Next, it must be pure, according to the example of Abraham, who drove the birds away from the sacrifice. Third, just; fourth, continual; fifth, humble; sixth, fervent—these two being contained in the grain of mustard seed; seventh, devout.

[Col. 0757]

## PARABLES COMMONLY ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT BERNARD

1245 **PARABLE I. On spiritual combat** [otherwise, *On the flight and return of the prodigal son*].

[Col. 0757B]

1. The rich and most mighty king, almighty God, made the human being whom he had created his son. Like a delicate child, he assigned him as pedagogues the Law, the Prophets, and the other guardians and stewards until the appointed time of his full maturity. He instructed and admonished him, made him lord of paradise, and showed and promised him all the treasures of his glory, provided that he did not desert him. And lest anything be lacking among his blessings, he also granted him free choice, so that his goodness might be voluntary rather than compelled. Having received freedom concerning good and evil, he began, through a desire to know good and evil, to grow weary of his blessings.

Having therefore departed from the paradise of a good conscience, seeking novelties which he did not know—though until then he had known nothing but good things—he abandoned his father’s [otherwise, native] laws and pedagogues, ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil contrary to the Father’s prohibition, and, wretchedly hiding himself and fleeing from the face of the Lord, the foolish child began to wander through the mountains of loftiness, the valleys of curiosity, the plains of license, the groves of lust, the marshes of carnal pleasures, and the waves of worldly cares.

[Col. 0757C] 2. But the ancient robber, seeing the wanton child wandering far from his Father’s house without a guardian or guide, approached him. Extending to him those little apples of disobedience by the hand of evil persuasion, and having drawn his consent from him, he attacked the wretch and hurled him down to earth—that is, into earthly desires. He bound his feet, that is, the affections of his mind, with the strongest chains of worldly desire, lest he rise again; and bound his hands of action and the eyes of his mind. He sent him aboard the ship of evil security and, with the wind of flattery blowing violently, carried him over into the far country of dissimilarity.

When he reached a country not his own, he became saleable to all who passed along the road. He learns to feed swine and to eat the swine’s husks. He unlearns all that he had learned, and learns what he had not known: servile works. Bound in the prison of despair, where the wicked walk in a circle, he is compelled to grind in the mill of impious circling the profits of an evil conscience.

[Col. 0757D] Alas for the child!

3. And where now is that most powerful, sweet, and generous father? Can he forget the son of his womb? Far be it, far be it! He does not forget, but has mercy; he grieves with him and laments the absence and ruin of his son. He sends orders to his friends, stirs up his servants, and rouses all to seek him.

One of the servants, Fear, following the footsteps of the runaway son at the Lord’s command, finds the king’s son in the depth of the prison, covered with the carnal filth of sins, bound with the fetters and chains of evil habit, wretched and out of his mind, secure and laughing amid his miseries. Urging him with words and blows to depart and return, Fear cast the wretch down into such confusion that he lay as one already near death and his belly clung to the earth.

Another immediately went forth, whose name was Hope. Seeing the king’s son not drawn out by Fear but buried by him, not aided but cast down, Hope approached gently. Raising the needy from the ground and lifting the poor from the dung heap, lifting his head, wiping his eyes and face with the garment of consolation gathered together into one, Hope said: “Alas! How many hired servants in your father’s house abound in bread, while you perish here from hunger! Rise, I beg you; go to your father and say to him: ‘Father, make me like one of your hired servants.’”

Then he, at last scarcely returning a little to himself, said: “Then it is you, Hope? And how could an entrance be opened for Hope into so great and so horrible a depth of my despair?”

“I,” Hope said, “yes, I am Hope, sent to you by your father, to help you and not to leave you until I bring you into your father’s house and into the chamber of your mother.”

“And,” he said, “O sweet relief of labors, sweet consolation

[Col. 0758C] of the wretched! O one—and not the least—of the three attendants of the royal chamber! You see the immense depth of my prison; you see the chains which, at your entrance, have nevertheless for the most part already been broken and loosed; you see the vast multitude, strength, speed, and cunning of my captors.

[Note: [Col. 0757D] That is, those holding captive, or those who have been captured.]

And what place is there here for you?”

But Hope said: “Do not be afraid. He who helps us is merciful; he who fights for us is almighty; and there are more with us

[Col. 0759A] than with them. Besides all this, I have brought the horse Desire, sent by the Father; when you have mounted it, under my guidance you will depart safely from all these.”

She spoke; and, laying down soft bedding of pious Devotion and adding spurs of good examples, she set the king’s son upon the horse Desire. But a bridle was lacking, so great was the haste of flight. Immediately the unbridled horse runs; Hope draws him forward, while Fear presses from behind with blows and threats.

Then, seeing this, “the princes of Edom were troubled; trembling seized the mighty men of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan grew stiff. Let fear and dread fall upon them; by the greatness of your arm let them become motionless as a stone, until your son passes over, O Lord, this son whom you have possessed” (Exod. 15:15–16). But while they are thus borne headlong, they do indeed escape, though not without danger, because they proceed without measure and without counsel.

[Col. 0759B] 4. Therefore Prudence, sent by the Father, came running up, one of the chief princes of the palace, having her friend Temperance in her company. Holding back those who were running, she said: “More sparingly, I beg you, more sparingly! For our Solomon says: ‘He who is hasty with his feet stumbles’” (Prov. 19:2). “If you run in this way, you stumble; if you stumble, you fall; if you fall, you hand over to the enemies the king’s son whom you undertook to free. For if he falls, their hand will immediately be upon him.”

As she spoke, she put the bridle Discretion upon that fiery horse Desire, and entrusted its reins to Temperance to govern. When Fear complained behind them about the proximity and power of the enemies and the slowness of their flight, Prudence said: “Go behind, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to us. The Lord is our strength and praise, and he has become our salvation.”

And behold, Fortitude, the outstanding soldier of God, came running through the field of Confidence with the drawn sword of Joy. “Do not be troubled,” she said; “there are more with us than with them.” Then Prudence, accustomed to the counsels of the heavenly court, said: “Take care, I beg you, because that inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning, as our Solomon says, will lack blessing in the end” (Prov. 20:21). “Proceed, therefore, not so much hastily as prudently. For the enemies are not on the road; rather, they are accustomed to set a stumbling-block beside the road, at forks and crossroads and bends in the way. Therefore I shall go ahead; but you, keep to the road of Justice, and we shall swiftly

[Col. 0759D] bring you into the camp of Wisdom, which is now not far from us. For this is the Wisdom of which it is said: ‘Desiring wisdom, learn justice’” (Ecclus. 1:33).

5. Thus, as they travel the road, Fear presses, Hope draws, Fortitude protects, Temperance moderates, Prudence foresees and instructs, and Justice leads and brings them through. The king’s son approaches the camp of Wisdom. Hearing of the new guest’s arrival, she goes before the one who desires her, meets him, and shows herself cheerfully in the ways.

A ditch of deep Humility surrounded the camp, above which a most strong and beautiful wall of Obedience had been built, piercing the heavens. It was wonderfully adorned on every side with painted histories of good examples. It was built

[Col. 0760A] with battlements: a thousand shields hung from it, all the armor of the strong. The gate of Profession stood open to all; the gatekeeper, standing on the threshold, admitted the worthy and cast out the unworthy. A herald cried out above the gate: “If anyone loves Wisdom, let him turn aside to me, and he shall find her; and when he has found her, he is blessed if he holds fast to her.”

Here the king’s son, led—indeed, carried in the arms—of Wisdom who came to meet him, surrounded by the services of the royal household, is brought to the citadel in the middle of the city. There Wisdom herself “built her house, hewed out seven columns,” subjected nations to herself, and by her own strength trampled upon the necks of the proud and lofty. There he is placed upon the bed of Wisdom, around which stand sixty mighty men from among the mighty men of Israel, each with his sword upon his thigh.

1247 David is present with tambourine and choir, with strings and organ;

[Col. 0760B] and the other companions of the heavenly court, rejoicing and exulting more over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance.

6. And behold, a wind of whirlwind and enveloping fire came from the north and shook the whole house, throwing Wisdom’s camp into disorder. For Pharaoh came forth with chariots and horsemen, pursuing fleeing Israel (Exod. 14:5, 8). “They also conspired together with one accord against him; they made a covenant: the tents of the Edomites and Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre. For Assur”—that great destroyer, the devil—“also came with them” (Ps. 82 [81]:6–9).

What more need be said? The city was besieged. The engines of temptations now rise up. On every side that enemy presses: a dragon in ambush, a lion in the open. He urges his allies, casts in fires, pierces the walls, raises wars, sends in ambushes, threatening the destruction of the entire city. But within there is fear and distress; and, at the violent and unexpected assault of the enemies, all were troubled, “and they reeled like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up; and they cried to the Lord in their affliction” (Ps. 107 [106]:27–28).

They run to the citadel of Wisdom; evil tidings are announced; counsel is sought. Prudence, having returned to herself, asks Wisdom what must be done. Wisdom declares that they must hasten and seek the aid of the supreme King. “And who,” Prudence asks, “will go for us?”

[Col. 0760D] Wisdom says: “Prayer. And lest she delay in going, let her mount the horse Faith.” Prayer was sought for a long time, and in so great a tumult was at last found only with difficulty. She mounts the horse Faith, proceeds along the way of heaven, and does not cease until she enters the gates of the Lord with confession and his courts with hymns. Like a familiar household servant, she approaches the throne of his grace with confidence and lays out the matter of her necessity.

When the king heard of his son’s peril, he turned to Charity, his consort in the kingdom: “O whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” But she said: “Behold, here I am; send me.” Then the king said: “Prevailing, you shall prevail, and you shall deliver him. Go forth and do so.”

Immediately the whole heavenly host accompanied Charity, queen of heaven, as she went forth from the Lord’s presence. Coming down into the camp,

[Col. 0761A] she immediately gladdened all things by the power and joy of her presence, set in order what was disturbed, and brought peace to what was troubled. Light was restored to the wretched; confidence to the fearful. Hope, who had almost fled, returned; Fortitude, who had almost collapsed, returned. The entire army of Wisdom recovered its steadfastness.

But the enemies besieging the city said: “What is this exultation in the camp? There was not such exultation yesterday or the day before. Woe to us! God has come into the camp! Woe to us! Let us flee Israel, for the Lord fights for them.” Thus, as the enemies fled, “the rush of God’s grace makes glad the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle. God is in her midst; she shall not be moved; God shall help her at the break of dawn. Nations were troubled and kingdoms bowed down; he uttered his voice and the earth was moved. The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector” (Ps. 46 [45]:5–8).

Therefore Queen Charity, receiving the child of God, her own child, raised him up to heaven and presented him to God the Father. The Father met him kindly and serenely and said: “Quickly bring out the first robe and put it on him; put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet. Bring out the fattened calf and kill it. For we must feast and rejoice, because this my son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:11–32).

[Col. 0761B] 7. Note here four stages in the deliverance of our child. First, repentance, but foolish repentance; second, flight, but rash and unreasonable flight; third, battle, but trembling and fearful battle; fourth, a strong and wise victory. You will find all these in every person fleeing from the world. At first he is needy [otherwise, dull] and foolish; afterward, headlong and rash in prosperity; then trembling and faint-hearted in adversity; finally, prudent, instructed, and perfect in the kingdom of charity.

1248 **PARABLE II. On spiritual combat** [otherwise, *On the conflict of vices and virtues*].

1. Between Babylon and Jerusalem there is no peace, but continual war. Each city has its own king. Christ the Lord is king of Jerusalem; the devil is king of Babylon. Since it delights one to reign in justice, the other in wickedness, the king of Babylon draws into Babylon such citizens of Jerusalem as he can seduce through his ministers, namely unclean spirits, so that he may make them “serve iniquity unto iniquity.”

[Col. 0761D] Therefore, when a watchman posted upon the walls of Jerusalem saw one of its citizens being dragged away, he announced to the king that captured spoil was being taken into Babylon. The king of Jerusalem summoned the spirit Fear, a vigorous soldier in such matters: “Go,” he said, “rescue our spoil.”

Always ready for every command, Fear pursued the enemies swiftly, and suddenly there came to be in their ears a sound like that of a mighty spirit approaching. For Fear thundered over them; at the voice of his power all the strength of the enemies trembled. Fear did not pursue them farther once they had turned to flight, but brought the rescued fellow citizen back to his own home.

Yet one of the adversaries, the spirit of Sadness,

[Col. 0762A] was not with them when Fear arrived. Seeing his companions suddenly fleeing, he quickly flew out from the ambush where he lay hidden.

“This has been done by Fear alone,” they said, “and it is a disgrace to us all.”

But he said: “Do not be afraid of this Fear. I know what must be done. I shall go and be a lying spirit in the corners of the paths, and I shall pretend to be Fear’s friend. For I know the man: he must not be dealt with by force, but by deceit. But you, wait for the outcome.”

He did as he had said. Taking shortcuts along the roads, he went ahead of Fear. Returning along the road by which Fear was walking, he met him and entered into friendly but wicked conversation with him, so that he began to deceive him; and Fear, unsuspecting, followed with good intention. He was already close to thrusting him into the pit of despair.

[Col. 0762B] But the watchman reports to the king what is happening. The king orders one of his soldiers, namely Hope, to be summoned, and commands him to hurry to Fear’s aid with the horse Desire and the sword Joy. The faithful soldier went out at the command; when he reached the place, he brandished the sword Joy and put Sadness to flight. Thus he led the freed fellow citizen, mounted upon the horse Desire, drawing him forward with the cord of promises; and Fear, following, pressed him onward with a scourge made from the cords of sins.

2. The horse went willingly, drawn from one side and driven from the other; but in such rapid running he had to fear an encounter. Therefore the Babylonian soldiers gathered in council and said: “What are we doing, since he thus escapes whom we already possessed almost securely? How has the applause of hell been turned into lamentation, and through only two soldiers is there joy in heaven over the liberation of their fellow citizen? How has the cunning of diabolical deceit perished?”

[Col. 0762C] But one among them, more wicked than the rest, being the contriver of this crime, offered a profane counsel: “You know nothing, nor do you consider that he is now easier to capture, and that if he is captured, he can be rescued only with greater difficulty. You, therefore, follow from afar. I shall transform myself into an angel of light, so that under the pretense of teaching I may deceive those ignorant of the way, as though they were strangers and pilgrims.”

When this deceit had thus been arranged, the watchman reports to our king that a man is coming, indeed mounted upon the horse Desire, but hurrying more than he ought because a bridle

[Col. 0762D] and saddle are lacking. “The enemies,” he says, “follow from afar; others, long practiced in evils, take shortcuts through the roads. Yet now I see one in whom the appearance of our weapons shines; nevertheless, he did not go out from us. It is necessary that someone go who knows how to question him: ‘Are you ours, or the adversaries’?’”

3. Now the king, whose mind is ever troubled by care for souls, sends out his two counselors, Prudence and Temperance. Temperance placed the bridle Discretion upon the horse and persuaded Hope to proceed more moderately. Prudence rebuked Fear and charged him with wrongdoing, warning him about the future. She put upon the horse the saddle Circumspection, so that its rider might not fall backward; rather, he should lean backward upon confession of past sin, forward upon meditation on judgment,

[Col. 0763A] on the left upon patience, and on the right upon humility. Hope and Fear then fitted spurs to the horse: Hope placed on the right foot expectation of reward, Fear on the left fear of punishment.

4. When there was delay and evening was drawing on and the day had already declined, the enemies again gathered in a multitude to fight against them. Fear trembles; Hope hastens forward; but at last Prudence and Temperance scarcely called them back to counsel. Prudence said: “You see that the day has passed and night has drawn near; and he who walks in darkness does not know where he is going. A great way still remains for you, and the multitude of enemies is not small. Yet there is a soldier of our king, most faithful, whom I know. He has a fortress situated near us, and it is a most firm dwelling, because

[Col. 0763B] he has placed his nest upon a rock. Let us turn aside to him, if it pleases you, for it is good to be there.”

When this pleased them all and they sought a guide for the journey, Prudence said: “My squire Reason shall go before us. He knows the roads and is known to Justice, as her kinsman.”

Therefore Reason went ahead, the others following. Reason arrived first; greeting Justice, he announced that guests were coming. She asks who they are, where they come from, and for what purpose. When she recognized the king, she rose with a cheerful face, met the fugitives with bread, came to meet them like an honored mother, took the received soul down from the horse, and eagerly placed it in the inner chambers of her house.

5. The hostile army follows, besieges the fortress, and searches everywhere to see whether some entrance might perhaps be open, circling like a lion seeking whom it may devour. But when they find it fortified on every side, they pitch their tents and post guards so that no one may enter or leave, intending at daybreak to destroy it with engines prepared for the purpose and rush upon them.

[Col. 0763C] Meanwhile Dread, diligent through fearfulness and anxiety and never secure, rouses his fellow soldiers. He consults Justice, asks about the fortification of the place and the preparation of weapons, adding also the concern that provisions might perhaps fail for their maintenance.

Justice replied: “As you can observe, the site is rocky and inaccessible, and it does not fear assault from the enemies either in arms or engines. But because it is dry, it has few native inhabitants, whom it sustains somehow with the dry food of barley bread. And now we have left five barley loaves and two fishes.”

[Col. 0763D] Fear said: “What are these among so many?” Thus he began to be more afraid and more distressed; blaming the soul because it had dismounted from the horse Desire, he repeatedly recalled the saying that “the last state of that man is worse than the first.” For that horse had been hastening toward the city in swift flight, now entrusted solely to the guidance of Reason. “You yourself can see,” he said, “whether it was not better for you then than now.”

6. Fear was already near to rising against Hope, who held the opposite view; but Temperance summoned Prudence. When Prudence had been called, she rebuked Fear’s wrongdoing: “Let your sword rage against the adversaries, O Fear. Do you not know that our king is the King of hosts, ‘the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle’?

[Col. 0764A] Therefore let a messenger go, one who may set forth the needs of his people, request help, and bring the helper.”

“But who,” Fear said, “can go? Darkness covers the land, the sleepless multitude of enemies besieges the walls, and we are ignorant of the way, as though in a far country.”

They therefore called upon Justice, their host. “If you can do anything,” they said, “help us.”

She said to them: “Be of good courage. For I have a most faithful messenger to the king, well known to the court: namely Prayer, who in the secrecy of night’s silence is skilled at penetrating heaven’s hidden places by unknown paths, at approaching the king’s chamber, and at bending the king’s merciful mind by fitting importunity; by pitiable supplication he is accustomed to obtain aid for those in distress. Let him go, if it pleases you; behold, he is ready.”

When they all replied,

1250 [Col. 0764B] “It pleases us,” Justice dictated to Prayer what she should communicate to the king, commanding her to act faithfully and not to return empty-handed. The others—and especially Fear—begged that she hasten on her way. Prayer was sent out through certain hidden exits of the wall. Penetrating the enemy ranks, swifter than every bird and secure, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, she reached the gates of the new Jerusalem.

Finding them closed, she knocked. Though the gatekeepers were annoyed because she filled the city with cries during the silence of untimely night and did not fear to be troublesome even to the king himself, she persisted in knocking and spoke more earnestly: “Open to me,” she said, “the gates of justice; having entered them I shall confess to the Lord our king with my mouth according to the multitude of my sorrows that are in my heart. This is the gate of my Lord.

[Col. 0764C] Justice sent me to you, that I may be brought before the king, because I have secrets to carry to him. The voice of a whirlwind has been heard in our land.”

7. When the king learned that she was Justice’s messenger, he commanded her to be admitted. Prayer entered before the king, worshiped, and said: “O king, live forever.”

And he said: “Is all well with your lord and with what belongs to him?”

Prayer said: “All is well, Lord, by your grace. Yet one thing is necessary. That servant of yours, rescued by the king’s command from the horns of unicorns, has turned aside to your soldier, my lord. And, my lord, that land is southern and dry, and has no food. May the Lord give blessing, and may our land yield its fruit. Behold, enemies have gathered in a multitude to fight against us. Give us, Lord,

[Col. 0764D] help in tribulation, for there is no one else who fights for us except you, our God.”

But our king, whose nature is goodness, moved by these tears, said: “Whom shall we send?”

Charity said to him: “Behold, Lord, here I am; send me.”

But the king asked concerning companions; Charity replied that her own household was sufficient. Therefore she goes forth with her noble company: Joy, Peace, Patience, Long-suffering, Kindness, Goodness, and Meekness. Surrounded by these, the illustrious leader advances, assured of victory. Raising the standard of triumph, she passes through the first and then the second guard of the enemies. When she came to the gate, it opened to her of its own accord. At her entrance great joy arose in the town.

[Col. 0765A] And when, at Joy’s urging, they all cried aloud and raised a shout, the sound that arose terrified the camp of the foreigners. They said: “What is this sound of exultation in our ears from the camp of Israel? It was not so yesterday or the day before. Perhaps help has come to them, and they will attack us. Let us therefore flee Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us.”

Meanwhile Charity, impatient of delay, commands that the army be drawn up, the gates opened, and the enemies pursued, openly declaring: “I shall go to the gates of hell.” Thus the entire army of Charity advances in a single assault. The Babylonians cannot withstand them and flee, but do not escape. A thousand fall at the side of Fear, and ten thousand at the right hand of Charity.

## PARABLE III. On spiritual combat

[Col. 0765B] 1. Battle lines are drawn up between Jerusalem and Babylon. On one side David, mighty in hand, leads forth and arranges the terrible and ordered battle line of virtues; on the other, Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon directs against it the spiritual powers of wickedness and his tumultuous army of vices.

A raw recruit comes forth from David’s camp, newly sworn into the king’s service, girded by the hands of the eternal David himself with the sword of the Word of God, equipped with spiritual arms, bearing a great heart, and—contrary to the king’s command—more impatient to make a name for himself than to conquer the enemy. His fiery horse was his own body, still strong, vigorous, and wanton from the sap of the world; his disposition matched it. Riding conspicuously upon it, despising the discipline of his camp and scorning his companions, he advanced far before the rest with a certain foolish presumption,

[Col. 0765C] burning and panting to make a name for himself.

David, seeing his impetuous presumption, commanded him through his son Solomon, with a threat: “Woe to the one who is alone, for if he falls, he will have no one to lift him up” (Eccles. 4:10). But he set little value upon these warnings. Seeking occasions to display great virtue in himself or to others, and plotting some brilliant exploit, he saw in the enemy’s quarter, far off, one of the enemies: strong in malice, crafty in wickedness, armed with fiery weapons and with hands full of fiery darts, wounding many, killing the wounded, trampling the slain, capturing easily and releasing with difficulty—the spirit of Fornication.

[Col. 0765D] 2. Presuming that he would display his splendid virtue against this spirit, he directed an attack upon him. Urging his ready horse with the lashes of fasts and the spurs of vigils, he rushed wholly at him. Prudence cries from behind, “Spare, spare!” Discretion cries, “Wait, wait!” The whole Davidic army rebukes him. Passing them all by with a deaf ear, the wretch rushes headlong into his own ruin and does not know it.

Nabuchodonosor, seeing this, roars and, preparing evil for him, sends deceit ahead. For two sisters, Pride and Vainglory, meet him from the side as he rushes headlong, crying deceitfully, “Well done, well done!” The poor fellow, far too credulous, rushes wholly onward and does not know what ambushes now surround him on every side.

[Col. 0766A] The spirit of Fornication, already often experienced in such attacks by such persons, feigns flight and provokes the deluded wretch to follow, until, having led him through an open gate into the middle of Babylon, he hands him over to his companions for mockery. Gluttony and Fornication claim the horse for themselves and no longer permit its master to have any right over it. For it was already failing; exhausted, it sought to turn aside. In the midst of battle it had fallen beneath its rider and, by its fall, had severely bruised him. The others refreshed it with Babylonian food, fattened it again, and subjected it to their service.

But Anger, Envy, and the rest of the crowd of vices rise up against the wretch; sinners confidently build upon his back. And Fornication, of whom he had thus far seen only the back as she fled,

[Col. 0766B] now rises against him with open face and shameless brow, hurls fiery darts into his heart, draws a sword against his neck, and, having cast him to the ground, tramples him. Handing him over to Nabuzardan, the cook of the Babylonian king, she subjects him to the cook’s unclean disgorgings for mockery. Nor does she now allow honorable vices to lay a hand upon him, but presents him for ridicule to the unclean buffoons from the king’s kitchen—that is, to foul and horrible vices. Thus, captured by enemies, he is bound with the cords of evil habit and cast into the prison of Despair.

3. But King David mourned with covered head, saying: “Absalom, my son! My son Absalom!” Calling one useful and proven for such matters from the royal household and court, namely Fear, he sends him to seek the man

[Col. 0766C] and orders Obedience to accompany him, so that Fear might entrust the rescued man from the prison to Obedience’s guardianship.

Sent forth, Fear comes and raises the wretch. Having rescued him from the prison’s locks and chains, he hands him over to Obedience as he had been commanded. He restores his horse to him, but it is fierce and rebellious and scarcely deigns any longer to acknowledge its master. Obedience seizes it and restrains it with an iron bridle, though it resists and kicks back greatly; she subjects it to its former master and teaches it to renew its strength.

4. Thus Obedience, taking in charge the soldier of Christ received from Fear, led him back to his own country by another road, and appointed his first lodging with Piety: so that Piety, like a father calling him back, might refresh his spirits, which Fear [Col. 0766D] had embittered. The second was with Knowledge, so that he might know whence and whither he must return; and might know how to use both Piety and Fear, lest Piety puff him up and Fear crush him. The third was with Fortitude, which might strengthen him to accomplish the journey of his return. The fourth was with Counsel, so that he might do everything with another’s counsel and in nothing turn aside from the guidance of obedience. The fifth was with Understanding, so that he might no longer rely only on the 1252 counsel of men, but might himself begin to understand what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of the Lord. The soldier of Christ came to the sixth lodging, that of Wisdom, his hosts accompanying him and not abandoning his journey, so that the good things of the Lord might now become sweet to him, and that thence, with Moses, as though from Mount Abarim, he might begin to contemplate [Col. 0767A] God’s promises (Deut. XXXII, 49). From there one comes at last to Jerusalem, to the kingdom and city of David, to the vision of peace: where the blessed peacemakers, children of God, having established peace in all things within and without, enter in and celebrate the joy of their Lord, the Sabbath of Sabbaths. Amen.

## PARABLE IV

> [Note: [Col. 0767] It is found among the Spurious Works in the older editions, as is the following.]

### On Christ and the Church

1. “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who was a king, who made a wedding for his son” (Matt. XXII, 2). When the wedding day drew near, the Father asked the Son whom he wished to marry. He replied that from eternity he had chosen and forechosen the Church. But the Father said: “She is held captive in Egypt, and there she serves in mud and brick” (Exod. I, 14), sold under sin. [Col. 0767B] “Pharaoh’s heart has been hardened against her, and his hand made heavy; nor will he release her except by a strong hand” (Exod. III). And the Son said: “I am your hand and the arm of your strength. I shall enter Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, and I shall set her free. And, so that I may stop the mouths of those who speak iniquity and redeem her from human accusations, I shall set in the balance, against the price for which she was sold under sin—that is, the will to sin—the price of my blood. She will be found to weigh less, and my judgment will attain victory.”

But the Father said: “Indeed it will attain it; yet the law of marriage requires the bride’s consent.” “It shall be sought,” he said. “I have found David my servant, a man according to my heart. I shall send him with a lyre, [Col. 0767C] that he may speak to her heart, summon her, and soothe her feelings, made accustomed and corrupt in Egypt’s mud.”

David, sent forth, enters Egypt; and, having prepared the most sweet wedding-song, he poured forth from his heart this good word: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house; and the king shall desire your beauty, because he is the Lord your God” (Ps. XLIV, 11–12).

Isaiah too is commanded immediately to follow. Seeing her in the chains of captivity, he says: “Awake, awake; put on the strength of the Lord’s arm. Lift yourself up, lift yourself up; arise, Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” (Isa. LI, 9; LII, 1–2).

2. When many other patriarchs and prophets had also entered, [Col. 0767D] all announcing the same things, at last she understood God’s grace; rising from the dust, she said: “You have remembered me, O Lord my God. You have mercy on whom you have mercy, and grant mercy to whom you will have shown mercy” (Exod. XXXIII, 19). Then, following the example of the wise Abigail, she said: “Who will make me the maidservant of my lord’s servants, that I may wash the feet of my lord’s servants?” (1 Sam. XXV, 41).

And at once, rising like Abigail herself, she mounted an ass—that is, subjected her flesh to herself—and followed the king’s servants. The bridegroom met her in festivity and gladness; taking her by the right hand, leading her according to his will, and receiving her with glory, [Col. 0768A] he introduced her into the city of his kingdom and into his mother’s chamber. Placing her on the bed of his charity, adorning her with the ornaments of his grace, putting his left hand beneath her head and embracing her with his right, he said: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not rouse or awaken my beloved until she herself wills it” (Song II, 6–7).

He placed sixty of Israel’s mightiest men around the bed, men most skilled in war, each with his sword upon his thigh because of terrors by night. Having kissed her with the kiss of his mouth (Song I, 1) and bidden her farewell, he went into a far country to receive a kingdom for himself and return. Through the prophet Hosea he commanded her: “For a long time you shall wait for me; and you shall have neither priest nor sacrifice” (Hos. III, 3–4).

[Col. 0768B] 3. Taking advantage of his absence, that Egyptian Pharaoh summoned his army and said: “Come, I shall pursue and overtake them; I shall divide the spoil; my soul shall be filled. 1253 I shall draw my sword; my hand shall kill them” (Exod. XV, 9). Rising with all the wickedness of his malice, he declared persecution against the Church. Immediately attacking her camps, he crucified Peter and his brother Andrew after seizing them; beheaded Paul; exiled John; flayed Bartholomew; stoned Stephen; burned Lawrence and Vincent; and filled all things with the deaths of saints and with kinds of deaths and tortures. “They gave the dead bodies of God’s servants as food to the birds of heaven, and the flesh of the saints to the beasts of the earth. They poured out [Col. 0768C] innocent blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them” (Ps. LXXVIII, 2–3).

Seeing her defenders made like sheep for slaughter, the Church groaned, and her bitterness became bitter. Yet the soil of the Church, enriched by the blood of martyrs, yielded crops of believers in manifold increase; and, returning a hundredfold or a thousandfold for the cutting down of one, she conquered through that by which she had been expected to be overcome.

4. When that barbarous wickedness of the enemy perceived this, it raged and, resorting to its familiar weapons of cunning, rested for a time from persecution, gathered its forces, recalled its sword, and changed its plan. “No enemy,” it said, “is worse than an enemy from within. Therefore I shall pour out contention upon their princes and make them wander in a trackless place, and not in the way [Col. 0768D] (Ps. CVI, 40). “And when they say, ‘Peace, peace,’ there shall be no peace” (Jer. VI, 14). “Rather, I shall stir up heresies and schisms among them, disturb everything by a kind of civil and internal war, and more easily cause them to perish by their own sword than by mine.”

It spoke, and at once that battle-line of the Church, hitherto terrible because ordered, became not terrible because disordered. For as they attacked one another with mutual wounds and struck each other down as enemies, while enemies stood far off and laughed, they occasioned laughter and derision to their enemies, but grief and unbearable pain to the Church. Her bitterness, bitter before, now became more bitter, as she lamented that her own entrails were being torn apart by a kind of viperous evil from her children.

But [Col. 0769A] immediately the outstanding soldiers of the Christian court, seeing the enemy’s crafty malice prevail, recovered their courage and seized the weapons of faith. Courageously removing the evil from among themselves, Alexander with many others slew Arius; Augustine, Manichaeus and many others; Jerome, the Epicurean Jovinian; and the rest, attacking the other plagues of heresies and schisms, either vigorously destroyed them or prudently drove them from the camp. Thus they restored peace and joy to the Church.

6. But alas, alas! Neither can the sea lack waves nor this life lack temptations; nor can peace be firm and solid except in its own country. For the sinner sees and angrily envies, gnashes his teeth and wastes away; and, preparing new wars, he turns to the spiritual weapons [Col. 0769B] of wickedness. Summoning the distinguished commanders of his army—the spirit of Fornication, the spirit of Gluttony, and the spirit of Avarice—he says: “You see that we achieve nothing, and now the whole world has gone after them. Yet those who boast that they have already escaped or eluded my arts must still experience our strength.”

He spoke, and sending them into the Church’s camp, finding all asleep and drunk by night—for “those who sleep sleep by night, and those who are drunk are drunk by night” (1 Thess. V, 7)—he immediately threw everything into confusion. For at once all became lovers of themselves, seeking what was their own rather than what was Jesus Christ’s. They claimed God’s sanctuary as their inheritance and defiled the tabernacle of his name (Ps. LXXIII, 7), serving there not God but their own wills and pleasures, and turning things offered or consecrated to God to their own uses.

For, making out of the names and offices of religion names and authorities for avarice, pride, and vanity, they stripped from the Church, despite her resistance and protest, that seamless garment of charity, woven from above throughout (John XIX, 23), and that purple mantle of faith dyed with precious blood, by which the Bridegroom had covered the bride’s nakedness, together with the other ornaments of religion. Having stripped her, yet not clothed themselves, they left naked her whom they ought to have guarded; and, driving her from her state of repose, compelled her, so far as lay in them, to flee from the world.

6. But she, crying, weeping, and exposed in her shame, [Col. 0769D] 1254 with her buttocks uncovered, lays bare before all, in lamentation, her hidden and shameful parts for their mockery. She prays to the children of her womb, and they do not pity her; she entreats, and is mocked. With both hands and all her strength, she draws tightly around her heart and those vital parts a few shreds of canonical or monastic religion, which had barely escaped the hands of the plunderers; she begs that at least these may be left to her, but she is not heard. For those who are hers attempt to plunder even these—not guardians, but thieves—so that, unable to bear her nakedness, she may flee from this world, or perish among them in the coldness of their malice.

Yet sometimes, pretending compassion, they try to sell her a garment woven on either side by the hand of Hypocrisy, from the pretence of Virtues and the concealment of Vices. Detesting and abhorring it, [Col. 0770A] she neither accepts nor recognizes it. She knows the one woven by Wisdom’s hands, dyed and consecrated by the blood of the Lamb, left to her by the Bridegroom and taken away by her children. She knows no other, but rejects and repels it. Therefore she is rejected, repelled, spat upon, and held in reproach by all.

7. These are our times, these are the perilous times of the Church, in which “in peace her bitterness became most bitter” (Isa. XXXVIII, 17). But three woes have passed; one woe still remains: namely, the angel of Satan, who will transform himself into an angel of light, sit in the temple of God, and show himself as though he were God. He already works the mysteries of iniquity (2 Thess. II, 3–10), while his forerunners assail the Church on every side, saying: “Behold, he is here,” and “behold, he is there” (Luke XVII, 23).

[Col. 0770B] But, O Bride of Christ, do not believe; do not go out. Rather, await your Bridegroom, who neither despises nor forgets you in tribulation, but in the fourth watch will come to you walking upon the sea (Matt. XIV, 25). And come, Lord; come to free her, O Lord God of hosts, who live and reign through all ages of ages. Amen.

## PARABLE V

### On Faith, Hope, and Charity

1. A noble and powerful king had three daughters: Faith, Hope, and Charity. To these he entrusted an excellent city, the human Soul. Since it has three citadels—Rationality, Desire, and Irascibility—he assigned one to each: the first to Faith, the second to Hope, the third to Charity.

[Col. 0770C] Faith is set over Rationality, because faith has no merit where human reason provides proof. Hope is set over Desire, because we are not permitted to desire what we see, but what we hope for; and hope that is seen is not hope. Charity is set over Irascibility: fervour over fervour, so that the fervour of virtue may rule the fervour of nature—indeed, so that natural fervour may raise itself into the fervour of virtue.

Having entered, each arranges and administers her own household according to her ability. Faith therefore appoints Prudence as keeper of her house in Rationality, so that she may preserve her right there and restrain reason beneath the laws of faith and within the limits laid down by faith. So that Prudence might act with confidence in the house, Faith added Obedience. So that Obedience might have perseverance in work and [Col. 0770D] endurance in labour, she placed Patience beneath her. So that she might also govern and administer properly the lower household of acts and senses, she supplied her with Administration itself. That all things might be done decently and in order, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. XIV, 40), she also added Order. Lest a curse enter the house—“every undisciplined house is cursed”—she set Discipline as gatekeeper.

2. In Desire, Hope placed Sobriety over her household, that Sobriety might preserve her right there and compel its ruling faculties always to serve her. So that Sobriety might be able to govern discreetly the lower household of wills and pleasures, Hope placed Discernment beneath her. Against the desire of the flesh, she added Continence; against the desire [Col. 0771A] of the eyes, Constancy; against worldly ambition, Humility. And lest poverty enter the house—for, as Solomon says, “where there are many words, there is much poverty” (Prov. XIV, 23)—she appointed Silence as keeper on the threshold.

3. But Charity entrusted her own house, situated toward the south and noon 1255, to her friend Piety; and gave all her right into Piety’s charge, placing under her service first Bodily Purity, then fitting exercises—namely, readings, meditations, prayers, and spiritual affections. And lest Misery, entering the house, disturb the Blessedness of God’s children, who, placed on the seventh step (Matt. V, 9), that is, in the perfection of blessedness, play and rejoice in Charity’s house, she appointed Peace herself as keeper [Col. 0771B] at the gate.

Their houses thus arranged, they appointed Free Will as a kind of governor and steward of the entire city.

4. When this had been done, the royal maidens returned to their father’s house. The enemy came upon the city; seeing and envying its order and glory, he devised treachery. Desiring to enter, he corrupted two of its chief citizens, Discernment and Administration, and brought in the whole army of his wickedness through the gates of Rationality and Desire.

Free Will, governor of the city, to whom had been entrusted the guardianship and direction of the whole city—for the householder, departing into a far country, had given his servants authority over each work—is bound with iron chains and [Col. 0771C] cast into prison. Once its guards have been hurled down from the citadel of Rationality, Blasphemy is immediately brought in against Faith. With it rush in contradictions, disturbances, confusions, and a whole crowd of such things; plundering everything for themselves and claiming whatever they pleased, they left nothing of reason in Rationality. Having slain the gatekeeper, Discipline, they gave everyone free access to enter and depart.

Moreover, once Mistress Luxury had entered the house of Hope—that is, Desire—and claimed everything for herself, she cast it down from its heights to the depths. She handed Continence over to be trampled and mocked by the desire of the flesh, Constancy by the desire of the eyes, and Humility by worldly Ambition. Having slain Silence, the gatekeeper, [Col. 0771D] she made the gate stand open to everyone entering and leaving. Sobriety and the virtues allied with sobriety she either killed, imprisoned, or sent into exile.

Then they ascend to the city’s highest citadel; and, after Peace, gatekeeper and guardian of supreme blessedness, has been slain, Misery enters. For immediately Mistress [Col. 0772A] Pride ascends the citadel—“the pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. LXXIII, 23)—and impiously drives Piety from it, condemning all the household of Piety and Peace to death or exile. Now whoever wishes enters God’s sanctuary; whatever is holy in it, whatever had until then been accessible and visible only to the sons of Levi, is now profaned, now plundered by enemies, and carried off to Babylon. The king of Babylon’s concubines drink from the temple vessels. Thus the entire city was taken and confounded; according to its glory, so its dishonour was made.

6. When all had been thrown into confusion, sad news of the ruined city reached the mistresses. Disturbed, they cast themselves at their Father’s feet, begging for help. As he reproached the negligence of Free Will, its guardian, [Col. 0772B] they said: “What, O Father, can Free Will do without assisting grace?” “I too,” he said, “shall give grace; but Fear must first be sent ahead. For he shall go before her to prepare her ways.”

Fear went forth from before the Lord and came to the city, carrying the rod of discipline in his hand. He found the gate of Difficulty barred and reinforced with the bolts of evil habit. At the gate stood the insolent and corrupt gatekeeper, the wantonness of the flesh, which was greatly hostile to Fear and wearied him with reproaches and insults. But making an assault in confidence, Fear broke the bolts of evil habit and tore down the gates of Difficulty. He seized that wretch and drove him with the rod of discipline which he held, even unto death. Immediately raising above the gates the sign of approaching [Col. 0772C] Grace, he turned the whole city to fear.

After him Grace enters the city, bringing with her that entire army of heavenly Virtues. At once the enemy party disappears, while the Virtues return to their accustomed strongholds. Discernment and Administration 1256 immediately come forward, accuse themselves of having been deceived, and beg forgiveness. Free Will comes forth from his chains and hastens to meet Lady Grace, at last hoping that under Grace’s rule he will be free.
