Dishes are prepared for the king’s daughters in their own house, and fitting tables are set. On Faith’s table is placed the bread of sorrow, the water of affliction, and the other dishes of penitence. On Hope’s table are strengthening bread, oil that makes the face glad, and the other dishes of consolation. On Charity’s table are the bread of life, wine that gives joy, and all the delights of paradise. Now they enter, feast, and guard the city. But “unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman keeps watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI, 1).

[Col. 0773]

## FORMULA OF PRIVATE CONFESSION

### Or a most devout prayer of a penitent to Christ, not improperly ascribed to Blessed Bernard

[Col. 0773A] 1. In union with your most bitter pain, you who assumed the cause of my pain and undertook amendment for my sins, Lord Jesus Christ, together with all who grieve, truly repent, and seek you in truth, I confess to you all my sins: the evils I have committed, the good things I have omitted, or have done neither purely nor diligently, as you know them better in number, weight, and measure; and the wasted days of my life, in which I offended you, diminished your praise, fell away from you, the supreme good, and drew my neighbour into ruin.

Receive, therefore, Lord, the remaining years of my wretched life. For those years which I lost by living badly, and in which I lived ruinously, do not despise, O God, a contrite and humbled heart. My days have declined and perished without fruit. It is impossible [Col. 0773B] for me to recall them; but may it please you that I should recall them in the bitterness of my soul. Lord, the deepest abyss of my misery calls upon the abyss of your most exalted mercy. Do not restrain your mercies in anger, and do not permit the inexhaustible fountain of your mercy to dry up around me because of my sins—you who have mercy on all and hate nothing that you have made, overlooking human sins for the sake of repentance.

It belongs to you, Lord, to forgive sins. Have mercy on me while it is the time of grace and mercy; and while it is the time of amendment, grant that I may merit the glory of blessing, lest on the day of consummation the word of curse strike me.

2. Make me, I beg you, Lord, leave behind the evils to which I am accustomed [Col. 0773C] and do what pleases you. Grant that, with your help, I may henceforth devote to your will the zeal which until now I exercised in sins, so that where transgression has abounded, your grace may abound still more.

I pray you, for your own sake, through the love of your most merciful mother, the glorious Virgin Mary, and through the intercession of all your saints and elect: forgive all my sins, negligences, and ignorances; do not destroy me together with all my iniquities, nor reserve my evils unto the end in anger. Remember, Lord Jesus, that it is not yours to destroy anything that your Father has given you; rather, [Col. 0774A] it is proper to you always to have mercy and spare, to destroy no one but to save. For your Father sent you into the world not to judge the world, but that we might have life through you; that you might be our propitiation and our advocate, not against us. For what we owed, you paid; what we sinned, you atoned for; what we neglected, you supplied.

3. Therefore let your complete—indeed, superabundant—satisfaction now avail me, Lord, even at my end: your most bitter death, the inestimable price of your shed blood, the remembrance of your satisfaction, and the venerable mystery of your body and blood, which is daily offered to you in the Church for the salvation of your faithful servants. In it you yourself are both priest and sacrifice: he who offers and he to whom the offering is made, and the very thing [Col. 0774B] which is offered. Let it avail for obtaining in the present the grace which I do not deserve, and in the future the rest and glory which your most bitter death obtained.

Your eyes saw my imperfection; yet you, merciful, compassionate, and more beneficent than malice, I beg you, do not impute it to me for eternal punishment—you who have most excellently, perfectly, and wisely preordained all things to the highest and perfect good. Do not allow me to be blotted out from the book of life; rather, grant me the portion that falls to me, namely the aid of your precious Passion, for which you willed humankind to be your co-heir in the land of the living.

4. [Col. 0774C] Therefore may consideration of human frailty move and incline you, Lord, to mercy—you who know what human substance is, and that you did not establish humanity vainly upon the earth. Preserve me, the work of your loving-kindness, lest you have laboured over it in vain and the shedding of your spotless blood prove fruitless in me. You who effect the purification of sinners, grant that, once the filth of sins has been cleansed away through you and my mind’s countenance illumined, I may know you; and, knowing you, may continually strive straight toward you, so that at last, with a happy end, I may merit to come to you, Jesus Christ, my God and my Lord, who live with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

[Col. 0775]

## OFFICE FOR SAINT VICTOR THE CONFESSOR

Composed by Saint Bernard at the request of Guy, abbot of Arremar.

> [Note: [Col. 0775D] See above, p. 715, letter 398; and p. 2078, the two sermons on St Victor.]

### AT FIRST VESPERS

[Col. 0775A]

### ANTIPHONS ON THE PSALMS

Victorious soul, you who, like a sparrow in flight, escaped the snares of hunters: grant that through your protection we may be delivered from them.

O veteran soldier, who after the contest received the rest due to you, look upon us, who amid hostile swords are occupied with your praises.

O Jesus, victor, whom we know to have won victory in our Victor: grant him so to glory in you on his own behalf that forgetfulness of us may not come upon him.

### CHAPTER

Saint Victor, beloved by God and humankind, whose memory is in blessing, was made like the saints in glory.

[Col. 0775B] **R.** (long responsory). O truly Victor, who from the moment you lived were victorious, from the womb to the tomb, continually meriting triumphs. Grant that, as we are inspired by your victories, we may also be fortified with weapons.

**V.** That we may be able to withstand in the evil day and stand perfect in all things. Grant to us, etc.

### HYMN

Victor’s life, illustrious in merits,  
Presents a man to the earth, one not of earth,  
As though given from heaven  
For imitation.

Christ lived in him, and not he himself;  
A mirror of life to those dead to the world,  
He offered himself as a heavenly man,  
Seeking those like himself.

[Col. 0775C] Professing, moreover, something holier,  
Victor became a pattern of sanctity,  
Keeping whole and uncorrupted  
The honour of uprightness.

Therefore he saw visions of God,  
And saw the heavens opened to him.  
For the heavenly vision seeks  
Chaste eyes.

Glory to God, the supreme Trinity;  
Glory, threefold yet one, of the Persons;  
The whole Godhead of each of the three is undivided,  
For the Three are One.

**Antiphon at the Magnificat.** Great is the might of your Lord, Victor, nor is his mercy less; and would that through you [Col. 0775D] he might be as merciful to us for salvation as he proved magnificent to you for virtue! Magnify, Victor, the Lord who did great things for you, making you great, that you might [Col. 0776A] do wonders in which you might become wonderful; he gave you to contend, that he might grant you to conquer and crown you as Victor.

**Collect.** Hear, Lord, we beseech you, the prayers of those who entreat you; and grant that we, whom you have made to glory in the bodily presence of your blessed confessor Victor, may everywhere be protected by his gracious intercession. Through the Lord Jesus, etc.

1258 ### AT MATINS

**Invitatory.** Take courage: Victor has conquered the world. Let us rejoice in his victory, that we too may conquer.

### HYMN

Rightly did a man in a weighty body  
Hear the sweet voices of angels,  
Slaying fleshly pleasures, while living  
[Col. 0776B] An angel in the flesh.

So it was fitting that the vessel already marked out  
For honour should remain holier,  
Whose sanctity was consecrated  
In its mother’s womb.

Finally, seeing the mother pregnant,  
They could not endure it, but fled in fear;  
They reveal his name and confess him holy,  
Though enclosed in the womb.

Nor did a secure life begrudge this tender child  
Glory so early;  
Rather, it increased it  
With abundant interest.

Glory to the supreme Trinity, etc.

[Col. 0776C]

### IN THE FIRST NOCTURN: ANTIPHONS

Blessed is the man who loved the law and did not seek a chair.

He served the Lord in fear, and now exults in him without trembling.

Lord, he walked in the light of your countenance, and now your sign has been set upon him.

Your words, Lord, Victor received with ears and heart, and through them he conquered.

Perfect praise was in Victor’s mouth, because perpetual peace was in his heart.

In vain did those who shoot in darkness at the upright in heart lay snares for one confident in the Lord.

### LESSON I

The life and glory of Victor, etc. See above among the Sermons [Col. 0776D] on the Saints, col. 371.

**R.** O man of outstanding holiness, who was holy before he was born, and Victor in deed before he was Victor in name, [Col. 0777A] so that, enclosed in the womb, he already triumphed over the enemy.

**V.** Lord, you went before him with blessings of sweetness. So that, etc.

### LESSON II

Let us have, most beloved, in the life of Victor, etc. See above in the place cited.

**R.** O delightful and unprecedented miracle! A roaring lion flees from the face of a little child who has not yet begun to cry.

**V.** As wax melts before fire, so may sinners perish before the face, etc.

### LESSON III

Let us feast, most beloved, called to the table of the rich man, etc. See above, col. 372.

**R.** O happy mother, whose womb felt a new thing [Col. 0777B] unknown to any mother since the days of John the Baptist.

**V.** None like him has been found since the days, etc.

### LESSON IV

Therefore, if I consider carefully, most reverend brethren, etc. See above, col. 373.

**R.** O good Jesus, yours is the power, yours the victory, that one little lamb drove out a multitude of wolves.

**V.** Before the child knew how to call father or mother, the wolves, etc.

### IN THE SECOND NOCTURN: ANTIPHONS

The wicked one was reduced to nothing in his sight, that Victor might preserve the truth of his name.

Lord, Victor shall rejoice in your strength, knowing that he won the victory not by his own strength.

He did not receive his soul in vain, who ruled his life by reason, and therefore ascended the mountain of the Lord.

You delivered, Lord, the soul of the saint from fear of the enemy; once victory was accomplished, no combat remains for him.

A hymn befits you, praise befits you, whose work it was that Victor, freed from flesh, should free the chained human being.

It is good to confess to the Lord, to whom the merits of saints belong as gifts; to whom Saint Victor confesses that he owes both his sanctity and his victory.

1259 ### LESSON V

Rejoice in the Lord, most beloved, who, etc. See above, col. 373.

[Col. 0777D] **R.** When the king of the Franks was passing by and came near where the hermit dwelt, he wondered at the things said about this man.

**V.** How great are the things we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us, concerning these things, etc.

### LESSON VI

The veteran soldier rests, and after his labours, etc. See above, col. 374.

**R.** Rumour, a telltale, had already disclosed the hidden treasure; it could not pass by the passing king, but he turned aside to the poor man’s hut, stirred by the report of his sanctity.

**V.** That he might see the works of the Lord and his wonders in the wilderness, stirred up, etc.

[Col. 0778A]

### LESSON VII

Brethren, the breadth of heaven enlarges hearts; it does not narrow them, etc. See above, col. 375.

**R.** When the king entered the poor man’s cell, the host was troubled because he had no wine. Blessing water drawn from a nearby spring, he changed it into wine. And the king drank, and those with him.

**V.** All were filled with wonder and ecstasy at what had happened to them. And he drank, etc.

### LESSON VIII

Small for battle, great for victory, etc. See above, col. 375.

**R.** A new kind of power! The water-jars grow red; at the command to pour forth wine, the water changed its origin.

**V.** The right hand of the Lord has shown power. Wine, etc.

[Col. 0778B]

### IN THE THIRD NOCTURN: ANTIPHONS

How gracious, how sweet, how pleasant, O Victor, in this place of affliction and in this body of death, to sing to you, honour you, and pray to you!

**R.** A certain man, not fearing to act maliciously against the saint, stole his wheat and hid it in the earth; and behold, the wretch is delivered to an evil spirit.

**V.** Cursed is the man who hides grain among the people. He is delivered, etc.

**R.** A sad miracle, but full of justice: that a man should endure the demon as both instigator and avenger of his crime.

**V.** You are just, Lord, and your judgment is right. That the one whom, etc.

**R.** The mysteries of iniquity are revealed: the demon compels the man, the man betrays the demon. Victor, standing between them, judges between them. As he drives out the demon and heals the man, he recovers the wheat through the very disclosure of the malice.

[Col. 0778C] **V.** He was present with him in the deceit of those who defrauded him, and made him honourable. As he drives out the demon, etc.

**R.** Looking up, Victor saw the heavens opened and a golden cross adorned with gems; and a voice said to him: “The gems are souls that attained the glory of the cross whose shame they bore.”

**V.** Let Israel rejoice in him who made him, and let the daughters of Zion exult in their king. Whose, etc.

### AT LAUDS: ANTIPHONS

Victor, dwelling on earth in body and in heaven in mind, sometimes heard angelic voices announcing something, sometimes pleasing angelic voices with the ineffable sweetness of song.

Now that he has entered the heavens, which he had formerly contemplated with open eyes, he now truly beholds the glory of God with unveiled face.

Blessed vision! By it, Victor, you are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.

Truly your soul, Victor, is one of the gems which appeared to you [Col. 0778D] on the 1260 cross; truly fixed to the cross and joined to divine glory, it puts on for itself the same image of brightness which it found.

Almighty Father, we have sinned against you and become children of strangers; yet we draw near in our Victor, who, having conquered his own desire, may conquer your wrath also and mightily restore us in grace.

[Col. 0779A] **R.** Daughters of Jerusalem, a holy soul departs. Go out to meet her.

**V.** She comes, coming with exultation. Go out, etc.

### HYMN

Wines flow from a spring, not from the vine;  
Coloured new wine runs in place of streams,  
By the hand of one who blesses  
Well used instead of a winepress.

A new flavour suddenly entering  
Compelled the waters to new uses;  
The king marvelled, where he had not expected  
A royal drink.

A man tortured by a demon reveals himself;  
[Col. 0779B] The wretch confesses his thefts, even unwillingly.  
The tormentor is expelled when the thief is discovered,  
Though himself also tortured.

These things sufficiently prove, along with many others,  
The prerogative of Victor’s glory,  
Not diminished because he was anticipated  
By the Holy Spirit.

Glory to the supreme Trinity, etc.

**Antiphon at the Benedictus.** Blessed is the generation for whom a light has arisen in darkness. Victor, give light to those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death.

**Another.** Blessed is the Lord God of Victor, who, setting him in the midst, raised up for us a horn of salvation, and, taking him again from our midst, placed him among princes, so that he may have one from among humankind to whom he may forgive human sins.

[Col. 0779C] **V.** This is the day of his great solemnity; this is the day of his people’s joy.  
**R.** Let us exult and rejoice in it.

### AT PRIME: ANTIPHON

Today, after laying aside the body, by which alone he seemed hindered [Col. 0780A] from entering into glory, Victor—rich in merits, renowned for signs—freely entered the holy places, made like the saints in glory.

### AT TERCE

Your name and remembrance, Victor, are a dripping honeycomb upon the lips of captives. Come then, mighty athlete, sweet patron, faithful advocate: rise to help us, that you may glory in complete victory.

### AT SEXT

He who gave his Spirit to the one contending opened his bosom to the conqueror. There, there, inspire him—you who are everywhere, O God—to think of the wretched; receive him, O God, as he pleads for the wretched; hear him, O God, as he intercedes for the wretched.

[Col. 0780B]

### AT NONE
Absorbed is Victor into the glory of the Son of God: cause him always to remember us, and to undertake and plead our cause at your dreadful judgment.

## AT SECOND VESPERS

Holy Victor, who can worthily set forth your praises—the glory of chastity, the strength of spirit, the purity of conscience?

Holy Victor, who will grant us that, together with the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness, the pattern of the uprightness of your life may dwell within us?

Holy Victor, send us help from the sanctuary, and from Zion defend us, who praise you from the earth.

Holy Victor, the more salutary your holiness and your victory are found to be for us, the more glorious they are for you.

[Col. 0780C] V. Behold, glorious Victor draws near; quickly bring forth the crown.

R. Now he enters into the joy of his Lord.

# THE FOURTH VOLUME OF THE WORKS OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, COMPRISING EIGHTY-SIX SERMONS ON THE SONG OF SONGS

(Collated with the manuscripts of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Jumièges, the Cistercians, Saint-Victor of Paris, the Celestines of Paris, Saint-Theodoric of Reims, Saint-Evroul, etc.)

[Col. 0779]

# PREFACE TO THE FOURTH VOLUME

1261–1263 I. Although all the works of Saint Bernard are filled with the rich substance of sound piety and doctrine, two above all ought to be held in esteem by everyone: namely, the books *On Consideration* and the sermons on the *Song of Songs*. For in those books is comprehended, in an elegant compendium, whatever is most holy in the sacred Scriptures and councils, and whatever is most salutary for the governance of the Church as prescribed in the writings of the ancient Fathers and in papal decrees. In these sermons, however, whatever is scattered throughout the other works of the holy doctor for the shaping of character and the kindling of piety—whatever concerns vices and virtues and the whole spiritual life—is treated more solidly and loftily; and from the coverings and figures of mystical allegories the secrets of all perfection are drawn forth, in a manner no less delightful and useful than elevated. Thus these sermons should be regarded as a kind of chaste delight for devout persons.

We call this manner of writing delightful and useful. For this is, in Bernard’s own testimony, “the altogether wonderful and pitiable condition of human souls: although they apprehend so many things outwardly through the liveliness of their intelligence, they nevertheless have complete need of certain figures and enigmas drawn from bodily likenesses, so that from visible and external things they may at least in some measure infer invisible and inward things.” [Note: [Col. 0781] Sermon 6 *On Various Subjects*, no. 1.] This is indeed accomplished most excellently in these sermons.

II. Bernard undertook this remarkable work in 1135, after his return from Aquitaine, as is evident from Book II, chapter 6, of his *Life*:

> “When the man of God had obtained some time of quiet, he occupied himself with other tasks; withdrawing into a little cell, interwoven with braided rushes, he resolved there alone to devote himself to divine meditations. And suddenly, while he stood in a humble lodging, as though beside the Lord’s manger, the Songs of Love and the dishes of spiritual nuptials met him. For a long time he poured out his soul in meditation upon these matters; and, as he expounded them in many ways, how much progress he himself made, who daily feasted upon those delights, and how much benefit he conferred upon us, for whom he preserved in writing the remnants of that same blessing, is clear to those who read it.”

Thus Geoffrey; who again, in chapter 8 of Book III, says: “In the sermons on the *Song of Songs*, he reveals himself both as an investigator of mysteries and as a magnificent builder of morals.” We understand that the work was begun during Advent of that same year, 1135, from the opening of the second sermon: “For behold how many will rejoice in this Nativity of his, which is soon to be celebrated,” etc.

III. It is established from Bernard’s Letter 153 to Bernard de Portes the Carthusian that he was, if not the author of this undertaking, at least its encourager. In that letter the holy man, when the latter earnestly requested an exposition of the *Song of Songs*, or some spiritual work, pleaded his own inadequacy; but at length he yielded to his insistence—whether this is to be understood of undertaking the work, or of publishing and sending the work already begun. The latter interpretation is preferable, especially because Geoffrey, in the passages just cited, does not say that Bernard de Portes intervened as the authority prompting Bernard to undertake this work; indeed, he sufficiently indicates that the holy man of his own accord applied his mind to this meditation.

The words of Letter 153 favor this view:

> “I yield to your importunity, that the offering may at least remove suspicion. It is a matter with a friend. I now spare no embarrassment: indeed, provided your wish is done, I shall not remember my folly. Behold, I am having copied for you a few sermons, recently dictated, on the beginning of Solomon’s *Song of Songs*, and, although I have not yet published them, I send them to you as quickly as possible. In this work, when I have gained time, Christ commanding my cares, I shall attempt to proceed.”

From these words one can infer only that Bernard of Portes had requested some spiritual work from our Bernard and that the first sermons on the *Song of Songs* were sent to him. I do not know whether the passage in Sermon 1, no. 3, ought to be explained with reference to this Bernard:

> “But I think that he who came to us from the road as a friend will no longer have anything with which to complain against us, when he has consumed this third loaf also.”

[Note: [Col. 0781] He alludes to Luke 11:5: “Friend, lend me three loaves.” Whether some commentary on these two books is indicated by these words is considered in the Preface to this volume.]

I leave this for others to judge. Finally, the earlier sermons were sent to Bernard of Portes with Letter 154, in which we read:

> “The sermons on the beginnings of the *Song of Songs*, which you requested and I had promised, I send to you. Having read them, I ask that, as soon as you conveniently can, you advise me by your reply whether I ought to proceed or to desist.”

This too may be understood of the actual transcription and sending of the work.

IV. Although Bernard delivered these sermons to his brethren at Clairvaux on almost uninterrupted days, he was unable to complete the work he had begun during the eighteen years that he survived, being repeatedly interrupted by various affairs of Church and kingdom, and even by the troublesome frequency of visitors, of which he complains more than once, as at the end of the third sermon:

> “But behold, the evil of the day calls us away. For those whose arrival has just been announced oblige us rather to break off than to finish the pleasant discourse. I shall go out to the guests, lest anything be lacking in the offices of that charity of which we are speaking.”

And in Sermon 52, no. 7: “A sufficiently rare hour of leisure from arrivals is granted me.”

It is indeed remarkable that the holy Father, distracted by the cares of a large household and pressing affairs, was equal to meditating on discourses of such profound wisdom and delivering them day after day. He himself attests this in Sermon 22, no. 2: “It is certainly a task and labor involving no small weariness, namely, to go forth daily and draw even from the plain streams of the Scriptures,” etc. For he delivered these sermons on days of leisure, and indeed almost continuously, as is clear from Sermon 83, where he says that for three successive days he had applied himself to explaining one passage. Moreover, he delivered these sermons orally. Thus, at the end of Sermon 42, he says: “My infirmity, as you know, does not permit me to proceed further.” And at the end of Sermon 44: “And enough on this matter. For my infirmity bids me rest, as it often does.”

V. The holy man certainly joined prayer to his meditation while arranging the matter of his sermons; but he sometimes drew them forth from the abundance and fullness of his mind before they had been written, as various passages prove. For many things in these sermons are said extemporaneously. For example, when in Sermon 36 he rebukes those who are sleepy, he says:

> “I thought to fulfill in one sermon what I promised concerning the twofold ignorance; and I would have done so, had it not seemed too long to the fastidious. For I see some yawning and some even sleeping. Nor is this surprising: the vigils of the preceding night—for they were very long—excuse them.”

But nothing proves those extemporaneous remarks so much as the passage from Sermon 9, no. 6: “Another meaning occurs to me, which I had not proposed, but I shall by no means pass over it.”

Furthermore, the holy man indicates that the sermons, after being delivered, were transcribed by disciples. “They have been written as they were spoken,” he says in Sermon 54, no. 1, “and, except for the style, like the other sermons, so that what may perhaps have escaped may easily be recovered.” To this belongs what is read in Sermon 77, no. 2: “But if perhaps the things we say are committed to writing, they will disdain to read them.”

VI. Bernard commonly delivered these sermons “in the assembly” of the brethren, and with novices present, according to Sermon 63, no. 6, but not lay brothers, who did not attend meetings of this kind. Hence he often suggests that his hearers were skilled in the sacred Scriptures; in Sermons 15, no. 2; 16, no. 1; and 39, no. 2, he testifies that they outstripped his words in intelligence.

Moreover, the hour at which these sermons were delivered was sometimes in the morning, before Mass—as has been said concerning other sermons in the preface to the preceding volume—and sometimes in the evening. Interpret as morning references the two passages in which he dismisses the discourse because of manual labor and the divine office. Thus, at the end of Sermon 1, he says: “But the hour passes, which urges us to go out to the work of our hands, both poverty and the rule of our order.” Still more explicit for this purpose is the passage in Sermon 47, which he interrupted because the hour of the divine office was at hand. Clear evidence for an evening time occurs in Sermon 71, no. 15: “For now, as I have discoursed at length, the day has declined.” But enough of such minutiae, though they are not ill-suited to this place.

VII. Bernard had completed altogether twenty-four sermons by 1137, the year in which he went to Italy to settle the schism. Returning thence in the following year, he again took up the interrupted work, repeating Sermon 34 with a different beginning and a different conclusion; from this arose the diversity of readings which we shall discuss in its place.

The holy man composed the sixty-fifth sermon and the following one, which begin with the exposition of the verse, “Catch for us the little foxes,” against the heretics of Cologne, on the occasion of a letter written to him by Everwin, provost of Steinfeld. For that reason it seemed appropriate to prefix that letter to those two sermons. Finally, the eightieth sermon was delivered after the Council of Reims in 1148, held in the presence of Eugenius, at which the error of Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, was condemned, as Bernard himself recalls in that sermon.

VIII. Most manuscripts contain eighty-six sermons; a few, eighty-seven—either because Sermon 24 is repeated, as in the Colbert manuscript, or because another sermon is divided, as in our Saint-Germain manuscript. Of five Vatican manuscripts examined at my request by our Jean Durand, one contains altogether eighty-six sermons; but another, marked no. 665, contains a preface found neither in printed editions nor in any manuscripts. Its opening runs thus:

> “Here begins the preface of blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, on the *Song of Songs*. God has set before virtue its supreme incentive, the delight of future blessedness; likewise, the devil devised delight as a vehement spur to error. Adam, the first man, placed by the Lord God in the paradise of delight in order that he might enjoy eternal happiness, gives evidence for both statements, as an inducement to virtue for future ages.”

It then adds that, through sin, innocence and consequently delight were lost, but that this delight is restored by the sweetness and harmony of psalms and songs. Nothing in that preface approaches Bernard’s style or genius.

Only eighty-three sermons are placed beneath the preface, under this title: “Here begins the exposition of blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, on the *Song of Songs*.” Another manuscript reads: “Here begins Bernard on the *Song of Songs*.” Others: “Here begins the treatise of blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, on the *Song of Songs*.” In one Colbert manuscript they are called *Treatises*, not *Sermons*, in accordance with ancient usage. But these are minor matters.

This exposition ends at chapter 3 of the *Song*, at the verse, “On my bed I sought by night”; from there Gilbert of Hoyland, likewise an Irish Cistercian, continued it as far as the verse in chapter 5, “My beloved is white and ruddy,” publishing forty-eight sermons. He was indeed a man not much inferior to Bernard in gravity and piety of speech. But death took him from human affairs while he was attempting to proceed further in exposition, as though indignant with him—if we believe Sixtus of Siena—for daring to continue again and bring to an end Bernard’s work, left unfinished by Bernard himself. Sixtus is mistaken in saying that Bernard’s work was begun “in the final year of his life.” We shall present Gilbert’s sermons in the following volume.

IX. Besides this exposition, Bernard dictated another, briefer one to William, abbot of Saint-Theodoric, as William himself testifies in Book I, chapter 12, of Bernard’s *Life*. But a more fitting place to speak of this will be in Volume V, where we shall reproduce a concise commentary from Bernard on the first two chapters of the *Song*.

X. In the first sermon of the fuller exposition Bernard seems to suggest that he had published commentaries on Solomon’s *Proverbs* and on *Ecclesiastes*. For thus he says in no. 2:

> “For from the words of Ecclesiastes you have, I think, by God’s grace been sufficiently instructed to know and despise the vanity of this world. And what of the Proverbs? Have not your life and character been sufficiently corrected and shaped according to the teaching found in them? Therefore, having first tasted those two loaves—which nevertheless you received as a loan from a friend’s storehouse—come also to this third loaf, that perhaps you may taste things more excellent.”

But these words seem to mean only that the monks of Clairvaux had devoted themselves to reading *Proverbs* and *Ecclesiastes*, and had conformed their conduct to their precepts. Certainly Geoffrey, who compiled a rather careful catalogue of Bernard’s works, and no ancient writer known to me, attributes commentaries of this kind to Bernard. Or perhaps by the name “friend” he means some other author of that time, such as Hugh of Saint-Victor, who composed nineteen homilies on *Ecclesiastes*.

XI. I return to the sermons on the *Song*, and the opinion held of them by Guerric, abbot of Igny, himself a most devout disciple of the holy doctor, is revealed in Sermon 3 for Saints Peter and Paul, which appears with others in Volume VI:

> “Our master, that interpreter of the Holy Spirit, undertook to speak of that whole nuptial song, and gave us hope from what he has already published that, if he comes to the passage about which you inquire—‘until the day breathes and the shadows decline’—he will bring the shadows themselves into the light of understanding; what was said, or will be said, in darkness, he will tell us in the light.”

Thus Guerric.

[Col. 0785]

# SERMONS OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, ON THE SONG OF SONGS

[Note: [Col. 0785C] begun in the year 1135.]

1266–1267

# SERMON I

## On the very title of the book: “The Song of Songs of Solomon”

[Col. 0785A]

1. Brothers, something different must be said to you from what is said to people in the world—or at least it must be said differently. For he who follows the Apostle’s pattern in teaching gives them milk to drink, not solid food (1 Cor. 3:2). But that more substantial fare ought to be set before spiritual persons, the Apostle likewise teaches by his own example: “We speak,” he says, “not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual”; and again: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2:13, 6). Such, surely, I trust you to be—unless perhaps you have long been occupied in vain with heavenly studies, your faculties exercised, and meditating day and night upon the law of God. Therefore prepare your throats, not for milk, but for bread. Solomon has bread, and it is exceedingly splendid and savory: I mean the book entitled the *Song of Songs*. Let it be brought forth, if you please, and broken.

2. For from the words of Ecclesiastes you have, I think, by God’s grace been sufficiently instructed to know and despise the vanity of this world. And what of the Proverbs? Have not your life and conduct been sufficiently corrected and shaped according to the teaching found in them? Therefore, having first tasted those two loaves, which nevertheless you received as a loan from a friend’s storehouse, come also to this third loaf, that perhaps you may taste things more excellent. [Note: [Col. 0785C] begun in the year 1135.]

For since there are two evils which either alone, or especially, wage war against the soul—namely, vain love of the world and excessive self-love—those two books are known to oppose these two plagues. One, with the hoe of discipline, cuts away everything distorted in moral conduct and the excesses of the flesh; the other, by the light of reason, shrewdly detects the counterfeit of vanity in all worldly glory and truthfully distinguishes it from the solidity of truth. Finally, it preferred fearing God and keeping his commandments to all human pursuits and worldly desires. And rightly so. For of true wisdom the former is the beginning and the latter the completion—provided you agree that true and perfected wisdom is nothing other than to turn away from evil and do good; and likewise that no one can perfectly turn away from evil without the fear of God, nor can any good work exist apart from keeping the commandments.

3. Therefore, once the two evils have been driven away by reading the two books, one approaches fittingly this sacred and contemplative discourse. Since it is the fruit of both books, it ought wholly to be entrusted only to sober minds and ears. Otherwise, before the flesh has been tamed by the pursuits of discipline and made subject to the spirit, before the pomp and burden of the world have been despised and cast aside, holy reading is unworthily undertaken by the impure. For as light is spread in vain around blind or closed eyes, so “the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (ibid., v. 14). Indeed, “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wis. 1:5), that is, an unrestrained life; nor will he ever have any part in the world’s vanity, since he is the Spirit of truth (John 14:17). For what fellowship is there between the wisdom which is from above and the wisdom of the world, which is “folly with God” (1 Cor. 3:19), or the wisdom of the flesh, which is itself hostile to God? (Rom. 8:7). But I think that he who came to us from the road as a friend will now no longer have anything with which to complain against us, when he has consumed this third loaf also.

4. But who will break it? The master of the house is present; recognize the Lord in the breaking of bread. For who else is fit for this? Certainly I shall not rashly claim this office for myself. Look to me in such a way that you do not expect it from me. For I too am one of those who wait, myself begging with you for the food of my soul, the nourishment of the spirit. Truly poor and needy, I knock at him who opens and no one shuts, concerning the most profound mystery of this discourse. “The eyes of all look to you in hope, O Lord.” The little children have asked for bread, and there is no one to break it for them; this is hoped for from your kindness. O most merciful one, break your bread for the hungry—by my hands, if you deign, but by your strength.

5. Tell us, I pray, by whom, concerning whom, or to whom is it said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1)? Or what kind of opening is this, so abrupt and suddenly produced from the middle of a discourse? For it bursts into these words as though it had first introduced someone speaking, and then brought in, as responding in due sequence, this person—whoever she may be—that asks for the kiss. Further, if she either asks or commands that she be kissed by someone unknown, why does she specify and name the mouth, and his own mouth, as though those kissing were accustomed to offer themselves some instrument other than a mouth, or an alien mouth rather than their own?

Yet she does not even say, “Let him kiss me with his mouth,” but something still more unusual: “With the kiss,” she says, “of his mouth.” This is indeed delightful speech, beginning with a kiss; and the charming face, as it were, of Scripture easily moves and draws one to read, so that what lies hidden in it is pleasing to investigate even with labor, and the possible difficulty of inquiry does not weary one where the sweetness of the language charms. But whom would not such a beginning without a beginning, and such novelty of expression in an ancient book, make deeply attentive? Hence it is clear that this work was so composed not by human ingenuity but by the art of the Spirit that, though difficult to understand, it is nevertheless delightful to investigate.

6. But what? Shall we pass over the title? We ought not omit even one iota (Matt. 5:18), when we are commanded to gather even the small fragments lest they perish (John 6:12). The title is this: “Here begin the Songs of Songs of Solomon.” First observe that the name of the Peaceful One—that is, Solomon—suits the beginning of the book, which begins with the sign of peace, namely a kiss. At the same time observe that, by such beginnings, only peaceful minds are invited to understand this Scripture: minds already able to free themselves from the disturbances of vices and the tumults of cares.

7. Then do not suppose it without significance that the inscription reads not simply “Songs,” but “Songs of Songs.” I have read many songs in Scripture, and I remember none of them to have been called in this manner. Israel sang a song to the Lord because it had at once escaped Pharaoh’s sword and yoke, wonderfully freed and avenged by the twofold service of the sea. Yet what it sang was not called the *Song of Songs*; rather, if I remember correctly, Scripture says: “Israel sang this song to the Lord” (Exod. 15:1). Deborah also sang (Judg. 5:1), Judith sang also (Judith 16:1), and Samuel’s mother sang also (1 Sam. 2:1). Certain prophets too sang, and none of them is read to have called his song the *Song of Songs*.

Certainly, as I think, you will find that they all sang because they themselves, or their own people, had received some benefit: for example, to obtain victory, to escape danger, or to attain some desired favor. Thus most sang, each for a particular reason, lest they should be found ungrateful for divine benefits, according to the saying: “He will praise you when you have done him good” (Ps. 48:19). But this king Solomon, singular in wisdom, exalted in glory, abounding in wealth, secure in peace, is known to have needed none of these things for receiving which he might have wished to sing such a song. Nor does Scripture itself anywhere seem to indicate anything of the sort concerning him.

8. Therefore, divinely inspired, he sang the praises of Christ and the Church, the grace of sacred love, and the mysteries of the eternal marriage. At the same time he expressed the longing of the holy soul and, rejoicing in the Spirit, composed in joyful praise a bridal song—yet figuratively. Indeed, like Moses, he too veiled his face (Exod. 3:6), perhaps shining no less brightly in this respect, because at that time there was no one, or scarcely anyone, able with unveiled face to behold that glory. Therefore, because of its excellence, I think this nuptial song was marked with such a title [variant: *marked beforehand*] that it might deservedly and uniquely be called the *Song of Songs*, just as he to whom it is sung has uniquely been called “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Tim. 6:15).

9. But you, if you attend to your own experience—did you not also sing to the Lord a new song in the victory by which your faith conquered the world, and in your departure from the pit of misery and the mire of filth, because he has done wonderful things?

[Note: [Col. 0787] The Cistercian manuscript adds, “what songs we ought to sing at each stage of progress”; this seems to be a lemma.]

Again, when he went on to set your feet upon a rock and direct your steps, I think that then too, because of the granted newness of life, a new song, a hymn to our God, was put into your mouth. And when, as you repented, he not only forgave your sins but also promised rewards besides, did you not much more, rejoicing in hope of future blessings, sing in the ways of the Lord, because great is the glory of the Lord?

But if something closed or obscure in the Scriptures has at times dawned upon any of you, then surely it is necessary that, because you have received the nourishment of heavenly bread, the sound of one feasting may delight the divine ears in a voice of exultation and thanksgiving. Further, amid the daily exercises and battles—never absent for a single hour from those who live devoutly in Christ—against the flesh, the world, and the devil, as you continually experience in yourselves that “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7:1), daily songs must necessarily be renewed for victories achieved. Whenever temptation is overcome, a vice subdued, an impending danger avoided, a snare of the enemy detected, any long-standing and inveterate passion of the soul healed once and perfectly, or a virtue greatly and long desired, often requested, is at length obtained through God’s gift—what follows except that thanksgiving and the voice of praise resound as often as this, according to the prophet (Isa. 51:3), and that in each individual benefit God is blessed in his gifts? Otherwise, at the time of judgment, one will be judged ungrateful if one cannot say to God: “Your statutes were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118:54).

10. I think that in yourselves you now recognize those songs which in the Psalter are called not the *Song of Songs* but the *Songs of Ascents*, because at each stage of your progress, according to the ascents that each has set in his heart, particular songs are to be drawn forth to the praise and glory of the One who advances him. Otherwise I do not see how that verse can be fulfilled: “The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous” (Ps. 117:15); or certainly that most beautiful and salutary exhortation of the Apostle: “Singing and making melody to the Lord in your hearts with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs” (Eph. 5:19).

11. But there is a song which, by its singular dignity and sweetness, deservedly excels all those we have mentioned, and any others there may be. I would rightly call this the *Song of Songs*, because it is itself the fruit of all the rest. Only anointing teaches a song of this kind; only experience learns it. Let those who have experienced it recognize it; let those who have not burn with desire—not so much to know it as to experience it. For it is not a sound of the mouth but a jubilation of the heart; not a sound of the lips but a movement of joys; a harmony of wills, not of voices. It is not heard outside, for it does not resound in public. Only she who sings hears it, and he to whom it is sung—that is, bride and bridegroom. For it is a nuptial song, expressing the chaste and joyful embraces of minds, the harmony of character, and the fitting mutual love of affections.

12. Yet it is not for a childish soul, still a novice and newly converted from the world, to sing or hear this song, but for a mind already advanced and instructed: one which, through its progress under God’s guidance, has so grown as to attain perfect maturity and, as it were, marriageable years—years, I mean, of merits, not of time—and has become fit for the marriage of the heavenly bridegroom, such as will be more fully described in its proper place.

But the hour passes, which urges us to go out to the work of our hands—both poverty and the rule of our order. Tomorrow, in the Lord’s name, we shall continue what we began concerning the kiss, since today’s sermon has finished with the title.

# SERMON II

## On the Incarnation of Christ, announced through the patriarchs and prophets and most ardently awaited by them

1. When I very often ponder the burning desire of the Fathers who sighed for Christ’s presence in the flesh, I am pierced and ashamed within myself; and now I can scarcely hold back tears, so ashamed am I of the wretched lukewarmness and torpor of these times. For to which one of us does the fulfillment of this grace bring as much joy as its promise had kindled desire in the saints of old? For behold how many will rejoice in this Nativity of his, which is soon to be celebrated—but would that it were for the Nativity, not for vanity!

The burning desire of those men, and the affection of their devout expectation, is breathed to me by this utterance: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). For whoever at that time could be spiritual had perceived in the Spirit how great the grace would be poured out upon those lips. Therefore, speaking in the desire of the soul, he said, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” desiring in every way not to be deprived of a share in such sweetness.

2. For every perfected person said: “What are these half-spoken utterances of the prophets to me? Rather, let him himself, fairer in form than the children of men, kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. I no longer hear Moses, for he has become too slow of speech for me (Exod. 4:10). Isaiah’s lips are unclean (Isa. 6:5); Jeremiah does not know how to speak, because he is a child (Jer. 1:6); and all the prophets are speechless. Let him himself—himself of whom they speak—speak; let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.

“Let him no longer speak to me in them or through them, because there is dark water in the clouds of the air; but let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, so that his gracious presence and the streams of his wondrous teaching may become within me a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. He whom the Father anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions (Ps. 44:8)—is not a more abundant grace poured out upon me from him, if only he deigns to kiss me with the kiss of his mouth?”

His speech, of course, living and effective, is a kiss to me—not the joining of lips, which sometimes falsely represents peace of mind, but rather an infusion of joys, a revelation of secrets, a wondrous and, in some way, undivided mingling of heavenly light and the enlightened mind. For “he who is joined to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 5:17). Therefore I rightly reject visions and dreams; I do not want figures and enigmas; I even disdain angelic appearances. For Jesus, my own Jesus, far surpasses even the angels in his form and beauty. Thus I ask not an angel or a human being, but him himself, to kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.

And certainly I do not presume that I shall be kissed by his very mouth—for that belongs to the unique blessedness and singular prerogative of the assumed man—but I ask more humbly to be kissed with the kiss of his mouth. This is indeed shared by many who can say: “And we all have received from his fullness” (John 1:16).

3. Attend. Let the mouth that kisses be the Word that assumes; the thing kissed, the flesh that is assumed; and the kiss, produced jointly by the kisser and the kissed, be the very person composed from both—namely, the man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and humankind. For this reason none of the saints presumed to say, “Let him kiss me with his mouth,” but only, “With the kiss of his mouth.” They preserved for him the prerogative which was uniquely and once for all granted to the one upon whom the mouth of the Word was then impressed, when the fullness of all divinity gave itself to him bodily.

Happy kiss, and wondrous through astonishing condescension, in which mouth is not pressed to mouth, but God is united to man! There indeed the touching of lips signifies the embrace of minds; here, however, the union of divine and human natures makes peace between things on earth and things in heaven. “For he himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). Therefore every saint of ancient times sighed for this kiss, because they sensed that delight and rejoicing were stored up over him, and that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden in him (Col. 2:3); and they too desired to receive from his fullness.

4. I perceive that what is said pleases you; but receive another interpretation as well. The saints, even before the Savior’s coming, were not unaware that God was thinking thoughts of peace concerning the race of mortals (Jer. 29:11). For he would not do a thing upon earth without revealing it to his servants the prophets (Amos 3:7). Yet this word was hidden from many (Luke 18:34). At that time faith was rare on earth, and hope was exceedingly faint even among most of those awaiting Israel’s redemption.

But those who foreknew it also foretold that Christ would come in the flesh, and that peace would come with him. Thus one of them says: “And there will be peace in our land when he comes” (Mic. 5:5). Indeed, they proclaimed, as they had received it from God, that through him human beings would recover the grace of God with complete confidence. John, the Lord’s forerunner, recognized and testified in his own time that this had been fulfilled: “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). And every Christian people now experiences that it is true.

5. Moreover, while they announced peace, but the Author of peace delayed, the faith of the people wavered, since there was none to redeem and none to save. Thus people complained of the delay, because that Prince of peace, so often proclaimed, had not yet come, as he had spoken through the mouth of his holy prophets from the beginning of the world; and, holding the promises in suspicion, they demanded the sign of the promised reconciliation, which is the kiss. It was as though any one of the people replied to the messengers of peace: “How long do you take away [Col. 0791D] our souls? Long ago you preached peace, yet it has not come; you promise good things, yet there is still disturbance. Behold, angels have announced this very thing to the fathers in many ways and by many means, and our fathers have announced it to us, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ and there is no peace” (Jer. 6:14). “If God wishes me to be persuaded that he answers by so frequent an embassy concerning the good pleasure of his will, yet does not fulfil what he announces, let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, and thus, in the sign of peace, make me secure concerning peace. For how am I now to trust words? Words need rather to be confirmed by deeds. Let God prove his messengers truthful—if indeed they are his messengers—and let him himself follow them, as they so often promised, because without him they can do nothing. He sent the boy, he carried the staff, and still there is neither voice nor life” (4 Kings 4:29–31). “I do not rise, I am not raised, I am not shaken from the dust, I do not breathe again in hope, unless the prophet himself comes down and kisses me with the kiss of his mouth.”

6. There is also this: he who professes himself to be our mediator with God is the Son of God, and is God (1 Tim. 2:5). And what is man, that God should make himself known to him, or the son of man, that he should take account of him? What confidence have I, that I should dare to entrust myself to so great a Majesty? Whence, I ask, do I, earth and ashes, presume that God has care for me? Moreover, he loves his Father, but has no need of me; he has no need of my goods. How then shall I be assured that my mediator is not partial [Col. 0792B]? Yet if, as you say, God has truly decreed to have mercy and intends henceforth to be more gracious, let him establish a covenant of peace and make an everlasting treaty with me in the kiss of his mouth. Let him not make void the things which proceed from his lips; let him empty himself, humble himself, bend down, and kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. So that, as a mediator suited equally to both parties, he may be suspect to neither, let God, the Son of God, become man; let him become the son of man, and make me certain of this in the kiss of his mouth. Securely I receive as mediator the Son of God, whom I recognize as also mine. He will plainly no longer be suspect to me: for he is my brother and my flesh. For I think that he can no longer despise me, bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.

[Col. 0792C]

7. Thus the ancient complaint demanded the most holy kiss—that is, the mystery of the incarnate Word—when faith, wearied by a long and burdensome expectation, was failing, and an unbelieving people, overcome by weariness, murmured against God’s promises. It is my invention, if you do not recognize this same thing from the Scriptures. From this surely came those complaining, murmuring voices: “Command, command again; wait, wait again; a little here, a little there” (Isa. 28:10). From this came those anxious and devout prayers: “Give a reward, Lord, to those who wait for you, that your prophets may be found faithful.” Likewise: “Raise up, Lord, the prayers [Note: [Col. 0791] This was formerly read in Bibles before Sixtus’s Roman correction. The Septuagint has: “the prophecies” (τὰς προφητείας).] spoken in your name by the earlier prophets” (Ecclus. 36:18, 17). From this came those gentle promises, full of consolation: “Behold, the Lord will appear and will not lie; if he delays, wait for him, because he who is coming will come and will not be late” (Hab. 2:3). Likewise: “The time for his coming is near, and his days shall not be prolonged” (Isa. 14:1). And, in the person of the One promised: “Behold, I,” he says, “bend toward you like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations” (Isa. 66:12). In these words both the urgency of the preachers and the distrust of the peoples are sufficiently apparent. Thus the populace murmured and faith wavered; and, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, “the angels of peace wept bitterly” (Isa. 33:7). Therefore, lest the whole human race should perish in despair while Christ delayed, because frail mortality suspected itself to be despised [Col. 0793A] and distrusted the grace of its reconciliation with God, so often promised, the saints who were certain concerning the Spirit desired certainty concerning the presence in flesh, and with all urgency sought the sign of peace to be restored, for the sake of the faint-hearted and unbelieving.

8. “O root of Jesse, who standest as a sign to the peoples!” (Isa. 11:10). How many kings and prophets wished to see you and did not see! Yet blessed above all was Simeon, whose old age was rich in mercy. For he rejoiced to see the sign of his desire; he saw it and rejoiced; and, having received the kiss of peace, he is dismissed in peace—yet first openly declaring that Jesus was born as a sign to be contradicted (Luke 2:25–35). It was altogether so. The rising sign of peace was contradicted, but by those who hate peace; for to persons of good will there is peace, but to the ill-disposed he is a rock of stumbling and a stone of offence (ibid., 14). Indeed Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him (Matt. 2:3); for he came unto his own, and his own did not receive him (John 1:11). Blessed are those shepherds in their night-watch, who were accounted worthy of the sight of this sign. Even then he hid himself from the wise and prudent and revealed himself to little ones. Herod too wished to see him; but because he did not wish with a good will, he did not deserve to do so. For this was the sign of peace, given only to persons of good will; but to Herod and those like him no sign shall be given except the sign of Jonah the prophet. But to the shepherds the angel says: “And this shall be a sign to you”—to you humble ones, to you obedient ones, [Col. 0793C] to you who do not aspire to high wisdom, to you who keep watch and meditate day and night on the law of God: “This,” he says, “is a sign to you.” What sign? What the angels promised, what the peoples sought, what the prophets foretold—this the Lord has now done and shown you, so that the unbelieving may receive faith, the faint-hearted hope, and the perfect assurance. Therefore this is a sign to you. A sign of what? Of pardon, grace, peace, and of peace without end. This, then, is the sign: “You shall find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger” (Luke 2:12). Yet God is in him, reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. 5:19). He shall die for your sins and rise again for your justification, so that, justified by faith, you may have peace [Col. 0793D] with God (Rom. 4:25; 5:1). Long ago the prophet offered this sign to King Ahaz, to be sought from the Lord his God either in the heights above or in the depths below. But the wicked king refused (Isa. 7:11–12), wretchedly not believing that in this sign things lowest and highest were to be joined in peace: so that both the underworld, when the Lord descends for its salvation, may receive for itself the sign of peace in the holy kiss; and the heavenly spirits likewise, when he has returned to heaven, may share it in eternal sweetness.

9. The discourse must be concluded. But, to gather briefly the substance of what has been argued in it: it is clear that this holy kiss was necessarily granted to the world for two reasons—both to give faith to the weak and to satisfy the longing [Col. 0794A] of the perfect. Moreover, the kiss itself is nothing other than the mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON III. On the kiss of the Lord’s foot, hand, and mouth, etc.

1. Today we read in the book of experience. Turn back into yourselves, and let each person attend to his conscience concerning what is to be said. I should like to ascertain whether it has ever been granted to any of you to say with conviction: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). For it does not belong to every person to say this from heartfelt affection; but if anyone has received, even once, a spiritual kiss from Christ’s mouth, his own experience surely impels him to seek it and gladly seek it again. I judge that no one can even know what it is unless he receives it. It is hidden manna, and only the one who eats it will still hunger. It is a sealed fountain, in which no stranger shares; but only the one who drinks will still thirst. Hear one who has experienced it, and how he seeks it: “Restore to me,” he says, “the joy of your salvation” (Ps. 50 [51]:14). Therefore let no soul like mine arrogate this to itself—burdened with sins and still subject to the passions of its flesh, having not yet felt the sweetness of the Spirit and wholly ignorant and inexperienced of inward joys.

2. Yet I show such a soul a place suitable to it in salvation. Let it not rashly rise to the mouth of the most serene Bridegroom; rather, let it lie with me in fear at the feet of the most stern Lord, and, with the publican, tremblingly look at the ground and not heaven [Col. 0794C] (Luke 18:13), lest a face accustomed to darkness, confounded by the lights of heaven, be overwhelmed by glory and, dazzled by the unfamiliar splendours of Majesty, be wrapped once more in the darker blindness of gloom. Let that place not seem lowly or contemptible to you, O soul, whoever you are, of such a kind—the place where the holy sinful woman put off sins and put on holiness. There the Ethiopian woman changed her skin and, restored to a new brightness, already then confidently and truthfully answered those who reproached her with the saying: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1:4). Do you wonder by what art she could have done this, or by what merits she obtained it? Receive the answer briefly. She wept bitterly, and, drawing long sighs from her inmost depths, shaken within by saving sobs, she vomited up her bitter humours. The heavenly physician came to her aid very swiftly, “because his word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147 [146–147]:15). Is not the word of God a draught? It certainly is: strong and powerful, searching hearts and kidneys [the inmost self] (Ps. 7:10). Finally, the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, joints also and marrow, and discerning thoughts (Heb. 4:12). Therefore, after the example of this blessed penitent, cast yourself down as well, O wretched one, that you may cease to be wretched. Cast yourself down upon the earth; embrace the feet, appease them with kisses, water them with tears—yet not so as to wash him, but yourself—so that you may become one of the flock of shorn ewes that come up from the washing (Song 4:2). Thus indeed [Col. 0795A] do not dare raise your face, suffused with shame and sorrow, until you too hear: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 7:37–48); until you hear: “Arise, arise, captive daughter of Zion; arise, shake yourself from the dust” (Isa. 52:1–2).

3. Having received the first kiss at the feet, even then you must not presume at once to rise to the kiss of the mouth. Rather, there shall be for you a step toward it: another, intermediate kiss, which you will receive second, at the hand. Hear also the reason for this. If Jesus says to me, “Your sins are forgiven,” what benefit is that unless I cease sinning? “I have put off my garment”; if I put it on again, how much have I gained? If I again defile my feet, which I had washed, will it avail me to have washed anything? Foul with every sort of vice, I lay long in the mire of dregs; but it will without doubt be worse for one who falls back than for one who lies there. Finally, I recall that he who made me whole said to me: “Behold, you have been made whole; go, sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14). He who gave me the will to repent must add the strength to persevere, lest I repeat what must be repented of and make my last state worse than the first. Woe to me even as a penitent if he immediately withdraws his hand, without whom I can do nothing. Nothing, I say, because I can neither repent nor persevere. Accordingly I hear the counsel of the Wise Man: “Do not repeat a word in prayer” (Ecclus. 7:15). I also fear what the Judge threatens against the tree that does not bear good fruit (Matt. 3:10). I confess that in such matters I am not at all content with the first grace, by which [Col. 0795C] I now repent of evil deeds, unless I receive also the second, so that I may produce fruits worthy of repentance and henceforth not return to the vomit.

4. Therefore this is what remains for me first to ask and receive before I presume to touch higher and more sacred things. I do not wish suddenly to become exalted; I wish to advance gradually. As greatly as the shamelessness of the sinner displeases God, so greatly does the modesty of the penitent please him. You appease him more quickly if you keep your measure and do not seek things higher than yourself. The leap from foot to mouth is long and steep, and not a fitting approach. What then? Still sprinkled with fresh dust, will you touch those sacred lips? Drawn from the mire yesterday, are you today presented to the face of glory? Let the passage be through the hand. Let that hand first wipe you clean; let it raise you up. How does it raise you? By giving you grounds for confidence. What is this? The beauty of self-restraint and fruits worthy of repentance, namely works of mercy. These will raise you from the dung-heap into hope of daring greater things. And certainly, in receiving the gift, kiss the hand: that is, give glory not to yourself but to his name. Give it once and give it again: both for sins forgiven and for virtues bestowed. Or else see how you will fortify your brow against these blows: “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

5. At last, then, having in the two kisses a twofold experience of divine condescension, perhaps you will not be ashamed to presume to holier things. For in proportion as you grow in grace, you are enlarged also in confidence. [Col. 0796A] Hence it comes about that you love more ardently and, because of what you feel is still lacking to you, knock more confidently. And to the one who knocks it shall be opened. That highest kiss—whatever it is—of supreme condescension and wondrous sweetness, I believe, will not be denied to one thus disposed. This is the way; this is the order. First we fall at the feet and weep before the Lord who made us, for the things we ourselves have done. Second, we seek the hand that raises us and strengthens our feeble knees. Finally, when we obtain these things by many prayers and tears, then at last we perhaps dare to lift our head to the very mouth of glory—not only, I say trembling and afraid, to behold it, but even to kiss it. For “Christ the Lord is the spirit before our face”; by cleaving to him in the holy kiss, we are made one spirit by his condescension.

[Col. 0796B]

6. To you, Lord Jesus, my heart rightly said: “My face has sought you; your face, Lord, I shall seek.” For in the morning you made me hear your mercy, when, first lying in the dust and kissing your venerable footprints, you forgave my evil life. Later, in the course of the day, you made the soul of your servant glad, when afterward, in the kiss of the hand, you bestowed also the grace of living well. And now, O good Lord, what remains except that, receiving me graciously now also to the kiss of the mouth, in the fullness of light and the fervour of the Spirit, you fill me with joy in your presence? Tell me, O sweetest, O most serene one, tell me where you pasture, where you rest at noon. Brothers, it is good for us to be here; but behold, the evil of the day calls us away. For those who are now reported to have arrived compel me pleasantly to break off this discourse rather than finish it. I shall go out to the guests, lest anything be lacking in the offices of that charity of which we speak, lest perhaps we too hear: “They say and do not do” (Matt. 23:3). Meanwhile pray that God may make the voluntary offerings of my mouth acceptable for your own edification and for the praise and glory of his name.

## SERMON IV. On the threefold progress of the soul, effected through the kiss of the Lord’s foot, hand, and mouth

1. Yesterday’s discourse treated a threefold progress of the soul under the designation of three kisses. Has it escaped you? I must pursue it in today’s discussion, insofar as God in his goodness shall deign to provide for his poor servant. We said, if you recall, that these kisses are received at the feet, at the hand, and at the mouth, each corresponding to a distinct stage. In the first, indeed, the beginnings of our conversion are consecrated; the second is granted to those making progress; the third, however, is experienced only by rare perfection. This Scripture which we have undertaken to expound began from the last of these alone; for its sake the other two were added by us. You will judge whether necessarily. I think the very form of the utterance readily indicates that these also are required. Yet it would be strange if you too did not notice that there truly must be another kiss or other kisses, from which the kiss of the mouth was meant to be distinguished by the one who said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). For why, when it would have sufficed simply to say, “Let him kiss me,” did she nevertheless, contrary to ordinary speech and usage, add distinctly and pointedly, “with the kiss of his mouth,” unless to show that the kiss which she sought was the highest, not the only one? Do we not ordinarily speak to one another in this way: “Kiss me,” or “Give me a kiss”? No one goes on to say, “With your mouth,” or “With the kiss of your mouth.” What then? When preparing to kiss one another, do we not turn our mouths toward each other, although we do not expressly ask them from one another by name? Finally, one who tells, for example, that the traitor was received by the Lord with a kiss says: “And he kissed him” (Mark 14:45); he does not add, “With his mouth,” or “With the kiss of his mouth.” Thus everyone, whether writing or speaking, is accustomed to do. Therefore these are three dispositions or advances of souls, sufficiently known and evident only to those who have experienced them: when they obtain either forgiveness for evil deeds, grace for doing good deeds, or even a vision of the presence of the very One who grants forgiveness and benefits them—so far, at least, as is possible in a frail body.

2. Moreover, understand more clearly why I have called the first and second kisses. We all know that a kiss is a sign of peace. But if, as Scripture says, our sins separate us from God (Isa. 59:2), remove the intervening thing and there is peace. Therefore, when we make satisfaction, so that, with the sin which separates removed, we are reconciled, what should I call the pardon we receive except a kind of kiss of peace? And this, for the present, is to be received nowhere but at the feet. For the satisfaction by which a proud transgression is amended ought to be humble and modest.

3. But when, in order to live more rightly and conduct ourselves more worthily toward God, we are endowed with the welcome familiarity of a more abundant grace, then with greater confidence we raise our head from the dust, to kiss, as is customary, the hand of the Giver—provided that in the gift received we seek not our own glory but that of the Author, and attribute his gifts to him rather than to ourselves. Otherwise, if you glory in yourself rather than in the Lord, you are plainly convicted of kissing your own hand rather than the Lord’s—a thing which, according to blessed Job’s judgment, is the greatest iniquity and a denial of God (Job 31:28). If, therefore, according to Scripture’s testimony, to seek one’s own glory is to kiss one’s own hand, then surely one who gives glory to God is not inappropriately said to kiss God’s hand. And we see that this is so among human beings: servants customarily kiss the feet of offended masters when asking their pardon, and the poor kiss the hands of the rich when receiving a gift from them.

4. But because God is spirit (John 4:24), and that simple substance is not distinguished by bodily members, perhaps someone will refuse entirely to accept any such thing concerning him, demand that I show him God’s hand or foot, and thereby prove what I have defined concerning the kiss of foot or hand. But what if I in turn ask this questioner about God’s mouth also, that he may demonstrate how what Scripture says of the kiss of the mouth belongs to God? Surely either God possesses a mouth along with hand and feet, or lacks a mouth together with them. Yet God has a mouth, by which he teaches knowledge to man; he has a hand, by which he gives food to all flesh; and he has feet, of which the earth is the footstool, at which sinners of the earth, turning and humbling themselves, make satisfaction. God has all these, I say, by effect, not by nature. With God, indeed, modest confession finds a place at which to cast itself down in humility; ready devotion, a place at which to be renewed and restored; and joyful contemplation, a place at which to rest in transcending itself. He who governs all things is all things to all, yet is nothing of all things in a proper sense. For, as he is in himself, “he dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16); “his peace surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4:7); “there is no number to his wisdom” (Ps. 146 [147]:5); “there is no end to his greatness” (Ps. 144 [145]:3); and “man cannot see him and live” (Exod. 33:20). This is not because he is far from each one, he who is the being of all things, without whom all things are nothing; but—to increase your wonder—nothing is more present than he, and nothing more incomprehensible. What is more present to any thing than its own being? Yet what is more incomprehensible to anything than the being of all things? Certainly, I call God the being of all things, not because those things are what he is, but because all things are from him, through him, and in him (Rom. 11:36). Therefore he, their Maker, is the being of all things that have been made, causally, not materially. In this manner, then, that Majesty deigns to be to his creatures what they are; to living beings, what they also live by; to rational beings, light; to those using reason rightly, virtue; and to conquerors, glory.

5. In creating, governing, administering, moving, advancing, renewing, and strengthening all these things, he needs no bodily instruments, for by his word alone he created both bodies and spirits. Souls need bodies and bodily senses in order to make themselves known to one another and have power to do so. But it is not so with almighty God, whose will alone affords swift efficacy both for creating things and ordering them as he wills. He can do what he wills, as much as he wills, without the service or ministry of bodily members. What? Do you suppose that, to behold what he himself has made, he requires the assistance of bodily sense? Absolutely nothing is hidden from, or escapes, the light that is present everywhere; yet to know anything he has no need of the service of a reporting sense. And he not only knows all things without a body, but makes himself known to the pure in heart without a body. I shall explain this more fully, so that it may become clearer. But perhaps, because the narrow limits of this discourse do not allow it now to be finished, it is better to defer the matter until tomorrow.

## SERMON V. On the four kinds of spirits: namely, God’s, the angelic, the human, and the animal

1. Four kinds of spirits are known to you: that of the animal, our own, the angelic, and that which created these. There is none among them for which a body, or the likeness of a body, is not necessary either for its own sake, for another’s sake, or for both—except only him to whom every creature, bodily as well as spiritual, rightly confesses and says: “You are my God, because you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15 [16]:2). It is clear, first, that the animal spirit needs a body in such a way that it cannot in any manner subsist without it. For when the animal dies, that spirit at once ceases both to give life and to live. We indeed live after the body; but no access to the things by which we live blessedly lies open to us except through the body. He perceived this who said: “The invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” (Rom. 1:20). For these very made things—that is, bodily and visible things—come into our knowledge only when perceived by the instrument of the body. Therefore the spiritual creature which we are has need of a body, without which it cannot acquire that knowledge which alone it has received as a step toward those things whose knowledge makes one blessed. If someone objects to me here concerning baptized infants, who, leaving the body without knowledge of bodily things, are nevertheless believed to pass into the blessed life, I reply briefly that grace, not nature, confers this upon them. And what has God’s miracle to do with me, who am discussing natural things?

2. That the spirits above heaven also need bodies is made especially certain for us by this true and truly divine saying: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. 1:14). How, then, do they perform their ministry without a body, especially among those who live in bodies? Indeed, moving about or passing from place to place belongs only to bodies; and authority, as unquestionable as it is well known, proves that angels do this frequently. Hence they were seen by the fathers, entered in to them, ate, and washed feet. Thus both lower and higher spirit need their own bodies, but only in order to help, not in order to be helped.

3. The animal, indeed, serves by the obligation of slavery and assists only in the uses of temporal and bodily necessities; therefore that spirit also passes away with time and fails with the body. For “the servant does not remain in the house for ever,” although those who use it well turn every use of this temporal servitude to the gain of eternal things. But the angel, in the freedom of spirit, takes care and strives to administer an office of mercy, offering himself as a ready and eager minister of future goods to mortals, since they are to be his citizens—or rather fellow-citizens—in eternity, and co-heirs of heavenly joy. Therefore the one, to serve by right; the other, to bring aid in mercy—both undoubtedly need their bodies in order to help. For I do not see how they are themselves helped by them, at least with respect to eternal advancement. For although the irrational spirit also takes in bodily things through the body, is it helped by its body so far that, through the bodily and sensible things which it perceives by it, it may advance and attain also to spiritual and intelligible things? Yet it is known to help toward the attainment of these those who, through their bodily and temporal service, turn every use of temporal things to the fruit of eternal things, using this world as though not using it.

4.
