The heavenly spirit, however, without the body’s aid and without observation of the things perceived through the body, is certainly sufficient, by the mere nearness and vitality of its nature, to apprehend the highest things and penetrate the deepest. Did not the Apostle understand this when, after saying, “The invisible things of God are understood through the things that are made,” he immediately added, “from the creation of the world”? Clearly, because not from the creation [Col. 0800B] of heaven. What the spirit clothed in flesh and dwelling on earth strives to attain gradually and, as it were, little by little, by advancing through consideration of sensible things, the inhabitant of heaven reaches by its innate subtlety and loftiness with all speed and ease—supported by no aid of bodily sense, assisted by no operation of bodily member, informed by no observation of any bodily thing. Why should it search among bodies for spiritual perceptions, when it reads them without contradiction in the book of life and understands them without difficulty? Why should it labour in the sweat of its face to shake grain from chaff, wine from grapes, and oil from olive pulp, when it has all these things sufficiently and abundantly at hand? Who would beg his food from other people’s houses when he has bread in abundance at home? [Col. 0800C] Who would take pains to dig a well and laboriously search out veins of water in the bowels of the earth, when a living fountain freely pours out clear waters to him in abundance? Therefore neither the animal nor the angelic spirit is helped by its body toward attaining those things which make a spiritual creature blessed: the former because, through innate dullness, it cannot receive them; the latter because, through the prerogative of a more excellent glory, it does not need them.

5. But it is clear that the human spirit, which holds a kind of middle place between the highest and the lowest, needs a body for both purposes to such an extent that without it it can neither advance itself nor benefit another. For, to say nothing of the other members of the body or their functions, how, I ask, do you instruct a hearer without a tongue, or receive instruction without ears?

6. Therefore, since without the body’s aid neither the animal spirit can pay the debt of its servile condition, nor the spiritual and heavenly creature fulfil the office of mercy, nor the rational soul adequately provide for the salvation both of its neighbour and of itself, it is clear that every created spirit needs bodily assistance altogether: either in order to help, or to be helped and also help. But what if some living things are found, so far as human use of them is concerned, to be inconvenient and suited to none of the uses of human needs? They are surely useful to sight, even if not to use; they may be more useful to minds that contemplate them than to bodies that employ them. Although they are harmful—even destructive, as is established—to the temporal welfare of human beings, their bodies nevertheless do not lack a way of cooperating for good with those saints called according to the purpose. If not by becoming food or offering service, then certainly by exercising the intellect, according to the advancement of common instruction, for which every means of use is surely at hand: namely, that “the invisible things of God are understood through the things that are made.” For the devil and his attendants, although their intention is always malicious, and although they always wish to harm, cannot harm good zealots, to whom it is said: “Who can harm you, if you are zealous for what is good?” (1 Pet. 3:13). Far from it that they should be able to do so; rather, even unwillingly, they are useful and cooperate for good with the good.

7. But whether angelic bodies are natural to their spirits, as human bodies are to human beings; whether angels are living beings as humans are, yet immortal—something humans are not yet; whether they alter and transform those bodies into whatever form and appearance they wish when they wish to appear, making them dense and solid to whatever degree they wish, though in their true nature they are, because of the subtlety of their nature and substance, impalpable and wholly inaccessible to our sight; or whether, subsisting as simple spiritual substances, they assume bodies when necessary and, their work completed, lay them aside again to be dissolved into the same matter from which they were taken—I do not wish you to ask me.

[Note: [Col. 0801C] Bernard raises the same doubt in *On Consideration*, book 5, chapter 4. Among the Fathers and leading doctors of the Church the matter was highly uncertain: some affirmed that angels are incorporeal, while others—no fewer—denied it. Thus the Master of the Sentences, book 2, distinction 8, considering this variety of opinions, did not dare define anything. I find that St Augustine spoke doubtfully on the matter, though he inclined more to the view that assigns bodies to angels. For, trained in Platonic learning, he mentions the Platonists’ opinion on angelic bodies in such a way as to seem to approve it—for example, in *The City of God*, book 8, chapters 14–16. Elsewhere, moreover, he frequently calls angels living beings and assigns bodies to them. In chapter 59 of the *Enchiridion* he says that the question of angelic bodies is very difficult. There is no time to indicate every passage: Estius noted very many in book 2 of the *Sentences*, distinction 8. Today, however, the certain and universally approved opinion is that angels are incorporeal and do not possess bodies naturally united to them. See St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 50, article 1; and question 51, articles 1 and 2. Whether this is a matter of faith or not is not agreed among all. See Estius at the cited place. Sixtus of Siena praises Bernard’s modesty in not daring to state an opinion in this question, indeed in professing ignorance: *Bibliotheca sancta*, book 3, annotation 8.]

The Fathers seem to have thought differently concerning such questions. It is not clear to me from what source I should teach either alternative, and I confess that I do not know. Nor do I think knowledge of these matters contributes much to your advancement [Col. 0801C].

8. But know this: no created spirit can of itself be applied to our minds, so as to be mingled with or infused into us without the mediation of any instrument belonging either to us or to its own body, in such a way that by participation in it we may become learned or more learned, good or better. No angel or soul is capable of containing me in this manner, nor am I capable of containing any of them. Nor do the angels themselves so receive one another. Let this prerogative therefore be reserved for the supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit, who alone, when he teaches knowledge to angel or human being, seeks no instrument of our bodily ear, any more than of his own mouth. He is infused through himself; through himself he becomes known; being pure, he is apprehended by the pure. He alone needs no one; and he alone is sufficient to himself and to all things by his omnipotent will alone.

> [Note: Col. 0801D] Bernard treats this argument correctly in Book V of *On Consideration*, no. 12: “The angel is present, suggesting good things but not inserting them; present, urging toward good but not creating the good. God is present in such a way as to affect, to infuse—or rather, to be infused and participated in—so that one would not fear to say that he is, as it were, one spirit with our spirit. The angel, then, is with the soul; God is in the soul.”
>
> That God is applied to human minds directly is expressed by others in different words: namely, that God alone can enter substantially into human souls or minds and fill them. This is expressly taught by Didymus, Book I *On the Holy Spirit*; Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, ch. 82; Bede, Commentary on Acts 5; and the Master, Book II, Distinction 8. Estius gives several explanations of this doctrine in Book II, Distinction 8, paragraph 12.
>
> “First,” he says, “it must be confessed that God alone fills the human mind according to substance: that is, God alone, by the presence of his nature, is inwardly present to the whole soul, containing, preserving, governing, and working within it. Secondly, he fills it with respect to the capacity of its desire; thirdly, by knowledge, because he searches and knows every inward chamber and recess of the heart; fourthly, God enters human minds in a certain special manner when, by the presence of his grace, he sanctifies them and makes them his dwelling and temple. Moreover, the devil is said already to enter, and sometimes even to fill, those who consent to demonic suggestion—not according to substance, in the manner explained above, but according to the effect of externally applied suggestion and according to the power of domination. The same must correspondingly be understood of good angels: they too are rightly said, through the effects of holy suggestions, to enter the human heart and work in it, according to that saying in Zechariah 1, ‘The angel was speaking in me.’ Bernard uses this passage for the matter in Book V of *On Consideration*, no. 12, where he expressly teaches this concerning good angels and clearly explains how it belongs differently to angels and to God.”
>
> Thus he speaks more fully in that place. Cassian also teaches the same thing weightily and soundly, *Conferences* VII, ch. 13. Compare likewise Sermon 31 on the Song of Songs, no. 6.

[Col. 0802B] 9. Yet he works immense and innumerable things through created beings subject to him, whether bodily or spiritual; but as one commanding, not as one begging. For example, he has now taken up my bodily tongue for his work—that is, to teach you—though beyond doubt he could do this more easily and sweetly through himself. This is surely indulgence, not need. For in your progress he seeks merit for me, not comfort for himself. Every person who works good ought to think thus, lest perhaps he glory in himself because of the Lord’s good gifts, and not in the Lord.

Yet there is one who works good unwillingly, whether an evil human being or an evil angel; and it is clear that what is done through him is not done on his account, since no good can benefit him against his will. To him, therefore, only a dispensation has been entrusted. But I know not how we experience as more welcome and delightful a good which is administered through an evil steward. This, then, is the reason why God does good things to the good even through evil people; not because he needs their works in doing good.

10. But who can doubt that God has still less need of things lacking reason or sense? Yet when these too cooperate in a good work, it is apparent that all things serve him who can rightly say, “The world and its fullness are mine” [Ps. 49:12]. Or rather, because he knows what things are more fittingly done through what means, he seeks not effectiveness from the service of bodily creation, but fitness. Suppose, then, that the services of bodies are often suitably applied to divine works—for example, rain to give life to seeds, multiply crops, or ripen fruits. What need, I ask, has he of a body of his own, when all heavenly and earthly bodies are plainly ready, without distinction, to obey his command in whatever work? He who finds no body foreign to himself would surely superfluously possess one of his own.

But if we wish to conclude in the present sermon everything that occurs to be said on this subject, the sermon will exceed its limits, and perhaps the strength of some. Therefore let us reserve what remains to be completed under another beginning.

> [Note: Col. 0803] Compare what is said on this argument in the little work *On Grace and Free Will*, ch. 13, nos. 44–45, in Volume II.

## SERMON VI. On the supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit, who is God; and how mercy and judgment are called the Lord’s feet.

1. That the following sermon may be joined to the preceding one: do you retain what was stated above, that the supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit alone has no need of the instrument or service of a body for anything that he wills to do or to have done [Col. 0803C]? Let us therefore safely grant to God alone, as immortality, so also incorporeality: for he alone among spirits so transcends the whole bodily nature that he needs no body for any work whatsoever, but by a spiritual nod alone, whenever he wills, is sufficient for doing whatever he wills.

That majesty alone requires no bodily instrument, either for itself or for another, whose omnipotent will finds every work immediately ready, before which everything high bows down, everything hostile yields, every created thing favors—even with no bodily or spiritual aid intervening or assisting. He teaches or admonishes without a tongue; he gives or holds without hands; without feet he runs and hastens to the aid of those perishing.

[Col. 0803D] 2. He was doing these things also among the fathers in earlier ages. Human beings experienced his constant benefits, but the benefactor was hidden from them. He indeed “reaches mightily from one end to the other”; but, “ordering all things sweetly,” he was not perceived by human beings. They rejoiced in the Lord’s gifts, yet were altogether unaware of the Lord of hosts, because he judged all things with tranquillity. They were from him, but not with him; through him they lived, but not for him; from him they had wisdom, but did not know him—alienated, ungrateful, senseless.

Thus it eventually came about that they did not attribute to their Maker what they were, what life they had, and what wisdom they possessed, but ascribed it to nature—or, more foolishly still, to fortune. Many also arrogated much to their own diligence and power. How much did deceitful spirits usurp for themselves! How much was given to the sun and moon! How much was attributed to earth and water, and even assigned to handmade and crafted works of mortal men! Herbs, shrubs, and the tiniest and most worthless seeds were honored as divinities.

3. Alas! Thus did human beings lose and exchange their glory for the likeness of a calf eating grass? [Ps. 106:20]. God, pitying their errors, deigned to come forth from the shadowy and dense mountain, and “set his tent in the sun” [Ps. 19:6]. He offered flesh to those who savor flesh, that through flesh they might learn to savor the Spirit as well. For while in the flesh [Col. 0804B] and through the flesh he performs works not of flesh but of God—commanding nature, overcoming fortune, making foolish the wisdom of human beings, and overthrowing the tyranny of demons—he clearly shows himself to be the one through whom these same things were done before, when they were done.

By working wonders powerfully and openly in the flesh and through the flesh, by speaking saving words and suffering indignities, he plainly showed that he himself was the one who had powerfully, though invisibly, created the ages, wisely governed them, and kindly protected them. Finally, while he preaches the Gospel to the ungrateful, gives signs to unbelievers, and prays for those who crucify him, does he not clearly declare himself to be the one who, together with his Father, daily makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and unjust? [Matt. 5:45]. For this is what he himself said: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me” [John 10:37].

4. Behold, he opens the mouth of his flesh, teaching his disciples on the mountain—the one who in silence teaches angels in heaven. Behold, at the touch of his bodily hand leprosy is healed, blindness driven away, hearing restored, the dumb tongue loosened, and the disciple nearly drowned is raised up. And he is undoubtedly recognized as the one to whom David had long before said: “You open your hand, and fill every living thing with blessing” [Ps. 145:16]; and again: “When you open your hand, all things shall be filled with goodness” [Ps. 104:28].

Behold, lying repentant beside bodily feet, the sinful woman hears, “Your sins are forgiven you” [Luke 7:48], and recognizes him of whom she had read long before: “The devil shall go forth before his feet” [Hab. 3:5]. For where sin is forgiven, there beyond doubt the devil is expelled from the sinner’s heart. Hence he says universally of all penitents: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” [John 12:31]: that is, God forgives sin to one humbly confessing, and the devil loses the dominion which he had seized in the human heart.

5. Finally, he walks upon the waves with bodily feet [Matt. 14:25], though the Psalmist, before he had yet been clothed with flesh, had already sung beforehand of him: “Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters” [Ps. 77:20]. That is: you trample the swelling hearts of the proud and restrain the unstable desires of the fleshly, justifying the ungodly [Col. 0805A] and humbling the proud. Yet because this is done invisibly, the carnal person does not perceive by whom it is done. Hence he adds: “And your footprints shall not be known” [Ps. 77:20].

Again, the Father says to the Son: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” [Ps. 110:1]. That is: until I subject to your will all who despise you, whether unwilling and miserable or willing and blessed. Therefore, because the flesh did not perceive this work of the Spirit—for “the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” [1 Cor. 2:14]—it was necessary that the sinful woman, lying bodily at bodily feet and kissing those same feet with bodily lips, should receive forgiveness of sins. Thus that “change of the right hand of the Most High” [Ps. 77:11], by which he wonderfully but invisibly justifies the ungodly, might become known even to carnal people.

6. Yet I ought not pass over those spiritual feet of God, which the penitent must first kiss spiritually. I know your curiosity, which passes over nothing entirely that has not been encrusted by its own will. Nor indeed should it be regarded as contemptible to know by what feet Scripture so frequently represents God: now standing, as there: “We shall worship in the place where his feet stood” [Ps. 132:7]; now walking, as there: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” [Lev. 26:12; 2 Cor. 6:16]; and now even running, according to: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” [Ps. 19:6].

If the Apostle rightly understood Christ’s head to refer to divinity [1 Cor. 11:3], I think it is not unfitting for us to understand the feet as referring to his humanity. Let us call one of them mercy, the other judgment. These two terms are familiar to you; and, if you consider it, both occur together in very many passages of Scripture. That God assumed the foot of mercy in the flesh which he united to himself is taught by the Epistle to the Hebrews, which declares that Christ was tempted in all respects according to our likeness, yet without sin, “that he might become merciful” [Heb. 4:15]. And does not the God-man himself plainly show that the other foot, called judgment, equally belongs to the humanity assumed, when he declares that the Father has given him authority to execute judgment “because he is the Son of Man” [John 5:27]?

7. With these two feet fittingly meeting under the one head of divinity, the invisible Emmanuel, born of a woman and made under the law, “was seen on earth and conversed with human beings” [Bar. 3:38]. By these feet he passes even now, doing good and healing all oppressed by the devil—but spiritually, invisibly. With these feet, I say, he walks through devout minds, ceaselessly examining and searching the hearts and inward parts of believers.

But see whether these may perhaps be those legs of the Bridegroom which the bride so magnificently commends later, comparing them, if I am not mistaken, to marble columns founded on bases of gold [Song 5:15]. Beautifully indeed: for in the incarnate Wisdom of God, which is signified by gold, “mercy and truth have met together” [Ps. 85:11]; and indeed, “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” [Ps. 25:10].

8. Blessed is the mind in which the Lord Jesus has once planted both feet! Recognize such a mind by two signs, which it necessarily bears within itself as one marked by divine footprints. They are fear and hope: the former represents the image of judgment, the latter that of mercy. Rightly does “the Lord take pleasure in those who fear him, and in those who hope in his mercy” [Ps. 147:11], since fear is the beginning of wisdom [Prov. 1:7], hope its progress, and love claims completion for itself.

Since these things are so, no small fruit belongs to this first kiss, received at the feet—provided only that you are deprived of neither of them. For if you are already pierced by sorrow for sin and fear of judgment, you have pressed your lips upon the footprint of truth and judgment. But if you temper fear and sorrow by contemplating divine goodness and by hope of obtaining forgiveness, know that you are also embracing the foot of mercy. Otherwise it is not beneficial to kiss one without the other: for remembrance of judgment alone casts one down into the abyss of despair, while the deceptive complacency of mercy produces the worst security.

9. It has also sometimes been granted to me, wretched man that I am, to sit beside the feet of the Lord Jesus, and with entire devotion to embrace now this foot, now that, insofar as his kindness deigned to admit me. But whenever, forgetful of mercy and driven by conscience, I clung too long to judgment [Col. 0806C], I was immediately cast down by incredible fear and miserable confusion; surrounded by gloomy horror, trembling, I cried from the depths only this: “Who knows the power of your anger, and who can number your wrath because of your fear?” [Ps. 90:11–12].

But if, leaving that foot, it happened that I held too much to the foot of mercy, I was, on the contrary, dissolved into such carelessness and negligence that at once my prayer seemed colder, my action more sluggish, my laughter more ready, my speech more incautious, and, finally, the whole disposition of both the inner and outer person more unstable. Therefore, taught by experience as my mistress, I shall sing not judgment alone, nor mercy alone, but “mercy and judgment” together to you, O Lord [Ps. 101:1]. I shall never forget these ordinances; both together shall be songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage, until mercy, exalted above judgment, silences misery, and thereafter my glory alone sings to you and I am no longer pierced with compunction.

## SERMON VII. On the burning love by which the soul loves God. Also, on the attention to be cultivated during prayer or psalmody.

1. I bring this labor upon myself, since I voluntarily provoke you to ask questions. Because, on the occasion of the first kiss, I took care to set forth the spiritual feet of God by particular definitions and names—and indeed more than sufficiently—you continue to inquire also about the hand, proposed as the second thing to be kissed. I consent; I yield to you. Indeed, I show not one hand but hands [Col. 0807A], and distinguish them by their proper names. Let one be called generosity, the other strength: because he both gives abundantly and powerfully defends what he has given. Surely whoever is not ungrateful will kiss them both, recognizing and confessing God as both giver and preserver of all good things. I think enough has been said about the two kisses. Let us see also about the third.

2. “Let him kiss me,” she says, “with the kiss of his mouth” [Song 1:1]. Who says this? The bride. And who is she? The soul thirsting for God. But let me posit different dispositions, so that the disposition properly belonging to the bride may shine forth more distinctly. If one is a slave, one fears before the face of the Lord; if a hired servant, one hopes for something from the Lord’s hand; if a disciple, one offers one’s ear to the teacher; if a son, one honors the father; but she who asks for a kiss loves.

This affection of love excels among the gifts of nature, especially when it returns to its own source, which is God. Nor have equally sweet names been found by which the mutual affections of the Word and the soul might be expressed as by bridegroom and bride. For they have all things in common, nothing their own, nothing divided from one another. One inheritance belongs to both, one house, one table, one bed, one flesh. Finally, for this reason he shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh [Gen. 2:24]. Likewise she is commanded to forget her people and her father’s house, that he may desire her beauty [Ps. 45:11–12]. Therefore, since loving especially and principally belongs to spouses, the soul which loves is not without reason designated by the name of bride.

It is the loving soul that asks for a kiss. She asks not for freedom, not for wages, not for an inheritance, nor even for teaching, but for a kiss—quite in the manner of the most chaste bride, breathing sacred love and altogether unable to conceal the flame she suffers. Observe how she seizes the opening of her speech. Though she is about to ask something great from one who is great, she nevertheless uses none of the adornment of flattery customary in such matters; she does not employ any circuitous approaches to attain what she desires. She makes no preface and seeks no favor; but, suddenly bursting forth from the abundance of her heart, quite plainly and boldly says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

3. Does she not seem plainly to say to you, “What have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” [Ps. 73:25]. Surely she loves chastely who seeks the very one she loves, and nothing else belonging to him. She loves holily, because not in fleshly desire but in purity of spirit. She loves ardently, because she is so intoxicated by her own love that she does not consider majesty. For what? He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble [Ps. 104:32], and she asks to be kissed by him! Is she drunk? Entirely drunk. Perhaps when she burst out in these words she had just come forth from the wine cellar, into which she afterward boasts that she had been brought [Song 1:3; 2:4]. For David also said to God concerning some: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” [Ps. 36:9]. O how great the power of love! How great the confidence of freedom in the spirit! What is clearer than that perfect love casts out fear? [1 John 4:18].

4. Yet modestly she does not address her speech to the bridegroom himself, but to others, as though he were absent: “Let him kiss me,” she says, “with the kiss of his mouth.” For a great thing is sought, and it is fitting that modesty accompany the prayer and commend the petitioner. Thus through household servants and intimates, access to the inner chamber is sought and an approach to the desired one pursued. Who are they? We believe that holy angels stand beside those who pray and offer to God the prayers and vows of human beings—where, however, they see pure hands lifted up without anger or disputing.

The angel speaking thus to Tobias proves this: “When you prayed with tears, buried the dead, left your meal, and hid the dead by day in your house and buried them by night, I offered your prayer to the Lord” [Tob. 12:12]. I think you are sufficiently persuaded of this also by other testimonies of Scripture. For that holy angels also customarily deign to join themselves to those singing psalms—what could be clearer than what the Psalmist says: “The princes went before, joined with those singing psalms, amid maidens playing tambourines” [Ps. 68:26]? Hence he also said: “In the presence of the angels I will sing psalms to you” [Ps. 138:1].

I therefore grieve that some of you are weighed down by heavy sleep during the sacred vigils and do not reverence the citizens of heaven, but appear as dead persons in the presence of princes, although those princes, moved by your eagerness, delight to take part in your solemn observances. I fear that, at some time, abhorring your sloth, they may depart in indignation.

> [Note: Col. 0807D] Sixtus of Siena, Book V of the *Sacred Library*, annotation 216, remarks on this passage as follows: “Scholastic writers commonly use Bernard’s words from the seventh homily on the Song of Songs when, for purposes of disputation, they contend that guardian angels sometimes abandon the guarding of those entrusted to their care. Albert the Great, in the first volume of the *Summa*, question 8, considering this passage, says that human beings are abandoned by guardian angels not with respect to place or local guardianship, but with respect to power and efficacy. This happens not through the angel’s negligence but through the human being’s fault, in the manner in which the saints say that a sinner departs from God into the region of unlikeness—not by distance of place, but through demerit.”

Then each one of you may too late say to God with groaning: “You have removed my acquaintances far from me; you have made me an abomination to them”; and: “You have removed friend and neighbor far from me, and my acquaintances because of misery” [Ps. 88:9, 19]; likewise: “Those near me stood afar off, and those who sought my life used violence” [Ps. 38:12–13]. For certainly, if good spirits withdraw from us, who will withstand the assaults of evil ones? Therefore I say to those who are such: “Cursed is he who does the work of God negligently” [Jer. 48:10]. And it is not I but the Lord who says: “Would that I had found you hot or cold! But because I found you lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you from my mouth” [Rev. 3:15–16].

Therefore attend to your princes when you stand to pray or sing psalms; stand with reverence and discipline, and glory because your angels daily see the face of the Father [Matt. 18:10]. Sent to minister for us, who receive the inheritance of salvation [Heb. 1:14], they bear our devotion upward and bring grace back. Let us take up the office of those whose fellowship we share, so that praise may be perfected “from the mouth of infants and sucklings” [Ps. 8:3]. Let us say to them: “Sing psalms to our God, sing psalms”; and let us hear them in turn replying: “Sing psalms to our King, sing psalms.”

5. Therefore, joining in common praise with the singers of heaven, as fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, “sing psalms wisely” [Ps. 47:7–8]. Food tastes in the mouth; a psalm tastes in the heart. Let the faithful and prudent soul not neglect to chew it with certain teeth of its understanding, lest perhaps, if it swallows it whole and unchewed, its palate be deprived of a desirable flavor, sweeter than honey and honeycomb. With the apostles at the heavenly banquet and the Lord’s table, let us offer a honeycomb [Luke 24:42]. Devotion is in the letter as honey is in wax. Otherwise the letter kills if you swallow it without the seasoning of the Spirit [2 Cor. 3:6]. But if, with the Apostle, you sing psalms in the spirit and also with the mind [1 Cor. 14:15], you too will know the truth of the saying that Jesus spoke: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” [John 6:64]; and likewise the saying we read Wisdom uttering: “My spirit is sweet above honey” [Sir. 24:27].

6. Thus your soul will delight in richness; thus your whole burnt offering will become fat. Thus you will appease the King; thus you will please the princes; thus, finally, you will make the whole court kindly disposed toward you. Having perceived in the heavenly places the fragrance of sweetness, they too will say of you: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a little column of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” [Song 3:6].

“The princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun; the princes of Naphtali” [Ps. 68:28]: that is, of those who confess, those who are continent, and those who contemplate. For our princes know that the confession of those singing psalms, the strength of those who are continent, and the purity of those who contemplate are acceptable to their King. They are solicitous to require from us such firstfruits of the Spirit, which indeed are nothing other than the first and purest fruits of wisdom.

For, as you know, Judah is interpreted “praising” or “confessing,” Zebulun “dwelling-place of strength,” and Naphtali “a hind let loose.” By the leaps of its agility the latter expresses the raptures of one contemplating; it is also accustomed to penetrate the dark places of forests, as the contemplative penetrates the obscurities of meanings. We know who said: “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me” [Ps. 50:23].

7. But if “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” [Sir. 15:9], do you not have a most necessary need of the virtue of continence, by which sin may not reign in your mortal body? Yet continence that seeks human glory has no merit before God. Therefore there is especially need also for purity of intention, by which your mind both desires to please God alone and is able to cleave to him. For to cleave to God is nothing other than to see God, a singular happiness granted only to the pure in heart.

David had a clean heart when he said to God: “My soul has clung after you” [Ps. 63:9]; and again: “But it is good for me to cling to God” [Ps. 73:28]. By seeing, he clung; and by clinging, he saw. To souls trained in these things the heavenly messengers show themselves familiar and frequent, especially if they have perceived the soul praying frequently [alternate reading: *prospiciant*, “observe her”]. “Who will grant me, through you, O kindly princes, that my petitions may become known before God?” Not before God himself, to whom even the thought of a human being confesses, but “before God”: that is, before those who are with God, both the blessed powers and spirits released from flesh. Who will raise me, needy, from the earth and lift up the poor from the dung-hill, that I may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory? I do not doubt that they gladly gather in the palace one whom they graciously visit on the dung-hill. Finally, they rejoiced at conversion: will they fail to recognize one at the assumption?

8. I think, then, that the bride addresses these beings while praying; and that she reveals the desire of her heart to them as the household servants and companions of the bridegroom when she says, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Observe the familiar and affectionate conversation of the soul, sighing in the flesh, with the heavenly powers. She longs for kisses and asks what she desires, yet does not name the one she loves, because she does not doubt that they know him, since she is accustomed to have frequent conversation with them concerning him. Therefore she does not say, “Let this one or that one kiss me,” but only, “Let him kiss me.” So too Mary Magdalene did not state by name whom she sought, but said only to him whom she supposed to be the gardener: “Lord, if you have taken him away” [John 20:15]. Whom does she mean by “him”? She does not say, because she believes it plain to everyone what cannot depart from her heart even for a moment.

So also this bride, speaking to the companions of her bridegroom as to those who knew her secret and to whom she knew herself to be manifest, suddenly bursts forth, without naming her beloved, into these words: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” I do not wish to detain you longer concerning this kiss; but tomorrow’s sermon will tell you whatever the anointing that teaches concerning all things may deign to suggest to me while you pray. For flesh and blood does not reveal this mystery, but the Holy Spirit, who searches the depths of God, proceeding from the Father and the Son and living and reigning with them alike for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. How the kiss of God’s mouth signifies the Holy Spirit, whom the Church asks to be given to her for knowledge of the Holy Trinity.

[Col. 0810D]

1. Today, as you remember from yesterday’s promise, I intend to speak to you about the highest kiss—that is, the kiss of the mouth. Listen more attentively to what is sweeter in savor, more rarely tasted, and more difficult to understand. To begin somewhat more deeply, it seems to me that he who said, “No one knows the Son except the Father; and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” [Matt. 11:27], indicated a certain kiss ineffable and unexperienced by every creature.

For the Father loves the Son and embraces him with a singular love: the highest embraces his equal, the eternal his coeternal, the one his only-begotten. Yet he is bound to the Father by no lesser affection; indeed, for love of him he even dies, as he himself testifies when he says, “That all may know that I love the Father, arise, let us go” [John 14:31]—undoubtedly to his passion. That mutual knowledge and love of begetter and begotten, then, what is it but the sweetest and most secret kiss?

2. I certainly believe that not even angelic creation is admitted to so great and holy a mystery of divine love. For, as Paul himself understands, that peace surpasses every understanding, even angelic understanding [Phil. 4:7]. Hence this bride, though presuming much, nevertheless does not dare to say, “Let him kiss me with his mouth,” reserving that expression for the Father alone; but asks for something less: “Let him kiss me,” she says, “with the kiss of his mouth.” See the new bride receiving a new kiss—not from the mouth, however, but from the kiss of the mouth.

“He breathed upon them,” it says—Jesus, undoubtedly, upon the apostles, that is, upon the primitive Church—and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” [John 20:22]. This was surely a kiss. What then? Was that breath bodily? No: it was the invisible Spirit. He was given in that breath of the Lord so that it might thereby be understood that he proceeds from him as well as from the Father, as truly the kiss common to both the one kissing and the one kissed. Therefore it is enough for the bride if she is kissed by the Bridegroom’s kiss, even though she is not kissed by his mouth. For she does not consider it a small or contemptible thing to be kissed by the kiss, which is nothing other than to be filled with the Holy Spirit. For if the Father is rightly understood as the one kissing and the Son as the one kissed, it is not inappropriate to understand the kiss as the Holy Spirit, since he is the undisturbed peace of Father and Son, their firm bond, indivisible love, and undivided unity.

3. Therefore the bride ventures to ask for him and confidently asks, under the name of a kiss, that he be infused into her. For she grasps something which gives her occasion not to lack confidence. When the Son said, “No one knows the Son except the Father; and no one knows the Father except the Son,” he added, “and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him.” The bride does not doubt that he wills this for her, if he wills it for anyone. Therefore she boldly asks that the kiss be given to her: that is, that Spirit in whom both the Son and the Father are revealed to her. For neither becomes known without the other. Hence: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” [John 14:9]; and John’s saying: “Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either; but whoever confesses the Son has the Father also” [1 John 2:23].

From these sayings it is clear that neither the Father is known without the Son nor the Son without the Father. Rightly, therefore, he who says, “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” [John 17:3], places the highest blessedness not in the knowledge of one alone, but of both. Finally, those who follow the Lamb are said to have his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads [Rev. 14:1]; that is, they glory in the knowledge of both.

4. But someone may say: “Then knowledge of the Holy Spirit is not necessary, since, when he said that eternal life is to know the Father and the Son, he said nothing about the Holy Spirit.” It is indeed necessary. But where Father and Son are perfectly known, how can the goodness of both, which is the Holy Spirit, be unknown? For one human being is not fully known to another so long as it remains hidden whether that person has a good or evil will.

Moreover, when it is said, “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent,” surely that sending manifests both the good pleasure of the Father who graciously sends and the voluntary obedience of the Son. Thus the Holy Spirit has not altogether been left unmentioned where such great grace of both has been mentioned. For the love and kindness of both is the Holy Spirit.

5. Therefore the bride asks that the grace of this threefold knowledge be poured into her, insofar as it can be received in mortal flesh, [Col. 0812B] when she asks for the kiss. But she asks it from the Son, because it belongs to the Son to reveal to whomever he wills. Thus the Son reveals himself to whomever he wills, and reveals the Father also. He reveals, without doubt, through the kiss—that is, through the Holy Spirit—as the Apostle testifies when he says: “God has revealed it to us through his Spirit” (1 Cor. 2:10). Yet in giving the Spirit through whom he reveals, he reveals the Spirit himself also: by giving, he reveals; and by revealing, he gives. Moreover, the revelation that takes place through the Holy Spirit not only enlightens for knowledge but also kindles love, as Paul says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

And perhaps this is why we do not read that those who, “though they knew God, did not glorify him as God,” knew him by the Holy Spirit’s revelation; [Col. 0812C] for, though they knew, they did not love. For thus you have it: “God revealed it to them.” And it is not added, “through his Spirit,” lest impious minds should arrogate to themselves the bride’s kiss—minds which, content with the knowledge that puffs up, did not know the love that builds up (1 Cor. 8:1). Finally, the Apostle himself tells by what means they knew: “They perceived through the things that were made, understood by the mind.” Hence it is clear that they did not know perfectly him whom they did not love at all. For had they known perfectly, they would not have been ignorant of the goodness by which he willed to be born and to die in the flesh for their redemption.

Hear, finally, what was revealed to them concerning God: “His eternal power,” he says, “and divinity” (Rom. 1:19–21). You see that they investigated, in the presumption of a spirit—not God’s Spirit, but their own—that which belongs to loftiness and majesty; but they did not understand that he is meek and humble of heart. Nor is this surprising, since their head, Behemoth, has nothing humble in him; rather, as is written of him, “he sees everything that is high” (Job 41:25). In contrast, David “did not walk in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for him” (Ps. 130:1–2), lest, as one who searches out majesty, he should be overwhelmed by glory (Prov. 25:27).

6. You also, if you would plant your foot cautiously in hidden meanings, always remember the admonition of the Wise Man: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, and do not investigate things stronger than yourself” (Ecclus. 3:22). Walk in these matters by the Spirit, and not by your own understanding. The Spirit’s teaching does not sharpen curiosity but kindles charity. Rightly, therefore, the bride, seeking him whom her soul loves, [Col. 0813A] does not entrust herself to the senses of her flesh or rest content with the empty reasonings of human curiosity; rather, she asks for the kiss—that is, she invokes the Holy Spirit, through whom she may receive both the savor of knowledge and the seasoning of grace.

And fittingly, the knowledge given in the kiss is received with love, because the kiss is a sign of love. Therefore knowledge that puffs up, being without charity, does not proceed from the kiss. Nor should those who have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, claim it for themselves in any way. For the grace of the kiss brings both gifts together: the light of knowledge and the richness of devotion. For it is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding who, like a bee carrying wax and honey, possesses both that by which he kindles the light of knowledge and that by which he imparts the flavor of grace.

Let neither, then, suppose that he has received the kiss: neither one who understands truth but does not love, nor one who loves but does not understand. Certainly, in this kiss there is room neither for error nor for lukewarmness. Therefore the bride, in order to receive the twofold grace of the most holy kiss, sets forth her two lips in response: the faculty of understanding and the will of wisdom, so that, glorying in the fullness of the kiss, she may deserve to hear: “Grace is poured out upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you for ever” (Ps. 44:3).

Thus, when the Father kisses the Son, he most fully pours forth to him the hidden things of his divinity [1287] and breathes forth the sweetness of love, as Scripture signifies when it says: “Day pours forth speech to day” (Ps. 18:3). To that eternal and uniquely blessed embrace, as has already been said, no creature at all is granted access: only the Spirit of them both is witness and conscious of their mutual [Col. 0813C] knowledge and love. “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11:34).

7. But perhaps someone will say to me: “How, then, did you learn that which you assert was entrusted to no creature?” Certainly the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, “has declared him” (John 1:18). I would say: not to me, wretched and unworthy as I am, but plainly to John, the friend of the Bridegroom, whose words these are; and not only to John the friend, but also to John the Evangelist, indeed the disciple whom Jesus loved. For his soul was pleasing to God, altogether worthy of the bride’s name and dowry, worthy of the Bridegroom’s embraces, worthy, finally, to recline upon the Lord’s breast. John drew from the bosom of the Only-Begotten what that Only-Begotten had drawn from the paternal bosom.

Yet not he alone, but also all those to whom the angel of great counsel said: “I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father” (John 15:15). Paul also drew from it, whose gospel “is not according to man”; nor did he receive it through man, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ (Gal. 1:11–12). Surely all these can say, as happily as truthfully: “The Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him to us.” And what was that declaration to them but a kiss? Yet it was a kiss from a kiss, not from the mouth.

Hear, then, the kiss from the mouth: “I and the Father are one”; likewise: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:30, 38). It is a kiss received mouth to mouth; but no one approaches it. Truly it is a kiss of love and peace; but that love surpasses [Col. 0814A] all knowledge, and that peace exceeds all understanding. Nevertheless, what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart, God revealed to Paul through his Spirit—that is, through the kiss of his mouth. Therefore, that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son is a kiss from the mouth. But what is written—“We have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12)—is indeed a kiss from a kiss.

8. And, that we may distinguish the two more clearly: he who receives the fullness receives a kiss from the mouth; but he who receives from the fullness receives a kiss from a kiss. Paul indeed was great; yet however high he may stretch his mouth, even if he extends himself as far as the third heaven, [Col. 0814B] he must nevertheless remain below the mouth of the Most High, be content according to his measure, and remain within himself. Since he cannot attain to the face of glory, he must humbly ask that the kiss be condescended to him and sent down from on high.

But he who “did not deem it robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. 2:6), so that he dares to say, “I and the Father are one,” because he is joined as an equal and embraces as an equal, does not beg for a kiss from a lower place; but, with equal loftiness, joins mouth to mouth [otherwise: “touches mouth with mouth”], and by a singular prerogative receives a kiss from the mouth. For Christ, then, the kiss is fullness; for Paul, participation—so that the one may glory that he is kissed from the mouth, while the other only from the kiss.

9. Blessed, nevertheless, is the kiss by which God is not merely known but the Father is also loved—for he is by no means fully known unless he is perfectly loved. What soul among you has at some time felt, in the secret place of her conscience, the Spirit of the Son crying, “Abba, Father”? (Gal. 4:6). Let that very soul presume herself to be loved with paternal affection, since she feels herself moved by the same Spirit as the Son. Take confidence, whoever you are; take confidence without hesitation. In the Spirit of the Son, know yourself to be the Father’s daughter, the Son’s bride or sister. You will find one such as this called by either name.

The proof is at hand; I shall not labor long over it. The Bridegroom’s voice is addressed to her: “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride” (Cant. 5:1). She is a sister because she is from one Father; a bride because she is in one Spirit. For if a carnal marriage makes two into one flesh, [Col. 0814D] why should not a spiritual union all the more join two in one spirit? Finally, “he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). But hear also how lovingly and [1288] worthily the Father calls her his daughter, and likewise invites her, as his own daughter-in-law, to the Son’s tender embraces: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty” (Ps. 44:11–12).

Behold from whom she asks this kiss. O holy soul, show reverence, for he is the Lord your God, and perhaps is not to be kissed, but to be adored with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IX. On the Bridegroom’s breasts, that is, Christ’s: one is his long-suffering in waiting for sinners; the other, his kindness or readiness in receiving them.

[Col. 0815A]

1. Let us now approach the book and give an account of the bride’s words and their sequence. For they hang suspended and precariously abrupt without a beginning. We must therefore supply that to which they suitably adhere. Let us suppose, then, that those whom we called the Bridegroom’s companions have come once more to the bride, as yesterday and the day before, to visit and greet her; that they found her murmuring and weary; that they wondered at the cause and addressed her somewhat in this manner:

“What new thing has happened? Why do we see you sadder than usual? What is the cause of this unexpected murmuring? Surely, when you went astray and alienated after your lovers, with whom you fared badly, and were at last compelled to return to your former husband, did you not persist with many prayers and tears, if only that you might deserve to touch his feet?”

“I remember,” she says.

“What then? Having obtained this, and having received in the kiss of the feet forgiveness for your offenses, did you not again become impatient, dissatisfied with so great a condescension, and, desiring greater intimacy, ask and obtain with the same persistence as before a second grace also, so that in the kiss of the hand you gained virtues not few and not small?”

“I do not deny it,” she says.

And they say to her: “Indeed, are you the one who used to swear and solemnly protest that, if you were ever granted to attain the kiss of the hand, it would be enough for you, and you would ask nothing further?”

“I am.”

“What then? Do you complain that anything of what you received has been taken away?”

“Nothing.”

“Or do you fear that what you had presumed upon from your former evil manner of life will be demanded back?”

“No.”

2. “Yet come: tell us how we may satisfy you.”

“I do not rest,” she says, “unless he kisses me with the kiss of his mouth. Thanks for the kiss of the feet; thanks also for that of the hand. But if he has any care for me, ‘Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth’” (Cant. 1:1). I am not ungrateful, but I love. I confess that I have received gifts greater than my merits, yet altogether less than my desires. I am carried by desire, not by reason. Do not, I beg you, charge me with presumption where affection presses me. Modesty indeed protests; but love prevails. Nor am I ignorant that “the king’s honor loves judgment” (Ps. 98:4); but headlong love neither waits for judgment, nor is moderated by counsel, restrained by shame, or subjected to reason.

I ask, I entreat, I demand: let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. Behold, by his grace I have now for many years endeavored to live chastely and soberly; I persist in reading, resist vices, devote myself frequently to prayer; I keep watch against temptations and recall my years in the bitterness of my soul. So far as lies in me, I judge that I live blamelessly among the brethren; I am subject to higher authorities, going out and coming in at the command of the elder. I do not covet another’s possessions; rather, I have given both what is mine and myself. I eat my bread in the sweat of my face. [Col. 0816A] Yet all that there is in these things consists in habit; of sweetness there is nothing. What am I but, according to the prophet, “Ephraim, a heifer taught to love threshing” (Hos. 10:11)? Finally, in the Gospel, one who does only what he ought to do is accounted an unprofitable servant (Luke 17:10). Perhaps I fulfill the commandments in some fashion; but in them my soul is like land without water. Therefore, that my burnt offering may become rich: let him, I beseech you, kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.

3. Many of you also, as I remember, are accustomed to complain to me in your private confessions of this sort of [1289] dryness of spirit, languor, and dullness of the sluggish mind: namely, that you cannot penetrate the lofty and subtle things of God, and that you feel either nothing or little of the Spirit’s sweetness. What do these people do but [Col. 0816B] sigh for the kiss?

> [Note: [Col. 0815D] In private confessions of this kind they disclosed even their negligences, as Bernard calls them in Sermon 1 on the Circumcision, no. 5. Cuigo, Prior of the Charterhouse V, calls “private” those confessions that took place in private cells; “common” those made by all every Saturday, though individually. Compare Book 1 of the *Life of St Bernard*, no. 28.]

They surely sigh and yearn for the Spirit of wisdom and understanding: for understanding, indeed, that they may attain; for wisdom, that they may taste what they have apprehended by understanding. I think that the Prophet prayed in this very desire when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with fatness and richness, and with lips of exultation my mouth shall praise you” (Ps. 62:6). He was plainly asking for the kiss, and for that kiss by whose touch, when his lips were suffused with the richness of special [otherwise: spiritual] grace, there would follow what he elsewhere prays: “Let my mouth be filled with praise, that I may sing your glory, your greatness all the day long” (Ps. 70:8). Finally, he poured forth speech when he had tasted: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden [Col. 0816C] for those who fear you” (Ps. 30:20).

This kiss has detained us long enough; and yet, to speak truthfully, I do not trust that I have expressed it worthily enough. But let us pass on to what remains, because it is known better by being impressed upon one than by being expressed.

4. It follows: “Because your breasts are better than wine, more fragrant than the finest ointments” (Cant. 1:1–2). The author does not say whose words these are, leaving us free to consider to which person they are most fitting. I, however, have no lack of grounds for assigning them suitably either to the bride, or to the Bridegroom, or even to the Bridegroom’s companions. First I shall show how they suit the bride.

Meanwhile, while she and they were conversing together, he of whom they were speaking drew near. He gladly approaches those who speak of him. Such is his custom. Thus, when they were going to Emmaus and conversing with one another, he showed himself a pleasant and eloquent companion (Luke 24:15). For this is what he promises in the Gospel: “Where two or three are gathered together in my name, I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20); and through the prophet: “Before they call,” he says, “I will answer; and while they are still speaking, I will say: Behold, I am here” (Isa. 65:24).

Thus he was now present without being summoned; delighted by their words, he anticipated their prayers. I think that sometimes he does not even wait for words, but is summoned by thoughts alone. Finally, the man found [Col. 0817A] according to God’s heart says: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart” (Ps. 9:17). Attend also to yourselves in every place, knowing that God, who searches hearts and reins, knows all that belongs to you—he who fashioned each of your hearts individually and understands all your works.

Therefore, sensing that the Bridegroom was present, the bride fell silent. For she is ashamed of the presumption in which she realizes that she has been caught; she had imagined that it was more modest to pursue her purpose through intermediaries. Then, turning immediately to him, she attempts, as best she can, to excuse her boldness: “Because your breasts are better,” she says, “than wine, more fragrant than the finest ointments.” It is as if she said: “If I seem to think lofty thoughts, you have done this, O Bridegroom, by nursing me in such sweetness from your breasts, with so great a condescension, that, all fear driven away by love for you, not by my own rashness, I dare perhaps more than is fitting. I dare indeed, mindful of your mercy and forgetful of your majesty.” Let this suffice as an explanation of the connection of the words.

5. Let us now see what this praise of the Bridegroom’s breasts means. The Bridegroom has two breasts; in him they are two evidences of uncreated gentleness: that he patiently waits for the sinner and mercifully receives the penitent. A twofold sweetness of graciousness overflows, I say, in the breast of the Lord Jesus: long-suffering in waiting, and readiness in giving.

And hear that this is not my invention. You read concerning long-suffering: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering?” Likewise: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2:4). For this reason he long postpones the sentence of vengeance upon one who despises him: that at some point he may grant the grace of forgiveness to one who repents. For he does not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.

Let us give examples also of the other breast, that is, the readiness to forgive. You read of it: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, his sin shall be forgiven him” (Ezek. 33:11–12). You read: “Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him; and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiving” (Isa. 55:7). David beautifully embraces both in few words, saying: “Long-suffering and [1290] [Col. 0817D] greatly merciful” (Ps. 102:10).

By experience of this twofold goodness, therefore, the bride confesses that she has grown into such confidence as to dare ask for the kiss. “What wonder,” she says, “if I presume thus of you, O Bridegroom, when I have experienced from your breasts such an abundance of sweetness? Therefore it is the sweetness of your breasts that encourages me to dare, not confidence in my own merits.”

6. When she says, “Your breasts are better than wine,” this is what she means: “The richness of grace that flows from your breasts is more effective for my spiritual progress than the biting reproach of prelates.” And they are not only better than wine, but “more fragrant than the finest ointments,” because you not only nourish those present with the milk of inward sweetness, but also sprinkle those absent with the pleasant fragrance of a good reputation, having a good testimony both from those within [Col. 0818A] and from those outside. You have milk within, I say, and ointments without; for there would be no one for you to refresh with milk if you had not first drawn them by your fragrance.

We shall see later, when we reach the subsequent words, “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Cant. 1:3), whether these ointments contain anything worthy of consideration. Now, according to our promise, let us see whether these very words, which have been assigned to the bride, also suit the Bridegroom.

7. While the bride speaks of the Bridegroom, he suddenly appears, as I said; he grants her wish, gives the kiss, and fulfills in her the saying that is written: “You have given him his heart’s desire, and have not withheld from him the request of his lips” (Ps. 20:3). This he proves by the filling of her breasts. For the holy kiss is of such power that the bride immediately conceives when she has received it; her breasts swell and, as it were, become full of milk as a sign.

Those who strive to pray frequently have experienced what I say. We often approach the altar with a lukewarm and dry heart, and devote ourselves to prayer. But as we persist, grace is suddenly poured in; the breast becomes rich, a flood of devotion fills the inward parts; and if there is someone to press them, the breasts will not delay in pouring forth abundantly the milk of conceived sweetness. Let him say, therefore: “You have, bride, what you asked for; and this is your sign, that your breasts have become better than wine. By this you may know that you have received the kiss: you feel that you have conceived. Hence your breasts have swelled and, in their abundance of milk, have become better than the wine of secular knowledge, [Col. 0818C] which indeed intoxicates, but with curiosity, not charity; fills, but does not nourish; puffs up, but does not build up; gluts, but does not strengthen.”

8. But let us also allow the companions to speak these words. “You complain unjustly,” they say, “against the Bridegroom, because what he has already given is of greater value than what you ask. What you seek indeed delights you; but the breasts by which you nourish the little ones whom you also bear are better—that is, more necessary—than the wine of contemplation. For one thing gladdens the heart of a single person, another builds up many. For although Rachel is more beautiful, Leah is more fruitful. Do not, then, press too hard for the kisses of contemplation, because the breasts of preaching are better.”

[Col. 0818D]

9. Another meaning occurs to me, which I had not intended to propose, but which I shall by no means pass over. Why should we not say that these words suit rather those over whom she presides in care, as a mother or nurse over little children? For young and still tender souls do not patiently endure her leisure in quiet, when they desire to be more fully instructed by her teaching and formed by her examples. Is not the restlessness of such persons, finally, checked in what follows, where, under a solemn charge, they are forbidden to awaken the beloved until she herself wills it? (Cant. 2:7.)

Thus, when these souls perceive that the bride yearns for kisses, seeks a private retreat, avoids public life and declines crowds, and prefers her own rest to care for them, they say: “Do not, do not; for there is greater fruit in the breasts than in embraces. For by them you vindicate us from carnal desires that wage war against the soul; you rescue us from the world and gain us for God.” This, therefore, is what they mean when they say: “Your breasts are better than wine.” “The spiritual delights,” they say, “which your breasts distill upon us, overcome the pleasure of the flesh by which we were held shortly before, as though drunk with wine.”

10. And they aptly compare carnal affection to wine. For just as a grape, once pressed, has nothing left to pour out again, but is condemned to perpetual dryness, so the flesh, in the pressure of death, is dried up utterly from all its delight and does not again grow green for lusts. Thus the prophet says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass. The grass has dried up and the flower has fallen” (Isa. 40:6–7); and the Apostle: “He who sows in the flesh shall also reap corruption from the flesh” (Gal. 6:8); and again: “Food for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. 6:13).

But consider whether this comparison perhaps applies not only to the flesh but also to the world. For the world too passes away, and its desire; and although all things that are in the world have an end, their end will not be an end. But the breasts are not so. Once exhausted, they draw again from the fountain of the maternal breast what they may offer to those who suck. Rightly, therefore, the bride’s breasts are declared better than love of the flesh or the world, for no number of those who nurse ever dries them up; rather, they always abound from the depths of charity, so as to flow again. For “rivers flow from her belly,” and in her there comes to be “a fountain of living water springing up into eternal life” [Col. 0819C] (John 7:38; 4:14).

The praise of the breasts is then heightened by the fragrance of ointments: they not only feed by the savor of words, but also give off fragrance through the reputation of deeds. What the breasts are, with what milk they are swollen, and with what ointments they are anointed, we shall show, Christ helping us, at the beginning of another sermon: he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[1291]

## SERMON X. On three spiritual ointments: those of contrition, devotion, and compassion.

1. I am not of deep understanding or such penetrating ability as to be able to discover any new thing from myself; but Paul’s mouth is a great and unfailing fountain, open to us. From it I now draw, as I often do, in showing the bride’s breasts. “Rejoice,” he says, “with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15). Maternal affections are briefly expressed, because little children can neither suffer nor thrive without her who bore them: in either case she must conform herself to the feelings of her children.

Accordingly, following Paul’s judgment [otherwise: wisdom], I shall assign these two affections to the bride’s two breasts: compassion to one, rejoicing with others to the other. Otherwise she is a little girl and not yet marriageable, if her breasts have not yet appeared—that is, if she does not find herself ready to rejoice with others or inclined to suffer with them. If such a person is perhaps appointed to the care of souls or the office of preaching, she benefits others not at all, while harming herself greatly. And to thrust oneself forward in this way—what great impudence it is!

2. But let us return to the bride’s breasts; and, according to the distinction of the breasts, let us set forth different kinds of milk. Rejoicing with others pours out the milk of exhortation; compassion, the milk of consolation. The spiritual mother, moreover, feels that both kinds are abundantly sprinkled from heaven upon her devout breast as often as she receives the kiss. You may see her immediately bend over the little ones to nurse them with full breasts, ministering more abundantly from one consoling milk and from the other exhorting milk, as she sees is suitable for each.

For example, if she finds any one of those whom she has begotten in the Gospel shaken by some severe temptation, troubled and sad because of it, and made faint-hearted, so that he can no longer bear the force of temptation—how she suffers with him, how she soothes him! How she laments, how she consoles! How many arguments of compassion she immediately discovers by which to raise one who is desolate! Conversely, if she knows someone to be ready, cheerful, and progressing well, she rejoices, approaches him with wholesome counsels, kindles him yet more, instructs him, so far as she can, to persevere, and exhorts him always [1292] to advance to better things. She conforms herself to all, takes upon herself the feelings of all, and proves herself a mother no less to those who fail than to those who advance.

3. How many today show themselves disposed otherwise! I speak of those who have undertaken to govern souls. For, to say what cannot be said without grievous groaning, they melt down Christ’s reproaches, spittle, scourges, nails, lance, cross, and death—all these things—in the furnace of avarice, squander them in pursuit of shameful gain, and hasten to enclose the price of the whole universe in their purses. They differ from Judas Iscariot only in this: he reckoned all the profit from these things at the number of a few denarii; these, with greedier hunger for gain, demand limitless sums of money.

They yearn for these with insatiable desire; for their sake they fear lest they lose them; when they lose them, they grieve; and in love of them they find rest, insofar as they are free from the care of keeping or increasing them. They take no account of the fall or salvation of souls. They are surely not mothers: though they have grown excessively fat, corpulent, and swollen from the patrimony of the Crucified, they do not suffer with the ruin of Joseph [Col. 0820D] (Amos 6:6).

A true mother does not conceal herself; she has breasts, and they are not empty. She knows how to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep; she does not cease to press from the breast of rejoicing with others the milk of exhortation, and from the breast of compassion the milk of consolation. Let this suffice concerning the bride’s breasts or their milk.

4. I shall now show with what ointments the same breasts give forth fragrance—if indeed I am helped by your prayers, so that what I have been given to feel about this may also be given me to speak worthily for the profit of the hearers. The Bridegroom’s ointments are one thing and the bride’s another, just as each has its own breasts. But where the Bridegroom’s are to be treated has been set forth above; now let us attend to the bride’s ointments, and more carefully, since Scripture has commended them not moderately, declaring them not simply good but the best.

I shall set forth various sorts of ointment, so that from among many we may select those most suited to the bride’s breasts. There is an ointment of contrition, an ointment of devotion, and one of compassion. The first is pungent, causing pain; the second moderating, soothing pain; the third healing, even expelling disease. Let us now discuss each more fully.

5. There is, then, an ointment which a soul entangled in many crimes prepares for itself when it begins to consider its ways: it gathers, piles together, and crushes in the mortar of conscience the many and varied spices of its sins; then, in the pot of its burning breast, cooks them all together over a certain fire of repentance and grief, so that it may say with the Prophet: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire shall be kindled” [Col. 0821B] (Ps. 38:4). Behold, this is one ointment with which the sinful soul ought to season the beginnings of its conversion and apply it to its fresh wounds.

For the first sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit. Therefore, while, poor and needy as it is, it has nothing with which to compound for itself a better and more precious ointment, let it not neglect meanwhile to prepare this one, even though from lowly spices; for “a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:19). It will appear less lowly in the sight of God in proportion as the soul has made itself more lowly in remembering its sins.

6. Yet if we say that this invisible and spiritual ointment was prefigured by that visible ointment with which, visibly, the bodily feet of God are said in the Gospel to have been anointed by the sinful woman, [Col. 0821C] we cannot consider it altogether lowly. For what is written of that ointment? “And the house,” it says, “was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12:3).

> [Note: [Col. 0821D] In this passage—as also elsewhere more than once, in Sermon 3 on the Assumption, etc.—the sinful woman mentioned in Luke, chapter 7, is confused with Mary, sister of Lazarus and Martha, who anointed the feet of Christ the Lord with ointment in the village of Bethany in John, chapter 12, where the house is said to have been filled with the fragrance of the ointment. But most of the ancients before Gregory the Great, indeed not a few more recent writers, distinguish the one from the other by weighty arguments, and distinguish both also from Mary Magdalene, from whom Christ cast out seven demons, according to Mark, chapter 16; she followed Christ with others in Luke, chapter 8, and before the sinful woman’s conversion, as they think. Compare Sermon 12 below, no. 6.]

It was distilled by the hands of a sinful woman and poured upon the lowest members of the body, that is, the feet; [1293] yet it was not so contemptible or lowly that the power of its spices and the sweetness of its fragrance did not fill the whole house. And if we consider how great a fragrance is spread through the Church at the conversion of one sinner, and how great an aroma of life unto life any penitent becomes if he repents publicly and perfectly, we shall surely pronounce with no less certainty concerning this ointment too: “The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.”

Finally, the fragrance of repentance reaches even the heavenly dwellings of the blessed, so that, as Truth himself testifies, there is great joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10). Rejoice, penitents; take courage, faint-hearted persons. I speak to you who, recently converted from the world and turning away from your crooked ways, are immediately seized by bitterness and confusion of a repentant soul, and are tortured and troubled, as it were, by the excessive pain of still-fresh wounds. Let your hands securely distill the bitterness of myrrh into this wholesome anointing; [Col. 0822A] for God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart. Such an anointing is not at all to be despised or deemed lowly; its fragrance not only urges people toward amendment but also invites angels to exult.

7. But there is an ointment certainly much more precious than this one, because it is composed of better spices. That its spices may not have to be sought far away, we find them among ourselves without difficulty and can readily take an abundant supply of them from our own gardens whenever necessity requires. For who, if he does not conceal them, does not have his own iniquities and sins sufficiently at hand whenever he wishes? These, as you recognize, are the spices of the first ointment, which I have already described.

But the spices of this second ointment are not produced by our earth; rather, we seek them far off, from the ends of the earth. For “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17). This ointment is made from the divine benefits bestowed upon the human race. Blessed is the person who takes care diligently to gather these for himself and bring them back before the eyes of his mind with worthy thanksgiving. Certainly, when they have been pounded and crushed in the vessel of the breast by the pestle of frequent meditation, then all cooked together over the fire of holy desire and finally enriched with the oil of gladness, the anointing will be far more precious and excellent than the former.

The testimony of him who says, “A sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Ps. 49:23), is sufficient proof of this. Nor is there any doubt that the remembrance of benefits incites one to praise.

8. Moreover, since Scripture testifies of that other ointment only that it is not despised, it is clear that this one is more highly commended, because it even honors. Finally, the former is applied to the feet; this one to the head. For if in Christ the head is to be referred to divinity, as Paul says, “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3), then without doubt one who gives thanks anoints the head, because he touches God, not man.

This is not because he who is God is not man—for Christ is one, both God and man—but because every good thing is from God, not from man, even the good that is administered through a human being. For “it is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” [Col. 0822D] (John 6:64). Therefore “cursed is the man who puts his hope in man” (Jer. 17:5). For although all our hope deservedly rests upon the God-man, it rests upon him not because he is man, but because he is God.

Thus the former is offered to the feet, this to the head: because the humiliation of a contrite heart corresponds to the lowliness of the flesh, while glorification befits majesty. Behold what ointment I have set before you—an ointment by which that awful head does not deem itself dishonored when touched, even by principalities; indeed, it judges it a mark of honor, saying: “A sacrifice of praise will honor me.”

9. For this reason it is not for a soul that is poor and needy, or small of heart, to prepare an anointing of this kind—an anointing whose spices and ingredients are possessed by confidence alone, though it descends from the freedom of the spirit and purity of heart. For a faint-hearted mind and one of little faith is constrained by the scantiness of its material resources; and, because of poverty, it cannot find leisure to devote itself to divine praises, or to the contemplation of those benefits which give rise to praise. And if at some time it does indeed attempt to rise, it is immediately recalled to its own concerns by the pressing anxieties of domestic necessities, and compelled by its own want to contract into itself.

If the cause of this misery is sought from me, I shall say what you yourselves, unless I am mistaken, will recognize either to be or to have been in you. This sickness and distrust of mind seem to arise from two causes: either from the newness of conversion, or from lukewarmness in one’s manner of life, even though one may have been long in conversion. Both certainly humble and cast down the conscience, and make it restless, while it still feels, whether owing to recent conversion or to lukewarmness, the old passions of the soul not yet dead within it. And thus, being obliged to attend to cutting out from the garden of the heart the thorns of wickedness and the nettles of desires, it is not permitted to wander far from itself.

For what? Can one who labours in groaning at the same time exult in the praises of God?
