How will that saying of Isaiah—namely, “thanksgiving and the voice of praise” (Isa. 51:3)—sound alike in the mouth of one groaning and weeping? For, as we learn from the Wise Man: “Music in mourning is an untimely tale” (Ecclus. 22:6). Thanksgiving follows a benefit; it does not precede it. But a soul still in sorrow does not rejoice in a benefit; rather, it is in need. It therefore has something for which to offer prayers, but not something for which to render thanks. For how shall it call to mind a benefit which it has not received? Rightly, then, I said that it does not belong to a poor soul to prepare this ointment, which ought to be composed from the recollection of divine benefits; for it cannot see the light while it is looking upon darkness. It is in bitterness: the sad remembrance of sins occupies its memory, and it has no wish to admit anything joyful at the same time.

Therefore the prophetic Spirit declares to such persons: “It is vain for you to rise before the light” (Ps. 127:2). That is: You rise in vain to contemplate benefits that delight, unless you first receive the light of consolation concerning the offences which trouble you. This ointment, then, is not for the poor.

10. But see who may deservedly glory in its abundance. “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41). They had indeed absorbed much of the richness of the Spirit, whose gentleness yielded, I do not say to words, but not even to blows. For they were rich in charity, which no expenditure exhausts, and from it they could readily offer rich holocausts. Their sweating breasts poured abroad everywhere the holy liquid with which they were most fully imbued, when they spoke in diverse tongues “the mighty works of God, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:11, 4).

Nor is there any doubt that those also abounded in the same ointments to whom the Apostle bore witness, saying: “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God which was given to you in Christ Jesus; because in all things you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you, so that you lack no grace” (1 Cor. 1:4–7). Would that I too might render these same thanks on your behalf: that I might see you rich in virtues, eager in the praises of God, and more abundantly overflowing in this spiritual richness in Christ Jesus our Lord.

## SERMON XI. On the two matters—namely, the fruit and the manner—belonging to the work of human redemption.

[Col. 0824B]

1. At the end of the sermon I said—and I do not shrink from repeating it—that I desire you all to become participants in the sacred anointing: that, namely, in which holy devotion recalls God’s benefits with joy and thanksgiving. This is good, both because it lightens the labours of this present life, which are certainly made more bearable for us when we exult in God’s praise; and because nothing represents on earth so properly a state of the heavenly dwelling as does the gladness of those who praise God. For Scripture says: “Blessed are they who dwell in thy house, O Lord; they shall praise thee for ever and ever” (Ps. 84:5).

I think that it was especially of this ointment that the Prophet said: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity; like ointment upon the head” (Ps. 133:1). For it does not seem capable of applying to the former ointment. That ointment, though good, is not pleasant, because the recollection of sins produces bitterness, not delight. Nor do those who make it dwell together in unity, since each person mourns and laments his own sins. But those who occupy themselves with thanksgiving look upon and think only of God; and in this respect they truly dwell together in unity. What they do is good, because they most justly preserve for him the glory that is his; and it is no less pleasant, because it delights.

2. Therefore, my friends, I advise you occasionally to turn back your foot from the burdensome and anxious recollection of your own ways, and to escape into the smoother paths of the more serene remembrance of God’s benefits, so that you who are ashamed when you look at yourselves may breathe again when you look upon him. I wish you to experience what the holy Prophet counsels, saying: “Delight thyself in the Lord, and he will give thee the petitions of thy heart” (Ps. 37:4).

Sorrow for sins is indeed necessary, but it must not be unceasing. Let it certainly be interspersed with a more joyful recollection of divine goodness, lest the heart perhaps become hardened through sadness and perish the more through despair. Let us mix honey with wormwood, so that wholesome bitterness may then confer health when, moderated by an added sweetness, it can be drunk. Hear, finally, how God himself tempers the bitterness of a contrite heart; how he recalls the faint-hearted from the abyss of despair; how, with the honey of a gentle and faithful promise, he consoles the mourner and raises the distrustful.

He says through the prophet: “I will bridle thy mouth with my praise, lest thou perish” (Isa. 48:9). That is: “Lest, by looking upon your crimes, you fall into excessive sorrow and, like an unbridled horse, rush desperately over a precipice and perish, I shall restrain you,” he says, “with the bridle of my forgiveness, and I shall raise you up by my praises. You will breathe again in my blessings, though you are ashamed of your own evils, since you will find me more merciful than you are guilty.” Had Cain been bridled with this bridle, he would never in despair have said: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve to be forgiven” (Gen. 4:13). Far be it, far be it. For God’s mercy is greater than any iniquity.

Therefore the righteous man is an accuser of himself not continuously, but only “at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17); afterwards he is accustomed to close the end of his speech with God’s praises. See, then, the righteous man proceeding in this order: “I considered my ways, and turned my feet unto thy testimonies” (Ps. 119:59), so that he who had suffered contrition and misery in his own ways might delight in the way of God’s testimonies as in all riches. You likewise, then, following the example of the righteous man, if you think of yourselves with humility, think also of the Lord with goodness. For thus you read in the Book of Wisdom: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1:1).

The frequent—indeed continual—recollection of divine generosity [or: magnificence] readily persuades the mind of this. Otherwise, how will that apostolic saying be fulfilled: “Giving thanks in all things” (1 Thess. 5:17), if the things for which thanks are owed have departed from the heart? I do not want you to be marked with the Jewish reproach, of whom Scripture testifies that “they remembered not his benefits, nor his wonders which he showed them” (Ps. 78:11).

3. But since it is impossible for any person to recall and gather together all the good things which the merciful and compassionate Lord never ceases to bestow upon mortals—for “who shall declare the powers of the Lord, or make known all his praises?” (Ps. 106:2)—let at least that work which is chief and greatest, namely the work of our redemption, not altogether depart from the memory of the redeemed.

In this work I shall endeavour to set before your attention two matters which now occur to me, and to do so as briefly and concisely as I can, mindful of that saying: “Give occasion to a wise man, and he will be wiser still” (Prov. 9:9). These two matters are the manner and the fruit. The manner is God’s emptying of himself; the fruit is our being filled from him. To meditate on the latter is the seedbed of holy hope; to meditate on the former is the incentive of highest love. Both are necessary for our advancement, lest hope be mercenary if it is not accompanied by love, or love grow lukewarm if it is thought fruitless.

4. We expect such a fruit of our love as he whom we love has promised: “A measure, full and pressed down and shaken together and overflowing, they shall give into your bosom” (Luke 6:38). This measure, as I hear, will be without measure. But I should like to know of what thing that measure—or rather that immensity which is promised—will consist. “Eye hath not seen, O God, besides thee, what things thou hast prepared for them that love thee” (Isa. 64:4). Tell us, thou who preparest: what dost thou prepare?

We believe and trust, truly, as thou promisest: “We shall be filled with the good things of thy house” (Ps. 65:5). But with what goods, I ask, or of what kind? Perhaps with grain, wine, and oil; gold and silver; or precious stones? But these we know and have seen; we see them, and we are weary of them. We seek that which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the heart of man. Whatever it may be, that is what it pleases us, what tastes sweet to us, what delights us to seek. “They shall all be taught by God” (John 6:45), and “he shall be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28). As I hear it, the fullness which we await from God will be nothing but God.

5. Who can comprehend how great a multitude of sweetness is contained in this brief saying: “God shall be all in all”? To say nothing of the body, I discern three things in the soul: reason, will, and memory; and these three are the soul itself. Everyone who walks in the Spirit feels [or: knows] how much each of these lacks, in this present age, of its integrity and perfection. Why is this, except because God is not yet all in all?

Hence reason very often errs in its judgments; the will is tossed by a fourfold disturbance; and memory is confused by manifold forgetfulness. This noble creature is subjected unwillingly to this threefold vanity, yet in hope. For he who will fill the desire of the soul with good things will be for reason fullness of light; he will be for the will an abundance of peace; he will be for memory the continuance of eternity. O truth, charity, eternity! O blessed and beatifying Trinity! To thee my wretched trinity sighs most miserably, because it is unhappily exiled from thee. In departing from thee, into how many errors, sorrows, and fears it has entangled itself! Alas for me! What a trinity have we exchanged for thee!

“My heart is troubled,” and from this comes sorrow; “my strength hath forsaken me,” and from this comes fear; “and the light of mine eyes is not with me” (Ps. 38:11), and from this comes error. Behold, O trinity of my soul, what a dissimilar trinity you have displayed in your exile.

6. Yet why art thou sad, O my soul? And why dost thou trouble me? “Hope in God, for I shall yet give thanks to him” (Ps. 42:6), when error has departed from reason, sorrow from the will, and every fear from memory; and when there succeeds that wondrous serenity which we hope for, full sweetness, and eternal security. The first will be effected by God the Truth; the second by God the Charity; the third by God the supreme Power: so that God may be all in all, with reason receiving unquenchable light, will attaining undisturbed peace, and memory adhering eternally to the unfailing fountain.

Consider whether you rightly assign the first to the Son, the second to the Holy Spirit, and the last to the Father—yet in such a way that you take none of these things away from Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, lest the distinction diminish the fullness of any person or perfection abolish a proper characteristic. Observe also what likeness the children of this age experience through the enticements of the flesh, the spectacles of the world, and the pomps of Satan. Yet this entire thing is that by which the present life deceives its wretched lovers, as John says: “All that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (1 John 2:16).

This is concerning the fruit of redemption.

7. In the manner also—which, if you remember, we defined as God’s emptying of himself—I commend [or: entrust] three matters especially to your consideration. For that emptying was neither simple nor slight; rather, “he emptied himself” unto flesh, unto death, unto the cross (Phil. 2:7–8). Who can worthily weigh how great was the humility, gentleness, and condescension involved in the Lord of majesty being clothed with flesh, punished by death, and disgraced by the cross?

But someone says: “Could not the Creator restore his work without this difficulty?” He could; but he preferred to do so at injury to himself, lest the utterly worst and most hateful vice of ingratitude find any further occasion in man. He willingly undertook much weariness in order to hold man indebted for great love; and so that the difficulty of redemption might remind of thanksgiving one whom the ease of creation had made less devout.

For what did the created and ungrateful man say? “I was certainly created freely, but with no burden or labour on the Creator’s part. For he spoke, and I was made, just as all things were. What great matter is it, however great the things you have given through the ease of a word?” Thus human impiety, diminishing the benefit of creation, drew from it material for ingratitude where it ought to have had a reason for love [*habere debuerat*, “ought to have had”; variant: *debebat*, “was bound to have”], and used this “to make excuses in sins.” But the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped.

It is clearer than light how great a loss he has now suffered for you, O man: from Lord to servant, from rich to poor, from Word to flesh, and from Son of God to son of man, he did not disdain to become. Remember now that although you were made from nothing, you were not redeemed for nothing. In six days he created all things, including you among all things. But for a full thirty years he worked your salvation in the midst of the earth. O how greatly he laboured and endured! The necessities of flesh and the temptations of the enemy—did he not make them heavier for himself by the disgrace of the cross and add to them the terror of death? This was necessary indeed. Thus, thus hast thou saved men and beasts, O Lord: according as thou hast multiplied thy mercy, O God (Ps. 36:7–8).

8. Meditate upon these things; occupy yourselves with them. Refresh your inward parts with such perfumes, which the more offensive smell of sins has long tortured, so that you may abound also in these ointments, no less sweet than salutary. Yet do not suppose that you have already attained those best ointments which are commended in the bride’s breasts. The narrowness imposed by the sermon’s approaching conclusion prevents me from beginning upon them now. Keep in memory what has been said concerning the others; prove it in life. And aid me concerning these by your prayers, that I may worthily speak what is worthy of the bride’s so great delights, and may build up your souls unto love of the Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

## SERMON XII. On the precious ointment of mercy, and on the reverence to be shown by subjects toward their prelates.

[Col. 0828A]

1. I remember that I have delivered to you two ointments: one of contrition, embracing many sins; the other of devotion, containing many benefits. Both are salutary, but not both sweet. The first is felt to be pungent, because the bitter recollection of sins moves to compunction and produces sorrow. The second, which follows, is soothing, because the contemplation of divine goodness gives consolation and calms sorrow.

But there is an ointment which far surpasses both. You may call it the ointment of mercy, because it is made from the needs of the poor, the anxieties of the oppressed, the disturbances of the sorrowful, the faults of offenders, and finally from every misery of all wretched persons, even if they are enemies. These ingredients appear contemptible; but the ointment prepared from them is above all perfumes. It is healing, for “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7).

Thus many miseries, gathered together and considered with the eye of compassion, are themselves the ingredients from which the best ointments are composed, worthy of the bride’s breasts and pleasing to the Bridegroom’s senses. Blessed is the mind which has taken care to enrich and fatten itself by collecting such perfumes, pouring them into the oil of mercy and boiling them with the fire of charity. Who, think you, is “the gracious man who hath mercy and lendeth” (Ps. 112:5)? One inclined to compassion, prompt to help, judging it more blessed to give than to receive; quick to forgive, slow to anger, wholly unwilling to take revenge; and in all things regarding the needs of neighbours as he does his own.

O soul, whoever you are, thus disposed, thus steeped in the dew of mercy, thus overflowing with bowels of compassion, thus making yourself all things to all, thus making yourself like a ruined vessel, so that you may everywhere and always be ready to meet and assist others; thus, finally, dead to yourself so that you may live for all: you indeed happily possess the third and best ointment, and your hands have distilled a liquid of every sweetness. It shall not dry up in an evil time, nor shall the heat of persecution drink it up. Rather, God shall always remember every sacrifice of yours, and your holocaust shall become rich.

2. There are men of riches in the city of the Lord of hosts. I ask whether these ointments may be found in any of them. First there occurs to me, as is his custom everywhere, Paul, the vessel of election: truly an aromatic vessel, a fragrant vessel, filled with every powder of spices. For he was “the good odour of Christ unto God in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15). That breast, which had been so affected by concern for all the churches, certainly diffused the fragrance of much sweetness far and wide.

See what ingredients and perfumes he had heaped up for himself: “I die daily by your glory” (1 Cor. 15:31); and again, “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Cor. 11:29). This rich man abounded in many such things, well known to you, for compounding the best ointments. For it befitted the breasts which nourished Christ’s members—of whom Paul was certainly a mother, travailing once and again until Christ should be formed in them (Gal. 4:19), and the members be re-formed to their Head—to exhale the scent of the first and purest perfumes.

3. Hear also of another rich man, how he had at hand choice ingredients from which to prepare the best ointments. “The stranger did not remain outside; my door was open to the traveller” (Job 31:32). Likewise: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor; I broke the jaws of the wicked man and drew the prey out of his teeth” (Job 29:15–17). “If I denied to the poor what they desired, and made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat of it; if I despised the passer-by—

> [Note: [Col. 0829] This is the old reading; the Vulgate now has “the perishing man” (*pereuntem*), according to the Hebrew text and the Greek of the Seventy Interpreters.]

—because he had no garment, or the poor man without a covering; if his sides did not bless me, and he was not warmed by the fleeces of my sheep” (Job 31:16–20).

How great an odour, we think, did this man scatter over the earth by these works! Each work was a separate perfume. With these he filled his own conscience, so that by an exhalation of inner sweetness he might temper for himself the stench of putrid flesh.

4. After Joseph had made the whole of Egypt run after him through the odour of his ointments, he at last offered that same fragrance even to those who had sold him. He indeed spoke words of rebuke with an angry expression; but tears burst forth from the richness of his heart (Gen. 43:30; 45:2), not signs of anger but disclosures of favour. Samuel mourned Saul (1 Kings [Col. 0829C] 4:35), who sought to kill him; and, as his breast grew warm with the fire of charity and melted inwardly, the fat of mercy flowed outward through his eyes.

Finally, because of the good odour of his reputation which he diffused everywhere, Scripture reports of him that “all Israel, from Dan even to Bersheba, knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord” (1 Sam. 3:20). What shall I say of Moses? With how much fat and richness had he too filled his inward parts! Not even that provoking house in which he lived for a time could ever, amid all its murmuring and fury, drive out the anointing of the Spirit with which he had once been imbued, so as to prevent him, amid continual quarrels and daily disputes, from persevering in his gentleness.

Rightly the Holy Spirit testified of him that he was “the meekest of all men who dwelt upon the earth” (Num. 12:3). For with those who hated peace he was peaceable (Ps. 120:7), so much so that he not only did not grow angry with the ungrateful and rebellious people, but by his intercession even softened an angry God, as it is written: “He said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath lest he should destroy them” (Ps. 106:23). Finally he says: “If thou wilt forgive them, forgive; but if not, blot me out of thy book which thou hast written” (Exod. 32:31–32).

O truly a man anointed with the anointing of mercy! He plainly speaks with a parent’s affection: no happiness can delight him apart from those whom he brought forth. For example, suppose a rich man says to a poor woman: “Come in to my banquet, but leave outside the little child whom you carry, because he cries and is troublesome to us.” Would she do it? Would she not rather choose to fast than, having abandoned her dear pledge, dine alone with the rich man? So Moses cannot bear to be admitted alone into the joy of his Lord while the people remain outside—a people to whom, though restless and ungrateful, he clings equally in the role and affection of a mother. His inward parts suffer pain, yet he judges the torture more tolerable than the tearing away.

5. What was gentler than David, who mourned the death of one who had always thirsted for his own? (2 Sam. 1:11.) What was more kindly than that he should grieve at the death of the man whose successor in the kingdom he became? And how reluctantly did he accept consolation for the death of his parricidal son? (2 Sam. 19:4.) Such affection plainly displayed a great abundance of the best ointment. Therefore he prayed confidently: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness” (Ps. 132:1).

Therefore all these possessed the best ointments, by which they even today give forth the sweetest fragrance throughout all the churches. Nor only they, but all who in this life have shown themselves so benevolent and beneficent, who have sought to live humanely among men in such a way that they did not keep to themselves whatever grace they seemed to possess, but brought it into common use—considering themselves debtors alike to friends and enemies, wise and foolish. Being useful to all, humble in all things, and above all beloved by God and men, their fragrance is in blessing.

All such persons, I say, who have gone before have been fragrant with the best ointments in their own times, and are fragrant with them today. You too, if you gladly share with us who dwell with you the gift which you have received from above; if you show yourself among us everywhere serviceable, affectionate, grateful, approachable, and humble, will receive testimony from all that you too exhale the fragrance of the best ointments.

Everyone among you who not only bears patiently the infirmities of the brethren, both of body and soul, but also, when permitted and able, assists them by services, strengthens them by words, instructs them by counsel [the variant adds: “and relieves them”]; or, if discipline prevents this, at least does not cease to comfort the infirm person by earnest prayers—everyone, I say, who does such things among you spreads a good odour among the brethren, an odour from the best ointments. Such a brother is balm in the mouth of the congregation; he is pointed out, and all say of him: “This is a lover of the brethren and of the people of Israel; this is he who prays much for the people and for the whole holy city” (2 Macc. 15:14).

6. But let us return to the Gospel and seek something which may perhaps bear upon these ointments also. “Mary Magdalene, and Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, that, coming, they might anoint Jesus” (Mark 16:1). What ointments are these, so precious that they are prepared and procured for Christ’s body, so abundant that they suffice for the whole of it? For neither of the two preceding ointments is read to have been bought, or specially made for the Lord’s service, or poured over his whole body.

> [Note: [Col. 0831D] Several manuscripts omit “bought” (*emptum*).]

But suddenly a woman is introduced, in one place kissing his feet and anointing them with ointment (Luke 7:38; John 12:3); in another place, either the same woman or another, having an alabaster flask of ointment and pouring it upon his head (Mark 14:3). But now, he says, “They bought spices, that, coming, they might anoint Jesus.” They buy not ointments but spices; and the anointing is not one made for the Lord’s service and then taken up, but a new one is prepared. Nor is it for anointing only some part of the body, such as the feet or head; but, as it is written, “that, coming, they might anoint Jesus”: this is an embracing of the whole, not a distinction of a part.

7. You also, if you put on bowels of mercy and show yourself generous and kind—not merely toward your parents or relatives, or those whom you count your benefactors or hope will become such, for “the Gentiles also do this” (Matt. 5:47)—but, in accordance with Paul’s counsel, strive “to work good toward all” (Gal. 6:10), so that for God’s sake you judge that no bodily or spiritual office of humanity is to be denied or withheld even from an enemy: it is clear that you too abound in the best ointments. You have undertaken to anoint not merely the Lord’s head or feet but, wherever you can, his whole body, which is the Church.

And perhaps for this reason the Lord Jesus did not wish an anointing prepared for him to be expended upon his dead body: he wished to preserve it for his living body. For the Church lives, which eats the living bread that came down from heaven. She is Christ’s more cherished body; no Christian is unaware that, so that she might not taste death, that other body was handed over to death. He desires that she be anointed and cherished; he desires that her infirm members be raised by more attentive care.

Therefore he retained the precious ointments for her. Anticipating the hour and hastening glory, he did not frustrate the devotion of the women but instructed it. He refused to be anointed, but spared rather than despised it; he did not reject the service but reserved its usefulness. I mean usefulness not of this material and bodily ointment, but plainly of the spiritual ointment signified by it. Thus the Master of mercy spared the best ointments of mercy, which he entirely desired to be supplied to his needy members both bodily and spiritually.

For shortly before, when ointment, itself quite precious, was poured upon his head or even upon his feet, did he forbid it? On the contrary, he even opposed those who forbade it. To Simon, who was indignant that he allowed himself to be touched by a sinful woman, he delivered an extended parable of rebuke; and to others, who complained of the waste of ointment, he answered: “Why do you trouble this woman?”

8. Sometimes, to make a slight digression, when I sat mourning at Jesus’ feet, offering the sacrifice of an afflicted spirit in remembrance of my sins; or when, if only rarely, I stood at his head and exulted in remembrance of his benefits, I heard people saying: “Why this waste?” They alleged, that is, that I lived for myself alone, though, as they thought, I might benefit many people. And they said: “It could have been sold for much and given to the poor” (Matt. 26:8–10).

But it is no good bargain for me, even if I gain the whole world, to lose myself and suffer loss of myself. Recognizing these words as those “dying flies” of which Scripture speaks, which spoil the sweetness of ointment (Eccles. 10:1), I remembered that divine sentence: “My people, they who call thee blessed lead thee into error” (Isa. 3:12). But let those who accuse me as though I were idle hear the Lord excusing and answering on my behalf: “Why,” he says, “do you trouble this woman?” That is: “You see according to outward appearance, and therefore judge according to outward appearance. He is not a man, as you suppose, able to put his hand to mighty deeds, but a woman. Why do you attempt to lay upon him a yoke for which I see that he is insufficient? He does a good work in me. Let him remain in what is good until he grows strong enough for what is better. When he has advanced from womanhood into manhood, into the perfect man, he may also be taken up into the work of perfection.”

9. Brothers, let us reverence bishops, but let us fear their labours. If we weigh their labours, we shall not covet their honours. Let us acknowledge the inequality of our strength, and let us not delight to place soft and womanly shoulders under the burdens of men. Let us not scrutinize them, but honour them. For you inhumanely censure the works of those whose burdens you refuse. A woman spinning at home rashly rebukes a man returning from battle.

I say this: if one who is in a cloister finds one who lives among the people sometimes acting less strictly or less circumspectly—for example, in speech, food, sleep, laughter, anger, or judgment—let him not immediately leap forward to judge, but remember what is written: “Better is the iniquity of a man than a beneficent woman” (Ecclus. 42:14). For you, indeed, do well in keeping watch over yourself; but he who helps many does better and acts more manfully. If he cannot accomplish this without some iniquity—that is, without a certain inequality in his life and manner of living—remember that “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

Let these things be said against the twofold temptation by which religious men are often stirred, through diabolical promptings, either to seek the glory of bishops or rashly to judge their excesses.

10. But let us return to the bride’s ointments. Do you see how this ointment of mercy is to be preferred above the others, since of it alone it is not permitted to make a waste? So far is there no waste made of it that even the gift of a cup of cold water is not allowed to go unrewarded (Matt. 10:42).

The ointment of contrition, however, which is made from the remembrance of sins and poured upon the Lord’s feet, is good, because “a contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Ps. 51:19). Yet I judge far better that which is called the ointment of devotion, made from remembrance of God’s benefits, since it is reckoned worthy even for the head, so that God says of it: “The sacrifice of praise shall glorify me” (Ps. 50:23).

But the anointing of mercy surpasses both: it is made from regard for the wretched and spread throughout Christ’s whole body. I mean not the body that was crucified, but that which was acquired by his passion. This is truly the best ointment, in comparison with which he who says, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Matt. 9:13), shows that he does not even look upon the others. Therefore I think that, among the bride’s virtues, her breasts especially breathe the odour of mercy, since she desires in every respect to conform to the Bridegroom’s will. Did not Tabitha give forth the fragrance of mercy even in death? And therefore she quickly recovered from death (Acts 9:39–41), because the odour of life prevailed.

11. But hear a brief word upon the present chapter. Whoever both intoxicates with words and gives forth fragrance in good deeds should understand the words as addressed to himself: “Because thy breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the best ointments” (Song 1:1–2). Yet who is sufficient for these things? Which one of us possesses even one of them wholly and perfectly, so as not sometimes to be less fruitful in speaking and more lukewarm in acting?

But there is one who deservedly and without doubt glories in this praise: namely, the Church, who never lacks in her entirety both that by which she may intoxicate and that by which she may give fragrance. For what is lacking to her in one person she possesses in another, according to the measure of Christ’s gift and the distribution of the Spirit, who divides to each as he wills (Eph. 4:7; 1 Cor. 12:11). The Church is fragrant in those who make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity; she intoxicates in ministers of the word, who pour the wine of spiritual joy upon the earth, make it drunk, and bear fruit in patience.

She boldly and confidently calls herself the bride, as one who truly possesses breasts better than wine and fragrant with the best ointments. Though none of us should presume to claim this for himself, so that he would dare to call his own soul the bride of the Lord, yet because we belong to the Church—which deservedly glories both in this name and in the reality denoted by the name—we rightly claim a share in this glory. For what we all together possess fully and wholly, each of us shares without contradiction.

Thanks be to thee, Lord Jesus, who hast deigned to join us to thy most beloved Church, not only that we might be faithful, but also that we might be united to thee, in the bride’s role, in embraces joyful, chaste, and eternal; we too with unveiled face beholding thy glory, which thou dost share alike with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. On glory and praise always to be attributed to God for all his good things bestowed upon us.

1. The sea is the source of all springs and rivers; [Col. 0834A] the Lord Jesus Christ is the source of virtues and kinds of knowledge. For who is the Lord of hosts except he, the King of glory? And, according to Hannah’s song, this same God is the Lord of knowledge (1 Kings 2:3). Bodily continence, diligence of heart, rectitude of will—all flow from that fountain. Nor only these: if anyone is acute in intellect, distinguished in speech, or pleasing in character, that too comes from it. From it come knowledge and the word of wisdom. For all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden there (Col. 2:3). What then? Are not chaste counsels, just judgments, holy desires, 1302 streams of that fountain? And if abundant waters constantly return to the seas through hidden underground courses, so that from there they may again burst forth, in unceasing and tireless service, for our sight and use, why should not [Col. 0834B] spiritual streams likewise be returned, without deceit and without interruption, to their own fountain, so that they may never cease watering the fields of minds? Let the rivers of grace return to the place from which they issue, that they may flow again. Let the heavenly outpouring be sent back to its source, so that it may be poured out upon the earth more abundantly. “How?” you ask. As the Apostle says: “Giving thanks in all things” (1 Thess. 5:18). Whatever wisdom or virtue you are confident you possess, ascribe it to Christ, God’s power and God’s wisdom.

2. “And who,” you say, “is so mad as to presume otherwise?” Certainly no one—so much so that even the Pharisee gives thanks (Luke 18:11), though the praise of his righteousness is not from God. For, if you remember the Gospel rightly, that act of thanksgiving does not make him more acceptable. Why? Because whatever devoutness may sound upon his lips does not [Col. 0834C] suffice to excuse the swelling of his heart before him who knows the lofty from afar (Ps. 137:6). God, O Pharisee, is not mocked. Do you suppose that you possess anything which you have not received? “Nothing,” you say; “and therefore I give thanks to the giver.” If absolutely nothing, then no merit whatever preceded in you by which you received those things in which you boast. If you acknowledge even this, first, you are vainly puffed up against the tax collector, who does not have what you have because he has not received as you have. Then see also whether you do not fail to surrender God’s gifts wholly to God; for, by bending some part of his glory and honour back toward yourself, you deserve to be charged with fraud—fraud against God.

For if you should perhaps claim for yourself something, from yourself, in the things of which you boast, I would think that you were deceived rather than willing to defraud, and I would correct your error. [Col. 0834D] But now, because in giving thanks you show that you prudently recognize that you attribute nothing to yourself and that your merits are God’s gifts, yet by despising others you reveal what you have said in your heart: with one heart lending the tongue to falsehood, with the other arrogating the glory of truth. For you would not judge the tax collector to be contemptible in comparison with yourself unless you considered yourself worthy of honour above him. But what do you answer to the Apostle, who prescribes and says: “To God alone be honour and glory” (1 Tim. 1:17)? What to the angel, who distinguishes and teaches what God chooses to retain for himself and what he deigns to share with human beings? For he says: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). Do you see the Pharisee, in giving thanks, honouring God with his lips indeed, but himself in the judgment of his heart?

[Col. 0835A] Thus one may observe thanksgiving resounding in the mouths of many more by habit than by understanding or affection—so much so that even the most wicked people are accustomed to give thanks to God for their crimes and misdeeds, because, as they themselves imagine, success has attended the fulfilment of their perverse wishes. You may hear, for example, a thief, when he has carried off the desired spoils of an impious scheme, exulting aloud and saying: “Thanks be to God: I did not keep watch in vain; I have not lost my night’s labour.” Likewise, one who has killed a man—does he not boast and give thanks because he prevailed over his rival or avenged himself upon an enemy? And no less does the adulterer, dancing with delight, rejoice in God’s praises because he has at last obtained the long-desired intercourse [Col. 0835B] of adultery.

3. Therefore not every act of thanksgiving is acceptable to God, but only that which proceeds from the chaste and unalloyed simplicity of the heart. I say “chaste,” certainly, because of those who, glorying even in their evil deeds, are accustomed to give God thanks as though God delighted with them when they do evil and rejoiced in their most wicked acts. Such a person will hear: “You wickedly imagined that I should be like you; I will rebuke you and set you before your own face” (Ps. 49:21). I added “unalloyed” because of hypocrites, who indeed glorify God for their good things, but only in words: in their heart they keep back what they offered with their mouth. Since they act deceitfully in his sight, their iniquity is found worthy of hatred. Those people impiously attribute their evils to God; [Col. 0835C] these fraudulently twist God’s good things toward themselves.

The first evil is indeed so foolish, so worldly, and in some sense even bestial, that I need not warn you about it. But the second commonly lies in wait especially for religious and spiritual people. It is surely a great and rare virtue that, although you do great things, you do not know yourself to be great; and that, though your holiness is manifest to all, you alone remain unaware of it. To appear admirable and yet consider yourself contemptible—I judge this more admirable than the virtues themselves. You are truly a faithful servant if, from your Lord’s abundant glory, even though it does not proceed from you but passes through you, nothing happens to cling to your hands. Then, according to the prophet, you cast away avarice—gain from oppression—and shake your hands free from every bribe (Isa. 33:15). Then, according to [Col. 0835D] the Lord’s command, your light shines before people, not to glorify you, but your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16). And, as an imitator of Paul and of faithful preachers who do not preach themselves, you likewise seek not your own interests but those of Jesus Christ (2 Cor. 4:5; Phil. 2:21). Therefore you too will hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much” (Matt. 25:21).

4. Joseph, although he knew that the house and all the goods of his Egyptian master had been entrusted to him, knew that his mistress was excepted; and therefore he did not consent to touch her. “Among all my master’s goods,” he says, “there is nothing which is not in my power, or which he has not entrusted to me, except [Col. 0836A] you, because you are his wife” (Gen. 39:9). He knew that a woman is the glory of her husband, and judged it unjust to render dishonourable, by an opposite exchange, the man who had made him glorious. The man of God, prudent in wisdom, observed that a husband strongly guards his wife as his own glory, reserving her for his own keeping and entrusting her to no one else; and he did not presume to stretch out his hand toward what had not been granted.

What then? A human being is jealous for his own glory, and does one dare to wish to defraud God of his glory as though he were not jealous for it? But hear what he says: “My glory,” he says, “I will not give to another” (Isa. 48:11). What then will you give, Lord? What will you give us? “Peace,” he says, “I give to you; my peace I leave to you” (John 14:27). It is enough for me. I gratefully receive what you leave, and I leave what you retain. Thus it pleases me; thus I do not doubt that it serves my interest.

[Col. 0836B] I utterly renounce glory, lest perhaps, if I seize what has not been granted, I deservedly lose even what has been offered. I want peace; I desire peace, and nothing more. Whoever is not satisfied with peace is not satisfied with you. For you are our peace, who have made both one (Eph. 2:14). This is necessary for me; this is enough: to be reconciled to you and reconciled to myself. For since you have set me in opposition to you, I have become burdensome even to myself (Job 7:20). I am careful neither to be ungrateful for the benefit of peace bestowed, nor sacrilegiously to invade your glory. Let your glory, Lord—your glory—remain inviolate; all is well with me if I have peace.

5. When Goliath had been struck down, the people rejoiced at peace restored; but David alone proved glorious. Joshua, Jephthah, Gideon, Samson, and Judith too, though a woman, triumphed gloriously over their enemies in their days; but while the others enjoyed peace with joy, no one shared their glory. Judas Maccabaeus too was illustrious for many victories; when, by fighting bravely, he repeatedly secured peace for a rejoicing people, did he ever share his glory with anyone? Finally, it says, “there was not glory but great joy among the people” (1 Macc. 4:58). By what lesser measure than all these did the Creator of all things act, that he should not himself also glory uniquely? He alone created all things; he alone triumphed over the enemy; he alone freed the captives—and will he have a partner in glory? “My arm,” he says, “has helped me”; and again: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and from among the nations no man was with me” (Isa. 63:5, 3).

[Col. 0836D] What then have I to do with victory, if I was not even in the battle? With the greatest insolence I claim for myself either glory without victory or victory without battle. But, mountains, receive peace for the people; receive peace for yourselves, not glory—keeping glory for him alone who alone both fought and conquered. So, I pray, let it be: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” But the person who is not of good but plainly of unjust will, dissatisfied with peace, restlessly pants with proud eye and insatiable heart even for God’s glory; and therefore he neither retains peace nor grasps glory. Who would believe a wall if it said that it gave birth to the ray which it receives through a window? Or if clouds boasted that they had generated rain, who would not laugh at them? It is perfectly clear to me that streams of water are not born from channels, [Col. 0837A] nor words of wisdom from lips or teeth, even if an understanding beyond the bodily sense does not reach this point [variant: “does not” omitted].

6. If I behold anything in the saints worthy of praise or admiration, examining it in the clear light of truth, I surely find that one thing appears praiseworthy or wonderful, and another is so in reality. Thus I praise God in his saints, whether Elisha or that great Elijah, raisers of the dead as they were. They themselves display outwardly to us things new and unheard-of, not by their own command but by their ministry; but God, abiding in them, himself performs the works. Invisible and inaccessible in himself, he is visible and wonderful in his own people—and he alone is wonderful, “who alone does wondrous things” (Ps. 71:18). The praise is not the pen’s when a painting or writing is praiseworthy; nor is a good discourse the glory of the tongue or lips.

It is time also for the prophet to speak. “Does the axe,” he says, “boast against the one who cuts with it? Or is the saw exalted against the one by whom it is drawn? As if a rod should lift itself against the one who raises it, and a staff—which is certainly wood—should exalt itself” (Isa. 10:15). So every person who boasts boasts against the Lord if he does not boast in the Lord (2 Cor. 10:17). If one is to boast, Paul has taught me whence and in whom. “This,” he says, “is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). I boast securely if, with conscience as witness, I claim for myself nothing of the Creator’s glory; securely indeed, because then I boast not against the Lord but in the Lord. This boasting is not only not forbidden us, but is even encouraged, when it is said: “You seek glory from one another, and do not [Col. 0837C] desire the glory that comes from God alone” (John 5:44). Truly, to boast in God alone comes only from God alone. Nor is this a mediocre glory: it is so true, being from truth, and so rare in truth, that scarcely even a small number of the perfect boast perfectly in it.

Let vain children of men go, then—lying children of men; let them go and deceive one another in vanity itself (Ps. 61:10). But the wise person who boasts will test his own work and carefully examine it in the light of truth; and thus he will have glory in himself, not in another’s mouth. I am foolish if I entrust my glory to the little casket of your lips and begin to beg it from you when I want to possess it. Is it not within your discretion to approve or disapprove me as you wish? But I keep it with myself; I myself guard it for myself more faithfully. Indeed, I do not entrust it even to myself: rather, I lay it up for the keeping of him who is able to guard my deposit until that day (2 Tim. 1:12), cautious in guarding and faithful in restoring it. Then each person’s praise from God will be secure—only for those who have despised human praises. For theirs is glory in shame who set their minds on earthly things; David also says: “Those who please human beings have been put to shame, because God has despised them” (Ps. 52:6).

7. Brothers, if you know these things, let none of you wish to be praised in this life; for whatever favour you gain here which you do not refer back to God, you steal from him. For whence comes glory to you, foul dust—whence to you? From holiness of life? But it is the Spirit who sanctifies: the Spirit, I say, not yours but God’s. Even if you shine with wonders and signs, [Col. 0838A] they are performed through your hand, but by God’s power. Does popular acclaim flatter you because you have perhaps delivered a good word well? But Christ gave you mouth and wisdom. For what is your tongue but a scribe’s pen? And you received even that on loan. A talent has been entrusted to you, to be demanded back with interest. If you are found diligent in work and faithful in producing fruit, you will receive a reward for your labour. If not, the talent will be taken from you; the profit will nevertheless be demanded, and you will be called a wicked and slothful servant.

Therefore let every praise for the good things of the manifold grace displayed in you be returned to him, the author and giver of all praiseworthy things. And let this be done not falsely, as by hypocrites; nor merely from habit, as by worldly people; nor under compulsion, as beasts are harnessed [Col. 0838B] to bear burdens; but as befits saints: with faithful sincerity, attentive devotion, grateful but not frivolous cheerfulness. Therefore, offering the sacrifice of praise and fulfilling our vows day by day, let us take every care to unite understanding to practice, affection to understanding, exultation to affection, seriousness to exultation, humility to seriousness, and freedom to humility. Thus at times, with the free steps of a purified mind, we may advance and, through certain unfamiliar spiritual affections, pass beyond ourselves into joys amid the delights of jubilation—in God’s light, in sweetness, in the Holy Spirit—proving ourselves to be included among those whom the prophet beheld when he said: “Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance; in your name they shall exult all day long, and in your righteousness they shall be exalted” (Ps. 88:16–17).

8. But perhaps someone will say to me: “You admonish well, but only if you were saying things suited to your purpose.” Wait a little; I have not forgotten. Is it not our task to discuss the saying, “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1:2)? This is the work; this is the labour. Whether what we set beforehand was necessary, you may judge. But now, as far as concerns me, give brief attention to why these things are not irrelevant. Do you not remember that the final excellence commended in the bride’s breasts was the sweet fragrance of ointments? What follows more fittingly than that the bride should recognize the same fragrance as a benefit from the bridegroom, lest she be thought to arrogate it to herself? You recognize [Col. 0838D] that all which we have set forth serves precisely this meaning. “That my breasts,” she says, “smell so sweetly and are so pleasing, I do not ascribe to my own efforts or merits; rather, O bridegroom, I attribute it to your generosity—from the oil poured out, namely, your name.” This is the connection according to the letter.

9. But the explanation of the chapter itself, on whose occasion we have spun out this present sermon to such length concerning the utterly wicked vice of ingratitude, requires another time and another beginning to the sermon. For now, let it suffice that you have been admonished of this alone: if the bride does not dare to arrogate to herself anything whatever from all her virtue or grace, how much less should the young women—perhaps we ourselves? Let us therefore, following in the bride’s footsteps, say: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. [Col. 0839A] 113:1). Let us say it not only in word and tongue, but in deed and truth, lest perhaps—as I greatly fear—it may be said of us too: “They loved him with their mouth and lied to him with their tongue; but their heart was not right with him, nor were they found faithful in his covenant” (Ps. 77:36–37). Therefore let us say it—let us say it—crying out more with the marrow of our heart than with the lips of our mouth: “Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations, that we may confess your holy name, not our own; and glory in praise, not our own but yours” (Ps. 105:47), for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. On the Church of faithful Christians and the Synagogue of unbelieving Jews.

[Col. 0839B]

1. “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75:2). The people of the nations, who walked in darkness, saw a great light (Isa. 9:2), which was in Judah and in Israel; and they wished to approach and be enlightened, so that those who once were not a people might now be a people (1 Pet. 2:10), and so that the one cornerstone might receive into himself the two walls coming from opposite directions, and thereafter his dwelling-place might be in peace. Moreover, the voice of the one inviting them, which had already sounded, gave confidence: “Rejoice, O nations, with his people” (Deut. 32, according to the Septuagint; Rom. 15:10). Therefore they wished to approach; but the Synagogue forbade them, maintaining that the Church from the nations was unclean and unworthy, reproaching it with the dregs of idolatry and the blindness of ignorance. It said: “By what merit do you have this? Do not [Col. 0839C] touch me.” Why, it says? “Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also of nations?” (Rom. 3:29). Even if merit is certainly lacking to me, mercy is not lacking to him. Is he only just? He is also merciful. “Let your mercies come to me, Lord, and I shall live”; and again: “Your mercies are many, Lord; give me life according to your judgment” (Ps. 118:77, 156)—a judgment that is mercy because it is tempered by mercy.

What will the Lord, who is just and merciful, do when one party glories in the law, applauds its own righteousness, needs no mercy, and despises the one who does need it; while the other, conversely, recognizes its own sins, acknowledges its unworthiness, refuses judgment, and implores mercy? What, I say, will the judge do—and that judge for whom both judging and showing mercy are so characteristic that neither is more characteristic than the other? What could be more fitting than that each should receive according to its own desire: judgment for the former, mercy for the latter? The Jew seeks judgment: let him have it. But let the nations glorify God for mercy. And this is judgment: that those who despise God’s merciful righteousness and wish to establish their own—which certainly does not justify but accuses—should be left to that same righteousness of their own, to be oppressed by it rather than justified.

2. For righteousness from the law has never brought anyone to perfection; it is a yoke which neither they nor their fathers were ever able to bear. But the Synagogue is strong: it does not care for the light burden or the sweet yoke. It is healthy: it has no need of a physician [Col. 0840A] or of the Spirit’s anointing. It trusts in the law; let the law save it, if it can. Yet no law was given that could give life; indeed, it kills: “For the letter kills” (2 Cor. 3:6). “Therefore,” he says, “I tell you: you will die in your sins” (John 8:24). This, then, O Synagogue, is the judgment which your error demands. Blind and contentious, you are abandoned until the fullness of the nations—whom you proudly despise and enviously exclude—shall enter in, and until you yourself also acknowledge him who is “God known in Judah,” and that “his name is great in Israel.” For Jesus came into this world for judgment: “that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

Yet only in part, because “the Lord will not cast off his people” (Ps. 93:14), preserving for himself, as seed, the apostles and the multitude of believers [Col. 0840B] whose heart and soul were one. Nor will he cast them off forever, for he will save a remnant. For he will again receive Israel his child, and remember his mercy (Luke 1:54), so that mercy, the companion of judgment, may not abandon judgment even where mercy itself finds no place. Otherwise, if Israel received according to its merits, judgment would indeed be without mercy for one who has not shown mercy (Jas. 2:13). Judah possesses much oil of divine knowledge, but greedily keeps it locked up in itself as in a closed vessel. I ask, and it has no mercy; it does not lend. Alone it wishes to possess God’s worship, knowledge, and his great name; it does not zealously claim these for itself, but begrudges them to me.

3. Therefore, Lord, judge my case, and let your great name be magnified still further, and let the oil, which is abundant, be multiplied more abundantly. Let it increase, bubble over, be poured out, and be conveyed even to the nations; and let all flesh perceive God’s salvation. How can the saving anointing, as the ungrateful Jew wishes, remain wholly in Aaron’s beard? It belongs not to the beard, but to the head. And the head belongs not only to the beard, but also to the whole body. Let the beard indeed receive it first, but not alone. Let it pour down upon the lower members what it has itself received from above. Let the heavenly liquid descend—descend even into the Church’s breasts (for the Church, greatly eager, does not disdain to press it out for itself from the beard); and, drenched with the dew of grace, let it show itself not ungrateful by saying: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1:2).

But let it overflow further, I pray, and reach even to the hem of the garment—to me, namely, the very last and most unworthy of all, though still of the garment. For I too, as a little child in Christ, rightly demand this from my mother’s breasts by the law of filial affection. If the person whose eye is evil because of goodness grumbles, Lord, answer for me: let my judgment come forth from your countenance, not from Israel’s haughty brow. Indeed, answer for yourself and say to the accuser—for he accuses you because you give freely—say then to him: “I will give to this last one also in the same way” (Matt. 20:14). The Pharisee is displeased. Why do you mutter? It is my right; it is the will of the judge. What is more just in relation to desert, or richer in relation to reward? Is he not permitted to do what he wills? Mercy is shown to me, certainly, but no wrong at all is done to you. Take what is yours and go. If he decides to save me too, what do you lose?

[Col. 0841A] 1307 4. Exaggerate your merits as much as you please and magnify your labours: “the mercy of the Lord is better than lives” (Ps. 62:4). I confess that I have not borne the burden of the day and the heat; but, by the good pleasure of the householder, I bear a sweet yoke and a light burden. My work is scarcely that of a single hour; and if it is more [variant: “of greater value”], I do not perceive it because of love. Let the Jew exert his own powers; I desire to prove what is the Lord’s good, pleasing, and perfect will. From it I make good the losses of labour and time. He relies upon the agreed contract; I upon the pleasure of the will. I believe—and not to my folly, for life is in his will. That will reconciles the Father to me and restores my inheritance with even more abundant grace; it calls forth for me the most splendid joys of music, song, feasting, and the whole rejoicing household.

If my elder brother is indignant—the one who prefers to eat a goat with his friends outside rather than a fatted calf with me in the father’s house—he will be answered: “It was fitting to feast and rejoice, because this my son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32). The Synagogue still feasts outside with its friends, the demons. It greatly pleases them that, in its folly, it devours and swallows the goat of sin and, in a manner, hides it and stores it in the belly of its sluggishness and foolishness, while, despising God’s righteousness and wishing to establish its own, it says that it has no sin and has no need of the death of the fatted calf, since it considers itself clean and righteous through works of the law.

But the Church, after the veil of the killing letter was torn at the death of the crucified Word, boldly breaks into his inner sanctuary, led forward by the spirit of freedom. It is acknowledged, finds favour, receives its rival’s place, becomes a bride, and enjoys the embraces it has seized beforehand. Clinging in the heat of the Spirit to Christ the Lord, to whom it presses close, while his oil of exultation drips and pours out on every side, it receives this above its companions and says: “Your name is oil poured out.” What wonder that she is anointed, since she embraces the Anointed One?

5. The Church, then, reclines within—but for the present, the Church of the perfect. Yet there is hope for us too. Let us keep watch outside the doors, we who are less perfect, rejoicing in hope. For the present let bridegroom and bride alone be inside, enjoying their mutual and secret embraces, with no noise of fleshly desires and no tumult of bodily [Col. 0841D] images disturbing them. But let the crowd of young women, who cannot yet be without such disturbances, wait outside; and let them wait securely, knowing that this concerns them which they read: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you” (Ps. 44:15).

And let each know to what kind of spirit she belongs. By “virgins” I mean those who, betrothed to Christ before they were defiled by the embraces of the world, steadfastly persevere with him to whom they devoted themselves all the more happily because they did so earlier. By “companions” I mean those who, ashamed at last and departing from their former ugliness—in which, once conformed to this world, they had shamefully prostituted themselves to the rulers of the world, that is, to unclean spirits, in every fleshly desire—hasten to be re-formed into the likeness of the new [Col. 0842A] human being, all the more sincerely because later. Let both these and those progress; let them not fail or grow weary, even if they do not yet fully feel within themselves that from which they too may say: “Your name is oil poured out.” For the young women do not dare to address the bridegroom in their own words. Yet if they strive to cling more closely to the mistress’s footsteps, they will at least delight in the fragrance of the oil poured out, and by perceiving its scent will be stirred also to desire and seek greater things.

6. I myself frequently—something I am not ashamed to confess—especially at the beginning of my conversion, was hard and cold in heart, seeking him whom my soul wished to love. For it could not yet love him whom it had not yet found; or at least it loved him less than it wished, and therefore sought him in order to love him more. Yet it would not seek him unless it had already loved him in some measure. When, then, I sought him in whom my spirit, benumbed and languishing, might be warmed and find rest, and no one at all appeared who could help—through whom, that is, the frozen winter [variant: “the frozen frost”], which bound the feelings between us, might be dissolved and that spring sweetness and spiritual loveliness return—then my soul languished more and more; it grew weary and slept; and through weariness it was sad, almost despairing, and muttering to itself: “Who can endure before this cold?” (Ps. 147:17).

But when suddenly, perhaps through the speech or even the sight of some spiritual and perfect man, and sometimes through the mere remembrance of one dead or absent, the Spirit blew and waters flowed, [Col. 0842C] those tears were bread to me day and night. What was this but the fragrance of the anointing exhaled by the one who was saturated with it? It was not the anointing itself, which plainly could not reach me except through the mediation of a human being. Therefore, although I rejoiced in the gift, I was nevertheless ashamed and humbled because only a thin exhalation, not a rich sprinkling, had reached me. Delighted by smell rather than touch, I recognized myself consequently as unworthy for God to become sweet to me in himself.

Even now, if this happens, I eagerly receive the granted gift and count it welcome; but I grieve with sorrow that I did not deserve it through myself and, as the saying goes, did not receive it directly, though I earnestly asked for it. It shames me, indeed, to be moved more by the remembrance of a human being than of God. Then I cry with groaning: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3). I think that some of you have experienced the same thing, and perhaps still experience it from time to time. What ought we to think in this matter except that either our pride is convicted, our humility is preserved, brotherly love is nourished, or desire is stirred? One and the same food is medicine for the sick and a regimen for convalescents; moreover, it strengthens the weak and delights the strong. The same food both heals languor and preserves health; it nourishes the body and pleases the palate.

7. But let us return to the bride’s words, and let us take care to hear what she says in such a way that we strive also to taste what she tastes. The bride, as I said, is the Church. She is the one to whom more has been forgiven and who loves more. What her rival casts at her as an insult, she turns to her own advantage. From it she becomes gentler under correction, more patient in labour, more ardent in love, more perceptive in caution, more humble because of conscience, more acceptable because of modesty, more ready to obey, and more devout and attentive in thanksgiving. Finally, while the other, as was said, murmurs and recounts her merits, labours, and the burden and heat of the day, the Church recalls the benefit, saying: “Your name is oil poured out.”

8. This truly is Israel’s testimony in confessing the Lord’s name—yet not Israel according to the flesh, but Israel according to the Spirit. For how can the former say this? Not because it does not possess oil, but because it does not possess it poured out. It has it, but stored away; it has it [Col. 0843B] in books, but not in hearts. It clings outwardly to the letter; it handles with its hands a vessel that is full yet closed, and does not open it to be anointed. Within—within is the Spirit’s anointing: open it and anoint yourself, and you will no longer be a rebellious house. What use is oil in vessels if you do not feel it also in your limbs? What benefit is it to you to read repeatedly in books the merciful name of the Savior, but not to have mercy in your conduct? It is oil: pour it out, and you will experience its power, which is threefold. But the Jew disdains these things; you, listen.

I wish to explain why the bridegroom’s name is compared with oil, which I have not yet explained. Three reasons for this occur to me. But because he is called by many names, since none can be found by which he may be named properly—for he is ineffable—we must first invoke the Holy Spirit, that he may deign by himself to disclose to us from among the many the one name meant in this place, since it was not thought fit to designate it in writing. But this too must await another occasion. For even if everything were now ready to hand, and neither you burdened nor I tired, the hour nevertheless announces an end. Retain the point on which I have made you attentive, so that there will be no need to repeat it tomorrow. This is the task before us; this is what is in hand: to teach why the bridegroom’s name is compared to oil, and what is meant concerning the names. And because I cannot say anything from myself, prayer has been appointed, that the bridegroom himself may reveal it to us through his Spirit—Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XV. How the name Jesus is health-giving medicine for faithful Christians in every adversity.

[Col. 0843D]

1. The Spirit of wisdom is gracious (Wis. 1:6), and is not accustomed to be difficult toward those who call upon him; often, even before he is invoked, he says: “Behold, I am here” (Isa. 65:24). Hear now what, in answer to your prayers, he deigns to indicate through me concerning what we postponed yesterday for this very purpose; and receive the timely fruit of your prayers. Behold, I show you a name rightly compared to oil, and I shall say why it is rightly so compared. You read many names of the Bridegroom scattered throughout all the divine page, but I shall include them all for you under two headings. I think you will find none [Col. 0844A] which does not signify either the grace of mercy or the power of majesty. The Spirit says this also through an instrument more familiar to himself: “These two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and mercy to you, O Lord” (Ps. 61:12–13).

Accordingly, with reference to majesty: “Holy and terrible is his name” (Ps. 110:9); with reference to mercy: “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings in which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). But this will become clearer by examples. “This,” he says, “is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord, our righteousness” (Jer. 23:6). It is a name of power. Again: “His name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14); it indicates mercy. Again, he himself says of himself: “You call me Master and Lord” (John 13:13). The first belongs to grace, the second to majesty. For it is no less merciful to instruct the soul in knowledge than to provide food for the body.

Again the prophet says: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9:6). The first, third, and fourth signify majesty; the others, mercy. Which of these, then, is poured out? Surely the name of majesty and power is, in a certain manner, poured into that which belongs to mercy and grace; and it is poured out abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior. For example, does not the name “God” melt and dissolve into “God with us” (Matt. 1:23), that is, into Emmanuel? Thus “Wonderful” becomes “Counselor”; thus “God” and “Mighty” become “Father of the age to come” and “Prince of Peace”; and “the Lord, our righteousness” becomes “the Lord, merciful and compassionate” (Ps. 110:4). I say nothing new: formerly Abram was likewise poured out into Abraham, and Sarai into Sarah (Gen. 17:5, 15); and we recall that even then the mystery of the saving outpouring was celebrated and prefigured.

2. Where now is that saying which among the ancients used to resound so terribly and so often: “I am the Lord, I am the Lord” (Exod. 20:2)? A prayer is dictated to me whose opening, with the sweet paternal name, supplies confidence for obtaining the petitions that follow. Servants are called friends (John 15:14–15), and the resurrection is announced not merely to disciples but to brothers (Matt. 28:10) [Note: Col. 0843D: Thus the manuscripts; elsewhere, “only.”]. Nor am I surprised that, when the fullness of time came, there was an outpouring of the Name: for God fulfilled what he had promised through Joel, [Col. 0844D] pouring out his Spirit upon all flesh (Joel 2:28). For I read that something of this sort happened long ago also among the Hebrews. I believe you anticipate me and already know what I mean to say. What was it, I ask, that was first answered to Moses when he inquired: “I am who I am,” and, “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14)? I do not know whether even Moses himself could have grasped it in this way, unless it had, that is, been poured out. But it was poured forth and grasped; nor merely poured forth, but poured out: for it had already been infused. Heaven already possessed it; it had already been made known to the angels. Yet it was sent abroad; and what had been so infused into the angels as to be their private possession was also poured out upon human beings, so that already then one might rightly cry from earth: [Col. 0845A] “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1:2)—had not the hateful obstinacy of an ungrateful people stood in the way. For he says: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:6, 15).

3. Run, nations: salvation is at hand; the Name has been poured out, and whoever calls upon it shall be saved. The God of angels also names himself the God of human beings. He sent oil into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel. Say to your brothers: “Give us some of your oil” (Matt. 25:8). If they refuse, ask the Lord of oil to send it to you also. Say: “Take away our reproach” (Isa. 4:1). Do not, I beg you, let the ill-wisher mock your beloved, whom you were pleased to summon from the ends of the earth—so much the more worthily, surely, as she was less worthy. Is it fitting, I ask, that a wicked servant [Col. 0845B] should exclude those invited by a kindly master of the household? “I am,” you say, “the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” And no more? Pour out, pour out; open your hand still further, and fill every living creature with blessing.

Let them come from east and west, and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 8:11). Let them come, let the tribes come, the tribes of the Lord, Israel’s testimony, to give thanks to the name of the Lord (Ps. 121:4). Let them come and recline; let them feast and delight in joy; and everywhere let one sound resound in the voice of exultation and thanksgiving—the sound of one feasting (Ps. 41:5): “Your name is oil poured out.” One thing I know: if we have Philip and Andrew as gatekeepers, none of us who ask for oil, none of us who wish to see Jesus, will be turned away. Without hesitation Philip will tell Andrew; and Andrew [Col. 0845C] and Philip will tell Jesus. And what will Jesus do? Surely, what Jesus does. “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:22–25). Let the grain therefore die, and let the harvest of the nations rise. Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and repentance and forgiveness of sins were to be preached in his name, not only in Judaea but also among all nations; so that from the one name, Christ, thousands upon thousands of believers might be called Christians and say: “Your name is oil poured out.”

4. For I recognize the name which I read in Isaiah: “He shall call his servants by another name, in which he who is blessed [Col. 0845D] upon earth shall be blessed in the Lord, amen” (Isa. 65:15–16). O blessed Name! O oil poured out everywhere! How far? It runs from heaven into Judaea, and from there throughout all the earth; and from the whole world the Church cries: “Your name is oil poured out.” Truly poured out: it has not only drenched heaven and earth, but has sprinkled even the underworld, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess (Phil. 2:10–11), saying: “Your name is oil poured out.”

Behold Christ, behold Jesus: both infused into the angels, both poured out upon human beings—those human beings who had rotted like beasts in their own dung. God saves human beings and beasts, according as he has multiplied his mercy. How precious, [Col. 0846A] how lowly! Lowly, yet life-giving. If it were not lowly, it would not be poured out for me; if it were not life-giving, it would not gain me. I share in the Name, and I share also in the inheritance: I am a Christian; I am Christ’s brother. If I am what I am called, I am God’s heir and Christ’s co-heir (Rom. 8:17). And what wonder that the bridegroom’s Name was poured out, when he himself too was poured out? For “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7). Finally, he says: “I am poured out like water” (Ps. 21:15). The fullness of divinity was poured out, dwelling bodily upon earth, so that from that fullness all of us who bear the body of death might receive, and, filled with a life-giving fragrance, might say: “Your name is oil poured out.” See what Name was poured out, and how, and how far.

[Col. 0846B] But why oil? For I have not yet said this. In the previous sermon I had begun to speak of it, but something else suddenly intervened which seemed fit to be preached. Yet I interrupted the matter longer than I had expected. I think this was nothing other than that the strong woman, Wisdom, put her hand to the distaff and her fingers grasped the spindle. For she knows how to draw a small quantity of wool or flax into a long thread, stretch it across the breadth of the loom, and thus clothe all her household in double garments (Prov. 31:19, 21). Without doubt there is a likeness between oil and the bridegroom’s Name; nor did the Holy Spirit compare them idly. I, however, find it in a threefold quality of oil: it gives light, nourishment, and anointing—unless you have a better explanation. It sustains fire, feeds flesh, and eases pain: light, food, [Col. 0846C] medicine. Now consider the same things in the bridegroom’s Name. Preached, it gives light; recalled, it feeds; invoked, it eases and anoints. Let us take these one by one.

6. Whence, do you suppose, came such great and sudden light of faith throughout the world, except from the preaching of Jesus? Was it not in the light of this Name that God called us into his marvelous light? Enlightened by it, and seeing light in this light, Paul may rightly say: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). This same apostle was commanded to bear this Name before kings, nations, and the children of Israel (Acts 9:15); he bore the Name as a light, illumined his country, and cried everywhere: “The night has passed; [Col. 0846D] the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. 13:12–13). He set the lamp upon its stand for all to see, proclaiming in every place Jesus—and him crucified.

How this light flashed and struck the eyes of all who beheld it when, issuing from Peter’s mouth like lightning, it strengthened the bodily soles and ankles of one lame man and enlightened many who were spiritually blind! Did he not scatter fire when he said: “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6)? Nor is the name of Jesus only light; it is also food. Are you not strengthened as often as you remember it? What equally fattens the mind that contemplates? What so restores the exercised faculties, strengthens virtues, quickens [Col. 0847A] good and honorable habits, and cherishes chaste affections? Every food of the soul is dry if this oil is not poured into it; it is tasteless if it is not seasoned with this salt. If you write, it has no savor for me unless I read Jesus there. If you dispute or converse, it has no savor for me unless Jesus sounds there.

> [Note: Col. 0847D] Augustine, in Book III of the *Confessions*, chapter 4, says that the same thing happened to him while reading the *Hortensius*: “This alone,” he says, “checked me amid such ardor: that the name of Christ was not there … and whatever was without this Name, however learned, polished, and true it might be, did not wholly seize me.” [Col. 0848D]

Jesus is honey in the mouth, melody in the ear, jubilation in the heart. But he is also medicine. Is any one of you sad? Let Jesus enter the heart, and from there leap into the mouth; and behold: at the rising of that Name’s light, every cloud flees and serenity returns. Does someone fall into sin and then run further, by despair, into the noose of death? If he invokes the Name of life, will he not immediately breathe again into life?
