Before whose face has hardness of heart ever stood, as it often does; or the numbness of sloth, bitterness of spirit, the sickness of acedia? Whose dried-up fountain of tears, [Col. 0847B] upon invoking Jesus, did not immediately burst forth more abundantly and flow more sweetly? To whom, trembling and quaking amid dangers, has the invoked Name of power not at once given confidence and driven away fear? To whom, I ask, fevered and tossed amid doubts, has certainty not suddenly shone forth at the invocation of the radiant Name? To whom, distrustful in adversity and already on the point of failing, if the Name of Help sounded, did strength fail? These indeed are diseases and infirmities of the soul; that Name is their medicine.

Indeed, you may test it: “Call upon me,” he says, “in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. 49:15). Nothing so restrains an outburst of anger, calms the swelling of pride, heals the wound of envy, checks the flow of lust, extinguishes the flame of sexual desire, moderates the thirst of avarice, [Col. 0847C] and drives away every itch of shamefulness. For when I name Jesus, I set before myself a man meek and humble of heart, kind, temperate, chaste, merciful, and, finally, conspicuous in every virtue and holiness; and this same man is almighty God, who both heals me by his example and strengthens me by his aid. All these things sound together for me when Jesus sounds. Thus I take my examples from the man and aid from the Mighty One: the former as aromatic ingredients, the latter as that by which I sharpen them; and I make a preparation such as no physician can make.

7. You have this electuary, O my soul, stored in the vessel of this word, Jesus: assuredly health-giving, and never found ineffective against any [Col. 0847D] plague of yours. Let it always be in your bosom, always in your hand, so that all your thoughts and actions may be directed toward Jesus. Indeed, you are invited: “Set me,” he says, “as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song 8:6). But of this elsewhere. For now, in the name of Jesus, you have that by which to heal both arm and heart: that is, by which to correct your actions when evil, or complete them when less than perfect; likewise, by which to preserve your thoughts from corruption, or, if corrupted, heal them.

8. Judaea too had certain “Jesuses,” in whose empty [Col. 0848A] names she boasts. For they neither illumine, nourish, nor heal. Therefore the Synagogue remains in darkness still, suffering hunger and weakness; nor will it be healed or satisfied until it knows that my Jesus rules Jacob and the ends of the earth, and until it turns at evening, suffers hunger like dogs, and goes about the city (Ps. 58:14, 7). Those others were sent ahead, like the staff that preceded the prophet to the dead child, and they could not interpret their own names, for they were empty. The staff was laid upon the dead child, and there was neither voice nor perception, because it was a staff. He who had sent the staff came down (4 Kings 4:29–35), and immediately saved his people from their sins, proving himself to be what he was called: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” [Col. 0848B] (Luke 7:49). Surely he is the one who says: “I am the salvation of the people” (Ps. 34:3).

Now there is voice; now there is perception; and it is clear that he does not bear an empty name like the former ones. The salvation infused within is felt, and its benefit is not kept silent. Within, perception; without, voice. I am pierced with compunction, and I confess; and confession shows life: “For from one dead, as from one who is not, confession perishes” (Ecclus. 17:26). Behold life; behold perception. I have been perfectly raised; the resurrection is complete. What else is bodily death than the deprivation of perception and life? Sin, which is the death of the soul, had left me neither the perception of compunction nor the voice of confession, and I was dead. He who forgives sins came, restored both, and says to my soul: “I am your salvation.” What wonder if death yields where life descends? [Col. 0848C] Now the heart believes unto righteousness, and confession with the mouth is made unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). Now the child yawns, and yawns seven times (4 Kings 4:35), and says: “Seven times a day I have offered praise to you” (Ps. 118:164), O Lord.

Observe this sevenfold number. It is sacred; it is not without meaning. But we reserve this better for another sermon, so that we may approach such excellent fare hungry and not fastidious, invited by the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. On contrition of heart and the three kinds of true confession

1. What, then, does this sevenfold number mean? For I do not know [Col. 0848D] whether anyone among us is so simple as to think these repetitions meaningless, or this number accidental. I also do not think it meaningless that the prophet, bending over the dead child, contracted himself to the measure of the child’s body, joining his mouth to the child’s mouth, his eyes to the child’s eyes, and his hands to the child’s hands (4 Kings 4). The Holy Spirit caused all these things to be done and written for the instruction, without doubt, of those spirits whom the faithless companionship of a corruptible body deceives and whom the foolish wisdom of the world teaches to become foolish. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” [Col. 0849A] (Wis. 9:15).

Therefore let no one wonder or take it ill if I am inquisitive in examining these things, as though they were certain storehouses of the Holy Spirit; for I know that this is how one lives, and that the life of my spirit lies in such things. Yet I say to those who, swift in intellect, in every discourse almost demand the end before they grasp the beginning: I am a debtor also—and especially—to the slower. Nor is my purpose so much to expound words as to imbue hearts. I must both draw and pour out; and this is not done by rushing quickly through, but by careful treatment and frequent exhortation.

Yet, contrary even to my own expectation, our discussion of the mysteries has detained us long. I thought, I confess, that one sermon would suffice, and that we should quickly pass through this shadowy and hidden forest [Col. 0849B] of allegories and reach the plain of moral meanings in something like a day’s journey. But it happened otherwise. We have already spent two days on it, and the road still remains. The glance of the eye flew over from afar the tops of branches and mountain peaks; but the expanse of the valleys lying beneath and the density of the thickets frustrated our sight. Could I, for example, have foreseen Elisha’s miracle, that, while we were discussing the calling of the nations and the rejection of the Jews, it would suddenly leap into our midst? And now that we have encountered it, let us not begrudge spending a little time on it; afterward we shall return to what we interrupted, since this too is food for souls. Even dogs and hunters often [Col. 0849C] leave the beast they had pursued and follow another which unexpectedly happens to meet them.

2. It gives me no small strengthening of confidence that that great man, the prophet, mighty in deed and word, descending from the lofty mountain of heaven, has deigned to visit me, though I am ashes and dust: to have mercy on the dead, bend down to the prostrate, contract himself and make himself equal to the little one, share with the blind the light of his own eyes, loosen the dumb mouth by the kiss of his own mouth, and strengthen weak hands by the touch of his own [Col. 0849D]. I sweetly meditate upon these things; my inward parts are filled, my interior is made fat, and all my bones break forth in praise. What he bestowed once upon all humanity, we feel being enacted daily in each of us: namely, that light of understanding is given to the heart, a word of edification to the mouth, and a work of righteousness to the hands. He gives faithful perception, useful utterance, and effective accomplishment. And it is a threefold cord, not easily broken, for drawing souls out of the devil’s prison and drawing them after itself toward the kingdoms of heaven—if you think rightly, speak worthily, and confirm it by your life.

He touched my eyes with his own, adorning the brow of the inner person with bright lights: faith and understanding. He joined his mouth to mine and impressed upon the dead man the sign of peace; for while we were still sinners, dead to righteousness, he reconciled us to God. He placed mouth upon mouth, again breathing into my face the breath of life, but holier than at first. For at first [Col. 0850A] he created me a living soul; the second time he refashioned me into a life-giving spirit. He placed his hands upon mine, giving an example of good works and a pattern of obedience. Or rather, he stretched his hands toward mighty deeds, to teach my hands for battle and my fingers for war.

3. “And the child yawned seven times” (4 Kings 4:35). To manifest the glory of the miracle, one yawn would have sufficed; but its repetition and remarkable number point to a mystery. If you consider that first, vast, lifeless body of the whole human race, you see the Church everywhere, having received life through the prophet bending over it, as though yawning seven times, because it is accustomed to say praise seven times a day. If you consider yourself, you will know that you live this spiritual life, [Col. 0850B] and fulfill this mystical number if you subject the fivefold number of your senses to the twofold number of charity, and, according to the Apostle, present your members as servants to righteousness unto sanctification, which you formerly presented as servants to iniquity unto iniquity (Rom. 6:19). Or again, if, sharing that same fivefold number for the salvation of your neighbors, you add these two in order to complete the sevenfold number: namely, to sing mercy and judgment to God.

4. I have also another set of seven yawns: namely, seven experiences without which the true and certain salvation of the revived spirit is by no means established. Four concern the perception of compunction; three, the utterance of confession. If you live, if there is voice and perception, you too recognize these same things in yourself. You should know that you have fully recovered perception if you feel your conscience [Col. 0850C] bitten by a fourfold compunction: by a twofold shame and a twofold fear. For three kinds of confession testify to life and complete the sevenfold number, of which we shall speak later.

Does not holy Jeremiah also observe this number in his lament? Therefore, in your own lamentation for yourself, taking the prophet as your model, think of God as your Maker; think also of him as your Benefactor; think of him as Father; think of him as Lord. You are guilty in regard to all these; weep over each separately. Let fear answer to the first and the last; shame to the two in the middle. A father, certainly, is not feared merely as a father. For it belongs to a father always to have mercy and to spare. Even if he strikes, he strikes with a rod, not a club; and when he has struck, he heals. It is the voice of a father: “I will strike, and I will heal” [Col. 0850D] (Deut. 32:39). Thus there is no reason to fear a father who, even if he sometimes wounds in order to correct, never does so in order to take vengeance.

But when I reflect that I have offended my Father, there is surely cause for shame, even if not for terror. He begot me willingly by the word of truth; he did not cast me forth by the impulse of fleshly desire, as did the father of my flesh. Moreover, he did not spare his Only-begotten for one whom he thus begot. Thus he showed himself a Father to me, but I did not in return show myself a son to him. With what face can I now lift my eyes to the countenance of so good a Father, I so evil a son? I am ashamed to have acted unworthily of my lineage; ashamed to have lived degenerate beneath so great a Father. “Let my eyes bring down streams of water”; let confusion cover my face, let shame suffuse my countenance, and let darkness seize [Col. 0851A] me. Let my life fail in sorrow and my years in groaning. Alas for shame! “What fruit had I then in those things of which I am now ashamed?” If I have sown in the flesh, I shall reap from the flesh nothing but corruption (Gal. 6:8); if in the world, it too passes away, and its desire (1 John 2:17). What? I did not blush to prefer to the love and honor of the eternal Father things that are passing, vain, nearly nothing, and whose end is death—wretched and insane that I was. I am confounded, confounded to hear: “If I am a father, where is my honor?” (Mal. 1:6).

5. But even if he were not Father, he would overwhelm me with benefits. Against me he raises witnesses: to omit countless others, the nourishment of this body, the use of this present time, and above all the blood of the beloved Son [Col. 0851B] crying from the earth. I am ashamed of ingratitude; though, to increase my confusion, I am also accused of repaying evil for good and hatred for love. Indeed, I need no more fear a Benefactor than a Father. For he is truly bountiful, giving generously and without reproach (Jas. 1:5). He does not reproach me with gifts, because they are gifts; and he gave me his benefits, he did not sell them. Indeed, his gifts are without repentance. Yet the more kindly I must think of him, the more unworthily I am compelled to think of myself. Be ashamed, and nevertheless grieve, O my soul; for though it be fitting for him neither to demand repayment nor to reproach, it is altogether unfitting for us to have proved ungrateful and forgetful. Alas! What, even now at last, shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?

[Col. 0851C] 6. But if shame is perhaps too sluggish to perform its office sufficiently, let fear be summoned to assist. Let it be summoned, that it may arouse. Set aside for a while the kindly names of Benefactor and Father, and turn to harsher ones. He is indeed called “the Father of mercies and God of all consolation” (2 Cor. 1:3); but he is also called “the Lord, God of vengeance” (Ps. 93:1); “God, a just and mighty judge” (Ps. 7:12); “terrible in counsel above the children of men” (Ps. 65:5); and “a jealous God” (Exod. 20:5). That he is Father, that he is Benefactor, is for you; that he is Lord and Creator, is for himself. For, as Scripture testifies, he made all things for himself (Prov. 16:4). Do you suppose that he who defends and preserves for you what is yours will never also be zealous for himself? Do you suppose he will not require the honor due to his sovereignty? “The wicked has provoked God, because he has said in his heart: ‘He will not require it’” [Col. 0851D] (Ps. 9:13). And what is it to say in one’s heart, “He will not require it,” except not to fear that he will require it? Yet he will require it to the last farthing; he will require it and repay abundantly those who act proudly (Ps. 30:24). He will require service from the redeemed, honor and glory from the one whom he formed.

7. Suppose the Father overlooks it and the Benefactor forgives: the Lord and Creator will not; he who spares the son will not spare the thing he fashioned, nor spare the wicked servant. Consider what fear and horror it is to have despised your Maker and the Maker of all, and offended the Lord of majesty. Majesty must be feared; the Lord must be feared—[Col. 0852A] especially this Majesty and this Lord. For if one guilty of royal majesty, though human, is by human laws decreed to be punished by death, what end awaits those who despise divine omnipotence? “He touches the mountains, and they smoke” (Ps. 143:5); and does a vile speck of dust, soon to be scattered by a single light breath and never gathered again, dare to provoke so dreadful a Majesty? He, he must be feared, who, after killing the body, has power also to cast into Gehenna (Luke 12:5).

I fear Gehenna; I fear the face of the Judge, dreadful even to the angelic powers themselves. I tremble before the wrath of the Mighty One, before the face of his fury, before the crash of the falling world, the conflagration of the elements, the violent storm, the voice of the archangel, and the harsh word. I tremble before the teeth of the infernal beast, the belly of hell, and those roaring creatures prepared for food. [Col. 0852B] I shrink from the gnawing worm and the rushing fire, smoke, vapor, sulphur, and stormy blast; I shrink from the outer darkness. “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes” (Jer. 9:1), that I may forestall with weeping the weeping, the gnashing of teeth, the harsh bonds of hands and feet, and the weight of chains that press, constrict, burn, and do not consume? Alas for me, my mother! Why did you bear me, a son of sorrow, a son of bitterness, indignation, and eternal lamentation? Why was I received upon knees? Why nursed at breasts—born for burning and food for fire?

8. One so affected has without doubt recovered perception; and in this twofold fear, as also in that equally twofold shame, he has four yawns [Col. 0852C]. He will add the remaining three, which belong to the voice of confession; and it will no longer be said of him that there is neither voice nor perception, provided that confession proceeds from a heart humble, simple, and faithful. Therefore confess humbly, purely, and faithfully everything that stings your conscience; and you will have completed these repetitions.

There are those who glory when they have done evil and exult in utterly wicked things (Prov. 2:14). Marking them, the prophet says: “They have proclaimed their sins like Sodom” (Isa. 3:9). But I exclude these from the present discussion as worldly persons; for what have we to do with those who are outside?

9. Yet even among those clothed in religious dress and professing religious life, we have sometimes heard certain people recalling and most shamelessly boasting of their former [Col. 0852D] evils: for example, acts they once performed with force in gladiatorial conflict, or cleverly in literary contention, or something else favorable according to the vanity of the world but harmful, ruinous, and destructive to the salvation of the soul. This is a sign of a still worldly mind; and the humble garb worn by such people is not the merit of holy newness but a covering for ancient oldness. Some recall such things as though grieving and repenting; yet, seeking glory by their intention, they do not wash away their deeds but deceive themselves. For God is not mocked (Gal. 6:7). They have not put off the old man, but cloak him with the new. By that confession the old leaven is neither exposed nor cast away; rather, it is established, [Col. 0853A] according to the saying: “My bones grew old while I cried all day long” (Ps. 31:3).

I am ashamed to recall the insolence of some, so great that they are not ashamed to boast exultantly of things that ought to be lamented: that, even after taking on the holy habit, they craftily tripped someone up and cheated a brother in business; or that they boldly rendered retaliation for an insult or curse—that is, evil for evil or curse for curse.

10. But there is a confession more dangerously harmful because more subtly vain: when we do not fear to reveal even our disgraceful and shameful acts, not because we are humble, but in order to be thought humble. To seek praise for humility is not humility’s virtue but its overthrow. The truly humble person wishes to be considered lowly, not to be proclaimed humble. He rejoices in contempt for himself [Col. 0853B]; in this alone is he proud: that he despises praise. What could be more perverse or unworthy than for confession, the guardian of humility, to serve pride, and for you to wish to seem better by that through which you seem worse? It is a marvelous kind of boasting: you cannot be thought holy unless you appear criminal.

Such a confession, having the appearance but not the virtue of humility, not only does not deserve pardon but provokes wrath. Did it profit Saul that, when Samuel reproved him, he confessed that he had sinned? (1 Sam. 15:30). Without doubt that confession was blameworthy, for it did not wash away the fault. For when would the teacher of humility despise a humble confession, he whose nature it certainly is to give grace to the humble? He could not possibly fail to be appeased if the humility that sounded in the mouth [Col. 0853C] had shone forth in the heart. See why I said confession must be humble.

11. It must also be simple. Let no one delight in excusing an intention—perhaps because it is hidden from people—if it is guilty; nor in making light of a grave fault; nor in shading one’s own guilt by another’s advice, when no one compelled one unwilling. The first is not confession but defense; it does not appease but provokes. The second shows ingratitude: the less the fault is considered, the more the glory of the pardoner is diminished. A benefit is given less gladly when it is felt to be received less gratefully or less necessarily. Thus one deprives oneself of pardon who diminishes the giver’s gift; and everyone does this who seeks to lessen his guilt [Col. 0853D] in words.

Let the example of the first man at the beginning deter you: though he did not deny his fault, he nevertheless did not obtain pardon—undoubtedly because he implicated the woman in his guilt (Gen. 3:2). It is a kind of excuse, when you are accused, to accuse another. Ask holy David how unprofitable—and even harmful—it is to wish to excuse yourself when corrected. He calls them “words of wickedness, excuses in sins,” praying and pleading that his heart may not incline to them (Ps. 140:4). And rightly so. For one sins against one’s own soul who excuses himself, thereby rejecting from himself the medicine of pardon and thus shutting off life from himself by his own mouth. What greater wickedness is there than to arm yourself against your own salvation and pierce yourself with the blade of your own tongue? [Col. 0854A] “He who is wicked to himself, to whom is he good?” (Ecclus. 14:5).

12. Let confession also be faithful: confess in hope, in no way despairing of pardon, lest by your own mouth you condemn yourself rather than justify yourself. Judas, the Lord’s betrayer, and Cain, the fratricide, confessed and despaired. The one said: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:4); the other: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve pardon for” (Gen. 4:13). Though their confession was true, its unfaithfulness profited them nothing. These, then, are the three observances of confession; joined to the four previously mentioned kinds of compunction, they complete the sevenfold number.

13. Now, once you have thus been pierced by compunction and thus confessed, and therefore are certain in yourself of life, you are likewise [Col. 0854B] certain, I think, that Jesus is not called by an empty name—the one who has been able and willing to work such things in you—and that the staff he sent ahead did not come uselessly. He did not come empty, because he did not come as one empty. For how could he be empty, in whom fullness dwelt? The Spirit was not given to him by measure. Indeed, he came in the fullness of time (Gal. 4:4), thereby showing that he came full. He came fittingly full: the Father anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions (Ps. 44:8), and anointed and sent him full of grace and truth (John 1:14). He anointed him so that he might anoint. All who deserved to receive from his fullness were anointed by him. Therefore he says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim good news to the meek, to heal the contrite of heart, [Col. 0854C] to proclaim pardon to captives and opening to those confined, to proclaim the year acceptable to the Lord” (Isa. 61:1–2).

He came, as you hear, to anoint our contritions and soothe our pains; and therefore he came anointed, gentle and mild, and abundant in mercy toward all who call upon him. He knew that he was descending to the sick, and he showed himself such as was fitting. Since there were many infirmities, the provident physician took care to bring many remedies. He brought the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord.

14. Do you see how many vials full of perfumes the heavenly physician prepared to heal the wounds of that [Col. 0854D] wretched man who fell among robbers? They are seven in number, perhaps suited to awaken the seven yawns spoken of above. For the spirit of life was in the vials. From them he surely poured oil into my wounds; he also poured in wine, but less of it than oil. This was fitting for my infirmities: he made mercy prevail over judgment, as oil is poured in above wine. He therefore brought five vessels of oil, but only two of wine. For wine was only fear and strength; the other five designate oil by their own sweetness.

Thus, in the spirit of strength, “like a mighty man roused from wine” (Ps. 77:65), he descended into hell, shattered the bronze gates and broke the iron bars; he bound the strong man and snatched away the vessels of captivity. [Col. 0855A] Yet he descended also in the spirit of fear—but as one to be feared, not as one afraid.

15. O Wisdom! With what art of healing you restore health to my soul through wine and oil—strongly sweet and sweetly strong: strong for me and sweet to me! For you reach from end to end mightily and order all things sweetly, driving back the enemy and cherishing the weak. Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; I shall sing and confess your Name, and say: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1:2). Not wine poured out—for I do not wish you to enter into judgment with your servant—but oil, because you crown me with mercy and compassion (Ps. 102:4).

Truly oil: because, as it floats above every liquid [Col. 0855B] with which it is mixed, it clearly signifies that Name which is above every name. O Name most pleasant and most sweet! O Name most radiant, most choice, most exalted, and exalted above all for ever! This is truly the oil which makes the face of a human being glad, which makes fat the head of one fasting, so that he may not feel the oil of the sinner. This is the new Name which the mouth of the Lord has named (Isa. 62:2), and which was called by the angel before it was conceived in the womb (Luke 2:21). Not only the Jew, but whoever calls upon this Name shall be saved (Joel 2:32): so completely has it been poured out everywhere. The Father gave it to the Son, the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. On observing the coming and departure of the Holy Spirit, and on the devil’s envy toward the human race

[Col. 0855C]

1. Do we think that we have advanced far enough into the sanctuary of God while searching out this wondrous mystery, or do we dare to follow the Spirit farther inward, to investigate whatever may remain? For this Spirit searches not only human hearts and reins, but also the deep things of God; and whether to our own concerns or to the heights [Note: [Col. 0855D] Thus the manuscripts; not “to other things.”], I safely follow him wherever he goes. Only may he guard our hearts and minds, lest, when he is absent, we suppose him present and, straying, follow our own understanding in place of his.

For he comes and goes as he wills, and no one readily knows whence he comes or whither he goes (John 3:8). Perhaps it is possible to be ignorant of this without harm to salvation; but to be ignorant of when he comes, [Col. 0855D] or when he goes, is plainly most dangerous. For when these providential alternations of the Holy Spirit in relation to us are not watched with the utmost vigilance, it follows that one neither longs for him when absent nor glorifies him when present. He withdraws precisely in order that he may be sought more eagerly; but how is he sought, if his absence is unknown? And again, he graciously returns in order to console; but how is he worthily received in accordance with his majesty, if his presence is not even perceived? Thus the mind that does not recognize his departure lies open to deception; and the mind that does not observe his return will be ungrateful for his visitation.

2. Elisha once asked something of his master [Col. 0856A] when he perceived that his departure was near; and, as you know, he did not obtain it except on the condition that he should see when his master was taken from him (4 Kings [2 Kings] 2:9–10). This happened to them figuratively, but it was written for our sake. By this prophetic example we are taught and admonished to be watchful and attentive concerning the work of our salvation—a work which the Spirit unceasingly carries on in the depths of us with the marvelous subtlety and sweetness of his divine art.

May that anointing, which teaches concerning all things, never be taken from us without our awareness, if we wish not to be deprived of the double gift. And when it comes, may it never find us unprepared, but always with faces uplifted and bosoms opened wide for the Lord’s abundant blessing. For what sort of people does he seek? Those like men awaiting [Col. 0856B] their lord when he returns from the wedding feast (Luke 12:36); and certainly he never returns empty-handed from the abundant delights of that heavenly table. Therefore we must keep watch—indeed, keep watch every hour—because we do not know at what hour the Spirit will come, or depart again.

The Spirit goes and returns; whoever stands while he sustains him must fall when he abandons him. Yet he is not dashed down, because the Lord again puts his hand beneath him. He does not cease to alternate these changes in those who are spiritual, or rather in those whom for this very reason he intends to make spiritual, visiting them in the morning and suddenly testing them. Indeed, the righteous person falls seven times and rises seven times (Prov. 24:16), provided that he falls in the day, so that he sees himself falling, knows that he has fallen, desires to rise, seeks the helping hand, and says: “Lord, in your good pleasure you bestowed strength upon my beauty; you turned your face away from me, and I was troubled” (Ps. 29:8 [30:7]).

3. It is one thing to doubt the truth, which one must suffer when the Spirit is not breathing; it is another to hold falsehood as true, which you readily avoid if you do not fail to recognize your own ignorance, so that you too may say: “And if I have been ignorant of anything, my ignorance remains with me” (Job 19:4). This is the saying of holy Job; recognize it.

Ignorance, a most evil mother, has likewise two most evil daughters: falsehood and doubt. The former is more wretched; the latter more pitiable. The former is more destructive; the latter more troublesome. When the Spirit speaks, both give way; and there is not merely truth, but certain truth. For he is the [Col. 0856D] Spirit of truth, to which falsehood is contrary; he is also the Spirit of wisdom, which, being the brightness of eternal life and reaching everywhere because of its purity, admits no obscurity of uncertainty.

When this Spirit does not speak, one must indeed beware: if doubt is not troublesome, falsehood is certainly detestable. For it is one thing, under uncertainty, to think that this or that may be so; it is another rashly to affirm what one does not know. Therefore either let the Spirit always speak—which assuredly is not in our power—or, when he chooses to be silent, let him make that very fact known, and at least let his silence speak, lest, falsely supposing that he goes before us, we confidently but wrongly follow our own error in his place. And if he leaves us in uncertainty, let him not abandon us to [Col. 0857A] falsehood.

There is one who states a falsehood uncertainly and does not lie; and there is one who affirms as true a truth he does not know, and lies. For the former does not say that what is not is; rather, he says truly that he believes what he believes, even though the thing he believes may not be true. But the latter, when he says that he is certain of what he is not certain, does not speak truly, even though the thing he asserts may itself be true.

4. Having prefaced these warnings for the caution of the inexperienced, I shall now follow the Spirit, as I trust, going before me—yet with the same caution, if I can, which I have just set forth. And I shall try myself to do what I teach, lest it be said also to me: “You who teach others, do you not teach yourself?” (Rom. 2:21). We must certainly distinguish between what is manifest and what is doubtful: the former must not be brought into doubt, nor the latter rashly affirmed. [Col. 0857B] This, indeed, is itself to be hoped for from the Spirit’s teaching; for our own diligence by no means suffices for it.

Who among men knows whether that judgment, disclosed in the preceding discourse—this, if I remember rightly, being the fourth—which God has made among human beings, had not already been preceded by a judgment made in heaven? [Note: [Col. 0857] In most copies, with the parenthesis removed, the text reads: “had preceded—whether, namely, Lucifer, who,” etc., as in the following section; so the first edition also reads.]

5. What I mean is this. Do you suppose that Lucifer, who rose in the morning but was lifted up too soon, before he was turned into darkness, envied the human race even the infusion [variant: “effusion”] of the oil, so that already then he muttered indignantly to himself, as it were saying inwardly: “Why this waste?” I do not assert that the Spirit says this; neither do I say that he contradicts it. For I do not know.

Yet it might have happened, [Col. 0857C] if it is not thought incredible, that he who was full of wisdom and perfect in beauty could have foreknown that human beings would come to be, and would also advance to equal glory. But if he foreknew it, he undoubtedly saw it in the Word of God; he envied it in his malice; and, scorning to have companions, he devised to have subjects. “They are weaker,” he says, “and lower in nature; it is not fitting that they should be fellow citizens or equals in glory.”

Or perhaps that presumptuous ascent and enthronement reveal this impious design of his, the sitting signifying teaching: “I will ascend,” he says, “above the high mountain, and I will sit on the sides of the north” (Isa. 14:13), in order thus to obtain the likeness of the Most High: just as the latter, seated above the cherubim, governs every angelic creature, so he himself might sit on high and rule the human race? Far be it! He devised iniquity upon his bed; let iniquity lie to itself.

We recognize no judge but the Creator. It is not the devil but the Lord who will judge the world, and he is our God for ever and ever; he himself will rule us for the ages.

6. Therefore in heaven he conceived sorrow, and in paradise he gave birth to iniquity: the offspring of malice, the mother of death and miseries, and the first parent of all sins—pride. For although “through the envy of the devil death entered into the world” (Wis. 2:24), nevertheless “the beginning of all sin is pride” (Sir. 10:15). But what did it profit him? Nevertheless, [Col. 0858A] you are in us, O Lord, and your name is invoked over us. And the people of your possession says—the Church of the redeemed says—“Your name is oil poured forth.”

When I am cast out, you pour it out after me and into me, because, when you are angry, you remember mercy. Yet Satan received dominion over all the children of pride, becoming the prince of these darknesses; so that pride itself might serve the kingdom of humility, while, under his one temporal dominion—a dominion of that kind—he makes many humble persons lofty and eternal kings. A delightful judgment: that proud hammerer of the humble unknowingly forges for them everlasting crowns, attacking all and being overcome by all.

For everywhere and always the Lord will judge the peoples; he will save the children of the poor and humble [Col. 0858B] the slanderer. Everywhere and always he will defend his own, repel their enemies, and remove the rod of sinners from above the lot of the righteous, “lest the righteous stretch forth their hands unto iniquity” (Ps. 124:3 [125:3]). And it shall finally come to pass that he utterly breaks the bow, shatters the weapons, and burns the shields with fire.

You, wretch, establish your seat in the north, a cloudy and cold quarter; and behold, the needy are raised from the dust and the poor from the dungheap, that they may sit with princes and possess the throne of glory. And you grieve to see fulfilled: “The poor and needy shall praise your name” (Ps. 73:21 [74:21]).

7. Thanks be to you, Father of orphans and Judge of the fatherless: the curdled mountain, the rich mountain, has grown warm over us; the heavens have distilled at the presence of God of Sinai; the oil has been poured out, [Col. 0858C] and the name has been enlarged—the name bestowed on us and begrudged us by the wicked one. Enlarged, I say, even to the hearts and mouths of little children; and in the mouth of infants and nursing babes praise is perfected.

Moreover, the sinner shall see and be angry; and as his anger is implacable, so shall be the unquenchable flame, already prepared for him and his angels. The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall accomplish this. How do you love me, my God, my love? How do you love me, remembering me everywhere, everywhere zealous for the salvation of the needy and poor—not only against proud human beings, but even against exalted angels? In heaven and on earth, O Lord, you judge those who injure me; you overthrow those who attack me. Everywhere you help; everywhere you stand by; everywhere you are at my right hand, O Lord, that I may not be moved.

[Col. 0858D] “I will sing these things to the Lord during my life; I will sing psalms to my God while I exist.” These are his powers; these are the wonders he has done. This is the first and greatest judgment, which that virgin Mary, privy to the secrets, disclosed to me, saying: “He has cast down the mighty from their throne and exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1:52–53).

And the second is like it, which you have now heard: “that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). In these two judgments let the poor person console himself and say: “I remembered your judgments from of old, O Lord, and was comforted” (Ps. 118:52 [119:52]).

8. But let us return to ourselves and search [Col. 0859A] our ways. And that we may do so in truth, let us invoke the Spirit of truth and call him back from on high, whither he had led us, so that he may go before us also into ourselves; for without him we can do nothing. Nor need we fear that he will disdain to descend to us; rather, if we attempt even some small thing without him, he is offended.

For he is not one who goes and does not return, but leads us and brings us back “from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord,” at times drawing us up to himself in his light, at times [variant addition: “to us”] tempering himself to us and enlightening our darkness, so that whether above ourselves or within ourselves, we may always walk in the light, always as children of light.

We have passed through the shadows of allegory; we must now investigate moral matters. Faith has been built up; let life be instructed. The understanding has been exercised; let action be prescribed [variant: “enriched”]. [Col. 0859B] For “good understanding belongs to all who practice it” (Ps. 110:10 [111:10]), provided that both action and understanding are directed to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. On the Two Operations of the Holy Spirit, One Called Effusion and the Other Infusion

1. “Your name is oil poured forth” (Song 1:2). What certainty does the Holy Spirit show us concerning himself in us on the occasion of this passage? Surely, as first occurs, an experience of a twofold operation of his: one by which he first strengthens us inwardly with virtues unto salvation; the other by which he also adorns us outwardly with gifts for the benefit of others. We receive the former for ourselves; the latter for our neighbours.

For example, faith, hope, and charity are given to us for our own sake, since without them we cannot be saved. But a word of knowledge or wisdom, the gift of healing, prophecy, and similar gifts—gifts which we can lack without loss even of our own salvation—are undoubtedly given to be expended for our neighbours’ salvation. Let us call these operations of the Holy Spirit, which we experience either in ourselves or in others, by names derived from their effect: “infusion” and “effusion,” if you please.

To which of these does “Your name is oil poured forth” belong? Is it not to effusion? For concerning infusion he would have said “poured in” rather than “poured forth.” [Note: [Col. 0859D] In Horstius and elsewhere the following sentence is inserted here: “Finally, the phrase ‘Your name is oil poured forth’ was uttered concerning the fragrance breathing outwardly from the breasts, not concerning the bride’s inward virtues. Finally, because of the good [Col. 0860D] fragrance,” etc. But most manuscripts and the first edition omit it. The Utica manuscript contains it, but omits the following sentence, “Finally, because of the good,” etc. In truth, one of the two is superfluous.]

Finally, because of the sweet fragrance of her breasts anointed outwardly, the bride says: “Your name is [Col. 0859D] oil poured forth,” ascribing that fragrance to the bridegroom’s name, as though to oil poured over her breasts. And whoever feels himself anointed with an outward gift of grace, through which he can also pour back something upon others—to him too it is fitting to say: “Your name is oil poured forth.”

2. Yet in these matters we must beware either of giving away what we have received for ourselves, or of retaining what we have received in order to distribute. You keep your neighbour’s property for yourself if, for example, though full of virtues and nevertheless adorned outwardly with gifts of knowledge and eloquence, you bind in useless—indeed, damnable—silence a good word that could benefit many, perhaps through fear, laziness, or an insufficiently discerning humility. Certainly you are cursed because you hide grain from the peoples (Prov. 11:26).

Conversely, you scatter and lose what is your own if, before you have been wholly filled, you hasten to pour forth while half-full—ploughing contrary to the law with the firstborn of an ox and shearing the firstborn of a sheep (Deut. 15:19). Assuredly, while giving another life and salvation, you defraud yourself, when, empty of sound intention, you swell with the wind of vain glory or are infected by the poison of earthly desire; and, swollen with a deadly abscess, you perish.

3. Therefore, if you are wise, you will present yourself as a basin, not as a channel. A channel almost simultaneously receives and pours back; the basin, however, waits until it is filled and then shares what overflows without loss to itself, knowing that cursed is the one who makes his own portion worse.

And lest you consider my counsel contemptible, hear one wiser than I: “The fool,” Solomon says, “utters all his spirit at once; the wise man reserves it for the future” (Prov. 29:11). Yet today we have many channels in the Church, but very few basins. So great is the charity of those through whom heavenly streams flow to us that they wish to pour out before they have been filled, are readier to speak than to listen, eager to teach what they have not learned, and desirous of ruling others though they do not know how to rule themselves.

I judge that no step of piety leading to salvation should be placed before the step established by the Wise Man when he says: “Have mercy on your own soul by pleasing God” (Sir. 30:24). But if I have only a little oil with which to anoint myself, do you think I ought to give it to you and remain empty? I keep it for myself and do not bring it forth at all except at the prophet’s command. If some press me with requests—those perhaps who think of me beyond what they see in me or hear from me—they will be answered: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go rather to those who sell and buy for yourselves” (Matt. 25:9).

“But charity,” you say, “does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5). And do you know why? It does not seek what is its own because it does not lack it. Who seeks what he possesses? Charity never lacks what is its own, that is, what is necessary for its own salvation; nor does it merely possess it, but it abounds. It wishes to abound for itself in order that it may be able to abound for all; it keeps enough for itself that it may fail no one. Otherwise, if it is not full, it is not perfect.

4. But you, brother, whose own salvation is not yet sufficiently secure, whose charity is still either nonexistent or so frail and reed-like that it yields to every breath, believes every spirit, and is carried about by every wind of doctrine—indeed, whose charity is so great that, beyond the commandment, you love your neighbour more than yourself, and yet so small that, contrary to the commandment, it melts through favour, fails through fear, is disturbed by sorrow, is constricted by avarice, is stretched out by ambition, is disquieted by suspicions, harassed by insults, torn open by cares, swells with honours, and wastes away through envy: you, I say, who experience yourself thus in your own concerns, by what madness, I ask, do you either aspire to, or consent to, care for another’s?

But hear the counsel of cautious and watchful charity: “Not that there should be relief for others and affliction for you, but by equality” (2 Cor. 8:13). “Do not be overly righteous” (Eccl. 7:17 [7:16]). It is enough that you love your neighbour as yourself; for this is according to equality.

David says: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness, and my mouth shall praise with lips of rejoicing” (Ps. 62:6 [63:5]). He wishes first to be infused and then to pour forth; not only first to be infused, but also to be filled, so that he may belch forth from fullness, not gape from emptiness. Prudently indeed, lest what was relief to others should be affliction to himself; yet chastely as well, imitating him from whose fullness we have all received.

Learn, then, to pour forth only from fullness, and do not wish to be more generous than God. Let the basin imitate the fountain. It does not flow into a stream or extend into a lake until it is filled with its own waters. Let the basin not be ashamed not to be more lavish than its fountain.

Finally, the very fountain of life, full in itself and full of itself—did it not first, bubbling and leaping into the nearest hidden places of heaven, fill all things with goodness? And only then, when the higher and more secret regions had been filled, did it burst forth to the earth and, from its abundance, save human beings and beasts, as it multiplied its mercy. It first filled the inner regions; and then, overflowing in its many mercies, it visited [Col. 0861C] the earth, watered it abundantly, and multiplied its riches. Therefore do likewise: first fill yourself, then take care in pouring forth.

Kind and prudent charity is accustomed to overflow, not to flow away. “My son,” Solomon says, “do not flow away utterly”; and the Apostle says: “Therefore we ought to pay closer attention to what has been said, lest perhaps we flow away” (Heb. 2:1). What then? Is Paul holier than Solomon, or wiser? In any case, I do not wish to be enriched by your being emptied. For if you are bad to yourself, to whom will you be good? Help me from your surplus, if you can; but if not, spare yourself.

5. But now hear what and how great are the things necessary for one’s own salvation, what and how great must be infused before we presume to pour forth—so far as I can gather them briefly at the present time. For the hour has already advanced far, and urges the discourse toward its close.

The physician comes to the wounded man, the Spirit to the soul. For what soul does he not find wounded by the devil’s sword, even after the wound of its ancient offence has been healed by the medicine of baptism? Therefore, when the Spirit approaches that soul which says: “My scars have become putrid and corrupt because of my foolishness” (Ps. 37:6 [38:5]), what is first necessary? That the swelling or [uncertain reading: *nicus*] which perhaps has grown over the wound and can obstruct healing should before all things be cut away.

Let the ulcer of inveterate habit, then, be cut out by the blade of sharp compunction. But the pain is bitter; let it therefore be soothed with the ointment of devotion, which is nothing other than the exultation conceived from hope in pardon. [Col. 0862A] This produces the power of self-restraint and victory over sin. Now the soul gives thanks and says: “You have broken my bonds; I will offer you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115:16–17 [116:16–17]).

Then is applied the medicine of repentance: the poultice of fasts, vigils, prayers, and any other exercises belonging to penitents. In its labour the soul must be fed with the food of good works, lest it fail. That work is food, you learn from this: “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34). Therefore let works of piety accompany and strengthen the labours of repentance. “Almsgiving,” it says, “provides great confidence before the Most High” (Tob. 4:12).

Food arouses thirst, and the soul must be given drink. Let the drink of prayer accompany the food of good work, composing in the stomach of conscience what has been well done and commending it to God. In prayer is drunk the wine that gladdens the human heart—the wine of the Spirit—which intoxicates and causes forgetfulness of carnal pleasures. It moistens the inner parts of the parched conscience, digests the foods of good deeds, and conveys them through certain members of the soul, strengthening faith, fortifying hope, quickening and ordering charity, and enriching one’s character.

6. Having taken food and drink, what remains except that the sick person rest and give himself to the repose of contemplation after the labours of action? Sleeping in contemplation, he dreams of God; for the present he beholds him through a mirror and in an enigma, not face to face. Yet thus, not so much seen as conjectured, and perceived swiftly as though beneath a flash from a passing spark, scarcely and faintly touched, he burns [Col. 0862C] with love and says: “My soul desired you in the night; indeed, my spirit within me” (Isa. 26:9).

Such love is zealous. Such zeal befits the friend of the bridegroom; this must burn in the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has set over his household. This love fills, burns fervently, boils over, and now pours itself out securely, overflowing and bursting forth, saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

Let him preach, bear fruit, renew signs, and work changes in wonders. There is no place for vanity to intrude where charity occupies everything. For charity is the fullness of the law and of the heart (Rom. 13:10), provided it is full. Finally, “God is charity” (1 John 4:16), and nothing in created things can fill a creature made in God’s image except charity—God—who alone is greater than that creature.

One who has not yet attained this is promoted most dangerously, however great the other virtues by which he seems to excel. If he possesses all knowledge, if he gives all his substance to the poor, if he delivers his body so that it is burned—without charity he is empty. Behold how much must first be infused [Col. 0862D] before we dare to pour forth, giving from fullness rather than want: first, compunction; then devotion; third, the labour of repentance; fourth, a work of piety; fifth, devotion to prayer; sixth, the leisure of contemplation; seventh, fullness of love.

All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit in accordance with the operation called infusion, so that the operation called effusion may thereafter be administered purely and, for that reason, safely, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIX. On the Nature, Manner, and Properties of Angelic Love toward God, According to the Several Orders of Angels

1. The bride still speaks lovingly; she still continues further to pursue the praises of the bridegroom, and invites grace by showing that the grace she had already received was not idle in her. Hear, then, what she adds next: “Therefore,” she says, “the young maidens loved you exceedingly” (Song 1:2).

As though she said: “Not uselessly or vainly, O bridegroom, has your name been emptied and poured out upon my breasts; for therefore the young maidens loved you exceedingly.” For what reason? Because of the name poured out, and because of the breasts anointed by it. For from these they were aroused to love of the bridegroom, and from these they received the means to love.

When the bride received the infused gift, they immediately perceived its fragrance, since they could not be far from their mother; and, filled with that sweetness, they say: “The charity of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Therefore the bride, commending their devotion, says: “This, O bridegroom, is the fruit of your name poured out: therefore the young maidens loved you.”

For they perceive it as poured out because they could not receive it whole; therefore they loved you. Effusion makes the name capable of being received; what is received [variant: “the thing received”] becomes lovable—but only for the young maidens. Those who are more capable rejoice in it whole and do not need it poured out.

2. The angelic creature, with the unobstructed gaze of the mind, beholds the profound abyss of the divine judgments. Blessed by the ineffable delight of their supreme equity, it also rejoices that these judgments are entrusted to its ministry for accomplishment and public manifestation; and therefore it rightly loves the Lord Christ. “Are they not all ministering spirits,” he says, “sent for ministry on behalf of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. 1:14).

But the archangels—to attribute to them something more distinctive than to those who are simply angels—are, I believe, wonderfully delighted because they too are admitted more intimately to the counsels of eternal Wisdom, and because through them those counsels are administered, with supreme ordering, in their proper places and times. This also is why they love the Lord Christ.

Those blessed beings also, perhaps called “Virtues” because, by divine appointment, they investigate and wonder at the hidden and perpetual causes of powers and wonders with happy curiosity, and can mightily produce signs from all the elements of the earth when and where they will—these too are thereby not without reason inflamed with love for the Lord of powers, Christ the power of God. For it is full of sweetness and grace to behold in Wisdom itself the mysterious and hidden things of wisdom; and likewise full of honour and glory to direct visibly in their own hands effects of causes hidden in God’s Word, for the world to behold and wonder at.

3. Likewise, those spirits called Powers, delighting to behold and magnify the divine omnipotence of our Crucified One, which reaches mightily everywhere, receive power to drive out and defeat the hostile powers of demons and human beings on behalf of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation. Do these not also have the most just cause to love the Lord Jesus?

Above these are Principalities. Beholding him more loftily and clearly perceiving that he is the principle of the universe and the firstborn of every creature, they are accordingly granted such dignity of principality that throughout the earth they have power, as from a supreme pivot of things, to change and order kingdoms, principalities, and every rank as they will; according to each person’s merits, to make first persons last and last persons first; to cast down the mighty from their throne and exalt the humble. This too is their reason for loving him.

The Dominations also love him. Why? They are borne, with a praiseworthy presumption, to investigate something more subtle and more sublime concerning Christ’s unbounded and irresistible lordship: namely, that, present everywhere in the universe no less than powerful, he compels the courses of time, movements of bodies, and impulses of minds, above and below, to obey his most righteous will in a most beautiful order. He does so with such vigilant care that not even a point or an iota, as the saying goes, can in any way withdraw from the service due from all these things; yet he works with such ease that the Governor feels no disturbance or anxiety whatsoever.

Therefore, while they behold the Lord of hosts judging all things with such tranquillity, they are carried away, in the exceeding but intelligent wonder of an intensely attentive and sweet contemplation, into that vast sea of divine brightness. They withdraw into a more secret retreat of wondrous tranquillity, where they enjoy such peace and security that, as they rest, all the remaining multitude seems, in reverence for their prerogative, to minister and serve them as truly Dominations.

4. God sits in the Thrones. And I think that these spirits have, above all those mentioned, both a more just cause and fuller matter for love. For if you enter the palace of any human king, do you not see it filled with stools, benches, and chairs, while the royal seat is set in a high place? You need not ask where the king customarily sits: his seat is immediately apparent, higher and more ornate than the other seats.

Thus understand that these spirits surpass all the others in every adornment of beauty, since in them the divine majesty has chosen to reside through a special gift of astonishing condescension. And if sitting signifies teaching, I think that Christ, the Wisdom of God, he who alone is our teacher in heaven and on earth, although elsewhere reaching everywhere because of his purity, enlightens these more specially and more chiefly by his presence as his own seat; and from there, as from a formal teaching hall, instructs angel and human being in knowledge.

From there angels receive knowledge of divine judgments; from there archangels receive knowledge of counsels; there Virtues hear when, where, and what signs they are to produce. There, finally, all—whether Powers, Principalities, or Dominations—learn what they ought to perform by office, what they may undertake by rank, and, above all, what is enjoined on everyone: not to misuse for personal will or glory the power they have received.

5. Yet those heavenly hosts called Cherubim, if the interpretation of their name is retained for them, I judge have nothing which they receive from others or through others; since they may draw in full from the fountain itself, the Lord Jesus himself graciously leading them in person into all fullness of truth and most abundantly revealing the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, all of which are hidden in him.

The Seraphim likewise have no such need, since God, who is charity itself, has drawn and absorbed them into himself so completely and carried them into the same ardour of holy affection that they seem to be one spirit with God. It is like fire which, when it enkindles air, impresses all its heat upon it and clothes it with its colour, so that the air is seen to have become not merely ignited, but fire.

Accordingly, the former spirits especially love to contemplate in God the knowledge “of which there is no number”; the latter, the charity that never fails. Thus each has received its name from that in which it seems to excel: Cherubim means “fullness of knowledge,” while Seraphim means “burning ones” or “those set aflame.”

[Col. 0865C] 6. Therefore God is loved by the angels because of the supreme equity of his judgments; by the archangels because of the supreme moderation of his counsels; by the Virtues because of his most gracious performance of miracles, through which he most kindly draws unbelievers to faith; by the Powers because of that force of most righteous might through which he is accustomed to repel and restrain from the devout the cruelty of malicious beings.

He is loved by the Principalities because of that eternal and original power by which, reaching mightily from end to end, he gives being and the principle of being to every higher and lower creature, spiritual and bodily. He is loved by the Dominations because of his most tranquil will, by which, although he rules everywhere in the strength of his arm, he nevertheless orders all things sweetly through a power made still greater by his innate gentleness and undisturbed tranquillity.

He is loved by the Thrones because of the benevolence of Wisdom as teacher, communicating itself without envy, and of the anointing that freely teaches concerning all things. But he is loved by the Cherubim because he is the Lord of knowledges and, knowing what each needs for salvation, discreetly and providently distributes his gifts, as he knows to be expedient, to those who worthily ask. And he is loved by the Seraphim because he is charity, hates none of the things he has made, and wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth.

7. All these, then, love according to their capacity. But the young maidens, since they understand less, also receive less [Col. 0866A], and are altogether unequal to such sublime things; for they are little children in Christ, to be nourished with milk and oil. Therefore they must draw from the bride’s breasts that by which they may love. The bride has oil poured out, by the fragrance of which they are stirred to taste and perceive how sweet the Lord is. And when she has perceived that they are aflame with love, turning to the Bridegroom she says: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens loved you exceedingly.” What is “exceedingly”? Greatly, vehemently, ardently.

Or perhaps the spiritual discourse indirectly touches you who have recently come, rebuking that less discerning vehemence of yours—which we too have often tried to restrain—or rather, that wholly immoderate stubbornness. You do not wish to be content with the common life. The regular [Col. 0866B] fast is not enough for you; nor the customary vigils, nor the prescribed discipline, nor the measure we assign you in clothing and food. You prefer private observances to common ones. Having once entrusted your care to us, why do you again take yourselves into your own keeping? For that self-will of yours, by which you have so often offended God—your consciences bearing witness—behold, you now again have as your teacher, not me. It teaches you to spare not nature, to yield not to reason, to obey neither the counsel nor the example of the elders, and not to obey us.

Do you not know that obedience is better than sacrifices? (1 Sam. 15:22.) Have you not read in your Rule that whatever is done without the will or consent of the spiritual father shall be reckoned to vainglory, not to reward? (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 49.) [Col. 0866C] Have you not read in the Gospel what model of obedience the boy Jesus handed down to holy children? For when he remained in Jerusalem and said that he must be occupied with the things of his Father, yet, when his parents did not accept this, he did not disdain to follow them to Nazareth: the Master followed disciples, God followed human beings, the Word and Wisdom followed a craftsman and a woman. What more? Sacred history even adds: “And he was subject to them” (Luke 2:43–51).

How long will you be wise in your own eyes? God entrusts and subjects himself to mortals, and do you still walk in your own ways? You received a good spirit, but you do not use it well. I fear that you may receive another in place of it, one who may overthrow you under the appearance of good; and that, having begun in the Spirit, you may be completed in the flesh. Or [Col. 0866D] do you not know that the angel of Satan very often transforms himself into an angel of light? (2 Cor. 11:14.) God is wisdom, and he wishes to be loved not only sweetly but wisely. Hence the Apostle says: “Your reasonable service” (Rom. 12:1). Otherwise the spirit of error will very easily mock you through your zeal if you neglect knowledge; nor does the crafty enemy possess any device 1326 more effective for removing love from the heart than if he can bring it about that love is pursued incautiously and not according to reason.

For this reason I intend to set before you certain ways which those who love God would do well to observe. But because this discourse calls for an end here, tomorrow, if God preserves for me life and the leisure we now have for discussion, I shall attempt to explain them. Then, with your minds refreshed by the night’s [Col. 0867A] rest, and, what is most important, made more eager by prayer offered beforehand, we shall fittingly assemble for a discourse on love, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XX. On the threefold manner in which we love God

1. Let the discourse take its beginning from the Master’s words: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema” (1 Cor. 16:22). He is altogether greatly to be loved by me, through whom I am, live, and understand. If I am ungrateful, I am unworthy. He plainly deserves death who refuses, Lord Jesus, to live for you—and is dead; and whoever does not savor you is foolish; and whoever is concerned to exist except for your sake is of no account and is nothing. Finally, what is man, unless [Col. 0867B] you have made yourself known to him? (Ps. 143:3.)

For your own sake, God, you made all things; and one who wishes to exist for oneself and not for you begins to be nothing among all things. “Fear God and keep his commandments; this,” Scripture says, “is the whole of man” (Eccl. 12:13). Therefore, if this is the whole of man, without this the whole of man is nothing. Bend toward yourself, O God, this little thing which you have deigned to make me; and receive, I beseech you, from my wretched life the remainder of my years. For those years which I lost by living, because I lived ruinously, do not despise, O God, a contrite and humbled heart. My days have declined like a shadow and have passed without fruit. I cannot call them back; let it please you that I should recall them before you in the bitterness of my soul.

Now, concerning wisdom, all my desire and the purpose of my heart are before you; [Col. 0867C] if there were any in me, I would preserve it for you. But, God, you know my foolishness; unless perhaps this itself is wisdom, that I recognize it—and that indeed by your gift. Increase this in me: I am by no means ungrateful for the small gift, but anxious about what is lacking. Therefore I love you in this way, as much as I can.

2. But there is something that moves me more, presses me more, kindles me more. Above all, I say, what renders you lovable to me, good Jesus, is the cup which you drank, the work of our redemption. This readily claims our whole love for itself. This, I say, both attracts our devotion more sweetly, demands it more justly, binds it more tightly, and affects it more powerfully. For in this the Savior labored greatly; nor in the whole fabric of the world did the Creator undertake so much weariness. Indeed, he spoke, and things were made; he commanded, and they were created (Ps. 32:9). But here he endured opponents in his words, watchers in his deeds, mockers in his torments, and reproachers in his death. Behold how he loved.

Add that he did not repay this very love, but added it. For who first gave to him, and shall be repaid? (Rom. 11:35.) But as Saint John the Evangelist says: “Not because we loved God, but because he first loved us” (1 John 4:10). Indeed, he loved even those who did not exist; but he further added love for those who resisted, according to Paul’s testimony: “For while we were still enemies, we were reconciled to God by the blood of his Son” (Rom. [Col. 0868A] 5:10). Otherwise, if he had not loved enemies, he would not yet have possessed friends, just as there would not yet have been those whom he might so love if he had not loved those who did not yet exist.

3. He loved sweetly, wisely, and strongly. I call it sweet because he clothed himself in flesh; cautious because he avoided sin; strong because he endured death. For although he visited in the flesh those whom he visited, he by no means loved carnally, but in the prudence of the Spirit. “Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face” (Lam. 4:20), being jealous for us with God’s jealousy, not a human jealousy—and certainly with a sounder jealousy than the first Adam had for his Eve. Thus those whom he sought in the flesh, he loved in the Spirit and redeemed in power. It is truly full of every sweetness to see the Creator of man as man.

But while he prudently selected human nature apart from sin, he also powerfully drove death from that nature. In assuming flesh he condescended to me; in avoiding sin he provided for himself; in accepting death he made satisfaction to the Father: a sweet friend, a prudent counsellor, a strong helper. I safely entrust myself to him who wills, knows, and is able to save me. The one whom he sought, he also called by his grace; will he cast out one who comes? Certainly I fear neither force nor fraud capable of snatching me from his hand. For he conquered death, which conquers all things; and by a holier art he deceived the serpent, the deceiver of the whole world—wiser than that serpent, more powerful than it.

He assumed the reality of flesh, but the likeness of sin: in the former offering sweet consolation to the weak, and in the latter prudently concealing from the devil the snare of deception. [Col. 0868C] Moreover, in order to reconcile us to the Father, he boldly underwent and subdued death, pouring out his own blood as the price of our redemption. Therefore, unless he had loved sweetly, that Majesty would not have sought me in prison; but he joined wisdom to affection, by which he might deceive the tyrant, and he joined patience also, by which he might appease God the offended Father. These are the ways I promised you; but I set them first before you in Christ, that you might receive them with greater commendation.

4. Learn, O Christian, from Christ how you should love Christ. Learn to love sweetly, to love wisely, to love strongly: sweetly, lest you be enticed; wisely, lest you be deceived; strongly, lest you be turned away from the love of the Lord by oppression. That you may not be drawn away by the glory of the world or pleasures of the flesh, let Christ, who is wisdom, be sweeter to you than these. That you may not be deceived by the spirit of falsehood and error, let Christ, who is truth, shine upon you. That you may not be worn down by adversities, let Christ, the power of God, strengthen you.

Let charity inflame your zeal, knowledge give it form, and steadfastness make it firm. Let it be fervent, watchful, and unconquered. Let it have no lukewarmness, lack no discernment, and be no coward. Consider whether perhaps these three things were also handed down to you in the Law, when God says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. 6:5). It seems to me—if no more fitting interpretation of this threefold distinction occurs—that love of the heart pertains to a certain zealousness of affection; love of the soul to the diligence or judgment of reason; and love with one’s strength [Col. 0869A] to the capacity, steadfastness, or vigor of the mind.

Love, then, the Lord your God with the whole and full affection of your heart; love him with all the vigilance and circumspection of reason; and love him also with all your strength, so that you need not fear even to die for his love, as is written later: “Love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as hell” (Song 8:6). Let the Lord Jesus be sweet and delightful to your affection, against the wrongly sweet enticements of carnal life; and let sweetness overcome sweetness, just as one nail drives out another. But let Christ be, no less, light preceding the understanding and guide to reason—not only in order to avoid the traps of heretical deceit and preserve the purity of faith from their cunning, but also so that you may carefully avoid in your conduct excessive and undiscerning vehemence. Let your love also be strong and constant, neither yielding to terrors nor succumbing to labors.

Therefore let us love affectionately, circumspectly, and mightily, knowing that the love of the heart, which we call affectionate, without that called the love of the soul, is indeed sweet but susceptible to deception; while the latter, without that belonging to strength, is reasonable but fragile.

5. And see that this is so, as we say, in plain examples. When the disciples were distressed because they heard from the Master himself of his approaching departure by ascension, they heard: “If you loved me, you would indeed rejoice because I am going to the Father” (John 14:28). What then? Did they not love him at whose departure they grieved? They loved him in a certain manner, and did not love him. They loved sweetly, but not wisely enough; they loved carnally, [Col. 0869C] but not reasonably. In short, they loved with their whole heart, but not with their whole soul. Their love was contrary to their salvation; therefore he said: “It is expedient for you that I go” (John 16:7), blaming their judgment, not their affection.

Likewise, when he spoke of his future death, Peter, who loved him by wishing to hold him back, tried to oppose him. When, as you remember, Christ restrained him by rebuke, what else did he condemn in him but imprudence? Finally, what does “You do not savor the things that are of God” mean (Mark 8:32–33), except: “You do not love wisely, following human affection against the divine purpose”? And he called him Satan because, though unknowingly, he opposed salvation by forbidding the Savior to die.

Therefore, once corrected, Peter did not thereafter forbid him to die when he repeated the sorrowful saying, but promised that he himself would die with him. Yet he did not fulfill this, because he had not yet arrived at the third degree, in which one loves with all one’s strength. He had been taught to love with his whole soul, but was still weak; well instructed, but insufficiently aided; not ignorant of the mystery, but afraid of martyrdom. That love strong as death had not yet then existed, for it yielded to death. But it existed afterward, when, clothed with power from on high according to the promise of Jesus Christ, he at last began to love with such strength that, when forbidden in the council to preach the holy name, he steadfastly replied to those forbidding him: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Then at last he loved with all his strength, when he did not spare even his life for love. For “no one has greater charity than this: that someone lay down [Col. 0870A] his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Although he did not then lay it down, he had already put it at risk.

Therefore, to love with one’s whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength is not to be drawn away by flatteries, deceived by falsehoods, or broken by injuries.

6. Notice that love of the heart is in a certain sense carnal, because it affects the human heart chiefly toward Christ’s flesh and toward what Christ did or commanded in the flesh. Whoever is filled with this love is readily pierced by every discourse concerning such matters. Nothing is heard more gladly, read more eagerly, recalled more frequently, or meditated upon more sweetly. From this source the person enriches the whole burnt offerings of prayer, as it were, with the fat of a well-fed calf.

Before one praying stands the sacred image of the God-Man: now being born, now nursing, now teaching, now dying, [Col. 0870B] now rising, now ascending. Whatever such representation occurs must either bind the mind to the love of virtues or drive out the vices of the flesh, banish enticements, and quiet desires. I judge this to have been the principal reason, for the invisible God, why he wished to be seen in the flesh and, as man, to live among human beings: namely, that he might first draw all the affections of carnal persons—who could not otherwise be loved except carnally—toward the saving love of his flesh, and thus lead them step by step to spiritual love.

Were not those still standing at this degree who said: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you”? (Matt. 19:27.) Certainly, through love of his bodily presence alone they had left everything, so much so that they could not even endure with composure to hear of the saving passion and death to come, nor afterward behold—or, according to another reading, receive—the glory of his ascension except with profound grief. For this is what he said to them: “Because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart” (John 16:6). Thus, for the time being, in the grace of his present flesh alone, he had withdrawn them from the love of all flesh.

7. But afterward he showed them a higher degree of love when he said: “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:64). I think that the one who said, “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16), had already ascended to this degree. Perhaps the prophet likewise stood at this very point when he said: “Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face.” For what he adds—[Col. 0870D] “Under his shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lam. 4:20)—seems to me to have been added in the person of beginners, so that those who feel themselves too weak to bear the burning heat of the sun may at least rest in the shadow and be nourished by the sweetness of the flesh, while they are not yet able to receive the things that are of God’s Spirit.

For I take the shadow of Christ to be his flesh, by which Mary too was overshadowed (Luke 1:35), so that, through its interposition, the heat and brilliance of the Spirit might be tempered for her. Therefore let the person who does not yet possess the life-giving Spirit meanwhile be consoled in devotion to the flesh—yet only in the manner in which those possess it who say, “Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face,” and likewise, “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer.” For otherwise Christ is by no means loved even in the flesh without the Holy Spirit, though not with that fullness.

The measure of this devotion, however, is that this sweetness should occupy the whole heart and wholly claim it for itself from the love of every flesh and every carnal enticement. For this is to love with the whole heart.
