Otherwise, if I perhaps prefer any blood relationship or pleasure of my own flesh to the flesh of my Lord, so that I am less able to fulfill what, remaining in the flesh, he taught me by word and example, does it not plainly follow that I do not love with my whole heart? For, having it divided, I appear to give one part to his flesh and turn another toward my own. Finally, he says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

Therefore, to put it briefly, to love with the whole heart is to place beneath the love of his most holy flesh everything that flatters from one’s own flesh or another’s. And under this I likewise include the glory of the world, because worldly glory is the glory of the flesh, and there is no doubt that those who delight in it are carnal.

8. Although devotion of this kind toward Christ’s flesh is a gift—and a great gift—of the Spirit, I would nevertheless call this love carnal in comparison with that love in which one tastes not so much the Word made flesh as the Word who is wisdom, the Word who is righteousness, the Word who is truth, the Word who is holiness, piety, power, and whatever else of this kind may be said. For Christ is all these things, having been made for us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption (1 Cor. 1:30).

[Col. 0871C] Do the following seem to you equally and in the same way disposed? On the one hand, one who compassionately sympathizes with Christ suffering, is pierced and readily moved by the remembrance of the injuries he endured, feeds upon the sweetness of this devotion, and is strengthened for whatever is healthful, honorable, and pious. On the other hand, one who is always inflamed with zeal for righteousness, who everywhere is zealous for truth, who burns with devotion to the pursuit of wisdom; to whom holiness of life and discipline of conduct are beloved; whose habits blush at boasting, abhor detraction, know nothing of envy, detest pride, flee not only but also disdain and despise all human glory; who most vehemently abominates and persecutes every impurity of flesh and heart within oneself; who, finally, as though by nature, rejects every evil and embraces what is good. If you compare the affections of the two, is it not evident that the former, compared with the latter, loves in a certain sense carnally?

9. Yet this carnal love is good, through which carnal life is excluded, the world despised and conquered. It advances when it becomes rational, and is perfected when it becomes spiritual also. It is rational, moreover, when, in everything that ought to be believed concerning Christ, the reasoning of faith is held so firmly that one departs in no degree from the purity of ecclesiastical understanding through any appearance of truth or any heretical or diabolical deception. Likewise, it is rational when one’s personal manner of life keeps such caution that the boundary of discernment is exceeded by no superstition, frivolity, or vehemence of a seemingly more fervent spirit. And this, as we said above, is to love God with one’s whole soul.

But if the strength of the assisting Spirit is added so greatly that righteousness is never abandoned through fear of labors, torments, or even death, then God is loved also with all one’s strength, and love is spiritual. I think this name is especially fitting for this love because of the privilege of that fullness of Spirit by which it excels.

And let this suffice concerning what the bride says: “Therefore the young maidens loved you exceedingly” (Song 1:[Col. 0872B] 2). In what follows, may Jesus Christ our Lord himself, the keeper of the treasures of his mercy, deign to open them to us—he who lives and reigns with the Father, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXI. How the bride—that is, the Church—desires to be drawn after the Bridegroom—that is, Christ

1. “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance [Note: [Col. 0871D] Thus the old books and the first editions; not “into the fragrance,” as in other printed editions, as has already been noted. For we run not “into the fragrance,” but “we shall run while the ointments breathe forth fragrance,” no. 4; “stirred by the fragrance,” [Col. 0872D] no. 9; “we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments,” not trusting in our own merits. Further: “You run in the anointing itself; we shall run in its fragrance—you in fullness, we in fragrance,” no. 11.] of your ointments” (Song 1:3).

What? Does the bride, then, need to be drawn—and drawn after the Bridegroom? As though she follows him unwillingly rather than gladly. But not everyone who is drawn is drawn unwillingly. A sick or weak person, namely one unable to walk without help, does not resent being taken to the baths or to a meal, although a guilty person resents being dragged to judgment or punishment. Indeed, she wishes to be drawn, since she asks for this; but she would not ask if she could follow her beloved by herself as she wished.

Why, then, can she not? Shall we confess that the bride too is weak? If any one of the young maidens called herself weak and asked to be drawn, we should not be at all surprised. But concerning the bride, who, as strong and perfect, seemed sufficiently able even to draw others—who does not find it hard to hear that she too must be drawn, as though weak or feeble? Of what soul, then, may we be confident that it is strong and sound, if we consent that she should be called weak who, because of her singular perfection and superior virtue, is called the bride of the Lord?

Or perhaps the Church said this when she beheld her Beloved ascending, yearning to follow him and be taken up with him in glory. Yet even a soul of whatever perfection, so long as it groans under the body of this death and is held enclosed in the prison of this evil age, bound by necessities and tormented by sins, must rise more slowly and sluggishly to contemplate sublime things; nor is it wholly free to follow the Bridegroom wherever he goes. Hence that tearful cry of one groaning: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24.) Hence that suppliant prayer: “Bring my soul out [Col. 0873A] of prison” (Ps. 141:8).

Therefore let the bride also say—say it with groaning—“Draw me after you,” because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). Or does she say this because she desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ, especially when she sees that those for whose sake it seemed necessary for her to remain in the flesh (Phil. 1:23–24) are advancing well in love for the Bridegroom and stand secure in charity? For she had said beforehand: “Therefore the young maidens loved you.” Now, then, she speaks as if saying: “Behold, the young maidens love you and by loving cling firmly to you; they no longer need me, and I have no reason to remain further in this life.” Therefore she says, “Draw me after you.”

2. I would understand it so if she had said, “Draw me to you.” But now, since she says “after you,” it seems to me that she rather asks to be enabled to follow the footprints of his manner of life, to imitate virtue, preserve the rule of life, and attain the discipline of conduct. For in these things especially she needs assistance, so that she may deny herself, take up her cross, and thus follow Christ. Here the bride truly needs to be drawn—and certainly drawn by no other than him who himself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

“I know,” she says, “that I cannot arrive at you except by walking after you; nor can I do even this unless aided by you. Therefore I pray that you draw me after you.” Blessed indeed is the one whose help is from you, who has arranged ascents in the heart in the valley of tears [Col. 0873C] (Ps. 83:6), and who will someday come to you on the mountains of joys. How few, O Lord Jesus, are willing to go after you! Yet there is no one who does not wish to arrive at you, since all know that “delights are at your right hand forever” (Ps. 15:11). Therefore all wish to enjoy you, but not likewise to imitate you; they desire to reign with you but not to suffer with you.

Of these was the one who said: “Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like theirs” (Num. 23:10). He desired for himself the end of the righteous, but not likewise their beginning. Even carnal people desire for themselves the death of spiritual people, whose life they nevertheless abhor. They know that the death of the saints is precious, because, “when he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126:2–3); and because “blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14:13), whereas, on the contrary, according to the prophet’s saying, “the death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. 33:22). They do not care to seek him whom they nevertheless desire to find; they wish to attain him, but not to follow him.

Not so those to whom he said: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22:28). Blessed are those judged worthy of your testimony, gracious Jesus! They truly went after you both in their steps and in their affections. You made known to them the ways of life, calling them after you, because you are the way and the life; and you say: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19); likewise, “Whoever serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also shall my servant be” (John 12:26). Therefore they said in glory: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27).

3. So too your beloved, having left all things for your sake, longs always to go after you, always to cling to your footsteps, and to follow you wherever you go. For she knows that your ways are lovely ways and all your paths are peaceful, and that whoever follows you does not walk in darkness. But she prays to be drawn because your righteousness is like the mountains of God, and she does not suffice for it by her own strength. She prays to be drawn, as is customary, because no one comes to you unless your Father draws him (John 6:44). Moreover, those whom the Father draws, you too draw. For the works that the Father does, these the Son also does likewise.

But she more familiarly asks to be drawn by the Son, as by her own [Col. 0874B] Bridegroom [Note: [Col. 0873] Some manuscripts add: “who desired her beauty.”], whom the Father sent to meet her as her guide and teacher: to go before her in the way of conduct, prepare the path of virtues, instruct her as himself, teach her the way of prudence, and hand over to her the law of life and discipline; and thus he would deservedly desire her beauty.

4. “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” Therefore I need to be drawn, because the fire of your love has cooled for a little while in us; nor are we now able, because of this cold, to run as we did yesterday and the day before. But we shall run afterward, when you restore the joy of your salvation; when a better tempering of grace returns; when the Sun of righteousness is warm again and the cloud of temptation—which is seen to cover him for an hour—has passed away; and when, at the gentle breath of a more favorable breeze, the ointments begin to melt as usual, the aromatics to flow, and to give forth their fragrance. Then we shall run; in that fragrance we shall run.

We shall run, I say, while the ointments breathe forth fragrance, because the present sluggishness will depart, devotion will return, and we shall no longer need to be drawn, since, stirred by the fragrance, we shall run of our own accord. But for now, draw me after you. Do you see that the one who walks in the Spirit does not remain in one condition or always advance with the same ease, and that one’s way is not in one’s own power? Rather, the governing Spirit, as he wills, dispenses it so that one now more slowly, now more eagerly, forgets what lies behind and stretches forth toward what lies ahead. I think that, if you attend to this very point, your inward experience answers you concerning what I speak outwardly.

5. [Col. 0874D] Therefore, when you feel yourself affected by lethargy, sloth, or weariness, do not for that reason despair or desist from spiritual endeavor. Instead, seek the helping hand, begging to be drawn, after the example of the bride, until grace once again awakens you and makes you more ready and eager, so that you run and say: “I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118:32).

But while grace is present, delight in it in such a way that you do not imagine that you possess God’s gift by hereditary right, secure in it as though you could never lose it. Otherwise, when he suddenly perhaps withdraws his hand and removes the gift, you may collapse in spirit and become more sorrowful [Col. 0875A] 1332 than you ought. Do not say in your abundance, “I shall never be moved,” lest you also be compelled to say with groaning what follows: “You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (Ps. 29:7–8). If you are wise, you will rather follow the counsel of the Wise Man: in days of evil, do not forget good things; and in days of good things, do not forget evil things (Ecclus. 11:27).

6. Therefore, in the day of your strength do not be secure, but cry to God with the Prophet and say: “When my strength fails, do not forsake me” (Ps. 70:9). In a time of temptation, however, take comfort and say with the bride: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” Thus hope will not abandon you in evil times, nor will prudence be absent in good times. Amid the adversities and prosperities of changing seasons, you will possess a certain image of eternity: namely, the inviolable and unmoved equanimity of a steadfast mind. You will bless the Lord at every time, and so, even among the uncertain events and sure failures of this unstable age, you will claim for yourself a state somehow of perennial unchangeableness, as you begin to renew and reform yourself into that ancient mark of likeness to the eternal God, “with whom there is no change or shadow of turning” (James 1:17).

For as he is, so shall you be in this world: neither timid in adversities nor undisciplined in prosperities. In this, I say, the noble creature made in the image and likeness of its Maker shows that it is recovering—indeed, already beginning to regain—the dignity of its ancient honor, when it judges itself unworthy to be conformed to this falling age and strives rather, according to Paul’s teaching, to be reformed in the newness of its mind (Rom. 12:2), into that likeness in which it knows itself to have been created. In this way it also compels, as is fitting, this age—which was made for its sake—to be conformed to it in a marvelous reversal, when all things begin to work together for its good, as though, having cast aside their degenerate appearance and resumed their own natural form, they recognize their Lord, for whose service they were created.

7. Hence I judge that the saying which the Only-Begotten spoke concerning himself—namely, that if he were lifted up from the earth, he would draw all things to himself—can also belong in common to all his brothers, those whom the Father foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Thus I too, if I am lifted up from the earth, boldly say: “I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). For I do not rashly appropriate to myself, my brothers, the voice of the one whose likeness I put on.

If this is so, let the rich of this age not suppose that Christ’s brothers possess heavenly things alone because they hear him say: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). Let them not, I say, suppose that those who hear only heavenly things in the promise possess heavenly things alone. They possess earthly things too, indeed “as having nothing, yet possessing all things”: possessing not as needy beggars, but as masters—certainly more truly masters to the degree that they are less covetous. For to a faithful person the whole world is wealth. Truly the whole world: because adversities and prosperities alike, all things equally serve such a person and work together for good.

8. Therefore the avaricious person hungers for earthly things as a beggar; the faithful person despises them as a master. The former begs by possessing; the latter keeps by despising. Ask any of those who with an insatiable heart crave temporal gain whether people act wisely who sell their possessions and give to the poor, purchasing the kingdom of heaven with earthly property. Without doubt he will answer: “Wisely.” Ask likewise why he himself does not do what he approves. “I cannot,” he will say. Why? Certainly because his mistress, avarice, does not permit it; because he is not free; because the things which he appears to possess are not his, nor is he master even of himself.

If they are truly yours, spend them for gain and exchange earthly things for heavenly. If you cannot do so, confess that you are not the master of your money but its slave; its keeper, not its possessor. Finally, you are conformed to your purse as a servant to her mistress: just as a servant necessarily both rejoices with her rejoicing and grieves with her grieving, so you too grow in spirit together with your growing purse and diminish with your diminishing one. For you are contracted with sadness when it is emptied, and relaxed with joy—or at least puffed up with pride—when it is filled. This is the case with that person.

But let us strive to imitate the bride’s freedom and steadfastness. Well instructed in all things and wise of heart, she knows how to abound and how to endure want. When she asks to be drawn, she shows what she lacks: not money, but virtue. Again, when she nevertheless consoles herself with the hope of returning grace, she shows that although she may fail, she does not despair.

9. She says, therefore: “Draw me after you; we will run in the fragrance of your ointments.” And what wonder if she needs to be drawn, she who runs after a giant, who strives to overtake him who leaps upon the mountains and bounds over the hills? “His word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147:15). She cannot run abreast of him, cannot contend with equal speed with him who “rejoices as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6); she cannot do so by her own strength, and therefore asks to be drawn. “I am weary,” she says, “I fail; do not abandon me, but draw me after you, lest I begin to wander after other lovers, lest I run as though without a sure aim. Draw me after you; for it is better for me [Col. 0876D] that you should draw me—that is, that you should inflict upon me whatever force is needed, whether by frightening threats or by chastening scourges—than that, sparing me, you should leave me disastrously secure in my sluggishness. Draw me, in a sense, unwilling, that you may make me willing; draw me while sluggish, that you may make me run. A time will come when I shall not need one to draw me, since we shall run willingly and with all eagerness. I shall not run alone, though I have asked that I alone be drawn: the young maidens too will run with me. We shall run together, we shall run at the same time: I in the fragrance of your ointments, they stirred by my example and encouragement; and thus we shall all run in the fragrance of your ointments. The bride has imitators, just as she herself is an imitator of Christ. Therefore she does not say in the singular, ‘I shall run,’ but, ‘We shall run.’”

[Col. 0877A] 10. But a question arises: why, when she asked to be drawn, did she not likewise join the young maidens to herself, so as to say not “Draw me,” but “Draw us”? What then? Does the bride perhaps need to be drawn, while the young maidens do not? O fair one, O happy one, O blessed one! Explain to us the reason for this distinction. You say, “Draw me.” Why “me,” and not “us”? Do you begrudge us this good? Far be it! For you would not immediately have said that the young maidens would run with you, if you had wished to go after the Bridegroom alone. Why, then, after adding at once in the plural, “We shall run,” did you ask in the singular that you be drawn? “Charity,” she says, “asked it so.” Learn from this word of mine to hope for a twofold help from above in spiritual exercise: correction and consolation. One disciplines outwardly; the other visits inwardly. The former restrains [Col. 0877B] insolence; the latter raises one to confidence. The former produces humility; the latter consoles faintheartedness. The former makes people cautious; the latter devout. The former teaches the fear of the Lord; the latter tempers fear itself with an infused joy of salvation, as it is written: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Ps. 85:11); and again: “Serve the Lord with fear, and exult before him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11).

11. We are drawn when we are exercised by temptations and tribulations; we run when, visited by inward consolations and inspirations, we breathe as it were amid sweet-smelling ointments. Therefore I reserve for myself, as strong, as sound, as perfect, that which seems austere and hard, and say in the singular, “Draw me.” That which is pleasant and sweet I share with you as with the weak, [Col. 0877C] and say, “We shall run.” I know that the young maidens are delicate and tender, and less fit to endure temptations; therefore I wish them to run with me, but not to be drawn with me. I wish to have companions in consolation, but not likewise in labor. Why? Because they are weak, and I fear that they may fail and collapse. “Correct me,” she says, “exercise me, test me, draw me after you, O Bridegroom; for I am ready for scourges and able to endure them. Yet we shall run together: I alone shall be drawn, but together we shall run. 1334 We shall run, we shall run—but in the fragrance of your ointments, not trusting in our own merits. Nor do we trust that we run by the greatness of our own strength, but by the multitude of your mercies. For even if at some time we have run and have been willing, it was not of one who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16). Let mercy return, and we shall run. You indeed run in your strength, as a giant and mighty one; we shall not run unless your ointments breathe forth their fragrance. You, whom the Father anointed with the oil of gladness above your companions (Ps. 44:8), run in the anointing itself; we shall run in its fragrance: you in fullness, we in fragrance. It would be time for me to fulfill what I remember having promised long above concerning the Bridegroom’s ointments, if the length of this sermon did not forbid it. I therefore postpone it; for the dignity of the subject does not allow itself to be compressed into an irksome brevity. Pray to the Lord of anointing that he may deign to make the free offerings of my mouth pleasing, so as to bring to your desires the remembrance of the abundance of his sweetness, [Col. 0878A] which is in Jesus Christ our Lord, the Bridegroom of the Church. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. On the Bridegroom’s Four Ointments, and the Four Cardinal Virtues

1. If the Bride’s ointments were found to be so precious and magnificent, as you heard when they were discussed, what sort, then, are the Bridegroom’s? And although we are not able adequately to explain them as they deserve, there is nevertheless no doubt that the power is more excellent and the grace more effective in those whose fragrance alone stirs not only the young maidens, but even the Bride herself to run. For, if you observe, she dared promise nothing comparable concerning her own ointments. Indeed, she boasts that they are excellent; yet she does not say that she had run or would run in them, [Col. 0878B] whereas she promises this in the fragrance alone of his ointments. What if she felt the very anointing poured out upon herself, when she is so moved by its faint fragrance that she runs? It would be surprising if she did not fly as well.

But someone says: “Stop praising them now. It will be sufficiently clear what they are once you begin to identify them.” No; I make no such promise. Indeed, believe me, I still confess that I do not know whether even these are the things which come to mind to be said. For I think the Bridegroom possesses many and various kinds of spices and ointments, and not a few: some in which the Bride alone delights, as one nearer and more intimate; others which reach even to the young maidens; and still others which extend even to those far away and strangers, so that there is no one who can hide from his warmth. Yet although the Lord is sweet to all, he is sweetest to those of his household; and the more familiarly anyone approaches him through merits of life and purity of mind, the more I think that person perceives the fragrance of fresher spices and a sweeter anointing.

2. In matters of this kind, understanding grasps only as much as experience attains. I certainly would not rashly claim for myself the Bride’s prerogative. The Bridegroom knows with what delights of the spirit he cherishes his beloved, by what inspirations he singularly refreshes her senses, and with what perfumes he soothes her. “Let your spring be your own, in which no stranger shares, nor any unworthy person drinks”; for it is “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song 4:12). Yet its waters are drawn out into the streets. I confess that I have these at hand, provided no one is troublesome or ungrateful to me if I draw from the public source and offer drink from it. For, to commend my ministry in this respect for a moment, it is surely no small weariness and labor to go out daily and draw even from the open streams of Scripture, and from them serve the needs of individuals, so that each of you may have ready at hand, without personal labor, spiritual waters for every purpose: for washing, for drinking, for cooking food. The divine word is indeed the water of saving wisdom, not only giving drink but also washing, as the Lord says: “You are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15:3). Moreover, divine speech cooks the raw thoughts of the flesh by the fire kindled by the Holy Spirit, and turns them into spiritual meanings and [Col. 0879A] food for the mind, so that you may say: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire shall blaze” (Ps. 38:4).

3. Those who, with a purer mind, are able by themselves to grasp loftier matters than those set forth through us, I not only do not prohibit, but warmly congratulate—provided they too allow us to minister simpler things to simpler people. Who will grant me that all may prophesy? Would that I did not have to occupy myself with these matters! Would that this care lay upon another, or rather, what I would prefer, that there were no one among you who needed them, but that all were taught by God, and I could be free to contemplate and see that the Bridegroom is God! But now, since for the present I am not permitted even to inquire into him—much less, I do not say to behold him—and I say this not without tears: the King in his beauty, seated above the cherubim, seated upon a throne high and exalted, in that form in which, equal to the Father, he was begotten before the morning star amid the splendors of the saints, in which the angels ever desire to look upon him, God with God—at least I, a human being, speak to human beings of that same one as man, according to that form in which, to make himself manifest through his exceeding condescension and love, being made lower than the angels, he placed his tent in the sun and himself came forth “as a bridegroom from his chamber” (Ps. 18:6). I speak of him as sweet rather than sublime, as anointed rather than lofty: in short, as the one whom the Spirit of the Lord anointed and sent “to preach good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim pardon to captives and opening to those who are shut up, to proclaim [Col. 0879C] the year acceptable to the Lord” (Ps. 61:1–2).

4. Therefore, while preserving for each person whatever loftier and subtler understanding concerning the Bridegroom’s ointments may perhaps have been granted them by a special gift to feel and experience, I set forth publicly what I have received in common. For he himself is the fountain of life, himself the sealed fountain; bursting forth from within the enclosed garden, he poured himself out through the mouth of Paul, his channel, as that true Wisdom which, according to blessed Job’s saying, “is drawn from hidden places” (Job 38:18), into four streams, and directed them into the streets. There Paul assigns to us that Christ was made by God “wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30). From these four streams, as from most precious ointments—for nothing prevents both meanings being understood: water, because they cleanse; anointing, because they give fragrance—from these four things just mentioned, I say, as from most precious ointments, prepared from heavenly ingredients upon the mountains of spices, such sweetness of fragrance filled the Church’s nostrils that, immediately stirred by that sweetness from the four quarters of the world, she hastened upward to the Bridegroom, like that Queen of the South who hastened from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, provoked by the fragrance, as it were, of his reputation (1 Kgs. 10:1–7).

5. Indeed, the Church could not run in the fragrance of her Solomon until he who from eternity was Wisdom from the Father was in time made Wisdom for her by the Father, so that she might perceive his fragrance. [Col. 0880A] In the same way he was made righteousness, sanctification, and redemption for her, so that she might run in the fragrance of these also, although he had equally been all these things in himself before all things. For “in the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1); but the shepherds came hastening to see him only when it was announced that he had been made. Finally, they say to one another: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this word which has been made, which the Lord has made and shown to us.” And it follows that they came hastening (Luke 2:15–16). Previously they did not move, while the Word was only with God. But when the Word which was became made, when the Lord made and showed this, then they came hastening; then they ran. Therefore, just as in the beginning the Word was, but the Word was with God, and was made so as to begin to be also with human beings, so likewise in the beginning wisdom was, righteousness was, sanctification and redemption were—but for angels. In order that he might be these things also for human beings, the Father made him all these things, and made what the Father did. Finally, “he who was made,” he says, “wisdom for us [Col. 0880B] from God” (1 Cor. 1:30). He does not say simply, “who was made wisdom,” but “who was made wisdom for us,” because he who was for angels was made also for us.

6. “But,” you say, “I do not see how he was redemption for angels. For nowhere does the authority of Scripture seem to maintain that they were ever captive to sin or subject to death, and thus needed redemption—except, at any rate, those who, falling through an irreparable lapse of pride, do not thereafter deserve to be redeemed. If, therefore, angels were never redeemed—some because they had no need, others because they could not merit it; the former because they did not fall, the latter because they are irrevocable—how do you say that the Lord Jesus Christ was redemption for them?” Listen briefly. He who raised fallen humanity gave the standing angel [variant: “a state”] the gift not to fall; thus rescuing the one from captivity and preserving the other from captivity. In this respect he was redemption equally for both: releasing the one and keeping the other safe. It is clear, therefore, that the Lord Christ was redemption to the holy angels, as he was righteousness, wisdom, and sanctification; and nevertheless that these same four things were made for human beings, [Col. 0880D] who can perceive and discern the invisible things of God only through things that have been made (Rom. 1:20). Thus everything that he was for angels he was made for us. What? Wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, redemption: wisdom in preaching; righteousness in the forgiveness of sins; sanctification in the life he led among sinners; redemption in the passion which he endured for sinners. When, therefore, he was made these things by God, then the Church perceived the fragrance; then she ran.

7. See now the fourfold anointing; see the most abundant and immeasurable sweetness of him whom the Father anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. You sat, O human being, in darkness [variant: “dark places”] and the shadow of death through ignorance of the truth; you sat [Col. 0881A] bound in chains of sins. He descended to you in prison, not to torment, but to rescue you from the power of darkness. First, as teacher of truth, he drove away the shadow of your ignorance by the light of his wisdom. Then, by the righteousness which is from faith, he loosed the cords of sins, freely justifying the sinner. By this twofold benefit he fulfilled that saying of holy David: “The Lord frees those in chains; the Lord enlightens the blind” (Ps. 145:7–8). He added, moreover, holy life among sinners, and thus gave the pattern of life, as of the road by which you might return to your homeland. Finally, to crown his mercy, he gave up his soul to death and brought forth from his own side the price of satisfaction by which he might appease the Father; by this he plainly drew to himself that verse: “With the Lord is mercy, and with him abundant redemption” (Ps. 129:7). Truly abundant, because not a drop but a wave of blood flowed freely from the five parts of his body.

8. What ought he to have done for you and did not do? He enlightened the blind, freed the bound, brought back the wandering, reconciled the guilty. Who would not willingly and eagerly run after him, who both frees from error and overlooks errors; who then gives merits by his life and wins rewards by his death? What excuse has one who does not run in the fragrance of these ointments, unless perhaps the fragrance has not reached that person? Yet the fragrance of life has gone out into all the earth, for “the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy, and his mercies are over all his works.” Therefore whoever does not perceive this life-giving fragrance scattered everywhere and consequently does not run is either dead or foul-smelling [variant: “rotten”].

The fragrance is reputation. The fragrance of report reaches [variant: “goes before”], stirs one to run, leads one to the experience of anointing, to the prize of vision. One is the voice of all who rejoice, of all who arrive: “As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts” (Ps. 47:9). Assuredly, because of the gentleness proclaimed in you, we run after you, Lord Jesus, hearing that you do not despise the poor or shrink from the sinner. You did not shrink from the thief confessing, the sinful woman weeping, the Canaanite woman pleading, the woman caught in adultery, the man sitting [Col. 0881D] at the tax booth, the publican praying, the disciple denying you, the persecutor of your disciples, or your very crucifiers. We run in the fragrance of these things.

Moreover, we perceive the fragrance of your wisdom from what we have heard: that if anyone lacks wisdom, that person should ask it from you, and you will give it. For they say that you give to all abundantly and do not reproach them (Jas. 1:5). But the fragrance of your righteousness is spread everywhere so abundantly that you are called not only righteous, but righteousness itself, and righteousness making righteous. Finally, you are as powerful to justify as you are abundant in forgiving. Therefore, whoever, pierced with sorrow for sins, hungers and thirsts for righteousness, should believe in you who justify the ungodly; and, justified by faith alone, that person will have peace with God.

Your life indeed gives forth most sweetly and abundantly the fragrance of holiness—not only your manner of life, but also your conception. For you neither committed sin [Col. 0882A] nor contracted it. Therefore those who desire and resolve to pursue holiness from him who justifies from sins, without which no one shall see God, should hear you crying: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 19:2). Let them consider your ways and learn from you that you are righteous in all your ways and holy in all your works (Ps. 144:17). And how many does the fragrance of redemption make run? When you are lifted up from the earth, then indeed you draw all things to yourself. Your passion is the final refuge, the unique remedy. When wisdom fails, when righteousness is insufficient, when the merits of holiness collapse, it comes to aid. For who would presume that one’s own wisdom, righteousness, or holiness is sufficient for salvation? “Not,” he says, “that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5). Therefore, when my strength fails, I am not disturbed, I do not despair. I know what I shall do: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:13). “Enlighten my eyes, O Lord, that I may know what is pleasing before you at all times” (Wis. 9:10), and I am wise. “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. 24:7), and I am righteous. “Lead me, O Lord, in your way” (Ps. 85:11), and I am holy. Yet unless your blood pleads for me, I am not saved. For all these things we run after you: forgive us, for we cry after you.

9. Nor do we all run equally in the fragrance of every ointment. Rather, you may see some burning more intensely with zeal for wisdom; others more strongly encouraged to repentance by hope of pardon; others more abundantly stirred to the practice of virtues by the example of his life and conduct; and still others more inflamed to devotion by remembrance of his passion. Do we think that we can find examples of each?

Those sent by the Pharisees ran in the fragrance of wisdom when they returned and said: “Never has any man spoken thus” (John 7:46), undoubtedly admiring his teaching and confessing his wisdom. Holy Nicodemus too ran in this very fragrance when he came to Jesus by night (John 3:2); in the great splendor of wisdom, he departed instructed and taught in many things. But Mary Magdalene ran in the fragrance of righteousness, she whose many sins were forgiven because she loved much [Col. 0882D] (Luke 7:47). Surely she was righteous and holy, and no longer a sinner, as the Pharisee reproached her, not knowing that righteousness and holiness are God’s gift, not a human achievement; and that one is not only righteous but blessed to whom the Lord will not impute sin. Had he forgotten how, by touching either his own bodily leprosy or another’s, Christ drove it away rather than contracted it? Thus, touched by a sinful woman, the righteous one bestows righteousness; he does not lose it. Nor is he defiled by the filth of sin by which he cleanses her.

The publican also ran: when he humbly implored propitiation for his sins, he went down justified, as Righteousness itself testified (Luke 18:14). Peter ran, who, having fallen, wept bitterly (Luke 22:62), so that he might wash away guilt and recover righteousness. David ran, who, acknowledging and confessing his guilt, deserved to hear: “And the Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Sam. 12:13).

Paul, moreover, testifies that he runs in the fragrance of sanctification when he boasts that he is an imitator of Christ, saying to his disciples: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1). All who said, “Behold, we have left [Col. 0883A] everything and followed you” (Matt. 19:27), also ran; for from desire to follow Christ they had left everything. This saying generally exhorts all to the same fragrance: “Whoever says that he abides in Christ ought also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). Finally, if you wish to hear who ran in the fragrance of his passion, take all the martyrs. Behold, you have the four ointments identified: first, wisdom; second, righteousness; third, sanctification; fourth, redemption. Retain the names, receive the fruit; but do not ask for the method of composition or the number of ingredients from which they were prepared. Such things are not readily available to us in the Bridegroom’s ointments as they were in the preceding ointments of the Bride. For in Christ there is fullness of things without number and without measure. “There is no number of his wisdom” (Ps. 146:5); his righteousness is “like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35:7), like everlasting mountains; his holiness is unique, and his redemption inexplicable.

10. This too must be said: the wise people of this age disputed much in vain concerning the four virtues, though they could not grasp them at all, because they did not know him who was made for us by God: wisdom, teaching prudence; righteousness, forgiving sins; sanctification, living continently as an example of temperance; and redemption, dying bravely as an example of fortitude. Perhaps someone says: “The other correspondences fit well, but sanctification seems less properly referred to temperance.” To this it is first answered that continence is the same thing as temperance. Then, in Scripture it is customary for sanctification to be used for continence or purity. Finally, what were those very frequent sanctifications among Moses other than certain purifications of persons restraining themselves from food, drink, sexual intercourse, and similar things? But hear especially the Apostle himself, how habitually he uses or employs “sanctification” in this sense. “This,” he says, “is the will of God: your sanctification—that each of you may know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification, and not in the passion of desire”; again: “For God has not called us to uncleanness, but to sanctification” (1 Thess. 4:3–7). It is clear that he uses sanctification for temperance.

11. Having therefore brought into the light what seemed somewhat obscure, I return to the point from which I had digressed. What have you to do with virtues, when you do not know Christ, the power of God? Where, I ask, is true prudence except in Christ’s teaching? Whence comes true righteousness except from Christ’s mercy? Where is true temperance except in Christ’s life? Where is true fortitude except in Christ’s passion? Therefore only those imbued with his teaching ought to be called prudent; [Col. 0884A] only those who have obtained forgiveness of sins from his mercy, righteous; only those who strive to imitate his life, temperate; only those who steadfastly hold to the examples of his patience amid adversity, strong. Consequently, anyone labors in vain to acquire virtues if that person thinks they are to be hoped for from some source other than the Lord of virtues: whose teaching is the seedbed of prudence, whose mercy is the work of righteousness, whose life is the mirror of temperance, whose death is the emblem of fortitude. To him be honor and glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. On Three Modes of Contemplation Concerning God, Under the Figure of Three Chambers

1. “The king has brought me into his storerooms.” See whence the fragrance comes; see whither one runs. She had said that one must run, [Col. 0884B] and in what one must run; but she had not said where one must run. Therefore one runs to the storerooms, and runs in the fragrance which proceeds from them, the Bride, in her customary discernment, foreseeing it and desiring to be brought into its fullness. But what are we to think of these storerooms? For the moment, let us regard them as certain fragrant places belonging to the Bridegroom, full of perfumes and overflowing with delights. In such a storehouse, the choicest things from the garden or field are laid away for preservation. There, therefore, they run together. Who? Souls fervent in spirit. The Bride runs; the young maidens run. But she who loves more ardently runs more swiftly and arrives sooner. Upon arriving, she suffers neither rebuff nor even delay. Without delay it is opened to her, as to one of the household, one most dear, specially beloved, and singularly welcome.

What then of the young maidens? They follow from afar; for, while still weak, they cannot run with the Bride in equal devotion, nor entirely imitate her desire and fervor. Thus, arriving later, they remain outside. But the Bride’s charity does not rest, nor does she become arrogant, as often happens, through her success, so as to forget them. Rather, she consoles and encourages them to patience, that they may bear with equanimity both their own exclusion and her absence. Finally, she tells them of the joy she has received, and for no other reason than that they may rejoice with her, confident that whatever grace has come to their mother will in no way be foreign to themselves. For she does not so care for her own progress as to neglect care for them; nor does she judge her own advancement to be helped by their loss. Therefore, wherever the prerogative of merits may lift her above them, charity and loving concern necessarily keep her always with them. In the end, she must imitate her Bridegroom, who indeed ascended to heaven and nevertheless promised that he would be with his own on earth until the end of the age. Thus she too, however much she advances or progresses, is never removed by care, providence, and affection from those whom she bore in the Gospel; she never forgets her own children.

2. Let her therefore say to them: “Rejoice; be confident. The king has brought me into his storerooms [variant: ‘chamber’]: consider yourselves also brought in with me. I seem to have been brought in alone; but it will not benefit me alone. All my advancement is yours: I advance for you; I will share with you whatever additional thing I may perhaps merit for you.” Do you wish to know beyond doubt that she spoke with this meaning and affection? Hear what they reply: “We will exult and rejoice in you.” “In you,” they say, “we will exult and rejoice; for in ourselves we do not yet deserve it.” And they add: “Remembering your breasts”—that is, we patiently endure until you come, knowing that you will return to us with full breasts. Then we trust that we shall exult and rejoice, meanwhile remembering your breasts. By adding “more than wine” (Song 1:3), they indicate that, because of their imperfection, they are still assailed by the remembrance of carnal desires, signified by wine; yet these desires are overcome by the recollection of the abundance of sweetness [Col. 0885B] which they have already experienced flowing from those breasts. I would speak of the breasts, if I did not remember that I had spoken sufficiently about them above (Sermon 9).

Now you see how they trust in their mother, how they count her gains and joys as their own, consoling the injury of their own exclusion by her admission. They would never trust so, unless they recognized her as their mother. Let prelates hear this, who always wish to inspire fear in those entrusted to them, but seldom seek their benefit. “Be instructed, you who judge the earth.” Learn that you ought to be mothers of your subjects, not masters; strive rather to be loved than feared. And if severity is sometimes necessary, let it be fatherly, not tyrannical. Show yourselves mothers by cherishing, fathers by correcting. Become gentle; set aside fierceness; suspend the lash, bring forth the breasts. Let your breasts grow rich with milk, not swell with pride. Why do you make your yoke heavy upon those whose burdens you ought rather to bear? Why does a little one bitten by a serpent flee the conscience of the priest, when he ought rather to run to it as to a mother’s bosom? If you are spiritual, “restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, each considering himself, lest he too be tempted” (Gal. 6:1). Otherwise, that person will die in sin; but “I will require his blood from your hand,” he says (Ezek. 3:20). But of this elsewhere.

3. Now, since the sequence of the text is clear from what we have already set forth, let us see what we ought spiritually to understand by the storerooms. In what follows, there is mention also of the garden and of the chamber; I now join both of these to the storerooms and take them up for the present discussion, for when treated together they will become better known through one another. Let us inquire, if you please, into these three things in Holy Scripture: garden, storeroom, and chamber. For the soul thirsting for God willingly moves and remains in them, knowing that there, without doubt, it will find him for whom it thirsts. Let the garden, then, be plain and simple history; the storeroom, the moral sense; the chamber, the secret place of contemplative insight.

4. First, I think history is not undeservedly assigned to the garden, because in it are found men of virtue, like fruitful trees in the Bridegroom’s garden and in God’s paradise; and from their good deeds and manners you gather as many examples as you pluck fruits. Or does anyone doubt that a good human being is God’s planting? Hear what holy David sings concerning the good man: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall yield its fruit in its season, and whose leaf shall not fall” (Ps. 1:3). Hear Jeremiah singing in the same spirit and in almost the same words: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which sends out its roots toward moisture and shall not fear when heat comes” (Jer. 17:8). Again, the Prophet: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree; he shall multiply like the cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. 91:13). And of himself: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. 51:10). History, therefore, is a garden, and it is itself threefold. For it contains the creation of heaven and earth, reconciliation, and restoration. [Col. 0886B] Creation is like the sowing or planting of a garden. Reconciliation is like the germination of what has been sown or planted. For in its season, when the heavens dropped dew from above and the clouds rained down the righteous one, the earth opened and brought forth the Savior (Isa. 45:8), through whom the reconciliation of heaven and earth was accomplished. For “he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14), making peace through his blood between things on earth and things in heaven (Col. 1:20). Restoration, moreover, will come at the end of the age. For there will be a new heaven and a new earth; and the good will be gathered out from the midst of the evil, like fruit from a garden, to be stored in God’s granaries. “In that day,” as it is written, “the branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth exalted” (Isa. 4:2). Thus you have three times in the garden of the historical sense.

5. In moral instruction likewise, three things are to be observed, as it were three cells in one storeroom. Perhaps for this reason she said “storerooms” in the plural rather than “storeroom,” having in mind this number of cells. For below she boasts that she has been brought into the wine-cellar (Song 2:4). Since we read, “Give an occasion to the wise, and he will become wiser” (Prov. 9:9), let us take occasion from the name which the Holy Spirit judged fit to give to this cell and give names also to the other two: let one be the spice-cellar, and the other the ointment-cellar. We shall see the reasons for these names later. For now observe that all things found with the Bridegroom are health-giving, all are sweet: wine, ointments, spices. Wine, Scripture testifies, gladdens the human heart [Col. 0886D] (Ps. 103:15). Likewise the face is said to be made cheerful with oil (ibid.); into this, of course, powder of spices is poured, so that ointments may be made. Spices are useful not only through the pleasant sweetness of their fragrance, but also through their healing power. Rightly does the Bride rejoice that she has been brought in there, where such abundance of grace overflows.

6. But I think I have other names also, which convey a clearer rationale. And, to name them in their proper order, I would call the first the chamber of discipline; the second, of nature; the last, of grace. In the first you learn, according to the moral order, to be inferior; in the second, equal; in the third, superior: that is, under another, with another, over another; or thus: to be subject, to coexist, to preside. First, therefore, you learn to be a disciple; second, a companion; third, also a master.

Indeed, nature brought forth all human beings equal. But because pride, corrupting the good of nature in their morals, has made people impatient of equality—striving to be made superior to one another, desiring to outstrip each other, vainly ambitious, envying and provoking one another—then, first of all, in the first chamber, the insolence of their conduct must be subdued beneath the yoke of discipline, until their stiff-necked will, worn down by the harsh and prolonged rules of their elders, is humbled and healed; and until, by obedience, they recover in themselves that good of nature which they had lost through pride. Thus, guided now by natural affection alone rather than by fear of discipline, they learn, as far as lies in them, to conduct themselves peaceably and sociably with all the companions of their nature—that is, with all human beings—and at last pass into the chamber of nature, experiencing what is written: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity! It is like ointment upon the head” (Ps. 132:1–2).

To disciplined conduct, as to spices that have been crushed, there is added the oil of gladness, the good of nature; and so the ointment becomes good and pleasant. Anointed, as it were, with this, a person becomes gentle and mild, blameless, cheating no one, oppressing no one, injuring no one, exalting or preferring himself above no one, and moreover gladly sharing in matters of giving and receiving.

7. I think that, if you have rightly understood the properties of both chambers, you will testify that I have not inappropriately called this one the ointment-chamber and that one the spice-chamber. For in the latter, just as violent pounding draws out and extracts the strength and fragrance of spices by the force of the pestle, so the power of teaching and the strictness of discipline somehow draw forth and express the natural power of upright conduct. In the former, however, the pleasing gentleness of a voluntary, as it were inborn, affection spontaneously hastens to perform its service, precisely like the ointment on the head, which at the light touch of warmth runs down and spreads throughout the whole body.

Thus, in the chamber of discipline are contained the dry and simple kinds of spices; and for this reason I judged that it ought to be called the spice-chamber. But in that which is called the chamber of nature, because ointments are already stored and kept there as though prepared, it likewise receives its name from the thing itself and is called the ointment-chamber.

Nor do I think that the wine-chamber bears any rationale for its name other than this: that there is stored in it the wine of zeal burning in charity. No one at all ought to preside over others who has not yet deserved to be introduced into it. He who rules others must indeed burn with this wine, as the Teacher of the Gentiles burned when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29). Otherwise, you quite improperly desire to preside over those whose benefit you do not seek; and, when you do not zealously desire their salvation, you claim their submission for yourself with excessive ambition.

I have called this chamber too the chamber of grace—not because anyone can obtain either of the other two without grace, but because of the fullness that is received in this one in a singular manner. For “the fullness of the law is charity,” and “he who loves his brother has fulfilled the law” (Rom. 13:10, 8).

8. You have seen the rationale of the names; see also the difference between the chambers. For it is not equally easy or equally within one’s power to restrain, by fear of the master and by the rigid censure of discipline, the unruly and wandering senses and the unbridled appetite of the flesh; and to live well in harmony with one’s companions through spontaneous affection; to live with one’s conduct chastened under the rod, and to behave agreeably toward one’s equals under the sole instruction of the will.

Nor, again, may anyone say that living sociably and presiding usefully are of one and the same merit or virtue. How many live quietly under a teacher who, if you release them from the yoke, prove unable to remain quiet or in any way to keep themselves harmless among equals! Likewise, you will see countless people living simply and blamelessly among their brethren, yet over their brethren not merely uselessly but foolishly and wickedly. Such persons are content with a certain good mediocrity, according to the measure of grace God has apportioned to them: they do not need a master, yet are not fit for mastery.

Those in the latter condition surpass the former in conduct; but those who know how to be superiors stand above both. For those who govern well receive in promise that they shall be “set over all the goods of their Lord” (Matt. 24:48). Yet few indeed preside usefully; fewer still preside both usefully and humbly. Nevertheless, the person who has perfectly attained discernment, the mother of virtues, accomplishes both easily—provided that he is also made drunk with the wine of charity, unto contempt for his own glory, unto forgetfulness of himself, and so as not to seek his own interests. This is attained only by the singular and wondrous instruction of the Holy Spirit within the wine-chamber.

For the virtue of discernment lies inert without the ardor of charity, while vehement ardor rushes headlong without the restraint of discernment. Therefore praiseworthy is the one in whom neither is lacking: so that ardor may raise up discernment, and discernment may govern ardor. Such, then, ought to be the conduct of one who presides.

But I would call the best in conduct, and the one who has perfectly grasped the summit of this discipline, the person to whom it has been granted to pass through and traverse all these chambers without stumbling: resisting his superiors in nothing whatsoever, envying his equals in nothing, and neither failing his subjects in care nor ruling them in pride; obedient to those set over him, well fitted to his companions, usefully condescending to those subject to him. This, indeed, I would without hesitation judge to be the mark of perfection in the bride. The saying she uttered also indicates it: “The king brought me into his chambers,” because she shows herself introduced not into one particular chamber, but into chambers in the plural.

9. Let us now come to the bedchamber. What is this also? And do I presume to know what it is? Far be it from me to claim experience of so great a matter, or to boast of a prerogative reserved for the blessed Bride alone. I take care, in accordance with the Greek saying, to know myself, so that I may know with the Prophet also what I lack (Ps. 38:5). Yet if I knew nothing at all, I would say nothing. What I know, I do not begrudge you or withhold; what I do not know, may he who teaches human beings knowledge teach you (Ps. 93:10).

I said—and you remember—that the bedchamber is to be sought in the secret place of contemplative vision belonging to the King. But just as I know that I have said concerning ointments that many and diverse ones are with the Bridegroom, that not all are available to everyone, but particular gifts are granted to each according to the diversity of merits, so too I think that the King has not one bedchamber but many. For surely there is not one queen only, but many; there are many concubines also, and maidens without number. And each finds her own secret place with the Bridegroom and says: “My secret is for myself, my secret is for myself” (Isa. 24:16).

Not all are granted enjoyment in one place of the Bridegroom’s welcome and secret presence, but each as it has been prepared for her by his Father. For we did not choose him; rather, he chose us and appointed us; and where each is appointed by him, there she is. Thus one contrite woman obtained a place beside the feet of the Lord Jesus (Luke 7:38), while another found the fruit of her devotion at his head (Matt. 26:7), if indeed the latter—

> **[Note: Col. 0889C]** These are the same words as Augustine’s, *Tractates on John*, tractate 9, no. 3. Whether the woman who is read to have anointed the Lord more than once, and who was Martha’s sister, was one woman or several, was a major controversy among the ancients. Among others, see Jansen of Ghent, *Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 48, where he treats the matter thoroughly in his customary manner.
>
> Some, especially Greeks, among them Origen and Theophylact, think that there were three different women: first, the unnamed sinner mentioned in Luke chapter 7; second, another unnamed woman, mentioned in Matthew chapter 26 and Mark chapter 14; third, the woman called Martha’s sister, mentioned in John chapter 12.
>
> Chrysostom, however, in Homily 81, thinks there were only two: namely, one and the same woman, who is read to have performed the office of anointing Christ once and again, and another who was Martha’s sister. Saint Jerome, conversely, on Matthew chapter 26, holds that the woman who poured ointment over Christ’s head was the same as Martha’s sister, but different from the woman who anointed his feet in the Pharisee’s house; Saint Ambrose, on Luke, appears to favor this opinion.
>
> Gregory the Great admits one woman everywhere, and most support him. Ambrose, on Luke—where he does not object to their being considered different—writes, meanwhile, that the same woman may appear to have been different only according to the difference of time and merit: “Thus she is still that sinner, yet already more perfect. For although the Church or the soul does not change its person, it changes in its progress.”
>
> Whatever the case, Bernard raises the same doubt in Sermon 12 on the Song of Songs; but in Sermon 3 on the Assumption, no. 2, he expressly asserts that the woman dealt with in Luke chapter 7 is the same as the one in Matthew chapter 26, Mark chapter 14, and John chapter 12. For he says: “See Mary’s prerogative: what an advocate she has in every case. For the Pharisee is indignant” (namely, in Luke chapter 7), “the sister complains” (John chapter 12), “and even the disciples murmur” (Matthew chapter 26 and Mark chapter 14); “everywhere Mary is silent, and Christ speaks for her.” Read Vossius, *Evangelical Harmony*, book 1, chapter 3, and other interpreters.

Moreover, Thomas at his side, John at his breast, Peter in the bosom of the Father, and Paul in the third heaven obtained the grace of this secret.

10. Which of us can adequately distinguish these varieties of merits—or rather, rewards? Yet, lest we seem to have entirely passed over what we ourselves know [variant: “have set in motion”], the first woman made her bed for herself in the security of humility; the second, on the throne of hope; Thomas, on the firmness of faith; John, on the breadth of charity; Paul, in the depth of wisdom; Peter, in the light of truth.

Thus there are many dwelling places with the Bridegroom; and whether she be a queen, a concubine, or even one among the maidens, each receives there a fitting place and limit according to her merits—how far she may advance in contemplation, enter into the joy of her Lord, and search out the sweet secrets of the Bridegroom. In its place, I shall try to demonstrate this more distinctly, insofar as he himself deigns to suggest it. For now it is enough to know that no maiden, no concubine, and no queen at all has access to that secret of the bedchamber which the Bridegroom reserves uniquely for his one fair and perfect dove.

Nor indeed am I indignant if I am not admitted to it, especially since I know that not even the Bride herself has yet meanwhile reached every secret she desires. For she too asks that it be shown to her where he feeds, where he rests at noon (Song 1:6).

11. But hear how far I have reached, or thought that I had reached. It should not be accounted boastfulness that I disclose this for your advancement. There is a place with the Bridegroom where the Governor of the universe himself decrees his laws and disposes his counsels, establishing laws for every creature—weight, measure, and number. This place is lofty and hidden, but by no means quiet. For although, as far as he himself is concerned, he disposes all things sweetly, he nevertheless disposes them; and he does not permit the contemplator who perhaps reaches that place to rest. Rather, while searching and marveling, he wonderfully—though delightfully—wearies him and renders him restless.

The Bride aptly expresses both in what follows: both the delight of such contemplation and its restlessness, when she confesses that she sleeps and that her heart watches (Song 5:2). For by sleep she signifies that she feels rest in a most sweet stupor and peaceful wonder; by watchfulness, that she suffers the fatigue of restless inquiry and laborious exercise.

Hence blessed Job says: “If I sleep, I say, ‘When shall I arise?’ and again I wait for evening” (Job 7:4). Do you perceive in these words a holy soul wishing at times to escape a sweetness that is in some manner burdensome, and then again desiring that sweet burden? For he would not have said, “When shall I arise?” if that rest of contemplation had pleased him altogether; but if it had altogether displeased him, neither would he await anew the hour of rest, that is, evening. This, then, is not the place of the bedchamber, where one rests in every respect.

12. There is likewise a place from which the most secret and severe judgment of the righteous Judge, God, keeps immovable watch over rational creatures indeed rejected—he who is terrible in his counsels over the children of men. In this place, I say, the reverent contemplator beholds God, by his just but hidden judgment, neither wiping away the evils of the reprobate nor accepting their goods; indeed, he hardens their hearts lest perhaps they should grieve, repent, be converted, and he heal them. And this is not without a certain and eternal reason, which is known to be all the more dreadful because it stands immovably fixed in eternity.

What we read concerning such people in the prophet is greatly to be feared. There, speaking to his angels, God says: “Let us have mercy on the wicked.” When they tremble and ask, “Will he not then learn to do justice?” “No,” he says, adding the reason: “In the land of the saints he has acted wickedly, and he shall not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. 26:10).

Let clerics fear; let ministers of the Church fear—those who, in the lands of the saints which they possess, act so wickedly that, not content with stipends which ought to suffice them, they impiously and sacrilegiously keep for themselves surplus funds by which the needy ought to be supported; nor do they fear to consume, for the uses of their own pride and luxury, the sustenance of the poor. Surely they sin with a double injustice: they both plunder what belongs to others and misuse sacred things for their own vanities and shameful practices.

13. Since, therefore, he whose judgments are a great abyss is seen for the present to spare and pity such people lest he spare them eternally, who would seek rest in this place? This vision contains the trembling [variant: terror] of judgment, not the security of the bedchamber. This is a terrible place, wholly devoid of rest.

Whenever I have been caught up into it, I have shuddered altogether, repeating with trembling that saying to myself: “Who knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred?” (Eccl. 9:1). Nor is it surprising that I stagger there—I who am indeed a leaf carried by the wind and dry stubble (Job 13:25)—when that greatest contemplator too confessed that his feet were almost moved and his steps almost slipped, saying: “I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners. Why? Because they are not in the labor of men, nor are they scourged with men; therefore pride has held them fast” (Ps. 72:3–6), so that they may not be humbled to repentance but may be condemned for pride with the proud devil and his angels.

For those who are not in the labor of human beings shall surely be in the labor of demons, as the Judge says: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). Yet this too is a place of God, plainly none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven. Here, indeed, God is said to be feared; here are his holy and terrible name and, as it were, the entrance of glory: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:9–10).

14. Do not be troubled because I have assigned the beginning of wisdom to this place at last, and not to the former. There, in a kind of lecture hall of her own, we hear Wisdom, our teacher, teaching concerning all things; here, we receive her. There we are instructed; here we are affected. Instruction makes learned persons; affection makes wise persons.

The sun does not warm all those upon whom it shines. So Wisdom does not immediately kindle to action all those whom she teaches what ought to be done. It is one thing to know of many riches, another to possess them; knowledge does not make a person rich, but possession does. In precisely the same way, it is one thing to know God, another to fear him; knowledge does not make one wise, but fear does, because it affects one.

Would you call wise the person whom his knowledge puffs up? Who but the most foolish would call wise those who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks? I agree rather with the Apostle, who plainly pronounces their heart foolish (Rom. 1:21).

And well is the fear of the Lord called the beginning of wisdom, because God first becomes sweet to the soul when he moves it to fear, not when he instructs it to know. You fear God’s justice; you fear his power; and the just and powerful God tastes sweet to you, because fear is a taste. Moreover, taste makes one wise, as knowledge makes one knowing and riches make one rich.

What, then, is the former place? It merely prepares for wisdom. There you are prepared so that here you may be initiated. Preparation is knowledge of things. But swelling pride most easily follows this, unless fear restrains it. Hence it is rightly said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” for it first opposes itself to the plague of folly. There, therefore, is a certain approach to wisdom; here there is entrance. Yet neither here nor there is perfect rest for the contemplator, because there God appears as if concerned, here as if troubled. Do not, then, seek the bedchamber in these places, of which one appears rather as the lecture hall of a teacher, the other as the tribunal of a judge.

15. But there is a place where God is seen truly resting and at rest: a place altogether not of a judge, not of a teacher, but of a Bridegroom. To me at least—for I do not know about others—it is plainly a bedchamber whenever I happen to be brought into it. But alas, the hour is rare and the stay brief!

There the mercy of the Lord is clearly known to be from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him. Blessed is the one who can say: “I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments” (Ps. 118:63). God’s purpose stands firm; his sentence of peace stands firm over those who fear him, both overlooking their evils and rewarding their goods, so that in a wonderful way not only their good things but even their evil things work together for good.

O he alone is truly blessed to whom the Lord will not impute sin! (Ps. 31:2). For no one exists who has no sin. “All have sinned, and all need the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23). Yet who shall accuse God’s elect? (Rom. 8:33). For every righteousness it is enough for me to have him alone propitious, against whom alone I have sinned. Everything which he himself has determined not to impute to me is as though it had not been. Not to sin is God’s righteousness; God’s forgiveness is human righteousness.

I saw these things and understood the truth of that saying: “Everyone born of God does not sin, because the heavenly generation preserves him” (1 John 3:9). The heavenly generation is eternal predestination, by which God loved his elect and bestowed grace on them in his beloved Son before the foundation of the world. Thus they appear holy before him, so that they might see his power and glory, become fellow-heirs of his inheritance, and appear conformed to his image.

I perceived these, then, as though they had never sinned; for even if they seem to have committed some fault in time, they do not appear so in eternity, because the charity of their Father covers a multitude of sins.

> **[Note: Col. 0891D; 0892D; 0893D]** In the same sense, in *On Grace and Free Will*, no. 29, the sins of the predestined are said to be “hidden in charity,” namely, God’s charity. Compare Sermon 4 *On Various Subjects*, no. 5, and Sermon 1 for Septuagesima, with the notes.

And he called blessed those “whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31:1). Suddenly such confidence concerning myself arose within me, and such joy was poured in, as great as the fear that had not preceded in the place of horror—that is, in the place of the second vision—so that I seemed to myself to be one of those blessed ones. O if it had endured! Again and again visit me, Lord, with your salvation, that I may see the prosperity of your elect and rejoice in the joy of your people (Ps. 105:4–5).

16. O place of true rest, which I would not undeservedly judge worthy of the name “bedchamber”! In it God is seen neither as troubled by anger nor as stretched taut by care; rather, his will is proved in it to be good, well-pleasing, and perfect. This vision does not terrify but soothes; it does not stir restless curiosity but calms it; it does not weary the senses but makes them tranquil. Here one truly rests.

The tranquil God makes all things tranquil; and to behold what is at rest is to rest. It is to see the King, after the day’s quasi-forensic disputes of cases, sending away the crowds, avoiding the troubles of his cares, seeking a lodging for the night, and entering his bedchamber with those whom he deems worthy of this secret and this familiarity. He rests all the more securely because more secretly; he is all the more serene because he looks more peacefully upon those whom he loves alone.

If perhaps one of you should at some hour be caught up and hidden in this mystery and sanctuary of God in such a way that neither an active sensation, nor a troubling care, nor a biting fault, nor even the phantasms of bodily images that rush in and are harder to remove, should distract or disturb him—then, when he returns to us, he may indeed glory and say: “The king brought me into his bedchamber” (Song 1:3). Yet I would not rashly affirm that this is precisely the bedchamber concerning which the Bride rejoices. It is nevertheless a bedchamber, and the King’s bedchamber; for, among the three places assigned to the threefold vision, this alone has become a place of peace.

For, as has clearly been shown, little rest is perceived in the first and none in the second: in the former, God appearing as wondrous exercises curiosity in the effort of investigation; in the latter, God making himself known as terrible shakes human weakness. But in this third place he deigns to appear neither truly terrible nor so much wondrous as lovable: serene and calm, sweet and gentle, and abounding in mercy toward all who behold him [variant: “call upon him”].

17. Now, that your memory may retain a summary of this longer discussion concerning the storehouse, garden, and bedchamber, remember three periods, three merits, and three, as it were, rewards. In the garden observe the periods; in the storehouse, the merits; in the threefold contemplation that seeks the bedchamber, the rewards. Let this suffice concerning the storehouse. As for the garden or the bedchamber, if anything is to be added, or if anything else besides what has been said should occur as requiring attention, let us not pass it over in its place. Otherwise, let what has been said suffice and not be repeated, lest those things which are offered for the praise and glory of the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ—who is God over all, blessed forever—ever come, God forbid, to disgust us. Amen.

## SERMON XXIV

> **[Note: Col. 0893D]** Delivered in the year 1138, after the schism had been settled, following his return from Italy.

It deals chiefly with the detestable vice of detraction, or slander, and with the matter in which human rectitude chiefly consists.

1. Brothers, on this third occasion of our return from the City, a more merciful eye looked down upon us from heaven, and at last a more serene countenance smiled upon us from above. The Leonine fury has ceased; wickedness has come to an end; the Church has received peace. The evil man who had troubled her for nearly eight years by a dreadful schism has been reduced to nothing in God’s sight.

Am I then restored to you freely after such great perils? I have been granted to your desires; I prepare myself for your advancement. By your merits I live; I desire to live for your zeal and salvation. And since you wish me to continue what I began long ago on the Song of Songs, I gladly accept it and judge it fitting to mend the interrupted discourse rather than to begin something new.

Yet I fear that a mind long unused to this task and habitually distracted in the meantime—not only by such different things, but even by such unworthy ones—may not admit the dignity of the subject as it ought. But if I give you what I have, God may also grant, in return for my faithful service, that I may give what I do not have. If not, let my ability indeed be blamed, not my will.

2. The passage from which we must begin is, I think, this: “The upright love you.” But before we begin to explain it, let us see what it is, whose utterance it is, and who precisely says it. For we are required to supply what the author does not say. Perhaps it is better that we give it to the maidens, so that they may add this also in their own words.

> **[Note: Col. 0893D–0894D]** From the beginning of the sermon to this place there is a notable variation in the manuscripts. In some, this opening is omitted and the sermon begins thus: “The upright love you.” “And to what person do we judge this especially fitting? If to the maidens, they surely say it to their mother; for after saying to her, ‘We will exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts more than wine,’ they add this too in continuous speech: ‘The upright,’ etc.” Other manuscripts have our reading.
>
> From this variation great confusion arose in most printed editions, in which both openings are reported, but incorrectly.
