The variation arose because Bernard delivered this same sermon twice: first, with the shorter opening, in 1137, before departing for Rome for the third time; and second, upon returning thence in 1138, he repeated it with the other opening, in order to resume the interrupted work from this final sermon. One Royal manuscript, no. 4511, accordingly repeats the same sermon under two openings; likewise, one manuscript of Thou and Colbert gives it once here with one opening and again after Sermon 60 with the other.

For after they had said, “We will exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts more than wine”—and there is no doubt that they were speaking to their mother—they add this also in continuous speech: “The upright love you” (Song 1:3).

I think this is because some among their number, though they appeared to run together, did not think alike: seeking their own interests, not walking simply or sincerely, but envying the mother’s distinctive glory and looking for an occasion to murmur against her because she alone had entered the storehouses. This is none other than what the Apostle calls “danger among false brothers” (2 Cor. 11:26). These are the very persons in reply to whose reproaches she is repeatedly compelled to defend herself when she says: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1:4).

Therefore, because of those who murmur and blaspheme, the good, simple, humble, gentle maidens say to the Bride in order to console her: “The upright love you.” “Do not,” they say, “be concerned about the unjust reproach of these blasphemers, since it is certain that the upright love you.” It is surely good consolation, when evildoers blaspheme us for doing good, if the upright love us. Against the mouth that speaks iniquity, the good opinion of good people together with the testimony of conscience entirely suffices. “My soul shall be praised in the Lord; let the meek hear and rejoice.” “Let the meek,” he says, “rejoice” (Ps. 33:2). Let me please the meek, and I shall hear with equanimity whatever the envy of the wicked wishes to hurl against me.

3. Therefore, I think that “The upright love you” has been added in this sense. Nor is this unreasonable, in my judgment, since throughout almost every choir of maidens there are such persons as scrutinize the Bride’s actions out of curiosity, not in order to imitate them but to disparage them. They are tormented by the good qualities of their elders and feed upon their faults. You may see them walking apart, gathering and sitting together, then immediately loosening their shameless tongues into detestable whispering. One attaches herself to another, and there is no breath between them; so great is their appetite for slandering or for hearing someone slander.

They enter into familiarity in order to speak evil, harmonize in discord, unite among themselves most hostile friendships, and celebrate an odious conference in a shared and mutually agreeing disposition of malice. Herod and Pilate once acted no differently; the Gospel relates that “they became friends that day” (Luke 23:12), that is, on the day of the Lord’s Passion.

When people thus come together, they are not eating the Lord’s supper; rather, they are offering and drinking the cup of demons. With insolent tongues they bring the poison of another’s destruction, while others gladly receive into their ears the death that enters. Thus, according to the prophet, “death enters through our windows” (Jer. 9:21), when, with itching ears and mouths, we strive to administer to one another the deadly drink of detraction. Let not my soul enter the council of slanderers, for God hates them, as the Apostle says: “Slanderers hateful to God” (Rom. 1:30). Hear how God himself, speaking in the psalm, confirms this sentence: “The one who slandered his neighbor, him I pursued” (Ps. 100:5).

4. Nor is this surprising, since this vice is known above all to attack and persecute charity, which is God, and more sharply than other vices, as you yourselves can observe. Everyone who slanders first shows himself to be empty of charity. Then what else does he intend by slandering except that the person whom he slanders should become hateful or contemptible to those before whom he slanders him?

Therefore the evil-speaking tongue wounds charity in all who hear it and, so far as it can, utterly kills and extinguishes it; and not only in them, but in all absent persons to whom the flying word may perhaps come through those who are present. You see how easily and in a short time swiftly moving speech can infect a vast multitude of souls with the contagion of this evil.

Therefore the prophetic Spirit says of such persons: “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood” (Ps. 13:3). Certainly they are as swift as speech itself runs. One person speaks and utters only one word; yet that one word, in one moment, while it infects the ears of a multitude of hearers, kills their souls.

For a heart made bitter by the gall of envy can scatter through the instrument of the tongue nothing but bitter things, as the Lord says: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45). There are kinds of this plague. Some openly and irreverently vomit the poison of detraction as it comes to their lips. Others, however, try to disguise with a certain show of feigned modesty the conceived malice which they cannot keep in.

You may see deep sighs offered beforehand; then, with a certain gravity and slowness, with mournful face, lowered brows, and a plaintive voice, the slander comes forth—indeed, all the more persuasive because hearers believe it to be uttered reluctantly and more from the feeling of one who sympathizes than from malice. “I grieve greatly,” one says, “because I love him greatly, and I was never able to correct him in this matter.” Another says: “For my part, I had ascertained this fact about him; but it would never have become known through me. Yet since the matter has been disclosed by another, I cannot deny the truth. I say it sorrowfully: it is truly so.” And he adds: “What a great loss! For in other respects he is indeed effective in many ways; but in this point, to speak the truth, he cannot at all be excused.”

5. Having said these few things against this most malicious vice, let us return to the order of exposition and show who are to be understood here by “the upright.” For I do not think anyone of sound understanding supposes that those who love the Bride are called upright in body. We must therefore demonstrate spiritual—that is, mental or heartfelt—uprightness.

It is the Spirit who speaks, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. Therefore God made the human being upright according to the soul, not according to earthly and foul material. For he created him in his own image and likeness (Gen. 1:27). And he himself, as you sing, is upright: “The Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him” (Ps. 91:16). Thus the upright God made the human being upright, like himself—that is, without iniquity, just as there is no iniquity in him.

Moreover, iniquity is a vice of the heart, not of the flesh. By this you may know that God’s likeness must be preserved or restored in the spiritual part of yourself, not in the gross and muddy substance. For God is spirit; and those who wish either to remain like him or to become like him must enter into the heart and conduct this work in the spirit. There, “with unveiled face beholding the glory of God,” they are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18).

6. Although God also gave the human body an upright stature—perhaps so that this bodily uprightness of the external and lesser creature might remind the inner man, who was made in God’s image, to preserve his own spiritual uprightness, and so that the beauty of the clay might rebuke the deformity of the soul. For what is more unseemly than to carry a bent mind in an upright body? It is a perverse and ugly thing that the clay vessel, which is the body from earth, should have its eyes raised upward, freely behold the heavens, [Col. 0897B] and delight its gaze in the lights of heaven; while the spiritual and heavenly creature, conversely, drags its own eyes—that is, its inward senses and affections—downward to earth; and, though it ought to have been nourished amid saffron, clings to mud like one of the swine and embraces dung (Lam. 4:5).

Blush, my soul, at having exchanged the divine likeness for a bestial one; blush at wallowing in filth, you who are from heaven. “Blush, soul,” says the body, “when you consider me. Created upright, like your Creator, you received me also as an assistance like yourself—certainly according to the outlines of bodily uprightness. Whichever way you turn, whether upward toward God or downward toward me (for no one ever hated his own flesh), everywhere the appearance of your beauty meets you; everywhere, in keeping with the rank of your dignity, [Col. 0897C] you have in the teaching of wisdom a familiar admonition. While I retain and preserve the prerogative which I received for your sake, how are you not ashamed to have lost your own? Why does the Creator behold in you his likeness obliterated, when in me he preserves yours for you and continually presents it anew? You have now turned into your own confusion every assistance that was owed you from me; you abuse my service, you inhabit the human body unworthily—a brutish and bestial spirit.”

7. Souls thus bent cannot love the Bride, because they are not friends of the Bridegroom, since they belong to the world. “Whoever wishes,” he says, “to be a friend of this world makes himself an enemy of God” (James 4:4). Therefore, to seek and relish things that are upon the earth is the soul’s crookedness; and conversely, to meditate upon and desire things above is uprightness. And for that uprightness to be perfect [Note: [Col. 0897D] Here too, for the reason stated above, the disagreement of the old manuscripts has disturbed the printed editions. In those manuscripts in which the prologue of this sermon is more extensively absent, the text is given here as follows: “uprightness. And this uprightness, in order to be perfect in all respects, must necessarily be found in understanding and agreement. I should truly call him upright in heart who both understands rightly in all things and in no respect dissents from what he has rightly understood. Behold those of whom it is said to the Bride: ‘The upright love you,’ namely, those who in all things both judge rightly and assent to what is right.” The sermon then concludes with these words: “Would that we too might be among them, numbered among the lovers of the Bridegroom, through the favor of the same Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages. Amen.” Other manuscripts, however, prefer our reading.], it must be defined in judgment and in agreement. I shall call you upright in truth if you judge rightly in all things and do not dissent in your deeds. Let faith and action declare the invisible state of the soul. Judge a person upright if you have found him catholic in faith and just in deed. If he falls short in either respect, do not hesitate to consider him crooked.

For thus you have it: “If you offer rightly and do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. 4:7). You do indeed rightly offer either of these, but you do not rightly separate them from one another. Do not be an upright offerer and a perverse divider. Why do you divide action from faith? You divide unjustly, killing your faith; for “faith without works is dead” (James 2:20). Do you offer God a dead gift? For if devotion itself is in some sense the soul of faith, what is faith that does not work through love but an inanimate corpse? Do you honor God well with a fetid offering? Do you propitiate well the slayer of your faith? How can there be a peace-offering where such savage discord exists? It is no wonder that Cain rose against his brother, since he had first killed his own faith. Why are you astonished, O Cain, that he who despises you does not look upon your offerings? (Gen. 4:5.) Nor [Col. 0898B] is it strange that he does not look upon you, who are so divided within yourself. If you give your hand to devotion, why do you give your mind to envy? You do not reconcile God to yourself when you are at odds with yourself; you do not propitiate him, but sin—not yet, indeed, by an impious offering, yet nonetheless by an improper division. Though not yet a fratricide, you are already held guilty as a killer of faith. Are you upright, even when you stretch out your hand to God, whose heart envy and hatred of a brother drag down to earth? How are you upright, whose faith is dead, whose work is death, whose devotion is nonexistent, whose bitterness is great? Faith was indeed present in the offerer, but love was not in the faith; the offering was upright, but the division cruel.

8. The death of faith is the separation of love. Do you believe in Christ? Perform Christ’s works, that your faith may live. Let love animate your faith; let action prove it. Let not [Col. 0898C] an earthly work bend down one whom faith raises toward heavenly things. Whoever says that he abides in Christ ought also to walk as Christ himself walked. But if you seek your own glory, envy one who flourishes, disparage one who is absent, retaliate against one who injures you: Christ did not do this. You confess that you know God, but by your works you deny him. You have plainly acted not rightly but impiously: you have given your tongue to Christ and your soul to the devil. Hear, then, what he says: “This people honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13). Certainly you are not upright when you divide so improperly. You cannot lift a head pressed down beneath the devil’s yoke. You are unable to raise yourself up while iniquity rules you. “Your iniquities have gone over your head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon you” (Ps. 37:5). Finally, “Wickedness sits upon a talent of lead” (Zech. 5:7).

You see that even right faith does not make a person upright if it does not work through love. But one without love has nothing with which to love the Bride. Yet works, though upright, are likewise insufficient to make the heart upright without faith. For who would call upright a person who does not please God? “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6). Whoever does not please [Col. 0899A] God cannot find God pleasing. For one to whom God is pleasing cannot displease God. But one to whom God is not pleasing finds neither his Bride pleasing. How, then, is he upright who loves neither God nor the Church of God, to whom it is said: “The upright love you”? Therefore, since neither faith without works nor works without faith suffice for the uprightness of the soul, let us, brethren who believe in Christ, strive to make our ways and our pursuits upright. Let us lift up our hearts together with our hands to God, that we may be found wholly upright, proving the uprightness of our faith by upright deeds—lovers of the Bride, beloved by the Bridegroom, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. On the Blackness and Beauty of the Bride, That Is, the Church

[Col. 0899B] 1. Here is what I said in the sermon: that the Bride was compelled to respond to the provocations of her rivals, who seem indeed to belong bodily to the company of maidens, but are far removed from it in spirit. For she says: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1:4). Clearly they disparaged her by reproaching her blackness. But observe the Bride’s patience and kindness. Not only did she not return curse for curse, but she even blessed them, calling them daughters of Jerusalem, though they deserved rather, on account of their wickedness, to be called daughters of Babylon, or daughters of Baal, or by whatever other name of reproach might have occurred.

Certainly she had learned from the prophet—or rather from that anointing itself which teaches gentleness—that the bruised reed must not be broken and the smoking flax must not be quenched (Isa. 42:3). Therefore [Col. 0899C] she thought that persons already sufficiently stirred up should not be provoked further, nor should anything be added to the goads of the envy by which they were tormented. Rather, with those who hated peace, she strove to be peaceable, knowing herself to be a debtor even to the foolish. She preferred, then, to soothe them with a favorable name, because she was concerned to labor for the salvation of the weak rather than for her own revenge.

2. This perfection is indeed to be desired by all; but it is especially the model of the best prelates. Good and faithful superiors know that the care entrusted to them is that of sick souls, not an occasion for display. And when, by the indication of a complaining voice, they discover inward murmuring in one of them—even when it breaks out against themselves in insults and abuse—recognizing themselves as physicians [Col. 0899D] rather than masters, they promptly prepare a remedy, not vengeance, against the frenzy of the soul. This, therefore, is why the Bride calls daughters of Jerusalem those very persons whom she endures as ill-disposed and abusive: namely, that by gentle speech she may soothe their murmuring, calm their agitation, and heal their envy. For it is written: “A peaceable tongue restrains disputes” (Prov. 25:15).

In another sense, those who are such are in some manner truly daughters of Jerusalem, nor does the Bride call them so falsely. Whether because of the sacraments of the Church, which they receive indiscriminately along with the good; or because of the equally shared confession of faith; or on account at least of their bodily fellowship with the faithful; or even because of the hope of future salvation, from which they are not altogether excluded as long as they live here, even if, being such as they are, they live most despairingly—[Col. 0900A] they are not inappropriately called daughters of Jerusalem.

3. Let us now see what it was to say, “I am black, but beautiful.” Is there any contradiction in these words? Far from it! I say this for the sake of the simple, who do not know how to distinguish color from form, though form pertains to arrangement and blackness is a color. For not everything that is black is immediately ugly. Blackness, for example, does not detract from the pupil of the eye; certain black stones please in ornaments; and black hair even increases the beauty and charm of fair faces. You may readily notice the same thing in countless other cases. For innumerable things are found which are indeed discolored on their surface but beautiful in their composition.

Perhaps in such a way the Bride may, together with beauty of composition, possess a blemish of blackness—but certainly in the place of her pilgrimage. Otherwise, when the Bridegroom of glory presents her to himself glorious in her homeland, she will have neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind. But now, if she said that she had no blackness, she would deceive herself and truth would not be in her. Therefore do not wonder that she says, “I am black,” and nevertheless glories that she is beautiful. For how is she not beautiful to whom it is said, “Come, my beautiful one”? (Song 2:10.) But she to whom it is said, “Come,” had not yet arrived—lest anyone suppose that this was said not to this black one, who is still laboring as she comes along the way, but to that blessed one, already reigning in her homeland wholly without blackness.

[Col. 0900C] 4. But hear why she calls herself black and why beautiful. Is she black on account of the foul manner of life which she formerly had under the prince of this world, still bearing the image of the earthly man; and beautiful because of the heavenly likeness which she afterward assumed, now walking in newness of life? But if this is so, why does she not say rather of the past, “I was black,” and not “I am black”? Yet if this interpretation pleases anyone, what follows—“like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon” (Song 1:4)—must be understood thus: she calls herself Kedar on account of her old way of life, and Solomon’s tent on account of her new one. For that skins signify the same thing as tent, the prophet shows when he says: “Suddenly my tents were devastated, suddenly my skins” [Col. 0900D] (Jer. 4:20). Thus, she was first black, like Kedar’s most lowly tents; afterward beautiful, like the skins of a glorious king.

5. But let us see how both rather refer to the condition of a superior life. If we consider the outward bearing of the saints—that which appears on the face—how lowly, abject, and, as it were, neglected it is, while inwardly they repeatedly behold with unveiled face the glory of God and are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18): would not any such soul rightly seem able to answer those who reproach it with blackness, “I am black, but beautiful”? Do you wish, then, that I should show you a soul both black and beautiful? “His letters,” they say, [Col. 0901A] “are weighty, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible” (2 Cor. 10:10). This was Paul.

Thus you, O daughters of Jerusalem, judge Paul by the presence of his body, and despise him as discolored and ugly because you see this little man afflicted by hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, by many labors, exceeding beatings, and frequent deaths (2 Cor. 11:23, 27). These are the things which blacken Paul. On account of such things the teacher of the nations is accounted inglorious, ignoble, black, obscure—as indeed the refuse of this world. Yet is he not the very one who is caught up into paradise, who, passing through the first heaven and the second, penetrates by his purity even to the third? O truly most beautiful soul! Though it inhabited a feeble little body, heavenly beauty did not disdain to admit it, angelic sublimity did not reject it, divine splendor did not repel it. Do you call this soul black? It is black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem: black by your judgment, beautiful by the divine and angelic judgment. If it is black, it is so outwardly. Yet it matters little to Paul that he is judged by you or by those who judge according to appearances. For man sees what is in the face, but God looks upon the heart (1 Sam. 16:7). Thus, though black outwardly, he is beautiful within, so as to please him before whom he proved himself—not you; for if he still pleased you, he would not be Christ’s servant. Blessed blackness, which produces the whiteness of the mind, the light of knowledge, and purity of conscience.

6. Hear, finally, what God promises through the prophet to blacks of this kind—those whom either the humility of repentance or the zeal of love seems to have discolored like the heat of the sun: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and though they be red as crimson, they shall be white as wool” (Isa. 1:18). This outward blackness in the saints, which works inward whiteness and thereby prepares a seat for wisdom, is by no means to be despised. For wisdom is the brightness of eternal life, as the Wise Man defines it (Wis. 7:26); and the soul in which wisdom chooses to take its seat must be bright. But if the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom, I shall without doubt say that the soul of the righteous is bright. And perhaps righteousness itself is brightness.

Paul was righteous, and for him the crown of righteousness was laid up (2 Tim. 4:8). Therefore Paul’s soul was bright, and wisdom sat within it, so that he spoke wisdom among the perfect: wisdom hidden in a mystery, which none of the rulers of this world knew. Moreover, that outward blackness arising from the weakness of Paul’s bodily presence, from his many labors, from his many fasts and vigils, either produced or merited this brightness of wisdom and righteousness within him. Thus what is black in Paul is more beautiful than every external adornment, even than all royal finery. No degree of bodily beauty can compare with it: no smooth skin destined to burn, no painted face close to decay, no costly garment liable to wear out, no appearance of gold or sparkle of jewels, nor anything of the kind, all of which are subject to corruption.

7. Rightly, therefore, the whole concern of the saints, despising the superfluous adornment and cultivation of their outward man, which indeed is perishing, applies and occupies itself with all diligence in cultivating and adorning that inward man which is according to God’s image and is renewed day by day. For they are certain that nothing can be more acceptable to God than his own image if it has been restored to its proper beauty. Therefore all their glory is inward, not outward: that is, not in the flower of grass or in popular acclaim, but in the Lord. Hence they say, “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12), because God alone is the judge of conscience; they desire to please him alone, and to please him is the only true and highest glory.

That inward glory is no slight glory, since the Lord of glory himself deigns to glory in it, David saying: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is from within” [Col. 0902B] (Ps. 44:14). And each person’s glory is safer when he has it in himself and not in another. Yet perhaps one should glory not only in inward brightness but also in outward blackness, so that nothing at all may be lost to the saints, but all things may work together for good. Thus, not only in hope, but also in tribulations we should glory. “Gladly,” he says, “will I glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me.” An infirmity is desirable when it is compensated by Christ’s power. Who will grant me not merely to be infirm, but even to be deprived and to fail utterly in myself, that I may be established by the power of the Lord of hosts? For power is perfected in weakness. Finally, he says: “When I am weak, then I am strong and powerful” (2 Cor. 12:9–10).

8. This being so, the Bride beautifully turns to her own glory what her rivals cast at her as a reproach, glorying not only that she is beautiful but also that she is black. For she is not ashamed of the blackness which she knows also preceded her in the Bridegroom; and to be made like him is a matter of what great glory! Therefore she considers nothing more glorious than bearing Christ’s reproach. Hence that utterance wholly of exultation and salvation: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!” (Gal. 6:14.) The ignominy of the cross is welcome to one who is not ungrateful to the Crucified. It is blackness, but it is the form and likeness of the Lord.

Go to holy Isaiah, and he will describe for you what kind of man he saw him to be in the Spirit. Of whom else, indeed, does he say that he was “a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity,” and that “he had neither form nor beauty”? And he adds: “We considered him as leprous, struck by God, and humbled. But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our crimes; and by his bruise we were healed” (Isa. 53:3, 5). Behold the source of his blackness. Add also that saying of holy David: “Beautiful in form above the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3), and you have in the Bridegroom in full what the Bride has testified concerning herself in this passage.

9. Does it not seem to you that he too, in accordance with what has been said, might rightly answer his Jewish rivals: “I am black, but beautiful, sons of Jerusalem”? Black indeed: he to whom there was neither form nor beauty; black because he was “a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21:7). Finally, he made himself sin (2 Cor. 5:21); should I hesitate to call him black? Look upon him filthy in garments, bruised by wounds, smeared with spittle, pale in death; then indeed you will acknowledge him to be black. Question also the apostles as to what sort of person they saw him to be upon the mountain; or, indeed, the angels as to what kind of person they long to behold; and you will nevertheless marvel that he is beautiful.

Therefore, he is beautiful in himself, black on your account. How beautiful I recognize you, Lord Jesus, in my own form—not only because of the divine miracles in which you shine forth, but also because of truth, meekness, and righteousness. Blessed is the one who, carefully observing you as a man dwelling among men in these things, offers himself, so far as he can, as your imitator. Your beautiful one has already received this gift of blessedness as the first-fruits of her dowry: she is not sluggish in imitating what is beautiful in you, nor ashamed to endure what is black. Hence she said: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem,” [Col. 0903B] and added the comparison: “Like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.”

But this is obscure and must not at all be approached by those who are weary. You have time to knock. If you do not neglect it, he who reveals mysteries will be present; nor will he delay in opening, he who invites us also to knock. For he is the one who opens and no one shuts (Rev. 3:7): Jesus Christ our Lord, Bridegroom of the Church, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI [Note: [Col. 0903D] Delivered in the year 1138.]. In Which Blessed Bernard Mourns the Death of His Brother Gerard

1. “Like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon” (Song 1:4). We must begin from this point, because the preceding sermon ended here. You expect to hear what this means and how it is joined to the verse considered last, because it is a comparison. For it may have been appended in such a way that both parts of the comparison answer only to what preceded there: “I am black.” Or it may be understood in such a way that these two terms correspond to those two—that is, each one to each one. The former meaning is simpler, the latter more obscure. But let us attempt both, and first the one that appears more difficult.

The difficulty, however, lies not in the first two terms, but only in the last two. For Kedar, which is interpreted “darkness,” appears clearly enough to agree with blackness; but the skins of Solomon do not agree so readily with beauty. Yet who does not see that tents nonetheless converge upon the same correspondence? For what are tents but our bodies, in which we are pilgrims? “For here we have no abiding city, but seek one to come” (Heb. 13:14). We also serve as soldiers in them, as in tents—indeed, forcing our way toward the kingdom. Finally, “the life of man upon earth is a warfare” (Job [Col. 0904A] 7:1); and as long as we serve in this body, we are pilgrims from the Lord, that is, from the light. For the Lord is light; and insofar as anyone is not with him, so far is he in darkness—that is, in Kedar. Let him therefore recognize as his own that lamenting utterance: “Alas for me, that my sojourning has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner” (Ps. 119:5–6).

Thus this dwelling of our body is not the residence of a citizen or the house of a native, but either the tent of a soldier or the lodging of a traveler. This body, I say, is a tent, and a tent of Kedar, because it now, as it were by its obstruction, deprives the soul of the sight of unbounded light and does not allow it to see that light except “through a mirror, in an enigma,” not face to face (1 Cor. 13:12).

2. Do you see the source of the Church’s blackness, the source from which some rust has clung even to the most beautiful souls? It comes, certainly, from the tent of Kedar; from the exertion of laborious warfare; from the long duration of miserable sojourn; from the straits of grievous exile; finally, from the frail and heavy body. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). Therefore they desire to be released, that, freed from the body, they may fly to Christ’s embrace. Thus one of the afflicted said with groaning: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24.) One who is such knows that in the tent of Kedar one cannot be altogether without spot or wrinkle, without some degree of blackness, however slight; and he longs to depart so that he may cast it off.

This is the reason why the Bride calls herself black like the tents of Kedar. But how is she beautiful like the skins of Solomon? I sense some lofty and sacred meaning wrapped up in these skins, which I should not dare at all to touch except at the bidding of him who has stored it up and sealed it. For I have read: “He who searches out majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25:27). Therefore I refrain and defer the matter. Meanwhile, let it be your concern, according to custom, to obtain favor by your prayers, so that we may return to a subject requiring more attentive minds with greater eagerness as our confidence is greater. And perhaps a devout knocker will find what a rash searcher could not. Yet grief and the calamity [Col. 0904D] that I endure command an end.

3. For how long shall I dissemble [Note: [Col. 0903D] Here begins Bernard’s funeral oration for his brother Gerard, which Berengar, that shameless disciple of Abelard, unjustly criticizes—first because Bernard allegedly “joined sorrowful things with joyful,” and then because he uses certain words of Ambrose, taken “syllable by syllable” from Ambrose’s funeral oration on the death of his brother Satyrus. But these words are not found in this sermon; and even if they were, they would do Bernard no injury. It is worthwhile to cite two passages. Here is the first: “My brother has departed from life—or rather, to speak more correctly, he has left death for life. My brother, I say, has departed: the support of conscience, the mirror of conduct, the bond of religious life. Who henceforth will encourage me to labor? Who will thereafter soothe me in grief?” The second is this: “An ox seeks an ox, and, thinking itself alone, gives proof of its dutiful affection by frequent lowing. An ox, I say, seeks the ox with whom it was accustomed to draw the plow by the neck.” The latter passage does occur after the beginning in Ambrose; neither occurs in Bernard. Berengar cautiously prefaced his assertion with “if I am not mistaken,” lest he be accused of lying and imposture. For Gerard’s conversion, see William, *Life of Bernard*, book I, nos. 11 and 12. He was cellarer at Clairvaux: ibid., no. 27. His death fell in 1138, after his return from Italy with Bernard: here, no. 14. A similar funeral oration for Humbert is found in volume III.]? How long shall the fire which I conceal within myself burn my sorrowful breast and consume my inward parts? The more confined it is, the more widely it spreads; the more fiercely it rages. What have I to do with this song, I who am in bitterness? The force of grief draws away my attention, and the indignation of the Lord has drained my spirit. For when he was taken away through whom my endeavors in the Lord were customarily in some measure free, my own heart at the same time forsook me.

Yet I forced my mind and concealed my feeling until now, lest affection seem to overcome faith. For while others wept, I, as you were able to observe, followed that unwelcome funeral with dry eyes; with dry eyes I stood at the tomb until all the solemn rites of burial had been completed. Clothed in priestly vestments, I finished with my own mouth the customary prayers over him; according to custom, with my own hands I cast earth upon the body of my beloved, soon itself to be earth. Those who watched me wept and wondered that I myself did not weep, since all pitied not him but rather me, who had lost him. [Col. 0905B] For whose breast, even if iron, would not then have been moved at the sight of me surviving Gerard? It was a common loss, but it was not considered comparable to my misfortune.

But I struggled, with whatever strength of faith I could, against affection, striving, though unwillingly, not to be moved by the vain attachment of nature, by the debt owed to all, by the usage of our condition, by the command of the powerful one, by the judgment of the just one, by the scourge of the terrible one, by the will of the Lord. For such reasons, from that time onward, I continually required of myself that I not give way to much weeping, though I was greatly troubled and sad. Yet I could not command my grief, though I could command my tears; rather, as it is written: “I was troubled, and I did not speak” (Ps. 76:5). But the suppressed grief struck roots more deeply within and, as I feel, became more bitter because it was not permitted to emerge. I confess: I have been overcome. What I suffer within must come forth. Let it come forth before the eyes of my sons, so that, knowing the loss, they may judge the mourning more humanely and console me more sweetly.

4. You know, my sons, how just is my grief, how grievous my wound. You see what a companion has left me on this road upon which I walked: one not sluggish in work, so gracious in character. Who was so necessary to me? To whom was I equally beloved? He was a brother by blood, but more truly a brother by religious fellowship. Grieve, I beg you, for my loss, you to whom these things are known. I was weak in body, and he carried me; I was faint of heart, and he strengthened me; I was sluggish and negligent, and he roused me; I was improvident and forgetful, and he reminded me. Why have you been torn away from me? Why snatched from my hands, man of one mind with me, man after [Col. 0905D] my own heart? We loved each other in life; how are we divided in death? Most bitter separation! And it could not have been effected at all except by death. For when, while living, would you have left me living? It is wholly death’s work: a dreadful divorce. For who would not have spared so sweet a bond of our mutual love, except death, the enemy of all sweetness? Death was rightfully called death: in madly taking one, it killed two.

Is it not death also to me? Indeed, it is worse for me, since a life more unhappy than any death has been preserved for me. I live in order to die while living; and shall I call this life? How much more gently, O harsh death, would you have deprived me of the use of life than of its fruit! For life without fruit is a graver death. Finally, a double evil is prepared for an unfruitful tree: axe and fire (Matt. 3:10). Therefore, envying my labors, you took away from me my friend and neighbor, by whose zeal they were, whenever they were so, fruitful. It would therefore have been better for me to risk my life than to lose your presence, O Gerard: you were the solicitous encourager of my endeavors in the Lord, a faithful [variant: strong] helper, a prudent examiner.

Why, I ask, did we either love or lose one another? The condition is hard, but mine is the lamentable lot, not his. For you, dear brother, if you lost those dear to you, received persons dearer still. [Col. 0906B] But what consolation now remains for me, a wretch, after you—my sole comfort? We both found the fellowship of our bodies pleasing because of our harmony of character; but the separation has wounded me alone. What was pleasant was shared; what is sorrowful and mournful is mine: wrath has passed into me; fury has been established in me. The presence of each was agreeable to the other; companionship was sweet; conversation delightful. But I have lost such great delights of us both, while you have exchanged them. And in exchange for those things, indeed, your recompense is abundant.

5. By what an immense return of joys and what a heap of blessings you abound today without us, dearest brother [Note: [Col. 0906D] Some manuscript and printed copies add *tanto* here, to correspond with *quanto*, but incorrectly.]! In place of my insignificant presence, you certainly have Christ’s presence reserved for you; and, mingled among the choirs of angels, you do not feel the loss of your absence from us. Therefore you have no cause to complain that our presence has, as it were, been taken from you, since the Lord of majesty has graciously granted you an abundant sufficiency of himself and his own.

But what do I have in place of you? How I wish to know what you now think of me, your only one, wavering amid cares and pains, deprived of you, the staff of my weakness—if indeed it is still permitted you to think of the wretched after entering the abyss of light and being absorbed in that ocean of eternal blessedness. Perhaps, although you knew us according to the flesh, you now know us no longer; and because you have entered into the powers of the Lord, you remember his righteousness alone, forgetful of us.

Yet he who is joined to God is one spirit with him (1 Cor. 6:17), and is wholly transformed into a certain divine affection; he can now neither feel nor savor anything except God, and what God feels and savors, being filled with God. But God is love; and the more closely anyone is joined to God, the fuller he is of love. Moreover, God is incapable of suffering, but not incapable of compassion; for it is his own property always to have mercy and to spare. Therefore you too must be merciful, who cling to the merciful one, though you yourself are no longer miserable; and though you do not suffer, you nevertheless suffer with others. Thus your affection has not been diminished but transformed; nor, because you have put on God, have you put off concern for us [Note: [Col. 0906D] This concern may be inferred from Gerard’s two appearances in *The Life of Bernard*, book IV, no. 10, and book V, no. 8.]; for he himself has care for us (1 Pet. 5:7). You have cast off what was weak, but not what was loving. For “love never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8): you will not forget me forever.

6. I seem almost to hear my brother saying: “Can a mother forget the child of her womb? Even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isa. 49:15). It is utterly unfitting. You know where I dwell, where I lie, where you left me; there is no one to stretch out a hand. At every difficulty that arises, I look for Gerard as I used to, and he is not there. Alas! Then I groan in misery, like a man without help. Whom shall I consult in uncertainties? In adversities, in whom shall I trust? Who will carry the burdens? Who will ward off dangers? Did not Gerard’s eyes everywhere go before my steps [variant: encourage them]? Did not your breast, Gerard, know my anxieties better than my own did [Col. 0907B], encounter them more familiarly, press upon them more urgently? [Note: [Col. 0907] Bernard’s rebuke of Gerard concerning miracles, lest he grow proud on their account, bears witness to this; *Life*, book I, no. 43.] Did you not, by your conciliating and powerful tongue, very often rescue me from worldly conversations, 1356 and restore me to the silence of a friend? The Lord had given him a learned tongue, so that he knew when he ought to utter a word. Thus, finally, in the prudence of his replies, in the grace bestowed on him from above, he satisfied both those of the household and outsiders, so that scarcely anyone sought me out if Gerard had perhaps met him first.

He met those who were arriving, setting himself in their way so that they might not suddenly invade my leisure. If he could not satisfactorily deal with certain persons himself, he brought these to me; the rest he sent away. O industrious man! O faithful friend! He accommodated himself to his friend and did not fail in the offices of charity. [Col. 0907C] Who departed from him empty-handed? If rich, he carried away counsel; if poor, assistance. Nor did he seek his own interests, he who threw himself into the midst of anxieties so that I might have leisure. For, being most humble, he hoped for a greater fruit from our quiet than if he himself had leisure.

Yet from time to time he asked to be relieved and to yield the task to another, as though someone else could provide better. But where was such a man to be found? Nor was he held to this duty by any restless zeal for office, as often happens, but by charity alone. Indeed, he laboured more than all and received less than all; so that often, while supplying others with necessities, he himself lacked many things—for example, food or clothing. Finally, when he felt that he was approaching death, he said: “God, you know that, so far as lay in me [Col. 0907D], I always desired quiet: to attend to myself, to be free for you. But your fear, the will of the brothers, the zeal of obedience, and above all the genuine love alike of an abbot and a brother, kept me entangled.”

So it is. I thank you, brother, for every fruit—if there be any—in the Lord, of my labours. To you I owe it if I have made progress, if I have been useful. You became entangled, and through your kindness I sat at leisure for myself, or rather was more holily occupied in divine service, or applied myself more profitably to instructing the sons. Why should I not have been secure within, when I knew that you were acting outside as my right hand, the light of my eyes, [Col. 0908A] my heart, and my tongue? And indeed an untiring hand, an unclouded eye, a heart of counsel, a tongue speaking judgment, as it is written: “The mouth of the righteous meditates wisdom, and his tongue speaks judgment” (Ps. 36:30).

7. But why did I say that he acted outside, as though Gerard did not know inward things and lacked spiritual gifts? Those who knew him spiritually know how his words breathed the Spirit. Those who lived with him know how his habits and pursuits savoured not of the flesh but burned in the Spirit. Who was more strict than he in observing discipline? Who more severe in chastising his body, more rapt or more exalted in contemplation, more subtle in reasoning? How often, while discussing matters with him, did I learn things that I did not know; and I who had come to teach went away better taught [Col. 0908B]! Nor is this surprising in my case, since great and wise men likewise testify that this very thing happened to them through him.

He did not know literary learning; but he possessed the understanding of the inventor of letters, and he possessed the enlightening Spirit. Nor was he great only in great things, but greatest also in the least. What, for example, in buildings, fields, gardens, waters—in short, in every art or work of countrymen? What, I ask, in this whole class of things escaped Gerard’s expertise? He was readily a master to masons, smiths, farmers, gardeners, shoemakers, and weavers. Though in everyone’s judgment he was wiser than all, in his own eyes alone he was not wise. Would that the same curse touched many people no more, even if they were less wise: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes” (Isa. 5:21)!

I speak to those who know these things, [Col. 0908C] and who have discovered still more and greater things concerning him. Yet I spare him, because he is my flesh and my brother. But I safely add this: he was useful to me in all things and above all others; useful in small and great matters, in private and public affairs, outside and within. Rightly I depended wholly on him, since he was my whole support. 1357 He had left me almost nothing except the honour and name of steward: for he did the work itself. I was called abbot, but he presided in solicitude. Rightly did my spirit rest in him, through whom I was free to delight in the Lord, to preach more freely, to pray more securely. Through you, I say, my brother, I had a sober mind and welcome repose, more effective speech, richer prayer, more frequent reading, and more fervent affection.

[Col. 0908D] 8. Alas! You have been taken away, and all these things with you. Together with you all my delights and joys have departed. Now cares rush in; now troubles assail me from every side; and distresses from all quarters have found me alone. They alone remain to me now that you have gone; alone beneath the burden I groan. I must either lay it down or be crushed, because you have withdrawn your shoulders.

Who will grant that I may die quickly after you? For I would not die in your place, nor rob you of your glory. But to outlive you is labour and pain. I shall live, as long as I live, in bitterness; I shall live in mourning; and let this be my consolation, that I am afflicted by mourning. I shall not spare myself, and I shall assist the hand of the Lord; for the hand [Col. 0909A] of the Lord has touched me. Me, I say, it has touched and struck—not him, whom it summoned to rest. It killed me when it cut him down. For who would call him slain whom it planted in life? But what was for him the gate of life is plainly death to me; and by that death I would call myself dead, not him who fell asleep in the Lord.

Come forth, come forth, tears long desiring to flow; come forth, because he who had blocked your passage has passed away. Let the floodgates of my wretched head be opened; let fountains of waters burst forth, if perhaps they may suffice to wash away the filth of the sins by which I deserved wrath. When the Lord has comforted me, then perhaps I too may deserve to be comforted—provided that I do not spare myself mourning; for “those who mourn shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

Therefore let every saint condescend to me, and let the spiritual person bear with one who laments [Col. 0909B] in a spirit of gentleness. I ask that my mourning be weighed by human feeling, not by customary practice. For we see the dead daily mourning their dead: much weeping, and no fruit. We do not blame the feeling, except when it exceeds its measure; rather, we blame its cause. The former belongs to nature, and its disturbance is the penalty of sin; the latter is vanity and sin. For there, unless I am mistaken, people mourn only losses to bodily glory and the disadvantages of the present life. And those who thus mourn ought themselves to be mourned.

Am I such a one? My feeling is similar, but its cause is different, and its intention unlike. Certainly I have no complaint concerning all that belongs to the world. In those things that belong to God, I grieve for faithful help taken away, for wholesome counsel. I mourn Gerard: [Col. 0909C] Gerard is the cause—my brother in flesh, but neighbour in spirit, companion in purpose.

9. My soul was joined to his soul; and not blood relationship but unity of mind made one out of two. The bond of flesh was indeed not absent, but fellowship of spirit, agreement of minds, and conformity of character joined us more closely. Therefore, since we were one heart and one soul, a sword passed through this soul which was both mine and his, and, cleaving it, placed one half in heaven and left the other half in mire. I, I am that wretched portion lying in the mud, cut off from its own part—and the better part at that—and am told: “Will you not weep?” My entrails have been torn from me, and I am told: “Will you not feel it?”

I do feel it, I feel it even against my will, for neither is my strength the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze; [Col. 0909D] I certainly feel it and grieve, and my pain is always before me. The one who strikes cannot accuse us of hardness and insensibility, as he accused those of whom he said: “I struck them, and they did not grieve” (Jer. 5:3). I have confessed my feeling and have not denied it. Let anyone call it fleshly: I do not deny that it is human, any more than I deny that I am human. If even this does not suffice, neither shall I deny that it is fleshly. For I too am fleshly, sold under sin, subject to death, liable to punishments and miseries. I confess that I am not insensitive to suffering; I dread death, my own and that of my loved ones.

Gerard was mine, wholly mine. Was he not mine, he who was my brother by blood, my son by profession, 1358 my father by solicitude, my companion in spirit [variant: harmonious with me in spirit], most intimate in affection? He has gone away from me. I feel it; I am wounded, and grievously so.

[Col. 0910A] 10. Forgive me, sons; indeed, if you are sons, grieve in return for your father. “Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you who are my friends” (Job 19:21), who surely consider how grievous are the things I have received from the Lord’s hand for my sins. With the rod of his indignation he has struck me—justly according to my deserts, harshly according to my strength. Would anyone call it a light thing for me to live without Gerard, unless he does not know what Gerard was to me?

Yet I do not dispute the words of the Holy One; nor do I blame the judgment by which each has received what he deserved: he, the crown he merited; I, the punishment that I owed. Does my feeling the punishment mean that I blame the sentence? The former is human; the latter impious. It is human, I say, and inevitable to be affected toward loved ones: delightfully when they are present, painfully when they are absent. Social intercourse, especially [Col. 0910B] between friends, is not without effect; and what mutual love accomplishes in those present to one another is shown by the horror of separation and the pain of those separated from each other.

I grieve for you, dearest Gerard, not because you are to be mourned, but because you have been taken away. And so perhaps I ought rather to be mourned for, since I drink the cup of bitterness. And I alone am to be mourned, because I drink it alone; for you do not drink it too. I alone suffer what those who love one another ordinarily suffer together when they lose one another.

11. Would that I have not lost you, but sent you ahead! Would that, even late, I may someday follow you wherever you have gone! For there is no doubt that you have gone to those whom, around the middle of your final night, you summoned to praise, when suddenly, with face and voice rejoicing, you burst forth [Col. 0910C] into those words of David—to the astonishment of those standing by: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights” (Ps. 148:1).

Already for you, my brother, while it was still midnight, day was beginning to dawn, and the night was illuminated like the day. Truly that night was illumination amid your delights. I was summoned to witness this miracle: to see a man rejoicing in death and triumphing over death. “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” No longer a sting, but jubilation. Now the man dies singing and, in dying, sings. You are enlisted for joy, mother of mourning; enlisted for glory, enemy of glory; enlisted as an entrance into the kingdom, gate of hell; and as the pit of perdition, for the discovery of salvation—and this by a sinful man.

Justly indeed, because you wickedly and rashly usurped power over the innocent and righteous man. [Col. 0910D] You are dead, O death, and pierced by the hook which you unwittingly swallowed; his is that voice in the prophet: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13:14). Pierced, I say, by that hook, you open to the faithful passing through your midst a broad and joyful way out into life. Gerard does not fear you, phantom image. Gerard passes through the midst of your jaws to his homeland, not only secure but joyful and praising.

When I arrived, and he had already, in my hearing, completed the final words of the psalm in a clear voice, he looked up to heaven and said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). Repeating the same words and saying again and again, “Father, Father,” he turned to me with a cheerful face and said: “How great [Col. 0911A] is God’s condescension, that he should be the Father of human beings! How great is the glory of human beings, to be God’s children and God’s heirs! For if children, then heirs.” Thus sang the one whom we mourn; and in this, I confess, he almost turned my mourning into song, while, intent upon his glory, I nearly forget my own misery.

12. But piercing pain calls me back to myself, and sharp anxiety easily awakens me from that serene vision, as from a light sleep. Therefore I shall weep—but for myself, since reason now forbids me to weep for him. For I think that, if an opportunity were given him, he would now say to us: “Do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves.”

David rightly wept for his parricidal son (2 Sam. 19:1), since he knew that the enormity of his crime had forever barred his way out from the womb of death. Rightly he wept for Saul and [Col. 0911B] Jonathan (2 Sam. 1:17), who, once equally swallowed up, are no longer hoped to emerge. [Note: [Col. 0911D] Thus all manuscripts, together with the earliest editions; later editions read, “was hoped.”] And indeed they will rise again, but not unto life—or rather, unto life, so that, living, they may die more unhappily in death.

Yet concerning Jonathan’s fate one may not unreasonably hesitate. [Note: [Col. 0911D] Bernard seems to doubt Jonathan’s salvation. But other Fathers and interpreters affirm that he is in heaven. See Rangolius, on chapter 31 of book I of Kings, vol. 2; Salianus, under the year of the world 2979, no. 135; Abulensis, on the cited chapter. His unhappy death with his father Saul ought not to trouble anyone. The impious die badly, however they depart; the pious die well and happily, whatever kind of death they undergo.]

But though I do not have that reason for weeping, I do not lack every reason. First I mourn for my own wound and for the loss to this house; then I mourn for the needs of the poor, whose father Gerard was; certainly I mourn also for the whole condition of our Order and profession, which derived no small strength from your zeal, counsel, and example, Gerard. Finally, though not over you, yet because of you I mourn. This, indeed, this deeply moves me, [Col. 0911C] because I love intensely.

And let no one trouble me by saying that I ought not to be affected in this way, since kindly Samuel over the rejected king (1 Sam. 16:1), and devout David over his parricidal son, gave satisfaction to their feeling, without injury to faith or insult to the judgment above. “Absalom, my son,” says holy David, “my son Absalom” (2 Sam. 18:33); and behold, here is more than Absalom. The Saviour too, seeing the city of Jerusalem and foreseeing its fall, wept over it (Luke 19:41). And shall I not feel my own desolation, the desolation presently before me? Shall I not grieve for my fresh and grievous wound? He wept in compassion, and shall I not dare to weep in suffering?

Certainly, at Lazarus’s tomb, he neither rebuked those who wept nor forbade weeping; indeed, he himself wept with those who wept: “Jesus wept,” it says [Col. 0911D] (John 11:35). Those tears were surely witnesses to nature, not indications of unbelief. Finally, the one who was dead immediately came forth at his voice, lest you should at once think that grieving feeling prejudices faith.

13. Thus our weeping too is not a sign of unbelief, but an indication of our condition; nor, because I weep when struck, do I accuse him who strikes, but I appeal to compassion and strive to bend severity. Hence my words are full of pain, but not of murmuring. Have I not uttered what is full of justice, namely, that by the completion of one sentence both he who deserved it was punished and he who merited it was crowned? And I still say: The sweet and upright Lord did both well. “I shall sing to you, Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 101:1). Let the mercy which you showed to your servant Gerard sing to you; let the judgment which we bear sing also. In the one you will be praised as good, in the other as just.

Is praise due to goodness alone? It is due to justice also. “You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Ps. 119:137). You gave Gerard; you took Gerard away. And although we grieve that he has been taken away, we do not forget that he was given, and we give thanks that we deserved to have him—though we do not wish to be without him [Col. 0912B] so far as it is not expedient.

14. I remember, Lord, my agreement and your mercy, that you may be more justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. When, last year, we were at Viterbo on the business of the Church, [Note: [Col. 0912D] Bernard made two stays at Viterbo in Italy: the first in 1133, as Letter 151 testifies; the second in 1137, which is mentioned here.] he fell ill; and as his sickness worsened, when his summons seemed near at hand, I bore it with the greatest distress that I should leave my companion in travel, that companion, in a foreign land, and not restore him to those who had entrusted him to me, since he was loved by all, as he was very lovable. Turning to prayer with tears and groaning, I said: “Wait, Lord, until our return. Restore him to his friends; then take him, if you will, and I shall not complain.”

You heard me, God. He recovered; we completed the work [Col. 0912C] that you had enjoined; we returned with rejoicing, carrying the sheaves of peace. But I had almost forgotten my agreement; you had not. I am ashamed of these sobs, which convict me of breaking faith. What more shall I say? You reclaimed what had been entrusted to you; you received what was yours. Tears put an end to my words; you, Lord, set an end and measure to them.

1360 **SERMON XXVII. On the Bride’s Adornment, and How a Holy Soul Is Said to Be Heaven.**

1. Since we have attended to the duties owed by humanity in accompanying our friend as he returned to his homeland, I return, brothers, to the proposed work of edification which I had interrupted. For it is unfitting to weep long over one who rejoices, and troublesome to bring many tears to one sitting at a feast. [Col. 0912D] Yet even if we weep over our own miseries, we ought not do even that excessively, lest we seem to have loved him less than we sought our own advantages through him. Let the joy of the beloved moderate the sorrow of those left desolate; and let what we cannot have with us become more bearable because he is with God.

Relying, therefore, upon your prayers, I wish, if I can, to bring to light whatever it is that I perceive hidden beneath those skins which were brought forward as an image of the bride’s beauty. This, if you remember [variant: as indeed you remember], was touched upon but left undiscussed; whereas it has been discussed and explained how she is black like the tents of Kedar. How then is she beautiful like the skins of Solomon (Song 1:4), as though Solomon in all his glory had anything worthy to match the beauty of the bride and the glory of her adornment?

Indeed, if we said that these unspecified skins, like the tents of Kedar, referred not to the bride’s beauty but rather to her blackness, perhaps it would fit, and we should not lack the means to show its appropriateness, as we shall show. But if we think that the beauty of any skins is to be compared with the bride’s brightness, we certainly need here the help of him upon whom you have knocked, so that we may worthily unfold this mystery.

For what among things that shine outwardly, if compared with the inward beauty of some holy soul, would not appear cheap and ugly to a right judge? What, I ask, does that passing form of this world display in itself that could equal the beauty of that soul which, having stripped off the old age of the earthly human being, has put on the splendour of him who is from heaven—adorned with the finest moral qualities in place of necklaces, purer than the ether itself and also higher, more splendid than the sun? Therefore, when you seek to discover to what skins the bride glories in comparing herself in beauty, do not look to this Solomon.

2. What, then, does she mean when she says: “I am beautiful like the skins of Solomon”? It is something great and wonderful, as I judge—provided we attend here not to this Solomon, but to him of whom it is said: “Behold, here is more than Solomon” (Matt. 12:42). For my Solomon is so much Solomon that he is called not merely peaceful—for this is what *Solomon* means—but peace itself, Paul testifying that “he himself is our peace” (Eph. 2:14).

With this Solomon I do not doubt that what I do not hesitate at all to compare with the bride’s beauty can be found. Especially consider his skins in the Psalm: “Stretching out heaven like a skin” (Ps. 104:2), it says. Certainly it was not that Solomon, however wise and powerful, who stretched out heaven like a skin; rather, it was he who is not so much wise as Wisdom itself, who indeed stretched it out and created it.

For that saying belongs to this one, not to the other: “When he prepared the heavens”—that is, God the Father—“I was present.” Undoubtedly his power and wisdom were present with him who prepared the heavens. Nor should you think that Wisdom stood by idly, merely to observe, because it said, “I was present,” rather than “I was preparing.” Look a little further down, and you will find it openly added: “I was with him, composing all things” (Prov. 8:27–30). Finally he says: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5:19). Thus he too stretched out heaven like a skin.

A most beautiful skin, which, like some vast tent covering the whole face of the earth, delights human sight by the so splendid variety of sun, moon, and stars. What skin is more beautiful than this? What is more adorned than heaven? Yet it is in no way to be compared with the glory and beauty of the bride, failing precisely because this form too passes away, being bodily and subject to bodily senses. For “the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18).

3. But the bride possesses a rational beauty and a spiritual likeness, itself eternal, because it is an image of eternity. Her adornment, for example, is charity; and charity, as you read, “never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8). There is also justice: “His justice,” it says, “endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 112:3). There is patience as well; and you likewise read that “the patience of the poor shall not perish for ever” (Ps. 9:19). What of voluntary poverty? What of humility? Does not the one merit the eternal kingdom (Matt. 5:3), and the other likewise eternal exaltation? (Luke 14:11). To this also belongs the holy fear of the Lord, “enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. 19:10).

Thus prudence, temperance, fortitude, and whatever other virtues there are—what are they but certain pearls in the bride’s adornment, gleaming with perpetual splendour? Perpetual, I say, because they are the seat and foundation of perpetuity. For there is no place at all for a perpetual and blessed life in a soul except with virtues placed as intermediaries. Hence the Prophet says to God, who is certainly blessed life: “Justice and judgment are the preparation of your throne” (Ps. 89:15). And the Apostle says that Christ dwells—not in every way, indeed, but notably—through faith in our hearts (Eph. 3:17).

When the Lord was to sit upon the ass, the disciples laid their garments beneath him (Matt. 21:7–8), signifying that the Saviour, or salvation, by no means sits upon a naked soul—that is, a soul not found clothed in the teaching and morals of the apostles. Therefore the Church, possessing the promise of future blessedness, meanwhile takes care to prepare and adorn herself “in garments of gold, surrounded by variety” (Ps. 45:10), with graces and virtues, [Note: [Col. 0913] Horstius adds, “which indeed we have described in part”; these words are absent from the earliest editions and from all our manuscripts.] so that she may be found worthy and capable of the fullness of grace.

4. But I would by no means compare in beauty this visible and bodily heaven, however beautiful in its own kind through the variety of its stars, with that spiritual variety so beautiful which the bride has meanwhile received from the first robe in a certain garment of her sanctification. [Col. 0914D] Yet there is a heaven of heaven, of which the Prophet says: “Sing to the Lord, who ascends above the heaven of heaven from the east” (Ps. 68:33–34). This heaven is intellectual and spiritual; and he “who made the heavens in understanding” (Ps. 136:5) created it, established it for ever, and himself inhabits it.

Do not suppose, moreover, that the bride’s devotion remains short of that heaven in which she knows her beloved dwells: for “where her treasure is, there is her heart also” (Matt. 6:21). [Col. 0915A] She indeed emulates those who stand before the face for which she longs; and those with whom she is not yet able to be united by seeing, she strives to resemble by living, crying out more by her conduct than by words: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. 26:8).

5. Certainly she does not think it beneath her to draw a likeness from this heaven. It is stretched out like a skin—not by expanses of places, but by the affections of minds; and it is marked out by the wonderful and varied works of its artificer. Its divisions, however, are not divisions of colours [Note: [Col. 0915D] All our manuscripts read *colorum*, “of colours,” except one from Jumièges, which reads *locorum*, “of places”; the printed editions read *coelorum*, “of heavens.”], but of blessedness. For he has appointed some as angels, others as archangels, others as virtues, others as dominions, others as principalities, others as powers, others as thrones, others as cherubim, and others as seraphim. Thus this heaven is studded with stars; thus this skin is painted.

[Col. 0915B] This is one of the skins of my Solomon, and this is foremost among the whole adornment of his manifold glory. But this great skin contains within itself very many skins of Solomon as well, because every blessed and holy one who is there is certainly a skin of Solomon. For they are gracious and stretched out in charity, reaching even to us. They do not begrudge us the glory which they possess, but desire it for us; so that, for this very purpose, they do not count it burdensome to linger among us, being diligent around us and caring for us: “all are ministering spirits, sent for service on account of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation” (Heb. 1:14).

Therefore, just as that entire gathered multitude of the blessed is called, in the singular, the heaven of heaven, so they are called heavens of heavens on account of the individual persons, who are themselves heavens; and to each belongs what is said: “Stretching out heaven like a skin” (Ps. 104:2). You see, I think, what those skins are, and whose Solomon they belong to, whose likeness the bride glories in possessing.

6. Now consider her glory, she who compares herself to heaven—and to that heaven which is so much more glorious as it is more divine. Nor does she improperly take a likeness from that from which she derives her origin. [Note: [Col. 0915D] Berengar, Abelard’s disciple, in the *Apology* which he published for his master against the Council of Sens and Bernard himself, mocks these words as though the holy doctor had thought souls were created in heaven and afterward infused into bodies. Thus he shamelessly insults the most holy man: “You have truly erred,” he says, “in asserting that the origin of souls is from heaven. Since it is useful and easy to ascertain how you maintain this in your book, I shall retrace it for the discerning reader from a more fundamental starting point. There is a book which the Hebrew calls *Firasirim* (*Schirbaschirim*), and Latin calls the *Song of Songs*, whose letter sweats forth, for wakeful souls, the secret of a certain divine understanding.” And below: “Your words, subtly examined, taste of heresy to the palate of a Christian mind. For if you maintain that the soul’s origin is from heaven because it will someday be blessed in heaven, then by the same reasoning the body’s origin will be in heaven, because it too will someday be blessed in heaven. Or if you ascribe a heavenly origin to the soul because it once arose—that is, was made—in heaven, which indeed is the evident intention of such words, you incur the error of Origen.” Thus that rash apologist. But why should a soul not be called heavenly, when it has a heavenly Father, when its manner of life ought to be in heaven, when its homeland is in heaven, and when its substance transcends all earthly things? Hence St Augustine, book II *Against Julian*: “Since we possess a body from earth and a spirit from heaven, we ourselves are earth and heaven.” But away with that foul slanderer Berengar.]

For if, because of the body that she has from earth, she compares herself to the tents of Kedar, why should she not also glory that she is like heaven because of her soul, which is from heaven? Especially since her life bears witness to her origin, to the dignity of her nature and homeland. She worships and serves one God, as [Col. 0915D] the angels do; she loves Christ above all things, as [Col. 0916A] the angels do; she is chaste, as the angels are—and this in sinful flesh and a frail body, which the angels do not have. Finally, she seeks and savours what is with them, not what is on the earth.

What clearer mark of heavenly origin can there be than to retain innate likeness in the region of unlikeness; to claim on earth the glory of a celibate life, even while in exile; finally, to live as an angel in a body almost bestial? These are powers of heaven, not of earth; and they openly show that the soul capable of them is truly from heaven.

Listen, however, more clearly: “I saw,” he says, “the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven, prepared by God as a bride adorned for her husband”; and he added: “And I heard a great voice from the throne saying: ‘Behold, the tabernacle of God with human beings, and he will dwell with them’” (Rev. [Col. 0916B] 21:2–3). For what purpose? I think, to acquire for himself a bride from among human beings. A wonderful thing! He was coming to the bride, and yet he was not coming without a bride. He sought a bride, and the bride was with him. Were there two brides? Far from it! “My dove is one,” he says. But just as he willed to make one flock from different flocks of sheep, “that there may be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10:16), so, although he had from the beginning the multitude of angels as a bride cleaving to him, it pleased him also to call the Church from among human beings and unite it to her who is from heaven, so that there might be one bride and one bridegroom.

Therefore, by this addition the former bride was perfected, not doubled; and she recognizes the saying spoken of herself: “My perfect one is one” (Song 6:8). Conformity makes them one: now, indeed, in similar devotion; later, also in equal glory.

[Col. 0916C] 7. Thus you have both from heaven: the bridegroom, namely Jesus, and the bride, Jerusalem. He, so as to be seen, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of human beings and found in outward appearance as a human being (Phil. 2:7). But in what form or appearance, we may ask, or in what outward habit did he who saw her see her descending? Perhaps in the multitude of angels whom he saw descending and ascending above the Son of Man? (John 1:51).

But we say better that he then saw the bride when he saw the Word in flesh, recognizing two in one flesh. For while that holy Emmanuel brought to earth the teaching of heavenly discipline; while through him and in him a visible image and likeness of the beauty of that Jerusalem above, which is our mother, was made known to us—what did we see except the bride in the bridegroom, admiring one and the same Lord of glory, both bridegroom adorned with a crown and bride adorned with her necklaces? Therefore he who descended is the same who ascended, so that no one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven: one and the same Lord, bridegroom in the head, 1363 and bride in the body.

Nor was the heavenly human being seen on earth without purpose, since from earthly persons he made very many like himself, heavenly persons, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “As is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly ones” (1 Cor. 15:48). From then on, therefore, life is lived on earth in the manner of heavenly beings, while this community too—which came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon—likewise cleaves in chaste love to the heavenly man, after the likeness of that blessed creation above. Though it is not yet joined to him by sight as that creation is, it is betrothed by faith, according to God’s promise spoken through the prophet: “I will betroth you to myself in mercy and compassions, and I will betroth you to myself in faith” (Hos. 2:19).

Accordingly, it strives ever more and more to be conformed to the form that came from heaven, learning from it to be modest and sober, learning to be chaste and holy, learning to be patient and compassionate, and finally learning to be gentle and humble in heart. Thus by conduct of this kind it strives, even while absent, to please him into whom angels desire to look; so that, burning with angelic desire, it may prove itself a fellow citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household, prove itself beloved, prove itself a bride.

8. I think that every such soul is not only heavenly by origin, but may also deservedly be called heaven itself by imitation. And then it clearly shows that its origin is truly from heaven when its manner of life is in heaven. Thus a certain holy soul is a heaven, having the sun as understanding, the moon as faith, and the stars as virtues. Or, more precisely, the sun is zeal for justice or fervent charity, and the moon self-restraint. For just as, they say, the brightness of the moon comes only from the sun, so without charity or justice there is no merit in self-restraint. Hence the Wise Man says: “O how beautiful is a chaste generation with charity!” (Wis. 4:1). Nor do I regret calling virtues stars, when I consider the aptness of the comparison. For as stars shine at night and are hidden by day, so true virtue, often unapparent in prosperity, stands out in adversity. The former is a matter of caution; the latter, of necessity. Therefore virtue is a star, and a man of virtues is a heaven. Unless perhaps someone, reading that God said through the prophet, “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1), thinks that this visible, revolving heaven is meant, rather than that of which Scripture speaks more plainly elsewhere: “The soul of the just person is the seat of wisdom.”

> [Note: Col. 0917D] The same passage is cited in Sermon 1 on the Purification, no. 4, and Sermon 5 on the First Sunday of November, no. 5; likewise above, Sermon 25, no. 6. Besides Bernard, Augustine and Gregory the Great frequently cite it from Scripture. Yet I have not so far found it in the Bible according to the Vulgate translation, although those Fathers frequently cite it under the name of Scripture. St Augustine, indeed, in his Exposition of Psalm 46, on verse 9, and in Sermon 200, no. 1, says: “Why should we not recognize as heavens those who have been made the seats of God? As it is written: ‘The soul of the just person is the seat of wisdom.’” St Gregory, *Morals*, Book 29, chapter 15: “What else should heaven here be understood to mean but the exalted life of the saints? … Of this heaven the Lord says: ‘Heaven is my throne.’ And elsewhere it is written of that seat: ‘The soul of the just person is the seat of wisdom.’” Again, in Homily 38 on the Gospels, at the beginning: “For the assembly of the righteous is called the kingdom of heaven.
