Since the Lord says through the prophet [Col. 0918D], ‘Heaven is my throne’; and Solomon says, ‘The soul of the just person is the seat of wisdom,’” etc. Thus the saying is attributed to Solomon; indeed, in the margin Wisdom, chapter 7, is noted. The Book of Wisdom was attributed to Solomon by many ancient Fathers. But there at verse 7 I read: “I prayed, and the spirit of wisdom came into me.” From these words the cited saying, famous among the Fathers, may seem to have been formed. Let the reader accept this conjecture until finding a better one. Let him further observe that many sayings of Scripture are cited by the Fathers according to the translation of the Seventy Interpreters [the Septuagint]; many of these we have noted throughout Bernard’s works. But this should not be applied to the present passage, since the Book of Wisdom was first written in Greek, or at least its Hebrew text no longer exists. Some bring in here Proverbs 12:28: “In the path of righteousness is life.”

But whoever, from the teaching of the Savior, understands that God is spirit and must be worshipped in spirit (John 4:24), does not hesitate to assign him a spiritual seat. I myself would confidently do this no less in the righteous human being than in an angelic spirit. Above all, I am confirmed in this sense by that faithful promise: “I and the Father,” says the Son, “will come to him”—that is, to the holy person—“and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). I also think that the prophet spoke of no other heaven: “But you dwell in the holy one, O praise of Israel” (Ps. 21:4). The Apostle plainly says that Christ dwells through faith in our hearts (Eph. 3:17).

9. Nor is it surprising if the Lord Jesus gladly dwells in this heaven, which he did not merely command to come into being, as he did the rest, but fought to acquire and died to redeem. Therefore, having attained his desire after labor, he says: “This is my rest for ever and ever; here will I dwell, for I have chosen her” (Ps. 131:14). Blessed is she to whom it is said: “Come, my chosen one, and I will place my throne in you.” Why are you now sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me? Do you think you too may find within yourself a place for the Lord? And what place within us is fit for such glory, sufficient for such majesty? Would that I might at least deserve to worship in the place where his feet stood. Who will grant me at least to cling to the footprints of some holy soul whom he has chosen for his dwelling? Yet if he deigns to fill my soul also with the anointing of his mercy, and so stretch it out like a skin—which, when anointed, is certainly expanded—then I too may say: “I ran the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118:32). Perhaps I too shall be able to show in myself, if not “a large furnished upper room” where he may recline with his disciples, at least somewhere to lay his head. From afar I gaze upon those blessed ones of whom it is said: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Cor. 6:16).

10. O how great the breadth of that soul, and how great the prerogative of its merits, which is found worthy to receive the divine presence within itself and sufficient to contain it! What of the soul that also has broad walks available for the work of Majesty?

> [Col. 0918D–0919A; variant: “spaces”]

Certainly it is not entangled in lawsuits or secular cares; nor is it devoted to belly and luxury. Nor is it curious for spectacles, wholly eager to rule, or puffed up by dominion. For first the soul must be empty of all these things, if it is to become heaven and God’s dwelling-place. Otherwise, how can it be at leisure and know that he is God? Nor must it yield at all to hatred, envy, or rancor, since “wisdom will not enter a malicious soul” (Wis. 1:4). Then it must grow and be enlarged, so as to be capable of God. Its breadth, moreover, is its love, as the Apostle says: “Be enlarged in charity” (2 Cor. 6:13). For though the soul, being spirit, does not receive bodily magnitude, grace grants it what nature has denied. It grows indeed and is extended, but spiritually; it grows not in substance but in virtue; it grows also in glory; it grows into a holy temple in the Lord; finally, it grows and advances “to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13).

Therefore let the size of every soul be measured by the amount of charity it possesses. For example, one that has much charity is great; one that has little is small; but one that has none is nothing, as Paul says: “If I do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). If it has begun to possess however little, so that it takes care at least to love those who love it, and to greet its brothers and those who greet it, I would call that soul something: it still retains at least a social charity in the matter of giving and receiving. Yet, according to the Lord’s saying, “What more are you doing?” (Matt. 5:47). Accordingly, I would judge narrow and small—not broad or great—the soul which I knew to have such scant charity.

11. But if it grows and advances, so that, passing beyond the bounds of this narrow and self-interested love, it grasps in all the freedom of the spirit the broad limits of gratuitous goodness, and in the ample bosom of good will takes care to extend itself to every neighbor, loving each one as itself—will it then rightly be told, “What more are you doing?” It makes itself so broad. Broad, I say, is the bosom of charity which embraces all, even those with whom it knows itself joined by no tie of flesh; which is enticed by no hope of gaining any advantage; which is obligated by no repayment received; and finally is bound by no debt at all, except that of which it is said: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom. 13:8).

But if you add that you exert all your strength upon the kingdom of charity, so that as a pious invader you prevail in occupying it as far as its furthest bounds, judging that even to enemies the bowels of compassion must not be closed—doing good also to those who hate you, praying for those who persecute and slander you, and striving to be peaceable even with those who hate peace—then indeed the breadth of heaven is the breadth of your soul; its height is not unlike, nor its beauty dissimilar. Then at last is fulfilled in it what is said: “Stretching out the heavens like a skin” (Ps. 103:2). In this heaven of marvelous breadth, height, and beauty, the supreme, immeasurable, and glorious One not only graciously dwells, but walks about spaciously.

12. Do you see what heavens the Church contains within herself, while she herself nevertheless, in her universality, is a vast heaven, stretched “from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth”? See further to whom you may compare her in this very respect, if you have not forgotten the example of this matter mentioned a little earlier: the heaven of heaven, and the heavens of heavens (above, no. 9). Therefore, following the example of her mother who is above, this Church also, still on pilgrimage, has her heavens: spiritual people conspicuous in life and reputation, pure in faith, steadfast in hope, broad in charity, uplifted in contemplation. These, raining down the saving rain of the word, thunder in rebukes and flash with miracles. These proclaim the glory of God; stretched out like skins over the whole earth, they show in themselves the law of life and discipline, written indeed by God’s finger, to give knowledge of salvation to his people. They also display the Gospel of peace, because they are Solomon’s skins.

13. Recognize now in these skins the image of those heavenly skins that were described not far above in the Bridegroom’s adornment (above, no. 3). Recognize likewise the queen standing at his right hand, clothed with similar ornaments, though not equal ones (Ps. 44:10). For although even here, in the place of her pilgrimage and on the day of her strength, among the splendors of the saints, she has no small share of brightness and beauty, nevertheless the integrity and consummation of the blessed ones’ glory crown that beauty in a different manner.

Yet I would call the Bride perfect and blessed, but only in part. For she is in part the tent of Kedar, though beautiful: whether in that portion of herself which already reigns in blessedness, or in the illustrious men by whose wisdom and virtues she is adorned, even in this night, as heaven is adorned with its stars. Hence the prophet says: “Those who are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, as stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12:3).

14. O humility! O sublimity! Both a tent of Kedar and the sanctuary of God; both an earthly dwelling and a heavenly palace; both a house of clay and a royal court; both a body of death and a temple of light; finally, an object of scorn to the proud and the bride of Christ. “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem”: though labor and the pain of long exile discolor her, a heavenly beauty adorns her; Solomon’s skins adorn her. If you shrink from her blackness, marvel also at her beauty; if you despise her lowliness, reverence her exaltation. How prudent, how full of counsel, discrimination, and fittingness is this very fact: in the Bride this lowliness and this loftiness are so tempered together according to the time, that amid the changes of this world loftiness raises the humble lest she fail in adversity, while humility restrains the exalted lest she vanish in prosperity. Although wholly opposed to each other, these two things cooperate together for the Bride’s good and serve her salvation.

15. This has been said because the Bride seems to introduce a comparison with Solomon’s skins. Yet there remains to be opened that meaning of the same chapter which I mentioned and promised at the beginning: namely, how the whole comparison is to be referred to blackness alone. You are not to be deprived of that promised explanation. But it must be deferred to the beginning of another sermon, both because the length of this one now demands it, and so that, as is customary, prayer may come first: prayer to be offered in praise and glory of the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

1366

## SERMON XXVIII

### On the Bridegroom’s Blackness and Beauty, and How Hearing Rather Than Sight Has Force in Matters of Faith and for the Knowledge of Truth

1. You understand, I think, what Solomon’s skins and whose skins I take the Bride’s beauty to have been compared with, provided that the comparison drawn from them is referred to the displaying and commending of beauty. But if it is thought rather to concern blackness, as does that concerning the tents of Kedar, no explanation of such Solomon’s skins occurs to me except perhaps those which the king used to take for the use of a tent whenever he chose to dwell in encampments. Such skins, if there were any, would necessarily have been dark and dingy, exposed daily to sun and to the violence of frequent rains.

> [Note: Col. 0921D] Three manuscripts read differently after “thought”: “those skins with which Solomon formerly covered the tent must be recalled to mind. They were undoubtedly black, exposed daily to sun [Col. 0922D] and to the violence of daily rains. Nor was this without purpose,” etc.

Nor was this without purpose, but so that the adornment stored within might be kept brighter. By this example the Bride does not deny her blackness, but excuses it; nor does she regard as disgraceful any condition which charity shapes and the judgment of truth does not disapprove. For “who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29). She puts on the blemish of compassion, so as to relieve or heal in another the sickness of suffering; she becomes dark through zeal for brightness, for the gain of beauty.

2. The darkening of one makes many white, not when it is stained by guilt, but when it is affected by care. “It is expedient,” he says, “that one man die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish” (John 11:50). It is expedient that one be darkened for all in the likeness of sinful flesh, lest the whole nation be condemned in the blackness of sin; that the brightness and image of God’s substance be shadowed in the form of a servant for the servant’s life; that the brightness of eternal life be darkened in flesh in order to cleanse flesh; that he who is “beautiful in form above the children of men” be obscured in suffering, made ugly on the cross, and made pale in death, in order to enlighten the children of men. Let him have no beauty or comeliness at all, that he may acquire for himself the Church as a beautiful and comely Bride, without spot or wrinkle.

I recognize Solomon’s skin—indeed, I embrace Solomon himself in a black skin. Solomon too has blackness, but in the skin: black outwardly, black in the hide, not within. Otherwise “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:3, 14). Within are the brightness of divinity, the beauty of virtues, the splendor of glory [variant: grace], and purity of innocence. But these things are covered by the more contemptible color of weakness, and his face is, as it were, hidden and despised while he is tempted in all things according to our likeness, without sin.

I recognize the form of nature made dark; I recognize those garments of skin, the clothing of the sinful first parents (Gen. 3:21). Thus he made himself dark, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found in outward appearance as a man (Phil. 2:7). Under the skin of a goat, which signifies sin, I recognize the hand that committed no sin, and the neck through which no evil thought passed; therefore no deceit was found in his mouth (Isa. 53:9). I know that by nature you are gentle, meek and humble of heart, gracious in appearance, sweet in spirit, and indeed anointed with the oil of gladness above your companions (Ps. 44:8). Whence then are you now hairy and rough, like Esau? Whose wrinkled and hideous image is this, and where do these hairs come from? They are mine: for the likeness of hairy hands expresses the sinner. I recognize these hairs as mine, and in my skin I see God my Savior.

3. Yet Rebekah did not so clothe him, but Mary did: by as much the worthier to receive the blessing as she who bore him was holier. And he is rightly in my clothing, because the blessing is claimed for me and the inheritance is sought for me. For he had heard: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2:8). “Your inheritance,” he says, “and your possession I will give you.” How will you give it to him if it is his? And how do you bid him ask for what is his? Or how is it his if he must ask for it? Therefore he asks for me, who puts on my form for this purpose, that he may undertake my cause. For “the discipline of our peace was upon him,” as the prophet says, “and the Lord laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isa. 53:5–6). Hence, as the Apostle says, he had to be made like his brethren in all things, that he might become merciful (Heb. 2:17).

Therefore “the voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands” (Gen. 27:22). What is heard from him is his; what is seen in him is ours. What he speaks is spirit and life; what appears is mortality and death. One thing is seen, another believed. Sense reports blackness; faith proves him white and beautiful. He is black, but to the eyes of the foolish; to the minds of believers he is exceedingly beautiful. He is black, but beautiful: black in Herod’s estimation, beautiful in the thief’s confession and in the centurion’s faith.

4. How beautiful did he perceive him to be who cried out, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” But consider how he perceived it. If he had attended to what appeared, how could he see him as beautiful, how as the Son of God? What but ugliness and blackness presented itself to onlookers’ eyes when, with hands outstretched on the cross, he hung between two criminals, providing mockery for the malicious and tears for the faithful? He alone was made an object of mockery, though he alone could have been an object of terror and alone should have received honor. Whence then did he perceive the beauty of the Crucified One, and that he was the Son of God who “was reckoned among the wicked” (Isa. 53:12)? It is neither lawful nor necessary for us to give our own answer, for the evangelist did not omit the matter through carelessness. For this is what you have: “But the centurion who stood opposite him, seeing that he had expired with such a cry, said: Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark 15:39). Therefore he believed because of the voice; from the voice he recognized the Son of God, not from the face. Perhaps he was one of his sheep, of whom he says: “My sheep hear my voice” (John 10:17).

> [Note: Col. 0923D] Two manuscripts read thus. Another, with the printed editions, adds: “and I know mine, and mine know me.” The Colbert manuscript has only: “and mine know me.”

5. Hearing found what sight did not; appearance deceived the eye, while truth poured itself into the ear. The eye declared him weak, the eye ugly, the eye miserable, the eye condemned to a most shameful death. To the ear he became known as the Son of God, to the ear as beautiful—but not to the ear of the Jews, for they were uncircumcised in ears. Peter rightly cut off the servant’s ear, to make a way for truth, and so that truth might free him—that is, make him free. That centurion was uncircumcised, but not in ear: at the single cry of the dying man, amid so many indications of weakness, he recognized the Lord of Majesty. Therefore he did not despise what he saw, because he believed what he did not see. Yet he did not believe from what he saw, but undoubtedly from what he heard, because “faith comes by hearing” (Rom. 10:17).

It would indeed have been fitting for truth to enter the soul through the upper windows of the eyes; but this, O soul, is reserved for us in the future, when we shall see face to face. For now, however, let the remedy enter by the same route by which the disease crept in; and through the same footsteps let life follow death, light darkness, and the antidote of truth the serpent’s poison. Let it heal the eye that has become disordered, so that when clear it may see him whom, while disordered, it cannot see. Let the ear, the first gate of death, be the first opened also to life; let hearing, which caused the loss, restore sight, for unless we believe, we shall not understand. Therefore hearing belongs to merit, sight to reward. Hence the Prophet says: “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing” (Ps. 50:10): the blessed vision is the faithful hearing’s reward, and faithful hearing is the merit of blessed vision. “Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). The eye that is to see God must, moreover, be cleansed by faith, as you have it: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9).

6. Therefore meanwhile, while sight is not yet ready, let hearing be awakened; let hearing be exercised; let hearing receive truth.

> [Note: Col. 0924D] Some copies lack “let hearing be exercised.” Perhaps this is an addition by a scribe who, uncertain which reading ought to be adopted, wrote both.

Blessed is he to whom Truth bears witness, saying: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me” (Ps. 17:45). I shall be worthy to see, if I am found to have obeyed before I see; I shall safely see him whom the gift of my obedience has preceded. How blessed is he who says: “The Lord God opened my ear, and I do not resist; I have not turned back” (Isa. 50:5). Here you have both the form of voluntary obedience and an example of perseverance. For one who does not resist is willing, and one who has not turned back perseveres. Both are necessary, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7), and “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

Would that the Lord might open my ear also; that the word of truth might enter my heart, cleanse my eye, and prepare it for a joyful vision, so that I too may say to God: “Your ear has heard the preparation of my heart” (Ps. 9:17); so that I too, with the other obedient ones, may hear from God: “And you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15:3). Not all who hear are cleansed, but those who obey: “Blessed are they who hear and keep it” (Luke 11:28). Such hearing is required by him who commands, saying: “Hear, O Israel” (Deut. 6:3); such hearing is offered by him who says: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears” (1 Sam. 3:9); such hearing is promised by him who says: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me” (Ps. 84:9).

7. And so that you may know that the Holy Spirit also observes this order in the soul’s spiritual progress—namely, first forming hearing and then gladdening sight—he says: “Hear, daughter, and see” (Ps. 44:11). Why strain your eye? Prepare your ear. Do you desire to see Christ? You must first hear him, hear about him, so that when you see, you may say: “As we have heard, so have we seen” (Ps. 47:9). The brightness is immense, the vision majestic, and you cannot attain it. You can attain it by hearing, but not by sight. When God cried, “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9), I, now a sinner, did not see him, but I still heard him. Yet hearing will restore sight, if it comes first devoutly, vigilantly, and faithfully. Faith will cleanse the one whom impiety disturbed; obedience will open the one whom disobedience closed. Thus he says: “From your commandments I have understood” (Ps. 118:104), because observance of the commandments restores the understanding which transgression took away.

Observe further in holy Isaac how, when he was already old, hearing remained strong above the other senses. The patriarch’s eyes grow dim; his palate is deceived; his hand is misled; his ear is not misled. What wonder if the ear perceives truth, when faith comes by hearing, hearing by the word of God (Rom. 10:17), and the word of God is truth? “The voice,” he says, “is Jacob’s voice.” Nothing is truer. “But the hands are Esau’s hands” (Gen. 27:22). Nothing is falser. You are deceived: the likeness of the hands has deceived you. Nor is there truth in taste, though there is sweetness. For how does one have truth who thinks that he is eating game, when he is feeding on the flesh of domestic kids? Still less does the eye have it, since it sees nothing. There is no truth in the eye, no wisdom. “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes!” he says (Isa. 5:21). That wisdom is not good which is cursed. It belongs to the world and is therefore folly with God (1 Cor. 3:19).

8. Good and true wisdom is drawn from hidden things, as blessed Job knows (Job 28:18). Why do you seek it outside, in bodily sense? Taste is in the palate; wisdom is in the heart. Do not seek wisdom in the eye of flesh, for flesh and blood do not reveal it, but the Spirit does (Matt. 16:17). Not in the taste of the mouth, for it “is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job 28:13). Not in the touch of the hand, since the holy man says: “If I have kissed my hand with my mouth, which is a very great iniquity and a denial of God” (Job 31:27–28). I think this occurs when the gift of God, which is wisdom, is ascribed not to God but to the merits of one’s actions.

Isaac was wise, but nevertheless erred in his senses. Hearing alone possesses truth, because it perceives the Word. For good reason the woman who thinks carnally is forbidden to touch the risen flesh of the Word: she gives more to the eye than to the oracle—that is, to bodily sense than to God’s word. The one whom she saw dead she did not believe resurrected [variant: about to rise], though he himself had promised this. Thus her eye did not rest until sight had been satisfied, because there was no consolation of faith and no firm confidence in God’s promise. Do not heaven and earth, and everything whatever that the eye of flesh can reach, sooner pass away and perish than one iota or one stroke of all that God has spoken? Yet she ceased weeping at the sight of her eyes, though she refused to be consoled by the Lord’s word, valuing experience more highly than faith. But experience is deceptive.

9. Therefore she is sent to the more certain knowledge of faith, which indeed grasps what sense does not know and experience does not discover. “Do not touch me,” he says; that is: Withdraw from this deceptive sense; rely on the word, become accustomed to faith. Faith, incapable of deception and comprehending things invisible, does not feel the poverty of the senses. Indeed, it passes beyond even the limits of human reason, the course of nature, and the boundaries of experience. Why do you question the eye about what it cannot attain? Why does the hand attempt to investigate what is above it? Whatever either reports is less. Let faith indeed speak of me, faith which detracts nothing from majesty. Learn to hold as more certain and follow more safely that which faith has advised.

“Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17). As though, once he had ascended, he would then wish or be able to be touched by her. He will indeed be able to be touched, but by affection, not hand; by longing, not eye; by faith, not senses. Why, he says, do you now seek to touch me, you who judge the glory of resurrection by bodily sense? Do you not know that, even in the time of my mortality, the disciples’ eyes could not endure the glory of my body, transfigured for a moment and yet destined to die? (Matt. 17:6). For the present I still accommodate your senses by presenting the servant’s form which you recognize by familiarity. But my glory has become wonderful from you; it has been strengthened, and you cannot attain it. Therefore defer judgment, suspend your sentence, and do not entrust the definition of so great a reality to sense; reserve it for faith. Faith will define it more worthily and more certainly, because it comprehends it more fully. For in its mystical and profound bosom it comprehends what is the length, breadth, height, and depth. What eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, faith bears within itself as though sealed up in a certain envelope and keeps it guarded.

10. Therefore faith will touch me worthily when it receives me seated with the Father, no longer in a lowly condition but in a heavenly one: with the same flesh, yet under another appearance. Why do you wish to touch me ugly? Wait until you touch me beautiful. For he who is ugly now will then be beautiful: ugly to touch, ugly to sight; ugly, finally, to you who are yourself ugly, because you cling more to the senses and less to faith. Become beautiful, and touch me; become faithful, and you are beautiful. Being beautiful, you will touch the Beautiful One more worthily and more happily. You will touch him with the hand of faith, the finger of desire, the embrace of devotion; you will touch him with the eye of the mind.

But will he still be black? Far from it! Your Beloved is white and ruddy. He is indeed beautiful, surrounded by the flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys—that is, the choirs of martyrs and virgins—and seated in the midst, differing from neither choir: virgin and martyr. How could I fail to belong with the white choirs of virgins, being a virgin, the Son of a Virgin, and the Bridegroom of a virgin? How could I fail to belong with the rose-red choirs of martyrs, being the cause, strength, fruit, and model of martyrdom? Touch such a one in such a manner, and say: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands” (Cant. 5:10).

Thousands of thousands are with the Beloved, and ten times a hundred thousand around the Beloved, yet none is the Beloved. Will you fear that, while seeking the one you love, you may perhaps mistakenly fall upon someone from the crowd? You will not at all hesitate whom to choose. The one chosen from among thousands, more conspicuous than all, will easily meet you, and you will say: “This one is beautiful in his robe, walking in the greatness of his strength” (Isa. 63:1). Therefore he will not be in the black skin which hitherto had to be presented to persecutors’ eyes so that they might despise one to be killed, or even to friends’ eyes so that they might recognize one restored to life. No, I say, he will no longer meet you in a black skin, but in a white garment: beautiful in form, not only above the children of men, but even above the countenances of angels. Why do you wish to touch me in a lowly condition, in a servant’s form, in a contemptible appearance? Touch him beautiful in heavenly appearance, crowned with glory and honor—terrible indeed in divine majesty, but welcome and gentle in innate serenity.

11. In all this observe the Bride’s prudence and the depth of her sayings. Under the figure of Solomon’s skins—that is, in the flesh—she discerned God; in death, life; amid reproaches, the summit of glory and honor; and, finally, beneath the black condition of the Crucified One, the brightness of innocence and the splendor of virtues. For those skins, though black and despised, preserved within themselves the precious and dazzlingly white ornaments of the exceedingly wealthy king. She rightly does not despise blackness in the skins, perceiving the beauty beneath the skins. And therefore some despised her because they did not recognize him; “for if they had known him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

Herod did not recognize him and therefore despised him. The Synagogue did not recognize him; reproaching him with the blackness of suffering and weakness, it said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. Let Christ, the King of Israel, now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 27:42). But the thief recognized him from the cross, though himself on the cross; he confessed both the purity of his innocence: “What evil has this man done?” and the glory of his royal majesty: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:41–42). The centurion recognized him, crying that he was the Son of God (Matt. 27:54). The Church recognizes him, and imitates his blackness in order to share his beauty. She is not ashamed to appear black or to be called black, so that she may say to her Beloved: “The reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me” (Ps. 68:10).

Yet she is black like Solomon’s skins: outwardly, that is, and not inwardly. For my Solomon has no blackness within. Thus she does not say, “I am black like Solomon,” but “like Solomon’s skins,” because the blackness of the Peaceful One is true only on the surface. The blackness of sin is within; guilt first stains the inner parts before it comes forth to the eyes. For from the heart proceed evil thoughts, thefts, murders, adulteries, blasphemies; “and these are what defile a person” (Matt. 15:19–20). But far be it from Solomon! You will find no such defilements whatever in the true Peaceful One. For he who takes away the sins of the world must be without sin, so that, being found fit to reconcile sinners, he may rightly claim for himself the name Solomon.

12. But there is a blackness of afflicting repentance, when mourning is undertaken for sins. Perhaps Solomon will not abhor this in me, if I willingly put it on for my sins, because “God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:19). There is also the blackness of compassionate fellow-feeling, if you grieve with one who is afflicted and your brother’s misfortune discolors you. Our Peaceful One certainly does not judge this to be rejected, since he himself graciously put it on for us, he “who bore our sins in his body upon the tree” (1 Pet. 2:24). There is also the blackness of persecution, which is regarded as a supreme adornment if it is received for righteousness and truth. Hence: “The disciples went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were considered worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41); and again: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10). I think that the Church especially glories in this blackness and more willingly imitates it from the Bridegroom’s skins. For she has this also in promise: “If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15:20).

13. Therefore the bride adds: “Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me” (Song 1:5); that is: Do not mark me as though misshapen, because you see me, under the pressure of persecution, less flourishing and less adorned with the color of worldly glory. Why do you reproach me for a darkness brought on by the heat of persecution, not by the shamefulness of my conduct? Or she calls “sun” the zeal of righteousness, by which one rises and girds oneself against evildoers, saying to God: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68:10); and: “My zeal has made me waste away, because my enemies have forgotten your words”; likewise: “Faintness seized me because of sinners who forsake your law” (Ps. 118:139, 53); and again: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away over your enemies?” (Ps. 138:21). She also carefully observes the saying of the Wise Man: “Daughters, he says, do you have? Do not show them a cheerful face” (Sir. 7:26): so that toward those who are lax, soft, and fleeing discipline, she may display not the brightness of serenity but the darkness of severity. Or to be discolored by the [Col. 0928B] sun is to be inflamed with brotherly love: to weep with those who weep, to be weak with the weak, to burn at each person’s stumbling.

Or thus: Christ, the Sun of righteousness, has discolored me, for whose love I languish. This languishing is a kind of loss of color and a failing of the soul in longing; hence she says: “I remembered God and was delighted; I was exercised, and my spirit failed” (Ps. 76:3). Thus the ardor of desire, like a burning sun, discolors one who is a pilgrim in the body: while longing for the countenance of glory, it makes one impatient at being repulsed, and delay tortures the lover. Which of us burns with such holy love that, out of desire to see Christ, he disdains and lays aside every color of present glory and joy, protesting to him in that prophetic voice: “I did not desire the day of man; you know it” [Col. 0928C] (Jer. 17:16); and again with holy David: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76:7), that is, it scorns to be adorned by the empty delight of present goods?

Or certainly, “the sun has discolored me” by comparison with its own splendor: as I draw near to it, I find myself dark by contrast, discover myself black, and regard myself as ugly. At other times, indeed, I am beautiful; why do you call me dark when I yield only to the beauty of the sun alone? Yet what follows seems to agree more with the former meaning. For she adds: “The sons of my mother fought against me,” plainly indicating that she has suffered persecution. But from this point we shall begin another discourse, since what we have received on this occasion concerning the glory of the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0928D] may suffice—by his own gift, who is God, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX. On the Church’s complaint against her attackers, or against those who assail brotherly unity

1. “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song 1:5). Annas, Caiaphas, and Judas Iscariot were sons of the Synagogue; and they fought most bitterly against the Church, likewise a daughter of the Synagogue, at the very beginning of her existence, hanging her gatherer, Jesus, upon the wood. For already then God fulfilled through them what he had long before foreshown through the prophet, saying: “I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered” (Zech. 13:7). Perhaps that voice in Hezekiah’s song is hers: “My life is cut off like cloth from the loom; [Col. 0929A] while I was still beginning to weave, he cut me off” (Isa. 38:12). Therefore understand the bride’s saying, “The sons of my mother fought against me,” to refer to these and to the others from that people who are known to have opposed the Christian name.

She aptly calls them sons of her mother, but not also sons of her father; for they did not have God as their Father, but were of the devil their father—murderers, certainly, just as he was a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44). Therefore she does not say, “My brothers,” or, “The sons of my father”; rather, she says, “The sons of my mother fought against me.” Otherwise, if she did not make this distinction, the Apostle Paul would seem also to be included among those of whom she complains, since he too once persecuted the Church of God (1 Cor. 15:9). Yet he obtained mercy because he did this ignorantly, [Col. 0929B] remaining in unbelief (1 Tim. 1:13); and he proved that God was his Father, and that he was a brother of the Church both on the father’s and the mother’s side.

2. But observe how she names and accuses only the sons of her mother, as though they alone were guilty. How much she suffered also from outsiders! As the prophet says: “Often they attacked me from my youth,” and, “Sinners built upon my back” (Ps. 128:1–3). Why, then, do you complain particularly of the sons of your mother, when you well know that you have been most often attacked by many other nations as well? “When you are invited to the table of a rich man,” he says, “consider carefully what is set before you.” Brothers, we sit at Solomon’s table. Who is richer than Solomon? I do not mean earthly riches, although Solomon abounded even in those; [Col. 0929C] rather, behold this present table, how full it is of heavenly delicacies. What is set before us on it is spiritual and divine. “Consider carefully,” therefore, he says, “what is set before you, knowing that you ought to prepare such things” (Prov. 23:1–2).

For my part, insofar as I am able, I carefully observe that in these words of the bride something is set before me which directly concerns my instruction and warning: persecution by those of one’s own household is explicitly and exclusively named, while the many and grievous sufferings which she is known to have endured throughout the world from every nation under heaven—from unbelievers, heretics, and schismatics—are passed over in silence. I know the bride’s wisdom; I would not suppose that she omitted these things by chance or from forgetfulness. [Col. 0929D] Rather, she laments more expressly what she feels more acutely and what she judges we must guard against more vigilantly. What is it? An internal and domestic evil. The Savior himself expresses this plainly in the Gospel when he says: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. 10:36). The prophet says the same: “The man of my peace, who ate my bread, has magnified his treachery against me” (Ps. 40:10); and again: “If my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken great things against me, perhaps I would have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food” (Ps. 54:13–15). That is: What I suffer from you, my table-companion and fellow-dweller, [Col. 0930A] I feel more painfully and bear more heavily. You know whose complaint this is, and concerning whom.

3. Recognize, then, that the bride also complains of the sons of her mother with the same feeling, because she speaks in the same Spirit when she says: “The sons of my mother fought against me.” Hence elsewhere she says: “My friends and my neighbors drew near and stood against me” (Ps. 37:12). I beg you: always keep this utterly abominable and detestable evil far from yourselves—you who have experienced, and daily experience, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity (Ps. 132:1), provided that they dwell in unity and not in scandal. Otherwise it is certainly neither pleasant nor good, but most evil and most troublesome. Woe to that man through whom the pleasant bond of unity is disturbed! Whoever he may be, he shall certainly bear judgment.

May it happen to me first to die rather than to hear anyone among you justly crying: “The sons of my mother fought against me.” Are you not all sons of the present congregation as of one mother, each of you a brother to the other? What then can trouble or distress you from outside if you are well within and rejoice in brotherly peace? “Who,” he says, “will be able to harm you, if you are zealous for what is good?” (1 Pet. 3:13). Therefore be zealous for the better gifts (1 Cor. 12:31), so that you may prove yourselves zealous for good things.

The most desirable gift is love: truly incomparable. The heavenly Bridegroom of the new bride took care to impress it upon her repeatedly, at one time saying: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, [Col. 0930C] if you have love for one another”; at another: “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another” (John 13:35, 34); and, “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15:12); and likewise praying that they might be one, as he and the Father are one (John 17:11). See whether Paul himself, who invites you to the better gifts, does not place love above all else: whether, with faith and hope, he calls it greater and surpassing knowledge; or whether, after enumerating many marvelous gifts of heavenly grace, he finally directs us to a more excellent way—surely defining it as none other than love. What, finally, should we judge comparable to it, when it is preferred even to martyrdom and to faith that moves mountains? (1 Cor. 12:31; 13:3).

This, therefore, is what I say: Let peace among yourselves be yours; then whatever may seem threatening from outside does not terrify, because it does no harm. Conversely, whatever may appear attractive from outside affords no consolation if, God forbid, a seedbed of discord has sprung up within.

4. Therefore, beloved, have peace among yourselves, and do not injure one another—not by deed, not by word, not by any sign whatever—lest anyone, perhaps embittered and overtaken by faintness of spirit and storm, be compelled to appeal to God against those who have hurt or distressed him, and happen to break forth into that grave utterance: “The sons of my mother fought against me.” For in sinning thus against a brother, [Col. 0931A] you sin against Christ, who says: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40, 45).

Nor must one guard only against graver offenses, for example open abuse or cursing, but also against every covert and venomous whisper. It is not enough, I say, to keep one’s mouth from these and similar things; even small matters must be avoided—if indeed anything you undertake against a brother with the intention of hurting him ought to be called small, when by this alone, if you are angry with him, you are held guilty of divine judgment (Matt. 5:22). And rightly so. For what you consider slight, and consequently treat more lightly, another often understands differently, like a person who sees according to appearances and judges according to appearances, ready to suspect a beam in a straw and to think a spark a furnace. For not everyone has that love which “believes all things” [Col. 0931B] (1 Cor. 13:7).

Human perceptions and thoughts are inclined to suspect evil rather than believe good, especially where the discipline of silence permits neither you, who are the cause, to excuse yourself, nor the other man to disclose the wound of suspicion he suffers, so that it may be cured. Thus he burns and dies with a closed and lethal wound, groaning within himself; since wholly occupied with anger and contention, in silence he can turn over nothing else in his mind but the injury he has received. He cannot pray, cannot read, cannot meditate upon anything holy or spiritual; and so, with its vital breath cut off, while the soul for which Christ died goes to death deprived of its nourishment, what disposition, I ask, do you have in the meantime? What savor do your prayer or whatever work you do then have for you, when Christ anxiously cries out from the breast of the brother whom you have distressed: “A son of my mother fights against me, and he who together with me took sweet food has filled me with bitterness”?

5. If you say that he ought not to have been so grievously disturbed for so slight a cause, I reply: The slighter it is, the more easily you could have avoided doing it. Yet I do not know how you can call slight, as I have already said, anything exceeding anger, when you have received from the Judge’s own mouth that even anger itself is liable to judgment. What then? Would you call slight that in which Christ is offended, and on account of which you may be dragged before God’s judgment, when “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God”? (Heb. 10:31.)

Therefore, if you have perhaps received an injury—which indeed it is difficult never to encounter in such communities—do not immediately, in the manner of the world, hasten to strike your brother in return with an indirect answer. Nor, under the pretext of correcting him, dare in any way to pierce with a sharp and burning word the soul for which Christ deigned to be fixed to the cross. Do not grumble as though rebuking; do not mutter with your lips as though murmuring; do not wrinkle your nose or laugh scornfully as though mocking; do not furrow your brow as though attacking or threatening. Let your agitation die where it arises, and do not allow that which bears death to go out and kill; so that you too may say with the Prophet: “I was troubled, and I did not speak” (Ps. 76:5).

6. I have understood some to take this more deeply, as though it were said of the devil and his angels, who, although they too were sons of that Jerusalem above which is our mother, have not ceased since their fall to attack their sister, the Church. But neither do I contend against anyone who applies this also in a good sense: namely, that the spiritual persons in the Church fight against their carnal brothers with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 6:17), wounding them for salvation and advancing them toward spiritual things by such assaults. “May the righteous man rebuke me in mercy and correct me,” striking and healing, killing and making alive, so that I too may dare to say: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). “Be in agreement with your adversary while you are with him on the way, lest he hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the torturer” (Matt. 5:25). A good adversary indeed, [Col. 0932B] with whom, if I agree, there will be no ground for either judge or torturer to charge me.

For my part, if I have ever distressed any of you for such reasons, I do not regret it; for they were distressed unto salvation. Indeed, I do not know that I have ever done this without great sadness also on my own part, according to the saying: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow” (John 16:21). Yet far be it from me now to remember the anguish, while I hold the fruit of my pain and see Christ likewise formed in the offspring. I do not know how it is, but those who finally recovered from weakness after and through rebukes are bound to me even more tenderly than those who remained strong from the beginning and had no need of this sort of medicine.

7. Therefore, in this sense the Church—or a soul that loves God—may say that the sun has discolored [Col. 0932C] her, namely by sending and arming sons of her mother who would beneficially assail her and lead her captive to faith and love of him, pierced, indeed, by the many arrows of which it is written: “Sharp arrows of the mighty one” (Ps. 119:4); and again: “Your arrows have been fixed in me. Therefore,” it follows, “there is no health in my flesh” (Ps. 37:3–4), so that, becoming healthier and consequently stronger in soul, she may say: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41); and with the Apostle: “For when I am weak, then I am powerful and strong” (2 Cor. 12:10).

You see that weakness of the flesh increases the strength of the spirit and supplies it with power. Conversely, know that strength of the flesh produces weakness of spirit. And what wonder, if, when your enemy is weakened, [Col. 0932D] you become stronger? Unless, perhaps, you are so utterly mad as to regard as your friend that which never ceases to desire against the spirit (Gal. 5:17). See, then, whether the saint does not wisely ask to be shot at and beneficially assaulted, when he says in prayer: “Pierce my flesh with your fear” (Ps. 118:120). This fear is an excellent arrow, which pierces and kills the desires of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved. And one who chastises his body and reduces it to slavery—does he not seem to you himself to assist the hand that fights against him?

8. The word of God, living and effective, more piercing than every two-edged sword, is also an arrow (Heb. 4:12); concerning it the Savior says: “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34). The chosen arrow is also the love of Christ, which not only pierced Mary’s soul, [Col. 0933A] but passed through it, so as to leave no portion of her virgin breast empty of love: rather, she loved with her whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength, and was full of grace. Or certainly it passed through her in order to come even to us, so that all of us might receive from that fullness and she might become the mother of love, whose Father is God, who is love—giving birth and setting his tent in the sun—so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says: “I have given you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. 49:6).

For this was fulfilled through Mary, who brought forth visibly in flesh him whom she received invisibly neither from flesh nor with flesh. She, indeed, received throughout her whole being a great and sweet wound of love. But I should count myself happy if I felt myself touched, as it were, only by the tip of this sword, so that, having received even a small wound of love, my soul too might say: “I am wounded by love” (Song 2:5). Who will grant me to be wounded in this way—not only wounded, but wholly conquered, even to the destruction of that color and heat which wages war against the soul?

9. If the daughters of this world reproach a soul of this kind, calling it pale and colorless, will it not seem fitting to you that it may answer: “Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me”? And if it remembers that it has come to this through the exhortations or rebukes of certain servants of God, who are zealous for it with God’s zeal, will it not consequently and truthfully add [Col. 0933C] that “the sons of my mother fought against me”? The sense, then, according to what has been said, will be that the Church or any earnest soul says this not as grieving or complaining, but as rejoicing, giving thanks, and even glorying that, for the name and love of Christ, it is worthy to be dark or discolored and to be called so. And it ascribes this very thing not to its own industry, but to the grace and mercy that goes before it and sends preachers to it. “For how are they to believe without one who preaches? And how are they to preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10:14–15). It mentions that the sons of its mother fought against it, not in anger, but not ungratefully.

Hence it follows: “They set me as a keeper in the vineyards.” If this phrase is examined spiritually, I think it will appear to contain nothing of complaint or [Col. 0933D] resentment, but rather to breathe something favorable. Yet before we dare put our hand to it—for the place is holy—we must first, with our customary prayers, win the favor of the Sun and then consult that Spirit who searches the deep things of God; or rather, the Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXX. How the people of the faithful, or the souls of the elect, are signified by vineyards, of which the Church is called keeper; and on the prudence of the flesh, which is death

1. “They set me as a keeper in the vineyards” (Song 1:5). Who did? Those attackers whom you mentioned just before? Hear and understand whether she does not confess that she was promoted by the very persons from whom she suffered. Yet it is no wonder if the purpose of fighting was correction. Who does not know that many people have often been assailed in a friendly and beneficial manner? How many do we daily find advancing to better things and rising to higher ones through the pious assaults of their superiors?

Let us rather show, if we can, how the sons of her mother fought against the Church both with hostile intention and to beneficial effect. For it is more pleasing when those who intend harm help against their will. The preceding interpretation embraces both senses: for there were those who were zealous for her well and those who were zealous ill, fighting with differing intentions; but both benefited her. Indeed, she glories that she profited so greatly from what she suffered from her rivals that, in exchange for the one vineyard which they seemed to have taken from her, she rejoices to have been placed over many. “This,” she says, “they accomplished for me by fighting against me and against my vineyard, they who say: ‘Empty it, empty it, even to its foundation’” (Ps. 136:7), “so that I might exchange one for many.” For this is what she adds: “I did not keep my vineyard,” as though giving the reason why this happened to her—why she was set as keeper not now over one vineyard, but over many. And this is the literal sense.

2. But if we follow it simply, content with only what seems to sound upon the surface, we shall think that in Holy Scripture we are reading about those bodily and earthly vineyards which we see daily receiving from the dew of heaven [Col. 0934C] and the fatness of the earth, whence they pour forth wine in which is excess. Thus we shall seem to have drawn from such holy and divine Scripture something worthy, I do not say of the Lord’s bride, but not even suitable to any of the rest. For what connection is there between a bride and the keeping of vineyards? Even if such a connection were supposed, how could we show that the Church was ever assigned such an office? Does God have care for vineyards? But if in a spiritual sense we interpret vineyards as churches—that is, as faithful peoples—according to the prophet’s meaning when he says, “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7), perhaps it will begin to become clear to us how it is by no means unworthy of the bride to be made keeper of vineyards.

[Col. 0934D] 3. I think that in this very point a no small privilege will further appear, if someone takes diligent care to observe how greatly throughout the world she has extended her borders into vineyards of this sort from the day when she was attacked and driven out from Jerusalem by the sons of her mother, together with her first young planting—that is, the multitude of believers, who are recorded as having had one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32). This is the vineyard which she now confesses that she did not keep, yet not to her own folly. For she was not so uprooted from it in persecution that she was not planted elsewhere and entrusted to other cultivators who would render its fruits in their seasons. She certainly did not perish, but migrated; she even grew and was enlarged, as one whom the Lord has blessed.

“Lift up your eyes,” indeed, “and see whether its shadow has not covered the mountains and its branches the cedars of God; whether it has not stretched out its shoots to the sea and its offshoots to the river” [Col. 0935A] (Ps. 79:11–12). Nor is this surprising: for it is God’s building and God’s cultivation (1 Cor. 3:9). He makes it fruitful, he propagates it, he prunes and purges it so that it may bear more fruit. When would he abandon the care or labor of what his right hand planted? Certainly it is not to be neglected, since the apostles are its branches, the Lord its vine, and his Father its husbandman (John 15:2, 5, 1). It is planted in faith, sends down roots in love, is dug with the hoe of discipline, manured with the tears of penitents, watered with the words of preachers; and thus it abounds with wine in which there is joy but not excess—wine of every sweetness and no lustfulness.

This wine certainly gladdens the human heart; and it is agreed that angels drink it with joy as well. For they rejoice at the conversion and repentance of sinners, thirsting for human salvation. The tears of penitents are their wine, because in those tears are the fragrance of life, the savor of grace, the taste of pardon, the joy of reconciliation, the health of restored innocence, and the sweetness of a conscience made serene.

4. Therefore, from that one vineyard which the storm of savage persecution seemed to have destroyed, how many vineyards have sprung up and flowered again throughout the whole earth! And in all of them the bride has been set as keeper, so that she need not grieve that she did not keep the first vineyard. Take comfort, daughter Zion: if blindness has happened in part to [Col. 0935C] Israel, what do you lose? Wonder at the mystery, and do not lament the loss. Enlarge your bosom and gather in the fullness of the nations. Say to the cities of Judah: “It was necessary for the word of God to be spoken first to you; but since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts 13:46).

Moses was certainly offered by God the possibility, if he were willing to dismiss the transgressing people and expose them to divine vengeance, of becoming himself a great nation; but he refused (Exod. 32:9–13). Why? Certainly because of the excessive love by which he was firmly bound to that people, and because he did not seek what was his own but God’s honor, nor what would benefit himself but what would benefit many. Such was Moses.

5. But by a more hidden counsel I think that God reserved this gift, in accordance with its greatness, for the bride herself: that she, rather than Moses, should be sent into a great nation. For it was not fitting that the bridegroom’s friend should snatch the bride’s blessing beforehand. Therefore it was not Moses, but the new bride—to whom it is said, “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15)—who was sent into a great nation. Could she have been sent into any nation greater than the whole human race? And the whole human race readily yielded to one bearing peace and offering grace.

But grace is not like the Law. How differently the sweetness of the former and the severity of the latter present themselves to every conscience! Who could regard with equal favor one who condemns and one who consoles, one who exacts and one who pardons, one who punishes and one who embraces? Shadow and light, wrath and peace, judgment and mercy, figure and truth, rod and inheritance, bridle and kiss, will surely not be received with equal desire. Moses’ hands were heavy, as Aaron and Hur testify (Exod. 17:12); the yoke of the Law was heavy, as the apostles themselves testify when they declare it unbearable both to themselves and to their fathers (Acts 15:10); the yoke was heavy, and the reward was paltry, for the promise was earthly land.

Moses was not sent into a great nation for such things. But you, Mother Church, possessing the promise of life both now and to come, readily obtain reception from all people through a double grace: because your yoke is easy and your kingdom exalted. Driven out of one city, you are received by the whole world, because what you promise attracts so powerfully that what you impose does not frighten. Why do you still lament the loss of one vineyard, [Col. 0936B] when it has been compensated for you with such great interest? “Instead of your being abandoned and hated, with no one passing through you, I shall make you the pride of ages, a joy from generation to generation. You shall suck the milk of the nations and nurse at the breasts of kings; and you shall know that I, the Lord, am your savior and your redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob” (Isa. 60:15–16). In this way, therefore, the bride says that she has been set as keeper in the vineyards and that she did not keep her own vineyard.

6. On the occasion of this passage, I am accustomed to reproach myself because I have undertaken the care of souls when I was not sufficient to keep my own, interpreting vineyards as souls. If you also approve this interpretation of ours, see further whether we rightly say that faith is the vine, virtues the branches, [Col. 0936C] a work the cluster, and devotion the wine. For a branch is nothing without the vine, and a virtue is nothing without faith. “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6); perhaps it is even necessary to displease him. For “everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23).

Those who set me as keeper in the vineyards ought therefore to have considered whether I was keeping my own. Yet for how long it lay uncultivated and deserted, reduced to a wilderness! Its wine had entirely failed, its branches of virtue dried up through the barrenness of faith. Faith was present, but dead. How could it not be dead without works? This was so in my secular life. But after I turned to the Lord, I began, I confess, to keep it somewhat better, though not as I ought. And who, indeed, is equal to this? Not even the holy Prophet, who says: “Unless the Lord keeps the city, the watchman keeps watch in vain” (Ps. 126:1).

How many snares I remember suffering even then from him who shoots the spotless person from hidden places! How much, O my vineyard, was secretly stolen from us by his contrivances precisely at the time when we began to apply ourselves more vigilantly to our care and keeping! How many and what clusters of devout works were either choked by anger, carried away by boastfulness, or defiled by vain glory! How much we endured from the enticement of gluttony, from the spirit of sloth, from faintness of spirit and storm! Such was I; and nevertheless they set me as keeper in the vineyards, not considering what I was doing or had done with my own, nor listening to [Col. 0937A] the reproving teacher saying: “If anyone does not know how to govern his own house, how will he have care for the Church of God?” (1 Tim. 3:5).

7. I marvel at the audacity of many whom we see gathering from their own vineyards nothing but thorns and briars, yet who do not fear to thrust themselves into the Lord’s vineyards. They are thieves and robbers, not keepers or cultivators. So much for them. But woe is me even now because of the danger to my vineyard! Indeed, more now, when, attending to many vineyards, I am compelled to become less diligent and less solicitous about the one. I am unable to set a hedge around it or dig a winepress in it. Alas! “Its hedge has been broken down, and all who pass along the road plunder it” (Ps. 79:13). It lies open and exposed to sadness, anger, and impatience.

Certain busy little foxes of pressing necessities demolish [Col. 0937B] it; anxieties, suspicions, and cares break in from every side; the uproar of those who disagree and the burdens of lawsuits are seldom absent even for an hour. I have no power to prevent them, no means of avoiding them, not even time for prayer. With what shower of tears shall I sufficiently moisten the barrenness of my soul? (Ps. 34:12). I meant to say “my vineyard,” but the phrase came from the Psalm through habit, and the meaning is the same. Nor do I regret the error that reminds us of the comparison, because the discourse is not about a vineyard but about the soul. Therefore let the soul be understood whenever a vineyard is read; for under the image and name of the former, the barrenness of the latter is lamented.

With what tears, then, shall I water the barrenness of my vineyard? All its branches have dried up from lack; they lie fruitless because they have no moisture. Good Jesus, what bundles of twigs from them does the fire of my contrite heart consume in your daily sacrifice, you being witness? Let, I beseech you, a crushed spirit be a sacrifice to you; “a contrite and humbled heart, O God, do not despise” (Ps. 50:19).

8. Thus I draw this present passage to myself because of my own imperfection. But everyone will be perfect who can say in another sense, “I did not keep my vineyard,” namely in the sense in which the Savior says in the Gospel: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it” (Matt. 10:39). He is plainly fit and worthy to be set as keeper in vineyards whose care for his own vineyard does not hinder or delay diligence and solicitude for those entrusted to him, because he does not seek what is his own [Col. 0937D] or what benefits himself, but what benefits many.

For this reason that care was entrusted to Peter over so many vineyards among the circumcised: he was a man prepared to go both to prison and to death (Luke 22:33), so little held back by love for his own vineyard—that is, his own soul—that it did not prevent him from attending to the care of those entrusted to him. Likewise, among the Gentiles so vast a forest of vineyards was entrusted to Paul because he too was found by no means over-concerned with keeping his own vineyard; so much so that he was prepared not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 21:13). Finally, he says: “I fear none of these things, nor do I make my soul more precious [Col. 0938A] than myself” (Acts 20:24). An excellent appraiser of things, who judges that none of his possessions is to be preferred to himself.

9. How many have preferred a small and most worthless sum of money to their own salvation! Paul did not even prefer his soul. “I do not,” he says, “make it more precious than myself.” Do you then make a distinction between yourself and your soul? Wisely indeed you value yourself more highly than anything belonging to you. But how is your soul not you?

I think that, because Paul already walked then in the spirit and consented in his mind to the law of God because it is good (Rom. 7:16), he judged this very mind of his, as the principal and highest part of himself, worthy to be designated rather by the name of himself than by the name of any possession of his. The remainder, however—namely, the soul, which is evidently of an inferior nature and therefore of a lower and less worthy essence, because it adheres to the body not only in the office of giving it life and sensation but also in the desire to cherish and nourish it—the spiritual man judged sensory and carnal, unworthy of being called “himself,” and reckoned it rather among his possessions than as that by which he personally expressed himself.

“When I say ‘I,’” he says, “understand the higher thing that is in me, in which I stand through God’s grace: that is, my mind and reason. When I speak of ‘my soul,’ understand the lower thing which you see fitted to animate the flesh and even joined to it in concupiscence. I recognize that this indeed was myself, but that I am so no longer, because I no longer walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit” (Rom. 8:4). “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). According to the mind I am myself; according to the flesh I am not myself.

What if the soul even now desires carnally? “It is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Rom. 7:17). Therefore I would call that which has a carnal savor in me not myself, but nevertheless mine; and it is nothing other than the soul itself. For the carnal affection of the soul and the life which it administers to the body are truly a portion of the soul. Paul therefore despised this soul of his in comparison with himself, prepared for the Lord not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem, and thus to lose his soul according to the Lord’s counsel.

10. You too, if you abandon your own will, if you wholly renounce the pleasures of the body, if you crucify your flesh with its vices and desires, [Col. 0938D] and also put to death your members which are upon the earth, will prove yourself an imitator of Paul: you will not make your soul more precious than yourself. You will prove yourself also a disciple of Christ, by even losing it in a saving manner. Indeed, you lose it more wisely in order to keep it than you keep it in order to lose it. For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it (Matt. 16:25). What do you say to this, you observers of foods and neglecters of morals? [Note: [Col. 0937D] See notes on Epistle 345, note 910.] Hippocrates and his followers teach men to save their souls in this world; Christ and his disciples, to lose them. Which master of the two do you choose to follow? He who argues thus plainly shows himself: “This harms the eyes, this the head, and that the chest [Col. 0939A] or stomach.” Surely each person brings forward what he learned from his own master. Have you read these distinctions in the Gospel, or in the prophets, or in the writings of the apostles? Flesh and blood, certainly, revealed this wisdom to you, not the Spirit of the Father; for this is wisdom of the flesh. But hear what our physicians think of it. “The wisdom,” they say, “of the flesh is death”; likewise: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God” (Rom. 8:6–7). Ought I to have set before you the opinion of Hippocrates or Galen, or indeed something from the school of Epicurus? I am a disciple of Christ; I speak to Christ’s disciples. If I introduce an alien doctrine, I myself have sinned. Epicurus prefers bodily pleasure, Hippocrates bodily soundness; my Master proclaims contempt for both. [Col. 0939B] The latter anxiously investigates what will sustain the soul’s life in the body, the former what will also delight it; the Savior urges that it be lost.

11. For what else has sounded in your ears from Christ’s teaching, when a little earlier there was the cry: “He who loves his soul will lose it” (John 12:25)? He said, “will lose it,” whether by laying it down as a martyr or by afflicting it as a penitent. Yet it is a kind of martyrdom to put to death, by the spirit, the deeds of the flesh: milder in horror than that in which limbs are cut by the sword, but more burdensome in its duration. Do you see how, by this saying of my Master, the wisdom of the flesh is condemned—the wisdom by which one either dissolves into indulgence in pleasure, or seeks even bodily health itself beyond what is fitting? Finally, that true wisdom does not dissolve into pleasures you have surely heard from the Wise Man: it is not even found in the land of those who live pleasantly (Job 23:13). But he who found it says: “I loved wisdom above health and all beauty” (Wis. 7:10). If above health and beauty, how much more above pleasure and ugliness? Yet what is the good of refraining from pleasures while spending one’s daily care in investigating the various bodily constitutions and searching out varieties of foods? “Legumes,” he says, “cause wind; cheese weighs down the stomach; milk harms the head; the chest cannot bear water as a drink; cabbages nourish melancholy; leeks inflame bile; fish from a pond or muddy water do not at all suit my constitution.” What kind of thing is this—that in [Col. 0939D] all the rivers, fields, gardens, and storehouses one can scarcely find something for you to eat?

12. Consider yourself, I beg you, a monk, not a physician; one who must judge not of bodily constitution but of profession. Spare, I beseech you, first your own peace; then spare the labor of those who serve; spare the burden upon the household; spare consciences. I mean not your own conscience, but another’s: namely, that of the man sitting nearby and eating what is set before him, who murmurs at your exceptional fast. For either your hateful superstition is a scandal to him, or the harshness which he perhaps attributes to the man responsible for providing for you. Your singularity, I say, offends the brother who judges you superstitious, as one [Col. 0940A] seeking superfluities; or else he blames me as harsh because I do not search out necessities for your diet. Certain persons vainly flatter themselves with Paul’s example, when he urges his disciple not to drink water but to use a little wine because of his stomach and his frequent infirmities (1 Tim. 5:23). Such persons ought first to observe that the Apostle was by no means recommending such a thing to himself, nor was the disciple demanding it for himself. Secondly, this was not said to a monk, but to a bishop, whose life was most necessary to the still tender and nascent Church. This was Timothy. Give me another Timothy, and I will feed him, if you wish, even with gold, and give him balsam to drink. But you are your own steward, taking pity on yourself. I confess that your stewardship of yourself is suspect to me; and I fear that the prudence of the flesh is deceiving you under [Col. 0940B] the cover and name of discernment. At least I want you to be warned of this: if the Apostle’s authority concerning drinking wine pleases you so much, do not omit the word “little,” which he added. Enough on this point. But let us return to the bride, and learn from her that it is useful for her not to keep her own vineyards [Note: [Col. 0939] That is, for her own benefit. Thus the older manuscripts and first printed editions; Horstius and others read: “for us usefully to keep our own [vineyards].”], especially we who appear to have been appointed guardians in the vineyards of the Bridegroom, the Church of Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXI. On the excellence of the divine vision; and how, in the present life, saints’ experience of the divine presence varies according to the varied desires of the soul.

1. “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed, [Col. 0940C] where you rest at midday” (Song 1:6). The Word, the Bridegroom, frequently appears to eager minds, and not under one form. Why is this? Certainly because he is not yet seen as he is. For that vision is fixed, because the form then seen is fixed; for it is, and admits no change from what it was or will be. Remove, indeed, “was” and “will be”: whence then can come change or the shadow of alteration? But whatever, coming from what “was,” does not cease to tend toward what “will be,” has indeed a passage through “is,” but is not truly at all. For how can that be which never remains in the same state? Therefore that alone truly is which is neither cut off from “was” nor blotted out by “will be”; but “is” alone remains to it, invincible, and it remains what it is. Nor does “was” take from it eternal being, nor does “will be” [Col. 0940D] take from it everlasting being; and by this it claims true being—that is, uncreated, without end, unchangeable. Therefore, when he who thus is—rather, who does not exist “thus” or “so,” but simply is—is seen as he is, that vision, as I have said, is fixed, because no alteration interrupts it. Then the single denarius of the Gospel is paid to all who see thus (Matt. 20:9), in the one form presented. For what appears, as it is unchangeable in itself, is also unchangeably present to those who behold it; and those to whom it appears desire to see nothing more desirable, and can find delight in nothing more delightful. When, then, will that eagerness grow weary, or that sweetness withdraw itself, or truth deceive, or eternity fail? But if both the power of seeing and the will to see extend into eternity, [Col. 0941A] how can happiness not be complete? For nothing is lacking to those who always see, and nothing remains beyond the desire of those who always will.

2. But such a vision does not belong to the present life; it is reserved for the last things, for those alone who can say: “We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Even now, indeed, he appears to whom he wills; but as he wills, not as he is. No wise man, saint, or prophet can—or could—see him as he is in this mortal body [Note: [Col. 0941D] Compare what Bernard says of St Benedict in Sermon 9 on Various Subjects, and below concerning Moses, [Col. 0942D] in Sermon 33 on the Song of Songs, no. 6, and Sermon 34, no. 1.]; but he will be able to do so in an immortal body, if found worthy. Thus he is seen here also, but as he is seen by the beholder, not as he is in himself. For you have never seen even this great luminary—I mean the sun which you see every day—as it is; you see it only as it illuminates, for example, the air, a mountain, or a wall. Nor could you even do this in any degree unless the light of your bodily eye, by its innate clearness and transparency, were in some respect like the heavenly light. No other bodily member is capable of light, because of its great dissimilarity. Nor, indeed, can the eye itself approach the light when it is clouded, because it has lost its likeness to it. Therefore, the clouded eye sees the clear sun not at all because of dissimilarity; the clear eye sees it in some degree because of a certain likeness. Certainly, if it possessed precisely equal purity, it would see it with unobstructed sight as it is, because of complete likeness. So too one illuminated can see in this world the Sun of righteousness, who enlightens every person coming into [Col. 0941C] this world, as he enlightens—being already in some degree like him; but cannot at all see him as he is, since he is not yet perfectly like him. Therefore he says: “Draw near to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded” (Ps. 33:6 [34:5]). Yes, provided that we are enlightened sufficiently, so that, with unveiled face beholding the glory of God as in a mirror, we may be transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18).

3. Therefore we must draw near to him, not rush upon him, lest an irreverent searcher of majesty be overwhelmed by glory (Prov. 25:27). We must draw near not by places but by brightnesses; and those not bodily but spiritual, as by the Spirit of the Lord. Truly by the Lord’s Spirit, and [Col. 0941D] not by our own, although it is in us. Thus the brighter one is, the nearer one is; and to be most bright is to have arrived. Moreover, for those already present, to see as he is is nothing other than to be as he is, and not to be obscured by any dissimilarity. But this, as I said, belongs to that time. Meanwhile, what are this great variety of forms and multitude of appearances in created things but rays, as it were, of the Godhead, showing indeed that he from whom they are truly exists, yet not fully defining what he is? Thus you see something concerning him, but not him himself. Yet when you see other things from him whom you do not see, you know beyond doubt that he exists, whom you ought to seek, so that grace may not disappoint one who seeks, nor ignorance excuse one who neglects to seek. But this kind of seeing is common. For, according to the Apostle, it is readily available to everyone who uses reason: to behold the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made (Rom. 1:20).

4.
