Undoubtedly another mode is that by which, formerly, that frequent and abundant familiarity of the divine presence was graciously granted to the Fathers—though not even to them as he is, but as he deigned to be. Nor was it in one way to all; rather, as the Apostle says, “in many portions and in many ways” (Heb. 1:1), although he is one in himself, according to his own saying to Israel: “The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). This manifestation was not common, but it was still external: it was displayed through images appearing outwardly [Col. 0942B] or through sounding voices. But there is a divine beholding, differing from these precisely because it is more inward: God himself deigns to visit the soul that seeks him, provided that it has devoted its whole self to seeking through desire and love. And the sign of such a coming, as we are taught by one who experienced it, is this: “Fire shall go before him, and shall burn up his enemies round about” (Ps. 96:3 [97:3]). For the ardor of holy desire must precede his face in every soul to which he is about to come, so that it may consume all the rust of vices and thus prepare a place for the Lord. Then the soul knows that the Lord is near when it feels itself kindled by that fire and says with the prophet: “From on high he sent fire into my bones, and instructed me” (Lam. 1:13); and again: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire shall blaze” [Col. 0942C] (Ps. 38:4 [39:3]).

5. When, to a soul that sighs in this way, prays frequently—indeed, without ceasing—and afflicts itself with desire, that Desired One whom it seeks so earnestly sometimes comes compassionately to meet it, I think it may fittingly say from its own experience with holy Jeremiah: “You are good, O Lord, to those who hope in you, to the soul that seeks you” (Lam. 3:25). And his angel, one of the Bridegroom’s companions, appointed for this very task—the minister and mediator, certainly, of this secret mutual greeting—how does that angel rejoice, how does he exult and share in the delight! Turning to the Lord, he says: “I give you thanks, Lord of majesty, because you have granted her the desire of her heart and have not disappointed her of the will of her lips!” [Col. 0942D] He is the one who, everywhere a diligent attendant of the soul, does not cease to spur her on and to admonish her by continual promptings, saying: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart”; and again: “Wait for the Lord and keep his way” (Ps. 36:4, 34 [37:4, 34]); likewise: “If he delays, wait for him, because he will surely come and will not be late” (Hab. 2:3). But to the Lord he says: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so this soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. 41:2 [42:1]). “She has desired you in the night, and also your spirit within her has watched for you in the morning” (Isa. 26:9). And again: [Col. 0943A] “All day she has stretched out her hands to you” (Ps. 87:10 [88:9]); “dismiss her, for she cries after you” (Matt. 15:23); “turn again a little, and be entreated concerning her” (Ps. 89:13 [90:13]). Look down from heaven, see, and visit the desolate one. A faithful friend of the Bridegroom, conscious of their mutual love but not envious, seeking not his own interest but the Lord’s favor, he runs back and forth between beloved and beloved, offering prayers and bringing back gifts. He stirs up the one and appeases the other. Sometimes also, though rarely, he presents them together to each other, either snatching up the soul or bringing down the Lord; for he is a member of the household and known in the palace, and does not fear rejection, since he daily sees the Father’s face.

6. But take care not to suppose that in this union of the Word and the soul we mean anything bodily or imaginary. We say what the Apostle says: “He who is joined to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). The ecstasy of a pure mind into God, or God’s gracious descent [Col. 0943B] into the soul, we express in whatever words we can, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. Therefore this union takes place in the spirit, because God is spirit; and he desires the beauty of that soul which he finds walking in the spirit and making no provision for the flesh in its desires, especially if he sees it burning with love for himself. Therefore a soul so disposed and so beloved will not be satisfied merely with the manifestation of the Bridegroom which is made to many through created things, or that which is made to few through visions and dreams, unless, by a special prerogative, it receives him entering from heaven into its inmost affections and the very marrow of the heart [Col. 0943C] and has present the one it desires—not figured but infused, not appearing but affecting; and, without doubt, the more delightful because he is within rather than without. For the Word does not merely sound but penetrates; he is not wordy but effective; he does not clamour in the ears but gently wins the affections. His face is not formed but forming; it does not strike the bodily eyes but makes glad the face of the heart: pleasing, indeed, through love’s gift, not through color.

7. Yet I would not say that he even then appears as he is, although in this manner he displays nothing entirely different from what he is. For he will not be continuously present even to the most devout minds, nor uniformly present to all. Rather, according to the various desires of souls, the experience of the divine presence must vary, and the infused savor of heavenly sweetness must delight the palate of the desiring mind in different ways. For you have observed in this song of love how often he changes his countenance, and in how great a multitude of his sweetness he has deigned to transform himself before his beloved; how now, indeed, like a modest bridegroom, he seeks the secret embraces of the holy soul and delights in kisses; but now appears as a physician in oil and ointments, undoubtedly because tender and weak souls still need such fomentations and medicines. Hence they are designated by the delicate name of maidens. Should anyone murmur, he will hear that “those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12). Again, [Col. 0944A] at times, like some traveller, joining the bride and the maidens as they journey, he relieves the whole company from the toil of the road by his most delightful conversation, so that when he departs they say: “Was not our heart burning within us while Jesus spoke to us on the way?” (Luke 24:32). An eloquent companion, who by the sweetness of his speech and character, as by the fragrance of sweet-smelling ointments, makes all run after him; hence they say: “We will run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3). At another time he meets them as a very wealthy householder, who has abundance of bread in his house; or rather as a magnificent and powerful king, who seems to raise the faint-heartedness of his poor bride and awaken her desire, showing her every desirable thing of his glory—the riches of presses and storehouses, the abundance of gardens and fields—and finally even bringing her into the secrets of the chamber itself. Surely her husband’s heart trusts in her, and there is nothing that he thinks should be hidden from her whom he redeemed while poor, proved faithful, and embraces as beloved. Thus, by this or that inward mode, he does not cease continually to appear to the sight of those who seek him, so that the saying may be fulfilled which he uttered: “Behold, I am with you unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

8. In all these things he is sweet, gentle, and abundant in mercy. In kisses, indeed, he is affectionate and tender; in oil, spices, and ointments, merciful and overflowing with the bowels of pity and compassion; on the road, cheerful, approachable, [Col. 0944C] full of grace and consolation; but in the display of riches and possessions, he shows himself munificent and generous, a rewarder in royal liberality. Thus throughout the whole course of this song you will find the Word portrayed by such likenesses. This, I think, is what is signified in the prophet where he says: “Christ the Lord, the spirit before our face; in his shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lam. 4:20). That is, we now see through a mirror and in an enigma, and not yet face to face. This is so, indeed, while we live among the nations; among the angels it is otherwise. For then we too, in happiness wholly undifferentiated from theirs, shall see him as he is—in the form of God, not in a shadow. For just as we say that among those of old there existed shadow and figure, while for us the truth itself shines forth through the grace of Christ present in the flesh, so no one will deny, in relation to the age to come, that we now live meanwhile in a certain shadow of truth—unless he refuses assent to the Apostle’s saying: “We know in part and prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13:9), and: “I do not reckon that I have apprehended” (Phil. 3:13). For how can there not be a distinction between one who walks by faith and one who walks by sight? Therefore the righteous person lives by faith (Hab. 2:4); the blessed exults in sight. Thus the holy human being lives meanwhile in Christ’s shadow, while the holy angel glories in the radiance of the face of glory.

9. The shadow of faith is good: it tempers light for the dim eye and prepares the eye for light. For it is written: [Col. 0945A] “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). Faith, therefore, does not extinguish light but preserves it. Whatever it is that the angel sees, the shadow of faith keeps it for me, laid up in its faithful bosom to be revealed in due time. Is it not beneficial to hold, though veiled, what you cannot grasp unveiled? Finally, the Mother of the Lord also lived in faith’s shadow, she to whom it was said: “Blessed are you who believed.” She also had a shadow from Christ’s body, she who heard: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35, 45). Nor is the shadow lowly that is formed from the power of the Most High. Truly it was power in Christ’s flesh, which overshadowed the Virgin, so that what was impossible for a mortal woman, she might nevertheless, by the interposition of the covering of the life-giving body, bear the presence of majesty and endure inaccessible light. It was power indeed, in which every opposing force was defeated; power and shadow driving away demons and protecting human beings; or rather, power giving life and shadow giving refreshment.

10. Therefore we who walk by faith live in Christ’s shadow, and feed upon his flesh in order to live. For Christ’s flesh is truly food (John 6:56). And see whether this is why he is here described as appearing in a pastoral figure, where the bride seems to address him as one among the shepherds, saying: “Tell me where you feed, where you rest at midday.” The good Shepherd gives his soul for his sheep (John 10:11): his soul for them, his flesh to them—the one as a price, the other as food. A wonderful thing! He himself is shepherd, he himself is pasture, he himself is redemption. But the discourse runs to length, because the passage is ample and contains great things, and cannot be unfolded in a few words. Therefore necessity seems to me to require that it be broken off rather than concluded. Yet, since the matter remains pending, memory must stay awake, so that where we pause, there we may soon resume and examine it, as the Lord shall grant: Jesus Christ, Bridegroom of the Church, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII. How Christ is received by the holy soul as bridegroom, and by the weak soul as physician. Also, on the distinction of thoughts and the sources from which they arise.

1. “Tell me where you feed, where you rest at midday” (Song 1:6). Here we are; from here we proceed. But [Col. 0945D] before this vision and address begins to be discussed, I think we should briefly recapitulate the other visions which preceded it, and how they may be spiritually applied to us according to the desires and merits of individuals. If we grasp these, should this nevertheless be granted, understanding may shine forth more easily in the examination of this vision also. But this is very difficult. For although the words by which those visions or likenesses themselves are described seem to sound of bodies and bodily things, the things ministered to us through them are spiritual; and therefore their causes and meanings must also be sought in the spirit. And who is adequate to investigate and comprehend [Col. 0946A] so many dispositions and advances of the soul, according to which this grace, so manifold in the Bridegroom’s presence, is dispensed? Yet if we enter into ourselves, and if the Holy Spirit in his light deigns to show us what he does not disdain continually to work in us through his own operation, I think we shall not remain entirely without understanding in these matters. For I trust that we have received not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God (1 Cor. 2:12).

2. Therefore, if it is good for any of us, with the holy Prophet, to cleave to God (Ps. 72:28 [73:28]), and, to speak more plainly, if anyone among us is so much a man of desire that he longs to be dissolved and to be with Christ—longs vehemently, thirsts ardently, and meditates continually—then surely he will receive the Word in the form of a bridegroom at the time of visitation: namely, at the hour when he feels himself inwardly bound by certain arms of wisdom and thereby receives the sweetness of holy love poured into him. For the desire of his heart will be granted him, even though he is still a pilgrim in the body, yet only in part, for a time, and a short time. For when the One sought by vigils, prayers, much labour [Note: [Col. 0945D] “Labour” is absent from certain manuscripts.], and a rain of tears has come, he suddenly slips away just when he is thought to be held. Then, coming again to meet the weeping and pursuing soul, he allows himself to be grasped but by no means held, since he suddenly slips once more, as it were, from its hands. If the devout soul persists in prayers and tears, he will return again and will not disappoint it of the will of its lips; but [Col. 0946C] he will soon disappear again and will not be seen unless he is sought once more with the whole desire of the heart. Thus even in this body there can be frequent joy from the Bridegroom’s presence, but not abundance; for visitation brings joy, but alternation causes distress. The beloved must suffer this until, once the burden of bodily weight has been laid down, she too flies away, lifted on the wings of her desires, freely making her way through the fields of contemplation and following with an unencumbered mind the Beloved wherever he goes.

3. Yet even on this journey he will not be present to every soul in this manner, but only to one whom great devotion, vehement longing, and a most sweet affection prove to be a bride and worthy of receiving the Word, who assumes the Bridegroom’s form when he comes by the grace of visitation. But one who is not yet found so disposed, who is rather pierced by the remembrance of his deeds and says to God in the bitterness of his soul, “Do not condemn me” (Job 10:2), or who perhaps is still dangerously tempted, drawn away and enticed by his own desire—such a person does not seek a bridegroom but a physician. Accordingly, he will receive not kisses or embraces but only remedies for his wounds, in oil and ointments. Do we not often feel and experience this in prayer—we who are still tempted by our present daily transgressions and bitten by those of the past? From what bitterness have you often delivered me when you came, good Jesus? How often, after anxious tears, unutterable groans, and sobs, have you anointed my wounded conscience with the ointment of your mercy and poured over me the oil of joy? How often has prayer, which received me almost despairing, restored me exultant and confident of forgiveness? Those who are affected similarly know that the Lord Jesus is truly a physician, who heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds (Ps. 146:3 [147:3]). Those who have not experienced it should believe him when he says: “The Spirit of the Lord has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted” (Isa. 61:2; Luke 4:17, 21). If they still doubt, let them approach and taste, and thus learn in themselves what this means: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Matt. 9:13). But let us consider the rest as well.

4. There are people who, worn out in spiritual pursuits, become lukewarm and sink into a certain weakness of spirit. They walk sadly in the ways of the Lord; with hearts dry and weary they undertake whatever has been commanded them; they murmur often, complain of long days and long nights, saying with holy Job: “When I lie down, I say, ‘When shall I arise?’ And again I wait for evening” (Job 7:4). Therefore, when it happens that we suffer something of this kind, if the Lord in mercy draws near to us on the way in which we walk and begins to speak from heaven, he who is from heaven, and also to sing us some gracious thing from the songs of Zion—to tell us of the city of God, the peace of the city, the eternity of peace, [Col. 0947C] and the condition of eternity—I tell you that this joyful account will be like a conveyance for the sleeping and sluggish soul: it will drive all weariness from the hearer’s mind and fatigue from the body. Does he seem to you either to suffer or to seek anything else who says: “My soul has slumbered because of weariness; strengthen me by your words”? And when he receives this, will he not cry: “How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all day” (Ps. 118:97, 28 [119:97, 28])? For certain words of the Word, the Bridegroom, to us are our meditations concerning him and his glory, beauty, power, and majesty. And not only this: when with eager mind we ponder his testimonies and the judgments of his mouth, and meditate upon his law day and night, let us know with certainty that the Bridegroom is present and speaking to us, so that, delighted by his words, we may not grow weary in our labors.

5. Therefore, when you feel thoughts of this kind turning in your mind, do not think them your own thought; recognize instead that he is speaking who says in the prophet: “I am he who speaks righteousness” (Isa. 63:1). For the thoughts of our mind are very like the words of Truth speaking within us; and no one readily discerns what his own heart inwardly produces and what it hears, unless he wisely attends to the Lord speaking in the Gospel: “Evil thoughts come forth from the heart” (Matt. 15:19); and: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4); and: “He who speaks a lie speaks from his own” (John 8:44). But the Apostle says: “Not that we are sufficient,” he says, “to think anything from [Col. 0948A] ourselves as from ourselves”—understand, anything good—“but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5). Therefore, when we entertain evil in the heart, it is our own thought; if it is good, it is God’s word. The former our heart speaks; the latter it hears. “I will hear,” he says, “what the Lord God will speak in me, for he will speak peace to his people” (Ps. 84:9 [85:8]). Thus God speaks peace, mercy, and righteousness in us; we do not think such things from ourselves but hear them within us. But murders, adulteries, thefts, blasphemies, and things like these come forth from the heart (Matt. 15:19): we do not hear them but speak them. Finally, “the fool said in his heart: ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13:1 [14:1]). And therefore the wicked man provoked God, because he said in his heart: “He will not require it” (Ps. 9:13 [10:13]). But there is, besides, something felt in the heart which is not nevertheless the heart’s word. For it does not come forth from the heart as our own thought does, yet neither is it what we said is made to the heart—the word, namely, of the Word—since it is evil. Rather, it is sent in by hostile powers, as incursions are made through evil angels; such, for example, was that which we read the devil put into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray the Lord (John 13:2).

6. But who is such a wakeful and diligent observer of his inward movements, whether occurring within him or originating from himself, that he can clearly distinguish, in each unlawful impression felt in his heart, between a disease of the mind and the serpent’s bite? I think this impossible for any mortal person unless, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, he has received that special gift which the Apostle, among the other charisms he enumerates, calls the discernment of spirits (1 Cor. 12:10). However much a person may, according to Solomon, guard his heart with all vigilance (Prov. 4:23), and observe with most watchful attention all that moves within him—even if he has perhaps had long practice in these things and frequent experience—he still cannot perfectly recognize or distinguish from one another the evil native to him and evil sown in him. “For who understands transgressions?” Nor does it matter greatly for us to know whence evil is present in us, provided that we know it is present. Rather, we must watch and pray, whatever its source, lest we consent to it. Finally, the prophet prays against both evils, saying: “Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from alien ones” (Ps. 18:13–14 [19:12–13]). And I cannot give you what I have not received. I have not received, I confess, the means of assigning a certain criterion between what the heart brings forth and the enemy’s seedbed. For both are evil, both are from evil; both are in the heart, but not both are from the heart. This much is certain to me concerning myself, though I am uncertain what to attribute to the heart and what to the enemy. And this, as I have said, is without danger.

7. But there is a case in which error is dangerous—indeed, damnable—and there rightly a sure rule is prescribed for us: that we do not give to ourselves what is God’s in us, supposing the visitation of the Word to be our own thought. Therefore, as far as good differs from evil, so far do these two differ from each other: for evil cannot come from the Word, nor can good come from the heart, unless perhaps it has first conceived it from the Word. For a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit (Matt. 7:18). But I think enough has been said concerning what in our heart is God’s and what is ours; and not superfluously, in my judgment, so that the enemies of grace [Note: [Col. 0949D] He seems, I think, to mean Abelard, who almost reduced the grace of Christ to reason and example, as was stated in volume III, Opuscule XI.] may know that without grace the human heart is not sufficient even to think what is good, but that its sufficiency is from God; and that the good which is thought is God’s voice, not the offspring of the heart. Therefore, if you hear his voice, do not now fail to know whence it comes or where it goes: knowing that it goes out from God and goes to the heart. See, moreover, how the word that goes forth from God’s mouth does not return to him empty, but prospers and accomplishes all that for which he sent it, so that you too may say: “The grace of God in me was not empty” (1 Cor. 15:10). Happy is the mind to which the Word, an inseparable companion, everywhere shows himself gracious, and which, continually delighted by the sweetness of his eloquence, frees itself at every hour from the burdens and vices of the flesh, redeeming the time from evil days (Eph. 5:16). It will not grow weary or be distressed, because, as Scripture says: “Whatever happens to him will not grieve the righteous person” (Prov. 12:21).

8. But now I think that the pattern of the great Householder, or of royal majesty, is apparent to those who, approaching [variant: ascending] the lofty heart, have become more magnanimous through greater liberty of spirit and purity of conscience. They are accustomed to dare greater things, being altogether restless and eager to penetrate more secret matters, grasp loftier things, and attempt more perfect things—not only of the senses, but also of the virtues. For, because of the greatness of their faith, they are found worthy to be led into all fullness; nor is there, in all the storehouses of wisdom, anything from which God, the Lord of knowledge, judges that those who desire truth and are unaware of vanity should be excluded. Such was Moses, who dared to say to God: “If I have found favor in your eyes, show me yourself” (Exod. 33:13, 18). Such was Philip, who demanded that the Father be shown to himself and his fellow disciples (John 14:8); and such also Thomas, who refused to believe unless he touched with his own hand the wound and the pierced side (John 20:25). His faith was small, but in a wonderful way it proceeded from greatness of spirit.

> [Note: Col. 0949D] How can it proceed from greatness of spirit if it proceeds from smallness of faith? Yet in this statement of the apostle Thomas, St Bernard distinguishes two things: first, that he declined to believe, in which there was a defect of faith; second, the condition without which he refused to believe—namely, unless he saw the scars of the wounds. Since this is something great, it pertains to greatness of spirit, whose characteristic is to dare great things. Bernard’s interpretation is especially supported by Sermon 162 in the Appendix to the Works of St Augustine [Col. 0950D], where one reads:
>
> “Although a man of little faith, although a Christian of weak understanding, could never have equalled his concern with Thomas’s inquiry. For after recognizing him, associating with him, and hearing him speak, he would never have dared to request that he might investigate Christ by touch as well; that, in the very man whom he saw, he might examine the body of a man; and that he might believe in his resurrection not so much because of the glory of miraculous works as because it was proved by the injury of his passion,” etc.
>
> Thus it is there. See the same thought in William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, *On the Contemplation of God*, book I, chapter 1, no. 3, here.

Such also was David, who himself said to God: “My heart has said to you: My face has sought you; your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. 26:8). Therefore such people dare great things because they are great; and what they dare, they obtain, according to the word of promise made to them: “Every place upon which your foot shall tread shall be yours” (Deut. 11:24). For great faith merits great things; and as far as you extend the foot of confidence into the Lord’s good gifts, so far will you possess.

9. Finally, God speaks to Moses mouth to mouth; and Moses merits to see the Lord openly, not through riddles and figures, whereas God says that he appears to other prophets only in a vision and speaks through a dream (Num. 12:6–8). The Father too was shown to Philip, according to his heart’s request, in the Son—undoubtedly in that he immediately heard: “Philip, he who sees me sees the Father”; and, “Because I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:9–10). To Thomas also, according to the desire of his heart, he offered himself to be touched (John 20:27), and did not defraud him of the desire of his lips. What of David? Does he not likewise indicate that he was not wholly disappointed of his vow, when he says that he will not give sleep to his eyes nor slumber to his eyelids until he finds a place for the Lord? (Ps. 131:4–5).

Therefore the Bridegroom will meet such great spirits in a great manner, and will do great things with them, sending forth his light and his truth, leading and bringing them to his holy mountain and to his tabernacles, so that one such as this may say: “He who is mighty has done great things for me” (Luke 1:49). His eyes shall see the King in his beauty (Isa. 33:17), going before them to the lovely places of the wilderness, to flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys, to the pleasantness of gardens, the waters of springs, the delights of wine-cellars, and the fragrances of spices; finally, to the very secrets of the bridal chamber.

10. These are the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden with the Bridegroom; these are the pastures of life prepared for the refreshment of holy souls. Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire from them. Let him only be warned not to wish to possess alone what can suffice for many. For perhaps this is why, after all these things, the Bridegroom is described as appearing like a shepherd: so that the recipient of such great gifts may thereby be admonished to feed the flock of simpler persons, who are as unable to grasp these things by themselves as sheep dare not go out into pasture without a shepherd.

Indeed, the bride, wisely observing this very point, asks to be told where he feeds and rests beneath the noonday heat, prepared—as may be understood from this—to be fed and to feed with him and under him. For she does not think it safe to keep the flock far from the chief Shepherd, especially because of the attacks of wolves—above all, those who come to us in sheep’s clothing. Therefore she strives to pasture in the same fields with him and to rest in the shade. And she gives the reason: “Lest,” she says, “I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.” These are those who wish to seem friends of the Bridegroom, but are not; and although their concern is to feed their own flocks, not his, they nevertheless lie in wait on every side and say: “Behold, here is Christ; behold, there he is” (Mark 13:21), so as to deceive many, lead them away from Christ’s flocks, and join them to their own.

This is according to the literal sense of the text. But await, under another opening of discourse, the spiritual sense hidden in it—whatever it may be which, through your prayers, the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, may deign in his mercy to impart to me for you: he who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIII. On the Things a Devout Mind Must Always Pursue; What Noon Is; and the Four Kinds of Temptation Always to Be Avoided

1. “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you rest at noon” (Song 1:6). Another says: “Tell me why you judge me thus” (Job 10:2). He does not indeed complain of the judgment, but investigates its cause, seeking to be instructed by scourges, not delivered from them. Another likewise prays, saying: “Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths” (Ps. 24:4). Elsewhere he makes clear what ways or paths he means: “He has led me,” he says, “upon the paths of righteousness” (Ps. 22:3).

Thus the inquiring soul never ceases to seek three things from God: righteousness, judgment, and the place where the Bridegroom’s glory dwells—namely, a way in which it may walk, a safeguard by which it may walk, and the dwelling toward which it may walk. Of that dwelling the prophet says: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this shall I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4); and again: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. 25:8). Concerning the other two, he says: “Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne” (Ps. 88:15).

A devout mind rightly seeks these three things: God’s throne and the preparation of that throne. And all of them beautifully converge in the bride’s prerogative for the perfection of the virtues: that she may be beautiful through the form of righteousness, cautious through knowledge of judgments, and chaste through desire for the Bridegroom’s presence or glory. Such indeed ought the bride of the Lord to be: beautiful, instructed, and chaste. The petition which I placed last belongs to the present passage. For she asks him whom her soul loves to show her where he feeds and where he rests at noon.

2. First observe how elegantly she distinguishes the love of the spirit from carnal affection. Wishing to designate her beloved more by affection itself than by name, she does not simply say, “Whom I love,” but: “O you whom my soul loves,” thereby indicating spiritual love. Then attend carefully to what delights her so greatly in the place of pasture. Nor should you pass over the mention of the noonday hour, or the fact that she particularly asks concerning the place where he who feeds also rests: this is a sign of great security.

I think that “rests” was added for this reason: in that place there is no need for him to stand and keep watch over the flock, when the flock may nevertheless roam freely through the pastures even while the shepherd rests and takes repose in the shade. Happy is the region in which sheep enter and go out at will, and there is none to terrify them. Who will grant me to see you and myself feeding together in the mountains with those ninety-nine whom we read were left there when their shepherd graciously descended to the one which had strayed? (Matt. 18:12). Certainly he rests securely nearby who did not hesitate to go far away, knowing that he left them safe.

Rightly the bride sighs for that place; rightly she longs for a pasture that is at once peace, quiet, security, exultation, admiration, and astonishment. For even to me—alas, wretched me!—who remain far away and greet it from afar, its very remembrance draws tears, altogether in accord with the feeling and words of those who said: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, Zion” (Ps. 136:1). I too desire to cry out with the bride and with the Prophet: “Praise your God, O Zion, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you. He has made your borders peace, and satisfies you with the fat of wheat” (Ps. 147:12–14). Who would not ardently desire to be fed there, because of its peace, its richness, and its fullness? There nothing is feared, nothing is wearisome, nothing is lacking. Paradise is a secure dwelling; the Word is sweet food; eternity is exceedingly abundant wealth.

3. I too possess the Word, but in the flesh; truth too is set before me, but in a sacrament. The angel is fattened by the fat of wheat and satisfied by the naked grain; for the present I must be content with a certain sacramental rind, the bran of flesh, the chaff of the letter, the veil of faith. And things of this kind, if tasted, bring death unless they receive some seasoning, however small, from the firstfruits of the Spirit. Truly, there is death in my pot unless it is sweetened by the prophet’s meal (4 Kings 4:40–41). For without the Spirit even the sacrament is received unto judgment; the flesh profits nothing; the letter kills; and faith is dead. But it is the Spirit who gives life, so that I may live in these things.

Yet, however richly these things are made fat by the Spirit, the sacramental rind and the fat of wheat, faith and sight [variant, wrongly: hope], remembrance and presence, eternity and time, face and mirror, the image of God and the form of a servant, are not received with equal delight. In all these things faith is rich for me, understanding poor. But is the taste of understanding and faith equal, when the latter belongs to merit and the former to reward? You see, therefore, that the difference between the foods is as great as the difference between the places; and that, as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so those dwelling in them abound in better goods.

4. Let us hasten, then, children; let us hasten to the safer place, the sweeter pasture, the richer and more fertile field. Let us hasten, that we may dwell without fear, abound without want, and feast without weariness. For you, O Lord of hosts, who judge all things with tranquillity, likewise feed all things there in security. You are at once Lord of hosts and shepherd of sheep. Therefore you feed and rest together—but not here. For you were standing when, looking down from heaven, you saw one of your little sheep—I mean Stephen—surrounded on earth by wolves (Acts 7:55).

And therefore, I beg you, tell me where you feed, where you rest at noon—that is, throughout the whole day; for that noon is an entire day and knows no evening. Therefore that one day in your courts is better than thousands (Ps. 83:11), because it knows no sunset. Yet perhaps it had a morning, namely when the sanctified day first dawned upon us through the tender mercy of our God, whereby the Dayspring from on high visited us (Luke 1:78). Then indeed we received, O God, your mercy in the midst of your temple (Ps. 47:10), when in the midst of the shadow of death the light of morning rose upon us, and in the morning we saw the glory of the Lord. How many kings and prophets desired to see it and did not see it! Why? Because it was night, and that awaited morning, to which mercy had been promised, had not yet come. Hence one prayed, saying: “Make me hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you” (Ps. 142:8).

5. There was indeed a kind of dawn of this day from the time when the Sun of righteousness was announced to earth through the archangel Gabriel, and the Virgin conceived God in her womb by the Holy Spirit and gave birth as a virgin; and thereafter, for as long as he was seen on earth and lived among men. Throughout that entire period the light appeared so small, and truly like the light of dawn, that almost all humanity remained unaware that it was day. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8). Even to those few disciples it was said: “Yet a little light is in you” (John 12:35), because it was dawn—the beginning, or rather the indication, of the day—while the Sun still concealed his rays and scarcely scattered them over the earth.

Paul too said: “The night has gone before, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:12), indicating that the light was then still so small that he preferred to say that the day had drawn near rather than that it had come. But when did he say this? Certainly when the Sun, returned from the lower regions, had already raised himself to the heights of heaven. How much more, then, while the likeness of sinful flesh still covered the dawn like a dense cloud, in all the passions of our body, so that neither bitter death nor the shameful cross was lacking! How much more, I say, was the light then scant and exceedingly faint, seeming to proceed from the presence of dawn rather than from that of the Sun?

6. Therefore all Christ’s earthly life was dawn, and a rather shadowed dawn, until, setting and rising again, he drove away the dawn by the clearer light of his solar presence; and, when morning came, the night was swallowed up in victory. Thus we read: “Very early on the first day of the week, they come to the tomb, the sun having already risen” (Mark 16:2). Was it not morning when the Sun rose? But he brought from the resurrection a new beauty and a light clearer than usual: “Even though we knew him according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16).

It is written in the Prophet: “He has put on beauty, he has put on strength, and girded himself” (Ps. 92:1), because he shook off the infirmities of flesh as though they were clouds and put on the robe of glory. From then on the Sun was raised high; and, gradually spreading his rays over the earth, he began little by little to appear brighter and to be felt more fervently everywhere. Yet, however much he grows warm and strong, multiplies and extends his rays through the entire course of our mortality—for he will be with us until the end of the age (Matt. 28:20)—the light will not reach noon, nor will he now be seen in that fullness in which he is to be seen hereafter by those alone whom he himself deigns to make worthy of this vision.

O true noon: fullness of heat and light; the Sun standing still; the banishment of shadows; the drying up of marshes; the driving away of foul odors! O perpetual solstice, when the day will no longer decline! O noonday light, O springtime mildness, O summer beauty, O autumn abundance; and, lest I seem to have omitted anything, O winter rest and holiday! Or rather, if you prefer it, then winter alone has passed away and withdrawn.

“Tell me,” she says, “of this place of such brightness, peace, and fullness, so that, as Jacob while still remaining in the body saw the Lord face to face and his soul was saved (Gen. 32:30); or as Moses saw him, not through figures and riddles or dreams, as other prophets did, but in a manner plainly excelling and unknown to others, known to himself and to God (Num. 12:6–8); or as Isaiah, with the eyes of his heart unveiled, saw him upon a throne high and lifted up (Isa. 6:1); or even as Paul, caught up into paradise, heard ineffable words (2 Cor. 12:4) and saw his Lord Jesus Christ with his own eyes—so may I also deserve, by an ecstasy of mind, to contemplate you in your light and beauty, feeding more abundantly and resting more securely.”

7. For here too you feed, but not to fullness; nor is one permitted to rest, but one must stand and watch because of terrors by night. Alas! there is neither clear light, nor complete refreshment, nor secure dwelling. Therefore, tell me where you feed, where you rest at noon. You call me blessed when I hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt. 5:6). What is this compared with the blessedness of those who “are filled with the good things of your house” (Ps. 64:5), who feast and exult before God and delight in joy? (Ps. 67:4). And if I suffer anything for righteousness’ sake, you nevertheless pronounce me blessed (Matt. 5:9). Certainly, to feed where one fears suffering has delight, but not security. But to feed and suffer at once—is it not a burdensome delight?

Here all things fall short of perfection for me; many things are contrary to my desire; and nothing is secure. When will you fill me with joy in your presence? (Ps. 15:11). “Your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. 26:8). Your face is noon. Tell me where you feed, where you rest at noon. I know well enough where you feed without resting; tell me where you both feed and rest. I do not fail to know where you are accustomed to feed at other times; but I would know where you feed at noon.

For in the time of my mortality and in the place of my pilgrimage, I have indeed been accustomed, under your protection, to be fed and to feed in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning you; I have likewise found rest in Gospel pastures and among the Apostles. I have also often, as I could, begged food for myself and those entrusted to me from the deeds, sayings, and writings of the saints. More often, however—because it was more readily at hand—I ate the bread of sorrow and drank the wine of compunction; my tears became my bread day and night, while it was said to me daily: “Where is your God?” (Ps. 41:4). Except that, from your table—since “you have prepared before me a table against those who trouble me” (Ps. 22:5)—from that table, I say, through the benefit of your mercy, I receive that in which I somehow recover breath whenever my soul is sad and whenever it is troubled within me. These pastures I know and have frequented, following you as shepherd; but show me, I beg, also those which I do not know.

8. There are indeed other shepherds who say they are your companions, but are not. They have their own flocks and their own territories, full of the fodder of death; in these they feed neither with you nor through you. I have neither entered their boundaries nor come near them. These are the ones who say: “Behold, here is Christ; behold, there he is” (Mark 13:21), promising richer pastures of wisdom and knowledge. They are believed, and many flock to them; and they make them children of Gehenna twice as much as themselves.

Why is this so, except because there is no noon there, no clear light by which truth may be plainly known? Falsehood is readily accepted in its place because of its likeness to truth; and in darkness it is not easily distinguished from the truth—especially since stolen waters are sweeter and hidden bread more pleasant (Prov. 9:17). Therefore I beg you to show me where you feed, where you rest at noon—that is, openly—lest, deceived, I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions, just as they themselves wander, stable in no certainty of truth, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth (2 Tim. 3:7). The bride says this because of the diverse and empty doctrines of philosophers and heretics.

9. But it seems to me that she says it not only because of these things, but also because of the deceits of invisible powers—such as seducing spirits, who sit in ambush and prepare their arrows in the quiver in order to shoot the upright in heart in darkness. Because of these, I say, and especially because of these, noon seems desirable also for us: that by clear light we may detect the devil’s stratagems and most easily distinguish from our angel that angel of Satan who transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14). For we cannot otherwise sufficiently guard ourselves against “the attack and the noonday demon” (Ps. 90:6), unless we too are in noonday light.

I think that this demon is called “noonday” because some among the number of the wicked, though by the merit of their dark and obstinate will they are night, indeed perpetual night, nevertheless know how to counterfeit day in order to deceive—indeed, not merely day, but noon. Thus their prince, not content to be equal to God, also opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or worshipped as God (2 Thess. 2:4). Therefore, unless the true noon—the Dayspring from on high—has shone upon the heart of one whom some such noonday demon has undertaken to tempt, exposing and proving falsehood, he can in no way be guarded against it. The demon will certainly tempt and overthrow him under the appearance of good, persuading the unwary and unwatchful person to accept evil in place of good. Then the noonday demon—that is, a greater brightness—appears as a tempter, when it presents, as it were, an image of a greater good.

10. How often, for example, has he suggested that one anticipate the vigils, so that he might mock a sleeping monk at the brethren’s liturgical observances? How often that fasts should be prolonged, so that he might make someone so much the less fit for divine services as he made him weaker? How often, envying those who were making good progress in monasteries, has he persuaded them, under a pretext of greater purity, to seek the desert; and at last the wretched learned how true was the saying which they had read in vain: “Woe to him who is alone, because, if he falls, he has none to lift him up” (Eccl. 4:10)? How often has he urged someone to manual work beyond what was necessary, and made one whose strength was broken incapable of the other regular observances? How many has he persuaded to an immoderate bodily exercise—though, according to the Apostle, it profits little (1 Tim. 4:8)—and thereby defrauded them of godliness?

Finally, you yourselves have experienced how certain persons—to the shame of those, I say, who formerly could not be restrained, for in a violent spirit they were carried away to almost everything—afterward came to such sloth that, according to the Apostle’s saying, having begun in the Spirit they are now consumed in the flesh (Gal. 3:3). What a shameful treaty they have entered into with their bodies, against which they had previously proclaimed cruel war! You may see them—shameful to say!—importunately demanding superfluities, though formerly they most obstinately refused necessities.

Yet if any perhaps persist in their unconquered obstinacy, abstaining without discernment and by a conspicuous singularity troubling those with whom they ought to live harmoniously in one house, I do not know whether they think they retain godliness, since such persons seem to me to have cast it away even farther. For those who have resolved to be wise in their own eyes, neither yielding to counsel nor obeying command, should see what answer they will make—not to me, but to him who says: “To resist is like the sin of divination, and refusing to submit is like the crime of idolatry.” He had first said that obedience is better than sacrifice, and hearkening than offering the fat of rams (1 Sam. 15:22–23): that is, than the abstinence of the obstinate. Hence the Lord says through the Prophet: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 49:13), signifying that the fasts of the proud or impure are by no means acceptable to him.

11. But I truly fear lest, while condemning the superstitious, we seem to loosen the reins for gluttons; and lest they hear, to their danger, what is said to these as a remedy. Therefore hear, both parties, that there are four kinds of temptation, described to us in the prophetic utterance as follows: “His truth shall surround you with a shield; you shall not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the business that walks in darkness, the attack and the noonday demon” (Ps. 90:5–6).

You others also, attend to what I hope will benefit everyone. All of us who have turned to the Lord feel and have felt within ourselves what Holy Scripture says: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). Thus, at the beginning of our conversion, according to common experience, the first thing that agitates us is fear: immediately upon entering, the dread of a stricter life and the severity of an unfamiliar discipline are impressed upon us. This is called “terror by night,” either because night in Scripture ordinarily signifies adversities, or because what we undertake to endure adversity for has not yet been revealed.

For if that day shone in whose light we should see alike our labors and their rewards, no fear of any labors would remain in the face of desire for the rewards, when it appeared in clear light that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). But now, because these things are hidden from our eyes, and it is as yet night in this respect, we are tempted by terror by night, and for the sake of good things which we do not see, we fear to endure adversities that are presently before us. Therefore, at the outset, we must watch and pray against this first temptation, lest, suddenly overcome by faintness of spirit and storm, we should—God forbid!—draw back from the good work begun.

12. Once this temptation has been overcome, let us nevertheless arm ourselves against human praise, which finds its material chiefly in a praiseworthy life. Otherwise we shall lie open to the wound from “the arrow flying by day,” which is empty glory. For fame flies; and it is by day because it proceeds from works of light. If this is blown away like an empty breeze, something more substantial is offered—riches and worldly honors—if perhaps the person who does not care for praise may desire dignities.

See whether this order of temptation was not observed in our Lord: after the precipice was proposed to him for sheer vanity, all the kingdoms of the world were displayed and offered to him (Matt. 4:6, 8). You therefore, following the Lord’s example, reject these things as well. Otherwise you must be ensnared by “the business that walks in darkness,” which is hypocrisy. For it descends from ambition, and its dwelling is in darkness: it hides what it is and falsely claims what it is not. It traffics at all times, retaining the appearance of godliness in order to conceal itself, while laying claim to its power and purchasing honors.

13. The final temptation is the noonday demon, which is especially accustomed to lie in wait for the perfect—those, namely, who, as men of virtues, have conquered everything: pleasures, favor, honors. For what remains to the tempter, in which he can openly fight against such persons? Therefore he comes secretly, because he does not dare to come openly; and, having thoroughly found that they abhor every evident evil, he strives to overthrow them by a false good.

Those who can say with the Apostle, “We are not ignorant of his devices” (2 Cor. 2:11), become, the more they progress, the more careful to avoid this snare. Thus Mary is troubled by the angelic greeting (Luke 1:29), suspecting deceit, I think; and Joshua does not receive the angel as a friend until he knows him to be a friend. He asks whether he is on his side or on the side of his adversaries (Josh. 5:13–15), as one who has experienced the cunning of the noonday demon.

The Apostles too, when they were laboring at the oars while the wind was contrary and tossed their little boat, saw the Lord walking on the sea and thought him a phantom, crying out in fear. Did they not show an evident suspicion of the noonday demon? Recall that Scripture says he came to them, walking upon the sea, in the fourth watch of the night. Therefore this temptation should be feared fourth—that is, finally—and the more anyone sees himself standing on high, the more watchfully he should understand that he must guard himself against the attack and the noonday demon. But the true noon manifested himself to the disciples when they heard: “It is I; do not fear” (Matt. 14:25–27), and their suspicion of a false apparition was removed.

Would that, whenever disguised falsehood seeks to creep in upon us, the Dayspring from on high—the true noon—would send forth his light and truth to expose it, and divide light from darkness, lest we be marked by the prophet as those who make light darkness and darkness light (Isa. 5:20).

14. Further, unless the length of the discourse is wearisome, I shall attempt to assign these four temptations, in their order, to the body of Christ, which is the Church. And behold, I shall run through it as briefly as possible. Look at the primitive Church: was it not first sharply pervaded by terror by night? For it was night when everyone who killed the saints thought that he was rendering service to God. But when this temptation had been conquered and the storm calmed, the Church became illustrious and, in accordance with the promise made to her, was quickly made the pride of the ages.

The enemy, grieving that he had been frustrated, cunningly turned from terror by night to the arrow flying by day, and wounded some persons within the Church by it. Vain men arose, desirous of glory, and wished to make a name for themselves; departing from the Church, they long afflicted their same mother through diverse and perverse doctrines. But this plague too was driven away by the wisdom of the saints, just as the first had been by the patience of the martyrs.

15. Behold, these times are indeed free, by God’s mercy, from both those evils; but they are plainly foul with the business that walks in darkness. Woe to this generation because of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy!—if, indeed, that ought to be called hypocrisy which is no longer able to conceal itself because of its abundance, and does not seek concealment because of its shamelessness.

Today a putrid corruption creeps through the whole body of the Church; the more widely it spreads, the more desperate it is, and the more dangerous because it is more inward. For if an openly heretical enemy arose, he would be cast out and wither away; if a violent enemy, the Church might perhaps hide herself from him. But now whom shall she cast out, or from whom shall she hide herself? All are friends, and all are enemies; all are necessary, and all are adversaries; all are members of the household, and none are peaceable; all are near, and all seek their own interests. They are ministers of Christ and serve Antichrist. They proceed in honor from the goods of the Lord, yet render no honor to the Lord.

Hence the meretricious splendor you see daily, the theatrical attire, the royal display. Hence gold on bridles, saddles, and spurs; and spurs gleam more brightly than altars. Hence splendid tables, food, and cups; hence revelry and drunkenness; hence harp, lyre, and flute; hence winepresses overflowing and storehouses full, pouring out from one thing into another. Hence jars of spices; hence purses stuffed full. For the sake of such things, men desire to be—and are made—leaders of churches: provosts, deans, archdeacons, bishops, archbishops. These offices are not granted for merit, but by that business which walks in darkness.

16. It was foretold long ago, and now the time of fulfillment has come: “Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” (Isa. 38:17). Bitter first in the killing of martyrs; more bitter afterward in conflict with heretics; now most bitter in the conduct of those within the household. The Church cannot drive them away or flee from them; so strong have they become, and so multiplied beyond number. The Church’s wound is internal and incurable; and therefore in peace her bitterness is most bitter.

But in what peace? There is peace, and there is no peace. Peace from pagans and peace from heretics; but certainly not from her children. The voice of one weeping is heard in this time: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1:2). They have despised and defiled me by a shameful life, shameful gain, shameful commerce—in short, by the business that walks in darkness.

It remains that the noonday demon should now come forth from the midst to deceive any who remain in Christ, still abiding in their simplicity. For “he has swallowed up the rivers of the wise and the torrents of the mighty, and is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job 40:18): that is, the simple and humble who are in the Church. For he is Antichrist, who will pretend to be not only day but also noon, and will exalt himself above all that is called God or worshipped as God; whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming (2 Thess. 2:4, 8). He is the true and eternal Noon, Bridegroom and Advocate of the Church, God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIV. In Which Humility and Patience Are Treated
1. “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go forth, and follow after the flocks of your companions, and pasture your kids beside the shepherds’ tents” (Song 1:7). Long ago holy Moses, because he presumed greatly upon the grace and familiarity which he had found with God, [Col. 0960A] aspired to a certain great vision, so that he said to God: “If I have found grace in your eyes, show me yourself.” Yet in place of it he received a vision far inferior, through which nevertheless he might at some time attain the vision he desired (Exod. 33:13–23). Likewise the sons of Zebedee, walking in the simplicity of their hearts, ventured upon something great; yet they too were reduced to the step by which they had to ascend (Matt. 20:21–23). So now too the Bride, because she seems to ask for a great thing, is indeed checked by a rather stern answer, but one plainly useful and faithful.

For one striving toward higher things must think humbly of oneself, lest, while being lifted above oneself, one fall away from oneself—unless one has first been firmly established in oneself through true humility. And because [Col. 0960B] the greatest things are by no means obtained except through the merit of humility, the person who is to be advanced is humbled by rebuke and earns advancement by humility. Therefore, when you see yourself being humbled, take it altogether as a favorable sign, an indication that grace is drawing near. For just as “the heart is lifted up before ruin” (Prov. 16:18), so it is humbled before exaltation. Certainly you read both that God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4:6). Did he not, finally, when he judged that his servant Job’s great and well-tested patience, after its notable triumph, should be rewarded with abundant blessing, first take care to humble him through many searching and rigorous questions, and thus prepare a way for the blessing? (Job 38 ff.).

2. But it is little when God humbles us [Col. 0960C] by himself, even if we then receive it willingly, unless, when he does this through another, we understand it in the same way. Therefore receive a remarkable example of this matter from holy David. Once he was cursed even by a servant; but he did not feel the added injury, because he foresaw grace. “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?” he says (2 Sam. 16:10). O truly a man after God’s heart, who thought that he should be angered with the one taking vengeance upon him rather than with one reproaching him! Hence, with a secure conscience, he said: “If I have repaid evils to those who repaid me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. 7:4).

He therefore forbade the abusive curser to be restrained, reckoning curses a gain. And he adds: “The Lord sent him to curse David” (2 Sam. 16:10). [Col. 0960D] Truly a man after God’s heart, who drew his judgment from God’s heart. A cursing tongue raged, but David attended to what God was doing in secret. The voice of the curser was in his ears, while his spirit bent itself toward blessing. Was God in the mouth of the blasphemer? Far be it! But he used him to humble David. This was not hidden from the Prophet, to whom God had revealed the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom (Ps. 50:8); and therefore he says: “It is good for me that you humbled me, that I might learn your ordinances” (Ps. 118:71).

3. Do you see that humility justifies us? I said humility, not humiliation. How many are humiliated who are not humble! Some are humiliated resentfully, others patiently, and others even willingly. The first are guilty; the second innocent; the last righteous. Although innocence too [Col. 0961A] is a portion of righteousness, its perfection belongs to the humble person. But the one who can say, “It is good for me that you humbled me,” is truly humble. One who endures unwillingly cannot say this, much less one who murmurs.

We promise grace to neither of these merely because he is humbled, although these two differ greatly: one indeed possesses his soul in patience, while the other perishes in his murmuring. Yet although the one escapes wrath, neither earns grace; for God gives grace not to those who are humiliated but to the humble. The humble person is one who turns humiliation into humility; and this is the person who says to God: “It is good for me that you humbled me.” What one bears patiently is by no means pleasant to anyone; it is plainly distressing. But we know that God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7).

[Col. 0961B] Hence, when we fast, we are commanded to anoint our head with oil and wash our face (Matt. 6:17), so that our good work may be seasoned with a certain spiritual joy and our burnt offering may become rich. For only a joyful and unreserved humility merits the grace which it displays. A humility that is compelled or forced—such as belongs to that patient man who possesses his soul—obtains life because of patience, but, because of sadness, will not possess grace.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] This is evidently the special grace promised to truly humble persons in the words, “God gives grace to the humble”: a special grace, I say, not only inward but also outward—namely, exaltation even in this life.]

For the Scriptural saying does not fit such a person: “Let the humble glory in his exaltation” (Jas. 1:9), because he is not humbled voluntarily or willingly.

4. Do you wish to see one who is humble rightly glorying, and truly worthy of glory? “Most gladly,” he says, “will I glory in [Col. 0961C] my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:9). He does not say that he bears his weaknesses patiently, but that he glories in them—and glories in them gladly—proving that it is good for him to be humbled. Nor is it at all enough for him to possess his soul as one humbled patiently, unless he also receives grace as one humbled voluntarily.

Hear, then, the general rule: “Everyone who humbles himself,” he says, “shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11). He plainly signifies that not every humility is to be exalted, but only that which proceeds from the will, not from sorrow or necessity. For conversely, not everyone who is exalted will be humbled, but only the one who exalts himself will be humbled—namely, because of voluntary vanity. Thus it is not the person who is humbled, but the one who humbles [Col. 0961D] himself voluntarily, who will be exalted, certainly because of the merit of his will.

For even if the material of humility is supplied by another—for instance, insults, losses, or punishments—the person who has resolved to undergo all these things for God’s sake with a silent and joyful conscience will nevertheless rightly be said to be humbled not by another but by himself.

5. But where are we going? Patiently, as I perceive, you endure this digression on humility and patience; but let us return to the passage from which we departed. For this came to us on the occasion of the Bridegroom’s answer, [Col. 0962A] by which he judged that the Bride, presuming great things, should be checked—not to make her foolish, but so that an opportunity might thereby be given for a more commendable and greater humility, through which she might become worthier and more capable of higher things, even of the things she herself asked for.

Nevertheless, since we are still at the threshold of the present chapter, let us begin its examination at the beginning of another sermon, if you please—especially lest the Bridegroom’s words either be repeated with weariness or heard with weariness. May Jesus Christ our Lord avert this from his servants, he who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXV. On the severe rebuke which the Bridegroom gives the Bride; and on the twofold ignorance which must greatly be feared and avoided.

[Col. 0962B]

1. “If you do not know yourself,” he says, “go forth” (Song 1:7). It is a hard and harsh rebuke when he says, “Go forth.” For servants are accustomed to hear this word from masters who are greatly angered and indignant, or maidservants from their mistresses when they have gravely offended them: “Get out of here; get away from me; depart from my sight and from this house.” Thus the Bridegroom now uses this harsh, bitter, and exceedingly reproachful word against his beloved, though under the condition that she should not know herself.

For he could direct nothing more powerful or effective toward frightening her than the threat that she must go forth. You too can perceive this if you attend carefully from where and to where she is commanded to go out. From where, and to where, do you suppose, except from spirit to flesh; from the goods of the soul to worldly desires; [Col. 0962C] from the inward repose of the mind to the noise of the world and the restlessness of outward cares? In all these there is nothing but labor, pain, and affliction of spirit.

For what soul, once it has learned and received from the Lord how to enter into itself, how in its inmost depths to sigh for God’s presence and always seek his face—for God is spirit, and those who seek him must walk in spirit, not live according to the flesh—would, I do not know whether, judge even the experience of hell itself for a time more dreadful and more painful than, after having once tasted the sweetness of this spiritual pursuit, going out again to the allurements—or rather the troubles—of the flesh and returning to the insatiable curiosity of the senses? For Ecclesiastes says: “The eye is not filled with seeing, nor the ear with hearing” (Eccl. 1:8).

Hear, then, a man experienced in what we say: “You are good, O Lord, to those who hope in you, to the soul that seeks you” (Lam. 3:25). If anyone tried to turn that holy soul away from this good, I think she would receive it no differently than if she saw herself cast down from paradise and from the very entrance to glory. Hear also another like him: “My heart has said to you: my face has sought you; your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. 26:8). Hence he said: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 72:28); and again, speaking to his soul, he says: [Col. 0963A] “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt generously with you” (Ps. 114:7).

Therefore I tell you: there is nothing that anyone who has once received this benefit fears so greatly as that, abandoned by grace, he may be compelled once more to go out to fleshly consolations—indeed, desolations—and again endure the tumult of carnal senses.

2. Therefore the threat is terrible and exceedingly dreadful: “Go forth, and pasture your kids.” Its meaning is: Know yourself unworthy of that familiar and sweet contemplation of heavenly, intelligible, divine realities. Therefore go forth from my sanctuary, which is your heart, where you used sweetly to draw secret and sacred perceptions of truth and wisdom; and, rather as one of worldly people, involve yourself in feeding and pleasing the senses [Col. 0963B] of your flesh.

For by “kids”—which signify sin and are to be placed at the left in judgment—he means the wandering and wanton bodily senses, through which sin entered the soul, as death through windows. And what follows in Scripture fits well: “Beside the shepherds’ tents.” For kids, unlike lambs, are fed not above but beside the shepherds’ tents.

The shepherds, insofar as they are true shepherds, although in the days of their present service they have tents from the earth and on the earth, namely their bodies, nevertheless are accustomed to feed the Lord’s flocks from heavenly pastures, not from the earth; for they preach not their own will but the Lord’s. But the kids, which are the bodily senses, do not seek heavenly things; rather, beside the shepherds’ tents—that is, amid all the sensible goods of this world, which is the realm of bodies—they obtain material that does not so much satisfy as stimulate their desires.

3. A shameful change of pursuits! A soul whose pursuit formerly was to feed itself, while a pilgrim and exile, on sacred meditations as on heavenly goods; to investigate what pleases God and the mysteries of his will; to penetrate heaven in devotion and range through the heavenly dwellings in mind; to greet the patriarchs and apostles, the choirs of prophets; to marvel at the triumphs of martyrs; and to be amazed at the most beautiful orders of angels—now, abandoning all these things, it enslaves itself to the shameful service of the body: to obey the flesh, satisfy belly and gluttony, and beg throughout [Col. 0963D] the whole earth for something from the passing form of this world that may in some measure console its perpetually hungry curiosity.

“Let streams of waters run down from my eyes” over such a soul, which, though “nourished in saffron,” at last embraces dung (Lam. 4:5). For, in the saying of the blessed man, “he has fed the barren woman who had no children, and has not done good to the widow” (Job 24:21). And observe that he does not simply say, “Go forth,” but: “Go forth,” he says, “and follow after the flocks of your companions, and pasture your kids.” In this, as it seems to me, he warns us of some great matter.

What is it? Alas, that a noble creature, long ago made one of the flock and now miserably falling into worse things, is not even permitted to remain among the flocks, [Col. 0964A] but is commanded to go behind them. “How?” you ask. Just as you read: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). See how a noble creature became one of the flock. I think the beasts would say, if it were permitted them to speak: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” (Gen. 3:22).

“He was in honor,” it says. In what honor, you ask? He dwelt in paradise, and his dwelling was in a place of delight. He experienced neither trouble nor want, surrounded by fragrant apples, supported by flowers, crowned with glory and honor, and set over the works of his Maker’s hands. But above all he excelled through the distinction of the divine likeness; he had his lot and fellowship with the people of angels and with all the host of the heavenly army.

[Col. 0964B]

4. But he changed this glory of God into the likeness of a calf eating hay. Hence the bread of angels became hay, placed in a manger and set before us like beasts. For “the Word was made flesh” (John 1:14), and according to the prophet, “All flesh is hay.” Yet this hay did not wither, nor did its flower fall, because the Spirit of the Lord rested upon it. For the end once came upon all flesh because the spirit of life had departed. Thus he says: “My spirit shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh” (Gen. 6:3).

Understand that here “flesh” denotes vice, not nature; for nature does not drive out the spirit, but vice does. Therefore because of vice all flesh is hay, and [Col. 0964C] all its glory like the flower of hay. “The hay has withered,” he says, “and the flower has fallen”; but not that flower which sprang from the shoot and root of Jesse, because the Spirit of the Lord rested upon him (Isa. 11:1–2); nor that hay which the Word became, because the prophet continues: “But the word of the Lord remains for ever” (Isa. 40:6–8).

For if the Word is hay and the Word remains for ever, then the hay too must necessarily remain for ever. Otherwise how does it give eternal life if it does not itself remain for ever? For he says: “If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever.” And he makes clear which bread he means when he adds: “And the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52). How then is that not eternal by which one lives eternally?

[Col. 0964D] 5. But recall with me now the voice of the Son speaking to the Father in the psalm: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10). Without doubt he speaks of the body lying lifeless in the tomb. For this is the holy thing of which the angel who announced to the Virgin also spoke, saying: “And that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

How, then, could holy hay see corruption—hay which sprang from the ever-green pastures of an incorrupt womb, and which can hold fast upon itself even the eager gaze of angels, delighting them without satiety? Let the hay indeed lose its greenness if Mary loses her virginity. Therefore the food of man changed itself into fodder for cattle because man changed into cattle.

Alas, sad and tearful [Col. 0965A] change! The man who was an inhabitant of paradise, lord of the earth, citizen of heaven, member of the household of the Lord of hosts, brother of blessed spirits, and co-heir of heavenly powers, found himself through a sudden transformation lying in a stable because of weakness, needing hay because of his beast-like likeness, and bound to a manger because of untamed wildness, as it is written: “With bit and bridle bind fast the jaws of those who do not draw near to you” (Ps. 31:9).

Yet acknowledge, O ox, your owner; and you, ass, your lord’s manger, so that God’s faithful prophets may be found true, who foretold these marvels of God. Know, O beast, him whom you did not know as a human being; adore in the stable him from whom you fled in paradise; honor the manger whose rule you despised; eat the hay—him who is bread, the bread of angels, whom you disdained.

[Col. 0965B]

6. But what, you ask, was the cause of so great a fall? Certainly that man, when he was in honor, did not understand. What did he not understand? The text does not say; let us say it. Set in honor, he did not understand that he was mud, delighted by the height of honor. And immediately he experienced in himself what, much later, a man among the children of captivity both wisely perceived and truly declared: “He who thinks himself something when he is nothing deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3).

Woe to the miserable man, because there was no one then to say to him: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10:9). From this came the noble creature’s joining to the flock; from this, God’s likeness was changed into a bestial likeness; from this, fellowship with beasts was entered upon in place of communion [Col. 0965C] with angels. Do you see how this ignorance must be avoided by us, from which so many thousands of evils have come upon our entire race? For it says that man was compared to senseless beasts because he did not understand.

Therefore ignorance must be avoided in every way, lest perhaps, if we are still found without understanding even after affliction, many more and graver evils than the former should overtake us, and it should be said of us: “We healed Babylon, and she was not healed” (Jer. 51:9). Deservedly so, because not even affliction has given understanding to hearing.

[Col. 0965D]

7. And observe whether perhaps for this reason too, when the Bridegroom deterred his beloved from ignorance with so thunderous a rebuke, he did not say: “Go forth with the flocks,” or “Go forth to the flocks,” but, “Go forth,” he says, “after the flocks of your companions.” Why is this? Surely in order to show that the second ignorance is more to be feared and shamed than the first: the first made man equal to beasts, while this makes him lower even than they.

For human beings who, deservedly because of ignorance, are themselves not known—that is, rejected—must stand before that dreadful judgment and be handed over to everlasting fire; beasts do not. And without doubt it will be worse for those who are thus than for those who do not exist at all. “It would have been better for that man,” he says, “if he had not been born” (Mark 14:21)—not indeed if he had not been born altogether, but if he had not been born a human being; but, for example, as a beast or some other creature. Since it would not have judgment, it would not come to judgment, and therefore not [Col. 0966A] to punishment.

Let the rational soul, then, which blushes over the first ignorance, know that beasts are its companions in enjoying the goods of earth, but will not likewise be its companions in bearing the torments of hell. At last it will be driven disgracefully even from the flocks of these its beastly companions; it will no longer go even with them, but distinctly behind them, when they feel no evil and it is exposed to every evil. It will never be delivered from these, if it adds the second ignorance.

Thus man goes forth and goes alone behind the flocks of his companions when he is thrust alone into the lowest hell. Does not one who is cast, hands and feet bound, into outer darkness seem to you to occupy the lower place? And indeed the last condition [Col. 0966B] of that man will be worse than the first, when he who was formerly made equal to beasts is now even placed after them.

8. I think that even in the present life, if you attend well, you will judge a human being to go behind beasts. For does not a man endowed with reason and yet not living according to reason seem in some manner more beastly than beasts themselves? A beast, indeed, if it does not govern itself by reason, has an excuse from nature, which wholly denied it this gift; a human being has no such excuse, since he was endowed with it as a special prerogative.

Thus man is rightly judged, for that very reason, to go forth and follow behind herd animals: alone among animals, through a degenerate manner of life he transgresses nature’s laws, and though possessed of reason imitates creatures without reason in habits and affections.
