Therefore man is proved to go behind the flocks—now [Col. 0966C] indeed through the corruption of nature, and later through the extremity of punishment.

[Col. 0966D]

9. See how the person found to possess ignorance of God will be cursed. Shall I say ignorance of God, or of oneself? Both, without doubt: both ignorances are damnable; either is sufficient for perdition. Do you wish to know that this is so? You have no doubt concerning ignorance of God, if it is established for you that eternal life is nothing other than knowing the Father as the true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent (John 17:3).

Hear, then, the Bridegroom clearly and openly condemning in the soul ignorance even of itself. For what does he say? Not, “If you do not know God,” but: “If you do not know yourself,” he says, and so forth. It is evident, therefore, that one who is ignorant will be ignored (1 Cor. 14:38), whether it happens that one is ignorant of oneself or of God.

Concerning both ignorances, if God nevertheless lends his hand, we shall have a very useful discussion. But not now, lest, being tired and without the customary prayer first offered, either I pursue a necessary matter less carefully or you hear with less attention matters which must be received only with great desire. For if bodily food, when you take it without appetite and already satiated, not only does no good but does very great harm, much more will the bread of the soul, taken with distaste, bring not nourishment of knowledge but rather torment of conscience. May Jesus Christ, Bridegroom of the Church, avert this from us—he who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVI. That knowledge of letters is good for instruction, but knowledge of one’s own weakness is more useful for salvation.

[Col. 0967A]

1. Here I am, true to my promise; here I am, responding to your desires; here I am also in the service I owe to God. As you see, I am compelled to speak for a threefold reason: fidelity to an agreement, brotherly love, and fear of the Lord. If I keep silent, my mouth will condemn me. But what if I speak? Certainly I fear the same judgment, lest my mouth again condemn me as one who speaks and does not act.

Help me with your prayers, that I may always both speak what I ought and fulfill in deed what I say. You know that today’s proposed discourse concerns ignorance, or rather ignorances, [Col. 0967B] since, as you remember, two were proposed: one concerning ourselves, the other concerning God. We have warned that both must be avoided, because both are damnable. It remains for me to make this clearer and explain it more fully.

But first I think we must ask whether every ignorance is damnable. It seems to me that it is not. For not every ignorance condemns; rather, there are many, indeed innumerable, things which one may fail to know without any diminution of salvation. For example, if you do not know the craft of a smith, carpenter, or mason, or any other such arts practised by people for the uses of this present life, does this hinder salvation?

Even without all those arts called liberal—[Col. 0967C] although they are learned and practised in more honorable and useful pursuits—very many people have been saved, pleasing God through their character and deeds. The Apostle lists many such persons in the Epistle to the Hebrews: they became beloved not through literary knowledge but through a pure conscience and unfeigned faith (Heb. 11). All pleased God in their lives by the merits of life, not by knowledge.

Peter, Andrew, the sons of Zebedee, and all the other disciples were not chosen from the school of rhetoricians or philosophers; and yet through them the Savior worked salvation in the midst of the earth. He made them saved, holy, and teachers not through a wisdom in them greater than in all who had lived (Eccl. 1:16), as some saint confessed of himself, but through their faith and gentleness. Finally, they made known to the world [Col. 0967D] the ways of life, not with loftiness of speech or learned words of human wisdom, but because, since the world did not know God through its own wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of their preaching to save believers (1 Cor. 2:1; 1:17, 21).

2. Perhaps I may seem excessive in disparaging knowledge, as though I condemned learned persons and prohibited literary studies. Far from it! I do not fail to know how much learned persons have benefited, and do benefit, the Church: both in refuting opponents and in instructing the simple. For I have read: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I too will reject you, so that you may not exercise priesthood for me” (Hos. 4:6). I have read: “Those who have been learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many in righteousness, [Col. 0968A] like stars for everlasting ages” (Dan. 12:3).

But I also know where I read: “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1); and again: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclus. 1:18). You see that there is a difference between kinds of knowledge, since one puffs up and another causes sorrow. But I would have you know which of these seems more useful or necessary for salvation: the knowledge which swells, or that which grieves. I do not doubt that you prefer the grieving knowledge to the swelling one, because pain seeks the health which swelling pretends to possess. But one who seeks approaches salvation, because whoever asks receives (Luke 11:10).

Indeed, he who heals the broken in heart rejects the swollen, as Wisdom says: God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4:6). And the Apostle said: “By the grace given to me, I say [Col. 0968B] to all who are among you not to think more highly than they ought to think, but to think soberly” (Rom. 12:3). He does not forbid thinking, but thinking more highly than one ought. But what is it to think soberly? To observe with greatest vigilance what one ought to know more, and first.

For time is short. In itself, every kind of knowledge is good, provided it rests upon truth. But you who hasten, in the shortness of time, to work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, take care to know preferably and more fully those things which you recognize as nearer to salvation. Do not physicians of bodies prescribe a measured choice in taking food—what ought to be taken first, what afterwards, and how each thing ought to be taken? For although the foods created by God are certainly good, you make them plainly not good for yourself if, in taking them, [Col. 0968C] you do not observe measure and order. Therefore understand of forms of knowledge what I say concerning foods.

3. But I will send you rather to the Teacher. This judgment is not mine but his—or rather, it is ours because it is Truth’s. “If anyone thinks that he knows something,” he says, “he does not yet know how he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2). Do you see that he does not approve one who knows much if he does not know the manner of knowing? Do you see, I say, how he places the fruit and usefulness of knowledge in the manner of knowing?

What, then, does he call the manner of knowing? What but that you know in what order, with what zeal, and for what end each thing ought to be known? In what order: that you first know what ripens more quickly toward salvation; with what zeal: that you know more ardently what more forcefully leads toward love; for what end: not for empty [Col. 0968D] glory, curiosity, or anything similar, but only for your own edification or that of your neighbor.

For there are those who wish to know solely in order to know: that is shameful curiosity. And there are those who wish to know in order that they themselves may be known: that is shameful vanity. Such people will certainly not escape the satirist’s mockery, as he sings of a person of this kind:

> Your knowledge is nothing, unless another knows that you know it.  
> —Persius, *Satires* 1.27

There are also those who wish to know in order to sell their knowledge—for money or for honors, for example: that is shameful gain. But there are also those who wish to know in order to edify: that is charity. And likewise those who wish to know in order to be edified: that is prudence.

[Col. 0969A]

4. Of all these, only the last two are not found abusing knowledge, since they wish to understand for the sake of doing good. Thus: “Good understanding belongs to all who do it” (Ps. 110:10). Let all the rest hear: “To one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (Jas. 4:17). It is as though he said by analogy: “For one who takes food and does not digest it, it is harmful.”

For undigested food, and food which has not been properly cooked, produces bad humors, corrupts the body, and does not nourish it. So too, if much knowledge is poured into the stomach of the soul, which is memory, and is not cooked by the fire of charity and then poured out and digested through certain limbs of the soul—namely, character and actions—so that the soul itself may be made good by the good things it has known, as its life and conduct bear witness, [Col. 0969B] will not that knowledge be reckoned as sin, like food turned into perverse and harmful humors?

Is not sin a bad humor? Are not bad humors evil habits? Will not such a person—one who knows the good and does not do it—endure swellings and torments in conscience? Will he not have within himself, as often as the word God spoke comes to mind, the sentence of death and condemnation: that the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do what is worthy will be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47)?

And perhaps the prophet, speaking in the person of such a soul, lamented: “My belly pains me, my belly pains me” (Jer. 4:19). Yet the repetition itself seems to suggest a double meaning, so that, besides the meaning we have given, we should seek another. [Col. 0969C] I think the Prophet could have said this in his own person: namely, that he was full of knowledge, burning with charity, and altogether wishing to pour himself out, but found no one willing to hear; and so his own knowledge was a burden to him because he could not share it.

The devout teacher of the Church therefore laments both those who despise to learn how they ought to live and those who, though knowing, nevertheless live badly. And this is why the Prophet repeats the same utterance.

[Col. 0969D]

5. Do you now perceive how truly the Apostle said that knowledge puffs up? Therefore I want the soul, first of all, to know itself, because both usefulness and order require this. Order requires it because what we are is first for us; usefulness because such knowledge does not puff up but humbles, and is a certain preparation for building. For a spiritual building cannot stand unless it rests upon the stable foundation of humility.

Moreover, the soul can find nothing more vigorous or better suited for humbling itself than finding itself in truth—provided only that it does not dissemble, that there is no deceit in its spirit, that it sets itself before its own gaze and is not drawn away from itself. Does it not, looking at itself thus in the clear light of truth, find itself in a region of unlikeness? And, sighing miserably—for it can no longer hide from itself that it is truly miserable—will it not cry with the Prophet to the Lord: “In your truth [Col. 0970A] you have humbled me”? (Ps. 118:75).

For how will it not be truly humbled in this true knowledge of itself, when it perceives itself burdened with sins, weighed down by the mass of this mortal body, entangled in earthly cares, infected with the dregs of carnal desires, blind, bent, weak, involved in many errors, exposed to a thousand dangers, trembling amid a thousand fears, anxious amid a thousand difficulties, liable to a thousand suspicions, miserable amid a thousand necessities, prone to vices, and feeble for virtues? From where, then, can it have haughty eyes? From where can it raise its head?

Will it not rather turn in its misery while it is pierced by the thorn? (Ps. 31:4). It will turn, I say, to tears; it will turn to lamentation and groans; it will turn to the Lord; and in humility [Col. 0970B] it will cry: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5). But once turned to the Lord, it will receive consolation, because he is the Father of mercies and God of all consolation.

6. So long as I look into myself, my eye remains in bitterness. But if I look up and raise my eyes to the help of divine mercy, the joyful vision of God will at once temper the bitter vision of myself. To him I say: “My soul is troubled within me; therefore I shall remember you” (Ps. 41:7). Nor is it a slight vision of God to experience him as gracious and ready to be entreated, as he truly is kind, merciful, and “ready to relent from evil” (Joel 2:13)—for goodness is his nature, and it is proper to him always to have mercy and to spare.

[Col. 0970C] Thus God becomes known savingly through this experience and in this order: first, a human being knows oneself as placed in need; then one cries to the Lord, and he hears, saying: “I will deliver you, and you shall honor me” (Ps. 49:15). In this way, knowledge of yourself will be a step toward knowledge of God. And he will be seen from his image, renewed in you, while you, beholding the Lord’s glory with unveiled face and confidence, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18).

7. But now at last observe how each knowledge is necessary for your salvation, so that you cannot lack either of them and retain salvation. For if you do not know yourself, you will not have the fear of God within you, nor humility. But whether you presume upon salvation without the fear of God and without humility, you may judge. You did well to signify by your grunting that you think nothing of the kind—indeed, that you are not so foolish as that—so that we need not linger over what is obvious. But attend to what remains. Or should we rather pause on account of the sleepy? I thought I should fulfil in one discourse what I had promised concerning the twofold ignorance; and I would have done so, had it not seemed too long for the fastidious. For I see some yawning and others even sleeping. Nor is this surprising: the vigils of the preceding night—very long, indeed—excuse them.

> [Note: Col. 0969D. Thus he calls what we term the office of Matins, in accordance with the mind of St Benedict.]

But what shall I say of those who slept then and nonetheless sleep now? Yet I will not go on further to shame them now; it is enough to have touched upon it. I think that hereafter they will keep better watch, fearing the cautery of our observation. In this hope, we indulge them on this occasion; and, though the argument remains unfinished, we divide what reason required to be continued out of charity toward them, making an end where there was no end. Let them, for the indulgence shown them, glorify with us the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVII. On the twofold knowledge and the twofold ignorance, and on the evils or losses which they produce.

1. I think we now have no need to exhort you to wakefulness, since that stinging discourse is doubtless still awake—being still fresh—which we delivered yesterday in charity and which thoroughly roused some people. You remember, then, that I hold your agreement that no one is saved without knowledge of himself. From this knowledge arise humility, the mother of salvation, and the fear of the Lord, which is both the beginning of wisdom and likewise of salvation. No one, I say, is saved without that knowledge, provided that he has the age and capacity for knowing. I say this because of little children and the mentally incapable, whose case is different.

But what if you do not know God? Can there be hope of salvation with ignorance of God? Not even then. For you can neither love one whom you do not know, nor possess one whom you have not loved. Know yourself, therefore, that you may fear God; know him, that you may equally appease him. In the one knowledge you are initiated into wisdom; in the other you are perfected, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10), and “love is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. 13:10). Thus you must avoid both ignorances, just as salvation cannot exist without the fear and love of God. All other things are indifferent: whether known, they bring no salvation; whether unknown, no condemnation.

2. Yet I do not say that the learning of letters should be despised or neglected. It adorns the soul, instructs it, and makes it able to instruct others also. But those two things ought, and it is advantageous, to come first—the things in which the preceding reasoning showed that the sum of salvation consists. See whether he who said this did not both discern and teach this order: “Sow for yourselves unto righteousness; reap the hope of life; and then at last,” he says, “make for yourselves the light of knowledge shine” (Hos. 10:12). He placed knowledge last, like a painting that cannot stand upon emptiness; and therefore he first set forth those two things and subjected knowledge to them, as though laying some solid ground beneath a picture.

I may now safely apply myself to knowledge, if I have first received, through the benefit of hope, security of life. You therefore have sown for yourself unto righteousness if, from true self-knowledge, you have awakened to fear God, humbled yourself, shed tears, poured out alms, devoted yourself to the other works of piety; if you have afflicted your body with fasts and vigils, wearied your breast with beatings and heaven with cries. This indeed is to sow unto righteousness. Good works and good pursuits are seeds; tears are seeds. “They went forth,” he says, “and wept, scattering their seeds.” But what? Shall they always weep? Far from it. “They shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:6). Rightly with rejoicing, when they bring back sheaves of glory.

You say: “This will happen at the resurrection on the last day, and the waiting is exceedingly long.” Do not be broken in spirit; do not fail through faintness of heart. Meanwhile you have, from the firstfruits of the Spirit, something that you reap now in rejoicing. “Sow for yourselves unto righteousness; reap the hope of life.” He does not send you merely to the last day, when the thing will already be possessed and no longer hoped for; he speaks of the present. Great joy indeed, and abundant, exceeding exultation, come when life comes.

3. But will the hope of such great joy exist without joy? “Rejoicing in hope,” says the Apostle (Rom. 12:12). And David said not that he would rejoice, but that he had rejoiced because he hoped to go into the house of the Lord (Ps. 121:1). He did not yet possess life, but he had certainly reaped the hope of life; and in himself he experienced the truth of Scripture’s testimony that not only the reward but even the expectation of the righteous is joy.

This joy is produced in the mind of one who has sown for himself unto righteousness by the presumed forgiveness of sins—provided that the effectiveness of grace received bears witness to that forgiveness by a holier life thereafter. Everyone among you who feels these things being wrought within him knows what the Spirit says, whose voice and operation never disagree with one another. Therefore he understands what is said, because he feels inwardly what he hears outwardly. For the Spirit who speaks in us and works in you is one and the same Spirit, “distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11): to some, indeed, the gift of speaking; to others, that of doing what is good.

4. Therefore, whoever among you, after those bitter and tearful beginnings of conversion, rejoices that he has drawn breath into hope and, lifted on the wings of grace, flown forth into a certain clear serenity of heavenly consolation—such a person is already reaping, receiving the temporal fruit of his tears; and he has seen God and heard the voice saying: “Give her of the fruit of her hands” (Prov. 31:31). For how has he not seen God who has “tasted and seen that the Lord is sweet”? How sweet and gracious he has found you, Lord Jesus, he to whom you have not only forgiven sins, but also granted the gift of holiness; and not this alone, but, to crown these goods, have besides added the promise of eternal life!

Blessed is he who has already reaped so much, having for the present his fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life! Rightly, he who wept when he found himself rejoiced when he saw the Lord; at the sight of whose mercy he has now raised so many sheaves: forgiveness, sanctification, and the hope of life. O how true is the saying read in the Prophet: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in rejoicing” (Ps. 125:5). Here both kinds of knowledge are briefly comprised: knowledge of ourselves, sowing in tears; and knowledge of God, reaping in joy.

5. Therefore, when this twofold knowledge goes before us, whatever knowledge may further grow up in us does not puff us up, since it can bring nothing of earthly advantage or honour that is not plainly inferior to the hope conceived and to the joy of hope now more deeply rooted in the soul. “Hope does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). It does not put to shame because this love imparts certainty. For through it the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God (Rom. 8:16). What, then, can come to us from however great our learning that is not less than this glory, by which we are numbered among God’s children? I have said too little: even the world itself and its fullness cannot be regarded in comparison with it, even if the whole world should fall to any one of us as a possession.

But if ignorance of God holds us, how do we hope in one whom we do not know? If ignorance of ourselves holds us, how shall we be humble, while thinking ourselves something when we are nothing? And we know that neither the proud nor the despairing have part or fellowship in the lot of the saints.

6. Consider with me now how great the care and concern with which we ought to drive away from ourselves these two ignorances, of which one produces the beginning of every sin, the other its completion. Conversely, of the two kinds of knowledge one produces the beginning of wisdom, the other its perfection: the former, fear of the Lord; the latter, love. This concerning knowledge has been shown above. Now observe it concerning ignorance. For just as “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Sir. 1:16), so “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Sir. 10:15); and just as the love of God claims for itself the perfection of wisdom, so despair claims for itself the completion of all wickedness. And just as from knowledge of yourself the fear of God comes into you, and likewise from knowledge of God the love of God, so, conversely, from ignorance of yourself comes pride, and from ignorance of God comes despair.

Ignorance of yourself gives birth to pride in you when your thought—deceived and itself deceiving—lies to you that you are better than you are. For this is pride, and this the beginning of every sin: when you are greater in your own eyes than before God and than in truth. Therefore, concerning the first who sinned this great sin—I speak of the devil—it was said that “he did not stand in the truth, but is a liar from the beginning” (John 8:44), because what he was in his own thought, he was not in truth.

What if he had differed from the truth by thinking himself lesser and more lowly than truth held him to be? His ignorance would undoubtedly have excused him, and he would not at all have been reckoned proud; perhaps humility would have found favour rather than his iniquity being discovered for hatred. For if we clearly knew in what state God holds each of us, we ought neither to move above nor fall below that state, acquiescing in truth in all things.

> [Note: Col. 0973. This is a notable conception of humility, whose rationale consists in truth itself. Compare Sermon 20 *On Various Subjects*.]

But now, because “he has made darkness his hiding-place” and the word is hidden from us, so that no one knows “whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Eccl. 9:1), it is surely more just and safer, in accordance with the counsel of Truth himself, to choose for ourselves the lowest place, from which we may afterwards be brought up higher with honour, than to presume upon a higher place, from which we must soon withdraw in shame (Luke 14:10, 9).

7. Therefore there is no danger, however much you humble yourself, however much you judge yourself less than you are—that is, less than truth holds you to be. But it is a great evil and a dreadful danger if you exalt yourself even a little above the truth: if, that is, you prefer yourself in your thought to even one person whom perhaps truth judges your equal or even your superior. For just as, if you pass through a doorway whose lintel, to speak figuratively, is excessively low, it does no harm however far you stoop; but it does harm if you raise yourself even by the breadth of a finger beyond what the doorway permits, so that you strike against it and are dashed with a wounded head—so in the soul no degree of humiliation is to be feared, whereas the slightest rashly presumed elevation is dreadful and greatly to be feared.

Therefore, man, do not compare yourself with those greater than you; do not compare yourself with those lesser than you; do not compare yourself with anyone—not even with one person. For what do you know, O man? Perhaps this one whom you regard as the vilest and most wretched of all, whose life you abhor as most criminal and uniquely foul, and whom for that reason you think contemptible not merely in comparison with yourself—who perhaps already trust that you live soberly, justly, and piously—but even in comparison with all other criminals, as the most criminal of all: what do you know, I say, whether by a change effected by the right hand of the Most High he will be better than you and them in himself hereafter, but already is so in God?

For this reason he did not command us to choose a place that was merely not middling, or even next-to-last, or at least among the lowest; rather, “recline,” he says, “in the lowest place,” so that you may sit alone as the very last of all, and may dare neither—I do not say—to put yourself before anyone, nor even to compare yourself with anyone. See how great an evil comes from ignorance of ourselves: namely, the devil’s sin and the beginning of every sin, pride. What ignorance of God likewise brings forth we shall see another time. For the brevity of the hour does not permit it now, since we assembled late today. Let it suffice, then, that each person has now been admonished not to be ignorant of himself, not only by our discourse but also by the condescension of the Bridegroom of the Church himself, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVIII. How despair is born from ignorance of God, and how the Bride is called beautiful among women.

1. What, then, does ignorance of God bring forth? For this is where we must begin, as you remember that yesterday’s discussion ended here. What, then, does it bring forth? We said despair; let us now say how. Perhaps someone, returning to himself and displeased with himself in all the evils he has done, considers repenting and returning from every evil way and from his carnal manner of life. If he does not know how good God is, how kind and gentle, and how abundant in forgiveness, will not his carnal thought rebuke him and say:

“What are you doing? Do you wish to lose both this life and the life to come? Your sins are enormous and exceedingly numerous. You will by no means suffice to make satisfaction for so many and such great sins, even if you flay yourself. Your constitution is weak, your life has been luxurious, and you will overcome habit only with difficulty.”

Because of these and similar thoughts, the miserable man, in despair, recoils, not knowing how easily almighty Goodness—who, alternatively, the Almighty One—willing that no one should perish, could dissolve all these obstacles. Impenitence follows, which is the greatest sin and unforgivable blasphemy. Or he is overwhelmed and swallowed up by excessive sorrow, and carried down into the abyss, never to emerge so as to receive consolation, as it is written: “When the wicked man comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). Or else, disguising matters and flattering himself with some plausible argument, he irrevocably calls himself back into the world, to enjoy and delight in all its goods as long as he may. But “when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction shall come upon them, as travail upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape” (1 Thess. 5:3). Thus from ignorance of God comes also the completion of all wickedness, which is despair.

2. The Apostle says that some “have ignorance of God” (1 Cor. 15:34). But I say that all who refuse to turn to God are ignorant of God. For beyond doubt they refuse for no other reason than that they imagine him burdensome and severe, though he is loving; harsh and implacable, though he is merciful; savage and terrible, though he is lovable. Thus iniquity lies to itself, fashioning for itself an idol in place of what he is not.

Why do you of little faith fear? That he will not wish to forgive sins? But he fastened them to the cross with his own hands. That you are frail and delicate? But he knows our frame. That you are badly habituated and bound by the custom of sinning? But “the Lord sets the fettered free” (Ps. 145:7). Or perhaps you fear that, angered by the enormity and multitude of your crimes, he will hesitate to stretch out a helping hand? But “where sin abounded, grace has been accustomed to abound still more” (Rom. 5:20). Are you anxious about clothing, food, and the other necessities of your body, and therefore hesitate to leave what is yours? But he knows that you need all these things (Matt. 6:25–32).

What more do you want? What now prevents salvation? But this is what I say: you do not know God, and you do not believe our report. I wish that you would at least believe those who have experienced it; for unless you believe, you will not understand. But faith is not everyone’s.

3. Yet far be it from us to suppose that the Bride is warned about such ignorance—that is, ignorance of God. She has been granted such knowledge, indeed not merely knowledge but friendship and familiarity, with her Bridegroom and God, that she has deserved his frequent conversations and kisses, and now speaks with familiar boldness: “Tell me where you pasture, where you lie down at noon” (Cant. 1:6–7). Here she asks to be told, not himself, but the place where his glory dwells, although he himself, his place, and his glory are not different things.

But she is judged deserving of rebuke for presumption and must be reminded of self-knowledge, in which she evidently seemed to be somewhat clouded, since she thought herself fit for so great a vision—whether because, in her ecstasy, she attended too little to the fact that she was in the body, or because she vainly hoped that, while still remaining in the body, she could approach that inaccessible brightness. Therefore she is immediately recalled to herself, convicted of ignorance, and chastened for presumption. “If you do not know yourself,” he says, “go forth” (Cant. 1:6–7). The Bridegroom thunders terribly at his beloved, not as a bridegroom but as a teacher; and not as if angry, but so that, frightened, she might be purified, and, purified, be made fit for the very vision for which she longs. For that vision is reserved for the pure in heart.

4. Beautifully, moreover, he calls her beautiful—not beautiful in every respect, but “beautiful among women”: that is, with a distinction. By this also she may be more fully checked and know what she lacks. For I think that by the name “women” in this place are meant carnal and worldly souls, having nothing manly in themselves, displaying perhaps nothing strong or steadfast in their actions, but living and doing everything lax, feminine, and soft.

A spiritual soul, however, although already beautiful in that it walks not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit, nevertheless, because it still lives in the body, has not yet attained perfect beauty. Accordingly, it is not beautiful in every respect, but beautiful among women—that is, among earthly souls that are not spiritual as it is—not, however, among angelic blessednesses, virtues, powers, and dominions.

Just as one of the fathers of old was found and called “righteous in his generation” (Gen. 6:9), that is, above all those of his time and generation; and Tamar is said to have been justified “from Judah” (Gen. 38:26), that is, above Judah; and in the Gospel the tax collector is reported to have gone down from the temple justified, but justified in comparison with the Pharisee (Luke 18:14); and just as the great John was once magnificently commended because he had no superior—but this was “among those born of women” (Luke 7:28), not among the choirs of blessed heavenly spirits—so the Bride is now called beautiful, but for the present only beautiful among women, and not among the heavenly blessednesses.

5. Therefore, while she is on earth, let her cease inquisitively investigating what belongs to heaven, lest one who scrutinizes majesty be overwhelmed by glory. Let her cease, I say, while she lives among women, from inquiring into what belongs to those exalted powers, things perceptible only to them and lawful only to them, as heavenly things are to be seen by heavenly beings.

This vision which you ask to have shown you, O Bride, has become wonderful beyond you; for you are not yet able to behold the noonday and wondrous brightness in which I dwell. For you said: “Tell me where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.” But to be brought into the clouds, to penetrate the fullness of light, to burst into the abysses of brightness, and to dwell in inaccessible light—this belongs neither to the present time nor to the body. It is reserved for you at the last, when I shall present you to myself glorious, “not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing.”

Do you not know that, as long as you live in this body, you are a pilgrim away from the light? How do you, who are not yet wholly beautiful, think yourself fit to contemplate the totality of beauty? How, finally, do you seek to see me in my brightness while you still do not know yourself? For if you knew yourself more fully, you would surely know that, burdened by a corruptible body, you could in no way lift up your eyes and fix them upon that splendour into which angels desire to look.

It shall be, when I appear, that you will be wholly beautiful, as I am wholly beautiful; and, made most like me, you will see me as I am. Then you will hear: “You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no spot in you” (Cant. 4:7). But now, although in part already like me, in part you are still unlike me: be content to know in part. Attend to yourself, and “do not seek things higher than yourself, nor search out things stronger than yourself” (Sir. 3:22). Otherwise, if you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women (Cant. 1:7)—for I too call you beautiful, but among women, that is, in part; but “when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 13:10)—if, therefore, you do not know yourself; but what follows has already been said and need not be said again.

I had promised to discuss the twofold ignorance usefully. If I seem not to have fulfilled this promise, grant pardon to one who is willing. For “to will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish,” except insofar as the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever, deigns in his goodness to grant it for your edification. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIX. On Pharaoh’s chariots—that is, the devil’s—and the princes of his army, who are Malice, Lust, and Avarice.

1. “I have compared you, my friend, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots” (Cant. 1:8). Above all, in these words we gladly receive the fact that the type of the Church went beforehand in the fathers, and that the sacraments of our salvation were prefigured. In Israel’s departure from Egypt and in that twofold service of the wondrous sea—giving passage to the people and vengeance upon their enemies—the grace of baptism is clearly expressed: it saves human beings and drowns their sins. “All,” he says, “were under the cloud, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10:1–2).

But we must, as is our custom, mark the sequence of the words and join what follows to what precedes; and then, if we can, draw out something sweet that profits the instruction of conduct. Therefore, when the Bride’s presumption had been checked with a hard and stern rebuke, lest she remain too sad, some good things already received are recalled to her memory and some things not yet received are promised to her. She is again called beautiful and named friend. “Though I spoke harshly to you, my friend, do not suspect hatred or resentment in me toward you. The evident signs of my love for you are the very gifts by which I honoured and adorned you. I do not intend to withdraw them, but rather to add greater things.

“Or thus: Do not take it ill, my friend, that you do not now receive what you ask, since you have already received so much from me; and you shall receive greater things than these if you walk in my commandments and persevere in my love.” This is the sequence according to the letter.

2. Now let us see what the things are which he recalls having given her. First, he compared her to his cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots: that is, by freeing her from the yoke of sin and putting to death all works of the flesh, just as that people was freed from Egyptian slavery when all Pharaoh’s chariots were overthrown and submerged (Exod. 14:28). This indeed is the greatest mercy, in which I too, if I wish to glory, do not speak foolishly; for I shall speak the truth. I confess and shall confess: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul had almost dwelt in hell” (Ps. 93:17). I am not ungrateful; I have not forgotten: “I shall sing the mercies of the Lord for ever” (Ps. 88:1).

But so far I am with the Bride. Thereafter, by a singular act of condescension, once freed she is admitted as a friend; she is clothed with beauty as the Lord’s Bride, though meanwhile only in cheeks and neck. Then little necklaces are promised her for adornment, made of gold for their value and marked with silver for their beauty. Who would not be greatly pleased by the order of these gifts? First, she is mercifully freed; second, she is graciously loved; third, she is kindly washed and cleansed; finally, she receives the promise of most excellent ornament.

3. I do not doubt that some of you already recognize in yourselves what is being said and, admonished by your own experience, hasten ahead to understand it. Yet, mindful of that verse, “The unfolding of your words gives light and gives understanding to the little ones” (Ps. 118:130), I judge it fitting to explain these matters somewhat more fully for such persons. For the Spirit of wisdom is gracious (Wis. 1:6), and he is pleased by a teacher who is gracious and diligent, who desires to satisfy the eager in such a way that he does not refuse to accommodate the slower. Indeed Wisdom herself says: “Those who make me clear shall have eternal life” (Sir. 24:31); and I would not wish to be deprived of that reward. Moreover, even in things that seem plain, matters sometimes lie hidden which it will not be useless to explain more carefully even to those who seem more capable and swift in intellect.

4. But now observe the comparison involving Pharaoh and his army, and the Lord’s cavalry. The comparison is not made between the armies themselves, but from them. For what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what share has the believer with the unbeliever? But there is indeed a comparison between the holy and spiritual soul and the Lord’s cavalry, and between Pharaoh and the devil, and their respective armies.

Nor will you wonder that one soul is compared to a host of cavalry if you consider how many battle-lines of virtues are present in that one soul, provided it is holy; how much order in its affections, how much discipline in its conduct, how much armour in its prayers, how much strength in its actions, how much terror in its zeal, and, finally, how unceasing its conflicts with the enemy and how numerous its triumphs. Thus we read later: “Terrible as an army arrayed in battle” (Cant. 6:3); and again: “What will you see,” he says, “in the Shulammite, but the choirs of armies?” (Cant. 7:1).

Or, if this does not please you, know that such a soul is never without the guardianship of angels. They are jealous for her with God’s jealousy, anxious to preserve her for her husband and to present a chaste virgin to Christ. And do not say in your heart, “Where are they? Who has seen them?” The prophet Elisha saw them and, moreover, by prayer caused Gehazi also to see them (4 Kgs. 6:16–17). You do not see them because you are neither a prophet nor the servant of a prophet. The patriarch Jacob saw them and said: “These are the camps of God” (Gen. 32:2). The teacher of the nations also saw them, who said: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to minister for those who shall inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14).

5. Therefore, upheld by angelic ministries and surrounded by a heavenly host, the Bride as she proceeds is like the Lord’s cavalry—the cavalry which once triumphed among Pharaoh’s chariots by so astonishing a miracle of divine help. For if you attend carefully, you will find no less worthy of wonder here all that you admire as magnificently accomplished there. Except that the triumph is now more glorious, because what was there prefigured bodily is here fulfilled spiritually.

Does it not seem to you far stronger and more glorious to cast down the devil than Pharaoh, and to defeat aerial powers than to overthrow Pharaoh’s chariots? There the struggle was against flesh and blood; here it is “against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). Now follow with me each element of the correspondence. There the people is brought out of Egypt; here the human being is brought out of the world. There Pharaoh is cast down; here the devil. There Pharaoh’s chariots are overthrown; here carnal and worldly desires, which wage war against the soul, are overthrown. Those are in the waves; these in weeping: those seawaters, these bitter tears.

I think that even now demons cry out, should they happen upon such a soul: “Let us flee from Israel, because the Lord fights for him” (Exod. 14:25). Would you like me also to point out to you by their proper names some of Pharaoh’s princes and describe their chariots, so that, after their pattern, you yourself may be able to discover any others there may be? Malice is certainly a great prince of the spiritual and invisible king of Egypt; Lust is great; Avarice is great. These possess their respective territories under their king, as each has been assigned. For Malice rules in every region of evil deeds and crimes; Lust presides over every uncleanness and shamefulness of the flesh; Avarice has received as its province the rule over plunder and fraud.

6. Hear now what chariots Pharaoh has prepared for these his princes in pursuit of God’s people. Malice has a chariot consisting of four wheels: Cruelty, Impatience, Audacity, and Shamelessness. This chariot is indeed very swift in shedding blood: innocence does not halt it, patience does not delay it, fear does not check it, shame does not restrain it. It is drawn by two exceedingly fleet horses, most ready for every ruin: earthly Power and worldly Pomp. For this four-horse chariot of malice runs very swiftly when, on the one hand, the resources of power are available to carry out malicious designs; and, on the other, the applause of pomp smiles upon crimes committed, so that the saying written may be fulfilled: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked is blessed” (Ps. 9:3); and again another Scripture: “This,” it says, “is your hour, and the power of darkness” (Luke 22:52).

Two charioteers preside over these two horses: Arrogance and Envy. Arrogance drives pomp; envy drives power. For he is carried headlong by love of diabolical displays whose heart has first swollen within him. A heart firmly standing under the constraint of fear, modest through seriousness, secure in humility, and sound in purity, is not lightly carried away by the breeze of this vanity. Likewise, is not the beast of earthly power driven by envy and, as it were, spurred on all sides by the goads of spite—namely, suspicion of being displaced and fear of being overthrown? For a successor is one thing that is suspected; an invader is another thing that is feared. By these spurs earthly power is continually driven. Such, then, is the chariot of Malice.

7. The chariot of Lust likewise rolls upon a four-horse team of vices: Gluttony of the belly, Lust of intercourse, Softness of clothing, and Dissolution in idleness and sleep. It is drawn by two horses likewise: Prosperity in life and Abundance of possessions. Two drivers preside over these: the Torpor of sloth and treacherous Security. For abundance loosens into sloth, and, according to Scripture, “the prosperity of fools shall destroy them” (Prov. 1:32), for no other reason than that it renders them wrongly secure: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction shall come upon them” (1 Thess. 5:3).

They have no spurs, whips, or anything of that kind; instead, they use a canopy to make shade and a fan to stir the wind.

> [Note: Col. 0979. In most printed editions there is added “a little butterfly,” but this is a marginal gloss in the manuscripts.]

The canopy is Dissimulation, making shade and protecting from the heat of cares. For it is characteristic of a soft and delicate soul to conceal even necessary cares, and, lest it feel burning anxieties, to hide beneath the shelter of dissimulation. The fan, however, is Extravagance, bringing the breeze of flattery. For the luxurious are lavish, buying with gold the breath from flatterers’ mouths. And enough on this matter.

8. Avarice in turn is borne on four wheels of vices: Faintheartedness, Inhumanity, Contempt of God, and Forgetfulness of death. Its draught animals are Tenacity and Rapacity; and one charioteer presides over both: Ardour for Possession. For Avarice alone, because it does not permit the hiring of more servants, is content with a single attendant. But he is an exceedingly prompt and tireless executor of the task entrusted to him; in driving the beasts, he uses most sharp whips: Desire of Acquiring and Fear of Losing.

9. There are also other princes of the king of Egypt, who likewise have their own chariots in their lord’s expedition: such as Pride, one of the greater princes; and Impiety, the enemy of faith, which likewise holds a great place in Pharaoh’s house and kingdom. There are still many other satraps and horsemen of lower rank, whose number in Pharaoh’s army is beyond counting. Their names and functions, and likewise their arms and equipment, I leave for your study, that you may exercise yourselves in these matters.

By the strength of these princes and their chariots, the invisible Pharaoh roams everywhere and, after the manner of a tyrant, rages with all his power against every household of the Lord; even in these days he pursues Israel as it comes out of Egypt. But Israel, neither borne upon chariots nor defended by arms, yet strengthened by the Lord’s hand alone, sings securely: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. 15:1); and again: “These in chariots and those on horses, but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. 19:8). Let this suffice concerning the comparison introduced between the Lord’s cavalry and Pharaoh’s chariots.

[Col. 0981C] 10. After this she is called a friend. For he was indeed a friend even before her deliverance; otherwise he would not have delivered one whom he had not loved. But by the benefit of deliverance she was brought to become a friend. Hear her confessing at last: “Not because we loved him,” she says, “but he first loved us” (1 John 4:10). Recall now for me Moses and the Ethiopian woman, and recognize that the marriage of the Word and the sinful soul was already prefigured there; and discern, if you can, what tastes sweeter to you in contemplating this most sweet mystery: the exceedingly gracious condescension of the Word, the inestimable glory of the soul, or the sinner’s unexpected confidence. But Moses could not change the Ethiopian woman’s skin; Christ could. For what follows is: “Your cheeks are lovely, like those of a dove.” But let this be reserved for another discourse, so that, always eagerly receiving what is set before us at the Bridegroom’s table, we may pour it forth in praise and glory of him, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XL. That intention is the face of the soul: what its beauty or deformity is; and what its solitude and boldness are.

1. “Your cheeks are lovely, like those of a turtle-dove” (Song 1:9). Tender is the Bride’s modesty; and, at the Bridegroom’s rebuke, I suppose that her face was suffused with blushes and appeared all the lovelier for it. At once she hears: “Your cheeks are lovely, like those of a turtle-dove.” But take care not to think carnally of the colour of decaying flesh, or of the discharge of yellow or bloody fluid lightly and evenly spread across the surface of translucent skin; when these are moderately mingled with one another, a pale-red blush is tempered into an effect of bodily beauty, to make the form of the cheeks attractive. That incorporeal and invisible substance of the soul, however, is neither marked out by bodily limbs nor coloured with visible hues.

Rather, if you can, grasp spiritual essence with spiritual sight; and, in order to fit the proposed comparison, consider the soul’s face to be the intention of the mind. For the rectitude of an action is judged from intention, just as bodily beauty is judged from the face. Understand modesty, moreover, as colour in the face, since this virtue especially imparts loveliness and increases grace. Thus, “Your cheeks are lovely, like those of a turtle-dove.” He might more ordinarily have said “face,” and described it as lovely, as one whose beauty is praised is customarily said to have a beautiful or comely face. But I do not know why he preferred to speak of “cheeks” in the plural, unless indeed I am to believe that this is by no means without purpose. For it is the Spirit of wisdom who speaks, and it is not permissible to attribute to him anything whatever, however slight, that is idle or said otherwise than it ought to be. There is therefore undoubtedly some reason, whatever it may be, why he preferred plural “cheeks” to singular “face.” If you have nothing better, I shall set forth what seems to me.

2. Two things are necessarily required in intention, which we have called the soul’s face: the thing and the cause—that is, what you intend and for what reason. Indeed, from these two the soul’s beauty or deformity is judged. Thus, for example, a soul which possesses both of these upright and modest may deservedly and truly be told: “Your cheeks are lovely, like those of a turtle-dove.” For no blemish deserving censure appears on either cheek. But if it lacks one of these two, it cannot be said of it that its cheeks are lovely like those of a turtle-dove, because of the deformity which remains in part. Much less can this apply to one found to possess neither of them in a praiseworthy form.

This will become clearer from examples. If, for instance, someone directs his mind to seeking truth, and does so solely from love of truth, does he not seem to you to have both an honourable object and an honourable cause, and rightly to claim for himself the words: “Your cheeks are lovely, like those of a dove”? For no blemish of blame appears on either of his cheeks. But if he turns toward truth not from desire for truth at all, but under the pretext either of vain glory or of some other temporal advantage, then, although he may seem to have one lovely cheek, you will nevertheless, I think, not hesitate to judge him deformed in part, since the baseness of his motive has disfigured his other face. But if you see a person pursuing no honourable endeavour, ensnared by fleshly pleasures, given over to the belly and to luxury—such as those “whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame, who savour earthly things” (Phil. 3:19)—what of him? Will you not judge him utterly foul on both sides, since in his intention both the object and the cause are found reprehensible?

[Col. 0983A] 3. Therefore, to direct one’s intention not toward God but toward the world belongs to a worldly soul, one that has no lovely cheek at all. To direct one’s intention, as it were, toward God, but not for God’s sake, plainly belongs to the hypocrite’s soul. Though one side of its face may seem comely, because it looks toward God with some sort of intention, yet that very pretence destroys all beauty in it and instead brings ugliness throughout it.

But if a person directs his intention to God only, or chiefly, for the necessities of this present life, then it is not foul with the stench of hypocrisy, but we call it somewhat darkened by the vice of faintheartedness and less acceptable. Conversely, to direct one’s intention toward something other than God, yet for God’s sake, is not Mary’s leisure but Martha’s work. Far be it from me to say that such a soul has anything deformed in it! Yet I would not affirm that it has attained perfect beauty: for it is still anxious and troubled about many things, and cannot avoid being sprinkled with even the light dust of earthly activities. Yet a chaste intention and the testimony of a good conscience toward God will quickly and easily wipe this away, even at the hour of holy death.

Therefore, to seek God alone for his own sake alone—this is truly to have both faces of the twofold intention most beautiful. This is the Bride’s particular and distinctive property; and it is fitting that, by a singular prerogative, she should hear: “Your cheeks are lovely, like those of a turtle-dove.”

4. But why “like those of a turtle-dove”? The turtle-dove is a chaste little bird, and is said to be content to live not among many but with one mate alone; if it loses that mate, it seeks no other but thereafter lives alone. Therefore you who hear these things—so that you may not hear idly what was written for your sake and is now handled and discussed for your sake—you, I say, if you are moved by such promptings of the Holy Spirit and burn to labour at making your soul God’s bride, strive to have both cheeks of your intention beautiful. As an imitator of that most chaste bird, sit alone, according to the prophet, “because you have lifted yourself above yourself” (Lam. 3:28).

It is altogether above you to be betrothed to the Lord of angels. Is it not above you to cling to God and be one spirit with him? Sit, then, alone like the turtle-dove. Let there be nothing between you and crowds, nothing between you and the multitude of others; indeed, “forget also your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty” (Ps. 44:11–12). O holy soul, be alone, that you may keep yourself for him alone, whom you have chosen for yourself from among all others. Flee the public throng; flee even those of your own household. Withdraw from friends and intimates, and even from the one who ministers to you. Do you not know that you have a modest Bridegroom, one who by no means wishes to grant you his presence while others are present?

Withdraw, therefore—but in mind, not in body; in intention, devotion, and spirit. For Christ the Lord is spirit before your face, and he seeks solitude of spirit, not of body—although at times you also separate yourself bodily not without purpose, when you can suitably do so, especially at the time of prayer. In this you have both the Bridegroom’s command and his example: “But when you pray,” he says, “enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray” (Matt. 6:6). What he said, he did. He spent the night alone in prayer, hiding himself not merely from crowds but admitting none at all of his disciples or household servants (Luke 6:12–13). Finally, when he was voluntarily hastening toward death, he had brought with him three intimates, but even from them he withdrew in order to pray (Matt. 26:37–39). Do likewise, then, whenever you wish to pray.

5. Beyond this, solitude of mind and spirit is prescribed for you. You are alone if you do not think common thoughts, do not desire present things, despise what many admire, disdain what all desire, avoid quarrels, do not feel losses, and do not remember injuries. Otherwise, even if you are bodily alone, you are not alone. Do you see that you can be alone while among many, and among many while alone? You are alone amid whatever multitude of people you may live, provided only that you take care not to be either a curious investigator or a rash judge of another’s conduct.

Even if you discover that something has been wrongly done, do not therefore judge your neighbour; rather, excuse him. Excuse his intention, if you cannot excuse the deed; suppose ignorance, suppose surprise, suppose accident. But if the certainty of the matter wholly refuses every such extenuation, nevertheless persuade yourself and say within yourself: “The temptation was exceedingly severe. What would it have done to me, if it had likewise obtained power over me?” Remember that I am now speaking to the Bride, not instructing the Bridegroom’s friend. For he has a different obligation: to take more careful care that no one sins, to investigate whether someone has sinned, and to correct him if he has sinned. From this necessity the Bride is free, living for herself alone and for him whom she loves, her Bridegroom and likewise her Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLI. How the Bride meanwhile receives great consolation from contemplation of divine brightness before she attains its clear vision.

1. “Your neck is like necklaces” (Song 1:9). A neck is customarily adorned with necklaces, not compared with them. But let those women do this who, because they have no beauty of their own, must borrow elsewhere the means by which they pretend to be beautiful. The Bride’s neck, however, is so beautiful in itself and so becomingly formed, as if by nature, that it seeks no ornament from without. For what need has one, whose own and, as it were, inborn beauty is sufficient, to apply the artificial colours of foreign adornment—so sufficient, indeed, that it can equal the brilliance of those necklaces which are sought for ornament?

This, surely, is what he meant when he said not that necklaces hung from the neck, as usual, but rather that the neck itself was like necklaces. We must now invoke the Holy Spirit, that, as by his gracious favour he enabled us to discover the Bride’s spiritual cheeks, so he may deign to reveal her spiritual neck as well. To my understanding—for it is my task to speak what I think—nothing meanwhile appears more likely or more plausible than that the soul’s understanding itself is denoted by the name “neck.” You too, I think, will approve this if you consider the logic of the comparison. Does not understanding seem in some manner to perform the office of a neck, through which your soul conveys vital nourishment of the spirit into itself and transfers it into, as it were, the inner organs of its dispositions and affections?

Thus the Bride’s neck—that is, pure and simple understanding—since it shines sufficiently of itself with naked and open truth, does not need ornament. Rather, like a precious necklace, it fittingly adorns the soul itself; and therefore it is described as resembling necklaces. Truth is a good necklace; purity or simplicity is a good necklace; to have sober understanding is plainly a good necklace. The understanding of philosophers or heretics has no such brightness of purity and truth within it; and therefore they take great care to colour and paint it with the trappings of words and the subtleties of syllogisms, lest, if it appeared naked, the ugliness of falsehood should appear as well.

2. It follows: “We will make for you golden ornaments, patterned with silver.” If he had said “I will make,” in the singular, rather than “we will make,” I should absolutely and without hesitation declare that the Bridegroom also speaks these words. But now take care lest we more fittingly assign them to his companions, as though they were consoling the Bride with this promise: until she attains the vision of him for whom she burns with such desire, they will make her lovely and precious ornaments—ornaments for the ears.

And this, I think, is because faith comes through hearing; and as long as we walk by faith and not by sight, care must be given to instructing hearing rather than to directing sight [variant: “exercising it”]. For the eye is directed in vain if it has not been cleansed by faith, since the power to see is promised only to those pure in heart (Matt. 5:8). Yet it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). Since, therefore, faith comes through hearing and sight is purified by faith, they rightly apply themselves to adorning the ears, while hearing, as reason has shown, is the preparation for sight.

“O Bride,” they say, “you yearn to behold the brightness of your Beloved; but that belongs to another time. For the present, however, we give ornaments to your ears. They will meanwhile be your consolation, and also your preparation for the very thing you ask—as though they said to her with the prophet: ‘Hear, O daughter, and see’ (Ps. 44:11). You desire to see, but hear first. Hearing is a step toward sight. Therefore hear, and incline your ear to the ornaments we make for you, so that through the obedience of hearing you may reach the glory of vision. We give joy and gladness to your hearing. For it is not ours to give to your sight—that in which there is fullness of joy and fulfilment of your desire—but belongs to him whom your soul loves. He himself, that your joy may be full, will show himself to you; he himself will fill you with gladness in his countenance. Meanwhile receive these ornaments from our hand as consolation; but delights are at his right hand for ever.”

3. Notice the kind of ornaments they offer her: “Golden,” he says, “and patterned with silver.” Gold is the splendour of divinity; gold is the wisdom which comes from above. With this gold those to whom this ministry belongs—the heavenly goldsmiths—promise to fashion certain shining marks, as it were, of truth, and to insert them into the inward ears of the soul. I think this is nothing other than weaving certain spiritual likenesses and bringing, in those likenesses, the utterly pure meanings of divine wisdom before the gaze of the contemplating soul, so that it may see, at least “through a mirror in an enigma,” what it is not yet able in any way to behold face to face.

These things are divine and utterly unknown except to those who have experienced them: namely, how, while still in this mortal body, while faith still has its place and the substance of clear light has not yet been disclosed, contemplation of pure truth may nevertheless already at times [variant: “meanwhile”] venture to perform its work within us, even if only in part. Thus one to whom this is granted from above may dare to appropriate the Apostle’s words: “Now I know in part”; likewise, “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13:12, 9).

But when something more divine has flashed swiftly, as in the speed of lightning, into the mind carried beyond itself in spirit, then—whether to temper excessive brightness or for the use of teaching—certain imaginative likenesses of lower things are immediately present, I know not whence, suitably adapted to the divinely infused meanings. By them that utterly pure and brilliant ray of truth is, as it were, shaded, so as to become more bearable for the soul itself and more capable of being communicated to those with whom it is intended to be shared. Yet I think that these likenesses are formed in us through the suggestions of holy angels, just as, conversely, there is no doubt that contrary and evil promptings are introduced through evil angels.

4. Perhaps this is the “mirror” and “enigma,” as I said, through which the Apostle saw (1 Cor. 5:12): fabricated, as it were, by the hands of angels from imaginings of this pure and beautiful kind. Thus we may understand that what is pure and seen without any phantasy of bodily images belongs to God; while we may attribute to angelic ministry any beautiful likeness in which it appears suitably clothed. Another translation seems to indicate this more expressly, saying: “We will make for you likenesses of gold, with markings of silver” (Song 1:10, according to the Septuagint).

“Markings of silver” and “patterned with silver” are one and the same. By this, it seems to me, he signifies not only that likenesses are suggested inwardly through angels, but also that the brightness of speech is supplied outwardly through them, so that, adorned suitably and becomingly, they may be more easily understood and more delightfully received by hearers. If you ask, “What have speech and silver to do with one another?” the prophet tells you: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11:7). Thus those heavenly ministering spirits make golden ornaments patterned with silver for the Bride who journeys upon earth.

5. Notice, however, how she desires one thing and receives another: while she strives for the repose of contemplation, the labour of preaching is imposed upon her; while she thirsts for the Bridegroom’s presence, the anxiety of bearing and nourishing the Bridegroom’s children is laid upon her. This does not happen to her only now. On another occasion, as I recall, when she sighed for the Bridegroom’s embraces and kisses, she was answered: “How much better are your breasts than wine” (Song 1:1), so that she might understand herself to be a mother and be recalled to give milk to little ones and nourish children. Perhaps, if you are not sluggish in searching, you may discover this same thing for yourself in other places of this Song.

Was not this matter once prefigured in the holy patriarch Jacob? Disappointed in his desired and long-awaited embraces of Rachel, he unwillingly and unknowingly received fruitful but bleary-eyed Leah instead of the barren and beautiful woman (Gen. 29:23, 23). Thus now, while the Bride wishes to know and asks where her Beloved feeds and rests at midday, she receives in return golden ornaments patterned with silver—that is, wisdom together with eloquence—undoubtedly for the work of preaching.

6. We are surely taught from this that sweet kisses must often be interrupted for the sake of nursing breasts, and that no one ought to live for himself but for all.

> [Note: [Col. 0987D] The earliest editions read: “but all ought to live for him who died for all.”]

Woe to those who have received the gift both of thinking and speaking well about God, if they regard piety as a means of gain; if they turn to vain glory what they received to distribute for God’s profit; if, thinking high things, they do not consent to the lowly. Let them fear what is read in the prophet, where the Lord says: “I gave them my gold and my silver, but they made Baal out of my silver and gold” (Hos. 2:8).

Hear then what the Bride, receiving rebuke on the one hand and promise on the other, answered. For she is neither puffed up by promises nor angered at refusal, but, as it is written, “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. 9:8); and likewise, concerning gifts and promises: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:20). Both points will become clearer from her answer. But, if you please, let the discussion of that answer be postponed to the beginning of another sermon; and let us glorify, for what has been said, the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLII. On two kinds of humility: one produced by truth, and the other kindled by charity.

1. “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1:11). These are the Bride’s words, which we postponed until today: this is the answer she gave when she was rebuked by the Bridegroom—not, however, to the Bridegroom, but to his companions. This is easily seen from the words themselves. For since she says not, as to the second person, “While you, the king, were at your table,” but “While the king was at his table,” it is clear that she speaks not to him but about him.

Suppose, then, that the Bridegroom, after reproving or restraining her as seemed fitting, perceived from the flushing of her cheeks her modesty, and withdrew so that in his absence she might speak more freely what she felt; and that, if she became more fearful than was fitting, as often happens, or too dejected in spirit, the consolations of his companions might raise her up. Yet he himself did not neglect to do this, insofar as he judged it suitable for the occasion. For, to make clear how much he was pleased by that rebuke—since he undoubtedly perceived that it had been received worthily and as it ought—he did not withdraw before he poured forth from the abundance of his heart into her praises and commended the beauty of her cheeks and neck. Therefore those who remain with her speak gently to her and offer gifts, knowing the Lord’s will. Her answer, then, is addressed to them. Such is the literal construction of the passage.

2. But before we begin to extract the kernel of the spirit from this shell, I shall say one thing briefly. Blessed is the person whose rebuke receives such an answer as we have in the present passage. Would that no one ever needed to be rebuked! That would be better. But since we all offend in many things, I may not be silent, since by office I am bound to rebuke sinners; indeed, charity presses me all the more.

But if I rebuke and do what is mine to do, while that rebuke, once issued, does not do what is its own work or accomplish that for which I sent it, but returns empty to me like a dart which strikes and rebounds—what state of mind do you think I am then in, brothers? Am I not distressed? Am I not tormented? And, that I may take something for myself from the words of the Master, though I cannot do so concerning my own wisdom:

> [Note: [Col. 0988D] Gemmet adds “my.”]

I am “hard pressed between the two” and do not know which to choose (Phil. 1:23, 22)—whether to be pleased with what I have said because I did what I ought, or to repent of my word because I did not obtain what I intended.

For I intended to destroy the enemy and rescue my brother; yet it did not happen so. Rather, the opposite occurred: I wounded a soul and increased its guilt, since contempt was added. “They will not hear you,” he says, “because they will not hear me” (Ezek. 3:7). You see what majesty is despised. Do not suppose that they have despised me alone. The Lord has spoken; and what he said to the prophet, he said also to the apostles: “He who despises you,” he says, “despises me” (Luke 10:16). I am not a prophet, I am not an apostle; yet I dare say that I fulfil the office of prophets and apostles. Though I am not their equal in merits, I am involved in their cares; and although it is to my great shame and great danger, I sit in Moses’ chair, though I neither claim Moses’ life for myself nor experience his grace. What then? Is honour not to be shown to the chair because it is occupied by one unworthy? Even if scribes and Pharisees sit in that seat, he says: “Do what they say” (Matt. 23:2–3).

3. Often impatience too is joined with contempt, so that someone not only does not care to be corrected when rebuked, but is also angry with the rebuker, like a madman repelling the physician’s hand. What astonishing perversity! He is angry with the one who treats him, though not angry with the one who shoots him! For there is one who “shoots in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. 10:3), and who has now shot you yourself to death; yet you are not moved against him? You are angry with me, who desire that you may become whole? “Be angry,” he says, “and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). If you are angry with sin, you not only do not sin at all, but you also destroy what you had sinned. But now, by rejecting the medicine, you retain the sin; and by being irrationally angry, you add sinning to sinning. Thus sin is sinning beyond measure.

4. At times shamelessness is added, so that a person not only bears impatiently the rebuke he receives, but shamelessly defends the very thing for which he is reproved. This is plainly despair. “You have become to me the forehead of a harlot; you refused to blush” (Jer. 3:3); and he says: “My zeal has departed from you; I shall be angry with you no longer” (Ezek. 16:42). I tremble at the very hearing of it. Do you perceive how dangerous, how dreadful and terrible, a thing the defence of sin is? Again he says: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3:19). Therefore, if zeal has abandoned you, love has too; nor will you be judged worthy of love if you are judged unworthy of chastisement.

You see that God is more angry when he is not angry. “Let the ungodly be shown mercy,” he says, “and he will not learn to do justice” (Isa. 26:10). I do not want this mercy. That compassion is worse than all wrath, hemming in for me the ways of justice. It is certainly better for me, according to the Prophet’s counsel, to “take hold of discipline, lest the Lord be angry and I perish from the righteous way” (Ps. 2:12). I want you to be angry with me, Father of mercies—but with the anger by which you correct one who has strayed, not that by which you drive him from the way. Your gracious correction produces the former for us; your dreadful forbearance nourishes the latter.

For when I know—not when I do not know—that you are angry, then I most confidently trust that you are merciful; for “when you are angry, you will remember mercy.” “God,” he says, “you were gracious to them, while avenging all their devices” (Ps. 98:8). He speaks of Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, whom he had just mentioned; and he calls it propitiation that God did not spare their transgressions. Go on, then: by defending error and accusing correction, shut this way out from yourself for ever. Is this not to call evil good and good evil? Will impenitence, the mother of despair, not immediately spring from this hateful shamelessness? For who repents of what he considers good? “Woe to them,” he says (Isa. 5:20). That woe is eternal.

It is one thing for a person to be drawn away and enticed by his own desire and thus tempted; another to seek evil voluntarily as though it were good, and to hurry to death as though to life in a false security. In such a case, I say, I would sometimes rather have been silent and overlooked what I discovered to be wrongly done than have rebuked it to such ruinous effect.

5. Perhaps you will tell me that my good returns to me, that I have delivered my soul, and that I am clean from the blood of the man to whom I announced and spoke, so that he might turn from his evil way and live. But even if you add countless things of that kind, they will not console me as I look upon the death of my son. As though I had sought my own deliverance by that rebuke, rather than his! What mother, even though she knows that she has given all possible care and attention to her sick son, if at last she sees herself frustrated and all her labour wholly ineffectual, would ever restrain her tears because he nevertheless dies? And she does this over temporal death. How much more, in the eternal death of my son, do abundant weeping and lamentation await me, even if I know of nothing by which I failed to warn him?

You see also from how great evils, conversely, the person saves both himself and us who answers rebuke gently, yields modestly, obeys humbly, and confesses with humility. To such a soul I profess myself a debtor in all things, its minister and servant, as to the most worthy Bride of my Lord, one who can truly say: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”

6. Good is the fragrance of humility, which rises from this valley of tears, scents all the surrounding regions, and sprinkles even the royal table with its pleasing sweetness. Nard is a lowly herb, and those who have investigated the powers of plants more carefully say that it is warm in nature. Therefore I think it not unsuitable to understand it here as the virtue of humility, but one that burns with the warmth of holy love. I say this because there is a humility which truth produces in us and which has no warmth; and there is a humility which charity forms and kindles. The latter lies in affection, the former in knowledge.

For if you examine yourself inwardly in the light of truth, without pretence, and judge yourself without flattery, I do not doubt that you too will be humbled in your own eyes, becoming more contemptible to yourself through this true knowledge of yourself, although perhaps you do not yet allow yourself to be so in the eyes of others. You will therefore be humble, but for the present by the work of truth, not yet by an infusion of love. For if, illuminated by the splendour of that very truth which has shown you yourself truly and beneficially to yourself, you had also been moved by its love, you would doubtless wish, so far as lies in you, that everyone should hold of you the same judgment which you know truth itself holds within you.

I say “so far as lies in you,” since it is often not expedient that all things we know about ourselves should become known to everyone; and the very love of truth and the truth of love forbid us to wish publicly disclosed what would harm the person who comes to know it. Otherwise, if held by private self-love you keep enclosed within yourself the judgment of truth, who can doubt that you love truth less, since you prefer either your own advantage or your own honour to it?

7. You see, then, that it is not the same thing for a person, convicted by the truth of light, no longer to think highly of himself, and, assisted by the gift of charity, voluntarily to consent to the lowly. The former belongs to necessity; the latter to will. “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7), and gave us the pattern of humility. He emptied himself; he humbled himself—not from the necessity of judgment, but from love for us. He could indeed show himself lowly and contemptible, but he could not judge himself to be so, since he knew himself.

Therefore he was humble by will, not by judgment: he presented himself as what he did not know himself to be.
