> [Note: [Col. 0991] Other editions read, “as what he did not know himself to be,” supplying “himself” from the next clause: that is, as what he understood himself not to be—namely, lowly and contemptible.]

Rather, he was pleased to be reckoned least, though he did not fail to know himself supreme. Finally, he says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). He said “of heart”—that is, by the affection of the heart, by will. Thus he excluded necessity by confessing will. For he was not like you or me, who find in truth that we deserve disgrace and contempt, every extremity and lowliness, even punishments and blows. He, I say, was not so; yet he underwent all these things because he willed it, as one humble in heart—humble, that is, with the humility prompted by the heart’s affection, not forced from him by truth’s examination.

8. Therefore I said that this form of voluntary humility is created within us not by truth’s rebuke but by the infusion of charity: because it belongs to the heart, to affection, and to will. Whether this is rightly said, judge for yourself. Let this also be equally examined by your judgment: whether I have worthily ascribed this humility to the Lord, who is known to have emptied himself through charity, to have been made lower than the angels through charity, to have been subject to his parents through charity, to have bowed under the Baptist’s hands through charity, to have suffered the weakness of flesh through charity, and finally through charity to have become subject to death and inglorious on the cross.

Let it also be for your consideration whether I have rightly understood this humility, so warm with charity, to be denoted by a lowly and warm herb—that is, nard. And if you approve all this—for you will approve it if you yield to the clearest reasoning—then, if you have already been humbled within yourself by that necessary humility which Truth, searching hearts and kidneys, impresses upon the senses of the wakeful soul, apply your will and make a virtue out of necessity. For there is no virtue without the consent of the will [variant: “the concurrence of the will”].

This will happen if you do not wish to appear outwardly other than you find yourself inwardly. Otherwise fear lest you read concerning yourself: “For he has acted deceitfully in his sight, so that his iniquity may be found unto hatred” (Ps. 35:3). “A weight and a weight,” he says, “are an abomination before God” (Prov. 20:10). What is this? You despise yourself in secret, weighed on truth’s scales; yet outwardly, pretending to be of another value, you sell yourself to us at a higher price than you received from truth itself. Fear God, and do not commit this most evil thing: that will should exalt the person whom truth humbles. For this is to resist truth; this is to fight against God.

Rather, yield to God, and let the will be subject to truth—not merely subject, but devoted. “Shall not my soul,” he says, “be subject to God?” (Ps. 61:2).

9. But it is not enough to be subject to God unless you are also subject, for God’s sake, to every human creature: whether to the abbot, as the superior; or to the priors, as appointed by him. I say more: submit to equals; submit also to inferiors. “Thus it is fitting for us,” he says, “to fulfil all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15). Go also to one lower than yourself, if you wish to be perfect in righteousness; yield to an inferior, bowing yourself before one younger than yourself [Col. 0992A]. By doing this, you too will draw to yourself the bride’s saying: “For my nard has given forth its fragrance.” Fragrance is devotion; fragrance is good repute, which reaches everyone, so that you may be Christ’s good fragrance in every place, conspicuous to all and beloved by all. This cannot be the case with the humble person whom truth compels to humility, because he keeps that humility to himself and does not allow it to go forth and exhale abroad. Indeed, he has no fragrance, because he has no devotion, since he does not humble himself freely or willingly. But the bride’s humility, like nard, diffuses its fragrance: warm with love, strong in devotion, sweet-smelling in repute. The bride’s humility is voluntary, enduring, fruitful. Its fragrance is destroyed neither by rebuke nor by praise. She had heard: “Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove, and your neck like necklaces” (Song 1:9). She had also received the promise of golden ornaments; nevertheless she answers with humility, and the more highly she hears herself praised, the more she humbles herself in all things. She does not glory in merits, nor amid her praises does she forget humility, which she humbly confesses under the name of nard; as though she spoke in the voice of the Virgin Mary: “I am conscious of no merit of mine for such condescension, except that God has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48). For what else is “my nard gave forth its fragrance” than “My humility was pleasing”? “Not my wisdom,” she says, “not my nobility, not my beauty”—for these were not mine—but the humility alone that was in me gave forth its fragrance, that is, its customary scent. God is customarily pleased by humility; indeed, the high Lord customarily and habitually looks upon the lowly. Therefore, when the King was at his table, that is, in his exalted dwelling-place, the fragrance of humility rose even there. “He dwells on high,” he says, “and looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 112:5–6).

10. Therefore, while the King was at his table, the bride’s nard gave forth its fragrance. The King’s table is the bosom of the Father, for the Son is always in the Father. Do not doubt that this King is merciful, for his perpetual resting-place is the abode of paternal kindness. Rightly does the cry of the humble rise to him whose dwelling is the fountain of compassion, whose familiar quality is sweetness, whose goodness is substantial—or rather consubstantial. Hence [Col. 0992D] all that he is is from the Father, so that the trembling of the humble may suspect absolutely nothing in the royal majesty except what is paternal. Thus: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I shall arise, says the Lord” (Ps. 11:6).

The bride, conscious of these things, being a member of the household and most beloved, does not think that she is to be shut out [variant: constrained] from the bridegroom’s grace through lack of merits, relying upon humility alone. In short, she calls him King, for, terrified by the rebuke, she does not yet dare call him Bridegroom; and she acknowledges that he dwells on high, yet humility does not thereby despair.

11. You may fittingly apply this utterance to the primitive Church, if you recall those days when the Lord had been taken up to where he was before and sat at the right hand of the Father, in that ancient, noble, and glorious resting-place of his; while the disciples were gathered together in one place, persevering unanimously in prayer with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brethren (Acts 1:13–14) [Col. 0993A]. Does it not seem to you that at that time the nard of the little and trembling bride truly gave forth its fragrance? Finally, when “there came suddenly from heaven a sound as of a mighty rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting” (Acts 2:2), could not that poor little bride deservedly then have said: “While the King was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance”? It was surely plain to all who remained in the place how grateful a fragrance of humility, and how well-pleasing, had ascended—a fragrance to which there was immediately returned so abundant and glorious a recompense.

Yet she was not ungrateful for the benefit. Listen to how, immediately filled with devotion, she prepares herself to endure every evil for his name: for it follows, “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts.” My weakness, as you know, does not permit me to proceed further. I say only this: under the name of myrrh she declares herself prepared, out of love for her beloved, to undergo the bitterness of tribulations. We shall pursue the rest of the chapter on another occasion, provided that the Holy Spirit, entreated by you, is present to make us understand the bride’s words—words which he himself formed by inspiration, as he knew fitting for the praises of him whose Spirit he is: the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen. [Col. 0993C]

## SERMON XLIII

**How reflection upon Christ’s passion and labours enables the bride—that is, the soul—to proceed unharmed amid this world’s prosperity and adversity.**

1. “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts” (Song 1:12). Before, he was King; now, Beloved. Before, he was at the royal table; now, between the bride’s breasts. Great is the power of humility, before which even the majesty of the Godhead so readily bows itself. Quickly the name of reverence has changed into a term of friendship; he who was far away has in a short time become near. “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh.” Myrrh is a bitter thing, signifying the harsh and rough character of tribulations [Col. 0993D]. Foreseeing these to be impending upon her for her beloved’s sake, she speaks rejoicingly, confident that she will undergo all things courageously. “The disciples,” it says, “went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

For this reason, she calls her beloved not a bundle but a little bundle: whatever labour and pain may threaten, she counts it light in comparison with love for him. Aptly, a little bundle, because “a little child has been born to us” (Isa. 9:6). Aptly, a little bundle, because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). “For,” he says, “this present momentary and light tribulation works in us beyond measure an eternal weight of glory on high” (2 Cor. 4:17) [Col. 0994A]. Therefore, there will one day be for us a vast accumulation of glory, which now is a little bundle of myrrh. Is it not a little bundle, whose yoke is sweet and whose burden light? (Matt. 11:30.) Not because it is light in itself—for the harshness of suffering and the bitterness of death are not light—but because it is light to one who loves. And therefore she does not merely say, “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh,” but, “To me,” she says, “who love him, he is a little bundle.”

Hence she calls him beloved, showing that the force of love overcomes the distress of every bitterness, and that “love is strong as death” (Song 8:6). And so that you may know that she glories not in herself but in the Lord, and expects strength not from her own power but from the Lord’s help, she says that he will dwell between her breasts, to whom she may confidently sing: “Even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, because you are with me” (Ps. 22:4) [Col. 0994B].

2. I recall that in one of the preceding sermons (Sermon 10, §1), following Paul’s teaching—“Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15)—I defined the bride’s two breasts as fellow-rejoicing and fellow-suffering. But because, moving amid adversity and prosperity, she knows that dangers are lacking in neither, she wishes to have her beloved in the midst of such breasts, protected by whose continual guardianship she may neither be lifted up by happy things nor cast down by sad ones.

You too, if you are wise, will imitate the bride’s prudence and will not allow this dearly beloved little bundle of myrrh to be torn from the chief place of your heart, even for an hour. Always retain in memory, and turn over in continual meditation, all those bitter things that he endured for you, so that you too may say: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts” [Col. 0994C].

3. And I, brethren, from the beginning of my conversion, knowing that I lacked a heap of merits, have taken care to bind together for myself this little bundle and place it between my breasts, gathered from all the anxieties and bitter sufferings of my Lord: namely, first, the necessities of his infancy; then the labours he bore in preaching, the weariness of travelling about, the vigils of prayer, the temptations of fasting, the tears of compassion, the snares amid conversation; finally, the dangers from false brethren [Col. 0994D], insults, spittings, blows, mockeries, reproaches, nails, and all such things as the evangelical forest is known to have brought forth in greatest abundance for the salvation of our race.

Among so many branches of this fragrant myrrh, I judged that the myrrh with which he was given to drink upon the cross should by no means be omitted; nor that with which he was anointed in burial. By the first he applied to himself the bitterness of my sins; by the second he consecrated the future incorruption of my body. “I shall utter the memory of the abundance of their sweetness” as long as I live; eternally I shall not forget these mercies, for by them I have been given life.

4. Long ago holy David sought these mercies with tears: “Let your mercies come to me,” he said, “and I shall live” (Ps. 118:77) [Col. 0995A]. Another of the saints also recalled them with groaning, saying: “The mercies of the Lord are many. How many kings and prophets desired to see and did not see! They laboured, and I entered into their labours; I have harvested the myrrh which they planted. This saving little bundle has been preserved for me; no one shall take it from me; it shall dwell between my breasts.”

I have called meditation upon these things wisdom; in them I have established for myself the perfection of righteousness; in them the fullness of knowledge; in them the riches of salvation; in them an abundance of merits. From them I sometimes receive a drink of saving bitterness; from them again a sweet anointing of consolation. They raise me up amid adversities and restrain me amid prosperities; and as I walk the royal way amid the joys and sorrows of this present life, they provide safe guidance on either side, driving away the evils that threaten from both directions [Col. 0995B].

They reconcile to me the Judge of the world, while they portray him—terrible to powers—as gentle and humble; while they present as not only propitiable but also imitable him who is inaccessible to principalities and terrible among the kings of the earth. Therefore, as you know, these things are often on my lips; as God knows, always in my heart; as appears, very familiar to my pen. Meanwhile this is my higher philosophy: to know Jesus, and him crucified. I do not seek, as the bride does, where he lies down at noon (Song 1:6), whom I joyfully embrace as dwelling between my breasts. I do not seek where he feeds at noon, whom I behold as Saviour on the cross. The former is more sublime; this is sweeter. The former is bread; this is milk. This refreshes the inward parts of little children; this fills the breasts of mothers. Therefore he shall dwell between my breasts [Col. 0995C].

5. You also, most beloved, gather for yourselves this most beloved little bundle; implant it in the marrow of your hearts; fortify with it the entrance of your breast, so that he too may dwell between your breasts. Always keep him not behind upon your shoulders but before your eyes, lest, carrying him without breathing in his fragrance, the burden press you down while the fragrance does not raise you up.

Remember that Simeon received him in his arms (Luke 2:28); Mary carried him in her womb and cherished him in her lap; the bride placed him between her breasts. And, lest I omit anything, “the word came through the hand of Zechariah the prophet,” and likewise through those of certain others. I suppose that Joseph, Mary’s husband, often smiled upon him on his knees [Col. 0995D]. All these had him before them, and none behind them. Let them therefore be examples to you, that you may do likewise. For if you have before your eyes him whom you carry, then surely, seeing the Lord’s distresses, you will bear your own more lightly, with the help of the Bridegroom of the Church, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLIV

**On moderating correction according to the disposition of sinners: the humble and compliant are to be corrected gently, the hard and obstinate severely.**

1. “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi” (Song 1:13). If the beloved is found in myrrh, much more is he found in the sweetness of the cluster. Therefore my Lord Jesus tempered himself for me as a most health-giving drink: myrrh for me in death, a cluster in resurrection, in tears kept within measure. “He died for our sins and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4:25), so that, dead to sins, we may live to righteousness (1 Pet. 2:24).

Thus, if you have bewailed your sins, you have drunk bitterness; but if you have now drawn breath in hope of life through a holier life, the bitterness of myrrh has been changed for you into wine, which gladdens the heart of man. And perhaps this was signified by the myrrhed wine offered to the Saviour on the cross [variant added: wine], which he therefore refused to drink because he thirsted for this. Therefore, after the bitterness of myrrh, as I have said, when you experience the wine of joy, you too may without rashness say: “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi” [Col. 0996B].

Engaddi has a double interpretation, and both serve one understanding. For it is said to mean “fountain of the kid,” and “baptism of the Gentiles”; and it plainly signifies the tears of penitents. It is also said to mean “eye of temptation,” which both sheds tears and foresees temptations—temptations that never fail in human life upon earth. Moreover, the people of the Gentiles, who walked in darkness, could never of themselves recognize the snares of temptations, and therefore could not escape them, until, through the grace of him who enlightens the blind, they received the eyes of faith; until they came to the Church, which has the eye of temptation; until they committed themselves to be instructed by spiritual men, who, enlightened by the spirit of wisdom and taught by their own experience, can truly say: “We are not ignorant of the wiles and thoughts of the devil” (2 Cor. 2:11) [Col. 0996C].

2. It is reported that little balsam trees grow at Engaddi, cultivated by the inhabitants in the manner of vineyards; and perhaps for this reason he called them vineyards. Otherwise, what would a cluster of Cyprus be doing in the vineyards of Engaddi? Who has ever transported clusters from vineyards into vineyards? Wine is ordinarily carried from elsewhere to a place where it is lacking, not to where it is present.

Therefore, by the vineyards of Engaddi he means the congregations of the Church, which possess the liquid of balsam, the spirit of gentleness. With it she tenderly cherishes those still weak in Christ and consoles the griefs of penitents. And if any brother is overtaken in some fault, the ecclesiastical man who has already received this spirit will take care at once to restore such a one in the same spirit of gentleness, considering himself lest he too be tempted (Gal. 6:1) [Col. 0996D]. Under this figure, the Church is accustomed also bodily to anoint with material oil all who are to be baptized.

3. Yet because the wounds of the man who fell among robbers and was carried upon the beast—the body—of the compassionate Samaritan into the Church’s inn are healed not by oil alone but by wine together with oil (Luke 10:30–34), the spiritual physician must also have the wine of fervent zeal together with the oil of gentleness. It is fitting for him not only to console the faint-hearted but also to rebuke the unruly.

For if he sees that the wounded man—that is, the sinner—is not corrected by the gentle and mild exhortations already lavished upon him, but perhaps even abuses the gentleness and patience shown him, becomes more negligent, and falls more securely asleep in his sin, then, after the oil of such sweet admonitions has been spent fruitlessly, he must use sharper remedies and pour in the wine of compunction. That is, he must deal with him through harsh rebukes and denunciations; and if the case requires it and the hardness is so great, he must even strike the despiser with the rod of ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 0997A].

But where is he to get this wine? Wine is not found in the vineyards of Engaddi, but oil. Let him seek it in Cyprus, for that island is rich in wine, and in excellent wine. Let him take from there for himself the great cluster which the Israelite scouts once bore upon a pole (Num. 13:24), the prophetic choir going before and the apostolic choir following, with Jesus in the middle, represented by a beautiful figure. Taking this cluster, then, let him say: “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus.”

4. We have seen the cluster; let us see how the wine of zeal is pressed from it. If a sinful human being does not become angry with another sinful human being, but rather, as one sweating a dew of sweetest balsam upon him, shows a compassionate affection, we know whence this comes. You have already heard it, though perhaps you did not notice it. For it was said that each person’s gentleness toward all arises from considering himself; when, by the counsel of most wise Paul, in order to know how to condescend compassionately to those overtaken in sin, a person considers himself lest he too be tempted (Gal. 6:1).

Does not love of neighbour draw its root from this source, that concerning which the Law commands: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself”? (Luke 10:27.) Brotherly love indeed draws the first beginnings of its birth from the innermost human affections; and from the natural sweetness implanted in a person toward himself, as from earthly moisture, it undoubtedly receives the growth and power by which, grace breathing from above, it bears the fruits of compassion. Thus, what the soul naturally desires for itself, it should not suppose—by a certain law of humanity—that it may withhold, where it can and ought, from one who shares its nature, that is, another human being; rather, it should freely and willingly impart it.

There is therefore in nature, if it has not become stale through sin, a kind of pleasant and excellent sweetness, causing it to feel and show itself more disposed to compassionate sinners gently than to be harshly indignant with them [Col. 0997C].

5. But because, according to the saying of the Wise Man, “dying flies destroy this ointment of sweetness” (Eccles. 10:1), and nature has no means in itself to restore it once lost, it finds itself, through a lamentable change, falling into that of which Scripture truthfully says: “The senses and thoughts of humankind are prone to evil from youth” (Gen. 8:21).

It is not a good youth in which the younger son asks that his portion of the paternal substance be set apart for him, and begins to desire the division of a good that is more sweetly possessed in common; to possess alone what is not diminished by sharing but is lost by partition. Thus: “He dissipated all his goods, living prodigally with harlots” (Luke 15:11, 13). Who are these harlots? Take care lest they be those same things that destroy the ointment of sweetness: namely, carnal desires, concerning which Scripture most beneficially warns you: “Do not go after your desires” (Ecclus. 18:30) [Col. 0998A]. And the Wise Man rightly describes them as destined to die, because “the world passes away, and its desire” (1 John 2:17).

While we wish to satisfy these alone, therefore, we deprive ourselves of the unique sweetness of social and common good. These are precisely the filthy, stinging flies that defile in us the beauty of nature, tear the mind with cares and anxieties, and destroy the sweetness of social grace. Hence a human being is called the younger son: because nature, corrupted by a certain slippery and irrational adolescence, has lost all the sap of manly maturity and wisdom; and, having turned harsh, with a parched mind despises everyone besides itself, becoming without affection.

6. Thus, from the beginning of this most evil and wretched youth, the senses and thoughts of humankind are prone to evil, and nature is readier to anger than to compassion. Hence a person, as though wholly stripped of humanity, does not wish to aid those human beings who are in need, although he wishes people to aid him when he is in need. Instead, sinful man judges, despises, and mocks human beings who err, without considering himself lest he too be tempted [Col. 0998B].

From this evil nature will by no means rise again of itself, as I have said; nor will it recover the oil of inborn gentleness once destroyed within it. Nevertheless, what nature cannot do, grace can do. Therefore, the person upon whom the anointing of the Spirit has had mercy and whom it deigns to bathe anew in its kindness will at once return to humanity; indeed, from grace he will receive something better than he received from nature. It will make him holy in faith and gentleness and will give him, not oil, but balsam in the vineyards of Engaddi [Col. 0998C].

7. For there is no doubt that better gifts flow from the fountain of the kid, whose anointing certainly turns kids into lambs and transfers sinners from the left hand to the right, having first more abundantly bathed them in the anointing of mercy, so that “where offences abounded, grace might abound still more” (Rom. 5:20).

Does it not truly seem to you that this person has in some way returned to humanity? Having put off the fierceness of a worldly soul, and having recovered—indeed, recovered with the added interest of grace—the anointing of human gentleness, which the flies of carnal desires had utterly destroyed in him, he takes from the human being he bears, or rather from that which he himself is, both the material and the manner of showing mercy to other people. Thus he abhors, as it were, a dreadful grimace [variant: “practice” rather than “grimace,” uncertain]: not only doing to any human being what he would not wish to suffer himself, but even failing to do for everyone all that he would wish done for himself [Col. 0998D].

8. Here, then, is the oil. Whence comes the wine? Assuredly from the cluster of Cyprus. For if you love the Lord Jesus with all your heart, all your soul, and all your strength, can you possibly bear with equanimity his injuries and contempt when you see them? Certainly not. At once seized by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning, and “like a mighty man overcome with wine” (Ps. 77:65), filled with the zeal of Phinehas, you will say with David: “My zeal has consumed me, because my enemies have forgotten your words” (Ps. 118:139); and with the Lord: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68:10; John 2:17).

This most fervent zeal, then, is wine pressed from the cluster of Cyprus; and Christ’s love is an intoxicating cup. For “our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24), and the prophet called the fire sent from on high into his bones (Lam. 1:13), because he burned with divine love [Col. 0999A]. Therefore, having from brotherly love the oil of gentleness, and from divine love the wine of zeal, approach confidently to heal the wounds of him who fell among robbers, as an excellent imitator of the most merciful Samaritan.

And confidently say with the bride: “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi.” That is: the zeal of righteousness, the love of my beloved, is to me amid affections of compassion.

And enough on this subject. For my weakness bids me rest, as it often does, so that I am often compelled, as you know, to leave discussions unfinished and reserve what remains of the chapters for another day. But what then? “I am ready for scourges” (Ps. 33:18), knowing that I still receive punishments far less than my deserts. Let me indeed be beaten, let me be beaten as an evildoer, if perhaps stripes may be reckoned as merits. Perhaps he will have mercy upon one who has been scourged, in whom he found no good to reward: Jesus Christ our Lord, Bridegroom of the Church, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen. [Col. 0999B]

## SERMON XLV

**On the soul’s twofold beauty; how the soul speaks to God the Word and the Word to the soul; and what their languages are.**

1. “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are those of doves” (Song 1:14) [Col. 0999C]. Beautifully and excellently, from love, came the bride’s presumption; from love came the bridegroom’s indignation. The outcome proves this. Rebuke followed presumption, amendment followed rebuke, and reward followed amendment. The beloved is present; the master is removed; the king disappears; dignity is laid aside; reverence is put away. For pride yields where affection grows strong. And as once Moses spoke, almost as a friend to a friend, and the Lord answered (Exod. 33:11), so now a most intimate conversation is held between the Word and the soul, as between two neighbours.

Nor is this surprising. From the one fountain of love there flows into both the loving of one another and mutual cherishing. Therefore words sweeter than honey fly back and forth, and mutual looks, bearing all sweetness in themselves, are exchanged: holy tokens of love. Thus he calls her friend, declares her beautiful, repeats that she is beautiful, receiving the same in return from her. Nor is the repetition idle: it confirms love and perhaps indicates something to be sought.

2. Let us seek the soul’s twofold beauty, for this, I think, is what it indicates. The soul’s beauty is humility. I do not say this on my own authority, since the prophet said first: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. 50:9), signifying humility by the lowly herb that cleanses the breast. By this the king and prophet trusted that he would be washed after his grave fall and thus recover a certain snowy brightness of innocence.

Yet in one who has sinned grievously, humility, though lovable, is not admirable. But if someone preserves innocence and nevertheless joins humility to it, does he not seem to you to possess the soul’s twofold beauty? Holy Mary did not lose holiness and did not lack humility; and therefore the King desired her beauty, because she joined humility to innocence. Thus she says: “He has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48). Blessed, then, are those who keep their garments clean—those of simplicity and innocence—provided that they also add the beauty of humility.

Certainly she who is found such will hear: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful.” Would that you might say even once to my soul, Lord Jesus: “Behold, you are beautiful.” Would that you would preserve humility in me! For I kept the first garment badly [Col. 1000B]. I am your servant. I do not dare to profess myself a friend, since I do not hear the repeated testimony to my beauty. It is enough for me if I hear it once. But what if even this is uncertain? I know what I shall do: as a servant, I shall revere the friend; as a deformed little man, I shall admire the beauty accumulated in her; I shall rejoice at the bridegroom’s voice, as he nevertheless admires so great a beauty. Who knows whether I may at least thereby find grace in the friend’s eyes, so that through her grace I too may be found among the friends? For “the friend of the bridegroom stands and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.” Behold, his voice is in the beloved’s ears; let us hear and rejoice. They are present to one another and speak together; let us stand with them. Let no care of the world draw us away from this conversation, no enticement of the body.

3. “Behold,” he says, “you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful” [Col. 1000C]. “Behold” is a word of admiration; the rest is praise. Rightly is she admirable: lost holiness did not bring her humility, but preserved holiness admitted it. Rightly is she found beautiful: neither beauty was lacking to her. It is a rare bird on earth either not to lose holiness or not to have humility excluded by holiness. Therefore blessed is she who retained both.

Finally, this has been proven: she is conscious of no fault and does not refuse rebuke. When we offend even grievously, we can scarcely bear reproof; but she calmly hears bitter things said against her while having committed no sin. For if she desires to see the bridegroom’s brightness, what evil is there in this? It is rather praiseworthy. Yet, rebuked, she does penance and says: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts” (Song 1:12). That is: “It is enough for me; now I wish to know nothing except Jesus, and him crucified.” Great humility! Innocent in deed, she takes on the disposition of a penitent; and she who has nothing for which to repent nevertheless has a disposition of repentance.

Why, then, you ask, was she rebuked if she did nothing wrong? Listen now to the bridegroom’s providence and prudence. As Abraham’s obedience was once indeed tested, so now the bride’s humility is tested. And as he, after fulfilling obedience, then heard, “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12), so she now hears, as it were in different words: “Now I know that you are humble.” For this is what he says: “Behold, you are beautiful.” And for this reason he repeats the praise, to signify that the beauty of humility has been added to the glory of holiness [Col. 1001A]. “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful.” Now I know that you are beautiful, not only through my love but also through your humility. I do not now call you beautiful among women, or beautiful in cheeks, or in neck, as I said before; I simply declare you beautiful—not beautiful by comparison, not with qualification, not in part.

4. And he adds: “Your eyes are those of doves.” Humility is plainly still being commended. For this refers to the fact that, when she was reproved for her lofty inquiry, she did not hesitate but immediately descended to simpler things, so that she said: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh.” There is indeed a great distance between the countenance of glory and a bundle of myrrh; and therefore it is a great mark of humility to consent to be recalled from the one to the other [Col. 1001B].

“Your eyes are those of doves.” “You no longer walk in great things nor in wonders above yourself; but like a most simple bird, you are content with simpler things, nesting in the clefts of the rock, dwelling in my wounds, and gladly gazing with a dove’s eye upon those things that concern me only as incarnate and suffering.”

5. Or, since the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of this bird (Matt. 3:16), perhaps it is her spiritual rather than her simple gaze that is commended under the name of the dove. If this interpretation pleases, you must connect the present chapter with the earlier statement that the companions promised to make her golden ornaments (Song 1:10), intending, as I taught then, not to adorn the bodily ears but to form the hearing of the heart (above, Sermon 41, §§2–4) [Col. 1001C]. It could therefore have happened that, with the heart more cleansed through faith—which comes by hearing—she was made more capable of seeing what she could not previously see.

And since, by means of the ornaments received, she seemed to have advanced through keener sight to spiritual understanding, this pleased the bridegroom, who always prefers, insofar as it lies in him, to be seen in the spirit. Adding this too to her praises, he says: “Your eyes are those of doves.” “Now,” he says, “look upon me in the Spirit, because Christ the Lord is Spirit before your face” (Lam. 4:20). And you have the means to do so, because your eyes are those of doves. Previously you did not have them, and therefore you had to be restrained; but now possess the ability to live, because your eyes are those of doves—that is, spiritual. Not, indeed, the ability you were seeking; for even now you are not yet capable of that, but an ability which can meanwhile suffice. You must indeed be led from brightness to brightness; therefore see now as much as you can, and when you can do more, you will see more [Col. 1001D].

6. I do not think, brethren, I do not think that this is a mediocre vision or one common to all, even though it is inferior to that in which he is to be seen in the future. Observe this from what follows. For it follows: “Behold, you are handsome, my beloved; behold, you are handsome.” You see how high she stands and how she has been raised to the lofty summit of the mind: she claims the Lord of the universe for herself in a certain personal manner as beloved.

Notice how she does not merely say, “Beloved,” but “my beloved,” to mark him as her own [Col. 1002A]. This is truly a great vision, from which she has grown into such confidence and authority that she does not know the Lord of all as Lord, but as Beloved. I think that on this occasion no images of flesh, cross, or any other bodily likenesses of infirmities were brought before her perceptions. For in these, according to the prophet, “he had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53:2). But she, beholding him, now declares him beautiful and comely, signifying that he appeared to her in a better vision.

For the bridegroom speaks mouth to mouth with her, as once with holy Moses (Exod. 33:11), and she sees God openly, not through riddles and figures. Accordingly, she declares him with her mouth as she beholds him with her mind—in a vision truly sublime and sweet. Her eyes saw the King in his beauty, yet not as King, but as Beloved. Someone may indeed have seen him seated upon a throne high and lifted up; another may have testified that he appeared to him face to face. Yet it seems to me that in this respect the bride is pre-eminent: there the Lord is read to have been seen, here the Beloved.

For thus you have: “I saw the Lord seated upon a throne high and lifted up” (Isa. 6:1); and likewise: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (Gen. 32:30) [Col. 1002B]. “But if I am Lord,” he says, “where is my fear?” (Mal. 1:6.) If revelation was made to those persons with fear, because where the Lord is, there is fear, then I, if the choice were given me, would embrace the bride’s vision so much more willingly and dearly because I perceive it to have been granted in the better affection, which is love. For fear has punishment, but perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

There is indeed a great difference between appearing “terrible in counsels above the children of men” (Ps. 65:15) and appearing “beautiful in form above the children of men” (Ps. 44:5). “Behold, you are handsome, my beloved, and comely.” These words clearly resound with love, not fear.

7. But perhaps thoughts arise in your heart, and you ask yourself in doubt, saying: “How can words spoken by the Word be referred to the soul, and again words of the soul to the Word—so that she hears the voice speaking to her and declaring that she is beautiful, and in turn immediately renders back the same praise to her praiser? How can these things be?” For we speak by means of a word; a word does not speak. Likewise, the soul has no means of speaking unless the mouth of the body forms words for it to utter [Col. 1002D]. You ask well; but consider that the Spirit speaks, and that what is said must be understood spiritually. Therefore, whenever you hear or read that the Word and the soul converse together and look upon one another, do not imagine bodily voices passing between them, nor bodily images of the speakers appearing. Rather, understand what you ought to think in such cases. The Word is spirit, and the soul is spirit; and they have their own tongues by which they address one another and make their presence known. The tongue of the Word is the favor of his condescension; that of the soul, the ardor of devotion. The soul that lacks it is tongueless and an infant, and can in no way hold discourse with the Word. Therefore, when the Word moves this his tongue, wishing to speak to the soul, the soul cannot fail to perceive it [Col. 1003A]. For the word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit (Heb. 4:12). And again, when the soul moves her own tongue [elsewhere incorrectly: “the soul”], the Word will be still less able to remain unaware of it—not merely because he is present everywhere, but especially because the tongue of devotion is not moved to speech unless he himself prompts it.

8. Therefore, for the Word to say to the soul, “You are beautiful,” and to call her friend, is to infuse that by which she may both love and presume herself loved. For the soul in turn to name the Word “beloved,” and to confess him beautiful, is to ascribe to him, without pretense or deceit, both that she loves and that she is loved; it is to wonder at his condescension and be astonished at grace. For his beauty is his love; and it is the greater because it comes first. Therefore, from the marrow of her heart and with the inward voices of her affections, she cries out all the more abundantly and ardently that he is to be loved, inasmuch as she first experienced herself loved rather than loving. Thus the Word’s speech is the infusion of a gift; the soul’s answer is amazement joined with thanksgiving. And for this reason she loves more, because she feels herself surpassed in loving; and she wonders more, because she recognizes that she has been anticipated. Hence she is not content to call him beautiful once, unless she repeats it, “and fair,” signifying by that repetition the excellence of his beauty.

9. Or rather, in Christ’s twofold substance she has expressed a beauty worthy of all admiration: in one, the beauty of nature; in the other, that of grace. How beautiful you are to your angels, Lord Jesus, in the form of God, in the day of your eternity, begotten before the morning star amid the splendors of the holy ones [Col. 1003C], the radiance and image of the Father’s substance, indeed the everlasting and wholly unfeigned brightness of eternal life! How fair you are to me, my Lord, in this very laying aside of your beauty! For where you emptied yourself, where you put off the unfailing light of your natural rays, there mercy shone forth more brightly, there love gleamed more fully, there grace radiated more abundantly. How brightly you rise for me, Star out of Jacob (Num. 24:17); how luminous a Flower you come forth from the root of Jesse (Isa. 11:1); how delightful a light you visited me amid darkness, Dayspring from on high! (Luke 1:78). How splendid and astonishing even to the heavenly Powers: in conception by the Spirit, in birth from the Virgin, in innocence of life, in the streams of teaching, in the flashing of miracles, in the revelations of mysteries! Finally, how radiant after your setting [Col. 1003D], Sun of righteousness, you rise from the heart of the earth! How beautiful at last in your robe (Isa. 63:1), King of glory, as you are received into the heights of heaven! How shall not all my bones say for all these things, “Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. 34:10).

10. Understand, then, that the Bride observed these and similar things while contemplating the Beloved, when she said: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and fair.” Nor only these, but beyond doubt something of the superior beauty of his nature, which wholly surpasses our sight and escapes experience. Thus the repetition of both terms indicated the beauty of his substance. Hear next how, at the sight and address of her beloved, she dances for joy and sings before him in a bridal song those things that rejoice in love [Col. 1004A]. For it follows: “Our bed is flowering; the beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings cypress.” But let us reserve the Bride’s song for a fresher beginning, so that we too, made more cheerful by rest, may more freely exult and rejoice in it, to the praise and glory of the Bridegroom himself, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLVI

On the condition and ordering of the whole Church. Also, how one comes through the active life, which is lived under obedience, to the contemplative life.

1. “Our bed is flowering; the beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings are cypress” (Song 1:15–16). She sings an epithalamium, beautifully describing the bed and bridal chambers [Col. 1004B]. She invites the Bridegroom to rest. For this is better: to rest and to be with Christ. Yet to go forth for gain, for the sake of those to be saved, is necessary. But now, when she thinks she has found the opportunity, she announces that the chamber is adorned, points out the bed, as it were, with her finger, and invites the Beloved, as I said, to rest. Unable, like those going to Emmaus, to endure the burning of her heart, she draws him into the lodging of her mind, compels him to remain with her through the night (Luke 24:29, 32), and speaks with Peter: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:4).

2. Let us now inquire what these things contain spiritually. In the Church, I think the bed in which rest is taken signifies cloisters and monasteries, in which people live quietly, free from the cares of the age and anxieties of life [Col. 1004C]. This bed is shown to be flowering when the conduct and life of the brethren shine with the examples and institutions of the Fathers, as though sprinkled with sweet-smelling flowers.

By “houses,” moreover, understand the popular assemblies of Christians. Those set in high places—namely Christian rulers of either rank—bind them firmly together, like beams holding walls, by just laws imposed upon them, lest each person, living by his own law or will, should fall apart from the others like leaning walls and a broken fence, and thus the whole structure of the building should collapse and be scattered. The ceilings, which hang firmly from the beams and notably adorn the houses, I think signify the gentle and disciplined conduct of a well-ordered clergy, and offices duly administered. For how will the ranks of clergy and their administrations stand [Col. 1004D], unless they are supported by the favor and generosity of rulers, as by beams, and protected by their power?

3. That the beams are described as cedar and the ceilings as cypress undoubtedly arises from qualities in those kinds of wood that suit the aforesaid orders. Cedar, being incorruptible, fragrant, and lofty in stature, sufficiently shows what kind of men ought to be chosen to serve in place of beams. Those set over others, therefore, must be strong and steadfast; they must also be long-suffering in hope and raise the summit of their minds toward things above. By spreading everywhere the fragrance of their good faith and conduct, they may say with the Apostle: “For we are the sweet savor of Christ unto God in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15) [Col. 1005A].

Cypress likewise, a wood both fragrant and incorruptible, shows that every member of the clergy should be of uncorrupted life and faith, so that he may deservedly be assigned to the beauty of the house and the adornment of its ceilings. For it is written: “Holiness befits your house, O Lord, unto length of days” (Ps. 93:5). Here both the beauty of sanctity and the explicit perseverance of unfailing grace are present. Therefore, the man chosen for the adornment and beauty of the house must be adorned with good conduct; and although he is always within, he must nevertheless have a good testimony even from those outside. There are other properties of these woods that suit the matters under spiritual discussion [Col. 1005B], but I pass them over for brevity’s sake.

4. It should be noted how beautifully the entire condition of the Church is comprehended in one short verse: the authority of prelates, the dignity of the clergy, the discipline of the people, and the repose of monks. When all these are rightly ordered, holy mother Church rejoices in contemplating them; and then she offers them also for the Beloved to behold, when she refers them all to his goodness as author of all, attributing none of them to herself. For her words “our” and “our houses” are not a sign of usurpation but of love: through the exceedingly confident trust of charity, she considers nothing belonging to him whom she loves greatly to be alien from herself. Nor does she think herself to be excluded from the Bridegroom’s companionship or from the fellowship of his rest, since she is always accustomed to seek not her own interests but his [Col. 1005C]. This is why she has ventured to declare the bed and the houses common to herself and her Bridegroom. She said: “Our bed,” “the beams of our houses,” and “our ceilings,” boldly associating herself with him in possession, since she does not doubt that she is joined to him in love.

Not so the woman who has not yet renounced her own will, but lies by herself and dwells by herself—or rather, not by herself, but lives luxuriously with harlots: I mean the desires of the flesh, with which she squanders her goods and the portion of substance that she demanded to be divided to her (Luke 15:12–13).

5. But you who hear or read these utterances of the Holy Spirit: do you think that you can apply any of what is said to yourself, and recognize in yourself something of the Bride’s blessedness, whose song of love is sung by the Spirit himself [Col. 1005D], lest it also be said to you that you hear his voice and do not know whence he comes or where he goes? Perhaps you too desire the repose of contemplation, and rightly so—provided only that you do not forget the flowers with which you read that the Bride’s bed is strewn. Therefore take care likewise to surround your own bed with flowers of good works, and by the exercise of virtues, as by flowers, to anticipate that fruit, holy leisure. Otherwise, if you desire rest without having been trained, you will wish to sleep in idle luxury; and, neglecting Leah’s fruitfulness, you will desire to delight only in Rachel’s embraces.

Moreover, it is a perverse order to demand the reward before merit and to take food before labor, when the Apostle says: “If anyone will not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3:10). “From your commandments,” he says, “I have received understanding” (Ps. 119:104), so that you may know that, apart from obedience to the commandments, the taste of contemplation is by no means owed. Therefore do not suppose that, for love of your own repose, any injury may be done to the works of holy obedience or to the traditions of the elders. Otherwise the Bridegroom will not sleep with you in one bed [elsewhere: “one little bed”], especially in that bed which you have strewed, in place of the flowers of obedience, with the hemlocks and nettles of disobedience. For this reason he will not hear your prayers, and, when called, will not come. So great a lover of obedience will not grant his presence to one who is disobedient—he who preferred to die rather than not obey [Col. 1006B]. Nor does he approve the empty leisure of your contemplation, he who says through the prophet: “I have labored, enduring” (Jer. 6:11), signifying the time when, exiled from heaven and the homeland of highest rest, he worked salvation in the midst of the earth.

Indeed, I fear rather that that dreadful sentence, thundered against the unbelief of the Jews, may also enfold you: “Your new moons and sabbaths and other feasts I will not endure”; and again: “My soul hates your new moons and your solemnities; they have become burdensome to me” (Isa. 1:13–14). The prophet too will mourn over you and say: “Her enemies saw her and mocked at her sabbaths” (Lam. 1:7). For why should the enemy not mock what the Beloved rejects?

6. I am greatly astonished at the shamelessness of certain persons among us who, although they have disturbed us all by their singularity, provoked us by their impatience, and despised us by their obstinacy and rebellion [Note: In the editions this is commonly supplemented here: “have defiled us by their disobedience.” But this clause is absent from most manuscripts, and indeed amounts to the same thing as the preceding phrase. In the earliest printed editions it is read, but with the preceding words, “have despised us by their obstinacy and rebellion,” omitted.], nevertheless dare to invite the Lord of all purity, with every urgency of prayer, to the utterly foul bed of their conscience. “When you stretch out your hands,” he says, “I will turn away my eyes; and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear” (Isa. 1:15). What then? The bed is not flowering; rather, it is foul-smelling—and you draw the King of glory there? Do you do this for rest, or for litigation?

The centurion forbids him to enter beneath his roof because of his own unworthiness, though his faith is fragrant throughout all Israel (Matt. 8:8, 10); and do you compel him to enter you, while you reek with the filth of so many vices? The chief of the apostles cries: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8); and do you say: “Enter to me, Lord, for I am holy”? “All of you,” he says, “be of one mind in prayer; love the brotherhood” (1 Pet. 2:17). And the vessel of election says: “Lifting up pure hands, without anger and dispute” (1 Tim. 2:8). Do you see how the chief of the apostles and the teacher of the Gentiles agree with one another and speak in the same spirit concerning the peace and tranquility of mind that the one who prays ought to possess? Go on then: stretch out your hands to God all day long, you who trouble the brethren all day long, attack unanimity, and separate yourself from unity [Col. 1006D].

7. “And what do you want me to do?” you ask. Certainly, first cleanse your conscience of every defilement of anger, dispute, murmuring, and envy; and hasten to remove from the dwelling-place of your heart whatever is recognized as hostile either to the peace of the brethren or to obedience toward the elders [Col. 1007A]. Then also surround yourself with the flowers of every good act and commendable pursuit, and with the fragrances of virtues: that is, whatever is true, whatever modest, whatever just, whatever holy, whatever lovable, whatever of good report; if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline—think on these things (Phil. 4:8), and take care to exercise yourself in them. To such things you will safely invite the Bridegroom. For when you have brought him in, you too will be able truthfully to say: “Our bed is flowering,” since your conscience gives off the fragrance of piety, peace, gentleness, justice, obedience, cheerfulness, and humility. So much concerning the bed [Col. 1007B].

8. Let each person recognize himself as the spiritual house of God, provided he no longer walks according to the flesh but according to the Spirit: “For the temple of God,” says the Apostle, “is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:17). Therefore, brothers, take care that this spiritual building—which you are—does not perhaps, when it begins to rise upward, shake and collapse because it has not been supported and bound together with strong beams. Take care, I say, to give it incorruptible and immovable beams: namely, the chaste fear of the Lord, which endures for ever and ever (Ps. 19:9); patience, of which it is written that “the patience of the poor shall not perish for ever” (Ps. 9:18); and long-suffering, which, persevering unbent beneath whatever weight of structure, stretches out into the endless ages of blessed life, as the Savior says in the Gospel: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). But above all, charity, which never fails, because “love is strong as death,” he says, “and jealousy hard as hell” (Song 8:6) [Col. 1007C].

Then endeavor to lay beneath and bind to these beams other woods equally precious and beautiful, which may be ready at hand for ceilings to adorn the house: namely, the word of wisdom or of knowledge, prophecy, the grace of healings, interpretation of utterances, and other such things. These are clearly known to be more suited to ornament than necessary for salvation [Col. 1007D]. Concerning these I have no command, but I give counsel. Since such woods are known to be laboriously sought, difficult to find, and dangerously worked upon—for our land is found to produce them rarely, especially in these times—I counsel and urge that they not be sought too eagerly. Rather, ceilings should be made from other woods, which, though they appear less splendid, are nevertheless proved no less strong; besides, they are more easily possessed and more safely so.

9. Would that I too had an abundance of those woods with which the Bridegroom’s garden, the Church, is richly thickened: peace, goodness, kindness, joy in the Holy Spirit, showing mercy with cheerfulness, giving with simplicity [Col. 1008A], rejoicing with those who rejoice, weeping with those who weep (Rom. 12:8, 15). Would you not judge that house—so far as its ceilings are concerned—sufficiently and abundantly adorned if you saw it adequately and harmoniously boarded with such woods? “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house” (Ps. 26:8). Always give me, I pray, these woods, by which I may always present to you an adorned chamber of conscience—of my own conscience, I mean, and of another’s. I shall be content with these. There will also be those willing to follow my counsel in this matter, because I think that you too will be content. I leave the rest to the holy apostles and apostolic men.

But you also, most beloved, although you do not have those woods, nevertheless, if you have these, be confident; nevertheless, with every confidence approach the highest, chosen, precious cornerstone [Col. 1008B]. Nevertheless, upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, be yourselves built up as living stones, spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (Eph. 2:19–22; 1 Pet. 2:4–9), the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLVII

On the threefold flower—namely, virginity, martyrdom, and good action—and on the devotion to be maintained in the divine office.

1. “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1). I think this refers to the Bride’s commendation of the bed strewn with flowers. Lest she should attribute to herself the flowers by which the bed seemed adorned and the chamber beautified, the Bridegroom adds that he is the flower of the field [Col. 1008C]. Flowers, he says, do not properly spring from the chamber, but from the field; whatever shines and gives fragrance does so through his gift and participation in him. Therefore, lest anyone should reproach her and say, “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7), he himself, as both the devoted lover of his beloved and her gracious instructor, piously and condescendingly shows her to whom she ought to attribute the brightness in which she gloried and the sweet fragrance of the bed. “I am the flower of the field,” he says: “what you glory in comes from me.” From this passage too we are most beneficially warned that one ought by no means to glory; and if anyone glories, “let him glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17) [Col. 1008D]. Thus far according to the letter; now let us, with the help of him of whom it speaks, investigate the spiritual meaning hidden in it.

2. First observe for me a certain threefold condition of the flower: in the field, in the garden, and in the chamber. Then it will be easier to discover why he especially chose to call himself the flower of the field. In the field and garden a flower grows; in the chamber it does not. In the chamber it gives fragrance and brightness, yet it is not upright and standing as in garden or field, but lies flat, as something brought in rather than born there. Therefore it is certainly necessary frequently to replace it and always to add fresher flowers, since they do not long retain either their fragrance or beauty. But if, as I said in another sermon, the bed strewn with flowers is the conscience filled with good works (preceding sermon, §7), you see clearly, in order that the comparison may be maintained, that it is by no means sufficient to do good once or twice unless you continually add new things to what came before, so that, sowing in blessings, you may also reap from blessings [Col. 1009A]. Otherwise the flower of good work lies and withers, and in a short time all its brightness and vigor perish, unless it is continually renewed by one act of piety after another laid upon it. This is true in the chamber.

3. In the garden, however, it is not so; nor is it so in the field. Once they have produced flowers from themselves, they continually supply the means by which their native beauty may long endure in them. Yet they differ from one another: the garden flowers through human labor and skill, whereas the field naturally produces flowers from itself, without any aid from human care. Do you think that you now perceive who that field is—neither furrowed by a plow, nor dug by a hoe, nor enriched with manure, nor sown by human hand [Col. 1009B], and yet nevertheless beautified [elsewhere: made lovely] by that noble flower upon which the Spirit of the Lord is known to have rested? “Behold,” he says, “the odor of my son is like the odor of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27). That flower of the field had not yet put on his visible form, and already he was giving forth his fragrance, when the holy and aged patriarch, worn out in body and dim in sight but keen in scent, perceived him by the Spirit and, in joy, cried this out. Therefore he ought not to have declared himself the flower of the chamber, for he is a flower perpetually flourishing; nor the flower of the garden, lest he should seem generated by human labor. But beautifully and most fittingly he says, “I am the flower of the field,” since he came forth without human skill, and once he had come forth, corruption thereafter had no dominion over him, so that the saying might be fulfilled: “You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 16:10) [Col. 1009C].

4. But, if you please, receive another explanation of this matter, one that I judge not to be despised. For the Spirit is not described by the Wise Man as manifold without reason; rather, beneath the single bark of the letter he is accustomed often to conceal diverse meanings of wisdom. Thus, according to the foregoing division of the flower’s condition, virginity is a flower, martyrdom is a flower, and good action is a flower. Virginity is in the garden, martyrdom in the field, and good work in the chamber. Virginity is rightly in the garden, for modesty is truly familiar to it: it avoids public view, delights in seclusion, and endures discipline. Indeed, in the garden the flower is enclosed; in the field it is exposed; in the chamber it is scattered. And you have: “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song 4:12). This enclosure signifies the barrier of modesty in a virgin, and the guarding of inviolate holiness—provided she is such as is holy in body and spirit. Martyrdom likewise is rightly in the field, since martyrs are exposed to the mockery of all and made a spectacle both to angels and to human beings. Is this not their lamentable voice in the psalm: “We have become a reproach to our neighbors, scorn and derision to those around us?” [Col. 1010A] (Ps. 79:4). Good action also belongs rightly in the chamber, because it makes the conscience both peaceful and secure. For after a good work one sleeps more safely in contemplation, and one undertakes to behold and investigate lofty things with so much the greater confidence as one knows oneself not to have failed in the works of charity through love of one’s own repose.

5. In some respect, the Lord Jesus is all these things. He himself is the flower of the garden: a virgin shoot begotten of a Virgin. He is likewise the flower of the field: a martyr, the crown of martyrs, the pattern of martyrdom. For he was led outside the city, suffered outside the camp, was lifted up on the wood, to be seen by people and mocked by all. He is also the flower of the chamber, the mirror and example of every beneficence, as he himself testified to the Jews, saying: “Many good works have I shown you from my Father” (John 10:32) [Col. 1010B]; and again Scripture says of him: “He went about doing good and healing all” (Acts 10:38). If, then, the Lord is these three things, why did he prefer among the three to call himself the flower of the field? Certainly in order to encourage her to endurance, since he knew that, if she wished to live piously in Christ, she would have to suffer persecution. He therefore declares himself more willingly to be that to which he especially wishes her to conform. This is what I said elsewhere: she always seeks repose, while he urges her to labor, declaring that “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14:21). Thus, when the Church, newly espoused to him upon earth, was preparing to return to the Father, he said to her: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is rendering service to God” (John 16:2); and again: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15:20) [Col. 1010C]. You can also gather many similar pronouncements in the Gospel concerning evils that must be endured.

6. “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” Thus while she points out the bed, he calls her to the field and challenges her to exercise. He judges that nothing will persuade her more effectively to enter the contest than to set himself before her either as an example for one who fights or as the prize. “I am the flower of the field.” Certainly either meaning can be understood in this saying: namely, either that he is the model of the combatant or the glory of the victor. You are both to me, Lord Jesus: both the mirror of suffering and the reward of the sufferer [Col. 1010D]. Each powerfully urges me on and vehemently kindles me. By the example of your strength you teach my hands for battle; after victory, by the presence of your majesty, you crown my head. Whether I look upon you as fighting, or await you not only as crowning but also as the crown, in both ways you wonderfully draw me to yourself; each is a most powerful cord for drawing. “Draw me after you”: I gladly follow you; more gladly do I enjoy you. If you are so good, Lord, to those who follow you, what will you be to those who attain you? “I am the flower of the field.” Let whoever loves me come into the field; let him not shrink from entering the contest with me and for me, so that he may say: “I have fought the good fight” (2 Tim. 4:7).

7. And because those fit for martyrdom are not the proud or arrogant, but rather the humble, who do not know how to presume upon themselves, he further adds that he is the lily of the valleys: that is, the crown of the humble. By the loftiness of this flower he signifies their special glory in the future exaltation [Col. 1011A]. For there will be a time when every valley shall be filled and every mountain and hill brought low (Isa. 40:4); and then that brightness of eternal life—that true lily—will appear, not as the lily of hills but of valleys. “The righteous shall blossom like a lily,” he says (Hos. 14:6). Who is righteous except the humble? Finally, when the Lord inclined himself before the hands of John the Baptist, his servant, and John trembled before his majesty, he said: “Allow it; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15), plainly placing the fulfillment of righteousness in the perfection of humility. Therefore the righteous person is humble; the righteous person is a valley. And if we are found humble [Col. 1011B], we too shall blossom like the lily and flourish forever before the Lord. Will he not especially prove himself then to be the lily of the valleys when he refashions the body of our humility, conformed to the body of his glory? (Phil. 3:21). He does not say “our body,” but “the body of our humility,” in order to signify that by the wondrous and everlasting whiteness of this lily only the humble will be illumined. Let this suffice concerning the Bridegroom’s declaration that he is the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.

8. It would now be good to hear what he next declares concerning his most beloved; but the hour does not allow it. For our Rule permits nothing to be preferred to the Work of God (Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 43). By this name Father Benedict wished the solemn offices of praise, daily rendered to God in the oratory [Col. 1011C], to be called, so as to make clearer how attentively he wished us to apply ourselves to that work. Therefore I exhort you, most beloved, always to be present at the divine praises with purity and energy. With energy, so that, as you stand before the Lord reverently, you may also do so cheerfully: not sluggish, sleepy, or yawning; not sparing your voices; not cutting words in half or skipping them entire; not uttering through the nose, in broken and feeble voices, some womanish stammering. Rather, with manly sound and affection, as is fitting, bring forth the utterances of the Holy Spirit.

With purity, so that while you sing psalms you think of nothing other than what you sing. I do not say merely that vain and idle thoughts are to be avoided. At that hour and in that place, even those thoughts must be avoided which brethren charged with external offices [Note: “Officials,” those assigned to external duties, are distinguished from cloistered brethren in Sermon 9 on Various Subjects, §4, and below, Sermon 57, §11.] are often compelled, as though necessarily, to entertain for the common need [Col. 1011D]. But I would certainly not counsel you then to receive even those thoughts which perhaps, while sitting in the cloister shortly before, you had read in books—such as those fresh matters from this audience of the Holy Spirit which you are now carrying away as I expound them aloud. They are salutary; but you do not meditate on them salutarily while singing psalms. For at that hour the Holy Spirit does not receive with favor whatever other thing you offer than what you ought, neglecting what you ought to offer. May we, by his inspiration, always be able to do his will in conformity with his will, through the grace and mercy of Jesus Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLVIII

On the reciprocal praise exchanged by Bridegroom and Bride, and how Christ’s body and faith are understood through his shadow.

1. “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters” (Song 2:2). The daughters who prick are not good daughters. Consider the worst offspring of our earth, to which the curse was pronounced: “When you cultivate it, it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18). Therefore, as long as the soul is in the flesh, it certainly dwells among thorns and must suffer the uneasiness of temptations and the stings of tribulations. If, according to the Bridegroom’s word, she is a lily [Col. 1012B], let her see how watchful and anxious she ought to be concerning her own protection, fenced about on every side with thorns that stretch out their stings from here and there. For the tenderness of the flower cannot endure even the slightest prick of a thorn; as soon as it is pressed even lightly, it is pierced.

You see how rightly and necessarily the prophet exhorts us to “serve the Lord with fear” (Ps. 2:11), and likewise the Apostle, “with fear and trembling work out your own salvation” (Phil. 2:12). As friends of the Bridegroom, they knew by their own experience the truth of this saying, and did not doubt at all that what is said applied to their own souls: “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.” For one of them says: “I was turned in my affliction while the thorn was fixed in me” (Ps. 32:4) [Col. 1012C]. He is well pierced who is thereby converted. You are well pricked if you are pierced to compunction. Many, when they feel punishment, correct fault; and such a person may say: “I was turned in my affliction while the thorn was fixed in me.” A thorn is fault; a thorn is punishment; a thorn is a false brother; a thorn is an evil neighbor.

2. “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.” O shining lily! O tender and delicate flower! Unbelievers and corrupters are with you: see how carefully you walk among thorns. The world is full of thorns: they are in the earth, in the air, and in your flesh. To live among them and remain uninjured is a work of divine power, not of your own virtue. “But take courage,” he says, “for I have conquered the world” (John 16:33). Therefore, though you see the stings of tribulations, like thistles, directed against you on every side [Col. 1012D], let not your heart be troubled or afraid, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience testing, testing hope, and hope does not put to shame (Rom. 5:3–5). Consider the lilies of the field, how they flourish and shine among thorns. If God so preserves the grass, which is here today and tomorrow cast into the oven (Matt. 6:28–30), how much more his dearest friend and Bride? For “the Lord preserves all who love him” (Ps. 145:20).

“As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.” It is certainly no ordinary title of virtue to live uprightly among the wicked and to retain the brightness of innocence and gentleness of conduct among those who act maliciously [Col. 1013A]—especially if you show yourself peaceable and friendly even to enemies who hate peace. This will rightly claim for you, as its own special property, the comparison drawn from the lily: that it does not cease to illuminate and beautify with its own whiteness the very thorns that prick it. Does not the lily therefore seem in some way to fulfill the perfection of the Gospel, by which we are commanded to pray for those who slander and persecute us, and to do good to those who hate us? (Luke 6:27–28). Therefore do likewise, and your soul will be the Lord’s friend; and he will praise you for yourself, saying: “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.”

3. It follows: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons” [Col. 1013B]. The bride returns the tribute of praise to the bridegroom who commends her: to be praised by him is to become praiseworthy; and to praise him is to recognize and admire one who is praiseworthy. And just as her praise is figured by the bridegroom from an outstanding flower, so she, conversely, displays his unique glory and pre-eminence from an excellent tree.

Yet this tree gives me pause, because it does not appear to be of such great excellence as some of the others, and therefore seems less fit to be taken up for the purpose of comparison, as though it were insufficient to repay praise in kind. “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.” Indeed, the bride herself does not seem to have esteemed it greatly, since she took pains to exalt it only among the trees of the forest—plainly barren trees, bearing no fruits fit for human food. Why then, with better and nobler trees omitted, is the mediocrity of this tree brought forward to form the bridegroom’s praise? Was he who did not receive the Spirit by measure to receive [1433] praise according to measure? This comparison drawn from that tree makes him seem to have one above him who has no equal. What shall we say to this? I confess: it is a small praise, because it is praise of the little one. For here the “great Lord, and exceedingly praiseworthy” is not proclaimed (Ps. 144:3), but the little Lord, exceedingly lovable: namely, the little child who was born to us (Isa. 9:6).

4. Therefore majesty is not exalted here, but humility is commended; and fittingly and reasonably “the weak and foolish thing of God” is preferred to human strength and wisdom [Col. 1013D]. For men are those wild and fruitless trees, because, according to the Prophet, “all have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:3). “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.” Among the trees of the forest the Lord Jesus alone is a tree bearing fruit—certainly according to his humanity: though set above men, yet made lower than the angels (Ps. 8:6). For in a wonderful way he, having become flesh, subjected himself even to angels; and remaining God, he kept angels subject to himself. Thus he says: “You shall see angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:51), so that in the one and same man, Christ Jesus, they both minister to weakness [Col. 1014A] and marvel at majesty.

Since, therefore, what diminishes itself tastes sweeter to the bride, she more gladly magnifies grace, prefers mercy, and marvels at condescension. Accordingly, she chose to admire the man among men, not God among angels: like an apple tree he excels among the trees of the forest, and not, plainly, among the plants of gardens. Nor does she think praise diminished where, in consideration of weakness, the goodness of compassion is exalted. For insofar as she moderates his praises in one respect, she praises him more in another, pursuing less the glory of his dignity so that the grace of his condescension may stand out.

Thus the Apostle says that what is foolish and weak in God is wiser and stronger than men (1 Cor. 1:25), but not than angels; and thus the Prophet declares him “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. [Col. 1014B] 44:3), but not beyond angels. So she too, certainly speaking in the same Spirit, wished here under the image of the fruitful tree and the forest trees to exalt the God-Man above every grace of men, but not above the excellence of angels.

5. “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.” And rightly “among the sons,” because, though he was the only Son of his Father, he strove without envy to acquire for him many sons, whom he is not ashamed to call brothers, so that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. Rightly is he who is Son by nature set above all who are adopted by grace. “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.” Rightly like an apple tree, because, after the manner of a fruit-bearing tree, he has both the shade of refreshment and the very best fruit.

[Col. 1014C] Is he not truly a fruitful tree, whose flowers are “the fruits of honor and uprightness”? (Ecclus. 24:23). Indeed, “he is a tree of life to those who lay hold of him” (Prov. 3:18). All the trees of the forest cannot be compared with this one; for although there may be beautiful and great trees which seem to bring help by praying, ministering, teaching, and assisting by examples, yet Christ alone, the Wisdom of God, is the tree of life; he alone is the living bread who came down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:41, 33).

6. Therefore she says: “Under his shadow whom I had desired I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2:3).
