Rightly she had desired his shadow, from whom she was to receive both refreshment and nourishment together [Col. 1014D]. For the other trees of the forest, although they have the shade of consolation, do not have the nourishment of life or the everlasting fruits of salvation. For there is one author of life, one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), who says to his bride: “I am your salvation” (Ps. 34:3). “Moses,” he says, “did not give you this bread from heaven; but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven” (John 6:32). Therefore she especially desired Christ’s shadow because he alone not only cools from the heat of vices, but also fills with the delight of virtues.

“Under his shadow whom I had desired I sat.” His shadow is his flesh; his shadow is faith. The flesh of her own Son overshadowed Mary; the faith of the Lord overshadows me. Yet how does his flesh not also overshadow me, who [Col. 1015A] eat it in the [1434] mystery? And the holy Virgin likewise experienced the shadow of faith, to whom it was said: “Blessed are you who believed” (Luke 1:45). “Under his shadow whom I had desired I sat.” And the prophet says: “The breath before our face is Christ the Lord; in his shadow we shall live [Note: [Col. 1015D] Rouauld, Tiraqueau, Horstius: ‘we live.’] among the nations” (Lam. 4:20).

In shadow among the nations; in light with the angels. We are in shadow so long as we walk by faith and not by sight; and therefore the righteous person is in shadow, who lives by faith. But one who lives by understanding is blessed, because he is no longer in shadow but in light. David was righteous and lived by faith when he said to God: “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments and live” (Ps. 118:73, 144), knowing that understanding would follow faith, that to understanding the light [Col. 1015B] of life would be revealed, and that life belongs to light. One must first come to the shadow, and thus pass over to that of which it is the shadow; for, he says, “unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

7. You see that faith is both life and the shadow of life. Conversely, a life spent in pleasures, because it is not from faith, is both death and the shadow of death. For “she who lives in pleasures,” he says, “is dead while living” (1 Tim. 5:6). Indeed, “the wisdom of the flesh is death” (Rom. 8:6). And it is the shadow of death: namely, of that death which torments eternally. We too once sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, living carnally and not living by faith: already dead to righteousness, and only a little short of being swallowed up by the second death [Col. 1015C]. For as closely as the shadow is joined to the body whose shadow it is, so surely had that life of ours drawn near to hell. Thus he says: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would soon have dwelt in hell” (Ps. 93:17).

But now we have passed from the shadow of death to the shadow of life—or rather, we have been transferred from death to life (1 John 3:14), living in Christ’s shadow, if indeed we are living and not dead. For I do not think that, merely because someone has been in his shadow, he necessarily lives in it; since not everyone who has faith lives by faith. Faith without works is dead and cannot give life when it does not itself possess life. Therefore, when the prophet had said, “Christ the Lord is the breath before our face,” he was not content to continue by saying, “We are in his shadow,” but said, “In his shadow we live among the nations” [Col. 1015D]. You therefore see to it that you live in his shadow after the prophet’s example, so that one day you may also reign in his light.

For he has not only shadow; he has light also. Through the flesh he is the shadow of faith; through the Spirit he is the light of understanding. For he is both flesh and spirit: flesh to those who remain in the flesh; spirit before our face—that is, in the future—provided we forget what lies behind and stretch ourselves toward what lies before, so that when we arrive there we may experience the truth of his saying: “The flesh profits nothing; it is the Spirit who gives life” (John 6:64). Nor am I unaware that one who was still remaining in the flesh said: “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, [Col. 1016A] yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). But that was he; whereas we, who have not yet deserved to be caught up into paradise, not yet into the third heaven, should meanwhile feed upon Christ’s flesh, revere the mysteries, follow the examples, keep the faith; and we truly live in shadow.

8. “Under his shadow whom I had desired I sat.” Perhaps she glories in having experienced something happier than the prophet did, in saying that she sat in the shadow: not that she lived, as the prophet says, but that she sat. For to sit is to rest. And to rest in shadow is more than to live in it, just as to live is more than merely to be in it. Thus the prophet, taking to himself what is common to many, says: “We live in his shadow”; but the bride, having a prerogative, glories also that she alone sat under it [Col. 1016B]. For he did not say in the plural, “We sit,” as he said, “We live”; nor did she say “I live,” but singularly, “I sat,” so that you may recognize the prerogative.

Where we live with labor, conscious of sins and serving under fear, she, devoted and loving, rests sweetly. For fear has punishment, but love has sweetness. Hence she says: “And his fruit was sweet to my throat,” signifying the savor of contemplation which she had obtained, sweetly raised up by love. Yet this is in shadow, because it is through a mirror and in an enigma. It will be otherwise when the shadows have declined as the light increases—or rather, when they have wholly vanished—and a vision, as clear as it is [1435] everlasting, enters in. Then there will be not merely sweetness in the throat but fullness in the belly, yet without satiety.

“Under his shadow whom I had desired [Col. 1016C] I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat.” Let us too rest where the bride rests, glorifying, for the taste we have received, the master of the household who invited us to such a feast: Jesus Christ our Lord, Bridegroom of the Church, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLIX. How love is ordered through discernment, so that all members of the Church—that is, the elect—are joined together mutually.

1. “The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered love within me” (Song 2:4). As the letter of the heading seems to mean, after the bride has had the sweet and very familiar conversation with her beloved that she wished, and he has departed, she returns to the young women [Col. 1016D], so restored and inflamed by his sight and speech that she seems like one intoxicated. And as though they were astonished at this novelty and asking its cause, she answered that it was not surprising if she burned with wine, since she had entered the wine-cellar. Such is the literal sense.

The spiritual sense also does not deny that she is intoxicated, but with love, not wine—except that love is wine. “The king brought me into the wine-cellar.” When the bridegroom is present and the bride addresses her speech to him, then he is called either bridegroom or beloved, or “he whom my soul loves”; but when she speaks of him to the young women, she calls him king. Why is this? I think it is because it suits the loving and beloved bride to use the more familiar names of love in speaking to him, while the young women, as needing discipline, require to be impressed with the reverent title of majesty.

2. “The king brought me into the wine-cellar.” I pass over what this wine-cellar is, because I remember having spoken of it. Yet, if the discourse is referred to the Church: when the disciples, filled with the Holy Spirit, were thought by the people to be drunk with new wine, then Peter, standing in their midst as the bridegroom’s friend for the bride, said: “These are not drunk as you suppose.” Observe meanwhile that he did not deny that they were altogether drunk, but only drunk as they were supposed to be by those people. They were drunk indeed, but with the Holy Spirit, not with new wine.

And as though they testified to the people that they had truly been brought into the wine-cellar, Peter again spoke for all: “But this,” he says, “is what was spoken through the prophet Joel: ‘And it shall come to pass in [Col. 1017B] the last days, says the Lord, that I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and daughters shall prophesy; your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams.’” Does not that house seem to you to have been a wine-cellar, in which the disciples were gathered together when suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty spirit coming, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting (Acts 2:13–17, 2), and fulfilled Joel’s prophecy? And did not each of them, going out intoxicated by the abundance of that house and made to drink from the torrent of such delight, rightly say: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar”?

3. You also, if, having recollected your spirit, with a sober mind free from cares, you enter alone into the house of prayer [Col. 1017C], and standing before God at one of the altars, touch the gate of heaven with the hand of holy desire; and, brought before the choirs of saints by your devotion penetrating there—for “the prayer of the righteous penetrates the heavens”—you deplore piteously in their presence the miseries and calamities you suffer; if by frequent sighs and unutterable groanings you disclose your need and implore mercy—if, I say, you do this, I trust in him who said, “Ask, and you shall receive” (Matt. 7:7), that if you persevere in knocking, you will not go away empty.

But when you return to us full of grace and love, you will not be able, fervent in spirit, to conceal the gift received, which you will share without envy. You will be pleasing to all in the grace given you [Col. 1017D], not merely acceptable, but perhaps even admirable; and you too may truly testify: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar”—provided only that you take care to glory not in yourself but in the Lord.

Nor would I [1436] say that every gift, however spiritual, proceeds from the wine-cellar, since the bridegroom has other cells or storehouses containing within themselves diverse gifts and charisms, according to the riches of his glory; concerning these cells I remember having discussed more fully elsewhere (above, Sermon 23). “Are not these things stored up with me,” he says, “and sealed in my treasuries?” (Deut. 32:34). Therefore, according to the diversity of the cells, there are divisions of graces, and “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each one for usefulness.” Although to one is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge, to another prophecy, to another the grace of healings [Col. 1018A], to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of utterances, and other similar gifts to others (1 Cor. 12:7–11), none of these persons can on this account say that he has been brought into the wine-cellar. Such things are taken from other cells or treasuries.

4. But if someone obtains in prayer an ecstasy of mind into the secret of God, from which he soon returns burning most vehemently with divine love and aflame with zeal for righteousness, and also exceedingly fervent in every spiritual pursuit and duty, so that he can say: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire is kindled” (Ps. 38:4)—such a person, when from the abundance of love he begins to belch forth a wholesome and salutary intoxication with the wine of joy, will not without reason be said to have entered the wine-cellar [Col. 1018B].

For there are two ecstasies of blessed contemplation: one in understanding, the other in affection; one in light, the other in fervor; one in knowledge, the other in devotion. A pious affection, then, a breast warm with love, an infusion of holy devotion, and a vehement spirit filled with zeal are certainly brought back from no other place than the wine-cellar. And whoever is granted to rise from prayer with an abundance of these things may truly say: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar.”

5. It follows: “He ordered love within me.” Most necessary indeed. Zeal without knowledge is unbearable. Therefore, where emulation is vehement, discernment is especially necessary; and this is the ordering of love. Zeal without knowledge is always found less effective and less useful; and often it is felt to be very harmful. The more fervent the zeal, the more vehement the spirit, and the more lavish the love, the more vigilant must be the knowledge that restrains zeal, tempers spirit, and orders love.

Therefore, lest the bride should be feared by the young women as excessive and unbearable because of the impulse of the spirit which she seems to have brought back from the wine-cellar, she adds that she also received discernment, namely the order of love [Col. 1018C]. For discernment gives order to every virtue; order gives measure, beauty, and also permanence. Thus it is said: “By your ordering the day endures” (Ps. 118:91), where “day” means virtue. Discernment, then, is not so much a virtue as a certain moderator and charioteer of virtues, an arranger of affections, and a teacher of conduct. Remove it, and virtue will become vice; even natural affection will be turned rather into disturbance and the destruction of nature.

“He ordered love within me.” This occurred when, in the Church, he gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints (Eph. 4:11–12). But one love must bind all these together and harmonize them into the unity of Christ’s body. It cannot do this at all unless it itself is ordered. For if each person is carried along by his own impulse according to the spirit he has received, and rushes without distinction to whatever he wishes, as he is affected, rather than by the judgment of reason [Col. 1019A], then, while no one is content with the office assigned to him but all alike attempt everything in indiscriminate administration, there will plainly be not unity but confusion.

6. “He ordered love within me.” Would that the Lord Jesus might order in me at least a little of the love he has given, so that all that belongs to him may concern me, yet that I may care before all else for what is known to belong especially to my purpose or office; but in such a way that, while this comes first, I am nevertheless more deeply moved by many things that do not specially concern me. For what must always be cared for first need not always be loved more, since what comes first [1437] in solicitude is often less in usefulness and, for that reason, ought also to be less in affection.

Thus what is put first because of a duty laid upon one is often set behind by judgment [Note: [Col. 1019] Thus all our manuscripts and the earliest printed editions. Later editions: “by God’s judgment,” etc. Horstius: “therefore what truth judges should be put first is, by judgment,” etc.]; and the order of love requires that what truth judges to be preferable should be embraced more dearly. Does not care for all of you, for example, rest upon me by reason of the charge committed to me? Whatever work I might happen to put before this task, so that I give less watchful and worthy attention to carrying it out according to my ability—even if I might seem to do it from love—the principle of order does not consent to it.

But if, as I ought, I devote myself before all else to this care, yet do not rejoice more in the greater gains of God which I learn may perhaps be accomplished through another, it is evident that I keep the order of love in part, but not at all in part. If, however, I show myself more diligent regarding that which lies more specially upon me, while nonetheless being more warmly affected toward that which is greater [Col. 1019C], then I am found to have attained the order of love in both respects; nor is there any reason why I too may not say, “He ordered love within me.”

7. But if you say that it is difficult for someone to rejoice more over another’s great good than over his own small good, you will see even from this the excellence of grace in the bride, and that not every soul can say: “He ordered love within me.” Why, then, have the faces of some of you fallen just now at this discourse? Your deep sighs bear witness to the sadness of your souls and the dejection of your consciences. Plainly, measuring ourselves by ourselves, some of us know from our experience of imperfection how rare a virtue it is not to envy another’s virtue [Col. 1019D], much less to rejoice in it, and still less for each person to rejoice in it more than in his own, by as much as he finds himself surpassed in virtue.

There is still a little light in us, brothers, all of us who think thus of ourselves. Let us walk while we have the light, lest darkness overtake us (John 12:35). To walk is to make progress. The Apostle was walking when he said: “I do not consider that I have attained”; and he adds: “But one thing: forgetting what lies behind, I stretch myself toward what lies before” (Phil. 3:13). What is this “but one thing”? “But one thing,” he says, as though one remedy, one hope, one consolation remained to him. What is it? Namely, “forgetting what lies behind, I stretch myself toward what lies before” [Col. 1020A]. Great confidence! The great Vessel of Election, refusing to call himself perfect, confesses progress.

I see danger not for the one walking, but for the one sitting, to be overtaken by the darkness of death. And who sits except the person who does not care to make progress? Beware of this; and if death overtakes you, you will be in refreshment. You will say to God: “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and nevertheless all shall be written in your book.” Who are “all”? Certainly those found in the desire to make progress. For it follows: “The days shall be formed, and no one in them” (Ps. 138:16); supply: “shall perish.” Understand by “days” those who make progress: if death overtakes them, they will be perfected in that which they lack. “They shall be formed,” and no one among them will be left unformed.

8. “And how,” you ask, “can I make progress when I envy a brother who is making progress?” If you grieve that you envy, you feel it but do not consent to it. It is a passion which must at some time be healed, not an action to be condemned. Only do not remain there, meditating iniquity upon your bed: namely, how you may foster the disease, satisfy the pestilence, persecute one who has done no wrong, by slandering, suppressing, distorting, and obstructing the good deeds he has done or will do [Col. 1020B].

Otherwise, it does not harm one who is walking and stretching toward better things that it is no longer he who acts, but sin dwelling in him (Rom. 7:20). Therefore there is no condemnation for one who does not give his members as weapons to unrighteousness: neither his tongue [1438] for detraction, nor any other part of his body to injure or harm in any way. Rather, he is ashamed that he is so wrongly affected; and, confessing, weeping over, and praying against a vice ingrained by long habit, he strives to cast it out. When he does not prevail, he is thereby found gentler toward all and humbler in himself [Col. 1020C]. What sound-minded person would condemn one who has learned from the Lord to be meek and humble of heart? (Matt. 11:29). Far be it that an imitator of the Savior should be found without a share in salvation: the Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON L. On two kinds of love, namely active and affective, and on their ordering.

1. Perhaps you expect the following words to be discussed, thinking the verse which was most recently treated finished [Col. 1020D]. But I intend something else, for I still have something to set before you from the fragments of yesterday’s feast, which I gathered lest they perish. They will perish, however, if I set them before no one; for if I wish to keep them alone, I myself shall perish. Therefore I do not wish to deprive you of your appetite for them, which I know well—especially since they are from the dish of love: the sweeter because subtler, the more savory because smaller. For it is altogether very contrary to love to deprive others of love itself. Thus here I am: “He ordered love within me” (Song 2:4).

2. There is love in act, and there is love in affection. Concerning that which consists in work, I think a law has been given to men and a command framed; for who can possess love in affection just as it is commanded? Therefore the former is commanded for merit; the latter is given as a reward. We do not deny that divine grace may allow its beginning, progress, and even a present experience of it in this life; but we maintain that its consummation belongs to future blessedness. How, then, could that be commanded which could in no way be fulfilled? Or, if you prefer that the command was given concerning affective love, I do not dispute it, provided that you in turn agree with me that no human being can or could fulfill it in this life [Note: [Col. 1021D] See *Treatise on Loving God*, ch. 10, no. 29.].

For who would dare arrogate to himself what Paul himself confesses that he has not attained? (Phil. 3:13). Nor was the Teacher ignorant that the weight of the command exceeds human powers; but he judged it useful that men should thereby be warned of their own insufficiency and should know to what end of righteousness they ought to strive according to their strength. Therefore, by commanding impossibilities, he did not make men transgressors but humble, so that every mouth might be stopped and the whole world made subject to God, because “by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified before him” (Rom. 3:19–20). For when we receive the command and recognize our sin, we shall cry out to heaven, and God will have mercy on us; and on that day we shall know that “not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3:5).

3. And I would say this if we had agreed that the affective law was commanded. But it appears to apply more properly to active love [Note: [Col. 1021D] Bernard’s view is that the command concerning love applies more properly to active than to affective love. By “affective” he understands that most perfect love which belongs only to the blessed—or at least to the perfect. By “active,” however, he means the love that does not stop at simple affection but breaks forth into action, while by no means excluding the inward act of love. “I do not say this,” he says in no. 4, “that we should be without affection”; rather, it includes inward love [Col. 1022D], which, though it does not yet sweetly refresh with that sweet love, nevertheless burns vehemently with love for love itself. This is the inward love with which active love is content; see no. 6. See the Admonition to the book *On Loving God*, above, vol. II.], especially because, after the Lord said, “Love your enemies,” he immediately adds works: “Do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6:27). Likewise Scripture says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink” (Rom. 12:20). Here you have action, not affection.

But hear the Lord likewise commanding love for himself: “If you love me,” he says, “keep my words” [Note: [Col. 1022D] “Where, then, are they to be kept? Undoubtedly in the heart,” Bernard says in Sermon 5 on Advent, no. 2; indeed also from the heart, as he explains there, so that they may be like food, which “passes into the affections and into conduct.”] (John 14:15). Here also we are directed toward works by the enjoined observance of the commandments. He would have warned us [1439] about work in vain if love were already in affection. Thus you must necessarily understand in the same way the command to “love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39), even though it is not so expressly stated. Would you not judge it sufficient for fulfilling this command concerning love of neighbor if you perfectly observe the rule rightly prescribed to every human being by the law of nature: “Do not do to another what you would not wish done to yourself”? (Tob. 4:16). And likewise: “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. 7:12).

4. I do not say this in order that we should be without affection and move only our hands to works with a dry heart. Among the other great and grave evils of men which the Apostle records, I have read this also listed: namely, to be “without affection” (Rom. 1:31). But there is an affection produced by the flesh; there is one governed by reason; and there is one formed by wisdom. The first is what the Apostle says is not subject to the law of God, nor can be (Rom. 8:7); the second, which he says on the contrary consents to the law of God, because it is good (Rom. 7:16). There is no doubt that contentious affection differs from harmonious affection. But the third differs far from both: it both tastes and knows that the Lord is sweet [Col. 1022B] (Ps. 33:9), eliminating the first and rewarding the second.

For the first is sweet but shameful; the second dry but strong; the last rich and sweet. Therefore works are done through the second, and in it love dwells—not that affective love which, seasoned with the salt of wisdom, grows rich and brings to the mind a great abundance of the Lord’s sweetness, but rather a kind of active love which, although it does not yet sweetly refresh with that sweet love, nevertheless burns vehemently with love for love itself. “Let us not love,” he says, “in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18).

5. You see how carefully he walks a middle course between vicious love and affective love, distinguishing this active and saving love equally from both [Col. 1022C]. In this love he admits neither the pretense of a lying tongue nor, again, demands the savor of wisdom that affects the heart. “Let us love,” he says, “in deed and truth”: that is, let us be moved to act well more by a certain impulse of living truth than by the affection of that savory love. “He ordered love within me.” Which of these kinds of love do you think? Both, but in opposite order. For active love puts lower things first; affective love, higher things.

For in a rightly disposed mind, there is no doubt, for example, that love of God is placed before love of man; among human beings, that the more perfect are preferred to the weaker; heaven to earth; eternity to time; soul to body. Yet in rightly ordered action, the opposite order is often, or even always, found. For in caring for one’s neighbor we are pressed more urgently and occupied more frequently; we attend to weaker brothers with more diligent care; through human obligation and necessity itself, we properly give more attention to the peace of earth than to the glory of heaven; the restless anxiety of temporal cares scarcely permits us to have any perception of eternal things; setting aside the care of the soul, we serve almost continually the infirmities of our body [Col. 1023A]; and finally, according to the Apostle’s teaching, we bestow more abundant honor upon the weaker members of our bodies (1 Cor. 12:23).

In this way we in some measure do the Lord’s word: “The last shall be first, and the first last” (Matt. 20:16). Who doubts that a person praying speaks with God? Yet how often are we drawn and torn away from this by love’s command, because of those who need our work or speech? How often does holy repose rightly yield to the tumult of business? How often is the book of a good conscience laid aside so that we may sweat at manual work? How often, in order to administer temporal affairs, do we most justly refrain even from celebrating the solemnities of Mass? [Note: [Col. 1023D] Among the Cistercians of old, the sacred rites were interrupted at harvest time. Thus Philip Augustus, having heard that at the monastery of Barbeaux, during harvest time, when the monks went to the granges, the solemnity of Mass was suspended on account of temporal affairs, commanded that the solemnities of Mass be celebrated there every morning for the soul of his father, who was buried there. Letters on this matter are extant in book VI of *De re diplomatica*, p. 603. Elsewhere Bernard very rarely interrupted the offering of the saving victim “until the very last extremity,” as Geoffrey testifies in book V of his *Life*, ch. 1.]

This is an inverted order; but necessity has no law. Thus [1440] active love follows its own order according to the command of the master of the household, beginning with the last (ibid., v. 8) [Col. 1023B]. It is certainly pious and just, because it does not show partiality and considers not the value of things but the necessities of persons.

6. Affective love is not so: it takes its order from the first things. For it is wisdom, by which each thing tastes to us according to what it is. Thus, for example, what has greater worth by nature is felt by affection also to be of greater worth; lesser things, less; the least, least of all. Truth establishes the former order of love; but love of truth claims the latter for itself. For love is true in this: that those who need more receive first; and conversely, truth appears dear when we maintain in affection the order which truth maintains in reason.

Therefore, if you love the Lord your God with all your heart, all your soul, and all your strength (Matt. 22:37); and, passing beyond with more fervent affection that “love for love” [Note: [Col. 1024D] In some manuscripts the words “for love” are absent here. But this is not contrary to Bernard’s meaning, for above, in no. 4, when speaking of active love, he says: “Nevertheless it burns vehemently with love for love itself.”] with which active love is content; if, receiving in the fullness of the Spirit the divine love itself at close hand, toward which that is a step, you are wholly set aflame: then God truly tastes sweet to you, though certainly not altogether worthily as he is—for this is impossible for every creature—but at least according to your capacity for tasting.

Then you too will taste sweet to yourself according to what you are, when you perceive that you have absolutely nothing by which you may love yourself except insofar as you are God’s; since you have poured out into him all that by which you love. You will, I say, taste sweet to yourself according to what you are when, by the very experience of your love and by the affection you will have toward yourself, you find nothing in yourself worthy of being loved even by yourself except on account of him, without whom you yourself are nothing.

7. Moreover, the neighbor whom you are truly bound to love as yourself, so that he too may be pleasing to you according to what he is, will assuredly be pleasing to you in no other way than you are pleasing to yourself; for he is what you are: a human being. Therefore, since you love yourself only because you love God, you consequently love as yourself all who likewise love him. But an enemy, because he is nothing insofar as he does not love God, cannot indeed be loved as yourself by one who loves God; nevertheless, you will love him so that he may love. Now, to love someone so that he may love is not the same as to love him because he loves. Hence, that he too may be pleasing to you according to what he is, what will be pleasing to you is not what he is—for certainly he is nothing—but what perhaps he will be, something close to nothing, since it still hangs in uncertainty. But one of whom it is established that he will never return to the love of God must necessarily be pleasing to you, not as something now close to nothing, but as nothing altogether, since he is eternally nothing. Excepting, therefore, that person who not only is no longer to be loved, but is even to be hated, according to the saying: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies?” (Ps. 138:21 [Vulgate]). Apart from him, charity—ambitious, indeed, in this respect—allows no human being, however hostile, to be denied even the slightest affection. “Who is wise, and will understand these things?”

8. Give me a person who, before all else, loves God wholly; who loves himself and his neighbor insofar as they love him; who loves his enemy as one who perhaps will one day love; who loves the parents of his flesh more tenderly because of nature, but his spiritual instructors more lavishly because of grace; and who in this fashion directs an ordered love toward every other thing of God, despising earth and looking up toward heaven, using this world as though not using it, and discerning, by a certain inward taste of the mind, between things to be used and things to be enjoyed; who treats transient things transiently, caring for them only so far as need requires and in the manner required, but embraces eternal things with eternal desire. Give me, I say, such a person, and I shall boldly pronounce him wise: one for whom each thing truly has its proper savor according to what it is, and who can glory truly and securely, saying: “He has ordered charity in me.”

But where is that person? Or when will this be? I say it weeping: how long shall we smell and not taste, behold the homeland from afar and not attain it, sigh for it and greet it from a distance? O Truth, homeland of exiles and end of exile! I see you, but am not permitted to enter, held back by the flesh; nor am I worthy to be admitted, stained by sins. O Wisdom, who reaches mightily from end to end in establishing and sustaining things, and orders all things sweetly in making affections blessed and rightly disposed! [Col. 1024D] Direct our actions as our temporal necessity requires; and order our affections as your eternal truth demands, so that each of us may securely glory in you and say: “He has ordered charity in me.” For you are the power of God and the wisdom of God, Christ, Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord, God blessed above all for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LI. How the bride asks that the fruits of good works be heaped up for her together with the flowers and fragrances of faith; likewise, concerning hope and fear.

1. “Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2:5). Love has increased, because more incentives to love than usual have appeared. You see how great on this occasion was the opportunity not only to behold, but also to converse. The vision itself seems to have been granted with a more serene countenance; the speech was more delightful, and the conversation longer and more extended. Nor was she merely delighted by the conversation; she also gloried in the praise bestowed upon her. Moreover, she was refreshed by the shade of him whom she had desired, fed with fruit, and given drink from the cup. For she must not be thought to have left the wine-cellar thirsty, into which she has just now gloried that she was brought. Or rather, she was thirsty, since, “He who drinks me,” says Wisdom, “will still thirst” (Ecclus. 24:29).

After all these things, when the bridegroom withdraws in his accustomed manner, she declares that she languishes with love—that is, because of love. For the more welcome his presence had proved to her, the more burdensome she afterward found his absence. The removal of a thing that one loves increases desire; and what you desire more ardently, you endure lacking more painfully. Therefore she asks in the meantime to be comforted with the fragrances of flowers and fruits, until he returns again, whose delay she bears most painfully. Such is the order of the discourse.

2. Let us now, under the Spirit’s guidance, endeavor to draw out the spiritual fruit contained in these words. If the common Church of the saints is here understood to be speaking, we are signified by the flowers and fruits, as are all who have been converted from the world throughout the whole world. In the flowers is represented the new and still tender manner of life of beginners; in the fruits, the strength of those making progress and the maturity of the perfect. Supported by these, the pilgrim and fruitful mother—whose life is Christ and whose death is gain—bears more equably the burden of her delay, because, according to Scripture, “the fruit of her hands is given to her,” as though from the firstfruits of the Spirit, and “her works praise her in the gates” (Prov. 31:31).

But if, in the moral sense, you wish both to be assigned to a single soul—flowers, namely, and fruits—understand faith as the flower and action as the fruit. Nor, I think, will this seem unsuitable to you if you observe how, just as a flower must precede fruit, so too a good work must be preceded by faith. Otherwise, “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6), as Paul testifies—or rather, himself teaches equally: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). Thus, no fruit without a flower, and no good work without faith. But “faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:20), just as a flower is useless where fruit does not follow. “Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love.”

Therefore a mind accustomed to repose receives consolation from good works rooted in unfeigned faith whenever, as often happens, the light of contemplation is withdrawn from it. For who, not to say continually but even for any length of time while remaining in this body, enjoys the light of contemplation? Yet whenever, as I have said, it falls away from contemplation, it returns to activity, intending thereby, as from nearby, to return more familiarly to the same contemplation; for these two are companions sharing one dwelling and inhabiting it together. Martha is Mary’s sister. Nor, although it falls away from the light of contemplation, does it at all allow itself to fall into the darkness of sin or the idleness of sloth; rather, it keeps itself in the light of good action. And so that you may know that works too are light: “Let your light shine before men” (Matt. 5:16)—which was undoubtedly said of works that people could see.

3. “Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love.” When what is loved is present, love flourishes; it languishes when that object is absent. This is nothing other than a kind of weariness arising from impatient desire, which must strongly affect a mind that loves intensely when the one it loves is absent. Entirely absorbed in expectation, it regards however great a haste as slowness. Therefore she asks that the fruits of good works be heaped up for her with the fragrances of faith, so that while the bridegroom delays she may rest among them.

I speak to you from my own experience—what I myself have experienced. Whenever I have found some of you to have advanced through my admonitions, then, I confess, I was not sorry to have preferred the care of preaching to my own leisure and quiet. For when, for example, after a sermon, an irascible person is found changed into a gentle one, a proud person into a humble one, a faint-hearted person into a courageous one; when the gentle, humble, and courageous have each grown in his own grace and are recognized to have become better than before; when those who perhaps had grown lukewarm and languid in spiritual endeavor, sluggish and asleep, seem to have been rekindled and awakened by the Lord’s fiery word; and when those who, having abandoned the fountain of wisdom, had dug for themselves cisterns of their own will that could not hold water, and therefore murmured with dry hearts at every task imposed on them, possessing in themselves no moisture of devotion—when these, I say, are proved to have blossomed again into works of obedience through the dew of the word and the voluntary rain which God set apart for his inheritance, becoming willing and devout in all things—then, I tell you, no sadness comes upon my mind as though because I have interrupted the pursuit of delightful contemplation, when I am surrounded by such flowers and fruits of piety.

I patiently tear myself away from the embraces of unfruitful Rachel, so that the fruits of your progress may abound for me from Leah. I shall not at all regret interrupted quiet [or, disturbed quiet] for the sake of preaching, when I see my seed germinating in you and the increase of the harvest of your righteousness growing from it. For charity, which “does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5), long ago easily persuaded me to set none of my desirable things before your benefit. Prayer, reading, writing, meditation, and whatever other gains belong to spiritual study—I have counted these losses for your sake.

4. “Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love.” The bride said this, then, to the young women in the bridegroom’s absence, warning them to advance in faith and good works until he comes; for she perceived that this would bring the bridegroom’s good pleasure, the daughters’ salvation, and her own consolation. I know that I explained this passage more fully in my book *On Loving God*, and under another interpretation. Let the reader who wishes to see both judge which is better or worse. I shall certainly not be judged by a prudent person on account of a diversity of meanings, provided truth supports us in both places, and charity—to which the Scriptures ought to be of service—edifies more people in proportion as it draws more true meanings from them for its work. For why should what we constantly experience in the uses of things displease us in the meanings of Scripture? Into how many uses, for example, is water alone put by our bodies? So likewise it will not be unfitting if a single divine saying produces diverse meanings suited to the diverse needs and uses of souls.

5. It follows: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” I remember that this too was discussed more fully in the aforementioned little work; but let us mark the sequence of the discourse. Clearly the bridegroom is again present, I believe, to raise her up by his presence as she languishes. For how could she fail to recover in his presence when his absence had cast her down? He cannot endure the distress of his beloved. He is present, for summoned by such desires he cannot delay. And because he found that, while he was absent, she had been faithful in works and diligent in gaining spiritual profit, in that she had commanded flowers and fruits to be gathered for her, this time he returned with an even more generous recompense of grace. At last, with one of his arms he supports the head of her as she lies down; the other he prepares for embracing, that he may cherish her in his bosom. Happy the soul that reclines upon Christ’s breast and rests between the arms of the Word. “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” She does not say, “He embraces me,” but “He will embrace me,” so that you may know that she is so far from being ungrateful for the earlier grace that she anticipates the second by thanksgiving.

6. Learn not to be slow or sluggish in rendering thanks; learn to give thanks for every gift. “Consider diligently,” Scripture says, “the things set before you” (Prov. 23:1), so that no gifts of God, great, moderate, or small, may be deprived of their due thanksgiving. We are commanded, indeed, to gather up the fragments lest they perish (John 6:12); that is, we are not to forget even the smallest benefits. Does not what is given to an ungrateful person perish? Ingratitude is an enemy of the soul, an emptying of merits, a scattering of virtues, a loss of benefits. Ingratitude is a scorching wind, drying up within itself the fountain of piety, the dew of mercy, and the streams of grace. Therefore, as soon as the bride felt the grace of the left hand, she gave thanks, not waiting for the fullness that is in the right. For when it was said that the left hand was already under her head, it did not also follow that she was similarly embraced by the right; rather, she says, “His right hand will embrace me.”

7. But what are we to suppose the left hand and the right hand to be for the Word, the Bridegroom? Does the word spoken by a human being have bodily parts of this sort, divided and outlined so as to distinguish left from right? How much more does he who is God and the Word of God admit no variation whatsoever, but is “he who is” (Exod. 3:14): in his nature so simple that he has no parts, so one that he has no number. For he is the wisdom of God, of whom it is written: “There is no number to his wisdom” (Ps. 146:5 [Vulgate]). But if what is unchangeable must also be incomprehensible, and hence ineffable, where, I ask, will you find words by which you might either adequately ascribe something to that majesty, properly express it, or suitably define it?

Still, let us speak as we can of what, by the Holy Spirit’s revelation, we understand as we can concerning it. We are taught by the authority of the Fathers and by the practice of Scripture that it is fitting to employ analogies from known things concerning realities unknown; and not to devise new words, but to borrow [or, transfer] familiar ones by which such analogies may suitably and fittingly be clothed. Otherwise, you would absurdly attempt to teach unknown things through unknown things.

8. Therefore, because adversity and prosperity are commonly signified by the left and right, it seems to me that here the Word’s left hand may be understood as the threat of punishment, and his right hand as the promise of the kingdom. Sometimes our mind is held down in servile fashion by fear of punishment; and then the left hand must by no means be said to be under the head, but over the head. A soul thus affected cannot at all say: “His left hand is under my head.” But if, making progress, it passes from this spirit of slavery into a worthier disposition of willing obedience—so that it is drawn rather by rewards than constrained by punishments, or rather, is moved by love of the good itself—then it can undoubtedly say: “His left hand is under my head.” For it has overcome, by a better and more excellent disposition of mind, that servile fear which is in the left hand, and through worthy desires has even approached the right hand itself, in which are all the promises; as the Prophet says to the Lord: “Delights are at your right hand for ever” (Ps. 15:11 [Vulgate]). Hence, having conceived a sure hope, it speaks confidently: “And his right hand will embrace me.”

9. Consider with me now whether, for a soul so disposed and having attained this place of such great sweetness, it is also fitting to borrow that saying from the Psalm, so that it may say: “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the selfsame state,” especially since the following reason is available: “For you, O Lord, have established me singularly in hope” (Ps. 4:9–10 [Vulgate]). Its meaning, indeed, is this. So long as someone is oppressed by the spirit of slavery and has little hope but very much fear, there is for him neither peace nor rest; his conscience fluctuates between hope and fear, especially because he is more abundantly tormented by overwhelming fear, for “fear has punishment.” Therefore he cannot say, “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the selfsame state,” when he cannot yet say that he has been established singularly in hope. But if, gradually through the increase of grace, fear begins to diminish and hope to grow; and when at last love, rising with all its strength to assist hope, casts fear outside—will not such a soul appear to be established singularly in hope, and therefore now also sleep and rest in peace in the selfsame state?

10. “If you sleep among the midst of the lots, the wings of the dove are silvered” (Ps. 67:14 [Vulgate]). I think this was said because there is a place between fear and security, as between left and right: namely, hope in the middle. In it mind and conscience rest most sweetly, with a soft bed of charity laid beneath them. Perhaps this very place is indicated later in this same Song, where, in the description of Solomon’s litter, you read among other things: “He paved its midst with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 3:10). For one who feels himself established singularly in hope no longer serves in fear, but rests in charity.

Finally, the bride rests and sleeps, concerning whom it is said: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields: do not stir up or awaken my beloved until she herself wills it.” Great and astonishing condescension: he causes the contemplating soul to rest in his bosom; moreover, he guards it from harassing cares, protects it from the disturbances of activity and the vexations of business, and does not permit it to be awakened except at her own will. But this must not be begun within the narrow limits of a discourse now coming to an end. Rather, let another begin from this point, so that this delightful passage may not be deprived of the diligence it deserves in treatment. Not that we shall then be sufficient to think anything from ourselves as though from ourselves, especially concerning so worthy, excellent, and altogether surpassing a subject; but our sufficiency is from God, Jesus Christ our Lord, Bridegroom of the Church, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LII. On the ecstasy called contemplation, in which the Bridegroom causes the holy soul to rest, being zealous for its repose.

1. “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields, that you do not stir up or awaken my beloved until she herself wills it” (Song 2:7). The young women are forbidden—for he calls them daughters of Jerusalem because, although delicate and soft, and still weak as it were in feminine dispositions and actions, they nevertheless cling to the bride in hope of making progress and journeying toward Jerusalem. They are forbidden, then, to harass the sleeping bride, lest they presume in any way to awaken her against her will. For this reason the most sweet Bridegroom placed his left hand under her head, according to what has been said before, so that he might make her rest and sleep in his bosom. And now, as Scripture continues, he himself, her guardian, most graciously and benevolently watches over her, lest she be compelled to awake, disturbed by the frequent and petty needs of the young women.

This is the literal coherence of the text. But that adjuration made by the roes and harts of the fields seems to have no rational consequence at all according to the letter; so completely does spiritual interpretation claim it for itself. Yet however that may be, for the present it is good for us to be here and to contemplate for a little while the goodness, sweetness, and condescension of the divine nature. What, indeed, have you, a human being, ever experienced among human affections sweeter than what is now expressed to you of the heart of the Most High? And it is expressed by him who searches the deep things of God and cannot fail to know what is in him, because he is his Spirit; nor can he speak anything except what he has seen with him, because he is the Spirit of truth.

2. Indeed, there is not lacking among our race one who has merited to be gladdened by this happy gift and thus to experience in himself this most sweet mystery—unless, that is, we altogether disbelieve the passage of Scripture before us. In it the heavenly Bridegroom is manifestly introduced as most ardently zealous for the repose of a certain beloved one of his, carefully preserving her as she sleeps between his own arms, lest she be disturbed from her sweetest sleep by some vexation or restlessness. I am beside myself with joy that that Majesty does not disdain to stoop to our weakness in such familiar and sweet companionship; that the Godhead on high does not disdain to enter into a marriage with an exiled soul and, captivated by the most ardent love of a bridegroom, to show it affection.

Yes, yes: I do not doubt that it is so in heaven as I read that it is on earth. The soul will assuredly experience what the page contains—except that these words wholly fail to express how much it will then be able to receive, or even how much it can already receive. What, do you suppose, will that soul receive there, when it is here granted such intimacy that it feels itself embraced by God’s arms, cherished in God’s bosom, and guarded by God’s care and zeal, lest while asleep it be awakened by anyone before it awakes of its own accord?

3. Come then, let us say, if we can, what is that sleep in which the Bridegroom wishes his beloved to fall asleep, and from which he permits her by no means to be awakened except at her own choice. Otherwise, when someone reads in the Apostle, “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13:11), or reads the Prophet praying God that his eyes might be enlightened, “lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 12:4 [Vulgate]), he may be confused by the ambiguity of the terms and find no way to form a worthy understanding of the bride’s sleep mentioned here. For even that saying is not like this one which the Lord says in the Gospel concerning Lazarus: “Our friend Lazarus sleeps; let us go and awaken him from sleep” (John 11:11). He said this about the death of Lazarus’s body, though the disciples thought it was said of ordinary sleep.

But the bride’s sleep is not the sleep of the body, whether the pleasant sleep that for a time sweetly lulls the bodily senses, or the dreadful sleep that commonly removes life entirely. Still more is it foreign to that death-sleep in which someone persists irrevocably in sin that is unto death. Rather, this kind of vital and wakeful sleep illuminates the inner sense and, death being driven away, grants eternal life. It is truly a sleep, yet one that does not dull perception but draws it away. It is also a death, as I would say without hesitation, because the Apostle, commending some who still live in the flesh, says: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3).

4. Accordingly, I too would not absurdly call the bride’s ecstasy a death: a death that, however, snatches her not from life but from life’s snares, so that she may say: “Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. 123:7 [Vulgate]). For in this life one walks among snares; and they are certainly not feared as often as the soul is carried away from itself by some holy and powerful thought—provided that it withdraws and flies so far in mind as to transcend even this common use and habit of thinking. “For the net is cast in vain before the eyes of the winged creatures” (Prov. 1:17). For why should sensual pleasure be feared where life itself is not felt? When the soul goes out of itself—not indeed out of life, but certainly out of the sense of life—it necessarily does not feel the temptation of life either.

“Who will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly and rest?” (Ps. 54:7 [Vulgate]). Would that I might often fall by this death, that I might escape the snares of death; that I might not feel the deadly allurements of luxuriant life; that I might be numbed to the sensation of lust, the heat of avarice, the stings of anger and impatience, the anxieties of cares, and the troubles of concerns! May my soul die the death of the righteous, so that no deceit may ensnare it and no iniquity delight it. Good is the death that does not take life away but transfers it to something better; good is that death in which the body does not fall, but the soul is lifted up.

5. But this is the death of human beings. Let my soul also die, if it may be so called, the death of angels: transcending the memory of present things, stripping itself not only of desires but even of likenesses of lower and bodily things, and having pure intercourse with those with whom it shares a likeness in purity. Such an ecstasy, I think, is called contemplation, either uniquely or most properly. For not to be held by the desires of things while living belongs to human virtue; but not to be entangled by images of bodies while contemplating belongs to angelic purity. Both, nevertheless, are gifts of God: in both, one goes beyond oneself; in both, one transcends oneself [or, in both, one strips oneself of oneself, etc.]; but one does so far, the other not far.

Blessed is one who can say: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. 54:8 [Vulgate]). He was not content merely to go out, unless he also went far away, that he might rest. You have passed beyond the pleasures of the flesh so as no longer to obey its desires or be held by its attractions: you have progressed and separated yourself, but you have not yet gone far away unless you can, by purity of mind, fly beyond the phantasms of bodily images that press in from every side. Until then, do not promise yourself rest. You are mistaken if you think that short of this you have found a place of repose, the secrecy of solitude, the serenity of light, the dwelling of peace.

But give me one who has reached that place, and without hesitation I confess him to be at rest, one who can rightly say: “Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you” (Ps. 114:7 [Vulgate]). This is truly the place in solitude and the dwelling in light: precisely as the Prophet says, “a tabernacle for shade by day from the heat, for safety and shelter from the whirlwind and rain” (Isa. 4:6); and as holy David says: “He hid me in his tabernacle in the day of evils; he protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle” (Ps. 26:5 [Vulgate]).

6. Suppose, then, that the bride has withdrawn into this solitude and there, amid the bridegroom’s embraces and the loveliness of the place, has sweetly fallen asleep—that is, has gone out of herself in spirit—when the young women are forbidden to awaken her until she herself wills it. But how is this so? They are not forbidden simply, nor with the light admonition customary in such cases, but by an altogether new and unusual adjuration: namely, by the roes and harts of the fields. By this kind of animal, it seems to me, are quite fittingly represented the holy souls stripped of their bodies, together with the angels who are with God, on account of keenness of sight and swiftness of leap. For we know that both qualities belong to both kinds of spirits: they easily seek the heights and penetrate the depths. Their dwelling in the fields likewise clearly signifies free and unencumbered movement in contemplation.

What, then, is the point of the adjuration made by them? Surely, that the restless young women may not dare on a slight pretext to call their beloved away from so venerable a fellowship, with which she undoubtedly mingles whenever she goes beyond herself in contemplation. They are fittingly frightened by the authority of those from whose society it is clear that she is torn away by their importunity. Let the young women consider whom they offend when they trouble their mother; and let them not so rely on maternal charity as not to fear entering, except in great necessity, upon that heavenly assembly. For this, they should think, is what they do whenever they are more troublesome than is just to one resting in contemplation.

It is left to her will both to have leisure for herself and to attend to their care as she judges fitting, when they are forbidden to awaken her until she herself wishes. The Bridegroom knows how ardently the bride burns with love even for her neighbors, and how much the mother is stirred by her own charity concerning her daughters’ progress. He knows that she will by no means withdraw herself from them or deny them what is needed, however much or however often it may be needed. Therefore he judged that this ordering could safely be entrusted to her discernment. For she is not like many whom we see branded by the Prophet’s rebuke: those who take what is fat and strong, but cast away what is weak (Ezek. 34:3–4). Does a physician seek the healthy rather than the sick? If it happens, perhaps he does so as a friend, but not as a physician. Whom, good Master, will you teach if you reject all the unlearned? To whom, I ask, will you give the care of discipline if you either drive all the undisciplined away or flee from them? In whom, I beg, will you prove your patience if you admit only the gentle and exclude the troublesome?

7. Yet there are some among those sitting here who, would that they observed the present chapter more attentively. They would surely reflect how great is the reverence owed to superiors, whom, by thoughtlessly troubling, they make even the citizens of heaven hostile toward themselves. Perhaps at last they would begin to spare us a little more than usual and would no longer thrust themselves upon us so irreverently and lightly when we are at leisure. As they well know, even when they themselves bear with me in all patience, I am granted very rarely an hour of respite from those who come in.

But I raise this complaint rather scrupulously, lest some faint-hearted person, fearing to disturb me, conceal needs that exceed the strength of his own patience. Therefore I desist, lest I seem rather to offer the weak an example of impatience. Those who believe in him are the Lord’s little ones; I cannot bear that they should suffer scandal through me (Matt. 18:6). I do not use this authority; rather, let them use me as they please, provided only that they may be saved. They will spare me if they do not spare me; and I shall rest more in this, if they do not fear to trouble me for their needs.

I shall comply with them as far as I can, and in them I shall serve my God for as long as I live, in unfeigned charity. I shall not seek what is my own; nor shall I consider useful to me what benefits me, but what benefits many. This alone I pray: that my ministry may be acceptable and fruitful to them, so that perhaps through this I may find mercy on the evil day in the eyes of their Father and of the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with him is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LIII. That the mountains and hills signify the heavenly spirits, whom the Bridegroom leaps over through his coming to earth, or through the mystery of his Incarnation.

1. “The voice of my beloved” (Song 2:8). The bride sees the young women’s new modesty and reverent fear: that they had lately begun not to dare to intrude upon her holy leisure, nor, as yesterday and the day before, presume to disturb her while she rested in contemplation. She recognizes that this has come to her through the bridegroom’s care and action; and, rejoicing in spirit, whether for their progress, because they are restrained from excessive and needless disturbance; or for her own freer rest in the future; or also for the bridegroom’s condescension and favor, since he is so zealous for this very repose of hers and so earnestly protects her sweetest leisure—or rather, her most fervent studies—she says that this is the voice of her beloved, uttered to them for this purpose.

For one who presides over others in care scarcely ever, or only rarely, has secure leisure for himself, because he always fears failing those under his charge and displeasing God by preferring his own repose and the sweetness of contemplation to the common good. Yet a person enjoying sweet leisure sometimes receives no small increase of joy and security when, through a certain divinely instilled fear and reverence toward him in the hearts of his subjects, he understands that his repose pleases God. God causes them to bear their own needs with more even minds rather than rashly daring to disturb their spiritual father’s welcome leisure. For the rightful trembling of the little ones clearly shows that inwardly they have heard, as it were, the threatening and rebuking voice of him who says through the Prophet: “I who speak righteousness” (Isa. 63:1). His voice is his inspiration and the instilling of righteous fear.

2. Having recognized this voice, the bride rejoices and exults: “The voice,” she says, “of my beloved.” It is friendly, and she rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. And she adds: “Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.” Having recognized through hearing the presence of her beloved, she immediately directs her keen and curious eyes to see him whom she had heard. Hearing leads to sight, because “faith comes by hearing” (Rom. 10:17), and through faith hearts are cleansed so that God may be seen; for thus it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9).

She therefore sees him coming whom she had heard speaking, while here also the Holy Spirit observes that order described in the Prophet: “Hear, O daughter, and see” (Ps. 44:11 [Vulgate]). And so that you may see more surely that hearing is put before sight here not by accident or chance, but deliberately and intentionally, for the reason we have stated, observe whether this same order of words is not found also in holy Job, when he says to God: “By the hearing of the ear I heard you, but now my eye sees you” (Job 42:5). Again, when the Holy Spirit is recorded as having descended upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost, is it not described that hearing preceded sight? For it says: “Suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a mighty wind coming”; and below: “There appeared to them divided tongues, as it were of fire” (Acts 2:2–3). Here too, therefore, hearing first and then sight is said to have perceived the coming of the Holy Spirit. But enough on this point; for you also, if you care to give attention to such an inquiry, may perhaps find some similar instances in other places of Scripture.

3. Let us now consider the matter that requires more careful inquiry and has more difficult approaches. For this, I confess, I wholly need the help of the Holy Spirit, so that I may bring to light who those mountains or hills are in which the Church beheld the Bridegroom leaping and leaping over them with joyful gaze, I believe, when he hastened to redeem her whose beauty he had desired. For I have understood this in that way, and not without reason, because something similar occurs to me from the Prophet, who plainly foresaw and expressed in the Spirit the coming of the Savior: “In the sun he has set his tabernacle, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber. He rejoiced like a giant to run his course; from the summit of heaven is his going forth, and his circuit unto its summit” (Ps. 18:6–7).

That course and return are very well known; and it is equally well known from whom and for what purpose the journey was undertaken and completed. What then? When reading these words either in the Psalms or in the present Song, shall we picture to ourselves a gigantic man of lofty stature, captivated by love for some absent little woman, and, as he hastens toward the embraces he desires, leaping over those mountains and hills which we see rising bodily above the earth’s plains to such a height that some of them appear to lift their summits even above the clouds? But it is not fitting to imagine such bodily fantasies, especially when we are treating this spiritual song; nor is it at all permitted to us, who remember reading in the Gospel that “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit” (John 4:24). [Col. 1034D]

4. Who, then, are these spiritual mountains and hills, so that afterward we may understand in due order what sort of leaps, and of what kind, the Bridegroom—who is God and therefore Spirit—made in them or over them? If we suppose them to be those among whom, according to the Gospel, the ninety-nine sheep were once left, when their merciful shepherd came on earth to seek the one that had perished (Matt. 18:12), the matter nonetheless remains obscure and the understanding hesitates, since it is difficult to discover what other spiritual [Note: [Col. 1035D] Thus Rouauld; Mabillon and the other printed editions read *illas* (“those”), rather than *illae* (“those”/“these”).] and supercelestial blessed beings—for without doubt they are the sheep mentioned there—have spiritual mountains or hills of their own in which to dwell or feed.

Yet if such beings did not truly exist, Truth would not have said this. Nor would the Prophet long before have declared of the heavenly city Jerusalem that “her foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. 86:1), unless holy mountains truly existed there. Finally, hear Isaiah saying that this heavenly dwelling has not only spiritual mountains and hills but living and rational ones: “Mountains and hills shall sing praises before God” (Isa. 55:12). [Col. 1035A]

5. Who, then, are these, except those very spirits who inhabit heaven, whom we have said are called sheep by the Lord’s own voice—so that the mountains themselves are sheep? Unless perhaps it seems absurd to you that mountains should feed among mountains, or sheep among sheep. According to the letter, certainly, it sounds harsh; but according to the spiritual understanding it has a sweet savor, if we carefully observe how Christ, the Wisdom of God and shepherd of both flocks of sheep, administers the one and same food of truth differently to his flocks on earth and in heaven.

For we mortal human beings, meanwhile in the place of our pilgrimage, must eat our bread in the sweat of our face, begging for it outside amid labor and hardship: that is, either from learned persons, or from sacred books, or indeed by perceiving through the things that have been made the invisible things of God. But the angels receive, in all fullness—though not from themselves, yet within themselves—with as much ease as happiness that by which they live blessedly. For all of them are taught by God. And it is promised with certain truth that the elect among human beings will one day attain this, though they are not yet granted the secure happiness of experiencing it. [Col. 1035B]

6. Thus mountains feed among mountains, or sheep among sheep, when those heavenly spiritual substances find abundantly within themselves, from the Word of life, that by which they perpetuate their blessed life. They are both mountains and sheep: mountains because of their fullness or height; sheep because of their gentleness. For, full of God, lofty in merits, heaped with virtues, they nevertheless submit and bow their uplifted heads in complete and humble obedience beneath the sovereignty of that majesty which far surpasses them, like most gentle sheep walking in all things at their shepherd’s beck and following him wherever he goes.

And in these truly holy mountains, according to the prophet David, the foundations of the city of the Lord, like wisdom first created of all things, stand firmly established from the beginning (Ps. 86:1). This city is indeed one in heaven and on earth, though partly in pilgrimage and partly reigning. And from these same beings, according to Isaiah, like life-giving cymbals sounding well, thanksgiving and the voice of praise resound from their heights (Isa. 51:3), as they fulfill with a sweet and unceasing voice what we recalled a little earlier from the same Prophet: “Mountains and hills shall sing praises before God.” Likewise, that other man says while speaking to the Lord God: “Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). [Col. 1036A–B]

7. These, then—to return to the point from which we have digressed somewhat, though, I think, necessarily—are the mountains and hills in which the Church saw the heavenly Bridegroom leaping with marvelous eagerness as he hastened to his own embraces; and not merely leaping, but also leaping over them. Do you wish me to show you these leaps from the writings of the prophets and apostles? [Col. 1036C] Not that I shall now begin to repeat all the testimonies concerning this matter that idle readers may find in them—for that would be long, and unnecessary—but I shall set down only those which seem briefly and clearly to establish what is said about the Bridegroom’s leaps.

David says of him that “he has set his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course; from the summit of heaven is his going forth” (Ps. 18:6–7). See what a leap he made: from the summit of heaven to earth. For indeed I find nowhere else where he set his tabernacle “in the sun,” that is, in light and openly—he who dwells in inaccessible light and deigned to manifest his presence—except surely on earth. Finally: “He was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings” (Baruch 3:38). [Col. 1036D]

On earth, I say, openly—that is what “in the sun” means—he set his tabernacle, namely, the body which he deigned to fashion for himself from the Virgin’s body, so that he who was invisible in himself might be seen in it. Thus all flesh saw the salvation of God when he came in the flesh.

8. Therefore he leapt in the mountains, that is, in those highest spirits, when he descended even to them, graciously disclosing to them the mystery hidden from the ages and the great mystery of godliness. But leaping over these higher and more exalted mountains—namely, the cherubim and seraphim, and likewise the dominions, principalities, powers, and virtues—he deigned to descend as far as the lower order of angels, as though to hills. [Col. 1037A] But did he remain even among them? He leapt over the hills also. For “he does not take hold of angels,” it says, “but of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2:16), which is surely beneath the angels, so that the saying of the aforementioned Prophet might be fulfilled, when he spoke thus to the Father concerning the Son: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6).

Although this may certainly be understood as said in commendation of human nature: humanity, made in the image and likeness of God and endowed beforehand with reason after the pattern of an angel, nevertheless differs a little from an angel because of the earthly body. But hear the Apostle Paul plainly proclaiming of him: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized; but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2:6–7); and again: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4:4–5). [Col. 1037B]

Therefore, he who was made of a woman and made under the law undoubtedly descended past not only the mountains—that is, the greater and higher blessed beings—but also the lesser angels, who are deservedly designated by the name of hills in comparison with those above them. Yet he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than anyone bearing flesh upon the earth, even if that person is the great John the Baptist (Luke 7:28). For although we confess God as man, and confess that even in his humanity he incomparably surpasses every principality and power, it is nonetheless certain that, although he precedes them in majesty, he yielded in weakness. [Col. 1037C]

Thus he leapt in the mountains and leapt over the hills when he most graciously displayed himself lower than not only the higher but also the lower spirits. Nor did he show himself subject merely to those heavenly spirits: even to those who inhabit houses of clay he subjected himself, leaping over and conquering by humility even human lowliness. For when he was twelve years old, he was subject to Mary and Joseph at Nazareth (Luke 2:51, 42); and at the Jordan, now a young man, he bowed himself beneath John’s hands (Matt. 3:13). But the day has declined, and I am not yet at all inclined to descend from these mountains. [Col. 1037D]

9. Yet if on this occasion we wished to explore at our pleasure all the delights of these mountains and search their hidden things, we must fear either that the discourse would lose its welcome brevity or that this rich and excellent subject matter would be deprived of due care by haste. Let us therefore rest today, if you please, upon these mountains; for it is good for us to be here, where, placed by Christ the Shepherd together with the holy angels in a place of pasture, we are fed both more delightfully and more abundantly. For we too are the sheep of his pasture.

Let us therefore chew the cud, like the clean animals of the good Shepherd, upon those things which we have swallowed with full eagerness in today’s discourse. In another discourse we shall receive more attentively the remainder of this same chapter, through the generosity of the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen. [Col. 1038A]

## SERMON LIV. How angels and human beings are again signified by mountains, and demons by hills. Also concerning the threefold fear by which each person ought to fear lest he lose the grace received from God for good works.

1. On the same chapter that was treated in yesterday’s sermon [elsewhere: “on the preceding day”], I shall give another interpretation which I reserved for today. Test it, and choose what is better. There is no need to repeat what has gone before, which I do not think has slipped from your memory in so short a time. But if it has, these things have been written down as they were spoken and taken down in shorthand, like the other sermons, so that whatever may perhaps have escaped may easily be recovered. Therefore receive another interpretation. [Col. 1038B]

“Behold, he comes,” he says, “leaping in the mountains, leaping over the hills” (Song 2:8). He speaks of the Bridegroom, who indeed leapt in the mountains when, sent by the Father to preach good news to the poor, he did not disdain to perform the office of angels, becoming the Angel of Great Counsel although he was Lord. He descended to earth in person, he who used to delegate others. In person the Lord made known his salvation; in person he revealed his righteousness before the nations (Ps. 97:2).

Since, according to Paul’s statement, all are “ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. 1:14), he who was above them became among them as one of them, disregarding the injury and increasing grace. But hear him himself: “I came not to be served, but to serve, and to give my life for many” (Matt. 20:28). No other has been found to have done this, so that he surpassed all who have seemed to minister by his devout and faithful services. [Col. 1038C]

A good minister indeed, who supplied his flesh as food, his blood as drink, and his life as the price. Truly good: lively in spirit, fervent in charity, devoted in piety; not only leaping in the mountains but also leaping over the hills—that is, surpassing and overcoming all in eagerness to minister—as one whom God, his God, anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions (Ps. 44:8). In him, indeed, he uniquely “rejoiced like a giant to run his course.” Finally, he leapt over Gabriel and came before him to the Virgin, as that same archangel testifies when he says: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28). [Note: [Col. 1037] The manuscripts read *praevenit* (“came before”); the printed editions have *pervenit* (“arrived”).] What? The one whom you have just left in heaven, you now find [elsewhere: “him”] in the womb.
