How? “He flew and flew ahead upon the wings of the winds.” You have been outdone, O archangel: he who sent you ahead leapt over you. [Col. 1038D]

2. Or rather, he was leaping in the mountains when in former times he appeared in angels to the fathers; and this seems more in keeping with the literal wording. For it does not say, “leaping onto the mountains,” but “leaping in the mountains,” so that he himself may be seen to leap in them, he who makes and enables them to leap; just as he speaks in the prophets and works in the righteous, giving words to the former and deeds to the latter. Add that some of them bore his person, so that each would speak not as an angel but as the Lord. For example, the angel who spoke with Moses said not, “I am of the Lord,” but “I am the Lord,” and repeated this more than once. [Col. 1039A]

Thus he leapt in the mountains, that is, in the angels, in whom he both spoke and manifested his presence to human beings. For he leapt toward human beings, but in angels, not in himself; not in his own nature but in a subject creature. For one who leaps moves from place to place, and this cannot be said of God. Thus he leapt in the mountains, that is, in the angels, because he could not leap in himself; and he leapt as far as the hills, that is, the patriarchs, prophets, and other spiritual persons on earth. But he leapt over the hills also when he deigned to speak and appear in angels not only to great and spiritual men, but also to certain ordinary people and even to some women. [Col. 1039B]

Or by “hills” he means the aerial powers, which are no longer counted among the mountains because through pride they fell away from the height of virtues; yet they do not subside through penitence to the low places of valleys, that is, to the valleys of the humble. Of these, I think, the Psalm says: “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord” (Ps. 96:5). These swollen and barren hills, placed as it were midway between the mountains of the perfect and the valleys of penitents, he undoubtedly leaps over—the one who leaps in the mountains. Passing and despising them, he descends to the valleys, so that the valleys may abound in grain. But they, conversely, are condemned to eternal dryness and barrenness, as you have the Prophet’s imprecation against them: “Let neither dew nor rain descend upon you.” And so that you may know that under the figure of the mountains of Gilboa he speaks these words concerning the angels who transgressed, he says: “There many wounded fell” (2 Sam. 1:21). [Col. 1039C] How many from the army of Israel fell from the beginning, and fall daily, upon these accursed mountains! Of them you also have the same Prophet speaking to the Lord: “Like the slain sleeping in graves, whom you remember no more, and who are cut off from your hand” (Ps. 87:6).

3. It is therefore no wonder if these remain barren and fruitless—not heavenly mountains, but aerial hills—upon which neither dew nor rain descends, since the author of grace and giver of blessings leaps over them and descends to the valleys, in order to drench with heavenly rain the humble who are upon the earth, so that they may bear fruit with patience: thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold (Matt. 13:8, 23; Luke 8:15). Finally, “He visited the earth and made it drunk; he multiplied it to enrich it” (Ps. 64:10). He visited the earth, not the air, because “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 32:5). Finally, “He has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73:12); did he also do so in the midst of the air? [Col. 1039D]

This is against Origen, who in an audacious falsehood crucifies anew in the air the Lord of glory for demons, whereas Paul, who knew this mystery, affirms that Christ, “having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9).

4. But he who leapt over the air did not visit earth alone; he also visited heaven, Scripture saying: “O Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches unto the clouds” (Ps. 35:6). For up to the clouds is the heaven inhabited by the holy angels, whom the Bridegroom did not leap over but in whom he leaps, so that he impresses upon them two footprints of his feet: mercy and truth. I remember having discussed these footprints of the Lord more fully in earlier sermons (Sermon 6). [Col. 1040A]

But from the clouds downward is the dwelling-place of demons, in this lowest and gloomy air. The Bridegroom does not leap in them, but leaps over and passes them by; nor do they retain any trace in themselves of the God who passes. For how can truth be in the devil, concerning whom the judgment of Truth itself stands in the Gospels: that he did not stand in the truth, but was a liar from the beginning? Nor would anyone call him merciful, whom the same truth of the Gospel convicts of having been a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44). Moreover, as is the master of the household, so are his household servants. Thus, when the Church sings beautifully of the Bridegroom that he “dwells on high and looks down upon the lowly in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 112:5–6), she makes no mention at all of those proud spirits who move about in the air, because “God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). [Col. 1040B]

5. Therefore she sees him leaping in the mountains and leaping over the hills, according to David’s imprecation: “May the Lord visit all the mountains round about it,” that is, round about Gilboa; “but let him pass over Gilboa” (2 Sam. 1:21). For around the devil, signified by Gilboa, are mountains on every side which the Lord visits: above, angels; below, human beings. For in punishment he received, when he fell from heaven, a place in this air, midway between heaven and earth, so that he may see and envy, and be tortured by that very envy, as Scripture says: “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away” (Ps. 111:10). [Col. 1040C]

How miserable he is when he looks up to heaven, where he beholds countless mountains shining with divine brightness, resounding with divine praises, exalted in glory, abounding in grace! How still more miserable when he looks toward the earth, which likewise possesses very many mountains from the people of God’s possession: firm in faith, lofty in hope, broad in charity, cultivated in virtues, filled with the fruits of good works, daily receiving from the dew of heaven—as from the Bridegroom’s leap—blessing! With how much pain and bitterness, we may suppose, does this most greedy seeker of glory look upon these mountains so glorious around him, when he sees himself and his own, in contrast, uncultivated, dark, barren of every good thing, so that he feels himself to be a reproach to humans and angels—he who used to reproach everyone—according to that saying in the Psalms: “This dragon whom you formed to be mocked” (Ps. 103:26). [Col. 1040D]

6. And this is because the Bridegroom leaps over them on account of their pride, while leaping in the mountains round about him, like a spring rising from the midst of paradise, watering all things and filling every creature with blessing. Blessed are those who sometimes or rarely deserve to drink from this torrent of delight, in whom, even if the water does not flow continually, the water of wisdom and the fountain of life at least leaps for a time, so that in them too there may be “a fountain of water leaping up into eternal life.” The rushing of this river indeed makes glad the city of God, perpetually and abundantly.

But may he not disdain to make occasional leaps like an overflowing flood into our mountains that are on earth, so that, sufficiently watered, they may in turn distill even sparse drops upon us who are valleys, lest we remain altogether dry and barren. Misery, poverty, and utter severe famine are in that region which is never moistened by such leaps or droppings, while the fountain of wisdom flows past it and leaps over it: “Because they did not possess wisdom,” it says, “they perished through their folly” (Baruch 3:28). [Col. 1041A]

7. “Behold, he comes, leaping in the mountains, leaping over the hills.” He leaps in order to leap over; he does not wish to reach all, for God is not pleased with all. Brothers, if, according to Paul’s wisdom, “these things were written for our correction” (1 Cor. 10:11), let us observe the Bridegroom’s discriminating and watchful leaps: how, both among the angels and among us, he leaps in the humble and leaps over the proud. For “the Lord is exalted, and looks upon the lowly; but he knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137:6). [Col. 1041B]

Let us attend to this, I say, that we may prudently prepare ourselves for the Bridegroom’s saving leaps, lest perhaps he pass over us as over the mountains of Gilboa, should he find us unworthy of his visitation. Why are you proud, earth and ashes? The Lord even leaps over angels, execrating their pride. Let the rejection of angels, therefore, become the correction of human beings; for it was written for their correction. May even the devil’s evil cooperate for my good, and may I wash my hands in the blood of the sinner. How, you ask? Listen.

A dreadful and terrifying curse is certainly inflicted upon the proud devil, when the prophet David says in the Spirit concerning him under the figure of Gilboa, as was recalled above: “May the Lord visit the mountains that are around it; but let him pass over Gilboa.” [Col. 1041C]

8. Indeed, when I read this and turn my eyes upon myself, looking carefully, I find myself infected with the very plague which the Lord so abhorred in the angel that for this reason he turned away from him, while he deemed all the mountains around him—whether angels or human beings—worthy of the grace of his visitation. Trembling and afraid, I say to myself: “If this was done to an angel, what will become of me, earth and ashes? He swelled with pride in heaven; I do so upon a dung-heap. Who would not judge pride more tolerable in a rich person than in a poor one? Woe to me! If punishment was inflicted so severely upon that mighty being because his heart was lifted up, nor did it avail him that pride is recognized as akin to the powerful, what shall be required of me, both wretched and proud?” [Col. 1041D]

Indeed, I am already paying the penalty; I am already being most bitterly scourged. Not without cause, surely, since yesterday and the day before yesterday this languor of soul, this dullness of mind, this unusual sluggishness of spirit have seized me. I was running well; but behold, a stone of stumbling lay in the way: I struck it and fell. Pride was found in me, and the Lord in anger turned aside from his servant. Hence this barrenness of my soul and this lack of devotion which I endure.

How has my heart so dried up? It has curdled like milk; it has become like earth without water. I cannot even be moved to tears; so great is the hardness of my heart. The psalm has no savor; I have no desire to read; prayer gives no delight; I do not find my customary meditations. Where is that inebriation of the spirit? Where are serenity of mind, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit? Therefore I am sluggish at manual work, sleepy at vigils, hasty to anger, stubborn in hatred, more indulgent toward tongue and stomach, more slow and dull in preaching. Alas! The Lord visits all the mountains around me, but does not come near me. Am I not one of the hills which the Bridegroom leaps over? [Col. 1042A]

For I see one person of exceptional abstinence, another of admirable patience, another of the highest humility and gentleness, another of great mercy and piety; one frequently transported in contemplation, another knocking upon and penetrating the heavens through persistence in prayer, and others excelling in other virtues. All these, I say, I behold fervent, devout, unanimous in Christ, overflowing with heavenly gifts and grace: truly spiritual mountains visited by the Lord and frequently receiving the Bridegroom leaping within them. But I, finding none of these things in myself, what else should I think myself to be but one of the mountains of Gilboa, whom in his anger and indignation that most gracious visitor of all the rest passes by? [Col. 1042B]

9. Little children, this reflection removes the haughtiness of the eyes, obtains grace, and prepares for the Bridegroom’s leaps. I have applied these things to myself for your sake, so that you may do likewise. Be imitators of me. I do not say this now concerning the practice of virtues, the discipline of morals, or the glory of holiness—for I would not rashly claim for myself anything of that kind as worthy of imitation—but I want you not to spare yourselves, but to accuse yourselves whenever you discover grace growing even slightly lukewarm in you, or virtue becoming weak, just as I accuse myself on account of such things.

This is what a person does who is a watchful observer of himself, a searcher of his ways and pursuits, and who always suspects in every matter that the vice of arrogance may creep in. In truth I have learned that nothing is so effective for obtaining, retaining, and recovering grace as to be found at all times before God not thinking highly of oneself, but fearing. “Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Prov. 28:14). Therefore fear when grace smiles upon you; fear when it departs; fear when it returns anew. This is to be always fearful. [Col. 1042C]

Let these three fears succeed one another in the mind, according as grace is graciously felt to be present, to depart in displeasure, or to return reconciled. When it is present, fear lest you fail to act worthily from it. For this is the Apostle’s warning: “See that you do not receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Cor. 6:1). And to his disciple: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you” (1 Tim. 4:14). Of himself he said: “The grace of God in me was not in vain” (1 Cor. 15:10).

That man, who possessed the counsel of God, knew that to neglect a gift bestowed and not expend it for the purpose for which it was given amounts to contempt for the giver; he judged this to be intolerable pride. Therefore he himself most diligently avoided this evil and taught that it must be avoided. But again, here is a hidden pit which I do not want to remain hidden from you, in which the same spirit of pride lies in wait—more dangerously because more secretly—as the Psalm says, “like a lion in his den” (Ps. 10:9). For if it cannot hinder the action, it assaults the intention, suggesting and persuading you to attribute to yourself the effect of grace. Do not doubt that this form of pride is far more intolerable than the former. For what is more hateful than the words spoken by certain persons: “Our hand is mighty; it is not the Lord who has done all these things” (Deut. 32:27)? [Col. 1042D–1043A]

10. If, therefore, there is cause for fear while grace remains, what if it departs? Is there not then much greater cause for fear? Certainly much greater; for when grace fails you, you fail. Hear what the giver of grace says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Therefore fear when grace has been withdrawn, as one about to fall at once; fear and tremble because God, as you feel, is angry with you; fear because your guardian has left you.

Do not doubt that pride is the cause, even if it does not appear and even if you are conscious of nothing. For God knows what you do not know, and he is the one who judges you. “For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends” (2 Cor. 10:18). Does God commend you when he deprives you of grace? Or will he who gives grace to the humble (James 4:6) take away what he has given from one who is humble? Therefore the deprivation of grace is evidence of pride.

Yet sometimes grace is withdrawn or held back, not because of pride already present, but because of pride that would arise if it were not withdrawn. You have clear proof of this in the Apostle, who endured against his will the goads of his flesh, not because he was exalted, but lest he should be exalted (2 Cor. 12:7). But whether already existing or not yet existing, pride will always be the cause of grace’s withdrawal. [Col. 1043B–C]

11. But if grace, reconciled anew, returns, then one must fear far more, lest perhaps a relapse occur, according to the Gospel saying: “Behold, you have been made well; go, and sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14). You hear that to relapse is worse than to fall in the first place. Therefore, as the danger grows greater, so also let fear grow greater. [Col. 1043D]

You are blessed if you fill your heart with this threefold fear: fearing indeed for grace received, more for grace lost, and much more for grace recovered. Do this, and you will be a water-jar at Christ’s wedding feast, filled to the brim, containing, to be sure, not merely two but three metretas (measures), so that you may deserve Christ’s blessing, which turns your waters into the wine of gladness, and “perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). [Col. 1044A]

12. What I mean is this. Water is fear, because it cools the heat of carnal desires. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10); and we read: “He gave him to drink the water of saving wisdom” (Ecclus. 15:3). If fear is wisdom, and wisdom is water, then fear is water. Finally: “The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life” (Prov. 14:7). Your mind, moreover, is the water-jar. “Each held two or three measures,” it says. The three measures are the three fears. “And they filled them,” it says, “to the brim” (John 2:6–7). Not one fear, nor merely two, but all three together fill it to the brim.

“Fear God at all times,” and with all your heart, and you have filled your water-jar to the brim. God loves an undivided gift, a full affection, a perfect sacrifice. Take care, then, to bring a full water-jar to the heavenly wedding, so that it may be said of you also: “Because he filled him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11:3). One who fears in this way neglects nothing. For how can negligence enter into fullness? Otherwise, what can still receive something is not full. [Col. 1044B]

For the same reason, a person cannot both fear in this manner and think highly of himself. There is no room in which to admit pride when one is filled with the fear of the Lord. The same must be understood concerning the other vices, because all of them must necessarily be excluded by the fullness of fear. Then at last, if you have feared fully and perfectly, charity will give savor to your waters through the Lord’s blessing. For without charity fear involves punishment. Charity, indeed, is wine “which gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103:15). But perfect charity casts out fear, so that where water had been, wine may begin to be, to the praise and glory of the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LV. How a person may escape God’s judgment through true penitence.

[Col. 1044C]

1. “My beloved is like a gazelle and a fawn of stags” (Song 2:9). This depends on the preceding verse. For the one whom she had just described as leaping and hastening, she subsequently compares to a gazelle and a fawn of stags. Aptly so, because this kind of animal is swift in running and agile in leaping. Moreover, the discourse is about the Bridegroom, and the Bridegroom is the Word. The Prophet says of God that “his word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147:15). This is certainly fitting for the present passage, where the Bridegroom, who is the Word of God, is described as leaping and leaping over, and is therefore made like a gazelle and a fawn of stags. [Col. 1044D]

This, then, is the reason for the comparison. But add this also, lest any small aspect of the comparison be idle: the gazelle excels not only in swiftness of running but also in keenness of sight. This properly concerns that part of the narrative in which the Bridegroom is said to appear not merely leaping but also leaping over, since without a sharp and penetrating gaze he could not at all discern—especially while running—upon whom he ought to leap and whom he ought to leap over.

Otherwise, for indicating the speed of one who hastens, the comparison with the fawn alone could suffice, since it is known to move with a swifter course. But because this Bridegroom, although ardently loving and seeming to rush swiftly into his beloved’s embraces, nevertheless knows how to direct his steps—or rather, his leaps—with prudent consideration, carefully placing his foot where it ought to be placed, it was surely necessary that, along with the fawn, a comparison also be made with the gazelle: so that the former might express the desire of the Savior, and the latter the judgment of the one who chooses. [Col. 1045A]

For Christ is righteous and merciful, Savior and judge. Because he loves, he “wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:4); and because he judges, he knows those who are his (2 Tim. 2:19), and he himself knows those whom he chose from the beginning (John 13:18).

2. Let us therefore understand, for the present, that these two good qualities of the Bridegroom—mercy and judgment—are commended to us by the Holy Spirit in these two animals, so that, in 1456 testimony to the integrity and perfection of our faith, we too, imitating the Prophet, may sing mercy and judgment to the Lord [Col. 1045B] (Ps. 100:1). I do not doubt that those who are curious and knowledgeable about such things can point out other features of these animals’ nature which may suitably and profitably be applied to the Bridegroom. But these, I think, may suffice to explain the comparison that has been introduced.

Beautifully, however, the Holy Spirit gave the comparison not of a stag, but of a fawn of stags: thereby he both mentioned the Fathers, from whom Christ came according to the flesh, and recalled the Savior’s infancy. For he who was born for us appeared as a little fawn (Isa. 9:6). But you who desire the Savior’s coming, fear the Judge’s investigation; fear the eyes of the roe; fear him who says through the prophet: “And it shall be in that day that I will search Jerusalem with lamps” [Col. 1045C] (Zeph. 1:12). His sight is keen; his eye will leave nothing unexamined. He will search heart and reins (Ps. 7:10), and the very thought of man will confess to him (Ps. 75:11).

What can be safe in Babylon if Jerusalem awaits investigation? For I think that here the prophet designates by the name Jerusalem those who lead a religious life in this world, imitating as far as they can, by upright and ordered conduct, the customs of that heavenly Jerusalem; not like those who belong to Babylon, wasting their lives amid the turmoil of vices and the confusion of crimes. Their sins, indeed, are manifest, going before them to judgment; they need not investigation, but punishment. But my sins—though I seem to be a monk and a citizen of Jerusalem—are surely hidden [Col. 1045D], shaded over by the name and habit of a monk. Therefore they must be sought out by a subtle examination and, as though lamps were brought near, brought forth from darkness into light.

3. We may also bring forward something from the Psalm to confirm what is said concerning the searching of Jerusalem. For the Lord says there in his own person: “When I receive the appointed time, I will judge justices” (Ps. 74:3). He says, I believe, that he will scrutinize and examine the ways of the righteous and their actions. It is greatly to be feared, when that point is reached, lest under so subtle an examination many things which are thought to be our righteous deeds should prove to be sins.

There is, however, one remedy: if we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged (1 Cor. 11:31). A good judgment is that which withdraws and hides me from that strict and divine judgment [Col. 1046A]. I utterly dread falling into the hands of the living God; I desire to be presented to the face of wrath as one already judged, not as one to be judged. “The spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:15).

Accordingly, I shall judge my evils, and I shall judge my goods as well. I shall strive to correct my evils by better actions, wash them away with tears, punish them with fasts and the other labors of holy discipline. Concerning my good deeds, I shall think humbly of myself and, according to the Lord’s command, reckon myself an unprofitable servant, who has done only what he ought to have done (Luke 17:10). I shall take care not to offer weeds instead of grain, nor chaff together with grain. I shall search my ways and my pursuits, so that he who is to search Jerusalem with lamps may find in me nothing unexamined or uninvestigated. For he will not judge the same matter twice.

[Col. 1046B]

4. Who will grant me so thoroughly to pursue and examine all my offenses that I need fear the roe’s eyes in nothing, and blush at the light of the lamps in nothing? Even now I seem to see, but I do not see. The eye to which all things lie open is present, although it itself is not manifest to me. The time will come when I shall know as I too am known; but now I know in part, whereas I am known not in part, but wholly.

I fear the gaze of that explorer who stands behind the wall. For Scripture adds this concerning him whom it likened to a roe because of the keenness of his sight: “Behold, he stands,” it says, “behind the wall, looking through the windows, peering through the lattices.” We shall consider this in its proper place. Thus I fear this hidden explorer of hidden things.

The Bride fears nothing, because [Col. 1046C] she is conscious of nothing against herself. For what should the friend, the dove, the beautiful one fear? You immediately hear: “Behold,” she says, “my beloved speaks to me.” He speaks nothing but good; and therefore I fear his gaze, because I do not have such testimony. What do you hear concerning yourself, O Bride? What does your Beloved say to you? “Arise,” 1457 he says, “make haste, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one” (Song 2:9–10).

But I shall reserve this too for another beginning, and shall not confine in brief compass matters requiring careful treatment, lest I too perhaps be found guilty in this respect, if you should not be found built up to understanding and love of the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LVI

### That sins and vices are like walls standing between God and the sinner

[Col. 1046D]

1. “Behold, he stands behind the wall, looking through the windows, peering through the lattices” (Song 2:9). According to the letter, the meaning seems to be that he who had been seen approaching with leaps had drawn near to the Bride’s dwelling; standing behind the wall, he looked more curiously within through the windows and cracks, and modestly did not presume to force his way in.

According to the spirit, however, he is likewise understood to have drawn near, but in another way—namely, in the manner befitting the action of a heavenly Bridegroom and the language of the Holy Spirit. For a true and spiritual understanding will admit nothing unworthy either of the author or of the narrator. Therefore he approached the wall when he joined himself to flesh. Flesh [Col. 1047A] is the wall; and the Bridegroom’s approach is the incarnation of the Word.

The lattices and windows through which he is said to look are, I think, the senses of the flesh and human affections, through which he acquired experience of every human need. Thus: “He himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53:4). He used human affections and bodily senses as apertures and windows, so that, having become man, he might know human miseries by experience and become merciful. He knew them before as well, but differently. The Lord of hosts knew the power of obedience; yet, as the Apostle testifies, “he learned obedience through what he suffered” (Heb. 5:8). In this manner he learned mercy also, although “the mercy of the Lord” is from eternity.

The same Teacher of the Gentiles teaches this too [Col. 1047B], when he declares that Christ was tempted in every respect according to our likeness, yet without sin, so that he might become merciful (Heb. 4:15). Do you see that he became what he was, learned what he knew, and sought for himself among us cracks and windows through which he might more carefully explore our calamities? For he found as many openings in our ruined wall, full of cracks, as he experienced in his own body trials of our weakness and corruption.

2. Thus the Bridegroom stood behind the wall, looking through the windows and lattices. And he is rightly said to stand, because he alone truly stood in the flesh who did not experience the sin of the flesh. We may also understand this faithfully: by the power of his divinity he stood, though through the weakness of the flesh he fell in death; as he himself said: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” [Col. 1047C] (Matt. 26:41).

I think that the following also supports this interpretation: holy David, in this mystery, as prophet of the Lord and prophesying, spoke of the Lord—speaking indeed of Moses, but beholding the Lord. For he is the true Moses, who truly came through water, and not through water only, but through water and blood. Thus the prophet mentioned above says: “He said that he would destroy them”—for he was speaking of the Father—“had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy them” (Ps. 105:23).

In what way, I ask, did Moses stand in the breach? How, I say, did he stand if he was broken? Or, if he stood, how was he broken [Col. 1047D]? But I shall show you, if you wish, who truly stood in the breach. I know no one else who could have done this except my Lord Jesus, who certainly lived in death; who, though his body was broken on the cross, stood with the Father in his divinity—supplicating with us in one respect, propitiating with the Father in another. And he stood behind the wall, while that in him which lay exposed was manifest in the flesh, and that by which he stood was hidden in him as though behind the flesh: one and the same man, manifest, and God, hidden.

1458 3. Moreover, for each of us who desires his coming, I think that he likewise stands behind the wall while this body of ours—which is certainly a body of sin—hides his face from us for the present and bars his presence. Thus: “While we are [Col. 1048A] in this body,” he says, “we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6). Not because we are in a body, but because we are in this body, which is indeed from sin and is not without sin.

And so that you may know that bodies do not obstruct, but sins, hear Scripture: “Our sins,” it says, “separate between us and God” (Isa. 59:2). Would that only the single wall of the body obstructed me, and that I suffered only the impediment which is sin in the flesh, rather than having many walls of vices intervene. For I fear that, beyond what belongs to nature, I have added very many barriers from my own iniquity, by whose interposition I have removed the Bridegroom too far from myself; so that, if I would speak truthfully, I must confess that he stands behind walls rather than behind a wall.

[Col. 1048B]

4. Let me state this more plainly. The Bridegroom is indeed equally and without distinction present everywhere, by the presence of his divine majesty and the greatness of his power. Yet by the granting or withholding of grace he is said to be far from some and near to others—namely, angels and human beings, that is, rational creatures. Thus, “Salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118:155). And holy David likewise says: “Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away?” (Ps. 9:1).

But from the saints, in a merciful dispensation, he sometimes makes himself far off for a time, not wholly, but in some respect. From sinners, however, of whom it is said, “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. 73:23), and again, “Their ways are defiled at all times” (Ps. 9:5), he is always and very far away [Col. 1048C]; and this is in wrath, not in mercy. Therefore the saint prays to God and says: “Do not turn away in anger from your servant” (Ps. 26:9), knowing that he may turn away also in mercy.

The Lord, then, is near to his saints and elect, even when he seems far away; and not equally near to all, but to some more, to others less, according to the diversity of their merits. For although the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth, and is close to those who are broken in heart, perhaps he is not near to all in such a way that they can say, “He stands behind the wall.” But how near he is to the Bride, from whom he is separated by only one wall! Therefore she longs to be dissolved, so that, once the dividing wall is broken down, she may be with him whom she trusts to be behind the wall.

[Col. 1048D]

5. But I, because I am a sinner, do not desire to be dissolved; rather, I fear it, knowing that “the death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. 33:22). How can death not be most evil where Life does not come to the aid? I fear to depart, and I tremble at the very entrance into the harbor, because I do not trust that he who receives one departing will stand near. For what? Do I depart safely if the Lord does not guard my going out? Alas! I shall become the sport of demons who intercept me, with no one standing by to redeem or save me.

Paul’s soul had nothing of this kind to fear. Only one wall opposed it to the sight and embrace of the Beloved: namely, the law of sin which he found in his members. This is the lust of the flesh, which he could not entirely lack while he remained in the flesh. With this single wall intervening, he was not far [Col. 1049A] from the Lord in his pilgrimage; and therefore he cried out in longing: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24), knowing that by the short path of death he would immediately come to life. Thus Paul confessed that he was held by this one law, namely lust, which, fixed immovably in his flesh, he endured unwillingly; but otherwise, he said, “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4:4).

6. But who is like Paul, who does not sometimes consent to this lust so as to obey sin? Let one who has consented to sin know that he has set another wall against himself: namely, that perverse and unlawful consent. Such a person cannot boast that the Bridegroom stands behind a wall for him, when there are now walls intervening, not a wall. Still less can he do so if consent proceeds [Col. 1049B] to affection, since then a third wall also keeps back and obstructs the Bridegroom’s approach—namely, the very act of sin.

What if habit perhaps carries sin into practice, or practice even into contempt? As it is written: “When the wicked man has 1459 come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). If you depart in such a condition, will you not be able to be devoured a thousand times over by roaring creatures prepared for prey before you reach the Bridegroom, shut off from you now not by one wall but by so great a multitude of walls? The first is lust; the second, consent; the third, act; the fourth, habit; the fifth, contempt.

Therefore take care to resist the first lust with all your strength, so that it may not draw you into consent; and then the whole structure of subsequent wickedness collapses. There is then nothing at all to prevent the Bridegroom [Col. 1049C] from drawing near to you except the single wall of the body, so that you too may glory, saying of him: “Behold, he stands behind the wall.”

7. You must also provide with all vigilance that he may always find open the windows and certain lattices of your confessions, through which he may kindly look upon you within; for his looking upon you is your progress. They say that lattices are narrower windows, such as copyists of books commonly arrange for themselves to admit light to their pages. From this, I think, those who are assigned by office to write documents are called *cancellarii* [clerks; literally, “lattice-men”].

Since there are two kinds of compunction, one in sorrow for our offenses, the other in exultation for divine gifts, whenever I make that confession of my sins which cannot occur without constriction of heart [Col. 1049D], I seem to myself to open a lattice—that is, a narrower window. And there is no doubt that the merciful explorer who stands behind the wall willingly looks through it, because “God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:19). Indeed, he exhorts us to this very thing: “Tell your iniquities first,” he says, “that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26).

But if, with a heart enlarged in charity, contemplating divine condescension and mercy, I am moved to release my soul in a voice of praise and thanksgiving, then I think that I open not a narrow but a very wide window to the Bridegroom standing behind the wall. Through this, I believe, he looks all the more willingly, the more abundantly “the sacrifice of praise” honors him [Col. 1050A]. Scripture readily proves both kinds of confession; but I speak to those who know these things, and you are not to be burdened with superfluities when you scarcely suffice for investigating necessary matters. So great are the mysteries of this bridal song and the praises celebrated in it of the Church and her Bridegroom, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LVII

### On observing the Lord’s visitations, and the indications or signs by which they may be recognized

1. “Behold, my Beloved speaks to me” (Song 2:10). See the progress of grace, and observe the stages of divine condescension. Consider the Bride’s devotion and attentiveness: with watchful eye she observes the Bridegroom’s coming [Col. 1050B], and thereafter contemplates all his actions more carefully. He comes, hastens, approaches, is present, looks, speaks; and none of these moments escapes the Bride’s diligent and anticipatory awareness.

He comes in the angels, hastens in the patriarchs, approaches in the prophets, is present in the flesh, looks in miracles, speaks in the apostles. Or thus: he comes in the affection and purpose of mercy; he hastens in zeal to help; he approaches by humbling himself; he is present to those present; he looks ahead to those to come; he speaks by teaching and persuading concerning the kingdom of God.

Such, then, is the Bridegroom’s coming. Blessings and the riches of salvation are with him, and all that belongs to him flows with delights, overflowing surely with joyful and saving mysteries. Now she who loves watches and observes. Blessed is she whom the Lord finds watching [Col. 1050C]. He will not pass her by or go past her; rather, he will stand and speak to her, and speak words of love—he will speak as a beloved one. For thus you have it: “Behold, my Beloved speaks to me.” Well is he called Beloved who comes to speak lovingly, not reproachfully.

2. For she is not among those who are rightly rebuked by the Lord because they knew how to discern the face of the sky, but did not know the time of his coming (Matt. 16:4). This Bride, so attentive, prudent, and watchful, saw him coming from afar; noticed his leaping because of his haste; most vigilantly observed his passing over the proud so that, by humility, he might draw near to her in her humility. Finally, when he had already stood and hidden himself behind the wall [Col. 1050D], she nevertheless recognized him as present, and perceived him looking through the windows and lattices. Now, as the reward for such devotion and religious diligence, she hears him speaking.

For if he had looked upon her and not spoken, that gaze might have seemed suspect—perhaps a gaze of indignation rather than love. Thus he looked upon Peter, and did not speak to him; and perhaps Peter wept (Luke 22:61–62) because he looked upon him but remained silent. But this Bride, because after his gaze she deserved also his address, not only does not weep but glories in joy, crying: “Behold, my Beloved speaks to me.”

You see that the Lord’s gaze, while he himself always remains the same, does not always have the same effect. It is conformed to the merits of those on whom he looks: in some it instills [Col. 1051A] fear; to others it brings rather consolation and assurance. Thus he looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; whereas, on the other hand, he looked upon Mary and poured grace into her. “He has looked,” she says, “upon the humility of his servant; for behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed” (Luke 1:48). These are not the words of one weeping or trembling, but of one rejoicing.

Likewise he looked upon the Bride in this passage, and she neither trembled nor wept after the manner of Peter, because, unlike him, she did not savor earthly things. Rather, he gave joy to her heart, testifying by his address with what affection he had looked upon her.

3. Finally, hear how the words he speaks are not those of one indignant, but of one loving. It follows: “Arise, make haste, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one.” Blessed the conscience which deserves to hear such things said of it!

[Col. 1051B] Who among us, do you think, is so watchful and attentive to the time of his visitation, so diligently observing the Bridegroom’s approach through every one of its stages, that when he comes and knocks, he opens to him at once? These things are not related of the Church in such a way that we individuals, who together constitute the Church, need not share in her blessings. For all of us, generally and without distinction, have been called to possess blessings as an inheritance.

Therefore the Psalmist dared to say to the Lord: “I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance for ever, for they are the joy of my heart” (Ps. 118:111)—by that inheritance, I think, through which he presumed himself to be a son of his Father who is in heaven. Now if a son, then an heir: an heir of God and co-heir with Christ.

He glories that by this inheritance he has acquired a great possession: the Lord’s testimonies. Would that I might deserve to possess even one testimony of the Lord concerning myself! For he rejoices not in one testimony, but in many. Thus he says again: “I have delighted in the way of your testimonies as in all riches” [Col. 1051C] (Ps. 118:14). And truly, what are the riches of salvation, the delights of the heart, the soul’s true and secure assurance, if not the Lord’s attestations? For “it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends” (2 Cor. 10:18).

4. Why have we until now still been deprived of these divine commendations or attestations and robbed of our paternal inheritance? Is it as though he had not also freely begotten us by the word of truth, that we remember no such commendation from him concerning ourselves and have received no testimony from him? Where is what the Apostle says: “The Spirit of God himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8:16)? How are we children if we lack the inheritance?

Our very poverty undoubtedly convicts us of negligence and carelessness. For if one of us, wholly and perfectly, according to the saying of the Wise Man, gives his heart to seeking the Lord who made him early in the morning and prays in the sight of the Most High [Col. 1051D] (Ecclus. 39:6), and with every desire strives, according to Isaiah the prophet, to prepare the ways of the Lord and make straight the paths of his God (Isa. 40:3), so that he can say with the Prophet, “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. 24:15), and, “I kept the Lord always before my sight” [Col. 1052A] (Ps. 15:8)—will he not receive blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior? (Ps. 23:5).

He will certainly be visited often, and he will never fail to know the time of his visitation, however hidden and stealthy he may come who visits in the spirit, as befits a modest lover. Thus the well-watchful soul will perceive him while he is still far away, with a sober mind; and then it will recognize everything which, at the Bridegroom’s coming, we have shown the Bride to have noticed as attentively as significantly. For he himself says: “Those who watch for me early in the morning shall find me” (Prov. 8:17).

It will recognize the desire of the one who hastens; it will immediately sense when he is near and when he is already present. It will behold with blessed eye the eye that looks upon it, like a ray of the sun entering through windows and cracks in the wall [Col. 1052B]. And finally it will hear words of exultation and love, being called friend, dove, and beautiful one.

5. Who is wise and shall understand these things, so as also worthily to distinguish them from one another, designate each particular thing, and define them for the understanding of others? If this is expected from me, I would rather hear it from one experienced and accustomed and practiced in such matters. But because everyone of this kind more modestly chooses to hide in silence what he perceives in silence, and considers it safer to keep his secret to himself, I, whose office is to speak and who am not permitted to remain silent, shall say whatever I retain from experience—my own or another’s—about such things, and whatever many can readily experience, leaving higher matters to those able to grasp them.

If, then, I am admonished—either outwardly by a human being or inwardly by the Spirit—to preserve justice and maintain equity, such a saving exhortation will surely be for me a forewarning of the Bridegroom’s imminent coming and a kind of preparation to receive worthily the heavenly visitor. The Prophet indicates this to me when he says that “justice shall walk before him” [Col. 1052C] (Ps. 84:14); and he also says to God: “Justice and judgment are the preparation of your throne” (Ps. 88:15).

The same hope will likewise smile upon me if I hear instruction about humility or patience, or about brotherly charity and the obedience to be rendered to superiors; especially about pursuing holiness and peace, and seeking purity of heart. For Scripture says: “Holiness becomes the house of the Lord” (Ps. 92:5); “His dwelling-place has been made in peace” (Ps. 75:3); and “The pure in heart shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Whatever, therefore, is suggested to my mind concerning these or any other virtues will, as I have said, signify that the visitation of the Lord of hosts is imminent for my soul.

6. If a righteous man rebukes me in mercy and reproves me, I shall understand the same thing, knowing that the righteous man’s zeal and goodwill make a way for him who ascends above the west [setting] (Ps. 67:5). It is a good setting when a man stands under a righteous person’s correction, a vice falls, and the Lord ascends over it, trampling it beneath his feet and crushing it so that it may not rise again.

Therefore the rebuke of a righteous person is not to be despised; it is the downfall of sin, the health of the heart, and also God’s way to the soul [Col. 1053A]. Nor should any discourse that builds up toward piety, virtues, and the best conduct ever be heard carelessly, because there too is the way by which the salvation of God is shown (Ps. 49:23).

But if a pleasing and agreeable discourse comes—[variant: *placidus*, “gentle”]—so that, with distaste driven away, it is heard with desire, then we must believe that the Bridegroom is not merely coming but hastening; that is, coming with desire. For his desire creates yours; and the fact that you hasten to receive his word comes from his own haste to enter. “It was not we,” he says, “who first loved him, but he first loved us” (1 John 4:10).

And if you feel that the word is fiery, and that your conscience is burned by the remembrance of sin, then remember him of whom Scripture says that “fire shall go before him” (Ps. [Col. 1053B] 95:3), and do not doubt that he is near. For “the Lord is near to those who are broken in heart” (Ps. 33:19).

7. But if you are not only pierced by that word but wholly turned to the Lord, swearing and resolving to keep the judgments of his righteousness, then know that he himself is already present—especially if you feel yourself growing fervent with love for him. For you read both that fire goes before him and that he himself is fire. Moses says of him that “he is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24).

Yet the fires differ: the fire sent beforehand has heat but not love; it cooks but does not thoroughly refine; it moves but does not advance. It is sent only to awaken and prepare, and at the same time to remind you what you are in yourself, so that afterward what you shall soon be from God may taste sweeter. But the fire which is God consumes indeed, but does not afflict; it burns sweetly and desolates happily. For it is truly a desolating coal, yet one which exerts the force of fire upon vices in such a way as to act as an anointing upon the soul.

Therefore recognize the Lord as present in the power by which you are changed and in the love by which you are inflamed. For “the right hand of the Lord works power” (Ps. 117:16). But this “change of the right hand of the Most High” [Col. 1053C] (Ps. 76:11) does not occur except in fervor of spirit and in unfeigned charity, so that such a person may say: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire blazes forth” (Ps. 38:4).

8. Further, when by this fire every stain of sin and rust of vice has been consumed, if upon a conscience now cleansed and made serene there follows a certain sudden and unusual spaciousness of mind, and an infusion of light illuminating the understanding either for knowledge of the Scriptures or for awareness of mysteries—the former, I think, given for our own delight, the latter for the building up of our neighbors—this is undoubtedly the eye of the one who looks upon us. It brings forth your righteousness as light and your judgment as midday, according to Isaiah the prophet’s saying: “Your light shall rise like the sun” [Col. 1053D] (Isa. 58:10), and so forth.

Yet this ray of such great brightness will enter not through open doors but through narrow openings, while this ruined wall of the body still stands. You are mistaken if you hope otherwise, however far you may advance in purity of heart, when that chief contemplative says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” [Col. 1054A] (1 Cor. 13:12).

9. After this gaze of such condescension and mercy follows a voice, gently and softly suggesting the divine will. This is nothing other than love itself, which cannot be idle, urging and counseling concerning the things of God. Thus the Bride hears that she is to arise and hasten—without doubt, for the gain of souls.

For true and chaste contemplation has this effect: it inflames the mind intensely with divine fire, and sometimes fills it with such zeal and desire to acquire for God others who love him in the same way that it most willingly interrupts the leisure of contemplation for the work of preaching. Then, having attained its aim, it returns with even greater ardor to the same contemplation, insofar as it remembers that its interruption was fruitful. Again, having received a taste of contemplation, it runs back with stronger vigor and its accustomed eagerness to seek its gains.

But amid these alternations the mind often fluctuates, fearing and greatly troubled lest, while pulled in different directions by its affections, it adhere more than is right to one of these pursuits, and thus deviate, even slightly, from the divine will in either. Perhaps holy Job suffered something of this kind when he said: “If I sleep, I say, ‘When shall I arise?’ and again I wait for evening” [Col. 1054B] (Job 7:4). That is: both when at rest, I accuse myself of neglecting work; and when occupied, I accuse myself likewise of disturbed rest.

You see the holy man severely distressed between the fruit of work and the sleep of contemplation. Though always engaged in good things, he nevertheless always does penance as though for evils, and at every moment seeks God’s will with groaning. The sole remedy or refuge in such a case is prayer and frequent groaning to God, that he may deign continually to show us what, when, and to what extent he wishes us to do.

You have, I think, these three things—preaching, prayer, and contemplation—commended and designated in three names. She is rightly called *friend* who zealously and faithfully seeks the Bridegroom’s gains through preaching, counsel, and service. She is rightly called a *dove* who, also groaning and pleading in prayer for her offenses, never ceases to win divine mercy for herself. She is likewise rightly called *beautiful* [Col. 1054D] who, shining with heavenly desire, clothes herself in the beauty of heavenly contemplation, at least at such hours as this can fittingly and suitably be done.

10. Consider also whether the account of those three persons dwelling together in one house, the Savior’s friends and very intimate companions, can be adapted to this threefold good of a single soul: Martha serving, Mary at leisure, and Lazarus as it were groaning beneath the stone and asking for the grace of resurrection (Luke 10:38–42; John 11).

These things have been said because the Bride is described as so attentive and watchful in observing the Bridegroom’s paths that she cannot fail to know when and with what haste he comes to her; so that no suddenness can forestall her awareness of when he is far away, when near [Col. 1055A], and when present. Therefore she has deserved not only to be looked upon mercifully, but also to be graciously gladdened by words of love and to rejoice with joy because of the Bridegroom’s voice.

11. We too have added, though boldly, that any soul among us, if it watches in like manner, will likewise be greeted as a friend, consoled as a dove, and embraced as beautiful. Everyone will be reckoned perfect in whose soul these three things are seen to concur suitably and seasonably: knowing how to groan for oneself, rejoice in God, and be able to help the needs of one’s neighbors—pleasing to God, watchful for oneself, useful to one’s own people.

But who is sufficient for these things? Would that they might be preserved among us all for long periods—if not all of them in each individual, then at least individual ones among different persons, as they seem to exist today [Col. 1055B]! For we have Martha, the Savior’s friend, in those who faithfully administer outward things. We also have Lazarus, the groaning dove, in novices who have recently died in sins and, because of their wounds still fresh, labor in their groaning under fear of judgment. Like the wounded sleeping in graves, of whom no one remembers any longer, they do not think themselves regarded until, at Christ’s command, the weight of fear is removed, like the mass of the pressing stone, and they are able to breathe again in hope of pardon.

We also have Mary contemplating in those who, after the passage of a longer time, through the cooperation of God’s grace, have been able to advance into something better and more joyful. Now, presuming upon forgiveness, they are less anxiously concerned to turn within themselves the sad image of their sins than insatiably delighted to meditate day and night upon the law of God. Sometimes also, with unveiled face, they behold the Bridegroom’s glory with ineffable joy and are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord [Col. 1055C] (2 Cor. 3:18).

In another discourse we shall consider why he who shortly before seemed to defend the Bride lest she be awakened while sleeping now exhorts her to arise and hasten. May he himself be present and deign to open for us the meaning of this mystery: Jesus Christ our Lord, Bridegroom of the Church, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LVIII

### How the Bridegroom exhorts the Bride—that is, perfect persons—to govern the imperfect; likewise, concerning the pruning of vices to be carried out in them so that virtues may grow

[Col. 1055D]

1. “Arise, make haste, my beloved, my dove, my beautiful one, and come” (Song of Songs 2:10). Who says this? Without doubt, the bridegroom. Yet is he not the very one who, a little earlier, so strongly forbade his beloved to be awakened? How then does he now command her not only to rise, but also to hasten? Something similar from the Gospel comes to mind. On the very night when the Lord was betrayed, after he had at last told the disciples who were with him—wearied by their prolonged vigils—to sleep and rest, at that very hour he said: “Rise, let us go; behold, he who will betray me has drawn near” (Matthew 26:46).

> [Note: At Col. 1055D more recent editions add, “he compels her to rise”; these words are absent from most manuscripts and from the earliest editions at Col. 1056D. Indeed, without them the reading is more pleasing and direct.]

So here likewise, in almost the same moment, he both forbids the bride to be awakened and awakens her: “Arise,” he says, “and come.” What, then, does this sudden change of will or purpose mean? Are we to think that the bridegroom acted frivolously, first willing something which he immediately ceased to will? Not at all. Rather, recognize those alternations—which, if you remember, I have already commended to you more than once—of holy rest and necessary activity. For in this life there is neither an abundance of contemplation nor a lasting leisure, where the more urgent and pressing usefulness of duty and work calls us.

Accordingly, in his customary manner, when the bridegroom perceives that his beloved has rested for a little while in his embrace, he does not hesitate to draw her anew to tasks that appear more useful. Yet not as though unwilling; for he himself would never in any way do what he had forbidden. Rather, for the bride to be drawn by the bridegroom is to receive from him the desire by which she is drawn: the desire for good works, the desire to bear fruit for the bridegroom—for her bridegroom is her life, and death her gain.

2. This is a vehement desire, which urges her not merely to rise, but to rise quickly. For thus you have it: “Arise, make haste, and come.” Nor is it a small encouragement that she hears, “Come,” rather than “Go”; by this she understands that she is not so much sent as led, and that the bridegroom himself will come with her. For what could she deem difficult with him as her companion? “Place me beside you,” he says, “and let the hand of anyone fight against me” (Job 17:3); and again: “Though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, because you are with me” (Psalm 22:4).

She is therefore not awakened except when she wishes it, because she is first brought to wish it. This is nothing other than an infused eagerness for holy gain. She is also encouraged for the work imposed upon her and made more cheerful by the favorable time. “It is time to act,” he says, O bride, “because winter has passed,” when no one could work. The rain too, which by its flooding covered the earth, impeded cultivation, and either destroyed what had been sown or prevented sowing—that rain, I say, has run its course, gone, and departed. Flowers have appeared in our land, signifying, surely, that the mildness of spring is present, the convenience of working, and the nearness of crops and fruits. Then he adds where and what must first be done: “The time for pruning has come” (Song of Songs 2:11–12).

She is therefore led out to cultivate the vineyards. In order that they may yield more abundant fruits to their husbandmen, it is necessary before all else to throw out barren branches, cut down harmful ones, and prune away what is superfluous. This is the literal sense.

3. Let us now see what we are spiritually given to understand under this apparently historical outline. I have already told you, and you have heard, that vineyards are souls or churches, together with the reason for this; you need not hear it again. A more perfect soul, then, is invited to inspect, correct, instruct, and save these vineyards—provided that it has received this ministry not through its own ambition, but through God’s call, like Aaron.

What, moreover, is this invitation except a certain inward prompting of charity, devoutly urging us to desire the salvation of our brethren, the beauty of the Lord’s house, the growth of its gains, the increase of its fruits of righteousness, and the praise and glory of his name? Whenever, therefore, one who has the charge of governing souls, or who is obliged by office to devote himself to the work of preaching, perceives his inward person stirred by such devout affections toward God, let him be certain that the bridegroom is present, certain that he is being invited by him to the vineyards. For what purpose, except “to pluck up and break down, to build and to plant”?

4. But since not every time is available or suitable for this work, just as for every other thing under heaven, he who gives the invitation adds that the time for pruning has come. He knew it to be present who said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation; giving no offence to anyone, that our ministry may not be blamed” (2 Corinthians 6:2–3). He was undoubtedly urging them now to prune and cut away what was defective and superfluous, and, in short, everything that might give offence or hinder the fruit of salvation, knowing that the time for pruning had arrived.

For this reason he also said to a faithful cultivator of vineyards: “Reprove, rebuke, exhort” (2 Timothy 4:2). In the first and second of these he enjoins pruning or uprooting; in the last, planting. These things, indeed, the bridegroom says through Paul’s mouth concerning the time for working. But hear what he said through his own mouth about considering the times, under a different image and name, when speaking with the new bride: “Do you not say, ‘There are four months, and then the harvest comes’? Behold, I say to you, lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest” (John 4:35); and again: “The harvest indeed is abundant, but the laborers are few. Pray the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 4:37–38).

Thus, just as there he showed that the time had come for reaping the harvest of souls, so here he announces that the time for pruning the equally intelligible vineyards—that is, souls or churches—has come. Perhaps he wishes the two matters to be distinguished by the diversity of terms, so that we understand harvests as the common people and vineyards as congregations of saints living together.

5. The wintertime which he signifies has passed seems to me to denote that period when the Lord Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews, because they had conspired against him, wishing to kill him. Hence he said to certain persons: “My time has not yet come; but your time is always ready”; and again: “Go up yourselves to this feast; I will not go up” (John 7:1–10). Yet afterward he too went up, not openly, but as it were in secret.

From then onward, up to the coming of the Holy Spirit—by whom the sluggish hearts of believers were warmed again, as by the fire which the Lord sent upon the earth for this very purpose (Luke 12:49)—it was winter. Would you deny that it was winter then, when Peter sat by the coals, his heart no less cold than his body? For, as it says, “It was cold” (John 18:18). Truly, a great cold had gripped the heart of him who denied.

Yet this is no wonder, since the fire had been withdrawn from him. A little before, indeed, he had borne no small zeal, being still near the fire; and, drawing his sword, lest he should lose the fire, he cut off the servant’s ear. But it was not the time for pruning; and therefore he heard: “Put your sword back into its place.” For it was the hour and power of darkness. Anyone among the disciples who then lifted the sword, whether of iron or of speech, would either have been cut down by the sword and gained no one, nor produced any fruit at all; or else he would have been compelled by the sword of fear to deny, and thus himself perish the more, according to the Lord’s word which he immediately added: “Everyone who takes the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matthew 26:51–52). For who among the rest would have stood fearless before the dreadful image of death, when their very leader trembled and gave way—he who had been strengthened by the encouraging voice of his commander and forewarned to strengthen others? (Luke 22:32.)

6. Moreover, neither he nor they had yet put on power from on high. For this reason it was not safe for them to go out into the vineyards, wield the hoe of the tongue, and with the sword of the Spirit prune the vines and cleanse the shoots, so that they might bear more fruit. Indeed, the Lord himself was silent during his Passion, and when questioned in many matters gave no answer (Matthew 27:12), becoming, according to the Prophet, “like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth” (Psalm 37:15).

But he said: “If I tell you, you will not believe me; and if I question you, you will not answer me” (Luke 22:67–68), knowing that the time for pruning had not yet come and that his vineyard would make absolutely no return for the labor spent upon it: that is, it would produce no fruit either of faith or of good work. Why? Because it was winter in the hearts of the faithless, and certain wintry rains of malice had occupied the ground, readier to choke than to nourish the sown seeds of the word; and they would likewise render futile every effort expended upon cultivating the vineyards.

7. Which rains do you suppose I now mean? Those which we see clouds, scattered through the air by a stormy wind, pour down upon the earth? It is not so. Rather, they are those whom men of turbulent spirit lift up from the earth into the air, setting their mouths against heaven, while their tongue passes over the earth. Like most bitter rain, this makes the very earth marshy and sterile, useless both for plants and for sown seed—not those visible and bodily plants given for our bodily uses, for God has no concern at all for these, any more than for oxen.

For which, then? Surely for those which the hand of God, not of man, has sown and planted: those which could either germinate or take root in faith and charity, and bring forth fruits of salvation, if they were watered by good and seasonable rains. In short, they are the souls for whom Christ died. Woe to the clouds that rain such showers upon them—showers which make mud and bring forth no fruit! For just as there are good and bad trees, each bearing fruits different according to its dissimilarity—the good good fruits, and the bad bad fruits—so I think there are good clouds which rain good showers, and bad clouds which rain bad ones.

Perhaps he who said, “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it”—doubtless upon the vineyard—“rain” (Isaiah 5:6), indicated to us this difference between clouds and rains. Why, do you think, did he pointedly add “my,” unless because there are also evil clouds which are not his? “Take him away, take him away, crucify him” (John 19:15). O violent and stormy clouds! O tempestuous rain! O torrent of iniquity, more fit to overthrow than to make fruitful!

No less evil, and no less bitter, though rushing down with less force, was the shower that followed: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. Let Christ, the king of Israel, now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matthew 27:42). The windy talkativeness of philosophers is not good rain; it has brought barrenness upon lands rather than fertility. Still more, the perverse teachings of heretics are evil rains, producing thorns and thistles instead of fruits. The traditions of the Pharisees, rebuked by the Savior, are also evil rains; and they themselves are evil clouds.

And unless you think that I do Moses an injury—for that is a good cloud—I will nevertheless say that not everything which even it rains is good, lest I contradict him who says: “I gave them,” that is, the Jews, “commands that were not good” (doubtless through Moses), “and ordinances in which they would not live” (Ezekiel 20:25). The literal observance, for example, of the Sabbath, which sounds forth rest but does not bestow it; the prescribed rite of sacrifices; the forbidden eating of pork; and certain similar things which Moses judges unclean—all this is rain descending from that cloud. Yet I do not wish it ever to descend upon my field or garden. It was indeed good in its own time; if it comes after its time, I no longer judge it good. Every gentle rain too, descending softly, is troublesome if it is unseasonable.

8. Therefore, so long as such pestilential waters occupied the earth and prevailed upon it, the vineyards did not have their season, nor was there occasion for the bride to be invited to prune the vineyards. But when those waters had run off, the earth appeared dry and flowers appeared upon it, signifying that the time for pruning had come. Do you ask when this was? When, do you think, except when Christ’s flesh bloomed again in the resurrection? Here is the first and greatest flower which appeared in our land. For Christ is “the firstfruits of those who sleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

He, I say, is Jesus, “the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1), thought to be the son of Joseph of Nazareth (Luke 3:23)—a name interpreted as “flower.” This flower therefore appeared first, but not alone. For many bodies also of saints who had slept rose at the same time; like certain most radiant flowers, they appeared together in our land. Indeed, “they came into the holy city and appeared to many” (Matthew 27:52–53).

Those who first believed from among the people, the firstfruits of the saints, were also flowers. Their miracles were their flowers, producing the fruit of faith as flowers do. For after that shower of unbelief had, to some extent or in part, gone and departed, there immediately followed the voluntary rain which God had set apart for his inheritance, and flowers began to appear. “The Lord gave goodness, and our land gave its flowers,” so that on one day three thousand and on another five thousand of the people believed (Acts 2:41; 4:4). So swiftly did the number of flowers—that is, the multitude of believers—increase. Nor could the frost of malice prevail against the flowers that appeared, nor snatch away, as it usually does, the fruit of life which they promised.

9. For when all who had believed were clothed with power from on high, men arose from among them who despised human threats and were strong in faith. They certainly suffered very many opponents, but did not yield or shrink back from doing and proclaiming the works of God. Thus, in the spiritual sense of that psalm: “They sowed fields and planted vineyards, and produced the fruit of increase” (Psalm 106:37).

In the course of time the storm was calmed, peace was restored to the lands, and the vineyards grew, spread, widened, and multiplied beyond number. Then at last the bride is invited to the vineyards—not to plant, but to prune that which had already been planted. This was timely, for such work required a time of peace. When, indeed, would it have been permitted in a time of persecution? To take into one’s hands two-edged swords, execute vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples, bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron shackles, and execute upon them the written judgment (Psalm 149:6–9)—for this is to prune the vineyards—all these things, I say, can scarcely be carried out in peace even in a time of peace. But enough of this.

10. The discourse might also have ended, had I first, according to my custom, admonished each of you concerning his own vineyard. For who has so completely cut away all superfluity from himself that he thinks he has nothing worthy of pruning? Believe me: even what has been pruned sprouts again; what has been driven away returns; what has been extinguished is rekindled; and what has been put to sleep is awakened anew. It is therefore too little to have pruned once; pruning must be done often—indeed, if possible, always. For you always find something that ought to be pruned, if you do not conceal it from yourself.

However much progress you make while remaining in this body, you are mistaken if you suppose that vices are dead rather than suppressed. Whether you wish it or not, the Jebusite dwells within your borders (Judges 1:21); he can be subdued, but not exterminated. “I know,” he says, “that no good dwells in me.” It is too little unless he also confesses that evil is present in him. For he says: “I do not do what I wish; but what I hate, that I do. But if I do what I hate, it is no longer I who do it, but the sin dwelling in me” (Romans 7:18–20).

> [Note: Thus the first editions and five better manuscripts; others add “good,” as in the Vulgate.]

Either, then, if you dare, prefer yourself to the Apostle—for this is his own utterance—or confess with him that you too are not free from vices. Virtue, indeed, occupies the middle ground among vices; and therefore you need diligent pruning, and circumcision as well. Otherwise there is danger that virtue, while you are unaware, may gradually languish from the vices licking around it—or rather gnawing at it on every side—or, if they grow over it, may be choked.

There is one counsel in so great a danger: watch carefully, and as soon as the heads of new growth appear, cut them off with ready severity. Virtue cannot grow together with vices. Therefore, if virtue is to flourish, do not permit those vices to grow. Remove what is superfluous, and what is wholesome springs up. Whatever you take away from desire is added to usefulness. Let us devote ourselves to pruning. Let desire be pruned, so that virtue may be strengthened.

11. For us, brothers, it is always the time for pruning, just as there is always work to be done. For I trust that winter has now passed for us. Do you know which winter I mean? That fear which is not in charity: it initiates all into wisdom, but brings no one to perfection, because charity, coming upon it, drives it out as summer drives out winter. For charity is summer; and if it has now come—indeed, because it has come, as it is right for me to think concerning you—it must have dried up every wintry shower, namely every tear of anxiety which bitter remembrance of sin and the fear of judgment formerly wrung from you.

Thus—I say this without hesitation, though not of all of you, certainly of most—the rain has now gone and departed. For flowers also appear, signs of a sweeter rain. Summer too has its sweet and abundant showers. What is sweeter than tears of charity? Charity weeps, indeed, but from love, not from sorrow; it weeps from longing; it weeps with those who weep. I do not doubt that the deeds of your obedience which I gladly behold are abundantly watered with such rain: not darkened by grumbling, not shadowed by sadness, but joyful and flowery with a certain spiritual gladness. You are as though you always carried flowers in your hands.

12. Therefore, if winter has passed and the rain has gone and departed; if, finally, flowers have appeared in our land, and, moreover, a certain springlike mildness of spiritual grace indicates the time for pruning: what remains except that henceforth we devote ourselves wholly to this work, so holy and so necessary? Let us search, according to the prophet, our ways (Lamentations 3:40) and our pursuits. Let each person judge that he has made progress, not when he finds nothing to criticize, but when he criticizes what he finds.

Then you have not searched yourself in vain if you perceive again that you need searching; and your inquiry has not deceived you as often as you judge it must be repeated. But if you always do this whenever it is needed, you do it always. Therefore remember that you always need the help from above and the mercy of the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LIX. On the groanings of the soul that sighs for its heavenly homeland, and on the commendation of chastity and widowhood

1. “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song of Songs 2:12). I can no longer conceal that, behold, for the second time he who is from heaven speaks of the earth—indeed, so graciously, so companionably, as though he were one from the earth. This is the bridegroom. When he first said that flowers had appeared “in the land,” he added “our”; and now likewise: “The voice,” he says, “of the turtledove has been heard in our land.”

Can language so unusual—indeed, not to say unworthy—of God lack reason? Nowhere, I think, will you find him speaking thus of heaven; nowhere else thus of earth. Observe, then, what sweetness it is for the God of heaven to say, “in our land.” You earthborn and children of men, listen: “The Lord has magnified his dealings with us” (Psalm 125:3). He has much to do with the earth, much with the bride whom he was pleased to take to himself from earthly things. “In our land,” he says. This expression plainly does not sound of lordship, but of partnership and intimacy. He speaks as a bridegroom, not as a Lord. What? He is the Creator, and counts himself her companion! Love speaks, and love knows no master. This is surely a song of love, and it ought to be supported only by things belonging to lovers.

God loves too; nor does he derive this from elsewhere, but he himself is the source from which he loves. And he loves more intensely, because he does not so much possess love as himself is love. Yet those whom he loves, he has as friends, not servants. Indeed, from being a teacher he becomes a friend; for he would not call his disciples friends unless they were such.

2. Do you see how even majesty yields to love? It is so, brothers: love looks up to no one, yet does not look down on anyone either. It regards all equally who love one another perfectly; in itself it harmonizes the high and the low, and makes them not only equals but one. Perhaps you think that God is still excepted from this rule of love; but “he who is joined to God is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

Why do you marvel at this? He himself became as one of us. I have said too little: not “as one,” but one. It is too little that he should be equal to human beings: he is a human being. From this he claims our earth for himself, yet as a homeland, not as a possession. Why should he not claim it? From it comes his bride; from it comes the substance of his body; from it comes the bridegroom himself; from it come the two in one flesh. If the flesh is one, why should the homeland not also be one? “The heaven of heaven is the Lord’s,” he says, “but he gave the earth to the children of men” (Psalm 113:16).

Thus, as Son of Man, he inherits the earth; as Lord, he subjects it; as Creator, he governs it; as bridegroom, he shares it. In saying, “in our land,” he certainly renounces exclusive ownership but does not reject fellowship. This much on the bridegroom’s gracious expression in deigning to say, “in our land.” Now let us consider the rest.

3. “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” This too is a sign that winter has passed, likewise announcing that the time for pruning has come. This is according to the letter. Otherwise, the turtledove’s voice is not particularly sweet in sound, but it signifies sweet things.
