The bird itself, if you buy it, is not worth much; if you examine it closely, it is of no small value. Its voice resembles one groaning more than one singing, and reminds us of our pilgrimage.

I gladly hear the voice of that teacher who moves not applause for himself but mourning in me. You truly present yourself as a turtledove if you teach others to groan; and if you wish to persuade, you must strive to do so more by groaning than by declaiming. Example, certainly in many other matters and especially in this one, is more effective than speech. You will give your voice the voice of power if it becomes known that you have first persuaded yourself of what you counsel. The voice of action is stronger than that of the mouth. Do as you say, and you will not only correct me more easily, but also free yourself from no light reproach. The saying will no longer apply to you: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on the shoulders of people, but they are unwilling to move them with their finger” (Matthew 23:4). Nor need you fear the other saying: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself?” (Romans 2:21).

4. “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” So long as people received for God’s worship only a reward on earth and only earth itself—namely, the land flowing with milk and honey—they did not know themselves to be strangers upon the earth, nor did they groan like the turtledove, recalling as it were their homeland. Rather, mistaking exile for their homeland, they gave themselves to eating rich foods and drinking sweet wine. Thus, for so long, the voice of the turtledove was not heard in our land.

But when the promise of the kingdom of heaven was made, people then understood that they did not have an enduring city here, and they began with all eagerness to seek the one to come. Then for the first time the voice of the turtledove clearly sounded in the land. For when every holy soul already sighed for Christ’s presence, bore with distress the delay of the kingdom, and greeted the desired homeland from afar with groans and sighs, does not every soul that acted thus on earth seem to you to perform the role of the mourning and most chaste turtledove? From then onward, therefore, the voice of the turtledove was heard in our land.

How could Christ’s absence fail to move in me frequent tears and daily groans? “Lord, all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you” (Psalm 37:10). “I have labored in my groaning,” you know; but blessed is the one who could say: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch” (Psalm 6:7). These groanings are known not only to me, but to all who love his coming. For this is what he himself said: “Can the children of the bridegroom mourn while the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they shall mourn” (Matthew 9:15)—as though he said: Then the voice of the turtledove will be heard.

5. It is so, good Jesus: those days have come. For “creation itself groans and labors in birth until now,” awaiting the revelation of the children of God. “And not only it, but we ourselves also groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption as children of God, the redemption of our body” (Romans 8:22–23), knowing that “while we are in this body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:1–6).

Nor are these empty groanings, to which such a merciful answer is made from heaven: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord” (Psalm 11:6). This voice of groaning existed also in the time of the Fathers, but it was rare, and each person had his own private groan. Hence one said: “My secret is for me, my secret is for me” (Isaiah 24:16). And he who said, “My groaning is not hidden from you,” surely showed that it was hidden, since it was hidden from all but God alone.

Therefore, it could not then be said: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land,” because what was still the secret of a few had not yet spread into a multitude. But when it was openly proclaimed, “Seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:1), this turtledove-like groaning began to belong to all, and all had one reason for groaning, because all knew the Lord, as is written in Jeremiah: “They shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 31:34).

6. But if many are groaning, what does the singular expression mean? “The voice of the turtledove,” he says. Why not “of the turtledoves”? Perhaps the Apostle resolves this when he says that the Spirit himself makes intercession for the saints with unutterable groanings (Romans 8:26). It is so: he is represented as groaning who makes others groan. And however many people you hear groaning in this way, one voice sounds through the lips of all. Why should it not be his voice, who forms it in the mouth of each according to the needs of each? For “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for usefulness” (1 Corinthians 12:7).

One’s own voice makes each person manifest and indicates that he is present. Hear from the Gospel also that the Holy Spirit has a voice: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice; but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John 3:8). Though the one who taught the killing letter—the dead teacher Nicodemus—did not know this, we should know it. Having been transferred from death to life through the life-giving Spirit, we prove by certain and daily experience, while he himself enlightens us, that our prayers and groanings come from him and go to him, and there find mercy in God’s sight. For when would God render the voice of his own Spirit ineffective? He himself knows what the Spirit desires, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to God.

7. Groanings alone do not commend the turtledove; chastity also commends it. Indeed, by reason of this, it was worthy to be given as an offering for a virginal birth. For thus you have it: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:24). Although the dove commonly signifies the Holy Spirit elsewhere, it was not fitting, because it is a lustful bird, for it to be offered in sacrifice to the Lord except at an age when it did not yet know lust. But no age is specified for the turtledove, because its chastity is recognized at every age.

Indeed, it is content with one mate; when that mate has been lost, it admits no other, reproving the multiplicity of marriages among human beings. For although perhaps the fault arising from incontinence is pardonable, such great incontinence is nevertheless shameful in itself. It is disgraceful that reason cannot achieve in a human being, in the matter of honorable conduct, what nature can achieve in a bird.

One may see the turtledove, in the time of its widowhood, vigorously and indefatigably carrying out the work of holy widowhood. You will see it everywhere alone and hear it everywhere groaning; nor will you ever observe it resting upon a green branch, so that you may learn from it to avoid the poisonous greenery of pleasures. Add that it more commonly dwells on mountain ridges and in the tops of trees, so that, as is especially fitting for the pursuit of chastity, it may teach us to despise earthly things and love heavenly ones.

8. From this it follows that the voice of the turtledove is also the preaching of chastity. For this voice was not heard on earth from the beginning; rather, the voice then was: “Increase, multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28). That voice of chastity would surely have sounded in vain before the homeland of those who rise again had been made known, in which people, far more happily, “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven” (Luke 20:35–36).

Would you say that the time for that voice had then come, when every barren woman in Israel lay under a curse; when the patriarchs themselves had several wives at once; when a brother was compelled by law to raise up offspring for his brother who had died childless? But when the heavenly turtledove proclaimed the commendation of eunuchs “who made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:12), and likewise when the counsel concerning virgins of that other most chaste turtledove prevailed everywhere (1 Corinthians 7:25), then for the first time it could truly be said that “the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.”

9. Therefore, if flowers have appeared in our land and the voice of the turtledove has been heard, then truth has certainly been recognized both by sight and by hearing. For a voice is heard, while a flower is seen. The flower is a miracle, according to our earlier interpretation; joining itself to the voice, it brings forth the fruit of faith. Though faith comes from hearing, it receives confirmation from sight.

The voice sounded, the flower shone, and “truth sprang up from the earth” (Psalm 84:12) through the confession of believers, word and sign running together as testimony to faith. These testimonies became exceedingly credible when the flower bore witness to the voice and the eye to the ear. Things heard are confirmed by things seen, so that the testimony of two witnesses—I mean the ear and the eye—may be valid.

Therefore the Lord said: “Go, report to John”—for he was speaking to John’s disciples—“what you have heard and seen” (Luke 7:22). The certainty of faith could not be conveyed to them either more briefly or more plainly. Indeed, the same conviction was quickly brought to the whole earth, and by the same concise argument: “What you have heard and seen.” O abbreviated word, yet living and effective! I unhesitatingly affirm what I have perceived with ears and eyes. The trumpet of salvation thunders, miracles flash forth, and the world believes. What is said is quickly accepted when what causes wonder is shown.

You have, moreover, that the apostles went out and preached everywhere, “the Lord cooperating and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16:20). You have him transfigured upon the mountain with wondrous brightness, and likewise attested by the voice from above (Matthew 17:2–5). You have likewise at the Jordan both the dove pointing him out and the voice bearing testimony (Matthew 3:16–17). Thus these two, voice and sign, everywhere work together through divine generosity to introduce faith, so that a way into the soul may lie open to truth as it enters through both windows.

10. It follows: “The fig tree has put forth its green figs.” Let us not eat from them, for they are unfit for eating because of their immaturity. They have the appearance of good figs, but only their likeness, not their flavor—perhaps signifying hypocrites. Yet let us not throw them away; perhaps we may need them for some other purpose. Otherwise they will readily and before their time fall of themselves, like “the grass of the roofs, which withered before it was plucked up” (Psalm 128:6), a saying which I think refers to hypocrites.

Yet it is not without reason that mention of them is made in the bridal song. They will undoubtedly have some use, even if not for food. Many things besides dishes must necessarily be provided at a wedding. I consider this matter far too important to pass over; but rather than discuss it amid the narrow limits at the end of this discourse, I defer it to another day and a freer hour. Whether that is necessary, you will then be able to discover—provided only that your prayers obtain for me the opportunity and ability to express what I think, for your own edification and for the praise and glory of the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LX. On the unbelief of the Jews, by which they filled up the measure of their fathers in killing Christ

1. “The fig tree has put forth its green figs” (Song of Songs 2:13). The present passage depends upon what precedes. For he had said that the time for pruning had come, maintaining this both from the flowers which had already appeared and from the voice of the turtledove that had been heard. He now affirms the same thing from the putting forth of green figs, because the season is recognized not only from flowers and the turtledove’s voice, but also from the fig tree. For the air is surely milder when the fig tree has put forth its green figs.

The fig tree has no flowers, but at the time when other trees are flowering it sends forth green figs in place of flowers. And as flowers appear and pass away, useful for nothing except as certain heralds of the fruits to follow, so also do green figs. They arise, but fall while immature and make way for those that are to ripen, being themselves wholly unfit to eat. Thus, as I have said, the bridegroom takes from this too an indication of the season and an argument for persuasion, so that the bride may not be slow to proceed to the vineyards, because work that comes in its season is not lost. And this is the literal sense.

2. But what does the spirit mean? Clearly, that in this passage we should look not at a fig tree, but at a people; for God’s concern is with human beings, not trees. Truly, the people are a fig tree: fragile in flesh, childish in understanding, lowly in spirit, whose first fruits—if for the moment we play upon the name—are certainly *grossi*, coarse and earthly. For it is not the way of the common crowd first to seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness (Matt. 6:33), but, as the Apostle says, to think of worldly matters, how men may please their wives, or women their husbands. Such persons will have tribulation in the flesh (1 Cor. 7:33, 28); yet in the end we do not deny [Col. 1067A] that they will attain the fruits of faith, if they have a good final confession, especially if they redeem works of the flesh by alms. Therefore the first fruits of the masses are not fruits at all, any more than the *grossi* of fig trees are. Finally, if later they produce fruits worthy of repentance—for “it is not the spiritual which is first, but the natural” (1 Cor. 15:46)—it will be said to them: “What fruit had you then from those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

3. Yet I do not think that in this place we are free to interpret just any people: one people is expressly indicated. For he did not say, “They produced,” as though speaking of several; rather, as of one, “the fig tree,” he says, “put forth its *grossi*”; and, as I understand it, this is the Jewish people. How often the Savior seems to speak of this people parabolically in the Gospel! [Col. 1067B] Thus: “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard” (Luke 13:6), and so forth; likewise: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees” (Luke 21:29); and Nathanael was told: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1:48). Again he curses the fig tree because he found no fruit on it (Mark 11:13–14).

A fitting fig tree indeed: although it sprang from the good root of the patriarchs, it nevertheless never chose to grow tall, never to raise itself above the earth, never to answer its root by the height of its branches, the nobility of its flowers, or the abundance of its fruit. You agree very badly with your root, little tree—crooked and knotty. For the root is holy. What worthy thing of it appears in your branches? “The fig tree,” he says, “put forth its *grossi*.” You did not draw these from that noble root, evil seed. What is in that root is from [Col. 1067C] the Holy Spirit, and is therefore wholly subtle and sweet. From where came these *grossi* to you? And truly, what was not coarse in that nation? Neither its actions, nor its affections, nor its understanding, nor even its manner of worshipping God. For its actions were wholly in wars, its affection in profits, its understanding in the grossness of the letter, and its worship in the blood of sheep and cattle.

4. But someone says: since that nation never ceased at any time to produce such *grossi*, then there was never a time of pruning, because one and the same time is said to belong to both things. That is not so. We say that women have produced children, not while they are in labor, but once they have already given birth. We also say that trees have brought forth their flowers, not when they begin to flower, but rather when they cease. So here too it is said [Col. 1067D] that the fig tree put forth its *grossi*, not when it produced some of them, but when it had produced them all—that is, when its production came to an end.

Do you ask at what time such completion befell that people? When it killed Christ, then its wickedness was completed, according to what he himself foretold to them: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matt. 21:32). Hence, as he was about to yield up his spirit upon the cross: “It is finished,” he said (John 19:30). O what a completion this accursed fig tree gave to its *grossi*, and was then condemned to everlasting barrenness! How much worse are the last things than the first! Beginning with useless things, it reached things destructive and poisonous. O coarse and viperish affection: to hate the man who heals human bodies and saves souls! O understanding no less [Col. 1068A] coarse, and certainly bovine, which did not understand God even in the works of God!

5. Perhaps the Jew will complain too much of my reproach, because I call his understanding bovine. But let him read Isaiah, and he will hear something worse than bovine: “The ox,” he says, “knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; Israel has not known me; my people have not understood” (Isa. 1:3). You see, Jew, that I am gentler toward you than your prophet. I compared you to beasts of burden; he puts you beneath them.

Yet the prophet did not say this in his own person, but in God’s, who proclaims himself to be God even by his works: “If you do not believe me,” he says, “believe the works; if I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe” (John 10:38, 37). Yet even so they do not take heed to understand. Neither the flight of demons, nor the obedience of [Col. 1068B] the elements, nor the life restored to the dead, could drive this beastly—and more than beastly—dullness from them. By a blindness no less astonishing than pitiable, they rushed into that deed so dreadful and so monstrously coarse, laying sacrilegious hands upon the Lord of majesty.

From that time, then, it could be said that the fig tree put forth its *grossi*, since the legal observances of that people had, as it were, begun to reach their final end; so that, when new things came upon them according to the ancient prophecy, the old things might be cast away (Lev. 26:10). Just as the *grossi* fall and yield place to the good figs beginning to grow. “So long,” he says, “as the fig tree did not cease to produce its *grossi*, I did not call you, O bride, knowing that the best figs could not come forth at the same time. [Col. 1068C] But now that those which had first to be produced have been produced, I invite you no longer unseasonably, since good and health-giving fruits are known to be near at hand, about to displace the useless ones.”

6. “For,” he says, “the flowering vineyards gave forth fragrance”; and this likewise indicates approaching fruit. This fragrance drives serpents away. They say that, when vineyards are in flower, every venomous creeping thing leaves the place and cannot at all endure the scent of the new flowers. Let our novices attend to this and act confidently, considering what kind of spirit they have received, whose first fruits demons cannot endure. If novice fervor is such, what will completed perfection be? Let the fruit be judged from the flower, and the power of its flavor be estimated from the strength of the fragrance. “The flowering vineyards gave forth fragrance.”

And so it was in the beginning. At the preaching of the new grace there followed newness of life in those who had believed; having their conduct good among the Gentiles, they were Christ’s good fragrance in every place (2 Cor. 2:14–15). A good fragrance is a good testimony. This fragrance proceeds from a good work as from a flower. And because, at the beginning of the faith then being born, faithful souls appeared adorned with such flower and such fragrance, like spiritual vineyards, having a good testimony even from those outside, we fittingly understand, I think, that it was said of them: “The flowering vineyards gave forth fragrance.” To what end? Surely so that those who had not yet believed, stirred by this fragrance as they considered their good works, might themselves glorify God, and thus the fragrance might begin to be for them a fragrance of life unto life. Therefore they are rightly said to have given forth fragrance, since they sought not their own glory but, through the good opinion held of them, the salvation of others. Otherwise they might, after the fashion of some, have regarded godliness as gain—for example, gain of display or reward. But that would not have been to give fragrance, but to sell it. Now, however, because they did everything in charity, they did not sell the fragrance at all, but gave it.

7. Moreover, if vineyards are souls, the flower a work, and the fragrance reputation, what is the fruit? Martyrdom. Truly the fruit of the vine is the martyr’s blood. “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, children are the inheritance of the Lord, the fruit of the womb a reward” (Ps. 126:2–3). I might almost have said: the fruit of the vine. Why should I not call the blood of the grape most unmixed wine—the blood of the innocent, the blood of the Just One? Why not red, proven, precious new wine, indeed from the vineyard of Sorech [otherwise, *Soreth*], pressed out in the winepress of suffering? For “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:5). This is regarding the words, “the flowering vineyards gave forth fragrance.”

8. Thus, if we prefer to refer this passage to the times of grace; or, if it pleases us, rather to refer it to the Fathers—for “the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7)—the meaning will be this: the prophets and patriarchs perceived that Christ would be born and die in the flesh, but they did not then give forth that same fragrance, because they did not present in the flesh the one whom they foresaw in the spirit. They did not give forth their fragrance, nor make their secret [Col. 1069C] public, waiting for it to be revealed in its own time. For who then could have grasped wisdom hidden in mystery when it had not been manifested in the body?

Thus the vineyards did not then give forth their fragrance. But later they gave it forth, when through the successive generations they brought forth into the world, by virgin birth, Christ born from themselves according to the flesh. Then indeed, I say, those spiritual vineyards gave forth their fragrance, when “the goodness and loving-kindness of God our Savior appeared” (Titus 3:4), and the world began to have present the one whom a few had previously perceived as absent. That man, for example, who, touching Jacob and sensing Christ, said: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” [Col. 1069D] (Gen. 27:27)—when he said this, he kept his delights to himself and communicated them to no one.

But when the fullness of time came, in which “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4:4–5), then the fragrance that was in him spread itself everywhere, so that the Church, sensing him from the ends of the earth, cried: “Your name is oil poured out,” and the young maidens ran in the fragrance of this oil (Song 1:2–3). Thus this vineyard gave forth its fragrance, and at that time the others also gave it forth, those in which this same fragrance of life had existed. Why should they not give it forth, from whom Christ came according to the flesh?

Therefore it was said that the vineyards gave forth fragrance, either because faithful souls spread everywhere [Col. 1070A] a good report of themselves, or because the oracles and revelations of the Fathers were made public to the world, and their fragrance went forth into all the earth, as the Apostle says: “Great indeed is the mystery of godliness: which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the Gentiles, believed in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16).

9. It would be remarkable if neither this fig tree nor these vineyards had anything that might build up moral character. I judge this passage to have a moral sense as well. I say that through the grace of God which is in us, we too have fig trees and vineyards. Fig trees are those who are gentler in their conduct; vineyards, those more fervent in spirit. Anyone among us who deals with others in a common and companionable way, and not only lives without reproach [Col. 1070B] among the brethren, but also makes himself a pleasure to all with great gentleness in every office of charity—why should I not most suitably say that he plays the part of a fig tree?

Yet he must first put forth and cast away his *grossi*: namely, the fear of judgment, which perfect charity casts out; and the bitterness of sins, which must yield to true confession, the infusion of grace, and the abundant outpouring of frequent tears; and other things of the same kind, which, like *grossi*, precede the sweetness of fruit. You yourselves can think of such things.

10. Yet, to add something further that occurs to me, see whether perhaps knowledge, prophecy, tongues, and similar things should also be counted among the *grossi*. For these, like *grossi*, are destined to fail [Col. 1070C] and yield to better things, as the Apostle says: knowledge shall be destroyed, prophecies shall be abolished, and tongues shall cease. Understanding will also exclude faith, and vision must take the place of hope. “For what a man sees, why does he hope for it?” Charity alone does not fail (1 Cor. 13:8)—that charity by which God is loved with all the heart, all the soul, and all the strength (Luke 10:27). Therefore I would by no means count this among the *grossi*, nor say that it belongs even to the fig tree, but rather to the vineyards.

Now those who are vineyards show themselves to us more severe than gentle, acting with vehement spirit, zealous for discipline, rebuking vices most sharply, and most suitably applying to themselves those words: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away over your enemies?” [Col. 1070D] (Ps. 138:21). Likewise: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68:10). The former, in my view, excel in love of neighbor; the latter in love of God. But I delight to rest beneath this vine and beneath this fig tree, where love of God and neighbor gives shade. I embrace both when I love you, Lord Jesus Christ, who are my neighbor because you are human and have shown mercy to me; and yet you are God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXI. How the Church found the riches of divine mercy in the openings of Christ’s wounds; and concerning the strength of the martyrs which they received from Christ

1. “Arise [Note: [Col. 1069] In the printed editions *hasten* is added; the word is absent from the manuscripts and the earliest editions.], my friend, my bride, and come” [Col. 1071A] (Song 2:13). The bridegroom commends his great love by repeating terms of affection. For repetition is an expression of feeling; and in again urging his beloved to the labor of the vineyards, he shows how solicitous he is for the salvation of souls. For you have already heard that vineyards are souls. Let us not linger needlessly over things already said. Consider what follows.

Yet nowhere, as I recall, had he openly called her “bride” thus far in this entire work, except now when they go to the vineyards, when they approach the wine of charity. When charity comes and is made perfect, it will effect a spiritual marriage; and the two will be one, not in one flesh, but in one spirit, as the Apostle says: “He who is joined to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

2. It follows: “My dove in the openings of the rock, [Col. 1071B] in the caverns of the wall, show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears.” He loves and continues to speak in the language of love. Again he tenderly calls her dove; he calls her his own and claims her as belonging to him. What he himself had been accustomed earnestly to ask of her, he now, in a reversal of roles, asks from her: both her presence and her conversation. He acts as a bridegroom; but, being modest, he is ashamed of public display and resolves to enjoy his delights in a secluded place—namely, in the openings of the rock and the caverns of the wall.

Suppose, then, that the bridegroom speaks thus: “Do not fear, beloved, as though this work of the vineyards to which we urge you will hinder or interrupt the business of love. It will surely serve in some way the purpose that we both desire. Vineyards indeed have walls, and these are pleasant retreats for the modest.” This is the literal play. Why should I not call it play? What seriousness does this sequence of the letter possess? What sounds outwardly is not even worthy of hearing, unless the Spirit within helps the weakness of our understanding.

Therefore let us not remain outside, lest, God forbid, we seem to be recounting the enticements of shameful loves. Bring chaste ears to the discourse now in hand concerning love; and when you think of the lovers themselves, you should understand not a man and a woman, but the Word and the soul. If I say Christ and the Church, it is the same thing—except that by the name “Church” is denoted not one soul but the unity, or rather the unanimity, of many souls. Nor should you think that the openings of the rock or the caverns of the wall are hiding places of evildoers, lest any suspicion at all arise of works [Col. 1071D] of darkness.

3. Another has explained this passage by interpreting the openings of the rock as the wounds of Christ. Entirely rightly; for the rock is Christ. Good openings these, which establish faith in the resurrection and in Christ’s divinity. “My Lord and my God,” he says (John 20:28). From where was that prophetic utterance obtained, if not from the openings of the rock? In them the sparrow finds a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest in which to place her young (Ps. 83:4); in them the dove shelters herself and fearlessly watches the circling hawk. Therefore he says: “My dove in the openings [Col. 1072A] of the rock.”

The dove’s voice is: “He set me on high upon a rock” (Ps. 26:6); and likewise: “He set,” he says, “my feet upon a rock” (Ps. 39:3). The wise man builds his house upon a rock, because there he need fear neither the assaults of winds nor of floods (Matt. 7:24–25). What good is not in the rock? Upon the rock I am exalted; upon the rock I am secure; upon the rock I stand firm. I am secure from the enemy, strong against falling; and this because I have been raised above the earth. For everything earthly is uncertain and liable to fall. Let our citizenship be in heaven, and we do not fear either falling or being cast down. The rock is in heaven; there are firmness and security. “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” (Ps. 103:18). And truly, where are weak people’s safe and secure protection and rest, if not in the wounds of the Savior? I dwell there all the more securely because he is more powerful [Col. 1072B] to save.

The world rages, the body presses upon me, the devil lies in wait: I do not fall, for I am founded upon the firm rock. I have committed a great sin: my conscience will be troubled, but it will not be dismayed, because I shall remember the Lord’s wounds. For he was wounded for our iniquities (Isa. 53:5). What is so deadly that it cannot be healed by Christ’s death? If, then, such a powerful and effective remedy comes to mind, I can no longer be terrified by the malignity of any disease.

4. It is therefore clear that he erred who said: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. 4:13). Except that he was not of Christ’s members, nor did Christ’s merit belong to him, so that he might claim it as his own and call his own what was Christ’s—as a member calls the possession of its head its own [Col. 1072C].

[Note: [Col. 1071D] The old books, together with the earlier editions, consistently read: “as a member, in the nominative, calls the possession of its head its own.” Horstius wrongly reads *reum capitis membrum* (“a member guilty of a capital charge”); Picard reads *veri capitis membrum* (“a member of the true head”). Our reading is genuine [Col. 1072D] and easy, if *membrum* is understood as a nominative, supplying *suam dicit* (“calls it its own”) from the preceding clause: thus the sense is, “As a member calls the possession of its head its own.”]

But I confidently appropriate for myself from the inner parts of the Lord whatever is lacking to me from myself, because they overflow with mercy; nor are there lacking openings through which it may flow out. They pierced his hands and feet, and opened his side with a lance; and through these clefts I am permitted to suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone—that is, to taste and see that the Lord is sweet. He thought thoughts of peace, and I did not know it. For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? But the nail that opens, the nail that pierces, has become for me a means of seeing the Lord’s will. Why should I not see through the opening? The nail cries out, the wound cries out, that truly God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. The iron passed through [Col. 1072D] his soul and came near to his heart, so that he now cannot fail to know compassion for my weaknesses. The secret of the heart lies open through the openings of the body; that great mystery of godliness lies open; the bowels of mercy of our God lie open, in which the Dayspring from on high visited us. Why should not the inward parts lie open through the wounds? For in what could it have shone forth more clearly than in your wounds, O Lord, that you are sweet and gentle and abundant in mercy? For no one has greater compassion than to lay down his life for persons condemned and given over to death.

[Col. 1073A] 5. Therefore the Lord’s compassion is my merit. I am not at all without merit so long as he is not without compassions. And if the Lord’s mercies are many, I too am correspondingly rich in merits. For what if I am conscious to myself of many sins? Surely where sin abounded, grace superabounded (Rom. 5:20). And if the mercies of the Lord are from eternity and unto eternity (Ps. 102:17), I too will sing the mercies of the Lord forever (Ps. 88:2). Shall I remember my own righteousnesses? “Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone” (Ps. 70:16). For it is also mine: you have been made righteousness from God for me. Need I fear that one righteousness will not suffice for us both? It is not a short blanket which, according to the prophet, cannot cover two (Isa. 28:20).

[Col. 1073B] “Your righteousness is righteousness forever” (Ps. 118:142). What extends farther than eternity? Your generous and eternal righteousness will abundantly cover both you and me. In me it covers a multitude of sins; but in you, Lord, what does it cover except treasures of loving devotion, riches of goodness? These are stored up for me in the openings of the rock. How great a multitude of your sweetness is in them—hidden, indeed, from those who perish! For why should what is holy be given to dogs, or pearls to swine? But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit; he has even brought us through the opened passages into the holy places. What a multitude of sweetness, what fullness of grace, what perfection of virtues is in them!

6. I will go to those chambers so richly stored, and, at the prophet’s admonition, leave the cities and dwell [Col. 1073C] in the rock (Jer. 48:28). I shall be like a dove nesting at the summit of an opening, so that, placed with Moses in the opening of the rock as the Lord passes by, I may deserve at least to behold his back (Exod. 33:22–23). For who can see the face of the One who stands—that is, the splendor of the Immutable One—unless he has already deserved to be brought not merely into the holy place, but into the Holy of Holies?

Yet the contemplation of the Lord’s back is neither trivial nor to be despised. Let Herod despise it; I despise it all the less because it showed itself more contemptible to Herod. The Lord’s back also has something delightful to behold. “Who knows whether God will turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him?” It will be so when he shows his face, and we shall be saved. But meanwhile, may he go before us with blessings of sweetness—those, indeed, which he is accustomed to leave behind him. Now let him show the back parts of his gracious condescension; later, in the glory of his dignity, he will show his face. Sublime in the kingdom, but sweet upon the cross. In this vision may he go before me; in that may he fulfill me. “You will fill me,” he says, “with joy by your countenance” (Ps. 15:11). Both visions are saving, both sweet; but that one is in sublimity, this in humility; that in splendor, this in pallor.

7. Finally, he says: “And the hind parts of his back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. 67:14). How could he fail to grow pale in death? Yet pale gold is better than shining bronze, and “what is foolish in God is wiser than men.” Gold is the Word; gold is Wisdom [Col. 1074A]. This gold discolored itself, concealing the form of God and assuming the form of a servant. It also discolored the Church, which says: “Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me” (Song 1:5).

Therefore her hind parts too are in the pallor of gold: she who did not blush at the blackness of the cross, did not recoil from the burning of suffering, and did not shrink from the bruising of wounds. She even takes pleasure in them and wishes her latter end to resemble them. Therefore she hears: “My dove in the openings of the rock,” because she dwells with entire devotion in Christ’s wounds and remains in them in continual meditation. From there comes her endurance in martyrdom; from there her great confidence before God Most High. The martyr need not fear to lift up to him a bloodless and bruised face, since by his bruising she has been healed; nor need the martyr fear to present the glorious likeness of his death, indeed in the pallor of gold.

[Col. 1074B] What should one fear to whom even the Lord says: “Show me your face”? For what purpose? As it seems to me, he wishes rather to show himself. So it is: he wishes to be seen, not to see. For what does he not see? He has no need that anyone should show himself to him, from whom nothing is hidden even if it hides itself. He therefore wishes to be seen; the gracious leader wishes the face and eyes of his devoted soldier to be lifted to his wounds, so that by this he may raise that soldier’s spirit and, by his own example, make him stronger to endure.

8. Indeed, the martyr will not feel his own wounds while he gazes upon Christ’s. The martyr stands dancing and triumphing, though his whole body is torn; and while iron tears open his sides, he sees the sacred blood gush from his flesh not merely bravely but joyfully. Where then is the martyr’s soul? Surely in safety; surely in the rock; surely in the inner parts of Jesus, the wounds being open for entry. If it were in its own inner parts, it would certainly feel the iron searching them; it would not endure the pain, but would yield and deny. But now, dwelling in the rock, what wonder if it has become hard like a rock? Nor is it surprising if, exiled from the body, it does not feel bodily pains. This is not caused by numbness, but by love. Sensation is subdued, not lost. Pain is not absent, but overcome and despised.

Thus the martyr’s strength comes from the rock; from there comes the power to drink the Lord’s cup. And how splendid is this cup that intoxicates! (Ps. 22:5). Splendid, I say, and no less delightful to the commander looking on [Col. 1074D] than to the soldier triumphing. For “the joy of the Lord is our strength” (2 Esdras 8:10). Why should he not rejoice at the sound of the strongest confession? Indeed, he seeks it eagerly: “Let your voice,” he says, “sound in my ears.” Nor will he delay to return the favor according to his promise: as soon as one has confessed him before men, he too will confess that person before his Father (Matt. 10:32).

Let us break off the sermon, for it cannot be finished now; lest it be without measure, if we wish to encompass in this one sermon all that remains in the chapter before us. Let us therefore reserve what remains for another beginning, so that the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord—God above all, blessed for ever—may rejoice in both our speech and its measure. Amen.

## SERMON LXII. What it means for the faithful soul to dwell “in the openings of the rock,” and what “in the caverns of the wall” means. Concerning searching God’s will rather than his majesty. Finally, concerning the purity of mind necessary for preaching the truth

[Col. 1075A]

1. “My dove in the openings of the rock, in the caverns of the wall” (Song 2:14). The dove finds a safe refuge not only in the openings of the rock; she finds one also in the caverns of the wall. If by “wall” we understand not a heap of stones but the communion of saints, let us see whether perhaps he meant by the caverns of the wall the places of angels who fell through pride, left, as it were, vacant [Col. 1075B] and destined to be filled from among human beings, like ruins to be restored with living stones. Hence the apostle Peter says: “Coming to the living stone, you yourselves also, as living stones, are built up into spiritual houses” (1 Pet. 2:4–5).

Nor do I think it irrelevant if we understand the guardianship of angels to perform the role of a wall in the vineyard of the Lord, which is the Church of the predestined; for Paul says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to minister for those who shall inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14); and the Prophet: “The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him” (Ps. 33:8). If this stands, the meaning will be that during the time and place of her pilgrimage the Church is consoled by two things: with regard to the past, the memory of Christ’s passion; with regard to the future, the thought and confidence that she will be received into the lot [Col. 1075C] of the saints. As though furnished with eyes both before and behind, she looks upon both with insatiable desire; and each sight is very pleasing to her, each a refuge from the tribulation and sorrow caused by evils. Her consolation is complete when she knows not only what is to be hoped for, but also from where that hope must be presumed. Her expectation is joyful and not doubtful, because it is established by Christ’s death. Why should she fear the greatness of the reward when she considers the worthiness of its price? How gladly she visits in mind the openings through which the price of the most holy blood flowed for her! How gladly she traverses the caverns, retreats, and dwellings which are the many and diverse mansions in the Father’s house, where he has a place to establish his children according to the differing character of their merits!

For now, indeed, insofar as she can for the present, she rests in them only in memory, already clothing herself in mind with the heavenly dwelling which is from above. But there will be a time when she fills the ruins, when she inhabits the caverns in body as well as in mind; when by the presence of her whole company she will illuminate the empty dwellings abandoned by their ancient inhabitants. Then no cavern at all will appear in the heavenly wall, which will thereafter rejoice in the happy perfection and completeness of itself.

2. Or, if you prefer this, we may say that these caverns are not found by zealous and devout minds, but made by them. [Col. 1076A] “How?” you ask. By thought and desire. For the devout wall yields, like a softer wall, to the desire of the soul; it yields to pure contemplation, it yields to frequent prayer. Indeed, “the prayer of the righteous pierces the heavens” (Ecclus. 35:21). It does not cleave the spacious heights of this bodily air as a bird in flight might with the rowing of its wings, nor does it pierce the solid and lofty summit of the firmament as a sharp sword might. Rather, there are holy, living, rational heavens, which declare the glory of God; and these gladly bend themselves toward our prayers in a kind of favorable compassion. As their affections curve toward the touch of our devotion, they receive us into their bosom whenever we knock upon them with worthy intention. “For to him who knocks it shall be opened.”

Thus each of us, even in this time [Col. 1076B] of our mortality, may hollow out for himself, wherever he wishes, caverns in the heavenly wall: now to revisit the patriarchs, now to greet the prophets, now to mingle with the senate of apostles, now to join the choirs of martyrs; and, by running through them with all the eagerness of the mind, to survey the ranks and dwelling places of the blessed powers from the least angel up to cherubim and seraphim, as each person’s devotion carries him. Wherever he is more deeply moved, as the Spirit moves within him according to his will, if he stands and knocks, it will immediately be opened to him. A cavern is thus made, as it were, in the mountains—or rather, in holy minds—as they freely bend themselves toward compassion; and he will rest with them for a little while.

For every soul acting thus, both face and voice are pleasing to God: the face because of purity, the voice [Col. 1076C] because of confession. For “confession and beauty are before him” (Ps. 95:6). Hence it is said to one who is such: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in your ears.” The voice is wonder in the mind of one contemplating; the voice is thanksgiving. God greatly delights in such caverns, from which there resounds to him a voice of thanksgiving, a voice of wonder and praise.

3. Blessed is the mind that has earnestly sought often to hollow out a place for itself in this wall; but happier still is the mind that does so in the rock. It is possible to hollow out a place even in the rock, but this requires a purer sharpness of the mind’s eye, a more powerful intensity of purpose, and greater merits of holiness [otherwise, “let us dig”].

[Note: Most manuscripts omit *sanctitatis* (“of holiness”), though all the editions, including the earliest, contain the word.]

And who is equal to these things? Surely he who said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; this was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2). Does he not seem to have immersed himself in the very inner chambers of the Word, and to have drawn from the hidden recesses of his breast a sacred marrow of deepest wisdom? What of the one who spoke wisdom among the perfect, wisdom hidden in mystery, which none of the rulers of this world knew? (1 Cor. 2:6, 8). Did not this devout searcher, having pierced one heaven and then another with keen but pious inquiry, at last bring it forth from the third heaven? Yet he did not keep it silent from us, faithfully imparting to the faithful, in such words as he could, [Col. 1077A] the things he had heard. But he heard ineffable words which it was not permitted him to speak (2 Cor. 12:2, 4)—not, certainly, to a human being, for he spoke them to himself and to God.

Suppose, then, that God comforts Paul’s anxious charity in this way and says: “Why are you troubled because human hearing cannot receive what you have conceived? Let your voice sound in my ears.” That is: “If you may not reveal to mortals what you perceive, take comfort nevertheless that your voice is able to delight divine ears.” Do you see the holy soul: now sober in charity for our sake, now surpassing itself in purity for God? (2 Cor. 5:13).

Consider also holy David, whether perhaps he himself is the very man of whom he speaks with God as though of another: “The thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thought shall keep festival for you” [Col. 1077B] (Ps. 75:11). Whatever from prophetic thought could be brought into public through the Prophet’s word and example, the Prophet immediately released into public confession; from this he confessed the Lord among the peoples, while reserving the rest for himself and God, and at the same time celebrating it festively in joy and exultation.

This, then, is what he wished to convey to us by the verse just mentioned. Whatever he could draw forth by that searching and eager thought of his from the secret place of wisdom, he imparted in careful preaching, so far as he could, for the salvation of peoples. What the crowds could not receive, he spent in festive jubilation in the praises of God. You see that nothing is lost to holy contemplation: whatever cannot be expended for the edification of the people becomes all the more a pleasing and fitting praise of God.

4. Since this is so, it is clear that there are two kinds of contemplation: one concerning the condition, blessedness, and glory of the heavenly city, and the vast multitude of its citizens—whether occupied in action or in repose; the other concerning the majesty, eternity, and divinity of the King himself. The former is in the wall; the latter in the rock. Yet the more difficult the latter is to excavate, the sweeter is what you draw forth from it. Nor should you fear what Scripture threatens against searchers of majesty (Prov. 25:27). Only bring a pure and simple eye: you will not be crushed by glory, but admitted to it—unless you seek not God’s glory but your own. Otherwise each is crushed by his own glory, not by God’s; while he is inclined toward the former, he is not permitted to raise his neck toward the latter, being made heavy, of course, by desire. Once that has been shaken off, let us safely search [variant: dig] in the Rock, in which are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3). If you still doubt, hear the Rock itself: “Those who work in me,” it says, “will not sin” (Ecclus. 24:30). “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly away and be at rest?” (Ps. 54:7). There the meek and simple person finds rest, where the deceitful—or the exalted—and the lover of empty glory is crushed. The Church is a dove, and therefore rests: a dove because innocent, because groaning. A dove, I say, because in meekness she receives the implanted word. And she rests in the Word—that is, in the rock; for the rock is the Word. Therefore the Church is in the clefts of the rock, through which she looks within and sees the glory of her Bridegroom; yet she is not crushed by the glory, because she does not claim it for herself. She is not crushed because she is not a searcher of majesty, but of will. For as regards majesty, she sometimes indeed dares to direct her gaze even upon it, but as one admiring, not as one searching. And if at any time she is carried away into it in ecstasy, this is the finger of God, graciously lifting up a human being—not human rashness insolently penetrating God’s heights. For when the Apostle recalls [variant: mentions] that he was caught up (2 Cor. 12), he does so to excuse his daring. What other mortal, then, would presume by his own efforts to entangle himself in that dreadful scrutiny of the divine majesty, or, as an importunate contemplator, to burst into fearful secrets? Therefore I think that “searchers of majesty” are called, as it were, intruders—not those who are caught up into it, but those who rush into it. These, then, are crushed by glory.

5. The searching of majesty, then, is fearful; but the searching of will is as safe as it is devout. Why should I not apply all diligence to searching out the mystery of the glory of that will, which I know I must obey in every respect? Sweet is that glory which proceeds from nothing other than contemplation of sweetness itself, from the beholding of abundant goodness and great mercy. “We have seen this glory,” indeed: “glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:14). For everything that appeared as glory in this respect was gracious and truly fatherly. This glory will not crush me, though I direct all my powers toward it; rather, I shall receive its imprint. For, “beholding with unveiled face, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18). We are transformed when we are conformed. Far be it that conformity of a human being to God should be presumed in the glory of majesty rather than in the modesty of will! This is my glory, if I should ever hear said of me: “I have found a man according to my heart.” The heart of the Bridegroom is the heart of his Father. What is it like? “Be merciful,” he says, “as your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6:36). This is the form he desires to see when he says to the Church: “Show me your face”—the form of devotion and meekness. With all confidence she raises this face to the Rock, to which she is like: “Come to him,” it says, “and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be put to shame” (Ps. 33:6). How can the humble be put to shame by the humble, the holy by the devout, or the modest by the meek? Certainly the pure face of the Bride will not recoil from the purity of the rock, any more than virtue recoils from virtue or light from light.

6. But because the Church cannot meanwhile approach the boring of the rock in every part of herself—for not all who are in the Church can look into the mysteries of the divine will or grasp the depths of God for themselves—she is shown to dwell not only in the clefts of the rock, but also in the hollows of the wall. Thus, in the perfect—those who dare, with purity of conscience, to explore and penetrate the mysteries of wisdom and who can do so by keenness of understanding—she dwells in the clefts of the rock. In the rest she dwells in the hollows of the wall, so that those who are unable, or do not presume, to dig in the rock for themselves may dig in the wall, content at least to contemplate in mind the glory of the saints. If even this is impossible for anyone, then Jesus is surely set before that person—and Jesus crucified—so that he too, without his own labor, may dwell in clefts of the rock in which he did not labor. The Jews labored in them, and he will enter into the labors of unbelievers, that he may become faithful. Nor need he fear being repelled who is also called to enter. “Enter into the rock,” it says, “and hide in the pit of the earth from the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty” (Isa. 2:10). To the still weak and sluggish soul—which, as a certain man confesses of himself in the Gospel, “cannot dig and is ashamed to beg” (Luke 16:3)—the pit of earth is shown in which it may hide, until it gains strength and advances, so that it too may bore for itself clefts in the rock through which it may enter into the inner things of the Word, by vigor and purity of mind.

7. And if we understand the pit of earth to be that which says, “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21:17), there will be no doubt that a wounded soul which lingers there will more quickly obtain healing. For what is so effective for healing the wounds of conscience and cleansing the mind’s sight as diligent meditation upon Christ’s wounds? Yet until it has been perfectly cleansed and healed, I do not see how the words “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears” can be applied to it. How, finally, can one dare to show her face or raise her voice when she is commanded to hide? “Hide,” it says, “in the pit of the earth.” Why? Because she is not fair of face and is not worthy to be seen. She will not be worthy to be seen so long as she is not fit to see. But when, through dwelling in the pit of earth, she has progressed so far in healing her inner eye that she too can behold with unveiled face the glory of God, then at last she will speak with confidence what she sees, pleasing in voice and face. The face that can direct its gaze toward God’s brightness must necessarily be pleasing. For it could not do so unless it itself were bright and pure, having been transformed into the same image of brightness that it beholds. Otherwise, repelled by its own dissimilarity, it would recoil from the unfamiliar reflected splendor. Therefore, when the pure woman can behold pure truth, then the Bridegroom will desire to see her face and consequently to hear her voice.

8. For how much the preaching of truth, joined with purity of mind, pleases him, he shows when he immediately adds: “For your voice is sweet.” And that a voice does not please when the face displeases, he shows when he at once adds: “And your face is lovely.” What is the beauty of the inner face except purity? In many persons this has pleased without the voice of preaching; but preaching without it has pleased in no one. Truth does not show itself to the impure; Wisdom does not entrust herself to them. Why, then, do they speak of what they have not seen? “We speak what we know,” he says, “and testify to what we have seen” (John 3:11). Go on, then: dare to testify to what you have not seen and to speak of what you do not know. Do you ask whom I call impure? One who seeks human praise; who does not offer the Gospel without charge; who preaches in order to eat; who regards godliness as gain; who seeks not fruit but a gift. Such people are impure. And although, owing to impurity, they have no means of seeing truth, they nevertheless have means of speaking it. Why do you act prematurely? Why do you not wait for the light? Why do you presume to perform the work of light before the light? “It is vain for you to rise before the light.” Light is purity; light is charity, which “does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5). Let this go first, and the foot of the tongue will not be set upon uncertain ground. Truth is not seen by the proud eye; it lies open to the sincere one. There is no reason for truth to refuse itself to a pure heart’s sight and therefore to its utterance. But God says to the sinner: “Why do you declare my righteous acts and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49:16). Many, neglecting purity, attempted to speak before seeing; and either erred grievously, not knowing what they were speaking about or what they were affirming, or became shamefully contemptible, because while teaching others they had not taught themselves. May the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord—God blessed above all for ever—preserve us always, at your prayers, from this twofold evil. Amen.

## Sermon LXIII

On the vineyard which a devout and wise person—that is, each person’s own life, or mind and conscience—must diligently cultivate; on the two kinds of foxes, namely flatterers and detractors; and on the temptations of novice monks.

1. “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, for our vineyard has blossomed” (Song 2:15). It is clear that the visit to the vineyards was not idle, since foxes destroying them were found there. Such is the letter. But what is the Spirit’s meaning? Before all else, we must utterly reject from this exposition the common and usual literal sense, as unsuitable and tasteless, wholly unworthy of acceptance in Scripture so holy and authoritative. Unless perhaps someone is so foolish and dull-minded as to think it a great thing to learn from it, after the manner of the children of this world, to care for earthly possessions and to guard and defend vineyards against the incursions of beasts, lest one perhaps lose the produce of wine, “in which is excess,” while labor and expense also perish. What a great loss, indeed, that we should read a holy book with such zeal and reverence merely in order to learn from it to guard vineyards against foxes, lest purses be emptied to no purpose in cultivating them if we have been lazy in guarding them! You are not so unlearned or so devoid of spiritual grace as to think in so carnal a fashion. Let us therefore seek these things in the Spirit. There we find, with a sound understanding and a meaning no less worthy, both flourishing vineyards and foxes destroying them; and in catching or removing these foxes one labors more honorably and more fruitfully. Do you doubt that minds must be guarded far more vigilantly than crops, and that spiritual wickednesses threatening them must be watched against far more carefully than deceitful little foxes threatening the crops?

2. But I must now show you these spiritual vines and foxes. It will be for you, my children, to care for your own vineyard, when, as I speak, you perceive what dangers and what assailants you must especially guard against. To a wise person his life is a vineyard, as are his mind and conscience. The wise person leaves nothing in himself uncultivated or deserted. The fool does not do so. With him you will find everything neglected, lying waste, uncultivated, and foul. A fool has no vineyard. How can there be a vineyard where nothing planted and nothing cultivated appears anywhere? The fool’s whole life is overgrown with thorns and thistles—and is that a vineyard? Even if it once was one, it is so no longer, having plainly been reduced to a wilderness. Where is the vine of virtue? Where is the cluster of good work? Where is the wine of spiritual joy? “I passed by the field of a lazy man,” it says, “and by the vineyard of a foolish man; and behold, nettles had filled it all, thorns had covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (Prov. 24:30–31). You hear the wise man mocking the fool because, through neglect, he has turned into a non-vineyard the goods of nature and gifts of grace that he perhaps received through the washing of regeneration—as his first vineyard, planted by God and not by man. Finally, there cannot be a vineyard where there is no life. For the life lived by a fool I would judge to be death rather than life. How can there be life with barrenness? Is not a tree, dry and become barren, judged dead? Its branches too are dead. “He destroyed their vineyards with hail” (Ps. 77:47), it says, showing that those deprived of life are condemned for barrenness. Thus the fool, precisely because he lives uselessly, is dead while living.

3. Therefore it belongs to the wise person alone to have—or rather, to be—a vineyard, because he has life. He is a fruitful tree in the house of God and therefore a living tree. Indeed, wisdom itself, by which he is called and is wise, “is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her” (Prov. 3:18). Why should the one who lays hold of her not live? He lives, but by faith. For the wise person is righteous, and “the righteous lives by faith” (Heb. 10:38). And if the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom, as it is, then the wise person is certainly the righteous person. Thus, whether you call him righteous or wise, he will never live without a vineyard, because he will never fail to live. For his vineyard is precisely his life. And good is the vineyard of the righteous—indeed, the righteous person is a good vineyard: virtue is its vine, action its branch, the testimony of conscience its wine, and the tongue its press for expression. Finally, “This is our glory,” he says, “the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). Do you see that nothing is idle in the wise person? Speech, thought, conduct, and whatever else belongs to him—why is not all of it God’s cultivation, God’s building, and the vineyard of the Lord of hosts? What of himself, finally, can perish for him, when even “his leaf shall not fall”?

4. Yet such a vineyard will never lack attacks or snares. “Where there are many riches, there are also many who consume them” (Eccles. 5:10). The wise person will be as careful to preserve his vineyard as to cultivate it, and will not allow it to be devoured by foxes. A hidden detractor is a most evil fox; but no less wicked is the smooth flatterer. The wise person will beware of them. He will make every effort in his power to catch those who do such things—but to catch them by benefits, acts of kindness, saving admonitions, and prayers to God for them. He will not cease to heap such coals of fire upon the head of the reviler (Rom. 12:20), and likewise upon that of the flatterer, until, if possible, he removes envy from the former’s heart and pretense from the latter’s, fulfilling the command of the Bridegroom: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.” Does not the man seem caught to you when his face is suffused with shame, since, ashamed of his own judgment, he himself bears witness to his confusion and repentance—whether because he hated a person most worthy of love, or because he loved only in word and tongue the one by whom he has at last learned himself to be loved in deed and truth? Certainly he is caught, and caught for the Lord, in accordance with the Lord’s express words: “Catch,” he says, “for us.” Would that I might thus catch all who oppose me without cause, so that I might either restore or gain them for Christ! “Thus, thus let those who seek my life be confounded and ashamed; let those who wish me evil be turned back and put to shame,” so that I too may be found obedient to the Bridegroom and may catch foxes—not for myself, but for him.

> **Note [Col. 1081].** Thus three manuscripts and two others together with the printed editions read: not only “in catching foxes,” but also “in catching them [the opponents] themselves.”

But let the discourse return to its beginning, so that the sequence of explanation may proceed in due order.

5. “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.” This is a moral passage; and in accordance with moral instruction we have now shown that these spiritual vineyards are nothing other than spiritual persons. Since all their inward parts are cultivated, sprouting, fruitful, and bringing forth the spirit of salvation—as was said of the kingdom of God—so we may equally say of these vineyards of the Lord of hosts that they are within us (Luke 17:21). For we read in the Gospel that “the kingdom of God will be given to a people producing its fruits” (Matt. 21:43). These are the fruits Paul enumerates: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, meekness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity” (Gal. 5:22–23). These fruits are our advances. They are welcome to the Bridegroom because he cares for us. Does God care for shrubs? The God-man loves human beings, not trees, and counts our advances as his own fruits. He carefully watches their season, smiles upon their appearance, and anxiously labors to prevent their perishing once they have appeared—or rather, to prevent their perishing for himself, since he counts himself as one with us. Therefore, in his providence, he commands the scheming little foxes to be caught for himself, lest they snatch away the tender fruits. “Catch for us,” he says, “the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.” And as though someone should say, “You fear too soon; the season of fruit has not yet come,” he answers: “It is not so, for our vineyard has blossomed.” After the flowers, there is no delay in the coming of fruit: while the flowers are still falling, the fruits at once burst forth and begin to appear.

6. This parable concerns the present time. Do you see these novices? They have come recently; they have converted recently. We cannot say of them, “Our vineyard has blossomed,” for it is blossoming. Meanwhile, what you see appearing in them is flower; the season of fruit has not yet arrived. The flower is their new manner of life; the flower is the fresh pattern of a more disciplined life. They have put on a disciplined appearance and a good bearing of the whole body. I admit that what is visible in their outward appearance is pleasing: more negligent, certainly, is the exterior care of the body—the clothing; speech is rarer, the countenance more cheerful, the look more modest, the step more sober. But since these things have only recently begun, they should be counted flowers by reason of their newness: a hope of fruits rather than fruits themselves. Concerning you, little children, we do not fear the deceit of foxes, which are known to envy fruits rather than flowers. Your danger lies elsewhere. I fear a scorching of the flowers—not a stealthy snatching, but a scorching by cold. The north wind and morning frosts are suspect to me, for they commonly destroy untimely flowers and take away fruits. Thus your evil opens from the north. “Who can endure the face of his cold?” (Ps. 147:17). If this cold has once penetrated the soul—through the soul’s negligence, as commonly happens, while the spirit sleeps—and if afterwards, God forbid, no one restrains it and it reaches the inner parts, descending into the entrails of the heart and the bosom of the mind, shaking the affections, taking possession of the paths of counsel, disturbing the light of judgment, and enslaving the freedom of the spirit, then, as commonly happens in fevered bodies, a certain stiffness of soul comes upon it: vigor slackens, a feebleness of strength is feigned, horror of austerity grows, fear of poverty torments it, the soul contracts, grace withdraws, the length of life stretches out, reason falls asleep, the spirit is extinguished, novice fervor cools, wearisome lukewarmness grows heavy, brotherly charity grows cold, pleasure flatters, security deceives, habit calls one back. Why say more? The law is disregarded; right is renounced [variant: right is adjudged]; what is lawful is proscribed; the fear of the Lord is abandoned. At last one gives one’s hand to shamelessness; that rash, shameful, utterly disgraceful leap is dared, full of ignominy and confusion: from the height into the abyss, from the pavement to the dungheap, from the throne to the sewer, from heaven to mire, from the cloister to the world, from paradise to hell. It is not the present occasion to show the beginning and origin of this plague, or the art by which it may be avoided, or the virtue by which it may be overcome. That will be for another time; now let us continue what we began.

7. The discourse must be turned back toward those more advanced and firm: toward the vineyard that has already blossomed. Although it has no reason to fear cold for its flowers, its fruits are not safe from foxes. We must explain more openly what these foxes spiritually are; why they are called small; why they are especially commanded to be caught rather than driven away or killed; and we must introduce the different kinds of these beasts, for greater knowledge and caution among the hearers—not in this sermon, however, lest satiety intervene, but so that the gladness of our devotion may continue in grace and in the confession of the glory of the great Bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, God blessed above all for ever. Amen.

## Sermon LXIV

On the temptations of more advanced monks, which they suffer from foxes—or rather, from temptations especially hostile to them. Also on heretics, the foxes of the Church, who must be caught.

1. I fulfill my promise. “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, for our vineyard has blossomed” (Song 2:15). Foxes are temptations. Temptations must come. For who will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully? (2 Tim. 2:3). Or how will they compete if no assailant is present? Therefore, you who approach the service of God, “stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1), certain that all who desire to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12). Moreover, temptations differ according to the different times of life. At our beginnings, like the tender flowers of newly planted vineyards, an evident force of cold bears down upon us; we spoke of this in another sermon and warned beginners against this plague (above, Sermon 63, §6). But the hostile powers do not dare openly to oppose those progressing in holier pursuits; rather, they commonly lie in secret ambush like deceitful little foxes—virtues in appearance, but vices in reality. How many have I found who entered the paths of life, advanced to better things, and were progressing well and securely upon the ways of righteousness, yet were shamefully overthrown by the deceit of these foxes and lamented, too late, the fruits of virtue stifled within them!

2. I have seen a man running well; and then a thought arose. Why should it not be a little fox? “How many people,” he says, “could I share the good that I alone enjoy with, if I were in my native country—brothers and kinsfolk, acquaintances and friends? They love me and would readily consent to my persuasion. Why should this be wasted? I will go there, save many of them, and myself along with them. Nor need I fear a change of place. For while I do good, what difference does the location make? Indeed, it will doubtless be better there, where I shall live more fruitfully.” What more? He goes, and the poor man perishes—not so much an exile returning to his native country as flesh returning to its vomit. Unhappy man: he has destroyed himself and gained none of his own. Here is one little fox: namely, the futile hope he placed in winning his relatives. You too can find or notice in yourself other foxes like this, if you do not neglect to do so.

3. Do you want me nevertheless to show you one more? I will do so; and I shall show a third and even a fourth, if I find you watchful in catching those which you perhaps notice in your own vineyard from these examples. Sometimes, when someone progressing well senses a more abundant sprinkling of heavenly grace upon himself, the desire to preach enters his mind—not indeed to his parents and relatives, according to the words, “Immediately I did not confer with flesh and blood” (Gal. 1:16), but, as though more purely, fruitfully, and strongly, to strangers everywhere and to everyone. Be wholly on your guard. He certainly fears to incur the prophetic curse if he hides among the people the grain he has received in secret (Prov. 11:26); and he fears acting contrary to the Gospel unless he preaches on the housetops what he has heard in the ear (Matt. 10:27). This is a fox, and more harmful than the former because it comes more secretly. But I will catch it for you. Moses says first: “You shall not plow with the firstborn of an ox” (Deut. 15:19). Paul interprets this: “Not a novice,” he says, “lest, lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Tim. 3:6). And again: “No one,” he says, “takes this honor to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5:4). Likewise he says: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10:15). And we know that the monk’s office is not to teach but to mourn. From these and similar passages I weave myself a net and catch the fox, lest it destroy the vineyard. For from them it is clear and certain that public preaching neither suits a monk, nor is expedient for a novice, nor is permitted to one not sent. What destruction of conscience, then, lies in acting contrary to these three points! Therefore, whatever of this sort is suggested to your mind—whether it is your own thought or a suggestion introduced by an evil angel—recognize it as a deceitful little fox: evil under the appearance of good.

4. But consider another. How many, fervent in spirit, has the solitude of the wilderness received from monasteries, only to cast them out lukewarm or to keep them, contrary to the law of the wilderness, not merely relaxed but dissolute? Thus it became apparent that a little fox was present where such devastation occurred in the vineyard—that is, such injury to a person’s life and conscience. He thought that, if he lived alone, he would receive much more abundant fruits of the Spirit, since in communal life he had experienced so much spiritual grace. His thought seemed good to him, but the outcome showed that the same thought had rather been a fox destroying him.

5. What of that conspicuous and superstitious abstinence of certain persons among us, which so often and so grievously disturbs us in this house, and by which they make themselves troublesome to everyone and everyone troublesome to themselves? How is this general discord not both a destruction of their own conscience and, so far as it lies in them, a great destruction of this vineyard planted by the Lord’s right hand—namely, the unanimity of you all? “Woe to the man through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18:7). “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble,” he says (Mark 9:41)—what follows is severe. How much harsher a punishment does one deserve who causes scandal to so great and holy a multitude? Whoever he may be, he will surely bear a most severe judgment. But this is for another time.

6. Now let us attend to what the Bridegroom says about these little and cunning animals that destroy the vineyards. I call them little not in malice but in subtlety. For by nature this kind of animal is cunning and especially ready to harm in secret. It seems to me most fittingly to designate certain very subtle vices disguised as virtues, examples of which I have just set forth, though briefly, for your recognition. For they cannot harm otherwise than by pretending to be virtues through a certain likeness to virtues. They are either vain human thoughts or suggestions made by evil angels, angels of Satan, who “transform themselves into angels of light” (2 Cor. 11:14), preparing their arrows in the quiver—that is, in secret—“to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. 10:2). I think they are called little for this reason also: while other vices display themselves openly with a kind of bulkiness, this kind, because of its subtlety, cannot easily be recognized and therefore cannot be guarded against except by the perfect and practiced—those who have the eyes of their heart enlightened for the discernment of good and evil, and especially for discernment of spirits, who can say with the Apostle, “We are not ignorant of Satan’s devices or of his thoughts” (2 Cor. 2:11). And perhaps this is why the Bridegroom commands them not to be exterminated, driven away, or killed, but caught: such spiritual and deceitful little beasts must be watched and examined with every vigilance and caution, and thus caught—that is, apprehended—in their own cunning. Therefore, when deceit is exposed, fraud uncovered, and falsehood convicted, then the little fox that was destroying the vineyard is most rightly said to have been caught. Indeed, we say that someone is caught in speech, as in the Gospel: “The Pharisees assembled together in order to catch Jesus in speech” (Matt. 22:15).

7. Thus the Bridegroom commands the little foxes that destroy vineyards to be caught—that is, detected, convicted, exposed. This kind of malice alone has the property that, once recognized, it does no harm, so that to be recognized is for it to be defeated. For who but a madman knowingly and deliberately puts his foot in a trap once discovered? It is enough, then, if things of this sort are caught—that is, if you expose them and bring them into public view—for to appear is to perish for them. Other vices are not like this. They come openly and harm openly; they take people captive who know what they are doing, and overcome those who resist, because they act by force, not deceit.
