Therefore against beasts of this kind, openly raging, there is need not of investigation but of restraint. These little foxes alone—the greatest deceivers—need only be brought into the light and caught in their cunning, because once exposed they no longer harm. For they have dens. For this reason, then, these foxes are commanded to be caught and are described as little. Or they are called little so that you may watch for vices as they arise and catch them at once in their very beginning, while they are still little, lest, as they grow, they harm more and become harder to catch.

8. And if, according to allegory, we understand the vineyards as Churches and the foxes as heresies—or rather as heretics themselves—the sense is straightforward: heretics should be caught rather than allowed to escape. They should be caught, I say, not with weapons but with arguments, by which their errors may be refuted; and they themselves, if possible, reconciled to the Catholic Church and recalled to the true faith.

> **Note [Cols. 1085D–1088D].** Augustine writes likewise in Letter 100 to Donatus, proconsul of Africa, §1: “We desire that they” (the Donatists) “be corrected, not killed; nor do we wish discipline against them to be neglected, nor that they be subjected to the punishments they deserve. Therefore restrain their sins in such a way that there may remain persons who repent of having sinned,” etc. In Letters 133, 134, and 139 he urges the prefects Marcellinus and Apringius to punish heretics without capital punishment, mindful of Christian gentleness. But in Letter 43 to Vincentius he argues at length that fear and the rigor of laws may beneficially constrain heretics to the Catholic faith. He says that he had once held the view that no force should be used against heretics and that only preaching should be employed; but, led by others’ opinions and examples, he changed his view and held that the laws and arms of rulers might rightly be invoked against heretics, provided this was done with the intention of correcting them. For this purpose he uses a very apt comparison of a madman running headlong to destruction, upon whom laying hands and chains ought to be judged a benefit. He confirms this with the example of the Circumcellions, many of whom the Catholic Church already had among its members: “Yet,” he says in §2, “they would not be brought to this health unless they were bound like madmen by the chains of those laws which displease you” (Vincentius Rogatianus). Hence, after much else, he adds in §17: “Yielding, therefore, to these examples set before me by my colleagues, I gave way. For my original opinion was that no one ought to be compelled to the unity of Christ; that action should be by word, contest by disputation, and victory by reason, lest we should have feigned Catholics whom we had known as open heretics. But this opinion of mine was overcome not by the words of opponents, but by examples that demonstrated the contrary. For first my own city was set against me: although entirely in Donatus’s party, it was converted to Catholic unity through fear of the imperial laws; now we see it so detest the ruinous fierceness of your party that one would suppose it had never belonged to it,” etc. The same letter briefly gives the reason why force and fear ought to be employed in addition to teaching: “For if they were taught,” he says in §3, “but not frightened, hardened by the antiquity of custom they would move more sluggishly toward taking up the way of salvation.” Thus Augustine, from whose footsteps Bernard does not usually depart. Hence, in Sermon 66 on the Song of Songs, §12, Bernard says: “Faith must be persuaded, not imposed. Yet undoubtedly it would be better for them to be restrained by the sword—namely, that of him who does not bear the sword without cause—than to be permitted to pierce many with their own error.” From this appears an easy way to reconcile the differing opinions in this question: those whose conversion may easily be hoped for should be treated more gently and taught rather than compelled. But those who endeavor to spread the poison of unbelief among many should be restrained by the severity of laws. Compare Letter 365.

For this is the will of him “who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth” (1 Tim. 2:4). Indeed, he declares that this is his will when he says not simply, “Catch the foxes,” but “Catch for us the foxes.” Thus he commands that these foxes be gained for himself and for his Bride—that is, the Catholic Church—when he says, “Catch them for us.” Therefore, a trained and learned member of the Church, when he undertakes to dispute with a heretic, ought to direct his intention to this end: to convict the erring person in such a manner as also to convert him, remembering the saying of the apostle James: “He who causes a sinner to turn from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:20). But if he refuses to return and, after a first and second admonition, is not refuted, since he is altogether perverted, then according to the Apostle he must be avoided (Titus 3:10). From that point, in my judgment, it is better that he be made to flee, or even bound, than that he be allowed to destroy the vineyards.

> **Note [Col. 1088D].** What it means in Bernard for a heretic to be “bound” is clear from §1 of the following sermon, where a heretic is said to be “bound outside, once impiety has been condemned and the impious person cast out.”

9. Nor should one who has defeated and convicted a heretic, refuted heresies, clearly and openly distinguished things that seem true from what is true, shown by plain and irrefutable reasoning that perverse doctrines are perverse, and finally reduced into captivity the perverse understanding that exalts itself against the knowledge of God—nor should such a person think that he has done nothing. For he has nonetheless caught a fox by doing these things, even if not to that fox’s salvation; and he has caught it for the Bridegroom and the bride, though in another way. For although the heretic has not risen from the dregs, the Church is nevertheless confirmed in faith; and [Col. 1087C] the Bridegroom undoubtedly rejoices in the progress of the bride. “For the joy of the Lord is our strength” (2 Esdras [Nehemiah] 8:10). Finally, he does not regard our gains as alien from himself, who so graciously associates himself with us when he commands that foxes be caught, not for himself, but for us together with him: “Catch them for us,” he says. Notice, indeed, that he says “for us.” What could be more companionable than this word? Does it not seem to you that he speaks as [Col. 1088A] a certain head of a household who possesses nothing separately, but holds all things in common with his wife, children, and household servants? And it is God who speaks—yet he does not speak this as God, but as the Bridegroom.

10. “Catch the foxes for us.” Do you see how companionably he speaks, though he has no companion? He could have said, “For me”; but, delighting in fellowship, he preferred “for us.” O sweetness! O grace! O power of love! Has he who is the one supreme being over all become one with all? Who has done this? Love: ignorant of rank, rich in condescension, mighty in affection, effectual in persuasion. What is more forceful? Love triumphs over God. Yet what is less violent? It is love. What, I ask, is this power—so forceful in victory, so overcome by force? Finally, “he emptied himself” (Philippians 2:7), so that you may know that it was love’s doing that fullness was poured out, height made equal, singularity joined in fellowship. With whom, O wondrous Bridegroom, is this union so intimate for you? “Catch for us,” you say. With whom together with you? With the Church drawn from the Gentiles? She has been gathered from mortals and sinners. We know who she is. But who are you, so devoted and so eager a lover of this Ethiopian woman? Certainly not another Moses, but more than Moses (Numbers 12:1). Are you he who is “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men”? (Psalm 44 [45]:3). I have said too little: you are the brightness of eternal life, the splendor and image of God’s substance (Hebrews 1:3); finally, God over all, blessed for ever. Amen (Romans 9:5).

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE TWO FOLLOWING SERMONS

We have assigned the letter of Everwin, hitherto printed here among the sermons, [Col. 1088C] a more suitable place among the letters of various persons to Bernard. See *Works*, vol. I, col. 676. EDITORS.

## SERMON LXV

On clandestine heretics, whose perverted religion and practice of concealing their mysteries, as well as their scandalous cohabitation with women, he censures.

1. I have delivered to you two sermons on one chapter; [Col. 1089A] I am preparing a third [otherwise: “I am preparing to deliver it”], if you are not weary of hearing. And I judge it necessary. For, as regards our own domestic vineyard—that is, yourselves—I believe that in two sermons I have done enough to fortify it against the snares of the threefold kind of foxes: flatterers, detractors, and certain deceitful spirits, skilled and accustomed to introduce evils under the appearance of good. But it is not so with the Lord’s vineyard. I mean that vineyard which has filled the earth, of which we too are a portion: a vineyard exceedingly great, planted by the Lord’s hand, redeemed by blood, watered by the word, extended by grace, made fruitful by the Spirit. Thus, giving greater care to what was my own, I have helped the common good less.

But I am moved on its behalf by the multitude of those destroying it, the fewness of its defenders, and the difficulty [Col. 1089B] of its defense. Concealment creates the difficulty. For although the Church has always had foxes from its beginning, they were soon all discovered and caught. The heretic fought openly—for he was chiefly a heretic in that he desired to prevail openly—and he was overcome. Thus those foxes were easily caught. For what if, truth having been brought into the light, the heretic remained in the darkness of his obstinacy, alone, bound outside and withering away?

**[1488–1491]** Nevertheless, the fox was accounted caught when impiety had been condemned and the impious man cast outside: displayed, indeed, as one now to be conquered, not as one bearing fruit. From this, according to the prophet, they had “dry breasts and a barren womb” (Hosea 9:14), because an error publicly refuted does not sprout again, and exposed falsehood bears no new growth.

2. What shall we do with these most malignant foxes, so that they may be caught—who prefer to do harm rather than to conquer, and do not even wish to appear, but to creep? All heretics have always had one purpose: to seek glory from the singularity of their knowledge. This heresy alone, more malignant and more cunning than the rest, feeds upon the losses of others, careless of its own glory. Taught, I suppose, by the examples of earlier heresies—which, once exposed, could not escape but were immediately caught—it has cautiously undertaken, by a new kind of wickedness, to work the mystery of iniquity, all the more freely because more secretly. In short, they have, as it is said, prescribed hiding places for themselves; “they have strengthened for themselves an evil discourse.” Swear, forswear yourself—but do not reveal the secret.

Yet at other times they will by no means consent even to swear lightly, on account of the Gospel saying, “Do not swear, neither by [Col. 1089D] heaven nor by earth” (Matthew 5:34–35), and so forth. O foolish and slow of heart, wholly filled with the Pharisaic spirit: straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel! (Matthew 23:24). Is it unlawful to swear, but lawful to commit perjury? Or is it in this one matter that both are lawful? From what passage of the Gospels do you produce this exception for me—you who boast falsely that you pass over not even an iota? Clearly, you observe the prohibition of oaths superstitiously and arrogate to yourselves perjury wickedly. O perversity! What was prescribed as a safeguard—not to swear—they observe with such contentiousness as though it were a command; and what was established by an unchanging law—not to commit perjury—they dispense with at their pleasure as though it were indifferent.

“No,” they say, “but lest we make the mystery public.” As though it were not God’s glory to reveal the word. Or do they begrudge God his glory? Yet I think rather that they are ashamed to disclose it, knowing it to be dishonorable. For they are said to do abominable and obscene things in secret; indeed, the hindquarters of foxes stink.

[Col. 1090B] 3. But I pass over matters which they would deny; let them answer concerning what is manifest. Do they, according to the Gospel, take care not to give what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine? (Matthew 7:6). But to confess this openly is to confess that they are not of the Church, since they judge all who belong to the Church to be dogs and swine. For, without exception, they think that their own possession, whatever it is, must be withheld from all who are not of their sect. Yet even if they think this, they will not answer, lest they become known—which they avoid in every way, but will not escape.

Answer me, O man who are wise beyond what is fitting and foolish beyond what can be said. Is the mystery that you conceal God’s, or not? If it is, why do you not disclose it to his glory? For “the glory of God is to reveal the word.” If it is not, why do you place faith in something that is not God’s, unless because you are a heretic? Therefore either let them disclose God’s secret to God’s glory; or let them deny that it is God’s mystery, and cease altogether to deny that they are heretics; or at least confess themselves manifest enemies of God’s glory, since they do not wish that to be made manifest which they know will bring him glory.

For the truth of Scripture stands: “The glory of kings is to conceal a word; the glory of God is to reveal a discourse” (Proverbs 25:2).

> **Note [Col. 1089D].** St. Gregory the Great understood these words of Scripture in a similar sense, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, book 1, homily 6, opening. Yet today they are read in the Vulgate edition in a plainly contrary sense: “It is the glory of God to conceal a word, and the glory of kings to search out a matter.” Hence Cornelius a Lapide, on this passage, warns that there is a gross error in Gregory; and he corrects not only the words of Scripture but also Gregory’s words, altering them, unless I am mistaken, contrary to Gregory’s thought and purpose. For Gregory’s meaning there is that prophetic mysteries are indeed obscure; nevertheless, because it pertains to God’s glory to open the mysteries of his word, this task ought to engage us, and so forth. Bernard uses these words in precisely the same sense in this sermon [Col. 1090D]. We say this not in order to criticize the genuine reading, but to show how the Fathers read it, since their text frequently differs in many places from our Vulgate. Who would suppose that they ought to be corrected in every place according to the Vulgate norm? We note incidentally that Solomon’s saying, according to the Fathers’ reading, agrees admirably with that of the angel Raphael to the two Tobits: “For it is good to conceal the secret of a king; but it is honorable to reveal the works of God” (Tobit 12:7). Otherwise, let interpreters consider how this saying is to be reconciled with Solomon’s maxim. The Greek Septuagint supports the Vulgate.

Do you refuse to reveal it? Then you refuse to glorify God. But perhaps you do not accept this Scripture. So it is: they profess themselves imitators of the Gospel alone, and of the Gospel only. Let them answer, then, to the Gospel: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matthew 10:27). It is no longer permissible to be silent. How long will that be kept hidden which God commands to be made public? How long is your Gospel covered? I suspect that it is yours, not Paul’s; for he confesses that his Gospel is not covered. “But even if our Gospel is covered,” he says, “it is covered in those who [Col. 1091A] perish” (2 Corinthians 4:3). Take care lest he meant you, among whom the Gospel is found covered. What could be clearer than that you are perishing? Or perhaps you do not even accept Paul? I have heard this of some among you. For you do not all agree among yourselves in every point, although all of you disagree with us.

4. Yet the words, writings, and traditions of those who were bodily with the Savior are, I suppose, all received by you with equal and indiscriminate Gospel authority. Did they keep their Gospel concealed? Did they keep silent concerning the weakness of flesh in God, the horrors of death, the disgrace of the cross? Indeed, “their sound went forth into all the earth” (Psalm 18 [19]:5). Where is the apostolic pattern and life of which you boast? They cry aloud; you whisper. They are in public; you are in a corner. [Col. 1091B] They fly like clouds (Isaiah 60:8); you hide in darkness and underground houses. What like them do you show in yourselves?

Is it that you do not, to be sure, lead women about with you, but shut them in with you? Escorting a woman is not equally open to suspicion as cohabiting with her. Yet who would have suspected anything sinister of those men who raised the dead? Do the like, and I shall suppose that the woman reclining with you is a man. Otherwise, you rashly claim for yourselves their dispensation, though you do not possess their holiness. To be always with a woman and not to know a woman—is that not greater than raising a dead person? You cannot do the lesser thing, and do you wish me to believe you in the greater?

Every day your side is beside the side of a young woman at table; your bed beside hers in the chamber; your eyes beside [Col. 1091C] her eyes in conversation; your hands beside her hands at work—and do you wish to be thought continent? Let it be that you are so; I am nevertheless not free from suspicion. You are a scandal to me. Remove the cause of scandal, so that you may prove yourself a true imitator of the Gospel, as you boast. Does not the Gospel condemn anyone who scandalizes one member of the Church? You scandalize the Church. You are a fox destroying the vineyard.

Help me, companions, that it may be caught—or rather, catch it yourselves for us, O holy angels. It is very cunning, veiled in its iniquity and impiety. It is indeed so small and subtle that it easily eludes human sight. But does it elude yours as well? Therefore that voice is addressed to you, as companions of the Bridegroom: “Catch for us the little foxes” (Song of Songs 2:15). Therefore do what you are commanded: [Col. 1091D] catch for us this most shape-shifting little fox, which, behold, we have long pursued in vain. Teach and suggest how its deceit may be detected. For this is to catch the fox: a false Catholic does much more harm than if he appeared as a true heretic.

> **Note [Col. 1091D].** Some manuscripts have the simpler reading: “than a true heretic.” The early printed editions prefer our reading, together with other written copies.

But no human being can know what is in a human being, unless perhaps he has for this very purpose either been enlightened by God’s Spirit or instructed by angelic skill. What sign will you give, so that this most evil heresy may be publicly exposed—a heresy trained to lie not merely with its tongue but with its life?

5. Indeed, the recent devastation of the vineyard indicates that a fox has been there; but by some art of pretense this most cunning animal so confuses its tracks [Col. 1092A] that a person can scarcely discover where it enters or leaves. Although its work is evident, its author does not appear; thus it conceals everything through things visible on the surface. In short, if you ask about faith, nothing is more Christian; if about manner of life, nothing more blameless. And it proves by deeds what it speaks. You may see a man frequently attending church in testimony of his faith, honoring priests, presenting his offering, making confession, sharing in the sacraments. What could be more faithful? Then, as regards his life and conduct, he cheats no one, overreaches no one, plunders no one. His face is pale from fasting; he does not eat bread idly, but works with his hands to sustain his life. Where, then, is the fox? We held it: how [Col. 1092B] did it escape from our hands? How did it vanish so suddenly? Let us press on; let us investigate. We shall know it by its fruits. And certainly the devastation of vineyards attests a fox. Women, leaving their husbands, and likewise men, dismissing their wives, resort to these people. Clerics and priests, having abandoned congregations and churches, are found among them, unshorn and bearded, most often among weavers and women weavers.

**[1493]** Is this not a grave devastation? Are these not the works of foxes?

6. Yet perhaps such things are not found so manifestly among all of them; and, if they are, there is no means of proving them. How shall we catch them? Let us return to this association and cohabitation with women: among them there is no one without it. I question one of these persons: “Ho, good man! Who is this [Col. 1092C] woman, and whence has she come to you? Is she your wife?” “No,” he says, “for that does not accord with my vow.” “Then is she your daughter?” “No.” “What then? Is she neither your sister nor niece, nor related to you by any degree at least of kinship or affinity?” “Not at all.” “And how is your continence secure with this woman?” Certainly you are not permitted this. If you do not know, the Church forbids the cohabitation of men and women in those who have vowed continence.

> **Note [Col. 1092D].** Chapter *A nobis*, “On the Cohabitation of Clerics”; Council of Nicaea, canon 3; compare chapter *Interdixit*, distinction 37, etc.

If you do not wish to scandalize the Church, send the woman away. Otherwise, from this one point alone, the rest—which are not so manifest—become undoubtedly credible.

7. “But in what place of the Gospel,” he says, “do you show me that this is forbidden?” You appealed to the Gospel; to the Gospel you shall go. If you obey the Gospel, you will not cause scandal; [Col. 1092D] for the Gospel plainly forbids scandal to occur. But you cause it by not removing this woman according to the Church’s ordinance. You were suspected; now you will manifestly be judged both a despiser of the Gospel and an opponent of the Church.

What do you judge, brothers? If he is so obstinate that he neither obeys the Gospel nor acquiesces in the Church, what evasive maneuver can remain to him? Does not the fraud seem to you plainly exposed and the fox caught? If he does not remove the woman, he does not remove the scandal; if he does not remove the scandal when he can remove it, he is held guilty as a transgressor of the Gospel. What is the Church to do except remove the one who refuses [Col. 1093A] to remove the scandal, lest it become similarly disobedient? For it has this command in the Gospel: not to spare an eye that causes it to stumble, nor a hand, nor a foot; to pluck out the former, cut off the latter, and cast them away from itself. “If he will not hear the Church,” it says, “let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector” (Matthew 18:6–9, 17).

8. Have we accomplished anything? I think we have. We have caught the fox, because we have perceived the fraud. Those who lay hidden are exposed as false Catholics, true plunderers of the Catholic Church. For while you took sweet food with me—I mean the body and blood of Christ—while “we walked in the house of God with one accord,” there was room for persuasion, indeed an opportunity for seduction, according to the saying of Wisdom: “A dissembler with his mouth deceives his friend” (Proverbs 11:9).

But now, according to Paul’s wisdom, [Col. 1093B] after one [otherwise: “the first”] and a second admonition, I shall readily avoid a heretical man, knowing that one of this kind is subverted (Titus 3:10–11), and therefore taking care lest he now be a subverter of others as well. Thus it is no small thing, according to the word of the Wise Man, that “the wicked are caught in their own snares” (Proverbs 11:6)—especially those wicked men who shrewdly use snares as weapons. For all contest and defense have departed from these people. This is indeed a base and rustic kind, unlearned and wholly unwarlike. In short, they are foxes, and little ones; but neither are the things in which they are said to think wrongly defensible, nor are they so subtle as they are persuasive—and persuasive only to rustic and ignorant little women, and to such as, indeed, I have found all to be who thus far belong to this sect.

For I do not recall having heard in any of their assertions—for they are many—anything new or unheard of, but only what is worn and long debated among ancient heretics, and crushed and dispersed by our people. Yet I must state, and shall state, what these absurdities are: partly those which they themselves confessed when, in answering Catholics who questioned them, they replied too incautiously; partly those [1494] which, divided from one another and disputing against one another, they betrayed concerning one another; and partly those which some of them, returning to the Church, disclosed. I do not mean to answer all of them—for that is unnecessary—but only to make them known. That, however, will be the work of another sermon, to the praise and glory of the name of the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXVI

On the errors of heretics concerning marriage, the baptism of infants, purgatory, prayers for the dead, and the invocation of saints.

[Col. 1093D]

1. “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song of Songs 2:15). Behold, I turn to these foxes. They are those who pass beyond the way and harvest the vineyard. They are not content to abandon the way unless they can also lay waste the vineyard, adding transgression to transgression. [Col. 1094A] It is not enough for them to be heretics unless they are also hypocrites, so that sin may become exceeding sinful. These are those who come in sheep’s clothing in order to strip the sheep and despoil the rams. Does not each thing seem fulfilled to you where both the people have been robbed of their faith and the priests have been robbed from the people? Who are these robbers? They are sheep in appearance, foxes in cunning, wolves in deed and cruelty. They wish to seem good, not to be good; to be evil, not to seem evil. They are evil and wish to seem good, lest they alone be evil; they fear to seem evil, lest they be too little evil. For wickedness has always done less harm openly, and no good person has ever been deceived except by a simulation of goodness. Thus the good strive to appear good to the harm of the good; the evil do not wish to appear evil, in order that they may have greater freedom to act maliciously.

For their concern is not to cultivate virtues, [Col. 1094B] but to color vices with a kind of vermilion of virtues. They label the impiety of superstition with the name of religion. They define innocence as merely not doing harm openly, and thus claim for themselves only the appearance of innocence. As a covering for shamefulness, they distinguish themselves by a vow of continence. But they think that shamefulness is to be imputed only to wives, although a wife is the sole cause that excuses shamefulness in sexual intercourse. They are rustic and ignorant people, utterly contemptible; yet, I tell you, they must not be dealt with carelessly. For they make great progress toward impiety, and “their speech spreads like a cancer” (2 Timothy 2:16–17).

2. Indeed, the Holy Spirit did not overlook them, having long ago prophesied so plainly concerning them, when the Apostle said: “But the Spirit expressly says that in the last times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their own conscience seared, forbidding marriage, and abstaining from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:1–3). He spoke precisely of these people—precisely of them. These forbid marriage; these abstain from foods which God created, concerning whom we shall see later.

But now observe whether this is not properly the delusion of demons, not of men, as the Spirit foretold. Ask them for the founder of their sect: they will name no one. What heresy did not derive from human beings its own heresiarch? The Manichaeans had Mani as leader and teacher; the Sabellians, Sabellius; [Col. 1094D] the Arians, Arius; the Eunomians, Eunomius; the Nestorians, Nestorius. Thus all other such plagues are known to have had individual human teachers, from whom they derived at once their origin and their name. By what name or title will you designate these people? By none.

> **Note [Col. 1093D].** I do not know whether Bernard would have said this had these Cologne heretics possessed Henry, from whom the Henrician heretics took their name, as their founder. Although the doctrines of both groups were similar, as is clear by comparing Letter 240. Everwin notes two classes among the Cologne heretics, which Bernard distinguishes only obscurely at the end of Sermon 65.

For their heresy is not from a human being, nor did they receive it through a human being. Yet far be it from us to say that they received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ; rather, and without doubt, as the Holy Spirit foretold, through the sending [1495] and fraud of demons [Col. 1095A] “speaking lies in hypocrisy, forbidding marriage.”

3. They certainly speak in hypocrisy and with fox-like deceit, pretending that they say this out of love of chastity, whereas they devised it rather as a means of fostering and multiplying shamefulness. The matter is nevertheless so obvious that I wonder how it could ever have been persuaded to any Christian person—unless these people are either so brutish that they do not observe how one who condemns marriage gives free rein to every uncleanness, or else are so full of wickedness and swallowed up in diabolical malice that, observing it, they dissemble and rejoice in the destruction of human beings.

Take from the Church honorable marriage and the undefiled bed (Hebrews 13:4): do you not fill it with concubinaries, incestuous persons, those who spill seed, effeminate persons, men who lie with males, [Col. 1095B] and every kind of unclean person? Choose, therefore, which you prefer: either that all these monstrous people be saved, or that the number of the saved be reduced to the small number of the continent. How sparing in the one case! How lavish in the other! Neither suits the Savior. What then? Shall shamefulness be crowned? Nothing less befits the author of honor. Shall the whole human race be condemned except for a few continent people? That is not to be a Savior. Continence is rare on earth; and that fullness did not empty itself for so small a gain. And how have we all received from that fullness, if it granted participation in itself to the continent alone?

There is nothing they can answer to this. Nor, I think, to the other point. If honor has a place in heaven, and if the honorable and the shameful have no fellowship, just as light has no fellowship with darkness, then certainly no unclean person has a place remaining in the place of salvation. If anyone thinks otherwise, the apostolic voice will rebuke him, declaring without any ambiguity: “Those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5:21). By what route will this treacherous little fox now come out of its den? I think it has been caught in the pit in which it has made for itself, as it were, two openings—one by which it enters, the other by which it exits. For this is its custom. See, then, how its exit is blocked on both sides. If it places only the continent in heaven, salvation for the greater part perishes; if it places all filth together with the continent, honor perishes. But more justly it itself perishes, unable to go out either this way or that, shut up forever and caught in the pit it made.

[Col. 1095D] 4. Some, however, disagreeing with others, admit that marriage can be contracted only between virgins. But I do not see what reasoning they can offer in this distinction—unless it be that each one of them endeavors, according to his own whim, to tear apart the sacraments of the Church, as a mother’s entrails, with a viper’s tooth. For what they are said to allege concerning the first married couple, namely, that they were virgins—how, I ask, does this prejudice the freedom of marriage, so that it may not also be contracted by non-virgins?

But they whisper that they have found something in the Gospel which they vainly suppose supports their absurdity. I believe it is this: when the Lord had first set forth the testimony from Genesis, “God created man in his own image and likeness; male and female he created them,” he afterward added, [Col. 1096A] “Therefore, what God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Genesis 1:27; Matthew 19:4, 6). “God joined these,” they say, “because both were virgins, and it was thereafter not lawful for them to be separated; but a union presumed otherwise will not be from God.”

Who told you that they were joined by God because they were virgins? Scripture does not say this. “Were they not virgins?” you ask. They were; but it is not the same thing to say that virgins were joined, and that they were joined because they were virgins. Indeed, you will not find even this expressly stated, that they were virgins, although they were. The distinction of the sexes, certainly, is expressly given, not virginity, when it says: “Male and female he created them.” And rightly so. For the marital union does not require bodily intactness, but suitability of the sexes. Therefore, when the Holy Spirit instituted it, he fittingly [Col. 1096B] expressed sex and kept silence about virginity, giving no occasion to these treacherous little foxes to hunt for a word.

They would certainly have gladly done so, though even then in vain. For what if it had said, “He created them virgins”? Would you thereby immediately have established that only virgins may be joined in marriage? Yet how you would have exulted at the mere occasion of a word! How you would have blown away second and third marriages! How you would have mocked the Catholic Church, which joins prostitutes and procurers together all the more readily because it does not doubt that they thereby pass from shamefulness to honor! Perhaps you would even have reproached God for commanding the prophet to take a prostitute as wife (Hosea 1:2). But now both the occasion is lacking and you choose to be a heretic gratuitously. For the testimony you appropriated to establish [Col. 1096C] your error has been found to have greater force to destroy it: it does nothing for you and much against you.

5. Now hear what either utterly confounds or corrects you, and altogether crushes and pulverizes your heresy. “A woman is bound to her husband as long as he lives; but if her husband falls asleep, she is released from the law of her husband; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). It is Paul who permits the widow to marry whom she wishes; while you command the contrary: “No woman except a virgin shall marry, and only a virgin,” so that not even she may marry whom she wishes. Why do you shorten God’s hand? Why do you restrict the lavish blessing of marriage? Why do you claim as peculiar to virginity what has been granted to the sex? Paul would not grant this unless it were lawful. But I say too little: he grants it and wills it. “I will,” he says, [Col. 1096D] “that the younger women marry” (1 Timothy 5:14); and there is no doubt that he means widows. What could be clearer? Therefore, he grants it because it is lawful; he also wills it because it is expedient. Does a heretic forbid what is lawful and expedient? He will prove nothing by this prohibition except that he is a heretic.

6. It remains for us to attack these people somewhat concerning the remainder of the apostolic prophecy. For, as he foretold, they abstain from foods “which God created to be received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:3), thus proving themselves heretics—not, certainly, because they abstain, but because they abstain heretically. For I too sometimes abstain; but my abstinence is satisfaction for sins, not superstition for impiety. Do we reprove Paul because he chastises his body and reduces it to slavery? (1 Corinthians 9:27). I shall abstain [Col. 1097A] from wine, because “in wine is excess” (Ephesians 5:18); or, if I am weak, I shall use a little, according to Paul’s counsel (1 Timothy 5:23). I shall abstain from meat, lest, while it nourishes the flesh too greatly, it nourish also the vices of the flesh. I shall endeavor to take even bread in measure, lest, with my stomach overloaded, I grow weary of standing for prayer, and lest the prophet reproach me too, because I have eaten my bread to fullness (Ezekiel 16:49). But I shall not accustom myself even to gorge on plain water, lest distension of the belly extend even to the arousal of lust.

The heretic acts otherwise. He abhors milk and everything made from it; in short, everything generated by sexual intercourse. This would be right and Christian if it were not because it comes from intercourse, but lest such things provoke intercourse.

7. But what does it mean that everything generated by intercourse is avoided so universally? This observance of foods, so emphatically stated, creates suspicion in me. Yet if you offer this to us as a medical rule, we do not condemn care for the flesh, which no one ever hated, provided it is not excessive. If it comes from the discipline of those who abstain—that is, the school of spiritual physicians—we approve also the virtue by which you subdue the flesh and restrain lust. But if, out of the madness of Mani,

> **Note [Col. 1097C].** All, or nearly all, the heretics of those times were crazed by Manichaean delusions, as was stated in the General Preface. It is therefore not surprising that they so strongly rejected the truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, since they denied that Christ had a true body.

you prescribe terms to God’s beneficence, so that what he created and gave to be received with thanksgiving you, not merely ungrateful but also a rash judge, declare unclean and abstain from as though it were evil—I shall certainly not praise your abstinence, but shall detest your blasphemy. I shall call you more unclean, because [Col. 1097C] you regard something as unclean. “All things are clean to the clean,” says the best judge of things; “and nothing is unclean except to the one who judges something unclean. But to the unclean and unbelieving nothing is clean, but their mind and conscience are defiled” (Titus 1:15).

Woe to you who reject foods which God created, judging unclean and unworthy to pass into your bodies the foods which God created—when, for this very reason, the body of Christ, which is the Church, will spew you out as polluted and unclean.

8. I am not ignorant that they boast that they alone are the body of Christ; but let those persuade themselves of this who are also persuaded [Col. 1098A] that they have power daily at their table to consecrate Christ’s body and blood,

> **Note [Col. 1097D].** In this passage Bernard may perhaps seem to some to deny heretics the power to consecrate. This approaches the heterodox opinion whose advocates were the Donatists, who said that sacraments were polluted by evil ministers and that their effect was impeded, teaching that whatever had been performed by such persons, especially heretics, was thereby defiled and had to be repeated. St. Augustine strongly refutes this error in various places, citing against them the ancient practice of the Church of not repeating the baptism of heretics, together with clear arguments and testimonies of Holy Scripture. Thus this canon, Session 7, canon 12, of the Council of Trent was rightly issued against that error: “If anyone shall say that a minister in mortal sin, provided that he observes all the essentials pertaining to the making or conferring of the sacrament, [Col. 1098C] does not make or confer the sacrament, let him be anathema.”

> “Since the teaching of this canon,” says Estius, in book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 1, part 25, “is general, it must be understood generally concerning any minister in any mortal sin, whether secretly evil or openly so; whether still Catholic or heretical, or whatever his condition.”

> Hence, in the following paragraph he answers this objection from Bernard as follows: “Bernard,” he says, “speaks of those who, while calling themselves apostolic and declaring themselves successors of the Apostles, had nevertheless not been sent or ordained by the true successors of the Apostles, and were therefore not true priests.” And it is certainly evident from what follows how far the holy Doctor was from this error, where he attacks the heretics for maintaining that sinners were fit neither to administer nor receive the sacraments. No difficulty at all remains in this passage when it is compared with Everwin’s preceding letter, which says that these heretics held the error that “every chosen person (as they say, every one baptized among them) has the power to consecrate Christ’s body and blood.” Bernard rightly rejects this.

in order to nourish themselves into Christ’s body and members. They boast, indeed, that they are successors of the apostles and call themselves apostolic, yet are unable to show any sign of their apostolate. How long shall the lamp be under a bushel? “You are the light of the world,” was said to the apostles; and therefore the apostles are set upon the lampstand, that they may shine upon the whole world. Let successors of the apostles be ashamed not to be the light of the world, but of the bushel—and instead to be the darkness of the world. Let us say to them, “You are the darkness of the world,” and pass to other matters.

They call themselves the Church. But they contradict him who says, “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:14–16). Do you really believe that the stone cut from the mountain without hands, made into a mountain [Col. 1098B] and filling the world (Daniel 2:34–35), is enclosed in your caves? Nor need we dwell on this point either. Their very opinion shrinks from being made public, content with its own whispering. Christ has and always will have his whole inheritance and his possession to the ends of the earth. Rather, those withdraw themselves from this great inheritance who endeavor to take it away from Christ.

9. Look upon the detractors; look upon the dogs. They mock us because we baptize infants, pray for the dead, and seek the intercessions of the saints. Among every class of persons and both sexes they hasten to outlaw Christ—in adults and little children, in the living and the dead: denying him, on the one hand, to infants because of nature’s incapacity, and on the other to adults because of the difficulty of continence [Col. 1098C]. Moreover, they defraud the dead of the help of the living, and likewise strip the living of the intercessions of the saints who have departed. Far be it! The Lord will not abandon his people, who are like the sand of the sea; nor will he be content that those heretics, whom he redeemed all, should be few. For with him redemption is not scanty but truly abundant. Yet what is the number of these people in comparison with the greatness of the price? Rather, they deprive themselves of that price, who endeavor to make it void.

For what if an infant cannot speak for himself, when for him the blood of his brother—and of such a brother—cries to God from the earth [Col. 1099A]? Mother Church too stands by and cries out. Yet what of the infant? Does he not himself seem to you in some manner to long after the fountains of the Savior, to cry aloud to God—

> [Note: [Col. 1099D] Some manuscripts, together with the earliest editions, omit *to long after* (*hiniare*) and read: “to you, in some manner, to cry aloud to God from the fountains of the Savior.”]

—and by his cries to call out: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me” (Isa. 38:14). He demands the help of grace because he suffers violence from nature [variant: from origin; variant: from sin]. The innocence of the wretched one cries out; the ignorance of the little child cries out; the weakness of one held captive cries out. Thus all these cry out: the blood of the brother, the faith of the mother, the destitution of the wretched one, and the misery of the destitute; and the cry is made to the Father. Now the Father cannot deny himself, for he is a father.

10. Let no one tell me that one to whom his mother imparts her own faith has no faith, enfolding him in the sacrament until he becomes capable of receiving it unfolded and pure by his own—not only understanding, [Col. 1099B] but assent as well. Is the cloak too small to cover both? Great is the faith of the Church. Is it less than the faith of the Canaanite woman, which plainly could suffice both for her daughter and for herself? Therefore she heard: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you have asked” (Matt. 15:28). Is it less than the faith of those who, lowering the paralytic through the tiles, obtained for him salvation both of soul and body? Indeed, you have: “When he saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you’”; and shortly afterwards: “Take up your bed and walk” (Matt. 9:2, 5, 6).

Whoever believes these things will readily be persuaded that the Church is right to presume, on the basis of her faith, salvation not only for baptized little children, but also the crown of martyrdom for infants killed for Christ [Col. 1099C]. Since this is so, those reborn will suffer no prejudice from the saying, “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6), since those who received the grace of baptism as a testimony of faith are not without faith. Nor is there any prejudice from the other saying: “But whoever does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16:16). For what is believing except having faith?

Thus the woman also shall be saved through childbearing, if she continues in faith with gentleness—

> [Note: [Col. 1099D] Variant reading at this place. The Gembloux manuscript has, with the Vulgate: “in faith and love with sanctification and sobriety”; the Colbert manuscript: “in faith with sobriety”; Saint-Germain prefers our reading, together with the earliest editions.]

—(1 Tim. 2:15); infants will be helped through the washing of regeneration; adults who cannot maintain continence will redeem themselves by the thirtyfold fruit of marriage; and the dead who need it and are worthy will receive, through angels acting as intermediaries, the prayers and offerings of the living [Col. 1099D]. Nor will those still living lack the consolations, through God who is everywhere and, in God, is nowhere absent in the affection of love from those who have departed. For Christ died and rose again for this purpose: that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead (Rom. 14:9). For this purpose too an infant was born, and advanced through every stage of life into manhood, so that no age might lack him.

[Col. 1100A] 11. They do not believe that a purifying fire remains after death, but hold that a soul released from the body immediately passes either to rest or to condemnation. Let them therefore ask him who said that there is a certain sin which will be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matt. 12:32), why he said this, if no remission or purification of sin remains in the future.

Furthermore, since they do not acknowledge the Church, it is no wonder that they disparage the Church’s orders, reject its institutions, despise its sacraments, and disobey its commands. “Apostolic men,” they say, “archbishops, bishops, and presbyters are sinners; and therefore they are fit neither to administer nor to receive sacraments. Can these two things ever coexist: to be a bishop and a sinner?” That is false. Caiaphas was a bishop, and yet [Col. 1100B] what a great sinner he was, who pronounced a sentence of death against the Lord. If you deny that he was a bishop, John’s testimony will refute you; John reports that, in testimony to his high-priestly office, he even prophesied (John 11:51).

Judas was an apostle; and although greedy and wicked, he was nevertheless chosen by the Lord. Do you doubt the apostolate of one whom the Lord chose? “Did I not,” he says, “choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:71). You hear that the same man was chosen as an apostle and became a devil; yet you deny that one who is a sinner can be a bishop? The scribes and Pharisees sat in Moses’ seat, and those who did not obey them as bishops were guilty of disobedience even against the Lord himself, who commanded and said: “Do what they say” (Matt. 23:2–3). It is therefore clear that, although [Col. 1100C] they were scribes, although Pharisees, although indeed the greatest sinners, still, because of Moses’ seat, the other saying likewise applied to them: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

12. Many other evils have indeed been persuaded upon this foolish and senseless people by spirits of error, speaking lies in hypocrisy; but there is no need to answer everything. For who knows everything? Besides, the labor would be endless and entirely unnecessary. As for these people, they are not convinced by arguments, because they do not understand; they are not corrected by authorities, because they do not accept them; nor are they moved by persuasion, because they are perverted. It has been proved: they choose rather to die than [Col. 1100D] to be converted. Their end is destruction; fire awaits them at last. Indeed, a figure of them was prefigured in the deed of Samson with the tails of the foxes set ablaze (Judg. 15:4–5).

Often the faithful, laying hands upon them, dragged some of them into public. When asked concerning the faith, they altogether denied, in their customary manner, all the matters of which they seemed suspect; when tested by the judgment of water, they were found to be liars.

> [Note: [Col. 1100D] Various ordeals were formerly used as testimony to innocence or for clearing alleged crimes: for example, by the sacred Eucharist, fire, hot iron, cold water, boiling water, single combat, and so forth. But all were prohibited and condemned by canons, councils, and decrees of the popes. Yet there were some who maintained that this ordeal mentioned here by Bernard—namely, the water ordeal—ought to be approved; indeed, some relied for this opinion on Bernard’s authority itself, and specifically on the present passage. Delrio, however, shows that they interpret Bernard’s words wrongly, *Disquisitiones Magicae*, book IV, chapter 4, question 5, section 2. Bernard does not approve it as something rightly and lawfully done; he reports what was commonly practiced, at a time when this method of examination or proof still prevailed in cases of heresy, while magistrates overlooked it and were insufficiently inclined to observe the canons. Thus far Horstius. Mabillon adds: The ancients do not so disapprove the water ordeal that Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, did not approve it in a special letter to Hildegarius of Meaux. The form of this test appears in volume I of our *Analecta*, where it is said to have been instituted by Eugenius II. [Col. 1101D]]

And when they could no longer deny it, since they had been detected and the water did not receive them, they took, as the saying goes, the bit in their teeth, and, as wretchedly as freely, did not confess their impiety but professed it—openly asserting their piety and ready to undergo death for it [Col. 1101A]. Nor were those standing by less ready to inflict death. Thus the populace rushed upon them and gave the heretics new martyrs of their own perfidy. We approve the zeal, but do not commend the deed, because faith is to be persuaded, not imposed. Yet undoubtedly it is better that they be restrained by the sword—namely, by the sword of him who does not bear it without cause—than that they be permitted to draw many into their error.

> [Note: [Col. 1101D] Bernard is in no way inconsistent with himself in the preceding Sermon 64, section 8, where he says that heretics should be seized “not by arms, but by arguments”—that is, if they keep to themselves and do not endeavor to subvert others. Otherwise, “they are undoubtedly better restrained by the sword than permitted to draw many into their error,” as in this passage. [Col. 1102D]]

For he is God’s minister, an avenger to execute wrath on the one who does evil (Rom. 13:4).

13. Some wonder that they were led to death not merely patiently but even, as it seemed, joyfully. But these do not sufficiently consider how great is the devil’s power, not only over human bodies but also over hearts which, once he has been allowed to enter, he possesses. Is it not a greater thing for a person to lay hands upon himself than willingly to suffer it at another’s hands? Yet we have frequently experienced the devil’s ability to do this in many who drowned or hanged themselves. Judas, indeed, hanged himself (Matt. 27:5), undoubtedly at the devil’s instigation. Yet I consider it a greater and more astonishing thing that the devil could put it into his heart to betray the Lord (John 13:2) than that he could make him hang himself.

Therefore the constancy of martyrs and the obstinacy of these people have nothing alike; for in the former contempt of death is wrought by piety, in the latter by hardness of heart.

> [Note: [Col. 1102D] Augustine expresses a similar judgment in book I of the unfinished work against Julian, and in *On Patience*, chapter 17; and from him Canon 17 of the Second Council of Orange: “Worldly desire produces the courage of the Gentiles; the love of God produces the courage of Christians.”]

And so perhaps the Prophet spoke in the person of a martyr [Col. 1101C]: “Their heart has congealed like milk, but I have meditated on your law” (Ps. 113:70), because, although the punishment seemed the same, the intention was very different: in the one case the heart endured against the Lord; in the other, the person meditated upon the law of the Lord.

14. Since this is so, there is no need, as I have said, to speak at length in vain against people most foolish and obstinate. It is enough that they have been made known in order that they may be avoided. Therefore, that they may be detected, they must be compelled either to dismiss their women or to leave the Church, since they scandalize the Church by living and lodging with women. It is deeply regrettable that not only lay princes but also, it is said, certain members of the clergy, and even members of the episcopal order—who ought rather to have persecuted them—tolerate them for profit, accepting gifts from them.

> [Note: [Col. 1102D] I do not know whether Henry, bishop of Toul, was among their number. In an unpublished letter to him, Hugh Metellus says that there are hidden in his diocese “pestilential men who detest marriage, abominate baptism, and mock the sacraments of the Church.”]

“But how,” they say, “shall we condemn persons neither convicted nor confessing?” This is sufficiently frivolous—not a reason, but an excuse. By this fact alone, even if there were nothing else, you can readily detect them: as I have said, separate from one another the men and women who say that they are continent; compel the women to live with others of their own sex and vow, and the men likewise with men of the same purpose. For in this way provision will be made both for the vow and the reputation of each group, since they will have both witnesses and guardians of their continence. But if they cannot endure this, they will most justly be expelled from the Church which they scandalize by a cohabitation not merely conspicuous but unlawful. Let these points therefore suffice for uncovering the wiles of these foxes, so as to give knowledge and caution to the beloved [Col. 1102B] and glorious bride of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ages. Amen.

1500

## SERMON LXVII

On the bride’s marvelous affection of love, which she pours forth because of her love for Christ the bridegroom.

1. “My beloved is for me, and I for him” (Song 2:16). Thus far are the bridegroom’s words. May he himself be present, so that we may worthily investigate the bride’s sayings for his glory and for our own salvation. For they are not such as we can examine and discuss as is fitting unless he himself is the guide of the word. They are as sweet in grace as they are fruitful in meanings, and as profound in mysteries. To what shall I compare them? For the moment, to some one banquet distinguished by a threefold excellence: delightful to the taste, substantial for nourishment, effective for healing. Thus, I say, every utterance of the bride both soothes the affection by its sweet sound, enriches and nourishes the mind by the abundance of its meanings, and, from the height of its mysteries, wondrously heals the swelling of puffed-up knowledge by making the understanding, the more it is exercised, the more afraid.

For if someone among those who perhaps think themselves wise applies himself too curiously to searching these matters, when he sees the powers of his intellect fail and perceives that every understanding is reduced to captivity, will he not be humbled and compelled to say with that voice: “Your knowledge has become wonderful beyond me; it has grown strong, and I cannot attain it” (Ps. 138:6)? [Col. 1103A] And now, what a mark of sweetness does the beginning of her words bear! Consider what a beginning she has given: “My beloved,” she says, “is for me, and I for him.” The expression seems simple because it sounds sweet; but this will be considered later.

2. But now she begins from love and continues concerning the beloved, indicating that she knows nothing other than the beloved. It is clear of whom she speaks; with whom, not so clear. For she is not permitted to feel as though she were with him himself, since he is no longer present. Nor is this doubtful: for she seems immediately to call him back and, as it were, cry after him, “Return, my beloved.” Hence we are led to infer nothing other than that, after finishing his words, he once more withdrew in his customary way, while she nevertheless remained speaking of him who is never absent from her. So it is: she retained upon her lips the one who did not depart from her heart, even when he departed. What comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and “from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45).

Therefore she speaks of the beloved, as one truly beloved and truly worthy of love, because she loves greatly. We ask with whom she speaks, for we know of whom. No answer occurs, unless perhaps it is with the young maidens, who cannot leave their mother when the bridegroom has departed. But, I think, we judge better that she spoke thus with herself rather than with another, especially because her expression is found truncated and incoherent, altogether insufficient to communicate understanding to a hearer—the very purpose for which we speak with one another. “My beloved is for me,” she says, “and I for him.” No more? The sentence hangs; indeed, it does not hang but fails. The hearer is held in suspense—not instructed, but lifted up.

[Col. 1103C] 3. What is this that she says: “He for me, and I for him”? We do not know what she says because we do not feel what she feels. O holy soul, what is that one to you, and what are you to him? What, I ask, is this exchange, passing so familiarly and graciously between you: he to you, and you in turn to him? But what? Are you to him the very thing that he is to you, or something else? If you are speaking to us, for our understanding, plainly declare what you feel. “How long will you take away our souls?” Or, according to the prophet, “Is your secret for yourself?” (Isa. 24:16).

So it is: affection spoke, not understanding, and therefore it was not spoken for understanding. For what, then? For nothing other than this: wonderfully delighted and intensely moved by the beloved’s desired utterances, when he ended, she could neither remain altogether silent [Col. 1103D] nor express what she felt. She did not speak in order to express it, but in order not to be silent. Her mouth spoke from the abundance of her heart, though not in proportion to that abundance. Affections have their own voices by which they betray themselves even when they do not wish to: fear, for example, anxious ones; grief, groaning ones; love, joyful ones.

Do custom create, reason call forth, deliberation arrange, or premeditation form the lamentations of the sorrowful, the sobbing or groaning of the mournful, the sudden and wild cries of those struck or terrified, or even the belchings of the sated? Such things certainly do not proceed at the mind’s command, but burst forth by an impulse. Thus burning and vehement love, especially divine love, when it cannot contain itself within, takes no care what order, rule, sequence, or brevity of words it uses in boiling over, provided it feels no loss of itself thereby. At times it requires no words; at times no sounds at all, being content for this purpose with sighs alone. Hence the bride, burning with holy love, and that in an incredible manner, in order to gain some little vent for the ardor she suffers, does not consider what or how she speaks; but whatever comes into her mouth, under the pressure of love, she does not utter but belches forth. Why should she not belch, being so refreshed and so filled?

4. Review the text of this epithalamium from its very beginning down to this point, and see whether, in all the bridegroom’s visits and speeches, such abundance as she receives this time was ever granted her; and whether she ever received from his mouth not merely so many but such delightful words. Therefore, since he had filled her desire with good things, what wonder if she produced a belch rather than speech? And if you think she produced speech, regard it as belched forth, not contrived [variant, wrongly: “subordinated”] or prearranged. For the bride does not think it robbery to appropriate the prophet’s saying, “My heart has poured forth a word” (Ps. 44:2), since she is filled with the same Spirit. “My beloved is for me, and I for him.” It has no sequence; something is lacking from the sentence. What then? It is a belch. Why do you seek the connections of sentences and the formalities of diction in a belch? What laws or rules do you impose upon your own belch? It does not accept your restraint, await composition from you, seek appropriateness, or require timeliness. Of itself it bursts from the depths, not only when you do not wish it, but when you do not know it—torn forth rather than sent out [Col. 1104C].

Yet a belch carries an odor: sometimes good, sometimes bad, according to the opposed qualities of the vessels from which it rises. Thus “a good person brings forth good from a good treasure, and an evil person evil” (Matt. 12:35). The bride of my Lord is a good vessel, and her odor is good to me.

5. I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus, because you have deemed me worthy at least to smell it. Yes, Lord, for “even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table” (Matt. 15:27). I confess: the belch of your beloved smells sweetly to me, and from her fullness I gratefully receive, even though it be only a little. She pours forth to me the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness; and in that saying, “My beloved is for me, and I for him,” I have smelled something ineffable of your condescension and love [Col. 1104D].

Let her, as is fitting, feast and rejoice in your presence, and delight in gladness; yet let her so go beyond herself toward you that she remains sober for us. Let her therefore be filled with the good things of your house and drink from the torrent of your delight; but, I beg, when she has been filled, let even a faint fragrance reach me in my poverty as she pours forth her belch. Moses poured forth sweetly for me, and in his belch is the good fragrance of creative power: “In the beginning,” he says, “God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). Isaiah likewise: he gave the most sweet fragrance of redeeming mercy when he thus poured forth: “He delivered his soul to death, and was numbered with the wicked; and he bore the sins of many, and prayed for transgressors” (Isa. 53:12), so that they might not perish. What smells equally of mercy?

There is also a good belch from Jeremiah, and a good one from David, who says: “My heart has poured forth a good word.” All were filled with the Holy Spirit, and in pouring forth they filled all things with goodness. Do you ask for Jeremiah’s belch? I have not forgotten; I was just preparing it: “It is good to await in silence the salvation of the Lord” (Lam. 3:26). It is his, if I am not mistaken. Apply it to your nostrils: the sweetness of the justice that rewards, which it conveys, surpasses balsam. He wishes me patiently to await the reward of righteousness in the future and not receive it in the present, because the reward of righteousness—salvation—is not of this world but of the Lord. “If he delays,” he says, “wait for him” (Hab. 2:3); and do not murmur, because it is good to wait in silence. Therefore I shall do what he urges: I shall wait for the Lord, my Savior.

[Col. 1105B] 6. But I am a sinner, and a great journey still remains for me, because salvation is far from sinners. Nevertheless I shall not murmur; meanwhile I shall console myself in the fragrance.

> [Note: [Col. 1105] Horstius adds “or pain,” but it is absent from the manuscripts and earliest editions.]

“The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord,” experiencing by taste what I perceive by smell. What the righteous person beholds, the sinner awaits; and awaiting is smelling. For “the expectation of the creation awaits the revelation of the children of God” (Rom. 8:19). To behold, moreover, is to taste and see that the Lord is sweet. Or rather, is the righteous person who awaits and already possesses blessed? Indeed, “the expectation of the righteous is joy” (Prov. 10:28). For the sinner awaits nothing. And he is a sinner precisely because, held fast by present goods and even content with them, he expects nothing for the future, deaf to that voice: “Wait for me,” says the Lord, “for the day of my resurrection in the future” (Zeph. 3:8).

And thus Simeon was righteous because he awaited and already smelled Christ in the Spirit, though he had not yet adored him in the flesh. He was blessed in his expectation because, through the fragrance of expectation, he came to the taste of contemplation. Thus he says: “My eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:25). Abraham too was righteous: he also waited to see the Lord’s day and was not disappointed in his expectation, for he saw and rejoiced (John 8:56). The apostles were righteous when they heard: “And you, be like people awaiting their master” (Luke 12:36, 30).

7. Why should David not also be righteous when he said: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord” (Ps. 39:2)? He is the fourth among my aforementioned pourers-forth, whom I had nearly passed over. That would not do. He “opened his mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118:131), and, filled, he not only poured forth but also sang. Good Jesus! How great a sweetness he poured into my nostrils and ears, in his outpouring and song, from the oil of gladness with which God, your God, anointed you above your companions; from myrrh, stacte, and cassia, from your garments, from ivory palaces, out of which the daughters of kings delighted you in your honor! (Ps. 44:8–10).

Would that you might deem me worthy, on the day of solemnity and gladness, to meet so great a prophet and your friend when he comes forth from your bridal chamber, singing his epithalamium on the sweet psaltery with the harp, abounding in delights [Col. 1106A], sprinkled with and sprinkling all things with such perfumed powder! On that day—or rather, in that hour: for it is an hour, if ever there is one; perhaps not even an hour, but half an hour, according to the Scripture: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8:1)—in that hour my mouth will be filled with joy and my tongue with exultation, when I perceive each, not merely of the psalms, but of the individual verses, to be an outpouring, and fragrant above every spice.

What is more fragrant than John’s outpouring, which smells to me of the eternity, generation, and divinity of the Word? What shall I say of Paul’s outpourings, with what sweetness they filled the world? Indeed, Christ’s good fragrance was in every place (2 Cor. 2:14–15). Though he does not utter the ineffable words for me to hear, he nevertheless offers them for me to desire, so that I may delight to smell what I am not permitted to hear (2 Cor. 12:4). For I do not know how it is that the more they are hidden, the more they please, and we long more eagerly for what is denied. But now observe a similar thing in the bride: how, in the present chapter, like Paul, she neither discloses the secret nor passes it over untouched, granting something, as it were, to our sense of smell which she may judge not yet suitable for our taste, whether because of our unworthiness or our incapacity.

8. “My beloved is for me, and I for him.” There is no doubt that the mutual love of two persons burns in this passage; but in that love the one’s happiness is supreme, the other’s condescension wondrous. For this agreement or embrace is not between equals. But what she glories to have bestowed upon her, by this privilege of love, and to have repaid in return [Col. 1106C]—who would presume clearly to know it unless, by a special purity of mind and holiness of body, he had deserved to experience something like it in himself? The matter belongs to the affections; it is not reached by reasoning but by conformity. How few are they who can say: “We all, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18).

9. But in order that what is read may be reduced to some kind of intelligible form—while preserving the bride’s own singular secret, to which for now access is not granted, especially to people such as we are—we should add something for ourselves, the more fitting to common understanding because more familiar, and which gives both sequence to the words and meaning to the little ones. It seems to me sufficient for our coarse and somewhat popular understanding if, in saying, “My beloved is for me,” we understand: “He attends,” so that the sense is: “My beloved attends to me, and I to him.”

Nor am I alone or the first to understand it so, since before me the Prophet said: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he attended to me.” You have plainly the Lord’s attention to the Prophet; and you also have the Prophet’s attention to the Lord in his saying, “Waiting, I waited.” For one who waits attends, and to wait is to attend. The Prophet and the bride express precisely the same sense, almost the same words; but the Prophet reverses them [Col. 1107A]. For he puts first what she puts later, and conversely.

10. Yet the bride spoke more correctly: she does not put forward merit, but first sets forth the benefit, confessing that she has been anticipated by the grace of her beloved. Entirely rightly. For “who has first given to him, and shall be repaid?” (Rom. 11:35). Listen also to what John thought concerning this in his Epistle: “In this is love,” he says, “not as though we had loved God, but that he first loved us” (1 John 4:10).

The Prophet, however, though he did not state the prevenience of grace, did not deny its following action; indeed, he did not leave it unstated. Receive, in another passage, his clearer confession on this matter: “And your mercy,” he says—addressing the Lord—“shall follow me all the days of my life” (Ps. 22:6). Hear likewise his no less certain and explicit knowledge of its prevenience: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58:11); and again, addressed to the Lord: “Let your mercies quickly come before us, for we have become exceedingly poor” (Ps. 78:8).

The bride later, I think, fittingly puts these same words in a different order, but she too follows the Prophet’s order, speaking thus: “I am for my beloved, and my beloved is for me.” Why so? Surely in order to show herself then more full of grace, when she ascribes everything to grace, assigning to it both the first part and the last. Otherwise, how could she be full of grace if she had anything not from grace? Grace has no place to enter where merit has already taken possession.

> [Note: [Col. 1107] Namely, “anything not from grace,” above; “that excludes grace,” below. Compare the following sermon, section 6; and Augustine, Letter 105; *On Grace and Free Will*, chapters 6–8; *Confessions*, book IX, chapter 13; *Enchiridion*, chapter 107; *Expositions on Psalms* 68 and 118, sermon 2, and Psalm 149. [Col. 1108D]]

Thus the full confession of grace signifies the fullness of grace itself in the soul that confesses it [Col. 1107C]. For if anything of one’s own is present, grace must give way to it to that extent. Whatever you attribute to merits is lacking to grace. I do not want a merit that excludes grace. I shrink from whatever is my own, lest I be my own—except perhaps that is more truly mine which makes me my own. Grace restores me to myself, freely justified, and thus freed from the slavery of sin. For where the Spirit is, there is freedom.

11. O foolish Synagogue-bride, who, despising the righteousness of God—that is, the grace of her bridegroom—and wishing to establish her own, was not subject to the righteousness of God! Therefore, unhappy woman, she was repudiated and is now no longer the bride, but the Church to whom it is said: “I have betrothed you to myself in faith; I have betrothed you to myself in judgment and righteousness; I have betrothed you to myself in mercy and compassions” [Col. 1107D] (Hos. 2:19–20). “You did not choose me, but I chose you”; nor, in choosing you, did I find your merits, but I went before you. Thus I have betrothed you to myself in faith, not in works of the law; and I have betrothed you in righteousness, but in the righteousness which is from faith, not from law.

It remains for you to judge a right judgment between me and you—the judgment in which I betrothed you to myself, where it is evident that not your merit but my good pleasure intervened. This judgment is that you do not exalt your merits, do not prefer works of the law, do not boast of the burden of the day and heat, since you are known to have been betrothed rather [Col. 1108A] in faith and in the righteousness which is from faith, and likewise in mercy and compassions.

12. She who is truly the bride recognizes these things and confesses both graces: first, the grace which comes first and by which she was anticipated; afterward, the grace that follows. Therefore she now says: “My beloved is for me, and I for him,” assigning the beginning to her beloved. In what follows, she says: “I am for my beloved, and my beloved is for me,” likewise yielding the consummation to him.

Now let us see what she means by “My beloved is for me.” For if we accept that we should understand “he attends,” as we have said, and as the Prophet says, “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he attended to me,” I perceive in this word something not at all slight, something of no ordinary privilege. But a matter worthy of every eagerness should not be forced upon weary ears and minds. If it is not burdensome, let it be deferred, though not for long; tomorrow’s discourse will begin from this point. Only pray that the grace and mercy of Jesus Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, our Lord, who is God over all, blessed for ages, may meanwhile protect us from encroaching occupations. Amen.

## SERMON LXVIII

How Christ the bridegroom attends to the Church his bride, and she to him; on the care which God has for the elect; likewise, on the Church’s merit and confidence.

1. Hear now what we deferred yesterday; hear the joy that I perceived. It is yours also: hear it joyfully. In a single word of the bride I perceived this joy and, as it were, smelled something hidden, which I shall present to you today with greater festivity because it is more timely [Col. 1108C]. The bride spoke and said that the bridegroom attends to her. Who is the bride, and who is the bridegroom? He is our God; and she, if I dare say so, is ourselves, together with the remaining multitude of captives known to him. Let us rejoice: this is our glory—

> [Note: [Col. 1108D] So the manuscripts. Horstius adds “the testimony of our conscience,” which has no relevance to this passage.]

—we are those to whom God attends. Yet how great the disparity! What are earthborn people and children of men before him? According to the prophet, they are as though they were not, and are reckoned by him as nothing and emptiness (Isa. 40:17). What, then, can this comparison between such unequal parties mean? Either she glories beyond measure, or he loves beyond measure. How wonderful that she claims his attention as though it were her own, saying: “My beloved is for me”! Yet not content with this, she goes further in glorying: she answers him as if on equal terms, complies with him, and returns his affection in kind [Col. 1108D]. For she continues: “And I for him” (Song 2:16). An extraordinary saying: “And I for him.” No less extraordinary is: “My beloved is for me”—except that both together are more extraordinary than either one.

2. Oh, what boldness belongs to a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith! “He attends to me,” she says. Is that Majesty truly attentive to her—that Majesty upon whom alike rests the governance and administration of the universe—and is the care of the ages transferred to the mere business, indeed leisure, of this love and desire? [Col. 1109A] Yes, indeed. For she is the Church of the elect, concerning whom the Apostle says: “All things are for the sake of the elect” (2 Tim. 2:10). And who can doubt that God’s grace and mercy are upon his saints, and his regard upon his elect? (Wis. 4:15). Therefore we do not deny providence to the other creatures; the Bride claims care for herself. “Is God concerned for oxen?” (1 Cor. 9:9). Nor is there any doubt that we may say the same concerning horses, camels, elephants, and all the beasts of the earth; likewise concerning the fish of the sea and the birds of heaven; finally, concerning everything upon the earth—excepting, of course, those to whom it is said: “Casting all your anxiety upon him, because he has care for you” (1 Pet. 5:7). 1505 Does it not seem to you that [Col. 1109B] these words virtually say: “Attend to him, because he attends to you”? And observe the Apostle Peter—for these are his words—whether he too has not observed the order of the Bride’s words.
