For he does not say: “Casting all your anxiety upon him, so that he may have care for you”; but, “because he has care for you.” He thus plainly shows not only how beloved the Church of the saints is, but also that she was loved first.

3. It is clear that what the Apostle said concerning oxen does not apply to her; for he who loved her and gave himself for her has care for her. Is she not that wandering sheep, whose care was preferred even to the care of the flocks above? At last, leaving those behind, the shepherd came down to this one; he diligently sought her; having found her, he did not merely lead her back but bore her back. With her [Col. 1109C] and because of her he brought into heaven a new festival of joy, inviting the hosts of angels to the celebration (Luke 15:4–7, 10). What then? He deigned to carry her back upon his own shoulders; and will he not have care for her? Therefore she is not ashamed to say: “The Lord is mindful of me” (Ps. 39:18). Nor does she think herself mistaken when she likewise says: “The Lord will repay for me” (Ps. 137:8); or in anything else that appears to signify God’s care for her. Hence she calls the Lord of hosts her Beloved, and glories that he who judges all things with tranquillity (Wis. 12:18) attends to her. Why should she not glory? She has heard him saying to her: “Can a mother forget, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? And even if she should forget, yet I will not forget [Col. 1109D] you” (Isa. 49:15). Finally, “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 33:16). And what is the Bride but the assembly of the righteous? What is she but the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the Bridegroom’s face? For he does not attend to her without her attending to him. Therefore she sets down both, saying: “He to me, and I to him.” He is to me because he is kind and merciful; I am to him because I am not ungrateful. He gives grace to me from grace; I give grace to him in return for grace. He is for my deliverance; I for his honor. He for my salvation; I for his will. He is for me, and for no other, because I am his one dove; I am for him, and for no other. For I do not listen to the voice of strangers, nor do I yield to those saying to me: “Look, here is the Christ,” or, “Look, there he is” (Mark 13:21). This is the Church.

[Col. 1110A]

4. But what of each one of us individually? Do we suppose that there is anyone among us to whom what is said can be applied? What did I say, “among us”? If anyone asks whether this may apply to any person established within the Church, I would not judge the question altogether blameworthy. For the case of one person is not the same as that of many. Indeed, God did and endured so many things when he “worked salvation in the midst of the earth,” not for one soul, but for many souls to be gathered into one Church and bound into one Bride. She is dearly beloved by the One; she clings to no other bridegroom and yields place to no other bride. What would she not dare with so eager a lover? What would she not hope from him who sought her from heaven and called her from the ends of the earth? Nor did he merely seek her, but acquired her. Add also the manner of her acquisition: in the blood [Col. 1110B] of her Acquirer.

Moreover, as is customary, she is the more confident for this reason: looking ahead, she knows that the Lord has need of her. You ask: for what? “To behold the goodness of his elect, to rejoice in the joy of his nation, that he may be praised with his inheritance” (Ps. 105:5). Do not think this a small work. I tell you, no work will remain complete if this should fail. Does not the end of all things depend upon the Church’s establishment and completion? Remove her, and this lower creation waits in vain for the revelation of the children of God. Remove her, and neither patriarchs nor prophets will be made perfect, since Paul declares that God so provided for us that they should not be made perfect without us (Heb. 11:40). Remove her, and even the glory of the holy angels will be impaired through the incompleteness of their [Col. 1110C] number, and the City of God will not rejoice in its own fullness.

5. From where, then, will the purpose of God, the mystery of his will, and that great sacrament of godliness be fulfilled? From where, finally, will you give me infants and nursing children, from whose mouths God may perfect his praise? (Ps. 8:3). Heaven has no infants; the Church has them, to whom she also says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2). And these are summoned by the Prophet as though to complete praise, when he says: “Praise the Lord, children” (Ps. 112:1). Do you suppose that our God will possess the full praise of his glory until those come who sing to him in the sight of angels: “We rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, for the years in which we saw evil”? (Ps. 89:15). The heavens did not know this kind of joy except through the children of the Church; no one ever rejoices in this way who has never ceased rejoicing. Joy fittingly follows sorrow, rest follows labor, and harbor follows shipwreck. Security pleases everyone, but more greatly the person who has been afraid. Light is delightful to all, but more delightful to one escaping from the power of darkness. To have passed from death to life doubles the grace of life.

This is my portion at the heavenly banquet, distinct from that of the blessed spirits themselves. I dare to say that blessed life itself is deprived of my blessedness—unless it deigns to acknowledge that through love it enjoys me in me and through me. Something, indeed, seems to have been added even to that perfection through me, and this is no small thing. For the angels rejoice at a sinner’s repentance. [Col. 1111A] If my tears are the delight of angels, what then is delight? Their entire work is to praise God; yet something is lacking to praise if there are lacking those who say: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment” (Ps. 65:12).

6. Blessed, therefore, in her universality is the Church, whose every ground for glory falls short of its cause—not only because of the things already done for her, but also because of those which must yet be done from her. For what concern has she about merits, who possesses a firmer and safer reason for glorying from God’s purpose? God cannot deny himself, nor fail to do what he has already done—as it is written: “who made the things that are to come” (Isa. 46:10). He will do it, he will do it, and God will not fail his purpose. Thus there is no reason now to ask by what merits we hope for [Col. 1111B] good things, especially when you hear the Prophet say: “Not for your sakes, but for my own sake I will act, says the Lord” (Ezek. 36:22).

To know that merits do not suffice is sufficient merit. But just as it is enough for merit not to presume upon merits, so to lack merits is enough for judgment. Yet among reborn infants no one lacks merits: they possess the merits of Christ. They nevertheless make themselves unworthy of these if, when they are able to add their own merits, they neglect to do so. That danger belongs to those already of adult age. Therefore make it your concern to possess merits; once possessed, recognize that they are gifts; hope for their fruit from God’s mercy. You will then have escaped every danger of poverty, ingratitude, and presumption. Pernicious poverty is a lack of merits; but presumption of spirit is deceitful riches. Therefore the Wise Man says: “Give me neither riches nor poverty, Lord” (Prov. 30:8). Blessed is the Church, to whom neither merits without presumption nor presumption without merits is lacking. She has grounds for confidence, but not in merits; she has merits, but for deserving, not for presuming. Is not this very refusal to presume a deserving? Therefore she has confidence all the more safely because she does not presume; nor need she be ashamed in the word of glory, since she has abundant material for glorying. The mercies of the Lord are many, and his truth endures forever.

7. Why should she not glory securely, when mercy and truth have met together as a testimony to her glory? (Ps. 84:11). Whether she says, “My Beloved is to me”; or, “I waited expectantly for the Lord, [Col. 1111D] and he attended to me”; or again, “The Lord is mindful of me” (Ps. 39:2, 18); or whatever other and different utterances there are of this sort which seem similarly to express some divine affection and singular favor toward someone—she will regard none of them as foreign to herself, whose ground of confidence is the Lord’s ordinance. This is especially so since she sees no other Bride, nor another Church, for whom things that must happen cannot happen. It is clear, then, in the case of the Church, that she will not hesitate truly to apply all these things to herself.

But concerning one soul, even though spiritual and holy, the question remains whether it may in any way dare such language. For one member of the multitude, however eminent in holiness, will not arrogate to itself all the prerogatives of that one catholic multitude for whose sake all things are done. Therefore, as I see it, it will be more difficult [Col. 1112A] to discover—if indeed it can be discovered—how this may be permitted. I think it necessary to attempt this in another sermon, and not merely to enter upon the paths of a scrupulous discussion, whose outcome we still do not know, unless we have first prayed concerning the hidden word to him who opens and no one shuts: Jesus Christ our Lord, the Bridegroom of the Church, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXIX

### How every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God is cast down; concerning the coming and abiding of the Father and the Word with the soul that loves, and concerning the intimacy thereby formed between God and the soul

1. “My Beloved is to me, and I to him” (Cant. 2:16). [Col. 1112B] The preceding sermon assigned this utterance to the universal Church because of the promises made to it by God—of the life that now is and of that which is to come. But a question has been raised concerning the individual soul, because one soul cannot claim for itself what the whole may dare, nor draw that saying to itself in any way. If it is not permitted, we must accordingly refer it to the Church in such a manner that it is not at all referred to an individual person. And this applies not only to this saying, but also to the other similar utterances which speak great things, for example: “I waited expectantly for the Lord, and he attended to me” (Ps. 39:2), and any others touched upon in the preceding sermon.

If anyone thinks it permitted, I do not deny it; but it matters to whom it is permitted, for it is not permitted to everyone. The Church of God certainly has its spiritual persons, who act in it not only faithfully but confidently, speaking with God as with a friend, while their conscience bears them testimony to his glory. Who they are is known to God; but hear what you ought to be if you wish to be such a person. What I shall say, however, I say not as one experienced, but as one desiring to have the experience.

Give me a soul which loves nothing except God and what ought to be loved for God’s sake; for which Christ is not merely life but has long been life; whose occupation and repose are to set the Lord always before its face; whose sole resolve is carefully to walk with the Lord its God, and which lacks no power to do so. Give me, I say, such a soul, and I do not deny that it is worthy of the Bridegroom’s care, the Majesty’s regard, the Ruler’s favor, and the Governor’s concern. And if it wishes to glory, it will not be foolish—provided only that the one who glories glories in the Lord. Thus, in the matter in which many dare, one person also dares, though for a different reason.

2. For the holy multitude is made confident by the reasons just mentioned; but a holy soul by a certain twofold reason. First, in the absolutely simple nature of the Bridegroom’s divinity, he regards many as though one, and one as though many. He is neither manifold because of a multitude nor rare because of fewness; neither divided by diversity nor confined to one; neither distressed by cares nor disturbed or agitated by concerns. Thus he attends to one without being detained, and to many without being dispersed.

Second, it is as delightful to experience as it is rare [elsewhere, erroneously, “dearest”] to have experienced such condescension of the Word and such benevolence of the Father of the Word toward a well-disposed and well-ordered soul—which disposition itself is the Father’s gift and the Word’s work—that they, having anticipated and prepared it for themselves by such a blessing, also deign to visit it with their presence; and in such a way that they not only come to it, but make their dwelling with it (John 14:23). For it is not enough that they show themselves; they must also impart the abundance of themselves.

What is the Word’s coming to the soul? To instruct it in wisdom. What is the Father’s coming? To dispose it to love wisdom, so that it may say: “I became a lover of her beauty” (Wis. 8:2). To love belongs to the Father; and therefore the Father’s coming is demonstrated by infused love. What would instruction accomplish without love? It would inflate. What would love accomplish without instruction? It would go astray. For those of whom it was said were going astray: “I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. [Col. 1113B] 10:2). It does not befit the Bride of the Word to be foolish; moreover, the Father does not endure her when she is proud.

For the Father 1508 loves the Son, and is always ready to cast down and destroy every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of the Word—whether by sending zeal or by directing it: the former belongs to mercy, the latter to judgment. Would that in me every exaltation might be restrained—indeed cast down and reduced to nothing—not by kindled wrath but by infused love! Would that I might learn not to be proud, with anointing rather than punishment as my teacher! Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, as you rebuked the angel exalting himself in heaven; nor correct me in your anger, as you corrected the man in paradise. Both devised iniquity, aspiring to height: the former to height of power, the latter to height of knowledge. For the foolish woman believed one who promised but deceived her: “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5). He to whom she persuaded that he would be like the Most High had already deceived himself (Isa. 14:14). For one who thinks himself something when he is nothing deceives himself (Gal. 6:3).

3. Yet both heights were cast down, though more mildly in the case of man, by the judgment of him who makes all things in weight and measure. For while the angel was punished—in fact, condemned—in fury, man experienced anger only, not fury. For when God was angry, he remembered mercy. Hence his seed are children of anger, not of fury, down to the present day. If I had not been born a child of anger, there would have been no need to be born again; if I had been born a child of fury, either being born again would not have occurred, or it would not have profited me.

Do you wish to see a child of fury? If you have seen Satan falling like lightning from heaven, that is one hurled down in the violence of fury; and you have known this from God’s fury. For he did not remember his mercy; because he will remember mercy when he has been angry, not when he has already blazed forth into fury. Woe to the children of unbelief! Woe also to those descended from Adam who, born children of anger, by diabolical obstinacy turn anger into fury for themselves, the rod into a staff—indeed, into a hammer. For they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath (Rom. 2:5). And what is accumulated anger but fury? [Col. 1114A] They have sinned the devil’s sin, and they are struck by the devil’s sentence.

Woe also—though more mildly—to certain children of anger, who, born in anger, did not wait to be born again in grace. For, dying in the state in which they were born, they will remain children of anger. I have said “of anger,” not “of fury”; because, as is most devoutly believed and most humanely lamented, the punishments are most mild for all who are bound by a guilt contracted from another source.

> **Note [Col. 1113D].** Augustine teaches the same in *On the Merits of Sins*, book I, chapter 16, where he writes that “infants who depart from the body without baptism will be in the mildest condemnation of all.” The same is found in book V, chapter 12, of *Against Julian*. Likewise Fulgentius, *On the Truth of Predestination*, book I, chapter 14, and *On the Incarnation*, chapter 30. Add to these the letter of Faricius, abbot of Abingdon, in *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 137.

4. Therefore the devil was judged in fury because his iniquity was found worthy of hatred; but man was judged unto anger, and is therefore corrected in anger. Thus every height has been broken down—both that which inflates and that which casts headlong—because the Father is zealous for the Son. In either case there is injury to the Son: in usurped power opposed to God’s power, which he himself is; and in knowledge presumptuously sought from another source than the wisdom of God, which he likewise himself is.

Lord, who is like you? Who but the brightness and express image of your substance? Who but your image? Alone in your form, alone not counting equality with you a thing to be seized, is the Most High Son of the Most High (Phil. 2:6). How is he not equal? You and he are indeed one. You seat him at your right hand, not beneath your feet. How can anyone dare to invade the place of your Only-Begotten? Let him be cast down. He sets his seat on high; let the chair of pestilence be overthrown.

Again, who teaches a human being knowledge? Is it not you, O Key of David, opening to whom you will and shutting to whom you will? How then was entrance—indeed, a forcible intrusion—into the treasures of wisdom and knowledge attempted without the key? Whoever does not enter through the door is a thief and a robber. Peter, therefore, will enter, because he received the keys. Yet not he alone: for, if he wills, he will introduce me too, and exclude another whom perhaps he wills, according to the knowledge and power given to him from above.

5. And what are these keys? The power of opening and shutting, and discernment between those to be excluded and those to be admitted. The treasures are not in the serpent but in Christ. Therefore the serpent could not give knowledge which it did not possess; but he who possessed it gave it. Nor could Peter himself possess 1509 a power which he had not received; but he who received it possessed it. Christ gave (Matt. 16:19); Peter received, neither inflated by knowledge nor liable to be cast down by power. Why? Because in neither does he exalt himself against the knowledge of God; he sought none of these things apart from God’s knowledge, unlike the one who acted deceitfully in his sight, “so that his iniquity might be found worthy of hatred” (Ps. 35:3). How, finally, could he act apart from God’s knowledge when he writes of himself as “an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the foreknowledge of God the Father”? (1 Pet. 1:1–2).

Let this be said concerning the zeal of God which he directs against the transgressing angel and man—for in both he found perversity—and concerning the manner in which, in his anger and fury, he destroyed every height exalting itself against the knowledge of God.

6. We must now turn to the zeal of mercy: that is, not the zeal which is directed, but that which is sent forth. For the zeal which is directed, as we have already said, belongs to judgment, and it has sufficiently frightened us through the examples just recalled of those so grievously punished. Therefore I shall go to my place of refuge from the face of the Lord’s fury: namely, to that zeal of loving-kindness, gently burning and effectively cleansing. Does not charity cleanse? It does so powerfully. I have read that it “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). But I ask: is it not fit and sufficient to cast down and humble every exaltation of eyes and heart? Most certainly; for charity does not exalt or inflate itself.

Therefore, if the Lord Jesus deigns to come to me—or rather, into me—not in zeal of fury, nor even in anger, but in charity and a spirit of gentleness, being zealous for me with God’s own zeal—for what is so truly God’s as charity? Indeed, God is charity—if, I say, he comes in this way, I shall know by this that he is not alone but that his Father too has come with him. For what is more fatherly? This is why he is called not only Father of the Word, but also Father of mercies (2 Cor. 1:3): because it belongs to his nature always to have mercy and spare.

If I feel my understanding opened so that I understand the Scriptures; or a word of wisdom, as it were, bubbling up from my inmost being; or mysteries revealed to me by light infused from above; or, at least, something like the most generous bosom of heaven opened out to me, and richer showers of meditations flowing down from above into my soul—I do not doubt that the Bridegroom is present. For these are the riches of the Word, and it is from his fullness that we receive them. But if along with these there is poured into me a humble yet rich devotion, like an inward sprinkling, so that love for recognized truth produces in me a necessary hatred and contempt for vanity, lest knowledge perhaps inflate me or the frequency of visitations exalt me—then I most certainly feel that I am being dealt with in a fatherly manner, and I do not doubt that the Father is present. And if I persevere in responding to this condescension with dispositions and acts worthy of it, so far as lies within me, and if the grace of God is not idle in me, then both the Father who nourishes and the Word who instructs will make their dwelling with me.

7. How great, do you think, is the grace of intimacy that arises between the soul and the Word from this dwelling, and how great the confidence that follows from intimacy? Such a soul, I think, need no longer fear to say, “My Beloved is to me.” For, because she feels that she loves him, and loves him intensely, she likewise has no doubt that she is intensely loved. And from her own singular attentiveness, concern, care, industry, diligence, and zeal—by which she watches incessantly and ardently to discover how she may please God—she recognizes beyond doubt all these same things in him, remembering his promise: “With what measure you have measured, it shall be measured to you again” (Matt. 7:2). Yet the prudent Bride is careful to claim the repayment of grace more for her Beloved’s side, knowing that she was rather forestalled by him. Hence she gives precedence to his activity, saying: “My Beloved is to me, and I to him.”

Thus she recognizes from what is her own what belongs to God; and, because she loves, she does not doubt that she is loved. It is so. God’s love produces the soul’s love, and his prior attentiveness makes the soul attentive, his concern makes it concerned. For by some, I know not what, affinity of nature, once the soul can behold the glory of God with unveiled face, it must immediately be conformed to him and transformed into the same image. Therefore, as you have prepared yourself for God, such must God appear to you. “With the holy, he will be holy; and with the innocent man, innocent” (Ps. 17:26). Why not likewise loving with the one who loves, at leisure with the one at leisure, attentive with the attentive, and concerned with the concerned?

8. Finally, he says: “I love those who love me, and those who watch for me early shall find me” (Prov. 8:17). You see how he makes you certain not only of his love, if you love him, but also of the concern he bears for you, if he finds you concerned for him. Are you watching? He watches too. Rise in the night, at the beginning of your watches; hasten even to anticipate the watches themselves as far as you can: you will find him, but you will not forestall him. In such a matter you rashly attribute to yourself either anything earlier or anything greater; he loves more, and he loves first.

If the soul knows these things—or rather, because she knows them—do you wonder that she glories that that Majesty, as though caring for no others, attends to her alone, when she alone, setting aside every other concern, keeps herself wholly for him with total devotion? The discourse calls for an end; but I say one thing to those among you who are spiritual: it is wonderful indeed, but true. A soul beholding God sees itself as though it alone were seen by God. With that confidence, therefore, it says that he attends to it and it to him, seeing nothing except itself and him. You are good, O Lord, to the soul that seeks you: you meet it, embrace it, show yourself as Bridegroom—you who are Lord, indeed who are God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXX

### Why the Bridegroom is called Beloved; and concerning truth, gentleness, justice, and the other virtues which are lilies among which he feeds

1. “My Beloved is to me, and I to him, who feeds among the lilies” (Cant. 2:16). Who will now charge her with presumption or insolence if she says that she has entered into fellowship with him who feeds among the lilies? Even if he grazed among the stars, the mere fact that he grazes might seem to make it no small thing to have such friendship or intimacy with him. “To graze” sounds decidedly lowly and humble. But now, when he is said to feed among lilies, the added abasement removes still further and repels the charge of rashness. For what are lilies? According to the Lord’s saying, grass which is here today and tomorrow cast into the furnace (Matt. 6:28–30). How great is this one who grazes upon grass, like one of the lambs or calves? Yet he is indeed both Lamb and fatted Calf.

But perhaps you have more carefully observed that food is not designated here, but place. For it is not said that he grazes *upon* lilies, but *among* lilies. Granted. He does not eat grass like an ox; nevertheless, what preeminence can there be in dwelling in grass and reclining upon grass like one of the crowd? And what glory is there for this woman in having that one as her Beloved who has done this? According to the letter, indeed, the Bride’s modesty and the caution of her wisdom in speaking are sufficiently apparent: she orders her words with judgment and tempers the glory of the realities by modesty of expression.

2. But otherwise she does not fail to know that the one who feeds and the one who feeds others are one and the same; that he who dwells among lilies also reigns over the stars. Yet she more willingly recalls the lowly things of her Beloved, certainly because of humility, as I said; but more because he began to be Beloved from the time when he began to graze. Not only from that point, but because of it. For he who is Lord in the highest is Beloved in the lowest; reigning above the stars, loving among the lilies. He loved above the stars too, because, being love, he could nowhere and never fail to love. But until he descended to the lilies and was known to graze among them, he was neither loved nor made Beloved.

What then? Was he not loved by the patriarchs and prophets? He was; but not before he was seen by them also feeding among the lilies. For they did not fail to see him whom they foresaw—unless one is so devoid of spirit as to suppose that one who sees in the Spirit sees nothing. Why, then, were they called Seers? For thus the prophets were called (1 Sam. 9:9), if they saw nothing. Hence it is that they wished to see him whom they did not see. For they could not have wished to see in the flesh one whom they had not seen in the Spirit. But I ask: all the prophets? As though all wished to see, or as though all possessed faith. Yet those who saw were either prophets or persons who assented to the prophets. For to have believed is also to have seen. Indeed, not only one who sees by the spirit of prophecy, but also one who sees by faith—if anyone says that this person too sees in the Spirit—I do not think he is mistaken.

3. Therefore, the fact that he who feeds all deigned to descend to the lilies and feed among the lilies made him Beloved, because he could not be loved before he was known. Accordingly, when mention was made of the Beloved, it was fitting also to mention that which was the cause of love and recognition. This feeding among lilies must be sought spiritually, for to imagine it bodily is absurd. Indeed, the lilies themselves must be shown by us to be spiritual, if we can. I think we must also say on what the Beloved grazes among the lilies: the lilies themselves, or other herbs or flowers hidden among the lilies.

And here the more difficult point seems to me to be that he is said to graze, not to feed others. For there is no doubt that he feeds others, nor is this unworthy of him; but to feed suggests need, and it seems difficult to assign this to Majesty even in a spiritual sense without injury. Indeed, I do not recall having noticed up to this point that food is anywhere said to be taken in this Song, whereas I think you remember with me that one who feeds is mentioned. For at one time she asked that it be shown her where he fed and rested at noon (Cant. 1:6). Now, however, she says that he feeds—something she had not said before—but does not likewise ask that the place be indicated to her. Rather, she herself points it out, saying: “among the lilies.” She knows this, but does not know the former, because what is lofty and on high cannot be equally at hand with what is lowly and upon the earth. The work is lofty and its place lofty; and up to now even the Bride herself has no access to it.

[Col. 1118A]

4. And therefore he emptied himself to this extent: that he, the Shepherd of all, might himself graze; and he was found among the lilies, was seen by the Church, was loved by the poor needy one, and became Beloved because of likeness. But this was not only because of likeness: it was also because of truth, gentleness, and justice—because through him the promises were fulfilled, iniquities forgiven, and proud demons with their prince judged. Thus he appeared as one rightly to be loved: true for himself, gentle toward human beings, just on behalf of human beings. O Bridegroom truly to be loved and embraced with all the marrow of the heart! Why should the Church now delay to entrust herself wholly, with entire devotion, to so faithful a rewarder, so merciful a pardoner, so just a defender?

The Prophet had already said: “In your splendor and your beauty, advance prosperously” (Ps. 44:5). Whence comes this splendor and beauty? I think it comes from the lilies. What is more beautiful than a lily? So nothing is more beautiful than the Bridegroom. What, then, are those lilies from which comes the beauty of his splendor? “Go forth,” he says, “and reign because of truth, gentleness, and justice” (Ps. 44:5). Lilies they are—lilies, I say—springing from the earth, gleaming upon the earth, standing out among the earth’s flowers, fragrant beyond the scent of spices. Therefore the Bridegroom is among these lilies, and altogether beautiful and fair because of them. Otherwise, in respect of the infirmity of the flesh, “he had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53:2).

5. Truth, however, is a good lily: conspicuous in whiteness and surpassing in fragrance. For it is “the brightness of eternal light,” the splendor and image of God’s substance (Wis. 7:26). It is indeed a lily which our earth produced for a new blessing, and which God prepared before the face of all peoples as “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:31–32). While the earth lay under the curse, it brought forth thorns and thistles. But now, the Lord blessing it, “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Ps. 84:12–13, 2): a most beautiful flower of the field and lily of the valleys.

Recognize the lily by its whiteness: at the very rising of the flower it immediately shone upon shepherds by night, as the Gospel says, “an angel of the Lord stood by them, and the glory of God shone around them” (Luke 2:9). Rightly the glory of God, not of the angel: it was the whiteness of the lily. The angel was present, but the lily’s radiance flashed forth from Bethlehem itself. Recognize the lily also by its fragrance, through which it became known even to those far away. A star indeed appeared, but those grave men would never have followed it unless they had been drawn by some inward sweetness of the lily that had arisen. And truth is truly a lily: its fragrance animates faith, and its brightness illuminates understanding.

Now raise your eyes to the very person of the Lord, who says in the Gospel: “I am the truth” (John 14:6), and see how fittingly truth is compared to a lily. If you have not observed it, observe the little golden rods, as it were, issuing from the center of this flower and encircled by a most white blossom, beautifully and suitably arranged like a crown. Recognize in Christ the golden divinity crowned by the purity of human nature: that is, Christ in the diadem with which his mother crowned him. But the diadem with which [Col. 1119A] his Father crowned him is the inaccessible light in which he dwells; and for the present you could not yet see him in it. But of this elsewhere.

6. But now the lily is truth; it is also gentleness. And gentleness is fittingly a lily, possessing the whiteness of innocence and the fragrance of hope: “for there are remnants,” he says, “for the peaceable man” (Ps. 36:37). The gentle man is a man of good hope, and no less, even in the present life, a bright example of social living. Is not that a lily which shines in duty and is fragrant with hope? Add that, just as truth sprang from the earth, so also did gentleness. Unless anyone doubts that the Lamb, ruler of the earth, sprang from the earth (Isa. 16:1)—that Lamb who “was led to slaughter and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). Nor did gentleness or truth alone spring from the earth, but righteousness also, as the prophet says: “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness spring up together” (Isa. 45:8). But that righteousness is a lily, remember from Scripture: “The righteous shall spring up like a lily, and shall flourish forever before the Lord” (Hos. 14:6). This is by no means a lily that is here today and cast into the oven tomorrow, for it shall flourish forever. And it shall flourish before the Lord: the righteous man “shall be in everlasting remembrance and shall not fear evil tidings” (Ps. 111:7)—that is, the tidings by which sinners are commanded to go into the furnace of fire. Moreover, for whom does this lily’s whiteness not shine, except one to whom it gives no pleasure? Indeed, it is a sun, but not the sun that rises upon good and evil alike. For those who will say, “The sun of righteousness has not risen upon us” (Wis. 5:6), never at any time saw its light. Yet all have seen it who heard: “For you who fear God, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. 4:2). Therefore this lily’s whiteness belongs among the righteous; its fragrance too is spread even to the wicked, though not for their good. For we have heard the righteous say, “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place”: to some indeed “a fragrance of life unto life,” to others “a fragrance of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:15–16). What man, however criminal, does not approve the reputation of a righteous person, though he does not love his conduct? And blessed is he if he does not judge himself in what he approves. But he does judge himself when he approves the good yet does not love it; and therefore he is plainly not blessed, but miserable, condemned by his own judgment. What is more miserable than one to whom the fragrance of life is not life’s herald, but death’s? Indeed, it is not even a herald, but its bearer.

7. With the Bridegroom there are many other lilies besides those which have occurred to us from the Prophet—truth, gentleness, and righteousness. I speak the truth: it will now be difficult for none of you to discover similar things for himself in the garden of so delightful a Bridegroom. He abounds and overabounds in such things: who can enumerate them? Indeed, as many virtues as there are, so many lilies there are. What limit is there to virtues in the Lord of virtues? And if in Christ is the fullness of virtues, there is also the fullness of lilies. Perhaps for this reason he called himself a lily: because he is wholly occupied among lilies and all that belongs to him is lily—his conception, birth, manner of life, words, miracles, mysteries, passion, death, resurrection, ascension. What among these is not white and most sweetly fragrant? In his conception, finally, such brightness of heavenly light shone forth from the abundance of the Spirit coming upon him that even the holy Virgin herself could not have endured it, had she not been overshadowed by the power of the Most High. His birth was made white by the incorrupt virginity of his mother; his life, by innocence; his sayings, by truth; his miracles, by purity of heart; his mysteries, by the hidden meaning of godliness; his passion, by the willingness to suffer; his death, by the freedom not to die; his resurrection, by the courage of the martyrs; his ascension, by the fulfilment of promises. How good is the fragrance of faith in each of these things, filling our times and hearts—we who have not seen the whiteness! “Blessed are they who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29). My portion in these is the fragrance of life that proceeds from them. Poured into my nostrils through the fitting instrument of faith—and more abundantly, indeed, in proportion to the multitude of lilies—it both relieves exile and continually renews in my heart the longing for my homeland.

8. Some of the Bridegroom’s companions also have lilies, but not in abundance. For all have received the Spirit by measure, and virtues and gifts by measure; he alone who possesses all things “does not have [the Spirit] by measure” (John 3:34). It is one thing to have lilies; another to have nothing but lilies. Whom among the children of captivity will you give me who is so innocent and holy that he has been able to fill all his land with flowers—and flowers of this kind? Certainly not even an infant of one day is without defilement upon the earth (Job 14:4–5, according to the Septuagint). Great is the person who can cultivate three or four lilies in his own land, amid such a dense growth of thorns and briars, which are the long-established shoots of the ancient curse. Yet with me, poor as I am, matters go well if I can ever reclaim from this most wretched crop—namely, iniquities and vices—so small a portion of my land by uprooting and cultivating it that I may produce at least one lily, so that perhaps he who feeds among lilies may deign sometimes to feed also with me.

9. But I have said too little: “one.” My mouth has spoken from the poverty of my heart. One absolutely does not suffice; at least two are necessary. I mean continence and innocence: neither of these, without the other, will save. In vain, therefore, shall I invite the Bridegroom to either one of them, since he is said to feed not at a lily but among lilies. I shall therefore strive to have lilies, lest he complain of the solitary nature of the lily—for he will feed only among lilies—and thus turn away in anger from his servant. I place innocence first of all; and if I can join continence to it, I shall count myself rich in the possession of lilies. But I shall be a king if I can add patience to these as a third. Indeed, the former may suffice; but because they can fail in temptations—for “the life of man upon earth is temptation” (Job 7:1)—there is certainly need of patience, which is, as it were, the nurse [or: guardian] and protector of both. I think that, if that lover of lilies comes and finds things thus, he will no longer disdain to feed with us and to keep Passover with us: where he will find much sweetness in the two, and great security because of the third. But how he who feeds all things is said to feed will be seen later. For now it is evident that the Bridegroom not only appears among lilies, but can never at all be found outside lilies, since all that concerns him—and he himself—is a lily: Jesus Christ our Lord, Bridegroom of the Church, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXI. On spiritual lilies, that is, good works, whose fragrance is a right conscience and whose color is reputation; and how the Bridegroom both feeds us and is fed by us. Also on the unity of God the Father with the Son, and of the holy soul with God.

1. The end of the preceding sermon is the beginning of this one. Therefore the Bridegroom is a lily, but not a lily among thorns, because he who committed no sin has no thorns. Indeed, he declared the Bride to be a lily among thorns; for if she herself should say that she has no thorns, she deceives herself and the truth is not in her. But he professed himself to be a flower and a lily, though not among thorns. Rather: “I,” he says, “am a flower of the field and a lily of the valleys” (Song 2:2, 1). And there is no mention of thorns, because he alone among men has no need to say: “I am turned in my distress while the thorn is fastened in me” (Ps. 31:4). Therefore he who is always without vices is never without lilies, because he is wholly and always white, “beautiful in form above the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3). You, then, who hear or read this, take care to have lilies with you if you wish to have dwelling in you this dweller among lilies. Let your work, your zeal, your desire, be shown to be lilies by a certain moral whiteness and fragrance in the things themselves. Moral qualities too have their colors and their fragrances. For color and fragrance are no more identical in spiritual things than they are in bodily things. Consult conscience concerning color, reputation concerning fragrance. “You have made our fragrance stink before Pharaoh and his servants,” they say (Exod. 5:21), speaking of reputation. The intention of the heart and conscience’s judgment give color to your work. Vices are black; virtue is white. Conscience, when consulted, distinguishes between the one and the other. The Lord’s judgment concerning the evil and clear eye stands firm (Matt. 6:22–23), for he has fixed definite boundaries between white and black and divided light from darkness. Therefore what proceeds from a pure heart and a good conscience is white and is virtue; but if good reputation follows as well, it is also a lily, for it lacks neither the lily’s whiteness nor its fragrance.

2. Virtue, moreover, though not greater for that reason, becomes more beautiful and more illustrious. But if there is a blemish in the conscience, that which proceeds from it will not lack a blemish either. For if the root is in vice, so is the branch. Accordingly, whatever it may be that a corrupted root produces from itself with the propagation of its vice—for example, speech, action, or prayer—even if reputation seems to applaud it, ought not to be called a lily, because although the fragrance seems to wink at it, the color does not. How can there be a lily with the blemish of impurity? Nor will reputation be able to vindicate for virtue what conscience has convicted of being vice. Virtue will indeed be content with the whiteness of conscience where the fragrance of reputation cannot follow; but the fragrance of reputation will not suffice to excuse the vice of a discolored conscience. Still, insofar as lies in him, the virtuous person will always “provide things good not only before God but also before men” (Rom. 12:17), so that he may truly be a lily.

3. But the soul’s whiteness is also God’s forgiveness, as he himself says through the prophet: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and though they be red as the crimson worm, they shall be as white wool” (Isa. 1:18). There is also the whiteness with which one clothes himself who shows mercy cheerfully. For if you look at the man whom the Prophet depicts as “a gracious man who shows mercy and lends” (Ps. 111:5), will he not seem to you, from the very gladness of his soul, to have bestowed a certain whiteness of compassion alike upon his face and upon his deed? Conversely, if someone gives out of sadness and as though from necessity, he displays in hand and brow a color not white but plainly gloomy. Therefore “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). Does he love a sad one too? Certainly, having looked upon Abel because of the whiteness of his gladness, he turned his face away from Cain because his countenance [or: face] had fallen (Gen. 4:4–5), plainly through sadness and envy. Observe what kind of color belongs to sadness or envy, since it turns God’s gaze away from itself. The whiteness of gladness in bestowing a benefit is beautifully and elegantly praised in the poet’s phrase: “Above all, the kindly faces were added” (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book VIII). Nor is only the cheerful giver loved by God, but also one “who gives in simplicity” (Rom. 12:8). Simplicity too is whiteness. We prove it by its opposite: doubleness is a blemish. I have said too little: it is a stain. What is doubleness but deceit? But “he who acted deceitfully in the sight of God, his iniquity was found unto hatred” (Ps. 35:3). Therefore blessed is he “to whom the Lord will not impute sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit” (Ps. 31:2). In a few words the Lord beautifully marked both stains, deceit and sadness: “Do not,” he says, “become sad like the hypocrites” (Matt. 6:16). Thus the Bridegroom, being virtue, takes delight in virtues; being a lily, gladly dwells among lilies; and being whiteness, delights in those who are white.

4. And perhaps this is what it means to be said to feed among lilies: to delight in the whiteness and fragrance of virtues. Indeed, he was once fed bodily with Mary and Martha, reclining bodily also among lilies—I mean those women, for they were lilies—while nonetheless refreshing his spirit with the devotion and virtues of the women. If at that hour a prophet, an angel, or any other spiritual person had entered, scarcely unaware of what majesty reclined there, would he not, astonished at the condescension and familiarity which he saw that majesty have with pure souls and chaste bodies, though earthly and of the weaker sex, rightly have testified: “I have seen him not only dwelling but also feeding among lilies”? Thus the Bridegroom was found to feed among lilies in both respects—both flesh and spirit, I mean. But I think that he in turn also fed them, though in the spirit. By the very fact that he was fed, how did he feed? How, I ask, did he strengthen the women’s timidity, gladden their humility, enrich their devotion? But if you have seen that for him to feed is to feed others, see now also whether perhaps, conversely, for him to feed others is to be fed. “Lord, who feeds me from my youth,” says the holy patriarch Jacob (Gen. 48:15). He is a good householder, who takes care of his household, especially in evil days, feeding them in famine with the bread of life and understanding and thus nourishing them unto eternal life. But while feeding, I think he is nonetheless himself fed—indeed, with the foods he gladly eats: our progress. For “the joy of the Lord is our strength.”

5. Thus both when he feeds he is fed, and when he is fed he feeds, at once refreshing us with his spiritual joy and rejoicing in our likewise spiritual progress. My repentance is his food; my salvation is his food; I myself am his food. Does he not eat ashes like bread? And because I am a sinner, I am ash, so that I may be eaten by him. I am chewed when I am reproved; swallowed when I am instructed; cooked down when I am changed; digested when I am transformed; united when I am conformed. Do not wonder at this: he eats us, and is eaten by us, that we may be bound to him more closely. Otherwise we are not perfectly united to him. For if I eat and am not eaten, he will seem to be in me, but I am not yet in him. If, however, I am eaten but do not eat, he will seem to have me in himself, but not also to be in me; and the union will not be perfect in either case. Rather, let him eat me, so that he may have me in himself; and let him in turn be eaten by me, so that he may be in me: in order that the bond may be whole and firm, when I am in him and he himself nevertheless is in me.

> **Note [Col. 1123D].** Thus the first editions, together with several manuscripts. Some read: “The bond and embrace will likewise be firm and whole.”

6. Do you wish me to show by an analogy what is meant? Raise your eyes now to a higher harmony, indeed, yet one similar to this. If the Bridegroom himself were in the Father in such a way that the Father were not in him, or if the Father were in him in such a way that he were not in the Father, I dare say that even their unity would remain short of perfection—if indeed it were already unity. But now, since both he is in the Father and the Father is in him, there is nothing by which their unity might be impaired; rather, he and the Father are truly and perfectly one. So, then, the soul for which “it is good to cleave to God” (Ps. 72:28) should not judge itself perfectly united to him until it perceives both that he abides in it and that it abides in him. This is not because it is then said to be one with God in the way that the Father and Son are one, although “he who cleaves to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). I have read this; I have not read the other. I do not speak merely of myself, who am nothing; rather, no one at all, unless mad, whether on earth or in heaven, will arrogate to himself that utterance of the Only-begotten: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Yet I, although dust and ashes, relying on Scripture’s authority, do not at all fear to say that I am one spirit with God—provided that I have at some time been convinced by sure experience that I cleave to God after the likeness of one of those who abide in love and therefore abide in God, with God abiding in them, eating God and being eaten by God.

> **Note [Col. 1124D].** One manuscript adds “in a certain manner”; but this is absent from others, including the first editions.

For I think that it was concerning such cleaving that it was said: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit.” What then? The Son says: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:11), and, “We are one” (John 10:30); a human being says: “I am in God and God is in me, and we are one spirit.”

7. But do the Father and Son, in order to be in one another and therefore one, eat one another as God and man pass into one another through a certain mutual eating of each other, so that by this, though not one, they nevertheless exist as one spirit? [Variant: “may exist.”] Far be it! For these and the others are not in one another in the same manner, nor is the unity of the two the same.

[Indeed, the diversity of the unities is indicated to you by *unus* (“one,” masculine) and *unum* (“one,” neuter): for neither *unus* can apply to the Father and Son nor *unum* to man and God. If you are wise, you will become wiser from the occasion given, carefully observing that there, by *unum*, is meant unity of substance or nature; here, by *unus*, unity likewise, yet one far different, because among substances and natures—namely, man and God—each has his own nature and substance, whereas it is certain that the Father and Son have wholly one. You see that this is not even unity when compared with that singular and supreme unity. For how can there be unity where there is a number of natures and diversity of substances? Yet the soul that cleaves to God is called, and is, one spirit with God; nor does the plurality of things prejudice this unity, which is constituted not by a confusion of natures but by agreement of wills. For this reason too many hearts are called one, and many souls one, as it is written: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). This, then, is also a unity.]

8. But what has this to do with that unity which consists not in uniting but subsists by eternity? Certainly no mutual eating such as this produces that unity, because it does not come to be: it simply is. Nor is there conjunction, quasi-composition, or anything of that sort, which belongs not to what is one. But the Father and Son have nature, essence, and will not merely “one” but “one thing.” For them, to be is precisely to be nature; to will is precisely to be, or to be nature. Therefore the unity by which Father and Son are one must not be said to be made from natures, essences, or wills, because they are not plural; nor must it be said to come to be, because it is. For it is not made, but native.

> **Note [Col. 1124D].** The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the Cistercian, Saint-Germain, and Jumièges manuscripts, but are found in others and in the first editions. Yet the second, longer parenthesis or addition, extending from the middle of §8 to the middle of §10, is absent from those earlier manuscripts but is found in the later ones. In fact, one or the other is superfluous. This variation occurred because Bernard revised this passage, so that the first parenthesis appears to belong to the earlier edition and the second to the later. Only the former is found in the first editions, not the latter. We leave judgment to the reader.

The Father and Son are in each other, mutually capable and comprehending themselves, not only in an ineffable but also in an incomprehensible manner; yet capable in such a way as not to be divisible, and comprehending in such a way as not to be sharers [variant: capable of participation]. For, as the Church sings in the hymn: “The whole Son is in the Father, and the whole Father in the Word” (*Hymn for Monday, Second Nocturn at Matins*). The Father is in the Son, in whom he has always been well pleased; and the Son is in the Father, from whom, as he was never not begotten, so he has never been separated. But through love man is in God and God in man, as John says: “He who abides in love abides in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16).

[This is a certain agreement, by which two are in one spirit—indeed, are one spirit. Do you see the difference? Consubstantiality and concord are plainly not the same. Yet, if you have observed, the difference of the unities themselves is sufficiently indicated to you by *unus* and *unum*: for neither *unus* can apply to Father and Son nor *unum* to man and God. Father and Son cannot be called *unus*, one masculine person, because one is Father and the other Son; yet they are called and are *unum*, one thing, because they have entirely one substance, not each his own. Conversely, man and God, because they are not of one substance or nature, cannot be called *unum*, one thing; yet, if they cleave to one another by the bond of love, they are called one spirit with certain and absolute truth. This unity is produced not so much by cohesion of essences as by harmony of wills.

9. It is clear enough, unless I am mistaken, not only that the unities differ but that they are unequal: the one existing in a single essence, the other in different essences. What is more distant from each other than the unity of many and the unity of one? Thus, as I have said, *unus* and *unum* distinguish between the unities: by *unum*, indeed, is denoted the unity of essence in Father and Son; but by *unus*, between God and man, not this but a certain harmonious devotion of affections. With an added term, however, Father and Son are also most soundly called *unus*: for example, one God, one Lord, and whatever else is said of each in relation to himself and not in relation to the other [variant: either other]. For their divinity or majesty is not diverse, any more than their substance, essence, or nature. Indeed, if you consider devoutly, all these things are not diverse or divided in them but are one. I have said too little: they are one, and one with them. What, then, is that unity by which many hearts are read to be one and many souls one? In comparison with this it ought not, I think, to be reckoned worthy even of the name of unity, for this unity does not unite many things but singularly signifies one thing. Therefore that unity is singular and supreme; it consists not in uniting but subsists by eternity. Nor, indeed, does the aforementioned spiritual eating make it, because it does not come to be: it is. Much less should any conjunction of essences, or agreement of wills, be thought to make it, because there are not plural essences or wills. For, as has been said, they have one essence and one will; but where there is one, there is no agreement, composition, conjunction, or anything of that kind. There must be at least two wills for there to be agreement, and likewise two essences for there to be conjunction or union through agreement. None of these things exists in Father and Son, who have neither two essences nor two wills. Both realities are one for them; or rather, as I recall having said above, these two things in them are one, and are one with them. And consequently, as they abide mutually in one another incomprehensibly, so also immutably [variant: incomparably], they are truly and singularly one. Yet if anyone says that there is agreement between Father and Son, I do not dispute, provided that he understands not a union of wills but the unity of will.]

10. But with God and man, since they exist and differ in their own wills and substances, we perceive that each abides in the other quite differently: that is, not confused in substances but harmonious in wills. This union for them is communion of wills and agreement in love. It is a happy union if you experience it; it is no union at all if you compare it with the other. The voice of one who has experienced it: “But for me it is good to cleave to God” (Ps. 72:28). It is plainly good if you cleave in every respect. Who cleaves perfectly to God except one who, abiding in God as beloved by God, has nevertheless drawn God into himself in return by loving him? Therefore, when man and God cleave to each other on every side—for they cleave on every side, joined inwardly to each other through mutual love—I would without hesitation say that God is in man and man in God. Yet man is in God from eternity, as loved from eternity, if he is among those who say that God “loved us and bestowed grace upon us in his beloved Son before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:6, 4); but God is in man from the time when he is loved by man. And if this is so, man is in God even when God is not in man; but God is not in a man who is not in God. For one who is not loved cannot abide in love, even if perhaps for a time he loves; but one who is loved may not yet love. Otherwise, how will this stand: “He first loved us” (1 John 4:10)? But when the one previously loved now also loves, both man is in God and God in man. One who never loves, however, plainly was never loved; and therefore neither is he in God nor God in him. Let these things be said to establish the difference between that connection by which Father and Son are one and that by which a soul cleaving to God is one spirit, lest perhaps, because it is read of a human being abiding in love that he abides in God and God in him, and likewise of the Son that he is in the Father and the Father in him, the adopted person’s prerogative should be thought equal to that of the Only-begotten.

11. With these matters concluded, we must return to him who feeds among lilies, because our digression began there and has extended thus far. Whether it was not without purpose, you shall judge. I had already proposed two interpretations of the passage: either that he who is virtue and whiteness feeds upon the virtues of those made white; or that he receives sinners into repentance in his body, which is the Church—sinners to incorporate whom, he who committed no sin made himself sin, so that the body of sin, to which sinners had once been joined, might be destroyed, and that they, justified freely in him, might become righteousness.

12. I add a third interpretation which occurs to me [in other copies: “I add a third which occurs”]; and I think it sufficient not only for the explanation of the passage but also for the end of the sermon. The Word of God is truth, and he himself is the Bridegroom. You know this; hear the rest. When he is heard yet not obeyed, he remains in some manner empty and hungry for the time being, altogether sad and complaining that he has been uttered in vain. But if he is obeyed, will the word not seem to you to have grown into a certain fullness of body, because a deed has been added to the word—as though refreshed by certain fruits of obedience, the fruits of righteousness? Hence he says in the Apocalypse: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I will enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3:20). This interpretation also seems approved by the Lord’s statement in the Prophet, where he says that his word “shall not return to him empty, but shall prosper and accomplish the purposes for which he sent it” (Isa. 55:12). “It shall not return to me,” he says, “empty or hungry; rather, as though acting prosperously in all things, it shall be satisfied by the good deeds of those who rest in it through love.” Finally, in ordinary speech a word is said to be fulfilled when it has been committed to effect; that is, so long as it is not completed in deed, it is empty and lean, and in a certain manner hungry.

13. But hear with what food he says that he is nourished. “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34). The Word’s word plainly declares that a good deed is his food, provided he finds it among lilies—that is, among virtues. Otherwise, if he finds it outside them, although the food in itself seems good, he who feeds among lilies will not touch it. For example, he does not receive alms from the hand of a robber or moneylender; nor from that of a hypocrite who, when he gives alms, has a trumpet sounded before him so as to be glorified by men. Nor will he in any way answer the prayer of one who loves to pray at the street corners so that he may be seen by men (Matt. 6:2, 5). Indeed, “the prayer of the sinner shall be abominable” (Prov. 28:9). In vain likewise does he offer his gift at the altar who knows that his brother has something against him (Matt. 5:23–24). Finally, God did not regard Cain’s gifts (Gen. 4:5), because he did not walk rightly with his brother. The holy Prophet testifies that God also abhorred the Sabbaths, new moons, and sacrifices of the Jews, so that he openly declared that his soul hated them, saying: “When you came before my presence, who required these things from your hands?” I believe those hands did not smell of lilies; therefore he who is accustomed to feed among lilies and not among thorns rejected their gift. Why should they not have had thorny hands, when he said to them: “Your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1:13–15)? And Esau’s hands were hairy, like thorns; therefore they were not admitted to minister to the Holy One.

14. I fear that there may be some among us whose gifts the Bridegroom does not accept because they do not smell of lilies. For if on the day of my fast my own will is found, the Bridegroom has not chosen such a fast; nor does my fast taste good to him, because it tastes not of the lily of obedience but of the vice of self-will. I mean this not only concerning fasting, but concerning silence, vigils, prayer, reading, manual work, and finally every observance of a monk: wherever one’s own will is found in it rather than obedience to one’s master, I judge the matter in the same way. I would by no means count such observances, although good in themselves, as reckoned among lilies—that is, among virtues. Rather, one of this kind will hear from the Prophet: “Is this the service that I have chosen, says the Lord?” And he will add: “On the day of your good things your own wills are found” (Isa. 58:3–5). Self-will is a great evil, by which it comes about that your good things are not good for you. Such things must therefore become lilies, because he who feeds among lilies will taste absolutely nothing that has been polluted by self-will. Wisdom “reaches everywhere because of her purity, and nothing defiled comes into her” (Wis. 7:24–25). Thus the Bridegroom loves to feed among lilies, that is, among pure and bright hearts. But how long? “Until the day breathes and the shadows decline.” This is a shady and dense place; let us not enter this forest of profound mystery except in the clear light of day. For as I have continued my discussion too long, the day has declined, while we are unwillingly drawn away from these lilies. Nor have I been overcome by prolixity [variant: “Nor have I feared prolixity”], since the fragrance of the flowers removed all weariness. A little seems to remain of the present chapter; but that little is too deeply hidden, as are all the rest of this song. Yet he who reveals mysteries will be present, I trust, when we begin to knock; and he will not close himself against the mouths of those who speak, for it is more his custom to open what is shut: Jesus Christ our Lord, Bridegroom of the Church, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXII. What are the breathing day and the declining shadows? Then the various days of human beings are explained, and the fact that a brighter day awaits the righteous, who live in light, while eternal night awaits the wicked, who occupy themselves with works of darkness.

1. “My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline” (Song 2:16–17). Only the final part of this chapter remains to be treated, and at the very outset I doubt to which of the two preceding clauses I should join it most properly; for I may connect it equally with either. For whether you say, “My beloved is mine and I am his until the day breathes and the shadows decline,” merely inserting, “who feeds among lilies”; or, following the order of the text, “who feeds among lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline,” either construction may suitably be assigned. This, however, makes a difference: if you connect “until” with the first clause, you must understand it inclusively; if with the middle clause, you must understand it exclusively. Suppose, then, that the Bridegroom is signified as feeding among lilies when the day has breathed: will he likewise cease to attend to the Bride, or she to him? Far from it! They will remain with each other forever, except that then more happily, because more intensely; and more intensely, because more freely. Therefore let this “until” be like that in Matthew, where Joseph is said not to have known Mary “until she bore her firstborn Son” (Matt. 1:25): for he did not know her afterward either. Or let it be like that in the Psalm: “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God until he has mercy on us” (Ps. 122:2): for they will not turn away when he begins to have mercy. Or again like the Lord’s saying to the apostles: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20): for afterward he will not cease to be with them. But this is so if you refer “until” to “my beloved is mine, and I am his.” If, however, you prefer it to refer to “who feeds among lilies,” it must be understood in another sense. It will require more effort to show how the Beloved ceases to feed when the day has breathed. For if this is the day of resurrection, why would it not be much more pleasant there to feed among lilies, where their abundance will be far greater? Let these things be said for adapting the sense to the sequence of the text.

2. Now observe with me that, although the whole kingdom is radiant with lilies [Col. 1129C], and the Bridegroom is present in its midst and delights there, nevertheless there will no longer be occasion for him to be said to feed, as he formerly used to do. For where then will be sinners for Christ to incorporate into himself—tamed and as it were bitten by certain teeth of stricter discipline, namely affliction of the flesh and contrition of heart? Nor will the Bridegroom Word then require food for himself from acts or works of obedience, where all activity will be repose, and the whole matter will consist solely in contemplation and love. To be sure, his food is to do the will of his Father; but that belongs here, not there. For what is there to do when it has already been done? And it is certain that then it will be perfect. Finally, it is then for all the saints to prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God. And certainly, after perfection, nothing remains to be done. [Col. 1129D] Henceforth there remains enjoyment, not doing; experience, not labor; living in these things, not being exercised in them. Is not this the very will which, taught indeed by the Lord, we ask in most earnest prayer to be fulfilled on earth as in heaven (Matt. 6:10), so that its fruit may then delight us and its performance not weary us? Therefore the Bridegroom Word will have no food of work, because every work must cease where wisdom is more fully received by all. For “those who are diminished in action receive it” (Ecclus. 38:25).

3. But let us now see whether what we say can stand also according to that interpretation by which some understand feeding among lilies to mean delight in the bright array of virtues; for we too did not pass over this interpretation among the others. Shall we say either that virtues will not then exist, or that they will in no way taste sweet to the Bridegroom? To think [Col. 1130A] either is madness. But perhaps he will delight in them otherwise; for it is certain that he delights in them, perhaps rather by drinking than by feeding. Certainly, in this present time and body, none of our virtues will be so wholly purified, none so sweet and unmixed, as to be fit for the Bridegroom to drink. But he who wills all people to be saved overlooks much; and from that which meanwhile he cannot swallow with the ease of drinking, he takes care to draw out at least something savory, as if by a certain skill and labor of chewing. The time will come when virtue will be drinkable: it will not be pressed by the tooth or weary the one who chews—or rather, it will not weary the chewer—but will delight the drinker without labor, as a drink and not food. Finally, you have the promise in the Gospel: “I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine,” he says, “until I drink [Col. 1130B] it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 26:29). There is no mention of food. But in the Prophet likewise one reads: “Like a mighty man made drunk with wine” (Ps. 77:65); and there too nothing whatsoever is found concerning food.

The Bride, therefore, knowing this mystery, when she had learned and declared that her Beloved feeds among the lilies, set the limit until which he would deign to do so—or rather, recognized the limit already set and declared it—saying: “Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” For she knew that afterward he would drink the virtues rather than feed upon them. The custom also seems to agree [variant: *convenire*, “to agree”] which ordinarily has drink taken after food. Therefore, he who eats here will drink there, swallowing then all the more sweetly because more securely even those very things which he now dissolves more scrupulously and, in a sense, more laboriously [Col. 1130C], as though by chewing.

4. Let us now apply ourselves to considering that day and its shadows: what the one is, what the others are; on what grounds that day is said to breathe toward us, and by what power these shadows are able to incline. It is certainly significant that it is said, “until the day breathes toward,” indeed, that it is said in the singular. For only in this passage, unless I am mistaken, will you find a day said to breathe toward. Breezes, not times, are said to breathe. A human being breathes; other animals breathe, to which air, constantly drawn in and out, sustains life. And what is this but wind? The Holy Spirit also breathes, and is therefore Spirit. In what manner, then, can a day breathe, since it is neither wind nor spirit nor animal? Yet it is not even called simply “breathing,” but, more significantly, “breathing toward.” No less unusual [Col. 1130D] is the expression, “and the shadows incline.” For at the rising of this bodily and visible light, shadows do not incline but vanish. These realities, therefore, must be sought outside bodies. And if we find a spiritual day and spiritual shadows, perhaps then both their inclination and its breathing toward will more readily become clear.

Whoever thinks that the day of which the Prophet says, “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11), is bodily, I do not know what he will not think bodily. There is also a day in an evil sense, which the prophets cursed (Job 3:3; Jer. 20:14). But far be it from us to suppose it among these visible things made by the Lord! It is therefore spiritual.

5. And who can doubt that the shadow is spiritual by which Mary was overshadowed when conceiving (Luke 1:35); and likewise that shadow mentioned thus in the prophet: “The breath before our face, Christ the Lord, under whose shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lam. 4:20)? Yet by the name of shadows in this place I think rather that the contrary powers are designated, which are called by the Apostle not only shadows or darknesses, but also “rulers of this darkness” (Eph. 6:12), together with those of our race who cling to them—namely, children of night and not of light or day. These shadows, indeed, when the day breathes toward us, will not altogether return to nothing, as we see bodily shadows not merely disappear but utterly perish before this bodily light. They will indeed exist—not as something more utterly nothing, but in a more wretched state. 1521 They will exist, but bowed down and subjected. Finally: “He shall bow down,” it says, “and fall” [Col. 1131B] (without doubt the prince of shadows), “when he has ruled over the poor” (Ps. 9:10). Therefore nature will not be destroyed, but power removed; substance will not perish, but the hour and power of darkness will pass away. They are removed lest they see the glory of God; they are not annihilated, that they may burn forever. Why should the shadows not incline, when the mighty are cast down from their seats and are made a footstool for the feet? (Rom. 13:12.) This must surely happen soon. It is the last hour; the night has passed, but the day has drawn near. The day will breathe toward us, and the night will breathe out its last.

The devil is night; the angel of Satan is night, even if he transforms himself into an angel of light. Antichrist likewise is night, whom the Lord will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming [Col. 1131C] (2 Thess. 2:8). Is not the Lord day? Certainly, a day that enlightens and breathes, who by the breath of his mouth drives away shadows and by the brightness of his coming destroys phantoms.

Or, if one prefers to take the word “inclination” simply, and to think that to incline means nothing other than to be annihilated, let us not fail even this interpretation. We say that the shadows are the figures and enigmas of Scripture, as well as sophistical forms of speech, verbal quibbles, and tangled arguments—all of which meanwhile overshadow the light of truth. “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.” But when the day breathes toward us, the shadows will incline, because, when the fullness of light occupies all things, no part of darkness can remain. Finally, “when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part shall be done away” [Col. 1131D] (1 Cor. 13:9–10).

6. Thus far this might have sufficed concerning these matters, if that day had been called “breathing” and not “breathing toward.” But now, though it is a slight addition, I think something further must be added in order to investigate the reason for this difference. For, to tell the truth, I have long been persuaded that in the text of sacred and precious speech not even the smallest particle is without significance. We commonly use this expression when we vehemently desire something; for example, when we say, “He aspires to that honor or that dignity.” By this word, therefore, is indicated the wondrous abundance and vehemence of spirit to come on that day, when not only hearts but bodies too will be spiritual in their own kind; and those found worthy will be inebriated by [Col. 1132A] the abundance of the Lord’s house and given drink from the torrent of his delight.

7. Or otherwise. The sanctified day has already dawned upon the holy angels, breathing upon them, with the unceasing force of an everlasting flow, the honey-sweet mysteries of eternal divinity. Finally, “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5); but it is the city to which it is said: “In you is the dwelling of all who rejoice” (Ps. 86:7). But when it adds breathing toward us also, who inhabit the earth, it will be not merely breathing, but breathing toward, because, with its bosom enlarged, it will receive us too.

Or, to begin somewhat higher and speak more fully: when humanity had been formed from the mud of the earth, the Creator, as truthful history relates, breathed into its face the breath of life (Gen. 2:7), and thus became for it a day breathing into it. And behold: the envious [Col. 1132B] night craftily dashed itself against this day with counterfeit light. For while it promised, as it were, a brighter light of knowledge, it poured the unforeseen darkness of a perverse counsel upon the new light, and at the beginnings of our origin introduced the black gloom of ruinous transgression. Alas, alas! They did not know, nor did they understand; they walk in darkness, not knowing, making darkness light and light darkness. Finally, the woman ate from the tree which the serpent had given her and God had forbidden; and she gave to her husband, and it began, as it were, to grow light for them anew. For immediately the eyes of both were opened, and the day became a day conspiring, driving out the day breathing into them and substituting one breathing out.

For the serpent’s cunning, the woman’s allurements, and the man’s weakness conspired and came together as one against the Lord and against his Christ [Col. 1132C]. Hence too the Lord and his Christ spoke to one another: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. 3), because Adam had yielded, to the injury of both, to sinners glorying in themselves.

8. In this day we are all born. For we all bear impressed upon us the brand of that ancient conspiracy; 1522 Eve, that is, lives in our flesh, and through hereditary concupiscence the serpent labors with diligent solicitude to claim our consent for his own faction.
