Therefore, as I said, the saints cursed this day, desiring it to be brief and quickly turned into darkness (Job 3:3; Jer. 20:14), because it is a day of strife and contradiction: in it the flesh does not cease to desire against the spirit, [Col. 1132D] and the law contrary to the law of the mind continually resists in the members with tireless rebellion. Thus it became a day breathing out. For from then onward, “what human being shall live and not see death?” (Ps. 88:49).

Let someone say that this was done in wrath; I think it no less an act of mercy, lest the elect, for whose sake all things are done, be long wearied by the troublesome contradiction through which they too are led captive under the law of sin that is in their members. They shudder at and endure with great distress this shameful captivity and mournful conflict.

9. Let us therefore hasten to breathe again from the ancient and wicked conspiracy, because the days of humanity are short (Job 14:5). Let the day that restores breath receive us before the sighing night swallows us up, to be wrapped in the outer darkness of everlasting gloom. You ask in what this recovery of breath consists. It consists in this: that the spirit should in turn begin to desire against the flesh. If you resist the flesh, you breathe again; if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you have breathed again; if you crucify it with its vices and desires, you have breathed again. “I chastise my body,” he says, “and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9:27). This is the voice of one breathing again—indeed, of one who had already breathed again. “Go, and do likewise” (Luke 10:37), that you may prove that you have breathed again, that you may know that the day once more breathing into you has dawned for you.

Nor will the night of death prevail against this revived day; rather, “the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” So far from thinking that the light of life yields even when life departs, I judge that to no one is the saying more fittingly assigned [Col. 1133B] than to one who dies thus: “And night shall be my illumination in my delights” (Ps. 138:11). Why should he not see more clearly, freed from the cloud—or rather, the dregs—of the body? Without doubt, released from bodily bonds, he will be free among the dead and seeing among the blind. For just as once, while every eye was darkened throughout all Egypt, the people who saw God—that is, the people Israel—alone saw clearly amid the darkness, Scripture saying that wherever Israel was, there was light (Exod. 10:23), so among the children of darkness the righteous will shine in the black gloom of death and will see, indeed all the more clearly because they have put off the shadows of bodies.

But those who did not first breathe again—for they did not seek the light of the day breathing into them, and the sun of righteousness did not rise for them—these, I say, will go from darkness [Col. 1133C] into denser darkness, so that those who are in darkness may become still darker, while those who see may see more.

10. Here perhaps the saying of the Lord may fittingly be brought forward: “To the one who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have shall be taken away from him” (Luke 19:26). So it is: at death more is added to those who see, and taken away from those who do not see. For the more and more these latter see less, the more and more the former see, until the sighing night receives the one group and the day breathing toward them receives the other. These are the final states of each: utter blindness and supreme brightness. From this point there is nothing at all left to be taken from those entirely empty, nor anything to be added to those full—except that the latter, in accordance with the promise made to them, expect to receive something beyond fullness itself [Col. 1133D].

And the word of promise is this: “They shall give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing” (Luke 6:38). Does not that which overflows seem in some sense to you to be more than full? Moreover, you will readily understand “full” and “more full” if you remember having read: “Forever and beyond” (Exod. 15:18). Therefore this overflowing abundance will belong to the day breathing toward us. It, I say, will add to the measure of inspired fullness, to the abundance of the day breathing into us, producing beyond measure an exalted weight of glory, so that the overflowing addition of glorification may spill over into the bodies. For this reason it is called not “breathing,” but “breathing toward”: by the added preposition *ad* (“toward”), the Holy Spirit signifies that those whom the former [Col. 1134A] illuminates within, the latter adorns without and clothes in a robe of glory.

1523 11. And this is enough to explain the term “breathing toward.” If you wish to know, the day breathing toward us is the Savior himself whom we await, “who will refashion the body of our humiliation, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20–21). For he is likewise the one breathing into us, according to the operation by which he first makes us breathe again in the light that he breathes into us, so that we too may be a day breathing again in him, insofar as “our inward human being is renewed day by day” and is renewed in the spirit of its mind according to the image of him who created it—thus becoming day from day and light from light.

Therefore, since three days precede in us: one breathing into us [Col. 1134B] for the life of the body; another breathing again in the grace of sanctification; and a third, still to come, breathing toward us in the glory of resurrection—it is plainly evident that what preceded in the head will someday be fulfilled in the body: namely, the great mystery of godliness and the testimony of the prophet, who says: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight. We shall know and follow on, that we may know the Lord” (Hos. 6:3). He is the one into whom angels desire to look, the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXIII. How Christ will come to judge in human form, so that he may appear gracious to the elect; and how he is both less than the angels and higher than they.

[Col. 1134C]

1. “Return; be like a roe or a fawn of stags, my Beloved” (Song 2:17). What? He is just going, and now you call him back? What suddenly arose in so brief a time? Have you forgotten something? Yes: she has forgotten everything that is not he—and herself as well. For although she is not devoid of reason, yet now, as it seems, she is not in command of her reason. Nor does any modesty at all appear in her behavior, though perhaps she has it in her manners. Unrestrained love does this. For it triumphs and takes captive within itself every sense of shame, the measure of propriety, the counsel of deliberation, and produces a certain neglect and carelessness toward all modesty and timeliness.

See now how, while he has scarcely begun to go, she nevertheless already begs him to return [Col. 1134D]. She even asks him to hasten—indeed, to run like some swiftly running beast of the woods, for example a roe or a fawn of stags. Such is the literal sequence, and such is the Jews’ portion.

2. But I, according to what I have received from the Lord, shall seek out for myself spirit and life in the deep bosom of sacred speech; and this is my portion, because I believe in Christ. Why should I not draw forth from the barren and tasteless letter a sweet and health-giving banquet of the Spirit, as grain from chaff, the kernel from its shell, marrow from bone? I have nothing to do with this letter, which when tasted savors of flesh and when swallowed brings death; rather, what lies hidden in it belongs to the Holy Spirit. And “the Spirit speaks mysteries,” as the Apostle testifies (1 Cor. 14:2); but Israel, in place of the mystery’s veil being removed, retains the veil of the mystery itself. Why, except because a veil still lies over its heart? Thus what the letter sounds is theirs; what it signifies [variant: *designat*, “designates”] is mine. Accordingly, for them it is a ministry of death in the letter, but for me life in the Spirit. For “the Spirit is what gives life” (John 6:64): it gives understanding. Is not understanding life? “Give me understanding, and I shall live,” says the Prophet to the Lord.

Understanding does not remain outside; it does not cling to the surface or, like a blind person, grope external things. Rather, it searches the depths, accustomed to seize and carry away for itself with all eagerness the most precious spoils of truth found there, and to say with the Prophet to the Lord: “I will rejoice over your words, as one who finds great spoil” (Ps. 118:144, 162). Thus the kingdom of truth suffers violence, and the violent seize it [Col. 1135B] (Matt. 11:12). But that elder brother, who came from the field and prefigured the old and earthly people, who, for the sake of an earthly inheritance, learned to love threshing, groans anxiously with his brow worn down beneath the heavy yoke of the Law and bears the burden of the day and its heat. Because he did not have understanding, he, I say, still stands outside and refuses, even when invited by his father, to enter the house of feasting, depriving himself even now of participation in the music, the dancing, and the fatted calf (Luke 15:25–30). Wretched man, who refuses to experience how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity. Let this be said to distinguish the portion of the Church from that of the Synagogue, so that the blindness of the latter may become clearer from the wisdom of the former, and the blessedness of the former may stand forth against the pitiable folly of the latter.

[Col. 1135C] 3. Let us now examine the Bride’s words, and endeavor to express the chaste affections of holy love in such a way that nothing in sacred speech may appear utterly devoid of reason, unbecoming, or untimely. And if there comes to mind that hour when the Lord Jesus—for he is the Bridegroom—was passing from this world to the Father (John 13:1), and at the same time what that household Church of his, newly wed, felt when it saw itself abandoned as a desolate widow by its sole hope—I mean the apostles, who had left all things and followed him, and had remained with him in his temptations—if, I say, we consider these things, it will, I think, seem neither undeserved nor incongruous that, as she was sorrowful at his departure, so she was anxious [Col. 1135D] for his return, especially being so devoted and so left.

Accordingly, this twofold consideration—love and need—gave her reason to remind the Beloved: since he could not be persuaded not to go and ascend where he was before, he should at least hasten anew his promised coming. Her desire and request that he be like swift-moving beasts, especially beasts that seem more agile in running, reveals a longing heart to which nothing can come quickly enough. Does she not ask this daily when she says in prayer, “May your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10)?

4. Yet beyond agility, I think no less significantly is expressed weakness: that of sex in the roe, that of age in the fawn. She wishes him, therefore, as it seems to me, though he comes with power, not to appear in judgment in the form of God, but indeed in that form in which he was not only born for us, but born a little child for us—and that solely from the weaker female sex. Why this? Certainly so that he may be reminded by both forms of weakness to become gentle on the day of wrath and remember in judgment that mercy triumphs over judgment. For if he marks iniquities, who, even among the elect, can endure it? (Ps. 129:3.) The stars are not clean in his sight, and he finds perversity even in his angels (Job 4:18). Hear, finally, what a holy and elect person says to God: “You,” he says, “have forgiven the impiety of my sin. Therefore every holy person shall pray to you at an opportune time” (Ps. 31:5–6). Thus even the saints need to pray concerning their sins, that they may be saved by mercy, not trusting in their own righteousness. For all have sinned, and all need mercy [variant adds: “of God”]. [Col. 1136B] Therefore, so that when he is angry he may remember mercy, she asks him to appear clothed in mercy, in that attire of which the Apostle says: “And being found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:7).

5. Necessarily so. For if, even with this moderation, there will be such equity in the judgment, such ferocity in the Judge, such sublimity in majesty, such novelty in the very appearance of things that, according to the prophet, “the day of his coming cannot be conceived” (Mal. 3:2), what, do you think, would happen if that consuming fire—I mean almighty God—came in the greatness, strength, and purity of his divinity, displaying his power against a leaf carried by the wind and pursuing dry stubble? (Job 13:25.) “And he is a man,” it says, “and who shall see him? And who shall stand to behold him?” [Col. 1136C] (Mal. 3:2). How much more could no human being endure God presenting himself to us without humanity: inaccessible in brightness, unattainable in height, incomprehensible in majesty?

But now, when “his wrath is kindled in a short time” (Ps. 2:13), how welcome, on account of the children of grace, will be that gentle vision of a human being: indeed, a foundation for faith, strength for hope, and increase of confidence, since “grace and mercy are upon his saints, and regard for his elect” (Wis. 4:15). Finally, God the Father himself gave the Son authority to judge, not because he is his Son, but because he is the Son of Man (John 5:27). O truly Father of mercies! He wills that human beings be judged by a human being, so that amid such trembling and confusion [Col. 1136D] at the evils, likeness of nature may give the elect confidence.

Holy David long ago foretold this, praying and prophesying together: “O God,” he says, “give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:2). Nor does the promise made through the angels disagree with this. When he had been taken up, they spoke thus to the apostles: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same manner as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11)—that is, in this very form and substance of body.

6. From all this it is clear that the Bride possesses within herself divine counsel and is by no means ignorant of the mystery of the heavenly will. Under the image of weak and feeble animals, she declares, both in the affection of one praying and the Spirit of one prophesying, that the weaker—or rather lower, because it will no longer be weak—nature is to be displayed in judgment, so that he who will shake heaven and earth in his power, girded with power against the senseless, may nevertheless appear gentle and mild, and as if altogether unarmed, for the elect. Here one may also add that, in order to distinguish one group from another, he will in some fashion need the leaps of the fawn and the sight of the roe, so that amid such a multitude and disturbance he may see and discern upon whom he ought to leap and whom he ought to leap over, lest perhaps the righteous be trampled together with the wicked when he crushes peoples in wrath.

For with respect to the wicked, David’s prophecy must be fulfilled—indeed, the Lord’s own word spoken through David’s mouth: “I shall crush them as dust before the face of the wind; I shall wipe them away as the mud of the streets” [Col. 1137B] (Ps. 17:43). Likewise another saying, foretold through another prophet, will then be known to have been fulfilled, when, turning to the angels, he says: “I have trodden them in my fury and trampled them in my wrath” (Isa. 63:3).

7. But if anyone thinks it more correct to understand that our fawn ought rather to leap over the evil and leap upon the good, I do not dispute it. Let him only consider that these leaps will be arranged for the separation of good and evil. For I too, if I remember correctly, said this in another sermon, where the same chapter appears earlier, having been set forth elsewhere by the author and likewise expounded by me (above, Sermon 54). But there, according to the dispensation of grace—which in the present life is given to some and not given to others, by God’s just though hidden judgment—the fawn was said to leap and leap over. Here, however, it is according to the final and diverse recompense of merits.

And perhaps the final phrase of this chapter, which I had almost forgotten, seems to support this sense. For after saying, “Be like a roe and a fawn of stags, my Beloved,” she adds, “upon the mountains of Bethel.” Now there are no evil mountains in the house of God, which is what Bethel means. Therefore, when the fawn leaps upon them, he does not trample them but gladdens them, so that the Scripture may be fulfilled which says: “Mountains and hills shall sing praises before God” (Isa. 55:12). There are indeed mountains which faith compared to a mustard seed removes, according to the Gospel (Matt. 17:19), but they are not mountains of Bethel. For whatever are Bethel, faith does not remove them but cultivates them.

[Col. 1137D] 8. But if principalities and powers, together with the other ranks of blessed spirits and the powers of heaven, are mountains of Bethel, so that we understand the saying, “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86:1), to refer to them, then this fawn is certainly not lowly and contemptible, who appeared upon mountains so lofty, having become so much better than the angels as he inherited a name more excellent than theirs (Heb. 1:4). For what if we read in the psalm that he was made lower than the angels? (Ps. 8:6.) He is not therefore not better because he was made lower; nor have the Apostle and Prophet spoken contrary things, since they have the same Spirit.

For if his being made lower was an act of condescension, it was not a necessity; nothing is detracted from goodness thereby, but something is attributed to it. Finally, the Prophet says that he was “made lower,” not “less,” exalting grace and repelling dishonor. For nature rejects inferiority, while the cause excuses being made lower. He was made lower because he himself willed it: he was made lower by his own will and through our necessity. To be made lower in this way was to show mercy. What loss is this? Surely whatever majesty seemed to lose accrued to compassion. Nor did the Apostle keep silent about this great secret of great mercy, but says: “We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Heb. 2:9).

[Col. 1138B] 9. We have said these things concerning the name and likeness of the fawn, in order that we might fittingly apply it to the Bridegroom in accordance with the Bride’s words without injury to majesty. Why do I say, “without injury to majesty,” when even weakness did not remain without honor? He is a fawn; he is little; he is also said to be like a roe, as one born of a woman. Yet he is upon the mountains of Bethel; yet he has “become higher than the heavens” (Heb. 7:26). It does not say, “being higher than the heavens” [Note: In all manuscripts and in the first printed editions, *ens* (“being”) is read here; in Horstius and others, *manens* (“remaining”). Thus *ens* occurs in Sermon 75, no. 11, where the printed editions have *sedens* (“sitting”) in its place. Here, however, a little later, manuscripts too read *manens* or *existens* (“existing”).] or “existing,” but “having become higher than the heavens,” lest anyone think this was said of that nature in which he is “the One who is.” Likewise, where he is preferred to angels, he is nevertheless said to have “become better,” and is not said to remain or exist better.

From this it is clear that not only in that which he is from eternity, but also in that which he became in time, he claims for himself every preeminence [Col. 1138C] above every principality and power, indeed above every creature, as the firstborn of every creature. Therefore “what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:25). This, indeed, is the Apostle’s statement. But I do not think one errs if one says that even God’s foolishness and weakness are in every respect to be preferred to the wisdom and strength of angels. Thus the present passage will fittingly be applied to the universal Church.

10. But as regards one individual soul—for even one soul is a bride if it loves God sweetly, wisely, and vehemently—any spiritual person can perceive within himself what particular answer his own experience gives him. As for me, I shall not be ashamed to speak openly whatever it is that has been granted me to experience in such matters. For even if, when heard, it perhaps seems trivial and contemptible, that does not concern me: whoever is spiritual will not despise me; whoever is less so will not understand me. Yet if I reserve this for another sermon, perhaps there will be those who are edified by what the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, entreated in the meantime, will inspire—he who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXIV. Concerning the visits of the Bridegroom Word: how secretly they take place in the holy soul; and how Bernard, by his own example, humbly and modestly declares this for the edification of his followers.

[Col. 1139A]

1. “Return,” she says (Song 2:17). It is clear that the one she calls back is not present, yet that he was present, and not long before; for while he is still going away, he seems to be called back. Such untimely recall indicates one person’s great love and the other’s great loveliness. Who are these cultivators of charity and such tireless pursuers of this loving business, one of whom love follows and the other it presses so restlessly? It falls to me, as I remember my promise, to assign this passage to the Word and the soul; but I confess that, in order to do this worthily, even in some small measure, I need the help of the Word himself.

Indeed, this sermon would have suited one more experienced and more conscious of holy and hidden love. But I cannot fail in my duty or wholly disappoint your wishes. I see my danger and do not avoid it; you compel me. You positively compel me to walk amid things great and wonderful beyond me. Alas! How I fear that I may presently hear: “Why do you recount my delights and take my covenant into your mouth?” Yet hear me—a man who trembles to speak and cannot be silent. Perhaps this very trembling of mine will excuse my boldness; still more will your edification, if it results. And perhaps these tears too will be seen as an excuse.

“Return,” she says. Well: he was going away, and he is called back. Who will disclose to me the mystery of this changeability? Who will worthily explain the going and returning of the Word? Does the Bridegroom act from fickleness? From where and to where could he come, or go again, who fills all things? What local movement could one have who is spirit? Or finally, what movement of any kind can you ascribe to one who is God? For he is altogether unchangeable.

2. But let the one who can receive this receive it. As for us, walking cautiously and simply in the exposition of sacred and mystical speech, let us follow the practice of Scripture, which speaks in our words of wisdom hidden in mystery; which, by depicting God through our affections, makes him known; which offers to human minds the precious, unknown, and invisible things of God in familiar likenesses of sensible things, as in cups made of humbler material. Let us therefore follow the custom of pure speech as well, and call the Word of God the Bridegroom of the soul, insofar as he wills both to come to the soul and again to leave it—provided only that we understand these things to occur by a movement of the soul’s perception, not by a movement of the Word.

For example, when the soul feels grace, it recognizes his presence; when it does not, it laments his absence and seeks his presence again, saying with the Prophet: “My face has sought you; your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. 26:8). Why should it not seek? For when so sweet a Bridegroom has withdrawn himself, it will meanwhile be pleased not merely to desire nothing else, but not even to think of anything else. It remains, then, for the soul diligently to seek the absent one and call back the one who is departing. Thus the Word is called back; he is called back by the soul’s desire, but by the desire of that soul to which he has once granted the sweetness of himself. Is not desire a voice? And a powerful one. Finally: “The Lord has heard,” it says, “the desire of the poor” (Ps. 9:17). Therefore, while the Word is departing, the soul has one unbroken and continuous voice—its continuous desire—as though one continuous and unceasing “Return,” until he comes.

3. And now give me a soul which the Word, its Bridegroom, is accustomed frequently to visit—a soul to which familiarity has given boldness, taste hunger, and contempt for all things leisure; and I shall unhesitatingly assign to such a one both the voice and the name of bride, nor shall I judge the passage now before us altogether foreign to her. For such a woman is here represented as speaking. For the one whom she calls back, she plainly shows that she has deserved his presence, though not its abundance. Otherwise she would not have recalled him, but called him. Now the word of recall is “Return.”

[Col. 1140B] And perhaps he withdrew precisely in order to be recalled more eagerly and held more firmly. For at times he also pretended that he was going farther, not because he wished this, but because he wished to hear, “Stay with us, Lord, for evening is drawing on” (Luke 24:28–29). And again, on another occasion, walking upon the sea while the apostles were sailing and labouring at the oars, he acted as though he wished to pass them by; yet even then he did not wish that, but rather wished to test their faith and draw forth their prayer. Finally, as the Evangelist says, “They were troubled and cried out, thinking that it was a phantom” (Mark 6:48–49).

Therefore, the Word who is spirit, in his spiritual manner, does not cease repeatedly [Col. 1140C] to enact with a soul devoted to him the same pious pretence—or rather, salutary dispensation—which the Word made flesh sometimes displayed bodily. Passing by, he wishes to be detained; departing, to be recalled. For this Word is not irrevocable. He goes and returns according to his good pleasure, as one visiting at dawn and suddenly testing. His going is in a certain sense dispensatory; his return is always voluntary; yet both are full of judgment. The reason for them rests with him.

4. Now it is evident that such alternations of the departing and returning Word take place in the soul, as he says: “I go, and I come to you” (John 14:28); and again: “A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me” (John 16:17). O “a little while” and “a little while”! O long little while! Tell me, Lord, do you call it a little while that we shall not see you? May the word of my Lord stand: it is long—indeed, exceedingly long. Yet both are true: little with respect to merits, and long with respect to longing [variant: “not little with respect to longing”].

[Col. 1140D] You have both in the prophet: “If he delays, wait for him; for he will surely come and will not be late” (Hab. 2:3). How will he not be late, if he delays, unless because what is sufficient for merit is not sufficient for longing? The loving soul is borne onward by its desires, 1528 drawn by its longings; it disregards merits, closes its eyes to majesty, opens them to delight, rests upon salvation, and acts confidently in it. Finally, fearless and unabashed, it calls the Word back and confidently demands again its delights, calling in its accustomed freedom not “Lord,” but “Beloved”: “Return, my beloved; and be like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bethel.” But of this later.

[Col. 1141A] 5. For now, bear with a little of my folly. I wish to say—for I have undertaken this also—how I am dealt with in such matters. It is not expedient, indeed. But I will certainly disclose myself so that I may be of use; and if you have made progress, I shall find consolation for my folly; if not, I shall confess my folly. I confess that the Word has come even to me—in folly, I say—and more than once. And though he has often entered into me, I have sometimes not felt him when he entered. I have felt him present; I remember that he has been present; sometimes I have even been able to foresee his entrance; but I have never felt it, nor indeed even his departure. For I confess that I still do not know whence he came into my soul, or whither he went when he again left it; nor by what way he entered or departed, according to that saying: “You do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3:8).

Nor is this surprising, since he is the one to whom it was said: “Your footsteps shall not be known” (Ps. 76:20). Certainly, he did not enter through the eyes, for he has no colour; nor through the ears, for he made no sound; nor through the nostrils, for he does not mingle with the air but with the mind; nor did he infect the air, but made it. Nor indeed did he enter through the throat, for he is not chewed or swallowed; nor did I discover him by touch, for he is not tangible. By what way, then, did he enter? Or perhaps he did not enter at all, since he did not come from outside. For he is not one of those things that are outside.

[Col. 1141B] Yet neither did he come from within me, since he is good, and I know that no good is in me. I ascended even above my higher self, and behold, I found the Word towering above it. Curious investigator that I was, I also descended to my lower self, and found him nonetheless below it. If I looked outward, I found him beyond all that was exterior to me; if inward, he was more inward still.

[Col. 1141C] And I knew that what I had read was true: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). But blessed is the person in whom he is: the one who lives for him and is moved by him.

6. You ask, then, since his ways are altogether unsearchable, how I know that he is present. He is living and effective; as soon as he comes within, he awakens my sleeping soul. He stirs, softens, and wounds my heart, because it was hard, stony, and in a bad state of health. He also begins to uproot and destroy, to build and plant; to water what is dry, illuminate what is dark, open what is shut, warm what is cold; and likewise to make crooked paths straight and rough places into level ways.

[Col. 1141D] Thus my soul blesses the Lord, and all that is within me blesses his holy name. Whenever the Word, the Bridegroom, enters me, he never makes his entrance known by any signs: not by voice, appearance, or step. In short, none of his motions made him known to me; none of my senses perceived him as he slipped into my inmost chambers. Only from the movement of my heart, as I have said, did I understand his presence; from the flight of vices and the restraint of carnal affections I observed the power of his virtue; from the scattering or rebuke of my hidden things I marvelled at the depth of his wisdom; from even the slightest improvement in my conduct I experienced the goodness of his gentleness; and from the renewal and reformation of the spirit of my mind—

[Col. 1142A] that is, of my inward person—I perceived, in some measure, the form of his beauty. Looking upon all these together, I was struck with awe at the multitude of his greatness.

7. But when the Word has withdrawn, all these things immediately begin to lie languid, numb, and cold, just as a boiling pot does when fire is removed from beneath it. This must necessarily be a sad sign of his departure for my soul, until he returns again and my heart grows warm within me as before; and that is the indication of his return. Since I have such experience of the Word, 1529 what wonder if I too claim for myself the bride’s voice in calling him back when he has made himself absent? For although I am carried by no equal longing, I am nevertheless carried by a similar longing, at least in part.

So long as I live, the word of recall—namely, “Return”—will be familiar to me for recalling the Word.

[Col. 1142B] Whenever he slips away, I shall repeat it; nor shall I cease to cry after the one who is departing, as though behind his back, with the burning desire of my heart, that he may return and restore to me the joy of his salvation, restore himself to me. I confess to you [variant: “I say to you”], children, that while that which alone pleases me is not present, nothing else pleases me at all. And this I pray: that he may come not empty, but “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), in his accustomed manner, as yesterday and the day before. In this I think that the likeness of the roe and the young hart may be displayed to me: for truth has the eyes of the roe, and grace the cheerfulness of the young hart.

8. Both are necessary to me: truth, indeed, from which I cannot hide; and grace, from which I would not wish to hide. Otherwise the visitation will not be complete without one or the other, since truth’s severity without grace may seem burdensome, and grace’s cheerfulness without truth lax. Truth without the seasoning of grace is bitter; while devotion itself, without truth’s bridle, is light, knows no measure, and is often insolent.

[Col. 1142C] How many have gained no benefit from receiving grace because they did not also receive the moderation supplied by truth! For this reason they took more pleasure in themselves than they ought through grace, because they did not fear truth’s gaze; they did not look to the roe’s maturity, but gave themselves wholly to the lightness and cheerfulness of the young hart. Hence it happened that they were deprived of the grace in which they had wished to exult privately. To them, even if late, it might be said: “Go and learn what this means: Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11).

For a certain holy soul had said in its abundance, “I shall never be moved”; but suddenly it felt the face of the Word turned away from it, and itself not merely moved but also troubled (Ps. 29:7–8). Thus in sorrow it learned that, along with the gift of devotion, it also needed the weight of truth. Therefore, fullness of grace is not in grace alone, nor even in truth alone. What use is it to know what you ought to do, if the will to do it is not also given? What if you are willing but wholly unable? How many have I found made sadder by acknowledged truth, and sadder especially because they could no longer flee to ignorance as an excuse—knowing, yet not doing what Truth urged them to do?

9. Since this is so, neither is sufficient without the other.

[Col. 1143A] I have said too little: neither is even advantageous without the other. How do we know this? “For the one who knows what is good and does not do it, it is sin” (James 4:17); likewise: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do what is worthy shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12:47). This concerns the side of truth. What of grace? It is written: “And after the morsel Satan entered into him” (John 13:27). This speaks of Judas, who, having received the gift of grace, gave the devil a place within himself because he did not walk in truth with the Master of truth—or rather, with Truth herself as mistress.

Listen further: “He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock.” Whom? “The enemies of the Lord lied to him” (Ps. 80:17, 16). Those whom he fed with honey and fat became his enemies and lied to him, because they did not join truth to grace. Of them elsewhere you have: “Foreign children lied to me; foreign children grew old and limped from their paths” (Ps. 17:46).

[Col. 1143B] Why should they not limp, content with one foot of grace and not adding truth? “Their time shall be for ever” (Ps. 80:16), as also that of their prince, who likewise “did not stand in the truth,” but “was a liar from the beginning” (John 8:44); and therefore heard: “You destroyed wisdom in your beauty” (Ezek. 28:17). I do not want beauty that takes wisdom from me.

10. You ask what beauty is so harmful and destructive? Your own. Are you perhaps still without understanding? Hear more plainly: private, personal beauty. We do not blame the gift, but its use. For, if you have noticed, he was said to have lost wisdom not in beauty but in *his own* beauty. And, unless I am mistaken, the beauty of an angel and of a soul is one and the same thing: wisdom itself.

[Col. 1143C] For what is either the one or the other without wisdom but raw and misshapen matter? By wisdom, therefore, he was not merely formed but made beautiful. Yet he lost it when he made it his own; so that to lose wisdom “in his own beauty” means nothing other than to lose wisdom in his own wisdom. Possessiveness is the cause. He was wise for himself; he did not give glory to God; he did not return grace for grace; he did not walk in it according to truth, but bent it to his own will. This is why he lost it—or rather, this is what lost it for him. For to possess it in that manner is to lose it.

“And if Abraham was justified by works,” it says, “he has glory, but not before God” (Rom. 4:2). And I say: I am not [variant: “therefore I am not”] secure. I have lost whatever I possess outside God.

[Col. 1143D] For what is so lost as that which lives in exile from God? What is death but deprivation of life? Thus nothing is loss but alienation from God. “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent before yourselves!” (Isa. 5:21). Of you it is said: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the prudent” (1 Cor. 1:19). They lost wisdom because their own wisdom lost them. What have those not lost who are themselves lost? Or are those not lost whom God does not know?

11. Moreover, the foolish virgins—whom I consider foolish for no other reason than that, “professing themselves wise, they became fools”—must hear from God: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Likewise those who appropriated the grace of miracles to their own glory will hear: “I never knew you” (Matt. 7:23).

[Col. 1144A] From these things it plainly appears that grace does not profit where truth is absent from one’s intention; indeed, it harms instead. Both things are in the Bridegroom’s keeping. For John the Baptist says: “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

If, therefore, the Lord Jesus Christ knocks at my door with either of these without the other—he is the Word of God, the Bridegroom of the soul—he will certainly enter not as Bridegroom but as Judge. Far be it! May this never happen. Let him not enter into judgment with his servant. Let him enter peacefully, pleasantly, and cheerfully; yet let him enter maturely and with gravity, so that by a certain sterner countenance of truth within me he may purify my joy while restraining insolence. Let him enter like a leaping young hart,

[Col. 1144B] like a watchful roe: passing over fault by overlooking it, looking upon punishment with pity. Let him enter as one descending from the mountains of Bethel, festive and radiant, and as one proceeding from the Father, sweet and gentle; let him not disdain to be called—and to become—the Bridegroom of the soul that seeks him, though he is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXV  
God must be sought at the fitting time, in the fitting manner, and in the fitting place; and the present is the acceptable time in which each person can find God by good works and work out his or her salvation.

1. “Upon my bed, by night, I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:1). The Bridegroom did not return in answer to the voice and desire of her who recalled him. Why? That longing might increase, affection be tested, and love’s business be exercised. It is therefore a feigned delay, not indignation. Yet he must be sought, so that perhaps he may be found when sought—the one who did not come when called—for the Lord says: “Everyone who seeks finds” (Matt. 7:8).

Now the word of recall is this: “Return; be like a roe, my beloved, or a young hart” (Song 2:17).

[Col. 1144C] Since he did not return at that voice, for the reasons already given, she who loved him became more eager and immediately gave herself wholly to seeking him with all ardour. First she seeks him in the bed, but does not find him. She rises from it, goes around the city, travels back and forth through streets and lanes, yet does not meet him or see him. Whoever happens to come by is questioned, but nothing certain is reported. Nor is this the search and frustration of a single street or a single night, for she says, “I sought by nights.”

What longing and ardour this is: rising at night, she is not ashamed to go into public, run through the city, and inquire openly and everywhere about her beloved; no argument can turn her aside from tracking his paths, no difficulty hinder her, no love of untimely rest hold her back, nor a bride’s modesty, nor even fear of the night. Yet in all these things she has thus far been frustrated of her desire. Ask what this obstinate and prolonged disappointment means: nurse of weariness, fuel of suspicion, torch of impatience, stepmother of love, mother of despair. If it is still a feigned delay, it is exceedingly painful.

[Col. 1145A] 2. Grant that it was piously and usefully feigned while the matter was still only one of calling or recalling. But now that he is sought—and sought in this fashion—what benefit can delay still bring? If the question concerns carnal bridegrooms and shameful loves, as the literal surface seems at first to suggest, and if such things can occur among them, it is no concern of mine: let them see to it themselves. But if, according to my small ability, I must answer and satisfy the minds and affections of souls seeking the Lord, then from Holy Scripture—in which they trust that they have life—there must surely be drawn forth something life-giving, and therefore spiritual, so that the poor may eat and be satisfied, and their hearts may live.

And what is so much the life of hearts as my Lord Jesus Christ? Of him the person who lived through him said: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4).

[Col. 1145B] Therefore let him come into our midst, so that it may truly be said to us: “But there stands one among you whom you do not know” (John 1:26). Yet I do not know how the Bridegroom who is Spirit can be unknown to spiritual persons who have so advanced in the Spirit that they may say with the prophet: “Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face” (Lam. 4:20), and with the Apostle: “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16).

Is this not he whom the bride sought? He truly is the Bridegroom—loving and lovable. He, I say, is truly Bridegroom, just as his flesh is truly food and his blood truly drink (John

[Col. 1145C] 6:56); and everything concerning him is true, since he himself is nothing other than Truth itself.

3. But why is this Bridegroom not found when sought so diligently and tirelessly—now in the bed, now in the city, or even in streets and lanes—when he himself says, “Seek, and you shall find,” and “Whoever seeks finds” (Matt. 7:7–8)? The prophet also says to him: “You are good, O Lord, to the soul that seeks you” (Lam. 3:25); and holy Isaiah likewise: “Seek the Lord while he may be found” (Isa. 55:6). How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled? For she who is here represented as seeking is not one of those to whom he says: “You shall seek me and shall not find me” (John 7:34).

But observe that there are three causes which commonly frustrate seekers: either they do not seek at the proper time, or not as they ought, or not where they ought.

[Col. 1145D] For if every time is suitable for seeking, why does the prophet say—as I have just recalled—“Seek the Lord while he may be found”? Without doubt, a time will come when he cannot be found; and therefore he adds that he should be invoked while he is near, because a time will come when he will no longer be near. For by whom then will he not be sought? “Every knee shall bend to me” (Isa. 45:24), and so forth. Yet he will not be found by the wicked, whom avenging angels will certainly bar and remove, lest they see the glory of God.

[Col. 1146A] Even the foolish virgins will cry out in vain; he does not come out to them at all, for the door is shut (Matt. 25:10). Let them therefore understand that it is said to them: “You shall seek me and shall not find me.”

4. But now is the acceptable time; now are the days of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2): plainly a time both for seeking and for invoking, when often he is felt to be present even before he is invoked. Hear, finally, what he promises: “Before you call upon me,” he says, “I shall say: Behold, I am here” (Isa. 65:24).

Nor was the kindness and accessibility of the present time unknown to the one who speaks in the psalm: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart” (Ps. 9:17).

[Col. 1146B] If God is sought by good works, therefore, “while we have time, let us do good to all” (Gal. 6:10), especially because the Lord plainly foretells that night is coming “when no one can work” (John 9:4). Will you find for yourself in the ages to come any other time to seek God and do what is good, apart from this one which God has appointed for you, in which he may remember you? Therefore these are days of salvation, because in them God himself, our King before the ages, “has worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73:12).

[Col. 1146C] 5. Go then, and in the midst of Gehenna wait for salvation which has already been accomplished in the midst of the earth.

> **Note:** [Col. 1145D] He seems here to criticize Origen, or at least an error attributed to him, as he criticizes others in Sermon 34 *On Various Matters* and Sermon 54 *On the Song of Songs*, no. 3. Compare Ambrose Autpert, Book X on the Apocalypse, on the verse, “Nothing defiled shall enter into it,” where he refutes this error.

What opportunity to obtain pardon amid eternal burnings do you dream will be granted you, when the time of mercy has already passed? No sacrifice for sins remains for you when you have died in sins. The Son of God is not crucified again: he died once and dies no more (Rom. 6:9). The blood that was shed upon the earth does not descend to hell. All sinners of the earth drank it; demons have no claim upon it by which to extinguish their fires, nor do human companions of demons.

He descended there once—not his blood, but his soul—and this was the portion of those who were in prison: that one visitation which was then made through the presence of his soul, while his lifeless body hung above the earth.

[Col. 1146D] His blood watered the dry ground, drenched the earth, and made it drunk; his blood reconciled things on earth and things in heaven, but not the things in hell—except that, once, as I have said, his soul went there and accomplished redemption in part, lest even for that moment the works of charity be idle.

> **Note:** [Col. 1145D] Thus the manuscripts and the first printed editions, except that some codices read *pietatis* (“of mercy”) for *charitatis* (“of charity”); Horstius, with others, reads *vacarent opera* (“the works might be idle”). Moreover, Bernard in this passage did not hold the view—as Horstius thought in his more extensive notes at [Col. 1146D]—that certain of the damned were liberated from hell by Christ; rather, he meant only that the Fathers were brought out of limbo, which the holy Doctor places “in hell itself”: both in Sermon 1 for Easter Day, no. 5, where he calls it “the prison of Gehenna,” and especially in Sermon 4 for the Feast of All Saints, no. 1. There, explaining Abraham’s bosom, he says that before Christ’s advent access to heaven was open to no saint at all, but that God had provided for them “in hell itself a place of rest and refreshment,” yet with a great chasm between them and the souls of the wicked.
>
> [Col. 1147C] “For although,” he says, “both were in darkness, both were not in punishments . . . Descending, therefore, into this place, the Saviour shattered the bronze gates and broke the iron bars, and brought the bound out from the prison-house,” etc. [Col. 1147D] These words remarkably illuminate the present passage.—Thus Mabillon. The note of Horstius that he mentions on this passage is as follows: “By these words he seems to hold that Christ, once in his descent into hell, rescued someone from among the damned.” Cyprian likewise suggests this—or rather Arnold, Abbot of Bonneval—in his sermon on the Lord’s Ascension, where he says:
>
> “God will no longer show mercy” (that is, to those once condemned to hell), “nor will he then hear the penitent. That confession will be too late; and when the door has been shut, those excluded who lack oil will cry out in vain. There is no refreshment there, no remedy. Christ descended into hell once; he will descend no further. Those sealed in darkness will see God no more. That sentence will be irreversible and the judgment unchangeable,” etc.
>
> Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration* 42, also seems to favour this view, and Clement of Alexandria, Book VI of the *Stromata* [Col. 1148C], affirms it absolutely. It should be understood, however, that although it is certainly de fide that the punishments of the damned are eternal, as theologians discuss more fully in Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 44, it is not certainly de fide whether, under this ordinary dispensation of God’s law, an exception is made or not. Those Fathers therefore speak not of law but of privilege; indeed, not even of this absolutely, but hypothetically, in this sense: if anyone has ever been delivered from hell, this must have taken place when Christ himself descended into hell. This proposition seems sufficiently consonant with reason; yet it remains compatible with the proposition that no one has been rescued from hell, because it was never necessary for anyone to be rescued. We do not acquit Clement of Alexandria of the error of Marcion. Writers differ concerning the soul of Trajan, allegedly delivered from hell through the prayers of St Gregory the Great. Some call the story fictitious; others interpret it in various ways. See Baronius, vol. VIII, year 604; Bellarmine, *On Purgatory*, Book II, chap. 8; Suárez, vol. II, in Part III, disputation 43, section 3; Mendoza, on 1 Kings, Book I, chap. 2, no. 6.

[Col. 1147A] But he will not add anything further. Therefore now is the acceptable time and a fitting time for seeking, in which indeed whoever seeks finds—provided that the person seeks where and as he ought. This, then, is one cause that can prevent the Bridegroom from being found by those who seek him: they do not seek at the suitable time. But it does not hinder the bride, who invokes and seeks at the suitable time. Nor does she seek him coldly, negligently, or perfunctorily; she seeks with a burning heart and with complete tirelessness, exactly as is fitting.

6. It remains to consider the third point: whether she perhaps seeks where she ought not. “Upon my bed I sought him whom my soul loves.” Perhaps he was not to be sought in the little bed (*lectulum*), but in the bed (*lectus*), since the world is narrow for him? But I do not shrink from the little bed, because I know him as little. For “a little one has been born to us” (Isa. 9:6).

[Col. 1147B] Rejoice and praise, O dwelling-place of Zion, because great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel (Isa. 12:6). Yet the same Lord who is great in Zion was found little among us, weak among us; from the one fact he has the capacity to lie down, and from the other, to lie even in a little bed. Is not the tomb a little bed? Is not the manger a little bed? Is not the Virgin’s womb a little bed? For the womb of the great Father is not a little bed but a great bed, concerning which he says to the Son: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

And perhaps even that womb ought not properly to be called a bed, since it is the place of one ruling rather than lying down. For remaining in the Father, he governs all things with the Father. Indeed, unhesitating faith holds that the Son does not lie down but sits at the Father’s right hand; and he himself declares heaven to be his seat,

[Col. 1147C] not his bed (Isa. 66:1), so that you may know that among his own—that is, in the heavenly places—he possesses no comforts of weakness at all, but the insignia of power.

7. The bride therefore rightly calls the little bed “mine,” because whatever weakness belongs to God plainly belongs to him not from what is his own, but from what is ours. From us he assumed what he endured for us: to be born, suckled, die, and be buried. The mortality of the one born is mine; the weakness of the little one is mine; the expiring of the crucified one is mine; the sleep of the buried one is mine. “The former things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new.”

“Upon my bed, by nights, I sought him whom my soul loves.” What? Did you seek in your own bed one who had already returned to his own? Had you not seen the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? He has already exchanged the tomb and stable for heaven, and do you still seek him in your own little bed?

[Col. 1148A] “He has risen; he is not here.” Why do you seek the mighty one in a bed, the great one in a bed, the glorified one in a stable? He has entered into the powers of the Lord; he has clothed himself with beauty and strength. Behold, he sits upon the cherubim who lay beneath a stone. From this point he no longer lies, but sits; and do you prepare aids as though for one lying down? Or, to state the truth more fully: he either sits in judgment or stands in help.

8. Thus you also, O good women, for whom, I ask, are you keeping vigil? For whom do you buy spices and prepare ointments? If you knew how great he is, and how free among the dead is this dead man whom you go to anoint, perhaps you would ask rather to be anointed by him. Is this not he whom his God “anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Ps. 44:8)?

[Col. 1148B] You will be blessed if, returning, you can boast and say, “From his fullness we also have received” (John 1:16). And indeed this came to pass. For those who came to be anointed truly return anointed. Why should they not return anointed by the joyful news of a new and fragrant resurrection? “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Rom. 10:15). Sent by the angel, they perform the work of evangelists; made apostles to the apostles, they hasten to announce the Lord’s mercy in the morning and say: “In the fragrance of your ointments we run.”

From then onward, therefore, the Bridegroom was sought in vain in the little bed; because, although the Church had known him according to the flesh—that is, according to the weakness of the flesh—now she knows him so no longer.

[Col. 1148C] For afterward Peter and John repeatedly sought him in the tomb but did not find him. Consider whether each of them might then aptly and fittingly have said: “Upon my bed I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him.” For the flesh that was not from the Father, about to go to the Father, first stripped itself through the glory of the resurrection of every weakness, girded itself with power, and clothed itself with light as with a garment—the glory and adornment in which it was fitting for it to be presented before the Father’s eyes.

9. The bride speaks beautifully: she says not, “Him whom I love,” but “Him whom my soul loves,” because that love by which one loves something spiritually—for example, God, an angel, or a soul—belongs truly and properly to the soul alone. So too does the love of justice, truth, piety, wisdom, and other virtues.

[Col. 1149A] But when the soul loves—or rather desires—something according to the flesh, for example food, clothing, lordship, and other bodily or earthly things, it should be called the love of the flesh rather than of the soul. This explains why the bride, less commonly but no less properly, says that her soul loves the Bridegroom: thereby showing that the Bridegroom is spirit and is loved by her not with carnal but spiritual love.

And rightly she says that she sought him “by nights.” For if, according to Paul, “those who sleep sleep by night, and those who are drunk are drunk by night” (1 Thess. 5:7), then it may not unreasonably be said, I think, that those who are ignorant are ignorant by night, and consequently those who seek seek by night. Who seeks what lies openly before them? Day makes manifest what night conceals, so that in the day you may find what you had sought in the night.

[Col. 1149B] Night therefore lasts while the Bridegroom is sought; for if it were day, he would cease to be hidden and would not be sought. This is sufficient on the matter—unless perhaps this plurality of nights indicates something further to be sought, since she says not “night,” but “nights.”

10. It seems to me, unless you have a better explanation, that the following account may be given. This world has its nights, and not a few. Why do I say that the world has nights, when almost the whole world itself is night and always moves in darkness? Jewish unbelief is night; the ignorance of the pagans is night; heretical perversity is night; even the carnal or merely natural conduct of Catholics is night. Is it not night where the things of the Spirit of God are not perceived?

[Col. 1149C] Further, among heretics and schismatics, as many sects as there are, so many nights there are. In vain do you seek through these nights the sun of righteousness and the light of truth—that is, the Bridegroom—for there is no fellowship between light and darkness.

But someone may say that the bride is not so foolish or blind as to seek light in darkness or to seek her beloved among those who are ignorant of him and do not love him. Yet she does not say that she is now seeking through the nights, but rather that she has sought. She says not, “I seek,” but “I sought by nights him whom my soul loves.” The meaning is that, while she was little, she thought as a little child, reasoned as a little child,

[Col. 1149D] and sought truth where it was not, wandering and not finding it, according to that saying in the psalm: “I have wandered like a lost sheep” (Ps. 118:176). Finally, she recalls that she was then still in the little bed, as one weak in age and childish in understanding.

11. Yet if you construe it thus: “In my little bed”—understand, “being” or “lying”—“I sought him whom my soul loves”; that is, I did not seek in the little bed, but, being in the little bed, I sought.

> **Note:** [Col. 1149D] Thus the manuscripts; not “sitting.”

That is: While I was still weak and feeble and altogether less able to follow the Bridegroom wherever he went, to follow him to the difficult and exalted heights of his sublimity, I encountered many people who, knowing my desire, said to me: “Behold, here is Christ; behold, there he is” (Mark 13:21).

[Col. 1150A] Yet he was neither here nor there. I encountered them, moreover, not to my own folly. For the nearer I came and the more carefully I examined, the more quickly and certainly I knew that truth was not with them at all. For I sought and did not find; and I discovered nights that falsely professed themselves days.

12. I said: “I will arise and go around the city; through the lanes and streets I will seek him whom my soul loves.” Observe even now that the one who says, “I will arise,” is lying down. This is altogether fitting. Why should she not arise, once she has learned of her beloved’s resurrection? But, O blessed woman, if you have risen with Christ, you ought to think of things above; you must seek Christ not below but above, where he sits at the Father’s right hand (Col. 3:1–2).

But you say, “I will go around the city.” To what end? “The wicked walk about in a circle.” Leave that to the Jews, concerning whom their own prophet foretold that “they shall suffer hunger like dogs and go around the city” (Ps. 58:7).

[Col. 1150B] And if you enter the city, behold, according to another prophet, they are wasted with hunger (Jer. 14:18); which would certainly not be so if the bread of life were there. He rose from the heart of the earth, but did not remain upon the earth. Rather, he ascended to where he was before. For he who descended is the same who ascended: the living bread who descended from heaven, the same Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXVI  
On the brightness of the Bridegroom, in which, coequal with the Father, he sits at the right hand of his glory; and on how good shepherds ought to be diligent, watchful, and discerning in feeding the souls entrusted to them.

[Col. 1150C]

1. “Through the streets and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:2). She still thinks like a little child. I suppose she imagined that, having left the tomb, he would immediately have gone out in public, to teach the people as usual, heal the sick, and reveal his glory in Israel—if perhaps they might receive him rising from death, though they had promised to receive him coming down from the cross. But he had completed the work which the Father had given him to do; and she ought certainly to have understood this even from the voice of the one hanging there, when, about to expire immediately, he said: “It is finished” (John 19:30). There was no longer any reason for him to entrust himself anew to the crowds, who perhaps would not have believed in him even then [Col. 1150D]. And he hastened to the Father, who was to say to him: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1). For, once lifted up from the earth, he would draw all things to himself more powerfully and more divinely. Yet she, eager to enjoy him but ignorant of the mystery, thought that he was to be sought through streets and squares. Frustrated once more, then, she repeats: “I sought him, and did not find him,” so that the saying he spoke might be fulfilled: “Because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me” (John 16:16).

2. Perhaps she says: “How then will they believe in him whom they do not see?” As though faith came by sight, rather than by hearing. What great thing is it to believe what [Col. 1151A] you have seen? And what praise is deserved by refusing to deny faith to your own eyes? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience; and patience is merit. Finally: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29). Therefore, lest the merit of faith be emptied of its value, let him withdraw himself from sight, giving place to virtue. Moreover, it is time for him now to return to his own place. You ask, “To which place of his own?” To the Father’s right hand. For he will not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, since he is in the form of God (Phil. 2:6). This, then, is the place of the Only-Begotten, in which every indignity done to him may be seen to have been repelled. Let him indeed sit beside the Father, not beneath him, so that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father. Here the equality of majesty will appear, if you regard him as neither inferior to the Father nor later than him. But meanwhile she notices none of these things; rather, as though drunk with love, running here and there, she seeks with her eyes him whom the eye can no longer reach, but faith can. For she does not suppose that Christ ought to enter into his glory in any other way than after the glory of the resurrection has publicly become known to the world: impiety refuted, the faithful rejoicing, disciples exulting, peoples converted, and finally he himself glorified by all, once the truth of the preacher has become evident to everyone through the presence of the risen one. You are mistaken, O bride. These things indeed must happen, but in their proper time.

3. But now, meanwhile, consider whether perhaps this is more worthy and more consonant with heavenly justice: that what is holy should not be given to dogs, nor pearls to swine; that rather, according to Scripture, “the wicked man should be removed, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10); that faith should not be deprived [Col. 1151C] of its merit, since it is then recognized as more approved when what is not seen is believed; that what is hidden from the unworthy should be preserved for the worthy by faith itself, so that those who are in filth may become still filthier, and the righteous may be justified still more (Rev. 22:11), lest they grow drowsy through weariness. Let the heavens and the heaven of heavens waste away and be confounded by their expectation, if the almighty Father is still longer frustrated of his heart’s desire; if, finally, the Only-Begotten is delayed any further from entering into his glory—which alone would be most unworthy. At what price, do you think, should whatever glory mortals possess be valued, so that it ought to keep him, even for a little while, from that glory which has been prepared for him by his Father from eternity? Add that there is no reason why the Son’s own petition should be prolonged any further [Col. 1151D]. You ask what petition I mean? Surely that in which he says, “Father, glorify your Son.” Yet I understand him to have asked this not as a suppliant, but as one who foreknew. One freely asks for what lies within one’s own power to receive. Therefore the Son’s petition is dispensatory, not necessary, since together with the Father he gives whatever he receives from the Father.

4. Here it must also be said that not only does the Father glorify the Son, but the Son glorifies the Father, lest anyone say that the Son is less than the Father because he seems to receive glory from the Father—when he himself glorifies the Father. For the Son says: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you.” But perhaps you still think that the Son must be subordinated, because he appears to receive glory from the Father as though he were without glory, only to return it to the Father. Hear [Col. 1152A] that it is not so: “Father,” he says, “glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was made” (John 17:1, 5). Therefore, if the glory of the Son is not later, since it is from eternity, Father and Son glorify one another equally. And if this is so, where is the Father’s primacy? There is surely equality where there is coeternity. Indeed, the equality is such that the glory of both is one, just as they themselves are one. Hence it seems to me that when he says again, “Father, glorify your name,” he seeks nothing other than his own glorification, in whom and through whom the Father’s name would without doubt be glorified; and he received this reply from the Father: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (John 12:28). That reply of the Father was itself no small glorification of the Son. Besides, at the streams of the Jordan he is recognized as having been glorified more abundantly and more augustly—by John’s testimony, by the sign of the dove, and by the Father’s voice saying: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:14, 16, 17). Likewise on the mountain, before three disciples, he was most magnificently glorified: both by the same voice again descending upon him from heaven, by that wondrous and surpassing transfiguration of his body, and also by the testimony of the two prophets who appeared there speaking with him (Matt. 17:2, 5).

5. It remains, then, that according to the Father’s promise he should be glorified once more; and that will be the fullness of glory, to which nothing further can be added. But where will that blessing be given? Certainly not, as she supposed, in streets or alleys, 1536 unless perhaps in those of which it is said: “Your streets, Jerusalem, shall be paved with pure gold, and through all your alleys alleluia shall be sung” (Tob. 13:22) [Col. 1152C]. There the Son truly received from the Father that glory for which no equal can be found, not even among heavenly beings. For to which of the angels was it ever said: “Sit at my right hand”? (Heb. 1:13). Not only among the number of angels, but even among all the remaining higher orders of the blessed, no one whatever is found fit to attain this surpassing glory. To none of them at all was that voice of singular glory addressed; to no one was it granted to experience the efficacy of that voice in himself. Whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers, they surely desire to look into him; they do not presume to compare themselves with him. Therefore it was said and granted uniquely to my Lord by the Lord that he should sit at the right hand of his glory [Col. 1152D]: in glory equal to his, in essence consubstantial with his, in generation like his, in majesty not unequal, in eternity not later. There, there whoever seeks him will find him and see his glory: not glory as of one of the rest, but plainly “glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John 1:14).

6. What will you do, O bride? Do you think that you can follow him there? Or do you dare—or are you able—to intrude yourself into so holy a secret, so hidden a sanctuary, as to behold the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son? Certainly not. Where he is, you cannot come now; but you will come afterward. Yet go on: follow; seek. Let neither that inaccessible glory nor that height deter you from seeking or make you despair of finding. If you can believe, “all things are possible to one who believes” [Col. 1153A] (Mark 9:22). “The word is near you,” he says, “in your mouth and in your heart” (Rom. 10:8). Believe, and you have found. For to believe is to have found. The faithful know that Christ dwells through faith in their hearts (Eph. 3:17). What is nearer? Seek, then, confidently; seek devoutly. “The Lord is good to the soul that seeks him” (Lam. 3:25). Seek with desires, follow by deeds, find through faith. What does faith not find? It reaches what is inaccessible, discovers what is unknown, comprehends what is immeasurable, grasps what is ultimate; finally, in some manner it encloses eternity itself within its vast bosom. I will confidently say: I believe the eternal and blessed Trinity, whom I do not understand; and by faith I hold what I cannot grasp with my mind.

7. But someone says: “How will they believe without a preacher [Col. 1153B], since faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of preaching?” (Rom. 10:14, 17). God will provide this. And behold, those are already at hand who will instruct and form the new bride, who is to marry the heavenly Bridegroom, in the matters needed: they will teach her faith and hand down the pattern of piety and religion. Hear, indeed, what she adds: “The watchmen who guard the city found me.” Who are these watchmen? Surely those whom the Savior in the Gospel declares blessed if, when he comes, he finds them watching (Luke 12:37). How good are the watchmen who, while we sleep, keep vigil for us, as though they must give account for our souls! How good are the guardians who, awake in mind and spending the night in prayer, shrewdly investigate the ambushes of enemies, anticipate the schemes of the malicious, detect snares, evade traps, scatter nets, and frustrate contrivances! These are lovers of the brethren and of the Christian people, who pray much for the people and for the whole holy city. These are they who, deeply concerned for the Lord’s sheep entrusted to them, give their heart to keeping watch early in the morning for the Lord who made them, and make supplication before the Most High. They watch and make supplication, knowing their own insufficiency in guarding the city, and that “unless the Lord guards the city, the guard watches in vain” (Ps. 136:1) [Col. 1153C].

8. Moreover, since the Lord thus commands: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Mark 16:38), it is clear that without this twofold practice of the faithful and this care of the guardians, neither city, bride, nor sheep can be secure [Col. 1153D]. You ask their difference? They are one thing. A city because of its gathering together, a bride because of love, sheep because of meekness. Do you wish to know that she is a bride who is a city? “I saw,” he says, “the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev. 21:2). You will likewise see this clearly also concerning the sheep, if you recall how attentively that first guardian—I mean Peter—was at the same time reminded about love when the sheep were first entrusted to him. Surely the wise creditor would not have exercised such care unless he knew himself to be the Bridegroom, as his inmost conscience assured him. Hear these things, friends of the Bridegroom—if indeed you are friends. Yet I have said too little: “friends”; they ought to be most intimate friends, who are granted the privilege of such great familiarity. It was not without purpose that “Peter, do you love me?” was repeated so often (John 21:15–17) when the sheep were entrusted to him [Col. 1154A]. And I think this signified much the same as if Jesus had said to him: “Unless your conscience bears witness to you that you love me—and love me greatly and perfectly, that is, more than your possessions, more than those dear to you, more even than yourself, so that the number of this repetition of mine may be fulfilled—you must by no means undertake this care or involve yourself with my sheep, for whom my blood was poured out.” It is a terrible saying, capable of shaking even the fearless hearts of any tyrants.

9. Therefore attend to yourselves, all of you who have received the task of this ministry; attend, I say, to yourselves [Col. 1154B] and to the precious deposit entrusted to you. It is a city: keep watch for its protection and concord. It is a bride: devote yourselves to her adornment. They are sheep: attend to their feeding. And perhaps these three things may not inappropriately be said to correspond to the Lord’s threefold question. Now, that the guarding of the city may be sufficient, it must be threefold: against the violence of tyrants, the deceit of heretics, and the temptations of demons. The bride’s adornment lies in good works, conduct, and proper order. The sheep are fed generally in the pastures of Scripture, as in the Lord’s inheritance; but there is a distinction within these. For there are commandments imposed on hard and fleshly minds from the law of life and discipline; there are vegetables of dispensations set before the weak and small of heart from regard for mercy; and there are the solid and strong things of counsels, offered from the inner depths of wisdom to the sound, who have their senses trained to discern good and evil [Col. 1154C]. For little ones, like lambs, are given the milk of exhortation to drink, not solid food. Beyond this, good and diligent shepherds do not cease to fatten the flock with good and cheerful examples, and with their own examples rather than those of others. For if the examples are others’ and not their own, it is shameful for them, and the flock does not thereby advance. For if, for example, I who seem among you to bear a shepherd’s care were to set before you Moses’ meekness, Job’s patience, Samuel’s mercy, David’s holiness, and any similar examples of good men, while I myself were harsh and impatient, unmerciful and far from holy, my speech, I fear, would turn out less savory [Col. 1154D], and you would receive it less eagerly. But I leave this to heavenly mercy: may it supply what is lacking to you from us, and correct what is done wrongly. Now the good shepherd will also see to it that, according to the Gospel, he is found to have salt in himself (Mark 9:49), knowing that speech seasoned with salt will benefit salvation as much as it pleases by its grace. Let this suffice for the present concerning the guarding of the city, the adornment of the bride, and the feeding of the sheep.

10. Yet I wish to set out these same matters a little more explicitly, because of those who, while too eagerly craving honors, too carelessly submit themselves to heavy burdens and expose themselves to dangers. Let them know why they have come, as it is written: “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26:50) [Col. 1155A]. Unless I am mistaken, for the guarding of the city alone, if it is to be adequately provided for, a man is needed who is strong, spiritual, and faithful: strong to repel injuries, spiritual to detect snares, faithful so as not to seek what is his own. Further, for the reforming or correcting of conduct—which certainly pertains to the bride’s beauty—who does not plainly recognize that a disciplinary censure is most necessary, together with great diligence? Therefore everyone upon whom this work rests ought to burn with that zeal with which the preeminent champion of the Lord’s bride, inflamed with ardor, said: “I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy; for I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2). Again, how will an unlearned shepherd lead the Lord’s flocks into the pastures of divine utterances? But even if he is learned, yet is not good, one must fear that he will harm by a barren life no less than he nourishes by abundant teaching. Thus this burden cannot be undertaken in this respect without learning together with a praiseworthy life. But behold, contrary to our wish, an end is imposed where there was no end. We are called away to another matter, and it seems unworthy that this subject should yield to it.

> [Note: Col. 1155D] By these words Bernard indicates that the sermon was interrupted by some necessity, and that its end was signaled by some sign—whether this was the signal for the common [Col. 1156D] table, or some other business to which he judges it unworthy that this subject should give way. Rather, the opening words of the following sermon indicate some business.

I am distressed on every side, and do not know which I should bear more painfully: to be torn away from this subject or to be stretched out upon that other; except that either way both are more burdensome together. O servitude! O necessity! I do not do what I wish, but I do what I hate. Yet note where we stop, so that as soon as we are free to return to it, we may immediately begin again from that point, in the name of the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed [Col. 1155C] for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXVII. On the evil shepherds of the Church; likewise, how the blessed in heaven, together with the angels, assist the elect who are still pilgrims.

1. Come now, we are free! In yesterday’s sermon we said what sort of guides we would wish to have on this way by which we travel, not what sort we actually have. We find them far different.
