Not all those whom today you see standing around the bride on every side, and who, as people commonly say, seem to “stand at her right hand,” are friends of the Bridegroom. Very few, among all those dear to her, do not seek what is their own. They love money and cannot love Christ at the same time, because they have given their hands to Mammon [Col. 1155D]. Look how they walk, sleek and adorned, clothed all around in varied garments, like a bride coming forth from her chamber. If you happened to see one of them suddenly approaching from a distance, would you not think him the bride rather than the bride’s guardian? From where, do you suppose, comes to them this overflowing abundance of possessions, this splendor of clothing, this luxury of tables, this heap of silver and golden vessels, unless from the bride’s goods? Hence she is left poor, needy, and naked, pitiable in appearance, unkempt, rough, bloodless. Therefore in this time the bride is not adorned but despoiled; she is not guarded but destroyed; not defended but exposed; not instructed but prostituted; the flock is not fed but slaughtered and devoured. Of them the Lord says: “They devour my people as food for bread” (Ps. 13:4; 52:5); and, “They have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling place” (Ps. 78:7); and in another prophet: “They will eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4:8)—as though he said: They exact the price of sins and do not give sinners the care due to them. Whom will you give me among the number of superiors who watches more diligently to uproot vices than to empty the purses of his subjects? Where is one who by prayer bends wrath, one who preaches the year acceptable to the Lord? We speak of lighter things; a weightier judgment awaits graver matters.

2. Yet we linger in vain over either these men or those, because they do not hear us [Col. 1156B]. But even if what we say should perhaps be committed to writing, they would disdain to read it; or if by chance they read it, they would be angry with me, though they ought more rightly to be angry with themselves. Therefore let us leave these men, not discoverers of the bride but sellers of her, and rather seek those by whom the bride says she was found. Indeed, these have inherited the place of their ministry, but not their zeal. All desire to be successors; few desire to be imitators. Would that they were found as watchful in their care as they run eagerly toward the chair! They would indeed keep watch, carefully preserving her whom those earlier men found and who was entrusted to them. Rather, they ought to awaken for their own sake and not allow it to be said of them: “My friends and my neighbors drew near against me and stood” [Col. 1156C] (Ps. 37:12). This is a wholly just complaint, and one more justly applicable to no age than to ours, 1539. It is too little that our watchmen do not preserve us, unless they actually destroy us as well. For sunk deep in the sleep of forgetfulness, they awaken at no thunderclap of the Lord’s threat, so as even to fear their own danger. Hence they spare not their own people, because they spare not themselves, destroying and perishing together.

3. But who, then, are those watchmen by whom the bride declares that she was found? Surely the apostles and apostolic men. Truly these are those who guard the city—that is, the very city which they found. They guard the Church, and all the more watchfully because they see her now endangered more gravely by a domestic and internal evil, as it is written: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Mic. 7:6) [Col. 1156D]. For they do not abandon without their protection the Church for which they resisted unto blood; rather, they protect and guard her day and night—that is, in their life and in their death. And if “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15), I do not doubt that they do this all the more powerfully in death, as their authority has been strengthened more fully in death itself (Ps. 138:17).

4. “You affirm these things,” someone says, “as though you had seen them with your own eyes; but they are removed from human sight.” To him I reply: If you consider the testimony of your eyes trustworthy, the testimony of God is greater. For he says: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night, forever, they shall not be silent” (Isa. 62:6) [Col. 1157A]. “But,” you say, “this was said of angels.” I do not deny it: all are ministering spirits (Heb. 1:14). But what prevents me from thinking the same also of these, who now are by no means inferior to angels in power and perhaps are more closely related to us in affection and mercy, insofar as they are more closely joined to us by nature? Add also their experience of the same sufferings and miseries in which we still live for a time. Will not the fact that they undoubtedly remember having passed through them themselves work greater compassion or concern for us in holy minds? Is not this their own voice: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment”? (Ps. 65:12). What? Have they passed through, and will they leave us amid fires or waves, not even deigning to stretch out a hand to their children in danger? It is not so. All is well with you, O mother Church; all is well with you in the place of your pilgrimage: help comes to you from heaven and earth. Those who guard you do not slumber nor sleep. Your guardians are holy angels; your watchmen are the spirits and souls of the righteous. Those are not mistaken who perceive that you were found by both kinds of spirits and are guarded by both alike. And each has its own reason for this concern: the former, because without you they will not be made complete; the latter, because unless they are restored from you to their fullness, they will not be fully renewed [Col. 1157C]. For who does not know that when Satan fell from heaven with his accomplices, the number of the heavenly multitude was diminished by no small portion? Therefore all await their completion from you: some, the completion of their number; others, that of their desire. Recognize accordingly the voice in the psalm: “The righteous await me, until you reward me” (Ps. 141:8).

5. And it should be observed that it is reported not that she found them, but rather that they found her; and, as I suppose, that they were appointed with zeal for this very purpose. For how will they preach unless they are sent? Indeed, you have one speaking in the Gospels: “Go; behold, I send you” (Luke 10:3); and, “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). Thus it is. She sought the Bridegroom, and the Bridegroom was not unaware of her. Surely he had stirred her up for this very purpose, that she should seek him; and he had given her a heart for the commandments, and the law [Col. 1157D] of life and discipline, provided there should be someone to instruct and teach her the way of prudence. And he sent to meet her planters and waterers, that they might nourish her and establish her in all certainty of truth—that is, point out the Beloved to her and make her certain of him; for truth is what she seeks, and what her soul truly loves. And indeed what faithful and true love of the soul is there except that by which truth is loved? I possess reason; I am capable of truth; but would that I were not, if love of truth were lacking. For this is the fruit of those branches, and I am the root. I am not secure from the axe if I am found without it. For in that gift of nature there undoubtedly shines forth the mark of the divine image, by which the soul excels the other living creatures [Col. 1158A]. Hence my soul dares to rise to the sweet and chaste embraces of truth, and thus to rest in love of it with all security and sweetness—if only it finds grace in the eyes of so great a Bridegroom, so that he judges it worthy to attain this glory; indeed, if he himself presents it to himself “without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind.” Of how great a fault, and deserving what punishment, do you think it is to keep so great a gift of God idle? But of this elsewhere.

6. Now the bride did not find him whom she sought, but was found by those whom she did not seek. Let those hear this who do not fear to enter the paths of life without a guide and teacher, being both disciples and masters to themselves in the spiritual art. Nor is this enough: they even heap up disciples for themselves, blind guides of the blind [Col. 1158B]. How many have been found through this to have wandered most dangerously from the straight path! Surely, because they did not know the wiles of Satan and his devices, it happened that those who began in the Spirit were brought to their completion in the flesh, shamefully led away and damnably fallen. Let such persons therefore see how cautiously they walk, and take their example from the bride, who could not in any way reach him whom she desired until those met her whose teaching she might use to gain knowledge of the Beloved—certainly, to learn the fear of the Lord. Whoever pretends not to yield himself to a teacher gives his hand to a deceiver. And whoever leaves sheep in pasture without a guardian is shepherd not of sheep but of wolves.

7. Let us now see how the bride says that she was found [Col. 1158C]. To me she seems to have used the word “finding” in a rather unusual way. For she speaks as though the Church came from one place. But according to the Lord’s word (Matt. 8:11), she comes from East and West, and from all the ends of the earth. Nor was she ever gathered together in one place, where apostles or angels could find her and lead or direct her to him whom her soul loves. Was she found before she was gathered? No, because she did not yet exist. Therefore, if she had said that she had been collected, gathered, or, indeed—what more properly suits the name Church—called together by preachers, I would have passed over it simply, without hesitation on any point. For they are God’s fellow workers, and they have heard him say: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” [Col. 1158D] (Matt. 12:30). Nor would it seem irrelevant to me if someone said that she was founded or built by them. For they did this with him who says in the Gospels: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18); and, “Because it was founded upon firm rock” (Matt. 7:25). But now, speaking of none of these things and declaring, contrary to ordinary usage, that she was found, she makes us hesitate somewhat and leads us to suspect that something lies hidden here which must be examined more carefully.

8. I confess that I wished to pass by and withdraw myself from an inquiry for which I did not feel sufficient. Yet, remembering how in many equally doubtful and obscure matters, while you lifted your hearts above, I have felt myself helped beyond even my hope, I am ashamed of my distrust; and reproving my fear, I undertake—not rashly—what I had timidly avoided. The customary help, I trust, will be present. But if not, even among kindly hearers what I intended will not be fruitless [Col. 1159A]. Yet the following sermon will take this as its beginning, for here we close the present one. May the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed for ever, grant you not merely to retain in memory the things said, but to love them ardently and fulfill them effectively. Amen.

## SERMON LXXVIII. That the bride, that is, the Church of the elect, was predestined by God before the ages, and was anticipated by him so that she might seek him and be converted.

1. If I remember correctly, we stopped and hesitated at the word “finding” [Col. 1159B], hearing with some concern that the bride said she had been found by her preachers. We have expressed the reasons for our hesitation and doubt, and it seemed that something needed to be investigated; but what was sought could not be explained at the end of the sermon, when we were already pressed for time. What remains except that we now discharge our debt? In the exposition of the great mystery—I mean that holy and chaste marriage which the Doctor of the Gentiles interpreted as concerning Christ and the Church (Eph. 5:32)—lies the work of our salvation itself. In this work, I say, three cooperate with one another: God, angel, and human being. And why should God not act and take charge of the wedding of his beloved Son? He himself indeed does so, and with his whole will.

> [Note: Col. 1159D] Supply from the preceding clause: “takes charge.”

And certainly he would suffice by himself and without their aid; but they can do nothing without him [Col. 1159C]. Therefore, in calling them into the work of this ministry, he sought not help for himself but benefit for them. For he assigned merits to human beings in the work, according to that saying: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7); and because each shall receive according to his own labor (1 Cor. 3:8), whether he plants in faith or waters what has been planted. But when he uses the ministry of angels for the salvation of the human race, does he not bring it about that angels are loved by human beings? For that human beings are loved by angels may be perceived especially from this: angels know that the ancient losses of their city will be repaired from human beings. Nor indeed could the kingdom of love fittingly be governed by laws other than the mutual pious loves and pure affections of those who are to reign together, both toward one another and toward God.

2. But there is much difference in their manner of working, according to the dignity of each worker. God, indeed, does whatever he wills by the mere ease of willing, without agitation, without motion, without constraint of place, time, cause, or person. For he is the Lord of hosts, who judges all things in tranquility (Wis. 12:18). He is also Wisdom, disposing all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1). But the angel does not work without motion, both local and temporal [Col. 1160A], though without agitation.

> [Note: Col. 1159D] In the manuscript of St. Germanus: “both local and bodily.” But I prefer “temporal,” as in the Cistercian manuscript, so that it answers the preceding period, where God is said to act without prejudice of [Col. 1160D] place or time.

A human being, however, is free in working neither from agitation of mind nor from motion of body and mind. Thus he is commanded to work out his own salvation with fear and trembling (Phil. 2:12), and to eat his bread in the sweat of his face (Gen. 3:19).

3. With these matters set forth, consider now with me that in this most magnificent work of our salvation there are three things which God the author claims for himself and in which he precedes all his helpers and fellow workers: predestination, creation, and inspiration. Predestination had its beginning not, I say, from the rising of the Church, nor even from the beginning of the world, nor indeed at this or that time: it is before times. Creation occurs with time; inspiration [Col. 1160B] already occurs in time, where and when God wills. Certainly, according to predestination, the Church of the elect has never not existed with God. If an unbeliever marvels at this, let him hear something at which to marvel more: she has never not been pleasing, never not beloved. Why should I not boldly speak of the secret which that ready messenger of heavenly counsels disclosed to me from the heart of God? I mean Paul, who, as in many other matters, so also in this was not afraid to publish the secret of the riches of God’s goodness: “He blessed us,” he says, “with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blemish before him in love”; and he adds: “Who predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in him, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he made us gracious in his beloved Son” (Eph. 1:3–6) [Col. 1160C]. There is no doubt that these words are spoken in the voice of all the elect; and they themselves are the Church. Therefore, in that most deep bosom of eternity, before she came forth into the light and work of this creation, who among the blessed spirits could in any way have found her, unless God, eternity itself, had wished to reveal her to someone?

> [Note: Col. 1160D] In other printed editions: *opus prodiret*, “the work came forth,” in the nominative; but the manuscripts more correctly have *opusque*, in the accusative, so that “Church” is referred to *prodiret*, “came forth.”

4. But even when, at the Creator’s command, she seemed already to have emerged into these made and visible species and forms, she was not immediately found by any human being or angel, because she was not recognized, being overshadowed by the image of the earthly man and covered by the darkness of death. No child of humankind entered this life without that universal veil of confusion [Col. 1160D], except the one who enters without stain. This is Emmanuel, who nevertheless, being from among us and for us, clothed himself in our curse and in the likeness—not the reality—of our sin. For thus you have it: “He appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, that through sin he might condemn sin in the flesh” (Rom. 8:3). Apart from this, there is one entrance in every respect for all, I mean the elect and the reprobate. For there is no distinction. All have sinned, and all wear the hood (*caputium*; variant: *pileum*, “cap”) of their shame. For this reason [Col. 1161A], then, although the Church already existed as created among created things, she nevertheless could not even so be found or recognized by any creature, hidden in a wondrous twofold manner: both within the bosom of blessed predestination and within the mass of miserable condemnation.

5. But her whom predestining Wisdom had concealed from eternity, and creating Power had by no means brought forth plainly from the beginning [Note: In the Germanensis manuscript: “nor had creating Power brought it sufficiently into the open.” The sense is the same.], visiting grace surely revealed in its own time, according to the operation which I called above “inspiration,” because something from the Bridegroom’s Spirit had been poured into human spirits in preparation for the Gospel of peace—that is, to prepare a way for the Lord, and for the Gospel of his glory, into the hearts of all who had been predestined to life. Watchmen would have labored in vain in preaching, unless this grace had gone before. But now, seeing the word run swiftly, the peoples of the nations turn to the Lord with every readiness, tribes and languages gather into the unity of faith, and the ends of the earth are collected into the one Catholic mother, they came to know the riches of grace, which had been kept hidden from the ages in the secret place of eternal predestination; and they rejoiced that they had found her whom the Lord had chosen before the ages as his bride.

6. From this, I think, it becomes clear that it is not idle that the Bride declared herself to have been found by them. She meant that she knew herself to have been gathered by them, not chosen; discovered, not converted. For each person’s conversion must be ascribed to him to whom all must necessarily say that verse from the psalm: “Convert us, O God of our salvation” (Ps. 84:5). Yet perhaps I would not as fittingly apply to him the language of finding as that of conversion. Indeed, that is so. For the Lord does not find; he goes before, and his going-before excludes finding. After all, what could he find who has never failed to know anything? “The Lord knows those who are his,” says one (2 Tim. 2:19). And he himself says: “I know whom I have chosen from the beginning” (John 13:18). Certainly, she whom he foreknew from eternity, chose, loved, and created, could not reasonably be said by him to have been found. Yet I would confidently say that she was prepared by him so as to be found. For he who saw bore witness, “and we know that his testimony is true” (John 19:35). “I saw,” he says, “the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven, prepared by God as a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev. 21:2). And he was one of the watchmen who guard the city. But hear its very preparer, as though pointing it out with his finger to the watchmen, though under another figure: “Lift up your eyes,” he says, “and see the fields, for they are already white”—that is, prepared—“for harvest” (John 4:35). On this account the householder invites laborers to the work, when he perceives that everything has been so prepared that, without much labor of their own, they can boast and say, “We are God’s fellow workers” (1 Cor. 3:9). For what are they going to do? Surely, seek the Bride and, when she is found, tell her of the Beloved. For they will not seek their own glory but that of the Bridegroom, since they are the Bridegroom’s friends. And they will not labor much in winning her for this end: he is at hand, and she already seeks him with whole-hearted devotion; so fully has her will been prepared by the Lord.

7. Finally, before they [variant: “the watchmen” is added] have yet said anything, she asks about the Beloved; herself anticipated, she forestalls her preachers, questioning and saying: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” (Song 3:3). Thus she fittingly testified that she had been found by those who guard the city, since she knew that she herself had already been foreknown and anticipated by the Lord of the city, so that they might find her thus prepared, not make her so. In this way Cornelius was found by Peter, and Paul by Ananias; for both had been anticipated and prepared by the Lord. [Col. 1162B] What was readier than Saul, who had already cried in suppliant mind and voice: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts 9:6). Nor was Cornelius less ready: by his alms and prayers—though the Lord himself had inspired them in him—he merited to attain faith (Acts 10:4). Philip likewise found Nathanael; but first the Lord had already seen him while he was under the fig tree. Was not the Lord’s seeing of him a preparation? Andrew too is reported to have found his brother Simon, but Simon had equally been foreseen and foreknown by the Lord, so that he might be called Cephas, as it were, “strong in faith” (John 1:45, 48, 41, 42).

8. We read of Mary that she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit (Matt. 1:18). I think that in this respect the Bride bears some likeness to the Lord’s own mother. For unless she too had been found to be with the Holy Spirit, she would never have asked those who found her so familiarly about him whose Spirit that is. She did not wait for them to state why they had come; she herself spoke, and indeed from the abundance of her heart: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” She knew that the eyes which had seen were blessed; and, marveling at those who had seen, she said: “Are you those to whom it has been granted to see him whom so many kings and prophets wished to see and did not see? Are you those who deserved to behold Wisdom in flesh, Truth in a body, God in a man? Many say, ‘Look, he is here,’ and ‘Look, he is there’; but I think it safer to give credence to you, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.” [Col. 1162D] Let this be said concerning what the Bride asked of the watchmen. If anything remains wanting, it will be supplied in another discourse. But now from this it is especially clear that she was anticipated by the Holy Spirit; whereas she was found and recognized by those who guard the city as truly she whom God foreknew and predestined before the ages, and prepared as everlasting delights through eternal ages for his beloved Son, that she might be holy and without blemish in his sight, springing up like a lily and flowering forever before the Lord, the Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, Bridegroom of the Church, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXIX. On the tenacious and indissoluble love by which the soul holds the Bridegroom; likewise, on the Bridegroom’s return at the end of the age to save the synagogue of the Jews.

[Col. 1163A]

1. “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” (Song 3:3). O headlong, vehement, burning, impetuous love! You permit no thought besides yourself; you reject all else, despise everything apart from yourself, content with yourself alone. You throw all order into confusion, disregard custom, know no measure; everything that seems to belong to expediency, reason, modesty, counsel, or judgment, you triumph over in yourself and reduce to captivity. See: all that this woman thinks and says sounds of you, breathes of you, and nothing else. Thus you have claimed for yourself both her heart and her tongue. She says: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” As though these men knew what she herself was thinking. You ask about him whom your soul loves? And he has no name? Who then are you, and who is he? I have said this because of the singularity of the expression and the remarkable carelessness of the words, by which the present Scripture appears quite unlike the rest. Hence in this bridal song words are not to be weighed, but affections. Why so, except because holy love—the single subject of this whole book, as is plain—is not to be assessed by word or tongue, but by deed and truth? Love speaks everywhere; and if anyone wishes to attain knowledge of what is read here, let him love. Otherwise, anyone who does not love approaches in vain to hear or read the song of love; for a cold breast cannot comprehend burning speech. Just as one who does not know Greek does not understand a Greek speaker, nor one who is not Latin understands a Latin speaker, and likewise with the rest, so the language of love will be foreign to one who does not love; it will be like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal (1 Cor. 13:1). But these men—I mean the watchmen—because they too have received from the Spirit so that they may love, know what the Spirit says; and, being thoroughly familiar with the utterances of love, they have ready an answer in a like language, that is, in the pursuits of love and the offices of devotion.

2. Accordingly, they instruct her so briefly concerning what she seeks that she says: “A little while after I had passed beyond them, I found him whom my soul loves.” Fittingly, “a little while,” because they made for her a shortened word, handing on the Creed of faith. [Col. 1163D] And what follows is of the same kind. The Bride indeed had to pass through those through whom she came to know the truth; yet she also had to pass beyond them. For unless she had passed beyond even them, she would not have found him whom she sought. And that she was persuaded of this by them you need not doubt. For they did not preach themselves but their Lord Jesus, who is undoubtedly both above and beyond them. Hence he says: “Pass over to me, all you who desire me” (Sir. 24:26). Nor was it enough to pass over; she is taught also to pass beyond. For he whom she was tracking had passed beyond. He had not merely passed from death to life, but had passed beyond into glory. Why should she not likewise have had to pass beyond? Otherwise, she could not lay hold of him unless she followed his footsteps wherever he had gone.

3. To make my meaning clearer: if my Lord Jesus had indeed risen from the dead but had not ascended to heaven, one could not say of him that he had “passed beyond,” but only that he had “passed”; and consequently the Bride seeking him would have had only to pass, not to pass beyond. But now, because in rising he had already passed, and had added passing beyond, namely by ascending, she rightly declared that she had not merely passed but had passed beyond them, since by faith and devotion she followed him even to heaven. Therefore, to believe in the resurrection is to pass; to believe also in the ascension is to pass beyond. And perhaps—as I remember having said one day when I expounded the matter [Sermon 1 for the feast of Easter]—she knew the former but did not know the latter. [Col. 1164B] Thus, instructed by them in what she lacked, namely that he who had risen had also ascended, she herself ascended with him—that is, she passed beyond—and found him. Why should she not find him, when in mind [variant: “by faith”] she reaches where he is in body? “A little while after I had passed beyond them.” And fittingly, “them”: for our Head has preceded and surpassed both them and his other members that are on earth by two stages—resurrection, as we have said, and ascension. For Christ is the firstfruits. And if he has gone before, so has our faith. Where would faith not follow him? “If he ascends into heaven, it is there; if he descends into hell, it is present; and if he takes his wings at dawn and dwells at the farthest bounds of the sea, ‘even there,’ it says, ‘your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me’” (Ps. 138:8–10). Finally, has not the almighty and supremely good Father of the Bridegroom, in accordance with this faith, raised us together and made us sit at his right hand [variant adds: “in the heavenly places”]? This corresponds to the Church’s saying that she had passed beyond them, since she had passed beyond herself, standing by faith where she had not yet arrived in fact. I think it is also clear why she preferred to say that she had “passed beyond” rather than merely “passed.” Let us also pass on to what follows.

4. “I held him, and I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.” Thus it is: from that time onward the Christian race does not fail, nor faith from the earth, nor charity from the Church. The rivers came, the winds blew, and they beat upon it, but it did not fall, because it was founded upon the rock (Matt. 7:25). And the rock is Christ. Therefore neither the verbosity of philosophers, nor the quibbles of heretics, nor the swords of persecutors could, or ever will, separate her from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:39). So firmly does she hold him whom her soul loves, so good it is for her to cleave to God. “It is good to glue,” says Isaiah (Isa. 41:7). What is more tenacious than glue, which is neither washed away by waters, dissolved by winds, nor severed by swords? Indeed, “many waters cannot quench charity” (Song 8:7). “I held him, and I will not let him go.” And the holy patriarch says: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. 32:26). Thus she does not wish to let him go, and perhaps she wishes this even more than the patriarch did, because not even for a blessing does she wish it. For he let him go after receiving the blessing, but she does not. “I do not want your blessing,” she says, “but you. What have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. 72:25). “I will not let you go, not even if you bless me.”

5. “I held him, and I will not let him go.” Perhaps he too wishes to be held, when he says: “My delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8:31); and when, making his promise, he says: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). What bond is stronger than this, established by the so vehement will of one of two? “I held him,” she says. Yet in turn she herself is held by him whom she holds, to whom she says elsewhere: “You have held my right hand” (Ps. 72:24). How can she who is held and holds now fall? She holds by the firmness of faith; she holds by the affection of devotion. But she could not hold long unless she were held. And she is held by the power and mercy of the Lord. “I held him, and I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.” Great is the Church’s charity, which does not begrudge even her rival, the Synagogue, her delights. What could be kinder than to be ready to share with an enemy the very one whom her soul loves? Yet this is no wonder, since “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22). Let the Savior return to the place from which he came, that the remnant of Israel may be saved. Let not the branches be ungrateful to the root, nor the children to their mother. Let not the branches envy the root what they received from it; let not the children envy their mother what they sucked from her breasts. Let the Church, then, firmly hold the salvation which Judaea lost and she herself seized, until the fullness of the Gentiles enter and thus all Israel is saved. Let her desire that the common salvation may come into common possession—a salvation so received by all that nothing is diminished for each. Indeed, this is what she does, and more. What more? She wishes the name and grace of Bride to be granted to her. This truly exceeds salvation.

6. Her charity would be incredible, if the word she herself spoke had not established its credibility. For, if you notice, she said that she wished to bring him whom she held not only into her mother’s house but also into the chamber, which signifies a prerogative. It was enough for salvation if he entered the house; but the secrecy of the chamber signifies grace. “Today salvation has come to this house,” he says (Luke 19:9). Why should salvation not come to those of the household when the Savior enters the house? But she who deserves to receive him into the chamber possesses a private secret reserved for herself. Salvation comes to the house; delights are stored away in the bridal chamber. “I will bring him into my mother’s house,” she says. Into what house, if not that concerning which he had long ago foretold the Jews: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Luke 13:35)? He did what he said, as you have his own testimony about it in the prophet: “I have left my house,” he says, “I have forsaken my inheritance” (Jer. 12:7). And now she promises to bring him back and restore the lost salvation of the house of her mother. And if this seems too little, hear what good she adds: “And into the chamber of her who bore me.” He who enters the bridal chamber is a bridegroom. Great is the power of love! The Savior had left his house and inheritance in indignation; now, softened and turned by her favor, he returns not merely as Savior but as Bridegroom. Blessed are you from the Lord, daughter, who restrain indignation and restore the inheritance. Blessed are you to your mother, by whose benefit wrath is turned aside, salvation returns, and he returns who says to her: “I am your salvation” (Ps. 34:3). This is not enough: let him add and say, “I will betroth you to myself in faith; I will betroth you to myself in judgment and justice; I will betroth you to myself in mercy and compassions” (Hos. 2:19–20). But remember that she who reconciles these friendships is the Bride. How, then, does she yield—or, not to say desire—her Bridegroom, and this Bridegroom, for another? It is not so. A good daughter indeed desires him for her mother, but not so as to yield him to her; rather, so as to share him. One is enough for two—except that now they were no longer two, but one in him. For he is our peace, who makes both one, so that there may be one Bride and one Bridegroom, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXX [Note: Delivered after the Council of Rheims in the year 1148, at which Gilbert was condemned.]. A subtle discussion of the image, or Word, of God, and of the soul which is according to the image; and of the error of Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers.

1. Some of you, as I have learned, bear it with less than an even mind that, for several days now, while I delight to linger over the astonishment and wonder of the sacraments, the discourse which we offer has either had no seasoning of moral instruction or only a very little. [Col. 1166C] This is indeed unusual. But may I review what has been said? I will not proceed unless I first go back over everything. Come then, tell me if you remember from what passage of Scripture this deprivation began, so that I may begin again from there. It is mine to repair the losses—indeed, the Lord’s, from whom we presume everything. From what beginning, then, must we resume? Was it from this: “On my bed I sought through the nights him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:1)? Unless I am mistaken, it was. From that point until now my one concern has been, after dispersing the dense darkness of these allegories, to bring into light the hidden delights of Christ and the Church. Let us therefore return to examining the moral sense. It will not be burdensome to me to do what is beneficial to you. And this will fittingly be done if we assign to the Word and the soul the same things that have been said concerning Christ and the Church.

2. But someone says to me: “Why do you join these two? What has the soul to do with the Word?” Very much, in every way. First, there is so great a kinship of natures, in that the one is the Image and the other is according to the image. Next, likeness bears witness to their kinship. For the soul was made not only according to the image but also according to the likeness. In what respect, you ask, is it like? Hear first about the Image. The Word is truth, wisdom, justice; and this is the Image. The image of what? Of justice, wisdom, and truth. For this Image is justice from justice, wisdom from wisdom, truth from truth, as light from light, God from God. The soul is none of these things, because it is not the Image. Yet it is capable of them, desires them, and perhaps is thereby according to the image. It is a lofty creature: in its capacity for majesty it bears a mark of distinction, and in its desire for uprightness. We read that “God made man upright” (Eccl. 7:30), and, as was said, its capacity proves that this is something great. For that which is according to the image must accord with the Image and must not share the name of image emptily; just as the Image itself is not called image by a bare or empty name. You have concerning him who is the Image that, “being in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized” (Phil. 2:6). Here you are plainly shown both his uprightness in the form of God and his majesty in equality, so that, when uprightness is compared with uprightness and greatness with greatness, that which is according to the image and the Image appear reciprocally to correspond harmoniously; just as the Image in both respects likewise corresponds to him whose Image it is. He is indeed the one of whom you heard holy David sing in the psalms, now: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power” (Ps. 146:5); now again: “The Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him” (Ps. 91:16). From this upright and great God his Image has that it too is upright and great; and the soul has this, being according to the image.

3. But I say: Does the Image, then, have nothing more than the soul which is according to the image, because we assign greatness and uprightness to this soul also? It has very much more. The soul received both by measure; the Image, in equality. Is that not more? Notice another point. Creation or condescension bestowed both qualities on the soul; generation bestowed them on the Image. And this is unquestionably more magnificent. But no one could deny that this too is more eminent: both qualities are from God in the soul, but in the Image they are also of God—that is, of God’s substance. For his Image is consubstantial with God, and everything that appears to be communicated to that same Image belongs substantially, not accidentally, to both. Observe one further point in which the Image is notably pre-eminent. Greatness and uprightness—two things which no one fails to know differ by nature—are one in the Image. Nor only that: they are one also with the Image. For in the Image not only is being upright identical with being great, but being great and upright is identical with being. It is not so with the soul. Its greatness and its uprightness are distinct from it and distinct from one another. For, as I taught above, the soul is great insofar as it is capable of eternal things, and upright insofar as it desires things above. A soul that neither seeks nor savors the things above, but the things upon earth, is certainly not upright but bent, though for this reason it does not cease to be great, since even so it remains capable of eternity. For it will never fail to be capable of it, even if it never comes to possess it; so that it may be as Scripture says: “Nevertheless, man passes in an image” (Ps. 38:7)—but only in part, so that the Word’s pre-eminence may be apparent precisely from its integrity. For how can the Word fall away from greatness or uprightness, when it possesses them in such a way that it is what it possesses? Or it is only in part lest, if man were deprived of the whole, no hope of salvation should remain. For if he ceased to be great and capable, what could he hope for? The soul’s greatness is measured by capacity, as I said. But what could one hope who were incapable?

4. Therefore, by the greatness which he retains even when uprightness is lost, man passes in an image, as if limping on one foot and made an alien son. Of such persons, I think, it was said: “Alien sons have lied to me; alien sons have grown old and limped from their paths” (Ps. 17:48). They are aptly called alien sons: sons because of retained greatness; alien because of lost uprightness. He would not have said, “They limped,” but “They fell,” or something similar, if human beings [variant: “man’s”] had wholly stripped off the image. But now, in respect of greatness, man passes in an image; whereas in respect of uprightness, limping as it were, he is troubled and cast down from the image, as Scripture says: “Nevertheless, man passes in an image; yet he is troubled in vain.” Utterly in vain, for it follows: “He heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it” (Ps. 38:7). Why does he not know, except because, bending himself down toward these low and earthly things, he heaps up earth for himself? He truly does not know, concerning what he entrusts to earth, for whom he gathers it: for the moth that destroys, or the thief that digs through; for an enemy that plunders, or fire that devours. Thus for the wretched person who bends and broods over earthly things comes that mournful cry from the psalm: “I have become wretched and bent down utterly; all day long I went about mourning” (Ps. 37:7). For he experiences in himself the truth of that saying of the Wise Man: “God made man upright, but he has entangled himself in many sorrows” (Eccl. 7:30). And immediately comes the voice of mockery addressed to him: “Bend down, that we may pass over” (Isa. 51:23).

5. But how did we arrive here? Certainly from our wish to teach that uprightness and greatness—the twofold good by which we had defined the Image—are neither one in the soul nor one with the soul, just as we have established with equally firm assertion that they are one in the Word and one with the Word. From what has been said, it is clear concerning uprightness that it is distinct both from the soul and from the soul’s greatness, since even when it is absent the soul remains, and remains great. But how is the distinction between the soul and its greatness to be shown? It cannot be shown by the same argument by which the distinction between uprightness and the soul was demonstrated, since the soul cannot be deprived of its greatness as it can be of its uprightness. Nevertheless, the soul is not its own greatness. For although the soul is not found without its greatness, greatness itself is also found outside the soul. You ask where? In angels. For angels are great for the same reason by which the soul’s greatness is established: namely, by their capacity for eternity. If it was proved that the soul differs from its uprightness because it can lack it, why should it not likewise be clear that it differs from its greatness, which it cannot claim as its own exclusive possession? Therefore, since neither uprightness is in every being nor greatness in the soul alone, it is plain that each alike differs from the soul. Again, no form is identical with that of which it is the form. But greatness is a form of the soul. Nor is it any less a form because it is inseparable from the soul. For this is true of all substantial differences, true not only of properties properly so called but also of certain proper attributes, and of countless other forms. Thus the soul is not its own greatness, no more than a raven is its own blackness, snow its own whiteness, or a human being his own capacity for laughter or rationality; although you never find a raven without blackness, snow without whiteness, or a human being who is not both capable of laughter and rational. So too the soul and the soul’s greatness, though inseparable, are nevertheless distinct from one another. How could they fail to be distinct, when the latter is in a subject, while the former is the subject and substance? Only the supreme and uncreated nature, which is the Trinity God, claims for itself the pure and unique simplicity of its essence, such that there is not one thing and another, nor one thing in one place and another elsewhere, nor even one thing at one time and another at another. Remaining in itself, it is what it has, and what it is, it is always and in one manner. In it many things are reduced to one, and diverse things to the same, so that it acquires no plurality from the number of things and experiences no alteration from their variety. It contains all places and orders each thing in its own place, while itself contained in no place. Times pass beneath it, not through it. It does not await future things, recall past things, or experience present things.

6. Let the new men depart from us, beloved; not dialecticians but heretics, who most wickedly argue that the greatness by which God is great, the goodness by which he is good, the wisdom by which he is wise, the justice by which he is just, and finally the divinity by which he is God, are not God. “God is God by divinity,” they say, “but divinity is not God.” Perhaps God does not deign to be that which is so great that it makes God. But if divinity is not God, what is it? It is either God, or something that is not God, or nothing. Certainly you do not grant that it is God; but, I think, you will not grant that it is nothing either, since you confess it to be so necessary to God that not only could God not exist without it, but he is it. But if it is something which is not God, it will be either less than God, greater than God, or equal to God. But how can it be less, when God is God by it? It remains that you must confess it either greater or equal. But if greater, it is the highest good, not God; if equal, there are two highest goods, not one. Catholic understanding rejects either conclusion. We judge the same in every respect concerning greatness, goodness, justice, and wisdom as concerning divinity: in God they are one, and one with God. For he is not good from one source and great from another; nor just or wise from a source other than that by which he is great and good; nor, finally, is he all these things together from any source other than that by which he is God—and this too only from himself.

7. But the heretic says: “What? Do you deny that God is by divinity?” [Note: Here the manuscript codices vary. Cisterciensis has *divinitatem*; Germanensis, “You do not deny that God is by divinity.” But our reading is sound; it is similar to *On Consideration*, book V, no. 15, where the same argument is discussed.] No; rather, I maintain that the very divinity by which he is, is nevertheless God, lest I admit that something is more excellent than God. Thus I say that he is great by greatness, but by the greatness that he himself is, lest I posit something greater than God; and I confess that he is good by goodness, but by no goodness other than himself, lest I seem to have found something better than him; and likewise regarding the rest. Securely and gladly I proceed, as they say, with unimpeded foot in the judgment of him who said: “God is great only by that greatness which is what he himself is. Otherwise that greatness will be greater than God.” This is Augustine, the most powerful hammer of heretics [Note: *On the Trinity*, book V, ch. 10, no. 11.]. Therefore, if anything may properly be said of God, it is more correct and fitting to say, “God is greatness, goodness, justice, wisdom,” than “God is great, good, just, or wise.”

8. Hence, not without reason, lately at the council which Pope Eugenius held at Rheims, both the pope himself and the other bishops regarded as perverse and wholly suspect that exposition in the book of Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, in which he commented upon Boethius’s most sound and Catholic words concerning the Trinity as follows: “The Father is truth, that is, true; the Son is truth, that is, true; the Holy Spirit is truth, that is, true. And these three together are not three truths, but one truth, that is, one true [being].” O obscure and perverse explanation! How much more truly and soundly he would have said the reverse: “The Father is true, that is, truth; the Son is true, that is, truth; the Holy Spirit is true, that is, truth. And these three are one true [being], that is, one truth.” He would indeed have done this if he had deigned to imitate holy Fulgentius, who says: “For the one truth of the one God—indeed, the one truth, the one God—does not permit the service and worship of Creator and creature to be joined” [Note: *On the Orthodox Faith, to Donatus*, ch. 5.]. He would have been a good corrector, speaking most truly about truth and holding a pious and Catholic understanding of the true and pure simplicity of the divine substance, in which there can be nothing that is not itself and itself God. Although in several other places that book of the aforementioned bishop seemed more plainly to depart from the rightness of faith; I offer one further example. For when the author said, “When ‘God, God, God’ is spoken, it pertains to substance,” our commentator added, “Not that which is, but that by which he is.” Far be it from the Catholic Church to agree that there is a substance, or indeed any thing at all, by which God is and which is not God!

9. But we are no longer speaking these things against Gilbert himself, since at that same assembly, humbly acquiescing in the judgment of the bishops, he condemned with his own mouth both these and the other things found worthy of censure. We speak rather because of those who are said still to copy and read that book, despite the apostolic prohibition promulgated there, obstinately persisting in following the bishop where he himself did not stand, and preferring to have him as teacher of error rather than of correction. We speak also for your sake. Taking occasion from the distinction between the Image and the soul made according to the image, I judged it worthwhile to make this digression, so that if any of you have perhaps at some time drunk anything from stolen waters, which seem sweeter (Prov. 9:17), you may take the antidote and vomit it out; and, with the stomach of your mind cleansed, may approach what remains, according to our promise, to be said concerning likeness, and henceforth joyfully draw purer things not from our own resources but from the fountains of the Savior, Jesus Christ our Lord, Bridegroom of the Church, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXI. On the agreement and likeness of the soul with the Word, according to identity of essence, immortality of life, and freedom of choice.

[Col. 1171B]

1. Earlier we inquired into the affinity of the soul with the Word, and necessarily so. For what agreement is there between such majesty and such poverty, that this sublimity and this humility should be said, in the manner and love of bridegrooms, to embrace one another as equals? If we say this truly, it is a cause for very joyful confidence; if falsely, for severely punishable audacity. Therefore we had to inquire into their agreement. Much agreement has already been found, though not all. For who, however dull, does not see how closely the Image and that which is according to the image look toward one another? Yesterday’s discourse, if you recall, assigned one thing to the one and another thing to the other. Nor was kinship shown there merely concerning the image: it was shown also concerning likeness, except that we have not yet explained in what respect or respects this likeness especially consists. Come, let us now attend to this explanation, so that the more fully the soul recognizes its own origin, the more it may blush to live a degenerate life; or rather, whatever it discovers in its nature to have been corrupted by sin, it may strive diligently to reform, and, governing itself worthily of its lineage—indeed by God’s gift—may confidently approach the embraces of the Word.

2. Let it observe, therefore, from this divine nobility of likeness that there is in it that natural simplicity of its substance by which for it to be is the same as to live; though it is not the same as to live well or to live blessedly, so that there is likeness, not equality. It is a near degree, yet only a degree. For to have being identical with living, and likewise to have being identical with living blessedly, are not of one excellence or an equal summit. Therefore, if the former belongs to the Word by reason of his sublimity, and the latter to the soul by reason of likeness, then—while the Word’s eminence remains intact—the kinship of their natures and the soul’s prerogative are manifest.

To make this clearer: for God alone, to be is to be blessed; and this is the first and utterly pure simplicity. Second, and like to this, is that to have being is to live; and this belongs to the soul. From this, though it is an inferior degree, one may rise not only to living well but also to living blessedly. This does not mean that, even then, for one who attains it, to be will be the same as to be blessed; so that, while it glories in likeness, it may nevertheless always, because of the disparity, have cause for all its bones to say: “Lord, who is like unto thee?” (Ps. 34:10). Yet this is a good degree for the soul, since from it—and from it alone—the ascent is made to the blessed life.

3. There are living things, and among them two kinds: those which have sensation and those which do not. Sensible things are preferred to insensible things; and life is that by which both are alive, and the former also feel. Life and a living thing do not stand together on one level; much less life and things without life. The soul is life: it is indeed living, but not from another source than itself; and consequently, properly speaking, it is not so much a living thing as life. Hence, when infused into the body, it gives that body life, so that by the presence of life the body is not life, but living.

It is clear, then, that even for a living body, to live is not the same as to be, since it can be and not live at all. Still less can things devoid of life rise to this degree. Yet not everything called, or actually being, life is at once able to attain it. There is the life of beasts, and also that of trees—the former thriving in sensation, the latter lacking it. Yet for neither is being the same as living. For, as many suppose,

> [Note: Col. 1171D: That is, the Empedocleans.]

they existed first in the elements, before the one existed in limbs and the other in branches. Accordingly, when they cease to give life, they at the same time cease to live, but do not cease to be. They are dissolved and broken up together, as things not merely bound together but also compounded. For none of these is one simple thing; each consists of several elements. Therefore it is not reduced to nothing, but is scattered into parts, so that each returns to its own principle: air to air, fire to fire, and the rest in the same manner. Thus for such life, being and living are by no means the same, since it exists even when it does not live.

4. Moreover, none of those things for which being is not the same as living will ever advance or rise to living well and blessedly, since it could not attain even this lower degree. The human soul alone is known to stand at this level. It was created in this dignity—life from life, simple from simple, immortal from immortal—so that it is not far from the highest degree, namely, that in which being is the same as living blessedly. There alone stands the blessed and only potent One, the King of kings and Lord of lords.

The soul therefore received in its creation, though not actual blessedness, yet the ability to be blessed; and thus it approaches, as far as it may, the highest degree, though it does not attain it. For neither will it ever be true even of the soul, as we said above, that to be is the same as to be blessed—not even when it is blessed. We admit likeness; we reject equality. For example, God is life, and the soul is life also: alike indeed, but unequal. Alike because it is life, because it lives through itself, because it is not merely living but also life-giving, just as he is all these things. Unequal by the entire interval between Creator and creature. Unequal because, as it would not exist unless created by him, so it would not live unless vivified by him. I mean that it would not live the spiritual life, not the natural life. For even what does not live spiritually must live immortally in the natural sense.

But what kind of life is that in which it would have been better not to have been born than not to die from it? It is rather death—and therefore the heavier death, because it belongs to sin, not to nature. “The death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. 33:22). Thus the soul that lives according to the flesh is “living dead” [1 Tim. 5:6]; for it would altogether have been better for it not to live than to live in that way. From this life-like death it will never rise unless through the word of life—indeed, through the Word who is life, living and life-giving.

5. In another respect also the soul is immortal and thus likewise resembles the Word, though it is not equal to him. For the immortality of the Godhead surpasses so greatly that the Apostle says of God: “Who alone hath immortality” (1 Tim. 6:16). I think this is said because God alone is unchangeable by nature, he who says: “I am the Lord, and I change not” (Mal. 3:6). True and complete immortality admits change no more than it admits an end, since every change is a kind of imitation of death. For everything that changes, when it passes from one mode of being to another, must in some way die to what it is, in order to begin to be what it is not. And if there are as many deaths as changes, where is immortality?

The creation itself “was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope” (Rom. 8:20). Nevertheless, the soul is immortal, since it is life to itself; and as there is nowhere for it to fall away from itself, so there is nowhere for it to fall away from life. Yet, since it is evidently changed by its affections, let it recognize that it resembles God in immortality in such a way as to know that it lacks no small part of immortality, yielding to God alone absolute and perfect immortality—he with whom “is no variableness, neither shadow of turning” (Jas. 1:17). Nevertheless, this discussion has discovered no mean dignity in the soul: by a twofold proximity of nature it seems to draw near to the Word, through simplicity of essence and perpetuity of life.

6. But one further point occurs which I shall by no means pass over. It makes the soul no less distinguished and no less like the Word—perhaps even more so. Freedom of choice is this: something plainly divine, shining forth in the soul like a jewel in gold. From this it possesses discernment in judging and the power of choosing between good and evil, between life and death, and likewise between light and darkness, as well as whatever other opposites appear to stand over against one another in the condition of the mind. Yet among these things an arbiter—that is, the eye of the soul—judges and distinguishes; and as it is an arbiter in discerning, so it is free in choosing. Hence it is called free choice, because it is permitted to move among these things at the judgment of the will.

From this, man is capable of deserving. For every good or evil deed which it was free for you not to do is rightly reckoned to your merit or demerit. Thus, justly praised is not only one who could have done evil but did not, but also one who could have failed to do good yet did it. Likewise, guilt is not absent either from one who could have avoided doing evil but did it, or from one who could have done good but did not. Where freedom is absent, merit is absent also. Therefore animals devoid of reason deserve nothing, because they lack freedom as they lack deliberation. They are led by sensation, carried by impulse, swept away by appetite. They have no judgment by which to judge or govern themselves—indeed, not even the instrument of judgment, namely reason. Hence they are not judged, because they do not judge. For by what right can an account be demanded from those who have received no faculty of accounting?

7. Man alone does not suffer this natural force, and therefore he alone among animals is free. Yet, with sin intervening, he too suffers a certain force—but from the will, not from nature—so that he is not even thus deprived of his inborn freedom. For what is voluntary is free. Sin has indeed caused “the corruptible body” to weigh down the soul; but it does so by love, not by weight. For the reason why the soul, which could fall by itself, can no longer rise by itself is the will. Enfeebled and prostrate through a corrupted and vicious love of the corruptible body, it at the same time refuses the love of righteousness.

Thus, in some strange and perverse way, the will itself—changed for the worse by sin—creates necessity for itself: necessity, because it is voluntary, cannot excuse the will; nor can the will, because it is ensnared, exclude necessity. This necessity is in some manner voluntary. It is a force that flatters while pressing and presses while flattering. Therefore, once it has consented to sin, the guilty will can neither shake this necessity off by itself nor in any way excuse itself before reason.

Hence that plaintive voice, as though groaning under the weight of this necessity: “O Lord, I suffer violence; answer thou for me.” Yet, knowing in turn that it could not justly complain against the Lord, since its own will was rather the cause, see what it immediately adds: “What shall I say, or what shall he answer me, when I myself have done it?”

> [Note: Col. 1173: The Vulgate has “he hath done it” (*fecerit*). Bernard gives both readings in Sermon 3 on Various Subjects, no. 6.]

(Isa. 38:14–15.) It was pressed beneath a yoke, but beneath no yoke other than a certain voluntary slavery. In respect of its slavery it was pitiable; in respect of its will, inexcusable. For it is the will which, while free, made itself the slave of sin by consenting to sin; and it is likewise the will which keeps itself under sin by serving voluntarily.

8. “Consider what you are saying,” someone says to me. “Do you call voluntary what is admittedly now necessary? It is true that the will has enslaved itself, but it does not itself hold itself fast; rather, it is held fast even unwillingly.” At least you rightly grant that it is held fast. But take care to retain that it is the will which you admit is held fast. Do you then speak of an unwilling will? Surely a will is not held unwillingly. For will belongs to one who wills, not to one unwilling. If it is held while willing, it holds itself. What then shall it say, or what shall it answer him, when it has itself done this? What has it done? It has made itself a slave; whence it is said: “Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin” (John 8:34). Therefore, when it sinned—for it sinned when it resolved to obey sin—it made itself a slave.

But it becomes free if it does not continue to act thus. Yet it does act thus, keeping itself in the same slavery. For the will is not held unwillingly: it is will. Therefore, because it wills, it has not merely made itself a slave but continues to make itself one. Rightly then, and as must often be recalled, what shall it answer him when it has itself done it and continues to do it?

9. “But,” you say, “you will not make me disbelieve the necessity I suffer, which I experience in myself and against which I struggle continually.” Where, I ask, do you feel this necessity? Is it not in the will? Then you do indeed will rather firmly that which you will necessarily. You strongly will what you cannot not will, even while struggling strongly against it. But where there is will, there is freedom.

Yet I say this of natural freedom, not spiritual freedom, that freedom by which, as the Apostle says, Christ has made us free (Gal. 4:31). For of the latter the same Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Cor. 3:17). Thus the soul, in a strange and evil way, under this voluntary and wrongly free necessity, is both enslaved and free: enslaved because of necessity; free because of will. And, what is stranger and more miserable, it is guilty insofar as it is free, enslaved insofar as it is guilty, and therefore enslaved insofar as it is free.

“Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the accusation of this shameful slavery?” Wretched, yet free. Free because human; wretched because a slave. Free because like God; wretched because opposed to God. “O thou Preserver of men, why hast thou set me as a mark against thee?” (Job 7:20). For you set me so when you did not prevent it; otherwise I set myself so, and “I am become burdensome to myself” (Job 7:20). Most justly: so that your enemy may be my enemy, and he who resists you may also resist me. But I, who have become opposed to you and to myself, and who find in my members what contradicts both my mind and your law—who will deliver me from my own hands? “For that which I would, that do I not”; but it is I, not another, who prevents me. “And what I hate, that do I”; but it is I, not another, who compels me (Rom. 7:15).

Would that this hindrance and compulsion were so violent as not to be voluntary: perhaps then I might be excused. Or would that they were so voluntary as not to be violent: certainly then I might be corrected. But now no way of escape lies open to the wretched man whom, as I have said, the will makes inexcusable and necessity makes incurable. “Who shall deliver me out of the hand of the sinner, and out of the hand of the transgressor of the law and of the unjust?” (Ps. 70:4).

10. Does someone ask of whom I complain? Of myself. I am that sinner, that transgressor of the law, that unjust one. A sinner, because I have sinned; a transgressor of the law, because I persist in acting against the law by my will. For my very will is a law in my members, resisting the divine law. And because the law of the Lord is the law of my mind, as it is written, “The law of his God is in his heart” (Ps. 36:31), my own will is thereby found opposed even to myself—which is the greatest injustice. For to whom is he not unjust who is unjust to himself? “He that is wicked to himself,” says Scripture, “to whom will he be good?” (Ecclus. 14:5).

I confess that I am not good, because “there is no good thing in me.” Yet I shall console myself, because this too is the voice of saints: “I know that there is no good thing in me,” he says. Yet he distinguishes what he says: “in me,” interpreting it as “in my flesh,” because of the opposing law which is in it. For he has a law also in his mind, and it is better. Is not the law of God good? If he is evil because of an evil law, how is he not good because of a good law? Is what belongs to his flesh his own evil, so that he is evil from the evil law, while he is not at all good from the good law? It is not so.

The law of God is in his mind, and so in his mind that it is also the law of his mind. He himself bears witness, saying: “I find another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind.” Is what belongs to his flesh his own, and what belongs to his mind not his own? I say even more. Why should I not say what the same teacher himself says? For when he says, “With the mind I myself serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin,” he plainly shows what he acknowledges to be more truly his own. He judges the evil in the flesh so foreign to himself that he says: “Now then it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me.” And perhaps for this reason he significantly says that he found “another” law in his members: he regarded it as alien and, as it were, adventitious.

Therefore I venture still further, not rashly: Paul is no longer evil because of the evil that he has in the flesh, but rather good because of the good that he has in the mind. Is he not good who consents to the law of God because it is good? For although he likewise acknowledges that he serves the law of sin, he does this in the flesh, not in the mind. Since he serves the law of God with the mind and the law of sin with the flesh, you may decide which of these should chiefly be imputed to Paul. For my own part, I readily believe that what belongs to the mind is of more account than what belongs to the flesh—not only to me, but also to Paul himself, as has already been said, who declares: “If then I do that which I would not, it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me” (Rom. 7:18, 23, 25, 20).

11. But let this suffice concerning freedom. In the little book I wrote, *On Grace and Free Choice*, perhaps different things are argued concerning image and likeness; but, I think, not contrary things. You have read those things; you have heard these. Which you approve more—or which should be preferred—I leave to your judgment; or, if you perceive something better than both, I rejoice and shall rejoice in it.

But however those matters stand, you now hold three principal points commended to you: simplicity, immortality, and freedom. And I think it is now clear to you that, by reason of its inborn and native likeness—which shines forth so remarkably in these—the soul has no slight kinship with the Word, the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXII

**How the soul, while remaining like God, has nevertheless through sin become unlike him in simplicity, immortality, and freedom.**

[Col. 1177A]

1. What do you think? Can we now return to the order of exposition from which we digressed, since the kinship of the Word and the soul, for the demonstration of which the digression was made, has become clear? We could, it seems to me, unless I felt that a small measure of uncertainty still remains in what has been said. I do not wish to steal anything away. I am unwilling to pass over what I judge useful to you. And how should I dare do so, especially in matters which I receive for your sake?

I know of a man who, while speaking, held back and reserved for himself something suggested by the Spirit—not with an unbelieving mind, but with one insufficiently trusting—in order that he might have something to say when he treated the subject again. And behold, as it seemed to him, a voice came to him: “So long as you keep this back, you shall receive nothing else.”

> [Note: Col. 1177D: Bernard means himself, in the manner of the Apostle Paul; Caesarius of Heisterbach bears witness to this in his sermon for the Octave of the Nativity. “When at one time,” he says, “he was dictating something—I know not what—and had readily at hand a testimony fitting the present place, and wished to reserve it for the end, fearing a lack there, he heard a voice from heaven saying: ‘If you reserve this, nothing else will be given you.’” Thus, says Manricus, it was not he himself who spoke, but God in him. See what he says on the same subject in Sermon 18 on the Song of Songs, no. 2.]

What if he had held it back, not by providing for his own lack, but by begrudging his brothers’ advancement? Would not even that which he seemed to have be rightly taken from him? May God, as he has always done, keep this far from your servant. May that unfailing fountain of saving wisdom deign continually to abound for me, just as I have without envy shared with you and poured forth whatever he has thus far deigned to pour into me. If I defraud you, from whom should I no longer fear being defrauded myself? Even from God.

2. There is, then, something in what has been said which, I fear, may give offense unless it is made level. And, unless I am mistaken, among those standing here are some whom the point I am about to make has troubled. You remember that we assigned to the soul a threefold likeness to the Word—or rather, observed that it was marked by it—and that we thought this likeness inseparably present in the soul. This may seem to some to conflict with testimonies of Scripture: for example, the words in the Psalms, “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he is compared to the senseless beasts, and is become like unto them” (Ps. 48:13, 21); and likewise, “They changed their glory into the likeness of a calf that eateth grass” (Ps. 105:20); and also what is openly spoken in God’s person: “Thou thoughtest wickedly that I should be like thee” (Ps. 49:21). Many other passages appear alike to assert that God’s likeness in man was erased after sin.

What, then, shall we say to these? That these three things are not at all in God, and that we must seek other things in which to assign the likeness? Or that they are in God indeed, but not in the soul, and that likeness is not found in them even so? Or that they are in the soul, but can also cease to be in it, and are therefore not inseparable? Far be it! They are in God and in the soul, and are always present; nor is there anything we have said of which we need repent, so wholly is it supported by truth certain and absolute.

But when Scripture speaks of an unlikeness that has arisen, it does not speak as though this likeness had been erased; it speaks because another unlikeness has been laid over it. The soul has not stripped off its native form; it has put on a foreign one over it. The latter was added, not the former lost. What came upon it could obscure what is inborn, but not destroy it. Thus the Apostle says: “Their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. 1:21); and the prophet: “How is the gold become dim! how is the most fine gold changed!” (Lam. 4:1). He laments the darkened gold, yet it remains gold; he laments the changed excellent color, but not the uprooting of the ground of that color. Simplicity remains wholly unmoved in its foundation, but does not appear, covered by the duplicity of human deceit, pretense, and hypocrisy.

3. How incongruously is duplicity mingled with simplicity! How unworthily is such a structure entrusted to such a foundation! The serpent had clothed itself in such craftiness when, in order to deceive, it presented itself as a counselor and pretended friendship. The inhabitants of Paradise, seduced by it, had likewise clothed themselves in such craftiness when they sought to cover their now shameful nakedness with the shade of a leafy tree, girdles of leaves, and words of excuse (Gen. 3). How widely from that time onward has the hereditary poison of hypocrisy infected all posterity! Name for me one among the children of Adam who is willing—not merely willing, but even able—to be seen as he is.

Nevertheless, in every soul, along with original duplicity, universal simplicity persists, so that shame may be heightened by the comparison. Immortality likewise persists, but dark and grim, as the gloomy mist of bodily death rushes in. For though the soul is not deprived of life, it can no longer secure the benefit of life even for its own body. And what of the fact that it does not retain even its own spiritual life? “The soul that sinneth, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:4). When this twofold death comes upon it, does not the kind of immortality it retains become sufficiently dark and wretched?

Add the desire for earthly things, all of which are destined for destruction: it thickens the darkness, so that in a soul living thus there can be seen in no part anything but a pale face and some image of death. Why should not that which is immortal desire things like itself, immortal and eternal, so that what it is may appear and what it has become may live? But instead it tastes and seeks contrary things; conforming itself to mortality by a degenerate manner of life, it blackens the brightness of immortality with the pitch-black color of a deadly habit. Why should the appetite for mortal things not make the immortal soul like mortal things and unlike immortal things? “He that toucheth pitch,” says the Wise Man, “shall be defiled therewith” (Ecclus. 13:1). By enjoying mortal things, it puts on mortality; and, as the likeness of death falls upon it, it discolors but does not put off the garment of immortality.

4. Observe Eve: how her immortal soul introduced the false coloring of mortality into the glory of its immortality by desiring mortal things. Why, being immortal, did she not despise mortal and transient things, content with what was like herself, immortal and eternal? “She saw,” it says, “that the tree was pleasant to the eyes, and delightful to behold, and sweet to eat” (Gen. 3:6). This sweetness, this delight, this beauty are not yours, O woman. They are yours only in respect of the clay that is your portion; they are not yours alone, but shared with all animals of the earth. What is yours—truly yours—comes from elsewhere and is something else: it is eternal, from eternity.

Why do you stamp another form upon your soul—indeed, a foreign deformity? For what delights one to possess, one also fears to lose; and fear is a color. As it stains freedom, it covers it and nevertheless makes it unlike itself. How much more worthily would the soul, faithful to its origin, desire nothing where it feared nothing, and thereby preserve for itself from this slavish fear the freedom native to it, remaining in its strength and beauty! Alas, it is not so: “the most fine color is changed.” You flee and hide yourself; you hear the voice of the Lord God and conceal yourself. Why, except because you fear him whom you loved, and the form of a slave has displaced the appearance of freedom?

5. That voluntary necessity and opposing law imposed upon the members, of which I spoke in the preceding sermon, also presses upon this same freedom. It entices a creature free by nature and, through its own will, subjects it to slavery, filling its face with shame, so that it serves the law of sin even in the flesh and against its will. Because it neglected to defend the native nobility of its nature by uprightness of conduct, it has come about, by the just judgment of its Creator, not that it should be stripped of its proper freedom, but that it should be clothed over, as with a double garment, in its own confusion (Ps. 108:29).

And fittingly “as with a double garment”: in a garment as though doubled, freedom remains because of the will, while servile conduct nevertheless proves necessity. This is how one must understand the soul’s simplicity and immortality. If you consider well, nothing will appear in it that is not covered with a double garment of this kind, both of likeness and of unlikeness.
