Is it not a double garment where deceit is not inborn but attached to simplicity, fastened to it as though by the needle of sin; where death is attached to immortality, and necessity to freedom? For duplicity of heart does not cancel the simplicity of essence; death—whether voluntary death through sin or necessary bodily death—does not cancel the immortality of nature; nor does the necessity of voluntary slavery cancel freedom of choice.

Thus evils foreign to the goods of nature do not replace but are added to them; they disfigure them, but do not destroy them; they disturb them, but do not cast them down. Hence the soul is unlike God, and hence unlike itself. Hence it is compared to senseless beasts and made like them; hence it is said to have changed its glory into the likeness of a calf feeding on grass; hence men, like foxes, possess dens of duplicity and deceit, and because they have made themselves the equals of foxes, they shall have the lot of foxes. Hence, according to Solomon, “one event happeneth to man and to beast” (Eccles. 3:19). Why should not he have a similar end who has lived similarly? He clung to earthly things in a beastly way; he will depart from the earth in a beastly death.

Hear another point. Why should it be surprising that we receive a similar end, since we also have a similar entrance? Whence comes to human beings, unless from beastly likeness, that excessive ardor in intercourse and that immoderate pain in childbirth? Thus, in conception and birth, in life and death, man is compared to senseless beasts and made like them.

6. What of the fact that the free creature does not govern as mistress the appetite subjected to it, but follows and obeys it as a slave? Does it not in this too assimilate and number itself with the other animals, which nature did not call to freedom but created in slavery—to serve their belly and obey appetite? Does it not thereby justly deserve the shame of being said or thought to be like God? Therefore he says: “Thou thoughtest wickedly that I should be like thee”; and he adds: “I will reprove thee, and set thee before thy face” (Ps. 49:21).

It is not the part of a soul that sees itself to imagine God like itself—at least a soul such as mine, sinful and unjust. Such a soul is reproved: “Thou thoughtest wickedly,” he says. He does not say, “Thou, soul, thoughtest,” or, “Thou, man, thoughtest that I should be like thee.” But if the unjust person is set before his own face, and if some diseased and foul countenance of his inner man is placed before him, so that he cannot dissemble or turn away from the impurity of his conscience but, even unwillingly, sees the filth of his sins and beholds the deformity of his vices, he will no longer be able to think God like himself. Rather, despairing at the great unlikeness he sees, I think he will cry out and say: “Lord, who is like unto thee?” (Ps. 34:10).

This is said because of that voluntary and newly acquired unlikeness. For the original likeness remains; and therefore the latter displeases the more, because the former remains. O how great a good is the one, and how great an evil the other! Yet, through their mutual comparison, each stands out more in its own kind.

7. Therefore, when the soul sees within itself so great a distance between these two realities, why should it not cry out, placed between hope and despair: “Lord, who is like unto thee?” It is drawn toward despair by so great an evil, yet called back to hope by so great a good. Hence, the more it is displeased with itself because of the evil it sees in itself, the more ardently it is drawn toward the good which it also beholds in itself. It desires to become what it was made to be: simple and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil. Why should it not be able to withdraw from that to which it was able to draw near? Why should it not be able to draw near to that from which it was able to withdraw?

Yet I would say that both must be hoped for from grace, not from nature—not even from human effort. For wisdom conquers malice (Wis. 7:30), not effort or nature. Nor is there lacking an occasion for hope: the soul’s conversion is to the Word. The soul’s noble kinship with the Word, of which we have now spoken for three days, and the enduring likeness which bears witness to that kinship, is not idle in the presence of the Word. He graciously receives into fellowship a spirit like himself in nature. And certainly, by the principle of nature, like seeks like.

The voice of one seeking says: “Return, Shulamite; return, that we may look upon thee” (Song 6:12). He will behold one like himself whom he did not behold while unlike; and he will also make himself available to be beheld. “We know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Take, then, that question, “Lord, who is like unto thee?” as arising more from difficulty than impossibility.

8. Or, if this pleases you more, it is the voice of one who marvels. That likeness is indeed wonderful and astonishing which is accompanied by the vision of God—rather, which is the vision of God; and I say that it consists in charity. Charity is that vision; charity is that likeness. Who would not marvel at the charity of God, who has been despised and yet calls back?

Rightly is the unjust person mentioned above reproved for claiming God’s likeness for himself; for by loving iniquity he can love neither himself nor God. For Scripture says: “He that loveth iniquity hateth his own soul” (Ps. 10:6). Therefore, once iniquity—the cause of this partial unlikeness—has been taken away, there shall be union of spirit, mutual vision, and mutual love. For when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away; and there shall be between the two a chaste and perfected love, full knowledge, clear vision, firm union, indivisible fellowship, and perfect likeness.

Then the soul shall know as it is known (1 Cor. 13:10, 12); then it shall love as it is loved; and the Bridegroom shall rejoice over the bride, knowing and known, loving and loved—Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXIII

**How the soul, however corrupted by vices, may nevertheless return through chaste and holy love to the likeness of the Bridegroom, that is, Christ.**

1. So far as the regular hour which we have set aside for speaking allowed, three days [variant: two days] have been spent demonstrating the kinship of the Word and the soul. What benefit is there in all this labor? This, indeed: we have taught that every soul, though laden with sins, entangled in vices, captured by seductions, captive in exile, imprisoned in the body, clinging to mud, embedded in slime, fastened to its members, nailed to its legs, stretched out by business, contracted by fears, afflicted with pains, wandering in errors, anxious with cares, restless with suspicions, and finally—according to the prophet’s words—an alien in the land of enemies, defiled among the dead and reckoned with those in hell (Bar. 3:11), though, I say, condemned and despairing in this manner, can nevertheless perceive in itself grounds not only for breathing again in hope of pardon and mercy, but even for daring to aspire to marriage with the Word. It need not tremble to enter a covenant of fellowship with God or fear to bear the sweet yoke of love with the King of angels.

For what can it not safely dare with him in whose image it sees itself marked, whose likeness it knows makes it illustrious? What need it fear from majesty when its origin gives it confidence? Only let it take care to preserve the native nobility of its nature by honorable living; indeed, let it strive to adorn and beautify with worthy colors of conduct and affections that heavenly dignity which is originally within it.

2. Why should diligence sleep? Nature itself is surely a great gift within us. If it does not fulfill its own role, will not all that remains of nature in us be thrown into disorder and covered, as it were, with the rust of age? That would indeed be an injury to the Creator. And surely God the Creator willed that this mark of divine nobility should be preserved perpetually in the soul for this purpose: that it might always possess in itself something from the Word, by which it might be reminded always either to stand with the Word or to return if it has been moved.

It is moved, not by changing places or walking with feet, but—as motion in a spiritual substance consists in its affections, or rather its defects—it goes in a certain manner from itself toward worse things when it makes itself unlike itself through the perversity of life and conduct, and becomes degenerate. Yet this unlikeness is not an abolition of nature but a defect: it exalts nature’s own good by comparison with itself, while disfiguring it by union with it. But the soul’s return is its conversion to the Word, that it may be reformed by him and conformed to him. In what? In charity. For he says: “Be ye imitators of God, as most dear children; and walk in love, as Christ also hath loved you” (Eph. 5:1–2).

[Col. 1182C] **3.** Such conformity weds the soul to the Word: the soul which is, to be sure, like him by nature, also makes itself like him by will, loving as it has been loved. Therefore, if it loves perfectly, it is married. What is more delightful than this conformity? What more desirable than charity, by which, not content with human instruction, you, O soul, confidently approach the Word by yourself; steadfastly cling to the Word; familiarly question the Word and consult it on every matter—so far as you are capable in understanding, so bold in desire? This is truly the covenant of a spiritual and holy marriage. I have said too little: it is a contract; it is an embrace. It is indeed an embrace, where willing the same thing and unwilling the same thing makes one spirit out of two. Nor need one fear that the disparity of persons will in any respect impair the harmony [Col. 1182D] [or, “the mutual accord”] of their wills, because love knows no reverence. For love takes its name from loving, not from honoring.

Let him honor, certainly, who dreads, who is awestruck, who fears, who marvels. All these dispositions are absent in the lover. Love is sufficient for itself; when love comes, it draws all the other affections into itself and takes them captive. Therefore the one who loves, loves, and knows nothing else. He who is rightly an object of honor, rightly of awe and wonder, nevertheless prefers to be loved. They are bridegroom and bride. What other bond or connection do you seek between bridegroom and bride besides being loved and loving? This bond surpasses even that which nature has bound most closely, the bond of parents and children. “For this reason,” he says, “a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his bride” (Matt. 19:5). You see how this affection in bridegroom and bride is more powerful not merely than other affections, but even than itself.

**4.** Add that this bridegroom is not only one who loves, but is Love itself. Is he honor? Let anyone maintain it if he wishes; I have not read it. But I have read that “God is charity” (1 John 4:16); I have not read that he is honor or dignity. This is not because God does not desire honor, for he says, “If I am a father, where is my honor?” That is the language of a Father. But if he presents himself as bridegroom, I think he will change his voice and say, “If I am a bridegroom, where is my love?” For earlier he spoke thus: “If I am Lord, where is my fear?” (Mal. 1:6).

God therefore requires fear as Lord, honor as Father, and love as bridegroom. Which excels among these? Surely love. Without it, fear has punishment, and honor [Col. 1183B] has no grace. Fear is slavish until it is set free by love. Honor which does not arise from love is not honor but flattery. Honor and glory indeed belong to God alone; yet God will accept neither unless they have been seasoned with the honey of love. Love is sufficient in itself; it pleases in itself and for its own sake. It is its own merit and its own reward. Love seeks no cause or fruit beyond itself. Its fruit is its exercise. I love because I love; I love in order to love.

Love is a great thing, provided that it returns to its own source; that, restored to its origin and poured back into its fountain, it continually draws from that source from which it may flow without cease. Among all the movements, senses, and affections of the soul, love alone is that in which the creature can—though not as an equal—answer the Creator or return a reciprocal response in likeness.

For example, if God is angry with me, shall I likewise be angry with him in return? Certainly not: I shall tremble, I shall shudder, I shall beg forgiveness. Likewise, if he rebukes me, he will not be rebuked by me; rather, he will be justified by me. Nor, if he judges me, shall I judge him; I shall adore him. And he who saves me does not ask to be saved by me, nor does he who delivers all need in turn to be delivered by anyone. If he rules, I ought to serve; if he commands, I ought to obey, and not in turn demand service or obedience from the Lord.

Now you see how different the case is with love. When God loves, he desires nothing other than to be loved; indeed, he loves for no other purpose than that he may be loved, knowing that those who love him are blessed by that very love.

**5.** Love is a great thing, but it has degrees. The bride stands at the highest degree. Children too love, but they think of their inheritance; and, fearing in some way to lose it, they revere more and love less the one from whom they expect the inheritance. I distrust a love which seems to be supported by the hope of obtaining something else. It is weak if, when hope is removed, it is either extinguished or diminished. It is impure if it desires something else as well. Pure love is not mercenary. Pure love does not draw its strength from hope; yet neither does it suffer the losses of distrust.

This belongs to the bride, because this is what every bride is. The bride’s possession and hope is one thing: love. In this the bride abounds; with this the bridegroom is content. He seeks nothing else, and she possesses nothing else. Hence he is bridegroom and she bride. This is proper to spouses, a privilege which no one else shares—not even a son. Thus he cries to children: [Col. 1184A] “Where is my honor?” He does not say, “Where is my love?” reserving the bride’s prerogative. A person is also commanded to honor father and mother (Deut. 5:16), and nothing is said of love—not because children ought not to love their parents, but because many children are more disposed to honor their parents than to love them.

Let the honor of a king, if you will, value judgment; but the love of a bridegroom—indeed, the Bridegroom who is Love—requires only love returned and fidelity. Let the beloved therefore be loved in return. Why should not a bride love—and a bride of Love? Why should Love not be loved?

**6.** Rightly, then, renouncing every other affection, she devotes herself wholly and solely to love, she who has love itself to answer Love by returning love. For even if she pours herself out wholly into love, what is this compared with the everlasting outpouring of that fountain? Lover and Love, soul and Word, bride and bridegroom, Creator and creature, do not flow with equal abundance—any more than one who thirsts and a fountain are equal.

What then? Shall the purpose of the one about to be wed, the longing of the sighing soul, the ardor of the lover, and the confidence of her presumption perish or be wholly emptied because she cannot run equally with the giant, contend in sweetness with honey, in gentleness with the lamb, in whiteness with the lily, in brightness with the sun, or in charity with him who is charity? No. Although the creature loves less, because it is less, nevertheless if it loves with its whole self, nothing is lacking where the whole is present.

Therefore, as I said, to be thus in love is to be married; for it cannot love in this way and be loved only a little, since in the consent of two persons a marriage stands whole and perfect. Unless anyone doubts that the soul is loved by the Word both earlier and more greatly. [Col. 1184C] It is altogether anticipated in loving and overcome in love. Happy is the soul that has deserved to be anticipated by so great a blessing of sweetness! Happy is she to whom it has been granted to experience the embrace of such delight! This is nothing other than holy and chaste love: love pleasant and sweet to her; love of as much serenity as sincerity; mutual, intimate, and powerful love, joining two not in one flesh but truly in one spirit, making two no longer two, but one. Thus Paul says: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

Let us now rather hear her concerning these matters, she whom the anointing has easily made a teacher in all things, together with frequent experience. Unless perhaps we should better reserve this for the beginning of another sermon, lest we confine a good subject [Col. 1184D] within the limits of one now almost ended. And, if you approve, I shall end even before the end, so that tomorrow, while hungry, we may come at the proper time to the delights of the holy soul, which the blessed soul deserves to enjoy with the Word and from the Word—her bridegroom, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXIV

**That the soul seeking God has been anticipated by him; and what is that seeking in which it has already been anticipated by him.**

**1.** “Upon my bed, by night, I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:1). To seek God is a great good. Among the goods of the soul, I judge it second to none. It is first among gifts and last among attainments. It yields to no virtue and is added to none. To what could it be added, when nothing precedes it? To what could it yield, when it is the consummation of all things? What virtue can be attributed to one who does not seek God? Or what limit is there to seeking God? “Seek his face always,” he says (Ps. 104:4).

I think that even when he has been found, seeking will not cease. God is sought not by steps of the feet, but by desires. Blessed finding does not blunt holy desire, but enlarges it. Is the fulfillment of joy the destruction of desire? Rather, it is oil to desire, for desire itself is flame. So it is: joy will be fulfilled, but desire will have no end, and consequently neither will seeking. Consider, if you can, this zeal of seeking without need, and desire without anxiety. Presence surely excludes the one; abundance excludes the other.

**2.** Now see why I have said these things beforehand. It is, of course, so that every soul among you seeking God may know itself to have been anticipated in him, and sought before it sought, lest it twist a great good into a great evil for itself. Thus no small evils commonly arise from great goods when, having been made eminent through the Lord’s gifts, we use gifts as though they had not been given and do not give glory to God. Thus those who seemed greatest because of grace received are considered least by God because it has not been returned.

But I spare you. I have used milder terms, “greatest” and “least,” and have not expressed what I think. I have veiled the distinction; I shall uncover it: I should have said “best” and “worst.” For truly and without doubt, each person is the worse to the degree that he is better, if he attributes to himself the very thing by which he is better. This is indeed the worst thing. If anyone says, “Far be it from me! I acknowledge that by God’s grace I am what I am,” but strives to catch a little glory for the grace he has received, is he not a thief and robber? Let such a one hear: “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke 19:22). What is more wicked than a servant appropriating to himself the glory of his lord?

**3.** “Upon my bed, by night, I sought him whom my soul loves.” The soul seeks the Word, but one first sought by the Word. Otherwise, once it has gone out or been cast out from the presence of the Word, its eye will not return to see good things unless it is sought by the Word. For what else is our soul than “a spirit that goes and does not return,” if it is left to itself? Hear the fugitive and wandering soul: what does it lament and what does it ask? “I have wandered like a lost sheep; seek your servant” (Ps. 118:176).

O human being, do you wish to return? But if the matter lies within your will, why do you ask for help? Why beg from elsewhere for what you abundantly possess in yourself? It is clear that it wills but cannot; it is a spirit that goes and does not return. This is so even in the case of one who goes farther away, one who does not even will to return. Yet I would not call that soul wholly abandoned or forsaken which desires to return and asks to be sought. For whence comes this will in it? From this, I think: it has already been visited and sought by the Word. Nor is this seeking idle, for it has produced the will without which return was impossible. But it is not enough to be sought once: so great is the soul’s weakness and so great the difficulty of its return. For what if it wills? The will lies helpless where capacity is lacking. “To will lies close at hand,” he says, “but I do not find the power to accomplish the good” (Rom. 7:18).

What, then, does the man introduced from the psalm seek? Nothing other than to be sought. He would not seek this unless he had been sought; and he would not seek it again if he had been sufficiently sought. This is also what he asks: “Seek your servant”—that he who gave the will may also give the accomplishment corresponding to good will.

**4.** Yet it does not seem to me that the present passage can belong to a soul of this kind, which has not yet received the second grace: it wills indeed, but cannot approach him whom its soul loves. For how can what follows suit it—that it should rise, go about the city, and seek its beloved through the lanes and squares [Col. 1186B] (Song 3:2)—when it itself needs to be sought? Let the one who can do this do it; only let her remember that she was first sought, just as she was first loved, and that from this comes both her seeking and her loving.

Let us too pray, beloved, that these mercies may quickly anticipate us, because we have become exceedingly poor. I do not say this of all of you. For I know that very many of you walk in the love with which Christ loved us, and seek him in simplicity of heart. But there are some—sadly I say it—who have as yet given us in themselves no sign of this most saving anticipation, and consequently none of their salvation: people loving themselves, not the Lord, and seeking what is their own, not what belongs to the Lord.

**5.** “I sought,” she says, “him whom my soul loves.” Surely this is what the kindness of him who anticipates you summons you toward: he who first sought you and first loved you. You would by no means seek unless first sought, just as neither would you love unless first loved. You have been anticipated not in one blessing only but in two: in love and in seeking. Love is the cause of seeking; seeking is the fruit and assurance of love. You were loved, lest you should suppose that you were sought rather for punishment; you were sought, lest you should complain that you were loved in vain. Once both sweetnesses have been discovered to be so friendly, they gave boldness, banished shame, persuaded the soul to return, and stirred its affection. Hence comes zeal; hence this ardor to seek him whom your soul loves. For assuredly, although you could seek while not yet sought, now, having been sought, you can seek.

[Col. 1186D] **6.** But do not forget whence you have come to this point. And, to apply what is said to myself instead—for that is safer—are you that soul, O my soul, which, leaving your former husband, with whom you had prospered, annulled your first pledge and went after your lovers? And now, after you have fornicated with them as long as you pleased, perhaps even after you were despised by them, do you dare, shameless and brazen, to wish to return to him whom in pride you despised? What? Though worthy of hiding places, do you seek the light? Do you run to the bridegroom, more worthy of blows than kisses? It would be no wonder if you encountered a judge instead of a bridegroom.

Happy is the person who has heard his soul reply to this: “I do not fear, because I love; I would certainly not do this if I were not loved.” Therefore love itself gives confidence. The beloved has nothing to fear. Let those who do not love be afraid. Why should they not continually suspect hostility? But I, who love, can no more doubt that I am loved than I can doubt that I love. I cannot fear the face whose affection I have experienced. In what? In this: he not only sought one such as I, but also moved her affections and thereby made her certain that she was sought. Why should I not answer him in seeking, when I answer him in affection? Will he be angry when sought, he who overlooked me even when I despised him? Rather, he will not reject one who seeks him, since he seeks even one who despises him.

The Spirit of the Word is gracious and announces gracious things to me, inwardly revealing and persuading me concerning the zeal and desire of the Word, which cannot, of course, be hidden from that Spirit. He searches the depths of God, being conscious of the thoughts which God thinks—thoughts of peace and not of affliction. Why should I not be encouraged to seek, having experienced mercy and been persuaded of peace?

**7.** Brothers, to have this urged upon one is to be sought by the Word; to be persuaded is to be found. But not all receive this word. What shall we do for our little ones? I mean those among us who are still beginners, though not foolish, since they hold the beginning of wisdom, being subject to one another in the fear of Christ. How, I ask, are we to assure them that these things are thus with the bride, when they have not yet experienced such dealings within themselves? I send them to one such person, to whom they ought not to refuse belief. Let them read in the book what, because they do not see it in another’s heart, they do not believe.

It is written in the prophets: “If a man puts away his wife, and she departs and takes another husband, shall he return to her again? Shall not that woman be polluted and defiled? But you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord, and I will receive you” [Col. 1187C] (Jer. 3:1). These are the Lord’s words; it is not lawful to withhold belief. Let them believe what they do not experience, so that in due time they may obtain, as the reward of faith, the fruit of experience.

I think it has been sufficiently explained what it is to be sought by the Word and how this necessity belongs not to the Word but to the soul—except that she who has experienced it knows these things more fully and more happily. It remains for us, in the following discourse, to teach thirsty souls to seek him by whom they have been sought; or rather, to learn this from her who is introduced in this passage as seeking him whom her soul loves, the bridegroom of the soul, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXV

**On the seven needs for which the soul seeks the Word; and how, finally reformed, it approaches to contemplate and enjoy his sweetness.**

[Col. 1187D]

**1.** “Upon my bed I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:1). For what purpose? It has been stated, and repetition is superfluous. Yet for the sake of some who were not present when it was discussed, I shall say something briefly—and perhaps even those who were present will not be unwilling to hear it. For not everything could then be said.

The soul seeks the Word: that it may agree with him for correction; that it may be enlightened by him for knowledge; that it may lean upon him for strength; that it may be reformed by him for wisdom; that it may be conformed to him for beauty; that it may be wed to him for fruitfulness; and that it may enjoy him for delight. For all these reasons the soul seeks the Word. I do not doubt that there are many others; but these occur to me for the present. Anyone whose heart is inclined to do so may easily observe yet others within himself. For our turnings-away are many; the soul’s needs are many and infinite; and anxieties are numberless. But the Word more richly and fully overflows with good things, as Wisdom conquering malice and conquering evils by good things.

Now receive the explanation of those causes which I have set out. First—and this is first—see how the Word is agreed with for correction. We read the Word speaking in the Gospels: “Be reconciled,” he says, “with your adversary while you are with him on the way, lest perhaps he deliver you to the judge, and the judge to the torturer” (Matt. 5:25). What counsel could be wiser? It is, I think, the counsel of the Word declaring himself to be an adversary, because he opposes our carnal desires when he says: “These always err in heart” (Ps. 94:10).

Therefore, if you hear these words and begin in fear to desire escape from the wrath to come, I think you will anxiously ask how you may agree with this adversary who appears to threaten you with that wrath so terribly. Yet this is impossible unless you disagree with yourself, oppose yourself, wage against yourself an unrelenting battle, grave and watchful, and finally bid farewell to ingrained habit and inborn inclination. This is indeed hard. If you attempt it by your own strength, it will be as though you tried to stop the rushing of a torrent with one finger, or to turn the Jordan back again upstream.

What will you do? Seek the Word with whom you may agree, he himself making you agree. Flee to him who opposes you, so that through him you may become one whom he no longer opposes; so that he who threatened may become gracious, and grace infused may prove more powerful to change you than wrath intensely directed against you.

[Col. 1188C] **2.** This is, I think, the first need for which the soul begins to seek the Word. But if you do not know what he wills, though you already agree with him in will, will it not be said of you too that “you have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2)? And lest you judge this a slight matter, remember the written saying: “The one who is ignorant shall be ignorant” (1 Cor. 14:38).

Do you wish to know what I advise in this need also? What I advised in the first. By my counsel you will again go to the Word, and he will teach you his ways, lest, even while willing good, through ignorance of it you should run astray, wander in a trackless place rather than on the way, and err. For the Word is light. “The unfolding of your words gives light and gives understanding to the little ones.” You are blessed if you too may say: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:130, 105).

Nor has your soul advanced only a little when its will has been changed and its reason enlightened, so that it both wills and knows the good. In the one it has received life; in the other, sight. For by willing evil it was dead, and by not knowing good it was blind.

**3.** Now it lives, now it sees, now it stands in the good—but by the aid and operation of the Word. Raised by the hand of the Word, it stands as it were on two feet: devotion and knowledge. It stands, I say, but let it think itself addressed by the saying: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12). Do you suppose it can stand by itself when it could not rise by itself? I do not think so. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32:6); and shall the earth stand without the Word? Why then, if it could stand by itself, did the man of earth pray: “Confirm me in your words” (Ps. 118:28)?

Indeed, he had experienced it. His was the voice: “I was thrust down so as to fall, and the Lord received me” (Ps. 117:13). Do you ask who the one thrusting him was? There is not just one. The devil thrusts; the world thrusts; a human being thrusts. Do you ask who this human being is? Each person himself. Do not be surprised. A person is so much his own assailant and precipitant that he need fear nothing from another assailant if he restrains his own hands from himself. “For who,” he says, “will be able to harm you if you are zealous for good?” (1 Pet. 3:13). Your hand is your consent.

If, when the devil suggests or the world urges what ought not to be done, you withhold your consent, do not yield your members as weapons of unrighteousness, and do not permit sin to reign in your mortal body, you prove yourself a zealous follower of good, whom malice has not harmed at all—indeed, see lest it may rather have benefited you. For it is written: “Do good, and you shall have praise from it” (Rom. 13:3). Those who sought your soul have been put to shame, while you will sing: “If they do not rule over me, then I shall be undefiled” (Ps. 18:14).

You have indeed shown the mark of one zealous for good if, according to the counsel of the Wise Man, you have mercy on your own soul (Ecclus. 30:24); if you guard your heart with all vigilance (Prov. 4:23); if, according to the Apostle, you keep yourself chaste (1 Tim. 5:22). Otherwise, even if you gain the whole world but suffer loss to your soul, we do not judge you zealous for good—nor does the Savior [Col. 1189C] (Matt. 16:26).

**4.** Since, therefore, three forces threaten one who stands [Note: [Col. 1189D] More recent editions add “overthrowers,” a word absent from the earliest and most manuscripts and apparently unnecessary.]: the devil, by the envy of malice; the world, by the wind of vanity; and a human being, himself, by the weight of his own corruption. The devil thrusts, but does not overthrow, provided you refuse him your help or consent. Thus it is written: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4:7). He is the envious one who thrust down and overthrew those standing in paradise—but because they consented, not because they resisted. He is the one who, proud and with no one thrusting him, cast himself down from heaven, so that you may know how much more a person lies under threat from his own fall when weighed down by the burden of his own substance.

The world too is an assailant, because it lies in wickedness. It thrusts against all, but overthrows only its own friends—that is, those who agree with it. I do not wish to be a friend of the world, lest I fall. For whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God (Jas. 4:7); and there is surely no fall more grievous. From these points it is sufficiently clear how a human being is the chief assailant of himself: he can fall through his own impulse without another’s, but cannot fall through another’s impulse without his own.

Which of these must especially be resisted? Surely this one, who is the more troublesome because more inward; he alone is sufficient to cast one down, whereas without him the others can accomplish nothing. Not without reason did the Wise Man prefer to a conqueror of cities the person who rules his own spirit [Col. 1190A] (Prov. 16:32). This concerns you greatly: you need strength—not just any strength, but that with which you may be clothed from on high. For strength itself, if perfect, readily makes the mind victorious over itself and thus renders it invincible against all things. For it is the vigor of the mind which refuses to yield in defending reason. Or, if you prefer, it is the vigor of the mind standing immovably with reason or for reason. Or again: vigor of mind is that which, so far as lies in it, compels or directs all things toward reason.

**5.** “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” Whoever undertakes to strive [or, “to climb”] toward the summit of this mountain—that is, toward perfection in virtue—will certainly know how arduous is the ascent, and how fruitless the effort [Note: [Col. 1190D] The printed editions read *casus concitus*, “a hasty fall”; but our manuscripts read *cassus conatus*, “fruitless effort,” and more correctly in view of what follows: “Otherwise one strives in vain if one does not lean.”] without the Word’s aid.

Happy the soul which, while angels watch, provides both joy and wonder concerning itself, so that they may hear them saying of her: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8:5). Otherwise one strives in vain if one does not lean. Indeed, by leaning even against itself it will prevail; made stronger than itself, it will compel all things to serve reason: it will govern anger, fear, desire, and joy, like a certain chariot of the mind, as a good charioteer; it will lead every carnal affection captive, and bring bodily sensation, at reason’s command, into obedience to virtue.

Why should not all things be possible to one who leans upon him who can do all things? What a word of confidence: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me!” (Phil. 9:13). Nothing demonstrates the Word’s omnipotence more clearly than that he makes omnipotent all who hope in him. Thus, “all things are possible to one who believes” [Col. 1190C] (Mark 9:22). Is not he omnipotent to whom all things are possible? Thus the mind, if it does not presume upon itself but is strengthened by the Word, can surely rule itself, so that no unrighteousness may rule over it. Thus, I say, leaning on the Word and clothed with strength from on high, no force, no deceit, no enticement will be able either to cast down one who stands or to subject one who rules.

**6.** Do you wish not to fear the assailant? “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and the hand of the one who thrusts shall not move me. There fell those who work iniquity” (Ps. 35:13). There the devil and his angels fell: though they were not thrust by anything outside themselves, they were nevertheless cast out and could not stand. For “he did not stand in the truth,” because he did not lean upon the Word, but trusted in his own strength. And perhaps, because he could not stand, he wished to sit. For he said: “I shall sit upon the mountain of the covenant” (Isa. 14:13). But God judged otherwise: he neither stood nor sat, but fell, as the Lord says: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18).

Therefore, whoever stands, if he does not wish to fall, should not trust in himself but lean upon the Word. The Word says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). So it is: we can neither rise to good nor stand in good without the Word. Therefore, you who stand, give glory to the Word [or, “to God”], and say: “He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” [Col. 1191A] (Ps. 39:3). By whose hand you are raised, by that one’s strength you must necessarily be held. This concerns what I said: that we need the Word upon whom we may lean for strength.

**7.** We must now consider what I also mentioned: namely, that through the Word we are likewise reformed unto wisdom. The Word is strength; the Word is wisdom. Let the soul therefore receive strength from strength and wisdom from wisdom, and attribute both gifts to the one Word. Otherwise, if it claims for itself either or both from another source, it denies at the same time either a stream from the fountain, wine from the vine, or light as arising from light.

The saying is trustworthy: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask it from God, who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach; and it shall be given to him” (Jas. 1:5). So he says. I would think no differently concerning strength. Strength is akin to wisdom. Strength belongs to the household of God and must be reckoned among the best gifts [or, “things given”]; it too descends from above from the Father of the Word. If anyone believes that in every respect it is identical with wisdom, I do not deny it—but in the Word, not in the soul.

For what, in the Word, is one because of the unique simplicity of his divine nature, does not produce one effect in the soul; rather, it accommodates itself, as though diverse, to be shared according to that soul’s varied and diverse needs. Accordingly, it is one thing for the mind to be impelled by strength and another to be ruled by wisdom; one thing to rule in strength and another to delight in sweetness. Although wisdom may be powerful and strength pleasant, still, to give each term its proper force, vigor indicates strength, [Col. 1191C] while wisdom indicates tranquillity of mind with a certain spiritual sweetness.

I think the Apostle designated this when, after many exhortations pertaining to strength, he added what pertains to wisdom: “in sweetness, in the Holy Spirit” (2 Cor. 6:6). Therefore, to stand, to resist, and to repel force by force—things certainly reckoned among the functions of strength—is honorable, but laborious. For it is not the same thing to defend one’s honor laboriously and to possess it in peace. It is not the same thing to be moved by strength and to enjoy strength. What strength works for, wisdom enjoys; and what wisdom orders, plans, and moderates, strength carries out.

**8.** “Write wisdom in leisure,” says the Wise Man (Ecclus. 38:25). Therefore wisdom’s leisure is its business, and the more at leisure wisdom is, the more it is exercised in its own kind. Conversely, strength is more glorious when exercised, and more proved the more active it is. If anyone defines wisdom as the love of strength, he does not seem to me to stray from the truth. Where love is, there is no labor but savor. Perhaps *sapientia* (“wisdom”) takes its name from *sapor* (“flavor”), because when it comes to strength it renders savory, as by a kind of seasoning, that which by itself was felt to be in some way tasteless and harsh. Nor would I think anyone blameworthy who defined wisdom as the savor of good.

We lost this savor almost at the very origin of our race. From the time when, as the sense of the flesh prevailed, the poison of the ancient serpent infected the palate of the heart, the soul began not to find good savory, and a harmful savor entered in. “The senses and thoughts of the human being are inclined to evil from youth” [Col. 1192A] (Gen. 8:21)—that is, from the foolishness of the first woman. Thus the woman’s foolishness excluded the savor of good, because the serpent’s malice deceived the woman’s foolishness. But from the very point at which malice appeared to have conquered for a time, it laments that it has been conquered for eternity. For behold, wisdom has again filled a woman’s heart and body, so that we who were misshapen into folly through a woman may be reformed unto wisdom through a woman.

And now wisdom continually conquers malice in the minds into which it enters, banishing by a better savor the savor of evil which that woman introduced. As wisdom enters, it makes foolish the sense of the flesh, purifies the understanding, and heals and restores the palate of the heart. When the palate is healthy, good is now savory; wisdom itself is savory—the best of all things good.

[Col. 1192B] **9.** How many good things are done and yet are not savory to those doing them! For they are impelled toward them not by the savor of good, but by reason, or by some occasion or necessity. Conversely, for many people the evils they do are not savory; they are led into them by fear or by desire for some thing, rather than by the savor of evil. But those who have passed into the affection of the heart are either wise, delighting in the savor of good itself; or malicious, taking pleasure in malice itself, even when no hope of another advantage flatters them. For what is malice but the savor of evil?

Blessed is the mind wholly claimed for itself by the savor of good and hatred of evil. This is to be reformed unto wisdom; this is happily to experience wisdom’s victory. For in what is wisdom more evidently proved to conquer malice than when, the savor of evil—which is nothing other than malice itself—having been excluded, a certain inward savor of good is felt to occupy the innermost mind with complete sweetness?

Thus it belongs to strength to endure tribulations bravely; to wisdom, to rejoice in tribulations. “Strengthen your heart and endure the Lord” belongs to strength; “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” belongs to wisdom. And so that both goods may appear more clearly from the good proper to each nature: moderation of mind proves the wise person, while steadfastness shows the person of strength. Wisdom rightly follows strength, because strength is like a stable foundation upon which wisdom builds her house. But knowledge of the good had to come first, because there is no fellowship between the light of wisdom and the darkness of ignorance. Good will too was necessary, because “wisdom will not enter into an ill-disposed soul” (Wis. 1:4).

10. Now, if in the change of the will the life restored to the soul has become known, in instruction its health, in virtue its stability, and finally in wisdom its maturity, it remains for us to find for it that beauty without which it cannot please him who is fairer in form than the sons of men. For it hears: “The king shall desire thy beauty” (Ps. 44:3, 12). We have enumerated many goods of the soul—the gifts of the Word: a good will, knowledge, virtue, wisdom—and yet we do not read that the royal Word desires any of these, but only: “The king,” he says, “shall desire thy beauty.” The Prophet says: “The Lord hath reigned; he hath put on beauty” (Ps. 92:1). Why should he not desire a like garment for his image and [Col. 1193A] bride alike? Certainly she will be dearer to him in proportion as she is more like him.

Where, then, is the soul’s beauty? Is it perhaps in what is called moral comeliness (*honestum*)? Let us think so for the present, unless something better occurs. But let outward conduct be questioned concerning moral comeliness—not because it proceeds from outward conduct, but through it. For its dwelling and its origin are in the conscience. Indeed, its brightness is the testimony of conscience. Nothing is clearer than this light; nothing more glorious than this testimony, when truth shines in the mind and the mind beholds itself in truth. But what sort of mind? Chaste, modest, fearful, watchful; admitting absolutely nothing which may diminish the glory of its witnessing conscience; conscious to itself of nothing for which it blushes before the presence of truth, or which compels it to turn away its face as though [Col. 1193B] ashamed and repelled by the light of God. This indeed—this is that comeliness which, above all the soul’s goods, delights the divine gaze; and we name and define it moral integrity.

11. But when charity has more abundantly filled the innermost parts of the heart with this beauty, it must necessarily come forth, like a lamp hidden beneath a bushel—or rather, light shining in darkness, unable to remain concealed. The body receives the image of the mind as it shines forth and, as it were, bursts out in certain rays of its own, and diffuses it through limbs and senses, so that every action, word, look, gait, and laugh—if it is indeed laughter—may thence reflect it, mingled with gravity and full of propriety.

When the movement, gesture, and use of these and the other limbs and senses appears restrained, pure, modest, wholly free from [Col. 1193C] insolence and wantonness, from frivolity and sloth, suited to equity and ready for works of mercy, then the beauty of the soul will be publicly manifest—provided that there is no deceit in its spirit. For all these things can be feigned, and not thus proceed from the abundance of the heart. And that this beauty of the soul may appear more clearly, let moral integrity itself, if you please—the quality in which we judged that this beauty should be placed—be defined thus: “The nobility of the mind, carefully preserving, together with a good conscience, the integrity of one’s reputation.” Or, according to the Apostle: “Providing things good, not only before God but also before men” (2 Cor. 8:21).

Blessed is the 1566 mind which clothes itself with this adornment of chastity and, as it were, with a certain white robe of heavenly innocence, by which it claims for itself [Col. 1193D] a glorious conformity—not to the world, but to the Word, of whom it is written that he is “the brightness of eternal life” (Wis. 7:26), “the splendor and image of the substance of God” (Heb. 1:3).

12. From this stage, a soul such as this now dares to think of marriage. Why should it not dare, seeing itself marriageable insofar as it sees itself like him? Loftiness does not terrify where likeness unites; love reconciles, profession joins in marriage. The form of this profession is: “I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of thy righteousness” (Ps. 118:106). Following this, the apostles said: “Behold, we have left all things and followed thee” (Matt. 19:27). Similar is that saying which, though spoken concerning a carnal marriage, signified the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church: “For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and [Col. 1194A] shall cleave to his wife; and the two shall be one flesh” (Eph. 5:31–32); and the boast of the married woman in the Prophet: “But for me it is good to cleave to God, to put my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72:28).

Therefore, whenever you see a soul which, having left all things, cleaves to the Word by all its vows; which lives by the Word, governs itself by the Word, conceives from the Word what it may bring forth for the Word; which can say, “To me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21)—regard it as a bride, married to the Word. The heart of her husband trusts in her, knowing her faithful, since she has despised everything before him and counts all things as dung, that she may gain him. He knew such a one of whom he said: “This man is unto me a chosen vessel” (Acts 9:15). Truly the soul of Paul was a devout mother and faithful to her husband when he said: “My little children, of whom I travail again until [Col. 1194B] Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

13. But observe that in spiritual marriage there are two kinds of bearing children, and consequently different offspring, though not opposed: holy mothers give birth either to souls through preaching, or to spiritual understandings through meditation. In this latter kind they sometimes pass beyond themselves and even withdraw from bodily senses, so that she who feels the Word no longer feels herself. This happens when the mind, enticed by the ineffable sweetness of the Word, in a certain manner steals itself away from itself—indeed, is seized and slips away from itself—in order to enjoy the Word.

The mind that bears fruit for the Word is affected in one way; the mind that enjoys the Word, in another. There, the need of one’s neighbor urges; here, the sweetness of the Word invites. The mother is indeed glad in her offspring, but the bride is happier in embraces. The pledges of children are dear; but kisses give greater delight. [Col. 1194C] It is good to save many; but to pass beyond oneself and be with the Word is far more delightful. But when does this happen, or for how long? It is a sweet intercourse, but a brief moment and a rare experience. This is what I remember having said above after other matters: the soul seeks the Word in order to enjoy him in delight.

14. Perhaps someone will go on to ask me what it is to enjoy the Word. I answer: let him seek an experienced person from whom to ask it. Or, even if experience were granted to me, do you suppose I could utter what is ineffable? Hear one who had experienced it: “Whether we be transported in mind, it is to God; or whether we be sober, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5:13). That is: One thing is mine with God, God alone being judge; another is mine with you. That I was permitted to experience, but by no means to speak; thus I accommodate myself to you, so that I may speak and you may understand.

O whoever you are, curious to know what this is—to enjoy the Word—prepare for him not a thing, but a mind. It is not the tongue that teaches this, but grace. It is hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to little ones. Great, brethren, great and lofty is humility: it merits what is not taught; it is worthy to attain what it cannot learn; worthy to conceive from the Word, and concerning the Word, what it cannot explain in its own words. Why is this so? Not because it is thus deserved, but because thus it has pleased the Father of the Word, the Bridegroom of the soul, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXVI  
### On the caution and modesty of the bride seeking the Word; and in praise of modesty

[Col. 1195A]

1. There is now no reason to ask me why the soul seeks the Word: this has been more than sufficiently explained above. Come, let us continue with the remaining matters in this present chapter, at least those which concern conduct. First, observe now the bride’s 1567 modesty, than which I do not know whether anything more pleasing can be observed in human conduct. I should like, before all else, in some manner to take it in my hands, pluck it like a beautiful flower from its place, and set it before our young people.

Not that it should not be retained with every care even in more advanced age—for it is certainly the ornament of every age—but because the grace of tender modesty shines out more fully and beautifully in a more tender [Col. 1195B] age. What is more lovable than a modest young man? How beautiful and splendid is this jewel of character in the life and countenance of a young person! How true and undoubted a messenger of good hope, an indication of good natural disposition! For him it is a rod of discipline, hanging over shameful impulses, restraining the motions of a slippery age and repressing insolent deeds. Why is it so averse to foul speech and every subsequent kind of foulness? It is the sister of self-control. There is no equally manifest mark of dovelike simplicity, and therefore it is also a witness to innocence. It is a lamp of the chaste mind, perpetually shining, so that nothing shameful or unbecoming may dare remain there without immediately being exposed by it. Thus, the eraser of evils and defender of native purity, it is the special glory of conscience, guardian of reputation, [Col. 1195C] adornment of life, seat of virtue, first-fruits of the virtues, praise of nature, and distinguishing mark of all moral propriety. How much grace and beauty does the very blush of the cheeks, perhaps brought on by modesty, commonly bring to the suffused countenance!

2. Modesty is so truly a natural good of the mind that even those who are not ashamed to act badly are nevertheless ashamed to be seen doing so, as the Lord says: “Every one that doeth evil hateth the light” (John 3:20). “They that sleep, sleep in the night; and they that are drunken, are drunken in the night” (1 Thess. 5:7): concealing in darkness works of darkness, fit for hiding. Yet there is this difference: the hidden disgraces which the modesty of such people is ashamed, not of possessing, but of disclosing, the bride’s modesty does not cover at all; rather, it spits them out and drives them away. Therefore the Wise Man says: “There is a shame that bringeth sin, and there is a shame that bringeth glory” (Sir. 4:25).

The bride seeks the Word modestly indeed, because she seeks in bed and by night; but this modesty brings glory, not sin. She seeks him for the purification of conscience; she seeks him for testimony, that she may say: “This is my glory, the testimony of my conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loveth” (Song 3:1). Modesty, if you observe, is marked both by place and by time. What is more congenial to a modest mind than secrecy? Now secrecy belongs to the night and to the bed. Finally, those who wish to pray are commanded to enter their chamber (Matt. 6:6), surely for the sake of privacy. This indeed is for caution, lest human praise, before those who see them pray, steal the fruit of prayer and [Col. 1196A] frustrate its effect. Yet this saying also teaches you modesty. What is more proper to modesty than to avoid one’s own praises, to avoid boastfulness? It is clear that the Son and teacher of modesty [variant: minister] expressly commanded those who pray to seek privacy also for the sake of modesty. What is more unbecoming, especially in a young person, than the display of holiness?

Yet particularly at this age a fitting and seasonable beginning in religious life may surely be undertaken, as Jeremiah says: “It is good for a man when he hath borne the yoke from his youth” (Lam. 3:27). It is a good commendation of the prayer that follows if you first set 1568 modesty before it, saying: “I am young and despised; I have not forgotten thy justifications” (Ps. 118:141).

[Col. 1196B]

3. Nor must one who wishes to pray observe merely the place, but also the time. A holiday time is more convenient and suitable; but especially when deep nocturnal sleep enjoins silence, then prayer rises more freely and more purely. “Arise in the night,” he says, “at the beginning of thy watches, and pour out thy heart like water before the face of the Lord thy God” (Lam. 2:19). How securely prayer rises in the night, God alone and the holy angel being its witnesses, who receives it for presentation upon the heavenly altar! How pleasing and bright it is, colored with the blush of modesty! How serene and calm, disturbed by no shout or noise! How finally clean and sincere, sprinkled with no dust of earthly anxiety and tempted by no praise or flattery from anyone looking on!

Therefore the bride, wishing to pray—that is, to seek the Word—sought the secrecy of bed and night no less modestly than cautiously. For the two are one. Otherwise you do not pray rightly if, in praying, you seek something besides the Word, or something which you do not seek for the Word’s sake, since all things are in him. There are remedies for wounds, help for necessities, restoration for defects, abundant means of progress; there, finally, is whatever it is advantageous for human beings to receive or possess, whatever is fitting, whatever is necessary. Thus it is in vain to seek anything other than the Word, since he himself is all things. For even if, when necessary, we seem to ask for temporal things, provided the Word is the reason for doing so—as indeed is right—we do not seek those things but rather him, for whose sake we ask for the others. Those know this who have become accustomed to direct every use of these [Col. 1196D] things toward obtaining the Word.

4. Yet let us not be reluctant further to explore the secrets of this bed and time, in case something spiritual may lie hidden in them which it is useful to bring forth. If, as may please us, by the name of bed human weakness is signified, and by the darkness of night human ignorance likewise, then it follows suitably enough that the Word, the power of God and the wisdom of God, should be sought more earnestly against both original evils. What is more fitting than that power should be set against weakness, wisdom against ignorance? And lest any doubt concerning this interpretation remain in simpler hearts, let them hear what the holy Prophet says concerning these matters: [Col. 1197A] “May the Lord help him upon the bed of his sorrow; thou hast turned all his bed in his infirmity” (Ps. 40:4).

That is concerning the bed. Now, concerning the night of ignorance, what could be more plain than what he says again in another psalm: “They have not known nor understood; they walk in darkness” (Ps. 81:5), certainly expressing that very ignorance in which the whole human race was born. This, I think, is that ignorance in which the blessed Apostle both confesses himself to have been born and glories that he was delivered from it, saying: “Who hath delivered us from the power of darkness” (Col. 1:13). Hence he also said: “We are not children of the night nor of darkness” (1 Thess. 5:5); and likewise to all the elect: “Walk as children of light” (Eph. 5:8).

> **Note:** [Col. 1197A] Thus far Saint Bernard. Prevented by death, he could not complete the remainder—indeed, not even this final sermon, shorter as it is than the others, [Col. 1198A] and lacking the customary concluding formula. See the continuation by Gilbert of Hoyland at the beginning of the following Volume V.

[Col. 1197]

## FLOWERS, OR SENTENCES, DRAWN FROM THE WORKS OF ST BERNARD

[Col. 1197B] 1569 Chastity is endangered by pleasures, humility by riches, piety by business, truth by much speaking, and charity in this wicked age. *On Conversion to Clerics*, no. 37.

Nothing is more precious than time; but, alas, nothing today is valued more cheaply. *Treatise on Contempt of the World, addressed to Clerics*, no. 55.

The days of salvation pass, and no one reflects; no one laments to himself that irrecoverable moments have been lost. *Ibid.*

Nothing is so hard that it does not yield to something harder. IV, *On Consideration*, ch. 3. Hence habit is conquered by habit.

Impute to yourself whatever you suffer from him who can do nothing without you. IV, *On Consideration*, no. 9.

The scorpion has nothing in its face that you fear, but it stings with its tail. *Ibid.*

[Col. 1197C] What does it profit you to be wise if you are not wise for yourself? II, *On Consideration*, 2.

A monkey on a roof; a foolish king sitting on a throne. *Ibid.*

Prosperity is to the unwary what fire is to wax and a ray of the sun to snow. II, *On Consideration*, ch. 12.

No misery is truer than false joy. *On Free Will*, no. 14.

We are plainly convinced that we will, since it would not occur if we did not will. [Col. 1197D] *Ibid.*

A mind poured abroad does not perceive its inward losses. *On Conversion to Clerics*, ch. 4, no. 5.

To flee persecution is not the fault of the fugitive but of the persecutor. Letter 1.

The will is reckoned as the deed where necessity prevents the deed. *Treatise addressed to Hugh*, no. 9.

[Col. 1198B] No one deserves wrath more than an enemy who pretends to be a friend. *On Conversion*, no. 33.

Those who lay up treasure for themselves in heaven have no reason to fear thieves. *On Conversion to Clerics*, no. 41.

He does not placate who is not himself pleasing. *Ibid.*, 33.

The mother of clerical insolence is the negligence of bishops. Letter 152.

One must accommodate oneself to friends, but not to one’s own death. Letter 215.

If the water of a river begins to stand still, it rots. Sermon 1 on Lent.

Everything that is in the world has an end; but their end will have no end. Sermon 9 on the Song of Songs.

You will give your voice the voice of power if you first persuade yourself of what you urge. Sermon 6 on the Song of Songs, no. 3.

[Col. 1198C] I gladly hear the voice of that teacher who moves not applause for himself but mourning in me. *Ibid.*

The dove’s voice does not sound sweet, but signifies sweet things—namely, love for its mate. *Ibid.*

Willing or unwilling, the Jebusite dwells within your borders: he may be subdued, but not exterminated. Sermon 57 on the Song of Songs, no. 10.

It is too little to have thought once; one must think often—indeed always. *Ibid.* For vices repeatedly sprout again.

Virtue cannot grow together with vices; prune desire, that virtue may be strengthened. *Ibid.*

Remove what is superfluous, and what is wholesome rises up. Whatever you take away from desire is added to usefulness. *Ibid.*

[Col. 1198D] A learned shepherd who is not good harms more by his barren life than he nourishes by his abundant teaching. Sermon 76 on the Song of Songs, no. 10.

Ambition satisfied in its wishes sometimes does less harm than ambition frustrated. Letter 126: for it turns to violent means.

1570 He who does not love approaches in vain to hear or read the song of love. [Col. 1199A] Sermon 79 on the Song of Songs, no. 1.

A cold breast cannot receive a burning utterance. *Ibid.* Just as one who does not know Greek does not understand a person speaking Greek.

Reputation cannot vindicate for virtue what conscience proves to be vice. Sermon 71 on the Song of Songs, no. 2.

Virtue is content with the brightness of conscience, even if the fragrance of reputation does not follow. *Ibid.*

Many things which you reject when idle you will take with desire after labor. Letter 1, no. 11. For hunger is the best seasoning of food.

The enemy presses more boldly from behind than he resists face to face. *Ibid.*, no. 12.

[Col. 1199B] To do evil, even at anyone’s command, is not obedience but disobedience. Letter 7, no. 3—namely, with respect to God.

Whatever each person honors above all else, that he is shown to have made his god. *Treatise on Contempt of the World, addressed to Clerics*, ch. 5, no. 17.

The pleasure of the throat, so highly valued today, scarcely occupies the breadth of two fingers. *On Conversion to Clerics*, no. 13.

The insatiable love of riches torments far more through desire than it refreshes through use. *Ibid.*, 14.

The use of riches is mostly for others; to the rich themselves belong only the name and the anxiety. *Ibid.*

[Col. 1203B] The devil lies in wait especially for perseverance alone, because he knows that alone among the virtues it is crowned. Letter 24.

Guarding of the mouth is always useful, provided it does not exclude the grace of affability. IV, *On Consideration*, ch. 6, no. 23.

A headlong tongue must everywhere be restrained, but especially at a banquet. *Ibid.*

That demeanor is more suitable if you are severe in deed, serene in countenance, and restrained in speech. *Ibid.*

He who already holds the throne has no need of ladders. V, *On Consideration*, no. 1.

Whether it is more damnable to slander or to listen to a slanderer, I would not easily say. II, *On Consideration*, no. 22.

Deliberating prudence suspends judgment. Sermon [Col. 1203C] on St Mary Magdalene, no. 1, now in Volume V.

Religious sorrow mourns either another’s sin or one’s own. *Ibid.*, no. 2.

[Col. 1204A] Recognize how greatly God has valued you from those things which he became for you. Sermon 1 on the Epiphany.

1574 It is the height of folly that we are shameless regarding obscenities and ashamed of repentance: wrongly eager for wounds, ashamed of remedies. Sermon on the Circumcision.

For the preservation of humility, divine mercy commonly orders things so that the more someone advances, the less he judges himself to have advanced. Sermon 15 on Divers Subjects, no. 4.

Both please God: the repentant sinner and the devout righteous person; but the ungrateful righteous person displeases him as much as the self-assured sinner. Sermon on Divers Subjects, 4.

The healthy person does not know what the sick person feels, nor the full person what the fasting person suffers. *Treatise on the Steps of Humility*, no. 6.

Humility is a glorious thing, since even pride itself desires to cloak itself with it, lest it be despised. *Ibid.*, no. 47.

It is an unhappy victory in which, overcoming a man, you succumb to a vice. *Exhortation to Knights*, no. 2.

“The wicked walk round about,” naturally seeking that by which they may end desire, and foolishly rejecting that by which they may approach the end. *On the Love of God*, no. 19.

A soul that loves God seeks no reward for its love other than God; or, if it seeks another, it loves that other, not God. *Ibid.*, no. 17.

By natural desire everyone seeks the highest good. Do you wish to arrive? Begin to leap over. *Treatise on Contempt of the World, addressed to Clerics*, no. 33. For if you become entangled in the lowest things, you will not arrive.

The way is winding and impassable; you will arrive more easily by despising all things than by acquiring them. *Ibid.*, 33.

[Col. 1204C] A miserable exchange, full of the utmost madness: to avoid human labor and choose eternal gnashing with the devil. *Ibid.*, 27.

[Col. 1203]

## INDEX OF SUBJECTS AND WORDS IN VOLUME ONE

The reader is referred to the numerical notes in heavier type. The letter II designates notes.

## A
ABAELARD, pupil and later adversary of William of Champeaux, 14 n. His rashness, writings, and errors, 181. His books, etc.: see Peter Abelard. An abbot addressed by the title “Blessedness,” 261; likewise “Holiness,” 211, 212, 340, 346; “Reverence,” 292; “Serenity,” 346; “Greatness,” 211; “Crown,” 213. An abbot-elect received the professions of monks, 298. An abbot’s promotion is the emancipation of a son, 92; yet he does not cease to be a monk, 475, and remains subject to the Rule, 24, 503, 504. He ought to be as one of the monks, 475, and not forget his profession, 1156. He was instituted not so much for the good as for the vicious, 75. He should be an observer of the commandments and a punisher of vices, 503. It is shameful for an abbot to be inwardly inferior to monks in virtue, 392. Learning is necessary to him, 287. He must teach humility and obedience by example, [Col. 1204] 475. What is permitted to him in dispensing the Rule, 503 ff. The luxury and superfluities of abbots are censured, 538 ff.; likewise those who perversely seek exemptions, 475 ff.; likewise those who covet pontifical insignia, 476. Whether an abbot should take food with guests, 218. This is disapproved in a Cistercian abbot, 391. Having heard the brethren’s opinions in Chapter, an abbot is not bound to await their consent, 356. It is a transgression against God whenever an abbot’s command is disregarded, 512. The abbot of Cîteaux may be chosen from all the abbots and monks of the order, 319. Abbots of the Cistercian Order may not undertake journeys without permission of the abbot of Cîteaux and of their own bishop, 19, 20. The abbot of La Spina laments the office imposed on him, 335. Relieving an abbot of his dignity is pious counsel, 92. See Shepherd; Prelate.

To bear abasement anxiously is a blemish upon a beautiful body, 247. The first promise concerning the Incarnation of the Word was made to ABRAHAM, 1035. Abraham’s bosom, or the limbo of the Fathers, is in hell, 1035. Whether Abraham’s bosom may be called the present rest of the saints, 1056. Renunciation in baptism, 1107.

ABSALON, archbishop of Lund, 349 n.

It is more useful to conceal than to display whatever good we possess, 727. Those absent from one another because of distance are not judged good; it is otherwise with the wicked even when living together, 148, 149. How a friend’s absence is to be borne, 74. The alternation of the Bridegroom’s absence and presence, 1384. How the Bridegroom’s absence lasts both a little while and not a little while, 1527.

Superstitious and undiscerning abstinence is condemned, 1485. The rigid and remarkable abstinence of a certain novice, 392. The difference between the abstinence of Catholics and that of heretics, 1496. The superstitious abstinence of Manichaeans from certain foods, 1496.

Abuses often become so prevalent that they are regarded as order, 535. They are maintained for a threefold motive, 535. Abuses in monks’ drinking are censured, 536. How great a sin is the misuse of Church property, 395. Misuse of the Church’s honors and goods is censured, 1253. Custom is vainly pleaded against abuses and vices, 436.

The Academics doubt everything, 650. Respect of persons must be avoided by a pope, 426. Favoritism toward the rich is censured, 437. Accidents in the Eucharist, 637.

Action is to be preferred to contemplation, 1527 ff. The beginning of salvation is from action, 1000. The alternation of action and contemplation, 1441, 1462, 1464. One must not give oneself wholly to action, 411. How our actions and passions should be ordered, 889. Motive causes vary actions, 505. The active life is more necessary than contemplation, 1290. Useful warning for practitioners of the active life, 1002. Some are more suited to the active, others to the contemplative life, 1210.

ADALBERO, bishop of Metz, 43 n. ADALBERTO, bishop of Verdun, 63 n., 173 n.

ADAM’s state before sin, 813. Adam’s condition in the state of integral nature, 1089. His sleep was an ecstatic rapture, 813. Whether Adam in paradise possessed a threefold liberty, 611 ff. By cleaving to him who always is and is blessed, we could always be and be blessed, 36. One must cleave to Christ the Head, 814 ff. Three classes of persons are devoid of divine help, 828 ff. Who dwell in the help of the Most High, 329.

Modesty befits young people, 1567. Ecclesiastical dignities are not to be granted to young men, 434. The adoption of Christians, 905.

Pope ADRIAN IV, 398, 399.

The air is the dwelling-place of demons, 573. Summer is charity; winter, servile fear, 1467. One who despises earthly things merits eternal things, 877. Perseverance is an image of eternity, 458. Human works are seeds of eternity, 485. The abundance of eternal recompense, 1522.

The affection of the Holy Spirit in us, 929. Our affection and understanding must be purified, 915. Affection was gradually purified through Christ in the apostles, 926 ff. The four affections with which one ought to pray, 1228 ff.

An elegant tropological interpretation of spiritual agriculture, 991.

Aildicourt, a monastery of Regular Canons, 13.

The cheerfulness of those praising God represents the condition of the heavenly dwelling, 1294. The wings with which the seraphim cover God’s head are admiration and reverence, 954. Those with which they cover the feet are prudence and faithfulness, 954. ALIENORA, queen of the Franks, 199 n. Wife of Louis the Younger, 209 n.

Alpine monks pass to the Cistercian Order, 147. They are praised, 147 ff.

The high, the deep, the long, and the broad must be guarded against, 423.

Alturnia, a city conquered by the Pisans, 146.

AMBITION is the worship of the devil, 837. It is compared with a dragon, 869. It avoids being seen, 133. It is sober, 133; blind and brazen, 133; liable to confusion and contempt, 133.
