AMBROSE of Milan, 143.

AMEDEUS, abbot of Hautecombe, 59 n. AMEDEUS, count of Geneva, 101. AMEDEUS, bishop of Lausanne, 713.

Friendship makes strangers and absent persons known and present, 107. True friendship sometimes includes rebuke, but never flattery, 242. It separates bodies for God’s sake, not minds, 301. It keeps nothing shut up in the mind, 211. Spiritual friendship is always and everywhere consistent with itself, 66. Friendships will then be true if they are bound together in fellowship with truth, 82. A person is unworthy of love who serves a friend against God, 265. A friend is another self, 59. The rule for true friends, 265. Among friends there should be no timid smoothing-over against truth, 48. A friend’s duty is to warn beneficially, 27. How a friend’s absence is to be borne, 74. Let no one doubt that he is loved who already loves, 114.

LOVE absorbs the other affections, 1558, especially conjugal love, 1558. It does not know “Lord,” 1468. It recognizes a son even in mitres, 408. Majesty yields to love, 1468. Love and hatred corrupt judgment, 565. One who clings to things that should be loved in due order does not neglect things to be feared, 1184. The force and energy of love, 408, 1543. Nothing is difficult to one who loves, 879. The force and vehemence of sorrow born from love, 1. Love’s ardor is impatient, 1288. What its voice and speech are like, 1501. When what is loved is present, love flourishes; it languishes when that thing is absent, 1442. Where [Col. 1208] love is, there is no labor, but delight, 1564. Love alone suffices for itself, 1558. The true rule of love, 88. Love is a great thing, but it has degrees, 1558. Its four degrees, 31. They are expounded, 601. The fourth is impossible in this life, 31, 601. The first degree of love is love of self, 593. It is not imposed by command but implanted by nature, 593. It is moderated by the command to love one’s neighbor and becomes social, 594. The second degree is to love God for one’s own sake, 594; the third, to love God for God’s own sake, 595; the fourth, to love oneself only for God’s sake, 595. The happiness of that state is brief in this life, 595. To be affected in this way is to be deified, 596.

Love is threefold: sweet, prudent, and strong, 1145; likewise carnal, rational, and spiritual, 1329. Love is fivefold according to the body’s five senses, 1106 ff. Love of an apparent good, 36. Sweet love excludes lust of the flesh; prudent love, curiosity; strong love, ambition, 1146 ff. Spiritual love begins from the flesh, 31. What chaste and just love is, 595. True love does not demand a reward but merits one, 591. True love is content with itself: it has a reward, namely, the thing loved, 591. The true and faithful love of the soul, by which truth is loved, 1539. The necessary union of love and knowledge, 1507. The power of love in God, 1487. God’s love toward humanity is strong and constant, 1018. It is a mark of predestination, 113. God’s love precedes ours, 1510; ours gladly follows it, 114. Our love is nothing when compared with the divine, 1559 ff. God’s love for human beings against demons, 1319. Two arguments for God’s love toward us, 154. The origin of love for God from gifts and tribulations, 594. Scourges are signs of God’s love, 39. No surer testimony of divine love exists than God’s rebuke, 1100. God is lovable, being the love by which you love and by which you are loved, 458. Love of God comes from God, 127. Love of God produces the soul’s love, 1509, and is a sign that God loves, 1509. God is satisfied by love alone, 1558. Its fruit and reward are its enjoyment, 1558. God prefers to be loved rather than feared and honored, 1558. Let all love and honor be rendered to him from whom comes to us all that enables us to honor or love, and through whom we deserve to be loved or honored, 863. Whoever neither thinks upon God’s majesty with fear nor contemplates his charity with love is displeasing to God, 721.

How greatly the debt of love lies upon Christians, 590 ff. The commandment of love binds the faithful of the new law more strongly than those of the old, 590. Without love of God, other loves are transitory, 1107. What true love of God is, 1328. The boldness of one who loves God and God’s condescension, 1504. Great security belongs to the lover, 1561. Pure love is not mercenary, 1558, though it is not without recompense, 1558. Unity between God and humanity consists in the glue of love, 1516. Whether love of God precedes love of neighbor, 1241. We are called by fear and justified by love, 112. To love in God is to possess charity; but to strive to be loved for God’s sake is to serve charity, 97. The bride’s love is chaste, holy, and ardent, 128. To the soul that loves God all things are shared with God, 1427. God must be loved not only sweetly but strongly, 1325; sweetly, prudently, and strongly, 1327 ff. Love will then be temperate and just if what is withheld from pleasure is not denied to the brethren’s need, 594. The measure of the fruit of our love is without measure, 1296. A soul loving God is called sister, bride, and daughter, 1287. A soul loving God unceasingly seeks the way on which it may walk, the caution by which it may walk, and the dwelling toward which it may walk, 1387.

Christ’s love for us, 915. How greatly Christ ought to be loved for his condescension toward the soul, 808. Whence the Bridegroom has gained for himself so great a love, 1521. Meditation on Christ’s Incarnation and Passion is an incentive to love, 1145 ff. Christ’s Passion is a great incentive to the love of God, 586. Christ should be loved more for the work of redemption than of creation, 1326. Carnal love toward Christ is described, 328. One who loves Jesus cannot bear his injuries, 1422. The disciples’ love before Christ’s Ascension was sweet but neither prudent nor strong, 1327. The Church’s love for Christ is constant, 1544. One should yield to Christ’s love rather than to death, 107. What our love for Christ ought to be, 1327. The different kinds of Christ’s lovers, 1329.

Mutual love among brethren, 1354. Love is especially required of shepherds, 1537. Love of one’s own opinion must be avoided, 216. How parental love should be ordered, 109. Parental love must yield to love of the Crucified One, 299. See Charity; Love. “He who loves me loves my dog too,” 1020.

The monastery of Saint Anastasius at Aquae Salviae, of the Cistercian Order, 178 n.

Praise of Saint ANDREW the Apostle, 1117. He is not frightened by threats or punishments, 1059. Andrew’s longing for the cross, 1059, 1064 ff. His Acts, cited from nine hundred years earlier, 1059 n. Saint Andrew’s faith like a grain of mustard seed, 1059. Fasting on the vigil of Saint Andrew, 1059.

[Col. 1209] ANDREW, uncle of Saint Bernard, 178 n. Most necessary to the Holy Land, and a Knight Templar, 277. ANDREW, Knight Templar, 172 n. The various orders of angels, 1361. What must be considered in each order, 449 ff. Whether angels are corporeal, 447, 1278. Their eminence and dignity, 1019. They are God’s throne, 951. They know creatures in the Creator, 1104. Their virtues come from God, 449 ff. On the names, offices, and distinctions of angels, 447 ff. Their orders and names are full of mysteries, 1051. The time of Christ’s Advent was unknown to them, 634. Christ is higher than they, 1525; how he was made lower than them, 1525. Christ surpasses angels in eagerness to minister, 1451. Christ became redemption even for angels, and how, 1336. Why humanity, not angels, was redeemed, 719. With how great a love angels are carried toward Christ, 1323.

The bride’s familiarity with angels, 1284. The bride is one body from angels and human beings, 1362. The Church desires to be assimilated to angels, 1363. Angels are guardians of the Church, 1539. Angelic guardianship fortifies churches, 1076; it is the Church’s wall, 1478. God’s goodness in the guardianship of angels, 862 ff. The two hands of guardian angels, 864. Angelic guardianship is always at hand for the devout soul, 1407. Faith proves that the presence of angels is not lacking to us, 864. How necessary angelic protection is to us, 863. The angels’ condescension and charity toward us, 1019, 1361. Their offices toward devout souls, 1381; toward humankind, 862. How eager and zealous angels are for our salvation, 759; how solicitous, 1020. Holy angels console, visit, and help us for God’s sake, for our sake, and for their own sake, 1020. They delight in concord and unity; they are provoked to indignation by discord and dissensions, 1021 ff. They stand by those praying, 744, 1283 ff. Our prayers become known to God through them, 1284. They mingle with those singing psalms, 80. The devotion of psalm-singers refreshes them, 1284. Why they should be honored, 1038. How carefully their offense must be avoided, 1020. Obstacles to angels’ love and concern for us, 1022. The Virgin Mary was entrusted to the angel Gabriel’s guardianship from the beginning, 636. Angels marveling at the Assumption of the Blessed Mary, 1003. The fall of proud angels, 946. Singularity, 909. The testimony in heaven for distinguishing blessed angels from reprobate ones, 908. Pride changed the prince of angels into the devil, 718. The fall of angel and human being through pride, 1508. Humanity was punished more mildly than the angel, 1508.

ANGILBERT, count, 282. The English are more dreamers than the French, 715.

The human soul is akin to angelic nature, 1020. The soul’s dignity consists in two things, 585. By what indications it may be known that the soul derives its origin from heaven, 1362. The whole soul is nothing other than reason, memory, and will, 483, 929, 1296. The soul can never live without memory, 456. The soul’s three benefits: dignity, knowledge, and virtue, 585. It is not in the body as in a place, 1202. It is in all members, but especially in the head, 830. It has a certain trace of the Trinity, 1180. The affinity or likeness of the Word and the soul, 1546, 1549, 1550 ff., 1551, 1553, 1554, 1555, 1556, 1557. The soul reflects the greatness and uprightness of the Image, or Word, 1557. Whence this is to be assessed, 1547. The difference between greatness and the soul, 1547. The distinction between the Image and [Col. 1210] the soul, 1546. It lost uprightness while retaining greatness, 1547. For the soul, being and living are the same, though not living well and blessedly, 1550. The soul is immortal, not in respect of spiritual death, 1550, but in respect of natural death, 1551, although mutable in its affections, 1551. The spiritual union of soul and Word, 1381 ff. The spiritual conversation of soul and Word, 1425. The soul is in one respect free and in another a servant, 1552. See Liberty and Free Will. Although corrupt, the soul is capable of great grace and happiness, 1557. Conformity marries the soul to the Word, 1557, 1566. Its spiritual fruitfulness, 1566 ff.

The union of soul and body, 779. How much the body contributes to the soul, 597; how much it owes it, 730. How much the soul provides for the body, 779. The soul in the body is a symbol of peace and concord, 1021. The soul’s three offices toward the body, 1205. The soul’s immortality and faith in the resurrection, 846. The soul’s life is knowledge, perception, and charity, 1234. The soul’s life is truth; its perception, charity, 1106. The soul’s skin, flesh, and bones, 1098. Its blood is its will, 1229. The soul’s twofold beauty: humility and innocence, 1423. Its adornment lies in moral goodness, 1565 ff. The soul’s tongue is the fervor of devotion, 1425. What its voice is, 1478—namely desire, 1527. The soul’s wings are hope and fear, 1236. The soul’s three citadels, 1254. The soul’s castle, 1204; in how many ways it is attacked, 1204. The soul is broad and narrow, 1364. Its size is in proportion to charity, 1364. Its breadth is its love, 1364. How it grows and diminishes, 1364. It is great insofar as it can contain eternal things, and upright insofar as it desires heavenly things, 1547.

The soul’s natural food is righteousness, 593. Its true food is understanding of spiritual things, 978; likewise mercy, righteousness, and grace, 979. Bread taken by the soul with disgust brings not nourishment of knowledge but torment of conscience, 1398. The soul’s food is threefold according to its three states, 561. The carnal portion of the soul is its affection and the life which it administers to the body, 1378. The soul’s languor and greed arise from pride, 1453. Christ cannot dwell in a soul not clothed with the apostles’ doctrine and morals, 1361. The rational soul has two places: the lower, which it rules, namely flesh; and the higher, in which it rests, namely God, 1205. It is more present where it loves than where it gives life, 523. Its bed, 104. God is soul to the soul, 1107. God is the soul’s true life, 552, 855, 1107. How the soul’s threefold power must be filled by God, 1037. The soul’s affection toward God, 458. God’s condescension toward the soul, 1445; his entrance into the soul, 1382. This belongs to God alone, 1279. How greatly Christ deigns to honor the soul, and how greatly he should therefore be loved, 808. The soul is Christ’s kingdom, 750; what tyranny and hostility it contains, 750. Christ’s marriage with the soul, 808. Why a holy soul is compared to cavalry, 1407. It is as though heaven, 1363; God dwells in it as in heaven, 1363. Seven reasons why the soul seeks the Word, 1561 ff. See Word. Wisdom’s affection in the soul, 1564. See Wisdom.

A devout soul is called a friend, 1409. What a devout and spiritual soul is, 1507. To what soul the name bride belongs, 1527, 1566. A loving soul is rightly called bride, 1282. A holy soul is called sister, bride, and daughter, 1287. Whether what belongs to the Church also belongs to the holy soul, 1506. In what respect a spiritual soul is beautiful, 1405. Nothing in this world can equal its beauty, 1360. A soul thirsting for God gladly remains in the garden, the cellar, and the chamber, 1340. It seeks a kiss of the mouth, 1282. The devout soul’s desire for the noonday of eternal light, 1389.

The soul’s evil is sin, 855. Its death is sin; its life, righteousness, 114. The soul’s likeness to God is not erased by sin, but another likeness is superimposed upon it, 1554. Its two evils: vain love of the world and excessive self-love, 1267. Its threefold enemy: flesh, the world, and the princes of darkness, 758. Its corruption is threefold, 1201. The soul’s miseries, 1079. Its threefold misery, 1180. It suffers from the fourfold disease of vices, 1234. How greatly the corruptible body weighs down the soul, 1050. Present consolation enfeebles it, 343. The soul will find its flesh such as it has shown itself toward God, 1026. A soul rebellious against God rightly experiences flesh as rebellious, 532. Complaint concerning arid souls, especially among Saint Bernard’s disciples, 1288 ff. Carnal souls are signified by the name women, 1405. Tender souls are like pregnant women, 467. The life of the soul must be preferred to that of the body, 468, and cared for before and more than the body, 729. Let us never forget the concern of our souls, 763. The soul’s salvation must be procured even at bodily loss, 980. The saints’ chief concern is the soul, 1351. Souls are signified by vineyards, 1464. The soul must not be entrusted to someone who has lost his own, 164. The world rightly deceives souls forgetful of their dignity, 484. It is unworthy for a soul to carry itself crookedly in an upright body, 1348. The soul’s crookedness is to seek and relish things upon the earth; its uprightness is to meditate on things above, 1348. The gravest punishment sends the soul away from God to creatures, 1395 ff. The body must cooperate with the soul, 730 ff. The body must be exposed for the soul, 843. Care for one’s own soul must be preferred to care for another’s, [Col. 1211] 1321 ff. How the soul knows itself, 1098. How the soul is to be lost, by Paul’s example, 1378. Why Paul distinguishes between the soul and himself, 1378. Let the soul dwell in heaven through thought and longing, 1478. He takes his soul in vain who does nothing worthy of immortality, 108. The soul seeks rest, but Christ urges it to labor, 1430.

To impede the salvation of souls is a greater sin than the sin of the Jews, 955. Eugenius III dissuades the Cistercians from the care of souls, 267. By what marks a vocation to the care of souls may be recognized, 1464. Who is fit for the guardianship of souls, 1377. Those seeking their care are censured, 1377. Bishops who give no account of souls are censured, 443 n. Shepherds are guardians of souls, 1536.

The soul’s three states, 597, 1033. In a mortal body the soul cannot see God, 1405. What vision of God a devout soul seeks, 1382. The souls of the dead are carried to heaven by angels’ hands, 864. The soul’s blessedness consists in three things, 1037. Blessed souls lack something of glory, but have absolutely nothing of misery, 607. The souls of saints, stripped of their bodies, are not fully blessed except after the resurrection, 1174. The souls’ love for their bodies, 596. Souls are not perfectly blessed before the resurrection, 1203, 1207. Without bodies, they neither wish nor can be consummated, 597. Separated from the body, they are borne toward God less perfectly, 1033. They dwell in the courts, 1077. The souls of the dead receive three places according to their differing merits, 1177. Praises of souls blessed in heaven, 965. Holy souls pray for their own consummation, 1034. Bernard’s opinion concerning the state of souls, 710. Having resumed the body, the soul is borne fully toward God, 597. See Mind; Intellect.

The soul of a brute does not live except while it gives life, 108. The life of animals, 1550. All living creatures, even those that seem harmful, are useful to humans, 1278; even those produced through sexual intercourse and used for food, 1496.

How the affections and passions of the mind should be ordered, 817. Equanimity of mind must be preserved, 1332. How God comes to dwell in it, 1364. The mind that does not presume upon itself can do all things, 1563. See Soul.

The circumstances of the Annunciation of the Lord are examined, 981 ff.

ANSELLUS, cleric, 193. ANSELM, formerly abbot of Saint Vincent at Laon and then bishop of Tournai, 473 n. ANSELM, archbishop-elect of Milan, deposed, 141 n. ANSELM, bishop of Laon, 14 n. ANSELM, canon of Laon, 302 n., 377. ANSELM, bishop of Rochester, 194 n. ANSERICUS, archbishop of Besançon, 189 n. He reforms the monks of Faverney, 350 n.

ANTELMUS, or NANTELMUS, formerly prior of Portes and bishop of Belley, 247 n., 263 n.

The advent of Antichrist foretold by Saint Norbert, 60.

The Gregorian Antiphonary of Metz, 693. The Cistercian Antiphonary corrected by Bernard and others, 692.

The rights of the bishop of Auxerre over the officials of the count of Nevers, 376. The possessions of the bishop of Auxerre must be guarded as one’s own, 376. The turbulent election of the bishop of Auxerre after Hugh’s death, 268 ff., 270, 272 ff. Bernard asks that Louis the Younger not oppose it, 273. The seal of the Church of Auxerre, 269 n.

Christ is compared to a bee, 722.

How religious persons should guard against apostasy, 833. Apostasy of heart, 833. Apostasy is descent from the greater promised good to a lesser one, 540. Transfer to laxer observance is reckoned apostasy, 2, 5, 6 n., 293 ff. Apostate novices falling away from the order, and likewise monks turning back to laxer observance, 353 n.

Heretics vainly boast that they are apostolic, 1497. The apostles provide us with four things, 995. They are alien from judicial affairs and earthly concerns, 411. Their affection was gradually purified by Christ, 926 ff. They received the Holy Spirit in different ways, 927. A twofold manifestation of the Holy Spirit was given to them, 928. Why they could not receive the Holy Spirit while Christ was present, 915, 928: namely, because, fixed upon Christ’s bodily presence, they were incapable of the Holy Spirit, 369. What their drunkenness was like after receiving the Holy Spirit, 1435; likewise what their transformation was like, 928. They were ignorant of the liberal arts, 1399. Why they bore Christ’s departure with difficulty, 912 ff., 915. Why they were called men of mercy, 993, 994. They taught us to live well, 989. Female apostles of the apostles
women, 1533. The Apostles and apostolic men are guardians of the Church, 1539. We are the seed of the Apostles, 995. The enduring righteousness of the Apostles, 995. Ambition treads the thresholds of the Apostles [Col. 1212] more than devotion does, 427. The twofold spirit of Elijah is a type of the Apostles, 927. The Apostolic See ought not to be a refuge for criminals, 158; but a refuge for the oppressed, 57. There faith cannot experience failure, 643. Appearances of Christ, 905. In them the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified, 905. It is not lawful to appeal from judges chosen by the parties, 183. An appeal is not an evasion but a refuge, 428. The necessity and usefulness of appeals, 429. When they are lawful, 353, 428. They are not to be undertaken rashly, 429. Every appeal to which a lack of justice has not compelled one is unjust, 428. An appeal unlawfully made should neither benefit the appellant nor harm the respondent, 428. An appeal from the whole world to the pope is testimony to his primacy, 428. Unjust appeals must be corrected, 428. Abuse of appeals, 174 n. Demonstrated by examples, 429 ff. The grounds of unjust appeals, 428 ff. Before judgment, an appeal is altogether improperly presumed, except on account of manifest injury, 428. To seek things which neither satisfy nor moderate desire is the height of madness, 592. The human appetite for the highest good, 591 ff. Appetite is a power in a living being, assigned to move the senses eagerly, 604. Volition differs from appetite, 604. The approval of good persons ought to suffice us, 1346. Apulia captured by Roger, 173. The water of wisdom: the divine word, 1334. Water of remission from the fountain of mercy; of discernment from the fountain of wisdom; of devotion from the fountain of grace; of fervour from the fountain of charity, 778. The Saviour’s water is threefold, and so likewise is that of man, 1057. Fear is compared to water, 1235, 1455. The ordeal of water, 1499 n. The north wind signifies reprobate men, 574. The monastery of Aquis Cinctus, 65, 66 n., 67. Free will. See *Liberty*. A tree frequently transplanted rarely puts down firm roots, 268. The life of trees, 1550. Christ, the mystical tree, 969. Fruitful and fruitless trees, 968. The distinction among spiritual trees, 968. The archangels are admitted more intimately into the counsels of divine wisdom, 1328.

ARCHEMBAUD, archdeacon of Orléans, killed, 155 n., 160 n. ARCHEMBALD of Saint-Aignan, Knight Templar, 541. Archdeacons should be ordained deacons, 434. An archdeaconry given to a little boy, 367 twice. The title of holiness given to an archbishop, 292, 391; likewise that of sublimity, 325, 348. Submission is commended even in an archbishop, 474. A stricter life is to be urged, not required, of those who have not professed it, 87. See *Apostasy*. It is better to burn than merely to shine, 948. Merely to shine is vain; merely to burn is too little; to burn and shine is perfect, 983.

ARDUTIO, bishop-elect of Geneva, 42; bishop, 43. ARDUTIUS of Faucigny, 42. Gold and silver are white and red earth, made precious solely by human error, 726. ARGRIMUS, archdeacon of Orléans, 201 n. Dryness of soul arises from pride, 1453. Those who persevere in prayer while dry become fervent, 1290. The monastery of Aripatorium, of the Cistercian Order, 712. The spiritual weapons by which the devil is defeated, 1074. Their necessity, 1065. Weapons must be taken up against the enemy, 1065. The weapons by which the fortress of the soul is defended, 1204. Bernard’s weapons: the prayers of the poor, 258. Armach, or Ardmach, city, 660, 669. Whether the bishops of Armagh, before the use of the pallium, were ever called archbishops and exercised metropolitan authority, 311 n.

ARNALD, abbot of Bonneval, how great a friend of Bernard’s, 290. ARNALD OF BRESCIA, 182 n., 282. A heretic, 187, 188. He adheres to Abelard, 187. Expelled from Italy and the kingdom of France, 187, 188, 189. Instigator of sedition at Rome, 437 n. The Arnoldists, heretics, 240 n. They maintain that sacraments administered by evil ministers are invalid, 240 n. ARNALD OF COLOGNE, simoniac, 431 n. ARNOLD, abbot of Morimond, 14 n. He leaves the monastery of Cîteaux without the permission of its Father-Abbot, 16. His disastrous end, 146. ARNULF, abbot of Latiniac, 225 n. ARNULF, count of Chisne, 173 n. ARNULF, bishop of Lisieux, praised by Bernard, 246, 715. Saint Bernard commends his election against the violence of the count of Anjou, 317 ff. ARNULF, prior of Saint Stephen at Dijon, 62 n. ARNULF OF MAJOLE, a deceitful and wicked man, 264, 271.

The three spices of the mind: brotherly compassion, zeal for justice, and discernment of spirits, 900. With what they are to be purchased, 900. The three spices [Col. 1213] of the hand: continence in relation to the flesh, mercy toward brothers, and patience in piety, 902. Purchase them with the coin of submission, 902. Likewise the three spices of the tongue: moderation in rebuking, abundance in exhorting, effectiveness in persuading, 901. Magnanimity does not make men arrogant, nor humility faint-hearted, 1011. Arrogance is to be guarded against more than ignorance, 585. It is the sixth degree of pride, 577. Consideration of oneself corrects it, 1454. The effects of arrogance and humility, 93. See *Pride*. The monastery of Arremare, of the Order of Saint Benedict, 357 n., 712.

ARTOLD, or ARTAUD, abbot of Preuilly, 76. He builds the monastery of Vallis Lucentis, 76 n. The Apostles did not know the liberal arts, 1399. ASCELIN, bishop of Rochester, 194 n.

THE ASCENSION of Christ consummates the other feasts, reveals their fruit, and increases grace, 918. It was not to be delayed, 1535. Faith in it, 1544. Our glorification is attributed to Christ’s Ascension, 972. Its praises, 912. Christ’s ascents are various, 920 ff. Our hope from Christ’s Ascension, 918. See *Christ*. A twofold ascent commended by the Apostle, 924. The four degrees of ascent, 1233; likewise seven degrees, 1234. How one must ascend to Christ, 1153. A saving ascent, by the example of Christ descending, 920. The obstinate and stubborn are like the asp, 865. Temptation concerning the necessities of life is compared to the asp, 868. How asps stop their ears, 865. Harsh words are displeasing, 180. What a harsh word is, 832. The rigour of religious life is not to be feared by the delicate, 118. Consideration of hell softens every harshness, 832. See *Austerity*.

The feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary received, 169. All priests celebrate on this feast, 1214. See *Mary*. ATENULF, abbot of Farfa, 314 n., 315 n. His affection for the Cistercians, 314, 315. The monastery of Athanac, 352 n. The abbot of Athanac unjustly deposed, 352, 353. The courts of souls released from the flesh, 1077. ATTO, bishop of Troyes, 39, 155, 194, 712. By distributing his goods to the poor, he is delivered from the danger of death, 40. The avarice of prelates is sharply censured, 1292, 1538; likewise that of clerics, 472. The chariot, horses, and driver of avarice, 1408. Avarice must be cut away from one’s household, 444. The miser is the slave and guardian of riches, 1332. He is like a dropsical man, 769. He hungers after earthly things like a beggar and despises the faithful like a lord, 1332. The qualities of an ecclesiastical author, 357. What authority in a steward ought to be, 443. How harmful it is to listen to idle talk, 1120. In every conversation two hearers must be considered, 1120. What hearing must be like for merit, 1368. Hearing is for merit, sight for reward, 1367. Let no one think that credence is to be denied to hearing and sight, 470. See *Ears*. What turning away from one’s purpose, and being overthrown in one’s purpose, mean, 167.

ARCHEGAUD, prior of Saint-Oyend, beloved by Bernard for his religious vocation, 279. AUFRID, chaplain of Thurstan, bishop of York, 389. SAINT AUGUSTINE, the greatest doctor after the Apostles, 217. Augustine, pillar of the Church, 629. Hammer of heretics, 1548. AUGUSTINE, apostle of the English, 427. Christ’s yoke compared with birds’ feathers, 343. The prerogative of the ears in the matter of faith, 1367. See *Hearing*. Dawn signifies humility, 1212. Spanish gold, 427. Gold and silver are red and white earth, made precious solely by human error, 726. The discipline of a more austere life frightens novices, 1391. The austerities of the Rule may, at charity’s command, be mitigated, 219. Austerities soften monastic life, 299. Because of the austerities of a purer life, monasteries are not to be avoided, 297. See *Harshness*, *Mortification*. Auvecourt, or Aviulficurtis, abbey of Regular Canons, 275 n. AUXENTIUS, the Arian at Milan, 1054. God’s aid is twofold: correction and consolation, 1333. What aid we ought to give our brothers in cloisters, 725. The Latins use unleavened bread in the sacrifice; the Greeks, leavened bread, 216.

## B

**A staff called “Jesus,”** kept at Armagh, 669. The sick among the Cluniacs carried a staff, 536. **BALDICIUS**, monk, 243. **BALDWIN**, Bernard’s secretary, cardinal, and archbishop of Pisa [Col. 1214], 149 n., 150, 192 n. He excommunicates the judge of Arvor, 243. **BALDWIN**, abbot of Châtillon, afterwards bishop of Noyon, 271 n., 359 n. Saint Bernard wittily commends a boy to him, 359. When leaving for Rome, he entrusts his affairs to Bernard, 271, 377. **BALDWIN**, abbot of the monastery of Rieti, greatly beloved by Bernard, 192. **BALDWIN**, king of Jerusalem, 172 n., 321, 540. Near Jerusalem he yields to the Cistercians the site of Saint Samuel, together with a thousand gold pieces, 250, 277 n. **BALDWIN of Wasia** grants offerings to the church of Trunchin, 368. Saint Bernard reconciles him with Goswin, abbot of Trunchin, 368. The monastery of Balerna, Cistercian Order, 151 n. The abbey of Balmes reduced to a priory by Eugenius III, 248 n. Balsam shrubs grow at En-gedi, 1420. The ban of the count of Nevers at Auxerre, 376.

**Baptism:** the beginning of all sacraments, 890. Its figures, 1406. The grace of baptism, 891. The precept concerning it is positive, not natural, 626. When its obligation began, 625 ff., 628 ff. Its form must not be altered, 360. Baptism was conferred by the Apostles in the name of Christ, 360. Whether it is valid when administered in the name of God and of the holy and true Cross, 359 ff. Faith supplies the place of baptism, 628, 629; likewise martyrdom, 628, 629 ff. For the desire for baptism, right faith, devout hope, and sincere charity suffice, 628. Renunciation in baptism, 1107. Triple immersion, 890, 1143. Baptism of infants, 879. It benefits them through another’s faith, 630. They are baptized in the faith of the Church, 1497. What punishment belongs to infants dying without baptism, 1508 n. The error of heretics concerning infant baptism, 1497. The Henricians denied it to them, 237. Another error concerning baptism, 1489. Christ’s humility in baptism, 798, 804 ff. He was baptized on the same day on which he was adored by the Magi, 520, 798. Religious profession is a second baptism, 248, 520, 1108 n., 1160.

**The testament of BARONIS**, Roman subdeacon, 347, 348. **BARTHOLOMEW**, bishop of Laon, 73 n., 199 n., 299 n. Callixtus II commends Saint Norbert to him, 385. He founds the Cistercian monastery of Foigny, 73 n. Under him nine monasteries were founded in the diocese of Laon; others were increased in wealth and religious observance, 385. He becomes a monk at Foigny, 266 n. His *Apology* to Samson, archbishop of Reims, 385 ff. **BARTHOLOMEW**, bishop of Soissons, 86 n.

**The basilisk** carries poison in its eye, 865, 869. A symbol of envy, 865; likewise of vain glory, 869. **BASIL**, prior of the Charterhouse, 27 n. Basse-Fontaine, house of Premonstratensians, 251, 965.

**Blessedness:** wherein it consists, 1036 ff. Its endowments and state, 877. It is light, peace, and a fountain, 768. Its three goods, 1078. It is a noon that knows no evening, 1388. In it there is a threefold enjoyment of God, 1036. Its goods with respect to the soul, 1037, 1296 ff.; with respect to the body, 1037. It will not be perfect until after the judgment, 759, 1031 ff., 1053 ff., 1174. Three means prescribed by Christ for recovering blessedness, 1194. It wholly consists in fearing God, 1039. Its summit is to know him, 1285. Justice alone makes blessed, 1037. The blessedness of angels increases through ours, 1506. See **Heaven**. The eight beatitudes are opposed to the eight sins, 1195 ff. The title “Blessedness” is given to an abbot, 261; likewise to monks, 247.

**BEATRICE**, a noble lady: her solicitude for Bernard, 126 ff. The happiness of the blessed in heaven, 966, 1388. Their threefold joy, 1032 ff. They are joined to the choirs of angels, 1355. They are solicitous for us, 1355. They are merciful, yet free from passions, 1155 ff. Blessed souls desire to resume their bodies, 597. Before the resurrection something of glory is lacking to them, but they have nothing of misery, 607. Nor do they attain the perfection of contemplation, 1204. Encomia of blessed souls, 965.

**Bede’s History** rendered into Saxon, 608. Belfort, a place on the river Vigor, 272 n. **BELINUS**, citizen of Bar, punished by Theobald, 51. Belle-Vallée, monastery of the Cistercian Order, 190 n.

**War** is harmful to enemies and friends, but especially to subjects, 210. Its cause is often trivial, 545. Its cause must be just, and the intention of the combatant upright, 545. Its fruit, 101. Allegorical description of the war between Babylon and Jerusalem, 1248 ff. Belle-Lieu, Premonstratensian monastery, 250 n., 361. The church of Beauvais, accustomed to be tried by vexations and tribulations, 271.

**The monastery of Bangor**, head of many monasteries, 664, 684. Restored by Saint Malachy, 664. Even after its destruction, abbots were appointed who retained its possessions, [Col. 1215] 664. There are two monasteries called Bangor, one in Wales and one in Ireland, 664 n., 675, 679. Monks of Bangor, 900. Slain by pirates, 664.

A threefold blessing is necessary: prevenient, assisting, and completing, 1201. **Benedictio Dei** (“Blessing of God”), monastery of the Cistercian Order, 168 n., 178 n.

**BENEDICT (Saint)** hid himself for three years, 969. He is compared to a fruitful tree, 968. His three fruits, 969. He feeds the Lord’s flock by life, teaching, and intercession, 969. His holiness, justice, and piety ought to refresh us, 967. Whether he saw God intuitively in this world, 1103 n., 1104. Encomium of the Rule of Saint Benedict, 387. It is called holy, 391; dictated by the Holy Spirit, 217; subordinated to charity, 219 ff.; neglected by monks, 390. The monastery of Saint Benedict at the Po, reformed by Innocent II, 153.

**BENEDICT**, first abbot of Casa-Maria, 344. **BENEDICT**, monk of Flavigny, received by Saint Bernard, 67, 70.

Ingratitude closes the hand of a benefactor, 1142. Beneficence ought to be gratuitous, 177. A benefit profits the giver more than the receiver, 105. The four benefits of God, 834 ff. The benefit of creation considered, 867, 1128 ff.; of preservation, 1128; of redemption, 1128; of reward, 1128. Likewise, the benefits of creation, redemption, and calling, 1124. God is accustomed to anticipate the wicked with his benefits, 257. Their burden, 939. Blessed is he who is distressed lest he be overwhelmed by benefits as well as by sins, 870. They ought to win our love for God, 585.

Benefices for ecclesiastical dignities, 355. **Ecclesiastical benefices:** Their grant to children is disapproved, 265. To whom they should be owed, 265. When plurality is lawful, 265. Censured, 472. How ecclesiastical benefices should be used, 12. Whatever a cleric retains from them beyond necessities is robbery and sacrilege, 12. He who does not serve it rejoices undeservedly in its income, 355. The transfer of ecclesiastical benefices from seculars to religious is a twofold good, 295. It is not lawful without the bishop’s consent, 295. Ecclesiastical benefices are to be received not from a lay hand but from the bishop’s, 367, three times.

God’s good pleasure must be sought and maintained in all things, 44. Roger takes Benevento, 173. The church of Saint Benignus at Dijon, the chief church of the city, 34 n. The burial-place of Saint Bernard’s parents adorned there, 34 n. Dear to him because of its ancient religious standing, 33 n., 34. Recommended by him to the supreme pontiff against the monks of Luxeuil, 34.

**BERENGARIUS**, formerly chancellor of Alfonso, bishop of the church of Salamanca, 198 n.

**Acts and sayings of Saint BERNARD.** His arrival among the Genoese, preaching, and its fruit, 138, 139. He attends the Council of Pisa, 142 n., 143. His three journeys to Italy, 149 n., 1346. Journey into Apulia, 150. His two stays at Viterbo, 155 n. On the sixth day after the extinction of the schism he returns from Rome to his own people, 296. Sent into Germany to Emperor Lothair, 155 n.

**Saint Bernard’s preaching**, 608. Its fruit, 251. While he spoke publicly, the Holy Spirit suggested words to him, 1554 n. By word and example he suffices for instruction in virtue, 128. Fruit of his preaching among the people of Toulouse, 238; likewise miracles, 239. Preaching for the holy expedition, 326 n. Chosen at Chartres as leader of the holy expedition, 258, 329 n. Its success, 246. He laments its unhappy outcome, 277.

Saint Bernard opposes errors, 48, 180, 181 ff. Invited by William, abbot of Saint Thierry, to resist Peter Abelard, 301 ff. He approves William’s book against Abelard’s errors, 303. He is an object of fear to Peter Abelard, 302. He examines Abelard’s books, 309, 310. Challenged by him to the council of Sens, 309. He excuses himself from coming, but nevertheless attends, 309; and there convicts Abelard of heresy, 310. He comes unwillingly, 180 n., 183, 309.

**Saint Bernard’s constant occupations**, 94, 97, 192, 348, 732, 822. His vigils, 732. He discourages the writing of letters, 95, 96. Frequency of his letters, 348. His letters falsified, 275. The nature of his seal, 275, 359. Fruits of his labours, 150, 151, 164. He asks to be released from business, 56, 58, 33.

Bernard’s favour with the pope, 168, 201, 235, 272, 300, 318. He becomes the pope’s vicar in reconciling Peter of Pisa, 198. He falls out of favour with Pope Innocent, 201, 227; likewise with Eugenius III, 287, 288. He fears for Eugenius III upon his attaining the supreme pontificate, 232 ff., 234 ff.; yet congratulates him on it, 233 ff. His admonitions to Eugenius, 235. He tries to reconcile the Romans with Eugenius, 240 ff. He tries to draw Conrad, king of the Romans, to Eugenius’s aid, 242 ff.

His favour with princes, 195, 196, 295. He makes Emperor Comnenus a participant in the suffrages of his house, 374. His fidelity to the king, 257, 273. He does not refuse to pay taxes, 127, [Col. 1216] 283. King Louis the Younger uses his counsel, 333. Bernard dissuades the marriage between Mary, the king’s daughter, and the son of the count of Anjou because of consanguinity, 333. He receives letters from the patriarch of Jerusalem, 172. He receives many benefits from Count Theobald, 42. Queen Sancia grants him the abbey of La Spine, 334 n., 335 n. His admonitions to the queen of Jerusalem, 278. His familiarity with her, 278. He desires frequent letters from the queen of Jerusalem, 195. He is chosen to advise Ermengard, countess of Brittany, on salvation, 125. The charity of the noble lady Beatrice toward him, 126 ff. His favour with the Milanese, 141. His affection and benefactions toward the Premonstratensians, 250 ff., 252 n. How greatly Haimo, archdeacon of Châlons, relied on his prayers, 382.

Saint Bernard dissuades princes from war, 101 ff., 127, 139 n., 203. He exhorts them to peace, 139, 209, 210 ff. He makes peace between the Milanese and their neighbours, 142. He settles disputes, 62 n.; lawsuits, 368, 375 ff., 177. He wishes lawsuits to be settled through arbitrators, 284. The kingdoms and churches of Gaul rely upon his counsel, 55 n. He writes to Innocent for the reconciliation of Peter of Pisa, 198.

He recommends and undertakes the causes of bishops before the supreme pontiffs, 54 ff., 57 ff., 174, 176, 197 ff., 198, 199 ff., 245 ff., 281, 285, 293 ff., 300 ff., 311, 312, 317 ff., 367, four times. He asks that the monks of Balmes be received into the favour of Eugenius III, 249. He intercedes for monks with the supreme pontiffs, 260, 261, 270, 275 ff., 276, 279, 281, 289. He recommends the poor to the same pope, 319. He asks that his kinsman be strengthened by the supreme pontiff’s blessing, 318. He recommends the church of Dijon to the pope, 34; to Cardinal Peter, 35; and to Chancellor Haimeric, 34. He recommends to Lothair, hostile to them, the Pisans who were devoted to the supreme pontiff, 145 ff.; likewise the church of Saint Gengulf, 142. He recommends bishops gathered for a council to Count Theobald, 51. In supplicating Theobald for Humbert, he suffers a refusal, 49, 60. He undertakes bishops’ causes before princes, 53 ff., 54; before them he also pleads for religious, 52, 271, 337; for regular canons, 50; and for the wretched, 46, 49 ff., 50 ff., 51, 60, 127, 271. He recommends the liberty of the church of Molesme to Henry, archbishop of Sens, 52, 53; he pleads for it before the bishop of Langres, 62. He recommends poor monks to Abbot Suger, the regent, 339. He seeks the duchess of Burgundy’s assent for the marriage of the son of Hugh of Bèze, 127. He undertakes the causes of bishops, 39, 58, 284, 288, 313 ff.; and of the poor, 361.

Saint Bernard reminds the supreme pontiff of his duty, 183, 198 ff., 235 ff., 294 ff., 318; bishops, 42, 43 ff., 44, 374 ff.; and superiors, 75 ff., 97 ff., 106, 192 ff.

Saint Bernard adheres to the Apostle’s doctrine, 622. He is devoted to the holy Fathers, 102. His reverence toward them, 520, 625, 929, 743, 1277. He commends reverence for the Apostolic See, 178. What he thinks of the honour of the papacy, 232. His reverence toward bishops, 207, 226, 461. He is subject to the bishop, 56. He refuses to impose penance for grave crimes except upon his own monks, 63. In doubtful matters he consults bishops, 63. How he conducts himself in giving counsel, 90, 99 ff., 520. In doubtful and dangerous matters he suspends judgment, 27. The weight he gives to revelations, 170. His counsel concerning the acceptance of ecclesiastical dignities, 26 ff. He disapproves the granting of ecclesiastical benefices to boys, 265. He dissuades resignation of pastoral care, 85 ff., 89, 90, 146 ff., 297. He advises war against the enemies of the Church, 140.

How pleasing to Bernard was intimacy with holy men, 29. His friendship with Saint Malachy, 322. He sends monks to him, 322. Dying, Malachy receives his blessing, 658. Friendship with Peter the Venerable, 152, 211, 212, 225, 261, 262, 270, 329, 345, 346, 348. Mutual love between them from youth, 347. Peter the Venerable eagerly reads and kisses Bernard’s letters, 212, 346. Bernard’s friendship with William, abbot of Saint Thierry, and William’s opinion of him, 95. With Bernard of Portes, Carthusian, 156, 157. Friendship with Suger, 262, 263. Bernard’s secretary, Cardinal Baldwin, 150. Gebwin, precentor and archdeacon of Troyes, writes down the words spoken by Bernard, 35. Mutual affection between Bernard and his brother Gerard, 1357. His studies are free through Gerard, 1354. Bernard is their encourager, helper, and examiner, 1355. He obtains a reprieve for Gerard when his life is in danger, 1359. He follows Gerard’s funeral with dry eyes, 1354.

He desires to visit the Carthusians, 157. Their letters inflame him, 28. He fears lest he disturb their quiet by his own concerns, 28. He commends himself to the prayers of the Cluniacs, 212. Why he preferred the Cistercian Order to others, 350. He calls the Cistercians poor, 43; the poor of Christ, 54, 59, 110, 150, 168, 283, 317, 318, 319, 342.

[Col. 1217] **Saint Bernard’s purpose of religious life**, 108 ff., 109 ff., 110 ff., 111 ff., 115 ff., 117 ff., 120 ff., 363 ff., 364 ff., 365. He gives domestic precepts to someone, 367, tenth letter. He persuades notorious clerics, 117 n. He converts noble men to Christ, 118; likewise courtiers, 82 n. Conversions effected by him, 77 n., 82 n., 117 n., 125 n., 137 n., 142 n., 289 n. He persuades repentant sinners to leave the world, 63. He refuses to receive a refined cleric unaccustomed to labour, 361. He does not refuse that his monks should be received elsewhere for the sake of greater perfection, 70. He disapproves transfer to another monastery, 45, 46, 251, 367, 518, 528, 540; likewise transfer to the hermitage, 124 ff. Why he received monks of other orders into his own, 24. How he received them, 66, 68, 69, 106, 251 ff., 280, 354. He does not receive them without permission from their own abbot, 106, 280. Saint Bernard recalls religious who have returned to the world to the cloister, and intercedes for them, 1 ff., 8 ff., 60, 72 ff., 282, 259. He asks that an expelled novice be received again, 364, 365 ff. His conduct toward the incorrigible, 106 ff., 282. He rebukes those who impede the purpose of religious life, 280 ff. He labours for the reform of monasteries, 55, 77 ff. He does not approve the construction of monasteries in distant kingdoms, 76, 250. What he thought concerning the obligation of monks, 392. He does not condemn the less strict observances of others, 25, 528. He works to settle controversies among monks, 274.

Saint Bernard’s love is pure, 105, 111, 155, 192. Desire of love, 1374. He is free from Stoic apathy, 1357. His weapons are prayers and tears, 228; the prayers of the poor, 258. His charity, 1, 5, 38, 116, 117, 151, 155, 192, 228, 233, 259, 365. How free he is from avarice, 366. His tender love for his own, 76, 148 ff., 149 ff., 155, 193, 196, 249, 259, 260, 315, 342, 408, 580, 1160, 1346, 1447. His charity and piety toward his nephew Robert, 1, 5. His humility, 1. His gentleness, 2. His compassion and clemency, 75, 244 ff., 249, 258, 294, 363. He consoles the afflicted, 84, 86 ff. He awaits consolation in affliction, 1357; in labours, 150, 152, 271, 294, 324.

Saint Bernard is distinguished in the duties of contemplative and active life, 128. His sighs for the heavenly homeland, 811 ff., 1388. His experience of the Bridegroom’s visitation, 1528. He laments the barrenness of his soul in himself, 1377. His devotion, 1300, 1307 ff. Devotion to Christ’s passion, 888, 1418 ff. Love for the cross, 1069, 1422. Devotion to the Mother of God, 89, 732, 755. He has discernment in divine matters, 60. His gratitude, 199, 340, 342 ff.

**Bernard’s humility**, 1, 2, 13, 14, 29, 32, 35, 37, 56 ff., 59, 66, 68, 73, 74 ff., 90, 93, 210, 248, 271, 290, 335, 345, 350, 357, 461, 476, 530, 582, 967, 1273, 1343, 1398, 1453 ff., 1456. He desires humiliation, 93. He shrinks from praise, 13, 73, 74 ff., 90, 262. He is moved neither by praise nor blame, 55. He refuses a bishopric, 167 n. He declines honours, 243. He professes himself a sinner, 33, 58, 145, 289, 292, 313, 350, 461, 1127; a sinner and unlearned, 63, 39, 42, 90; an unfruitful tree, 97. He asks that his books be examined, 95. He does not wish them to be copied, 94. He submits himself to others’ judgment, 603. He accepts reproaches as medicine for his conscience, 271. He prefers curses directed against himself rather than against God, 417. What he thought of himself, 1377. He calls himself depravity, 102, 129, 150, 153, 175; rusticity, 35, 37. He complains of the prelate’s office imposed upon him, 1376. He was utterly removed from present glory, 875. He preaches subjection, 92. He refuses the office of teaching, 96. He wishes to burden no one, 44, 127. He hates flattery, 81. His integrity, 268, 271. His jokes, 95, 359. His zeal for manual labour, 855. His gentleness, 2, 66 ff., 116, 228, 229. His modesty, 32, 35, 37, 38, 49, 66 ff., 35, 71, 88, 90, 93, 94, 96, 99, 124, 129 ff., 143, 150, 156 ff., 157, 229, 240, 262, 265, 271, 287, 330, 331, 1277. His love of silence, 38, 83, 96, 212, 1291, 1307 ff., 1357, 1526. His love of peace, 66, 68, 69, 87, 151, 153, 249, 251, 253 ff. In pursuit of peace he yields his own rights, 282 n. He suffers detractions, 55 ff., 286 ff. His sincerity, 199, 346. His love of solitude, 33, 35, 38, 56 ff., 155, 212. Unwillingly, he goes out for business, 33, 56 ff., 155. He proposes never to leave the cloister except for matters of his Order, unless summoned by the legate of the Apostolic See or by his own bishop, 35, 56, 243. Under pressing necessities he enters public life, 54, 56 ff., 212. He condemns pilgrimages undertaken by monks, 14 ff., 16 ff., 60, 356.

Bernard’s concern for his own, 822, 1447, 1528; for the imperfect, 106, 228 ff.; for brothers undergoing temptation, 4. He rejoices in the progress of his own, 872, 1442 ff. How deeply correction which did not succeed distressed him, 1414. His disposition in correcting, 1373. How merciful he is to offenders, 42 ff., 106. How patient with a perverse monk, 282.

[Col. 1218] **Bernard’s zeal**, 437 ff. Zeal for justice, 158 ff., 160, 161 ff., 164, 165 ff., 174 ff., 198, 203 ff., 204 ff., 207, 264, 271, 316, 353 ff. He wishes nothing to be granted him except what is just, 271. He admonishes and rebukes kings and princes, 137 ff., 138, 167 ff., 203 ff., 204 ff., 205, 210 ff., 321, 333 ff. He rebukes bishops, 177, 205 ff., 207 ff. He inveighs against clerics who are courtiers and entangled in royal service, 81 ff. He pursues simoniacal bishops, 229 ff., 230 ff., 235, 236 ff., 249 ff., 316 ff. He pursues heretics, 180 ff., 181 ff., 18 ff., 184 ff., 185 ff., 187 ff., 188 ff., 237, 238, 239, 305 ff., 306 ff., 307 ff., 308 ff., 309 ff. Zeal for removing scandal, 67, 161 ff., 163 ff., 165 ff. In promoting good prelates and removing bad ones, 33, 55, 161 ff., 163, 164, 165 ff., 166 ff., 192, 247, 263, 268 ff., 272 ff., 296, 303 ff., 304, 316 ff. What sort of shepherds he requires for the Church, 248. His love and affection for the Church, 147, 152, 164, 165, 167, 173, 207, 231, 235, 256 ff., 257 ff., 263, 296, 305, 306, 329 ff., 339. His labours for the Church, 164, 165, 198, 201, 272, 296. He labours to uphold Innocent’s pontificate, 129 ff., 130 ff., 131 ff., 137 ff., 139, 140 ff., 144, 145, 319. His zeal for discipline, 499; for regular observance, 97 ff., 227, 254 ff. A leave extorted or compelled is, he says, not leave but violence, 90. He writes to Wratislaus, duke of Bohemia, concerning undertaking the holy war, 367, eleventh letter.

Bernard’s reputation, 128, 362, 711. He clears himself of sinister suspicions, 46, 47, 105, 273, 366 ff. He defends himself against unjust accusations, 84, 206, 207, 250 ff., 286 ff.; likewise concerning execution of Cardinal Ivo’s testament, 201; and concerning his frequent writing to Innocent, 202.

**Encomium of Saint Bernard**, 225, 261, 326 n., 345, 378 ff., 382, 383, 710, 1487. He was called “of holy memory” while still living, 55 n.; and “saint,” 262, 347, 1487, 1488. Peter the Venerable attributes to him the title of holiness, 346; Haimo, archdeacon of Châlons, 382. Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, calls him “dearest brother,” 128; Peter the Venerable, “holy brother,” 262. Called an interpreter of the Holy Spirit, 1265. His tongue: “the pen of a swiftly writing scribe,” 143. His spoken words transcribed, 37. When he enters the curia, Cardinal Gregory of Tarquinia rises for him, 307. Berengarius, his adversary, acknowledges his miracles, 239 n.

**Bernard’s writings**, 49, 96. He writes an Office and two sermons on Saint Victor, 358. His book *On Grace and Free Will*, 1553. The esteem in which his sermons were held by the learned, 705. On what days they were delivered, 705; at what hour, 706, 1163, 1264. Whether they were delivered in French or Latin, 706 ff. Why some are short and others long, 845. Because of illness he sometimes made them short, 845. He preached sermons outside the custom of his Order, 811, 856. Critical appraisal of his sermons, 710 ff. Sermons on the Song of Songs, 155. In everyone’s mouth and bosom, 382. Selections from his writings, 1569 ff. Those writing in his stead sometimes sharpened the style excessively, 345, 347. The letters of Bernard to Gertrude and of Gertrude to Bernard are spurious, 126 n. He grants Queen G., aunt of the Spanish emperor, the suffrages of the brothers of Cîteaux, 367, ninth letter.

**Saint Bernard’s illnesses**, 150, 180, 196, 212, 237, 265, 277, 288, 290, 732, 1418, 1422. What his food was then, 392. He suffers from fever, 38, 93, 97, 126, 367, sixth letter. The king is concerned for his health, 285. He is visited in illness by Robert, brother of Louis the Younger, 285. He recovers from illness, 97, 126. He desires death, 290. Among his own at Clairvaux, 150, 151. Bernard’s death foretold by others, 344. He foresees its imminence for himself, 277. He fears his own death and that of his people, 1357. He learns that the souls of his brethren have flown to heaven, 1127. His parents are buried in the church at Dijon and thence transferred to Clairvaux, 34 n. His cowl is at Saint Victor’s, Paris, 362 n.

**BERNARD**, abbot of Saint Anastasius near Rome, 307 n. His patience and concern toward an undisciplined monk, 378. He becomes Pope Eugenius III, 178 n., 231 n., 232 n., 314 n., 316. He complains of the office imposed upon him, 314 ff. **BERNARD**, abbot of Grandselve, 238, 239 n. **BERNARD**, abbot of Tiron, 136 n. **BERNARD**, legate, 284 n. **BERNARD**, bishop of Pavia, 135. **BERNARD**, bishop of Parma, 135. **BERNARD**, formerly bishop of Belley, prior of Portes, 155 n., 247. Elected bishop of Pavia, 157 n. A man of God, 157. Beloved by God and human beings, 157. His frequent letters to Saint Bernard, 156. Their mutual friendship, 156, 157. **BERNARD**, prior of Portes, afterwards bishop of Die, 156. **BERNARD**, monk of Portes, cardinal, 155 n.

[Col. 1219] **BERNARD**, monk of Ambournay, first prior of the Charterhouse of Portes, 155 n. **BERNARD**, prior of Portes after Nantelmus, 156 n. **BERNARD**, priest, 377. **BERNERIUS**, abbot of Bonneval, 290 n.

The monastery of Saint Bertin entrusted to Saint Hugh of Cluny, 153 n. Its flourishing condition under him, 153. It throws off the Cluniac yoke, 153. Saint Bernard urges the monks of Saint Bertin toward perfection, 342 ff. The monastery of Bèze, Order of Saint Benedict, 127 n. Bethany, that is, “house of obedience,” 557. Bethlehem: the place of Christ’s birth foretold by the prophets, 634. Its happiness and glory, 756. Moral exposition of Bethlehem, 774, 775. It likewise means “house of bread,” 757. Bethphage is called “house of the cheek,” 556. The dean of Béthune recommended by Bernard to the supreme pontiff, 275. The Cistercians’ Bible corrected, 692.

Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is the unforgivable refusal to correct minor sins, 957. Bonneval, monastery in the territory of Chartres, 290. Arnold, abbot, 290.

**God’s goodness** in the restoration of humankind, 930 ff.; in seeking human salvation, 788; in the guardianship of angels, 862 ff. God alone does not wish to be better than himself, because he cannot be, 98. Human desire for the highest good, 591 ff. To know and will the good is perfect religion and religious perfection, 915. A good taste is an incitement to desire and a spur to love, 1027. A poor argument for good is drawn from a multitude, 316. Grace is necessary for willing the good, and it is twofold, 611. All things cooperate for good for the godly, 1086. Good things must be done well, 486. It is unsafe to hinder those doing good, 341. Those seeking a better good should not be hindered, 100. A better good once proposed must not be abandoned, 99. No one is too good, 97. He is not good who does not wish to be better, 98. One cannot descend from a greater good that has been promised to a lesser without apostasy, 540. A good work is vitiated by an evil conscience, 1514. God is the author of all goods, 1301. Good thoughts must be attributed to God, 1386. The glory of good works must be attributed to God, 143, 151, 195, 486, 1303 ff., 1429, 1454, 1560. Our goods, whether of nature or grace, are God’s, 108. It is more useful to hide a good than to display it, 727. Goods must be provided in the sight of God and human beings in three ways, 1149. Abundance of goods in heaven, 1117. Natural, spiritual, and eternal goods, 1115. Pure and intermediate goods, 18, 20. Temporal goods, if loved, are unlawful; if not loved, lawful; but in either case dangerous, 370. All goods of this life are vain in comparison with those to come, 1056. The goods of the world and body are vain and perishable, 111. Love of an apparent good, 36. At times one ought to rejoice more in another’s good than in one’s own, 1437. To be good among the wicked is an outstanding virtue, 1432. The wicked are always mixed among the good, 380. In every matter, the strongest argument for establishing belief in a doubtful question is always that which pleases the good and displeases the wicked, 318. It is a sign of goodness to please the good, not the wicked, 247. The good are exposed to the hatred of the wicked, 291.

**BONUS-AMICUS**, canon of Langres, 163, 166. **Bon-Mont**, abbey of the Cistercian Order, 43. The arms with which Christ embraced us, and with which we embrace him, 890. Braina, town on the Aisne, 251 n. **BRICCIUS**, successor of Saint Martin, 1054. The birthplace of Saint BRIGID: the village of Fochart, 682. Britain, fruitful in brave men, 373. Bruyère-l’Évêque, forest, 375.

**BRUNO**, archbishop-elect of Cologne, reveals in letters to Saint Bernard the deformity of his own life, 26. Archbishop, 16 n., 27, 28, 101 n. He dies in 1136. Buried at Bari in Italy, 25 n. **BRUNO**, abbot of Chiaravalle, 273. **BRUNO**, monk of Clairvaux, 163. Companion of Saint Bernard in Italy, 150. Father of many disciples in Sicily, 150 n. Bernard’s inseparable companion, father of many souls, 197.

The brute spirit does not live except insofar as it is given life, 108. Brute creatures do not merit, 1551. The abbey of Boulancourt, having canons, lay brothers (*conversi*), and women, was, when discipline had failed, handed over to the Cistercian Order, 383 ff. **BURCHARD**, bishop of Meaux, 460, 461. **BURCHARD**, abbot of Balerna, 151. **BURDINUS’s** rashness, 202. Burgundy distinct from France, 308 n. Busay, monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded by Ermengard, 125 n., 227.

[Col. 1220] **C**
The monks of Caen acknowledge Innocent as pope, 156. Cause of blindness: contempt for truth, 36. Its effect, 36. It is the punishment of those who know God but do not love him, 36. Profession of celibacy among ministers of the Church, 493. Of subdeacons, 193 n., 194. The celibate life of religious is heavenly and angelic, 1161. Why CAIN’s offering was rejected, 1349. Caladia, a Cistercian monastery: when built, 63 n. Nearly three hundred monks live there, 63 n. It is given to Guy, abbot of Trois-Fontaines, 64 n. Mist or darkness arising from anger and a softer affection, 424. The cup of demons, 12. Pope CALIXTUS II, 173 n. He commends St. Norbert to Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, 385. The Camaldolese or Camauldolese adhere to Innocent, 136. Origin of the name “chancellors,” 1459. A good chancellor is necessary to the pope, 273. Addressed by the title “Your Excellency,” 292. His authority in the Roman curia, 291. Chancellors, by virtue of their office, may always devote themselves to the gains of piety, 291. *Cancelli*: narrow windows, 1459. Lampstands in churches in the likeness of trees, 539. Brightness, the seat of wisdom, 1351. Various kinds of brightness, 1514. Canons must be observed, 434 ff. To what extent dispensation is lawful. See Dispensation. Regular canons are called brethren by outsiders, 229. The regular canons of Sparnacum were established on the advice of Bernard and his brother Guy, 102 n. Regular canons of Aildicourt, 13. Regular canons of Larzicourt, 51. Regular canons may lawfully transfer to monks, 14. Incorrigible regular canons imprisoned, 106 n. Various scriptural songs, 1268. The Song of Songs, splendid and savory bread, 1267. Dignity and sweetness of the Song of Songs, 1270. Likewise its solidity and efficacy, 1500. It breathes nothing but love, 1543. Its aim, 1269. This book is to be entrusted only to sober minds and ears, 1267, 1475. To expound it belongs to God alone, 1268. For it was composed not by human ingenuity but by the art of the Spirit, 1268. In order to understand it, imaginings must be laid aside, 1448. Why the Songs of Ascents are so called, 1269. Their own songs suit religious, 1269 ff. What ecclesiastical chant ought to be like, 357. It is no slight loss of spiritual grace to be drawn, by the pleasantness of singing, away from the usefulness of the meaning, 357. Cistercian zeal for chant, 693 ff. Chapel of a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, 295. Honor should be shown to the pope’s chaplains, 444. General chapters among the Black Monks, instituted by Innocent II, 97 n., 397 n., 398. The first held at Soissons, 97 n. Matters to be discussed there, 97. General chapter of the Cistercians, 1156 n. Chapter of the Premonstratensians, 252. The roe and stags of the fields signify angels, 1446. Israel’s captivity under Pharaoh, a type of our captivity under the devil, 1252. Capua captured by Roger, 173. For a person to hold his head high and his heart low is shameful, 1109. Cara-Vallis, a Cistercian monastery near Milan, 142 n., 273 n. A harsh prison: the monastery, 211. Incorrigible nuns are to be committed to prison, 106 n. CARDINALS addressed by the title “Your Excellency,” 35 n.; and “Your Holiness,” 35 n., 232. They are Rome’s eyes, 241. They should be chosen from the whole world, and what kind they should be, 439. A petitioner is to be excluded, 439. Proven men ought to be chosen, not men needing to be tested, 439. What sort they ought to be, 440. Named before bishops, 232. Called brethren, 55 n., 187. It is theirs to assist the supreme pontiff with counsel and aid, 233. The property of deceased cardinals belongs to the Church, 201. Cari-Locus, a Cistercian monastery, 190 n., 692. Assembly at Chartres for a holy expedition, 258, 229. Assembly at Chartres to provide assistance to the Eastern Church, 329. The flesh is a tent, 854. Delights of the flesh, corruptions of the spirit, 6. To what extent the flesh is to be loved, 854. Care of the flesh contrary to penance, 367. It is unworthy, after abandoning spiritual studies, to turn to fleshly matters, 1396 ff. Care of the flesh unworthy of a monk, 1379. The flesh ought to serve the spirit, not the spirit the flesh, 1131. The flesh, a domestic enemy greatly to be feared, 942. No enemy is nearer, 758. Our flesh, our Eve, 1027. A snare and an enemy, 822. The soul rebellious against God rightly finds the flesh rebellious, 552. What is troublesome to the flesh ought to be chosen as better and more useful, 782. Mortification of the flesh [Col. 1221] benefits the flesh itself no less than the spirit, 945. It is a kind of martyrdom, 1379. See Mortification. They truly love the flesh who mortify it, 855. Mortification of the flesh must be practiced secretly, freely, and discreetly, 1168 ff. Pleasure of the flesh is evil; affliction, however, is good, 782. Bodily weakness increases the strength of the spirit, and conversely, 1374. Renouncing fleshly delights is difficult at first and sweet afterward, 917 ff. Religious ought not to care for the frailty of the flesh, 370. Those devoted to the flesh rebuked, 854. See Body. Eating meat in Cistercian granges forbidden, 205 n. Who are carnal persons, 934. Carnal souls designated under the name of women, 1405. In a perverse order they seek joy, 1123. Christ has no savor for them, 12. The flesh does not perceive the things of God, 111 ff. Carnal people ridicule the hope of future things, 1231. Carnal and spiritual persons, the two sides of the Church, 842. Spiritual consolations cannot be joined to carnal ones, 12, 369. The carnal person is always in punishment, 857. Those living carnally are dead, 899 ff. Carnal affection like wine, 1291. Carnal love toward Christ described, 1328.

CHARLES, Duke Emmanuel of Savoy, 139 n. The monastery of Tholdanos is made subject to the monks of Carracceta by the infanta Elvira, 283 n. The Carthusians are called Saints, 28, 247. Their holy quiet, 28. Unceasing silence, 28. St. Bernard regards the Carthusians as saints, 217. Peter of Celle sends Carthusians to Denmark, 348 n. The Carthusians oppose the election at Grenoble, 347. No apostate is received by them without satisfaction, 264. Bernard profits from the Carthusians’ letters, 28. He fears disturbing their quiet by his own letters, 28. King Louis the Younger joins the monks of Casa-Dei in fraternity, 54 n. The same monks are entrusted with the reform of the abbey of Faverney, 350 n. Casa-Marii, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, united to the Cistercians, 344 n., 384. Meaning of *casamentum*, 51 n. Cashel, a city in Ireland, 679. Chastity, an angelic virtue, 1362. Chastity without charity, a lamp without oil, 465. Fivefold chastity, 1243. Chastity signified by the fullness of the moon, 1212. Guarding chastity is difficult, 747. It is endangered amid delights, 493. Preaching chastity is the turtle-dove’s voice, 1470. Praise of chastity, 464 ff. The spiritual castle needs a threefold equipment for its defense, 1074. In how many ways the castle of the soul is assaulted, and by what arms it is defended, 1024 ff. Treachery against the spiritual castle must be guarded against, 1074. How, 1075. Who the traitors are, 1075. Mystical explanation of a small fortress, 997. Clairvaux, Christ’s castle, 1075. How the falls of the godly and ungodly differ, 830. Louis the Younger does not permit a pastor to be set over the Church of Châlons, 205. The four feet of the chair of pestilence, and who sits in it, 1199. A false Catholic harms more than a genuine heretic, 1492. Catholic. See Church. CATHOLICUS, disciple of St. Malachy, 688. The case of the bishop-elect of Catania entrusted to the bishop of Limoges, 304. Whether he was of Cahors, 304 n. The tail of the victim signifies perseverance, 164. Cases should be decided promptly, especially those of the poor and widows, 415. See Lawsuits. Caziacum, a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, 262 n. Cedar: darkness, 1353. Cedar, an incorruptible, fragrant, and very tall wood, 1426. Threefold cell: of discipline, nature, and grace, 1214 ff., 1340. Wine-cellar, spice-room, and ointment-room, 1340. Their difference, 1341. Entrance into the wine-cellar, 1435–1436. Small cells outside the monastery, sometimes synagogues of Satan, 253. Cell of Clairmont, 34 n. Mystical meaning of the cellar, 1340. The title “Highness” attributed to kings, 203, 257, 289, 371. Highness has no cause for self-flattery where the greater responsibility lies, 418. See Dignity. CELSUS, bishop of Ireland, 661. Archbishop, 667, 672. As he dies, he sends his pastoral staff to Malachy, his successor, 668. What is the monks’ hundredfold reward, 807 n. The hundredfold promised to poverty, 370.
