The desires of the godly are not always fulfilled, 86. Worldly desires, 1187. Human desires rest upon three things: what is fitting, what is useful, and what is pleasant, 771. The desires of the Fathers for Christ’s Incarnation rebuke our sluggishness, 1270 ff. Holy desires increase when God has been found, 1559. God is sought by desires, not by the steps of the feet, 1559. Those who desire to advance will be saved, 1437. Vehement desire is a great cry in the ears of God, 873. Desire is the voice of the soul calling back the Bridegroom, 1527. And it is a drawing, 1464. Desire leads to perfect charity, 36. Desire for the heavenly homeland accords with the New Law, 1469 ff. The desire of blessed souls to resume the body, 597; see Appetite. A vehement desire cannot be adequately expressed by the tongue alone, 111. The desire of a devout soul for the noon of eternal light, 1389. Our sloth in the business of salvation rebuked, 1198. The cause and effect of despair, 1404. Ignorance of God produces it, 1403, 1404.

Detraction: how great an evil it is, 1119 ff. Its immense harms, 1347. It assaults and destroys charity, 1347. It kills three persons with a single blow, 1119. It is the cup of demons, 12. Various species and modes of detraction, 1347. It is unworthy of religious persons of stricter life to speak ill of others, 527. The tongue of the detractor is crueler than the spear, thorns, and nails of Christ, 1119. Detractors hateful to God, 1347. They persecute Christ, 956. They are foxes destroying the vineyards, 1482. How they are to be caught, 1482. The disposition and habits of detractors noted, 1346 ff. To speak ill of another, or to listen to one who does so, is equally damnable, 426.

The names of GOD once terrible, now delightful, 1309. What it is to know the name of God, 872. How it is said to be sanctified, 825. God is apprehended not by disputation but by holiness, 457. Scripture speaks of God in figures, 1527. What God is, 455. A noble conception of him, 646. One must always think the best of God, 452. He is that than which nothing better can be thought, 451. He is his own being, 450. And the being of all things, 450. How this is so, 1276. The perfections of all things are in God more eminently, not separately, 451, 1024. God is the highest usefulness, the highest glory, and the highest delight, 771. God is he from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things, 450. Neither is he distinct from his essence, nor are his attributes distinct from it, 1548. God is Trinity, 452. How he is three and one, 452. [Col. 1234] One to himself and in himself, 452. Many things in God are one, 451. God is simple, 451. He is simple insofar as he is one, 452. Yet why he receives different names, 1101. He is supremely simple, one, and immutable, 1548. The immutability of God, 1380. God is eternal, 450. God is immeasurable, 451. God’s place is God himself, 1405. God is everywhere; man is nowhere, 1094. He is everywhere, but in different ways, 1082. In creatures, in different ways, 745. He is in the saints not only through substance, but also with them by concord of will, 745. God glorious in the saints, 39. How he is in a human being, and how an angel is in a human being, 450. How God is in a human being, and a human being in God, 1517. Why he is especially said to be in heaven, 829. Nothing can be hidden from God, 485. He alone knows the capacity of each person, 1210. God’s will is done concerning all and through all, but not in all, 951. God loves, and is love itself, 1468. God alone does not will to be better than himself, because he cannot, 98. That he cannot be evil is not a necessity arising from weakness, but a will firm in good and a voluntary steadfastness, 616.

God’s providence in the ordering of things, 860, 1343. In governing temptations, 836. For our preservation, 856. God is as attentive to one as to many, 1507. God’s differing regard brings fear to some and consolation to others, 1460. God’s goodness in the guardianship of angels, 862 ff. His condescension toward the soul, 1445. Toward human beings, 584. How greatly he has loved humankind, 584. His love for humankind is strong and constant, 1018. God’s love precedes ours, 1560. Indeed, it surpasses ours, 1510. God’s love toward human beings against demons, 1319. God’s mercies are many, 786. He is the Father of mercies, 786. His mercy is offered to all, 959. His seven mercies toward the godly, 940 ff. His abundant goodness in procuring human salvation, 788. He preserves us from sins in three ways, 941. He supports the godly when they fall, 830. His goodness is mingled with justice, 573. His indulgence toward sinners in three respects, 942. His long-suffering and kindness toward them, 178, 942, 954, 1004, 1229, 1561. How he recalls a human being from sin, 1245 ff. His condescension in receiving the sinner, 1561. His kindness toward recent converts, 481. God’s love converts souls, 598. He delays punishment for sin in order to commend patience, fulfill election, and confirm charity, 941. His long-suffering increases the guilt of the obstinate, 1110.

God’s protection, 834. Each of the elect possesses God as his own amid temptations, 830. God tests in order to prove, not to reprobate, 1018. God’s correction is a certain testimony of his love, 1100. His indignation proceeds from mercy, 1097. For when he terrifies or strikes, his purpose is to make people willing, not to save them against their will, 617. God’s anger is most grievous when he permits sin to go unpunished, 1415 ff. “If zeal and love have abandoned you,” 1415. Bernard wishes God to be angry with him, 1415. The distinction between God’s anger and wrath, 1508. How bodily members are attributed to God, 1276 ff. Nothing bodily must be imagined in him, 953. He does not need a body for his operations, 1276, 1279. God’s length is eternity, breadth charity, height power, depth wisdom, 457 ff. What God’s right and left are, 1443. His face and his back parts, 1471. God’s head is divinity; his feet are judgments, 953. His voice is his inspiration and the instilling of righteous fear, 1447. God’s voice offers itself to all, 479. God’s hand is breadth and strength, 1282. His two feet are mercy and truth, 1206, 1209; or mercy and judgment, 1281. Their signs in the soul, 1281. Both must be kissed, 1281. God’s throne is the angels, 951. God’s kingdom is everywhere, 1088. How God is said to be especially present in some place, 1082. How he is said to have come into this world: see Christ, Incarnation.

God’s marvelous art in saving human beings, 327. His goodness in restoring humankind, 930 ff. His wisdom in redeeming humankind, 741 ff. God works the salvation of the elect through creatures in three ways, 620, 621. Three things are proper to God in the work of salvation: predestination, creation, and inspiration, 1541. His power appeared in creation, wisdom in the governance of things, and kindness in the Incarnation, 776. How he works repentance in us, 941. The beginning of salvation comes from God, 621. God alone is the solid refuge of our hope, 871 ff. We have from God creation, healing, salvation, and all else, 622. God is the author of every good thing, 1301. The efficient and final cause of good works, 850. Likewise, the author, rewarder, and entire reward of good works, 850. He divided his gifts into merits and rewards, 620. God’s gifts are our merits, 972. Whatever good things ennoble us belong to God, 108. Good thoughts must be ascribed to God, 1386. So too must our conversion, 1542. Therefore glory for good things must be rendered to God alone, 1303 ff., 560. God alone is the first principle, 450. He has no need of matter, 451. With God alone doing and saying are the same thing, 752. His power, wisdom, and kindness in the creation of the world, 934.

What the image [Col. 1235] and likeness of God in humankind are, 614. The Son of God reformed God’s likeness in humanity, and this belonged fittingly to him, 651 ff. Degrees of divine likeness in the first human being, the angels, and ourselves, 614. This likeness perishes in the damned, though the image remains, 974. How great is God’s condescension in being the Father of human beings, 1358. God’s condescension is known only by one who has experienced it, 1503. Who are the children of God, 369. God’s spiritual coming to us, 720. His entrance into the soul: see Soul. How the soul becomes God’s dwelling: see Soul. God’s house is the spiritual human being, 1428. A dwelling worthy of God is one whose reason has not been deceived, whose will has not been perverted, and whose memory has not been defiled, 1073. A temple must be built for God within us, and how, 1072 ff. God must always be contemplated as our inspector, 831. How useful is the thought of his presence, 831. Whence it is to be gathered, 1509. Signs of God’s presence in the soul, 1528. There is absolutely no surer testimony of God’s presence than the desire for fuller grace, 1064. One who loves God is present to God, 523. God is the true life of the soul, 855. A person to whom God is pleasing cannot be displeasing to God, 1349. A human being is satisfied by God alone, 593. Three bonds by which we are bound to God, 1095 ff. How this bond is born, grows, and is preserved in us, 1235. To cleave to God is nothing other than to see God, 1284. Purity is necessary for seeing God, 1380. To see God, the eye of the mind must be cleansed from threefold defilement, 1028. In this life God cannot be seen as he is, 1174, 1380, 1405. How Moses saw God, 882. How blessed and sweet is the vision of God in heaven, 1380; see Vision. The enjoyment of God is threefold in perfect blessedness, 1036. It is presented to the saints differently than to us, 1041. How far it is permissible to investigate God’s majesty, 1479. How he is to be seen in creatures, 1037. Creatures are a ladder to God, though not for the blessed, 445. How necessary is the knowledge of God, 1401. What we can know concerning him, 928. Knowledge of him follows knowledge of oneself, 1401. God is not perfectly known unless he is perfectly loved, 1287. Four differences between those who know God and those who do not, 1202. Philosophers did not know him perfectly, 1286. Why the Gentiles did not perceive God, 1280. A human being ignorant of God is nothing, 36. Religious persons cannot be ignorant of God, 724. God’s secret is disclosed to sons and friends, 162. God often reveals to a little one what he does not grant to a great person filled with many gifts, 344. God’s visitation: see Visitation.

How the three powers of the soul are to be filled by God, 1037. God tastes differently to us according to the diversity of our affections, 1200; and according to different merits, 1334. He has no savor for carnal persons, 12. God demands to be feared as Lord, honored as Father, and loved as Bridegroom, 1558. The affections of the mind toward God, 458. We owe him love and subjection, 111, 1116. How effective is the consideration of God’s love for us, 589, 721. God must be loved not only sweetly but wisely, 1325. He must be loved sweetly, prudently, and strongly, 1327 ff. God must be loved even by an unbeliever, 585. An unbeliever who does not love God is inexcusable, 586. God is the efficient and final cause of loving God, 593. God is not loved without reward, although he is to be loved without regard to reward, 591. The soul that loves God continually asks by what way, with what caution, and toward what dwelling it should walk, 1387. The punishment of those who know God but do not love him is blindness, 36. Honor and love due to God alone do not exclude honor or love for the saints, 863. It profits nothing to speak for God unless God is in the heart, 850; see Love of God. We owe thanksgiving to God in four ways, 866. No one ever renders him what is owed, 1154. He is to be praised in every state, 1092. His good pleasure must be sought and maintained in all things, 44. God’s praise and grateful remembrance must be frequent while his presence is delayed, 1017. The difference among those who confess to God, 598. God must be feared, since we can neither resist nor hide from him, 458. He must be feared all the more as we receive greater gifts from him, 828. How he commends a human being, 1100. He is both the punishment of sinners and the glory of the humble, 455 ff. Both please God: the contrite sinner and the devout just person, 1092.

God anticipates the prayers of the godly, 1289. He grants his own people sufficient temporal provision, 835. He promises great things in this age and the future one, 833. Why he sometimes gives sparingly what a human being desires, 835. He wills that even what he promises should be sought from him, 754. He is accustomed to heal the heart before the body, 1219. To be drawn by God does not injure freedom: see Grace, Drawing. How great a thing it is to seek God, 1094; see Desires, Seeking. We ought to offer ourselves to God, 963. We owe our whole selves to him as our author, 1130. Members consecrated to God cannot, without grave sacrilege, be employed for vanity and curiosity, 847. It is impossible to serve God and the world, 123; likewise God and riches, 539. Nothing can both be contrary to God and cleave to him, 456. Whoever wishes to agree with God must disagree with himself, 1562. God subjects us to himself by his grace; the devil, by our own will, 610. To serve God is not a burden but an honor, [Col. 1236] 364. Nothing in things can fill a creature except God, who is charity and alone greater than it, 1322. It is just that one who refused to be gently ruled by God should be painfully ruled by himself, 30. For the soul to be sent back from God to creatures is a most grievous punishment, 1395 ff. When God departs, all things grow cold, 1528. God’s word is harsh to some, 588; see Harsh, and Word. God’s twofold aid: correction and consolation, 1333. He is accustomed to forestall the wicked with his benefits, 257. To complete his glory, he in some fashion has need of us, 1505. Why he employs the works of creatures in his actions, 1279 ff.—namely, for the sake of our merits, 620. Here he gives us not glory but peace, 1303 ff. Five states of human beings under God, 1101, 1103 ff. Those taught by God ought to teach others, 1387.

Devotion is rejoicing conceived from hope of pardon, 1322. It is compared to wine, and fear to water, 810. It chastens fear, 31. Devotion and knowledge are the soul’s two wings, 949. The grace of devotion must be sought through Mary, 808. Of what the ointment of devotion is made, and to whom it belongs, 1293 ff. Good works must be seasoned with its fervor, 778. The water of devotion without distress, 1058. The devil is tormented by the devotion of monks, especially in Lent, 841. Devotion is lent to novices, not given, 795. The obstacle to devotion: excessive writing, 527. Vanity, curiosity, and pleasure destroy devotion, 1242. What right and left mean in Scripture, 842 ff. What right and left mean in God, 1443.

The DEVIL is prince of the proud, 1319. Author of scandals, 85. Enemy of humankind, 822. Different names of demons arise from their different evil deeds, 865. As a lion, he need not be feared by the godly, 866. The hammer of the heavenly craftsman, 1044. What wings and hands belong to devils, 954. Whether the devil foresaw his own fall in paradise, 574. Obstinacy closed the way of mercy to the devil, 859. The devil’s inability to breathe again toward good does not result from another’s violent oppression, but from his own will obstinately fixed in evil and voluntary obstinacy, 616. In what sense the devil set his seat in the north, 574. His fall should be humanity’s warning, 1453. Why his punishment is eternal, 614 ff. The punishment of demons at the happiness of angels and human beings, 1452; see Devil. They are represented by the mountains of Gilboa, 1452. As incapable of grace, 1452. Likewise by hills abandoned because of pride, 1451. Their faith, 467. Their dwelling in the air, 573, 1452. He conquered the first parents not by force but by artifice, 1128. The devil had power over humankind, 651. That power was just, 651. The devil’s will is always evil; his power is just and limited by God, 1205. The mystery of the Incarnation was hidden from the devil, 888. The devil attacked Christ with three temptations, 837. The analogy between the defeated devil and Pharaoh, 1407. The devil unknowingly and unwillingly serves the salvation of the elect, 954. Though unwilling, the devil benefits humanity, 1278. Why he is so hostile to humanity, 843. He attacks spiritual persons more fiercely, 842. Frustrated in attacking faith, he assaults charity, 220. He persuades people that God’s words are harsh, 1221. The demons’ ways: circling and circumventing, 861; ascent and descent, 861. Their strength is not to be feared, but their cunning is to be guarded against, 1128. God’s protection against them, 841. The devil unknowingly fashions crowns for the humble, 1319. He lies in wait against fasting, 819. He is tormented by the Lenten devotion of monks, 841. The snares by which the devil catches people, 1060. The devil beats us with our own staff, 822. He entices no one except one who consents, 1563. He lies especially in wait against perseverance, 1066. Why he is sometimes permitted to terrify the godly, 841. He deceives many under the appearance of good, 1391. Noon is to be desired in order to expose the devil’s frauds, 1390. We are subjected to the devil by our own will, to God by his grace, 610. The human being’s threefold state under the devil, 1102. To persevere in evil is diabolical, 719.

Deacons are not to be ordained before their twenty-fifth year, 661 n. It is unworthy that they should serve the table of princes, 81 ff. A deacon who has suffered a nocturnal emission ought not minister that day, 686. DIARMITIUS, count in Ireland, 679. *Dictare* used for “to write,” 285 n. DIDO, abbot of Sens, physician, 68 n.

Two mystical days: one of this age, the other of the future age, 761. The true day, which knows no sunset, is eternal truth and true eternity, 875. Three days: one under Adam, another in Christ, a third with Christ, 758. The breathing day, the aspirating day, the inspiring day, the expiring day, the conspiring day, the day cursed by the saints, 1521 ff., 1523. Length of days promised here is eternal life, 875. Difficulty increases a strong person’s courage, 257. *Diffidere*: to depart from promised faith, 205 n. The title “His Dignity” attributed to the pope, 417. Saint Bernard shuns titles of dignity, 73, 74. The title of dignity attributed to dukes, 102. Nature’s prerogative and the power of dominion alike demonstrate human dignity, 585. A person ignorant of his own dignity is like the beasts, [Col. 1237] 585. Dignity is dangerous, 234. It is a cause not so much of exaltation as of fear, 350. A monstrous thing: the highest rank with the lowest mind, 421. Ecclesiastical dignities require persons of many merits, 43. A prelate ought to have measured his strength before receiving dignity, 420. Dignity without knowledge profits nothing, 585. A person seeking ecclesiastical dignities must be excluded, 439. To whom ecclesiastical dignities ought to be given, 265. Sinners are not to be promoted to ecclesiastical dignities unless repentance has first taken place, 26. It is unworthy to place boys over ecclesiastical dignities, 434, 471. How unworthy it is for dignities to be held by unworthy persons, 421 ff. Concern for dignity rather than holiness rebuked, 437. Abuse of the Church’s dignities, 956; see Benefices.

Delay in repentance is dangerous, 117; likewise delay in fulfilling a vow, 116. On the way of life, the sooner one runs, the more easily one runs, 343. God’s love toward us: see Love of God, Charity, God. God’s love precedes ours, 1560. Love toward God is aroused and advanced by three affections, 1220. Four modes of loving, 1223. The cause for loving God is God; the measure is to love without measure, 583 n. God is the efficient and final cause of loving God, 593. What it is to love with the whole heart, 1329; likewise with the whole soul and with the whole strength, 1329. God must be loved even by an unbeliever, 585. The twofold cause for loving God: his merit and our benefit, 584. God is not loved without reward, though he must be loved without regard to reward, 591. “Seek the Beloved with prayers; follow him with deeds; find him by faith,” 1536. The Father is not perfectly known unless perfectly loved, 1287. The love of the spiritual bride is not carnal, 1533. Love is necessary to a pastor, 1147. True love of neighbor, 598. The truth of love is shown in the performance of a work, 180. Whence brotherly love arises, 1421. One does not live who does not love those among whom one lives, 1106. For love of neighbor to be just, God must be its cause, 594. Love of neighbor is exercised in three ways, 1220. To wish to be loved more than is just is less than just, 262. How and why an enemy must be loved, 1440; see Love, Charity.

DINAH’S harmful curiosity, 571. The monastery of Saint DENIS near Paris, ennobled by a vast multitude of holy martyrs, 79. It belongs to the pope, 275. The patrimony of Peter, 275. Its more relaxed condition, 79, 80 n. Its reform by Abbot Suger, 77 n. Its regular observance after the reform, 79 ff. Abbots Suger and Odo: see their respective entries. A proclaimed celebration at Saint Denis, 209 n. The Regular Canons of Saint Denis at Reims, 383. They grant the church of Mores for founding a monastery of the Order of Clairvaux, 383. Diocese used for province, 54. Visitation of a diocese, 676.

Discipline, guardian of holiness, modesty, and integrity, 444. Its necessity, 1340. It must not be neglected in the papal household, 444. A superior owes discipline and guardianship to an inferior, 725. The use of bodily discipline, 71; also among the Cistercians, 392. Disciples: see Apostles. Various ends of learners, 1241. How unworthy it is for divisions to exist among monks, 214 ff.; see Lawsuits. How greatly discord and scandals displease the angels, 1021 ff. Discord makes a place for the devil, just as peace makes one for God, 1075. A discordant person does not reconcile God, 1349. Causes of the disputes between Louis the Younger and Count Theobald, 205, 206 ff., 208. Discretion commended, 900, 1436. It is the ordering of charity, 1346. Mother of virtues and completion of perfection, 795. Without fervor it lies inert; fervor without discretion rushes headlong, 1342. It moderates zeal and clemency, 424. The necessity of discretion, 1436. Its use in mortification of the body, 795. The virtue of obedience should supply its deficiency, 795.

Rules subject to dispensation, 502. To whom authority to dispense belongs, 501. What is permitted to an abbot concerning dispensation from the Rule, 503 ff. A dispensation should be made where necessity presses, 502. Where necessity urges, dispensation is excusable; where usefulness requires it, praiseworthy; otherwise it is not dispensation but cruel dissipation, 433. Remission of a vow without necessity is not dispensation but transgression, 505. God is not apprehended by disputation, but by holiness, 457. Dissension among monks makes repentance void, 298. Nothing is more horrible in a congregation than dissension, 1216. Whoever wishes to agree with God must disagree with himself, 1562. Dissimulation is characteristic of the self-indulgent, 1408. A soul subject to distractions cannot be filled with God’s visitations, 916. Diversity of rites in the Church, 215. Diversity of customs ought not to injure charity, 215 ff. How one should speak of divine matters, 1443. The divine things that the children of this age do not perceive, 111 ff. Negligence [Col. 1238] concerning divine worship noted, 724; see Divine Office.

The monks of Saint Benignus at Dijon, dear to Bernard because of their ancient religious observance, 33 n., 34, 35. He commends them to the supreme pontiff, 34; likewise to Haimeric the chancellor, 34; and to Peter, cardinal priest, 35. A controversy between the monks of Dijon and Luxeuil, 34 n. Christ disregards the rich in his birth, 783. The preference of the rich over the poor rebuked, 437. The rich purchase heaven from the poor, 1222. Riches are a snare, 831. They are unworthy of a human being, 726. How much secular people do for their sake, 1176. It is truly a great abuse that a vile little worm should wish to be rich, when for its sake the Lord of majesty became poor, 903. It is impossible to pursue riches and God, 589. Riches are acquired with labor, possessed with fear, and lost with grief, 484, 1176. The greedy person hungers for them as a beggar; the faithful person despises them as a lord, 1332. Contempt for them commended in a bishop, 41. What the riches of the just are, 291. True riches are virtues, 726. Our riches are Christ’s garments, 767; likewise his blood and cross, 767.

A good teacher is not one who has not been a disciple, 660. Teaching should be by example rather than word, 1469. Forest and solitude teach more than books, 110. The title *master* attributed to teachers, 107 n., 108. The teaching of the Spirit does not sharpen curiosity but kindles charity, 1286. DODO, monk of Trunco-Berengarii, 366 ff. Dogmas: see Judgment. Threefold sorrow for sins, 1167 ff. The force and intensity of sorrow born from love, 1. Human frailty fears pain and shame, 766. What the eye does not see, the heart does not grieve, 1040; see Contrition. It is characteristic of a deceitful person to feign humility when seeking to obtain something, 439. It is a pastor’s task to tame wolves, not to lord it over sheep, 420. Domestic enemies are more dangerous, 305. It is unworthy of a bishop to attend to household affairs, 443. Evils inflicted by members of one’s household are more bitter, 1371. The lust for dominion must especially be avoided by a pontiff, 426. To minister is more glorious than to dominate, 419; see Taming. Dominion forbidden to the apostles, 419.

The house of God is the spiritual human being, 1428. It is formed of angels and human beings, 1072. Its preparation, 999. Its living stones should cleave together by the cement of knowledge and love, 1072. The House of God, a Cistercian monastery, 339. Saint Bernard asks Suger for aid in grain for it, 339. Three gifts of the Holy Spirit: the pledge of salvation, the strength of life, and the light of knowledge, 932. God divided his gifts into merits and rewards, 620. The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit in seven appearances of Christ, 905. God’s gifts are our merits, 972. How all things are given to a human being, 1085. What must be guarded against in God’s gifts, 1320. Fourfold sleep, 1244. Anger compared to a dragon, 866; likewise ambition, 869. DROGO of Clacy, 288 n. DROGO, archbishop-elect of Lyons, 230 n. DROGO, monk of Saint Nicaise at Reims, 45, 46, 47. His eulogy, 47. Abbot of Saint John at Laon, 56 n. Incestuous intercourse of DRAGONIS and Milis, 174.

Doubt and falsehood, the two daughters of ignorance, 1318. How one ought to behave in doubtful matters, 27. In doubtful matters, wise people trust another’s judgment rather than their own, 85. Nothing should rashly be pronounced concerning doubtful matters, 1318. Saint Bernard calls for duels to be suppressed, 337. Duels reproved, 327. Duels must be attributed to madness, not valor, 327. The punishment of a duel is blinding, 51. Solemn fairs for duels, 337 n. Duevania, a city in Ireland, 678. Sweetness is not a virtue without justice, 573. The monastery of Dunes, of the Cistercian Order, 178 n. Swallowed up by the sands of the sea, 301 n. Saint Malachy restored the episcopal see of Down, 672. God’s words seem harsh to many, 588. His word is harsh in the bark, sweet in the marrow, 1221. It is a demon’s imposture to regard God’s words and commands as harsh, 1221. Harsh and undevout religious persons compared to a beast of burden, 881. The harsh and stubborn must be corrected more harshly, 1420. How a pastor ought to show himself toward the harsh, 438. A description of hardness of heart, 409. Hardness of heart arises because a person meditates not on the law of the Lord but on his own will, 818. Degrees leading to hardness of heart, 409.

A duke is called an illustrious prince, 101; a nobleman, 102. The title “Excellency” attributed to dukes, 101; likewise the title “Dignity,” 102. The office of a vigorous duke, 78. One who advances on the spiritual way without a guide is in error, 1540.

[Col. 1239]

## E
Ebalus, bishop of Châlons, 33 n., 61 n. Twelve monks of St Mary’s, York, pass over to the Cistercians, 99 n., 101 n. Ebrard, master of the Knights Templar, 541. The holy intoxication of the apostles after receiving the Holy Spirit, 1435. Drunkenness, the cup of demons, 12. Relics of St Ebrulf at Rebais, 460. Edanus, bishop, 673. Eden is interpreted as “delight,” 1041. The Church, the vineyard of the Lord, 1464, 1490. It was drawn by the fragrance of the incarnate Word, 1335. Christ espouses her to himself, 1252. The marriage of the Church and the repudiation of the Synagogue, 1307. Dowries granted to the Church by Christ, 243. The distinction between Church and Synagogue, 1376. The Church’s charity toward the Synagogue, 1545. The Church’s prayer for the Jews, 330. Her prayers for the spread of evangelical grace, 1306 et seq. Her prerogative: expansion throughout the whole world, 1376. Compared to Joseph’s multicolored tunic, 529. She is one, although one part is on pilgrimage and another reigns, 1449. The unity of the Church compared to the seamless tunic, 307. The source of her blackness, 1353. When she is without spot and wrinkle, 1034. The Church’s two sides: spiritual and carnal persons, 842. The Church’s three orders: married persons, the continent, and prelates, 1156. Her children include the wicked also, and in what sense, 1350. The Church’s judgment is infallible in the use and application of Scripture, 761. God counts the Church’s gains as his own, 1487. Her guardians are the apostles and apostolic men, and also angels, 1539 et seq. The guardianship of angels fortifies churches, 1076, 1478. How dangerous it is to be deprived of the Church’s prayers, 581. Two things console the Church: Christ’s Passion concerning the past; concerning the future, her confidence that she will be received into the stronghold of the saints, 1478 et seq. [Col. 1243] 987 et seq. What sort of sermons are suitable on feast days, 801. On feast days secular persons prepare banquets for themselves; religious persons, the delights of the heart, 1023.
