PAGANUS of Mont-des-Désir, Knight Templar, 541. Palace: humility is rare there, 437. What a palfrey is, 108 n. The pallium: the fullness of archiepiscopal honor, 141, 672. Its use was lacking to the archbishops of Ireland before St. Malachy, 672. How highly he valued its dignity, 687 and following. Whether, before its use, the archbishops of Armagh exercised episcopal and metropolitan authority, 311 n. Cloaked iniquity: the temptation of the perfect, 1392 and following. Cistercian bread made from oats, 6 n., 391. The manifold bread of the soul, 1074. The seven mystical loaves, 939. The three loaves to be served to a friend: truth, charity, and fortitude, 910. The seven loaves with which the Lord mystically fed four thousand men, 1038. The apostles refreshed by five loaves, 883. Christ’s garments are our riches, 667.

Pope: vicar of Christ, 249, 474. Vicar of Peter, 178, 317. Vicar of Peter and Paul, 177 n., 242. Heir of the Apostles, 425. Bishop of the world, 236. A watchman set over all things, 419. He has no equal on earth, 417. To him has been given judgment concerning all matters, 198. His sword is twofold, 438. His keys, 270. The fullness of authority over all the Churches of the world has been given to him, 141. He alone possesses the fullness of authority, 236. One would have to travel throughout the world to discover matters not belonging to his care, 425. Every kind of reverence must be shown him, 141. He can punish every disobedience, 141. An appeal to him from the whole world attests the pope’s primacy, 428. He is the one shepherd not only of the sheep but also of all shepherds, 422. Reverence must be shown him by an archbishop, 474. He can make archbishops out of bishops, and the reverse; he can also establish new bishoprics, 141. He can depose and excommunicate bishops themselves, 422. The deposition of bishops belongs to him alone, 235. From the ends of the earth he can compel any ecclesiastical persons, whenever he sees it expedient, to appear before him, 141. He presides over princes, commands bishops, and disposes kingdoms and empires, 232. Injury done to him touches all Catholics, 240. The pope’s consent for Robert’s transfer to the Cluniacs, 3. Papal authority is not the only authority instituted by God, and it must not despoil the others [Col. 1276], 433 and following. He is not the lord of bishops, but as it were one of them, 444. The supreme pontiff is so called not by completion but by comparison, 421. What the pope’s care ought to be, 434. Especially with respect to heretics, schismatics, and unbelievers, 427 and following. It belongs to him to extinguish heresies at their birth, 184. It is his fault if guilt is not punished, 236. His judgment was sought from the Council of Sens against Peter Abelard’s errors and person, 310. The error of heretics concerning the pope, 1490. The pope’s endowments, 444. What his mind ought to be like, 442. What he ought to be toward the Church, 233. Let him preside in such a way that he benefits, 426. He ought to seek the advantage of his subjects, not his own, 430. How he should conduct himself in judgments, 416. He must avoid partiality, 426. It is unbecoming to act from power rather than reason, 432. What should be thought of a surreptitiously obtained or unjust license, 20. His burden is terrible even to angelic shoulders, 232. He must especially avoid the lust of domination, 426. The administration of the world has been entrusted to him, not ownership of it given, 425. His power concerns crimes, not possessions, 412. What kind of servitude is unworthy of a pontiff, 410. He should avoid the clamor of lawsuits, 409. It does not befit him to occupy himself with trivial matters, 442. He should not be easy toward traffickers, but terrible, 416. The pope should be unyielding against flesh and blood, 269. Not only soundness of life but also the adornment of reputation befits him, 138. He must not neglect the discipline of his household, 444. Let him provide for reputation and conscience, 431. It is not enough for him to be good unless he also has such assistants, 439. What manner of clerics his household retainers ought to be, 435. And his attendants, 438. He needs a good chancellor, 273. Neither antiquity nor reason supports preferring ministers to their fellow presbyters, 442. What kind of shepherds the Church of Rome once had, 436. Eulogies of the pope, 422. Called “Holy Father,” 264. Given the title “Holiness,” 271, 398, 646. “Sublimity,” 399. “Majesty,” 249, 260. “Serenity,” 207 n., 309. “Excellency,” 300. “Condescension,” 417. Pope riding a white horse, 437 n. Wearing a red cape, 232 n., 437 n., 438. The pope’s short life, 235. See *Apostolic See*, *Vicar*.

Proverbs of Solomon: how useful, 267. The Paraclete is Christ, 1062. See *Holy Spirit*. The blessedness of paradise, 1388. Its four spiritual springs, 1234. See *Blessedness*. The fall of the first parents arose from instability and the defect of charity, 1063. The devil defeated them not by force but by craft, 1108, 1128. How love for parents should be ordered, 109. It must yield to love for the Crucified One, 299. Parents are enemies in matters concerning their children’s salvation, 119 and following, 120. Flight from parents is commended, 115. To disregard them for Christ is most dutiful, 109. Their love must not be consulted where flight from the world is at issue, 109. Parents who turn their children away from entering religious life are reproved, 9 and following. Parents do not lose children who become religious, 118. How dangerous disordered parental love is for monks, 1484. Monks must cast off care for them, 809. Jesus must be sought far from one’s homeland and parents, 364. Paris, the noble royal city of Gaul, 430. The Church of Paris deprived of a pastor, 208. Parish used for diocese, 174 n., 252. What the better part is, 1001. Two births in spiritual marriage, 1566. PARVINUS, formerly a monk of St. Vincent of Laon, abbot of Cambrai, 55, 56 n. Twofold littleness: humility and meekness; yet each is no small virtue, 958. Passover: a passing over, 897. Not celebrated at the same time by all, 216. Paschal confession, 898. Likewise Communion, 898. How sweet it is to be fed by the Bridegroom, 1388. What it is to feed among lilies, 1514. The Bridegroom is fed when he is obeyed, 1518. See *Feeding*, *Spiritual Joy*. The Bride’s pastures, 1390. The evil pastures of certain shepherds, especially philosophers and heretics, 1390. A passage granted to Cistercian monks by the duke of Lorraine, 126.

Christ’s Passion merits our love, 114. A great incentive to love, 586, 1145 and following. The consolation of martyrs, 1477. A remedy for those under temptation, 299. How efficacious for Christian hope, 1476. It alone suffices for us, 883. The remembrance of Christ’s Passion is the best defense amid adversity and prosperity, 1418. The power and efficacy of Christ’s Passion, 884. Its fruit, 587. How useful meditation upon it is, 299, 1419. Where Christ sees the grace of his Passion recalled, there he is diligently and willingly present, 587. Bernard’s devotion to Christ’s Passion, 888, 1418 and following. The sign of Christ’s Passion bearing fruit in us, 889. The remission of sins is attributed to it, 972. The causes of our passions arise from disordered humors, 1038. How these are to be ordered, 817, 889. The sufferings of this present time are not commensurate with past guilt that is forgiven, present grace that is bestowed, or future glory that is promised, 494.

What feeding and resting at noon mean, 1387 and following. The feeding of the Bridegroom: our progress, 1515. The sheep’s feeding is threefold, 1537. Shepherds are the Bridegroom’s closest friends, 1537. They are, as it were, guardians and cultivators of the vineyard, 991. They fulfill Martha’s office, 1002. They were instituted for the sake of the imperfect, 1447. Nothing is more precious in the Church than a good shepherd, 247. It belongs to a good shepherd to provide rather for the salvation of the weak than for his own vengeance, 1350. Conditions of a good shepherd, 1342, 1537 and following, 1322 and following. He ought to be unlike the sheep, 463. His office is threefold, 900. His three endowments, 989. Love is above all necessary to a shepherd, 1147, 1537. Likewise vigilance, 1240. Carefulness, 214. Teaching should be by example rather than word, 1223, 1537. Shepherds of the Church ought to feed their sheep by word, example, and prayer, 193. Bernard requires Church shepherds to be learned and holy, 248. “Do the work of an evangelist, and you have fulfilled the work of a shepherd,” 438. What is required from shepherds is care, not cure, 435. For a devout shepherd, his own correction is insufficient if one under him is still in danger, 1415. How a shepherd ought to deal with harsh and refractory persons, 438. Shepherds must tame wolves, not lord it over sheep, 420. Negligent shepherds destroy themselves and their own, 1539. Persecution distinguishes the good from hirelings, 494. A shepherd should order the business of external affairs so as to know how to give precedence to care of souls, 61. How much rapacious shepherds suffer for temporal goods, 495. What delights good shepherds have, 1213. Those worthy must be drawn to pastoral care, 247. With what pastures true shepherds usually feed souls, 1396. The evil pastures of certain shepherds, 1390. It is dangerous to drive the flock apart from the Shepherd, 1387. See *Prelate*. Bernard does not approve abandoning pastoral care through love of quiet, 91. Among the early Cistercians pastoral care was not a great honor but a great burden, 324.

God the Father is not perfectly known except when perfectly loved, 1287. To the Father it does not belong to be sent or to descend from heaven, but to the Son or Holy Spirit, 569. Mercy belongs to him, 1314. From what the presence of the Father and the Word in us may be inferred, 1509. The Father’s affection for the Son, 65. St. Bernard bore the name “Father,” 74. The Fathers before Christ were saved by faith in the Messiah to come, 654. The longings of the ancient Fathers for Christ’s birth, 773. These longings rebuke our sluggishness, 1270 and following. Some deeds of the ancient Fathers are fair in significance, though foul in the deed itself, 807. Heretics who despise the Fathers, 183. Bernard’s reverence for the Fathers, 102. See *Bernard*. The title of fatherhood applied to a bishop, 354. St. Patrick, apostle of the Irish, 1045. His cult, 667. Cemetery, 687.

Patient: who is patient, 491. He needs a threefold providence, 989. One who patiently bears with others is worthy of every praise, 1029. To suffer and to be fed at once: a troublesome delight, 1390. A human being should be like a beast of burden in bearing Christ’s load, 839. Patience is necessary to those living devoutly, 981. It must be embraced amid hardship and adversity, 794. Yet not every patience is to be approved, 409. Christ is both the model of suffering and the reward of the sufferer, 1430. Patience is commended by Christ’s example, 944. See *Christ*. David’s patience under one who curses him considered, 1394. The summit of patience, 1157.

PAUL (St.): monastery at Verdun granted to canons after the monks had been expelled, 175 n. Bernard’s work yielded to Prémontré, 250. PAULINUS (St.), intimate with Saints Martin, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome, and praised in many commendations by them and by St. Gregory, 221. PAUL the Apostle: formerly converted many by preaching, and now converts them also by example, prayer, and teaching, 955. Brief in words but abundant in meaning, 1122. He values not human judgment but God’s, 1154. Heavenly pipe, 374. His mouth, God’s pipe, 1355. A great and unfailing spring, 1291. As many words as thunderclaps, 1123. Simply called “the Teacher,” 1414. Likewise called “Most Wise,” 1421. An aromatic vessel, 1298. Whence Paul’s merits come, 623. Paul’s blackness and beauty, 1351 and following. Paul’s devotion, 1298. The nature of his servitude, 410. His rapture explained, 568. Paul’s humility, 1394. His obedience and renunciation of his own will commended, 957. His meekness, 959. His eulogy, 988. God’s wonderful mercy toward Paul, 993. How the soul is to be lost, by Paul’s example, 1378. How he distinguishes between himself and his soul, 1378. How useful the commemoration of St. Paul’s conversion is, 955.

The poor are blessed, 1025. Yet not every poor person, even voluntarily poor, 1025. Rather, the poor in spirit, 483, 1026. Their dignity, 107. They are kings, 107, 196; indeed, kings of heaven, 727. They are as though unknown and abandoned by God, 1202. The same promise is made to the poor and to martyrs, 1029. The poor are secure at the future judgment, 850. [Col. 1278] The poor—but devout and religious poor—must especially be cherished, 100. Those who have abandoned themselves must not be abandoned, 267. The prayers of the poor are Bernard’s weapons, 258. The poor are supported from their own labor by the monks of Clairvaux, 833. The rich purchase heaven from the poor, 1222. The poor kiss the hands of the rich when they receive something from them, 1276. The value of loving and imitating the poor, 107. The causes of the poor must be cared for before others, 415. The poor complain of the luxury of prelates, 464 and following. Preference for the rich over the poor is censured, 437. Eulogy of poverty, 39. Voluntary poverty, Christ’s fortress, 1183. A safe way, 270. Christ made poverty precious by his birth, 757. Holy poverty, 100. Martyrdom, 1030. Religious poverty is happy and secure, 832. Evangelical poverty possesses both heavenly and earthly things, 1332. It is corrupted by attachment even to the smallest possessions, 1157. A hundredfold is promised to it, 370. Likewise the kingdom of heaven, 1026. This is not so much promised as given, 727. Poverty is free from envy, both its own and others’, 1183. Not poverty but love of poverty is reckoned a virtue, 105. It is more fitting to be content with want than to abound in burdensome plenty, 105. Voluntary poverty cuts away every superfluity, 790. The summit of poverty, 1157. Christ’s poverty, 903. See *Christ’s Poverty*. Love of poverty is commended in a bishop, 41. Poverty of St. Malachy, bishop, 676.

Peace and unity set before us the form of the heavenly city, 1021. The soul in the body is a symbol of peace and concord, 1021. Peace and concord are especially pleasing to angels, 1021. Peace and charity commended, 1372. A person must seek peace with God, with neighbor, and within himself—not glory, 1041. Glory is God’s portion; peace, humanity’s, 134. God speaks peace to three classes of people, 1105 and following. Peace in the world at Christ’s coming, 720. There is no peace when fear prevails, 1444. Perfect peace cannot be possessed here, 758. Full and perfect peace is reserved for the other life, 767. Peace and joy in heaven, 1123. The full peace of the heart is reserved for the future life, 924. Two things are necessary for peace, 1122. The peace owed to one’s neighbor must be nourished by charity and humility, 1124. Peace is manifold, 1233. Peace is fourfold, 1242. False, disordered, and Christian peace, 1122. The pursuit of peace represses quarrels, 1536. Ambition is the enemy of peace, 134. Peace is lost when God’s glory is despised, 134. Where peace is absent, God too is absent, 369. A few things with peace are more useful than many with scandal, 540 n. It belongs to the Apostolic See to procure peace for the Churches, 323.

A sinner becomes one with the devil, 968. He even hates his own flesh, 480. Why God did not immediately destroy a person who sins, 1050. The sinner cannot remain hidden, 485 and following. The sinner’s prison, torturers, and hell, 998. The counsel and end of sinners and righteous persons, 114. The sinner expects nothing, but is held fast and contented by present things, 1502. Sinners do not cease to be children of the Church, 1350. God’s mercy toward sinners, 178, 1004. His long-suffering, 954, 1289. His condescension in receiving the sinner, 1561. God’s indulgence toward sinners in three respects, 942. God delays punishment for sin in order to commend patience, fulfill election, and confirm charity, 941. At his calling let the sinner hear what he should fear; and thus, approaching the Sun of righteousness, let him, enlightened, see what he should love, 112. See *God’s Mercy* and *Mercy*. The example of Peter repenting stirs sinners to repentance, 994. How the sinner’s calling and illumination take place, 113 and following. To cast off the yoke of sin once assumed belongs to divine, not human, power, 941. The sinner’s conversion is a work of divine power, 902. A great miracle, 1070. A precious fruit of the Cross, 117. How great a good the sinner’s conversion is to him, 123. The condition of a sinner already raised up, 1004. Both please God: the contrite sinner and the devout righteous person, 1092. The sinner’s conversion is for God’s glory, the angels’ joy, and human example, 143. See *Conversion*. Bernard refers penitent sinners to bishops, 63. St. Bernard persuades penitent sinners to enter religious life, 63. Sinners must not be promoted to Church dignities without prior repentance, 26. The multitude of sinners does not make crimes unpunishable, 390. For those who are desperate one should not pray but mourn, 579.

Sin: a heavy burden, 870. It is an evil of the soul, 855. Sin must be avoided more than its punishment, 855. Sins are works of darkness, 769. The blackness of sin is inward, 1370. Sins are walls by which we are separated from Christ, 1458. Why the capacity to sin was given to humankind, 612. Adam’s and the devil’s sin against the Son, 1508. The first parents sinned not under compulsion but through deception, 1108. Eve’s sin is threefold: curiosity, pleasure, and vanity, 974. Through sin a human being was despoiled, 974. Sin’s devastation in body and soul, 998. Sins arise from a defect of faith, 1231. Sin is nothing unless voluntary, 71. Voluntarily accepted necessity does not excuse this, 1552. The thought of sin discolors the soul; affection wounds it; consent kills it, 1098. [Col. 1279] Sin’s pleasure is brief, its memory bitter, 479. Its pleasure passes away; its foulness remains, 456. The corruption of nature from sin, 759. A human being cannot avoid sinning, 612. Yet he has not lost free choice, 612. Not to sin is God’s righteousness, 1344. Prayer for sins is necessary even for saints, 1524. Consent, not sensation, makes sin, 1437. Consent to sin must be carefully guarded against, 1459. The gravity of sin derives not from its result but from its intention, 70. For the devout, even sins work together for good, 1086. How sin and punishment work together for our good, 1163. How one born of God does not sin, 811, 1095. Not all sins are equal, 510, 512. Two kinds of sins: shameful acts (*flagitia*) and crimes (*facinora*), 1193. Some sin in hope, others from despair, 1029. What abiding and reigning sin is, 855. The stages of sin explained by a fine comparison, 1149 and following. Original sin is greatest, 886. Original sin is not absent where lust is not absent, 171. Remedies for original sin before Christ, 627. Its remedy was formerly difficult, now easy, 804. For removing original sin in little children before Christ, the faith of parents sufficed, 627. Of those born of women, the Virgin Mary alone was free from actual sin, 170. Why we remain liable to venial sins, 892. Some sins are venial even where God’s commandments are transgressed, 510. Foot-washing removes these, 891 and following. Venial sins must not be neglected; nevertheless excessive anxiety over them must be avoided, 892. Refusing to correct light sins is the unforgivable blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, 957. It is impossible to be saved with venial sins except through Christ, 892. Deliberate sin destroys the soul, 1099. Some sins arise from ignorance, 632 and following. We are free from another’s sin if we do not consent to it and rebuke it, 320. How purity from others’ sins may be obtained, 1233. If the idle are to be punished, how much more sinners, 486. A kind of shame is found even in sinners, 1567. Spiritual sins are not well known to the newly converted, 481. Anger must be directed against sins alone, 866. A human being cannot rise from sin by his own will, 612. The sinner’s redemption through Christ, 998. Christ has vanquished sin and death, humanity’s two enemies, 777. Whether original sin, alien to Christ, was expiated by him, 806. The threefold kind of sin conquered by Christ’s death: original, personal, and particular, 886. In no sins whatever should one despair of God’s mercy, 370 and following. Christ has both the power and will to forgive sins, 553, 555. Forgiveness of sins is attributed to Christ’s Passion, 972. What is necessary for remission of venial and mortal sins, 1111. Hatred of sin, 1178. How a person is recalled from sin, 1245 and following. Nothing resists sin more effectively than shame or sorrow, 1110. The four-day period of the repentant sinner, 1004. Sin does not reign in a contrite mind, 1076. Anxious remembrance of sins should be interspersed with a more joyful remembrance of divine kindness, 1295 and following. How sin’s damages are to be repaired, 1093. The just punishment of sin must not be averted because of evil consequences, 203. Why sin is punished with eternal punishment, 255. The punishment of sinners is the glory of humble people, 455 and following. Sins must be uprooted completely, 998. The entrance for new sins must be blocked before old ones are purged, 481. One’s whole life must be devoted to expiating sins, 1129. Awareness of sin removes or lessens awareness of punishment, 1164. The death of sinners is evil in loss of the world, worse in separation from the flesh, and worst in the twofold torment of worm and fire, 110. How dangerous the defense of sin is, 1415. In how many ways it is usually done, 577. By habitual sin a person falls into the abyss of evils, 579. God’s anger is most severe when he permits sin without punishment, 1415 and following. To persist in sin is diabolical, 719. Those who boast of their sins are noted, 1315. How grave the habit of sin is, 1102. God’s long-suffering accumulates sin for the obstinate person, 110. The higher anyone has advanced, the more grievously, if he falls, is he shattered in falling, 1093. One who loves Jesus cannot endure insults to him, 1422. What spirit a beast has that needs a body, 1277 and following. Even animals serve humankind for the progress of eternity, 1277. Foot-washing removes venial sins, 891 and following. God’s feet: mercy and judgment, 1281. Their signs in the soul: fear and hope, 1281. Both must be kissed, 1281. What Solomon’s skins are, 1361.

Use of furs, 218. Also among monks, 532. Disapproved, 782, 945. Blamed among the Cluniacs, 6. The Cistercians’ tunics contrasted with their furs, 2. Pride clothed in skins is worse than pride clothed in tunics, 532. The dignity of the feast of Pentecost, 928. The commerce of heaven and earth at Pentecost, 933. St. Bernard disapproves pilgrimages by monks, 358. Description of the moral pilgrim, 826. The joy of pilgrims approaching Christ’s tomb, 556. [Col. 1280] How rare perfection is, 1118. In what human perfection consists, 1091. Apostolic perfection: to be content with food and clothing, 984. A certain imperfect perfection, 854. Perfection is to know oneself imperfect, 380. The way of perfection becomes smoother through practice, 343. Its pursuit knows no end, 233. On the path of perfection one must always run, 255 and following. Different ways to perfection, 530. Efforts toward perfection are vain without God, 1563. In the profession of perfection, appearing imperfect is a blemish, 247. The perfections of all things are most eminent in God, 1024. Who is perfect, 1023, 1463. One is not perfect who does not desire to be more perfect, 47, 421. No one is so perfect as not to need forgiveness, 775. It belongs to the perfect to glory in tribulation, 45. What must be done with perfect monks, 87. Union of the perfect with the Bridegroom, 1307. Cloaked iniquity: the temptation of the perfect, 1392 and following. Bernard refreshed by the remembrance of the perfect, 1307 and following. One dying while persistently pursuing perfection is reckoned perfect, 253.

The dangers of the present life, 874. Everything here is full of dangers, 825. Security amid the midst of dangers is dangerous, 7. Exchanges between churches without simony, 356. Persecution is never absent from a Christian—or indeed from Christ himself, 955. Few are willing to suffer persecution, 1029. The blackness of persecution, 1370. Persecution distinguishes hirelings from shepherds, 494. The Church is increased by persecution, 1375. Persecution of the faithful is reckoned Christ’s own, 955. Persecution is the last of temptations, 869. Christ suffers greater persecution from false brethren than from Jews, 955 and following. St. Norbert predicts a general persecution of the Church, 60. Why the Church calls her persecutors children of her mother rather than of her father, 1371.

Perseverance commended, 1173. Its eulogies, 139. It is an image of divine eternity, 1232. An image of eternity, 458. It is necessary for good works, 1429. It alone is crowned, 118. Through its absence many perish, 139. Signified by the tail of the sacrificial victim, 41 n., 164, 893. The devil lies in wait for it, 1066. Exhortation to perseverance, 82. Perseverance is produced by imitation of the saints, the brevity of time, and bodily frailty, 1169 and following. Perseverance in the cross and in repentance, 895. Christ’s perseverance on the cross, 893. Those persevering in prayer become fervent from dry, 1290. To persist in evil is diabolical, 719, 858. The effectiveness of persuasion, 901. The coin of confession: its defect, 901. Obstinacy in one’s own opinion censured, 204 and following. See *Counsel*. The four feet of the chair of pestilence, and who sits in it, 1199. The heart’s petitions are threefold, 824. Why Christ asks from us, 815. The clefts of the rock: Christ’s wounds, 1475.

Eulogy of Saints Peter and Paul, 988. They are two luminaries, teachers, and mediators, 988. St. Peter of Chartres: a monastery of great nobility, 497. St. Peter of Châlons: monastery, 61. St. Peter of the Mount: monastery of Regular Canons of St. Augustine, 77 n. PETER, brother of Alfonso, king of Portugal, serving as a soldier in Gaul and Lorraine: conversion, 289 n. Eulogy of PETER, bishop of Palencia, 334 and following. Reconciliation of PETER of Pisa through St. Bernard, 198. PETER of Roya, novice of Clairvaux: his life in the world, 393 and following. PETRONILLA, abbess of Fontevraud, 191 n. PETRONILLA, sister of Eleanor, queen of the French, 200 n.

PETER the Apostle: superior to the other apostles, 422. Prince of bishops, 670. His love, 1328. Christ’s keys given to him, 1508. His sword is twofold, 257. Swaying through fear, he began to sink, 937. His untimely zeal, 1465. He cut off the servant’s ear in order to make a way for truth, 1367. Peter’s coldness, 1465. His denial considered, 618 and following. He sinned not by hating Christ but by loving himself too much, 618. Why, when looked upon by Christ, he wept, 1460. God’s great mercy toward him, 994. The example of Peter’s repentance encourages sinners, 994. Peter knew neither pomp nor splendor, 437.

PETER, abbot of Celle, 280 n., 712, 714. Praised for a reformed monastery, 280 n. A pupil of Bernard, he defends Bernard’s opinion on the conception of the Blessed Mary, 280 n. He directs Carthusians to Denmark, 347 n. PETER, abbot of the monastery of All Saints, Regular Canons of St. Augustine, 61 n. PETER ABELARD, 180, 181, 304. Description of his character, [Col. 1281A] 185 and following. Also an ugly portrait, 306, 310 and following. Called a forerunner of Antichrist, 308. A dragon, 182, 305, 306. He is silent in Brittany; in France he conceives iniquity, 306. Author of new words and meanings, 302. His books monstrous in title and doctrine, 303. Errors, 305, 306, 307, 308, 311, 650. Concerning the Trinity, 637, 640, 645 and following. Concerning God’s power, 642. Concerning the Father’s omnipotence, 644. Concerning the Incarnation, 637, 641 and following, 653, 654 and following, 656. Concerning the Eucharist, 642. Concerning grace, 637, 641 and following. Concerning original sin, 642. Concerning the sin of delight, 644. Concerning the sin of the Jews who crucified Christ, 643. Concerning the power of binding and loosing, 644. Concerning good and evil works, 643. Concerning faith, 185, 645, 185. His writings, 185. While he sweats to make Plato a Christian, he proves himself a pagan, 650. He prefers his own opinion to all the holy Fathers, 650. His doctrines scattered widely throughout Gaul, 309. His books read in the Roman curia, 302, 305, 306, 308, 311. Disseminated everywhere, 302. William, abbot of St. Thierry, read them with indignation, 302. He was condemned at Soissons before the legate, 186, 306. Bernard privately, then before witnesses, admonished him and his followers to come to their senses, 309. Abelard himself challenged Bernard to a single contest, 183. At the Council [Col. 1281B] of Sens, 309. Yet afterward he refused to answer him, 310. And feared him, 302. Peter Abelard’s errors, while his person was spared, were condemned at the Council of Sens, 310. Appeal to the pope, 310. Articles of his errors, 302. Condemned by the holy Fathers, 185. And sent to the pope, 310. Bernard sends his books to Rome, 306. Abelard himself proceeds to the Roman curia, 307, 308. His doctrines condemned by Innocent, 187. His writings committed to the flames, 640. Especially the book *On the Trinity*, by a legate of the Roman Church, 184. Arnold of Brescia adheres to him, 187. He is said to resemble him, 305. He was fellow-student and opponent of Alberic of Reims, 33 n.

PETER, archbishop of Bourges, 200 n., 203 n., 245 n. PETER, archbishop of Lyons, 162 n. Eulogy of that legate of the Apostolic See, 352. Called a man of pious memory, 168. His presumption in appointing the bishop of Langres, 164, 165. PETER, dean of Troyes, 713. PETER, cardinal-deacon and legate, 35. PETER, bishop of Pavia, 143 n., 157 n. PETER, another bishop of Pavia, 143 n. [Col. 1281C] PETER, bishop of Salamanca, 197 n. His humility, 197, 198 and following. PETER, bishop of Senlis, 199 n. PETER the hermit, prior of Mont-Saint-Quentin near Péronne, 328 n. Preacher of the holy expedition, 328. PETER of Fontaines, cardinal, 35 n. PETER LEONIS, 305, 306. The beast of the Apocalypse, 130. He derived his origin from Judaism, 145 n. He was a Cluniac monk, 135 n. Cardinal and legate, 35 n. His usurpation, 134. He plundered the ornaments of churches, 241. His schism for eight years, 1346. Sudden death, 152 n. Lucanus, bishop, commends PETER Lombard to Bernard, 373 n. St. Bernard commends the same man, enduring necessities of food, to the Canons of St. Victor in Paris, 362. PETER, monk of Clairvaux, 280. PETER, cardinal-priest, 35. PETER of Treva, dean of St. Stephen’s at Besançon, 189 n. Hostile to the abbot of Charlieu, 189.

PETER THE VENERABLE, abbot of Cluny, 71, 329, 714. His eulogy, 262, 270, 329. A great man occupied with great affairs, 152. His continual occupations, 213. He improves the order, 270. His gentleness, 213. Humility, 345. He does not accept magnificent titles, [Col. 1281D] 216. Love of charity and concord, 213 and following. Readiness to forgive, 347. How free he was from covetousness, 347. He yields his right in the monastery of Saint-Bertin, 153 n. Beneficent toward the Cistercian Order, 270. He commends himself to their prayers, 347. The Cistercians commemorate him and his brethren in chapter as father and friend, 348. Friendship between him and Bernard, 152, 214, 212, 345, 346. From youth, 347. He asks St. Bernard for the book *On Precept and Dispensation*, 497. Having relinquished governance, he considers retiring to St. Bernard, 270 n. He eagerly reads and kisses Bernard’s letters, 212. He likewise takes pride in Bernard’s letters among foreign peoples, 152. Peter the Venerable excuses to St. Bernard the delay in his writing, 213 and following. Peter the Venerable was intimate with Guigo and Basil, priors of the Carthusians, 27 n. His journey into Spain, 211. St. Bernard invites him to the assembly at Chartres, 329 and following.

Phantasms must be laid aside in order to understand the Song of Songs, 1448. Comparison of Pharaoh and Herod, 907. Analogy between conquered Pharaoh and the devil, 1407. Pharaoh’s mystical princes: malice, luxury, and avarice, 1407. Likewise others, 1408. Pharaoh’s daughter signifies Egypt, 907. [Col. 1282A] The pride of the Pharisees, 566. Their empty arrogance and exaltation, 982. PHILIP, bishop of Taranto, deposed, afterward prior of Clairvaux, 258 n. Bernard intercedes for him with Eugenius III, 258 and following. PHILIP intruded into the Church of Tours, 134 n. How degenerate from his original disposition, 155. Gilbert’s nephew and heir in ambition, 154 n. St. Bernard declares his election null, three times, 367. PHILIP, son of Louis the Fat, 53 n. PHILIP, monk of Clairvaux, 64. PHILIP, provost of Cologne and the emperor’s chancellor, 713.

Which philosophy is nearer to truth, 1099. The philosophers’ rain is sterile, 1466. And their pastures evil, 1390. They were desirous of glory and praise, 1099. Vain and curious, 934. They refused to abound in earthly wealth in order to abound in their own understanding, 1026. They did not know God perfectly, 1286. Madmen: those who mourn young people embracing the purpose of religious life, 299. Vain pictures must be rejected from cloisters, 539 and following. [Col. 1282B] What piety is, 412. It consists in two things, 1187. Its ointment is compounded from many miseries, 1297. It must be possessed not in books but in conduct, 1308. It is endangered in business affairs, 493. Its fruits are desired even by the impious, 840. Various examples of piety, 1298 and following. For the devout all things work together for good, even sins, 1086. Their desires are not always fulfilled, 86. Spiced wines among monks disapproved, 536. For the slothful, disgust arises not from satiety but from hunger, 343. See *Sloth*. The daily use of fat for seasoning vegetables among the Cluniacs, 531 n. Pisa chosen by Innocent II in place of Rome, 140. The Pisans receive the supreme pontiff in exile, 146. Faithful to Innocent, they resist the threats and gifts of Roger, duke of Apulia, 140. They drive the tyrant Roger from the siege of Naples and capture four heavily fortified cities, 146. Bernard intercedes for them with Emperor Lothair, 145 and following. Council of Pisa, 142 n., 143, 144 n.

Three kinds of mystical fishes, 1061. The scales of fishes signify patience; their fins, cheerfulness, 1061. The first Cistercians abstained from fish, except when travelling, 6 n. God cannot be pleasing to one who is not pleasing to God, 1349. In the evils in which we have pleased, we cannot likewise please in good things, 81. *Placitare* used for “to litigate,” 51. Those who rashly mourn the dead are to be mourned, 1357. Christ’s yoke compared with birds’ feathers, 343. Plurality of benefices censured, 472.

There would be no punishment on earth if iniquity had not preceded it, 1153. Now punishment is drunk drop by drop; in recompense there is a torrent of delight, 1086. God exacts from us the punishments which we voluntarily take upon ourselves for others’ sins, 1154. The just punishment of sin must not be averted on account of evil consequences, 203. Awareness of sin removes or lessens awareness of punishment, 1164. Evil is always accompanied by punishment, 857. The carnal person is always under punishment, 857. In similar deeds guilt and punishment differ, 87.

Repentance is the beginning of returning to God, 929. It is reckoned as innocence, 1151. It is the first degree of mercy, 490. Of penitents—
Tears are the wine of angels, 1376. [Col. 1282D] To have repentance is to grieve; to do penance is the remedy for grief, 480. Although repentance be ever so slight, by it we can nevertheless be reconciled to God, 797. Repentance is not to be shunned, 494. Exhortation to it is harsh for secular persons, 832. But the Judge’s sentence is harsher, 1097. Whoever does not embrace repentance either believes that he does not need it or despairs of divine goodness, 758. Even if humility has nothing for which to repent, it nevertheless has reason to repent, 1423. Detraction from repentance is cruel compassion, 827. It is fruitless after death, 480. It is easier to preserve innocence than to perform fitting repentance, 1129. How this difficulty is to be overcome, 494. Men’s perverse shame concerning repentance, 789. How God works repentance in us, 941. A person is then born when the mind is stirred to love repentance and hate sin, 793. Repentance is threefold: for lost innocence; for innocence lost but not sought again; and for God’s patience neglected, 1166 et seq. Signs of true repentance, 578. A sign of false repentance: not fleeing occasions [of sin], 898. False repentance, and its punishment, 898. Perseverance in repentance, 895. Modesty is necessary for the penitent approaching God, 1274. The blackness of repentance, 1370. The kiss of the feet is fitting for penitents, 1273. One’s whole life is to be devoted to repentance, [Col. 1283] 820. Three things necessary for repentance: time, body, and place, 1227 et seq. The present time of repentance is the vigil of the eternal Sabbath-rest, 1058. The place of repentance is the monastery, 373. A monk performs repentance more rightly there than on pilgrimage, 358. It is dangerous to perform repentance amid the tumults of the world, 794. St Bernard refuses to impose penance for grave sins unless they have been committed against himself, 63. Adults are cleansed only by their own repentance, 1143. Comparison of the penitent with Lazarus, 1003. The penitent soul’s aspiration toward God, 1326. A woman is no longer a sinner when she is penitent, 1076. The repentance of St John the Baptist ought to stir us to repentance, 985.

Polygamy is perhaps a venial fault, but a shameful incontinence, 1470. The turtledove rebukes it, 1470. Concern for pomp and dignity rather than holiness is censured, 437. Peter knew neither pomp nor splendour, 437. Etymology and office of *pontifex* [pontiff], 465 et seq. See Pope; Bishop; Prelate. Pontifical insignia in abbots are disapproved, 476. Pontigny Abbey, Cistercian Order, 46. PONTIUS, abbot of Cluny and of Pontigny, 35 n. PONTIUS, abbot of Vézelay, 337. PONTIUS, archdeacon of Langres, 162 n., 163, 165. PONTIUS, bishop of Belley, 247 n. Who the people of Jesus are, 786. Why swine were forbidden to be offered in sacrifices, 968. Portes Charterhouse, 156 n. One who bears Christ is not burdened but honoured, 840. Other things are to be borne with sufficient equanimity when our own conscience does not accuse us, 320. Where power is joined with malice, one must presume something beyond the merely human, 444. Three kinds of power in the mystery of the Incarnation: what did not exist was created; what had perished was restored; and what was above all things was made a little lower than the angels, 780. Apostolic power is not the only power instituted by God, nor ought it to despoil others, 433 et seq. How great the evils to which the ambition for power and knowledge is liable, 919. Once power has been received, to prefer to use it for evil rather than for good is abuse, 245. POTHO, priest of Prüm, disapproves the feast of the Conception, 169 n. Some precepts of the law are moral, others figurative, 1196. Some are greater and others lesser; and this is determined by the intention of the Lawgiver, the usefulness of the command, and the authority of the one commanding, 506 et seq. To fulfil commandments reluctantly or with murmuring is not the virtue of obedience but a covering for malice, 794. Whoever pretends not to give his hand to a teacher gives it to a seducer, 1540. Candidates for religious life are called the Lord’s prey, 98. What predestination is, 1541. Its ordering, 112 et seq. It is preparation for justification, 114. How the predestined do not sin, 1344. The beginning and end of predestination belong solely to grace; its working must also be ascribed to us, 949. The means of predestination, 841. Its signs, 909. The chief sign: duly hearing the word of God, 811. Likewise, love of God, 113. Predestination is uncertain, 913. The blessed state of the predestined, 1344. Heavenly generation is eternal predestination, 1344.

Preachers are called prophets, 1217. They bear Christ in the womb, 1185. The mission of preachers, 1539. Preaching the word of God belongs to bishops, 312. Foreign preachers, not sent by their own bishop or by the supreme Pontiff, are not to be received, 239. How dangerous the desire to preach is for monks, 1485. A monk ought not undertake this without a mission, 330. Public preaching neither befits a monk, nor is expedient for a novice, nor is permitted to one who has not been sent, 1485. The office of preaching is imposed upon those eager for contemplation, 1413. Preaching must be persistently employed even toward the rebellious, 438. A useful admonition for preachers, 1469. Let the preacher be a shell, not a channel, 1321. The preacher’s threefold cord: right understanding, worthy utterance, and confirmation by life, 1313. Conduct must tend toward higher things, 1025. Purity of mind is necessary to them, 1481. Compassion and rejoicing with others, 1291. It belongs to the preacher liberally to pour out upon others what God has given, 1553. What happened to Bernard when he wished to act otherwise, 1554. Christ’s law is a fiery law, to be preached with fiery tongues, 928. The tongue of preachers is afflicted in accordance with the disposition of their hearers, 811. The preacher must avoid vanity and gain, 1413. The labour of preaching is not slight, 1334. Yet it is vain without God’s grace, 1213. All their progress must be attributed to God, 1213. The reward of preachers, 143. Signs of imperfect preachers, 1321. Who are impure, 1481. Robbers despoil bishops returning from the Council of Pisa, 144 n. No one ought to prefer himself to another, 1404. It is great pride to prefer oneself to an equal, 804. See Humility.

[Col. 1284] Prelates are established not so much for the good as for the wicked and the weak, 75. Their condition and office, 1157. Zeal is necessary to them, 1341. The union of discretion and fervour, 1342. Charity, purity of intention, and holiness of conversion, 1257. How charity should rightly be ordered in them, 1436. They must not flee the care of the sheep, 1290. Prelates who are solicitous scarcely have leisure for themselves, lest they withdraw themselves from their subjects, 1447. A good prelate’s affection for his children, 1291. Let prelates labour to be useful, 331. You wickedly seek to preside over those whom you do not care to be of use to, 1341. The prelate’s role is ministry, not dominion, 418 et seq. It is more glorious for a prelate to serve than to rule, 419. Let prelates regard themselves as mothers, not masters, of their subjects, 1339. A prelate will never lack material for labour, 419. Both lives are necessary for prelates, namely those of Mary and Martha, 1105. Let a prelate be irreproachable, 1158. It is shameful to be inferior in virtue to one’s subjects, 392. By a perverse example, a bad prelate kills his subjects, 15. It is a most beautiful order that the burden which a prelate lays upon others should first be borne by himself, 193. Few preside usefully; fewer still humbly, 1342. Commendation of humility in prelates, 421. It is more necessary to them than to others, 471. Contempt for subjection makes one unworthy of prelation, 474. The luxury of prelates is censured, 1538 et seq. Likewise their avarice, 1292, 1538. What nobility and what estate prelates of the Church should seek, 420. To what extent they may possess riches, 419. Their inheritance is the cross and labours, 420. Ungrateful prelates are admonished, 868. They should attend more to God’s laws than to Justinian’s, 410. As they are in outward conduct, so should they be in hidden thought, 1158. Their harmful shame, 192. Before attaining dignity, they ought to have measured their strength, 420. Many are good as private persons who are bad as prelates, 1341. How harmful it is for prelates to go out from the monastery, 15 et seq. It is dangerous to rule oneself, 92. In what matters prelates must be obeyed, 1171 et seq. Whether their commands are to be examined by subjects, 22. St Bernard’s inquiry concerning the prelation imposed on him, 1376 et seq. Likewise that of the abbot of La Spina, 335.

A reward is proposed to one who does not yet love, owed to one who loves, and rendered to one who perseveres, 591. Where the punishment is greater, the reward is greater, 75. Prémontré monastery, 83, 385 n. Its first inhabitant, Brother Wido, had ceded the place to the Cistercians, 250. Whether the place was granted to the Premonstratensians by the Cistercians or by Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, 249 n. St Bernard ceded the place to the Premonstratensians, 172 n. His love and benefactions toward the Premonstratensians, 250 et seq., 252 n. Eulogy of the Premonstratensians, 321. Their pact with the Cistercians, 250 n. In twenty years the Premonstratensian Order grew to nearly seventy abbeys, 60 n. It grows in Denmark, 348 n. Ten thousand nuns of the Premonstratensian Order, 249 n. Threefold preparation for receiving the Holy Spirit, 1179. A taste of the divine presence according to the varying affections of the soul, 1382. From what the presence of God in us may be inferred, 1509, 1528. Signs of the bridegroom’s presence in us, 1385. To whom it is granted, 1384. The alternation of the bridegroom’s presence and absence, 1384. Bodily presence is not to be greatly valued, 362. Preservation from sin occurs in three ways: by the removal of occasion, by strength given for resistance, and by soundness of affection, 941. Presumption and obstinacy are the path of demons, 858. Effects of presumption, 577. It is the seventh degree of pride, 577. Four steps toward it, 858. Two presumptions in the Church are detestable, 81 et seq. How greatly the companionship of the wicked must be avoided, 23. What the agreement of the wicked is like, 132. God anticipates the prayers of the devout, 1289. The prayers of the poor are Bernard’s weapons, 258. Priests are not to be ordained before their thirtieth year, 661 n. Priests ignorant of letters, 706. An evidence for the primacy of the supreme Pontiff is the appeal to him from the whole world, 428. The primacy of the archbishop of Sens, 471. Firstfruits of the Spirit, 1086. What they are, 620. Namely holiness in conduct, piety in intention, and virtue in struggle, 1077. The office of a prince, 137, 271. Princes are God’s vassals, 98 n. Their glory comes from almsgiving, 195. It is unworthy for deacons to serve at their tables, 81 et seq. A prince’s error harms as many as he himself rules, 137. What evil counsellors contrive among princes, 204. Nothing can be a beginning to itself, 450. Granting the privilege of liberty to an obstinate monk is disapproved, 227. A two-year probation before entering religious life, 4. Reproaches and insults are a remedy for the conscience, 271. The Holy Spirit’s double procession, 928.

[Col. 1285] Processions are rare among the Cistercians, 961 n. Tropological explanation of the procession on the feast of the Purification, 961 et seq. What the conjunction of procession and Passion on Palm Sunday signifies, 878, 879. The procession represents the heavenly [procession], 879. In it Christ receives threefold service, 879. Four orders in it, 881. The prodigality of the luxurious, 1408. Tropological explanation of the parable of the prodigal son, 1101 et seq. Why monastic profession is a second baptism, 520. It does not include a promise never to sin against the Rule, 513. Profession is not made *of* the Rule, but according to the Rule, 504, 518. Profession is made in the abbot’s presence, not at his pleasure: he is its witness, not its dictator, 24. A subject’s profession binds even the superior, 504. Profession makes no mention of the subjection to be rendered to an abbot, 23. For the professed, to halt at the holy Rule without its purity is not a safe step, 101. Memory must be fortified against evil thoughts by recollection of one’s own profession, 1149. A novice’s profession delayed, 301. Accelerated, 217. The same profession permits diverse modes of life, 519.

One must always make progress, 98, 1237. By Christ’s example, 342. Whoever does not advance in Christ’s school is unworthy of his teaching, 342. One of two things is necessary: either to advance or to decline, 98, 1156. To be unwilling to advance is to decline, 255, 342. Not to progress on the way of life is to go backward, 961. There is no middle ground between progress and decline, 255. There is danger that one who does not advance will be overtaken by the darkness of death, 1437. Those who desire to advance will be saved, 1437. Untiring zeal for advancement is reckoned perfection, 255. Our progress consists in never thinking that we have attained, 962. The progress of the elect is distinguished by four degrees, 1224. How progress is to be discerned, 424. Christ loves our advances as his own, 1483. Our advances are fruits of the Holy Spirit, 1483. Our progress is God’s regard, 1459. Our progress is the bridegroom’s nourishment, 1515. Progress from good to better is rare among religious persons, 101. The progress of children is not to be envied but promoted, 293. Those advancing and declining are signified by the angels ascending and descending, 98. The deep, the high, the long, and the broad are to be guarded against, 423. Why divine promises and threats move us so little, 1230. It is not permitted to depart from a promised good, 517. Bernard calls the promise or purpose of entering religious life a vow, 116 n. In the prophets, knowledge of mysteries is unequal, 631. Christ is the meaning of prophecy, 110. One kind of prophecy is to walk in the Spirit and live by faith, 1161. How cautiously near relatives and neighbours are to be governed, 435. A good purpose must be maintained, 368. What it is to be turned away from one’s purpose and overthrown in one’s purpose, 368. A monk who owns property must be compelled to leave either the property itself or the house in which he lives, 349. Excessive prosperity, even spiritual prosperity, is harmful, 880. Prosperity casts down more people than adversity, 1045. Although adversity breaks many, prosperity exalts far more, 880. The alternation of prosperity and adversity is useful, 143. The whole of human life is occupied with it, 882. Prostration at the reading from the Martyrology announcing Christ’s nativity, 773. God’s protection, 834. Compared to a shield, 835. It gives us security against demons, 841. With Christ as protector, nothing need be feared, 841 et seq. God’s providence, 1343. In the ordering of things, 860. For our safeguarding, 856. In moderating temptations, 836.

How we ought to love our neighbour, 1241. True love of neighbour, 598. Its source, 1421. For it to be just, God must be its cause, 594. What we owe our neighbour, 1152 et seq. Namely peace; but justice to God, 1124. Whether a neighbour’s possessions and temporal things may be preferred to God’s things, 1439 et seq. Fear of the Lord must be preferred to compassion for one’s neighbour, 978. We must ask God for that from which something may be given to our neighbour, 594. Private persons must avoid judging their neighbour, but not prelates, 1411. No injury to one’s neighbour is slight, 1372 et seq., 1373. Prudence is the mother of fortitude, 413. Pruliac Abbey, Cistercian Order, 75 n. The usefulness of psalmody, 1188. Whence savour and sweetness are imparted to the Psalms, 1283. Angelic spirits mingle with those who chant psalms, 80. Those refreshed by their devotion, 1284. Sleepy chanters are rebuked, 1283. Imposition of psalms and antiphons upon an undisciplined monk is forbidden, 378. The publican, fearing to raise his eyes to heaven, drew heaven itself down to himself, 1135. Heavenly vision seeks chaste eyes, 1257. Chaste ears are necessary for hearing the song of love, 1475. Shame for offending God, our Father and benefactor, 1314 et seq. Men’s perverse shame concerning repentance, [Col. 1286] 789. Human frailty fears shame and grief, 766. Good and harmful shame, 556. A prelate’s harmful shame, 192. A married boy called king, 207 n. It is unworthy that boys should be promoted to ecclesiastical dignities on account of birth, 471. Good boys are to be preferred to old men, 472. Spiritual combat, 350, 1238. Combat with Christ and for Christ is safe, 7. A cleric may not exhort others to battle, 145. Artificial beauty is condemned, 122. None is comparable to inward beauty, 1360. The soul’s twofold beauty: humility and innocence, 1423. Why the bride’s beauty is compared to a turtledove, 1410. The Rule of St Benedict forbids three or four dishes in a single day, 532. Pultaria Abbey, Order of St Benedict, 84 n. Christ gave us seven purifications, 903. Purgatory, 1070, 1116, 1117, 1177. What torment is there, 1144. Attacked by heretics, 1490, 1498. The rationale and institution of the Purification, 962. Why a turtledove was offered at the Purification, 1470. Mary was not subject to the law of Purification, 962 et seq. What her purification teaches us, 1185. The time of purification is this life, 809. Where purity of heart consists, 465. It is necessary for seeing God, 1380. Preaching requires it, 1481. See Heart; Cleanness. Faintheartedness, the first temptation of novices, 836 et seq. Its two causes: the newness of conversion and lukewarmness in religious life, 1294. Humility does not make persons fainthearted, nor does greatness of soul make them arrogant, 1011. The torment and misery of the fainthearted, 829. The depression of excessive faintheartedness is a kind of despairing engulfment, 424. Its remedies, 836 et seq. The fainthearted are censured, 866. What it is to prune vineyards, 1467. A fitting time for pruning must be observed, 1464. What that time is, 1466.

## Q

**Lent and Quinquagesima** signify the present and future life, 930. Lent, a time of silence, 95. The short days of Lent are to be spent earnestly, 827. The observance of Lent, 303, 381. Greater fervour in Lent, 820. The Lenten fast lasts until evening, 819. Its leaders: Moses, Elijah, Christ, 819. In the Lenten season the whole Church fights together against the devil, 827. By the Lenten devotion of monks the demon is tormented, 841.

**Complaints** by monks about the labours of the present life are unjust, 1130.

**Seeking God:** how greatly it matters, 1094. A great good, 1559. How God is to be sought, 446, 1162. Both fear of death and the dignity of reason ought to stir us to seek God, 364. He is more worthily sought by prayer than by disputation, and more easily found, 458. He is sought not by steps of the feet but by desires, 1559. We approach God not by places but by illuminations, 1480. Who are to be reckoned seekers of God, 1094. No one seeks who has not first found, 593. Those seeking God already possess Him, 1160 ff. The soul seeks God only after having first been sought by Him, 1560. God is never sought in vain, nor is He sought when He cannot be found, 455. He is sought in vain for three reasons, 1531. One seeking God must beware of ingratitude, 1559. He withdraws Himself so that He may be sought more eagerly and held more firmly, 1527, 1530. Seven reasons for which the soul seeks the Word, 1561.

**Seeking one’s own interests** is a poison to the Church, 427.

**Rest:** none exists in this life, 1031. The work of charity is true rest, 97. Bernard disapproves of laying aside pastoral care from love of quiet, 91.

**Quintiniacum**, a village, 62 n.

## R

**Radulfus, abbot of Latiniacum**, 226 n. His eulogy, 226. St Bernard undertakes his defence, 226 ff.

**Radulfus, abbot of Valcellis**, 180.

**Radulfus, abbot of St Urban**, formerly a Cluniac monk, 61.

**Radulfus, count of Vermandois**, 205, 338. His divorce, 199 n., 200. Excommunicated on that account, 186, 201, 203, 209.

**Radulfus, monk of Fontaines**, returns to a more lax life, 293 n.

**Radulfus, a certain monk, or hermit**, censured, 330 ff. St Bernard reproves three things in him, 350.

**Radulfus of Parrona**, tutor of Louis the Younger, 165 n., 166 n.

**Radulfus, patriarch of Antioch**, 350.

**Radulfus, patriarch of Jerusalem**, omitted by Papebroch, 171 n.

**Radulfus Viridis**, archbishop of Rheims, 46.

**Raimundus, count of Barcelona**, 237 n.

**Raimundus, bishop of Cahors**, 304 n.

**Raimundus, bishop of Nevers**, 268 n.

[Col. 1287] **Raimundus**, opponent of Odo, abbot of St Denis, wrongly censured by Bernard, 275, 276.

**Death of Rainaldus, abbot of Cîteaux**, 265 n.

**Rainaldus, abbot of Foigny**, 73, 74 n., 75. His eulogy, 74. His humility and charity, 364.

**Rainaldus, abbot of Morimond**, leaves his monastery and seeks Jerusalem, 324.

**Rainaldus, archbishop of Rheims**, 167. His letters to Bernard, 292. His death, 292 n.

**Rainaldus of Martigné**, formerly bishop of Angers and then archbishop of Rheims, 37 n., 191 n.

**Rainaldus, archdeacon of Auxerre**, 377.

**Rainaldus of Morin**, monk of Clairvaux, 396.

**Ramnulfus, abbot of the Dorat**, intruded into the see of Limoges, 132 n.

**Resentment** dishonours God, 940. Its harms, 1373.

**Reason** is the handmaid of the will, 604. It does not impose necessity upon the will, 604. Reason should humble the body; the body should strengthen reason, 418. The threefold fall of reason, 1180.

Bishops who prefer calculations of temporal things to reasons of spiritual things are censured, 443 n.

**The monastery of Rieti**, 400. A double monastery of the Cistercian order, 192 n.

**Rebellion** is the tenth degree of pride, 578. Rebellion is a cause of apostasy, 578. One must not cease preaching even to rebels, 438.

**Rebellis**, a city conquered by the Pisans, 146.

**Reconciliation** with God is easy now, difficult later, 797. The many ways in which reconciliation takes place, 1029. We must be reconciled with human beings, angels, and God, 1241.

It is unlawful for recluses to leave their cell. See **Anchorite**.

**Human uprightness:** wherein it consists, 1347, 1348. Who is upright, 1348. Why God created man upright in body, 1348.

**The benefit of redemption** considered, 867, 1128 ff. It comes not only from mercy but also from justice, 652. Christ’s power and wisdom are hidden in the work of redemption, 1190. Christ is to be loved more for the work of redemption than for that of creation, 1326. How arduous redemption was, 889. Why Christ redeemed us with such labour, 1296 ff. The work of redemption is especially to be meditated upon: above all, its manner and its fruit, 1295. One ungrateful for the benefit of redemption does not sleep, but is dead, 867. The price of human redemption bestowed upon Mary, 1014. The effect of human redemption: our reconciliation, 655. Christ became redemption even for angels, and in what manner, 1336. Why man, rather than an angel, was redeemed, 719. Man was redeemed on the same day on which he was created, 895.
