The harmony of the Scriptures in prefiguring Christ’s mysteries, 740. Scripture speaks of God in figures, 1527. The obscurities of Scripture are more pleasing, 1502. Nothing in it is idle, 1521. It must be interpreted not for the benefit of the flesh but of the spirit, 1482. The Church’s judgment is infallible in the use and application of Scripture, 761. To misuse it is diabolical, 828. The error of heretics concerning the Scriptures, 1491. To be ignorant of Scripture’s purer teaching on morals is almost heretical, 293. The threefold sense of Scripture, 1214. Whether and how several senses of the same Scripture are to be admitted, 1442. How it is lawful to scrutinize God’s majesty, 1479. Scrutiny of the will is safer than scrutiny of majesty, 1480 ff.

Jests are to be avoided, 1070. A jesting word must be banished not only from the mouth but also from the ear, 425. God’s protection is compared to a shield, 835. Withdrawal is necessary for one who prays, 922. God’s secret is disclosed to sons and friends, 112. There is no security here, 762, 1147. Security is ruinous, 7, 1065. Never be secure concerning present grace, 1331. To sit upon the seat is characteristic of one who presides, rules, and reigns, 951.

The Apostolic See is exalted by divine and royal privileges, 211. Its supreme authority and plenary power, 190. It possesses fullness of power over all the churches of the world, 141. It alone has the prerogative of revoking surreptitiously obtained decrees, 176. It is a refuge for the oppressed, 57; not for criminals, 158. Nothing better becomes it than to assist the oppressed, 190. It is its office to procure peace for the churches, 323. Contempt for bishops derogates from its authority, 174. Feasts are not to be instituted without consulting it, 171. Bernard submits to it his opinion concerning the conception of the Blessed Virgin, 172. See Pope.

He gives his hand to a deceiver who pretends that he gives none to a teacher, 1540. Christ, a pious deceiver, 897. We are the seed of the apostles, 995. What we ought to sow, 970. Mystical sowers, 970 ff. What semicinctia are, 714. The first Cistercians used them, 714. How unknown are the bridegroom’s paths, 1526. Senoina Church, a priory in the diocese of Sens, 52 n., 53. Primacy of the archbishops of Sens, 471. The Church of Sens is noble, 193. The metropolitan see of Sens is designated under the name of France, 308 n. Council of Sens, 460.

Sayings of sensual persons concerning foods, 1379. Sensual monks are more miserable than all other human beings, 343. Sense is a living movement vigorous within the body, 604. The fivefold sense is suited to fivefold love, 1106 ff. See Love. Order of dignity among the bodily senses, 1107. A fast must be imposed on each sense, 820. Deceptive sense is not faith, 1368. The historical sense is designated by the garden, the moral [Col. 1294] by the chamber, 1340. The spiritual sense is superior to the bark of the letter, 1523.

A judgment pronounced untimely must be revoked, 353. Love of one’s own opinion must be avoided, 216. Separation from friends is harsher than death, 1355. Abbey of Sept-Fontaines, Premonstratensian Order, 250. The sevenfold Spirit in Christ, 977. Septuagesima consists of the number ten and seven, because of the Ten Commandments and their seven impediments, 812. Burial rites, 1354.

Nothing is to be feared by one following Christ, 110. How Christ acts toward those following him, 1382. Christ is apprehended not by reading but by following him, 110.

*Seraphim* means “burning” or “kindling,” 947, 1324. The two seraphim seen by Isaiah signify the angelic and human creation, 947. Meaning of the multiplicity of their wings, 949, 952; likewise, of their covering of head and feet, 949. *Seraphim* is singular and *seraphin* plural, 946 n.

The title “Serenity” is assigned to the pope, 164, 207 n., 309; to a bishop, 207 n.; to an abbot, 346; and to a king, 207 n.

SERLO, abbot, joins Savigny Abbey with thirty other monasteries to the Cistercians, 136 n. SERLO, canon of York, 389. The Word of God is living bread, the food of the mind, 729. It ought to work two things, 1237. It is to be preserved not in memory alone, but in conduct, 729. It is hard in the bark and sweet in the marrow, 1221. The living and effective word is example, 193, 902, 969. Its threefold use, 1334. Threefold usefulness of sermons concerning the glory of saints, 1030. Good and useful discourse is threefold, 1017. How harmful it is to listen to idle speech, 1120. In what esteem St. Bernard’s sermons were held among the learned, 705. On what days they were preached, 705; at what hours, 706, 1163. Whether they were delivered in French or Latin, 706 ff. Their evaluation, 710 ff. Why they are sometimes brief and sometimes lengthy, 845. Sermons suitable for feast days, 801. Before the solemnities of Mass among the Cistercians, 1021, 1033. Sermon on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, 765. Sermons before outsiders at Clairvaux, 1049. Speech or conversation was rarer among the Cistercians, 1483. Blooming vines drive away serpents, 1473.

To serve God is not a burden but an honor, 364. God’s service is sweeter than every servitude, 1139. It is sweet to the willing, 850. It is impossible to serve God and the world, 123. What Paul’s servitude was, 410. What servitude is unworthy of a pope, 410. No slavery is baser or heavier than that of the Jews, 410. The condition of slaves described, 599. Who is the faithful servant, 1034. What is the law of servants and hired laborers, 30. Difference between servants, hired laborers, and sons, 1094 ff. How wrongs done to servants are to be avenged, 84. Among the Romans slaves precede their master, 442 n.

What Christ’s sitting at the Father’s right hand means, 1535. It belongs to Christ alone, 1536. Severity should be paternal, not tyrannical, 1339. Both sexes cooperate in our restoration, 1006.

SIEBAUD, abbot of St. Leo, 381. The seven seals of Christ, 896. Nature of the seal of abbots of the Cistercian Order, 275 n.; of the church of Auxerre, 269 n.; of St. Bernard, 359. His name and image impressed upon it, 207 n., 275 n. Holding a book in his right hand, with his feet to the left [reading uncertain], 275 n. Image of Peter, archbishop of Lyons, impressed on a wax seal, 162 n. What a sign is, 890. How the signs of believers described in the Gospel apply to individual faithful persons, 911 ff. At judgment signs will not be sought, but merits, 911.

SIGUIN of Tornella, knight, 377. Praise of silence, 96. It is the strength of the soul, 343; guardian of religious life, 343 n., 810. Continual silence compels meditation on heavenly things, 79. It must be interrupted for the sake of charity, 1439. Mary, diligent cultivator of silence, 1010. Silence is threefold, good, and praiseworthy: silence from boasting, from blasphemy, and from murmuring and detraction, 1017. Silence among the Cistercians, 1373. It was not continuous, 220. Continual silence in the monastery of St. Denis, 79. Wood and solitude teach more than books, 110.

Feast of SIMEON, 103. Simeon dies with secure joy and joyful security, 104. Degrees of the divine likeness in the first human, the angels, and ourselves, 614. Angels hold the highest degree, we the lowest; Adam the middle; demons none, 614. The Son of God restored God’s likeness in humankind, 615. This was fitting to him, 616.

SIMON, abbot of St. Bertin, 153 n. SIMON, abbot of Caziac, 247 n. A religious man and friend of St. Bernard, [Col. 1295] 261. His desire to transfer to Clairvaux, 281 n. Fulfilled after Bernard’s death, 281 n. SIMON, abbot of St. Nicholas in Silva-Vedogii, monk of St. Nicasius at Rheims, 85 n., 86. Friend of St. Bernard, 361. He suffers persecution from his own people, 86 n. He departs and is recalled by them, 86 n. SIMON, duke of Lorraine, beneficent toward Bernard, 128. SIMON, bishop of Noyon, 118 n.; and of Tournai, 90 n., 199 n., 368. SIMON of Oisy, 179 n. SIMON, son of the Castellan of Cambrai, 180.

Simony: an evil old in time, ever new to greed, 462. Exchanges between churches without simony, 356. No virtue is more necessary at the beginning of conversion than humble simplicity, 803. Feigned holiness is a double iniquity, 528. Marks of feigned confession, 578. Singularity is censured, 961; likewise monks who love singularity, 1325, 1391. Singularity is the fifth degree of pride, 576. It is hateful to Christ, 1018. Its marks and indications, 576. It must be avoided, 939. The singularity of reprobate angels, 909. Sobriety is twofold, 1187. Crimes of the Sodomites, 493.

The sun signifies charity, 1212. The darkening of the sun variously expounded, 1370 ff. Conditions of good solitaries, 990. Solitude is commended, especially solitude of mind, 1410. In what this consists, 1411. Dangers of solitude, 794. God’s throne: angels, 951. Sleepers are censured, 1401. Those asleep are reproved at vigils, 1283. Nature of the bride’s sleep, 1445 ff. SOPHIA, noble virgin, 120. Sleep is twofold: that of the first Adam and of the second, 813. Christ’s arose from charity; Adam’s was an ecstatic rapture, 813. Vanity of spectacles, 484. Theatrical spectacles incite lust, 93.

What true hope is, 890. How certain it is, 838. Hope outweighs all earthly things, 1403. Its goods are inconceivable, 854. It makes us capable of mercy, 979. It makes a human being omnipotent, 1563. Hope in God is the treasure of the pious person, 852; the harvest of life, 1402. In it the soul rests, 1444. Hope is born from the knowledge of God and oneself, 1403. Its material is fear of the Lord, 872. Its three elements, 943. Hope of pardon, grace, and glory, 1181. We hope not only in God, but for God himself, 853. One must hope in him for whom nothing is impossible, nothing difficult, and whose will to do good does not fail, 852. God alone is the firm support of our hope, 87 ff. Our hope from Christ’s Ascension, 918. Hope and faith have a close kinship, 853 ff. Carnal persons mock the hope of future goods, 1231. Temptation against hope is the gravest of all, 868. False hope, 979 ff. It is a foolish and ruinous dwelling-place to hope in one’s own merits, 829.

La Espina Abbey, Cistercian Order, in Spain, 335 n., 385 n. It is granted to St. Bernard by Queen Sancia, 334 n., 335 n. Bernard sends Nivard there as abbot, 284 n. What thorns are, 1432. Who are spiritual persons, 934. How they are known, 1071. Their four orders, 881. The devil attacks them more fiercely, 842. Spiritual and carnal persons are the two sides of the Church, 842. The sum of spiritual life, 992. Whoever advances in it without a guide goes astray, 1540. Its delights, 488 ff. Spiritual and carnal delights cannot coexist in one person, 12, 369. Understanding spiritual things is the true food of the soul, 978. Opportunities for spiritual gain are not to be neglected, 291. It is unworthy, having abandoned spiritual studies, to turn to carnal ones, 1396 ff. Temporal matters cannot be handled without detriment to spiritual things, 443. Spiritual things can scarcely be possessed without bodily things, 533. Spiritual things are to be preferred to bodily observances, 532. Spiritual prosperity can be harmful, 880.

The dove, symbol of the Holy Spirit, 1424. The Holy Spirit is the kiss of Father and Son, 1285, 1286. The Holy Spirit’s procession is twofold, 928. His coming upon Mary, 750. Without the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, Christ’s death is useless, 114. Why the apostles could not receive him while Christ was present, 915, 926. The apostles, fixed upon Christ’s bodily presence, were incapable of the Holy Spirit, 369. The apostles received the Holy Spirit in different ways, 927. The Holy Spirit’s manifestation to the disciples was twofold, 928. Why he appeared in fire, 932. Change in the apostles after receiving the Holy Spirit, 928. Effects of the Holy Spirit in us, 929. Signs of his indwelling in us, 935. His fruit, 1128—namely, our progress, 1483. His works, 933. Some he performs for us, others for our neighbors, 1208. Three things he accomplishes in us [Col. 1296] for turning away from evil: repentance, supplication, and forgiveness, 929 ff. Likewise three for doing good: he admonishes memory, teaches reason, and moves the will, 929 ff. He enlightens and kindles, 1286. His three gifts: the pledge of salvation, strength of life, and light of knowledge, 932. How he convicts the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment, 1239. He is said to groan because he makes people groan, 1470. He is given to few for fervor, 935. The house of the Holy Spirit, the kiss of the Church, 1285. Grace is twofold, 1320. His seven gifts, 1243. Applied to Christ’s seven appearances, 905, 1242. In the gifts of the Holy Spirit, a twofold danger must be avoided, 1208. The sevenfold Spirit against the seven vices of sin, 1111. The Holy Spirit is given to people in many ways, 935. The Holy Spirit is a guide necessary to us, 1320. Therefore he withdraws, that he may be sought more eagerly, 1317. His coming and going, 1174. It is not unknown without danger to salvation, 1317. Preparation for the Holy Spirit: namely, persevering prayer, 927. What the firstfruits of the Spirit are, 620. How great an evil it is to quench the Spirit, 124. Diverse kinds of spirits, 1131. Four kinds of spirits, 1277. Elijah’s spirit is twofold, 916, 927. Spirit is threefold, 934. Who the Holy Spirit is, 934. The upright Spirit, 935. The principal Spirit, 935. The spirit of flesh counsels soft things, the spirit of the world vain things, and the malignant spirit bitter things, 1131 ff., 1133. Our own spirit sometimes suggests temptations of itself, 1132. How the Spirit of God is recognized, 1132. The flesh ought to serve the spirit, not the spirit the flesh, 1131. Our spirit is no more present where it animates than where it loves, 523. What spirits of beast, human, and angel require a body, 1277 ff.

Fervor is to be preferred to splendor, 983. Threefold splendor in St. John the Baptist, 984. Vain splendor of virtues must be avoided, 1229. What the bride is mystically, 1527, 1566: the soul loving God, 1082 ff., 1282. The bride is one body composed of angels and human beings, 1362. It becomes the Lord’s bride to be beautiful, learned, and chaste, 1387. Her spiritual beauty is the adornment of virtues, and it is eternal, 1361. Likewise, it lies in good works, morals, and orders, 1537. The bride is partly fair and black, humble and exalted, 1365. Why she is black and fair, 1350. Why her beauty is compared to a turtledove, 1410. Her head is intention, 589. Her breasts are better than wine, 1291. These are congratulation and compassion, 1239, 1291, 1418. The bride’s love is chaste, holy, and ardent, 1283. Spiritual, not carnal, love, 1533. Her eagerness in seeking the bridegroom, 1530. Her devotion and diligence in observing his coming, 1459. The bride recognizes the bridegroom beneath bodily weakness, 1369. How great is her confidence before him, 1505. Her familiarity with angels, 1284. The two lots of Christ’s bride, 589. The bride’s gifts from the bridegroom, 1406. The bride’s varied manner of speaking about the bridegroom, 1435. Nature of the bride’s sleep, 1445 ff. Her pastures, 1390. From the day of betrothal until the time of marriage, brides among the Jews were entrusted to their bridegrooms for protection, 740.

Who bridegroom and bride are mystically, 1504. The names bridegroom and bride most fittingly express the affections of the Word and the soul, 1282. Some names of the bridegroom denote majesty, others mercy, 1309. Why the bridegroom is like a roe and a young hart, 1455; why like an apple tree, 1432. What the bridegroom’s lilies are, 1511 ff. The bridegroom’s four ointments, 1338. His various chambers, 1342. What his bed is, 1532. What is signified by seeking the bridegroom fruitlessly in bed, 1533. To whom the bridegroom’s presence is granted, 1384. His judgments in us, 1385. Those unfit for the bridegroom’s embraces should seek him as physician, 1384. To be betrothed to the Lord of angels is above humanity, 1410. To whom the bridegroom’s consolation is granted, 1384. How sweet it is to be fed by the bridegroom, 1388. The bridegroom is fed when he is obeyed, 1518. Mutual intention of bridegroom and bride, 1505. The bridegroom’s left hand is merits, his right hand rewards, 565. The bridegroom’s breasts are long-suffering and kindness, 1289. Whence the bridegroom won so great a love for himself, 1511. What the bridegroom’s leaps are, 1449. The bridegroom leaps among good angels, not evil ones, 1452. How unknown the bridegroom’s paths are, 1526.

Nature of the obligation of stability, 518. The mission of superiors does not conflict with the vow of stability, but diversity of observances does, 24. Without conversion of morals, it is useless to a monk, 70. Christ’s stable condemns the world’s vanity, 782. The respective station of Christ, angel, and human being, 952. The station of the seraphim signifies immutability, 948. Four states of human beings, 1125. Five states of human beings under God, 1101, 1103 ff. Threefold state of humanity under the devil, 1102. Four states of a human being before conversion, 1101. The state of unfallen nature, 1089; of corrupted nature, 1089; of glory after the resurrection, 1089. Virtues are compared to stars, 1363.

STEPHEN, saint and martyr among human beings, 787. STEPHEN, abbot of Cîteaux, 14 n., 53, 57. He corrects the Bible, 692. STEPHEN, abbot of St. John of Chartres and patriarch of Jerusalem, 48 n., 85 n., 171 n. [Col. 1297] STEPHEN, abbot of Reigny, 377. STEPHEN, bishop of Autun, 62 n. STEPHEN, bishop of Metz, 173 n., 331. In what year he was elected and died, 43 n. He restores peace to the Church, 44. STEPHEN, bishop of Paris, 159, 160, 460, 477. Harassed by the king of the Franks, 53 ff., 54. His controversy with Stephen of Garlande, 377. His death, 208 n. STEPHEN, bishop of Palestrina and cardinal, 202, 207 n., 208, 225, 228 n., 305. STEPHEN of Garlande, seneschal of King Louis VI, 53 n. Converted to Christ by Bernard, 81 n. Controversy between him and Stephen, bishop of Paris, 383. STEPHEN of St. Germanus, canon of Auxerre, 377. STEPHEN, deacon of Auxerre, 269. Author of Bishop Hugh’s irreligious testament, 269. STEPHEN of Mercœur, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, 190 n. STEPHEN, king of the English, 229 n. STEPHEN, son of Roric, 210 n. Monastery of St. Stephen at Caen, 136 n. Monastery of St. Stephen at Dijon, 62. When it was inhabited by regular canons, 62 n. Its church consecrated by Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, 166 n. Controversy between the canons of St. Stephen and the monks of St. Seine brought to rest, 62 n.

Sterility alone suffices for condemnation, 109. St. Bernard laments in himself the sterility of the soul, 1377. Various ends of students, 1400. What spiritual studies are, 1442. Study of letters ought not to delay the intention of religious life, 36. St. Bernard approves literary studies, 1399, 1402. Bernard’s studies were made possible through his brother Gerard, 1354. Gerard was their encourager, helper, and examiner, 1355. Christ’s sweetness draws all people, 1024. The first five abbots of the Cistercian Order confer the subdiaconate, 478 n. Celibacy of subdeacons, 193 n., 194.

Prelates ought to seek the advantage of their subjects, not their own, 430. Usefulness of subjection, 902. St. Bernard preaches it, 92. Contempt for subjection makes one unworthy of prelacy, 474. Subjection is commended even in an archbishop, 474. No mention of subjection owed to an abbot occurs in profession, 23. Subjection of our will is the summit of humility, 1138. Subjection is threefold, 1138. See Humility. The title “Sublimity” is assigned to the supreme pontiff, 399; to an archbishop, 325, 348; to an emperor, 374; to a king, 256, 373; and to Suger, abbot and regent, 338. The subprior among the Cluniacs, 212. Things obtained by fraud are to be annulled, 263, 264. The removal of a thing one loves increases desire; and what one desires more ardently, one lacks more painfully, 1441. God withdraws himself in order to be sought more eagerly and held more firmly, 1327, 1530. What it is to be subverted in one’s purpose and turned away from it, 367. Christ’s sweat in the garden, 883. Council of Soissons against Abelard, 640. In the election of the bishop of Soissons, the clergy do not agree, 273. Cases of suffragans must be decided by the metropolitan, 175.

The suffrages of saints are to be implored and hoped for on four grounds, 1042 ff. Suffrages for the dead, 689. Whoever does not comply with the counsel of good people is unworthy of their suffrages, 366. St. Bernard makes the emperor a participant in the suffrages of his house at Comines, 374.

SUGER, abbot of St. Denis, 205, 339, 538 n. Friend of Bernard, 209, 262. His ordination, 78 n. His excesses before conversion, 78, 79. His conversion, 77, 78. Eulogy of him, 262, 289 ff., 340. The title “Greatness” given to him, 332; likewise “Majesty,” 333 n.; “Sublimity,” 338; and “Holiness,” 340. Sent to Rome by King Louis, 78 n. He acts as the king’s representative in the kingdom of France, 333 n., 338. He summons an assembly of the realm, 338. Bernard exhorts him to prosecute the cause of the commonwealth courageously, 338 ff. His zeal and concern for the common good, 338. The misfortunes of the kingdom unfairly attributed to him, 340. The care of all churches entrusted to him, 332. At the Parisian church of St. Geneviève, he establishes regular canons in place of the monks whom Eugenius III had ordered to be introduced, 332 n. His death, 262 n.

How diligently evil suggestions must be rejected, 1132. Goliath, type of pride, 936. Pride is a great and thick beam, 532. The spirit of heretics, 1491. Pride is the appetite for one’s own excellence, 468, 565. It is the cup of demons, 12. Pride is this: when you are greater in your own eyes than before God and in truth, 1403. Likewise, pride is the gravest sin: to use gifts as though inborn and to usurp for oneself the glory in benefits received, [Col. 1298] 586. It cannot endure a companion, 1083. It is an obstacle to knowing truth, 565. The first sin in heaven, 1195. How foreign and hostile to heaven it is, 946. It changed the prince of angels into a devil, 718. Demons, because of—
abandoned because of pride, 1451. The fall of angels and of humankind through pride, 1508. Because of pride, demons are incapable of grace, 1452. Pride, whether present or future, is the cause of grace being withdrawn, 1454. The proof of pride: deprivation of grace, 1454. The Lord passes by the proud and visits the humble, 1453. The proud are to be humbled and the humble exalted, 236. Pride is detestable, 718, 768, 946. It is intolerable impudence that, where Majesty emptied himself, a little worm should swell and puff itself up, 776. St Bernard represents in himself the harms of pride, 1453. The proud person sins against God, 784; he exalts himself above God, 768. Ignorance of oneself produces pride, 1400. Impenitence accompanies it, 1084. Pride must be avoided, that you may be safe from ruin, 1066, 1568. It must be struck down by Christ’s example, 735. Five stones are to be cast against the vice of pride, 937. The temptation to pride arises from an occasion of patience, 795. Pride is threefold, 1243; likewise fourfold: of heart, speech, deed, and bearing, 1182. Its leprosy is sevenfold, 903. Pride is blind and vain, 468. The first degree of pride is curiosity, 571; the second, frivolity of mind, 575; the third, foolish merriment, 575; the fourth, boasting, 576; the fifth, singularity, 576; the sixth, arrogance, 577; the seventh, presumption, 577; the eighth, defence of sins, 577; the ninth, feigned confession, 577; the tenth, rebellion, 578; the eleventh, freedom to sin, 579; the twelfth, habit, 579. The twelve degrees of pride may be gathered into three, 578. The pride of Lucifer, 908; of the Pharisees, 566. The pride of certain monks is censured, 753. Nothing is more pitiable than a proud monk, 527. The devil is the prince of the proud, 1319. Pride has but one foot, 352. The superfluities of monks are censured, 534 and following.

Superiors are the apostles’ vicars, 938. Reverence and obedience must be shown even to unworthy superiors, 725. Contempt for them falls upon God himself, 1414. Those who pass judgment on their superiors’ commands while obeying are censured, 957. Superiors owe guardianship and discipline to their inferiors, 725. They were instituted not so much for the good as for the wicked and weak, 75. Their dangers, 725. See Abbot, Shepherd, Prelate. The monastery of Sury, 680. Suspension from table fellowship, 378.

Suspicions. Agreements are not to be broken on account of empty suspicions, 206. Even the slightest whisperings must be avoided, 1372.

Sycarius, priest of York, 673 and following.

The blindness and folly of the Synagogue, 1523; its presumption, 1307. It brought forth Christ, but cast him away, 776. It is repudiated when it places salvation in the works of the Law, 1503. The repudiation of the Synagogue and the marriage of the Church, 1307. The distinction between Synagogue and Church, 1376. The Church’s charity toward the Synagogue, 1545. Out of love for his bride, Christ was ready also to espouse the Synagogue to himself, 1545.

## T

The tabernacles are those of laborers and soldiers, 1202. The dark tabernacle is the human body, 1353. The talent must be used, 192. The toll-house of the city of Auxerre, 376. Temperance neither exceeds necessity nor cuts it short, 413. Justice is necessary to temperance, 413. Why the sanctity of churches ought to be honored, 1077. How a temple for God must be built within us, 1072 ff. How we are the temple of God, 1081. The Cistercians refuse to receive a Knight Templar as a monk, 260. The more strictly temporal things are held, the better, 835. They cannot be dealt with without detriment to spiritual things, 443. God grants His own sufficient temporal provision, 835. Pursuit of them gnaws at the conscience, 443. Likewise, their abundance produces a poverty of eternal things, 720. It is unworthy of a bishop to be occupied with temporal matters, 443 ff. See Earthly things. How greatly the wasting of time in idle words must be avoided, 1118 ff. How one should profit from the past, present, and future, 992, 993, 1029. Whoever practices repentance loses none of these, 1227. See Repentance. The works of darkness are sins, 769. Tenoliense monastery, Order of Prémontré, 385 n. Temptation is the whole of human life, 835, 836. Temptations are foxes, 1484. They must be borne patiently, 461. Their necessity, 1484. God tests in order to prove, not to reject, 1018. The alternation of temptation and consolation is useful to the devout, 1090. God mingles revelations with temptations in order to preserve humility, 574. Temptation does not impair freedom, 617. The devil’s deceit in temptation, from Scripture, 869. The enemy can stir up the movement of temptation [Col. 1299], but it lies within us to give or withhold consent, 822. One must not yield to temptations or adversities, 1018. God’s providence in moderating temptations, 836. Threefold temptation and its remedy, 907. Four temptations, 835, 836 ff., 1065, 1391. Four virtues are set against four temptations, 870. The temptation against hope is hidden but most grave, 868. How the temptation of vain glory is extinguished, 869. The four temptations of Christ, 868. In three temptations the devil assailed Christ, 837. The four temptations of the Church: those of tyrants, heretics, evil clerics, and Antichrist, 838 ff. The last of temptations is persecution, 869. The temptations of beginners are open; those of persons advancing are hidden, 1484 ff. Their various kinds, 1484. The devil tempts the perfect by persuading them to evil under the appearance of good, 837, 1390. The temptation of the perfect is veiled wickedness, 1392 ff. Another temptation of the former concerns length of life, 1085. The devil tempts monks, sometimes by urging greater austerities and sometimes looser practices, 1128 ff., 1133. Temptations of converts, 487. Sharp temptations arise at the beginning of conversion, 1004. Temptation concerning necessities of life, 868. It is compared to an asp, 868. For those leaving everything, the first temptation is usually the discomforts of the flesh, 1026. The first temptation of novices is faint-heartedness, 836. It arises from the rigor of religious life, 1218. Not affliction itself but fear of it is temptation, 836. The antidote to temptations, 830. How one should conduct oneself in consolation and temptation, 1332. The caution required of novices in temptations, 831. Resistance to temptation must begin at the outset, 822. One must have recourse to prayer, 822. In their temptations, each of the elect has God as his own, 830. The remedy for temptations is meditation upon Christ’s Passion, 299. One must flee to Mary, 743. Angels should be invoked, 864. Victory over temptation is testimony of heavenly birth, 906. Lukewarmness must be cast aside, 925. It is condemned in monks, 98. Its origin, 916. Its cause is weakness of faith, 1230. How destructive this lukewarmness is for religious, 101. The lukewarm religious person enjoys neither heavenly nor earthly consolation, 123 n. Signs of spiritual life, 890. God is the true life of the soul, 855. Jesus is the life of hearts, 1531.

We owe our life to Christ for many reasons, 1128 ff. He who gave his own life for ours claims our whole life for himself, 149, 150.  
One does not live who does not love those among whom one lives, 1106.  
Commendation of the mixed life, 1001.  
The life of the saints is like a table full of dishes, 964. The usefulness to us of saints’ lives, 657.  
For the wise person, his own life is a vineyard, 1482; the fool’s life is death, 1482.  
The life of the world is night, 760.  
Monastic life is sport to secular persons, 93.  
The life of trees and animals, 1350.  
Life proceeds from the heart in two ways, 1204.

Vine. See “Vineyard.”  
Vices do not cease to sprout within us, 1467 ff.  
The soul suffers from the fourfold sickness of vices, 1234. They must be continually cut away, 1467 ff.; extinguished at their beginning, 1486; and not concealed beneath the names of virtues, 21.  
The vices which deceive us under the appearance of virtue are foxes, 1485 ff.  
The difference between living in the shade and sitting, 1434.  
VIVIAN, abbot of Hautecombe, 59 n.  
The monks of Vézelay are harassed by the retainers of the countess of Nevers, 337; reformed by a strong hand, 153.  
One must not resist the divine calling, 241.  
By what signs a calling to care for souls may be recognized, 1464.  
What persons God calls to ministries of the Church, 492.  
A religious calling is from God, 724. How highly it must be valued, 1015, 1130 ff. Those called to religious life who do not acquiesce endanger their salvation, 9 n.  
How the calling and illumination of a sinner takes place, 113 ff. It begins with fear, 113.  
Will is a rational movement, presiding over sense and directed toward an object, 604.  
That properly is called will to which we assent and toward which free choice inclines itself, 903. Freedom belongs to it alone, and it cannot be deprived of that freedom, 605; nor can it be compelled, 1552, except by itself, 618.  
Yet vehement desire diminishes voluntariness, 1551.  
When will and work are valid, 788 ff.  
Will does not suffice for human salvation, although without it one cannot be saved, 617.  
To will belongs to free choice; to will the good belongs to grace, 610.  
Whether willing to have a good will, yet being unable to have it, prejudices freedom, 607.  
The will to return to God comes from grace, 1560.  
The voluntary differs from appetite, 604.  
To will is to go with the mind, 1200.  
The will alone is capable of misery or blessedness, 605. Its mutability, 92. Its twofold weakness, 619. Its threefold disease, 482. Its threefold ruin, 1180.

Two things demonstrate an unjust will: delighting either in sinning or in having sinned with impunity, 615.  
Its threefold good, 611.  
A sound will is the kingdom of God, 369.  
What a good will is, 1062. Whoever wishes to have it has it, 607. Its four degrees, 1237. Its impediments, 1257.

The union of a human being with God is a concord of wills, 1517. This conformity of wills marries the soul to the Word, 1557.  
God’s will is done concerning all things and through all persons, but not in all persons, 951. Its various impediments in us, 821 ff.  
What must be done when it is not certainly made known, 1158.  
Whether we ought to entrust eternal damnation to it, 359 n., 370.  
Investigation of the will is safer than investigation of majesty, 1480 ff.  
Christ abandoned his own will so that, from good, it might become better, 904.  
Renunciation of one’s own will, 763, 957, 1022 ff. It must be rendered to God for his greatest benefits, 1129.  
Its harms, 901, 903 ff., 1138, 1518. How cruel and unjust it is toward God, 904. It alone can tear us away from God, 1107. It subjects a human being to the devil, 1108. The fasting of one’s own will is displeasing to God, 1518.

One’s own will is that which is common neither to God nor to human beings, but is ours alone, 903. Common will is charity, 901.  
The will of the condemned is opposed to God, 455. An evil will persists in the condemned, 615.  
Christ’s crying and tears teach flight from pleasures, 782.  
Bodily pleasure is evil, but affliction is good, 782. There is no sincere pleasure in bodily goods, 609.  
The vanity of this world’s pleasures, 394. How slight they are, 483 ff.  
A small pleasure entails no small loss of piety, 345.  
The memory of sinful pleasure is brief and bitter, 479. Sinful pleasure passes away; foulness remains, 456.  
To make vows is voluntary; to pay vows is necessary, 501. A person who is not compelled to vow is justly required to fulfill the vow, 10.  
Delay in fulfilling a vow is dangerous, 116.  
One guilty of delaying or frustrating a vow injures God, not a human being, 117.  
Bernard calls a vow the intention to enter religious life, 116 n.

Lesser vows ought not to impede greater ones, 60.

The vow of virginity in Mary, 737, 746 ff., 750, 1009.

The voice of the soul is desire, 1527.  
The affections have their own voices, 1501.  
Voice and sign commonly cooperate to introduce faith, 1471.  
The force of countenance and of the living voice, 67.  
Christ’s wounds are signs of victory, 1016.  
Christ’s wounds are the clefts of the rock, 1475. In them is secure habitation, 1475. Their contemplation heals the soul’s wounds, 1480.

The foxes that destroy vineyards are flatterers and detractors, 1482.  
Foxes in the Church: heretics, 1486, 1490.

# Index of Exotic Words in Saint Bernard

[Note: In this index, Arabic numerals refer to the column numbers printed in bold type in the text. This index refers to the works of Bernard of Clairvaux in *Patrologia Latina* 182–183.]

[Col. 1307]

**Addextrare**, Sermon 77 on the Song of Songs, no. 1: to stand beside, now on one side and now on the other.  
**Angariare**, in Letter 258: to compel, to press into service.  
**Barricanus**, in the *Apology to William*, ch. 9: a kind of mat. See the notes there.  
**Cancellarius** (“chancellor”), in Letter 311, etc.; and **Capellanus** (“chaplain”), in Book IV of *On Consideration*, no. 22: both are noted and occur elsewhere.  
**Carenum**, Book II of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, ch. 1: a kind of sweet boiled wine.  
**Casamentum**, in Letter 39: a benefice estate.  
**Cassare**, Letter 178: to invalidate and weaken.  
**Charitative** (“charitably”), in Sermon 37 on the Song of Songs.  
**Colare**, Sermon 72 on the Song of Songs, no. 3, and *On Loving God*, ch. 11, no. 33: to draw out and drink, as in Matthew 23, “straining out a gnat.”  
**Complices**, Sermon 77 on the Song of Songs, no. 4: persons privy to and partners in crimes.  
**Cuculla**, in the *Apology*, ch. 1: a type of monastic garment.  
**Deplanctus**, Letter 407: abundant complaint.  
**Diffidare**, Letter 222: to declare war upon someone, to proclaim him an enemy.  
**Epilogare** (“to summarize”), Book IV of *On Consideration*, ch. 7.  
**Episcopari** (“to be made bishop”), Letter 272.  
**Episcopium**, Letter 131: bishopric.  
**Forefacere**, *Treatise on the Errors of Abelard*: to commit a crime.  
**Galabrunum**, in the *Apology*, ch. 9: a type of cloth. See the notes there.  
**Garciones**, ibid., ch. 10: servants.  
**Grangia**, Letter 253: a rural settlement, estate.  
**Grisea pellicea**, Letter 2, no. 11: dark-grey furs.  
**Grossae vestes**, Letter 209; *Apology*, ch. 9: coarse garments.  
**Grossus intellectus**, Sermon 60 on the Song of Songs, no. 5: dull understanding.

[Col. 1308]

**Guerra**, Letter 220 and elsewhere: war.  
**Gyrovagi**, Letter 58: wandering monks.  
**Homagium** or **hominium**, Letter 39: homage.  
**Imbanniri**, Letter 253, no. 9: to be proscribed, interdicted, excommunicated.  
**Induciare**, Letter 303: to spin out delays.  
**Isembrunum**, in the *Apology*, ch. 9: a kind of more precious cloth. Notes there.  
**Ligius**, Letter 317: bound to his lord against every person.  
**Maneries**, Letter 402: manner of acting.  
**Matta**: a kind of mat.  
**Monachari**, Letter 261: to become a monk.  
**Officiales**, Book IV of *On Consideration*, no. 23, and in the sermons on the Song of Songs: officials.  
**Palefridus**, Letter 104: a type of horse.  
**Passagium**, Letter 119: a kind of toll customarily exacted from travelers.  
**Pausare**, Sermon 18 on the Song of Songs: to rest.  
**Repatriare**, Letter 168; Book V of *On Consideration*, no. 2; Sermon on the Ascension: to return to one’s homeland.  
**Sapa**, Book II of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, ch. 1: a kind of drink.  
**Scaccorum ludus**, in the book *To the Knights Templar*, ch. 4, no. 7: the game of chess.  
**Summarii**, Book IV of *On Consideration*, no. 4: packhorses.  
**Torneamentum**, Book I of the *Life*, ch. 11: a kind of mock combat.  
**Transalpinare**, Letter 245 and Sermon 1 for Advent, no. 10: to cross the Alps.  
**Typhus**, Letter 247: pride.  
**Vadium**, Sermon 2, on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, no. 5: pledge.  
**Vanitare**, *Treatise on the Conduct of Bishops*, ch. 2: whence, in Augustine, *Vanitas vanitantium* (“vanity of vain persons”). Therefore **vanizare** should not be read here, as Juretus thinks in his notes on Ivo’s Letter 66.

[Col. 1307]
